## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**THE COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINT OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION WHICH HAVE SURVIVED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, VERY CAREFULLY CORRECTED FROM THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY THE ADDITION OF ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST COPIOUS EDITIONS PRODUCED IN THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING THE INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ORNAMENTED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH TITLES AT THE TOP MARGIN OF EACH PAGE INDICATING ITS SUBJECT MATTER; AUGMENTED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH YET POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO COPIOUS GENERAL INDEXES: ONE OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER any one of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY LEARN WHICH FATHERS HAVE COMMENTED ON INDIVIDUAL SCRIPTURAL TEXTS OF INDIVIDUAL BOOKS, AND IN WHAT PLACES OF THEIR WORKS. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one weighs: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the thoroughness of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient form of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the course of the work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, IN WHICH ARE PUBLISHED THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The two hundred and sixty volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand three hundred francs; the three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand eight hundred francs. The wholly Latin edition embraces all authors, Western as well as Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.**

# Continuation of the Works of St. Martin of León

[Col. 0009]

## Sermons on the Saints

### First Sermon: On the Death of St. Isidore

[Col. 0009A] Isidore, an eminent man, a Carthaginian by nationality, born of the father Severian, bishop of the Church of Seville, was the brother and most holy successor of Bishop Leander.  
[Note: [Col. 0009D] Thus the Toledo manuscript, published by Henschenius, nos. 5 and 42.]

This most blessed man was, from childhood, devoted to literary studies; instructed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters; trained in every kind of expression; graceful in speech; most outstanding in intellect; and distinguished alike in life and teaching. For he so shone forth, advancing from virtue to virtue, as an exceptional teacher, that, according to the capacity of his discourse, he was suited to instruct everyone—Latin, Greek, and Hebrew alike, wise persons and those of lesser understanding—and was vigorous in incomparable eloquence. So great were the wisdom, learning, and holiness of this most glorious man that it is rightly said of him: [Col. 0009B] “Behold, a great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous” (Ecclus. 44 and 50).

[Note: [Col. 0009D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 12.] The word *sacerdos* (“priest”) is compounded from Greek and Latin, and means, as it were, “one giving sacred things” (*sacrum dans*). Just as a king is so called from ruling, so a priest is called such from sanctifying and from giving sacred things. A person becomes a great priest for two reasons: first, because he lives well; second, because he teaches well. Although an ecclesiastical teacher may live well, if he does not teach well he is not great; and although he may teach well, if he does not live well he will by no means be great. [Note: [Col. 0010D] Id., *Sentences*, book III, chapter 36.] Teaching with a good life is therefore necessary: for teaching without a good [Col. 0009C] life makes the teacher arrogant, while life without teaching makes the teacher useless.

Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and thus teaches people shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). In this passage, the kingdom of heaven is the assembly of the elect. Scripture often calls the Church [Col. 0010A] of the faithful the kingdom of heaven because, since it longs for heavenly things, the Lord already reigns in it as though in heaven. Therefore whoever breaks one of the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, whoever does not fulfil it in deed—and teaches people to fulfil it, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven, namely in the assembly of the faithful. It is as though he said plainly: “Whoever neglects to fulfil my commandments, and teaches people to fulfil them, shall be called least,” that is, he shall be imperfect in the holy Church. Of such a person the Lord says elsewhere: “They speak and do not do” (Matt. 23).

It follows: “But whoever does,” that is, fulfils my commandments in deed, “and teaches people to fulfil them, shall be great,” that is, fit for service in the holy Church. Thus a priest’s preaching must be confirmed by works, so that what he teaches by word he may instruct by example.

That passage also aptly serves to confirm this testimony which is read in the Song of Songs: “Behold Solomon’s bed; sixty mighty men surround it, of the mightiest of Israel, all holding swords and most skilful in war; each man’s sword is upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night” (Song 3). [Note: [Col. 0010D] Gregory, on this passage.] Solomon, indeed, is interpreted “peaceful.” Who, then, is understood by Solomon but Christ, of whom it is written: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2)? Solomon’s bed—that is, Christ’s—is the holy Church, because when it withdraws from worldly concerns, when through penitence it does not cease to cleanse its heart from every earthly defilement, [Col. 0010C] and when with the whole desire of its mind it strives toward the heavenly homeland, it makes itself, as it were, a bed in which Christ delightfully rests. Hence he himself says affectionately to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). And again he says through the prophet: “I will walk among them and I will be in them, and they shall be my people, and [Col. 0011A] I shall be their God” (Lev. 26).

The sixty mighty men who surround Solomon’s bed signify the prelates of the Church, who fortify it by words and examples and repel from it visible and invisible enemies by prayers as well as preaching. “All,” he says, “hold swords and are most skilful in war.” What is signified by the sword except the word of God, and what by the hands with which they hold swords except action? For, as they fulfil in action the word of God which they know in their heart, ever more and more, taught by wisdom and strength, they conquer the enemies of the Church. They are most skilful in spiritual warfare because they know how first to cut away vices in themselves and then in those subject to them. They are most skilful in war because they carry out in deed the commandments of God which they preach in word. They are prudent and highly skilled in warfare because by the sword of discernment they cut away in themselves and in their subjects what is superfluous and the pleasures of this world.

Concerning them it is aptly added: “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.” What do we understand by the sword except strictness of life, and by the thigh except the appetite of the flesh? Therefore prelates of the Church, who have now arrived at perfection in virtue, always carry the sword upon their thigh, because by strictness of life they continually break the appetite of the flesh, lest the enemy whom they fear in the night of this world should come suddenly, find them weak and lax in God’s work, and more easily deceive both them and those subject to them through the softness of pleasure and delight of the flesh, [Col. 0011C] and lead them into graver sins.

Therefore he is called great in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the Church—who fulfils by good works what he preaches in words. Let it therefore be said of blessed Isidore: “Behold, a great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous.” Truly he was great, because he fulfilled in deeds the works of God which he preached in words. [Note: [Col. 0011D] Toledo manuscript in Henschenius, ch. 2, no. 43, about the middle.] He is rightly called a great priest whom God raised up in Spain in recent times, after so many declines, I believe to restore the wisdom of the men of old, which through excessive antiquity had almost already perished from human minds, lest the Christian people should grow old any longer in ignorance and rusticity.

Thus, full of love and wisdom, [Col. 0011D] he did not hide in the earth the talents entrusted to him, but distributed them among all for the common good and, as a good trader, brought them back doubled to the Lord (Matt. 25), while by preaching he stirred the minds of many to desire heavenly things. [Note: [Col. 0011D] Ibid., no. 44, near the end.] For just as Gregory became the successor of the teacher, the Apostle Peter, so blessed Isidore succeeded the Apostle James; for the seed of eternal life which the most blessed James sowed was sufficiently watered by this eminent teacher’s preaching, as though by one [Col. 0012A] of the four rivers of paradise. And he illumined all Spain, like a most splendid lamp, both by the example of good works and by the renown of holiness. [Note: [Col. 0011D] The edition there reads “a most splendid ray of the sun.” Dufresne says that *lampada*, in place of *lampades*, was used by Pollio; Salmasius observed it from manuscript codices … and in Plautus: “Hold this lamp.” Sermon 56 in the Appendix to Fulgentius uses the word: “O good lamp,” says the author, “not one that loves the world, but one that loves heaven”; and below: “There are many who call the day a lamp.”]

The prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of the four living creatures, says among other things: “The likeness of the living creatures and their appearance was like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps” (Ezek. 1). By these four living creatures the multitude of saints is figured; their appearance, however, is compared to coals of fire and burning lamps, because whoever is joined to holy men is kindled in love for the Creator through their imitation and teaching. [Note: [Col. 0012D] From Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 5, no. 6.]

Yet there is this difference between coals and lamps: coals burn, but do not drive away darkness from the [Col. 0012B] place in which they lie. Lamps, however, because they shine with the great light of flames, illuminate the darkness spread about them. From this it should be observed that there are many saints so simple and hidden, concealed in lesser places under profound silence, that their life scarcely seeks to be known by others. What then are these but coals? For though they possess heat through the fervour of the Spirit, they do not possess the renown of an example, nor do they enlighten the darkness of sins in other hearts, because they wholly conceal their life from others. They are kindled for themselves, but are not an example of light for others. Although these people burn with the fire of divine love, they do not kindle others either by the renown of holiness or by the word of preaching.

Lamps, on the other hand, shine farther away: though situated in one place, they shine in another, because whoever shines by the example of good work and the word of preaching, that person’s reputation shines far and wide like a lamp. When their neighbours hear of their good works, they rise through them to love heavenly goods. And when they display themselves in good works, they shine as though from a lamp’s light. Therefore, when holy men kindle certain persons near them, as if by contact, to love of the heavenly homeland, they are coals; but when they shine for persons far away, lest they fall in darkness through their sins, they become lamps for their journey.

Thus those are rightly called lamps who offer examples of virtue and show others the light of good work through life and word. Truly they shine as lamps who, through love of the Creator and the flame of sound preaching, drive the darkness of error from sinners’ hearts. Whoever therefore lives well in secret yet does not benefit others is a coal; but one who, established in the Church by imitation of holiness, offers the light of uprightness from himself to many is a lamp, because he burns for himself and shines for others.

This most blessed man is therefore rightly compared to a shining lamp, [Col. 0013A] since by both the word of preaching and the renown of holiness he enlightened those present and absent, and kindled them to love the heavenly homeland. He is fittingly compared to a burning lamp, since he burned in love of God and neighbour and drove the darkness of sins from others’ hearts. Whoever came to him received, through the constancy of seeing him, the practice of conversing with him, and the example of his good works, the light of truth, and burned with longing for eternal light.

[Note: [Col. 0013C] Toledo manuscript, no. 43, in Henschenius.] For among the other works of holiness which this most blessed man wisely performed in Christ’s Church, he confuted and destroyed the malignant heresy of the Acephali, who, denying two substances in Christ, proclaimed a single nature in his person, while [Col. 0013B] maintaining that he was not true God and the Son of God, but merely a pure human being. Having overcome Gregory, the leader of the aforesaid heresy, and convicted him by the authority of testimonies from the holy Scriptures, he taught that there were two natures in Christ: divine and human. Divine, by which he is ever coeternal and coequal with God the Father; human, by which for our salvation he deigned in time to become the Son of Man, that is, the Son of the Virgin.

And what shall I say of his holiness and wisdom? Certainly human speech does not suffice fully to recount how many good things God bestowed upon his Church through him, and how useful he was to an ignorant people and an aging world, when in his *Chronicle* he made known the ages of the world and the sequence of times. [Col. 0013C] *Chronica* is called in Latin “a sequence of times.” For *chronos* in Greek means “time” in Latin. Thus he revealed to an ignorant people the sequence of times and the ages of the world; he displayed the laws of sacred things; he expounded to priests ecclesiastical offices and the ranks of all orders; he established laws for kings and princes; he forbade avarice to judges; he instilled the discipline of the Christian religion in citizens and in all peoples of the household of faith; and finally, by writing, he disclosed the names, kinds, functions, and causes of sees, regions, places, and of all divine and human things, and whatever was obscure and almost already removed from human minds. [Note: [Col. 0013C] Ibid., no. 44.]

He flourished in wisdom and holiness in the times of the emperors Maurice and Phocas, under Reccared, king of the Goths. For he was generous in almsgiving, foremost in hospitality, stern in heart, truthful in pronouncement, just in judgment, assiduous in preaching, joyful in exhortation, zealous in winning souls for God, careful in expounding the Scriptures, prudent in counsel, humble in dress, temperate at table, devout in prayer, outstanding in integrity, and conspicuous in every goodness. Moreover, he was the father of clerics, comforter of the sorrowful, [Col. 0014B] protection of orphans and widows, relief of the oppressed, defender of citizens, persecutor of heretics, and hammer of the proud. What more shall I say? He became a mirror of every good thing to the world, and therefore, as we believe, now reigns without end with Christ.

He died in the time of the Emperor Heraclius and of Suinthila, [Note: [Col. 0013C] Unless the name of King Suinthila was inserted into our manuscript by an untrustworthy and later hand—and undoubtedly after the Salamanca exemplar, which has *Suintillae*—the king’s reign and the year of Isidore’s death, 622, or Era 660, would have been correctly fitted together. But since the Toledo manuscript has the same error in assigning the era, and later says that Isidore died under King Cintilla or Cintillan, we do not doubt that our manuscript suffered from the same error, which the corrector wished to heal. We say that the author or copyist of the Toledo codex was mistaken when he asserted that the year of St. Isidore’s death was six hundred and twenty-two; for all now agree on six hundred and thirty-six, relying upon the authority of Redemptus, clerk or archdeacon of the same holy bishop, St. Braulio, and St. Ildefonsus. Yet it is no wonder that the aforesaid author or copyist fell into that error, since he was so miserably blind in this matter that he first says Isidore died in the time of Cintillan, afterward that he flourished until Sisenand, and immediately that he died in the time of Suinthila, Era 660—namely, nine years before Sisenand began to reign and fourteen before Cintillan—which we are surprised Henschenius did not note.] king of Spain—namely that Heraclius who restored and exalted in its place at Jerusalem the Lord’s cross which the impious King Chosroes had carried away. Blessed Isidore slept with his fathers in Era 655. Superior to all in sound teaching and sound counsel, and abundant in works of love, he was buried in a good old age.

Meanwhile, dearest brethren, it is fitting that we pray more earnestly to this most holy confessor, so that he may be a continual intercessor before God for us wretched sinners, who are still placed amid dangers to our souls; that through his most sacred merits and prayers, after this life we may be able to attain the fellowship of God’s elect. May he grant it who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

### Second Sermon: On St. John the Baptist

[Col. 0013]

[Col. 0013D] The prophet Isaiah, a noble man and full of God’s grace, whose excellence in holiness and life was so great that he wore only one tunic of haircloth and, later, after casting it aside for the sin of the people, covered his limbs with sackcloth (Isa. 21); and who, preaching the mysteries of Christ and the Church more openly than the others, ought rather to be called an evangelist than a prophet—kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, says among other things in today’s reading: “The Lord called me from the womb; from my mother’s belly he remembered my name” (Isa. 49), and the rest.

Although, dearest brethren, these words of the prophet Isaiah pertain especially to Christ alone, yet because Christ is the head of the Church and the Church—that is, all Christ’s faithful—is his body, those things said of the head, that is, Christ, may also suitably, indeed fittingly, apply to the members. Let us therefore repeat what we have set forth: “The Lord called me from the womb; from my mother’s belly he remembered my name.”

That this was said of Christ is evident when the archangel Gabriel said to Joseph concerning the virginal birth: [Col. 0015B] “You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1). It is also shown to be especially fitting for blessed John as one of Christ’s chosen members by holy Elizabeth, who testifies that her son leaped within the enclosure of her womb at the Saviour’s coming, saying to the most blessed Mary: “For behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb” (Luke 1). The same archangel Gabriel also foreshadowed this when, announcing John’s name and manner of life before he was born, he added concerning the greatness of his virtue: “He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” “Truly this man was the most blessed of all little children: still enclosed within his mother’s womb, though not yet able to do so with his tongue, he showed with prophetic joy, being filled with the Holy Spirit, that the Saviour [Col. 0015C] of the world was present.” [Note: [Col. 0015] The words enclosed in quotation marks are those of St. Maximus, Homily 1, on the day of John’s birth.] The saying which Jeremiah uttered prophetically also aptly applies to John: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came out of the belly I sanctified you, and I gave you as a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1).

It follows: “And he made my mouth like a sharp sword” (Isa. 49). The mouth of God the Father, properly and principally, is Christ, through whom God the Father was made manifest to this world. Hence our same Lord Jesus Christ, speaking to God the Father in the Gospel, says: “I have made known your name to the people whom you gave me” (John 17). John also became the mouth of Christ, who announced Christ to the earth. The holy apostles likewise were Christ’s mouth, who preached Christ to the nations: “And he made my mouth like a sharp sword.”

Christ is the sharp sword, because “with the spirit of his mouth he shall slay the wicked” (Isa. 11). Of this sword it is said in the Gospel: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). It is as though he said: “I came to separate the evil from the good and to divide children from parents. I came,” he says, “to separate a man from his father, and a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law; and through hatred of my name, the members of a man’s household shall be his enemies” (ibid.). The Apostle plainly explains what this sword is: “Take,” he says, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6).

The sword of the Holy [Col. 0016A] Spirit is that which the Holy Spirit gives. For the word of God is a two-edged sharp sword, teaching about temporal and eternal matters: giving consolation in the Old Testament concerning the former, promising perfection in the New concerning the latter, and dividing whatever it strikes in this world. John also wrote of this sword in Revelation: “From the mouth of the Son of Man,” that is, Christ, “a sharp two-edged sword came forth” (Rev. 1)—namely from the mouth of preachers, because holy teachers are Christ’s mouth, like John, like the apostles, and like the other preachers. Thus from them, as they disclose Christ’s hidden things, went forth the sharp two-edged sword—that is, the divine word—because, as a sword separates soul from body, so the divine word separates a person from worldly and carnal love.

From Christ’s mouth came forth the two-edged sword, cutting apart bodily and spiritual vices; or according to the New and Old Testaments; or according to letter and spirit; or according to divinity and humanity. Alternatively, the sharp two-edged sword cuts away the vices both of the preacher and of the hearer. Of this sword it is read in the Psalm: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44). The ecclesiastical preacher is fittingly commanded to be girded with a sword upon his thigh, so that, while about to cut away vices in others, he may first endeavour to restrain in himself the impulses of fornication.

Therefore whoever desires to correct vices in others must first cut away excesses in himself, as we read the Apostle Paul saying: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest perhaps, after I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the mote out of your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7). Paul the Apostle also says: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one should not steal, do you steal? You who say that one should not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Rom. 2). And the Lord says in the Psalm: “You who hate discipline and cast my words behind you, why do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49).

Alas for wretched me, who do not cast the most grievous beams out of my own eyes and yet notice the small motes in the eyes of my brothers! I do not correct myself of the gravest sins, yet I rebuke my brothers for the slightest faults. Nevertheless, most beloved brethren, I urge you not to be unwilling, because of my sins and my infinite negligences, to hear the words of the Holy Spirit; for the Lord says to preachers: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10). Therefore do not despise the words of God which you have heard from me, but hasten as swiftly as possible to fulfil them in good works. Let us return, then, to the matters we proposed.

For this reason blessed John, in order to offer himself as a model of teaching to ecclesiastical preachers, first endeavoured to fulfil by good works what he was afterwards [Col. 0017A] to preach to others, so that he might not be reproved by his hearers for any fault. Hence he crucified his flesh with its vices and desires; dwelt in desert places; despised the luxuries of priests; subdued his body by exceedingly rough clothing; girded his loins with the belt of mortification; drank neither wine nor *sicera*—strong drink—nor anything that can intoxicate; was content with scant and simple food; and utterly despised this world’s riches. Thus, first chastising himself by the strictness of virtue, he ensured that, when he rebuked the evils of an unbelieving people, there should be nothing in his clothing or meals for which others might rightly reproach him.

Then, secure and strengthened by God’s grace, he rebukes the people for their wicked deeds. “Offspring of vipers,” he says, “who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Produce fruits worthy of repentance.” Why? “Because now the axe is laid at the roots of the tree. Every tree which does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3). The person who produces fruits worthy of repentance is one who, the more gravely he sins, does not cease through repentance to labour the more strenuously in acquiring the fruit of good works. For by repentance each person ought to seek proportionately greater gains of good works, according as he has inflicted greater losses upon himself through sin.

Again he adds, saying: “He protected me in the shadow of his hand” (Isa. 49). Christ was especially protected in the shadow of God’s hand, because the lowliness of his flesh was covered by the power of divinity, as the angel announced to the most glorious Virgin: “The Holy [Col. 0017C] Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). This power of divinity so overshadowed the most blessed Virgin against the heat of vices, strengthened her inwardly and outwardly with virtues, and so weakened her in outward actions [the reading is uncertain] that it never allowed her to sin in thought, speech, or action. Hence blessed Augustine says: “Whenever I dispute concerning sinners, I affirm that this one most blessed Virgin, and he who was born of her, are without sin.” [Note: [Col. 0017D] *On Nature and Grace against the Pelagian*, 42.]

Nor is it doubted that blessed John the Baptist was protected by the grace of God’s virtue, because he could be conquered neither in prosperity nor in adversity, being fortified, as it were, by the invincible shield of that same grace. Prosperity did not exalt him, nor adversity break him, as the testimony of Truth confirms, which in praising him declared that he was not a reed shaken by the wind (Matt. 11). Hence John himself is not without reason interpreted as “the grace of God.”

Then follows: “He made me like a chosen arrow” (Isa. XL). In calling him a chosen arrow, he shows that God has very many arrows. Yet among many arrows Christ is uniquely the one chosen arrow; just as among very many sons he is the singular and only-begotten Son. With this arrow the bride in the Song of Songs recalls that she has been wounded, saying: “I am wounded by love” (Cant. II). The other arrows of the Lord are the prophets and apostles, who range throughout the whole world, of whom the Psalm sings: “Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you, in the hearts of the king’s enemies” (Ps. XLIV). And again: “The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” (Ps. CXIX). In Holy Scripture arrows signify the same as a sword; for arrows are called preachings or words of God. Yet arrow and sword appear to differ in this: the sword strikes nearby, while arrows are sent farther away. Thus is shown the incomprehensible power of God, which no one can escape, whether situated far off or near at hand. These arrows are sharp because they penetrate even to the division of body and soul. Hence the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. IV).

Truly the word of God is effective and living—that is, the Son of God, whom the unbelieving people suppose to be dead—because he accomplishes all that he threatens; and it is more penetrating than any two-edged sword, because it penetrates not merely bodily members like a material sword, but by the stroke of its own power reaches even to the division of soul and spirit. In the divine Scriptures “soul” is often used for life; hence: “He who loves his soul shall lose it” (John XII). As though he said: He who loves the present life shall lose the eternal. Therefore, in this passage “soul” denotes carnal vices, which belong to bodily action, such as lust, theft, robbery, and the rest that are referred to bodily acts. [Col. 0018C] By “spirit,” however, spiritual vices are understood: pride, avarice, envy, and the rest that belong to the mind.

Therefore that word reaches even to the division of joints and marrow. As though he said: It is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart. By “joints” we understand thoughts, which are joined together with one another; by “marrow,” the most secret and inward intentions of the heart. The divine word divides these from one another when it discerns what kind of thought and what kind of intention there is. For often the things thought are good, but the intention is evil. Often, moreover, we think either good or evil; but in these things [Col. 0018D] the divine word does not err, taking good for evil or evil for good. Thus the divine word is a discerner of thoughts and intentions because by its subtlety it knows what each person does and with what disposition he acts. Hence the Psalmist says: “God searches hearts and reins” (Ps. VII). In the heart are thoughts, and in the reins are pleasures. God therefore searches hearts because he knows what each person thinks; he also searches the reins because he knows in what each person most delights, whether in chastity or in lust.

John too is not without reason a chosen arrow, because not only was he chosen through Christ with the other saints before the foundation of the world, but he was also foretold by an angel at his very conception, and, while in his mother’s womb, was greeted, sanctified, and undoubtedly chosen by Christ. “For, as blessed Maximus declares, a special election shone forth in him to such a degree that he deserved to announce the Lord before he had begun to be born or received the office of speech.” [Note: [Col. 0019C] Homily 1, on the day of John’s Nativity.]

The Lord also says of this most blessed man in the Gospel: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John V): burning, namely, with love; shining with speech. Filled with love of God and neighbour, he burned; filled with the Holy Spirit, he shone by the word of preaching. Through love of God he burned in desiring heavenly things; through love of neighbour he shone in preaching good things. Through charity toward God, despising earthly things, he longed for heavenly things; through charity toward his neighbour, by the word of exhortation, he enlightened human minds. Through charity toward God he mortified his own body in this world; through charity toward his neighbour, rebuking evils and announcing the coming of the Son of God, he raised human hearts toward heaven.

Yet, dearest brethren, John the Baptist did not display the brilliance of his virtues in his parents’ house, but outside, before the people; nor did he shine in a house, but in public. Let us compare him, if you please, to the Chalcedonian stone. The Chalcedonian stone is placed third among the twelve precious stones by which the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the great King, is founded and adorned (Rev. XXI). This stone, it is said, does not shine in a house, but under the open sky—that is, under the air, under the brightness [Col. 0019C] of day, outside in the open. For it is said to emit a radiance like that of a pale and burning lamp. In that it does not shine indoors, it signifies those who perform their good works in secret, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. VI). But in that this Chalcedonian stone does not shine indoors but outside in the open, it signifies those who, compelled by some unavoidable necessity, go out into public and there, willingly or unwillingly, as though constrained, display their good works to their neighbours. Hence it is written: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

This most blessed man belonged to their number, because as long as he dwelt in his parents’ house he concealed his good works for fear of self-exaltation. But after he went forth to preach, he enlightened the whole province—indeed, the whole Church—prepared the way for the Lord, and raised human minds from earth to heaven.

Dearest brethren, while we recall the virtues of blessed John the Baptist, it is necessary that we consider ourselves inwardly and outwardly, and wash our sins with daily tears. [Col. 0020B] God has set before our eyes the examples of the holy Fathers so that, following in their footsteps and aided by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we may deserve to obtain eternal joys. Thus no ignorance now excuses us from sin, because both God’s law daily strikes upon our ears and the example of the holy Fathers unceasingly invites us to do good works. Now therefore “the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Cant. II): that is, the voice of the apostles and holy Fathers preaching and admonishing us, by words and examples, to live well.

Therefore, most beloved brethren, God must be entreated that the virtues which he prepared for his saints as a crown may be for our advancement and not for our punishment. They will serve [Col. 0020C] our advancement if we are willing to imitate so many and such great examples of virtue. We must therefore, beloved, with all devotion implore God that through the intercession of blessed John the Baptist he may make us fear and love himself, keep his commandments in all things, and after our death attain the heavenly kingdom—he who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## THIRD SERMON. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF SAINT MARY

[Col. 0019]

[Col. 0019D] The Virgin Mary was assumed into the ethereal bridal chamber, where the King of kings sits upon a starry throne. Mary is called “illuminatrix,” because she is the gate of eternal light, through whom light has risen for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. For she bore the Son of the eternal Father, “who enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I). Mary is also interpreted as “star of the sea,” because through her this great and wide sea—that is, the present age—is illumined, and to us who sail upon it she points out the harbour of eternal [Col. 0020D] rest. For like a most brilliant star she enlightened the human race and, amid the darkness and storms of this wave-tossed sea, showed it the straight way by which it could reach the shore of everlasting stability.

Mary is also called *Domina*, “Lady,” in the Syrian language. She is quite fittingly called Lady, because through the Lord whom she bore she is Lady in heaven and on earth. She is fittingly called Lady in heaven and on earth because all things that serve Christ are subject to her with every devotion and reverence. Truly she is [Col. 0021A] Lady in heaven and on earth, because from the beginning she was foreshadowed in figures and riddles, and, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, foretold by patriarchs and prophets. From her very birth she was guarded and accompanied by the holy angels and reverently greeted. Moreover, God the Father most gloriously overshadowed her as a bride and enriched her with heavenly gifts; the Holy Spirit enlightened and filled her; Jesus Christ her Son dedicated and consecrated her in the integrity of perpetual virginity; and the evangelists displayed and made her known. John the Evangelist also, to whom Christ entrusted her from the cross (John XIX), guarded her until the end of her life, faithfully and devoutly ministered to her in her needs, and, as we believe, after her falling asleep laid her in a mausoleum situated in the middle of the valley [Col. 0021B] of Jehoshaphat and fittingly placed her there.

Mausoleums are the tombs or memorials of kings, so called after Mausolus, king of Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0021D] From blessed Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XV, chapter 11.] After the death of this king Mausolus, his wife the queen built over his body a tomb of extraordinary size and wonderful beauty, so that all the costly memorials of kings and princes in the regions of the East are called mausoleums after King Mausolus.

Thus we see fulfilled what the archangel Gabriel foretold to the most holy Virgin Mary: “Hail,” he says, “Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke I). Truly Mary was full of grace, to whom, as we said above, heavenly and earthly things ministered so devoutly. Truly [Col. 0021C] Mary was full of grace, by which she was able to bear the Son of the eternal Father and destroy all the perversity of heretics, magicians, and philosophers. It was fitting, therefore, that this most august Virgin should be endowed—that is, enriched—with such gifts, so that she might be full of grace and receive reverent angelic services: she who gave glory to heaven, God to earth, restored peace, faith to the nations, an end to vices, order to life, and discipline to morals.

She gave glory to heaven when the angel announced Christ to the shepherds and immediately the angelic choir sang glory to God in the highest and proclaimed that peace had been restored on earth to people of good will (ibid.). She gave God to earth because she bore for us the Son of almighty God, who redeemed us from the enemy’s hand by his precious blood and freed us from the danger of eternal condemnation. She restored peace because she reconciled human beings to God and recalled angels to peace with humankind. She gave faith to the nations because people who, in ignorance, had long served idols instead of the true God were converted by her childbirth to faith and knowledge of their Creator. She also gave an end to vices, because through baptism and the mystery of Christ’s most sacred body faithful peoples are absolved from the bonds of both original and actual sin—provided that thereafter they renounce the works of the devil and faithfully submit their necks to the gentle yoke of Christ’s service. [Col. 0022A] She gave order to life because Christ ordered his Church, established rulers, and commanded lesser persons to obey greater. Hence the apostle Paul says: “Whatever things are ordered are ordered by God”; and: “Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII). She gave discipline to morals because Christ, who was born of her, imposed penance upon sinners, so that one who after baptism has subjected himself to sins and vices and stained the garment of innocence may again obtain forgiveness of sins through pure prayers, tears, fasts, and his other good works. Hence the Lord himself says through the prophet: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezek. XVIII).

Truly this most noble Virgin was full of grace, [Col. 0022B] through whom holy Church received such great and innumerable goods. With what praises, then, can we worthily honour her through whom we deserved to receive the pledge of eternal salvation? Or what thanks can we render to her through whose childbirth we were able to find the entrance to the heavenly kingdom? Or what do we attempt to say in her praises, she who has been praised and glorified more excellently by divine and angelic proclamations? Surely human speech cannot set forth in words the praises of this most holy and most glorious Virgin, especially since neither life corresponds, nor eloquence suffices, nor knowledge abounds. Without doubt heaven trembles, earth is astonished, reason does not know, the human mind cannot comprehend; indeed, every creature marvels at what is announced to her through Gabriel the archangel and fulfilled in her through Christ.

Hence in the Song of Songs the Holy Spirit, speaking in the person of the heavenly citizens and marvelling at her ascent, says: “Who is this who ascends through the wilderness like a little column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense?” (Cant. III). She ascended through the wilderness of this world like a little column of smoke because she was indeed slender and delicate, and made lean by heavenly disciplines—namely abstinence, fasts, vigils, and prayers—since her manner of life was now no longer on earth but in heaven. The Holy Spirit is said to have marvelled when this most blessed Virgin was exalted above the choirs of angels. “Wilderness” means “abandoned.” Therefore she rightly ascended through the wilderness because she was abandoning [Col. 0022D] the present world with her whole mind and longing with all devotion for her heavenly homeland; she despised earthly things, raised all her desire to heaven, and, because she saw nothing sweet to her in lower things, turned her whole heart to love what is above. She despised the wealth of the world with all harmful covetousness and strove toward invisible things. Thus she ascended through the wilderness, because with her whole intention she abandoned the world.

She is rightly said to have ascended like a little column of smoke because she left to holy Church the fragrance of a good reputation and the example of perfection. For she urged all whom she could to live according to her example and admonished them to despise earthly things and love [Col. 0023A] heavenly things. She especially urged virgins to preserve integrity of mind and body, avoid the enticements of mortal nature, and faithfully await Christ until their dying day with lamps of good works alight. So sweet a fragrance of perfect conduct flowed from her that an innumerable multitude of both sexes followed in her footsteps; setting aside marriage and despising the propagation of children, they became devoted to Jesus Christ, her heavenly Bridegroom, through her most holy admonitions.

He continues: “Like a little column of smoke,” he says, “from the spices of myrrh and frankincense” (Cant. III). It should be noted that this smoke is said to be from the spices of myrrh and frankincense. Bodies of the dead are embalmed with myrrh lest they decay, while frankincense is burned in a censer so that it may emit fragrance. Therefore this most glorious Virgin, while she mortified her flesh away from the decay of vices and renounced all the world’s pleasures through continence, applied myrrh, as it were, to her mortal body and strove with all her might that after death it might remain unharmed by eternal corruption. But while she cast all superfluous thoughts from the chamber of her heart, she made her heart, as it were, a censer before God. In it, while through love of God and neighbour she gathered virtues, she arranged them like coals of fire in the censer; in it she kindled herself before God with the fire of charity. And while she sent fervent and pure prayers to God, she brought forth, as it were, aromatic smoke from the censer, [Col. 0023C] by which she gave forth a sweet fragrance before God; and by her good examples she did not cease to stir all her neighbours to the love of God.

Again, concerning her, the Holy Spirit, marvelling in the same Songs, says: “Who is this who ascends like the dawn rising, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an ordered battle line?” (Cant. VI). The souls of the saints marvelled with joy at who she might be, she who surpassed even the dignity of angels. “Who is this,” he says, “who ascends like the dawn rising?” Because the ever-Virgin Mary, having left behind the darkness of corruption, shone at her ascent with the newness of incorruption and perpetual immortality. Beautiful as the moon—indeed more beautiful than the moon—[Col. 0023D] because the moon sometimes waxes and sometimes wanes. But she, without the defect of corruption, illumines the darkness of holy Church, and in her the brightness of eternal blessedness endures. She is also rightly called chosen as the sun because the Sun of righteousness himself chose her, that he might be born of her. Hence David the prophet says: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII). In the sun—that is, in this most blessed Virgin—he made ready his bridal chamber.

She is said to be terrible as an ordered battle line because at her ascension she was surrounded on every side by angelic choirs and accompanied here and there by the spirits of the elect. We believe that on this present day the whole host of heaven, with companies of angels, came festively to meet this most blessed Mother of God, Mary; surrounded her with immense light; and led her, with praises and spiritual songs, as far as the throne predestined for her by God before the foundation of the world. Let no one, then, doubt that at the assumption of so illustrious a Virgin the whole heavenly Jerusalem exulted with ineffable joy, was gladdened by inestimable charity, and rejoiced with every expression of gladness at her companionship. Indeed, so far as can be understood, [Col. 0024B] Jesus Christ himself came to meet her in rejoicing and festivity and placed her with himself in the glory of the Father.

Meanwhile, dearest brethren, it is fitting, insofar as we can by God’s granting grace, that we fit ourselves with good morals and cleanse the inner chambers of our hearts from sins and vices, so that on this solemnity of the ever-Virgin Mary we may worthily praise God; for the way of our salvation consists in God’s praises. Hence the divine word says in the Psalms: “A sacrifice of praise shall honour me” (Ps. XLIX): namely, the sacrifice of a contrite heart and chaste body; the sacrifice of a clean mind and pure praise honours God. And there is the way by which “I shall show him the salvation of God” (ibid.). [Col. 0024C] This way is not walked with feet but with good morals; it is not completed by bodily steps but by good works. It is completed thus: the body is exercised in holy actions and the mind is devoted to God’s praises. Glorious is the way that leads the one who praises to the Creator of heaven and earth. Glorious is the path that leads a human being to eternal joys. Yet, beloved, we can in no way find this way unless God deigns to show it to us. Therefore we must with all earnestness entreat God to deign to show us the way of his praise, through which we ask to come to him.

But because by our merits we are unworthy to obtain what we can, let us seek the help of this most glorious [Col. 0024D] Queen of heaven and earth, so that, aided by her most holy prayers, we may deserve by the way of praises to attain the heavenly kingdom and behold in the Father’s glory the Salvation of God of whom we speak. May he grant this, he who with the same Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## FOURTH SERMON. II. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT MARY

[Col. 0025]

[Col. 0025A] The stations of the Israelites, counted from the first to the last, are forty-two in all. Through these stations the Hebrew hastened to leave the land of Egypt and reach the land of promise. Through these, too, the Christian ought figuratively to run, if he desires to leave Egypt—that is, the present age—and attain the land of promise, that is, the heavenly homeland. Nor should it seem strange if we arrive at the kingdoms of heaven under the mystery of that number, since our Lord and Saviour himself also, under that same number, came typically from the patriarch Abraham to the Virgin Mary, as though to the Jordan—a river flowing with a full current and overflowing with the grace of the Holy Spirit. The evangelist Matthew figuratively displays these stations in his Gospel [Col. 0025B] when, counting from the patriarch Abraham to Christ, he relates that there were forty-two generations (Matt. I).

Thus through these forty-two generations, from Abraham as through so many stations and descending in a straight line through David, Christ came to Mary when he chose to be incarnate in her for our redemption. Mary therefore shines forth as having arisen from royal stock, and we most devoutly believe that we are aided in mind and spirit by her prayers. The ever-Virgin Mary is always said to be of royal descent because she is reported to have arisen from the stock of King David. She descended from royal lineage because she derived her true origin from David’s line. In respect of human nature she came from royal descent, but by grace God adopted her as his daughter. According to [Col. 0025C] the flesh she was born of royal seed, but by the adoption of the most high God she is a daughter. From herself she bore Christ, God and man; yet Christ created her. She is therefore mother and daughter: mother, because she bore true God and true man; daughter, because God created her in order to be born from her.

She is noble by the lineage of an earthly parent, but far nobler through the grace of almighty God. As daughter of King David she was made glorious, but she is much more glorious because she was chosen by God. She is noble in parents, yet nobler in morals; noble in lineage, but nobler in holiness. Why? Because from infancy, through the prevenient grace of God, she began to despise earthly things and love heavenly things. From the beginning of her birth, illumined by the gift of heavenly grace, [Col. 0025D] she endeavoured to despise visible things and seek invisible things. She feared God with love and loved him with fear; she restrained her mouth from superfluous speech, rejected the delights of food, avoided the sight of people, and wished in face and bearing to please God rather than people. Moreover, she avoided anger and hatred as a kind of deadly plague; she fled enticements together with all this world’s blandishments. She kept the right faith: no foolish doctrine deceived her, no perverse religion corrupted her, no wickedness turned her from the state of uprightness, no iniquity separated her from the love of God. She abstained from everything forbidden by the law and carefully avoided everything prohibited by Scripture. Daily she persisted in prayer; day and night she humbly entreated God; in nocturnal vigils she remained in God’s praises. She was established in humility, judged herself least, called herself God’s handmaid, and laboured with watchful care to be worthy in God’s sight. In her step she showed simplicity; in movement, purity; in gesture, dignity; in gait, propriety.

But who can adequately or worthily recount the perfection of her holiness? Her whole life was full of virtues and clean from sins and vices. The Holy Spirit illumined and strengthened her with virtues, made her drunk from the abundance of God’s house, and purified her from every carnal pleasure, so that she might love God above all things and cling to him with all devotion. Thus, kindled by desire for heavenly love, scarcely anyone could imitate her in good works. She grew so greatly in virtues among the entire Jewish people and gave them such an example of good works that it may rightly be said of her: “As a thorn produces a rose, so Judea produced Mary.” Judea is fittingly compared to thorns because it always provoked God by its deeds. Scripture rightly compared the Jewish people to thorns because it was, as it were, inflicting bloody wounds when it cruelly shed the blood of prophets and neighbours. Hence the Lord says to it in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you” (Matt. XXIII). Elijah also, lamenting, said to God: “Lord, they have dug down your altars, killed your prophets, and I alone remain; and they seek my life to take it away” (III Kings XIX). This too was signified when the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush in flame. There was flame in the bush, that is, in the thorns, and the bush was not burned (Exod. III). The bush signifies the thorns of the Jews’ sins, while the flame signifies the law [Col. 0026D] of the divine commandments; and as the flame did not burn the bush, so the law did not at all consume the Jews’ sins.

The ever-Virgin Mary is therefore fittingly said to have arisen like a rose from thorns. Although she derived her origin from Jewish stock, through God’s grace she remained free from sins and vices; and while she gave both sexes—men and women—examples of perfect conduct, just as a rose adorns thorn-bushes, so she adorned Judea, indeed the whole Church. While she preserved herself in every gentleness and patience through love of God and neighbour; while she kept innocence and purity in word and deed; while she regarded everything on earth as nothing—she was like a fragrant rose, sweetly giving forth fragrance to her neighbours by offering them the scent of a good reputation. Hence that which the Holy Spirit says to her in the Song of Songs fittingly applies: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Cant. II).

In sacred speech, “daughters” denotes all who are negligent and lukewarm in God’s love. Since they foster effeminate [Col. 0027B] habits and, having lost manly dignity, are inwardly of such a kind, they are outwardly called by a feminine name. And because they confess Christ only in words, but in deeds pursue nothing but worldly concerns, they are rightly called not sons but daughters.

Therefore the most blessed Virgin Mary is deservedly described as a lily among thorns among daughters. Although she came forth from the root of human frailty, issued from the stock of mortality, and emerged from corrupted nature, she nevertheless, despising the ugliness of human life, raised herself to heavenly beauty; despising the blackness of Jewish conduct, she preserved purity’s whiteness in heart and body; abandoning the mountain of pride, [Col. 0027C] she planted herself in the valley of humility. Like a lily she refreshed her neighbours—indeed all believers—with the fragrance of a good reputation.

She is rightly reckoned in the dignity of a lily because from infancy she loved the whiteness of virginity and preserved purity of mind, through which she deserved to please almighty God above all virgins, as Scripture says: “God chose her and chose her beforehand” (Ps. CXXXI). He chose her, namely, above other virgins; and chose her beforehand above all virgins, by the privilege of greater dignity and singular love. For none before her was found like her, nor will any who follows be able to be made like her. Blessed Jerome also says of her: “She is found first among the foremost companies of the highest King.” [Col. 0027D] She is called first among all the virgin companies of the highest King, not only in time but also in dignity and holiness. She is found first in the court of the highest King because above all virgins—indeed, above all women—she is blessed. Truly she is blessed above all women because, among all women, she first offered God the most glorious gift of virginity. She is said to be found first in the court of the highest King because on earth she endeavoured to imitate the angelic life.

Hence the Prophet says: “Virgins shall be brought to the King after her; her companions shall be brought to you” (Ps. XLI). Other virgins shall be brought to the Lord King, not in the first but in the second [Col. 0028A] place, because none will equal her either in holiness or in reward. Virgins consecrated to God shall be brought to the King of heaven, not equally but after her, because none, however holy or worthy, can be made equal to her in reward. Other virgins consecrated to God can be her followers, not her companions, because this most noble Virgin is lady among handmaids, queen among sisters, and teacher among virgins. Without doubt she is the teacher of holy virgins, because she gave them examples of good living. She is also their mother because she bore them through the example of holy virtues. Hence Scripture says: “Each person is called the son of the one whose teaching he follows.” Certainly she is mother and teacher not only of virgins but also of all holy women, because above all women she was chosen and blessed by God.

To her the Holy Spirit says in the Song of Songs, in great glory: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no stain in you” (Cant. IV). But since it is written, “No one is without sin, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day” (Job XIV), what does it mean that this most holy Virgin is said to be wholly beautiful, with no stain found in her? Elsewhere indeed it is read: “The stars are not clean in God’s sight” (Job XXV); and elsewhere: “We all offend in many things” (Jas. III). And the apostle John says: “If we say that we have not sinned, we lie and do not do the truth” (I John I).

Yet the most blessed Virgin Mary, as she is called wholly beautiful and without stain by the Holy Spirit, is also proclaimed as such by the holy Fathers—something believed of no other saint. The Holy Spirit therefore fittingly declares her to be without stain because, going before her, he wholly cleansed her from sin, freed her from the tinder of sin, and utterly purified her from every unlawful thought, so that thereafter no occasion whatever for sinning remained for her. Hence blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0027D] *On Nature and Grace, against Pelagius*, no. 12]: “With the exception of the most holy Virgin, if all holy men and women were gathered together and were asked whether they had sin, what would they answer except what John says: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us’?”

But this most glorious Virgin was anticipated [Col. 0028D] and filled by the singular grace of the Holy Spirit so that she might have as the fruit of her womb him whom every creature had from the beginning as Lord. She is therefore rightly, and without any doubt, said to have been wholly beautiful and without stain: into whose womb the Word of the Father, through whom all things were made, deigned to descend, there mercifully joining our humanity to himself for the salvation of the whole world. Likewise, she was wholly beautiful and without stain, in whose womb the Son of God clothed himself with our flesh; in that flesh he suffered for our redemption as he willed, and with it powerfully defeated the ancient enemy and despoiled hell, although he descended there in soul alone. After his resurrection, on the fortieth day, he raised its spoils to heaven [Col. 0029A] and, as we believe, placed them in eternal blessedness.

Without doubt she was wholly beautiful and without stain, she who both obtained the dignity of motherhood and did not lose virginal chastity. A virgin gave birth because a virgin conceived. Blessed was that fruitfulness which by bearing gave light to the world, inherited heaven, repaired the losses of angels and human beings, and yet did not lose the veils of virginity. Blessed is that womb which knew how to bring forth without human seed and knew no corruption. Surely blessed, and most worthy of every praise, is this ever-Virgin, who brought forth for the world the heavenly bread—that is, Christ—upon whom the holy angels are nourished in heaven. From herself she brought forth to the world the living bread, by whom the souls [Col. 0029B] of believers are nourished; and yet she did not lose the seal of virginity.

For this reason it is said in the same Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed. Your offshoots are a paradise” (Song 4). It is altogether a garden of delights, in which every kind of flower and the fragrances of holy virtues have been planted: so perfectly enclosed that it can in no way be violated or corrupted by any thoughts or treacherous stratagems. It is rightly called an enclosed garden, because, while through good examples it begets many peoples, like a garden putting forth shoots it sends forth beautiful flowers. It is also a fountain sealed with the seal of the whole Trinity, from which proceeds the fountain of life, which both nourishes the angels in heaven from itself and refreshes the faithful, lest they grow weary on the way of this world. [Col. 0029C] Of this fountain the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 4). The issue of that womb also—namely, Christ—is the paradise of all the citizens above. *Paradisus* is Greek; in Latin it means “garden.” *Eden* is Hebrew; in Latin it is interpreted as “delights”; joined together, these make “the garden of delights.” Jesus Christ is fittingly compared in this place to a garden, because, although in his divinity he is uncircumscribed together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is nevertheless so circumscribed that a hypocrite, heretic, Jew, or pagan can never attain to him. He is rightly called a garden of delights, because in him are all the delights and [Col. 0030A] riches of the heavenly citizens. He is aptly called paradise, because he himself is refreshment and sweetness to those who run to him and to all who remain in heaven. Therefore he is called a garden of delights, because he is the food and joy of all the heavenly orders of blessed spirits and of all the souls of the saints.

Therefore, most beloved brethren, if we desire to reach these delights of which we speak—that is, Christ—it is necessary that we strive to serve him with all devotion, to please him in all our conduct, and to cling to him with our whole mind, so that we may rightly say with the Prophet: “But for me, it is good to cling to God; to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72). As if he were saying: It seems delightful and beneficial to me to despise the world [Col. 0030B] and cling to God, and to place my hope in him, rather than in temporal goods, which are certain to come to nothing with all swiftness. It is fitting, then, that we cling to him by chaste conduct and follow him by holy deeds, after first cleansing our hearts from unclean and shameful, vain and harmful thoughts; for no one can worthily contemplate him or perfectly follow him without these virtues. For in his own essence he is most holy and most subtle, and an unclean eye cannot see him. Let us therefore approach him with a clean heart and pure mind, loving him before all things and above all things, loving him in all things and through all things, and serving him with all diligence, [Col. 0030C] he who both gives himself to us as food lest we fail on the road of this world, and preserves the reward in which we may rejoice in the heavenly homeland. But because, through the demands of countless sins, we are unworthy of heavenly gifts, let us implore the help of the most blessed Mary ever-Virgin, so that, cleansed from all sins and vices by her most sacred prayers and merits, we may deserve to partake of eternal delights and attain the joys of everlasting blessedness; and there behold the same Jesus Christ, her Son, reigning at the right hand of God the Father: he who, with that same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON FIVE. ON THE HOLY CROSS.

[Col. 0029]

[Col. 0029D] Therefore, dearest brethren, our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to descend to us from heaven for our salvation, that he might afterwards lead us back from earth to heaven. For this reason, for our restoration he willed to humble himself even to death and to endure the contempt of the cross, so that he might free us from the enemy’s power and, through himself, who is the way, truth, and life, lead us to eternal blessedness—that is, to the vision of [Col. 0030D] his Father. Let us therefore hear from him how we ought to go after him and attain him, so that where he is, we too may be through him. For he says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16). Therefore, whoever wishes to run after Christ must first deny himself.

But what is it to deny oneself? It is, plainly, to renounce one’s own former habits. Thus one who was proud and inflicted evils upon his neighbours, once converted to the Lord, should do good according to his strength not only to friends but even to enemies. But one who was formerly wrathful should show himself gentle and kindly in all things, so that he bears all people with evenness of mind and patience. One who was formerly lustful should strive to be chaste in mind and body, so that not only the body is not defiled by touch, but the soul as well is not defiled even by an unclean thought. One devoted to avarice should not covet another’s goods, but for Christ’s love should give his own possessions to the needy, love poverty, and despise riches. Whoever renounces such self-will undoubtedly denies himself; yet this does not suffice for perfection unless, having taken up the cross, he proceeds after Christ. [Col. 0031B]

But what is it to bear the cross? It is, plainly, to mortify oneself. To bear the cross and not die is the pretence of hypocrites; but to bear the cross and die is the endeavour of God’s servants. Whoever therefore enters God’s service, if he has not yet died to sins and vices, appears to bear the cross but does not follow Christ. He truly bears the cross and follows Christ who, renouncing the world, withdraws from sins and vices, firmly binds himself to God’s service, opposes his own will in all things, and humbly submits himself to the command of his master—that is, his abbot. Such a person may rightly say with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6). [Col. 0031C] The world is undoubtedly crucified to one who despises the world with its pleasures. Conversely, one is crucified to the world when the world hates him for the sake of Christ’s love. It sometimes happens that a person does not hold the world in his mind, yet the world binds him with its occupations: the person is dead to the world, while the world, as though alive, beholds him and strives to carry away into its pursuits one who is intent upon something else. But Paul neither desires the world nor is desired by it, so that, with two dead things, neither sees the other. As though he said: “I desire nothing of the world, nor does the world recognize anything of its own in me.” Therefore, as has already been said, to bear the cross is to mortify oneself, [Col. 0031D] despise visible things, love invisible things, and bear with all devotion the sweet yoke of Christ’s discipline and the light burden of his commandments.

Let us therefore also glory, most beloved, in the life-giving cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was worthy to bear the price of this world, through whose mystery the devil was conquered and the world redeemed. We ought to glory greatly in it, because its benefits are neither recent nor newly discovered, but were prefigured and shown long ago through figures and enigmas. Figuratively, it made bitter waters sweet when, at Marah—the fifth stopping-place of the children of Israel—the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood, which Moses immediately cast into the most bitter waters, and by divine power at once changed them into sweetness (Exod. 15). [Note: [Col. 0031D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 21.] The bitter waters are understood to represent the Law and the letter that kills; if confession of the cross is cast into them and the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion joined to them, they become waters of wonderful sweetness, and the bitterness of the letter is changed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding. Hence it is written: “The Lord established for the people a law and judgments, and tested him” (Exod. 21). In another sense, the fact that waters of wondrous bitterness became sweet when they received the wood was an indication that the bitterness of the Gentiles would at some time be changed by the wood of the cross into the use of sweetness. But according to the former sense, it must be understood that Israel was first led to salty and bitter waters, and, once the wood had been shown [Col. 0032B] by the Lord, these were made sweet; afterwards it came to springs. For the people are first led to the letter of the Law; while they remain in it, they cannot depart from bitterness or taste the sweetness of the Gospel. But when it has been made sweet through the wood of life and the Law begins to be understood spiritually, then one comes from the Old Testament to the New, and comes to the twelve apostles, whom Scripture calls springs, from which the faithful people sufficiently draw the sweetest water—that is, spiritual teaching. There too are found seventy palm trees, because not only the twelve apostles preached Christ’s faith, but also the other seventy sent to preach God’s word, through whom the world might recognize the palms of Christ’s victory. Indeed, these twelve springs watering the seventy palm trees prefigured apostolic grace, the tenfold number watering them, so that at last, through the sevenfold Spirit, the Decalogue of the Law might be fulfilled.

Through the mystery of this holy cross, the doctrines of the philosophers too are destroyed figuratively. For what Egypt of old suffered bodily under diverse plagues is now enacted spiritually in us. Egypt is, indeed, an image of the world, in which the waters are turned into blood at the Lord’s command. The waters of Egypt signify the wandering and slippery doctrines of philosophers, which are rightly turned into blood because they are shown to think carnally about the causes of things. But when the cross of Christ showed this world the light of truth, [Col. 0032D] it reproved it by such corrections that, from the character of its punishments, it might recognize what it had done wrongly.

By this cross also, at the Lord’s command, the rock gave forth waters through Moses’ ministry. [Note: [Col. 0032D] Isidore, *Questions on Numbers*, ch. 33.] At the thirty-third stopping-place, namely Kadesh, Moses offended the Lord concerning the waters of contradiction and was forbidden to cross the Jordan and enter the promised land. Troubled by the people’s murmuring, he struck the rock doubtfully, as though God could not bring water forth from the rock (Num. 20). But what doubtful faith does Moses here suggest, that he hesitated to bring water from the rock? In this we undoubtedly understand a prophecy concerning Christ. For while Moses in the Holy Scriptures bears now one, now another personage according to the effects of events, here he signified the person of the Jewish people placed under the Law and represented it in a prophetic utterance. For just as Moses, striking the rock with a rod—which signifies the wood of the holy cross—doubted God’s power, so that people, held under the Law given through Moses, fastened Christ to the wood and did not believe him to be God’s power. But as the stricken rock flowed with water for the thirsty, so the wound of the Lord’s Passion became life for believers. [Note: [Col. 0033D] This is from the same Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 24.] The same rock that poured out water bore the figure of Christ; when it was opened, all things flowed forth, and in order that grace might flow out to believers, the wood of the cross came to it as a rod. For when the rock was struck, a spring flowed; [Col. 0033B] when Christ was struck upon the cross, he poured out upon the thirsty and believing the grace of the washing and the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle proves that this rock bore the figure of Christ when he says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and that rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). But when the thirsty people murmured against Moses for water, and God therefore commands him to show them the rock from which they might drink, what does this signify except [Note: [Col. 0033D] The corrupt passage should thus be restored from the edition: “except that, if anyone reading Moses murmurs against him and the Law written according to the letter troubles him, Moses also shows the rock, who is Christ, and brings him to it, that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst.”] that the Law of Moses murmurs against him—the Law which kills according to the letter? Moses therefore shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to it, that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst. [Note: [Col. 0034D] Again from *Questions on Numbers*, cited above.] God commands this carnal despair concerning Christ’s divinity to die upon [Col. 0033C] Christ’s height itself, when he commands Moses’ bodily death to take place upon a mountain. For as the rock signifies Christ, so the mountain also indicates Christ. The rock is humble strength; the mountain, exalted height. Thus, as the Lord himself says, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5), asserting himself to be the mountain and his faithful, founded in the glory of his name, to be the city. For the wisdom of the flesh lives when Christ’s humility, like a stricken rock, is despised upon the cross by unbelievers. For Christ crucified is indeed a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles (1 Cor. 1). Again, the wisdom of the flesh dies when Christ is recognized as exalted, like a mountain’s height; for to those who are called, Jews and Gentiles alike, Christ is the wisdom of God and the power of God.

[Col. 0033D] The two pieces of wood which the widow of Zarephath was gathering (3 Kings 17) also signified this adorable cross of Christ, which is not constructed from one piece of wood but consists of two. Both the name “wood” and the number of the pieces of wood express the sign of the cross. Heaven was shut when there was famine, because there was no abundance for knowing the Divinity; but in those times, when famine oppressed the whole human race, Elijah was sent to a widow. [Note: [Col. 0034D] From St Ambrose, *On Widows*, ch. 1, §3.] See, brethren, [Col. 0034A] how a grace proper to each is preserved: an angel is sent to a virgin (Luke 1), a prophet to a widow. There were many widows, but one is preferred above all. [Note: [Col. 0034D] This is from ch. 2, §7.] This widow is defined not merely by bodily abstinence, but marked by virtue. [Note: [Col. 0034D] Now from ch. 3, §14.] This holy widow was of great merit, because, although the famine was very great throughout the land, God’s care for her did not fail, since he sent a prophet to sustain her. This widow signifies the holy Church, which has been widowed by the death of her husband, namely Christ. Therefore this widow is not idly preferred among many widows, but is reasonably set above them all. What widow such as this, or where is she found, to whom so great a prophet, who was taken up to heaven, is sent? Especially at the time when heaven was shut for [Col. 0034B] three years and six months. What are these three years, if not perhaps those in which the Lord came to the earth and could find no fruit? Hence it is written: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none” (Luke 13). [Note: [Col. 0034D] What we enclose in parentheses is not by Ambrose.] (We know Solomon to have said of this woman: “Who shall find a strong woman? Her worth is from afar and from the uttermost bounds” [Prov. 31]. The price and reward of the holy Church is Christ, who came to her from the uttermost bounds—that is, from heaven—and purchased her with the price of his own blood.) This is surely the widow of whom it was said: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54). It is also well said to her through the prophet: [Col. 0034C] “You shall not remember the shame and widowhood of your youth, for I, the Lord, make you safe” (ibid.). This, then, is that widow for whose sake, when there was drought in the lands, prophets of the heavenly word were sent. Hence we do not regard as insignificant the person of him who watered the dry earth with the dew of the heavenly word. He opened the shut heaven not by human power but by divine power. For who can open heaven except Christ, to whom citizens of the Church are daily gathered in abundance from among sinners? Nor is it within human power to say: “The jar of flour shall not fail, nor shall the flask—that is, vessel—of oil diminish until the day when the Lord shall give rain upon the earth” (3 Kings 17). But what is “until the day when the Lord shall give [Col. 0034D] rain upon the earth,” except until the day when the Son of God descends like rain upon the fleece? (Ps. 71).

In Scripture these things lie hidden under figures; but now the powers and benefits of the cross stand revealed. What benefits? Kings believe in Christ and, laying aside their crowns and bending their knees, adore this most holy cross—those who formerly inflicted most grievous torments upon Christians out of hatred for the name of this same Lord Jesus Christ.
