Through the power of that same holy cross, that strong and proud armed man, who seemed to guard his court in peace and possess his goods (Luke 11), is justly and reasonably conquered; his goods, namely the hearts of the faithful in which he dwelt, are plundered; the weapons in which he trusted—namely pride and deceit—are broken; the human race is reconciled to God; temples of idols are destroyed; the holy Church is strengthened; Christians are made firm in faith; pagans are confounded because they worshipped idols; Jews are scandalized; the gates of hell are destroyed; captives long held there are transferred to the rest of everlasting light and peace; the gate of paradise is opened; the losses of the heavenly orders are restored; demons [Col. 0035B] are restrained; enemies are overcome; and, to say it briefly, without the cross no sacrament is performed in the holy Church.

By its sign the most sacred body of Christ is consecrated, the Church is dedicated to God, priests and every rank of the Church are ordained, infants are baptized, boys and youths are confirmed in the faith with holy chrism by bishops, the food of the faithful is sanctified, all Christian peoples are blessed, and the foreheads of both sexes and every age are fortified. Hence the saying: “There is no salvation in a house unless a person fortifies the doorposts with the cross.” Truly, there is no salvation in the house—that is, in the body, which is the dwelling of the soul—unless it bears the sign of the holy cross upon its forehead. Through its power the sick are healed, [Col. 0035C] the dead raised, the blind enlightened, lepers cleansed, paralytics cured, demons expelled from possessed bodies, wild beasts changed to gentleness, serpents put to flight, and fire extinguished; finally, prosperity is bestowed and every adversity repelled.

Let us therefore give thanks, most beloved, to almighty God, who through the Passion and cross of Jesus Christ his Son has bestowed such great and countless blessings upon the whole world. Proud Adam took many good things from us through the wood of transgression; but humble Christ gave us far greater things through the wood of the holy cross. For such was the humility in Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, as could suffice for the salvation of all his own; just as in the first man there was such [Col. 0035D] pride as could harm both himself and his descendants. Yet no one among men was found able to accomplish this, namely that human beings could be reconciled to God by their own merits, except the Lion from the tribe of Judah, who opened the book and loosed its seals by fulfilling in himself all righteousness (Rev. 5)—that is, humility most complete and most perfect, greater than which cannot exist. For other human beings were debtors, that is, guilty, and scarcely did each one’s own virtue or humility suffice for himself. Therefore none of them could offer a sacrifice sufficient for our reconciliation. But Christ, God and man, was the sufficient and perfect sacrifice, who humbled himself far more by tasting the bitterness of death than Adam exalted himself through eating the forbidden tree and enjoying harmful delight. Thus great gifts were bestowed upon us in the death of the Only-Begotten: namely, that we might be permitted to return to our homeland, just as formerly, at the death of the high priest, those who had fled to a city of refuge could safely return to their own homes (Num. 35).

But amid these things, dearest brethren, it is wonderful that the Son of God, who never sinned and from whose mouth no deceit proceeded, should have willed so lovingly and mercifully to ascend the cross and die upon it for us sinners. Did he deign to come to us and redeem us from the hand of the ancient enemy because our merits demanded it, so as to show us the straight way of reaching heaven? Did any good works precede, by which we deserved to receive gifts so great and incomparable, [Col. 0036B] namely that the Son of God should bear our sins on the cross? Certainly it was not our holiness that made him descend to us from the Father’s bosom, but his own supreme and incomparable mercy. That God the Father sent to us his only-begotten Son, coeternal with himself; that he redeemed us from the enemy’s power; that he poured his love into our hearts; that he granted us knowledge of himself; that he opened for us the entrance to the heavenly kingdom; that he admits us to contemplate his face—all this was not due to our merits but to his most lavish goodness. Just as we were not born into this world by our own providence, so neither were we redeemed from the enemy’s hand by our own choice, nor spiritually regenerated by our own counsel. For from him [Col. 0036C] we were created out of nothing, instructed to serve him spiritually, and mercifully aided so that we may be able to ascend to heaven. From him also we have received the power to rise from exile to our homeland, from the lowest things to those above, from misery to happiness, from darkness to light, and from tribulation to paradise.

The Bridegroom himself, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, affirms this when he says figuratively to his bride, that is, the holy Church: “Under the apple tree I raised you up” (Song 8). What is signified by the apple tree except the holy cross, which bore that apple of which the same bride says above: “As the apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons” (Song 2)? Christ undoubtedly raised up his bride beneath the apple tree, because, placed upon the cross, [Col. 0036D] he called the Church subject to him to life and stirred her to do good, that she might rise from the sleep of death and, crucifying herself with him, hasten toward a new resurrection. Hence the Apostle says to everyone dead in soul: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5), that is, shall shine upon you. What thanks, therefore, dearest brethren, can we render to almighty God, who deigned to bestow such gifts upon us sinners who deserved no good thing? With what honour or what praises can we worthily honour the same King of all ages, without whom we cannot not only do any good but even think any good? How can human frailty worthily glorify him, when it was not enough for him to bestow temporal goods upon us, [Col. 0037A] but, what is more blessed, he also called our humanity to the heavenly kingdoms? What thanks then can we offer him that are worthy, except that we always remember his commandments and, for love of him, willingly suffer adversity as he suffered for us? Therefore, most beloved, take up your cross without deceit; crucify your flesh with its vices and desires; cast away this world’s prosperity; bear adversities with evenness of mind; apply yourselves willingly to divine offices; regard as nothing injuries inflicted by neighbours; [Col. 0038A] give thanks to God at the loss of temporal possessions; reject temporal things; desire eternal things; follow Christ not in pretence but in truth, so that, dead in the flesh, you may live in the spirit and through the same shepherd of all the faithful, Jesus Christ, attain the heavenly homeland: he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON SIX. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] Everything said in the Apocalypse concerning Michael’s battle with the dragon is mystically applied by our author to the battle of Christ and his saints in the Church; thus it is not surprising if you find nothing here concerning the actual Michael.]

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0037B] I exhort you, dearest brethren, to deign to hear attentively those things which blessed John, apostle and evangelist, says in the Apocalypse for your instruction—indeed, for that of the whole Church: “There was,” he says, “a battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels; and they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven” (Rev. 12). [Note: [Col. 0038D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 8, ch. 1.] *Ecclesia* is a Greek term which in Latin is rendered “convocation,” because it calls all people to itself to serve God. The holy Church is also called *catholic* because it is spread universally throughout the whole world. For unlike the assemblies of heretics, it is not restricted to certain parts of regions, but is extended and spread throughout the whole circle of the earth. The Apostle also testifies to this in congratulating the Romans: “I give thanks,” he says, “to my God for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. 1). Scripture often calls the holy Church heaven, because, since it longs for heavenly things, the Lord already reigns in it as though in heaven. Hence the saying: “I saw a door opened in heaven” (Rev. 5). The open door denotes Christ, born and suffering in the Church. For he says of himself: “I am the door” (John 10). Likewise, in this place too it calls the Church heaven, in which it relates that the battle took place.

“There was,” it says, “a battle in heaven,” that is, in the Church, in which the aforesaid dragon fights with God’s saints by tempting them through many adversities. It calls Christ Michael, and his angels holy human beings, with whom in heaven—that is, in the Church—he fights without ceasing against the ancient dragon. [Note: [Col. 0038D] From the same Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 7, ch. 5.] They are called *angeloi* in Greek, *malaoth* in Hebrew, and in Latin are interpreted as “messengers,” because they announce the Lord’s will to peoples. In Greek, archangels are interpreted as [Col. 0038B] chief messengers. Those who announce small or lesser matters are called angels; those who announce great matters, archangels. Archangels are so called because they hold primacy among angels; for *archos* in Greek is interpreted “chief” in Latin. Accordingly, Christ is aptly understood here under the name Michael, for he is truly the Prince of the angelic host, to whom every knee bends, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2). For the prophet says of his sovereignty: “Sovereignty has been placed upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9). Our Lord Jesus Christ is undoubtedly the Prince of Peace, who reconciled the human race to God in his blood and restored true peace between angels and human beings, as the choir of angels sang at his birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

Jesus Christ is also called Prince of kings, as John testifies of him at the beginning of the book of the Apocalypse to the seven Churches—that is, to the whole Church: “Grace,” he says, “to you, and peace, from him who is, and who was, and who is to come; and from the seven spirits who are before his throne; and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the Prince of the kings of the earth” (Rev. 1). But why, although the Church is one, does John write to seven Churches, except to signify that the one catholic Church is filled with the sevenfold Spirit? Hence we know Solomon also said of Christ: [Col. 0038D] “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has cut out seven pillars” (Prov. 9). Yet these seven are not doubted to be one, as the Apostle testifies: “The Church of the living God, which is the pillar of truth” (1 Tim. 3). Nor should it seem burdensome to you, whoever you are, if Christ is called an angel by virtue of his work, since he is also called by the prophet the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. 9). Although he himself is God and Lord of angels, [Col. 0039A] nevertheless, because he announced the will of the Father and his own will to faithful peoples, he is called angel in the divine Scriptures. Hence he says in the Gospel: “Father, I have made your name known to people” (John 17). Again, the Psalmist speaks to God the Father in Christ’s person, saying: “I have announced your righteousness” (Ps. 39), that is, the faith that justifies, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2), “in the great Church”—that is, not only in Judaea, but in the Church of all nations. [Note: [Col. 0039D] Isidore, cited above.] Michael is interpreted “Who is like God?”—understand, “in powers.” For when some work of wondrous power is done in this world, this archangel is sent by God. His name comes from that work itself, because no one can do what God can do. Therefore Christ is rightly understood in this place under the name Michael, [Col. 0039B] because he truly presides over all angelic spirits and all heavenly heights; and on earth he is the Angel of Great Counsel through whom God the Father redeemed the human race. No one in heaven has angels except the Son of God; for although archangels preside over angels, he presides over all, according to the fact that God the Father subjected all things beneath his feet. And although in the very offices of the angels higher powers preside over lower ones, they do not possess this from themselves, but received from him the authority to preside.

Let it therefore be said: “There was a battle in heaven,” that is, in the Church. Michael and his angels—that is, Christ and his saints—fought with the dragon, that is, [Col. 0039C] with the devil. [Note: [Col. 0039D] From the same Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 18, ch. 11.] *Diabolus* is Hebrew; in Latin it is interpreted “flowing downward,” because he disdained to stand at rest upon heaven’s summit, but, pressed down by the weight of pride, fell downward. In Greek, however, *diabolus* is called “accuser,” either because he reports to God the crimes into which he himself entices people, or because he accuses the innocence of the elect with false charges. Hence it is said: “The accuser of our brethren, who accused them before our God day and night, has been cast down” (Rev. 12). Long before this battle, the Prophet joyfully said to Christ in the Psalm: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk; you shall trample the lion and dragon” (Ps. 90). By the asp he meant death, by the basilisk sin, by the lion the devil, and by the dragon hell. These names are fittingly applied to the devil; yet all were cast beneath the feet of our Lord Jesus Christ at his glorious coming. He walked upon the asp because, rising from the dead, he destroyed death; he walked upon the basilisk because he committed absolutely no sin; he trampled the lion because he conquered the devil, who held the dominion of death, delivered him to the flames, and bound him in the chains of hell. Hence he himself said in the Gospel: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12), that is, expelled from the Church. This fiercest lion seemed to hold dominion in this world, while he drew all alike—good [Col. 0040A] and evil, righteous and sinful—to destruction with himself by tyranny. He trampled the dragon, that is, hell, when, set upon the cross and commending his soul to God the Father, he descended in it to hell, broke its gates, and powerfully and mercifully drew out those of his own who were held captive there (Luke 23). [Note: [Col. 0040D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book 1, ch. 14.] That devil, the author of all wickedness, although he did not know the order of our liberation, nevertheless knew that Christ had come for humanity’s salvation; but he did not know that Christ would redeem us by his death, and therefore killed him. For if he had known that Christ would redeem the human race through death, he certainly would not have slain him. That the devil knew Christ had come for the salvation of humankind is taught by the Gospel’s testimony: when he saw Christ, he trembled in recognition and said, “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Mark 1). Before Christ’s coming, the devil, like a strong armed man, guarded and possessed his court in peace; but when true strength came, namely the Son of God, he conquered him, broke the weapons in which he trusted, divided the spoils he unjustly held, and carried them with him to heaven. With what weapons did the Son of God conquer him? Namely, humility and prudence.

Listen, I beseech you, brethren, to an apt comparison by which the Son of God and of the Virgin overthrew the enemy of humankind. In the eastern region, it is said, there is a bird which, armed with a great, very hard, weapon-like beak, when about to fight a dragon whom it provokes with bold hisses, deliberately seeks out mud. Fouled by wallowing in its squalid mire, it covers with clay the gems of diverse colours with which nature has painted it more beautifully and lavishly. Why? So that, being despised in its humble garb, it may both frighten the enemy by its unfamiliar appearance and deceive him, as it were, by the confidence inspired by its seeming worthlessness. Moreover, with a warrior’s art it sets its tail before its face like a shield, rises in a bold attack against the head of its raging adversary, and with the unexpected weapon of its beak pierces the brain of the astonished beast; and thus, by a device of wonderful cunning, it brings down its monstrous enemy.

So the Lord and our Redeemer, when about to fight against the spirit of the ancient serpent, the supplanter of humankind, girded himself publicly for the warfare of salvation with human weakness; he wrapped himself in the mud of our flesh, in order to deceive the impious deceiver by a holy stratagem. He concealed the former things beneath the latter—that is, he hid divinity by humanity—or, as it were, placed the tail of humanity before the face of divinity; and, as with a most powerful beak, he extinguished in the word of his mouth the poisonous malice of the ancient murderer. Hence the Apostle says: “By the word of his mouth he will slay the impious one” (2 Thess. 2). Yet it should be noted that the Son of God and of the Virgin did not fight this dragon alone, but with his angels—that is, with his saints.

[Col. 0041A] “There arose,” says the evangelist, “a battle in heaven”—that is, in the Church: Michael and his angels, that is, Christ and his saints, fought with the dragon. Christ therefore fought, and his saints; and every day he fights against the ancient enemy who accused humankind. Without doubt he was summoning his disciples to this battle when he said in the Gospel: “When you hear of wars and seditions, do not be afraid” (Luke 21); “for they will hand you over in councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you” (Matt. 10). And elsewhere: “If they persecuted me,” he says, “they will persecute you also” (John 15). Again, consoling them, he says: “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 21).

The chief of the apostles, Peter, exhorted the disciples to this battle, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you [Col. 0041B] an example, that you may follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2). And again: “Therefore, since Christ suffered, arm yourselves also with the same thought” (1 Pet. 4). Paul too, Christ’s most valiant soldier, called the faithful to this combat when he spoke to the Ephesians, saying: “Put on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil; for our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in heavenly places” (Eph. 6). And a little later: “Stand, having girded your loins with chastity, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in preparation for the gospel of peace; in all things taking the shield of faith, by which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation [Col. 0041C] and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (ibid.).

Therefore, for this struggle with Michael—that is, with Christ, to whom none is equal in powers—the angels, that is, all the saints, gather and make war with the dragon in heaven, that is, in the Church. But who is this evil dragon against whom Christ fights with his angels in heaven, that is, in the Church?

He is the enemy of humankind who, through envy, expelled man from the delights of paradise and miserably dragged him with himself to destruction. Since he disdained to be a glorious prince in the palace, God made him a laborious smith in this world, so that he who formerly did not wish happily [Col. 0041D] to devote himself to God may be compelled to serve with all his strength. Of him Scripture speaks to God: “I shall make him your servant for ever” (Job 40). Although the devil did not wish to be subject to God in heaven, nevertheless, cast down from there, he serves God’s ordering even unwillingly.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 5.]

For this reason the devil is called in the sacred writings Behemoth, that is, “beast,” because he fell from heaven down to earth. For this reason he is called Leviathan, that is, “serpent of the waters,” because he moves about in the sea of this age with twisting cunning. He is also called a bird because through pride he raises himself aloft. In this the devil serves the divine dispensation: his wickedness advances the benefit of the saints. Thus all things in heaven and on [Col. 0042A] earth are subject to divine power, so that even those who seek to oppose God’s will unknowingly carry out his purpose.

Thus the devil, full of envy and deceit, serves in this world, like a blackest smith, the interests of the saints without knowing it: through many tribulations he cleanses them from the defilements of sins, so that they may be judged worthy of the heavenly dwellings. The furnace of this smith is affliction and tribulation; his bellows are temptations and suggestions; his hammers, torturers; his tongs, persecutors; his files or saws, the tongues of those who curse and slander. By such a furnace and these instruments the evil enemy himself purifies the golden vessels of the heavenly King—that is, the elect—in whom he renews the image of the Creator. But the reprobate, who act against God, this torturer punishes as an enemy in hell.

[Col. 0042B] It follows: “And the dragon,” he says, “fought, and his angels.”

[Note: [Col. 0041D] St Beatus on this passage.]

Far be it from us to believe that the devil, with his angels, dared to fight in heaven—he who, in order to harm even one man, namely Job, asked the Lord’s permission. It must not be believed that this evil dragon dared to engage in war against the Word of God, Creator of all things, or against the companies of holy angels, when he did not presume, without permission, even to enter the herd of swine (Matt. 8). For how could he fight in heaven, when, as soon as he was created, he burst forth in pride against God and immediately fell? For according to the voice of truth, “from the beginning he was a liar, and he did not stand in the truth” (John 8), because as soon as he was made, he fell.

[Note: [Col. 0042D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 10.]

He was indeed created in truth, but, not standing fast, [Col. 0042C] he immediately fell away from truth. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). The devil held primacy among the angels; from that confidence he fell, so that he can no longer be restored. The prophet proclaims the excellence of his pre-eminence in these words: “The cedars were not taller than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his height; no tree in paradise was like him, because God made him more beautiful” (Ezek. 31). Understand by cedars and fir trees the powers of the heavenly orders, which seemed inferior in comparison with him. For it is written of him: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). Hence, in comparison with the angels, he was called an archangel. He was created first by pre-eminence of rank, not by priority in time.

This evil dragon, therefore, does not fight God and his angels in heaven, but in the Church against the Word of God clothed in flesh and against his saints.

But what does Scripture say? “And the dragon,” it says, “fought, and his angels; and they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven.” By “heaven,” namely, it means all the saints, who, believing in Christ, do not receive the devil once expelled, but repel him from themselves with their whole mind. Thus the evil dragon was expelled from heaven—that is, from the Church—[Col. 0043A] “the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, deceiving the world; he was cast out upon the earth, and his angels were cast down with him.”

[Note: [Col. 0043D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 11.]

The name *anguis* denotes the whole class of serpents, which can be folded and twisted. It is called *anguis* because it is angular and never straight. Thus the ancient enemy is rightly called a serpent, because in this age he moves about with crooked and shifting cunning. Of him it is said: “O twisting serpent, who by a thousand windings and winding deceits stir up tranquil hearts.”

[Note: [Col. 0043D] From the same Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 4.]

*Satanas* in Latin means “adversary” or “transgressor.” He is indeed the adversary, because he is the enemy of truth and always strives to oppose the virtues of the saints. He is the transgressor because, made a lawbreaker, he did not remain in the truth in which he was created.

The demons, they say, are called by the Greeks as though *demna*, that is, “skilled” and “knowing things.” For they foresee many future events, and thus are accustomed to give certain answers. They possess knowledge of things beyond human weakness, partly through the keenness of a subtler [supp. sense], partly through the experience of a very long life, and partly through angelic revelation at God’s command. They flourish by the nature of aerial bodies. Before their transgression, indeed, they bore heavenly bodies; but having fallen, they were changed into a varied condition. They were permitted to occupy not the more extensive [perhaps “purer”] regions of that air, but the gloomy regions near at hand, which are like a prison for them until the time of judgment, in which they are to be condemned.

This evil dragon who was expelled is the prince of all [Col. 0043C] evils, and his angels are wicked people and unclean spirits, who are expelled with him from heaven—that is, from the Church. For all who consent to him in evil are driven outside the Church with their prince, compelled by divine justice and power. By heaven we understand holy people, but by earth, sinners. Hence: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). Heaven signifies spiritual people, who meditate on heavenly things; earth, carnal people, who have not yet put off the earthly man—that is, earthly vices. So too the Lord said to the devil: “You shall eat earth” (Gen. 3), that is, those whom you overthrow by earthly desire shall belong to you. Again he said to sinful man: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (ibid.). Therefore they are excluded from the righteous themselves who desire heavenly things, and are cast down upon the earth to be trodden under the feet of the saints. Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions of the earth, and over all the power of Satan” (Luke 10). Not that the saints tread wicked people or demons under their bodily feet, since they ought not to repay evil for evil; but because the wicked desire earthly things while the saints pant after heavenly things and desire nothing earthly, bearing tribulation [Col. 0044A] and poverty patiently, they walk over them not bodily but, as it were, in mind.

Again he adds, saying: “Now has come salvation, and power, and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ” (Rev. 12).

[Note: [Col. 0043D] St Beatus on this passage.]

The loud voice in heaven is Christ’s victory and the salvation which he gave to his Church when he appeared in flesh. All the kingdoms of the world serve him—that is, the saints whom he redeemed with his own blood from the hand of the enemy. Truly salvation and power have come, because the Son of God expelled the ancient enemy from the Church, namely from the hearts of the saints. Now salvation, power, and the kingdom of our God have come, because the world, formerly subject to the devil through the worship of idols, is now subject to God through faith in Christ. “For,” it says, “the accuser of our brethren has been cast down, [Col. 0044B] who accused them before the presence of our God day and night; and they conquered him through the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony [supplemented ‘and’], and they did not love their lives even unto death” (ibid.).

This voice is not that of angels, as some think; for if it came from the higher heaven, it would by no means say “the accuser of our brethren,” but “our accuser.” If angels call righteous people on earth their brethren, then there could be no rejoicing that the devil had been sent to earth and that human beings dwell on earth. On that interpretation, dwelling on earth with demons would be a cause of joy for people. But, as we said above—

[Note: [Col. 0043D] Beatus asserts this well, as one who has said above [Col. 0044D] that this voice heard was that of Christ’s disciples; but Martin, in whom there had previously been no mention of the apostles, rendered these words far too carelessly.]

—we believe the voice to be that of the apostles, when they learned that the devil was held bound and that the Son of God, incarnate, reigned in his saints, [Col. 0044C] saying: “Now salvation and power have come,” and the rest which are now seen in the Church. For Holy Scripture often uses day for prosperity and night for adversity. Thus he does not cease to accuse by day and by night, because now in prosperity and now in adversity he tempts us and accuses us concerning our errors. He accuses by day when, amid prosperity, he suggests that we have sinned in thought, word, or deed; he accuses by night when, amid adversity, he shows that we lack patience.

It is fitting, therefore, beloved, that we render thanks to God the almighty Father, who through Michael, the chief archangel, to whom none is equal in powers—that is, through his most beloved Son—[Col. 0044D] expelled from heaven, namely from the Church, the evil dragon, the accuser of our brethren. Stand therefore, beloved, strong in spiritual warfare, and fight with the ancient serpent, so that after victory you may be able to attain the delights of paradise, of which the envy of that same ancient enemy deprived you and your parents. Act manfully, and take up spiritual weapons against the evil and invisible enemy.

Those who serve an earthly emperor strive to obey all his commands; how much more ought those who serve the heavenly Emperor to labour to fulfil the heavenly commandments?

[Note: [Col. 0045C] From the book *On Saving Precepts*, chapter 20.]

Earthly soldiers, wherever they are sent, are ready and prompt, nor can they excuse themselves for the sake of wives or children. Much more must Christ’s soldiers, without the encumbrance of this age, obey their Emperor, their Lord Jesus Christ, and fight with spiritual weapons against the powers of the air for love of him. Soldiers of this world go to war against a visible enemy; but you, taught by the example of your Emperor Jesus Christ, fight without ceasing against the devil, the master of all wickedness. Earthly soldiers strive against enemies using iron weapons; but for you the wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the princes and rulers of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in heavenly places [Col. 0045B] with spiritual weapons (Eph. 6). Secular soldiers wear iron helmets on their heads in battle; but against the evil dragon Christ is your helmet and defence. They wear iron breastplates so that enemies may not wound them; but you have put on Christ’s love as your breastplate. Soldiers of a mortal emperor do not cease to cast spears and arrows against their enemies; but you, soldiers of the eternal Emperor, send pure prayers against the invisible enemy. Until they finish the battle, they do not cast off their weapons lest adversaries wound them; you must never be without weapons, because your enemy is more cunning than theirs. Earthly soldiers fight against enemies for a time; but your enemies do not cease to fight with you as long as you live in the body. Their weapons are laborious and heavy to carry; yours, indeed, are light and pleasant. They receive an earthly gift for earthly labour; but for spiritual labour you shall receive a heavenly reward.

Therefore do not fear, beloved, to join battle with the dragon, [Col. 0046A] because the Lord Jesus Christ will come to your aid.

[Note: [Col. 0045C] Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 5.]

In the eyes of carnal people the devil is terrible; but in the eyes of spiritual people his terror is contemptible. He is feared by unbelievers as a lion; by those strong in faith he is despised and trodden down as a worm, and, when he appears, is driven away in a moment. As the Lord says: “No archer has put him to flight” (Job 41); yet he shall be put to flight by devout people who send pure prayers against him. “The stones of the sling are turned to stubble for him” (ibid.); yet he shall fear servants of God strong in faith. This evil enemy reckons iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood (ibid.); yet he shall fear people diligent in the law of the Lord and humble in holy conduct. “He regards the hammer as stubble [Col. 0046B] and laughs at the brandishing spear” (ibid.); yet he shall dread believers who keep perfect love of God and neighbour.

Therefore let love of God and neighbour remain in you, and frequently send the arrows of prayer against the evil dragon. Let love of God and neighbour always be in your heart, and let unceasing prayer from your mouth not fail in the assault upon the enemy. Let not the fire of love be extinguished in your breast, and let the darts of prayers be hurled unceasingly against the invisible enemy. Frequent prayer overcomes the devil’s darts. The frequency of prayers drives out unclean spirits.

[Note: [Col. 0046C] Isidore, *Synonyms*, book II, “On Prayer.”]

This is the first power against the assaults of demons. Demons are conquered by prayer. Therefore, beloved, love God above all things and call upon him without ceasing, that he may deign to grant you the strength to fight against the wiles [Col. 0046C] of the dragon, so that, aided by his grace, you may be able to ascend to that place from which that same evil enemy is known to have fallen—he granting it, who through that same most beloved Son deigned to cast him out from his Church. Amen.

## SERMON SEVEN. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

[Col. 0045]

[Col. 0045D] John the apostle and evangelist, the son of Zebedee, chosen by the Lord and loved more than the others, whom Christ removed from carnal embraces when he was intending to marry; who at supper, by divine dispensation, reclined upon the Master’s breast; and who, intoxicated from the fountain of that very breast of the Lord, watered the holy Church of the Word of God as one of the rivers of paradise—afterward, visited beforehand by divine grace, ascended in spirit to heaven on the Lord’s Day. There, with an angel showing them to him, he saw divine mysteries (Rev. 1), from which, for our instruction, he says among other things:

[Col. 0046D] “Behold, I John saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God” (Rev. 7). By the other angel ascending from the rising of the sun and having the seal of the living God, he means the Church, which rises from the passion of Christ, who is the true Sun of righteousness. For it took its beginning from his side as he hung upon the cross, and reverently received in baptism the sign of the whole Trinity. In Greek, *angelus*; in Latin, it is called *nuntius*, “messenger.” Thus the holy Church is rightly called an angel, because it announces God’s commandments to all peoples. At one time it promises the joys of paradise; at another it threatens the punishments of hell. It admonishes these people to seek good; it persuades those people to beware of evil. It exhorts these people to remain in good; it preaches to those people that they should swiftly withdraw from evil.

Therefore let it be said: “Behold, I John saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God”: namely, the holy Church having the seal of the living God upon its forehead. “And he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm earth and sea, saying: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God upon their foreheads” (ibid.). By these four angels we understand the devil, who dwells in wicked people in the four regions of the world. Yet from Christ’s passion until Antichrist he is bound and placed beneath the feet of the Church, lest he harm humankind as much as he wishes.

For so we read in the Gospel: “The Lord gave his disciples power over all demons and to cure diseases” (Luke 9). And again: “Who shall enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man?” (Matt. 12). The devil is therefore bound in his body—that is, in wicked people—so that he may not deceive the believing nations in the four regions of the world, namely the holy Church, which is Christ’s body.

This angel, that is, the Church, therefore rebukes him under the person of the four angels, that he may not harm earth and sea—that is, the congregation of the faithful—until the elect, predestined for the kingdom of heaven, are sealed. [Col. 0047C] For it was given to him, namely the devil, to harm earth and sea—that is, he has the power to tempt God’s Church. Yet he tempts the good for their testing, but the wicked for their condemnation. The devil’s temptation benefits the good by increasing their reward; but for the wicked it becomes an addition to their condemnation. The devil does not tempt the elect beyond what God permits him, for although by his evil will he always desires to bring temptations upon them, nevertheless, unless he receives power from God, he can by no means obtain what he desires. Thus, although his will is unjust, his power, God permitting it, is just. The strength of God’s elect could never endure demonic temptations if God did not restrain their malice by a merciful governance.

Hence it is now said: “Do not harm [Col. 0047D] the earth or the sea or the trees.” As though it said: Do not harm the earth, that is, those given over to earthly actions, or the Jews, now cultivated by the ploughshare of the Law; nor the sea, namely the Gentiles, embittered and flowing with diverse vices. For in this present Church good and evil people are mingled together. Therefore let it be said: Do not harm God’s Church beyond what has been granted to you, nor before the time appointed by God, so that both “the just may still be justified, and those who are in filth may still be defiled” (Rev. 22), until Christ comes for judgment. In that judgment your wickedness shall be more severely condemned, and the patience of the saints more gloriously crowned.

[Col. 0048A] It follows: “And I heard the number of those sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed, from every tribe of the sons of Israel” (Rev. 7). The one hundred and forty-four thousand are the whole Church, sealed in the image and likeness of its Creator. Hence the Prophet sings in the person of the same Church: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4).

[Note: [Col. 0047D] From St Beatus, p. 350.]

Indeed this is the whole Church, believed to be founded in so great a number of members through Christ, who is the firmest rock. For the number of saints is said to be innumerable, as one reads in the Psalm: “But your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured by me; their rule has been greatly strengthened. I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand” (Ps. 138). The number of all saints is unknown to us, because it is said to be multiplied above the sand; yet it is wholly known to almighty God, in whose image and likeness it is read to have been pre-signified. Every faithful soul, without doubt, if it follows the footsteps of its Creator and keeps his commandments with all devotion, bears the seal of the living God upon its forehead. Although one has been baptized in the Lord’s name and anointed with sacred chrism, nevertheless, if one is more occupied in evil works than in holy actions, one is not counted among the sealed. Whoever therefore desires to have the seal of the living God upon his forehead should show by good works the faith in God received in baptism.

Again he adds, saying: “After these things I saw a great [Col. 0048C] multitude, which no one could number, from all nations and tribes and peoples and tongues, standing before the throne” (Rev. 7). He did not say, “After these things I saw another people” or “another multitude,” but “I saw the people”—that is, the same people whom he had seen mystically as one hundred and forty-four thousand, he now saw as innumerable. And the one whom he saw from every tribe of the sons of Israel is the great multitude from every tribe, people, nation, and tongue.

The Lord makes clear in the Gospel that the whole Church, whether from Jews or Gentiles, is the twelve tribes of Israel: “You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). For the holy apostles shall judge the whole Church, which is not from circumcision alone, but from every [Col. 0048D] tribe and nation. These one hundred and forty-four thousand are not the infants whom Herod killed, as some think, because they were about two thousand from the tribe of Judah and few from the tribe of Benjamin; but these are from every tribe, nation, and tongue.

This, then, is the universal Church, founded upon the firm rock—that is, on Christ—and established in nine grades. In the first grade, the Church is founded on the Lord’s passion and is especially instructed by his example of poverty and love. It is also born again through the saving laver and perfected by the teaching of humility. Finally, it is fortified by the trophy of the cross and redeemed from captivity by his precious blood.

[Col. 0049A] In the second grade, the twelve apostles, like twelve gates—or indeed like the twelve hours of the bright day—shone with light throughout the whole world through the example of the one Master. Both acting by deeds and teaching by speech, they multiplied the abundant and immeasurable number of believers; and thus, triumphing in the contest of patience, love, and humility by the Saviour’s example, they entered the heavenly kingdom.

In the third grade, the countless companies of martyrs followed in the footsteps of the holy apostles. Taking up the arms of holy faith and putting on the breastplate of righteousness, they despised the delights of worldly desire, rejecting all visible things as dung for Christ’s name (Phil. 3), and gave up their bodies to death rather than serve idols. They too, crowned with blessed martyrdom, were assigned with the apostles in the kingdom.

In the fourth grade follows the devout and most faithful struggle of the blessed confessors. Amid the savage fury of pagans defending their idols, they confessed the Lord and Saviour of all, and themselves gained no small people for the Lord by the example of good conduct. They bore patiently the insults inflicted upon them for Christ’s love, and through love prayed to God for their enemies.

In the fifth grade comes the dignity of bishops and the other orders of Catholic priests, assuming [Col. 0049C] the place of the holy apostles in the governance of churches and in the regeneration through the laver of believing peoples of both sexes.

In the sixth grade follows the most sacred religious life of cenobites, monks, and virgins, who, separated from the tumult of the age, have been gathered to the holy service of almighty God. Remaining there most devoutly in complete abstinence and persevering until the end in a life of good conduct, they left worthy examples for posterity.

In the seventh grade follows the way of life of the holy fathers, the anchorites—that is, hermits—who withdraw from public society, penetrate the difficult solitudes of the desert, enjoy divine discourse, and end their life “desiring to be dissolved and to be [Col. 0049D] with Christ” (Phil. 1).

In the eighth grade follows the order of penitents and of those who bewail grievous crimes, who strive not to sin further and do not cease to lament what is past. As great as was the intention of their perverse mind in sinning, so great is the full devotion of humility and love that perseveres in them until the end.

This ninth and final grade associates with the preceding grades the infancy of little children in their earliest age, who finish the course of this present life before they incur the harmful guilt of sin. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). By these nine [Col. 0050A] grades of holy institutions, the Catholic—that is, universal—Church, gathered from the whole world, ascends from Christ’s passion, has entered and daily enters the kingdoms of heaven, and reigns with its head Jesus Christ for ever.

It follows: “Clothed,” he says, “in white robes, and palms in their hands” (Rev. 7). The white robe signifies an unstained life. What he says, “and palms in their hands,” is not without reason.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] From Beatus, p. 351.]

For the life of the righteous is compared with the palm. Below, the palm is rough to the touch and, as it were, wrapped in dry bark; above, it is beautiful both in appearance and fruit. Below it is constricted by the wrappings of its bark; above it spreads out in the breadth of lovely greenness. Such indeed is the life of the elect: lowly below, [Col. 0050B] beautiful above; worthless on earth, precious in heaven. The life of the righteous on earth—that is, in this life—is wrapped, as it were, in many barks when it is afflicted and constricted by innumerable tribulations. But in that highest eternity it is enlarged, as it were, by leaves of lovely greenness, when it receives from God the reward of eternal blessedness.

Yet the palm differs from the other kinds of trees in this: other trees are thicker in their strength near the ground, but become narrower above, around their branches; and the more they grow taller, the more slender they become on high. But the palm is confined and narrow near the earth, while above it is broad; beginning slender and delicate from below, it ascends in growth more broadly to the heights. To what, then, are other shrubs found to be like, if not earthly people who desire earthly gain? For without doubt all lovers of this age are strong in earthly pursuits but weak in heavenly things. They desire to toil even unto death for temporal glory, and they despise labouring for eternal life. Lovers of this temporal life often endure injuries for earthly gains, but refuse to bear even the insults of the smallest word for a heavenly reward. They labour tirelessly all day in an earthly lawsuit, but grow weary within a single hour of prayer before God.

On the contrary, the life of the righteous is compared to the palm because it is constricted on earth and enlarged in heaven. In earthly [Col. 0050D] pursuits they are weak, and in heavenly pursuits strong. Often the conduct of the elect makes greater progress in finishing than it promises at its beginning; and if, in fear, it sometimes begins the first things, it completes the last more fervently. For it always considers itself only beginning, and therefore perseveres tirelessly in good work. The prophet, seeing this perseverance of the righteous, said: “Those who trust in the Lord shall change their strength; they shall take up wings like eagles; they shall run and not labour; they shall walk and not fail” (Isa. 40).

Therefore, dearest brethren, if you desire to attain the rewards of eternal recompense, let your life resemble the palm. If you truly desire to reach eternal [Col. 0051A] blessedness, let your conduct have the likeness of the palm. Let your life be narrow in low things and broad in high things; let your conduct become strict below but broad above. For narrow is the way which leads to life, broad that which leads to death (Matt. 7). By the broad way the wicked descend to hell, but by the narrow way the righteous ascend to heaven. By the wide path lovers of the world go to destruction, but by the narrow road the friends of God come to the kingdom.

Therefore, beloved, let your hands be ready for good work and weighed down from evil by the chains of love of God and neighbour. Let your feet run swiftly to the service of almighty God, and be bound by the fetter of religion against running about through the streets of the city (Cant. 3). Restrain the eyes of your body, lest they see the vanity of this world; but open the eyes of your mind, so that you may contemplate God in spirit. Let your ears be opened devoutly to hear the word of God; and, lest the deadly poison of flattering or slanderous words enter through them, let them be hedged about with the thorns of fear of God. Let a guard be set over your mouth according to the Psalmist (Ps. 140), [Col. 0052A] lest murmuring, slander, or abuse proceed from it. Let the tongue of each of you be free in God’s praises, and lest it break out in insult against anyone, let it at a suitable time be bound by the bond of silence. Guard your mind with all diligence, and cleanse it from sins and vices through true confession, because there lies the source of good or evil thought. Let your heart be opened to Christ in meditations on the Scriptures, but shut against the devil by rejecting harmful and vain things. Let a measure also be imposed upon the belly, so that it is not excessively distended by an abundance of food, but may be moderately refreshed with sobriety.

Brethren and my lords, in this manner constrain your life in earthly activities after the likeness of the palm, and enlarge it in spiritual pursuits, if on the day of judgment you desire [Col. 0052B] to receive, with all the saints, the palms of your labours. Wash away also the stains of your life with daily tears, that after your death you may attain the heavenly kingdom and see the King of saints reigning in his splendour—he who, in perfect Trinity, lives and reigns as God for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON EIGHT. ON THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT ISIDORE

[Note: [Col. 0051D] Why this and the following sermon are entitled by the author “On the Translation of Isidore,” although they offer not a single word about that translation, is not easy to conjecture. The whole turns [Col. 0052D] upon a matter altogether marvellous, the credibility of which we leave to the reader.]

[Col. 0051]

[Col. 0051C] “She shall not fear for her household from the cold of snow, for all her household are clothed in double garments” (Prov. 31).

In approximately the year 1147 from the Incarnation of the Lord, a messenger of the supreme King—namely, the angel whom the Lord sends round about those who fear him (Ps. 33), one of those who always behold the face of the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 18)—brought joyful news in the court of the supreme Emperor, who commands the winds and the sea (Matt. 8): that the house of blessed Isidore of Seville, formerly metropolitan bishop, was being prepared—or rather restored—within the walls of the city of León for the order and habitation of religious clerics.

When this report had been received, the venerable Father Augustine, outstanding doctor of the Catholic Church, rejoicing and exulting, observed Lord Isidore, foremost among the confessors, pondering something within himself, and addressed him thus:

“What is this, venerable brother, that you are turning over in your mind? Are you perhaps meditating upon the exposition of the Scriptures? Yet in this homeland of spirits, heaven—that is, Scripture—is not stretched out like a skin (Ps. 103), but folded up like a book (Isa. 34); nor do you find peoples here in need of instruction, since here is fulfilled what is written: ‘A man shall not teach his neighbour, for all shall know me, from the least even to the greatest’ (Jer. 31). [Col. 0052C] But although, as it seems, you are concerned about the governance and ordering of churches, you ought nevertheless to be concerned about that church which affects you more spiritually [Note: [Col. 0052D] Perhaps, “more particularly.”] and more closely. I mean that which, within the walls of the city of León, contains the treasure of your body and is being prepared for religious clerics to inhabit.”

To this Lord Isidore replied: “I am concerned about these matters, but especially about the clothing of the clerics serving God in that house. For I have already provided, for the most part, what is necessary for their sustenance, and I shall make more ample provision for the rest; but that land does not abound in clothing. Yet I desire that, having food and clothing, they should be content with these (1 Tim. 6).”

To this Father Augustine said: “And I too shall provide garments for these sons of yours. For it is read in Solomon concerning a certain woman [Col. 0052D] that ‘she shall not fear for her household from the cold of snow,’ and so forth. And there it is further said of her: ‘She worked flax and wool’ (Prov. 31). In this manner, therefore, I shall give these sons and dependants of yours a double garment woven from flax and wool: namely, a surplice and a cope. In one I wish purity, and in the other humility, to be understood; and this may also be recognized from the colour and appearance of the garments themselves. For bodily purity has whiteness, while the blackness of the garment represents humility.

“You also know that the most blessed Virgin, Mother of the Lord, was especially clothed in both. Hence it is written of her: ‘The glory of Lebanon has been given to her, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon’ (Isa. 35). And she herself says of herself: ‘Because the Lord has regarded the humility of his handmaid’ (Luke 1). The same is also seen in the making of these garments. For a linen garment is made with much labour and difficulty, whereas a woollen garment is not so made. In this way, purity of body is beneficially attained and preserved by much labour and effort, since it is resisted by the law of the members, the tinder and weakness of nature, the sting of the flesh—which even the Apostle confesses that he endures (2 Cor. 12)—perverse and unstable habit, the enticing external temptation of another’s skin, and the inciting suggestion of the inward enemy.

[Col. 0053B] “Now concerning flax, it is plain that it is first pulled from the earth; then gathered into bundles, lowered into a pool, dried in the sun, cleansed of refuse and tow, drawn through the distaff into threads, wound into balls, stretched and woven into cloth, finally cut and sewn; and thus the surplice is fitted. Flax grows from the earth, and by it is signified the shining beauty of purity and bodily and spiritual chastity.

“Therefore flax is first pulled from the earth, because whoever desires to possess the purity of chastity out of fear and love of God must first leave earthly and secular conduct and join himself to the fellowship of religious men. It is also fitting that each person bodily depart from the place where he remembers having been enslaved to vices. For often, when the place is changed, the disposition of the mind is changed as well.

“Then flax is gathered into bundles, because one who previously, in carnal living, was dissipated through unlawful acts ought, bound by the bond of divine love, to gather himself again within the lodging of his own heart. Thereafter flax is lowered into a pool. By the pool, because it is always in the depths, compunction of heart is figured; for as flax is cleansed and washed in the pool, so the sinner is cleansed and washed of sins and vices in tears of compunction arising with deep groaning from the breast.

“Then it is dried in the sun. God is the true Sun of righteousness, from whose heat—that is, from whose knowledge—no one can hide. Thus, by the heat [Col. 0053D] of the eternal Sun, the unlawful moisture of lust is dried up in a person; for, kindled by knowledge of him and by the fervour of charity, one immediately withdraws from the intention of an evil deed. Flax is also cleansed of tow and refuse, because every convert is cleansed through penitence from unlawful and superfluous actions.

“Again, flax is drawn through the distaff into threads. The distaff is carried in the left hand, but the spindle in the right; and as threads descend from the distaff, so all the actions of God’s servant depend upon the judgment of his superior, so that he is permitted to do nothing without that superior’s counsel. Then it is wound into balls, because it is restrained under the rule of its head. Thereafter it is stretched and woven into cloth, when, at his superior’s command, going about outside and within, he performs whatever good he can. Finally, the cloth is cut and sewn, when God’s servant [Col. 0054A] perfectly despises the world, scorns visible things, and gathers himself inwardly in contemplation of his Creator. He is, as it were, cut off from the tumult of the present age, and sewn—that is, joined—by mind and desire to the citizens of the eternal homeland, so that he may at least taste by longing the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom which he cannot yet taste perfectly. Thus the surplice of complete purity and honourableness is fitted, because he is now made suitable for the fellowship of the perfect.

“By God’s grace, brothers, you now have a surplice; nevertheless, you still need a sheep’s-wool cope. The woollen and black garment signifies the humility of religious life. Wool is first shorn, then cleansed and washed, hung upon the distaff, drawn into threads, woven and sewn; and thus the cope is made.

[Col. 0054B] “In wool are shown God’s gifts, which are bestowed upon us by God in the present life. Wool is shorn when earthly property is cast aside for God’s sake. Wool is, as it were, cleansed and washed when a person is cleansed of sins by the giving of alms. Hence: ‘Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you’ (Luke 11). Wool is hung upon the distaff when one keeps the utmost watch lest anything be given for the sake of display or through love of vain glory. It is drawn into threads when almsgiving is bestowed with discernment. Wool is woven when one diligently persists in works of mercy. The cloth is cut when the desire to possess is completely expelled from the mind. Finally it is sewn, when every convert, ascending from the active life, [Col. 0054C] leaves all things behind and is inserted into and joined with the contemplative life. Thus the regular cope is made, when through good works one deserves from God the garment of eternal glory.”

Again the most blessed Augustine addressed holy Isidore, saying: “Venerable brother, behold: as I promised, I have clothed all your household in double garments. Therefore do not fear any longer for your household because of snowy cold, since all your household are clothed in double garments. First I fitted them with a surplice, by which purity of mind and body is signified; then with a cope woven of sheep’s wool, in which innocence of life and humility of conduct are displayed. You therefore, venerable brother Isidore, procure sufficient provisions for them, so that, while they abound in clothing, [Col. 0054D] they may serve God without want. It also belongs to you to warn them, since you are present in spirit and body, that they should strive with all devotion to fulfil the rule established for them by me. Preach to them also that they should diligently adhere to spiritual offices, lest—God forbid—delighted with earthly goods, they should be altogether deprived of eternal ones.”

To this our patron, Saint Isidore, replied: “O most reverend Father Augustine, it is fitting that you should thus exhort them to live well. We render thanks to almighty God, who has appointed you teacher of the holy churches.”

Behold, dearest brothers: by God’s grace you have been sufficiently instructed by blessed Augustine and clothed doubly in regular garments, namely the surplice and cope. In the surplice, as has already been said, [Col. 0055A] purity of mind and body is signified. Take care, therefore, brothers, that damnable fornication does not lie hidden beneath the surplice. Believe me: whoever is defiled by fornication does not wear the surplice. What does it profit to show before human eyes a surplice washed with water, while inwardly bearing before God’s eyes a body defiled by fornication? Or what does it profit to display outwardly, in people’s sight, the cleanliness of a garment, while concealing within the uncleanness of fornication? Nothing is hidden before God: he who made hidden things sees what is concealed. “All things are naked and laid open to his eyes” (Heb. 4). Therefore I warn you, beloved, that you must not wish to be whitewashed tombs, which indeed outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones, [Col. 0055B] worms, and every kind of filth (Matt. 23).

The cope is woven from sheep’s wool and therefore signifies the humility of religious life. Therefore, beloved, take diligent care lest a wolf lie hidden beneath sheep’s skin. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7). A wolf lies hidden beneath sheep’s skin when beneath the habit of regular life are hidden pretence, discord, and envy. A wolf also lies hidden beneath sheep’s skin when any hypocrite, under the appearance of religion, harms his neighbours. The wolf is ravenous within: outwardly feigning innocence, he does not cease, by detraction, murmuring, and whispering, [Col. 0056A] to eat in secret the flesh of his neighbours. Therefore, brothers, fulfil with good works the religious habit which you display in outward appearance. Do not seek to be one thing in private and another in public. Let the inward mind accord with your religious garments. Let life accord with speech. The habit is holy: let the mind be holy. The garments are holy: let your works be holy.

Therefore, beloved, having food and clothing, be content with them (1 Tim. 6), and retain nothing as your own among you. Without doubt, he commits theft who holds all things in common with the other brothers and yet keeps something hidden for himself. To possess all things in common with the other brothers and [Col. 0056B] to hide something else for oneself—what is this but to hand oneself over to punishments after death? He who shares food and clothing in common with the other brothers and retains something else hidden commits nothing other than manifest theft. Therefore, dearest brothers, despise riches, love poverty, scorn earthly things, desire heavenly things. Seek nothing superfluous, retain nothing for yourselves, hide nothing, if you desire to attain the common fellowship of God’s elect. May he deign to lead you there, he who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Ninth Sermon. Second Sermon for the Translation of Saint Isidore

[Col. 0055C] “She shall not fear for her household from the cold of snow, for all her household are clothed in double garments” (Prov. 31).

A messenger of the supreme King—namely, the angel whom the Lord sends round about those who fear him (Ps. 33), one of those who always behold the face of the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 18)—brought joyful news in the court of the supreme Emperor, who commands the winds and the sea (Matt. 8): that the house of blessed Isidore of Seville, formerly metropolitan bishop, was being prepared, or rather restored, within the walls of the city of León for the order and habitation of religious clerics.

When this report had been received, the venerable Father Augustine, outstanding doctor of the Catholic Church, rejoicing and exulting, observed Lord Isidore, Doctor of the Spains, pondering something within himself [Col. 0055D] and addressed him thus:

“What is this, venerable brother, that you are turning over in your mind? Are you perhaps meditating upon the exposition of the Scriptures? Yet in this homeland of spirits, heaven—that is, Scripture—is not stretched out like a skin (Ps. 103), but folded up, that is, rolled together like a book (Isa. 34); nor do you find peoples here in need of instruction, since here is fulfilled what is written: ‘A man shall not teach his neighbour; for all shall know me, from the least even to [Col. 0056C] the greatest’ (Jer. 31). But although, as it seems, you are concerned about the governance and ordering of churches, you ought nevertheless to be concerned about that church which affects you more particularly and more closely. I mean that which, within the walls of the city of León, contains the treasure of your body and is being prepared for religious clerics to inhabit.”

To this Lord Isidore replied: “I am concerned about these matters, but especially about the clothing of the clerics serving God in that house. For I have already provided, for the most part, what is necessary for their sustenance, and I shall make more ample provision for the rest; but that land does not abound in clothing. Yet I desire that, having food and clothing, they should be content with these (1 Tim. 6).”

To this Father Augustine said: “And I too shall provide [Col. 0056D] garments for these sons of yours. For it is read in Solomon concerning a certain woman that ‘she shall not fear for her household from the cold of snow,’ and so forth. And there it is further said of her: ‘She worked flax and wool’ (Prov. 31). In this manner, therefore, I shall give these sons and dependants of yours a double garment woven from wool and flax: namely, a surplice and a cope. In one I wish purity, and in the other humility, to be understood; and this may also be recognized from the colour and appearance [Col. 0057A] of the garments themselves. For bodily purity has whiteness, while the blackness of the garment represents humility.

“You also know that the most blessed Virgin, Mother of the Lord, was especially clothed in these garments. Hence it is written of her: ‘The glory of Lebanon has been given to her, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon’ (Isa. 35). And she herself says of herself: ‘Because the Lord has regarded the humility of his handmaid’ (Luke 1). The same is also seen in the making of these garments. For a linen garment is made with much labour and difficulty, whereas a woollen garment is not so made. In this way, purity of body is beneficially attained and preserved by much labour and effort, since it is resisted by the law of the members, the tinder and weakness of nature, the sting of the flesh—which even the Apostle confesses that he endures (2 Cor. 12)—perverse and unstable habit, [Col. 0057B] the enticing external temptation of another’s skin, and the inciting suggestion of the inward enemy.

“Now concerning flax, it is plain that it is first pulled from the earth; then gathered into bundles, lowered into a pool, dried in the sun, cleansed of refuse and tow, drawn through the distaff into threads, wound into balls, stretched and woven into cloth, finally cut and sewn; and thus the surplice is fitted. In this way one labours and sweats greatly so that the rust of the flesh may come out and its tenacious stickiness be overcome—the barbs of which a human being experienced after sin, before the motions of other sins, when streams of desires began to diffuse lawlessly through the members, though formerly they had been restrained by the law of nature lest they burst forth in disorder. Hence he was ashamed of [Col. 0057C] his nakedness and ran to the shade to cover his shamefulness (Gen. 3).

“The Apostle indicates the difficulty of overcoming this beast when he says: ‘Flee fornication’ (1 Cor. 6). It is a tribute, that is, of nature, pursuing even you yourselves more sharply and more closely. ‘For all its strength is in its loins, and its power in the navel of its belly’ (Job 40). This is Delilah, who sleeps in our bosom (Judg. 16), from whom the prophet commands us to guard the bars of our mouth (Mic. 7); for no pest is more effective in harming than a familiar enemy.

“Augustine: Therefore, so that a wedding garment may be prepared for the bridegroom, so that at every time the garments of these sons of yours, O brother Isidore, may be white (Eccl. 9), lest they walk naked: let the abomination of sordid pleasure and carnal filth first pull the flax [Col. 0057D] from the earth; let the strictness of regular order take care to gather it into bundles; let fear of punishment lower it into the pool; let the heat of desire for what is above dry it in the sun; let mortification of the flesh cleanse it of refuse and tow by bruising; let contemplation of heavenly things draw it through the distaff into threads; let frequent meditation wind it into balls; let sure expectation of future things stretch it into cloth; let the bond of charity weave it; let regular discipline cut it; let the strength of perseverance sew it.

“In the first of these, a person is displeased with himself; in the second, he denies himself to himself; in the third, he lets himself down beneath himself; in the fourth, he raises himself above himself; in the fifth, he restrains himself within himself; in the sixth, he surpasses himself in mind above himself; in the seventh, he gathers himself back to himself; in the eighth, he is strengthened from himself; in the ninth [Col. 0058A] he is joined both above and around himself; in the tenth, he is made strong; in the last, he is perfected and brought to completion.

“For when a person begins to consider within himself how brief is pleasure, which suffers hunger for itself and, cast aside in disgust, soon is either concealed, returns, or occasions repentance [the reading is uncertain]—for every pleasure has this quality: it drives the mad with its goads, and, like a swarm of flying bees, once it has poured out sweet honey, leaves its sting in the conscience—when, I say, a person considers these things, though made an animal bent downward and given over to belly and genitals, to whom God

> Gave a lofty face and commanded him to behold the heavens  
> and raise his upright gaze to the stars.

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 1),

let him shudder at the mire of sordid pleasure and abhor the wallowing-place of carnal filth; and thus flax is [Col. 0058B] pulled from the earth. For every sin whatever that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever fornicates sins against his own body (1 Cor. 6). Those to whom the Apostle said, ‘What fruit, then, did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?’ (Rom. 6), had pulled this flax from the earth.

“Next, when he arranges ascents in his heart (Ps. 83), so as to enter into the powers of the Lord (Ps. 70), he chooses rather to be lowly in the house of God than to dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83), and binds himself by a vow of continence and by the strictness of regular order. This binding is plainly such that he is gathered and tied into a bundle of myrrh; that he may be like Isaac, bound to the altar with a bundle of wood placed upon him (Gen. 22). For he has a mouth and shall not speak; he has eyes and shall not see (Ps. 113), and so forth, so that he may truly say: ‘I have been crucified with Christ’ (Gal. 2).

“But because he is still grinding between two millstones, which Moses forbids to be given as a pledge (Deut. 24), through the lower stone—like flax lowered into a pool—conscious of past things and fearful of future ones, he fears punishments for past sins he has committed and for future sins he may commit. For, says Solomon, ‘Blessed is the man who is always fearful’ (Prov. 28). And the Psalmist: ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom’ (Ps. 110). For fear of punishment is the gate of the kingdom.

“But since amid these things the man of desires burns with desire for heavenly things, desiring to eat that new Passover in the kingdom [Col. 0058D] of God (Luke 22), and is as though burned like a whole offering upon the altar, every carnal moisture in him is dried up as in the sun. Thus, as though God were praised on the tambourine, whatever belongs to the Paschal lamb is eaten roasted with fire alone (Exod. 12). Jeremiah burned with this fire when he said: ‘It became like a burning fire shut up in my bones’ (Jer. 20); and the disciples when they said: ‘Was not our heart burning within us?’ (Luke 24); and David: ‘My heart grew hot within me’ (Ps. 38), and so forth.

“Placed also between hammer and anvil, he is bruised by mortification of the flesh, but not broken. He is cleansed of superfluities, not deprived of necessities, so that if he pursues the enemy, the citizen may not be extinguished, according to the Apostle’s saying: ‘Make no provision for [Col. 0059A] the flesh in its desires’ (Rom. 13). For since the belly and genitals are joined both by location and by vice, and a belly inflamed by wine easily foams over into lust, no more effective medicine can be applied for preserving bodily purity than to serve moderation, restrain gluttony, constrain the belly, and mortify the flesh, lest it overflow and dissolve into shameful lust—like Lot, whom Sodom did not conquer, but wines conquered (Gen. 9). Hence the prophet says: ‘The sin of Sodom was fullness and abundance of bread’ (Ezek. 16). The first parent also, through eating the forbidden tree, set his own weapons against himself; he experienced it and made himself loin-cloths to cover the shamefulness he had recognized (Gen. 3). The chief of the cooks also destroyed the walls of Jerusalem (Jer. 52). Hence the Apostle: ‘Do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery’ (Eph. 5). And Solomon: ‘Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness insolent’ (Prov. 20); it also uncovered Noah’s thighs and showed them to his son for laughter (Gen. 9). Thus wine did not spare even its own author. Anyone may better read these things in the book of experience:

> Wines prepare the spirits and make them fit for passions.

“The contemplation of heavenly things produces most delicate threads, from which, according to Boethius, the garment of philosophy is woven: so that, like a column of smoke from spices, caught up into the third heaven (Song 3), he may hear words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12).

“Frequent meditation also winds these together and gathers them, as it were, into balls, as is read concerning the most glorious Virgin: ‘But Mary preserved all these words, comparing them in her heart’ [Col. 0059C] (Luke 2). And the Apostle says: ‘Meditate upon these things’ (1 Tim. 4), so that reason may keep watch, lest, while the gatekeeper sleeps, Ish-bosheth be struck in the groin and die (2 Sam. 4). For meditation on the Lord’s sayings gives understanding to the little ones (Ps. 118).

“The upper millstone, that is, expectation of future things, raises the cloth on high, so that one may say: ‘Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we await Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation, making it conformed to the body of his glory’ (Phil. 3).

“But charity begins and completes the weaving of the garment, so that it may be a seamless robe woven from above throughout, which is not torn but falls, by the lot of divine predestination (John 19), to those whom he predestined [Col. 0059D] and fore-chose to become conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8). This is the wedding garment. Blessed is he who keeps it, lest he walk naked (Rev. 16). Concerning the discipline of regular order in reading, prayer, and the other things belonging to Mary, who is praised as having chosen the better part; or in the instruction of the younger members and works of mercy, in which Martha is troubled and anxious about many things (Luke 10): you, being better trained in these matters, are more able to teach me than to learn anything from one who is unlearned.

“Perseverance must sew this many-coloured garment together, so that it may be Joseph’s long robe (Gen. 37), and so that the tail of the victim may be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice—or rather, in the whole offering (Lev. 7). For ‘he who perseveres to the end shall be saved’ (Matt. 10). Let your sons be clothed inwardly [Col. 0060A] with this surplice, with this white garment; for ‘all the glory of the king’s daughter is within’ (Ps. 44), so that her Nazarites may be white, made whiter than snow (Lam. 4). But in order that they may be perfectly protected from the cold of snow and clothed in double garments, I shall also prepare for them the cope of humility.

“Now, for the cope to be fitted, wool is first shorn from the animal, then drawn into threads, cloth is woven, the fabric dyed, cut, and sewn. Renunciation of what is one’s own therefore shears the wool for making the cope of humility; regular instruction draws it into threads; the profession of obedience weaves the cloth; consideration of one’s own weakness dyes the fabric; remembrance of death cuts it; certainty of recompense sews it. The first of these, therefore, frees; the second instructs; the third binds; the fourth casts down; the fifth [Col. 0060B] shakes; the sixth raises up. Certainly, since wealth customarily gives birth to and nourishes pride—as is evident in the angel and in the first human being, whose iniquity came forth from fatness (Ps. 72), just as the richness of the earth burst forth upon the earth (Ps. 140)—

“Wool is, as it were, shorn for weaving the garment of humility when a person renounces his own will, his own possession, his own liberty, and his own thought, so that he may say to father and mother: ‘I do not know you.’ And as, when an animal is shorn, the animal is relieved of its burden, the worms die, and the wool is plucked off, so in renouncing one’s own things the camel is relieved of its burden so that it may pass through the eye of a needle (Matt. 19). For human prosperity itself is sprinkled with many bitter things: it is acquired with labour, possessed with fear, and lost with pain (Matt. 13). Thus it is compared in the Gospel to thorns. Hence the Apostle: ‘Those who desire to become rich entangle themselves in many pains’ (1 Tim. 6). The worms of temporal anxiety also die, and those of Gehenna’s punishment. For Solomon says: ‘As a worm consumes wood, so sorrow consumes the mind of a man’ (Prov. 25). And Isaiah says to Nebuchadnezzar: ‘Moth shall be spread beneath you, and worms shall be your covering’ (Isa. 14). And again: ‘Their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be extinguished’ (Isa. 66).

“In regular instruction, wool is as it were drawn into threads for making the cope of humility: in silence, which according to Isaiah is the cultivation of righteousness (Isa. 32); [Col. 0060D] in prayer, reading, and the remaining things which are signs of humility, such as tonsure, frequent bowing of the head, asking pardon, mutual confession, the common use of all things, lowliness of clothing, and austerity of food.
