The Apostle wished this wool to be drawn into threads when he said: ‘Let all things among you be done honourably and according to order’ (1 Cor. 14). Countless examples of the Fathers, both in the Old and in the New Testament, likewise support this.

“The profession of obedience weaves the cloth of humility. For what is so effective in producing and preserving humility as to place a human being in God’s place over one’s own head, and so depend wholly upon another’s judgment? Thus, without a superior’s signal, one has a mouth and does not speak; one has eyes and [Col. 0061A] does not see; one has feet and does not walk; one has hands and does not stretch them out even to receive gifts. Therefore obedience is rightly preferred to sacrifices (1 Sam. 15). For in sacrifice another’s flesh is slain; in obedience one’s own flesh is slain—sometimes even to the shedding of blood—according to the saying: ‘Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death’ (Phil. 2). Conversely, what is thought about obedience’s praise is better understood. The disobedience of one person condemns his descendants to death and proscribed the whole human race. For, as Samuel says: ‘To refuse obedience is the crime of divination, and to refuse submission is the sin of idolatry’ (1 Sam. 15). Obedience alone, therefore, possesses the merit of faith. The Apostle exhorts to it, saying: ‘Obey your rulers’ (Heb. 13).

[Col. 0061B] “Consideration of one’s own weakness dyes the fabric black. For if a person considers what he was, what he is, and what he will be, he recognizes that he is vile semen, a vessel of excrement, food for worms. ‘Why then does earth and ash grow proud?’ (Sir. 10). Why is a dead skin stretched out?

> Why does a human being grow proud, whose conception is guilt,  
> whose birth is punishment, whose life is pain, and whose death is necessity?

Know yourself, a rotting corpse. From heaven comes *γνῶθι σεαυτόν*, that is, “know yourself.” “In all your ways remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Sir. 7). And this is what cuts the fabric for sewing the cope of humility.

For pride is cut down if one considers the condition of death imposed upon all, according to the saying: [Col. 0061C] “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3); and the threat of condemnation to be inflicted upon the reprobate, according to the saying: “Your pride has been brought down to hell” (Isa. 14); and: “Like sheep they are placed in hell” (Ps. 48), and so forth.

“But certainty of recompense sews this cope. For if a person considers what he is of himself, what he is by God’s gift, and what sort of person and who he will become through God’s recompense, his own acts of righteousness become to him like a menstrual cloth (Isa. 64). This is what is meant when winged creatures lay down their wings as a voice comes from above the firmament that is over their heads (Ezek. 1). The shepherd of the Church customarily warns us to sew this cope when he says: ‘Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation’ (1 Pet. 5). Therefore, dearest ones, [Col. 0062A] clothe yourselves in these double garments, so that you may not fear for your household from the cold of snow.

“These cold things of snow are mortal sins and the assaults of the ancient enemy, who is not inappropriately called snow. For just as snow descends from heaven and does not return there again, so the devil, falling from the heights through pride, shall not return again to the hand from which he was shaken off. And as snow, though it is water, is hardened in the air by the violence of the north wind, so the devil, according to Job, is hardened like a stone (Job 41). He is also called the cold north wind, that is, hard, although only in name ‘right-hand.’ Hence in the Song of Songs: ‘Arise, north wind, and come, south wind’ (Song 4). By the cold of this snow the charity of many grows cold, as the Lord says (Matt. 24). [Col. 0062B] And Solomon says: ‘Because of the cold, the sluggard would not plough’ (Prov. 20).

“Therefore, so that your household may not fear these things, clothe yourselves in these double garments, beloved, so that you may break the two horns of that ancient horned serpent, more prominent than the others. Job says of it: ‘It sleeps in the covert of reeds, in damp places’ (Job 40); and again: ‘The mountains bring it herbs’ (ibid.); and: ‘It is king over all the children of pride’ (Job 41). This queen, this greatest offence, this little beast, which killed more of Absalom’s army than David’s sword, is especially to be feared and guarded against by you even in the good things you do. For:

> Pride, added to outstanding character, defiles it.

Though heavenly by origin, it dwells in the minds of lofty persons, [Col. 0062C] lurking beneath ashes and haircloth; it is first among those departing from God and last among those returning. For:

> When you have fought well, when you think all things subdued,  
> the pride that remains to be conquered attacks afterward.

At times there is long pride in a short sleeve. Therefore clothe yourselves in these double garments, so that you may be clothed not in a double garment of shame but in the robe of double glorification; walking with the Lamb in white (Rev. 3), made like the angels of God, who neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matt. 22), and, through the humility which you now maintain, sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, with him who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0061]

## Sermons on Various Subjects

## First Sermon. At the Dedication of a Church

[Col. 0061D] John, apostle and evangelist, chosen and beloved by Christ, was preferred in so great a love of affection that at the supper he reclined upon Christ’s breast [Col. 0062D] (John 13); and Christ deigned to commend his own Mother to him alone as he stood by his cross (John 19). This was by provident dispensation: he entrusted the most glorious Virgin to the keeping of the one whom, when he had wished to marry, he had summoned to the embrace of virginity and chosen beforehand as undefiled in mind and body.

Accordingly, when John was sent into exile on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, there was shown to him by that same Christ the Apocalypse which he there recorded. In it, among other matters for our instruction, he speaks thus: “The angel said to me: ‘Come, I will show you the bride of the Lamb.’ And he carried me in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, adorned like a bride arrayed for her husband” (Rev. 21).

By the great and high mountain he means Christ, of whom the prophet says: “On that day the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be upon the summit of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills” [Col. 0063B] (Isa. 2), that is, above the prophets and apostles; for they are called mountains and hills because of the greatness of their virtues and the excellence of their merits. And when he says “on that day,” he shows that the period from Christ’s Passion to the end of the world is one day.

It follows: the heavenly Jerusalem is the multitude of the saints, which is said to be coming with the Lord, as the prophet Zechariah says: “Behold, our Lord will come, and all his saints with him” (Zech. XIV). They are prepared by God as a clean dwelling-place, that they may dwell with him, like a bride adorned for her husband. Christ is the head and husband of the whole Church. Thus Solomon, speaking of that same Church under the figure of a valiant woman, says: “Her husband is noble in the gates, [Col. 0063C] when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. XXXI). Christ is the husband of the holy Church; with the senators of the land—that is, with the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles—he will sit to judge the living and the dead on the day of judgment. He is rightly called noble, because among all the children of men none is like him. Therefore the whole Church—that is, all the saints—will go forth adorned, to be joined in holiness and righteousness to Jesus Christ, their bridegroom, and will remain with him for ever.

This city Jerusalem, that is, the holy Church, is aptly called new, because through the sacrament of baptism it is renewed day by day in Christ, who is the new man. For it descends daily from heaven in penitence, namely by imitating the Son of God in humility. Thus the Son of God, though he was in the form [Col. 0063D] of God, took the form of a servant and descended from heaven, because he humbled himself even unto death (Phil. II). The descent of the Son of God from heaven is his incarnation. Therefore this city Jerusalem descends daily from heaven by imitating God, because, following in the footsteps of Jesus Christ her bridegroom, she keeps herself in humility. In a wonderful manner, the more the holy Church, or any holy soul, descends in humility for God’s sake, the more it ascends through God’s grace. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. XXIII). Thus too our most eloquent Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0063D] Book II, *On Synonyms*, on humility]: “Descend, that you may ascend; humble yourself, [Col. 0064A] that you may be exalted, lest, having been exalted, you be humbled.”

Accordingly, each person will be more precious and exalted in God’s eyes to the extent that he has become more despised and lowly in his own estimation for the love of God. Why? Because “God looks upon the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. CXXXVII). Hence Scripture says elsewhere: “God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud” (Prov. III). Thus the Lord speaks to Saul, saying: “Was it not when you were little in your own eyes that I made you head over the tribes of Israel?” (I Sam. XV). As if he said: You were great to me when you were contemptible to yourself. But now, because you are great to yourself, you are contemptible to me.

“This city,” he says, “had twelve gates, and twelve corners above the gates, and the names of the twelve tribes of Israel inscribed upon them. Its brightness was like [Col. 0064B] a most precious stone, like crystal.” The prophet speaks to the same city, saying: “You shall no longer have the sun to shine by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon give you light; but the Lord shall be for you an everlasting light, and your God your great glory” (Isa. LX). For as a crystal stone is transparent through its natural brightness, so that city is described as being illuminated by no radiance of the stars, but by God’s light alone.

“It had a great and high wall.” Hence the prophet Zechariah says: “I shall be a wall around it, says the Lord” (Zech. II). The Lord of all majesty, therefore, is the light and guardian of that most glorious city. And when it says that it had twelve gates, each made of a single pearl, twelve corners at the gates, and [Col. 0064C] inscribed names, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel: we read also in the Gospel that the Lord said of himself, “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John X). Christ, therefore, is the gate of this city. The twelve gates and the twelve tribes of Israel are the twelve apostles and the twelve prophets, who signify the universal Church established in the number twelve. Yet these twelve gates lead to the one gate, which is Christ. The gates are each made of a pearl because the holy apostles, who are the gates of the Church, show the light of truth to those entering.

When it says that the city is square (Rev. XXI), it indicates the united multitude of the saints, in whom the Catholic faith could by no means waver. This city [Col. 0064D] is set in a square because the holy Church is firmly built upon the Lord’s incarnation, according to the order of the four Evangelists, and is established in the four regions of the world.

Again he adds: “And he who spoke with me had a measuring instrument, namely a golden reed.” In the golden reed he indicates faith in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who took the flesh of human frailty, in which he showed us an example of perfection and the way of our salvation. He alone is he through whom the measure of faith is distributed to each person and the fullness of the holy Trinity is known. “And he measured the city: twelve stadia. Its length, [Col. 0065A] breadth, and height are equal.” The faith of Christ and the integrity of the holy Church are known through these twelve stadia, that is, through the teaching of the apostles and the faith of the prophets, because in them nothing superfluous, nothing coming from outside, and nothing deficient is found.

It is further said: “Its wall was constructed of jasper; but the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass.” In another metal, whatever is contained within is hidden; but in glass, whatever liquid is held inside is displayed outside as it is. What else, therefore, do we understand in gold and glass but that heavenly homeland and the fellowship of blessed citizens, whose hearts shine toward one another with charity and are transparent with purity? Indeed, [Col. 0065B] each one’s brightness is mutually evident in the hearts of the others, because, when one looks upon a person’s face, one simultaneously penetrates that person’s conscience.

The precious stones from which the city is built signify holy men strong in persecution, who can be shaken from the standing of true faith neither by the storm of persecutors nor by the violence of rain—that is, tribulations. The street, said to be of the purest gold, signifies the hearts of the saints cleansed from every sin, in which the Lord walks. The river of life, which proceeded from the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev. XXII), signifies the grace of baptism. The tree of life on either bank signifies, according to the flesh, the coming of Christ, whose future coming and suffering the old Law foretold, and whose [Col. 0065C] arrival the Gospel has now made known. The twelve fruits for each of the months signify the manifold grace of the twelve apostles. Receiving it from the one tree of the cross, they restore with the nourishment of God’s word peoples consumed by hunger. “And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” The leaves of the tree, which serve the nations’ health, signify the powers of the holy cross. “There shall be no more sickness, because God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes; and the throne of God and of the Lamb was in it” (ibid.). *Thronus* is Greek, and in Latin means “seat.” Therefore the seat of God was in that city, that is, in the holy Church, as the Psalmist testifies: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Ps. XLIV). “And his servants shall serve him, and they shall see his face” (Rev. XXII).

Meanwhile, dearest brethren, you ought to know that [Col. 0065D] all saints enter this most noble city through three gates. The holy Church has only three gates, through which it happily enters the heavenly Jerusalem, which is built daily in its members as a city from living stones. The first is toward the east, the second toward the north, and the third toward the south. The gate in the east is faith, because through it the true light is born in the human mind. The gate [Col. 0066A] in the north is hope, because anyone living in sins, if he despairs of God’s mercy, utterly perishes. Therefore one who had already died through his own iniquity must be restored to life through the hope of mercy. Certainly the gate in the south is charity, because whoever loves God perfectly burns with the fire of divine love. For at the southern gate the sun rises high, because through charity the light of faith is raised in love of God and neighbour. Through these three gates—faith, hope, and charity—every believer is made firm in love of God and neighbour and is established as a citizen in that heavenly Jerusalem of which we speak.

Therefore now, dearest brethren, strive to enter through these three gates, and labour earnestly that you may deserve to be citizens in that city above. Whoever [Col. 0066B] among you has not fallen into the depths of vices after faith and the sacrament of baptism, let him give thanks to God and enter the kingdom of heaven through the eastern gate. But those who, after the first warmth and light of faith, have fallen into the coldness and darkness of their sins, should obtain pardon from God through the compunction of repentance and reach the joys of eternal reward through the northern gate. And those who, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, burn with holy desires and virtues, daily penetrate the mysteries of inward joy by spiritual understanding, and diligently keep watch so that they may enter the heavenly Jerusalem through the southern gate.

Therefore, my brethren and lords, [Col. 0066C] practise these things with one another. Turn them over in your minds with diligent meditation; and if it delights you to dwell in that city, count all things under heaven as nothing, and hasten to it as swiftly as possible by the steps of good works. Let no abundance of words hinder you as you hurry toward it; let no sweetness of food draw you back; let no softness of clothing make you turn back; let no beauty of flesh detain you; let no human appearance call you back; let no love of temporal pleasures delay you; let no concern for parents turn you aside from the straight path. Therefore tend toward it in vow and desire; sigh for it without ceasing from your heart’s depths; gladly shed tears in remembrance of it; and, that you may one day attain it, implore God with all your prayers.

May Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who [Col. 0066D] is the Father’s splendour and power, and who illumines that same city by the brightness of his face, grant that through himself we may attain it with all the saints and live there eternally in his most sacred praises—he who lives and reigns as God with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SECOND SERMON: ON THE DEDICATION OF THE CHURCH II

[Col. 0067]

[Col. 0067A] Dearest brethren, I ask that your charity may deign to listen attentively to what the venerable priest Bede speaks for your instruction—indeed, for that of the whole Church. For he says [Note: [Col. 0067D] *On Solomon’s Temple*, chap. I]:

> “The house [the House] which Solomon built was a figure of the Church, which is built daily, from the first elect person to the last, through the grace of the peaceful King, that is, Christ. Part of it journeys in exile from him on earth; part, after its pilgrimage, already reigns with him in heaven; and after the last judgment the whole will reign there. To this holy Church belong the angels, whose likeness is promised to us in the future. Hence it is said: ‘They shall be equal to the angels, and are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection’ (Luke XX). Christ belongs to it, as he himself says: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three [Col. 0067B] days I shall raise it up.’ For he said this concerning the temple of his body (John II). But the Apostle says concerning us: ‘Do you not know that you are the temple of God?’ (I Cor. III), etc. Therefore, if he was made a temple according to the flesh, we too are made temples through the indwelling Spirit. It is evident that that temple was a figure both of all of us and of the Lord himself—that is, of the members and the head: of him as the chosen, precious cornerstone, laid in the foundation (Isa. XXVIII); but of us as living stones built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (I Pet. II; Eph. II:20), that is, Christ. This will appear more clearly when the arrangement of the Temple’s construction itself is considered: in certain respects the figure pertains to Christ himself; in others, to all the elect; in others, it displays the blessedness of the angels in heaven; in others, the helps bestowed upon human beings; and in others, the struggles of human beings rewarded together with the angels.

“Therefore King Solomon chose workmen from all Israel (III Kings V). He did not choose workmen from all Israel without reason, because those who are to build God’s house by example and word are not to be chosen from the stock of the priest Aaron, but sought from the whole Church, and are to be promoted without respect of persons. When they are ordained to instruct unbelievers and call them into the fellowship of the Church, vigorous and chosen men are sent, as it were, to cut down the Temple’s materials in Lebanon—that is, cedars. ‘And the levy was thirty thousand men; and he sent them to Lebanon, ten thousand men each month in rotation, so that they were in their homes for two months’ (ibid.). The thirty thousand cutters signify those perfected in faith in the holy Trinity, which especially befits teachers. But because the thirty thousand were arranged so that ten thousand should apply themselves to the work each month, the mystery of the number ten must rather [Col. 0068A] be unfolded. Ten thousand are sent from Israel to cut timber for work on the house of the Lord. Those ordained for the instruction of the ignorant must themselves keep the ten commandments of the Law in all things and show their hearers that they must be kept; they must themselves look toward the rewards to come in heaven, which are represented by the number ten, and tell their hearers to hope for them. The three months’ interval assigned to each group of timber-cutters proclaims the perfection of the three Gospel virtues: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting. For almsgiving includes all that we willingly provide for our brethren in fulfilment of love of neighbour; prayer includes all by which we are joined to our Creator through inward compunction; [Col. 0068B] fasting includes all by which we are guarded from the contagion of vices and the enticements of the world, so that with free minds and chaste bodies we may always be able to cling to love of God and neighbour.

“Now Hiram, king of Tyre, whose name is interpreted ‘living on high,’ was in charge of this levy. ‘Living on high’ is Christ, who is set over the workers of the Temple, to arrange in which months each should go out to work and in which they should return to care for the house. So he more familiarly instructs the minds of preachers to discern when they should return to examine their own consciences, as though inspecting their own house, to see whether it is worthy of visitation through prayers and fasts. The overseers who were set over the works numbered three thousand three hundred, to signify the faith of the holy Trinity [Col. 0068C] proclaimed by holy Scripture. But because in Chronicles they are recorded as three thousand six hundred, this concerns their perfection (II Chron. II). For the number six, [supplied: *number*] in which the world’s adornment was completed, signifies perfect good works. And because holy Scripture teaches that works of righteousness must accompany faith in the truth, the overseers of the works rightly numbered three thousand six hundred. The overseers are the authors of holy Scripture, by whose teaching we learn to instruct the ignorant, rebuke the contemptuous, and bear one another’s burdens.

“Thus Solomon had seventy thousand burden-bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain, besides the overseers who were set over the individual [Col. 0068D] works, three thousand three hundred in number, giving orders to the people and to those doing the work. Therefore the seventy thousand burden-bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters, together with their overseers, were not Israelites but proselytes—that is, resident foreigners who lived [Col. 0069A] among them. Those were called *proselyti* in Greek who, after receiving circumcision, passed from other nations into the fellowship of God’s people. Therefore the workers of the house of the Lord came from Israel, from the proselytes, and from the Gentiles.”

[Note: [Col. 0069D] From the same Bede, chap. 4.] Again Scripture says: “The king commanded that great stones, precious stones, be brought, which Solomon’s masons and Hiram’s masons cut”: namely, men outstanding in conduct and holiness, who cling more closely to Christ, so that, the more firmly they hope in him, the more strongly they may be able to love the lives of others and bear the breadth of the foundation. These are the prophets and apostles, who visibly or invisibly received from the very Wisdom of God the word and sacraments of truth. The foundation of the Temple, that is, [Col. 0069B] of the holy Church, is Christ. Hence it is said: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III). He is rightly called the foundation of God’s house because, as Peter says: “There is no other name under heaven given to men in which we must be saved” (Acts IV). Hence also: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. II).

For this reason the saints cut these stones, that is, the faithful peoples: so that all might leave behind what is harmful and empty and present before God only the rule of righteousness, like the firm form of a square. For the building of the house of the Lord, timber and stones are first cut from the mountain, [Col. 0069C] because those whom we seek to instruct in faith must first be taught to renounce the devil and the transgression in which they were born. Then precious and great stones must be sought and placed in the foundation, so that, having renounced their former way of life, we may examine their life and character in all things and set them before hearers for imitation: those whom we know to cling especially to the Lord through the virtue of humility and whom we see, squared by steadfastness of mind, remaining immovable against every assault of temptation. They are great and precious in reputation and merit.

The Biblici [perhaps: Giblites] prepared timber and stones for building the house. Byblos [Giblos] is a city of Phoenicia, and its name means “defining” or “determining.” Those who prepare human hearts for the spiritual building [Col. 0069D] constructed from the virtues of the soul can teach their hearers faith and works of righteousness only if they have first been instructed by the sacred pages and have learned, with a definite determination of truth, what faith must be held and by what path of virtues one must walk. He who does not know the discernment of faith and good works vainly usurps for himself the office of teacher. He who presumes to teach what he himself has not learned builds not a sanctuary for the Lord but ruin for himself.

“And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel went out of the land of Egypt, [Col. 0070A] in the month Ziv, that is, May—the second month of the fourth year of King Solomon over Israel—that he began to build” (III Kings VI). [Note: [Col. 0069D] Bede, chap. 5.] March, [Note: [Col. 0069D] Edition: April.] in which Passover is celebrated, is the first month of the year among the Hebrews. Hence it is evident that he began to build the house of the Lord after Passover; and the people consecrated by the mystical solemnity set their hands to the mystical work. The worship and religion of the tabernacle endured for four hundred and eighty years, and thus the Temple began to be built. Holy Scripture of the Old Testament overflows with such perfection that whoever understands it well finds that it contains within itself all the mysteries of the New Testament. Moreover, many Fathers of the Old Testament lived so perfectly that they are considered inferior in no respect to the apostles and apostolic men. [Note: [Col. 0069D] These remarks are from chap. 4, near the end.] After the house’s foundation had been composed of such persons, [Col. 0070B] and after timber and stones had been prepared and arranged, being removed from their former position or root, there must, after the first rudiments of faith, [Note: [Col. 0070D] Supplied from the edition after “arranged”: “within us, in accordance with the example of exalted men, a foundation of humility must be added,” etc.] be added on high a wall of good works, like successive courses of stones advancing from virtue to virtue and laid one upon another.

[Note: [Col. 0070D] Now chap. 6.] “The house which King Solomon built was sixty cubits in length, twenty in width, and thirty in height. And the portico before the Temple was twenty cubits long.” The length of the house signifies the Church’s long-suffering, by which it patiently bears adversities until it reaches the heavenly homeland. This is represented by sixty cubits, [Col. 0070C] because the number six denotes the perfection of good works. The breadth of the house signifies charity, which, with the bosom of the mind enlarged, loves friends in God and enemies for God’s sake, until, after their conversion to peace or their utter destruction, it rejoices in God with friends alone. It had twenty cubits in height, on account of the twofold extent of charity by which we love God and neighbour. It also had thirty cubits in breadth, on account of faith in the Trinity, upon the vision of which all the desires of our hope depend. Each number is multiplied by ten, because through faith and observance of the Law patience is beneficially exercised, charity beneficially kindled, and hope exaltedly carried up to eternal joys. Height signifies hope of eternal or future reward, for the sake of [Col. 0070D] which it despises prosperity and adversity alike until it sees “the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI:29).

The Temple signifies the Church. The portico, however, which stood before the Temple and first received the sun’s light, signifies that part of the Church which preceded the Lord’s incarnation, in which were the patriarchs and prophets. They were the first to receive the Sun rising in righteousness and bore witness to the Lord’s birth in the flesh by living, preaching, being born, and dying. The ancient righteous waited in patience and long-suffering for the incarnate Lord to bring the grace of the Gospel, [Col. 0071A] seeing and greeting his promises from afar (Heb. XI). Thus the portico equalled the Temple’s length and breadth, because by long-suffering of mind they desired to come to the Church’s love, which is in Christ Jesus.

But in what place did Solomon begin to build the Temple? Namely, on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father on the threshing-floor of Ornan [perhaps: Ornan] the Jebusite. [Note: [Col. 0071D] Again from chap. 5.] The house of the Lord is built on a mountain, that is, on Christ, of whom it is said: “In that day the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit” (Isa. II), etc. For he is the mountain of mountains, who, sprung from the earth according to the flesh, surpasses in the height of his dignity the power and holiness of all earthly things. He is rightly called Mount Moriah, that is, “of vision,” because he deigns to see and help in this life those whom he preserves for the eternal vision [Col. 0071B] of glory.

The threshing-floor signifies the Church. Hence the Gospel saying: “The Son of God shall cleanse his threshing-floor,” that is, his Church; “he shall gather the wheat into his barn, but burn the chaff with fire” (Matt. III). Ornan, whose name means “illuminated,” a Jebusite by nation, signifies the Gentiles to be enlightened by the Lord and transformed into children of the Church. Hence: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V). Jebus is interpreted “trodden under foot,” while Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” While the Gentile Ornan reigns in it, it is called Jebus; when David buys in it a place for the burnt offering (I Chron. XXI) and Solomon builds the Temple of the Lord, [Col. 0071C] it is called Jerusalem. For the Gentile world, ignorant of divine worship, is trampled upon and mocked by demons; but when the Saviour’s grace looks upon it, it finds within itself a place and name of peace. Hence it is said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. V).

[Note: [Col. 0071D] These remarks are from St Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XV, chap. 7.] Solomon also made slanting windows in the Temple. Slanting windows are those whose outer part is narrow and whose inner part broad. They are called *fenestrae* because they lend (*fenerentur*) light. For “light” is called φῶς in Greek; others think that *fenestra* is so called because it supplies light to the house—a name, namely, compounded of Greek and Latin speech. In slanting windows, therefore, the portion through which light enters is narrow, but the inner portion that receives the light is broad, because the minds of contemplatives, although they see only a little [Col. 0071D] of the true light, are nevertheless expanded within themselves with great breadth; indeed, they can scarcely contain even the few things they behold.

[Note: [Col. 0071D] Again from Bede, chap. 5.] The door of the Temple is the Lord, because no one comes to the Father except through him, as he himself says. [Note: [Col. 0071D] Supplied from the edition: “Hence elsewhere he says:”] “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John X), etc. The Temple faced east, and the portico had a door on the east opposite the door of the Temple, so that the rising equinoctial sun, by straight lines of rays, might pour over the ark of the covenant through the three doors—those [Col. 0072A] of the portico, Temple, and oracle. On the first front of the portico were the earliest righteous: Abel, Seth, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other Fathers of the Old Testament. In its innermost sanctuary, as it were close to the Temple wall, [Note: [Col. 0071D] Edition: “the parents of the Lord’s forerunner, Simeon, [Col. 0072D] and Anna,” etc.] were the Lord’s forerunners—namely Simeon, Anna, and the others—who, although they deserved to see his birth, were nevertheless unable to hear his teaching or receive the sacraments. [Note: [Col. 0072D] Now from chap. 9.] The Temple had no roof-peak above, nor did the tabernacle; rather, it was flat, as houses are made in Palestine and Egypt. The roof covering the house signifies men eminent in the resurrection, who attain the summit of virtue through singular holiness. Of one such it is said: “Among those born of women none greater than John has arisen” (Matt. XI), etc.

[Note: [Col. 0072D] These remarks are from chap. 8.] It should be noted that the thirty cubits of height mentioned above reached to the middle upper chamber; then another thirty were added to the third level, until the roof which extended around the Temple from south, north, and west was reached, according to Josephus. Then sixty cubits were counted up to the Temple’s highest roof, and thus, according to Chronicles, the whole height of the Temple was completed at one hundred and twenty cubits. The fact that the entire height of the Temple was one hundred and twenty cubits signifies the primitive Church, which received the gift of the Holy Spirit in this number of men (Acts I). It is also fitting that the house of the Lord is completed at this third upper level, because after the present [Col. 0072C] labours of the faithful, and after the rest of souls received in the future, the complete blessedness of the whole Church will be brought to perfection in the resurrection.

Therefore Solomon built the house and completed it; and he built the inner walls of the house with cedar panelling. The inner walls are covered with cedar panels when the hearts of the faithful abound in love of virtues. [Note: [Col. 0072D] Again from chap. 9.] For as cedar signifies perfect men, so in suitable places it signifies the loftiness of virtues by which that perfection is attained. “From the floor of the house to the top, and as far as the ceiling, he covered the interior with wood.” Everything is covered with wood from the floor of the house to the top and to the ceiling when the elect labour in good works from [Col. 0072D] the first rudiments of faith to the perfection of good conduct and to the perfect entrance into the heavenly homeland; when, from the first righteous persons to the last at the end of the age, all devote themselves to virtues, so that they may deservedly dare to say: “We are the sweet savour of Christ to God” (II Cor. II).

“And he covered the floor of the house with fir boards.” This is written more fully in Chronicles: “He paved the floor of the Temple with very precious marble of great beauty” (II Chron. III). Hence it is clear that he did not place the fir boards [Col. 0073A] with which he covered the floor directly upon the earth; rather, he first covered it with marble, then laid boards upon it, and added a third covering of gold over those two. The evenness of the floor signifies the harmony and humility of the saints. [Note: [Col. 0073D] These remarks are from the chapter.] The stones of the wall or floor, the boards, and the gold signify the life of the saints. But the saints are living stones, cemented into one and the same rule by the strength of faith; cedar or fir boards, joined to one another in one faith by the breadth of diverse virtues according to the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The white marble from which the house was constructed signifies the pure conduct of the elect and a conscience disciplined against every stain of corruption. Hence: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, [Col. 0073B] perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (II Cor. VII). The sheets of gold are those who possess charity surpassing knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0073D] From Bede, chap. 10, in the work cited above.] “And he built cedar-panelled rooms twenty cubits deep at the rear part of the Temple, from the floor to the upper parts; and he made the inner house of the oracle into the Holy of Holies.” The outer house, into which the priests always entered to perform the offices of sacrifices, is the present Church, in which, daily persisting in devout works, we offer the Lord sacrifices of praise. But the inner house, made at the rear part of the Temple, signifies eternal life in heaven: inner, indeed, in relation to the course of our exile, because in the presence of the supreme King the everlasting solemnity of the blessed is celebrated. Hence it is said: “Enter [Col. 0073C] into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV). Yet it is later in time, because it follows the labours of this age.

Moreover, the Temple itself before the doors of the oracle was forty cubits long. “And the whole house was covered with cedar, having carved work and skilfully made joints.” This number signifies the labour of the present life, just as fifty signifies future rest and peace. There are ten commandments by which one reaches life; the number ten signifies the life which we desire and for which we labour. The square signifies the world in which we strive to obtain that life, as in the saying: “He gathered them from the regions, from the rising of the sun, from the north, and from the sea” (Ps. CVI). [Note: [Col. 0073D] Now from chap. 11.] The house has its carved work and skilfully made joints in cedar boards when [Col. 0073D] the elect are joined together by the most beautiful bond of charity, so that they have one heart and one soul. The carvings attached to the joints of the boards, so that all become one panelling, are the offices of charity by which the holy brotherhood is united and made into the one house of Christ throughout the whole world.

The oracle, where the ark stood, was twenty cubits in length, breadth, and height—thus square—because in the heavenly homeland, where the eyes of the saints see Christ the King, the grace of divine charity alone shines forth in all things. Hence it follows: “And he covered it and overlaid it with purest gold,” because [Col. 0074A] grace of charity filled the walls of the heavenly city.

[Note: [Col. 0074D] From chapter 12.] The altar of incense also, which stood before the oracle, concerning which it is added: “And he covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold.” [Note: [Col. 0074D] Supplement and correction from the edition: “But he also clad the altar with cedar.” “He means the altar of incense,” etc.] From this it is understood that the same altar, made of stone, was clad with cedar and then covered with gold.

The cedar wall of the inner house had a doorway above, extending all across it, through which the smoke of the incense might enter; because the eyes of the Lord are open over his house day and night, and his ears are attentive to the prayer of his servants, and these are spread throughout the whole breadth of the Church across the world.

The inner house signifies the secrets of heaven; the ark of the covenant signifies the Savior, in whom we have a covenant of peace with the Father. After rising again and ascending into heaven, he placed at the Father’s right hand the flesh taken from the Virgin. For a place is called an oracle when divine or angelic speech, together with the revelation of hidden things, is granted to human beings. Thus the oracle was rightly made in a hidden place, that is, in the inner house, because in the heavenly homeland the vision and speech of angels, and the very presence of God, will be revealed. Hence the saying: “The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall announce the Father to you openly” (John 16). And again: “I shall love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14).

He also covered the house before the oracle with purest gold, because the perfect in this life are not yet able to hear the parable concerning the Father, nor yet to see him openly; but they adorn the same work of righteousness, lest it appear dead or idle, with divine love, through which they may deserve the fullness of the knowledge of God.

The golden nails by which the golden plates were fastened are the commandments of charity and the promises of eternal glory. Through these, by the gift of Christ’s grace, we are held firm in the practice of the virtues, lest we fail.

“And he covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold.” This altar signifies the life of the perfect, who, placed as though near the oracle, have abandoned lower pleasures and direct their care solely toward entering the kingdom. Hence on this altar they burned not the flesh of victims but incense alone, because such people no longer need to slaughter in themselves the sins of the flesh and the allurements of thoughts; rather, through the fire of eternal love, they offer before the sight of the Creator the fragrances of prayers and spiritual desires.

“But when the house was being built, it was built of dressed and finished stones; and neither hammer, nor axe, nor any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built.” The faithful who belong to the heavenly building must not quarrel, murmur, slander, or contend over superfluous matters, but live in complete peace and concord. The house of God advances and is built in silence, because the congregation of the elect, which is the dwelling of the eternal King, ought to cease from all worldly tumult.

“And in the oracle he made two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high.” [Col. 0075A] [Note: [Col. 0075D] From chapter 13.]

Cherub is the name of an angelic rank: in the singular, cherub; in the plural, cherubim. The cherubim, therefore, can be understood as the angelic ministries that always stand before the Creator in heaven.

They are said to have been made of olive wood and to be ten cubits high because the angels are anointed with spiritual grace, so that they may never wither away from the love of God; and he who created them immediately filled them with the light of heavenly wisdom.

The two cherubim may also prefigure the two Testaments. They were made in the oracle because, in the counsel of divine providence—unapproachable and incomprehensible to us—it was arranged before the ages when, how, and through which authors Scripture would be composed.

Two cherubim were made to signify the fellowship of charity, because charity cannot exist with fewer than two. Hence the disciples too are sent out to preach two by two (Luke 10).

When wings are placed upon the minds of holy people, they signify their virtues, by which they fly toward heavenly things and live among them. When, however, they are used as a symbol of angels, they signify the grace of their perpetual and unfailing blessedness, since they remain always in heaven in the service of their Creator. Alternatively, they signify that angels are endowed with the lightness of spiritual nature, so that wherever they wish, they arrive at once, as though flying.

“One wing of a cherub was five cubits, and its other wing was five cubits.” In every changing variety of passing things, holy people extend the senses of their bodies in the service of the Creator: they keep their eyes always toward the Lord, desiring to hear his voice of praise and to declare all his wonders.

They are ten cubits high because they enjoy the denarius of eternal life, possessing the unimpaired image of the Creator and preserving the holiness, justice, and truth in which they were created. For the denarius consists of ten obols and commonly bears within itself the name and image of the king.

The two cherubim are of one workmanship and measure because there is no disagreement of will in the heavenly homeland, where all are illumined by one and the same vision and glory of the present God.

The inner wings of the cherubim therefore touched one another above the ark, because they agree in an equal testimony concerning the Lord. Their outer wings touched one wall on one side and the other wall on the other, because the Old Testament was written specifically for the ancient people of God, and the New for us, who came to faith after the Lord’s incarnation. We are compared to the second wall, that is, the northern one, because after the cold and darkness of idolatry we were granted knowledge of the light of truth.

They extend their wings toward one another above the ark when they refer to the praise of the Creator the good that they have received. They also extend their wings toward both walls of the oracle, because, rejoicing in the heavenly homeland, they stir the righteous of both peoples to praise the Creator by the vision of their own glory.

They rejoice not only in the blessedness of those righteous whom they have with them within, but also care for us, who are still placed outside and cry to the Lord from the depths. Hence it is written of them in Chronicles: “They stood on their feet, and their faces were turned toward the outer house” (2 Chronicles 3). For they have never strayed from the way of truth in which they were immediately established; and they desire that we, rescued from the misery of this pilgrimage, should come to share their fellowship.

Thus they stand with feet upright and extend wings covered with gold toward the walls of the oracle, while their faces are turned toward the outer house: for the angels preserve their own innocence perpetually and rejoice in heaven over the blessedness of holy souls, yet they do not cease to bring help even to those whom they see still journeying on earth, until they lead them to the heavenly homeland. For all are ministering spirits, sent into service for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation (Hebrews 1).

“And he carved all the walls of the temple round about with various carved work and turned work.” [Note: [Col. 0075D] From chapter 14.]

The walls are carved with turned work when the faithful are strong in their readiness to do what the Lord commands, saying in every circumstance: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33). And again: “My heart is ready, O God,” etc. (Psalm 56).

Because turned work surpasses other arts in speed and preserves for itself the rule by which it works without error, it rightly signifies the devout life of the saints, which is always ready for the Lord’s service and has learned, through long practice of the virtues, to fulfil this without turning aside into error.

He makes various pictures as though projecting from and emerging out of the wall when God grants the faithful manifold workings of the virtues: the bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, patience, modesty, and so forth; and above all, charity, which is the bond of perfection (Colossians 3).

The levelness of the pavement signifies the humble concord of brotherhood. Although there are Jews and Gentiles, barbarians and Scythians, free and enslaved, noble and ignoble, all glory in being brothers in Christ and having the same Father in heaven.

Solomon therefore covered the floor of the house with gold within, because Christ filled the angels and the souls of the righteous in heaven with the complete gift of perfection, and separated those journeying in the world from the baseness of mortals by the mark of eternal love, as citizens of the heavenly homeland.

“And at the entrance of the oracle he made two doors of olive wood, and five-sided doorposts at the corners.” [Note: [Col. 0076D] From chapter 15.]

There was one entrance, but it was closed by two doors and opened when those same doors were unfastened. Likewise the temple and the portico before the temple had only one entrance, because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Ephesians 4).

There are two doors because angels and holy people love God and their neighbor; and they cannot enter the door of life except through this twofold love.

The doorposts have five sides because the heavenly hall receives not only the souls of the elect but also opens its doors at the judgment to bodies endowed with immortal glory. For there are five bodily senses. Each doorpost of the oracle is therefore five cubits high, because the entrance to the heavenly homeland is opened only to those who serve the Lord with all the senses of heart and body.

“And he carved on the doors pictures of cherubim, palm trees, and very prominent relief work; and he covered them with gold, and overlaid both the cherubim and the palm trees and the rest with gold.”

*Anaglypha* is Greek; in Latin they are called carvings. The works of the virtues that the Church exercises throughout the world in holy and perfect men require those especially to whom the care of the faithful and the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been entrusted to apply themselves with complete diligence, so that, just as they surpass others in rank, they may also excel them in the merit of good action.

They have within them a carved picture of cherubim when, as far as they can, they imitate heavenly life on earth in mind and deed. They have the appearance of palm trees when they meditate with fixed intention upon the reward above, for the palm is the adornment of a victorious hand. They have very prominent relief work when they display the most certain proofs of good works—proofs that no one can interpret maliciously.

“And at the entrance of the temple he made four-sided doorposts of olive wood, and two doors of fir wood on either side; and each door was double and opened while holding the other.”

Just as the entrance of the oracle, by which one reaches the ark of the Lord and the cherubim, signifies the entrance into heaven, where we desire to be introduced to the vision of God and the citizens above, so the entrance into the temple signifies the beginnings of our conversion to God, when we enter the present Church. The former designates our entrance into faith; the latter, our entrance into sight.

Thus the doorposts of this entrance are four-sided because of the four books of the Gospel, by whose teaching we are instructed in the faith of truth.

Alternatively, they are said to be four-sided because of the four principal virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—upon whose most firm foundation the whole structure of good deeds rests.

Prudence is the virtue by which we learn what we ought to do and how we ought to live. Fortitude is that by which we fulfil what we have learned must be done. The Prophet rightly embraces these when he says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 26): light, so that he may teach us what we ought to do; salvation, so that he may strengthen us to do it.

Temperance is the virtue by which we discern that we should pursue prudence or fortitude neither more nor less than is right. And since whoever uses prudence, fortitude, and temperance is truly just, justice follows as the fourth virtue after prudence, fortitude, and temperance.

The entrance of the inner house had two doors, not double but single, because in eternal blessedness faith and hope will no longer be necessary, since there we shall see openly what we now believe and hope for.

A veil was added to these doors, as it is written in Chronicles: “He made a veil of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and wove cherubim into it” (2 Chronicles 3)—so that, among the gilded walls, even the woven silk would shine.

The diligent opening of this veil—that is, its revelation to those entering—signifies the opening of the law and of the heavenly kingdom, which was granted to us through Christ’s incarnation. Hence, when the Lord was baptized, the heavens were opened (Matthew 3), to show that through the baptism which he himself consecrated for us we must enter the door of heaven.

When he died, this same veil was torn in the middle from top to bottom (Matthew 27), showing that the figures of the law had now ended, and that the truth of the Gospel, the heavenly mysteries, and entry into heaven itself were no longer to be signified figuratively but immediately opened to all who, from the beginning of the world, had passed from the world in faith in the truth.

The same veil, then, under which one entered the oracle, was made of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and cherubim were woven into it.

Hyacinth, which imitates the color of heaven, is compared with desire for heavenly things. Purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and has a bloodlike appearance, signifies the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, which we ought to imitate by carrying our cross.

In scarlet, its red color expresses the power of the love of God. Hence it is said: “Was not our heart burning within us” [Note: [Col. 0077D] The editions rightly continue: “while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us”? But our manuscript, which writes this after the word “to us,” is plainly corrupt in the letters *i*, *d*, and so forth.] (Luke 24).

Fine linen, that is, flax, which rises green from the earth and through the long practice of craftsmen loses its greenness and is brought to whiteness, signifies the chastisement of the flesh. Hence the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” etc.—“fornication, uncleanness, lust,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0078D] The remainder is “and so forth.”] (Colossians 3). Again he wishes to lead us to white brilliance when he says: “I beseech you to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God,” etc. (Romans 12).

Cherubim are woven into it and made with these same colors when, in all that we do devoutly, we are protected, by the Lord’s gift, from the poisoned arrows of demons through the guardianship of angels.

After this he built the inner court with three rows of dressed stones and one row of cedar wood. [Note: [Col. 0078D] From chapter 16, around the middle.]

The building of the temple within the priests’ court signifies the life of the perfect in the Church, who draw near to the Lord through the excellence of their virtues and show others the way of salvation by word and deed.

For a priest is understood to be one who provides sacred guidance to those of lesser rank. By this name are meant not only ministers of the altar—that is, bishops and presbyters—but also all who excel in the height of their teaching and way of life, who benefit not themselves alone but also the peoples.

When they present their bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God (Romans 12), they exercise the priestly ministry spiritually. Hence Peter speaks to the whole Church: “But you are a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Peter 2).

We read that there were three courts around the temple. When the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, purified priests stood in the temple itself. The unpurified, together with the Levites, singers, and Jewish men, stood praying in the innermost court under the open sky—that is, in the open air—if the weather was clear; but if there was a storm, they withdrew into the nearest porticoes.

In the outer court were purified Jewish women. In the farthest court were Gentiles and Jews who had recently come from the Gentiles, up to the sixth day of purification.

Speaking beforehand of these courts, the Psalmist said: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 133).

In these courts and porticoes Jeremiah and the other prophets preached; in them the Lord and the apostles preached; and in one of them the Lord sat teaching when the adulterous woman was brought to him for judgment while the Pharisees were testing him (John 8).

In them stood those selling sheep, oxen, and doves, whom he drove out of the temple (John 2). In them Peter and John found and healed a lame man (Acts 3). In them the whole multitude of the people prayed when the angel appeared to Zechariah, who was offering incense, at the altar of incense, and taught him fully about the birth of the Lord’s precursor (Luke 1).

The crowd came as far as the priests’ court and brought victims to the door, where the priests received them; they followed with their eyes the sacrifices offered on the altar. They also looked from a distance at the temple itself when it was opened, but they could not enter even the priests’ court. From below they cried out to the Lord, because the simplicity of the carnal in the Church is not despised by the Lord when they faithfully offer the devout vows they are able to offer.

They look from a distance into the temple when they rejoice to learn and admire the life of the exalted. Those whom they cannot follow by imitating their virtues, they embrace with the devout affection of veneration.

The one row of cedar wood is good action displayed without the corruption of pretense, without whose addition faith, hope, and charity cannot be true. Cedar wood, because of its fragrance and the natural power by which it does not decay, signifies perseverance and the good reputation of devout action.

“In the fourth year of King Solomon, the house of the Lord was founded in the month of Ziv, that is, May; and in the eleventh year of the same king, in the month of Bul, that is, October, the house was completed in all its work and all its furnishings.” [Note: [Col. 0079D] From chapter 17.]

The fact that the house was completed in the eighth year and eighth month in all its work pertains to the future age and the day of judgment, so that nothing more can be found to be added to it. Then Christ will show us the Father, and that will be enough for us (John 14).

The day of judgment is symbolically expressed by the number eight because the age that is now proceeding follows seven days. He built it for seven years and completed it in the eighth, because throughout the whole period of this age, which is completed in a cycle of seven days, the Church is built from the souls of the elect, and at the end of the age it brings its growth to perfection.

Alternatively, this refers to the significance of spiritual grace, through which the Church receives the ability simply to be the Church. For without the gifts of the Holy Spirit no one can become faithful, preserve faith, or attain the crown of righteousness by the merit of faith.

Hiram the craftsman from Tyre, whom Solomon took as his assistant in the work, signifies preachers chosen from the Gentiles. His widowed mother signifies the present Church, for which Christ, her husband, tasted death and rose again; ascending into heaven, he left her journeying on earth. Her children are the preachers and all the faithful. Hence: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you,” etc. (Psalm 44).

“And he cast two bronze columns, one column eighteen cubits high, and the other column of the same height; and a line of twelve cubits encircled each column.” [Note: [Col. 0080D] From chapter 18.]

Three times six makes eighteen. Three pertains to faith, because of the Trinity; six to action, because the world was made in six days. Three is multiplied by six when “the righteous lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2) and adds the knowledge of devout faith to the security of good action.

The line of twelve cubits which encircled each column is the teaching of the apostles. Thus the standard of apostolic instruction encircles both columns when a teacher sent to preach to Jews or Gentiles takes care to do and teach only what he received through the apostles and learned from the Church.

For one who wishes to live or preach otherwise, and to despise apostolic decrees, is not a column in God’s temple. Since he scorns to follow apostolic ordinances, he does not fit the line of twelve cubits, whether through the thinness of sluggishness or the bulk of pride.

The two columns therefore signify the apostles and all teachers, strong in faith and work and raised up in contemplation. They are two so that, through preaching, they may bring circumcision and uncircumcision into the Church.

The columns placed on either side surround the temple door when ministers of the word show both peoples the entrance to heaven. The two capitals placed upon the heads of the columns are the two Testaments, to the meditation and observance of which teachers submit both mind and body.

Thus each capital is five cubits high, because Mosaic Scripture is contained in five books. The whole sequence of the Old Testament also encompasses the five ages of the world. But the New Testament preaches nothing other than what Moses foretold would be preached through it, and what the prophets foretold. Hence: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also” (John 5).

“And he made forms of network and chains wonderfully interwoven with one another.” [Note: [Col. 0081D] From the same chapter.]

The form of chains and the likeness of a net upon the capitals signify the variety of spiritual virtues in the saints. Hence: “The queen stood at your right hand,” etc. (Psalm 44), that is, in the garment of shining love, surrounded by the variety of diverse gifts.

Or the manifold interweaving of chains and spreading of the net signifies the many kinds of persons among the teachers. When they faithfully obey and adhere to the words of preachers, they are as though set above the heads of columns, and offer to all the marvel of a net and chainlet through their mutual union.

For these chains are wonderfully interwoven with one another because it was brought about by the wonderful grace of the Holy Spirit that the life of the faithful—greatly differing in place, time, rank, condition, sex, and age—should be joined in one faith and love.

“And there were seven rows of nettings on one capital, and seven on the other.” The number seven signifies spiritual grace. Hence it is said: “The seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Revelation 5). Thus there were seven rows of nettings on each capital because the Fathers of both Testaments received the grace of the one sevenfold Spirit in order that they might be elect.

“And he completed the columns, and two rows round about each netting, to cover the capitals that were above the tops of the pomegranates.”

These nettings were made to cover the capitals—that is, to surround them on every side—because all sacred Scripture, when rightly understood, everywhere speaks of the grace of love and peace.

The capitals are the divine books; the nets are the bonds of mutual love. The capitals are covered by the nettings when sacred utterances are shown to be clothed on every side in the gift of love. For in those things in Scripture which we do not understand, love lies hidden; and in those which we understand, it lies openly revealed.

“Now the capitals which were upon the heads of the columns were made as a work of lilies in the porch, four cubits.” By lilies is signified the brightness of the heavenly homeland and the delightful beauty of paradise fragrant with the flowers of immortality. By the four cubits is signified the Gospel proclamation, which promises entrance into eternal blessedness and shows the path by which it is reached.

Thus when holy teachers display to us, in the four books of the Gospel, the promised lights of the heavenly kingdom, they present, as it were, upon the heads of columns a lily-work of four cubits.

“And again there were other capitals on the tops of the columns, above, beside the network, according to the measure of the column.” The workmanship of these capitals signifies the loftiness of the everlasting kingdom, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 11 [as cited]).

After the lilies of four cubits other capitals were set up, of whose height nothing is said, because we read many things in the Gospel concerning heavenly blessedness: that there the pure in heart shall see God (Matthew 5); that they shall be equal to the angels of God, and “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22); that they can die no more (Luke 20); that where Christ is, there his ministers also shall be (John 12); and other such things which are perfectly clear only to the citizens of that kingdom.

Just as many grains are enclosed within the one outer rind of a pomegranate, so the holy Church includes innumerable companies of the elect within the one defense of faith.

The heads of the columns were fittingly surrounded in a circle by pomegranates because holy teachers recall to mind the lives of earlier faithful people and fortify their actions and words on every side with their examples, lest they go astray by living otherwise. Thus the entire Church is signified in the pomegranates.

Two hundred rows of pomegranates around each capital are said to have existed. The number one hundred, which first passes to the right, indicates eternal blessedness. This number of pomegranates is doubled around the second capital in order to signify that the people of both Testaments are to be united in Christ and brought into the eternal crown.

“And he set up the two columns in the porch of the temple; and when he had set up the right column, he called it by the name Jachin, that is, ‘firmness’; likewise he raised the second column and called its name Boaz, that is, ‘in strength.’”

The right-hand column therefore signifies those who foretold by prophecy that the Lord would come in the flesh; the second, those who testify that he has now come and redeemed the world.

Both columns receive a similar designation. One is called “firmness,” the other “in strength,” in order to show that one strength of faith and work ought to be present in all teachers, and silently to condemn the slothfulness of our own time. For some teachers, priests, and columns of God’s house wish to be seen and called such, although they possess in themselves neither steadfast faith to despise worldly displays and desire invisible goods, nor strength to correct errors, nor even diligence to understand the errors of those over whom they have been set.

“He also made the molten sea, ten cubits from rim to rim, round about.” [Note: [Col. 0082D] From chapter 19.]

The sea signifies baptism, because from the first person baptized in the manner—that is, in the form—of Jesus Christ to the last person who will believe and be baptized at the end of the age, the whole choir of believers ought to enter upon the same way of truth and hope from the Lord for the common crown of righteousness.

Its height was five cubits, because whatever we have sinned through sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, the grace of God remits to us through the washing of the life-giving font. But forgiveness of past sins is insufficient unless one afterward devotes oneself to good works. Otherwise, if the devil who went out of a person sees him empty of good works, he returns more abundantly and makes that person’s last state worse than the former (Matthew 12).

By the priests who washed in this sea are signified all the elect, who are members of Jesus Christ the high priest. Hence it is said: “You are a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Peter 2).

This vessel is rightly called a sea, namely in remembrance of the Red Sea, in which the figure of baptism previously occurred through the destruction of the Egyptians. Hence: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea,” etc. (1 Corinthians 10).

“And a cord of thirty cubits encircled it round about.” The cord signifies the discipline of heavenly commandments, by which we are bound back from worldly pleasures. Hence it is said: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Ecclesiastes 4), because observance of the commandments, established in the hearts of the elect by faith, hope, and love of the heavenly reward, cannot be undone by any obstacle.

The cord encircles the sea when we endeavor to protect by devout works the sacrament of baptism which we have received.

“A cord of thirty cubits encircled it round about,” because our Lord Jesus Christ came to baptism when he was thirty years old (Luke 3). Since by his baptism, received at thirty years of age, he consecrated our baptism, the sea which signified our baptism was rightly surrounded by a cord of thirty cubits.

There were also two rows of cast historical carvings. A historical carving is one which represents certain histories of events. Thus by the historical carvings which surround the sea are signified examples from former times, which we ought to observe, so that we may see by what works holy people from the beginning pleased God.

[Col. 0083C] Again Scripture says: “And beneath it stood twelve oxen, three looking northward, three eastward, three westward, and three southward; and the sea was above them, and all their hindquarters were concealed within.”

By these oxen we understand the apostles and evangelists—indeed, all ministers of the Word. Hence: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out grain,” etc. (Deuteronomy 25).

They bear the sea placed upon them when the apostles and their successors fulfil with ready devotion the office of the Gospel entrusted to them. “Three looked northward,” etc., because they preach faith in the Trinity to all four regions of the four-cornered world.

For this reason the twelve apostles too were chosen as four groups of three: preaching faith in and confession of the Trinity through the four parts of the world, they baptized all nations in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

We can readily see and know by reading the words, deeds, and sufferings of these persons and their successors in the present life. But what glory of recompense awaits them in the future we cannot yet see.

The thickness of the basin was three fingers’ breadth, because reception of baptism is fortified by the strength of faith, hope, and love. Nor is it shown to be beneficial to those receiving it except when firm assurance of these three virtues strengthens both their minds and their actions.

The rim of the sea was like the rim of a cup and the leaf of an opened lily. A lily, attended by the grace of fragrance, shows white splendor outside and golden brightness within. It therefore signifies the glory of his resurrection: he showed his disciples outwardly the immortality of his body and taught that within it there was also a soul shining with divine light.

Before his Passion Christ too was like a lily still closed, when he shone forth as a man illustrious in miracles. But after his resurrection and ascension he displayed himself as an opened lily to the birds of heaven—that is, to angels and all the saints—to whom, in his assumed humanity, he showed the power of divine brightness which he had before the world existed.

Hence it is said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2).

The rim of the sea in which the priests wash was therefore like the rim of a cup and the leaf of an opened lily, because baptism, by which we are made members of the high priest [Note: [Col. 0083D] The edition reads better: “we are made.”] cleanses us, purifies us from sins through faith in his Passion, and, once purified, brings us to the vision of his glory.

Since it has been said that a cord of thirty cubits surrounded the sea, and that a carving, again placed beneath the rim, encircled it with ten cubits, it is clear that the vessel was spread out and widened in the manner of a bowl, contracting from the thirty cubits of circumference which it had at the rim down to ten.

The sea held two thousand baths, or three thousand *metretae*. A bath held a measure and a half. The *bath* is a Hebrew measure, called *bath* among them, containing three *modii*. It is the same as the *ephah*, which they call *epha*; but the *ephah* belongs to the measure of grain, while the *bath* belongs to liquids, namely wine, water, and oil.

The bath, therefore, being a standard of fixed measure, signifies works of fairness and righteousness, in which those baptized for the remission of sins must necessarily be instructed.

The sea holds one thousand baths when the water of baptism washes the Jewish people and sends them on to the heavenly kingdom. It receives another thousand when it makes the Gentiles, reborn in the same font and strengthened in works of righteousness, sharers in that same kingdom.

And he made ten bronze bases, each base four cubits long, four cubits wide, and [Note: [Col. 0083D] The edition reads: “three,” as does the Vulgate.] four cubits high. And the workmanship of the bases was openwork, that is, hollow within. [Note: [Col. 0084D] From chapter 20.]

The same mysteries of our salvation are represented in many and various ways. For as the apostles and apostolic men are signified by the oxen bearing the sea, [Col. 0084D] so they are signified by the bases prepared to bear the basins; and the basins themselves, like the sea, signified a spiritual washing. For, according to Paralipomenon, they washed in them everything that they were about to offer as a burnt offering (2 Chronicles 4). The Lord’s burnt offering is generally understood to be the entire multitude of the elect, who are baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire. Therefore, just as the priests who washed in the sea signify those who, through baptism, become companions of the high priest, namely Christ, so the burnt offerings likewise signify these same persons when, through the washing of baptism, they are filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the victim is washed in the basin when a believer is sprinkled with baptism. [Col. 0085A] It is offered as a burnt offering when, through the bishop’s laying on of hands, it receives the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The bases were four cubits in length and breadth, because preachers—whether they endure outwardly the adversities of the world, the length of exile, and present labours, or inwardly expand their hearts in exultation through love of God and neighbour—always devote themselves to virtues: prudently discerning inner goods and evils, bravely bearing adversities, restraining the heart from the desire for pleasures, and maintaining justice in action.

There were also carvings between the joints by which the panels of the basins were joined together, so that one base was made from, namely, four or five panels. What carvings the bases had between these joints—[Col. 0085B] that is, on their sides before and behind, right and left, and also above the circular forms—he explains when he says: “Between the little crowns and braided work were lions, oxen, and cherubim; and likewise above upon the joints.” The panels from which the bases were made were square, and in them were round patterns called little crowns or braided works, in the middle of which were carvings. No surface of the base was flat in any part, but everywhere it was carved with mystical figures; for the minds of the saints—indeed, their whole manner of life—display the grace of virtues. No hour passes empty in which they are not occupied with devout works, words, or thoughts.

They have little crowns carved upon them when they pant with tireless [Col. 0085C] desire for entrance into everlasting life. They have braided work when, amid desires for the heavenly life which is above, they do not dissolve the bonds of fraternal charity which is beside them. Between the little crowns and braided work they have lions when they so raise their minds to hope for heavenly things and so enlarge them to love their neighbours that at times they sternly regard and correct those erring persons committed to their care. They have oxen also with the lions when, in correction, they mingle gentleness with severity. They do not cease to have a divided hoof, because they take the greatest care to preserve discernment in action and speech. They always chew the cud, because they never cease to turn over in their mouths the words of divine reading.

Cherubim are fittingly remembered as carved after the crowns and braided work, after the lions and oxen; they signify, namely, the multitude of knowledge in [Col. 0085D] the Scriptures. For the more diligently teachers of the faithful apply themselves to Holy Scripture, the more—in the severity of discernment by which they judge sinners and in the gentleness of mercy by which they pardon penitents—they fear God’s judgment, lest by binding or loosing unjustly they themselves be justly bound by him whose judgment cannot err. And above the lions and oxen hang, as it were, bronze straps. By the straps is shown the power of binding and loosing, granted by the Lord Jesus Christ to the rulers of the Church in Peter and his successors.

He adds again, saying: “And there were four wheels for each base, and bronze axles, upon which the bases stood; and on the four sides there were, as it were, cast little shoulders beneath the basin, facing one another, in order to carry it.” [Col. 0086A] The four wheels are the four books of the Gospels. For just as a revolving wheel runs most swiftly where it is driven, so, at the Lord’s command, they filled the whole world in a short time through the apostles. And as a wheel lifts a cart placed upon it from the ground and carries it wherever the driver directs, so the books of the Gospels raise the minds of the elect from earthly to heavenly things and lead them, by whatever advance in action or mystery of preaching grace wishes to assist spiritual persons; for it follows: “Such were the wheels as are usually made in a chariot.” Thus we also read concerning the saints: “The chariots of God are many thousands, thousands of those rejoicing; the Lord is among them” (Psalm 67).
