The little shoulders placed before the wheels, preventing them from slipping off the axles, are the proclamations of the prophets, by which evangelical and [Col. 0086B] apostolic Scripture is confirmed so that it may not become doubtful to any reader. Hence it is said: “We have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp in a dark place” (2 Peter 1). The axles of the wheels that bear the bases are the hearts of teachers, which by continual evangelical precepts lift them from below; and, as axles with wheels fitted to them, raise the bases higher from the earth.

The mouth of the basin, on the contrary, turned inward; its opening was one cubit; its base was a cubit and a half; while its belly is believed to have been four cubits, so that it might teach us that through baptism a path to heavenly things has been opened for us. What appeared outwardly from it was wholly round and one cubit in size, on account, that is, of the unity of confession and faith in which all are baptized in the confession of the Father, [Col. 0086C] the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Hence: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all” (Ephesians 4).

It also had one cubit and a half, on account, namely, of the perfection of action and the merit of contemplation. The whole cubit in the basin indicates the perfection of good action possessed by holy people through the help of divine grace. But at the corners of the columns—that is, on the sides of the bases—there were various carvings, and the middle portion between the columns was square, not round. By “the middle between the columns” he means the upper panel, which, like the others, was square and likewise carved; and at its summit it had a roundness of one and a half cubits, upon which [Col. 0086D] the basin was placed. The wheels likewise are measured at one cubit and a half, because Gospel Scripture shows how those who wish to be perfect ought to live and promises the gift of eternal recompense. But the bases had at their summit, where they received the basins, one cubit and a half of breadth, because teachers and ministers of the washing shone in this life, indeed perfect in action, but were [yet] limited in part by the light of contemplation. Hence it is said: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13).

One basin held forty baths. The number forty signifies great perfection, because four times ten make forty. There are ten commandments by which all our action is prescribed in God’s law. But there are four books of the Gospels, [Col. 0087A] in which, through the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, entrance into the heavenly homeland has been opened to us. And because all who belong to the mystery of baptism ought, together with faith and the sacraments of the Gospel, to show the fruit of right action, each basin in which the burnt offerings were washed held forty baths.

And he set up ten bases, five on the right side of the Temple and five on the left. By the right and left side of the Temple he does not mean inside the Temple itself, but before the Temple, on the eastern side—namely, in the inner court, which was properly called the court of the priests. He set five on the right side of the Temple for the Jews, who of old enjoyed the sun of righteousness through the teaching of the Law; and five [Col. 0087B] on the left for us, who for a long time, with blinded hearts, clung to him who said: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14). As if he said: “I desire to rest in those hearts which I wish to be estranged from the light of truth and the flame of divine charity.”

But the sea was placed on the right side of the Temple, in the same court. For those entering the court from the east first had to turn southward, where the sea stood in the very corner, ready for the priests to wash; then, as they proceeded inward, the basins placed on either side for washing the victims met them. Among these also was a bronze platform, five cubits long, five cubits [Col. 0087C] wide, and three cubits high, upon which Solomon stood when he dedicated the Temple.

Hiram also made basins—namely bronze vessels for receiving the altar’s ashes. He made bowls also, that is, bronze vessels equally wide at base and mouth, for heating. He made hooks as well, that is, vessels for offering wines. [Note: [Col. 0087D] From chapter 21.] The clayey earth from which the moulds for casting the vessels were made signifies Scripture, from which we take the rule for living well. For just as clay hardened by fires shapes vessels, so Scripture shows us the rule of righteousness that we are to follow. [Note: [Col. 0087D] From chapter 22.]

The golden table upon which the loaves were placed is Scripture, bright with spiritual understanding. Of it it is said: “You have prepared a table before me” (Psalm 22). The loaves of the Presence are holy [Col. 0087D] teachers, whose works or words, set before us as an example in the divine pages, whoever seeks well finds. Hence in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0087D] Thus also in the edition, but it would be better to say “in Leviticus,” where, at chapter 24, verse 5, one reads: “You shall take … fine flour, and bake from it twelve loaves,” etc.] twelve loaves were commanded to be made, on account, namely, of the twelve apostles through whom the Scripture of the New Testament was composed and the mysteries of the Old were revealed.

In the Books of Chronicles we read that Solomon made tables in the Temple, five on the right and five on the left, upon which they placed the Lord’s vessels: cups, bowls, censers, little mortars, incense, etc. (2 Chronicles 4). [Note: [Col. 0088D] From chapter 23.] Therefore, just as one table [Col. 0088A] laden with twelve loaves signifies the unanimous harmony of the Scripture by which we are fed, fortified by apostolic authority, so the ten tables signify the utterances of the Law and prophets, which set before us the examples of the faithful—like the Lord’s vessels placed upon them—in their brightness and miracles. The tables are fivefold because the Law embraces both the five books of Moses and the five ages of the world; twice five, because after the Lord’s incarnation it is entrusted to both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles.

“And he set ten golden lampstands, five on the right and five on the left opposite the oracle, of pure gold; and above, lamps of gold, like lily flowers.” [Note: [Col. 0088D] From chapter 24.] By “like lily flowers” he appears to mean the flower, because the upper part of the lampstands was fashioned in the shape of an open lily. By “golden lamps,” through that which is contained he indicates what contains it: namely, the golden little vessels in which the oil shone. Just as the tables are set forth as a type of Scripture because they administer the bread of the word and bear the vessels of ministry—that is, set before us the deeds of the righteous as examples—so the same things are figured by the lampstands because they bring forth the light of wisdom for those who wander. Hence Solomon says: “The commandment is a lamp, and the law a light” (Proverbs 6). Hence David says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Psalm 118). That the lampstands are five on the right and five on the left has the same meaning as was stated above concerning the tables. The oracle, where the ark was, is the entrance into the heavenly homeland, where Christ sits at the Father’s right hand, fully knowing the Father’s hidden counsels. The lampstands opposite the oracle indicate that God’s utterances look toward the dwelling-place of the [Col. 0088C] heavenly city, so as to kindle us to merit it.

And he made golden snuffers, that is, wick-trimmers with which the lamps were trimmed so that, restored, they might shine more brightly. The snuffers signify the two Testaments by which sins are cleansed and which are joined to one another in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Water-jars signify the inmost hearts of the saints, filled with the water of wisdom and the wine of compunction. The flesh-hooks by which meats are prepared signify preachers, who administer to their hearers the food of understanding; their office is to distribute the body and blood to believers, but to deny it to unbelievers. Bowls signify teachers full of useful waters. Little mortars are the labour of penitents and the suffering of endurance, by which their members upon the earth are mortified. [Col. 0088D] Censers of the purest gold indicate the virtues of works and the prayers of the saints, from whom an odour of sweetness ascends to the Lord through a good conscience and unfeigned faith [Note: [Col. 0088D] From chapter 25.] (1 Timothy 1). The hinges of both doors are the perceptions and hearts of angels and saints, which cling immovably to contemplation and love of the Creator, so that they rightly fulfil the ministry entrusted to them, since they never turn their eyes from the Lord’s will.

[Col. 0089A] And Solomon brought in what David his father had consecrated—gold, silver, and vessels—and placed them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord. David, Solomon’s father, consecrated silver when God the Father strengthens with the grace of his Spirit those who are eloquent, to speak God’s word. He consecrates gold when he enlightens those endowed with natural ability to understand the Law. He also consecrates vessels when he bestows the grace of the Holy Spirit upon all the children of the Church. Solomon offers these consecrated things in the Temple when the Lord, after judgment has been completed, introduces the company of teachers and of the remaining faithful into the joy of the heavenly kingdom.

And Solomon made all the vessels in the house of the Lord. Above it said that Hiram made all the vessels for Solomon; now Scripture adds that Solomon made the same things, [Col. 0089B] because Solomon made them by directing, Hiram by doing. In the plain of the Jordan the king cast the vessels of the Lord’s Temple in clayey ground. [Note: [Col. 0089D] From chapter 21.] For we do not otherwise become vessels of election and mercy unless, looking to his baptism, we endeavour to be washed in such a river. It should be noted, moreover, that it says the same vessels were made not only in the region of the Jordan but also in its plain, signifying the multiplication of the faithful that was to occur not only in Judaea but over the breadth of every land, according to the words: “The fields shall rejoice, and all that is in them” (Psalm 95). Therefore the king cast the vessels of the Lord’s house in the plain of the Jordan, because Christ spread throughout the whole breadth of the world the baptism of salvation from which he would make vessels of mercy.

[Col. 0089C] The feast which Solomon and all Israel celebrated signifies the joy which the saints have everlastingly with Christ, the true and peaceful king. Emath is interpreted “the Lord’s truth.” The stream or torrent of Egypt signifies temporal death, which no one remaining in Egypt—that is, in the darkness of this world—can escape. Therefore all Israel celebrates the feast with Solomon from the stream of Egypt to Emath when, after the end of this present life, the saints truly enjoy eternal joys with the Lord Jesus Christ.

The Temple of the Lord is the holy Church, according to the saying: “The Temple of the Lord is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3). King Christ dedicated it when he cleansed it with his blood from the filth of sins. [Col. 0089D] The children of Israel also dedicate it when the faithful, according to the gift bestowed upon them, benefit their neighbours by the word of preaching and the works of virtues.

What does it mean that Solomon consecrated the middle of the court, offering burnt offerings there because the bronze altar before the Temple doors could not hold all of them, unless it is that Christ now fully accomplishes in the Church what could not be accomplished in the Law because of the people’s weakness? For he himself is the court of the Lord’s house, because through him entrance into the heavenly Jerusalem lies open. Therefore, since burnt offerings and sacrifices could not be offered on the typical altar, because everything there was done figuratively, our king raised up the altar of faith [Col. 0090A] in the Church, upon which burnt offerings and sacrifices are offered spiritually every day. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “I have not desired burnt offerings and the blood of victims, goats, and bulls” (Isaiah 1).

The priests took the ark of the Lord, the tabernacle of the covenant, and all the vessels of the sanctuary that were in the tabernacle; and they brought the ark into the oracle of the Temple, into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim. Moses made two golden cherubim and placed them upon the mercy-seat that was over the ark (Exodus 25). Solomon, however, added two larger ones, beneath whose wings he is now said to have placed the ark, together with the mercy-seat and the two former cherubim. The outer house of the Temple signifies the Church in pilgrimage; the Holy of Holies signifies the happiness of the heavenly homeland. The ark brought into the Holy [Col. 0090B] of Holies shows the assumed humanity of Christ brought within the veil of the heavenly royal dwelling.

The poles by which the ark was carried are the preachers through whom Christ became known to the world. The ends of the poles appeared before the oracle, not always, but when the doors of the oracle were opened; nor to everyone, but only to those who approached more closely and earnestly endeavoured to gaze upon the inner things. The poles are hidden in the oracle because the elect who have departed are now in the hidden place of God’s countenance. Yet the ends of the poles are seen by those who draw near when the oracle is opened, when God’s grace grants to the more perfect—those purifying the oracle of the heart—some small glimpse to contemplate of heavenly joy. For to those who have withdrawn a little farther away, that is, whose minds wander more outwardly, contemplation is not granted.

There was in the ark a golden urn containing manna, because in the human being Christ all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Colossians 2). There was also Aaron’s rod, which after being cut off had flowered anew, because the power of judgment belongs to him whose judgment seemed to have been taken away in humility. There were also the tablets of the covenant, because in him all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God are hidden (ibid.). The poles by which it was carried clung to it, because teachers who labour in the word now rejoice in the present vision of Christ’s glory. Hence Paul says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Col. 0090D] (Philippians 1). What kind of ark it was, and how it was positioned, only those who entered the oracle were permitted to see, because only citizens of the heavenly homeland fully behold there the glory of the Redeemer.

A cloud filled the house of the Lord, that is, the Synagogue, because the darkness of unbelief filled their minds. And the priests could not minister because of the cloud, because, while they disdain to investigate the mystical senses covered by the veil of the letter and the mysteries of Christ’s birth, they lost the due ministry of faith through the cloud of their error, so that, as their merits require, they do not recognize the worship of faith.

[Col. 0091A] Solomon’s fleet is Christ’s Church, set upon the sea of the world and devoting its effort to acquiring the treasures of knowledge and wisdom, together with the riches of virtues. There are Hiram’s servants, sailors and men skilled in the sea, together with Solomon’s servants, when Gentiles trained in secular learning and wisdom are joined in unity of faith with those skilled in the Law of Moses. Our Solomon, that is, Christ, sends them to Ophir, which is interpreted “weakening,” that is, into lowliness, so that they may bring him the gold acquired there—that is, precious understanding. How much? Namely four hundred and thirty talents: history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy in the two Testaments. Ophir is the name of a province in India, named after Ophir, one of the descendants of Heber; it is also called the golden land [Col. 0091B] because it has mountains of gold, inhabited by lions and very savage beasts. No one dares approach them otherwise than by standing near the shore and taking into his ship whatever earth he finds dug up by the lions’ claws, so that, if the beasts perceive them, they may easily retreat to sea.

I also wish you, most beloved brothers, to know that the tabernacle which the Hebrew people built in the wilderness was a figure of this spiritual house. But because the tabernacle was erected during their journey toward the promised land, while this house was built in Jerusalem itself; because the former was carried from place to place by the frequent service of the Levites and finally brought into the promised land, while this one, built at once in the homeland itself and in the royal city, was to stand always upon an inviolable foundation until [Col. 0091C] it fulfilled the office of heavenly figures entrusted to it: in that tabernacle may be figured the labour and exile of the present Church, but in this house the rest and blessedness to come.

Or because the former was made only by the children of Israel, whereas this was made also by proselytes and Gentiles, the fathers of the Old Testament and the ancient people of God may principally be represented in the tabernacle, while in this house may be represented the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Nevertheless, when examined more fully, both buildings show in many ways that the daily labours of the present Church and the eternal rewards in the future joys of the heavenly kingdom, the election of the primitive Church, and the salvation of all nations in Christ are prefigured.

Therefore, dearest brothers, that handmade Temple [Col. 0091D] was built by Solomon as a figure of Jesus Christ and of all of us—that is, of the head and the members. You therefore belong to the building of the spiritual Temple when, by believing rightly and doing good works, you are members of Christ. When I say that you belong to the building of the Temple, however, I do not mean the temple which Nebuzaradan, servant of the king of Babylon, burned and despoiled of its treasures (4 Kings 25), but that Temple which God the Father decreed before all ages to make in his beloved and coeternal Son Jesus Christ, in the heavenly Jerusalem. Hence: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city,” etc. (Psalm 121). And again: “Jerusalem, the city of the great king” (Psalm 47). To that Temple, therefore, beloved ones, I wish and desire you to belong; in its inner house—that is, in the Holy [Col. 0092A] of Holies—the ark is placed, namely the Son of God, in whom we have a covenant of peace with the Father. Manna too is contained in the ark, because in Christ are all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2). To him also is entrusted Aaron’s rod which had flowered: namely, the authority given by God to rule the Israelite people—indeed, the whole Church—forever. The same Son of God, ascending into heaven after his resurrection, entered once for all into that spiritual Temple not made by hands, having been appointed by God judge of the living and the dead. We also consider the angels to belong to this Temple. [lacuna] in the inner part of that same Temple, namely before the face of Jesus Christ himself, the high priest, because they are always ready for [Col. 0092B] his service. Thus they stand with feet upright, and fix their eyes upon the mercy-seat, that is, upon him himself. Thus they preserve their innocence continually. Thus they rejoice in heaven over the blessedness of holy souls, so that they do not cease to bring aid to us, whom they see still journeying on earth, until, at God’s command, they bring us to the heavenly homeland.

I therefore exhort you, beloved, to devote yourselves diligently to the sacred Scriptures, so that you may be able to imitate these Cherubim, whose name is interpreted “multitude of knowledge.” For in the divine Scriptures you will find a multitude of knowledge if you seek diligently; spiritually intoxicated by it, you may despise earthly things, love heavenly things, scorn transient things, desire eternal things, and finally fix the eyes of the mind without ceasing upon the mercy-seat—that is, upon Christ. [Col. 0092C] Concerning this mercy-seat John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2). And the apostle Paul says: “For Jesus did not enter holy temples made by hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us” (Hebrews 9).

The Cherubim of God, strengthened by his grace, persevere perpetually in their innocence. So also you, beloved, keep continually and faithfully by good works the covenant which you made with God, whether on the day of baptism or also upon receiving an order. Keep chastity both of mind and body, which is acceptable to God and an imitation of the angelic life; [Col. 0092D] for to live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not an earthly but a heavenly life. Chastity too, if long-enduring and humble, will receive the reward of eternal blessedness, provided nevertheless that it perseveres in its purpose until the day of death (Matthew 10). Where the flesh can no longer be intact from intercourse, let the conscience be a virgin in faith.

Therefore, dearest ones, let no disordered thought suggest anything unlawful to you; let no uncleanness defile you; let not luxury render you guilty; let not greed kindle the mind in love of earthly things; let not anger injure your neighbours; let not arrogance raise the mind into pride; let not an injury inflicted by neighbours disturb you; let not pretence display holiness before human eyes; let not hypocrisy render you guilty before God; let not malice [Col. 0093A] deprive you of a place in the heavenly court; let no perversity repel you as unworthy from the fellowship of the citizens above. Thus also the Cherubim rejoice in heaven over the blessedness of holy souls, so that they do not cease to bring aid to us, whom they see still journeying on earth.

Therefore, beloved, frequently bring before the eyes of your mind the examples of these blessed spirits, namely the Cherubim; and what they do perfectly and without ceasing in heaven, do yourselves upon earth according to your measure, as charity directs. With God’s help, therefore, guard yourselves from the contagion of sin, and diligently pour out prayers to the Lord for the salvation of the whole world and of your neighbours. For all the faithful departed who are still held in places of punishment, [Col. 0093B] I urge you to offer to God prayers, sacrifices, sighs, and tears, so that, through the intercession of your compassion, delivered from the most bitter punishments, they may deserve [Col. 0094A] to pass to places of refreshment, light, and peace.

Nor do I wish you to be content with this alone, but also to render thanksgivings to the Lord for those whom he has already placed in the palace of heaven. Thus you ought to be concerned for your own advancement, while not neglecting your neighbours’ salvation. Inflict upon no one an evil which you do not wish to suffer; refuse no one the good which you desire to be done to yourselves. Love God above all things; love your neighbours in God as yourselves; patiently endure enemies for God’s sake; raise the eyes of your mind with all devotion to the heavenly homeland; and, that you may someday be able to attain it, pour out prayers with tears in the utmost earnestness. May he deign to lead you there—he who, through his same most beloved Son, [Col. 0094B] our Lord Jesus Christ, ordained before the ages to build an eternal Temple for his majesty from living and chosen stones. Amen.

## THIRD SERMON. TO THE BROTHERS: THAT THEY SHOULD POSSESS NOTHING OF THEIR OWN

[Col. 0093]

[Col. 0093B] Dearest brothers, since by God’s grace you have assembled together in order to order and reform the customs of your religious order, it is fitting that you recall what you promised to God and to your abbot [Col. 0093C] when you first entered the order. When you were first presented before the abbot, there were three things which, upon his questioning, you vowed to fulfil for God: obedience, chastity, and that you would possess nothing of your own. It was most fitting, beloved, that you promised God obedience and chastity, because without them you could in no way please God. And therefore, if it pleases you, let us say something to you about each of these, beginning with obedience.

Obedience is the virtue which implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves those it has implanted. [Note: [Col. 0093D] From Gregory, *Moralia*, book 35, chapter 15, no. 28.] Of it Paul says: “Brothers, obey your superiors and be subject to them, for they keep watch as those who will render an account for your souls” (Hebrews 13). Hence Solomon says: “An obedient man speaks victories” (Proverbs [Col. 0093D] 21). Truly the obedient man speaks victories, because he conquers himself when he puts another’s will before his own will. Thus we too, when we humbly obey our abbot, overcome ourselves in our hearts.

Hence the prophet Samuel also speaks, saying: “Obedience is better than victims; and to hearken is better than to offer the fat of rams. For to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to comply is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Kings 15). Truly obedience is better than victims, because in victims another’s flesh is slain, whereas in obedience one’s own will is restrained. [Note: [Col. 0093D] From Isidore, book 8.] Diviners are those who utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols and offer abominable sacrifices to demons. But idolatry is the service of idols. [Note: [Col. 0094D] *Etymologies*, chapters 9 and 11.] For *latria* is Greek; in Latin it is called “service.” This, therefore, is the supreme evil: that servants of God placed in a monastery incur through disobedience the sin of divination.

It seems to me a great evil that servants of God should live in a monastery under the habit of religion and commit through disobedience and obstinacy the crime of idolatry. It is great misery when religious men descend to hell by the path of virtues. This is the greatest misfortune: when ecclesiastical men, under the habit of religion, incur through disobedience the danger of eternal damnation.

Let us also hear the apostle Paul saying: “As through the disobedience of one man, namely Adam, many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man, namely Christ, many are made righteous” [Col. 0094D] (Romans 5). And just as through one man’s disobedience many descended into hell, so through the obedience of one man many have ascended and will ascend into heaven. Thus also we read concerning our Lord Jesus Christ: “Christ became obedient for us to the Father unto death” (Philippians 2). If, therefore, Jesus Christ, king of heaven and earth, deigned to obey God the Father unto death, why does a most wretched man placed in a monastery disdain to obey his abbot? And if our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true king of glory, obeyed God the Father unto death, why does a mortal man, food for worms, despise the commands [Col. 0095A] of his abbot?

Why, unless because he does not follow Christ so as to ascend with him into heaven, but follows Adam so as to descend with him through disobedience into hell? Why does he refuse to obey his abbot, unless because he despises Christ and follows the devil? Thus the Lord says in the Gospel to his servants, to whom he entrusted the governance of his Church: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10). It is as though he said: “Whoever obeys you obeys me also, and whoever scorns you scorns me.” Therefore, beloved brothers, call to mind this saying of our Lord Jesus Christ and consider it with diligent attention: whoever in a monastery is disobedient to his abbot is disobedient not only to the abbot but also to Christ. [Col. 0095B] And whoever despises his superior despises not only his superior but also Christ.

My brothers, in the second place, you promised chastity to God and to your abbot when you first came to the monastery. Unless you have kept it, you have laboured in vain in all your works. If you have not kept chastity from the day on which you promised it to God and to your abbot, you have spent the whole time of your life in vain. Whoever has promised chastity to God and to his abbot cannot be religious unless he keeps it in mind and body, or repairs this failure by the most rigorous repentance. Why? Because through one evil many good things perish. Through one fault many righteous acts are brought to nothing. Through one iniquity many good things can be overthrown. Evil mingled with good things contaminates very many of them [Col. 0095C]. A little gall turns the sweetness of honey into bitterness. A little fire sets a great forest ablaze (Jas. III). A little leaven corrupts the whole lump (1 Cor. V). Hence Scripture says: “Whoever has sinned in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. II), namely with respect to eternal life. As though he were entangled in every sin, so, if he remains in even one alone, he shall not enter the gate of eternal life. Thus a man can be condemned through one sin unless he repairs it by the most rigorous repentance; and especially through fornication, because without chastity no work is perfect, and without chastity no work is great. Hence blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0095D] Homily 13 on the Gospels]: “Neither is chastity great without good work, nor is any good work anything without chastity” [Col. 0095D]. Therefore the beauty of chastity must be loved [Note: [Col. 0096D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, ch. 40]. Chastity is the fruit of sweetness. Chastity is the unviolated virtue of the saints. Chastity is security of mind and health of body. Chastity is beloved by God and by all the saints. Of it it is written that without chastity no one shall see God (Heb. XII). Hence the venerable Bede says in a certain homily: “On the day of resurrection no one except those chaste in body will be able to be raised to heaven; after the resurrection no one except those pure in heart will be able to behold the essence of the divine majesty.”

In the third place, you promised God that you would possess nothing of your own. [Col. 0096A] In many ways the devil tempts toward acquiring many things those who promised to be content with little and few things. Many are converted from secular life to God, enter the monastery, gladly give all their riches to the poor and to monasteries, and thereafter, throughout their lives, love poverty more than riches, as the holy apostles did. Very many secular persons too are converted to God in the monastery, and presume to commit fraud or theft from the monastery’s goods, as Judas the betrayer did. Of him we read that he had the money-box and concealed and stole the things put into the common fund. Some also come from the world to the monastery and retain and conceal one portion of their riches which they possessed in the world, [Col. 0096B] fearing temporary want, while they hand over another portion with them to the monastery, as Ananias and Sapphira did. Of them it is indeed written that they sold a field and placed part of its price at the apostles’ feet, but concealed another part (Acts V). Some poor persons also come from secular life to the monastery; though they were poor in the world, they nevertheless wish to become rich in the monastery, as Gehazi, Elisha’s disciple, did. Elisha said to him: “Because you ran after Naaman and received riches from him, Naaman’s leprosy shall cleave to you for ever” (4 Kings V). Therefore all who, for God’s sake, despise everything that is in this world, as the holy apostles did, shall rejoice and be rewarded for ever with those apostles [Col. 0096C]. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). But he who passes from the world into a monastery and commits fraud or theft from the monastery’s goods is Judas, and with Judas he shall bear punishment in hell. Those who are converted from secular life to the service of the Lord, if they reserve part of what they possessed in the world for themselves and distribute another part, shall bear the sentence of cursing with Ananias and Sapphira. And he who comes from the world to the monastery, if he desires there the riches which he could not possess in the world, Naaman’s leprosy shall without doubt cleave to him; and what Gehazi suffered in body, this man shall suffer in soul. Therefore to those [Col. 0096D] who truly, for God’s sake and after the manner of the apostles, despise all that is in this world, belongs that saying of the Psalmist: “But for me it is good to cling to God; to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. LXXII). And this: “Cast thy thought upon the Lord, and he shall nourish thee” (Ps. LIV). But to Judas and his followers it is said: “They ascend even to the heavens and descend even to the depths; their soul wasted away in evils” (Ps. CVI). To Ananias and those like him belongs this: “Those who trust in their strength and glory in the multitude of their riches” (Ps. XLVIII). Gehazi and his companions are suited by this: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but [Col. 0097A] trusted in the multitude of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. LI).

But behold, dearest brothers, while we scrutinize the sins of others with such zeal, let us fear lest we offend the eyes of the divine majesty. It is fitting, then, that we who so carefully notice specks in the eyes of others should hasten to cast beams out of our own eyes (Matt. VII). What, then, should we do amid these things? Surely what the Psalmist says: “Make vows and render them to the Lord your God” (Ps. LXV); otherwise it would be much better not to vow than, after a vow, not to pay what was promised (Ecclus. V). Why? “Because, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0097A] *Synonyms*, book II, ‘On a Vow’], among the unbelievers [Col. 0098A] are to be found those who did not fulfil the good things they vowed to God.” Therefore, dearest brothers, turn inward to yourselves; and if you find that you have fulfilled in deed the things which you promised God, give thanks to God. But if you recognize that in the things you vowed to God you have been transgressors and negligent, seek pardon from almighty Jesus Christ through pure prayers and daily tears, so that on the day of his strict judgment he may not permit you to perish with the unbelievers, but may deign to bring you with his elect to the kingdom of heaven—he who with the same Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON FOURTH. ON THE PRELATES OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0097]

[Col. 0097B] Isidore, the teacher of the Spains, a man trained in every kind of expression so as to be suitable to the unlearned and the learned according to the character of his discourse, spoke among other things as follows for the instruction of priests [Note: [Col. 0097D] *Sentences*, book III, ch. 35]:

> “Just as sinners and the unrighteous are forbidden to undertake priestly ministry, so the unlearned and unskilled are kept back from such an office. The former, by living badly, corrupt the lives of the good by their depraved examples; the latter, through ignorance, do not know how to correct the wicked. For how shall they be able to teach what they themselves have not learned? [Note: [Col. 0097D] Ch. 36.] Therefore let him cease to undertake the place of teaching who does not know how to teach. Every teacher, accordingly, ought to devote himself both to good conduct and to good preaching, because either without the other makes him useless and imperfect.”

Therefore a prelate ought with all earnestness to proclaim to his subjects the sweetness and delightfulness of God, to stir them by his own examples to good works, and frequently to admonish them with sweet words, so that he may rightly be counted among the members of holy Church, as the bridegroom—that is, Christ—speaks to that same Church under the person of the bride in the Song of Songs:

> “Thy lips, O bride, drip honeycomb; honey and milk are under thy tongue” (Song IV).

[Note: [Col. 0098D] From Gregory, on this passage: why the aforesaid saint is compared to a honeycomb.] The preachers of the Church are rightly called the lips of the bride, because through them she speaks to the peoples and through them all little ones are instructed in the faith, while through them the hidden things of Scripture, as though the concealed things of the heart, are made manifest. In a honeycomb, however, honey lies hidden and wax is visible. Therefore the lips of the bride—that is, of holy Church—are rightly called a honeycomb, because, while great wisdom is possessed amid the frailty of the flesh, honey is as it were hidden in wax [Col. 0097D]. But when any elect person preaches, when he reveals heavenly joys to those who do not know them, then the honeycomb drips, because through the frailty of his mouth he makes known to his hearers how great a sweetness of wisdom lies concealed in his heart. Hence it is written: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. IV). Therefore there follows: “Honey and milk are under thy tongue.” Certainly false preachers carry honey upon their tongue, not beneath it: they sometimes preach heavenly joys as though they were true men, while they themselves seek earthly goods with all their desires. But the holy mind displays honey upon its tongue, because in speaking it shows others the sweetness of wisdom, and in preaching truthfully refreshes its hearers as with honey’s sweetness. The good shepherd bears milk beneath his tongue, because by teaching suited to himself he nourishes all the little ones in the Church. Yet he keeps all these things beneath his tongue for himself, because he constantly carries inward sweetness with him. For while he casts away earthly things, while he rejects the bitterness of vices, he feeds inwardly upon the sweetness of wisdom, which gathers strength so that, travelling toward eternal things, he may not grow weary in the labour of the way.

[Col. 0098C] By such preaching the prudent shepherd pours the sweetness and delightfulness of God into the hearts of his subjects, and raises them by examples of good conduct to desire heavenly things. Certainly he is a prudent shepherd who watches carefully over the flock entrusted to him; for, while he wisely surveys himself and his sheep on every side, he avoids the snares of enemies. Therefore let the negligent shepherd hear what the Lord says to him and to the prudent shepherd: “The good shepherd,” he says, “lays down his life for his sheep; but the hireling flees” (John X). He lays down his life for his sheep who, ascending the dangerous post of government, closes the door of silence and keeps the flock of cloistered brothers in peace. He lays down his life for his sheep who alone, managing worldly external affairs amid dangers, seeks what is necessary and useful for the brothers. He lays down his life who alone goes out to endure the disputes of household business and walks in the midst of flattering and slanderous tongues; who labours for the weak and feeds those who labour, comforts the faint-hearted, and contends by rebuking the proud. Such a shepherd can say with Christ and through Christ: “I know mine, and mine know me” [Col. 0099A] (John X). The sheep know the shepherd whom they often see present, whom familiarity makes known to the subject brothers, and whom benefits render a friend. The brothers know the prelate because, whether by bearing with them in charity, chastising them through zeal for justice, or providing outward necessities, he makes himself in every respect useful and kind to them. Subjects know their prelate when, like a father to his children, he prepares what is necessary for their present life, and like a teacher preaches spiritual things. The shepherd, however, knows his sheep when he carefully attends to the characters and deeds of his subjects. Hence it is written: “Consider diligently the countenance of thy cattle” (Prov. XXVII). He considers the countenance of the cattle who does not fail to know what each of his subjects is capable of. He diligently inspects the countenance of his flock who carefully investigates the qualities, deeds, and capacities of the brothers whose care belongs to him. Through confession the hearts of his subjects are made manifest to him; through visitation their deeds are known; experience shows what they can do, and the result shows what they wish to do. “And,” he says, “they shall hear my voice” (John X).

There are three voices of the shepherd: the gentle, the sweet, and the loud. The gentle voice belongs to the sick, the sweet to the dying, and the loud to the deaf—that is, to the disobedient. He is sick who is tempted. But he who despairs of God’s mercy is dying. He is deaf who does not hear—that is, who scorns to obey. At times the sick man, that is, he who is placed amid temptations, hears the gentle voice of his teacher’s consolation; he who, because of the greatness of his sins, despairs of God’s mercy hears the voice of entreaty; the deaf man, that is, the disobedient, hears the loud—that is, harsh—voice of rebuke.

Again it is said: “And mine follow me”: the sheep follow the shepherd. What shepherd do the sheep follow? Either a good one or a bad one. Where do they follow him? Wherever he goes before them. If the shepherd is good, the sheep follow him to life; but if he is bad, they follow him to death. “If the blind follow the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matt. XV). How does the good shepherd go before the sheep? By life and teaching, certainly. When an ecclesiastical teacher lives well and teaches rightly, then there comes to be one sheepfold and one shepherd. The shepherd ought to be one in himself and one with the flock, so that what he teaches in words he may fulfil in good works. He [Col. 0099D] ought to be one, so that anger does not change him from gentleness, prosperity does not exalt him, nor adversity break him; rather, he should remain the same in persevering patience. Therefore he truly maintains and loves the unity of brotherhood who rejoices in the service of charity, imitating the example of the true shepherd who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Matt. XX). Certainly he is a fit shepherd and governs the flock according to God who labours only to draw more persons with him to God by word and example; whom the honour of prelacy does not delight but its burden; charity rather than power; service rendered to others rather than service received from [Col. 0100A] others—according to Paul’s saying: “Though I was free from all, I made myself servant of all” (1 Cor. IX). The shepherd also maintains unity with the flock when he is not separated from it by more costly clothing or more delicate food; when through compassion he becomes one with the weak, and through prudent dispensation with the delicate. Thus the prelate ought to live so that he may rightly say with the Apostle: “I became all things to all men, that I might gain all” (ibid.).

But the negligent shepherd flees and withdraws from the flock. There are certain prelates who scorn to do the good things they command others to do. For when they impose heavy and unbearable burdens upon their subjects and will not move them with a finger, they scorn to bear what they command others to bear. They flee when they withdraw themselves from divine offices [Col. 0100B] and scorn to bear the burden of their order with the brothers. They flee when they wander about through other people’s houses, considering themselves happier the later they return to the cloister. They flee when they go farther away from the cloister in order to devote themselves more freely to idle talk, fill their stomachs more abundantly with food, and sleep more securely than they used to in the cloister. They flee when they seek not what is common to the brothers but what is their own. They flee when, even though present, they conceal themselves in silence upon seeing negligences. They flee when, removed from the community, they live at leisure; when they withdraw from the brothers’ common counsel; when they live badly and do not wish to be reproved. Hence blessed Gregory says: “It pleases them, when they do even unlawful things freely, that none of their subjects should oppose them.” And in the same work [Note: [Col. 0099D] *Morals*, book XXVI, no. 44]: “A prelate considers himself wiser than all those over whom he sees that he has greater power.” They love, that is, to appear wise and to be powerful. This was the cause of angelic and human ruin. “I shall set my throne,” says the angel, “toward the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). And through the serpent he said to man: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. III). Therefore let the prelate fear the ruin which man and angel deserved. For the angel fell because he wished to be more powerful; and man became foolish because he wished to be wiser. Moreover, there are certain prelates who live well yet permit their subjects to live badly. Some also live badly and compel their subjects to live well. And others live badly [Col. 0100D] and wish their subjects to live badly. Those, then, who live well but permit their subjects to live badly go before them in the example of good conduct; but, since they do not rebuke them by correcting them, they themselves also sin with those who err. For though they themselves live well, they must nevertheless render an account to the Lord concerning the flock entrusted to them. Why do such men undertake the care of the flock and refuse to bear the burden of labour? Or if they do not know how to govern the flock, why undertake the task of governing? Or, if they know but through negligence permit their subjects to sin—although they might live well by themselves—why do they incur eternal death by turning others’ life into a danger to their own souls? Such [Col. 0101A] prelates nourish the sons of Eli the priest, who sleep with the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle; who do not permit those coming to Shiloh to sacrifice, but before the fat is burned seize raw flesh (1 Kings II). They are like Eli’s sons who live dissolutely and negligently under prelates who live well, who sleep with women either by actually doing this or by joining themselves to fleshly desires. They also hinder those who come to Shiloh from sacrificing when by words and examples they turn recent converts away from the exercise of good works. They do not permit the fat to be burned because, having extinguished the fire of charity, they do not pour the sweetness of a good heart into good action. They seek not cooked but raw flesh because, fleeing the fire of tribulation, they withdraw themselves from poverty [Col. 0101B] and labour and do not wish to suffer adversity for the Lord. For the vices of the flesh are usually cooked away in the furnace of tribulation and poverty. They therefore desire raw flesh so that they may cook it for themselves when, how, how much, and of what sort they please. Such are certain men who remain in the cloister, as if in Shiloh, and do nothing except what they will, and as they will, and when they will, and as much as they will. Subjects remain as if in Shiloh when they hasten more to fulfil their own wills than the commands laid upon them by good prelates. Such men do not imitate Samuel, who first anointed kings in the kingdom of the Jews (1 Kings X); but imitate Hophni and Phinehas, through whose sin the ark of the Lord was carried away by the Allophyles into the land of the Philistines (1 Kings IV). But those who live badly and compel their subjects [Col. 0101C] to live well do indeed call the erring back from evil, but kill the strong—that is, those zealous in God’s service. They correct the perverse from their wickedness by words, but kill those who live religiously by their depraved examples. [Col. 0102A] They desire to appear religious because they have religious persons under them, but scorn to live religiously. They glory in the good works of their subjects, not in their own deeds. What they do not wish to perform, they command others to perform; they themselves perform what they do not think others are permitted to perform. They compel their subjects to work well, but do not wish to be compelled by anyone.

Therefore let the shepherd maintain unity with the flock, so that he may be able to arrive with it at the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Let him not be separated from it by more costly clothing, more delicate food, or the pursuit of empty glory. Let him be diligent concerning the flock entrusted to him; let him gently admonish the good so that they may advance to better things; let him carefully correct the bad so that they do not proceed to worse; let him endeavour often to visit the weak; let him not refuse gently and mildly to console the sorrowful [Col. 0102B]. Moreover, let him enter the cloister continually, urge the sluggish to good works, rebuke the negligent, and unceasingly proclaim to all alike the joys of paradise and the punishments of hell. Above all, let him not neglect first to fulfil himself the good things which he preaches to others; let him willingly bear the burden of his order with the other brothers; and let him provide for them, in spiritual as well as temporal matters, as a father for his children, knowing diligently that he must render an account for them to God. But beyond all these things, let him always pour forth prayers to the Lord for them, so that none of the flock entrusted to him may perish, nor may the ravening wolf find any wandering from the way of truth whom he may carry off; but let him zealously strive, with those same sheep and Christ as guide, to reach the ever-green pastures [Col. 0102C], through the grant of the same our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON FIFTH. ON OBEDIENCE

[Col. 0101]

[Col. 0101D] Let the provost be obeyed as a father, and still more the priest, who bears the care of you all. We ought to fear our prelate as the Lord, love him as a father, and believe that whatever good he commands us is for the profit of our soul. Here, under the name of “provost,” is indicated the prior of the cloister, or the steward of the monastery. If, in a community where canonical order is observed, there is neither bishop nor abbot, but a prior, he is designated by the name “priest.” But if there is a bishop or abbot in the community, he who is greater in it is understood under the name “priest.” For we are commanded to preserve obedience unto death, because without it all regular observance is reckoned as nothing. Yet it must be known [Col. 0102D] that through obedience no evil ought to be commanded by a prelate or performed by subjects. Hence the eminent teacher Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0101D] *Synonyms*, book II, chapter “On Evil Commands”]: “Do not obey any authority in evil, even if punishment compels you, even if tortures threaten.” Why? Because it is better to die than to carry out unlawful commands. Therefore whoever obeys a prelate in evil is disobedient to Christ, who said in the Gospel: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII). And whoever refuses to obey his prelate in evil is obedient to Christ, Lord of all, who through the Prophet commanded men to turn away from evil and do good (Ps. XXXVI). Therefore, if whoever commits sin is the slave of sin, we ought not to obey any authority in evil.

[Col. 0103A] It must also be especially understood that obedience is sometimes none at all if it has something of its own, but sometimes, if it has nothing of its own, it is very slight [Note: [Col. 0103D] From Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXV, no. 30]. For when worldly success is commanded, when a higher position is ordered, the man invited to receive these things empties obedience of its virtue for himself if he also longs for them from his own desire. Again, when a prelate commands one of his subjects to despise this world, when he orders him to undergo insults and reproaches, if the latter does not willingly desire this of himself, he diminishes the merit of his obedience, because he receives unwillingly and reluctantly those things which are despised in this life. Therefore obedience ought to have something of its own in adversities and more lowly things, and again to have absolutely nothing of its own in prosperity, so that in adversities and more contemptible things it may be so much the more glorious as it submits even from desire to the divine dispensation; and in prosperity so much the more humble as it utterly overcomes in mind the very present glory which it receives from God [Col. 0103B]. Just as pus issues from a wound, so the disease of disobedience proceeds from the swelling of pride and the ulcer of contempt. The disease of disobedience is an infirmity of the soul. He who does not wish to do good things, though he can, is alive; yet he is sick. He lives in capacity, but languishes in a corrupt will. The first man suffered from this disease. While he lived in capacity and was sound in good will, he was set over the beasts of earth, birds of air, and fishes of the sea (Gen. I); but, fallen through the fault of disobedience and cast down from the joys of paradise, he is even now exposed and subjected to flies and gnats. When bodily infirmity gathers into a swelling, it sometimes happens that it produces sickness. Thus the carnal mind, through the swelling of pride, very often incurs the sickness of disobedience.

There are two kinds of swelling: the hard and the soft. The hard kind of swelling in the flesh is the obstinacy of carnal persons in their manner of life. It is usually treated in three ways: by plaster, ointment, and iron—that is, by the example of good work, the word of admonition, and the discipline of correction. When the mind does not discharge the pus of perverse intention through confession, or does not promise amendment in response to admonition, it remains for it to receive an incision of iron [Col. 0103D], that is, the most rigorous correction of discipline. Hence the eminent teacher blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0104D] *Sentences*, book III, ch. 46]: “He who is not corrected after being chastised by a gentle word must necessarily be rebuked more sharply. For with pain must be cut away those things which cannot be healed gently. He who, privately admonished, neglects to correct himself of sin must be rebuked publicly, so that a wound which does not know how to be healed secretly may have to be amended openly.” But the swelling is soft when the inflated mind delights in luxurious foods, pursues idleness, is dulled by drowsiness, and rejoices in vain tales. From these, then, comes sickness of soul, when the proud mind, pressed by the hardness of obstinacy or dissolved by softness of delight, does no good [Col. 0104A]. Disobedience sometimes assumes for itself the name of obedience, so that it may glory in the name alone and not in the deed. But because “obedience” is spoken of in many ways, it is expedient that a fuller account of it be set forth.

For “obedience” is imposed in a command, a task, and a place: it indicates what is commanded, denotes what is done, and names the place in which one resides. With regard to a command, one says, “An obedience was imposed upon him”; with regard to a task, “He completed an obedience”; with regard to a place, “He resides at an obedience,” when he maintains some outlying house. The first is easy, the second difficult, and the third may be either. It is easy to command but difficult to fulfil; a place, however, sometimes pleases and sometimes displeases. An obedience pleases some, not so that they may exercise themselves in it in good works, nor because it abounds in brothers, but because it abounds in many feasts and varied delights [Col. 0104B]. An obedience pleases some, not so that they may serve God in it more diligently than in the cloister, but so that servants of various ages may give them more abundant attendance, and they may devote themselves more freely to idle tales and their own pleasures. This obedience pleases because, in the house, one man possesses everything alone, gives to others what he wishes, retains for himself what he wishes, and often prefers his own will to reason. Thus it happens that, in the case of a man who receives an obedience with a perverse will, it is called obedience when it is not. Many desire this obedience, not in order to obey God and their prelate with their whole mind, but in order that they may be able to be outside obedience [Col. 0104C]. Obedience is commonly sought by some in many ways: through the assistance of relatives, the counsel of brothers, or skill in pretence, so that what cannot be obtained through relatives’ threats or brothers’ exhortations may at least be secured through skill in pretence. This obedience, granted to someone through the threats of relatives or any form of pressure, through the deceitful exhortation of brothers, or even through a pretended display of good work, has the name of obedience but lacks the reality. It is called obedience outwardly, but inwardly it has no fruit of reward. Obedience of this sort is not acquired so that the body may be wearied in labours for God, but so that it may delight in the blandishments of the present life.

[Col. 0104D] One also arrives at this obedience by other means, so that what cannot be obtained by those three preceding means may be obtained by a promise of a gift. Thus Simon Magus still remains in the Church with Peter, and Ananias remains with Sapphira (Acts V). By Peter good prelates are understood; by Simon, Ananias, and Sapphira bad subjects are indicated. Simon wished to buy the grace of the Holy Spirit (Acts VIII); these men wish to buy an obedience. Simon wished to purchase with money the gift of the Holy Spirit; these men endeavour to acquire the Church’s revenues at a price. Therefore these men are not sons of the apostle Peter by teaching, but of Simon Magus [Col. 0105A] by avarice [Note: [Col. 0105D] From Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, ch. 12]. Each person is called the son of the one whose teaching he follows. From the originator of an error some derive both their name and their fault, so that they are designated by the very name of the man whose error they follow. Thus the Lord speaks through the prophet to Israel: “Thy father was an Amorite and thy mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI): certainly not by birth, but by imitation. Likewise, in the better sense, those who follow God’s commands with their whole mind are called sons of God. Therefore we too, not by nature but by adoption, cry to God in prayer, saying: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. VI). Therefore those who buy obediences or any ecclesiastical dignities for a price are rightly called sons of Simon the magician, not by nature but by imitation. Ananias and Sapphira concealed part of their property (Acts V); these men, however, engage in money-making business [Col. 0105B]. But as it is written: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in worldly business” (2 Tim. II). In this, then, it is clear that they do not serve Christ as soldiers but Mammon, because they pursue not spiritual riches but the profits of temporal life. They do not strive to please Jesus Christ, the heavenly king, but to become rich in temporal things. Avarice, which is the service of idols, reigns more in their hearts than voluntary poverty, which brings a man into the kingdom of heaven. Such men take greater delight in riding and hurrying through the streets of the city than in reciting psalms quietly in the cloister. This is obedience full of simony, avarice, and empty glory; it does not raise its lover to eternal joys but casts him down into Tartarus.

[Col. 0105C] There is another sort of obedience which is called obedience only. Of it it is said: “Because thou hast obeyed the voice of thy wife and eaten of the tree, cursed is the earth in thy work” (Gen. III). There are four voices: those of wife, world, devil, and God. “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. LXXXIV). Will the devil speak? Will the flesh? Will the world? The wife’s voice is the voice of the flesh; the voice of the flesh is pleasure; the voice of the world is vanity; the voice of God is goodness [Note: [Col. 0106D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 4]. We understand the devil’s suggestion as the serpent. The woman, however, is the sense of the animate body, that is, of the flesh, which we share with beasts and which is called the lower part of reason. [Col. 0105D] Therefore, when a suggestion of sin comes before us, it is as though the serpent speaks. But if the flesh takes delight in consenting to that perverse suggestion, it is as though the woman consents. If, however, the perverse suggestion is checked and cast out of thought, it is as though the woman alone eats the forbidden tree. But if the very sin which the serpent—that is, the devil—suggests, and which the flesh, that is, the lower part of reason, namely the woman, eats by taking delight in it, is also consented to by the human mind—that is, the higher part of reason—for its perpetration, then it is as though the man has been deceived. The woman has now given food to the man when the rational mind has granted consent to sin through the pleasures of the flesh. Therefore whoever [Col. 0106A] willingly hears the serpent’s voice—that is, the devil’s suggestion—and obeys the woman’s voice, namely the delight of his own flesh, immediately becomes disobedient to the voice of the Creator. Thus they obey the voice of the wife who do not resist fleshly pleasures and obey the pleasure of the flesh more than the voice of God. But the Creator’s voice says of prelates to subjects: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). He indicates that you should obey perverse prelates, since he commanded obedience even to those who act badly (1 Pet. II), so that with David you may go in and go out under Saul, and, with Samuel, honour the same man though rejected. Therefore prelates must be obeyed if they command what is right, even though they themselves live badly. Those who do not obey or venerate prelates, though they are perverse, thus show themselves to be disobedient and proud [Col. 0106B]. Hear also briefly what you ought to do and how you ought to obey prelates, whether good or bad. Do not obey good prelates in evil commands, nor oppose bad ones in good matters. Be obedient to bad prelates in good commands, and take care not to obey good ones in evil orders.

Meanwhile, dearest brothers, recall to mind the teaching of the apostle Paul, so that you may understand more perfectly the power of obedience. For he says: “Whatever things are ordained are ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13). He therefore resists God’s ordinance who despises the commands of his superior. [Col. 0106C] Whoever contradicts a prelate of the Church when he gives fitting commands proves rebellious and disobedient not only to man but also to God. Dathan and Abiram perished for this reason: they were disobedient to their superiors, namely Moses and Aaron, when in their obstinacy they usurped for themselves the right to offer sacrifice (Num. 16). Hence it is written in the book of Psalms: “The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram” (Ps. 105). For because of the audacity of their rashness, when the joints of the earth were broken apart, they were plunged alive into the deep abyss and delivered to the punishments of hell. Was not King Saul likewise rejected by the Lord because of the fault of disobedience, expelled from his royal throne, made subject to Satan’s dominion, and finally slain by the Philistines? [Col. 0106D] Consider, therefore, most beloved brothers, how grave is the fault of disobedience, for which not only souls are tormented in hell, but bodies too are punished in this present age. Reflect how grave a sin it is to resist God’s ordinance, for which punishment is exacted not only in the soul but also in the body. Let rebels therefore hear; let those disobedient to the commands of their elders fear, lest they be delivered with Dathan and Abiram to the torments of hell. Let them beware of following the footsteps of the seditious Korah, lest perhaps they be plunged with him into the depths of hell. Let them not wish to imitate seditious Korah, who through obstinacy and rebellion hurled many with himself into hell; but let them follow Christ, who, through humility, “obedient to God the Father [Col. 0107A] unto death” (Phil. 2), daily draws many after himself to the kingdom (John 12). Therefore, brothers and my lords, fear Christ; love him above all things; and show reverence for his ordinances. For he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14). Let love for him, then, appear in your deeds. Following his example, preserve humility in your manner of life; and, for love of him, be obedient to your superiors. Gladly obey the commands of your superiors in this life, that you may attain eternal freedom.

[Col. 0108A] Therefore submissively place your necks beneath the divine dispensation; renounce your own desires; prefer the will of your superior to your own wills; strive to fulfil his commands without murmuring, so that after this life you may reach the heavenly homeland and there rejoice eternally in the vision of God the Father: through him who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Sixth Sermon: On Discipline

[Col. 0107]

[Col. 0107B] Hear, dearest brothers, what our Lord Jesus Christ says in the Apocalypse for the instruction and consolation of his whole Church: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3). By these words he exhorts us, like a most loving Father, to endurance and discipline, that we may patiently bear with all gentleness everything commanded us either by him himself or by our superiors. For our sins and negligences the Lord rebukes and chastises us in this present age, both directly and through the ministers of holy Church, lest we be condemned with this world—that is, with the lovers of the world—in the age to come.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] From the book *On the Twelve Degrees of Abuse*, degree 11, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. VI.]

Whoever does not submit to God through the exercises of discipline will not be able to escape God without the severity of discipline. Therefore the Psalmist, counselling those who live undisciplined [Col. 0107C] lives, says: “Lay hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2). But what is discipline? Discipline is the ordered correction of conduct and the observance of the rule of one’s predecessors and elders. Of this discipline the apostle Paul speaks thus: “Persevere in discipline. God offers himself to you as to sons” (Heb. 12). “But if you are without discipline, of which all have become partakers, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.” Therefore those without discipline are illegitimate children and do not receive the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. But sons gladly endure the correction of paternal discipline, and do not despair of receiving entirely the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. Isaiah also preaches to the undisciplined people concerning this discipline, saying: “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. 1).

[Col. 0107D] And the Psalmist continues the same teaching, saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36). Hence Solomon also says: “He greatly errs who rejects discipline” (Wis. 3). Unhappy, therefore, is the person who rejects the discipline of a father—that is, the ordering of the Church. Just as the soldiers who crucified Christ did not divide his tunic (John 19), so we ought not to tear or divide the discipline of Christ’s Church.

[Col. 0108B] For just as the tunic covers the whole body except the head, so discipline adorns and covers the whole Church except Christ, who handed down that same discipline. That tunic, moreover, is described as woven from above throughout, because this same discipline of the Church is bestowed and made whole by the Lord from heaven. Of it the Lord spoke to his disciples after he had risen from the dead and before he ascended to the Father: “But remain here in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24). Therefore the tunic of Christ’s body is the discipline of the Church. But whoever is outside discipline is alienated from Christ’s body. Let us not, then, tear Christ’s tunic; rather, let us cast lots for it—that is, let us strive with all earnestness to preserve it whole,

[Col. 0108C] lest we remain deprived of a share in its wholeness. Let no one set aside anything from Christ’s commands; rather, let each remain with God in that condition in which he was called.

Whoever despises the discipline of Christ and of the catholic priests whom he himself has placed over his Church, while travelling along the various paths of error, falls into the snare of perdition. Hence, under the person of a transgressing people, the prophet laments the human race thus: “We have gone astray like sheep; each has turned aside into his own way” (Isa. 53).

[Note: [Col. 0108D] Ibid., degree 12.]

Of those also who reject the Lord’s discipline and follow their own will, Wisdom speaks through Solomon in this way: “Many ways seem right to human beings, but their end leads to death” (Prov. 14).

[Col. 0108D] These many paths of destruction surely follow when the one royal way—the law of God, which turns neither to the right nor to the left—is abandoned through negligence. Of this way, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is “the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10), declares: “I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). He invites all people together to this way, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11), because “there is no respect of persons with God” (Deut. 10).

[Col. 0109A] “Where there is neither Jew nor Greek, male nor female” (Gal. 3), slave nor free, barbarian nor Scythian, “but Christ is all things and in all” (Col. 3). Therefore all are one in Christ Jesus. Since Christ, then, is the end of the law (Rom. 10), those who are without law—that is, without discipline—become without Christ. Whoever is without instruction, therefore, does not follow Christ’s footsteps. It is unfitting and a departure from justice that, in the age of the Gospel, servants of God should become without Christ, when the apostles were granted authority to preach among all nations (Matt. 28); when the thunderclap—that is, the voice of the Gospel—resounded through every region of the world; when the nations attained the righteousness that they had not pursued (Rom. 9); when those who were far off became near in Christ’s blood (Eph. 2); when those once not a people are now a holy people in Christ (Hos. 2); when it is the acceptable time and the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6), and the times of refreshing in the presence of the Most High (Acts 3).

[Col. 0109B] When every nation has a witness of the resurrection, as the Lord testifies to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Let us therefore do nothing without Christ, lest Christ begin to be without us in the age to come.

[Col. 0109C] It is fitting, therefore, beloved, that we receive Christ’s discipline with every devotion and that we be obedient to our superiors for Christ’s sake. Discipline is truly necessary for adolescents and young people, so that they may submit to their elders’ commands with all humility and reverence. Thus in the Old Testament the Lord commanded the Levites to serve the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year and ordered them, from their fiftieth, to become guardians of the vessels (Num. 8).

[Note: [Col. 0109] From Gregory, *Moralia*, book 23, no. 21.]

For what is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth arises, except the very conflicts of vices against each person? And what is expressed by the fiftieth year, in which the repose of jubilee is contained, except the inward peace of a mind that has subdued its passions? And what do the vessels of the tabernacle signify

[Col. 0109D] but the souls of the faithful? Thus Levites serve the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year and become guardians of the vessels in their fiftieth, so that those who still endure the contests of assailing vices may not presume to take responsibility for others, but may strive to remain under the discipline of their elders. But when they subdue the battles of temptations, when they are already secure within themselves in deepest tranquillity, then, as persons trained in spiritual warfare, they undertake the guardianship of souls. Yet who can perfectly subdue these battles, when Paul—the most learned and valiant fighter—says: “I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin” (Rom. 7)?

[Col. 0110A] But it is one thing to endure battles bravely, another to be feebly overcome and laxly defeated by them.

In these strongest battles, therefore, the virtue of the young is exercised, lest it become exalted; but in the weak and lax such virtue is utterly extinguished, lest it endure. It is good, therefore, for adolescents and young people, while the heat of nature is burgeoning in their limbs and the vigour of age increases in their bodies, to serve the commands of their superiors with all humility.

[Note: [Col. 0109] From the aforementioned book *On the Twelve Degrees of Abuse*, degree 3.]

For how does one who refuses to render obedience to elders in adolescence hope that others will minister to him in old age? How can one who, in youth, refuses to be subject to the discipline of elders suppose that, when he has reached old age,

[Col. 0110B] reverence will be shown him by the younger? Thus there is among the ancients a proverb: those who previously denied service to someone do not wish to serve another. For this reason the Lord Jesus Christ, during the years of adolescence, while he had not yet reached the lawful age of a teacher, obediently rendered service to his parents. Indeed, in his youthful age he paid honour, reverence, and service to his parents in order to give young people an example of obedience and service (Luke 2). Therefore, just as sobriety and perfection of conduct are required in elders, so service, subjection, and obedience are rightly due from adolescents. Consequently, among the commands

[Col. 0110C] of the law, the first of those concerning human relations commands honour for father and mother (Exod. 20), because, even if a natural father is not living or is unworthy, the text shows that filial honour must nevertheless be rendered to some living father-figure until one reaches a mature and worthy age. Accordingly, until children reach lawful age, they are commanded to live under the discipline of their father or of some outsider, because no one who is undisciplined and untaught can possibly be a disciple of Christ.

For in the divine Scriptures fathers are called by five modes: namely, by nature, nation, admonition, age, and adoption. Jacob spoke of a father by nature to Laban: “Unless the fear of my father Isaac had been with me, you would have taken everything that was mine” (Gen.

[Col. 0110D] 31). A father is named by nation when the Lord spoke to Moses from the bush: “I am,” he says, “the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3). A person is called father by age and admonition when Moses speaks in the song of Deuteronomy: “Ask your father and he will tell you; your elders and they will speak to you” (Deut. 32). We call a father by adoption when, in prayer, we say: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6). Therefore, if one’s natural father is not alive or proves unworthy, adolescents must nevertheless render obedience to an elder who gives admonition.

[Col. 0111A] For how will one appear worthy of honour in old age who has not borne the labour of discipline in adolescence? “Whatever a person labours for, that also shall he reap” (Gal. 6). For all discipline at present seems not to bring joy but sorrow, not rest but labour; “but afterwards it yields the most peaceable fruit of righteousness to those exercised by it” (Heb. 12). Just as fruit is not found on a tree in which leaf or flower has not first appeared, so one who has not laboured in adolescence in the discipline of some good exercise will not be able lawfully to attain honour in old age. How, then, can discipline exist without obedience? An adolescent without obedience is an adolescent without discipline. Why? Because obedience itself,

[Col. 0111B] the mother and perfection of all virtues, requires great exercise, that it may show Christ the Lord the measure of its endeavour—he who, obedient to the Father unto death, willingly endured the disgrace of the cross for all his people (Phil. 2).

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 41.]

Yet the discipline of catholic teachers must be moderated, lest by excessive cruelty it wound those whom it ought to heal and make whole.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] From Gregory, book 24, no. 40.]

Proud teachers know rather how to wound than how to amend, as Solomon testifies: “In the mouth of the fool is the rod of pride” (Prov. 14).

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Isidore, as above, chapter 40.]

Truly, proud teachers bear in their mouth the rod of pride, because they strike harshly in rebuking and do not know how to show humble and merciful compassion. Angry teachers also, through the rage of wrath, transform the measure of discipline into the savagery of cruelty,

[Col. 0111C] and where they could amend, there they rather wound. Therefore an angry superior takes vengeance upon faults without measure, because his heart, scattered among worldly concerns, is not gathered into love of the one dignity. A mind unbound amid diverse things is not held fast by the chain of charity; but, badly loosened, it is badly moved at every occasion.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Ibid., chapter 46.]

Every superior must therefore observe very carefully that he acts toward those entrusted to him with greater caution in proportion as he fears to be judged more severely by Christ on their account. For, as it is written: “With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured to you” (Matt. 7).

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Ibid., chapter 24.]

Whoever is appointed to governance ought so to conduct himself in disciplining his subjects that he shines not only in authority but also

[Col. 0111D] in humility.
