Yet the virtue of humility must be present in him in such a way that the lives of his subjects do not dissolve into vices; and the authority of power must be present in such a way that severity does not become the swelling of immoderation through pride of heart. This, therefore, is true discernment in God’s priests: that they be neither proud through licence nor lax through humility.

[Note: [Col. 0112D] Ibid., chapter 42.]

It must also be known that one and the same teaching is not to be applied to all subjects; rather,

[Col. 0112A] the exhortation of teachers must vary according to the character of their conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0112D] Ibid., chapter 45.]

Open sins are not to be purged by secret correction. Those who do harm openly must be rebuked openly, so that when they are healed by public reproof, those who had sinned by imitating them may be corrected. When one person is rebuked, many are amended. For it is more useful that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through one person’s licence or example of depravity. A word should thus be spoken to an offender as the salvation of the one rebuked requires. For harsh rebuke corrects some, while gentle rebuke corrects others. Hence blessed Ambrose, a man of great reverence and outstanding conduct in Christ’s Church, says: “One chastised gently shows reverence to the chastiser;

[Col. 0112B] but one offended by the harshness of excessive rebuke receives neither the rebuke nor salvation.” So too blessed Isidore, that outstanding teacher, says:

[Note: [Col. 0112D] As above, chapter 43.]

“Just as skilled physicians treat various bodily diseases with different medicines, applying different remedies according to the character of wounds, so the teacher of the Church will apply to every individual the remedy of teaching suited to that person, and will declare what is fitting for each according to age, sex, and calling.

[Note: [Col. 0112D] Again from chapter 45.]

At times discerning teachers also strike their subjects with harsh rebukes, yet do not depart from love for those whom they rebuke. Often the Church’s censure seems proud to the arrogant, and what good persons do piously is thought by the wicked to be done cruelly, because they do not discern with a right eye what is done by the good with a right intention.”

[Note: [Col. 0112D] Ibid., from chapter 32.]

Moreover, some perverse people offer this excuse: when they are rebuked for their crimes, they reject the words of just superiors in order to avoid censure, reserving themselves for divine judgment, by which they are to be punished more severely because they despise being judged temporarily by human beings. Truth is burdensome to the wicked, and the discipline of justice bitter; they delight only in what pleases their own weakness—unfruitful in justice and barren of truth, blind to behold the light and sharp-eyed to see the error of darkness. You may see certain people of depravity [addition: *videas*, “you may see”] who, while neglecting to be corrected themselves from evil, disparage their corrector by false accusation and, as consolation for their own crime, seize upon anything they discover—even falsely—that they may cast against the good as a reproach.

[Col. 0112D] Hence one reads in Solomon: “The wicked man turns good into evil and lays a stain upon the elect” (Ecclus. 11). Many wicked people also defend those like themselves in evil and, by their patronage, take up the cause of the depraved against the correction of the good, lest they be amended in that for which they are displeasing. They add to themselves others’ offences, so that they may be condemned not only for their own evils but also for the crimes of those whose sins they defend. Ecclesiastical discipline, therefore, ought to be moderate and discerning,

[Col. 0113A] so that it may correct the negligent, strengthen the weak, and provoke the good to emulate the better gifts.

Therefore I exhort you, brothers and my lords, gladly to receive the discipline of our Lord Jesus Christ which is communicated to you through your superiors; strive to fulfil their commands according to your strength; and hasten in all things to prefer their will to your own wills. Let none of you say: “Why should I receive my abbot’s discipline, when I am more learned than he and have greater understanding of the Scriptures?” Or: “Why should I be subject to my superior’s disciplines, when he is of the lowest birth whereas I am the son of a more powerful and stronger man?” Or: “Why should I fulfil his commands when he is more negligent in conduct,

[Col. 0113B] and I live more holily?” Do not say these things to yourselves, dearest brothers, for neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom avails anything in the underworld (Eccl. 9). Let no one exalt himself because he is the son of some magnate, since on the day of the strict judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ nobility of birth will not be able to assist him.

[Note: [Col. 0113] From the book *On Saving Precepts*, chapter 32, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. VI.]

Nor should anyone, because of holiness granted him by God, rise in pride against his superior, because fasts of many seasons, almsgiving, vigils, tears, prayers, and all other good things, if they end in pride, are reckoned as nothing before God. Therefore be humble, and receive your superior’s discipline with every devotion, because it is more profitable to be reproved or chastised by a just person than deceived or

[Col. 0113C] flattered by a sinner. Hence the Psalmist says: “The just man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but the oil of the sinner shall not make my head fat” (Ps. 140). The sinner’s oil is the praise of a flatterer.

[Col. 0114A] Thus the head is anointed with a sinner’s oil when the mind of the hearer delights in flattery. For in the divine Scriptures the mind stands for the head. Therefore gladly submit your backs to the lash, that you may escape the torments of hell. Let it not seem harsh to you to be scourged by an abbot’s hand, so that you may be counted among the martyrs in the heavenly court. Is it not better for you to be beaten temporarily with rods by a superior for faults and negligences than to suffer eternal torments in Gehenna? Is it not much better and more bearable humbly to endure an abbot’s sentence in this age than, through pride and obstinacy, to suffer in hell the penalty of eternal damnation with the devil and his angels? Therefore, beloved, hold fast and preserve the discipline of your shepherd, that with him

[Col. 0114B] you may be heirs of eternal blessedness. Show reverence to the one who chastises you; love the one who reproves you; return honour to the one who admonishes you; give thanks to the one who scourges you; render obedience to the one who urges good things; in all things obey the one who commands what is regular and pleasing to God. Do not return evil for good; do not oppose a blessing with a curse; do not answer preaching with abuse; do not dishonour one who rebukes you. In all things show yourselves as ministers and disciples of God. Despise earthly things; love heavenly things; diligently mourn for your sins and for those of the persons whose alms you eat; fear the punishments of hell; desire the joys of eternal life, so that, following Christ’s footsteps without stumbling, you may be able to reach the heavenly homeland with the abbot who presides over you:

[Col. 0114C] through him who, with the same Father and Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Seventh Sermon: How Young Men Should Flee Idleness

[Col. 0113]

[Col. 0113D] It is fitting, brothers and my lords, that we hear together what Isidore, teacher of Spain, says for our instruction—indeed, for that of the whole Church. God gave us his body, as I believe, so that we might devoutly receive his most wholesome teaching and hasten to fulfil it in good works. Therefore we ought reverently to hear his admonition as though he were living bodily among us. For he says:

[Note: [Col. 0113D] *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 8.]

“Just as by reading we desire to know what we do not know, so, knowing the right things that we have learned, we ought to fulfil them in action.” A vigorous reader will be readier to fulfil in action what he has read than to learn what he does not know.

[Col. 0114D] God’s law has both reward and punishment for those who read it. It has reward for those who preserve it by living well, but punishment for those who despise it by living badly.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] These matters are from book 2, chapter 1.]

It adds to the accumulation of greater guilt for someone to know what he ought to follow and to refuse to follow what he knows. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12). And James says: “To one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4).

[Note: [Col. 0114D] Again from book 3, chapter 19.]

Therefore a servant of God ought without interruption to read, pray, and work, lest the spirit of fornication creep upon a mind devoted to idleness and provoke it to sin. Lust quickly takes possession of

[Col. 0115A] the person whom it finds idle; but a body wearied by labour takes less delight in vice. “Observe King Solomon: through idleness he was entangled in many fornications, and through the vice of fornication he fell even into idolatry” (3 Kings 11).

[Note: [Col. 0115D] From the same book, *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 7.]

“Therefore both things necessarily commend themselves greatly before God: activity must be supported by prayer, and prayer by activity. Hence Jeremiah also says: ‘Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God’ (Lam. 3). One lifts the heart with the hands who supports prayer with a good work. For whoever prays and does not work lifts the heart but does not lift the hands. But whoever works and does not pray lifts the hands to God but does not lift the heart. Since, however, both working and praying are necessary, it was well said with reference to both: ‘Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God.’”

[Col. 0115B] Therefore, dearest brothers, lest we be reproved in heart for neglect of the commandments while striving to obtain our salvation by prayer alone or by work alone, it is necessary that, after we perform a good work, tears of prayer be poured out, so that the humility of prayer may obtain the merit of a good action. Whoever therefore desires to please God in all his conduct should flee idleness; at one time he should give himself to prayer, and at another seek work useful to himself and others, because idleness increases folly while labour produces knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] These matters also are from Isidore’s *Sentences*, book 2, chapter 10.]

For this reason, in every good work, fraud and desires must be feared. We defraud God

[Col. 0115C] whenever we praise not God but ourselves for our good work. We act sluggishly whenever, through lethargy, we perform half-heartedly those things that belong to God. Every art of this world has energetic lovers, most ready to carry it out; and this is so because it has the immediate reward of its work. But the art of divine fear has many followers who are languid, lukewarm, frozen in the inactivity of sloth; and this is because their labour is deferred, not to a present reward but to a future one. Therefore, since recompense for their labour does not immediately follow, their hope relaxed, they almost grow faint in good work.

There is labour and idleness of the inward person, and there is labour and idleness of the outward person. The labour of the inward person

[Col. 0115D] is the labour of knowledge; the labour of the outward person is the exercise of action. The labour of knowledge is divided into three parts: the labour of discipline, of practice, and of teaching. In childhood there is the labour of discipline; in youth, the labour of practice; in old age, the labour of teaching. Thus the person who does not know may learn in childhood; the one who has learned may put it into use in youth; and what he has put into use he may teach in old age. There is another inward labour as well, namely that of thought and meditation, so that one may attain the repose of contemplation: whatever lies hidden and obscure under the cloud of doubt through forgetfulness may become clear in thought, clearer in meditation, and clearest in contemplation. For when memory offers the mind something concerning heavenly things,

[Col. 0116A] it is first seen in thought as though confused; afterwards it is distinguished by meditation; and finally it is recognized by contemplation. Thus thought is kindled by consideration, meditation is inflamed by discernment, and contemplation is illuminated by knowledge. Thought in the mind is like smoke in fire; meditation, like flame with smoke; contemplation, fire with flame and without smoke. But when the mind labours to consider heavenly things, thought is hindered by the occupation of temporal affairs; meditation, indeed, is disturbed by idleness; contemplation is recalled by curiosity. Thus it sometimes happens that an idle mind grows sluggish in pleasure and becomes subject to vices. Therefore, when the inward person lies in the bed of pleasure, grows torpid in the sleep of inertia, and is deluded by dreams of curiosity,

[Col. 0116B] he calls and exhorts the outward person to incline his ear to rumours, speak vanities, dress in soft garments, eat in the morning, and let the cock bring the reading to an end at supper. As they go off to sleep, let brothers rising for vigils meet them; while those brothers keep watch, let them sleep; and as the brothers return, let them rise. Yet perhaps it would be better if they said nothing than if, omitting syllables or words, they chanted the psalms. This is the sluggishness of idlers: they do nothing at the appointed hour, but always keep company with delay. They take greater pleasure in eating outside the community and rising late for the Hours. These are they who wait with the ass and do not ascend the mountain with Isaac: carrying straw and a goad, which belong to the ass,

[Col. 0116C] rather than fire and a sword, which belong to the sacrifice. For Abraham says to the servants: “Wait here with the ass. I and the boy, after we have worshipped, will return to you” (Gen. 22). The boys (*pueri*) are the childish faculties of the soul, and they wait with the ass because they always love slowness. The two *pueri* are said to be the idle and the lukewarm, carrying the goad of the flesh and the straw of frivolity. But Abraham—whose name is interpreted “father of many nations,” that is, the mind begetting many thoughts—ascends with the boy, that is, with a pure heart, carrying fire and sword in his hands. By fire we understand charity; by sword, the word of preaching. Therefore the person who carries fire and sword in his hands is one who fulfils in good works what he loves and preaches. “I,” he says, “and

[Col. 0116D] the boy will return to you.” Both must return: that is, the power of reason and purity of mind must return to undertake care of the flesh, not for its desires but for its necessities (Rom. 13). For the flesh always seeks an abundance of food and freedom for idleness. What is necessary, however, should be provided, not withheld. Yet lest it be idle while food is supplied, let those things suited to the ass follow, namely a rod and a burden (Ecclus. 33): the rod of correction and the burden of labour. Indeed, between the rod and the burden there is no place for idleness. Let the inward and outward person therefore labour, and let them apply themselves diligently to work, lest they be told: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” (Matt. 20).

[Col. 0117A] Those stand idle all day who, throughout the whole time of their life, cease from good works and persist in lethargy in the marketplace of vain glory. A community of brothers stands as though idle if the abbot does not invite them by preaching and admonition to labour—that is, to the practice of regular life. The people stand idle because neither bishop nor archdeacons hire them for good work. Yet let superiors hear the reason for this idleness: “No one,” they say, “has hired us” (ibid.). Bishops and priests do not hire the people; abbots and priors do not hire the community. To what, indeed, will they hire them? Perhaps to seek temporal honour and not spiritual labour. Perhaps they will more zealously hire them for the king’s court than for the Lord’s vineyard. There inquiry is more curious about the weight of money than about the measure

[Col. 0117B] of guilt. Their conversation arises from assaying silver, not from cleansing sin. Yet there are certain good superiors who hire labourers for work: they teach by word and lead by example. To this labour come persons of different kinds: boys, young men, and old men. They come at different ages and times, namely evening, morning, and midday. Boys come in the morning, young men at midday, old men in the evening; so to speak, Maurus comes in the morning, Paul at midday, Tranquillinus or Gentianus in the evening. Here we take “youth” broadly, including not merely adolescence but mature age as well. This is the age suited to labour, because no one will be able to work in the future life. “Night comes when no one can work” (John 9).

[Col. 0117C] At this age Paul, wishing to redeem the time, applied himself not only to contemplation but also to action.

Let us, if you please, bring forward the patriarch Issachar and take from him an example of exertion, perseverance, and perfection. Issachar, whose name is interpreted “wages,” refers to the people of the Gentiles, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] From Blessed Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 31.]

This Issachar is called a strong ass (Gen. 40), because previously the Gentile people was like a brutish and lustful animal serving idols. Truly it is now strong, submitting its neck to the yoke of the Lord Redeemer and bearing the burden of Gospel discipline. This Issachar, resting between the boundaries, “saw that rest was good and the land excellent; and he put his shoulder beneath the burden, and became a servant paying tribute” (ibid.).

[Col. 0117D] Therefore, beloved, we must pass from land to land: from a foreign land to our own land, from exile to homeland, from one nation to another, from a kingdom to another people, from the land of the dying to the land of the living, if we wish by experience to know true and inward joy.

We too should desire that land which this Issachar saw and desired. For if he had not seen it, he would not have known it; and if he had not known it, he would not have desired it (John 14). For the sake of this land, having become an ass and having become strong, he gladly put his shoulder under the burden, and became a servant paying tribute. He had suddenly become of very little account in his own eyes, since he considered himself an ass—that is, an animal almost more contemptible than all others. He greatly desired the land that he saw, for whose sake he endured every labor with strength. He saw indeed that, compared with the beauty of that land, all our righteousnesses were like the cloth of a menstruating woman (Isa. 64); nevertheless he saw that the sufferings of this present time are not comparable with the future glory that shall be revealed in us (Rom. 8). Thus, becoming lowly in one respect and strong in another, humbled by the one and strengthened by the other, he gladly bent the shoulder of his strength to every labor; and, in seeking divine glory rather than his own, he rendered to the true heavenly King the tribute due to him.

Do you wish to hear how another likewise became lowly in his own eyes, and yet grew strong for every labor? “I have become like a beast before you,” says David (Ps. 72). And elsewhere: “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Ps. 42). See how lowly he is; see how strong. Lowly as a beast, strong to mortify himself. Issachar, the strong ass dwelling between the boundaries, saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent. Therefore he had almost, though not wholly, grasped that land of the living, since he dwelt between the boundaries. Because he was content with the meanest and fewest goods of this life, he held the outermost edge of this wretched land. And because through frequent ecstasies of the mind he tasted beforehand the goods of everlasting life, he touched the beginnings of that blessed land. “I saw,” he says, “that rest was good.” Good rest, therefore, is there—that is, in the heavenly homeland—for if it were not there, he could never have seen it there; and if it were not good, he would never have put his shoulder under the burden for its sake.

“But the meek,” says the Prophet, “shall inherit the land and delight in an abundance of peace” (Ps. 36). See what kind of land it is: there are true rest and full peace; good rest, tranquil peace, peaceful repose. In that heavenly homeland there is no labor; yet no one can reach it without labor. For its sake one labors in this life, but in it labor is required from no one. Outside this land true rest is not found, because there is absolutely no toil in it. If, therefore, with Paul we desire to redeem the time and escape the evil days, we must often pray, work, and read in this present life (Eph. 5). Thus Jacob returns to his homeland with Rachel and Leah (Gen. 30); thus, through the prayers of Mary and Martha, Lazarus is helped unto life (John 11). Jacob returns with Rachel and Leah when someone advances with the desire of working well and is joined to the active and contemplative life. Lazarus, moreover, means “helped.” He is raised when a person is freed from the death of sin, on the one hand by good works and on the other by tears.

Therefore no one is excused from labor: not boys, not young men, not old men. Youth alone, however, bears the burden and heat of the day. Materially, it bears the burden of work and the heat of the sun. Morally, it bears the burden of fleshly frailty and endures the heat of lust. By the labor of the hands the burden of temptations is destroyed; by idleness the temptation of vices is multiplied. Through labor the flesh is afflicted; through idleness it is nourished. But a young man in idleness is like an untamed bullock without a yoke: since he is not held by the bond of obedience, he roams amid the equality of fraternal fellowship, as though with a wanton voice, through the desires of his own will.

I therefore urge you, dearest brothers, to deign to hear attentively what is said. In that good and excellent land—that is, in the heavenly homeland—there is no labor; yet no one can reach it without labor. Hence the saying: “Great rewards cannot be attained except through great labors.”  
[Note: Col. 0119B. Gregory, Homily 37 on the Gospels.]

And again: “He shall not be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2). The kingdom of heaven will not be given to the lukewarm, idle, and wandering, but to those trained in God’s service and diligently struggling against vices and temptations. Therefore raise the eyes of your mind toward that good and excellent land; for love of it despise everything that is in this world; and, that you may be able to acquire it as your inheritance, gladly put your shoulder under the burden of your order. Keep the commands of your prelates with your whole attention; and, that you may be able to attain that excellent land of the heavenly homeland, willingly submit your necks to the yoke of divine ordinance. Hold yourselves cheap for Christ’s love and show yourselves strong in God’s service. Despise present things; desire future goods; abhor fleshly things; love spiritual things; possess temporal things for necessity; desire eternal things for delight.

But a mind not yet wholly gathered toward eternal joy does not experience what true rest is. Woe is me, wretched that I am, for to this day I am a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth! A wanderer, by following desire; a fugitive, by avoiding misery. Desire makes me a wanderer; misery makes me a fugitive. This land is undoubtedly not stability of heart, but hardness and insensibility of mind. O happy person who has been able, even for an hour, to forget all evils and to possess, if only briefly, that inward peace or rest! Yet happier is the one to whom it is given to gather the dispersions of the heart into one and to fix desire in that fountain of true blessedness.

Let us therefore also pass over, beloved, with the patriarch Issachar in mind and deed: from the land of misery to the excellent land; from a foreign land to our own land; from exile to the homeland; from prison to the court; from unhappiness to glory; from captivity to freedom; from death to life; from darkness to light; from the theatre to the palace; from the workhouse to the kingdom; from the sewer to heaven; from the wallowing-place of vices to the fellowship of angels. May Jesus Christ deign to lead us there, he who with the same Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## EIGHTH SERMON. HOW OLD MEN AND YOUNG MEN OUGHT TO SERVE GOD

[Col. 0119]

[Col. 0119C] I urge you, dearest brothers, for the sake of your salvation, to deign attentively to hear the words of the most wise Solomon: “Grey hairs are the understanding of a human being, and an unstained life is old age” (Wis. 4). A man is therefore not truly called old because he is advanced in years, but because he is perfect in understanding. For old age is venerable not because it is long, nor because it is counted in a number of years (ibid.), but because life is innocent and pleasing to God. No one lacks childish age if he is little and frivolous in understanding. Hence the saying: “The child of a hundred years shall be accursed” (Isa. 65).  
[Note: Col. 0119D. From the book *On Salutary Instructions*, chapter 43.]

Although anyone may be young in years, if he is great in understanding he is to be counted not among the young but among the old. Thus it is written of Daniel: though young in age, he was old in knowledge and gentleness. David too, though a boy in age, was perfect in understanding: his heart and mind were fixed upon the Lord, and for this reason he was raised to be king. Saul, however, though he was of advanced age, because he possessed great wickedness and childish frivolity within himself, was expelled from the royal height. Our Lord and Savior is crucified by old men, but, entering Jerusalem, is praised by children. Likewise a tree many years old, if it is fruitless, is cut down; but if it is young and fruitful, it is cultivated so that it may produce still more abundant fruit.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we have set these comparisons before you so that none of you, whether young or old, may presume upon his own virtue or put confidence in his own works. Rather, he should always be fearful lest he displease God in some work, and always wary lest for some fault he be separated from him forever. What then? “Let him who glories glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1), and not in himself.

Yet it must be known that in some respects we ought to be children, and in others old men. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18). And the apostle Peter: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit” (1 Pet. 2). Paul likewise says: “Do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice, while in understanding be mature men” (1 Cor. 14).  
[Note: Col. 0120D. From the book *On the Twelve Degrees of Abuse*, degree 2.]

It is fitting for all people diligently to serve God and cleave to him by good works, but especially for old men, who already have their feet at the edge of the grave. Those whom the flower of the present age, now passed, is abandoning ought more than all others to give themselves to religion. For just as among trees that rejected tree is plainly seen which, after its blossoms, does not offer its cultivator excellent fruits, so among people he is rejected whom the flower of youth abandons and who nevertheless thinks little of producing ripe fruits of good works in the old age of his body.

What, then, could be more foolish or stupid than for the mind not to strive to hasten toward perfection when, its whole bodily condition worn out by old age, a person is hastening toward destruction? The eyes grow dim; the ears hear with difficulty or almost nothing; the hair falls out; the face changes to pallor; the fallen teeth diminish in number; the skin dries up and contracts in wrinkles; the breath no longer smells pleasant; the chest is oppressed; the cough burns and rattles; the knees tremble; swelling distends the ankles and feet. The inward person, who does not grow old, is weighed down by all these things; and all these swiftly announce the body’s house, now on the point of collapse. What then remains, except that, as the end of this life approaches, old men should think of nothing other than how they may obtain the blessings of entrance into the future life and escape the dangers of the soul? For the end of this life threatens the young uncertainly, but for every old person a more imminent departure from this light draws near.

Therefore a man must beware of two parts that do not grow old in his body and draw the whole person toward sin: namely, the heart and the tongue. For the heart never ceases to devise new thoughts, while the tongue eagerly speaks whatever it perceives the heart has devised. Let not the old man say: “I do not shed human blood; I do not burn my neighbors’ houses; I do not plunder another’s property.” For if he has not expelled superfluous and, what is worse, harmful thoughts from his heart, and has not set a guard upon his mouth, he will be guilty before Christ—the strict Judge—even for a single idle word. Let old age therefore beware lest these youthful parts, namely the unbridled tongue and the heart thinking useless and vain things, deceive the whole harmony of the person, mock the gravity of the rest of the body through foolish matters, and hand it over to the torments of Gehenna.

But the old man who is near death, who neither shrinks from nor fears the coming of death; who, as though stationed at this world’s door, looks on firmly and stubbornly, yet pays no heed to his departure from the present life or considers his entrance into the future one—such a man alienates himself from the company of the righteous. He hears death’s messengers and refuses to believe them. There are three messengers of death: accident, illness, and old age. Accident announces doubtful things; illness, grave things; old age, certain things. Accident announces hidden death; illness, visible death; old age, present death.

From the uncertainty of death, fear ought to follow; from the severity of illness, pain; from the certainty of old age, not stubbornness but humility and affliction. Yet perhaps the threefold cord by which an old man is bound is not easily broken (Eccl. 4). The threefold cord is the practice of a wicked habit, formed from three things, when among idle people thought is joined to speech and speech to action. For when from childhood pleasure has made a path in an old man’s mind through thought, vanity through speech, and perversity through action, what else happens but that these three are twisted into a habit? The snare in the cord is temporal sweetness in habit; the encircling of the cord is the hindrances of the flesh. Thus we are deceived by the sweetness of temporal things and bound by habit. But he had escaped the snare who said of himself and his companions: “Our soul has been delivered like a sparrow from the snare of hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. 123).

Absalom, clinging by his hair to an oak, signifies the hardness of anyone stubbornly set against good works. As he fled his father’s army, it happened that he became caught by his hair in a thick oak tree (2 Sam. 18). Absalom means “the father’s peace,” because his father endured him although he pursued him. He is not called “the son’s peace,” because he did not wish to endure his father. The oak is harder within, yet is found more fragile without. Absalom hangs clinging to it because inward obstinacy of mind is accompanied outwardly by frailty of flesh. He hangs by his hair because he is held fast by love of superfluity. But the mule on which he rode passed on, while he himself remained hanging, clinging to the oak; for both the luxury and deceit to which he had always been enslaved passed away, but the penalty of sin remained. His heart is pierced by three spears: avarice, pride, and lust. Hence even to this day a great heap of stones is cast upon him, because he is weighed down forever by a multitude of sins or punishments. Nor is it surprising that there should be a great heap of stones, since through obstinacy he bore an unrepentant heart to the end.

There are also three kinds of stubborn persons: first, those who improve through correction; second, those who become worse through admonition; third, those who promise amendment but do not fulfill what they promise. King Manasseh became better through correction (2 Chron. 33); Nabal became worse through admonition (1 Sam. 25); Pharaoh became harder through affliction (Exod. 7). Manasseh, put in prison and bound with chains and fetters, came to know God, whom formerly, when free, he had refused to know. Such are certain religious living in cloisters who, so long as they are their own masters, live perversely. But when they are held in the cloister like prisoners, bound with chains—that is, of obedience and fear—and fetters are added, because they are not allowed to wander about or go outside, it sometimes happens that, corrected, they love the God whom they had formerly despised. Having made servitude out of freedom, they make virtue out of necessity. Thus those whom their own freedom had made perverse are rendered devout by the correction of another’s authority.

Nabal, however, signifies certain teachers who become worse through the admonition of their subjects. They deny food to David’s young men because they do not offer God’s word to those who wish to live purely. But they prepare a feast for their shearers because they love the flattering conversations of those at leisure in idleness. Nabal accuses David and says: “Today the servants who flee from their masters have increased” (1 Sam. 25). Perversely disposed prelates indeed are grieved when they see the number of religious persons multiplying. They fear when they see David—that is, good subjects—anointed king, and Saul—that is, perverse prelates—deprived of the honor of prelacy. But why do they fear? Plainly, lest they too be deprived of their honors, lest someone better be appointed in their place.

And Abigail told Nabal all the words she had heard from David, “and his heart died within him, and he became like a stone” (ibid.), when someone is hardened unto eternal death. After Nabal’s death, Abigail is made queen, because one who has lived well under a perverse master may be raised to the governance of souls, so that he may obtain a temporal kingdom with David and reign eternally with Christ. For David sent messengers to Abigail, and she followed them. Abigail follows David’s messengers whenever any faithful person imitates the teachers of the Church in life and conduct. And five maiden attendants went with her. Her five attendants are the five bodily senses, which, like maiden servants, walk with Abigail when, through the purity of continence, they obediently serve every righteous person.

Pharaoh, who promised Moses that he would release God’s people yet did not release them, signifies those who promise amendment to a better life but neither abandon sin nor seek contrition in the spirit of a dove; rather, with the voice of a raven they seek delay. Their land is afflicted with diverse plagues and is not softened, but is hardened more and more through the habit of sinning. For the Lord then turns waters into blood when someone judges the causes of things carnally. The earth produces frogs when empty talk rules in a babbler. The dog-fly and gnats are assaults upon the harbor of the mind and dog-like habits. The death of cattle signifies the death of thoughts, which are commonly compared to cattle when they lack rational understanding; as it is written: “Man, being compared with senseless beasts, has become like them” (Ps. 48). The sixth plague occurs when blisters swell and the inner parts are corrupted; this happens when the inward parts of the mind swell with hatred and boil over with anger. The plague of hail in the crops signifies manifest wickedness in works. The plague of locusts is the instability of the soul, which wounds with its mouth when it slanders and leaps when it extends itself toward fleshly affections. The plague of darkness signifies the blindness of souls; it is proved tangible when the perverse things the mind thinks are perpetrated in action. For that is tangible which can be touched by the hand. Observe that the plague of locusts is placed between the plague of hail and the plague of darkness. From the wickedness signified by hail there comes, as it were, a locust’s leap into the blindness of eternal damnation. The final plague is the death of the firstborn. Morally understood, the firstborn of the mind are the will and intention of every person acting. When will and intention are corrupted, they are struck with death, as though they were the firstborn of the Egyptians.

By these plagues the obstinacy of the old man is afflicted: he delights in carnal things, rejoices in talkativeness, is troublesome and burdensome to everyone, is prone to vices after the fashion of cattle, swells with anger, is openly bent on injury, is changeable in everything, lacks the light of truth, and therefore gropes at himself.

Again, beloved, in compassion for the obstinate old man I return to speak to you. The old man who is invited to good work in the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hour—that is, in childhood, adolescence, youth, and old age—and scorns to come, what does he await except the night of eternal damnation, in which he will no longer be able to do any good? The old man who has stood idle all day and refused for God to bear the burden and heat of the day—what does he await except to be handed over shortly to everlasting punishments to be tormented? Hence the most blessed John the Baptist says: “Already the axe has been placed at the roots of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3). The fruitless tree is cut down and handed over to fire when the fruitless old man, obstinate against good works, is cut down by death and assigned to the fires of Gehenna.

How can the person who, having heard and scorned the voice of the Lord inviting him, despises coming to him through the practice of good works, believe that he will enter the marriage feast of the eternal King? All people ought indeed to persist in good works, and especially old men, whom it is certain that death’s compulsion will more swiftly remove from this life. An old man given to frivolity and unlawful acts will have to render an account not only of his own crimes but also of the sins of others, to whom throughout his life he furnished examples of evil living.

It is therefore necessary that the negligent old man, though late, return to himself, break the threefold cord by which he is tightly bound—that is, overcome evil habit—and rescue his soul from the snare of hunters by living well. Moreover, let him submit himself with all devotion to the discipline of the Church, not hypocritically, nor with the raven’s cry, “Tomorrow, tomorrow”—that is, by promising delay—but with the dove’s groaning: that is, in humility, by amending the evils he has done. Let him shear the hair of his head—that is, cast away the love of frivolity and superfluity—lest, by clinging to the oak, that is, to hardness and avarice of mind, he perish while hanging: that is, empty of good works, he perish from the fellowship of God’s elect.

Hear then, whoever you are, useless and fruitless old man: hear what I say, listen to what I speak, heed what I warn. Stop now increasing your sins and put an end to your crimes. It is now time for you to return to yourself and recognize what you are, why you were born, and for what purpose you were brought into the world. Did almighty God create you in this life so that you might spend your whole lifetime idly, rather than so that you might know him, serve him faithfully, and at last reign with him in heaven? Why then, by living perversely, do you depart from him who created you and all things from nothing, and expose yourself to the flames of Gehenna? Run, therefore, wretch, while you can, lest, if you refuse while you can, perhaps when you wish to do so you will no longer be able.  
[Note: Col. 0125D. *Book III of Sentences*, chapter 18.]

God is always ready to forgive our sins if we are converted to him with our whole heart and entreat him with a humble and simple mind. Therefore, while he waits patiently, let us hasten to be converted to him by good works, lest, if we delay, we provoke him to anger. For he predestined some to punishment, while to others he granted a great benefit; yet he did this not unjustly, but by his deep counsel and judgment. Cain committed murder (Gen. 3), and Job, God’s friend, was wounded (Job 2), and Abel was killed by his brother (Gen. 3). Yet he did not permit Job to suffer torment longer; he did not give Ananias an opportunity for pardon (Acts 5); he did not abandon Paul when he was buffeted, but made him strong by his grace (2 Cor. 12); he did not receive Judas when he repented (Matt. 27); nor did he abandon Peter when he wept (Luke 22). Thus the pious and merciful Lord, by his deep judgment, separates vessels of wrath from vessels of mercy.

O that we might consider wretched Judas, once a vessel made complete, brought to destruction: he could not contain the new wine of the Holy Spirit, and, when he received it, immediately burst, because a vessel wholly broken is useful or suitable for nothing. I have therefore set these examples before you, O old man grown old in days—would that they were examples of good!—so that you may no longer delay in turning to God, but may as speedily as possible humbly submit yourself to the yoke of Christ’s service. Hasten, then, while you still can, while God grants you leave to live, lest he who did not spare the natural branches perhaps not spare you either if you delay (Rom. 11). Do now what you ought. Look daily upon the end of your life. Set the memory of your death before yourself. Resolve not to sin further; determine not to offend again; beware of repeating your faults. Set before yourself the future judgment; recall the everlasting fires of hell; set before yourself the dreadful punishments of Gehenna. Pray continually with tears; pray without ceasing; entreat God by day and night that he may mercifully forgive your crimes. Confess your sins with tears, and hope without doubt in God’s mercy. Put away injustice, and place your confidence of pardon in God’s goodness.

Again I want you to know, dearest brothers, that the Son of God deigned to die not only for old men but also for all whom he predestined to eternal life. It is fitting, therefore, for all boys, adolescents, young men, old men, and every age among the faithful, to know him with the Father and the Holy Spirit as the one true God; to love him with fear and fear him with love; to cleave to him in a pure and devout mind; and to render him such service as they are able, pleasing to him. Therefore follow his footsteps diligently, as far as possible, that you may be able to see him reigning at the right hand of his Father; through him who with the same Father and Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## NINTH SERMON. THAT MONKS OR CANONS SHOULD NOT PRESUME TO FREQUENT THE KING’S COURT

[Col. 0125]

[Col. 0125C] I ask and urge you, my brothers and lords, to listen more attentively to the words of Isidore, teacher of the Spanish lands.  
[Note: Col. 0125D. From the book *On Salutary Instructions*, chapter 56.]

“Different,” he says, “are the precepts given to faithful persons living a common life in this world, and those given to persons renouncing this world. All who live a common life in this world are told to manage all their affairs well and justly; but those renouncing the world are commanded to leave all their possessions for Christ. The former—that is, all the faithful—are bound by general precepts; the latter—that is, religious persons—transcend general precepts by living them more perfectly. The former are told not to seize another’s property; the latter, to leave behind what they possess. The former are commanded not to kill; the latter, to hate no one but to pour out prayers to the Lord for their enemies. It is permitted to the former lawfully to take wives; but to the latter it is unlawful even to think anything about the marital act. The former are commanded not to bear false witness against anyone; the latter, to set a guard upon their mouth. All the faithful alike are permitted to use worldly things well; religious persons are told, having renounced everything, to delight in living for God alone.”

It belongs to secular persons to run here and there through the streets of the city doing good; it belongs to religious persons to flee the sight of people and shut themselves up within the walls of the cloister.  
[Note: Col. 0125D. From the same work, book III, chapter 21.]

Those, therefore, who renounce the world out of the fear of God and yet entangle themselves in the cares of household affairs, separate themselves from divine love in proportion as they occupy themselves with worldly business. Those who strive both to obey earthly cares and to exercise themselves in divine offices cannot embrace both at once, because two cares cannot dwell together in the human breast, and it is difficult for one serving two masters to please both.  
[Note: Col. 0126D. Ibid., chapter 16.]

The person who, after renouncing the world, longs for the heavenly homeland with holy desires is raised up from this earthly preoccupation as if upon wings; he sees with sorrow where he has fallen, and he fixes his earnest attention with great joy on the place he has reached. But one who, turning away from the repose of contemplation, falls into the vices of this age, immediately groans if he returns to self-awareness; from the very difficulty of his labor he recognizes both how tranquil the things were that he lost and how confused are the things into which he fell. For what in this life is more laborious than to burn with earthly desires? Or what here is safer than to desire nothing of this world? Those who love this world are disturbed by its turbulent cares and anxieties; but those who hate and do not pursue it, enjoying the tranquillity of inward rest, begin already in some measure to possess here the repose of future peace which they behold elsewhere.

[Note: Col. 0127D. Again, Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 13.]

A monk is so called by Greek etymology because he is solitary. For Greek *monas* means “singleness” in Latin. If, then, *monachus* means “solitary” by its name, what is he doing in a crowd who is alone, and why does he move about amid the people?  
[Note: Col. 0127D. This is from the same author, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 16.]

There are several kinds of monks. The first kind is that of cenobites, whom we may call persons living in common. For a cenobium consists of many persons, after the pattern of those holy people who, in the time of the apostles at Jerusalem, having sold all their possessions and distributed them to the needy, lived in a holy fellowship of life, calling nothing their own; rather, all things were common to them, and they were one soul and one heart in the Lord (Acts 2, 4). By their institution and example monasteries took their beginnings under the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

The second kind is that of hermits, who, withdrawing far from people, are said to inhabit desert and desolate places, in imitation of Elijah and John the Baptist, who penetrated the retreats of the wilderness. The third kind is that of anchorites, who, having been perfected in cenobitic life, shut themselves up in cells, removed from human sight and rarely allowing anyone access to them; they live solely in contemplation and communion with the Lord.  
[Note: Col. 0128D. From the cited passage of the *Etymologies*.]

*Abba* is a Syriac name and means “father” in Latin, as Paul explained when writing to the Romans: “In whom we cry, Abba (Father)” (Rom. 8), using two languages in one word. For he says “father” with a Syriac term and then again calls the same person “father” in Latin. Greek *kanōn* means “rule” in Latin. Hence regular canons are so called: they are those who live religiously and in common in monasteries according to the rule established under the holy apostles.

Monks, therefore, and canons in particular renounce the world for Christ’s love, separate themselves from the turmoil of secular life, and devoutly confine themselves within the walls of the cloister,

> lest even a light hunger should happen to stain their life,

[Note: Col. 0128D. Hymn from the Common of Holy Monks.]

and humbly entrust themselves to the judgment and governance of their superiors. These monks and canons, fleeing the sight of people, despising the conversations of secular persons, rejecting riches and worldly pleasures, putting away even their relatives for Christ’s love, and diligently giving themselves day and night to prayer, reading, and divine contemplation, establish for themselves a wilderness as it were among human beings, so that they may more freely serve God purely and carefully in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

Yet there are certain monks and canons—something we cannot say without deep groaning—who, having renounced the world, live in monasteries under the habit of religion and yet refuse to keep themselves within the cloister walls; instead, they desire to frequent the courts of kings and princes.

Since we are about to say something about the courtly monk, I acknowledge that we should hold the same view concerning the courtly canon or convert. Although their dress differs, the effect of religion ought to be the same: they should seek to please not by garments but by good conduct. Therefore, when one says “courtly monk” or “courtly canon,” the added word indicates something frivolous. For unless a monk were given to frivolity, he would never expose himself to the conversations of kings. Those who love the company of secular persons, willingly intrude themselves into princes’ councils, and become privy to secrets may be called courtiers. If you know the perverse counsels of princes and become their intermediary, I fear that you may consent and incur a stain upon your soul.

The order of the cloister and the order of the court are different. The order of the cloister is tranquil; that of the court is tumultuous. In the cloister there is peaceful and health-giving life; in the court, turbulent and dangerous dwelling. The inhabitants of the cloister propitiate God by doing good; the inhabitants of the court provoke him to anger by doing unlawful things. In the court “you sit in ambush with the rich in secret places, that you may kill the innocent” (Ps. 9); in the cloister you hear: “I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not enter in with those who do iniquity” (Ps. 25). There you lie in wait in order to seize the poor: “to seize the poor when you draw him in” (Ps. 9); here you say: “I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked” (Ps. 25). There your right hand is filled with gifts; here you wash your hands among the innocent. There the goods of the poor are violently taken away; here they are freely offered by princes. There “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed” (Ps. 9); but here “the Lord blesses the righteous” (Ps. 5). If, therefore, you wish to be a courtly monk or canon, you praise what you ought not, defend what is not expedient, do what is unlawful, and say what is unbecoming.

Yet there are two courts of secular princes: those of certain princes who build churches, and those of certain princes who destroy them. Although the presence of religious men may be necessary at either, that of courtly monks is useless and dangerous. This is David’s court; that, Absalom’s. In both, however, the counsel of Hushai is necessary. I read that Ahithophel was once David’s counselor, but that he left him and remained with Absalom (2 Sam. 15). There is occasion, perhaps, for us to speak more fully of the example that has been introduced.

For there are two courts, that of David and that of Absalom. In each, however, the counsel of Hushai prevailed, not the counsel of Ahithophel. Hushai means “silence”; Ahithophel is interpreted “the ruin of a brother” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 17). “A man of tongue shall not be established upon the earth; evils shall seize the unjust man unto destruction” (Psalm 139 [140]). But if you love to see good days, “keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Psalm 33 [34]). This is the counsel of Hushai; that is Ahithophel’s. For the tongue dwells in moisture, and in that ruin of brothers. But in silence peace is nourished; David is preserved from death. As it is written, Hushai was David’s friend (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 15). But how did he love him? “I was struck dumb,” he says, “and humbled, and I kept silence even from good things” (Psalm 38 [39]). Thus [Col. 0129B] the righteous man loves the fruit of silence, so that he is silent even about certain good things. Thus he loves the counsel of Hushai: he sets a guard upon his mouth, speaking only by permission.

David sings a psalm concerning the words of Hushai (Psalm 7). The words of Hushai are words of silence; words of silence are words of mystery. There are, however, three silences: the silence of the mouth, tranquillity of mind, and the veil of mystery. The words of the first silence are distinct; those of the second, secret; the words of the third silence are the revelation of mystery. You know the history: observe the mystery; draw out the moral meaning. Absalom pursued David; Judas pursued Christ; the appetite of the flesh pursues the soul. Absalom burned with desire to reign. “Covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6): it is the head from which hangs the whole luxuriant growth of vices. This is the hair [Col. 0129C] which Absalom grew, which weighed him down, and which he cut only once a year; then he weighed his hair at two hundred shekels by the public weight (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 14).

Absalom is interpreted “the peace of the father”; he is also Judas the traitor. Hear the father’s peace: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he shall betray me” (Matthew 26). Hear the son’s peace: “Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him” (ibid.). With a kiss he promises peace and inflicts affliction. He grew his hair. But how? “He was a thief, and kept the money-box” (John 12). Yet he cut it once a year, when once he returned thirty pieces of silver and cast them into the Temple. He weighed his hair at two hundred shekels—a number belonging to the unclean—because, moved to repentance, he said: “I have sinned in betraying the righteous man” [Col. 0129D] (Matthew 27). Had he known the injustice of that weight—that is, the price of blood—he would not have run to the noose, but would have hastened humbly to the Lord’s cross.

But he weighed by the public weight, not by the weight of the sanctuary: he set down the talent of lead upon which the devil sits, not the light weight of mercy beneath which the Lord sets His hand. He set down the weight of despair, not of mercy: for he possessed the former and lacked the latter. And perhaps, because he was unwilling to show mercy, he hesitated to seek mercy’s pardon. Hear the sanctuary’s weight: “I have sinned; I made my offence known to you, and I did not conceal my injustice. I said: I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Psalm 31 [32]). O just weight, abounding in [Col. 0130A] mercy! He makes known his offence; he confesses his injustice; and the more his sin is uncovered by him, the more it is covered by God. Hear Cain’s public weight, for he said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve pardon for” (Genesis 3 [the reference appears erroneous; cf. Genesis 4:13]). He weighed his own wickedness more heavily than God’s mercy.

The appetite of the flesh, too, grows hair, because it produces an excess of thoughts. This hair weighs down the mind, while “the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 14 [probably Wisdom 9:15]). A man cuts it once a year and weighs his hair at two hundred shekels when, in the whole span of his life, he renounces his desires only once, and at the end denies fleshly desires. For only then is he stripped of what he possesses, when by the succession of final death he is separated from earthly things. [Col. 0130B] He weighs earth more heavily than heaven: he loves more to be in a house of clay than in the house not made by hands, which is in heaven; more in the transitory than in the eternal. And he does this by the public weight, not the sanctuary’s weight—that is, not for love of God, but from earthly desire.

Hear the sanctuary’s weight, namely Paul’s weight: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1). Hear the public weight: “Woe to those dwelling upon the earth” (Revelation 8)—not those who dwell there in body, but those who love it in heart; not those who reside bodily upon earth while in thought and longing they have their life in heaven, but those who are made drunk by the cup of earthly pleasure.

Therefore let a monk or canon who belongs to a court love the counsel of Hushai, namely the silence of the cloister; but let him reject [Col. 0130C] Ahithophel’s counsel, so that he may not love the business of princes or restlessly seek access to secular persons. Let him love the precepts of the Rule, through which he can obtain the gift of heavenly grace; and let him flee the rumours of the court and the froth of superfluous talk. Let him love the fellowship of humble brothers in the monastery more than that of proud knights in the king’s palace. Let it please him more to hear the praises of God with his fellow brothers in church than useless and idle conversations at the king’s court. It is more fitting for a canon or courtly monk to take part in the divine offices in the house of God than to mingle in secular affairs in the king’s house.

Jeremiah the prophet laments in a tearful voice over such canons and courtly monks—those who despise monasteries, thrust themselves improperly into secular crowds, and frequent the courts of princes and the streets of cities—saying: “How has the gold grown dark, how has its finest colour been changed! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations 4:1). By gold we understand religious men, separated from worldly clamour and practised in God’s service, who ought to illuminate the whole world through the wisdom and holiness granted them by God. To them the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5). Concerning their wisdom, too, which is signified by gold, Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Proverbs 21:20). Therefore they ought to be wise and holy, so that [Col. 0131A] by the word of preaching they may drive darkness from others’ hearts and, by the example of good conduct, show them the straight path to heaven.

Churchmen are rightly compared with gold. For as gold is more brilliant than all metals, so the order of clerics, through wisdom and discernment, is a light to all laypeople. Hence a certain wise man said: “As far as heaven is from earth, so far is the discernment of clerics from the discernment of laypeople.” Therefore the ecclesiastical order ought to shine before all believers with the splendour of holiness and give light through the preaching of evangelical teaching. Thus it is said: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

If, then, churchmen are the light of the world, as the Lord says, what [Col. 0131B] does Jeremiah mean by his preceding words: “How has the gold grown dark, its finest colour changed?” Undoubtedly the truthful prophet pronounced a true judgment concerning us and our times. What he understood spiritually would come to pass, we see fulfilled before us. Truly this prophecy is fulfilled in us today when our life is shown reprobate by lowly actions. The finest colour of gold is the habit of religious life. Thus gold has grown dark today when religious men, who ought to be an example of good works to others, become an example of depravity. The finest colour of gold is changed whenever the habit of holiness falls into contempt and disgrace. Without doubt the finest colour of gold—that is, the habit of religion—is changed when a wolf lies hidden beneath a sheep’s skin. The finest colour of gold—the habit of religious men—is likewise turned to contempt in the eyes of observers when perverse conduct is concealed inwardly but is not unknown outwardly to the people.

Most beloved brothers, do people despise us without cause? Not at all. They rightly despise us, because we are one thing within and another without. We conceal one thing inwardly and display another outwardly. Pride and empty glory are hidden within; humility is pretended without. The poison of hatred and discord lies hidden inside; the outward appearance of holiness and innocence is plainly visible. Within we conceal a will to possess riches; without we put on a show of voluntary poverty.

[Col. 0131D] It continues: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street.” The stones of the sanctuary are religious men founded upon the foundation of the Church. The stones [Col. 0132A] of the sanctuary, then, are scattered at the head of every street when churchmen wander abroad in pursuit of vain and useless things. And they are indeed scattered at the head of every street, because now they are found in the market-place, now in a city street, now at the king’s court. The stones—that is, churchmen—are scattered abroad when those who ought to remain within through pure prayer and divine contemplation go out with lovers of the world to fulfil the anxious cares of their own desire. Observe the phrase, “at the head of every street”: they have become the head of error, though they ought to have been a mirror of truth and an example of perfection.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since by God’s grace you have despised the world and chosen the monastery, I admonish you not to presume to frequent the king’s court except [Col. 0132B] when unavoidable necessity compels you. For love of God confine yourselves within the walls of the cloister. Read the books of Holy Scripture continually; devote yourselves unceasingly to prayer; keep silence at the appropriate time; apply yourselves to meditation and divine contemplation; and keep the closest watch, so that you may taste and see how sweet and pleasant the Lord is. Let vegetables in the refectory be sweeter to you than dishes of many foods at the king’s court. Let it be more delightful for you to inspect books on diverse subjects in the cloister than, in the palace, dogs of various breeds and hawks borne on the hands of knights of different ages. Let the consolations of brothers in the house of the Lord be more lovable to you than the greetings of princes [Col. 0132C] before the people.

Yet if you truly seek to be courtiers, hasten with the highest desire to the court of the supreme King. If you truly delight to behold soldiers of great nobility, strive by the steps of good works to reach the palace of the eternal Emperor, where the entire host of heaven serves that Emperor without end. Therefore, beloved, shake every gift from your hands; hedge your ears about with the thorns of the fear of God; set a guard upon your mouth; with all diligence cleanse the eyes of your heart from anger, envy, hatred, and every evil will, so that after this life you may reach your heavenly homeland and behold the King of all saints Himself reigning in His splendour. May He deign, in His freely bestowed goodness, to grant this—He who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity [Col. 0132D] through all ages of ages. Amen.

## TENTH SERMON. THAT MONKS OR CANONS SHOULD NOT DESIRE TO KNOW THE SECRETS OF PRINCES.

[Col. 0131]

[Col. 0131D] I admonish you, dearest brothers, to hear diligently the words of our Lord Jesus Christ. For He says: “He who serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also shall my servant be” (John 12:26). It is indeed fitting [Col. 0132D] and very necessary to follow Christ and serve Him, because He brings His followers and servants all the way to Himself. What, then, could be worthier or happier than to follow Christ with all devotion—Christ who knows how to reward His servants so nobly in the presence of Himself and God the Father? [Note: [Col. 0133D] From the book *On Salutary Teachings*, chapter 8.]

What glory or happiness, I ask, could be greater for us than to be servants and friends of that Emperor who is above all emperors and crowns His soldiers with unfading crowns? The greater our Emperor is in omnipotence and power, the greater should be our diligence and observance of His commands in holiness, justice, and humility. [Note: [Col. 0133D] Ibid., chapter 9.] Let us therefore recognize and consider with every care the honour with which His embassy ought to be received by us. If an embassy came to us from a king, or a seal or a written notice, would we not immediately, setting aside other concerns, receive the letters eagerly and with all devotion, [Col. 0133B] and, having read them, strive to carry them out?

And behold: the King of kings and Lord of lords—indeed, our Redeemer—has deigned to send us His letters from heaven through the prophets and apostles, not because He sought from us any service necessary to Himself, but in order to make known those things which can benefit us for salvation and glory. Nor did He choose to be content with this alone. Rather, what is more wonderful and merciful, He deigned to come to us Himself and to show us the straight way by which we may reach Him. It is fitting, therefore, that we follow Him with our whole mind by the steps of good works and serve Him with all devotion; for if we refuse to do this, we shall be in peril before His strict judgment.

But what is it to serve Christ? It is to persevere without deceit in good works for love of Him. Yet perhaps someone asks: “How do we deal deceitfully with Christ?” Whoever says this should listen carefully to what blessed Isidore says: [Note: [Col. 0134D] Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 10.] “We deal deceitfully with God when we praise, not God, but ourselves for good works.” Some likewise practise deceit against Christ when they glory inwardly in the merits of chastity and abstinence. For one who gives alms for the sake of empty glory commits deceit. So also the person who is arrogant because of wisdom; who seeks a reward for justice; or who turns any gift of God that he has deserved to his own praise or employs it for evil uses—without doubt, he deals deceitfully with Christ. Those who transform such virtues into [Col. 0133D] vices do not serve Christ, because for good works they desire to gain human temporal praise more than eternal reward from Christ. Such servants are not rewarded by Christ but condemned, because they perform their good works, not for Him, but for temporal praise. To them He Himself will say at the judgment: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know where you are from” (Luke 13:27).

Therefore let the children of the Church strive to serve Christ without deceit or pretence, not for the vain glory of men but for eternal blessedness. Let them flee honour from men sought for empty glory. [Col. 0134A] Let them separate themselves from the company of secular people and apply themselves devoutly to reading and prayer in God’s house.

Yet there are some—though it cannot be said without deep grief—who, after renouncing the world, love temporal things more than eternal, fleshly things more than spiritual, the conversations of the wealthy more than the chanting of psalms, and riding out to look upon secular affairs more than sitting in the cloister to read. It also sometimes happens that monks or canons who frequent courts hear cases and investigate legal disputes, so that if at any time the necessities of their own cases arise, they may resort to court with greater confidence. Such men now defend not only their own causes but also those of others. Because they love these things, they frequent them. They love decrees of councils, [Col. 0134B] not the secrets of mysteries; they do not recite psalms but chew over decrees. They become advocates in lawsuits and employ rhetorical embellishments. They seek praise because they speak for many; but a monk or canon who speaks much displeases many.

They arrange unlawful marriages, and sometimes dissolve lawful ones. Often they name as ancestors fathers and great-grandfathers whom they do not know, recount degrees of kinship, affirm that this man descended from that one, decide upon uncertainties, and very often testify to what they do not know. If, indeed, they sometimes join unlawful marriages, they put forward the common good as their pretext. They promise peace for churches, peace for the people, and safety for the country. But if the matter cannot thus be brought to its result, the monk or canon who is an advocate prepares a journey so that what could not be done elsewhere may be done at Rome. For a secular prince he willingly endures Alpine cold and Italian heat—things he would perhaps not endure, though far lighter, for a spiritual superior, that is, an abbot. Burdened with charters and supported by authorities, he returns; he appoints a day for the case and introduces persons who, if you wish, are ready to swear that a thing is so, and, if you wish, to swear again that it is not so. These are the affairs of princes.

Now hear again John the Baptist’s judgment in a similar case: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18). What, then, shall I say? Does not the monk who is an advocate prefer reclining at table with Herod to being held in chains and prison with John? At that banquet, though he may not see John’s head, [Col. 0134D] he nonetheless sees what is acquired by shed blood: namely, the widow’s cow and the poor man’s pig. In the prince’s prison a poor man dies; yet the monk or canon who eats from the poor man’s substance flatters the prince.

But I too, beloved, sometimes recline morally at the banquet with Herod: I observe the dancing girl; I behold John’s severed head on a dish. Herod is interpreted “glory.” For all the glory of the daughters of Zion is from within, but the glory of the daughters of the world is from without. Thus I sit at banquet with Herod when, amid delight in vices, I seek the favour of vain [Col. 0135A] glory. I behold Herodias’s daughter dancing when the vanity of curiosity pleases me. These are the two things that remove John’s head: delight in vices and the favour of curiosity. John is interpreted “God’s grace.” God is the head of this grace. The head, then, is separated from the body when someone ascribes to himself rather than to God the good that he does. Such people find no grace with God, because they do not seek it. For the proud seek to be great among men; the humble seek grace with God. Thus Paul says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10), and so forth.

Let the canon or monk who is an advocate hear the apostle saying: “Do not demand back what is yours” (Luke 6:30); let him hear it and determine cases. “Do not demand it back,” He says: do not pursue it with litigation or vexation. And yet, if anything is taken from him, he does not refuse to go to judgment; he does not avoid the danger of perjury when either someone swears for himself or another swears for him. Hence the Apostle complains that we are unwilling to suffer fraud, that we contend in courts, and that, inflamed with anger, we avenge ourselves (1 Corinthians 6), saying: “Beloved, do not defend yourselves, but give place to wrath” (Romans 12:19), and so forth.

Alas! Where will true religion, wholeness of perfection, and the foundation of charity be found? Perhaps among cloistered persons, who judge themselves, accuse themselves daily, fear the sentence of the supreme Judge, and constantly cry with a deep groan of heart: “Enter not into judgment with your servant, O Lord” (Psalm 142 [143]), and so forth. For cloistered persons investigate the true judgments of God, not secular judgments. [Col. 0135C] They keep the law of the Lord by living, meditating, and loving. By living, purity of conscience is usually attained; by meditating, fullness of knowledge; by loving, perfection of charity.

The law of cloistered persons also has its judges, witnesses, and counsellors. In the law of the Lord there are two witnesses: life and conscience; two judges: meditation and knowledge; two counsellors: love of God and love of neighbour. Conscience is a witness before God; life, before men. Knowledge and meditation agree in judgments when what is done or said is provided for by careful consideration. The whole justice of the aforesaid law depends on the two counsellors mentioned before. “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matthew 22:40).

[Col. 0135D] Therefore, if anything of perfection exists in this world, it can be found among cloistered persons. Yet wholeness of perfection cannot be preserved unless poverty is loved with the whole intention. For those who abound in riches, if they set their hearts upon them, are weighed down by cares and entangled in business. He is therefore seduced by dangerous vanity who, after renouncing the world, again becomes entangled in earthly cares. The higher the ascent, the more dangerous the fall. He falls from on high who, having tasted the sweetness of contemplation, returns again to secular things without any compulsion. A dog returns to its vomit; a monk or canon returns to secular business. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one who puts his [Col. 0136A] hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

Therefore he incurs a great evil who ought to have ascended but descends. He incurs a great evil who ought, through the exercise of spiritual life, to advance toward what is better, but through desire for temporal glory daily declines toward what is worse. Although God protects the life of His elect amid secular people, it is nevertheless impossible for anyone situated amid worldly pleasures to remain untouched by vices. We know some who departed from the cloister and were immediately enslaved to the contagions of vices; they departed from love of the Creator and thereby found the condemnation of their souls. Whoever, therefore, desires to preserve an unstained life should remain within the walls of the cloister, and should not go out [Col. 0136B] except when compelled by his abbot’s command, remembering what the bride—that is, the holy soul—says in the Song of Songs in answer to her calling bridegroom, namely Christ: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them again?” (Song of Songs 5:3). [Note: [Col. 0135D] Gregory on this passage.]

The bride—that is, the holy soul—has stripped herself of her tunic because she has cast aside all external things with which she was adorned. She has stripped off her tunic because, renouncing the world with its pleasures, she desires to live for God alone. The bride has also washed her feet because, while the soul lives in holy leisure, she carefully calls her works to mind and mourns with daily tears and groans whatever uncleanness she discovers in them through examination. She has washed her feet because she cleanses with tears the past deeds by which [Col. 0136C] she had walked disorderly through this world. She has washed her feet because, washing sins away with tears, she desires to appear clean in the sight of her Beloved. She fears to defile these feet again because she is very anxious that, if she should become further entangled in secular business, stained by the dust of earth, she might be base and reprobate in the eyes of Jesus Christ, her bridegroom. Therefore she shrinks from leaving spiritual leisure, because, being far from the waves of the sea—that is, from the tumult of the world—she lives more securely, as though placed upon the shore.

Therefore, beloved, do these things among yourselves; ponder them with diligent meditation; and do not wish to put on again the tunic—that is, the earthly substance—from which you once stripped yourselves for Christ’s love. Fear to defile your feet [Col. 0136D] again—that is, the stains of your former life—which you have already washed with tears and frequent sobs: in other words, fear to commit similar sins. Do not wish to pursue the cases and affairs of princes; flee quarrels and disputes; refuse to contend in court. Thus the Lord says: “Do not resist evil” (Matthew 5:39). And shortly afterward: “If anyone wishes to contend with you in judgment and take away your tunic, leave him your cloak also” (ibid., Matthew 5:40).

If you, therefore, beloved, are Christ’s disciples [the source reads *discipul?*, probably *discipuli*], show Christ’s discipline not only in words but also in good works. Do not seek to defend yourselves, but give place to wrath. Why? Because vengeance belongs to the Lord: He repays each according to his works [Col. 0137A] and delivers you from the hand of those who hate you. Therefore I admonish you, beloved, to strive more to investigate the secrets of mysteries than decrees of councils; to sing psalms in choir rather than settle cases concerning temporal matters at court; and to persist more in prayer, reading, and divine contemplation, at the day and night hours in God’s house, than to take part in diverse business and conflicts in a prince’s house. The former lift the mind to heavenly things; the latter estrange it from God. The former refresh the soul with heavenly banquets; the latter entangle it in sins and vices. The former satisfy the soul with spiritual delights; the latter strip it of virtues.

In the cloister, therefore, the spiritual table—namely, divine reading—is set, from which the minds of God’s servants are refreshed, lest amid the dangers of this present [Col. 0137B] life they grow weak from spiritual hunger, but rather may be raised with greater strength to the joys of the heavenly homeland. At the table of Holy Scripture, a little one—that is, one newly converted to God or of lesser understanding—finds milk, namely gentle and sweet teaching by which he may be nourished unto good works.
