The strong person, that is, one practised in God’s service or more perfectly instructed in divine knowledge, finds bread by which he may be refreshed: namely, loftier precepts, by which he may apply himself more diligently to God’s service.

There God’s servant learns how to withdraw from worldly pleasures; there he begins to taste how sweet and pleasant the Lord is. There he learns how the present age is to be despised and in what order God and neighbour are to be loved. There he discovers the wiles and temptations of the ancient enemy, and the desires of his own flesh against the spirit. There he finds the good he should do and the evil he should avoid: how he should renounce vices [Col. 0137C] and cleave to virtues; forgetting what lies behind and stretching himself toward what lies ahead; setting a guard on his mouth; closing his ears lest he hear evil; turning away his eyes lest they see vanity; returning no evil for evil; inflicting on no one what he does not wish to suffer; and doing to others what he wishes to be done to himself. Above all these things, however, at this spiritual table he can find the way by which he may attain the heavenly homeland.

Therefore, beloved, come more diligently than usual to this spiritual table, and, according to the understanding granted you by God, take spiritual food from it, lest you grow weary from hunger for the word of God in this pilgrimage. “For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). [Col. 0138B] For Holy Scripture varies according to the understanding of each reader, like manna, which gave the ancient people a varied taste according to each person’s delight. According to their capacity of perception—that is, their understanding—the word of the Lord is suited to individuals; and, though it differs according to the understanding of each person, it yet remains one in itself.

Therefore, beloved, despise outward things; take care to desire inward things. Contemn visible things; love invisible ones. Refuse to go to the court of an earthly prince unless great necessity requires it. Hasten as swiftly as possible to the palace of the eternal King by the steps of good works. And, that you may there behold your same Redeemer reigning at the Father’s right hand, pour forth tears unceasingly with deep groaning of heart. May He deign to grant this—He who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## ELEVENTH SERMON, ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

[Col. 0137]

[Col. 0137C] Luke the Evangelist and writer of the apostolic history, a Syrian by nation, a physician by profession, educated in Greek speech, disciple of the Apostle Paul and his inseparable companion in travel, was, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, most chaste from childhood. At the beginning of the rising Church, he speaks to Theophilus, [Note: [Col. 0137D] Who this Theophilus was is uncertain; but still more uncertain is whether he was a bishop and Luke’s fellow disciple. No interpreter mentions this latter designation, as may be seen in Maldonatus and Calmet on chapter 1 of the Gospel according to Luke.] his fellow disciple and bishop [Col. 0137D], saying: “The first account indeed I made, O Theophilus, concerning all that Jesus began to do and to teach, until the day on which, giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom He had chosen, He was taken up” (Acts 1:1–2).

It should be noted that he first said, “what Jesus began to do,” and then added, “and to teach,” because, as a perfect teacher, He first did what He afterward taught. He lived without stain and taught without falsehood. Throughout His entire life He committed no sin and preached nothing that could rightly be reproved. He lived innocently among the Jews and taught truthfully the crowds of people running to Him. Luke therefore rightly said first that he had composed an account of those things which Jesus began to do and teach, because Jesus gave a model of perfection to His disciples, whom He was going to send to teach all nations—indeed, to all [Col. 0138D] rulers of the Church.

This is the pattern of ecclesiastical religion: every preacher must first strive to live well and then to teach well, so that those whom he begets in faith by words he may nourish by example. Thus the Son of God and man lived incomparably in this world, taught with saving effect the crowds of people streaming to Him, and sufficiently refreshed them with the bread of the heavenly word, until the day when, having commanded through the Holy Spirit the apostles whom He had chosen [Col. 0139A] to preach the Gospel to every creature, He was taken up into heaven, whence He had descended.

He chose a few through whom He gained many. He chose the poor through whom He subjected to Himself the rich and powerful. He humbled the proud, checked the exalted, laid low tyrants, and subjected to the yoke of His faith all who were predestined to eternal life. He chose unlearned and fearful men, whom, as has been said, He taught through the Holy Spirit to preach and strengthened to endure the persecutions of the perverse. Certainly the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ were afraid when they dared neither to preach nor, for fear of the Jews, to move a foot beyond the threshold of the house. And unless divine grace had enlightened them, how could they preach, since they did not know letters or the languages of nations? In those same apostles, indeed, the primitive [Col. 0139B] Church then existed tender, fearful, and unlearned, as Solomon had long before foretold in the Song of Love under the person of the bridegroom, namely Jesus Christ.

“Our sister,” he says, “is little, and has no breasts” (Song of Songs 8:8). [Note: [Col. 0139D] Gregory on this passage.] Christ calls the Church His sister, He who said of the apostles themselves: “Go, tell my brothers to go into Galilee; there they shall see me” (Matthew 28:10). The Church, however, was a little sister and had no breasts when she existed only in the apostles, because she could nourish neither herself nor others with the milk of preaching. What could Peter preach to others when, denying, swearing, and protesting, he declared himself not to be Christ’s disciple at the voice of a single servant-girl? (Matthew 26.) The Church, therefore, was little and had no breasts, because after Christ’s resurrection she was shut up in one house and, among her persecutors, feared not merely to preach but even to be seen. [Col. 0139C]

Again the Son of God and the Virgin adds: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken to?” (Song of Songs 8:8). Christ spoke to this same sister when He sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles and, speaking inwardly, taught them all the languages of the world by a manifold distribution, and strengthened them to endure adversities. For he cannot be a perfect preacher who fears to preach the good things he has learned, any more than an unlearned man can be one who presumes to preach things he does not know. Therefore the Son of God strengthened and taught His disciples, that is, His Church, so that it might preach good things boldly and endure evil things patiently.

This was aptly prefigured by the patriarch Jacob when, blessing his son Zebulun, he said figuratively: “Zebulun shall dwell by the shore of the sea and at the station of ships” (Genesis 49:13). [Note: [Col. 0140D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 31.] Zebulun, whose name is interpreted “dwelling of strength,” signifies the Church, most strong for enduring every suffering. She dwells by the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, so that she may show believers a refuge and those in peril the harbour of true faith. Strengthened with immovable and unshaken firmness against every storm [Col. 0140A] of the age, she looks upon the shipwreck of Jews and heretics and upon all the storms that are borne about. Though beaten by waves, she breaks the waves themselves and is broken by none. She yields to no storms of heresy and, shaken by no wind of schism, does not collapse.

Moreover, she extends as far as Sidon—that is, she reaches the peoples of the nations. We also read in the Gospel that some of the apostles were taken from there, and that the Lord often taught in those places. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali” (Psalm 67 [68]:28). This is as though it said more plainly: “The princes of Judah, their leaders”—that is, the princes of faith, namely the holy apostles—will be leaders of those who are in [Col. 0140B] the Church; “and the princes of Zebulun,” that is, the princes of hope; “and the princes of Naphtali,” namely of charity. This charity is called “expansion,” because in charity some of them were extended so far as even to pray for their enemies.

It follows: “Command, O God, your strength; confirm, O God, what you have accomplished in us” (ibid.). As though he said: Command, O God, your strength—namely, that the faithful converted through the apostles may bless you in the churches. Or, as though it were said: O God the Father, command—that is, entrust—your strength, namely your incarnate Word, which is your strength. Hence Paul says: “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). Or, command that blessing to your strength, so that every blessing may be accomplished through your power. Or, command your strength [Col. 0140C], that is, the charity which you had toward humankind; for while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

Again he says: “Confirm, O God, what you have accomplished in us” (Rom. 5); that is, confirm the grace which you have bestowed upon us: make it firm both in us and among the nations, beginning from your temple, which is in Jerusalem; for there the word of God was first preached. But because the blinded Jews refused humbly to receive it, the preachers—that is, the holy apostles—turned to the nations. “Confirm,” he says, “O God, what you have accomplished in us”; for if you confirm it, kings—that is, your apostles—will bring you gifts. Peter will offer you converts from the circumcision; Paul, from the uncircumcision; [Col. 0140D] Thomas, Indians; James, Spaniards; Matthew, Ethiopians; John, Asians; Mark, Egyptians; and each apostle those among whom he will preach.

Otherwise: “The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.” Cassiodorus indicates by these tribal names Christ and his apostles. Augustine says: “Perhaps the apostles were from these tribes, and these are the leaders of those who bless God in the churches.” But the interpretation drawn from the meanings of the names, which suits the Church, is more pleasing. Judah means “confession”; Zebulun, [Col. 0141A] “dwelling-place of strength”; Naphtali, “expansion”—meanings appropriate to the princes of the Church. For in martyrdoms confession comes first, for whose sake whatever happens must be borne bravely. Then, when the straits are ended, expansiveness follows as the reward. Thus: “There are the princes of Judah,” that is, of confession; “the princes of Zebulun,” that is, of strength; “and the princes of Naphtali,” that is, of expansiveness.

Or this may be understood as referring to the three virtues signified by these interpretations of names: confession is in faith, strength in hope, expansiveness in charity. The sense is: Bless God—you who have drunk from the fountains of Israel, that is, from the teaching of the apostles—as is fitting; because there are the princes of Judah, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali, that is, the princes of faith, hope, and charity. These are the leaders [Col. 0141B] of those who are in the churches; and in this respect each of them is Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand”; a youth, having put off the old age of malice; in ecstasy of mind, that is, with the mind borne upward. “There is Benjamin, a youth, in ecstasy of mind.”

Cassiodorus: “There,” that is, among the fountains of living water, or in the churches, “is Benjamin,” that is, the last of the apostles; “a youth,” that is, one taken up last, who was from the tribe of Benjamin. Hence it is said: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoil” (Gen. 49). This is Paul, who in the morning of his life persecuted the saints, but in the evening of his conversion to God distributed through various offices the spoils wrested from the devil.

Augustine: He is in ecstasy of mind, his mind being withdrawn [Col. 0141C] from bodily senses, as when he was caught up to the third heaven; or in the terror of his mind. Our Lord Jesus Christ, coming into this world, broke the powers of the devil and chose, from humble ways of life, the disciples through whom he taught his Church. First he taught the synagogue through patriarchs, prophets, and teachers of the law; but at last, after destroying the prince of death and granting eternal peace, he taught the holy Church through the holy apostles and their successors. Hence the prophet Micah introduces the Lord speaking, as though declaring that there shall truly be peace for the holy Church and that the devil will be easily crushed at Christ’s coming. Therefore let almighty God, who is three in persons and one in divinity, say:

[Col. 0141D] “We shall raise up against the Assyrian seven shepherds and eight princes. And they shall shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod with their spears; and he shall deliver his people from Assyria; and there shall be peace in the land when he comes” (Mic. 5).

As though God the Father said: I, and my most beloved Son, coeternal with me, whom before all ages I begot from the womb before the morning star; and the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with us—we shall raise up over, that is, against, the Assyrian seven shepherds: namely all the patriarchs, prophets, and saints of the Old Testament, in which the Sabbath was observed; [Col. 0142A] and eight princes: namely the apostles, evangelists, and other teachers of the New Testament. “They shall shepherd the land,” that is, they shall tear down and lay waste Assyria with the sword of the divine word, which was sent into the earth in order to divide two into three. They shall lay waste also the land of Nimrod with their spears, that is, with the darts of Christ’s preaching, he who is our peace; and he shall deliver his people from Assyria, that is, from the devil.

Nimrod means “tyrant,” or “descending temptation.” For he was the first to seize upon an unprecedented tyranny among peoples, and he himself undertook to build a tower of impiety against God [Note: [Col. 0141D] Thus Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 7, chapter [uncertain]. A Lapide, on Genesis 10, says: “Nimrod was the author, instigator, and founder of the tower.” St Augustine, *City of God*, book 16, chapter 4: “Nimrod with his peoples erected a tower against [Col. 0142D] the Lord.” But see Calmet’s dissertation *On the Tower of Babel*.] signifying him who said: “I will set my seat in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Nimrod also means “descending temptation” and signifies him who fell from heaven like lightning [Col. 0142B] (Luke 10), and who continually roams among the beasts like a hunter. He ranges through fruitless trees and groves—that is, human beings barren of good works.

But the holy teachers of the Old and New Testaments—the patriarchs and prophets, apostles and evangelists—sent by God, lay waste the devil’s land as he accuses and tempts; and thus God delivers his people from the hand of Assyria, that is, of the same devil who longs to trample the boundaries of Israel, namely the holy Church. And because this same malicious enemy strives to destroy God’s household, he is wounded by Christ and his ministers and, according to the Gospel, is bound in his own house.

Again he says: “The remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many peoples like dew from the Lord, and like drops upon the grass, which does not wait for a man and does not [Col. 0142C] look for the sons of men” (Mic. 5). What we read as having been accomplished historically in the three boys, the teaching of the apostles accomplished universally among all nations (Dan. 3). “And like drops,” he says, “upon the grass,” which grass does not wait for a man—that is, does not await human help, but that of God alone—“and does not look for the sons of men,” but for the Son of God from heaven.

Therefore, when we have been delivered from Assyria, that is, from the devil’s power, by God, who raised up against him seven [Note: [Col. 0142D] Perhaps one should read here: “seven shepherds and eight princes.”] and eight shepherds, namely patriarchs and prophets, apostles and evangelists, then the remnant of Jacob—that is, the apostles and the primitive Church, which took its beginning from the Jews—will be among the peoples as dew, to extinguish the fiery darts of the devil in human hearts [Col. 0142D].

It follows: “The remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, and like a lion’s whelp among herds of swine.” As though he said: The apostles will be strong and invincible in sufferings, like a lion’s whelp among herds of swine. Christ, the lion and lion’s whelp, granted this to the apostles: just as a lion cannot be resisted in seizing beasts or sheep, so the apostles, delivered from the hand of the Assyrian—that is, the devil—snatch and separate beasts, that is, simple people, from unbelievers so that they may be saved.

[Col. 0143A] Gideon, the strongest of men, prefigured these invincible soldiers of Christ, namely the holy apostles and martyrs, when he overcame the Midianites not by arms but by jars, lamps, and trumpets (Judg. 7). [Note: [Col. 0143D] Isidore, *Questions on Judges*, chapter 5.] Thus Gideon, when he was preparing to fight the Midianites and leading out the multitude of his army to war, removed from the conflict of battle all whom he saw drawing water with bent knees. He remained with only three hundred men, who had drawn water with their hands while standing. With these Gideon goes to battle, and arms them not with weapons but with trumpets, jars, and lamps. For, as it is written, they placed lighted lamps inside the jars, held trumpets in the right hand and jars in the left, and, coming close upon their enemies, sounded the trumpets; [Col. 0143B] then the lamps appeared. Terrified by the sound of the trumpets on one side and by the flashing of the lamps on the other, the enemies turned to flight.

What does it mean that such a battle is brought forward by the prophet? Did the prophet intend to show us that that battle under Gideon’s leadership signified our Redeemer’s coming against the devil? For such things were certainly done there as, the more they surpass ordinary warfare, the less they depart from the mystery of prophecy. Who ever came to battle with jars and lamps? Who, coming against weapons, cast weapons aside? These things would indeed be ridiculous [“ridiculous,” perhaps an OCR variant] to us, if they had not been terrifying to the enemy. But the victory itself attesting it, we have learned not to regard what was done as insignificant.

For Gideon, coming to battle, signifies [Col. 0143C] the coming of the Redeemer, of whom it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes; be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23). And again: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord mighty in battle” (ibid.). He prophesied our Redeemer not only by deed but also by name. Gideon means “going about in the womb.” For the Lord by the power of his majesty embraces all things, yet by the grace of the dispensation entered the Virgin’s womb. What, then, is “going about in the womb,” except that Christ, almighty God, was within the womb by the substance of weakness and beyond the world by the power of divinity? Midian means “God’s judgment.”

[Col. 0143D] For the fact that his enemies were to be driven back and destroyed came not from a defect in the one repelling them, but from the judgment of the Judge. Therefore the Midianites are called “God’s judgment,” because, estranged from the Redeemer’s grace, they bear in the very designation of their name a just cause of condemnation. Gideon goes to battle against the enemies with three hundred men. The fullness of perfection is customarily understood in [Note: [Col. 0143D] The edition reads: “the hundredfold number.”] the number three hundred. What, then, is signified by [Note: [Col. 0144D] Ibid.: “the hundredfold number taken three times.”] the number three hundred, except perfect knowledge of the Trinity? With such people our Redeemer destroys the adversaries of faith; with them he descends to the battles of preaching—those who can know divine things and know how to think perfectly concerning the Trinity, who is God.

It should further be noted that this number three hundred is contained in the letter tau, which bears the form of the cross. If the part projecting above the transverse line, which appears on the cross, were added to it, it would no longer be the form of a cross but the cross itself. Therefore, since the number three hundred is contained in the letter tau, and since, as we have said, the letter tau displays the form of the cross, those who followed Gideon among these three hundred fittingly signify those to whom it is said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16). Those who follow Christ bear the cross more truly in proportion as they discipline themselves more strictly and are afflicted by compassion of charity toward their neighbors [Col. 0144B]. Hence the prophet Ezekiel says: “Mark tau upon the foreheads [of the men]” (Ezek. 9), namely of those who mourn and grieve. Or certainly, in these three hundred, contained in the letter tau, this is expressed: that the iron of enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross.

They were therefore brought to the river to drink water, and whoever drew water with bent knees was removed from the military expedition. By water is understood the teaching of wisdom; by those standing [the reading is: “but of the standing knee”] is signified upright conduct. Therefore, those said to have bent the knee while drinking water, and who withdrew barred from the conflict of battles, are those who do not draw doctrine together with upright works. But those who draw the streams of doctrine so that they may in no way be bent carnally into evil works—[Col. 0144C] these, with Christ as leader, go to battle against the enemies of faith.

They go, then, with trumpets and jars, because this, as we have said, was the order of battle. They sounded the trumpets; lamps were placed within the jars; when the jars were broken, the lamps were revealed; and terrified by the flashing light of these lamps, the enemies fled. Thus the trumpets signify the cry of preaching—namely that of apostles, evangelists, and holy martyrs; the lamps, the brightness of miracles; and the jars, the frailty of bodies. For our leader Jesus Christ led such soldiers with him to battle: men who, despising the safety of their bodies, struck down their enemies by dying and overcame their swords not by weapons but by patience.

Our martyrs came armed for battle under their Judge with trumpets, [Col. 0144D] jars, and lamps. They sounded the trumpets while preaching; they broke the jars while exposing their bodies, to be dissolved in sufferings, to hostile swords; the lamps shone when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they flashed with miracles. Immediately the enemies turned to flight, because, when they saw the bodies of the dead martyrs shining with miracles, they were shattered by the light of truth which they had attacked.

Therefore they sounded trumpets so that the jars might be broken; the jars were broken so that the lamps might appear; the lamps appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight. That is, the martyrs preached until their bodies [Col. 0145A] were dissolved in death; their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might shine with miracles; they shone with miracles so that they might strike down their enemies by divine light. It should be noted that the enemies stood fast before the jars and fled before the lamps: persecutors of the holy faith resisted preachers while they were still in the body, but after their bodies’ dissolution, when miracles appeared, they turned to flight because, terrified [the reading is “terrified”] into ceasing, they stopped persecuting the faithful.

It should also be observed that Scripture says they held the trumpets in the right hand and the jars in the left, because Christ’s martyrs regarded the grace of preaching as great, but the usefulness of their bodies as very small. Whoever values bodily usefulness more than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in the left hand and the jar in the right. If the grace of preaching is regarded in first place and bodily usefulness in second, it is certain that the trumpets are held in the right hands and the jars in the left. Therefore, as said above, Christ’s soldiers—the apostles and martyrs—conquered the persecutors of the Church not by inflicting evils, but by patiently enduring adversities and shining with miracles.

Divine grace permitted these men to be expelled from Judaea and caused them to migrate to the peoples of the nations, as blessed Job, considering among God’s other great and ineffable works, says: “He removed mountains, and they did not know it” (Job 9). Gregory [Note: [Col. 0145D] *Morals*, book 9, chapter 2.] says:

> “In Sacred Scripture, the name ‘mountains’ signifies the exalted rank of preachers, [Col. 0145C] concerning whom the Psalmist says: ‘Let the mountains receive peace for your people, and the hills justice’ (Ps. 71). The elect preachers of the eternal homeland are rightly called mountains, because by the height of their life they leave the low places of earth and become near to heaven. But God removed the mountains, that is, the preachers, by withdrawing them from the obduracy of Judaea. Hence the Psalmist again rightly says: ‘The mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea’ (Ps. 45). The mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea when the preaching apostles, driven away by Judaea’s unbelief, came to the understanding of the nations.
>
> “Thus they themselves say in the Acts: ‘It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but because you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations’ (Acts [Col. 0145D] 13). But those who were overthrown in the Lord’s wrath did not know this very transfer of the mountains. When the Hebrews drove the apostles from their territory, they thought that they had gained something by losing the light of preaching. Struck by a just punishment demanded by their merits, they were blinded by so great an error of understanding that they thought it a joy to lose the light.
>
> “But when the apostles had been driven away, Judaea was immediately destroyed by the Roman ruler Titus and, dispersed among all nations, scattered abroad. Hence, after the mountains’ removal, it is rightly added: ‘He moves the earth from its place, and its pillars shall be shaken’ (Job 9). The earth was moved from its place when the Israelite people, uprooted from the territories of Judaea, bowed their necks to the nations, though they had refused to submit to their Creator. That earth once had pillars, because in its priests, princes of the law, teachers, and Pharisees the structure of its impending obstinacy had been raised. In them the edifice of the letter stood, and in the time of its peace it bore the burdens of carnal sacrifices as though they were laid upon a superimposed structure.
>
> “But when the mountains were removed, the pillars were shaken, because, after the apostles were taken from Judaea, even those who had expelled its preachers of life were not permitted to live in it. It was fitting that, conquered, they should lose the earthly homeland for whose love they had not feared to attack the soldiers of the heavenly homeland. But after the holy teachers had been expelled, Judaea [Col. 0146B] became wholly numb and, by the just judgment of the Judge, closed the eyes of its mind in the darkness of error. Hence it is further added:
>
> “‘He commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he shuts up the stars as under a seal’ (Job 9). Sometimes, in sacred discourse, the name ‘sun’ signifies the quality of preachers, as John says: ‘The sun became like a sackcloth of hair’ (Rev. 6). At the end of time the sun is shown like a haircloth sack, because the shining life of preachers is displayed as harsh and contemptible before the eyes of the reprobate. They are also represented by the brightness of stars, because, while they preach what is right, they illuminate the darkness of our night. Hence, when the preachers have been withdrawn, the prophet says: ‘The stars of rain have been withheld’ (Jer. 3). Literally, the stars of rain are Orion, Arcturus, and the Hyades, which bring rain.
>
> “Since the sun shines by day while the stars illuminate the darkness of night, sacred discourse often designates the eternal homeland by ‘day’ and the present life by ‘night.’ Holy preachers therefore become a sun to our eyes when they open to us contemplation of the true light; and they shine like stars in darkness when, so as to be useful in active life, they arrange earthly matters for our needs. They flash like the sun by day when they lift the gaze of our mind to contemplate the homeland of inward brightness; and they gleam like stars by night because, even while they carry out earthly affairs, they direct the foot of our work, which might stumble, by the example [Col. 0146D] of their uprightness.
>
> “But because, once the preachers had been expelled, there remained no one to show the Jewish people, persisting in the night of its unbelief, either the brightness of contemplation or the light of active life, Truth—which that people had rejected—abandoned it and, having withdrawn the light of preaching, deservedly blinded it through its own perversity. Therefore it is rightly said: ‘He commands the sun, and it does not rise; and he shuts up the stars as under a seal.’ For he was unwilling for the sun to rise upon the people from whom he turned aside the minds of preachers. And he shut up the stars as under a seal, because by holding his preachers within themselves in silence he hid heavenly light from the blind minds of the wicked.
>
> “It should be considered, however, that we shut something under a seal in order to bring it forth when the appropriate time comes. From the testimony of sacred Scripture we have learned that Judaea, now abandoned, will be gathered into the bosom of faith at the end. Thus Isaiah says: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved’ (Isa. 10). Thus Paul says: ‘Until the fullness of the nations should enter, and so all Israel might be saved’ (Rom. 9). Therefore he who now withdraws his preachers from the eyes of Judaea but will later reveal them, shuts up the stars as under a seal: so that, hidden at first and later shining with rays of spiritual stars, the night of its unbelief may neither see them while it rejects them now nor fail to discover them when it is then illumined.
>
> “For this reason two outstanding preachers have been withdrawn by a deferred death, so that they may be recalled to the work of preaching at the end: these are ‘the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth’ (Rev. 11). Of one of them Truth himself promises in the Gospel, saying: ‘Elijah is to come and will restore all things’ (Matt. 17). Thus the stars have been shut up as under a seal: they are hidden now so as not to appear, and later they will appear in order to be useful. Yet the Israelite people, which will be gathered abundantly at the end, was cruelly hardened at the very beginnings of the holy Church: it rejected the preachers of truth and despised words of help. Nevertheless, this comes about through the wonderful ordering of the Creator, so that the glory of the preachers, which if received in one people could have remained hidden, might through rejection be spread abroad among all nations.”

Therefore the teaching of the Gospel went out through the apostles into all [Col. 0147C] nations and, like good seed, filled the whole world. As the prophet Micah foretold long before: “From Zion,” he says, “shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Mic. 4). Zion means “watching.” The holy Church is called Zion because, contemplating heavenly things, doing good, and avoiding adversity, it unceasingly watches for entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore let this holy prophet say here: From Zion, that is, from the primitive Church, in which that teacher and high priest is the Son of God and of the Virgin, the spiritual law shall go forth through the apostles to the nations; and the word of the Lord, that is, the proclamation of preaching, shall go forth from Jerusalem throughout the world. Hence it is said: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends [Col. 0147D] of the world” (Ps. 18).

It follows: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning-hooks” (Mic. 4). Allegorically, through faith in Christ, unbridled anger and insults are laid aside, so that each may put his hand to the plough, as the apostles exhort, and not look back; and so that, when the darts of persecutions and reproaches have been broken, Christ may reap spiritual grain through the angels. No one aims to overthrow the hearers or to prohibit the preachers, namely the apostles, because it is the time for planting.

Again he adds: “Nation shall not take up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.” A man shall sit beneath the vine, in order to press the wine of spiritual understanding, which gladdens the human heart; and beneath the fig tree, in order to pluck the rich [“sweet,” according to the Gloss] fruits [Col. 0148A] of the Holy Spirit. Before Christ’s birth, almost the whole world was full of blood; Rome also was torn apart in civil wars. But after Rome received a single empire in accordance with Christ’s command, the world was made ready beforehand for the apostles’ journey; city gates were opened to the apostles, and a single empire was established for the preaching of the one God.

Almighty God, through his most beloved Son, by sending apostles throughout the world, mercifully called all nations to knowledge and love of himself, as he himself foretold through the prophet Zechariah:

“I shall whistle for them and gather them, I who redeemed them; and I shall multiply them as they were multiplied before. [Col. 0148B] I shall sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me; they shall live with their children and return. I shall bring them back from the land of Egypt and gather them from the Assyrians; I shall bring them to the land of Gilead and Lebanon, and no place shall be found for them” (Zech. 10).

Allegorically, the Lord indicates by his mercy to those captive in sins that they should gather to him as to Redemption, saying: “Take my yoke upon you,” etc. (Matt. 11). He multiplies these saints, namely the apostles, not with a carnal but a spiritual blessing. They are sown among the peoples, to whom it is said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Through these disciples of Christ, sown among all [Col. 0148C] nations, peoples far removed through idolatry will remember the Lord, in whose presence all families of the nations shall worship. They shall live with their children, whom they acquired for the Lord by preaching; and they shall return, so that, having formerly been dead in unbelief, they may live spiritually. These are the children to whom Paul administered milk.

It follows: “I shall bring them back from the land of Egypt and from the Assyrians”: namely, from the land ruled by King Pharaoh, who said, “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezek. 29), and from the land ruled by the king of Assyria—that is, “great intellect,” namely the proud devil, who calls himself great and is also interpreted as “one accusing” or “one convicting.” Such persons are brought into the land of Gilead, [Col. 0148D] that is, from earthly things to spiritual. For Gilead means “testimony of migration.” Through the apostles the faithful are also brought to Lebanon, that is, to whitening, so that, led forth from the darkness of this world, they may be made white. Then no place shall be found for them, because they will not be confined by the narrowness of earth but will enjoy heaven’s breadth.

Through these apostles God also poured into the hearts of believers great sweetness from his goodness, as the prophet Joel, exulting and speaking figuratively, foretold:

“It shall be in that day: the mountains shall drip sweetness, the hills shall flow with milk, and waters shall run through all the streams of Judah” (Joel 3). After the Lord’s resurrection and ascension into heaven, the mountains—that is, the apostles, and after them the Church’s teachers, lofty [Col. 0149A] in mind—shall abound in the pleasantness and sweetness of wisdom and divine discourse; spiritual graces shall drip from them. And the hills—that is, those who do not possess so great a fullness of understanding—shall send forth milk, by which the infancy of the Church is nourished. Waters shall abound through all the streams of Judah, that is, over the believing children of the Church: the preachings of apostles and evangelists and gifts of charisms, because nothing in them will be dry.

It follows: “A fountain shall go forth from the house of the Lord, and it shall water the torrent of thorns.” “From the house of the Lord,” he says, that is, from the primitive Church, shall go forth the fountain of baptism and spiritual teaching. It waters the hearts of the nations, which were pierced by the thorns of vices and the stings of evil thoughts, so that flowers of virtues may spring up where formerly there sprang [Col. 0149B] the pricks of vices. This fountain then went out from the house of the Lord when the Lord said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Then too the mountains and hills dripped sweetness—that is, the honey of wisdom and spiritual understanding—and the hills milk—that is, the teaching by which the Church’s little ones are nourished in the knowledge of God—when the holy apostles and their successors watered the whole Church by words and examples, and by the most truthful writings of the Gospels and Epistles. Similar is what the prophet Zechariah, foreseeing in spirit the time of Christ’s resurrection and ascension, joyfully said:

[Col. 0149C] “In that day living waters shall go out from Jerusalem: half of them to the western [eastern] sea, and half of them to the last sea, in summer and winter” (Zech. 14). As though he spoke more plainly concerning Christ’s first coming and his Church: There shall be, on that day known to God alone, living waters going out from Jerusalem. The waters are called living because through Christ’s grace they bestow life. For from Christ’s first coming until the second there is, as it were, one day and one time. “Half of them,” he says, “to the western [eastern] sea,” which is called Dead because it kills living creatures, or because nothing can live in its waters; “and half of them to the last sea,” which is called the Great Sea.

Or, allegorically, the two seas signify the two Testaments, which, unless they are sweetened by the stream of spiritual understanding, are bitter, the letter killing and the spirit not giving life. “In summer,” he says, “and winter”—as though he said: the waters which go out from Jerusalem, that is, from the Church, will neither be dried by heat nor frozen in winter. The waters which go out from Jerusalem, that is, from the Church, are the Savior’s teaching, namely baptism. One part goes to the western [eastern] sea, that is, to the people of the circumcision, chosen in the apostles and through the apostles; [Col. 0149D] and one part to the last sea, because from east and west those will come who shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0150A] (Matt. 8). These waters shall not cease either in the summer of prosperity or in the winter of persecution.

It follows: “And the Lord shall be king over all the earth.” As though it were said: when such waters have entered both seas and softened the bitter waters with a sweet stream, the Lord, namely Christ, shall be king over all the earth. Then that most mighty king shall be recognized, of whom it was said: “O Lord our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth!” (Ps. 8).

Again he adds, saying: “In that day the Lord shall be one, and his name one; and all the land shall return as far as the wilderness, from the hill of Adremon to the south, and Jerusalem shall be exalted [Note: [Col. 0149D] It seems more correct to read, according to the Vulgate: ‘from the hill of Rimmon to the south of Jerusalem, and it shall be exalted,’ [Col. 0150D] etc.], and it shall dwell [Col. 0150B] in its own place”—that is, it shall be rebuilt in its former site—“from the gate of Benjamin to the place of the former gate, and to the gate of the corners; and from the tower of Hananel to the king’s winepresses. They shall dwell in it, and there shall be no anathema any more.”

When the Lord Jesus Christ is king over all the earth, then there shall be one Lord, of whom it is written: “Know that the Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 79). And the Lord’s name shall be one, when the perverse religion of idols has been trampled down. Then all the land in which the Jews dwelt shall return as far as the wilderness, that is, as far as the people of the nations, who were formerly deserted because without knowledge of the law; and from the hill to Adremon, that is, to the height, because from the earth and the wilderness we shall rise to the hills, and from the hills [Col. 0150C] to the mountains; then on to the south of full light. Thus, ascending, the Church shall be exalted and dwell in the place of which it is written: “He has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22).

And from the gate of Benjamin, beginning with the virtue signified by the right hand, it shall reach the former gate, so as to enter through it to the others. Next comes the gate of the corners, where is the cornerstone, namely Christ, who joins two walls into one. Next comes the tower of Hananel, which is called “most gracious of God.” Of this tower David says to God: “You have become my hope, a tower of strength against the enemy” (Ps. 60). Nothing is more welcome than this tower to a person who, amid the labors of the world, sighs for God. From there one comes [Col. 0150D] to the king’s winepresses, so that imitators of Christ’s passion may drink the wine which gladdens the human heart, having been brought into God’s wine cellar, where is the wine of Gospel preaching. Those intoxicated by winepresses of this kind shall dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem, in which there will be no anathema—that is, no curse or separation from God—but secure rest for those who trust in God.

Therefore, as stated above, living waters went out from Jerusalem because the holy apostles watered the whole world with the teaching of Gospel preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.] Certainly, the patriarch Jacob [Col. 0151A] prefigured these apostles of Christ when, in blessing his son Naphtali, he figuratively called him “a hind let loose.” Naphtali, therefore—whose name means “expansion”—signifies the apostles and the other preachers, whose teaching has been spread across the whole extent of the world. For apostles came from this tribe, and they are the princes and leaders of the Churches. Thus also what is read in the Psalm—namely, “the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali”—undoubtedly refers to the persons of the apostles (Ps. 67). They are the sons of those who have been shaken out—that is, of the prophets—who, placed in the hand of almighty God, like arrows shot forth, reached even to the ends of the earth. Thus Naphtali is rightly written here as “a stag let loose,” because the apostles, and likewise the other preachers, springing forth with a swift leap after the [Col. 0151B] manner of hinds, transcend the entanglements of this age. Thus they meditate upon exalted and sublime utterances of beauty—that is, they preach to all nations the grace of God the Saviour. Therefore God expanded the holy apostles throughout the whole world, because through them he made his name known to every nation, as blessed Job foretold among the many things that he said concerning God’s omnipotence. For he says:

> Who alone stretches out the heavens and walks upon the waves of the sea. (Job 9)

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0151D] *Morals on Job*, book IX, ch. 4]: “What is denoted by the name of the heavens but the heavenly course of the holy apostles and other preachers? Of them the Psalmist says: ‘The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands’ (Ps. 18). These heavens are also called the sun [Col. 0151C]: heavens, indeed, because they protect through intercession; but sun, because through preaching they reveal the power of light. The heavens, therefore, were stretched out, because when Judaea raged with the force of persecution, the Lord extended the lives of the apostles into the knowledge of all nations. And she, by a just judgment, is scattered captive throughout the world; while they, by grace, are everywhere spread abroad in honour. For the heavens were narrow when one people contained so many outstanding preachers. Who among the Gentiles would have known Peter, if he had remained in the preaching of the Israelite people alone? Who would have recognized Paul’s mighty works, unless Judaea, by persecuting him, had sent him on to our notice? Behold: those who were driven away with scourges and insults by the Israelite people [Col. 0151D] are now adorned throughout the ends of the world. Thus the Lord alone stretches out the heavens: by the wonderful dispensation of his hidden counsel, where he permitted his preachers to be oppressed among one nation, he caused them thereby to be extended to the farthest regions of the world.

“But this Gentile world too, given over to the present age, did not gladly receive the words of life when the tongue of the apostles rebuked its sins. It immediately swelled with the pride of contradiction and stirred itself to the cruelty of persecution. Yet that which strives to oppose the words of preaching is soon calmed by astonishment at signs. Therefore the text fittingly adds in praise of its Maker: ‘And he walks upon the waves of the sea.’ [Note: [Col. 0152D] Gregory, ch. 5.] What is signified by the sea except the [Col. 0152A] bitterness of this world, raging for the death of the good? Of this the Psalmist says: ‘Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin’ (Ps. 32). The Lord gathers the waters of the sea as in a wineskin when, ordering all things by wondrous governance, he restrains within their own hearts the threats of carnal people. Thus the Lord walks upon the waves of the sea, because when the storms of persecution rise up, they are broken by amazement at his miracles. He who calms the swellings of human madness is, as it were, standing upon a mound and treading down the wave.

“For when the Gentile world saw its customs destroyed by a new manner of life; when the rich of this world saw the deeds of the poor opposing their pride; when the wise of the age weighed the words of the unlearned, hostile to themselves—they immediately swelled into the tempest of persecution [Col. 0152B]. But those who, disturbed by opposition to their words, leap into storms of persecution are calmed, as we have said, by amazement at signs. Therefore the Lord set as many steps upon these waves as he showed miracles to proud persecutors. Hence the Psalmist again rightly says: ‘Wonderful are the surges of the sea; wonderful on high is the Lord’ (Ps. 92). For when the world wonderfully raised itself against the life of the elect into waves of persecution, the Creator of heavenly things more wonderfully laid it low by the exalted power of the preachers. For he showed that his servants could accomplish through miracles what earthly powers had swollen to accomplish through anger.”

The Lord also fittingly says through Jeremiah, outwardly describing while inwardly declaring:

> I have set the [Col. 0152C] sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting ordinance which it shall not pass; and they shall be moved and shall not prevail; its waves shall swell and shall not pass over it. (Jer. 5)

The Lord set sand as a boundary for the sea because, to break the glory of the world, he chose the lowly and poor. The waves of this sea swell when worldly powers leap up into the tumult of persecution. But they cannot cross the sand, because they are broken by the miracles and humility of the despised apostles and martyrs. Yet while the sea rages, while it rises in the waves of its madness, and while it is trodden down by the manifestation of inward power, the holy Church advances and, through the successive stages of time, rises to the condition proper to its order.

[Col. 0152D] Truly, the apostles of Jesus Christ and the holy martyrs, by Gospel preaching and by the shedding of the blood of their own bodies, recalled the whole world to the worship of God; and, like cultivators of fields, from land they have cultivated they render to God even today fruit most sweet. Rejoicing in the Holy Spirit, the prophet Amos spoke of them:

> Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when the ploughman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes the sower of seed; the mountains shall drip sweetness, and all the hills shall be cultivated. (Amos 9)

By all these is figured the entire order of preachers—namely, apostles and ecclesiastical men. Allegorically, the days are coming, that is, after the resurrection and ascension of the Lord [Col. 0153A], in which the ploughman—that is, the order of teachers, namely the apostles and the other teachers—shall plough up their own hearts and those of others with faith and love, drive out the hardness of unbelief, and bring forth the fruit of good works. These ploughmen, namely the holy apostles, overtake the reapers: that is, those who, by preaching the word of God, tear people away from worldly cares so as to store them in the holy Church.

By the treader of grapes are understood the apostles and holy martyrs, who, trampling death and the devil himself, pour out the must of their blood by suffering for Christ’s name, in order to offer others examples of virtue. God sends all these into the Church so that they may sow the seed of God’s word in the hearts of the elect, separate them from worldly cares, and themselves lay down their lives for the flocks entrusted to them [Col. 0153B]. And one takes hold of another because one succeeds another. Therefore, as has already been said, the Son of God and of the Virgin foretold through the prophets that his resurrection would take place, and showed us through the apostles that it had taken place. Hence he speaks to his Church through the prophet Zephaniah, saying:

> Wait for me on the day of my resurrection to come, for my judgment is to gather the nations—namely, to the faith—and to assemble kingdoms, that is, the leaders of perverse doctrines, who shall be consumed by divine fire; and I shall pour out upon them my indignation and all the wrath of my fury. (Zeph. 3)

As though the Son of God and of the Virgin were speaking more plainly to the holy Church, his bride: “Wait for me, casting idols away from yourself; and on the future day of my resurrection, when I rise from the death which I shall suffer for your redemption, I shall regenerate you through baptism to eternal life; I shall illuminate the eyes of your heart by the Holy Spirit so that you may know me; I shall strengthen you with the bread of the heavenly word; I shall make you drunk with the wine of Gospel preaching. Therefore, O bride, wait for me, so that you may rightly be able to say with the Prophet: ‘My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I shall sing and make melody in my glory’” (Ps. 56).

These things may also be understood allegorically of the first coming, when the devil was trampled down, every error removed, and even earthly works destroyed, and the apostles spoke in all tongues. It was then also that, after vices and sins, God seemed to rise in us; all are gathered to the faith [Col. 0153D], and are kindled by fear of God’s wrath with the divine fire by which every earthly work in them is devoured. Again the Lord speaks, saying:

> For in the fire of my zeal the whole earth shall be devoured. For then I shall restore to the peoples a chosen speech, that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder. (Zeph. 3)

“And it shall be restored,” he says, “to all, one language, so that each person, having laid aside his error, may return to the ancient speech of confession of God; so that with one mouth they may call upon God, confessing that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father, at whose name every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2).

[Note: [Col. 0153D] These words are not the text but the Gloss; this must be observed lest anyone be confused.]

[Col. 0154A] These may also be spoken of the second coming, when, after the vices of the present age, as the Church awaits the coming of the bridegroom, the nations will be gathered for judgment and kings assembled in the place of punishments. Then the wrath of God will be poured out, punishing every evil, where the mighty shall endure mighty torments, while the one who has sinned less shall quickly obtain pardon. “In the fire of my zeal,” he says, “the earth shall be devoured,” because, with nations gathered for judgment and kings for punishments, whatever is earthly and belongs to works of the flesh shall be consumed throughout the whole world; so that, when briars and thorns have been burned in all who are saved, each of them may return to the ancient speech of confession of God, praising God for ever and ever and, with united zeal, serve him continually in his temple.

[Col. 0154B] It is most fitting that thanks and praise should be rendered to him by angels and human beings not only in the present life but also in the life to come: for he does not cease mercifully to call to himself through the prophets and apostles all people, though unworthy—that is, the whole Church. Thus, through the prophet Hosea, displaying the sweetness of his love and kindness, he speaks to that same Church, saying:

> I shall betroth you to myself for ever; I shall betroth you to myself in righteousness and judgment, and in mercy and compassion. (Hos. 2)

Circumcision given to Abraham was a sign between God and his seed. It follows:

> And I shall betroth you to myself in faith, and you shall know that I am the Lord.

Observe the mercy of the husband, namely God. A harlot, long given to fornication, returns to her husband [Col. 0154C], and is said not merely to be reconciled to her husband but to be betrothed. Observe also the difference between God’s marriages and human marriages: human beings make virgins corrupt; God, united to harlots, restores them as virgins.

Again he says:

> And it shall be on that day: I shall hear, says the Lord, and I shall hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth. And the earth shall hear the grain, wine, and oil.

As though he said: “It shall be on that day, namely, when I have betrothed you to myself in faith: I shall hear the heavens, that is, the apostles; and they shall hear the earth, namely that earth from which truth has sprung, and in which the master of the household—that is, Christ—sows good seed; and they shall water it with the rain of the heavenly word. And the earth shall hear the grain, wine, and oil.” This pertains particularly to the apostles, who, beginning from Jerusalem, by their preaching [Col. 0154D] and miracles make the hearts of hearers bear fruit everywhere. They are seed when they hear from the Lord; they are sowers when “their sound has gone forth into all the earth.”

He continues: “And I shall betroth you to myself for ever.” First, God the Father betrothed her to himself in Abraham, or when he led her out of Egypt, that he might have her as an everlasting wife. Second, on Mount Sinai, he gave her the righteousness and judgment of the Law as a bridal gift, joining mercy to the Law, so that if she sinned she might be taken captive, but if she repented she might be recalled. Third, he betrothed her to himself in the coming of his Son: this is in faith in the holy Trinity, in which faith believers at once know him whom formerly they denied. Thus this harlot [Col. 0155A], who had formerly been joined in the everlasting embrace of her husband, because she worshipped idols in Egypt, is received again through the Law; but because she transgressed it, and the prophets, as it were the bridegroom’s companions, were killed, the Son came a third time.

When he had been crucified and had risen from the dead, the Church was betrothed—no longer in the righteousness of the Law, but in the faith and grace of the Gospel and in knowledge of the truth. Jerome: “According to the letter, it may be understood that temporal goods are promised to believers at Christ’s coming, so that through him, who is God’s seed, all things may run in their proper order, as they were created from the beginning, and may serve the benefit of humankind. Yet after such great goods the Jews still await the Antichrist bodily. Spiritually, the heavens, which declare [Col. 0155B] God’s glory, were heard when they pleaded for the Canaanite woman (Matt. 15) and for Peter’s mother-in-law (Luke 4). And the heavens—that is, the apostles—hear the earth, namely human beings, who are the Church: though not yet perfect, nevertheless keeping God’s commandments.

“And the earth—that is, the Church—hears the grain, wine, and oil: that is, it so furnishes spiritual understanding of the Old and New Testaments as to gladden the hearts of its hearers, adapting its teaching to the capacity of each. And all these—the heaven and the earth, namely the apostles and the universal Church—shall hear Israel: that is, they shall bring the seed of God’s word to the effect of action, so that one seed may yield a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold” (Matt. 13).

Certainly the seed, that is, the teaching of the apostles, brought forth a hundredfold fruit, because through their preaching a multitude of Gentiles and a certain part of the Jews came to faith in Christ. At the passion and resurrection of the Son of God and of the Virgin, although the Jews saw innumerable signs and miracles, one part of them nevertheless remained damnably in its wickedness, while another obtained the grace of baptism.

These two baskets indeed prefigured them, which the prophet Jeremiah foretold had been shown to him by the Lord before the temple of the Lord. For he says:

> The Lord showed me, and behold, two baskets—that is, two hampers—full of figs before the temple of the Lord. And one basket had very good figs; but the other basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten. (Jer. 24)

Some interpret the two baskets of good and bad figs as the Synagogue and the Church in the Law and the Gospel, the Jewish and Christian peoples, hell and the kingdom of heaven: one of these pertains to the punishments of sinners, the other to the dwelling-place of the saints. But we, holding with the Apostle that the Law is good and holy and the commandment good and holy, and that the God of both Testaments is one (Rom. 7), should refer these things to the Jews who either believed or did not believe at the Lord’s coming. Thus those who cried to Pilate, “Crucify, crucify him” [Col. 0156A] (Matt. 27), are the basket of bad figs; while those who believed should be referred to the good figs and the excellent basket.

The basket of good figs, therefore, consisted of Peter and Paul, John and James, Andrew and Thomas, the other apostles, and all the disciples, who sowed the word of life throughout the world. But the basket of bad figs consisted of Caiaphas, Annas, and the other unbelievers, who condemned themselves and their children before those children were born, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (ibid.). The sweetness of the good figs therefore signifies the sweetness and pleasantness of the Gospels. The bitterness of the bad figs, which could not be eaten, foreshadows the cunning and unbelief of the Jews. In Christ’s Church, then, the basket of good [Col. 0156B] figs was the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who resisted his adversaries courageously and willingly shed their blood in order to bring it to a state of uprightness.

Mystically, Gedaliah [Note: [Col. 0155D] These remarks are drawn from the Gloss on Jeremiah, ch. 40.], whose name means “made great by the Lord,” prefigured these most noble preachers of the Church. By the Lord’s will they are perfected, so that those who fear the Lord may have in them refuge and consolation. They lay down their lives for those subject to them, and against the faithless they set up shields of protection after the example of Jesus Christ, their master. Persisting faithfully in their office unto death, they are persecuted by the wicked, just as the innocent Gedaliah was killed by the treacherous Ishmael. Therefore God established the holy Church for the praise and glory of his name [Col. 0156C], set holy apostles in it for its guardianship and defence, gave it glorious martyrs as models of virtue, and, when the time of persecution had passed, bestowed upon it eminent teachers of the Old and New Testaments to water it abundantly with the rains of heavenly teaching.

Praising God in his works, blessed Job speaks figuratively of all these as though of heavenly stars, saying:

> Who makes Arcturus, Orion, the Hyades, and the inner regions of the south. (Job 9)

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0156D] *Morals on Job*, book IX, ch. 6]: “The discourse of truth does not follow the empty fables of Hesiod, Aratus, and Callimachus [Note: [Col. 0156D] The manuscripts corruptly read ‘Calli and Marci.’], as though, in naming Arcturus, it imagined the last of seven stars to be the tail of a bear, or as though Orion, a mad lover, held a sword [Col. 0156D]. These names of stars were invented by worshippers of carnal wisdom. But Sacred Scripture uses these same words so that the matters it seeks to convey may be expressed through familiar names. For if it named the stars of which it wished to speak by names unknown to us, then the human being for whom Scripture itself was made would doubtless not know what he heard.

“Thus, in sacred discourse, God’s wise people draw their speech from the wise of the world; just as, in Scripture, God himself—the Creator of all things—takes upon himself the language of human passion for humanity’s benefit, saying: ‘For I repent that I made human beings upon the earth’ [Col. 0157A] (Gen. 6). Yet it is certainly established that he who sees all things before they come to pass never reconsiders in repentance after doing anything. What wonder, then, if spiritual persons use the words of carnal people, when the ineffable Spirit himself, Creator of all things, frames in himself the language of flesh in order to draw flesh toward his own understanding?

“Therefore, when we hear familiar names of stars in Sacred Scripture, we know what stars are being discussed; but once we consider the stars that are described, it remains for us to rise from their movements to the mysteries of spiritual understanding. For, according to the letter, nothing remarkable is said in declaring that God made Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades, since it is undoubtedly true that there is absolutely nothing in the world which he did not make. Thus the holy man [Col. 0157B] says that the Lord made these things because he understands that they signify those realities which occur spiritually.

“For what is expressed by the name Arcturus, which is set upon the axis of heaven and shines with the rays of seven stars, except the universal Church, which in John’s Apocalypse is represented by seven Churches and seven lampstands? (Rev. 1). Because it contains within itself the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit of grace, illuminated by the brightness of supreme power, it shines as though from the axis of truth. It should also be considered that Arcturus constantly turns and never sets, because the holy Church unceasingly endures the persecutions of the wicked yet continues without failure until the end of the world. For often the reprobate who persecuted it even to extermination thought that they had wholly extinguished it; but it returned all the more completely to the condition proper to it because it had laboured by dying in the hands of persecutors [Col. 0157C]. Thus Arcturus, while turning, rises; for then the holy Church advances more powerfully in virtue when it is more ardently wearied for the truth.

“Therefore Orion is fittingly added immediately after Arcturus. Orions arise in the very season of winter; by their rising they stir up storms and trouble sea and land. What, then, is signified after Arcturus by the Orions except the martyrs? For when the holy Church rises to the condition of preaching, the martyrs, destined to endure the afflictions of persecutors, came before the face of heaven as though in winter. When they arose, sea and land were disturbed, because the Gentile world, grieving that its customs were destroyed by the appearance of their strength, stirred up against their death not only the angry and turbulent but even the peaceful. Thus winter grew fierce from the Orions, because, when the steadfastness of the holy apostles and martyrs shone forth, the cold minds of unbelievers were aroused into the storm of persecution. Therefore heaven brought forth Orions when the holy Church sent martyrs. Because they dared to speak what was right to the unlearned, they fully bore the weight of the adversity of cold.

“He then fittingly adds the Hyades, which come forth before the face of heaven as spring grows young and appear when the sun is already exerting the strength of its heat [Col. 0158A]. They adhere to the beginning of that constellation which the wise of the world call Taurus, from which the sun begins to increase and rises more fervently to extend the length of the day. What, then, is signified after the Orions by the name of the Hyades except the teachers of the holy Church? After the martyrs had departed, they came into the world’s notice at the time when the Church shines more clearly and, with the winter of unbelief driven away, the sun of truth burns more intensely in believers’ hearts. When the storm of persecution had been removed and the long nights of unbelief ended, they arose in the holy Church when the brighter springtime of faith was already opening for it.

“Nor without reason are the holy teachers signified by the name Hyades. In Greek, *hyetos* (ὑετός) means ‘rain,’ and the Hyades received their name from rains [Col. 0158B] because, when they rise, they undoubtedly bring showers. They are fittingly expressed by the title Hyades: brought forth, as it were, before the face of heaven for the established condition of the universal Church, they pour the rain of Gospel teaching upon the dry ground of the human breast. For if the utterance of holy preaching were not rain, Moses would never have said: ‘Let my speech be awaited like rain’ (Deut. 32); nor would the Lord have said through Isaiah: ‘I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it’ (Isa. 5). And again: ‘The stars—or drops—of rain have been withheld’ (Jer. 3): namely Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades, which bring rains.”

[Note: [Col. 0157D] The words enclosed in parentheses are absent here in the edition, which reads only: “And that which we cited a little [Col. 0158D] earlier (ch. 3), concerning why the stars of rain were forbidden.”]

“Therefore, as the Hyades come with rains, the sun is drawn to higher expanses of heaven, because, as the learning of teachers appears and our mind is watered by the rain of preaching, the warmth of faith increases. And the watered earth advances to fruitfulness when the light of heaven glows: for we bring forth more abundant fruits of good work when, through the flame of sacred instruction, we burn more brightly in the heart. As heavenly knowledge is shown to us more and more daily through them, the springtime of inward light opens to us, so that a new warmth may shine in our minds and, known to us by their words, may daily gleam brighter through itself. For as the world’s end presses on, heavenly knowledge advances and grows more abundantly with time. Hence Daniel says: ‘Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied’ (Dan. 12). Hence, in the earlier part of the Revelation, the angel says to John: ‘Seal up what the seven thunders spoke’ (Rev. 10). Yet at the end of the same Revelation he commands: ‘Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book’ (Rev. 22). The earlier part of Revelation is commanded to be sealed, while this is prohibited at its end, because whatever lay hidden in the beginnings of the holy Church is daily revealed by the end.

“Some, however, think that the Hyades are named from the Greek letter called Y. If this is so, it does not oppose the meaning which we have stated, for teachers are not unfittingly represented by those stars which take their name from letters. Yet although the Hyades do not differ from the appearance of that letter, it is nevertheless certain that *hyetos* means rain and that, when they rise, they bring rains.”

Let us hear also what blessed Isidore, teacher of Spain and our patron, says concerning these same stars [Note: [Col. 0159D] *Etymologies*, book III, ch. 71]:

> The first of the constellations is Arctos, fixed upon the axis and revolving with seven stars that turn within it. Its name is Greek; in Latin it is called *Ursa* [Bear]. Because it turns in the manner of a wagon, our people called it *Septentrio* [the northern constellation]. For *triones* are properly ploughing oxen, so called because they wear down the earth, as though *teriones*. The proximity of the axis causes the Septentriones not to set, because they are fixed upon it.
>
> It is called Arctophylax because it follows Arctos—that is, Helice, the Bear. It is also called Boötes because it clings to the wagon: a constellation visible by many stars, among which is Arcturus [Col. 0159B]. Arcturus is a star placed after the tail of the Greater Bear in the constellation Boötes; hence it is called Arcturus, as if *ἄρκτου οὖρα* [“the Bear’s tail”], because it is set at Boötes’ breast. It rises in the autumnal season.
>
> Orion shines before the tracks of Taurus and is called Orion from *urina* [water, urine], that is, from an inundation of waters. Rising in winter, it disturbs sea and land with waters and storms. The Latins call it *Jugulum* [the Collarbone], because it is armed like a sword and terrible and brilliant with starlight. If all its stars shine, fair weather is foretold; if its blade is darkened, a storm is seen to be imminent.
>
> The Hyades are so called *ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑεῖν*, that is, from moisture and rains. For rains in Greek are called *hyetos* (ὑετός). By their rising they produce rains; hence the Latins also called them *Suculae* [Little Sows], because when they rise the signs of rains appear. Of them Virgil says:
>
> > Arcturus and the rainy Hyades.
>
> There are seven stars in the brow of Taurus, and they rise in the springtime.

Having heard these things taught by blessed Isidore, we must return again to those matters which we left above.

Thus holy Job, contemplating in the Spirit the order of our redemption and considering the differing offices of teachers—namely evangelists, apostles, martyrs, and confessors—marvels; and, marvelling, cries out:

> Who alone stretches out the heavens, who makes Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades.

Gregory: “For when the heavens had been stretched out, the Lord formed Arcturus [Col. 0159D], because, having brought the apostles into honour, he founded the Church in heavenly conduct. When Arcturus had been formed, he made Orion, because, after strengthening the faith of the universal Church, he brought forth martyrs against the storms of the world. And when Orions had been brought forth, he produced the Hyades, because, as martyrs became strong against adversities, he bestowed the teaching of masters to water the dryness of human hearts. These, therefore, are the orders of spiritual stars, which, while eminent in supreme virtues, always shine from heavenly places.

“But after these things, what remains except that the holy Church, receiving the fruit of its labour, should attain to see the inner places of the heavenly homeland? Therefore, after saying fittingly, ‘Who makes Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades,’ he immediately adds: ‘and the inner regions of the south’ [Col. 0160A]. What, in this passage, is signified by the south but the fervour of the Holy Spirit? When anyone is filled with this, that person burns with love for the spiritual homeland. Hence, in the Bridegroom’s voice, it is said in the Song of Songs: ‘Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and let its spices flow’ (Song 4). When the south wind comes, the north wind rises and departs: with the coming of the Holy Spirit, the ancient enemy is driven out and leaves the mind which he had bound in numbness. The south wind breathes upon the Bridegroom’s garden so that its spices may flow, because when the Holy Spirit fills the holy Church with the powers of his gifts, it scatters from her far and wide the fragrances of good works.

“The inner regions of the south [Col. 0160B] are those hidden orders of angels and the most secret recesses of the heavenly homeland, which the warmth of the Holy Spirit fills. The souls of the saints attain there, both now when stripped of their bodies and afterwards when their bodies are restored; and there, like stars, they are hidden in secret places. There, as by day and as at burning noon, the fire of the sun is kindled more ardently, because the brightness of the Creator, the darkness of our mortality now pressed down, is seen more openly; and, like the ray of a sphere, it rises to higher expanses when Truth illuminates us more subtly concerning itself. There the light of inward contemplation is seen without the intervening shadow of changeability; there the heat of supreme light endures without any darkness of numbness; there the invisible choirs of angels gleam like stars in hidden places [Col. 0160C], and cannot now be seen by human beings precisely because they are more deeply suffused with the flame of true light.

“Therefore it is very wonderful that, after sending forth the apostles, the Lord stretched out the heavens; that, walking upon the waves of the sea, he restrained the swelling violence of persecution and calmed it; that, when the Church was established, he set Arcturus; that, after martyrs had been strengthened against adversities, he sent Orions; that, after teachers had been filled in tranquility, he supplied Hyades. But after these things it is still more wonderful that he restored for us the bosom of the heavenly homeland, as though the inner regions of the south. All this which is seen, as it were, upon the face of heaven in the divine dispensation is beautiful; but there something far more beautiful and incomparable is found.

“Thus the Bridegroom again rightly says in praise of his bride: ‘How beautiful you are, my friend; how beautiful you are! Your eyes are like doves, apart from that which lies hidden within’ (Song 4) [Col. 0160D]. He declares her beautiful and repeats that she is beautiful, because one beauty of hers is that of conduct, in which she is now seen, and another is that of rewards, in which she will then be raised through the sight of her Creator. Her members—that is, all the elect—walk in simplicity toward all things; therefore her eyes are called doves, because they are irradiated with great light and shine with the miracles of signs. But however great is every miracle that can be seen, more wonderful is that inward miracle which cannot now be seen; therefore it is fittingly added there: ‘apart from that which lies hidden within.’ Thus blessed Job makes this known to us [Col. 0161A] when he commends the inner regions of the south.”

Therefore, with the Bridegroom absent, the holy Church groans amid the straits of this present world, as Jeremiah laments in her person, saying:

They heard that I groan, and there is none to comfort me (Lam. 1). As though the holy Church said more plainly: “My enemies have heard that I groan, while Jesus Christ, my Bridegroom, is absent, and there is none to comfort me,” namely because the Holy Spirit has been driven away. Allegorically, the Church laments her own evils and those of her people—namely persecutions and martyrdoms. Hence the letter *Sin* is placed before this passage, a letter sounding like the teeth: this is the weeping of teeth, of which we read in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep” (Song 4), etc. These are those who do not require the milk of infancy but eat solid [Col. 0161B] bread, as was said to Peter: “Slay and eat” (Acts 10). It is as though He said: “I have set before you not only bread to eat, but also creeping things.” For such persons, by the sharpness of doctrine, know how to slay vices and to transfer creeping things—that is, people of diverse nations—into Christ’s body.

The functions of teeth, however, differ: some cut, some grind, some form sounds. So too among the mystical teeth, some are like flocks of shorn sheep: stripped of old age, they provide their offspring with the milk of doctrine and the garments of virtues. Others, whiter than milk, are adorned by the beauty of their office and serve the word to their hearers with the utmost refinement. Hence the Apostle says: “Solid food is for the mature, who have their senses exercised” (Heb. 5)—namely the holy [Col. 0161C] apostles and the doctors of the Church.

For he says: “They heard that I groan, and there is none to comfort me.” The enemies hear the Bride—that is, the holy Church—weeping, for she feels that the Bridegroom is absent. Though He is always present in majesty, He nevertheless permits His Bride to be shaken by temptations, so that she may always be watchful and fearful lest she accept the corruptor’s suggestion. “They heard,” he says, “that I groan”: what they had always desired, what they had never expected. “There is none to comfort me,” because the Holy Spirit does not dwell in a body subject to sins; and daily my evil is multiplied—namely the temptations of my children and the perils of the present age.
