Again she says: “All my enemies heard of my evil; they rejoiced” (Lam. 1), etc. The enemies of the Church are demons, [Col. 0161D] heretics, false Christians, and pagan persecutors. For the Jews grievously afflicted her in her very Head, Christ, and in His members—that is, in the apostles, martyrs, and other faithful—because, after killing some, they drove others from their territories. Therefore let Christ’s Bride, as though making complaint of her enemies, say to her Bridegroom: “All my enemies heard of my evil”: that is, demons and the other persecutors heard of the persecutions of the apostles, the sufferings of Stephen and of the other martyrs, and the afflictions of my members. “They rejoiced, because You did it,” that is, by a just judgment You permitted it to happen. Hence it is said: “I am the Lord making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45), that is, permitting it by just judgment. He permitted this so that [Col. 0162A] the Church might suffer on earth, at the hands of adversaries, hatred for His name, and might thereby be crowned by Him more gloriously in heaven.

It follows: “You have brought the day of consolation, and they shall become like me” (Lam. 1). As though Christ’s Bride, namely the holy Church, entirely awaiting consolation from that same heavenly Bridegroom and not doubting that those who afflicted her will be punished by Him, said: “You have brought the day of consolation,” that is, You will bring the day of judgment; and those who persecuted me “shall become like me,” namely captive and afflicted, as I was. This applies more particularly to the Church, because after the final captivity no consolation remains for the Jews and the other persecutors of the Church. On the day of judgment the Lord will render consolation to the good and punishments to the evil.

In this [Col. 0162B] present life the soul laments its losses of virtues, saying: “They heard that I groan”—namely the enemies, concerning the evils I endure. “There is none,” it says, “to comfort me”: the sorrow of the distressed soul is increased because the One in whom it hopes delays His help. It also grieves unspeakably because the invisible enemies, who formerly flattered it, now mock it. Conscience, moreover, insults it more severely by accusing it, and the vices that formerly seemed sweet are revealed as bitter. Those who previously seemed friends, and who ought to feel compassion, if perhaps they know its crimes, mock it as enemies. Hence David says: “Those who watched over my soul took counsel together, saying: ‘God has forsaken him’” (Ps. 70).

Cassiodorus: “A burden which is not shared is heavier.” [Col. 0162C] They themselves said by common counsel: “God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him.” As though they said among themselves in their proper sequence: “That God whom he makes his God has forsaken him.” Seeing him worn down by calamities, they suppose that he has been abandoned by God. Therefore pursue him as one slow to escape, and seize him as one weak; for there is no one to rescue him once seized. But every servant of God conquers all the adversities of the present world with God’s aid. The soul therefore, as was said, has teeth—namely virtues and discerning thoughts—which know how to divide prosperity from adversity, seek the consoling Holy Spirit, and hope in God’s mercy.

Therefore it added: “You have brought the day of consolation,” etc. [Col. 0162D] For the faithful soul knows that, after afflictions, pardon is given to the penitent and punishments are repaid to those who mock. Thus God the Father, from the beginning, through His Word coeternal and consubstantial with Himself, has never ceased to choose prophets and apostles, and through them to console His Church and separate it from unbelievers. This Word, coeternal with God the Father, came from the Lord to Jeremiah the prophet, in order to urge those same apostles and teachers to preach, saying: “Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Jer. 11), etc.

As though He said more plainly: “Hear the Word which was in the beginning with God, and the Word was God.” It is as though God the Father spoke to the prophets, apostles, and other teachers of the Church, saying: “Hear the word of this covenant,” namely of My only-begotten Son, sent from Me to you for your salvation. Therefore obey Him in all things whatsoever He shall say to you. Of Him Moses says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like myself; you shall hear Him according to all that He shall speak to you” (Deut. 18). Of Him also God the Father said to the three disciples—Peter, James, and John—when they saw Him transfigured on the mountain: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear Him” (Matt. 17). As though He said: “Keep and do everything whatsoever He shall say to you.” For this is the benefit of preachers: that God’s word should come to each individual. For what profit is it to me to have come into the world, if I do not possess that Word which came to the prophets? [Col. 0163B] And He said to the disciples: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

Therefore let God the Father say to the prophets, apostles, and ecclesiastical persons: “Hear the word of this covenant,” that is, of the great counsel; “and speak to the men of Judah,” namely Christians, who are truly confessors of Christ; “and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem,” namely of the Church, which is the city of the great King and the vision of peace. For peace is multiplied and seen in her through Christ Himself, who is the Father’s Word. “Jews” is interpreted as “confessors,” from Judah the patriarch, from whose tribe the Lord arose; and of him it is truly said: “Judah, your brethren shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies” (Gen. 49). Therefore, when the word of preaching is commanded to be addressed to the men of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, it refers to Christians who are truly confessors of Christ.

Let the prophets and apostles, then, speak the word of the Lord’s covenant: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Cursed is the man who has not heard the words of this covenant, which I commanded your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying: Hear My voice, and do all that I command you; and you shall be My people, and I will be your God” (Jer. 11). [Col. 0163C] As though He said: “Not by privilege of descent, not by the prerogative of circumcision, not by sabbath rest, but because of obedience does Israel become My people and I become its God.” Here, that is, in the Law, He speaks to servants; but in the Gospel, to friends: “You are My friends,” He says, “if you do what I command you” (John 15). And again: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends; because the servant does not know what his master does” (ibid.). When, however, they have become friends, they pass from being friends to being sons. “But as many as received Him, He gave them power to become the sons of God” (John 1), etc. To friends and sons He commands: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5). In naming perfection, He signifies not equality but likeness. In the Law obedience to commandments is commanded; in the Gospel likeness to God is promised to the Church’s children.

“Cursed,” He says, “is the man who has not heard the word of this covenant.” [Col. 0164A] The Jews, therefore, are cursed because they did not hear God’s testament when He brought them out of Egypt. But we who believe in Christ obey His testament handed down through Moses, because we are blessed in the seed of Abraham—that is, in Christ. For this purpose the Son of God chose the holy apostles and sent them to preach throughout every region of the world: so that, like clouds pouring water, they might pour the words of this covenant into the hearts of all nations under heaven—namely, that they should believe Him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to be one true God. He also commanded these same disciples to preach profound and mystical things to the more perfect, but plain things to the unlearned, that is, to those of lesser understanding.

Hence blessed Job, praising God in His works, says:

> “Who binds the waters in the clouds, so that they do not burst forth together downward” (Job 26).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0163D] Book XVII of the *Morals*, chapter 14]: “What is meant here by water but knowledge, and what by clouds but preachers—that is, the holy apostles? That water is sometimes called knowledge in sacred discourse, we learn from the testimony of Solomon, who says: ‘Deep water is speech from a man’s mouth; and an overflowing torrent is a fountain of wisdom’ (Prov. 18). David the prophet testifies that water signifies knowledge, saying: ‘Dark water in the clouds of the air’ (Ps. 17), that is, hidden knowledge in the prophets. For before the Lord’s coming, while pregnant with immense mysteries in hidden sacraments, their understanding was dark to the eyes of beholders. By the name of clouds, however, what else is denoted here but preachers, namely the holy apostles? Sent throughout the regions of the world, they knew how to rain in words, flash in miracles, and terrify by threats. Foreseeing this long before, the prophet Isaiah said: ‘Who are these that fly like clouds?’ (Isa. 60).

“Since, therefore, blessed Job, filled with the prophetic spirit, in this saying of his desires the beginnings of the nascent Church to arise for God’s praise, he endeavors to set forth its order beginning with the apostles’ preaching: for they took the greatest care to preach what was plain and comprehensible to unlearned peoples, not what was sublime and difficult. For if they had poured forth in speech the holy knowledge—which is here denoted by the name water—as they drew it into their hearts through the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0164D] they would have overwhelmed their hearers by its immensity rather than watered them. Hence, with knowledge bound up within so that it might not burst forth all together downward, that cloud, nourishing its hearers by the dripping of words, said: ‘I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal. As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food’ (1 Cor. 3).

“For who could have endured it if one caught up to the third heaven, caught up into paradise, and hearing even secret words which it would not be permitted a human being to utter, had opened such immense depths of heavenly knowledge? Or whose strength as a hearer would not be overwhelmed if the immensity of this water, which could be drawn within, had flowed out in a flood to the extent that the tongue of flesh was able? But so that unlearned hearers may advance not by a flood of knowledge but by the measured dripping of preaching, God binds the waters in the clouds, so that they do not burst forth together downward. That is, He moderates the preaching of teachers, so that the weakness of hearers, nourished by the teachers’ dew, may grow strong.

“This is aptly related in the Gospel by a mystical narrative, where it is said: ‘Jesus entered Peter’s boat and asked him to put out a little from the land; and, sitting, He taught the crowds’ (Luke 5). What else is represented by Peter’s boat than the Church entrusted to Peter? So that the Lord may preach from it to the crowds gathering together, He commands it to be moved a little from land. He commands it not to be taken into the deep, yet to be removed from land; thereby clearly indicating that His preachers ought to proclaim to unlearned peoples neither things too lofty concerning heaven nor yet earthly things. Thus water is bound in clouds because, when the knowledge of preachers speaks to weak minds, it is forbidden to say as much as it is able to perceive. For often, if the hearers’ heart is injured by the immensity of the word, the teacher’s tongue is punished for indiscretion.

“Hence it is written: ‘If anyone opens a cistern, or digs one and does not cover it, and an ox or an ass falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall pay the price of the animals’ (Exod. 21). What is it to open a cistern but to penetrate the mysteries of Holy Scripture by strong understanding? And what is understood by the ox and the ass—that is, the clean and the unclean animal—but the believer and unbeliever? Therefore, whoever digs a cistern must cover it lest an ox or ass fall into it. That is, whoever now understands high things in sacred discourse should cover its lofty senses with silence for those unable to receive them, lest by the scandal of the mind he destroy either a little believer or an unbeliever who might have believed. For he owes the price because of the death of the animals, since he has allowed that for which he is held guilty and bound to do penance. Therefore the cistern must be covered, because lofty knowledge must be concealed before immature minds, lest that by which the hearts of teachers are raised to the heights become the means by which the weakness of hearers falls into the depths.

“Thus it is rightly said: ‘Who binds the waters in the clouds, so that they do not burst forth together downward.’ For they would burst forth all together if all the knowledge possessed issued from the speaker’s mouth before weak hearers—if the whole fullness of preaching were poured out at once and retained nothing for those advancing. It is fitting, then, that one who preaches should consider the capacity of the hearer, so that the preaching itself may grow together with the growth of its hearer. Every preacher should act in the way God acts with him: he should by no means disclose to the weak everything he understands, because, for as long as he is himself weakened by mortal flesh, he does not understand all heavenly things. He should therefore not preach to the unlearned as much as he knows, because he himself is unable to know how great the heavenly mysteries are.

“The preachers of the holy Church, therefore, should preach according to the capacity of their hearers, as has been said, so that in their hearts they may cut away vices, nurture virtues, impose upon all the measure of the Christian religion, and render them fit for the building of heavenly Jerusalem. For God gives the teachers of the Old and New Testaments a measure for preaching, as the prophet Ezekiel speaks figuratively of them, saying:

> ‘I saw a man standing in the gate, who had a measuring rod in his hand; and he measured the building and its gates, and he measured the threshold of the gate, beside the inner vestibule of the gate, with one rod’ (Ezek. 40).

“This man is Christ, who holds in His hand the measuring rod—that is, the measure of Holy Scripture—in His power. With it He measures each threshold, the inner and the outer; that is, He orders the life of the saints of the Old and New Testaments, and through them governs the conduct of all the faithful and corrects vices.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0165D] These passages are taken from Gregory, *Homily 15 on Ezekiel*. But Martin copies the Gloss rather than the Supreme Pontiff, as he likewise does in what follows]: “By the outer threshold we understand the fathers of the Old Testament, by whose preaching perverse deeds were punished; and by the inner threshold, the teachers of the New Testament, by whose doctrine the mind is restrained from unlawful thoughts. Those were outside because they did not see Christ in the flesh; yet they were not separated from the holy Church, because in mind, deed, and preaching they possessed these sacraments of faith. For as we are saved through faith in Christ’s past Passion, so they were saved through faith in that same Passion yet to come. They were outside, not outside [Col. 0166C] the mystery but outside its time. Evil shepherds, however, were never within but always without, and therefore were cast out by the Lord.”

Since, then, through the Passion and Resurrection of Jesus Christ His Son, the Lord had determined to cast from His presence the shepherds of the Synagogue—not shepherds, I say, but transgressors of the Law, namely the scribes and Pharisees—because of their iniquities, and to appoint the apostles in their place, He took care to declare this to them through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: “You have scattered My flock, driven them away, and have not visited them; and because you have done this, behold, I will visit upon you the evil of your deeds, says the Lord” (Jer. 23). Since every hope of the Jewish kingdom had failed, the discourse passes to the leaders of the Church: the Synagogue, [Col. 0166D] abandoned and condemned with her shepherds, and the word is addressed to the apostles, concerning whom it is said: “I will raise up shepherds over them,” etc.

“Behold,” He says, “I will gather the remnant of My people from all the lands to which I had driven them, and I will bring them back to their fields; and they shall increase and multiply” (ibid.). As though He said: “Behold, I and no other shall gather the remnant of My flock”—namely the Gentile people, wandering far and wide in sin—“from all the lands to which, because their sins demanded it, I had driven them; and I will bring them back to their fields,” that is, to the holy Church, so that there they may feed upon the verdant grasses of the holy Scriptures; “and there shall be one fold and one shepherd,” and they shall increase in virtues and multiply in a spiritual and new offspring.

Again He says: “And I will raise up shepherds over them, and they shall feed them.” With the shepherds of the Synagogue—namely the scribes and Pharisees—cast out, I will raise up over My people shepherds, namely apostles and ecclesiastical persons; and they shall feed them with the bread of God’s word. We can understand this tropologically of the Church’s rulers who do not govern the Lord’s sheep worthily. Once they are cast out and condemned, the people entrusted to good shepherds is saved, and the remnant is saved. Shepherds who teach heresy destroy the sheep; those who make schisms tear them apart and scatter them; those who persecute unjustly and act proudly drive them from the Church; they do not visit the weak in faith, and they withdraw their hand from the penitent. [Col. 0167B] The Lord has mercy upon all these, restoring their former pastures and removing evil shepherds. Good shepherds refresh holy animals—that is, faithful peoples—with their preaching, like angelic delicacies. The teaching of the holy Fathers, therefore, is a table of heavenly sweetness.

Hence Ezekiel the prophet, in a vision divinely shown to him, speaks figuratively, saying: “I saw in the vestibule of the inner gate two tables on this side and two on that, that upon them might be sacrificed the burnt offering for transgression and for sin” (Ezek. 40). Gregory: “Our gate, that is, the Catholic faith, has four tables in its inner vestibule, because the holy Church has received four orders of rulers for the instruction of the faithful. Hence the most blessed Paul says: ‘He,’ namely God, ‘gave some indeed as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers’ (Eph. 4); the latter are one order. Therefore, while these preach, they satisfy the Lord’s flock—that is, the faithful people—with spiritual sweetness.

“The outer gate also has four tables, namely the Synagogue: the chief priests, elders of the people, scribes, and Pharisees; these Pharisees were called teachers of the Law. Thus in each gate there are two tables on this side and two on that, because at its beginning the holy Church had apostles and prophets, namely prophets arising after the apostles. But now it has evangelists and teachers. Evangelists are those who announce to the peoples the joys of the heavenly homeland. The tables of the inner gate—that is, of the holy Church—have a burnt offering, because whether in the hearts of the apostles and prophets or in the minds of evangelists and teachers, the fire of the Holy Spirit has blazed and burns, consuming every intention and thought. The flame of God’s love, like a whole burnt offering, burns up at once all that it finds.

“These tables are made from squared stones, because, while they meditate daily on the words of sacred discourse, they are, as it were, built from squared stones for offering the burnt offering of prayer to the Lord. For the words of Holy Scripture are squared stones: they stand firm everywhere and are nowhere refuted. For in everything they narrate as past, in everything they proclaim as future, in everything they sound spiritually, and in everything they announce morally, [Col. 0168A] they stand firm, as it were, on a different side. Thus the hearts of saints are God’s tables, built from squared stones for a whole burnt offering, because those who always meditate upon the Lord’s words sacrifice themselves to the Lord from carnal life. Hence it is said: ‘The law of his God is in his heart’ (Ps. 36), etc.”

Cassiodorus: “ ‘The law of his God,’ that is, God’s commands, are in his heart, and, as it were, the heart accords with the tongue. And what does this avail him? Namely, that his steps shall not be tripped up. To trip up is to set before one’s feet the pit of an ambush. The sense is: the word in the heart frees one from the snares of the sinner, so that the steps of one who praises God may not be tripped up.”

Beyond doubt, one who meditates upon the law of the Lord day and night may also say with the Prophet: “In [Col. 0168B] my heart I have hidden Your sayings, that I may not sin against You” (Ps. 118). As though he said: “I have sought out Your commandments and committed them even to memory”; and this is “I have hidden Your sayings in my heart”: I have hidden what is stored up, namely from swine and dogs. Cassiodorus: “For it is a kind of sin to preach to the obstinate; and therefore, ‘I have hidden Your sayings, that I may not sin against You,’ who say: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine’ (Matt. 7). For it is a fault to make secret mysteries public to the unworthy, and, as it were, show the treasures of the Lord’s house to Babylonians. One does this either by flattery, to please the person to whom one reveals them; by greed, to gain something; by boastfulness, to appear to know more; or by careless loquacity, when a word once uttered without judgment flies forth irrevocably.”

[Col. 0168C] The discipline of silence must therefore be adopted, so that one first keeps silent before speaking. Hence it is said: “Let every person be swift to hear, but slow to speak and slow to anger” (Jas. 1). Therefore Isaiah, when the Lord said to him, “Cry out,” did not cry out until he had heard what he ought to cry, saying: “What shall I cry?” (Isa. 40). In the Gospel the Lord also compares the kingdom of heaven to a treasure hidden in a field. This is the treasure of wisdom and knowledge: when a person has found it, he hides it in his heart and does not disclose it (Matt. 13), as Mary kept all the Lord’s words, pondering them in her heart (Luke 2).

Therefore, as has been said, the hearts of saints are God’s tables: they meditate without ceasing on the Lord’s words, and from them refresh the Church’s little ones. Concerning these stones it is said through Isaiah: “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones” (Isa. 9). As though He said more plainly: “The bricks have fallen,” that is, the Jews; “but we shall build with squared stones,” that is, with the holy apostles, martyrs, and doctors of the Church, by whom the building of heavenly Jerusalem is constructed from living and chosen stones. From these the Christian people—that is, the vestibule—has four tables constructed, because it takes from the lives of the saints faith, upright life, patience, and kindness as an example.

Therefore God alone is to be adored, glorified, and loved above all by human beings and by every order of blessed spirits in heaven: He who, in the Son of His love, that is, in Christ, restored all things among angels and holy human beings. Concerning Him Jeremiah the prophet, taught by the Holy Spirit, says:

> “He makes the earth by His strength, prepares the world by His wisdom, and stretches out the heavens by His prudence” (Jer. 10).

As though he said: God the Father makes the earth by His strength—that is, He makes sinners righteous and holy; He prepares the world to serve Him by His wisdom, that is, by the Son, who is His strength, power, and wisdom; and by His prudence He stretches out the heavens, that is, He spreads the teaching of the apostles widely through the whole world. For He spoke and they were made; He commanded and they were created (Ps. 148), speaking thus to the Son: “Let Us make man in Our image and likeness” [Col. 0169B] (Gen. 1).

Of Him the prophet rightly adds again: “At His voice He gives a multitude of waters in heaven, and He raises clouds from the extremities of the earth” (Jer. 10). Every teaching of the Lord flows from heavenly things. Hence it is said: “The earth was moved, for the heavens distilled from the presence of God of Sinai, from the presence of God of Israel” (Ps. 67). Augustine: “ ‘The earth was moved,’ that is, earthly persons were stirred to faith in Christ. But from where did this come? ‘For,’ that is, because ‘the heavens’—namely the apostles—distilled rain, that is, grace; and this came ‘from the presence of God,’ that is, not from themselves but from God who is in them. It follows: ‘Mount Sinai, from the presence of the God of Israel’; understand: it distilled from the presence of God, and more than the others.

“Another reading has: ‘Mount Sinai distilled from the presence of the God of Israel’; that is, Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles, who distilled drops of doctrine more than all others. He is rightly signified by Mount Sinai because he was formerly brought forth into slavery from the Law which was given on Mount Sinai. Or according to the same reading: ‘which Mount Sinai distilled from the presence of the God of Israel.’ The heavens and mountains are the same: namely, the apostles are signified alike by heavens and mountains. Yet it does not say ‘mountains’ but ‘mount,’ expressing in the singular what it means in the plural, just as elsewhere it is said: ‘The heavens declare, and the firmament proclaims’ (Ps. 18): it signifies the same thing by ‘heavens’ and ‘firmament.’ The meaning is: ‘Mount Sinai,’ that is, the apostles, distilled from the presence of the God of Israel.

“Some Greek and Latin books, however, do not have this reading, namely, ‘Mount Sinai, from the presence of the God of Israel,’ but have: ‘from the presence of the God of Sinai, from the presence of the God of Israel.’ The sense is: the heavens—that is, the apostles—distilled from the presence of God. Of which God? Namely, the God of Sinai, the God of Israel: that is, the God who gave the Law to the people of Israel. For He who gave the Law through Moses in order to terrify also gives blessing through the apostles in order to deliver.”

What did the heavens distill? Rain: namely the voluntary doctrine of the grace of the Holy Spirit, given without merits by God’s will alone. “For He begot us voluntarily by the word of truth” (Jas. 1). “You will set apart this rain, O God, for Your inheritance,” namely the faithful, upon whom the rain descends in a flowing irrigation. That inheritance was weakened—that is, it recognized that it was nothing [Col. 0170A] of itself—but You perfected it, because strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12).

Alternatively: “You will set apart voluntary rain, O God, for Your inheritance.” And how will this happen? “For the heavens distilled,” that is, the apostles will distill “from the presence of the God of Sinai,” that is, from the knowledge of God who gives the Law on Sinai, “from the presence of the God of Israel.” I mean Israel not according to the flesh, but the true Israel, receiving grace and not relying upon carnal observance. For He gave the Law to terrify those relying on themselves; He also gave blessing to deliver those who hope in Him. Let David, king and prophet, therefore say: “You will set apart voluntary rain, O God, for Your inheritance.” “The heavens,” he says, “will distill.” And what will they distill? Voluntary rain: the shower of God’s word, bestowed voluntarily and not according to human merits, which You, O God, will set apart for Your inheritance—that is, for Your chosen ones. You will commend that rain only to such persons, because faith is not possessed by all; and the inheritance has been weakened, recognizing its sins and perceiving that nothing is to be attributed to itself. It is weakened, but You—in reality—have made it perfect. Hence the Apostle says: “I, who was a persecutor and a blasphemer, received mercy” (1 Tim. 1). Or thus: the inheritance was weakened in itself for enduring tribulations, but You strengthened it and so made it perfect.

Therefore let Jeremiah say of God’s omnipotence: “At His voice He gives a multitude of waters in heaven, and He raises clouds from the extremities of the earth” (Jer. 10). As though he said more plainly: By His voice God gives in heaven—that is, in the Church—a multitude [Col. 0170C] of waters, namely the manifold doctrine of the holy Scriptures. Hence comes the saying: “In the voice of Your cataracts” (Ps. 41), that is, of the apostles and prophets. “And He raises clouds from the extremities of the earth,” because He chose as preachers not the proud but the humble, not the rich but the poor: namely the contemptible apostles, who were fishermen, in order to destroy the swelling arguments of heretics and philosophers. Hence it is said: “God chose the weak and contemptible things of this world in order to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1).

Whoever therefore raises his mind in pride should not presume to preach to his neighbors. He alone will be able worthily to announce the Lord’s righteousness to others who has been grounded in humility. Hence: “Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be last of all” (Mark 9). Otherwise no one can be a cloud—that is, otherwise no one will be fit to water the hearts of hearers with the doctrine of heavenly rain.

Isidore [Note: [Col. 0169D] Book XIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 10]: “*Nebula* [mist] is so called from the same source as *nubila* [cloudiness], from *obnubere*, ‘to cover,’ that is, to cover the earth; or because it makes a cloud while flying. For moist valleys exhale mists, and they become clouds; hence cloudiness and snow. Mists seek the low places when the sky is clear, but the high places when it is cloudy.”

The Lord, therefore, as was said, raises clouds from the ends of the earth: clouds, I say, which know upon whom to bestow rain and from whom to withhold it—namely the holy apostles and [Col. 0171A] their successors, who, according to the grace and authority entrusted to them, water the hearts of the faithful with spiritual showers. These know well when and to whom they ought to bring forth the word of preaching. Of them it is said: “I shall command My clouds not to rain rain upon her” (Isa. 5), that is, not to rain the teaching of salvation upon the sinful nation. Again, to those doing God’s will it is promised: “I will give you rains in their seasons” (Lev. 26).

Moses, like a cloud, poured rain down from above, saying: “Let my discourse be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew upon the grass” (Deut. 32). And Isaiah says: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, because the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1). God does not bring forth the rain of heavenly doctrine from proud counselors, leaders, or rich persons, but from the humble hearts of preachers—namely apostles and teachers—because blessed are the poor in spirit, since to them has been entrusted the governance of the holy Church, which is called the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5; Luke 6). Hence in the Gospel the Lord, glorifying God the Father, said: “I confess to You, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11), that is, to the humble and simple, who rely not upon themselves but upon Your mercy.

Again Jeremiah adds in praise of the Creator: “He makes lightnings into rain and brings forth winds from His treasuries” (Jer. 10). God makes lightnings into rain when He terrifies and satisfies the parched hearts of human beings with flashing doctrine. As they report, lightnings arise from the collision of clouds, just as fire escapes from the middle when harder flints are struck together. Moses and Joshua were clouds, because while they spoke with each other, lightnings flashed from their words. Jeremiah likewise and Baruch, conversing together, send forth gleaming lightnings.

The Psalmist too, considering God’s omnipotence, said: “He brings forth clouds from the farthest end of the earth; he made lightning into rain” (Ps. 134). Augustine: “God sent these clouds not only from Israel, but raises them up from the farthest end of the earth and sends them to the ends of the world.” But what does he accomplish by means of these clouds themselves? He made lightning into rain—that is, he turned threats toward mercy; from terrors he brought watering. For preachers [Col. 0171D] both frighten and soothe. They frighten when they threaten eternal punishments; they soothe by promising eternal joys. Therefore we read that manna melted in the sun and hardened in the fire (Exod. 16; Wisd. 16). For manna, given from heaven, is a figure of the divine word. It melts in the sun when it glorifies the minds of the faithful by the promise of future brightness, when it says: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 13). But manna hardens in the fire when it warns the minds of sinners who are ignorant, by the threat of future punishment, saying: “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” [Col. 0172A] (Matt. 3). Therefore in the garment of the high priest under the old Law there was scarlet twice dyed, which has the appearance of fire (Exod. 28).

Fire, however, does two things: it burns and it shines. Thus a preacher ought to burn the heart of sinners with lightning and the terror of threatening, and to cherish the minds of the devout with the promise of eternal light. Hence the pontiff’s staff pricks at its lower end and extends forward above: because the preacher ought to pierce the vices of the flesh and direct the powers of the mind toward what lies ahead—yet so that he always returns to consideration of himself, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become reprobate (1 Cor. 9). And at the beginning of his discourse he should be his own accuser, lest, carrying a beam in his own eye, he see the speck in another’s eye (Matt. 7). Therefore God, as was promised, makes lightning into rain, because in preaching he satisfies the hearts of humble hearers with spiritual teaching and terrifies them by fear of punishments.

He soothes them by the promise of rewards and frightens them by the announcement of punishments. Isidore [Note: [Col. 0171D] *Etymologies*, Book XIII, ch. 7]: “Clouds (*nubes*) are so called from veiling over (*obnubere*), that is, covering the sky; hence brides (*nuptae*) are so called because they veil their faces. Neptune too is so named because he veils (*nubat*), that is, covers sea and land. A density of air produces a cloud. For winds mass the air together and make clouds. Hence the line: ‘And the air is gathered into a cloud.’” [Note: [Col. 0171D] Id., ch. 8.] “Thunder (*tonitruum*) is so called because its sound terrifies; for *tonus* means ‘sound.’ It sometimes shakes everything so violently that the sky seems to have been split apart, because when a storm of very violent wind suddenly throws itself into the clouds, and, its whirl strengthening and seeking an outlet, cuts through the cloud which it has hollowed out with great force, it thus reaches the ears with a dreadful crash. No one should wonder at this, since even a small animal bladder, when burst, gives forth a great sound. Lightning appears together with thunder, but lightning is seen more quickly because it is bright, whereas thunder reaches the ears more slowly. The light which appears before thunder is called *fulgetra*; as we have said, it is seen first because the light is bright.” [Note: [Col. 0172D] Ch. 9.] “Lightning-flash (*fulgur*) and thunderbolt (*fulmen*) are named from the striking of a heavenly missile. For to flash (*fulgere*) is to strike and smite. Colliding clouds produce thunderbolts; for the collision of things [Col. 0172D] creates fire, as we see in stones, in the friction of wheels, and among the trees of forests. In a similar manner fire arises in clouds; hence there are clouds first, then fires. Thunderbolts are said to be made in clouds from wind and fire and to be discharged by the force of winds. The fire of a thunderbolt has greater power to penetrate than our fire, which serves our use, because it is made from subtler elements. It has three names: *fulgur*, *fulgor*, and *fulmen*. It is *fulgur* because it touches; *fulgor* because it kindles and burns; *fulmen* because it splits; and for that reason it is depicted with three rays.”

[Col. 0173A] Again the prophet Jeremiah adds concerning the works of almighty God, saying: “And he brings forth the wind from his treasuries” (Jer. 10): that is, from the hearts of the humble he brings forth the wind of wisdom, and sends those same simple and humble persons to preach the teaching of his faith. For in them are hidden the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God. God therefore brings forth wind from his treasuries when, through these humble persons—namely apostles, evangelists, and other teachers—he proclaims the mysteries of his secrets to all peoples throughout the world. The winds which blow over the earth indeed bear the figure of these spiritual winds. Similar is the Psalmist’s saying: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries” (Ps. 134). Preachers are clouds and winds: clouds, indeed, because of the flesh; winds because of the spirit. Clouds are seen; winds are felt and are not seen. And because flesh is from the earth, it is said that he raises clouds from the farthest end of the earth; but where the human spirit comes from is unknown. Hence it is rightly said: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries.” Or the apostles are called winds for another reason, namely because they swiftly traverse the whole world.

In the literal sense, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0173D] *Etymologies*, Book XIII, ch. 11]: “Wind is air set in motion and stirred; and it receives different names according to the different regions of the sky. It is called *ventus* because it is vehement and violent. Its force is so great that it not only uproots rocks and trees, but also disturbs sky and earth and stirs the seas. There are four principal winds, whose first blows from the east, Subsolanus; from the south, Auster; from the west [Col. 0173C], Favonius; and from the north, the wind bearing the same name, Septentrio. On either side these have paired winds. Subsolanus has Vulturnus at its right and Eurus at its left; Auster has Euroauster at its right and Austroafricus at its left. Favonius has Africus on the right and Corus on the left. Septentrio, moreover, has Circius at its right and Aquilo at its left. These twelve winds turn about the globe of the world, and their names are marked by their proper causes.

“Subsolanus is called thus because it arises beneath the rising sun. Eurus is so called because it blows from *Eous* [Mss.: *ab eo fiat*, ‘because it comes from it’], that is, from the east; for it is joined to Subsolanus. Vulturnus is so called because it thunders loudly; concerning it Lucretius says:

[Col. 0173D]

> Loud-thundering Vulturnus, and Auster mighty with lightning.  
> (*Lucretius*, V.744)

“Auster is called from drawing up waters; hence it makes the air thick and nourishes clouds. In Greek it is called νότος (*notos*, ‘south wind’), because it sometimes corrupts the air. For the blowing Auster carries into other regions the pestilence which arises from corrupted air; but as Auster produces pestilence, so Aquilo drives it away. Euroauster is so called because it has Eurus on one side and Auster on the other. Austroafricus, because it is joined on either side to Auster and Africus. It is also Libonotus, because it has Libs on one side and Notus on the other. Zephyrus is called by a Greek name because flowers and shoots [Col. 0174A] are enlivened by its breath. In Latin it is called Favonius because it cherishes what is born. Flowers are opened by Auster and produced by Zephyrus, that is, Favonius. Favonius is so called because it cherishes crops and flowers. In Greek it is called Ζέφυρος (*Zephyros*), because it usually blows in spring. Hence the line:

> And the crumbling clod loosens itself beneath Zephyrus.  
> (*Virgil*, *Georgics*, I.43)

“Africus is named from its own region, for it begins to blow in Africa. Corus is the wind which blows from the summer west; it is called Corus because it closes the circuit of the winds and makes, as it were, a choir (*chorus*). Septentrio is so called because it rises from the circle of seven stars, which, as the world turns, seem to be carried about with their heads thrown back. Circius is so called because it is joined to Corus. The Spaniards call it Gallecus because it blows upon them from the direction of Galicia. Aquilo is so called because it binds the waters and disperses clouds; for it is a cold and dry wind. It is also called Boreas because it blows from the Hyperborean mountains. There is the origin of that wind, and therefore it is cold. For the nature of all northern winds is cold and dry, that of southern winds moist and warm. But among all winds there are two cardinal winds: Aquilo [Septentrio], namely, and Auster.”

Having briefly stated these matters concerning the natures and varieties of winds from blessed Isidore, we must return to what we omitted above. The winds which blow over the earth, then, are not in God’s treasuries, because their nature is manifest; but there are treasures of winds—that is, of spirits: namely, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11). These treasures are most fully hidden in Christ, who is the source of all good things. They are also in the hearts of his servants in part. From the fullness of that supreme treasury it comes about that one person is wise, another faithful, another humble, another chaste, another full of charity, another sober, another devoted to prayer and divine contemplation, another generous in almsgiving, another intent on hospitality and works of mercy, another patiently enduring this world’s adversities, another despising riches and willingly embracing poverty for the sake of eternal reward [Col. 0174D].

Let Jeremiah the prophet again speak of the strength, wisdom, and prudence of God the Father: “He makes,” he says, “the earth by his strength, establishes the world by his wisdom, and stretches out the heavens by his prudence.” The prophet, taking up in some fashion three powers—strength, wisdom, and prudence—assigns to each its proper works: the earth to strength, the world to wisdom, heaven to prudence. Therefore, in our earth, concerning which it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3), we need the strength of God, without which it is impossible to carry out what resists the flesh. But when, as the Apostle says, our members upon the earth have been mortified [Col. 0175A] (Col. 3), then the flesh will obey the will of the spirit. For the deeds of the flesh are mortified by the Spirit, because, as is written in Job, God set the earth upon nothing; hence it is evident that by his strength the mass of earth is sustained in the midst of the world.

“He stretches out,” he says, “the north over the void, and hangs the earth upon nothing” (Job 26). Gregory [Note: [Col. 0175D] *Morals*, Book XVII, no. 34]: “In sacred language the devil is commonly denoted by the name of the north, who, in order to bind the hearts of the nations with the cold of torpor, said: ‘I shall sit on the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north’ (Isa. 14). He is stretched out over the void because he possesses those hearts which are not filled by the grace of divine love. Yet it is within the power of almighty God, by the gift of his grace, to fill even vessels of the devil that are empty of all [Col. 0175B] virtues, and to place in them the firmness of divine fear—those whom he sees strengthened by no act of righteousness. Hence it fittingly follows: ‘He hangs the earth upon nothing.’ For what is signified by the name of earth except the holy Church, which, when it receives the words of preaching, yields the fruit of good work? Of it Moses says: ‘Let the earth hear the words from my mouth’ (Deut. 32). And again: ‘Let my speech be awaited like rain’ (ibid.). And what is signified by ‘nothing’ except the Gentile peoples? Of them Isaiah says: ‘All nations are reckoned before him as nothing and emptiness’ (Isa. 40). Thus earth is suspended upon that nothing which was formerly held empty by the north, because the hearts of the Gentiles, formerly oppressed [Col. 0175C] by the devil’s torpor, have been filled with God’s charity.”

Let us therefore mortify our members which are upon the earth—that is, the vices of the flesh—and let virtues be made alive by God’s grace in the soul of each one of us, so that the dwelling-place of our heart may be shut against the devil and opened to Christ. By this void, moreover, the unbelief of the Jews may be signified; and by the earth, as we have said, the fruitfulness of the holy Church. Let the holy man therefore behold the cause of perishing Judah and discern the merits of the Gentile world returning to pardon; and let him say: “He stretches out the north over the void, and hangs the earth upon nothing.” For because the hearts of the Jews, empty of faith, are subject to the devil, he stretches out the north over the void. But because the Lord founded the Church among the nations when no merits existed—nations which the Prophet called nothing before their conversion—he fittingly added: “He hangs the earth upon nothing.” Here too may fit very well what the Psalmist says: “For nothing you will save them” (Ps. 55).

If, then, as was said above, we have mortified our members which are upon the earth, the north wind will be driven farther from us, we shall be numbered among the members of the Church, and our soul will be inhabited by the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0175D] Something seems to be lacking here.] The inhabited world is called in Greek *ciromines* [probably corrupt; *oikoumenē*], that is, “the inhabited [world].” I know a soul that is inhabited, and I know one that is deserted. For if it does not possess God the Father, [Col. 0176A] and the Son who says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and, “We shall come to my lover and make our dwelling with him” (John 14), and the Holy Spirit who proceeds from both, it is truly deserted. But that soul is inhabited which is full of God and possesses Christ and the Spirit of the Lord. Hence David says in the Psalm of confession: “Strengthen me with a steadfast spirit. Renew a right spirit within my inward parts. Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50).

We have brought these things forward as proof that the inhabited world—that is, the world—was fashioned in God’s wisdom. For, as it is written: “Wisdom helps the righteous person more than ten rulers in a city” (Eccl. 7). But one who rejects wisdom and instruction is unhappy; his hope is vain, his labours senseless, and his works useless (Wisd. 3). Therefore, dearest brethren, let us labour that our soul may be inhabited by God the Father, his Son, and the Holy Spirit, and may be raised up by his wisdom. For it fell when we came down from the height into this pit of miseries, after we sinned. Indeed, whoever is in this world fell before being corrected. For through sin we all fell into the inhabited world; but the Lord raised up those who lay fallen, and by his prudence stretched out the heavens, that is, minds. Strength and wisdom were not employed in stretching out the heaven. Hence it is said: “The Lord founded the earth, but established the heavens by prudence” (Prov. 3).

There is therefore a certain prudence of God, which I do not wish you to seek outside Christ, because Christ is all that belongs to God [Col. 0176C] (Col. 3). He himself is wisdom, he himself strength, he himself justice and holiness; it is his prudence. Yet though he is one in underlying reality, he is called by different names according to the variety of meanings. Wisdom signifies one thing and justice another. When he is called wisdom, he instructs you in the disciplines of human and divine things; when justice, he is signified as the distributor and judge of merits. Thus understand his prudence here when there is teaching and a showing of good or evil things, or of both. For thus he is said to have stretched out heaven in his prudence. Hence it is said: “I stretched out my words, and you did not attend” (Prov. 1). For it asserts that there is a certain extension of words, like that of the heavens. Thus it is written:

[Col. 0176D]

> Stretching out the heaven like a skin;  
> you cover its upper parts with waters.  
> (Ps. 103)

As though he said: You are God, stretching out the heaven. In the literal sense God stretches out heaven as the roof of the world; for he makes the firmament broad to cover the world, and does this like a skin—that is, not with some labour, as you, a human being, stretch out your own roof, but as easily as someone [stretches] a skin. But when he says “like a skin,” he also indicates that he himself is the maker [Note: [Col. 0175D] Read here: “the maker of all things,” or “the maker [who covers] all things.” The interlinear gloss on the words “you cover with waters” explains: “the covering of all things.”] of all things that are around all things.

It may also be read mystically, and it depends upon the statement mentioned above, that he clothed himself with the Church. But how he caused himself to be clothed with her, he explains by turning his speech toward him, saying: “You are stretching out the heaven like a skin.” He sets this forth by figurative mysteries when the Church was made light and without spot or wrinkle. For by heaven sacred Scripture is understood; by skin, which is stripped from dead animals, the mortality of preachers is understood. Hence our first parents, Adam and Eve, after their transgression and having become mortal, were clothed in garments of skin. Yet the Word of God is eternal and is God with God. And because the world did not know God in the wisdom of God, God saves believers through the foolishness of preaching—that is, through mortal preachers who seemed foolish—and in mortal humanity makes the immortal Word known (1 Cor. 1). Preachers are also well compared to skins, because, just as skins are of greater use after animals have died, so the Word of God became known through preachers, indeed even more after them [Col. 0177B]. For the prophets and apostles have died, but what they said remains. Yet their discourse is now called the speech of the dead, because after death they themselves became better known. Living prophets were possessed by Judaea alone; all nations possess them dead, to whom their speech was extended, so that we may read in it until the book is rolled up.

And the sense is: When you caused yourself to be clothed. Behold, you are God, stretching out heaven—that is, sacred Scripture—so that it may cover the whole world and through it God’s eternal Word may be known. You stretch it out, I say, like a skin—that is, through mortal preachers. For the Word of God, which was everywhere but the world did not know (John 1), began to be known through mortals, and became better known after them.

Our soul, therefore, is stretched out, as was said above, whereas it was formerly contracted. Those who bear the heavenly man are heavens. But if it is said to the sinner, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3), why is it not said to the righteous: “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go”? Or if, because of intercourse, it is said to one who bears the image of the earthly man: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” why, because of the heavenly man, is it not said to one who bears the image of the heavenly one: “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go”? Each one of us has either heavenly deeds or earthly ones. If they are earthly, they lead to its kindred earth the person who stores treasure on earth and not in heaven; but if they are heavenly, they bring their treasurer to the region near to themselves [Col. 0177D].

For this purpose God the Father sent his holy apostles through all parts of the world by his most beloved Son: that they might make heavenly persons out of earthly, spiritual persons out of carnal, and righteous persons out of sinners, and might instruct their conduct to serve God spiritually. Thus blessed Job, foreseeing in the Spirit the rejection from Judaea of those same apostles, said:

[Col. 0178A]

> The sons of instructors (*institutorum*) did not tread it,  
> nor did the lioness pass through it.  
> (Job 28)

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0177D] *Morals*, Book XVIII, no. 55]: “In all Latin manuscripts we find ‘instructors’ (*institutores*), but in the Greek we find ‘traders’ (*negotiatores*). From this one may infer that, in this passage, scribes ignorantly wrote *institutores* for *institores* [dealers, traders]. For we call merchants *institores*, because they press on with the work they pursue. Yet the two expressions, though differing in sound, do not differ in meaning, because all who train the conduct of believers conduct a spiritual business: when they offer preaching to their hearers, they receive from them faith and upright works. Thus it is written of the holy Church: ‘She made linen cloth and sold it’ (Prov. 31). And a little later it is added there: ‘She saw that her trading was good’ [Col. 0178B]. What, then, are the *institores* here but the holy prophets, who strove by prophecy to train the conduct of the Synagogue toward faith? Their sons are rightly called the holy apostles, who were begotten into the same faith by their preaching, in order that they might believe God to be human. Of them it is said to the holy Church through the Psalmist: ‘In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall make them rulers over all the earth’ (Ps. 44).”

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Here our manuscripts may be seen to agree with all the evidence that the Benedictines adduce in this place for restoring the true reading in the most corrupt edition, since *enstitores* was read here, and below *institores* stood for *negotiatores*, in place of *institutores* for *institores*. Yet although Gregory the Great asserts that Latin manuscripts incorrectly read *institutores* for *institores*, these same manuscripts wrongly retained here the corrupt reading *institutorum* for *institorum*, though afterwards they adopt the correct reading.]

Cassiodorus: “Here he says by what great increase the bride, that is, the holy Church, has advanced. He commends her from her offspring, as if to say: ‘They shall be brought’; for in place of your fathers—that is, your ancient fathers, worshippers of idols—sons have been born to you, namely the apostles, princes of preaching.”

Augustine: “‘In place of your fathers sons have been born to you’: that is, after the prophets came the apostles, and after the apostles and in place of the apostles came bishops and other teachers whom the Church bore and established in the seat of the Fathers. Hence follows: ‘You shall make them rulers over all the earth,’ and so forth. Thus in place of patriarchs and prophets sons were born to the holy Church, namely the holy apostles. But because, rejected by the Jews, they went out from the bounds of the Synagogue, it is rightly now said: ‘The sons of traders did not tread it’—namely, the Synagogue. If her holy preachers pressed down the vices of that Synagogue with the foot of virtue, they would surely tread her. But if by traders we understand the same preachers of the holy Church, then by the sons of traders [we understand] the pastors and teachers who followed the way of the apostles. There is no obstacle to understanding that they did not tread the Synagogue, because when their fathers—that is, the apostles—were rejected by it, they too ceased from recalling it.

“Through this Synagogue the lioness did not pass through, because the holy Church, devoted to gathering the Gentiles, did not occupy herself any longer with that people of Judaea. The Church is rightly called a lioness, because by the mouth of holy preaching she killed those who lived wickedly in vices. Hence to the first preacher himself, as if to the mouth of this lioness, it is said: ‘Kill and eat’ (Acts 10). What is killed is put to death from life; but what is eaten is changed into the body of the eater. ‘Kill and eat,’ therefore, means: kill them from the sin in which they live and turn them from themselves into your members. Since this Church is the body of the Lord, the Lord himself is called a lion in Jacob’s voice from himself, and a lioness from his body, when under the figure of Judah it is said to him: ‘You have gone up to the prey, my son; crouching, you lay down like a lion, and like a lioness—who shall rouse him?’ (Gen. 49).

“This lioness, then, is not said not to have passed Judaea; rather, she is said not to have passed *through* it. Thus blessed Job says: ‘The lioness did not pass through it’ (Job 28). For when the apostles preached, three thousand first believed from Judaea, and afterwards five thousand (Acts 2, 4). The lioness, therefore—that is, the Church—passes through the Synagogue but did not pass through it entirely: she snatched some from it into faith, but did not utterly extinguish that unbelieving people’s perfidy. But, as we have often said, the lioness—that is, the primitive Church—turned away from the unbelief of the Jews to the calling of the Gentiles. Hence it is further said of that same lioness, the holy Church: ‘She stretched out her hand to the rock; she overturned mountains from their roots’ (Job 28). The lioness stretches out her hand to the rock because the Church sent forth the arm of her preaching toward the hardness of the Gentiles. Thus the same blessed Job, foreseeing that the history of his suffering would be woven among us Gentiles, said: ‘Let these things be written with an iron stylus upon a plate of lead, or be carved with a chisel in rock’ (Job 19). And what are mountains here, except the powers of this age, which swell high because of earthly wealth? Of them the Psalmist says: ‘Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke’ (Ps. 143).”

Cassiodorus: “Lord, by your grace touch the mountains—that is, the earthly great ones [reading uncertain], that is, the proud—and they shall smoke: that is, they shall confess their sins.”

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0179D] In the place cited above]: “The mountains were overthrown from their roots because, when the holy Church preached, the highest powers of this age fell from their inmost thought into adoration of almighty God. For the roots of mountains are the inward thoughts of the proud; and mountains fall from their roots because the powers of the age are prostrated from their inmost thoughts to worship God. Let blessed Job, then, say of the lioness—that is, of the primitive Church—‘She stretched out her hand to the rock; she overturned mountains from their roots’: because, when the holy preaching of the apostles sought out the hardness of the Gentiles, it utterly uprooted the height of the proud.”

For this purpose the Son of God sent his disciples: that among both the exalted and the lowly people of this world they might cut away vices with the sword of God’s word, order their conduct, and utterly uproot from their hearts useless and perverse thoughts. Thus Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the man who keeps back his sword [Col. 0180A] from blood” (Jer. 48). As if he said: Cursed is the person who neglects by God’s word to cut away carnal vices, both in himself and in those subject to him. Hence blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0179D] *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, ch. 25]: “To keep back the sword from blood is to withhold the word of preaching from the killing of the carnal life. Of it it is said: ‘My sword shall devour flesh.’” [Note: [Col. 0179D] The edition reads “shall eat.” But Martin here follows the Vulgate, which some manuscripts also follow, as may be seen in the Benedictines at this place.] (Deut. 32).

Hence Paul says: “I testify this day that I am clean from the blood of all. For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20). This may also apply to those who live carnally, follow worldly luxury, and neglect to chastise and subject their body to slavery, according to the saying: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5). For without the shedding [Col. 0180B] of blood there is no remission of sins (Heb. 9). Flesh and blood also cannot possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15). Cursed, therefore, is the one who keeps back the sword—that is, the word of God—from the blood by which the matter of sins is animated.

We must know, therefore, that whatever carnal and earthly growth has arisen in our members must be cut away by the sword of God’s word. But what we cannot say without deep sorrow is that some ecclesiastical men gladly speak useless things and negligently keep silent about things that could benefit many hearers. For the love of God and neighbour should make them continually silent about superfluities and freely speak good things without ceasing. Certainly that man willingly preached God’s commands to the peoples who said: “I shall proclaim your righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I shall not restrain my lips. Lord, you know” [Col. 0180C] (Ps. 39).

As if he said: I have proclaimed it. He says this in the members—that is, in the person of the members—as though to say: I first spoke through myself, and afterwards through the members I proclaimed to others that your righteousness exists, that is, the righteousness which is from you. “I proclaimed your righteousness in the great Church,” which is throughout the whole world, not small as it was formerly; and if anything should rise up against me, fear will not prevent me from speaking. This is: “Behold, I shall not restrain my lips from speaking.” As if he said: I do not keep it in my heart alone so as to be silent through fear. He says this against worldly fear, as though to say: I shall do this without pretence also, because, Lord, you knew my heart. As if he said: My lips sound to human beings, but you, Lord, [Col. 0180D] know my heart. He says this lest the proclamation be in lips alone, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). And he says it against pretence.

Or thus: O Lord, I shall not restrain my lips; you know that fear does not prevent me from speaking. Or thus: I shall not restrain my lips, and this is from you, because you, Lord, knew—that is, you predestined that it would be so. And for this I am not idle: I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart, but have spoken your truth and your salvation. “I have not hidden in my heart,” when I could benefit others, “your righteousness,” or mine: that is, I confessed the faith; “nor have I concealed your salvation,” that is, I spoke your salvation. Augustine: “Or ‘your truth and your salvation,’ that is, Christ, I spoke—that is, I preached—and I did not desist because of many seeking to conciliate me.”

Ecclesiastical men, therefore, as was said above, ought gladly to preach God’s righteousness to the people and take the greatest care lest, being unlearned, they utter disordered things, or negligently keep necessary matters silent from their hearers. Rather, they should strive in all things to be able to follow the rule of apostolic teaching.

These chosen preachers from among the Gentiles were prefigured by Hiram the craftsman of Tyre, whom King Solomon took as a helper in his work (1 Kings 7; 2 Chron. 2). His mother, a widow, signified the present Church, for whom the Son of God and of the Virgin mercifully laid down his life; and, ascending into heaven, he left her as a widow wandering on earth. Her sons are the preachers chosen after the apostles. Hence it is said: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you” (Ps. 44), and so forth. And Hiram set up two bronze columns, eighteen cubits high; and a line of twelve cubits encircled each column (1 Kings 7). Therefore the line of twelve cubits which encircled each column is the teaching of the apostles. The standard of apostolic instruction surrounds both columns when holy teachers, commanded to preach to Jews and Gentiles, take care to do and teach only what the Church received and learned through the apostles.

For one who wishes to live or teach otherwise, and to despise apostolic teaching, is not a column in God’s temple. Since he scorns to follow apostolic ordinances, he does not fit the line of twelve cubits, whether through the thinness of sloth or the bulk of pride [Col. 0181C]. The two columns, therefore, signify the apostles and all teachers of the Church, strong in faith and work and upright in contemplation. They are two in order that by preaching they may introduce into the Church both uncircumcision and circumcision. Therefore God, who wished to build a temple to the glory of his name not only through Jews but also through Gentiles, himself chose, after the apostles, distinguished teachers from among the Gentiles to build his Church, as blessed Job, praising God, says among other things:

He who removes the stars of rain and pours out showers like [Col. 0181D] torrents flowing from the clouds (Job 36). Gregory [Note: [Col. 0181D] Book XXVII of the *Moralia*, no. 12]: “There are two kinds of righteous persons in this life: one, namely, those who live well but teach nothing; the other, those who live rightly and teach those same right things. Thus on the face of heaven certain stars appear which are followed by no rains; others, however, drench the parched earth with great showers, such as Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades. Therefore, whenever certain persons in holy Church live rightly but do not know how to preach that same rectitude, they are indeed stars, but born amid the dryness of the air; for by the example of their good life they can shine for others, [Col. 0182A] but they cannot rain forth the word of preaching. But when certain persons in her both live rightly and pour that same rectitude into others by words of preaching, then, as though stars were produced in heaven to bring forth rain, there appear stars which shine by the merits of their lives in such a way that they also rain by the discourse of preaching. Was not Moses a rain-bearing star in this heaven, who, when he shone forth from on high, drenched the hearts of sinners—like earth parched below—with the rain of holy exhortation, bringing them to the fruitfulness of germination? Was not Isaiah shown to be a rain-bearing star, who, insofar as he beheld and held fast the light of truth beforehand, watered by prophecy the dryness of unbelievers which he proclaimed? Were not Jeremiah and the other prophets, set as it were in heaven, stars of rain, who, raised to the height of preaching, dared freely to rebuke the perversity of sinners [Col. 0182B] and thus, as it were, pressed down the dust of human blindness by watering it with drops of words? Since the judgments above remove their souls, taken up from this corruptible flesh, from the present life, the rain-bearing stars are, as it were, withdrawn from the face of heaven. And the stars return secretly when, their courses completed, the souls of the saints are hidden away in the treasuries of the innermost providential ordering. But the earth would dry out if, once the stars had been removed, the heavenly streams of rain ceased altogether [Note: [Col. 0181D] Here the edition rightly supplies: “He who removes the stars of rain,” etc. For when he removed the prophets, [Col. 0182D] the Lord sent the apostles in their place, that they might rain in the likeness of torrents, after those had been withdrawn, etc.], that is, if, after the ancient fathers had been taken away, the outward proclamations of the Law had fallen silent. Therefore he hid the stars of rain and poured out showers like torrents, because [the text has *quia*, “because”] when he brought the preachers of the Law into secret and inward places, a more abundant power of preaching flowed forth through the words of those who followed.

[Col. 0182C] The holy Apostles, too, may be denoted by the stars of rain, concerning whom it is said through Jeremiah of rejected Judaea: “The stars of rain have been withheld, and there was no latter rain” (Jer. 3). Therefore the Lord withdrew the stars of rain and poured out showers like torrents, because, when he removed the preaching apostles from Judaea, the teaching of new grace watered the world. Both events can suitably be understood as taking place in the Church. For when, with their bodies dissolved, he transferred the souls of the Apostles to the hidden bosom of heavenly things, he hid the rain-bearing stars, as it were, from the face of heaven. But, after the stars of rain had been taken away, he gave showers in the manner of torrents, because, even after the Apostles had been brought back to heavenly things, he opened up with fuller outpouring, through the tongues of succeeding interpreters, the streams of divine [Col. 0182D] knowledge that had long been hidden. For what they spoke briefly, these expound at length and establish in many ways. Hence the preaching of the interpreters themselves is not undeservedly compared to torrents: while they collect the sayings of many predecessors, they themselves are expanded more deeply in what they establish. For while they join testimonies to testimonies, they make torrents, as it were, from torrents; and while the Gentiles are daily instructed by their words, the mind of the sinner receives heavenly knowledge, so that water standing upon the earth, as it were, displays torrents. Yet, because the interpreters by no means set themselves above those same Apostles in knowledge [Col. 0183A], when they speak more fully in exposition they must continually remember through whom they received the transmissions of that knowledge. Hence it is fittingly added: “Which flow from the clouds.” These torrents flow from clouds because, unless the power of understanding had begun from the holy Apostles, it could never have flowed more abundantly through the mouths of teachers.

For in sacred Scripture clouds sometimes signify changeable human beings, sometimes prophets, and sometimes Apostles. Human fickleness is expressed through clouds, as Solomon says: “He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who watches the clouds will never reap” (Eccles. 11). By “wind” he undoubtedly means the unclean spirit, and by “clouds” the people subject to him, whom he drives and draws back now here, now there, as often as [Col. 0183B] his temptation alternates the hearts of those people by the gusts of suggestions. Therefore he who watches the wind does not sow, because the person who fears coming temptations does not set good works before his heart. [Note: [Col. 0183C] The edition reads: “sets before.”] And he who considers the clouds does not reap, because one who trembles beforehand at the fear of human changeability deprives himself of the reward of eternal recompense. Prophets are signified through clouds, as it is said through the Psalmist:

> “Dark water was in the clouds of the air” (Psalm 17).

Augustine: “Dark water in the clouds of the air means obscure teaching in the prophets and in all preachers who, raised above earthly things, rain down the word of God upon those below. I call it obscure in comparison with the brilliance that will be in his presence—that is, in comparison with the brilliance that will be in his manifestation. For now we see through a mirror, [Col. 0183C] but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

Cassiodorus: “Therefore let no one suppose that he is already in the future light merely because he understands Scripture correctly.”

It continues: “The clouds passed over.” Water is as it were dark in the clouds; and those clouds—that is, the preachers of the divine word—passed over to the Gentiles and are no longer in Judaea. Alternatively: “He bowed the heavens,” that is, he humbled the preachers from the contemplative life to the service of the active life, so that Rachel might yield her husband to Leah (Gen. 29), and he himself might descend through their teaching into the understanding of certain simple people who cannot grasp greater things. Thus he says, “He descended,” or “He bowed the heavens”: that is, he humbled the preachers so that they might endure troubles, and he, the Bridegroom of the Church, descended, suffering in those with whom he is one.

[Col. 0184A] “The Apostles also are signified through clouds, as blessed Gregory said above, just as it is said through Isaiah: ‘I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it’ (Isa. 5). Thus they themselves are stars, shining by the merits of their lives; they themselves are clouds, because they water the parched earth of our breast with the rains of heavenly understanding. For if they were not clouds, the prophet would never have said when he beheld them: ‘Who are these who fly like clouds?’ (Isa. 60). Therefore torrents of rain flow from clouds because the profound preachings of succeeding interpreters received the origin of their understanding from the holy Apostles.”

For these disciples of the truest truth are, after their most glorious master Christ, themselves the beginning of preaching. To them it was said: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every [Col. 0184B] creature” (Mark 16). They were commanded to go throughout the world and baptize all nations into faith in the supreme and undivided Trinity (Matt. 28). What they heard in the ear, they preached upon the rooftops; and what they learned from the Lord in darkness—that is, in secret—they proclaimed in all cities, indeed among every people throughout the world. They cast selected grains of seed upon rational ground, that is, upon the hearts of humankind, and brought back to God a hundredfold fruit, namely holy souls. When the Son of God and of the Virgin went away into a far country—that is, ascended into heaven—he divided his goods among them for trading, entrusting them with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, in order that, when he returned to settle accounts with them, namely at the judgment, he might know how much each had gained by trading. But they, as faithful and most devoted servants, entrusted the talents committed to them at interest to all nations under heaven, and brought immense profits of holy souls back to that master of the household. Their same most loving Master foretold that at the end of the world they would sit with him and judge the twelve tribes of Israel. Therefore, dearest brothers, so far as divine grace grants, let us follow in the footsteps of these holy Apostles, so that, aided by their merits and prayers, we may deserve to attain eternal joys, through him who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0183]

## EXPOSITION OF SAINT MARTIN, PRIEST OF LEÓN, ON THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JAMES

[Col. 0183D] I want you to know, dearest brothers, that the friends of God, perfectly despising this present world and following Christ’s footsteps with every devotion by the steps of good [Col. 0184D] works, endure innumerable temptations of mind and body—namely inwardly and outwardly—until they reach the long-desired entrance into [Col. 0185A] the heavenly homeland. Within, the ancient enemy suggests unlawful things; without, wicked people stir up adversities. The invisible enemy raises within the titillations of the flesh, while ungodly persons outside plunder the resources of temporal life. Within, God’s servant endures incentives to lust; outside, insults and reproaches from neighbours. Within are contests with vices; outside, losses of temporal possessions (2 Cor. 7). Why say more? Battles without, fears within; raging people without, and within the natural impulses of seductive flesh do not permit the despisers of the world to live quietly. Blessed James consoles and exhorts such people not to fail in faith amid temptations; he rebukes sinners and warns them to refrain from sins [Col. 0185B] and strive to advance in virtues. For he says in the canonical, or catholic, Epistle: “Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into diverse temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience. But patience has a perfect work, that you may be perfect and whole, deficient in nothing” (James 1).

These Epistles are called catholic, that is, universal, because they do not depart from the faith of the universal Church. They are also called canonical, that is, regular, in distinction from those made by pseudo-apostles under the names of the holy Apostles. Therefore let it be said: “Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into diverse temptations.” As though he said: Tribulation produces righteousness in the present and increases the crown in the future; therefore there is nothing [Col. 0185C] for which you ought to grieve. You are tempted by adversities, whether by a persecutor or by desire, which tempts in diverse ways, so that through this you may prove that you bear firm faith in future recompense in your heart. This is to understand [Note: [Col. 0185D] Perhaps the following, which the *Glossa* has, is missing here: “the virtue of patience itself.”] what your faith requires. Therefore do not be indignant if evil people flourish in the world while you suffer; for it is not compatible with Christian dignity to be exalted in temporal things, but rather to be brought low. The wicked have nothing in heaven; the good have nothing in the world. Yet, in the hope of that good toward which you are proceeding, you ought to rejoice in whatever happens on the way. “Knowing,” he says, “that the tribulation of your faith produces patience,” that is, makes you understand and possess the virtue of patience itself. The same thought, but in reverse order, is read in Paul. “Knowing,” he says, “that tribulation produces patience, and patience testing” (Rom. 5), because one whose patience is not overcome [Col. 0185D] is proved perfect. [Note: [Col. 0185D] Another manuscript adds here, with the *Glossa*: “through tribulations.”] The same thought is expressed here as well. Patience has a perfect work, and testing produces patience; that is: tribulation, which is given for the testing of faith, causes a person to be exercised through patience, by which faith is proved perfect. Therefore patience has a perfect work, that is, it makes those who practise it perfect, because of what follows: “That you may be perfect and whole, deficient in nothing.” As though he said: That you may be perfect, not failing amid [Col. 0186A] tortures, and whole in the future, receiving full blessedness.
