Again he adds, saying: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach” (James 1). As though he said: If any of you lacks wisdom concerning how the tribulation of this present world is useful, let him ask God for the illuminating Spirit, who gives generously to all who ask piously, because his gifts are not measured; he does not reproach the weakness of the petitioner, and that wisdom which comes from heaven will be given to him. “Not everyone who says, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7); nor does God give every righteous person what he asks if he asks against his own salvation, as was said to Paul when he asked: “My grace is sufficient for you; for strength is made perfect in [Col. 0186B] weakness” (2 Cor. 12). So great is the usefulness of tribulations. If anyone, not yet enlightened by the Holy Spirit, does not know it, let him ask that his understanding may be opened through the Holy Spirit; and he will know with what loving care the Father corrects the children whom he receives. Nor should anyone, conscious of his own weakness, despair, because he gives to all and does not reproach.

Hence the Psalmist: “He has blessed all who fear the Lord, the little with the great” (Psalm 113). Cassiodorus: “No class of human beings is excluded from blessing, when he blessed the little together with the great.” It follows: “May the Lord add to you: to you and to your children.” As though he said: May the Lord add blessing to you, O Jews, and to you, O Gentiles, and to your children. [Col. 0186C] Augustine: Or he distinguishes fathers from children in this way, namely masters from disciples, saying: O fathers, O teachers, may the Lord add to you—that is, add many others to your number. And this has happened, because the number of teachers increased. And may he add to your children—which also has happened, because the number of followers increased, when children of Abraham are raised up from stones. For the faith of all nations was added, and the number increased not only of wise bishops but also of obedient peoples. Therefore, as was said above, the Lord has blessed all, because in his most perfect dispensation he grants eternal goods to all who live rightly and ask rightly in faith.

[Col. 0186D] And because, as we have said, many ask [Note: [Col. 0186D] The *Glossa*: “who do not.”] who deserve to receive, he therefore adds how they ought to ask. “Let him ask,” he says, “in faith, doubting nothing.” As though he said more plainly: Let him believe and live in such a way as to be worthy of being heard, because “he who stops his ear lest he hear the law, his prayer shall be abominable” (Prov. 28). But the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, moved and carried about by the wind. One weighed down by awareness of sin, who doubts the heavenly rewards, easily abandons the state of faith when the wind of temptation comes upon him and, according to the tempter’s will, is drawn [Col. 0187A] into error and becomes estranged from God. It follows: “Let not that person therefore suppose that he will receive anything from God.” The carnal person who doubts will receive nothing from God, either here or in the future. “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.” [Note: [Col. 0187D] The material enclosed in brackets is adduced by the *Glossa* to expound the words, “Blessed is the man who endures temptation,” etc.; and it says: “You ought to endure not only blows … but also losses,” etc.] The one who doubts receives nothing, because the one who doubts is double-minded, and the double-minded person receives nothing. For he is easily frightened by adversities and entangled by prosperity, so as to turn aside from truth. A double-minded man is one who bends his knee in prayer and, as conscience bites, despairs of obtaining his request. He too is double-minded who wishes to rejoice here with the world and eternally with God, and who seeks from the good things he does not God but favour. Hence it is said: “Woe to him who enters the land by two ways” (Ecclus. 2). Therefore let the humble brother glory in his exaltation, but the rich man in his humiliation, [Col. 0187B] because he will pass away like the flower of grass.

As though he said: Let the humble brother, made poor and lowly, glory and understand this humiliation as exaltation before God. As though he said: “Not only blows and imprisonments and the loss of possessions, which are worthless and transient, and those who love them, are to be punished.” Let the rich man, he says, glory in his humiliation, because he will pass away like the flower of grass. Or “let him glory” is said ironically: it is as though he ought not glory in the glory by which he is proud and oppresses others, because it must end and be humbled in hell. Or, let him glory in his humiliation, that is, let him not be proud, but serve the humble [Note: [Col. 0188D] The *Glossa*: “let him humble himself.”] and minister to others out of his wealth. If he does not do so, his glory will quickly pass away like the flower of grass. He calls rich the person who places all his hope in riches. [Col. 0187C] It does not harm one to possess riches, but to love them. [Note: [Col. 0188D] “For it is desire for the world, rather than possessions, that harms.” Bernard, or Geoffrey, *Declamation on Simon’s Conversation with Jesus.*] Therefore the righteous flourishes like a palm tree (Psalm 91), while the unrighteous dries up like grass: the former remains, the latter quickly passes away. The flower of the righteous is hope, which awaits fruit; the root of the righteous is charity, which remains unmoved. The root of the evil person is greed; his flower is delight in temporal things.

“Then the sun rose with its burning heat and dried up the grass; its flower fell, and the beauty of its appearance perished.” Truly the flower quickly passes away, because Christ, the Sun of righteousness, rises with burning heat, dries up the grass, and then its flower falls. When the flower falls, all the beauty of the grass perishes; the beauty of its appearance perishes—that is, worldly honour, friendship, and other such things. The sun’s burning heat is the coming of the severe Judge, either unexpected in the death of each person [Col. 0187D] or universally at the judgment, in which the righteous person will remain like a fruitful tree. “So also the rich man will wither in his ways.” The ways of the rich are temporal goods by which he seeks to be made happy, and which will quickly be destroyed. Therefore in his ways the rich man will wither, that is, he will perish in his deeds, because he neglected to walk uprightly in the Lord’s way.

Therefore, as stated above, Christ’s faithful ought to count it all joy when they fall into diverse temptations. For if the mind does not yield to temptation, everyone who is tempted gains from it a great reward, as blessed James [Col. 0188A] subsequently says here: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation; for when he has been proved, he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him.” Because it is difficult to exhort people to despise the world, he therefore added concerning the greatness of the reward. As though he said: Truly every faithful person ought to endure temptation, since, after being tested through it, he will receive, as conquerors do, the crown of life, which God promised through prophets and Apostles to those who love him. The person proved through the exercise of temptation is perfect in faith; this is why he is also tempted.

It follows: “Let no one, when tempted, say that he is tempted by God.” Up to this point he has dealt with outward temptations; now he treats those which we endure inwardly, through the devil’s instigation or even through the weakness of nature. Here he also destroys the error of those [Col. 0188B] who said that evil thoughts, just like good thoughts, are inspired in us by God, and that a person sins as though by necessity. Therefore let it be said more plainly: Let no one, when tempted—that is, when seized by inward temptation—say that he is tempted by God, as though God sends evil thoughts. God indeed sends outward temptation to test his own people; but he does not send the inward temptation by which theft, adultery, and murder are often conceived.

Again he says: “For God is not a tempter of evils.” As though he said: God is not one who sends temptations. Temptation occurs in three ways: through the suggestion of the enemy, through delight, or through the consent of our weakness.

If we do not consent to suggestion, temptation turns to victory for us. But if suggestion allures [Col. 0188C] by delight, we have already offended, but have not yet incurred death. If the delight of the wicked deed conceived in the heart is followed by the birth of a wrong action, the victorious enemy then departs, leaving us liable to death. It follows: He himself, namely God, tempts no one—that is, he leads no one into temptation. There are two kinds of temptation: one tests the tempted person, as God tested Abraham (Gen. 22); the other deceives, in which sense God tempts no one. He then reveals where temptation arises, adding: “Each person is tempted, drawn away and enticed by his own desire.” As though it were said more plainly: No one is tempted by God; rather, each person is tempted by his own desire, whether when the flesh seeks pleasures for itself or when the devil introduces incentives, being drawn away from the straight path and enticed [Col. 0188D] to evil. “Then,” he says, “when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin”—that is, when it has conceived through delight or consent, it openly brings a person to the act. It follows: “But sin, when it has been completed, brings forth death,” that is, when it has been carried out and completed through habit, it brings forth death. For just as the person who overcomes while tempted gains the reward of life, so the person enticed and overcome by desires deservedly incurs the ruin of death. When we build wood, hay, and stubble upon the foundation, the devil puts [Col. 0189A] fire beneath it. But if we build gold, silver, and precious stones, he does not dare to tempt; nevertheless, he does not altogether desist, but “sits in secret places in order to kill the innocent” (Psalm 9).

Cassiodorus: He sits, as though waiting, in ambush with the rich of this world, whom he will enrich and heap with gifts, displaying their false happiness in order to deceive others. He is said to be in ambush “in secret places,” that is, in ambiguous matters, where it is not easy to understand what ought and ought not to be desired. This can be understood, as stated above, of the devil; it may also be applied to any ungodly person who lies in wait for the faithful of the Church. Augustine: For what purpose does the ungodly person sit in ambush? Namely, in order to kill the innocent by making him harmful out of innocent. He then explains his ambushes [Col. 0189B] saying: “His eyes look upon the poor; he lies in wait like a lion in his den” (ibid.). As though he said: His eyes look upon the poor with apparent mercy and affection. Or he deceives others in this way, because his eyes look cruelly upon the poor in spirit, whose is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5), because he especially lies in wait for the righteous and poor in spirit. He lies in wait in secret, because the deceived person does not know it. He is, I say, like a lion because of his force; he is in his den, namely because of his deceit.

Again blessed James consoles and exhorts the faithful, saying: “Therefore do not err, my most beloved brothers.” As though he said: Do not err by supposing that the promptings of vices proceed from God; and therefore you ought not dissent from us, because I advise nothing useless but what is [Col. 0189C] necessary for you. And because sins are not from God but virtues are, he fittingly adds, saying: “Every good gift and every perfect donation is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of turning.” Having shown that vices come not from God but from ourselves, he conversely shows that whatever good we do comes not from ourselves but from God. Hence he calls him the Father of lights, that is, the author of all spiritual gifts. Let it therefore be said more plainly: Since evils arise not from God but goods rather, every good gift—namely chastity and the other virtues—and every perfect donation—that is, the exercise of those virtues, or eternal life, which is perfect—comes from above, descending [Col. 0189D] from the Father of lights like a ray from the sun. With him there is no change, that is, in whose nature there is no mutability but sameness; and this is true not only of his nature but also of his bestowal of gifts, because he sends only gifts of light and not the darkness of errors. Nor is there a shadow of turning, because no shadow interrupts his light so that he might send any evils; rather, he always sends good gifts of light. In us there are at times gifts of God which ensuing sins overshadow; such sins are not in God. “Gift” refers to nature; “donation” to grace. The gift is customarily ascribed to the human person himself, the donation to God’s grace; yet the good of nature also comes from God.

Again he recalls God’s benefits to mind when he adds: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be some firstfruits of his creation.” [Col. 0190A] As though he said: Every good is from God, and we have not attained this by our merits, but by the grace of the divine will alone. Let it therefore be said more plainly: Of his own will, after the children of darkness, he begot us through the water of regeneration as children of light, by the word of truth, in the teaching of the Gospel, so that we might be some firstfruits of his creation. Thus, through this begetting, we must not suppose that we are what he himself is; rather, by adoption he granted us a certain primacy among creatures. In a certain way, the human being is ruler of all creatures under heaven. Hence another translator says: “That we might be some firstfruits of his creatures.” Above he advised endurance in temptations; next he instructs them with moral precepts. For he says: “You know, my most beloved brothers.” As though he said: You know that you had from [Col. 0190B] yourselves the ability to fall into vices, but from the Lord illumination by heavenly grace; and, since you have been begotten as some firstfruits of creation, let this remain in you.

It follows: “But let every person be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” As though he said: Let everyone be slow to speak, lest he presume to teach before the proper time; and slow to anger, that is, let him not rashly become angry without cause, whether against sinful subjects, against any brothers, or against the prosperity of evil people, because the maturity of wisdom is received only by a tranquil mind. One who judges in anger, even if he judges what is just, nevertheless cannot imitate the justice of the divine judgment, into which disturbance does not enter. Why? Because “the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God.”

[Col. 0190C] An angry person, even if he seems righteous before people, is nevertheless unrighteous before God. Therefore, he says, “putting away all uncleanness and abundance of malice, receive with meekness the implanted word which can save your souls.” He advised them to seek teaching; so that they may receive it and profit through it, he exhorts them to purity of body and soul, because one who does not turn away from evil cannot do good. Let it therefore be said more plainly: Therefore—that is, because of what was said above—you ought first to be attentive in hearing, then in teaching, putting away every uncleanness, namely of soul and body, and abundance of malice. Malice properly concerns the perversity of the inward person [Col. 0190D]. Or “abundance” means evil people abounding in evils. In meekness—that is, contrary to anger—receive with great honour the implanted word which we lay upon your hearts by preaching. Or, receive the word implanted and sown on the day of redemption, when God begot you; it can save your souls even if you suffer temptation or death in the body. And receive it not only by hearing, but fulfil it also in deed, because “not the hearers of the Law are righteous, but the doers” (Rom. 2).

Again, in giving counsel, he adds: “Be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.” As though he said: Now receive more perfectly and fulfil in works what you hold in mystery. As though he [Col. 0191A] said openly: Be doers of the word in deed, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves if you suppose that you will be saved through hearing alone. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he shall be compared to a man considering the face of his birth in a mirror, namely a bodily mirror in which a mere shadow shines.

Allegorically: One who sets before his mind the consideration in the Scriptures, as in a mirror, of the face of his birth—namely, how he is born human, how frail he is, what he will become, how brief his life is, and amid how many miseries he is placed—takes on great compunction and a desire to repent. Yet, immediately deceived by some temptation, he forgets his compunction and returns to sins. Such a person’s inconstancy is compared to that of one who gladly hears the word but neglects to fulfil it. [Col. 0191B] There is a likeness between the person who, of his own accord and without a teacher, applied himself to the Scriptures and the person who hears the Scriptures from another, if neither fulfils them.

It follows: “He considered himself, went away, and immediately forgot what sort of person he was,” because he saw not the reality but only its shadow—like one who has only the shadow of words and not the body of action. When a child is born, it cries; this signifies the pain of the soul entering life amid the miseries of the flesh, a pain which it later forgets when accustomed to the enticements of the flesh.

It follows: “But whoever has looked into the perfect law of liberty and continued in it, becoming not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, that person will be blessed in his deed.” As though he said: Whoever thinks himself saved by hearing alone is deceived; but whoever has looked into the perfect law of liberty—that is, [Col. 0191C] by hearing the word of the Gospel—and has continued in it by persistence in work, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, will be blessed in the future, not in hearing but in his deed, even if he is miserable here. He calls the grace of the Gospel the perfect law of liberty, because it perfectly frees people from the slavery of fear. Those who kept the Law served in fear, because whoever transgressed it was stoned without mercy. This Law brought no one to perfection, because, though it compelled service by fear, it did not give grace so that it might be fulfilled in love, and it could not free people from the punishments of hell (Heb. 7). But the charity given in the Gospel casts out fear and leads to life (1 John 4).

Again, for their instruction, he adds, [Col. 0191D] saying: “If anyone thinks himself religious, while not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, that person’s religion is vain.” Above he warned that they should not merely hear God’s word, but also fulfil it. Now, in order to make them protected on every side, he adds that all these things are of no value unless the tongue too is restrained from detractions, lies, blasphemies, foolish speech, and excessive talk, because “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). Let it therefore be said more plainly: If anyone thinks himself religious through the faith he possesses and the works of faith, while not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart—not understanding that he will be punished for sins of the tongue—his religion is vain, that is, useless or not pure. As though he said: Do not merely be doers of the word, but also restrain your tongue.

[Col. 0192A] Again, commending works of mercy, he adds, saying: “Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself undefiled from this world.” As though he said more plainly: Religion pure in the intention of the heart and undefiled in the performance of work, before God and the Father—who is not deceived in discerning, as human beings are, and who lovingly cares and repays his children—is this: to visit orphans, that is, assist those lacking the protection of fathers, and widows, who lack the comfort of husbands, in their affliction, that is, at the time of need; concerning them it is said: “As long as you did it to one of these least of my brothers, you did it to me” (Matt. 25). And keep yourself undefiled from this world [Col. 0192B] by preserving purity of heart and fleeing wicked deeds. Since he had called the doer blessed, he now says which deeds especially please God: mercy and innocence. For in commanding that orphans and widows be visited, he indicates everything which we ought to do for our neighbour; and in commanding that we be kept undefiled from the world, he shows all things in which it is fitting for us to keep ourselves chaste, including those which he previously warned us to observe: to be slow to speak and slow to anger.

It follows: “My brethren, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with partiality.” Why? Because the world rejects the poor and honors the rich; the faith of Christ, on the contrary, teaches that all the glory of the rich is “like the flower of grass” (1 Pet. 1), while mercy toward the poor flourishes eternally. By these words blessed James shows that those to whom he was writing were imbued with faith but devoid of works; and that the alms which they preached they gave, not to the poor for eternal goods, but to the rich for temporal advantage. Therefore, rebuking them, he calls Christ the Lord of glory, so that they may obey the commands of him who rewards with everlasting glory whatever is given to the poor for love of him. Whoever chooses a rich person because of riches and rejects a poor person because of poverty sins in both respects. Hence he rightly adds: “For if there comes into your presence a man with a gold ring, in white clothing, and there also comes in a poor man in filthy clothing, and you look upon the one wearing the fine garment, and say to him, ‘Sit here in a good place’; but to the poor man, ‘Stand there,’ or, ‘Sit beneath my footstool’” (Jas. 2:2–3).

Augustine: If we refer this difference between sitting and standing to ecclesiastical offices, it must not be thought a slight sin to hold the faith of the Lord of glory with partiality. For who could endure a rich man being chosen for the seat of honor in the Church while a poorer man, more learned and holier, is despised? But if he speaks of everyday gatherings, in which we receive rich and poor differently, who does not sin here? Yet one does not sin unless one inwardly judges thus within oneself: that the other seems better in proportion as he is richer. For this appears to be what he signifies by adding: “Have you not judged among yourselves and become judges of evil thoughts?”—that is, human thoughts.

[Col. 0193A] “Listen, my beloved brethren,” he says, “has not God chosen the poor in this world, but rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to those who love him?” God chose the poor when he said: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12). For he himself, the Son of God and of the Virgin, chose poor parents, by whose care he might be nourished according to the flesh. Let it therefore be said more plainly: “Listen, my beloved brethren”—that is, attend more diligently—because those who are richer in this world are not better in the divine judgment, and therefore are not to be preferred to the poor. For God chose not the rich but the poor—that is, the humble, because of their contempt for visible things; in faith, however, they appear contemptible to the world because of the riches that are invisible. Yet he has made these illustrious and noble by the hope [Col. 0193B] of the kingdom to come.

“But you,” he says, “have dishonored the poor,” namely by saying: “Stand there,” or, “Sit beneath my footstool.” It follows: “Do not the rich oppress you by their power, and do they not themselves drag you into courts?” As if he said: The rich oppress you by their power, taking away your goods and inflicting blows; they themselves even drag you into courts and cause you to be condemned without cause. Here he shows more plainly whom he above called rich: namely, those who prefer riches to Christ. They, being themselves strangers to the faith, oppress believers by their power and drag them before the courts of the powerful. There is also another reason why the rich are not to be chosen: namely, because they bring evils upon the faith. “Do they not,” he says, “blaspheme the good name which [Col. 0193C] has been invoked upon us?” In the times of the apostles many among the Gentiles and the Jews, especially their leaders, are found to have done this. They blaspheme the good name—that is, the saving name of Christ, which has been invoked upon us for our perfection.

Again he says: “If, however, you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, namely, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’ you do well; but if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.” As if he spoke more plainly, saying: If you fulfill the royal law—that is, the law preeminent among others—according to the Scriptures, according to what the Scriptures testify, namely this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Since above he had spoken harshly about contempt for the world and seemed in some measure opposed to the divine law, which commands that all be loved, lest the rich should be thought wholly to be despised, he adds: They are not to be chosen for the reasons stated; yet if you fulfill this law which says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19), you do well. For although the rich are not to be chosen because of their riches, nevertheless they are not to be loved less because of God. But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors; for the law says: “Do not favor the person of the poor, nor honor the countenance of the powerful” (ibid.). And in the Old Testament it is said: “There shall be no distinction of persons: you shall hear the small as well as the great, because the judgment is God’s” (Deut. 1).

Therefore, lest those to whom he spoke should think it a contemptible sin to transgress the law in this single matter, he added consequently, saying: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.”

As if it were said: Whoever keeps the whole law—that is, proposes in his mind to keep it—but stumbles in one point, not from human frailty but because he regards it as slight, has become guilty of all before God, who leaves nothing unpunished and knows how necessary the law is which he gave. For he who said, “You shall not commit adultery,” also said, “You shall not kill.” Whoever neglects a commandment believes that it was vainly established by God. But if you do not commit adultery and yet kill, you have become a transgressor of the law, and thus a despiser of the Lawgiver.

Let us consider this statement by a similar example. If someone offended me, he would offend in me all my brothers and friends, and in some measure would sin against them all. So one who neglects one commandment renders useless to himself the other commandments which appeared to have been fulfilled. Truly, whoever stumbles in one point is a transgressor of the whole law, because he sins both against the author of the law, whom he neglects in his law, and against charity, which is the cause and, as it were, the mother of the whole law.

Or otherwise: charity is the fulfillment of the law, and on its precepts the whole law hangs (Matt. 22). Whoever therefore acts against charity is deservedly guilty of all. But no one sins unless he acts against charity, because he neither truly loves God, whose law he loves, nor his neighbor, against whom he sins. Therefore, because above he had shown that they sinned against charity when they said to the poor man, “Stand [Col. 0194C] there,” he appropriately adds: Whoever stumbles in one point—that is, in charity, which is the root of all commandments—is accused by all the commandments, which are the children of charity. Are sins therefore not said to be equal, except perhaps because the one who sins more grievously acts more against charity, and the one who sins more lightly acts less against it?

It follows: “So speak and so act, as those beginning to be judged by the law of liberty.” As if he said: Speak thus to your neighbors and be so merciful to them as God is to you. Or otherwise: One who despises the law of Moses is judged more severely than one who despises the natural law; likewise, one who despises the law of grace more severely than one who despises the law of Moses. As if he said: Speak well and act well, because, if you neglect this, you will be condemned more severely [Col. 0194D] than those who lived in Moses’ time; for from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required.

Since, then, it is evil to choose a rich man because of riches and to reject a poor man, and since it is good even to love the rich for God’s sake and to visit orphans and widows, therefore so speak and so act. Take care to speak and act in these ways, so that, by loving your neighbors, you may deserve to be loved by God; by showing mercy, you may be found worthy of mercy. “Beginning,” he says, “to be judged as by the law of liberty.” The law of liberty is the law of charity, which above he called royal, the law in which it is said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” By this law God judges you when he grants abundant mercy, because you are not judged by the law of punishments and servitude but by the law of grace, which calls people freely to repentance and forgives sins.

“Judgment,” he says, “is without mercy to one who has not shown mercy.” As if it were said more plainly: You must act mercifully, because one who could have shown mercy but did not do so before being judged will be judged without mercy. The greater mercy anyone receives from the Lord, the more unjustly he denies mercy to a needy neighbor, and the more justly he pays the penalties of impiety.

Again, commending works of mercy to believers, he says: “Mercy exalts itself above judgment” (Matt. 5)—that is, it is set beneath judgment. Mercy, as it were, illuminates judgment, because judgment joined with mercy is more commendable and more pleasing through mercy itself. As one who did not show mercy will grieve in judgment, [Col. 0195B] so the one who did show it will rejoice and exult when rewarded. Or otherwise: “Mercy exalts itself above judgment,” that is, mercy is set beneath judgment, because where a work of mercy is found, even if there is something for which a person deserves punishment in judgment, the wave of mercy extinguishes the fire of sin. Or otherwise: mercy exalts itself above judgment. Many are gathered through mercy—but those who have shown mercy. For “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (ibid.).

It follows: “What will it profit, my brethren, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?” As if he said: You ought to do good, because those who believe faith alone sufficient are deceived when they have opportunity to act. Faith alone indeed saves a person—but faith which works through love. Just as words of piety alone do not relieve a naked or hungry brother or sister unless food or clothing is provided, so faith maintained merely in words does not save.

Here he speaks more fully of works of mercy, in order to console those whom he had terrified by the preceding statement, teaching them by what remedies daily sins—without which this present life is not lived—are expiated, lest those who stumble not only in one point but in many should be found guilty of all in judgment. The text, “Whoever believes,” namely, “and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16), must be understood of perfect faith, which works through love. Therefore faith, if it does not have works by which it may be revived, is dead in itself—that is, against itself—because it has not fulfilled in works what it promised in words.

But someone will say, namely in mockery of you: “You have faith, and I have works.” As if blessed James said: You ought to be stirred up to good works not only for the reasons already stated, but also lest you endure reproach from others; for someone confidently relying on his own works, in order to show that faith alone has no force, may say reproachfully: “You have faith without works, while I have works of faith.”

Since, therefore, you do not have works, show me, if you can, your faith without works, by some certain signs so that I may believe you are faithful. But because you cannot, when works are lacking, I will show you by the works I have my faith, through which works [Col. 0196A] I can prove myself faithful.

Here blessed James has proved that those who did not have works did not have true faith. Now he reveals what sort of faith they do have, lest they think highly of such faith. For he says: “You believe that God is one: you do well; the demons also believe, and tremble.” For it is written: “Demons went out from many, crying out and saying, ‘You are the Son of God’” (Luke 4). And the legion which besieged the man cried out in fear: “What have we to do with you, Son of the Most High God? Have you come before the time to destroy us? We adjure you by God, do not torment us” (Matt. 8; Luke 8). Those, then, who do not believe that God exists, or who do not fear him whom they believe in, are slower and more insolent than demons.

Let it therefore be said more plainly: “You believe that God is one: you do well”—that is, I do not condemn this, but it is nevertheless not enough. And lest you think that you accomplish anything great in this: even demons believe that God is one, and, what is more, tremble.

Having proved that faith without works is dead, in order to invite them more evidently to good action, he sets before those who believed on account of circumcision an elegant example of good action in the patriarch Abraham, so that, like good sons, they may imitate their good father in trial and action. For he says: “Do you wish to know, empty man, that faith without works is dead? Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar?” He employs not only arguments but also example and authority. Although Abraham was righteous through the faith which he had, [Col. 0196C] yet through the works which he added he was justified more fully; had he not done them, he would have lost the merit of his earlier faith.

Abraham reasoned, when he offered his son upon the altar, that God was able even to raise the dead (Heb. 11). Great was the trial when he was commanded to kill his son; great the faith when he believed that even from one dead he could receive offspring; great the work when he did not hesitate to offer his most beloved son. Therefore, because he offered the one in whom he had received the promise, the great power of faith is evident: even if he offered him, he believed the promise would be fulfilled, because he believed God able even to raise the dead.

When Abraham is said to have been justified through faith without works, this must be understood of works which had preceded: for he was not righteous through the works which he had done, [Col. 0196D] but through faith alone (Rom. 4). Here the subject is works which follow faith, through which he is justified more fully after he had already been righteous through faith. Hence Paul says: “By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tried” (Heb. 2). This offering is a work and a testimony of faith and righteousness. Paul praises in Abraham the constancy of faith; James praises the greatness of his works. For Abraham was perfect in both, and in both he is set forth as an example.

And lest the Christian disciples to whom Saint James wrote should be unable to imitate the works of so great a father—especially since no one now compels them to offer their children—he adds the example of a sinful woman, who through works of mercy and hospitality was freed from sins, enrolled among the citizens of the Israelite people, and numbered among the generations of the Savior. For he says: “Likewise also Rahab the prostitute, was she not justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way?” As if he said more plainly: Likewise—that is, not only Abraham through his greater works, but Rahab too through her lesser works—was justified, receiving Joshua’s messengers and sending them out by another way, lest they should be killed by the men of Jericho.

Rahab is interpreted “breadth” and signifies the Church enlarged through faith. By her example he urges them to escape the destruction of their perishing homeland through works of mercy, to receive and protect Christ’s messengers and send them on to Jesus, as blessed Gamaliel is recorded to have done (Acts 5).

There were some in the apostles’ time who came down from Judea [Col. 0197B] to Antioch, insufficiently instructed in the law of faith, and taught that Gentile believers ought to be circumcised; and they introduced other errors which caused no small labor and dispute to the true preachers (Acts 15). Blessed James therefore removes these persons from the office of the word, lest they hinder true preachers. Let him then say: As I have urged you, he says, to perform works of mercy, so I urge you to avoid foolish teaching. “Therefore, my brethren, do not become many teachers, [knowing] that you receive a greater judgment.” One who is unlearned and usurps the office of teaching, and does not proclaim Christ sincerely, deserves greater condemnation than if he alone perished in his own crime; just as, on the contrary, one who ministers well acquires for himself a good rank.

Thus this holy Apostle speaks more plainly: “Do not become many teachers, my brethren.” Why? “Because we all stumble in many ways.” This is truly dangerous, because not only you, who are less instructed, but we all—preachers who are even greater—stumble in many ways: some by living badly, others by teaching badly. In these and other ways he counts himself among them, so that he may rebuke them more freely.

The righteous person stumbles in one manner, the wicked person in another. The righteous person stumbles through the frailty of the flesh, yet does not cease to be righteous. Hence Solomon says: “The righteous man will fall seven times in a day and rise again” (Prov. 24). Therefore, just as stumbling is daily, so daily healing through prayers and good works is necessary for all. But after stumbling the ungodly fall into evil.

It follows: “If anyone does not stumble in word, that person is a perfect [Col. 0197D] man.” That is, in speech whose offense human frailty can avoid, such as the speech of detraction, pride, boasting, or idle and superfluous talk. Whoever does not stumble in these is a perfect man. As if he spoke more plainly, saying: We stumble in many ways, by these and many other means, and therefore we are not perfect; for only the person who does not stumble in word is perfect. By this statement he wishes to show that verbal offense is unavoidable, so that he may deter the unlearned from desiring preeminence; for one who desires to preside must be more perfect than others, lest he stumble while he ought to be of benefit.

Again he says: “If we put bits into horses’ mouths so that they obey us”—understand: much more ought we to put them [Col. 0198A] into our own mouths. In drawing the comparison from horses to the tongue, he shows both the appropriateness and the possibility of restraining the tongue. As if he said: It is fitting that we put the bits of self-control into our mouths, so that we may obey our Creator and, through guarding the tongue, attain uprightness of conduct as well.

He next offers another comparison from ships when he says: “Behold, though ships are large and are threatened by strong winds,” and so forth. Allegorically, large ships on the sea are human minds in the world; the winds by which they are driven are the mind’s desires, through which people are naturally compelled to do something whereby they may arrive at a good or an evil end. The rudder is the intention of the heart, by which the good, having crossed the waves of the world, find the harbor of salvation, while the reprobate perish as though in Scylla or Charybdis.

Scylla and Charybdis are two rocks at Sicily by which ships are swallowed up or damaged. [Note: [Col. 0197D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book II, chapter 3.] “They also say that Scylla was a woman girded with dog-heads, because of the great barking beside the strait of the Sicilian Sea—that is, Sicily—in which sailors, terrified by the whirlpools of waves rushing together, suppose the waves to bark, when the gulf of the engulfing tide dashes them about.”

Thus, as stated above, Scylla and Charybdis are two rocks in the Sicilian Sea—that is, at Sicily—having countless cavities around them which alternately swallow and disgorge water. When they sometimes swallow and disgorge it, they seem to passersby like the voices of many barking dogs. Hence the proverb: “If you have escaped Scylla, beware lest you fall into Charybdis.” Therefore, as stated above, good intention is the rudder of the heart by which the good find the harbor of salvation; but the reprobate perish, as if in Scylla or Charybdis, through evil intention. Since, then, the good find the harbor of salvation and the wicked swiftly perish, he rightly adds:

“So also the tongue is a little member, but it exalts great things”—that is, great rewards, if the impulse of the one directing it steers it well; but if badly, it exalts great destruction for itself and its own. Hence Solomon: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. 18). The tongue exalts life if it teaches the Church well; [Col. 0198D] but it exalts death if it teaches badly. For he is dealing with those who lacked life and knowledge and yet presumed to teach. Some books have: “and boasts great things,” because, despising the words and thoughts of others, it boasts that it alone is wise and eloquent. Hence it is said: “Do not multiply proud words in your boasting” (1 Sam. 2).

Again he presents a very fitting example from fire, adding: “See how great a forest a small fire kindles! And the tongue is a fire, the whole world of iniquity.” So too an unrestrained tongue causes a great store of good works to perish; and since it is almost impossible for even the perfect to avoid sin, not just anyone ought to seek the ministry. “And the tongue,” he says, “is a fire, a world of iniquity,” because by evil speech it devours, as it were, the forest of virtues; and through it nearly all crimes are either arranged, such as robberies and adulteries; or committed, such as perjuries and false testimony; or defended, as when any impure person, excusing the crime he has committed, pretends to possess a good which he has not done.

It follows: “The tongue is situated among our members, defiling the whole body, and setting aflame the wheel of our birth, itself set aflame by Gehenna”: that is, it contaminates the entire course of temporal life, as long as we are driven onward toward death, like a turning wheel. Or he calls it the wheel of our birth because, deservedly cast out of inward stability by the first transgression, we are carried here and there by a wandering mind [Col. 0199B] and are wholly ignorant where danger or salvation lies. This wheel of birth is set aflame by the fire of the tongue when the fault of inborn disturbance is further defiled by foolish and harmful speech.

“Set aflame by Gehenna,” he says. As Gehenna always burns, so the devil, for whom it was made, wherever he may be—whether in the air or beneath the earth—carries with him the torments and flames of his punishments. Stirred by this punishment, he suggests the flame of vices to human beings; and the things which he has suggested to them through envy, he reveals through the tongue’s lack of restraint and compels them to bring to effect through their other members.

Again, showing more plainly the malice of the untamed tongue, he says: “Every kind of beasts, birds, serpents, and other creatures is tamed and has been tamed by human nature; but no human being can tame the tongue, an unquiet evil, full of deadly poison.” The tongue of the wicked surpasses beasts in fierceness, birds in levity, and serpents in venomousness. Some are beastlike, who “sharpen their tongues like a sword” (Ps. 63); some are flighty, who “set their mouth in heaven” and whose mouth “has spoken vanity” (Ps. 72); some are serpent-like, of whom it is said: “The poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 13).

We read in Pliny that an exceedingly savage asp in Egypt was tamed by a householder; it came daily out of its cave and was accustomed to receive food from his table. We read in Marcellinus of a tiger made tame and sent from India to the emperor Anastasius. [Col. 0199D] Some are beastlike in thought and deed; some are like birds in instability; others serpents in their cunning to do harm. Their tongue is difficult for a teacher to restrain. Therefore no human being can tame the tongue—that is, no teacher can restrain the tongue of loquacious subjects. It is an unquiet evil—that is, it cannot be tamed, because it does not rest in one place, so that the talkative person alone sins, but spreads like poison as it passes from one person to another.

Because Pliny’s account above has recalled to our memory the tamed asp, let us, if you please, hear a little more fully concerning the nature of this same serpent, as blessed Isidore teaches. [Col. 0200A] [Note: [Col. 0199D] *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 4; and see Grialius’s notes on this passage.]

“The asp,” he says, “is so called because it introduces and spreads poison by its bite; for the Greeks call poison *ios* (ἴος), and hence *aspis*, because it kills by its poisonous bite. There are diverse kinds and species of this serpent, with different effects in doing harm. It is said, however, that when an asp begins to suffer an enchanter, who summons it from its cave by certain spells, if it does not wish to come out, it presses one ear to the ground and stops and covers the other with its tail; and thus, not hearing those magical words, it does not come out to the enchanter.

“Dipsas is a kind of asp, called in Latin *situla* [‘water-vessel’], because one whom it bites dies of thirst. Hypnalis is a kind of asp so called because it kills by sleep; Cleopatra applied this to herself and so was released by death as if by sleep. [Col. 0200B] The asp called haemorrhois causes the person struck by it to sweat blood, so that, as the veins are dissolved, it draws out through the blood whatever life there is. For blood is called *haima* (αἷμα) in Greek. The asp *prester* always runs with open, steaming mouth; the poet mentions it thus:

> “And the greedy *prester*, stretching its smoking jaws.”

Whomever this creature strikes is distended and killed by monstrous swelling; for putrefaction follows the swelling. The *seps*, a wasting asp, when it bites a human being immediately consumes him, so that he wholly melts away in the serpent’s mouth.”

Having said this briefly concerning the kinds of asps, let the teacher of the Spains, Isidore, again tell us something about the nature of the tiger, of which Marcellinus above made mention, for those of us who desire to hear it to the praise of God, who is always wonderful in his creatures and works. [Col. 0200C] [Note: [Col. 0200D] *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 2.]

“The tiger,” he says, “is called so because of its swift flight; for the Persians and Medes call an arrow by this name. It is a beast marked with varied spots, wonderful in strength and speed. The river Tigris is named from it because it is the swiftest of all rivers.” The region of Hyrcania, situated beside the river Phison, produces these especially. Moreover, they are accustomed to tie female dogs—that is, bitches—at night in the woods and expose them to tigers. The tigers leap upon them, and from the same litter there are born dogs so fierce and strong that they throw down lions in their embrace.

[Col. 0200D] Therefore, as stated above, the tongue of the wicked surpasses beasts in fierceness, birds in levity, and serpents in venomousness, because beasts are tamed by human nature, while the tongues of the wicked cannot be tamed even by more perfect teachers. For this reason we have included these most ferocious beasts in this reading, so that the prudent reader may readily understand how grave and deadly a plague the untamed tongue is toward itself and its neighbors.

“With it,” as blessed James says, “we bless God and the Father; and with it we curse human beings, who have been made in the likeness of God.” As if he said: With it we bless God and the Father, namely by giving thanks and praise; and with it, by speaking ill, we curse human beings. For whoever speaks ill of a brother provokes him to curse in return. He then adds much concerning the severity of this poison, because in censuring the creature we offend the Creator.

“With it we curse rational human beings” [Note: [Col. 0201D] Interlinear Gloss: “rational,” as he himself is. Or, “as he himself,” etc. See it in this place if you wish to grasp the sense of our author, for, as always, he transcribes both glosses closely.]—that is, those truly possessing the knowledge of God. Or: just as he himself has supreme rule over all, so human beings, made in his likeness, preside over the other creatures.

It follows: “Does a spring send forth from the same opening sweet and bitter water?” A preacher ought sometimes to employ sweet and sometimes bitter preaching, attracting and rebuking; it is quite difficult to do both, with different words directed to the same end. “These things,” he says, “ought not to be so, brethren.” Truly, we ought not with the same [Col. 0201B] mouth to bless the Head and curse the members, because the sweetness of blessing is consumed by the bitterness of cursing, as we show better by a comparison. If you mix sweet and bitter water together and they issue through the same opening, the sweet turns bitter by mixture with the bitter; the bitter does not turn sweet by mixture with the sweet. So the tongue’s sweetness is not pleasing if mixed with bitterness, because “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5), and “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15).

Again he sets forth other examples, saying: “Can a fig tree, my brethren, bear grapes, or a vine figs?” As if he said: Just as a tree which has lost its natural fruit does not bear another tree’s fruit, [Col. 0201C] so cursing, even if it appears to speak well, nevertheless does not bear the fruit of blessing. Why? Because sweet things are more easily changed into bitter than bitter things into sweet.

Must a teacher be a fig tree by the sweetness of the blessedness to which he exhorts and employ sweet words, and also be a vine that causes all temporal things to be forgotten, in which he must use harsh words? But can the same teacher be a fig tree, attracting by sweetness, and a vine, withdrawing people from love of earthly things by greater harshness? It is as difficult as making salt water sweet: that is, a preacher who sharply bites at the morals of others cannot in the same teaching be sweet toward those same people.

It follows: “Who is wise and instructed among you? Let him show his works by good conduct in the meekness of wisdom.” Having refuted those who had neither holiness of life nor control of the tongue, he urges those who seemed wise to themselves—and those who were wise—that they should demonstrate their wisdom more by disciplined living than by teaching others. For one more inclined to teach than to act sometimes falls into boasting or strife, or envy against other teachers, and many other evils.

As if he said more plainly to those presuming to preach: You ought not quickly become teachers, because which of you is so wise in understanding and so disciplined in the practice of life that he dares assume the teaching office? Let him first learn [Col. 0202A] to act well before teaching others, so that through good conduct among you he may be able to be an example for others; and let this be done with meekness, lest he despise others because of his wisdom and good works.

Again inviting them to charity and peace, he says: “But if you have bitter zeal and contentions in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth.” As if he said: If, having zeal for God, you do good things, yet from the consciousness of good works are bitter toward your neighbors, despise them, and cast them down with angry words—and, what is less, if contentions are in your hearts although they do not break forth into words—then do not boast and lie against the truth. That is, do not lie to God, to whom in baptism you promised to renounce [Col. 0202B] the pomps of the devil—something you do not do when you are proud of a good work. Do not think that you will receive glory for deeds done from pride and for the humiliation of others, but punishment.

“This wisdom,” he says, “does not descend from above, but is earthly, animal, demonic.” As if he said: This swollen and resentful wisdom does not descend from above, from God, who is teacher and giver of spiritual goods; rather, it is earthly, animal, demonic—desirous of earthly glory, not spiritual, but seeking only sensible things in the manner of animals. This earthly and demonic wisdom knows and does only what the devil has infused into human nature because of transgression: namely, it turns itself toward mad and harmful things.

It follows: “Where jealousy [Col. 0202C] and contention are, there are instability and every evil work.” As if it were said more plainly: Truly earthly wisdom is not from God, because where there is zeal for God and contention against one’s neighbors in speech, there is instability of a mind fluctuating here and there, because it neglects to fasten itself to the one anchor of heavenly contemplation; and there is every evil work in God’s sight, even though it may appear right to human beings.

Again he adds: “But the wisdom which is from above is first indeed chaste, then peaceable, moderate, compliant, agreeing with the good, full of mercy and good fruits.” This is the meekness which above he commanded them to possess, opposed to bitter zeal and contention. Unless chastity first takes its seat in the mind, no perfection follows in action. Therefore wisdom from above is first chaste, because it understands and acts chastely; then peaceable, because through self-exaltation it does not separate itself from God or from fellowship with neighbors. It is moderate—that is, in all things it neither exceeds nor falls short of the measure; compliant, because if in any matter it acts inadequately, whether through ignorance or negligence, it assents to the persuasion of the good; agreeing with the good—that is, what it sees pleases the good does not displease it; full of mercy, namely in disposition, and of good fruits—that is, works of mercy, namely fasts, vigils, and prayers; judging without pretense, because it does not desire to appear [Col. 0203A] holier or more learned than it is, nor tear down its neighbor for its own commendation, as contentious wisdom often does.

As if he said: You ought to seek wisdom of this sort not only for the reasons stated, but also because for those who make peace, as though sowing this seed, the fruit of eternal blessedness—that is, the reward of righteousness bestowed for righteous works—is sown and prepared in peace. Whoever here devotes himself to peace and, as it were, scatters the soil of his heart with works of peace as with seed, it is just that he should possess eternal peace as the fruit of that seed.

It follows: “Whence are wars and quarrels among you?” As though he were saying: From true wisdom peace arises, both here and in the world to come; but, on the contrary, whence among you are wars and quarrels, except from jealousy and contention? “Do they not,” he says, “come from your desires, which wage war in your members?” [Col. 0203B] For what a corrupt mind suggests, hand and tongue strive to carry out. “You desire,” he says, “and do not possess; you kill and are jealous, and you cannot obtain.” As though he said: Truly, quarrels arise among you from desires, and in this order: what you desire, you do not possess; you kill in order to possess, you are jealous, and yet cannot obtain. “You quarrel,” he says, “and wage war, and you do not have because you have not asked.” “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, in order that you may spend it upon your desires.”

Above he had forbidden jealousy and contention; therefore he also discusses them more fully, adding other vices which follow from them—namely, the contentions of desire, and from desires, wars and quarrels. For one who desires to be preferred to others, or to abound in temporal goods, [Col. 0203C] hates, envies, and kills. Hence he now adds: “You quarrel and wage war for temporal glory, and you do not have because you have not asked. You ask for superfluity and do not receive, because you love earthly things more than God. Because you ask wrongly,” that is, you are ungrateful to God the giver. “For this reason,” he says, “you do not receive what you ask, because you do not ask God worthily. For if you asked him with a devout intention, he would give you not only everlasting things, but also temporal necessities for your use.” Those to whom the apostle James wrote this could have said: “You say that we do not ask—yet certainly we ask every day.” He answered them: “You do indeed sometimes ask, and yet do not receive, because you ask wrongly.”

[Col. 0203D] Again he adds, saying: “Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity toward God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God.” Above he had spoken of God’s open enemies: “Do not the rich oppress you by their power, and themselves drag you before courts?” and so forth. But lest these alone should be thought to be enemies—those who openly blaspheme and persecute—he here treats also of all lovers of the world, declaring that they are enemies of God. As though he said: You ought not to spend yourselves upon desires, that is, to persist in them or consume your life in them, because by this you are shown to be lovers of the world, and thus adulterers: having abandoned love for heavenly wisdom, you turn aside to the embrace of this world, and thereby make yourselves enemies of God.

Again he adds: “Or do you think that [Col. 0204A] Scripture speaks in vain: ‘The spirit which dwells in you desires unto envy’?” Scripture, which restrains us from association with the wicked, speaks thus through Moses: “You shall not make a covenant with the people of that land, nor with their gods” (Deut. 7). And again: “You shall not do their works, but shall break down their statues” (Exod. 23). Let blessed James therefore say: You ought not to quarrel, for the spirit which is in you does not desire toward envy, but rather makes you harmonious.

Alternatively: “The spirit which dwells in you desires unto envy,” that is, it desires that you should envy the world. Or: the spirit desires “unto envy,” that is, against envy; it desires, namely, that envy be removed. Or it desires that you should envy the world and not love it. Or the spirit of every human being desires temporal things unto envy, [Col. 0204B] because it envies others what it does not possess.

It follows: “He gives greater grace. Therefore it says: ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (Prov. 3). As though he said: The Spirit of grace does not make one envious; rather, it gives grace, that is, gifts freely bestowed, greater than the riches of this age. “Therefore,” that is, so that we may know to whom he gives and to whom he does not give, Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” As though it were said more plainly: God punishes all evil persons; but he is said especially to resist the proud because he strikes with greater punishment those who neglect to submit to God through repentance. But he gives grace to the humble, who submit themselves to the hands of the true physician amid the wounds of their sins. “He gives grace to the humble,” that is, eternal life and good works.

Again he adds, [Col. 0204C] saying: “Be subject therefore to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you.” As though he said: Because God gives grace to the humble, be subject to God—that is, fulfil his will. Resist the devil when he suggests evil, and thus he himself will flee from you. Draw near to the Lord through humility and the other good works; and he will draw near to you, giving grace so that you may advance to what is better, and delivering you from distress.

Again, desiring to lead them to perfection, he says: “Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.” As though he said: If you truly wish to draw near to God, you who until now have been sinners, purify and cleanse your hearts, and possess innocence of hands, [Col. 0204D] lest you be double-minded, loving eternal and temporal things at the same time. “Be wretched,” he says, “and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow.” As though he said: Be wretched and mourn, mindful of your crimes. You who have made others wretched, endure the miseries and poverty of this world, and grieve inwardly for what you have committed. Let your laughter, which arose from the frivolity of the world, be turned into mourning, and the joy of the mind occasioned by committing some sin into sorrow.

It follows: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” As though he said more plainly: Humble yourselves in every way, bearing poverty and tribulation for love of him, casting yourselves down, and he will exalt you in eternal life.

Again he says: “Do not speak evil of one another, brothers. For he who speaks evil of a brother or judges a brother speaks evil of the law and judges the law.” As though he said: Not only should you conduct yourselves thus toward God, but also restrain your tongues from the vice of detraction. The vice of detraction belongs to the poison of the tongue. Therefore one who speaks evil of, or judges, a brother [Col. 0205A] on account of some slight sin, lesser knowledge, or anything of that sort, speaks evil of the law which forbade detraction and judges the law, as though saying: “The law did not act rightly.”

Or otherwise: He who speaks evil of a brother carrying out the law speaks evil of the law and judges the law, asking why it gave such commands as order injuries done by brothers to be forgotten. And lest they should think that it is a slight sin to speak evil of the law, he added that they are to be punished as transgressors, saying: “Whoever judges the law is not a doer of the law, but its judge”—that is, [Col. 0205B] its critic.

Again, adding almost as a threat, he says: “There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to destroy and to deliver.” As though he said more plainly: You ought not judge, because you will be judged by God. For he who gave the law to be fulfilled is himself able to judge those who do not fulfil it. The lawgiver and judge himself, he says, is able to destroy and to deliver: to destroy those who do not fulfil it and to deliver those who do.

It follows: “But who are you, that you judge your neighbour?” As though he said: You are worse and more wicked than he, and may be cast down into greater sins, while he may rise to good things. As though it were said more plainly: You ought to avoid detractions not only so that you may not be judged by God as a transgressor of the law, but also because perhaps in no respect [Col. 0205C] do you excel those whom you criticize.

Again, for their correction, he adds, saying: “Behold, you who now say: ‘Today or tomorrow we shall go to that city, spend a year there, trade, and make a profit’—you who do not know what tomorrow will bring.” After reproving detraction, he condemns the rashness of those who, lacking certainty of life, promise themselves life and profit in the future through desire for temporal things. “Behold,” he says, “you are those who say: ‘Today or tomorrow we shall go to that city,’” and so forth. He had said that detraction must be avoided, and behold another vice: foolish lightness of mind, setting out for themselves a span of life. Here he notes their manifold folly: they plan an increase of gains, assume that they will live a long time, think it lies within their own power [Col. 0205D] where they will spend a year, and in all this disdain to recall to mind the judgment of the heavenly Judge.

“For what,” he says, “is your life?” He does not agree with those who say that there is nothing after death; rather, he teaches that the life of the wicked is brief in the present, though eternal death follows it in the future. As though he said: You ought not promise yourselves these things, because your life is brief—a vapour appearing for a little while and then vanishing—instead of saying: “If the Lord wills,” and, “If we live, we shall do this or that.” As though it were said more plainly: I say all these things to you so that, in hope of a longer life, you may not promise yourselves the gains of a future time, but rather leave all things to God’s will and power.

It follows: “But now you exult in your boastings, and every such exultation [Col. 0206A] is evil.” As though he said: Not only do you promise yourselves a span of life and the profits of a future time; you also exult in your boastings—that is, in riches which make people proud. Such exultation is evil because it is directed to the humiliation of others.

Again he adds, saying: “To one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin.” Throughout the text of the Epistle he shows that those to whom he wrote had knowledge of doing good and had learned the right faith, so that they presumed to make themselves teachers of others. Yet they had attained neither perfection in works, humility of mind, nor restraint in speech. Therefore, amid other words of rebuke and exhortation, he now greatly frightens them, because those who know how to do good and do not do it have greater [Col. 0206B] sin than if they did not know, although ignorance of good itself is a great sin, since it is written: “The ignorant person shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14). Let it therefore be said: “To one who knows good and does not do it, it is sin.” As though he said: You exult and are proud, and therefore will be grievously punished, because you know the good and do not do it.

Again he adds, saying: “Come now, you rich; weep, howling over the miseries which will come upon you.” As though it were said more plainly: Now, in this acceptable time and day of salvation, redeem future punishments through tears and almsgiving. Up to this point you have sinned; but now do penance. “Come now, you rich,” namely in money and in sins; “weep in your heart, howling in miseries,” that is, with outward expression of voice and deed, [Col. 0206C] in view of the future miseries which will come upon you.

It follows: “Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted; and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire.” Not only will the invisible fire of Gehenna burn up the flesh of merciless rich persons, when it begins to rage against them because they did not redeem their faults by almsgiving; it will also torment their souls.

Hence it is said: “Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16). Behold: the rust of money is turned into testimony of wickedness and an increase of punishment, because a person realizes that he wickedly gathered things which he did not need for the use of life, and is therefore punished more severely. Let it therefore be said [Col. 0206D] more plainly: Your riches, in which you trusted and which you gathered superfluously, have rotted; and your garments, with which you could have clothed those in need, have not been worn out by necessary use but eaten by moths. Your gold and silver—namely, that which is more precious and more enduring among riches, which you did not gather for the use of life—will rust, that is, fail through its own frailty. Their rust, namely their superfluous accumulation, which rotted because it was gathered though unnecessary, will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh—that is, your bodies or fleshly desires—like fire. For the outwardly raging flame will torment luxurious souls, and the inwardly piercing pain of their avarice will accuse them.

“You have stored up,” he says, [Col. 0207A] “wrath for yourselves in the last days.” As though he said: Truly you will suffer thus, because when, neglecting care for the poor, you gather treasures of money, you heap up for yourselves the wrath of the inward Judge. It does not yet appear, as it were, but in the last days it certainly remains.

It follows: “Behold, the wages of the labourers who harvested your fields, which have been withheld by you, cry out; and their cry has entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth.” It is a great injustice when rich people refuse mercifully to receive the poor; but it is much greater when they also refuse to render to hired workers and servants the wages due for their labour.

Thus blessed Job says: “If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep; and if I have eaten its fruits [Col. 0207B] without payment” (Job 31). For the land cries out when its workers murmur against the greedy and proud owner of the land because of wages promised but not paid. Although furrows are distinguished from land by the word used, they are nevertheless land. Therefore the furrows weep when those same workers, afflicted by prolonged labour and deprived of the wages promised them, complain of the man who hires them for work. The owner of the field himself also eats the fruits of the land without payment when he does not pay his workers the wage which he owes by agreement.

Gregory, however, expounding this saying mystically, says [Note: [Col. 0207D] *Morals*, Book 22, ch. 15]:

“What does it mean for the land to cry out, the furrows to weep, [Col. 0207C] and a man to eat his own fruits by purchase? Who ever needs to buy what is his? Who has heard a land crying? Who has seen furrows weeping? And since the furrows of the land are always themselves land, why are the land said, in distinct expression, to have cried out, and its furrows to weep with it? For since a furrow is nothing other than land, it is not without a reason of great distinction that he adds: ‘And its furrows weep with it.’ In this matter, because the sequence of the historical sense fails, the mystical meaning displays itself to us as though flowers had now opened. It cries out plainly, as it were: ‘Because you recognize that the reasoning of the letter has failed, it remains for you undoubtedly to return to me.’

“Everyone, indeed, whether he governs a household by private right, or presides over communities of the faithful for the common good, in possessing the rights of rule over the faithful entrusted to him, holds what else but land to be cultivated? For by divine dispensation each person is set over others for this purpose: that the mind of those subject to him, like tilled earth, may be made fruitful by the seed of his preaching. But the land cries out against its owner if either a private household or the holy Church murmurs justly against the one set over it. For the land’s crying out is the reasonable grief of subjects against the injustice of their ruler. Hence it is rightly added: ‘And its furrows weep with it.’

[Col. 0208A] “Land, even uncultivated by any labour, often produces some food for human use; but when ploughed, it bears crops for fullness. There are some who, not cut by the ploughshare of reading or exhortation, bring forth certain goods from themselves, however small, like land not yet ploughed. There are also some who are ever intent on hearing and retaining holy preaching; having been split from their former hardness of mind by the ploughshare, as it were, of the tongue, they receive the seeds of exhortation and render the fruits of good work through the furrows of voluntary affliction.

“But it often happens that those in authority commit some injustice and thus harm those whom they should have benefited. When the untrained see this, they are stirred against [Col. 0208B] their rulers and murmur, yet do not strongly grieve for their neighbour through compassion. But when those who have already been broken by the plough of reading and cultivated for the fruit of good work see innocent persons oppressed even in small matters, they immediately turn to lamentation through compassion, because they mourn as their own what their neighbours suffer unjustly. For the more the perfect are moved by spiritual concerns, the more they know how to groan over others’ bodily injuries, having now been taught not to grieve over their own.

“Therefore every ruler who acts perversely toward those subject to him causes the land to cry out against him and the furrows to weep: the untrained peoples break forth into murmuring voices against his injustice, but all who are perfect afflict themselves in tears because of his wrongful deed. What the inexperienced cry out and do not grieve over, subjects of more approved life weep over in silence. The land—that is, the inexperienced—cries out at the errors of the prelate and does not grieve. The furrows—that is, people of more perfect life—weep and are silent. Thus, for the furrows to lament along with the crying land is for subjects of holier and wiser life to come to lamentation on account of the very thing for which the multitude of the faithful justly complain against their ruler.

[Col. 0208C] “The furrows, therefore, are from the land, yet are distinguished from the land by name, because those in the holy Church who cultivate their minds by the labour of sacred meditation are better than the other faithful in proportion as, through the seeds they have received, they yield more fruitful harvests of works. There are some set over holy congregations who receive the provisions of life from ecclesiastical bounty but do not render the ministry of exhortation which they owe. Against these, the example of the holy man is still rightly added when he immediately says: ‘If I have eaten its fruits without payment.’ To eat the fruits of the land without payment is indeed to receive the sustenance of life from the Church, but not to offer that Church the payment of preaching.

“Whether, then, according to the letter or according to the mystical sense, it is a grave sin to eat the fruits of the land without payment: that is, to defraud labourers of their wages or not to water the faithful people with holy preaching. Even if the labourers, patiently bearing everything, do not cry out against [Col. 0209A] the owner of the land, the withheld wage nevertheless cries out.”

“Their cry,” he says, “has entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth,” that is, the Lord of hosts, for the condemnation of those who suppose that the poor have no protector; but the almighty Lord observes the cases of each individual.

Again he adds, saying: “You have feasted upon the earth, and have nourished your hearts in luxury.” It is evident that he addresses those rich persons to whom he says, “Come now, you rich,” who had conspired in the death of the Lord and had not yet received the faith by which they might be saved. Of them he also speaks above to believers: “Do not the rich oppress you by power and drag you before courts? Do they not moreover blaspheme the good name invoked over us?” And because he writes to the twelve [Col. 0209B] tribes in the Dispersion, he exhorts believers to perform works of faith in such a way that he urges those who had not yet believed to be converted to faith and works.

As though he were speaking more plainly to those same rich persons who crucified Christ and drove the holy apostles from their territories, he says: Neglecting heavenly joys, to which one must come through fasting and afflictions, you love fleshly feasts. Such hunger and thirst will follow them in the future that not even a drop of water will be found by which a burning tongue may be cooled (Luke 16). Nor have you sinned only by gathering superfluities and seizing others’ goods, but also by spending superfluously. You have used every pleasure and had no concern for feeding the poor.

Again he rebukes them for the Saviour’s Passion, saying: “In the day of slaughter [Col. 0209C] you condemned and killed the righteous one, and he did not resist you.” Here he reproaches them with the death of the Son of God; and, as though they had done no evil, they lived luxuriously and greedily. To them properly applies his saying that greed will consume their flesh like fire and that they have stored up wrath for themselves in the last days.

Let it therefore be said more plainly: “In the day of slaughter,” that is, when power to kill had been granted you, you brought Jesus Christ the righteous one before judgment and killed him. But he, like a sheep led to slaughter, did not resist you (Isa. 53). This wrath of God which they stored up for themselves was fulfilled in them not only in the future life but also in the present, when Jerusalem—indeed, all Judaea—was conquered and laid waste [Col. 0209D] by the Romans in vengeance for the Lord’s blood and the other crimes they committed.

Again he speaks for the consolation of the faithful, saying: “Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord.”

As though he said: Because you see that unbelieving rich persons are to be punished, be patient until the coming of the Lord, which begins at each person’s end. “Behold,” he says, “the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the earth, patiently enduring until he receives the early and the late rain.” As though he said more plainly: If a farmer works so patiently for the fruit of the earth which he hopes for, how much more should you do so for the heavenly fruit? “Until he receives,” he says, “the early and the late.” As though he said: Like the farmer, [Col. 0210A] you will receive the early fruit, that is, the life of the soul after death, and the late fruit, namely the incorruption of the flesh. Or, the early fruit is in works of righteousness, the late in the reward of labours. Hence the Apostle: “You have your fruit in sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6).
