Having rebuked the proud and unbelieving, he again turns to those oppressed by the wickedness of such people, inviting them to repentance, because their oppressions will soon end—either because the righteous are taken to the Lord, or because persecutors are deprived of power—saying: “Be patient also yourselves, and strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord is near.” As though he plainly says: Although the Lord delays, nevertheless be patient like the farmer and strengthen your hearts, [Col. 0210B] even if grievous things are inflicted upon you, because the coming of the Lord is near, so that you may be taken to glory and they to punishment.

It follows: “Do not groan, brothers, against one another, lest you be judged.” As though he said: Do not groan as though you suffer greater things than you deserve, while your persecutors, though they do evil, seem to suffer no adversity. “Lest you be judged,” he says, that is, lest you be condemned because you criticize the just Judge as though he did not judge fairly. “Behold,” he says, “the judge stands before the door,” who will give you rewards and your enemies punishment. He stands before the door because he is either near to know what you do, or will soon come to repay you and them according to your merits.

Again he urges them to imitate the earlier Fathers, who patiently endured adversities for righteousness’ sake, saying: “Take, brothers, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord as an example of an evil outcome, long-suffering, labour, and patience.” The prophets were holy, so that the Spirit of God spoke his mysteries through them; yet they appeared to have an evil end, suffering death at the hands of unbelievers in the Old and New Testaments, such as Zechariah, John, Stephen, and many others. Nevertheless, they did not groan because of this end, but wished to bear it with long-suffering. Others endured long labours without murmuring: Noah in the building of the ark, Moses in governing and leading the people, Joseph in slavery, David in exile from his homeland. “Behold,” he says, “we call blessed those who endured,” because [Col. 0210D] we regard them as great and venerate them.

“You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord, because the Lord is merciful and compassionate.” “You have heard,” he says, “of Job’s endurance,” namely in the reading; with your eyes you have seen the Lord patiently enduring on the cross; and you have learned through Gospel preaching of the glory of his resurrection and ascension. To each he adds a firm and “immitabille” [Note: [Col. 0209D] Perhaps *immutabile*, “unchangeable,” as in the *Glossa*.] example: Job concerning labours, the Lord concerning the outcome of death. He does not say, “You have heard the end of Job,” whose temporal possessions were restored, but “the patience of Job and the end of the Lord,” because he invites them to suffering by Job’s example, yet not so that they may receive temporal things, as Job the old man did, but eternal things, as Christ the new man did.

“Because,” he says, [Col. 0211A] “the Lord is merciful and compassionate.” As though he said: You ought rather to imitate him because he is merciful in his nature and in his bestowals of graces: either he delivers his own from temptations in the present and, through steadfastness of faith, glorifies them even before human beings while they live; or after death he crowns them secretly and does not even then take from human beings the remembrance of the praise they earned.

Desiring wholly to cut away from them the vices of the tongue, he again adds, saying:

“Before all things, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven nor by earth nor by any other oath.” Because he desires the deadly poison of the tongue to be entirely drained away in his hearers, [Col. 0211B] he who forbade them to speak evil of one another, prohibited judging a neighbour, and forbade groaning in adversities—manifest sins—also adds this which seems slight to some, in order to abolish the habit of swearing. For “of every idle word which people have spoken, they will render account for it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12).

He then instructs them how they ought to speak, saying: “Let your speech be ‘yes, yes,’ ‘no, no,’ lest you fall under judgment.” As though he plainly says: For this reason I restrain you from the fault of swearing: lest, by frequently swearing truthfully, you should at some time fall into perjury. Rather, keep so far from perjury that you do not even wish to swear to what is true unless unavoidable necessity compels you. Yet one also falls under the judgment of guilt who, although he has never perjured himself, nevertheless swears truth more readily than is necessary.

Again he teaches sorrowful and grieving persons how they ought to conduct themselves, saying: “Is anyone among you sorrowful”—namely, because of an injury inflicted, some fault, loss within the household, or any other matter—“let him pray with an even mind and sing psalms.” Since he forbade them to groan in afflictions, he now shows, conversely, what they ought to do. Let it therefore be said more plainly: Is anyone among you sorrowful? Let him not murmur or criticize God’s judgments; rather, let him hasten to the Church and, kneeling, pray that God may send him consolation, lest worldly sorrow, which works death (2 Cor. 7), swallow him up; and let him drive from his heart the harmful plague of sorrow by the frequent sweetness of psalmody.

It follows: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with holy oil in [Col. 0211D] the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.” As he gave counsel to the sorrowful, so he gives counsel to the sick person how to guard himself from the folly of murmuring and to apply a remedy proportionate to the wound. Let the sorrowful pray for himself; let one sick in body or faith—because he suffers a greater wound—remember to seek healing through the assistance of many, and especially of elders.

As though he plainly says: Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, lest he lay the cause of his weakness before younger and less learned persons and perhaps receive from them some harmful speech or counsel. “And let them pray over him, anointing him with holy oil,” that is, consecrated oil. “And the prayer of faith,” by which the name of the Lord is continually invoked, [Col. 0212A] “will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up” from bodily illness. “And if he is in sins,” that is, even if it happens that he dies, they will be forgiven him. Many are also punished with bodily death on account of sins. Therefore, if sick persons are in sins, confess these to presbyters, abandon them with a perfect heart, and diligently strive to amend them; then they will be forgiven. For sins cannot be forgiven without confession and amendment.

Hence he rightly adds: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved.” As though he said more plainly: Confess to one another—that is, to equals, namely presbyters—your daily and light sins; but the uncleanness of a more serious leprosy confess to a priest, that is, an abbot or bishop, and take care to purge it with all devotion for as long [Col. 0212B] as he commands. “And pray for one another, that you may be saved, because the persistent prayer of a righteous person has great power.” Notice: “righteous” and “persistent.”

It follows: “Elijah was a human being subject to suffering like ourselves; and he prayed in prayer that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and heaven gave rain and the earth gave its fruit.” He establishes by example how powerful the persistent prayer of a righteous person is: by one prayer Elijah held back the heavens for so long, withheld rain from the earth, and denied fruits to mortals.

As though he said: Elijah was a human being—although no human being was second to him in virtue—like us in his bodily origin, not yet translated, subject to suffering like us through frailty of mind and flesh. “And he prayed in prayer that it might not rain [Col. 0212C] upon the earth,” namely, in order to convict the pride of the king and the hardness of the idolatrous people. But when he perceived the time, when he saw that the heart of the proud king and idolatrous people had been bent to repentance by the wasting of prolonged famine, he prayed one prayer and restored to the lands the crops and waters which he had withheld.

He sets Elijah before us as an example, lest our frailty should tremble and judge itself unable to say things comparable to so great a prophet, who deserved to be carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot (4 Kings 2). Intending deliberately to speak of his prayer, he began with humility, saying: “Subject to suffering like ourselves.” Elijah, weak in body, was fed by a widow (3 Kings 17); weak in mind, frightened by the threats of a single little woman, he fled through the wilderness (3 Kings 19). If one Elijah obtained such great things by one prayer, what then may many faithful persons obtain by many prayers?

Having shown the efficacy of prayer, he shows how great is the merit of praying for brothers and restoring them to safety. Therefore, he who in the earlier part of this Epistle removed malicious and idle speech from our tongue now commends the usefulness of correcting those who err, saying: “If anyone among you has wandered from the truth and someone converts him, [Col. 0212D] he should know that whoever causes a sinner to be converted from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.”

At the end of the Epistle he shows what we ought to speak: we should pray and sing psalms whenever we are struck by adversities; we should confess sins and pray for one another, that we may be saved; for the salvation of our neighbours—not merely temporal, but rather eternal—we should devoutly pour out prayers to the Lord. For if it is a great reward to snatch from death flesh which will altogether die, how much greater a merit is it to free from death a soul which will live without end in the heavenly homeland?

Let it therefore be said more plainly: If anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone converts him, either by sound admonition or by displaying examples of good conduct with a silent tongue, he will save that soul from death and cover a multitude of sins: by the practice of a better life he conceals them from the sight of the inward Judge. Some manuscripts read: “He will save his own soul from death.” And indeed, one who corrects a wanderer thereby gains for himself fuller joys of heavenly life.

Therefore, dearest brothers, love the practice of prayer, which will be useful to you from your neighbours: namely, a consolation of both the present [Col. 0213B] and the future life. Let your persistent prayer be relief for the sick, and let it cover a multitude of sins both in yourselves and in them. Let your prayer be so pure, so devout, and so removed from every worldly disturbance that it may obtain health for the sick in mind and body, forgiveness for sinners, and eternal blessedness for all the faithful.

Yet, beloved, I do not wish you to be unaware that whoever is entangled in earthly desires or activities cannot give himself perfectly to prayer. A mind occupied with earthly affairs or fleshly desires understands spiritual things less, cannot speak perfectly with God in prayer, and cannot receive with the ear of the heart the voice of God speaking to it in the Scriptures, because the dust of earthly activity closes that person’s eyes. One who prays truly and devoutly speaks with God. But one who, withdrawn from worldly disturbance, diligently studies the books of Holy Scripture and desires in them to know the divine will—God speaks with him. Hence Elihu is read to have spoken angrily against Job when he said:

“God speaks once to human beings in a dream, in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon them and they slumber in bed, and [a second time] he does not repeat the same thing” (Job 33). Gregory [Note: [Col. 0213D] *Morals*, Book XXIII, ch. 11]: “God speaks once, and a second time he does not repeat the same thing.” This can be understood subtly: God the Father begot the only-begotten Son, consubstantial with himself. For God’s speaking is his begetting the Word. To speak once, therefore, is to have no Word other than the only-begotten one. Hence it is openly added: “And a second time he does not repeat the same thing,” because he begot this very Word—that is, the Son—as one only. It follows: “In a dream, in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon human beings and they slumber in bed.” [Note: [Col. 0214D] Ch. 12.] What does it mean that the utterance of the Godhead becomes known to us through a dream, unless that we do not know God’s secrets while we are wakeful amid earthly desires? In sleep the outward senses are asleep, while inward things are perceived. Therefore, if we wish to contemplate inward things, we must sleep with respect to outward entanglements. The voice of God is, as it were, heard in a dream when the tranquil mind rests from the business of this age [Col. 0214A] and, in the very silence of the mind, divine commandments are weighed. For when the mind is lulled to sleep from outward actions, then it more fully recognizes the weight of God’s commandments; then the mind penetrates God’s words more vividly; then his voice is heard more clearly by the ear of the heart, and his will is known more perfectly, when it refuses to admit within itself the tumult of worldly cares.

A person is wrongly wakeful when the turmoil of worldly business shamelessly disturbs him. For the crowd of earthly thoughts, as it clamors around, closes the ear of the heart; and the less the sound of tumultuous cares is restrained in the inner chamber of the mind, the less the voice of the presiding Judge is heard. A human being is not fully capable when divided between both; but while he desires to be taught inwardly and is nevertheless [Col. 0214B] entangled outwardly, that by which he opens himself to outward hearing makes him inwardly deaf. Moses, mingled among the Egyptians, was as though awake, and therefore, while in Egypt, did not hear the Lord’s voice. But after killing the Egyptian and fleeing into the wilderness, there, while he remained for forty years, he as though fell asleep from the restless tumults of earthly desires, and therefore deserved to receive the divine voice. For, through heavenly grace, the more he became numb to the pursuit of outward things, the more truly he awoke to the knowledge of inward things. Again, when he was set over the crowds of the Israelite people, he was led up the mountain to receive the commandments of the law; and, that he might penetrate inward things, he was hidden from outward tumults.

Therefore holy people who are compelled by the necessity of their office to serve in outward ministries [Col. 0214C] always diligently flee to the secrets of the heart. There they ascend to the summit of their innermost thought and receive the law, as it were, on the mountain, while, setting aside the tumults of temporal affairs, they investigate upon the height of their contemplation the decree of the heavenly will. Hence Moses himself repeatedly returns to the tabernacle concerning doubtful matters; there he privately consults the Lord and learns what decision he should make with greater certainty. For to leave the crowds and return to the tabernacle is to set aside outward tumults and enter the secret place of the mind. There the Lord is consulted, and what must publicly be done outside is silently heard within.

This is what good teachers do every day: when they recognize that they cannot discern doubtful matters, they return to the secret place of the mind as to [Col. 0214D] a certain tabernacle. Having considered the divine law, as though the ark were set before them, they consult the Lord; and what they first hear inwardly in silence, they afterwards make known outwardly by their actions. For, in order to serve outward duties without offense, they take continual care to return to the secrets of the heart. Thus they hear God’s voice as though in a dream, while in meditation of mind they are withdrawn from carnal senses.

Hence the bride in the *Song of Songs* heard the Bridegroom’s voice as though in a dream, saying: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5). It is as though she said: While I lull my outward senses to sleep from the anxieties of this life, with the mind free I know inward things more vividly. [Col. 0215A] I sleep outwardly, but inwardly my heart is awake, because, while I scarcely perceive outward things, I keenly apprehend inward things. Elihu therefore rightly says that God speaks through a dream; and aptly adds, “in a vision of the night.” For in a nocturnal vision contemplation of the mind is accustomed to appear under certain images. In daylight we see more certainly; in a nocturnal vision, however, we see hesitantly. And because all saints, so long as they are in this life, behold the secrets of the divine nature as though under a certain image—that is, because they do not yet contemplate them more openly as they are—Elihu properly added “in a vision of the night” after saying that God speaks to us through a dream.

For the present life is night, in which, as long as we remain, we are darkened by uncertain images even through that by which we behold inward things. The prophet felt himself oppressed by a certain darkness in seeking to see God, saying: “My soul desired you in the night” (Isa. 26). It is as though he said: In this darkness of the present life I seek to see you, but I am still enclosed by the cloud of infirmity.

David also, avoiding the darkness of this night and awaiting the brightness of the true light, says: “In the morning I shall stand before you and see you, because you are not a God who wills iniquity” (Ps. 5). Blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 0215D] Our author, following the Gloss, attributes this exposition to Augustine; but the holy bishop says literally: “What does ‘I shall stand’ mean except ‘I shall not lie down’? And what else is lying down except resting upon the earth—that is, seeking blessedness in earthly pleasures? Therefore one must not cling to earthly things if one wishes to see God, who is beheld with a pure heart.”] expounds this verse as follows: “In the morning I shall stand before you,” that is, in the morning I shall not be transient, but shall stand before you perseveringly, and this through purity of life; I shall not lie down seeking blessedness in earthly things. For by saying, “I shall stand,” he indicates two things: namely, [Col. 0215C] the direction of the mind toward eternal things, and perseverance. “And I shall see,” that is, I shall know that you are properly the one who, remaining stable, gives all things motion, because you are God; and therefore you do not will iniquity—that is, I shall know that being God and willing iniquity can never be compatible.

Note each word. He says, “You are,” which properly belongs to God. Likewise: “I shall stand before you.” One stands before God as present when one is pure—and this “in the morning,” that is, as soon as one abandons the darkness of vices [perhaps read: “night”]. Or thus: “In the morning I shall stand before you”: this does not change, and then I shall see you. For the one who clings to earthly things does not see God, but the one who stands before God in the morning of virtues does. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Therefore I shall stand in the morning so that I may see you, because you are God, not willing impurity. Iniquity, falsehood, murder, and deceit [Col. 0215D] are night; when this has passed, morning comes, so that God may be seen.

[Col. 0216A] And he gives the reason why he will stand in the morning and see: because God does not will iniquity. For if he did will it, he could be seen by the wicked without the morning of good works. Therefore one who desires the future morning in order to see God recognizes that he still sees him only imperfectly in the night.

But because, as we have said, to cease from outward action is to sleep, Elihu rightly adds: “When sleep falls upon human beings.” And because holy persons, while they serve outward action, rest within the chambers of the mind, he aptly adds: “And they sleep in bed.” For holy persons to sleep in bed is to rest in the chamber of their own mind. Hence it is written: “The saints shall exult in glory, and shall rejoice in their beds” (Ps. 149). Glory is the frequent praise of good [Col. 0216B] deeds. The righteous shall rejoice. Where? Not outside in popular favor, but in their beds—that is, in their conscience. Thus they have so good a Lord, who gives grace to sinners and eternal life to the undeserving. But the fool rejoices outside, in people’s tales. The saints, however, have this manner of joy: that they refer their good things to him who gave them.

Let it therefore be said that God speaks to us once through a dream in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon human beings and they sleep in bed, because we surely then know the secrets of the Godhead when we separate ourselves from the tumultuous desire of this world into the chambers of our mind. But since, as we have often said, the tumult of worldly affairs closes the ear of the heart [Col. 0216C] and the repose of hidden contemplation opens it, it is fitting, beloved, that you reject visible and perishable things and cleave with supreme desire to spiritual pursuits. Therefore conduct yourselves in God’s service in accordance with the counsel of the blessed Apostle James, so that your continual prayer may be heard by God and may avail many amid the straits of the present time. Let the frequency of your prayers be medicine both for bodies and for souls. In imitation of Jesus Christ, the supreme and true shepherd, raise up by the constancy of pure prayer those dead in sins, so that, delivered from eternal punishments, you may be able to bring them with you into the fellowship of the elect; through him who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity for all ages of ages. [Col. 0216D] Amen.

[Col. 0217]

## EXPOSITION OF SAINT MARTIN, PRIEST OF LEÓN, ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER

[Col. 0217A] At the time when, after the passion, resurrection, and ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Church began, certain persons from the Gentiles, who had passed over to Judaism, believed in God, suffered for Christ’s faith, and were scattered abroad. The apostle Peter comforts them, writing to them from Rome in the time of the Emperor Claudius, saying: “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen sojourners of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace be multiplied” (1 Pet. 1).

All these provinces named above are Greek provinces in Asia; but there is also another Bithynia in Europe, from which those in Asia derived their origin. That Bithynia [Col. 0217B] which is in Asia is called Greater Phrygia, and is bounded off from Galatia by the river Hiera. [Note: [Col. 0217C] The manuscripts incorrectly read: *determinatur*, “is delimited.”] In Latin, *advenae* (“sojourners”) are called *proselyti* in Greek. Thus they called those who, born from the Gentiles, wished to believe in God and, after receiving circumcision, to live in Jewish fashion according to God’s law. He calls them sojourners expelled from Judaea, who came from Gentile status to acceptance of the law and afterwards to acceptance of the faith.

But if we too truly wish to say with the Prophet, “We are sojourners with you in the land, and pilgrims, as all our fathers were” (Ps. 38), we ought to believe that the Epistles of the blessed Apostle Peter were written as though to us, and to read them as sent to us. For in those Epistles he admonishes us as people whose homeland is elsewhere, where he says: “Beloved, I beseech you, as sojourners and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires which wage war against the soul.” Let it therefore be stated more plainly:

“Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ”—that is, the well-known name—“to the chosen sojourners of the dispersion,” that is, to sojourners scattered from Jerusalem in the persecution which arose under Stephen (Acts 8), or in many other persecutions, both from Jews and from Gentiles; afflicted for Christ’s faith and often driven from their homes. “According to the foreknowledge of God the Father,” that is, not according to our merits, but those whom he foreknew and predestined to become conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8). “Chosen in sanctification of the Spirit,” namely for this purpose: that through the gift of the Holy Spirit they might be sanctified, cleansed from all sins; that they might begin [Col. 0218A] to obey Christ, whom they had lost through disobedience; and that, sprinkled with Christ’s blood, they might escape the devil’s power, as Israel departed Egypt through the blood of the lamb. In the old law, whatever was to be sanctified was customarily sprinkled with the blood of victims (Exod. 12; Heb. 3).

“Grace,” he says, “and peace be multiplied to you”—namely, so that you may perfectly fulfill what you have well begun, because without Christ’s grace one does not come to the peace of his reconciliation, and nothing can be peaceable for us.

It follows: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who through his great mercy has regenerated us into the hope of life, through Christ’s resurrection from the dead, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept [Col. 0218B] in heaven for you, who are guarded by the power of God through faith for salvation, ready to be revealed in the last time.” It is as though he said: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ—namely, of the Son born as a human being in the world and consubstantial with him—who through his great mercy regenerated us into hope of life. Though by our merits we were born for death, by his mercy he regenerated us for life. He loved our life so much that he determined that his Son should die for it; and, death having been destroyed through resurrection, he showed us hope and an example of rising again. He died, that we might not fear death; he rose, that we might hope to rise; and this through his resurrection from the dead, where we shall be touched neither by old age, illness, nor any other sorrow.

“Into an incorruptible inheritance,” namely, so that we may not be corrupted by grave sins; “undefiled,” so that we may not be defiled even by lesser sins; “unfading,” so that we may not wither through daily and venial sins; “kept in heaven,” so that we may be preserved in soul and body in such a way that through purity we may be heaven and God’s dwelling-place. “Undefiled,” he says, because even in the minds of blessed people that heavenly mode of life can never become cheap through long familiarity, just as neither can the delight [Note: [Col. 0218C] Gloss: “just as luxury.”] of this present world ever turn into weariness through long use. “Unfading, kept in heaven”: not to be given in the present time, but to be rendered to you in heaven at the predestined time—you, I say, who are guarded by God’s power through faith unto salvation, and so forth.

No one can be kept in good things by the power of free choice [Col. 0219A] unless he accomplishes it from whom you have the beginning of good action [Note: [Col. 0219D] The Gloss states more clearly: “from whom you have the righteousness of good action. Strive from faith, through faith, toward the end to come,” etc.] and have begun to strive toward the end, through faith, to come into eternal salvation. Though it does not now appear, it is nevertheless ready to be revealed if we are ready. “For you,” he says, “who are guarded by the power of God”: he who gave you who believe the power to become children of God (John 1) has placed in you that perseverance through which you may receive the inheritance in heaven, because one who has not kept the Father’s discipline does not deserve to receive his inheritance (Prov. 15). But he begot you for this purpose in the present life: that you might be his inheritance, whom he might possess as a person possesses an inheritance. First he regenerated us from matter; afterwards, according to the progress of life, he regenerated us. “For salvation,” he says, “ready to be revealed in the last [Col. 0219B] time, in which you shall exult.” It is as though he said: At the time when the last enemy, death, will be destroyed, you shall exult as conquerors.

It follows: “For a little while, if it is necessary, you are grieved in various tribulations, so that the testing of your faith may be found much more precious than gold which is tested by fire.” Where eternal recompense is granted, that which seemed everlasting and burdensome amid the tribulations of the world appears brief and light. The patience of the saints is compared with gold, because, as among metals nothing is more precious than gold, so this is most worthy of all praise before God. For just as gold is tested in a furnace, and when brought out its brightness is seen, so the steadfastness of believers appears contemptible amid the pressures of the present life; but, when the contest is ended, at the judgment it will be shown how great its glory is. [Col. 0219C] Hence it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115).

Let it therefore be stated more plainly: “Now, if it is necessary, you are grieved in various tribulations,” that is, because no one can come to joy except through sorrow; you ought not to be distressed in various tribulations, whether outward or inward—not because they are for your harm, but so that the testing of your faith may be manifest, and so that you, proven faithful in the furnace of tribulation, with every rust of the old nature burned away, may appear in the future. Let your faith please God, the supreme craftsman, more than material gold pleases any craftsman.

“May it be found unto praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ; whom, though you do not see him, you love; in whom, though you do not now see him, you nevertheless believe; [Col. 0219D] and believing, you exult with inexpressible and glorified joy, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls.” “The testing of your faith,” he says, “may be found unto praise”—that is, that you may be praiseworthy and glorious through steadfastness at the revelation of Jesus Christ, namely, on the day of judgment, when it will be revealed how great God’s power is. It is as though he plainly said: The testing of your faith will be found unto praise when the Judge, praising it, says: “I was hungry and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matt. 25). It will be found unto glory when, glorifying it, he says: “Come, blessed ones [Col. 0220A] of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.). It will be found unto honor when it is said: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God”; and then the righteous will go into eternal life (ibid.). Hence it is said: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” (John 12).

“You shall exult,” he says, “with inexpressible joy,” because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2). “Receiving the end of your faith”: namely, God himself, who is the end of every consummation. “The salvation of your souls”: because you will suffer no further infirmity. This salvation is greatly to be loved, because many have diligently sought much concerning this salvation—when, or in what manner, eternal salvation would come into the world. Hence it is said: [Col. 0220B] “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10).

Thus it is now said: “Concerning which salvation the prophets who prophesied concerning the grace to come to you inquired and searched diligently, searching what or what kind of time it signified.” [Note: [Col. 0220D] Old Latin: “which the Spirit of Christ who was in them signified.”] For the Spirit of Christ in them foretold the sufferings which are in Christ and the glories that would follow. It is as though he said more plainly: Concerning this eternal salvation—that is, concerning Christ’s coming—the prophets searched in secret, namely from the Lord or from angels. Hence one of them, because of his great love of saving knowledge, deserved to be called by an angel “a man of desires” (Dan. 9). “Who prophesied,” he says, “concerning the grace to come to you”: namely, by speaking openly to people and expounding [Col. 0220C] what they themselves had known secretly in inward contemplation. “Searching what or what kind of time it signified”: in what year, under what ruler, whether warlike or peaceful, whether through the Virgin’s childbirth or by some other manner.

“The Spirit of Christ in them, foretelling the sufferings which are in Christ and the glories that would follow.” It is as though he said: Although the Spirit of Christ was in them, foretelling not only his coming but also the delayed and long-desired sufferings which belong both to the head himself and to his members, and that he was to be ended by the cross and buried. He calls the archangels and the angels near to them the Spirit of Christ, through whom the Lord works and who are subject to Christ. “And the glories that would follow,” he says. There are two glorifications of the Lord according to the form of the human being he assumed: one, namely, by which he rose from the dead; the other, by which he ascended most gloriously into heaven before the disciples’ eyes. A third remains, likewise before human eyes, when he comes in his majesty to render to each according to his works (Matt. 16). These are the subsequent glories which blessed Peter declares to have been revealed to the prophets through the Spirit of Christ.

Hence it follows: “To whom it was revealed”—namely, to the prophets—“that they ministered not to themselves, but to you, those things which have been announced to you through those who preached the Gospel to you, with the Holy Spirit [Col. 0221A] sent from heaven—things into which angels desire to look.” He says this in order to urge them to take care for the salvation offered to them, which the earlier saints loved so greatly. It is as though it were more plainly said: To the prophets who searched the other hidden things, this too was revealed: that this salvation was to come, not for themselves—that is, not in their own days—but rather in yours, who are born at the end of the ages. “But they ministered to you those things which have been announced to you”: they themselves were not lords of salvation, but your ministers, foretelling all the mysteries of redemption which are now fulfilled and proclaimed, though hidden from many. I say, proclaimed through those who preached the Gospel to you, with the Holy Spirit sent from heaven—that is, through messengers of such power, namely the holy apostles, who proclaimed Christ neither falsely nor deceptively, but at the Holy Spirit’s dictation.

The Spirit is seen in prophets and apostles in this way: prophets and apostles announce the same salvation—the former as future, the latter as fulfilled. Therefore there is one Church: one part preceded Christ’s coming; the other follows it.

“Into whom angels desire to look,” he says. It is as though he said: So great is the subsequent glory of the man who suffered for us that even the angelic powers in heaven, though perfected in eternal salvation, rejoice continually to behold not only the magnificence of his immortal Godhead but also the splendor of his assumed humanity. But why do they desire to behold him whose face they never cease to behold, unless because contemplation of the divine presence so blesses the angels that they ever hunger insatiably for its sweetness as though it were new? Or: angels desire to look into the Holy Spirit, whose majesty and glory are so great that angels continually desire the vision of him, just as they desire that of the Father and the Son. Him divine merciful grace sent down to earth for the sake of human salvation and poured into the minds of believers to enlighten them; they are satisfied by the glory which they continually behold.

It follows: “Therefore, having girded the loins of your mind, being sober, hope perfectly for the grace offered to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ; as children of obedience, not conformed to the former desires of [Col. 0221D] your ignorance, but according to the Holy One who called you, be yourselves holy in all manner of life.” “Therefore,” he says, “having girded the loins of your mind”—that is, because such great grace is promised you that you will openly see him whom angels now see, take all the more care to be worthy. “Having girded the loins of your mind”: that you may cut away even superfluous pleasures from the heart and be able to receive that grace. “Being sober, hope perfectly,” steadfastly persevering, “for the grace offered to you”: that is, wait confidently, chaste in mind and body. For one who does not know that he pleases the Lord rightly, being without hope of good things, rightly fears lest he come soon. Grace is offered at Christ’s revelation—that is, it is made manifest, to be freely given by Christ to believers.

[Col. 0222A] As children of obedience, persevere in goodness, so that you may wait securely and be obedient children to the Father who corrects you: “Not conformed to the former desires of your ignorance,” that is, do not be dogs returning to their vomit (2 Pet. 2). For in this respect you were in some measure excusable before, but now you know the truth, according to him—that is, according to the example of Christ—who called you, the Holy One: that is, sanctified and sanctifying you, so that you may be holy in all conduct. Hence it is said: “You also be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5). For this purpose he called you: that you yourselves may be holy—that is, his children—in all conduct, steadfast against vices and against tribulations, because it is written: “Be holy, for I am holy” [Col. 0222B] (Lev. 11). It is as though he said: I am your Father, and I desire you to be such as I am.

It follows:

“And if you invoke as Father him who judges according to each person’s work without respect of persons, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourning.” It is as though he said more plainly: If you invoke as Father him to whom you say in prayer, “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matt. 6), who judges without respect of persons—that is, not like a carnal father, accustomed to spare his sinful children more indulgently than his servants; rather, God the Father adopts as children obedient servants, indeed even enemies who submit themselves to him, while those who appeared honorable under the name of children he makes strangers to the inheritance because of their disobedience—then conduct yourselves in fear throughout the time of your sojourning, because he judges according to the work of each person.

[Col. 0222C] It is as though he said: Take care lest through negligence and sloth you prove unworthy of so great a Father, and lest, while you are secure during the time of your exile, you should—God forbid!—be unable to attain the homeland of blessedness. Therefore, that you may be holy, conduct yourselves in the fear of God throughout the whole time of your sojourning, that is, as long as you are in the exile of this world. “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. 28). It is as though he said more plainly: You do not rightly invoke God at all if you are not fearful and watchful.

“Knowing that you were redeemed not with corruptible gold or silver from your vain manner of life handed down by your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of an immaculate and undefiled Lamb, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world but manifested [Col. 0222D] in the last times for your sake, who are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be in God.” It is as though he said: The greater the price by which you were redeemed from the corruption of carnal life, the more you must fear lest, by returning to the corruption of vices, you offend your Redeemer.

Let it again be stated more plainly: Conduct yourselves in the fear and watchfulness of God, knowing that you were redeemed not with corruptible gold or silver—by which prices sins are customarily remitted among human beings—from your vain manner of life received by ancestral tradition, even from transgression of the law, but with precious blood: because Christ was free from actual sin, like a lamb undefiled in any act, and immaculate from original sin; namely, the gentle lamb who did not [Col. 0223A] open his mouth (Acts 8), who clothes you with his wool—that is, instructs you with his preaching and refreshes you with love. Here he touches upon Levitical and priestly observances and signifies a soul made clean through the righteousness offered to God.

“You were redeemed,” he says, “with Christ’s precious blood, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world”: that is, ordained beforehand by God, so that redemption might take place through him; “but manifested in the last times” through the assumed humanity, for the sake of saving you, who through him—that is, through his justification—are believers in God as members of his body. God raised him from the dead on the third day and gave him glory in the ascension. All this was not because he himself needed it, but so that your faith and hope might be in God—that is, so that through him you might hope to possess the same glory.

[Col. 0223B] “Purifying your souls,” he says, “in obedience to love, for brotherly affection, love one another earnestly from a simple heart, having been born again not from corruptible seed but incorruptible, through the word of the living and abiding God; because all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.” It is as though he said: Therefore love one another, purifying your souls so that they may keep faith with one bridegroom, in obedience to love—that is, be obedient out of love for God in enduring all things in brotherly affection, even if brothers injure you. “From a simple heart,” that is, not for some advantage or disadvantage; “love one another earnestly,” because up to this point you have been reborn, not from corruptible but from incorruptible seed.

Or, as he plainly says: Do this because you were born “not of blood, [Col. 0223C] nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1). “Not from corruptible seed,” that is, not from the law, which fails in many respects, but in the unchangeable Gospel. “Through the word of the living and abiding God,” he says: that is, through the Son of God, or through the Gospel which cannot be corrupted. As corruptible flesh, which perishes, is born from corruptible seed, so life, which knows no end, is bestowed through water consecrated by God’s word.

He also confirms this openly by prophetic testimony, saying: “Because all flesh is grass,” that is, transitory; “and all its glory,” that is, all the delights of the flesh, “is like the flower of grass. For the grass has withered,” that is, through care, illness, or death; “and its flower,” that is, its glory, “has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains forever.” The glory of the flesh is called a flower because it promises something from itself and yet produces no fruit from itself.

[Col. 0223D] As the price of the Lord’s passion by which we were redeemed is incorruptible, so also is the sacrament of the sacred font by which we are reborn. These are so joined to one another that neither can confer salvation without the other. For in the time of his incarnation the Lord redeemed all by his blood in such a way that we too, in our own time, may deserve through the regeneration of baptism to attain fellowship in that same regeneration. Therefore, as one corruptible being generates another corruptible being, so the Word which abides forever gives eternal life to those reborn of water and the Holy Spirit in body [Col. 0224A] and soul (John 3). Again he adds, saying: “And this is the word which has been preached to you”—namely, through me and through the other apostles.

Therefore, putting away all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all slanders, like newborn infants desire the rational, guileless milk, that by it you may grow unto salvation.

As though he said: Since you have thus been reborn and made children of the eternal Father, be such through zeal for good conduct as infants newly born are by the condition of their age. Let it therefore be said more plainly: putting away all malice, that is, the will to harm others; and all guile, that is, deception; and hypocrisies, lest you harbour one thing in the heart and another on the lips; and envy of heart at others’ prosperity; and all [Col. 0224B] slanders of speech, like newborn infants, rational and without the wrinkle of duplicity, desire milk—that is, seek the simple rudiments of faith from the breasts of Mother Church, namely from the teachers of both Testaments who wrote the divine utterances or preach them orally—that by it you may grow unto salvation; that is, by learning well, through the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation, you may attain to contemplation of the divine majesty.

Like newborn infants, rational, without guile. As though he said: Though infants because malice has been removed, nevertheless rational through wisdom, lest reason draw you toward the craftiness of the world; rather, be without guile. Hence it is said: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10). Desire milk, that by it you may grow unto salvation. Here [Col. 0224C] he touches upon those who come reluctantly to hear the sacred readings, being ignorant of that thirst and hunger of which the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0223] Maximus of Turin reads thus in Homily IV, *On the Fast of Lent*, near the end.] (Matt. 5). Therefore they arrive more slowly at the perfect advances of salvation, by which they may be refreshed with the solid food of the word—that is, may know divine mysteries or perform greater good works.

It follows: “If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet; coming to whom, the living stone, rejected indeed by men but chosen by God and honoured.”

As though he said: With the malice of the heart thus cleansed away, desire the nourishing food of Christ, if you know by experience how great divine sweetness is. For he who tastes nothing of that sweetness [Col. 0224D] need not be wondered at if he does not avoid defiling himself with earthly desires. Therefore draw near to him, and, drawing near through faith, be built upon Christ, the most firm foundation; for “no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3).

Let it therefore be said more plainly: coming to him in faith and imitation, to the living stone upon which the heavenly city is founded—not a material but a living stone—who, as he could not be cast down by any blows, so neither can those founded upon him be deceived. Rejected by men, namely when they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 10); but chosen by God, who is not [Col. 0225A] mistaken in his ordering, “that he might make both one” (Eph. 2); and honoured, namely in miracles and in the Ascension.

Again he adds: “You yourselves also, as living stones, be built into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.”

Men through unbelief are hard and senseless stones; but when instructed through discernment they are made living and are fitted to be joined together in love in God’s building. As though he said more plainly: You also, like stones solid in faith and living in good works, be built into spiritual houses against rains, winds, and floods: a holy priesthood—that is, all of you are priests, anointed with the oil of gladness—to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus [Col. 0225B] Christ our Lord. That is, not as under the old Law; rather, be built up to offer good works—alms, prayers, and yourselves—through Jesus Christ. This applies to all things.

As though he said: Be built up, because you are priests and offer sacrifices; and all this is through Jesus Christ, by whose grace you have all things.

Again, to confirm that the Lord is rightly called a stone because of his steadfastness, he says: “Therefore Scripture contains: ‘Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, precious; and he who believes in him shall not be put to shame.’”

As though he said openly: Behold, I lay in Zion—because he was born in Judaea—a solid stone, chief, that is, more perfect than all others; a corner-stone, joining the two peoples in himself; chosen [Col. 0225C] from among all; precious, because he is given as the price of redemption. And he who believes in him, namely by imitating him, shall not be put to shame: neither will he now be ashamed because of a fall, nor in the future be without reward.

It follows: “To you therefore who believe is honour; but to those who do not believe, ‘the stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner’; and ‘a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence,’ for those who stumble at the word and do not believe, wherein also they were appointed.”

The Son of God is honour to believers; but to unbelievers he is the stone rejected by the builders. He was rejected by these men as by those others. And that stone has become the head of the corner for these—that is, for believers—and for unbelievers is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence. He has become, for unbelievers, the stone rejected by the builders, because as they rejected him in their building, so he in his coming rejected them from being received into the building of his house, which is in heaven.

Let it therefore be said more plainly: Honour is yours who believe, because the Father honours those who believe in the Son, and they shall not be put to shame at the coming of the Son. But for those who do not believe is the stone rejected by the builders: the stone which they, namely the Jews, would not place in the foundation of their hearts, confirming their own Law to be observed carnally and all wishing to establish their own righteousness. Yet this stone has become the head of the corner, that is, in the Christian building. [Col. 0225D] [Col. 0226A] This stone has also become a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence. Though it is the stone on which the good are supported and rest securely, it will be a cause of stumbling for unbelievers, because they do not now believe in him and therefore will fall from vice into vice; and in the future it will be a rock of offence, because their steps will strike against him whom they trampled underfoot in humility, and they will fall into hell.

“For those,” he says, “who stumble at the word and do not believe, wherein also they were appointed.” He stumbles at the word who, because he has heard the word, is offended in mind, while not believing what he has heard. The writer heightens the folly of the one who does not believe in that—or in what—for which he was made. By nature human beings were made to believe in God and obey his will. “Wherein also they were appointed,” because “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17).

[Col. 0226B] Again he says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvellous light.”

The apostle gives to the nations this testimony of praise, once given through Moses to the ancient people, because they believe in Christ, who, like a corner-stone, united the nations to the salvation which Israel had possessed in himself (Exod. 19). From this it is proved that he writes this Epistle to those who had come to the faith from among the nations. These verses are taken [Note: [Col. 0225D] The verses taken from Hosea are not, namely, “You are a chosen race,” etc., but those explained below: “Who once were not a people, but now [Col. 0226D] are the people of God.” Or, as Hosea 2:24 reads: “And I shall say to that which was not my people: You are my people.”] from the prophecy of Hosea, which deals with the calling of the nations.

Let it therefore be said more plainly: You are a chosen race, chosen through faith and distinguished from those who, rejecting Christ the stone, became rejected; a royal priesthood, [Col. 0226C] united to the body of the supreme Priest, who ought both to hope for a kingdom and to offer to God the sacrifices of an unstained manner of life; a holy nation, no longer living in the passions of desire but living holily and justly; a people for possession, acquired, namely, by the blood of the Redeemer—as the people of Israel were once redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the lamb.

Thus in the following verse he also recalls mystically the ancient history and teaches that it has been spiritually fulfilled in the new people. “That you may proclaim his virtues”: as those delivered from Egypt sang a triumphant song to the Lord (Exod. 15), so we, after darkness has been dispelled, after receiving forgiveness through Christ, who are to be led to the homeland of eternal brightness, ought [Col. 0226D] to render God worthy thanks for his heavenly benefits—he who called us from darkness into his marvellous light, just as he also led them by a pillar of fire (Exod. 13).

It follows: “Who once were not a people, but now are the people of God.” As though he said: You who were once alienated from the commonwealth of God’s people are now the people of God: in the time of grace you have been joined to his people. “Who had not obtained mercy”: that is, you who did not even know how to hope for mercy, “but now have obtained mercy.”

Again he adds: “Beloved, I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly [Col. 0227A] desires, which wage war against the soul; maintaining good conduct among the nations, so that, in the matter in which they speak against you as evildoers, observing you from your good works, they may glorify God on the day of visitation.”

Up to this point blessed Peter has generally instructed the Church, explaining both the benefits by which God deigned to call us to salvation and the gifts by which he once deigned to honour the Jews and now us. Here he carefully exhorts the different classes of believers not, by living carnally, to render themselves unworthy of such great grace of the Holy Spirit, and not to decline from the glory of the nobility promised them. First he teaches free persons and slaves, then men and women, and finally elders and young people, how they ought to conduct themselves. He appropriately warns free persons [Col. 0227B] to abstain from fleshly desires, because the liberty of a less restrained life is accustomed to suffer greater dangers from enticing allurements.

Let it therefore be said more plainly: Beloved, I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly desires. As though he said: Since you have now obtained mercy, subject your mind to earthly things all the less, remembering that you have your homeland in heaven. The reprobate have their homeland here, whose desires they eagerly pursue; therefore they will be banished into perpetual exile, deprived of pleasures. “Which wage war,” he says, “against the soul,” because when the flesh is weakly subjected to flattering desires, the army of vices is now strongly armed against the soul.

Maintain good conduct among the nations, namely by doing good works; so that [Col. 0227C] in that in which they speak against you as evildoers—that is, in that they think you foolish because you have abandoned their gods and afflict yourselves in the world on account of your sins—observing you from your good works, that is, from your chaste conduct, observing you, that is, your worthiness, they may glorify God on the day of visitation, namely at the time of recompense.

As though he said: Even now unbelievers know how great a glory God is to grant you, when they see that you steadfastly follow him through every danger. Or, “on the day of visitation,” when God visits them by converting them from evil to good. It often happened that pagans who condemned the faith of Christians later, observing their good [Col. 0227D] conduct, began to praise Christ.

It follows: “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake: whether to the king as supreme, or to governors, as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.”

As though he said: That your conduct may please all, be subject to every human creature, both believers and unbelievers, for God’s sake: that is, resist no human dignity or authority to which God willed you to be subject. For “there is no authority except from God, and he who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13). He explains “creature” in its parts when he says: “Whether to the king as supreme,” lest even in this respect anything be said against Christian faith and religion, namely that through it the laws of the established order are disturbed.

Be subject also [Col. 0228A] to governors as sent by him—that is, by the king or by God—for the punishment, that is, the penalty, of evildoers, and for praise of the good. Not that it is always so, but he simply states what a governor’s function ought to be. Even if such a ruler condemns the good, what he does belongs no less to their praise, if the good patiently endure his wickedness and wisely resist his cunning. God often permits an evil man to exercise tyranny, so that both the wicked may be put to shame and the good more fully tested.

Again he says: “For such is the will of God, that by doing good you may silence the ignorance of foolish men.” As though he said more plainly: Truly, whatever governors do, the good gain praise, because this is willed by God, who even uses evil men for good; so that you too, [Col. 0228B] using them for good whether they are good or evil, may silence their ignorance and foolishness. That is, those governors, being ignorant how you use them for good and gain praise through them, may find nothing to blame in you, while you honour and endure even them, however unclean and unworthy they may be.

“As free persons,” he says, “and not as having freedom for a covering of malice, but as servants of God.” As though he said plainly: The greater the freedom you enjoy among human beings, the more freely be subjected to divine service. Do not have your freedom as a covering for malice: that is, let your freedom not darken your hearts, so that you sin more freely in proportion as you are less burdened by the yoke of servitude; and do not conceal your fault under the name of freedom. [Col. 0228C] The apostle wants them to be free from servitude to sins, so that they may remain good and faithful servants of the Creator. Therefore he added: “But as servants of God.” Service of God requires humility.

It follows: “Honour all; love the brotherhood.” As though he said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matt. 22), and honour each person according to his station. Love the brotherhood: that is, above all love the brethren; love even those who are subject to you in temporal condition as brothers in Christ.

Again he says: “Fear God; honour the king.” As though he said: Fear God, so that the fear of God may come first in every act of obedience; honour the king, namely revere him as supreme with greater honour.

Up to this point he has exhorted [Col. 0228D] free persons to submission; now he speaks to slaves, that they too may be subject to their masters, saying: “Slaves, be subject in all fear to your masters,” so that you may neither offend God nor refuse obedience to your masters; “not only to the good,” namely in faith, life, and character, “and gentle,” that is, commanding moderately and forgivingly, “but also to the harsh” (*dyscolis*), that is, the undisciplined.

*Schola* is called in Greek a place where people gathered to hear teachers of the liberal arts. Hence *schola* is interpreted as “leisure,” because there they were free for study. *Scholastici*, therefore, are learned persons, while *dyscoli* are unlearned and uncultivated persons.

See how he warned above that one must be subject to every human creature for God’s sake. If, for God’s sake—God knowing his good intention—someone patiently endures unjust blows from his master [Col. 0229A] while serving him well, that is, considers such sorrows slight, this is grace: that is, by these things he becomes pleasing to God, and this is what the grace of faith requires. Hence he adds: “For this is grace, if for the sake of consciousness of God one endures sorrow while suffering unjustly.”

As though he said: If you suffer unjustly, you acquire God’s grace. “For what grace is it, if, when you sin and are beaten, you endure?” As though he said: If you patiently endure punishments inflicted by masters—you who sin by refusing to obey them—and are struck by those masters, that is, repeatedly corrected by them so that blows may induce you to obedience, what grace will you have from this? You will receive nothing from God on this account. But if, while doing good, you patiently endure—that is, although you have done well, you endure evils inflicted by masters—[Col. 0229B] this is grace before God.

He greatly exalts the condition of slaves, affirming that those who do good and are beaten without fault by cruel and wicked masters are imitators of the Lord’s Passion.

It follows: “For to this you were called, because Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps—he who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.”

As though he said: You were called to this, namely to suffer, and by Christ’s example, because Christ suffered for us. You rejoice also in this, because Christ died for you; observe what follows: “Leaving you an example”—namely of tribulations, insults, scourges, the cross, and death—“that you may follow his footsteps,” of him who did no sin although he suffered, [Col. 0229C] “neither was guile found in his mouth,” namely by the Jews and Pharisees who watched him, because he did not sin even in speech.

“When he was reviled,” as a deceiver and one possessed by a demon, “he did not revile”: that is, he did not reproach them with the evils truly present in them. “When he suffered,” namely from the Jews, “he did not threaten them. But he gave himself up to the one judging him unjustly; he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness; by whose wound you were healed.”

He handed himself over to those judging unjustly, namely those who judged according to an unjust sentence although he was utterly just; or he handed over to God the Father those judging unjustly—that is, those who most wickedly condemned him and insisted upon his death—that, undergoing punishments, they might be instructed. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree: that is, he bore on the tree the punishment commonly due for the sins of all, so that, dead to sins as he himself died bodily, we may live to righteousness as he lives a new life. “By whose bruise you were healed”: namely by love alone, or by his flesh made bruised in the Passion.

Having instructed slaves spiritually above, [Col. 0229D] he now instructs the whole Church, so that he may also recall to masters what their advocate endured for their liberation.

It follows: “For you were like wandering sheep, but [Note: [Col. 0229D] Another manuscript incorrectly reads ‘unless.’] now you have been converted to the shepherd and bishop of your souls.”

He touches upon the Gospel parable in which the kindly [Col. 0230A] shepherd, leaving ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, comes to visit the one which had wandered (Matt. 18). Let it therefore be said more plainly: You were like wandering sheep, without a shepherd through vices, torn by the thorns of vices; but now you have been converted to the shepherd. Namely, in Christ’s Passion you have returned in body and soul to him who feeds you with the word of truth, and to the bishop—or visitor—of your souls, which is the same thing.

“Now the title *episcopatus*, as blessed Isidore says, is derived from the fact that he who is set over others watches over them, namely by caring for his subjects; for *skopein* in Greek is called *intendere*, ‘to direct one’s attention,’ in Latin. *Episcopi*, moreover, are interpreted in Latin as ‘watchers’; for the watcher is the one placed over the Church, so called because he watches and looks ahead to the conduct and life [Col. 0230B] of the peoples placed beneath him.” [Note: *Etymologies*, Book VII, ch. 12.]

Jesus Christ is therefore most rightly called bishop, that is, overseer, because: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayers” (Ps. 33).

Cassiodorus: Here the Prophet treats of the recompenses of good and evil, lest in sufferings or dangers the righteous person grow faint through any uncertainty. As though he said: Turn aside from evil; seek peace; and do not despair because of your weakness, for the eyes of the Lord—that is, God’s merciful regard—are upon the righteous. Even if, like a physician, he cuts and burns, and thereby seems not to hear, he does this in order to heal and spare forever. And his ears are in their prayers, that he may give what they ask, namely grace for grace. Note that he did not say “toward their prayers,” but “in their prayers,” by which [Col. 0230C] the swiftness of his hearing is indicated.

Augustine: Perhaps an evil man says: “I do evil securely, because the eyes of the Lord are not over me. God attends to the righteous, and does not see me.” Therefore he adds: “But the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.” As though he said: God looks upon the righteous; but let not the evil man think himself unknown, for the face of the Lord—that is, God’s knowledge—is upon those who do evil. Yet he does not look upon them mercifully so as to hear them; he knows them in order to punish them. Hence he adds: “To destroy their memory from the earth,” namely so that not even remembrance—that is, intercession—may be made for them among the good, because God’s justice pleases them. Thus Abraham says to the rich man in the Gospel: “A great chasm has been fixed between us and you” [Col. 0230D] (Luke 16), so that the good cannot descend to them with any compassion because of the shameful sins which they committed.

And truly the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, because the righteous—such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joshua, Samuel, David, and the rest—cried to the Lord, and he heard them and delivered them from all their tribulations. Thus also the prophet Zechariah says: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1).

Again blessed Peter adds: “Likewise let women be subject to their own husbands, so that even if some do not believe the word, they may be gained without a word through the conduct of their wives, observing in fear your holy conduct. Let their adornment not be outward—braiding of hair, or the wearing around of gold, or the attire of garments—but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich in the sight of God.”

It seems that the women of those who were in tribulation despised their husbands and adorned themselves beautifully to please others; and he forbids this. He wishes good women to be so subject to unbelieving husbands that they not only do nothing evil at their command, but remain moreover invincible in such holy conduct that they may be examples of love and faith even to their husbands.

As though he says openly: As slaves ought to be subject to their masters for God’s sake, so likewise let patient women be subject to their spouses, even to those spouses themselves—not [Col. 0231B] to adulterers, but to their own husbands—so that husbands who do not believe the word of the Gospel may, by the conduct of women who behave well and humbly endure all things, be gained—that is, converted to the faith—without a word of preaching, merely observing in fear your holy conduct, maintained in the fear of God.

Let their adornment not be braiding of hair or gold worn around them; nor let the adornment consist in the attire of garments—let there not be festive garments with which they are clothed—but let your ornament be the inward person of the heart, known to God alone, in incorruptibility of spirit: a spirit quiet from the assaults of vices, and modest, lest it become proud; “which is rich in the sight of God,” because such a spirit, even if it is not manifest to human beings, is rich [Col. 0231C] in God’s sight.

As Cyprian says: “Women clothed in silk and purple cannot clothe themselves with Christ. Adorned with gold, pearls, and necklaces, they have lost the ornaments of heart and breast. But if Peter also warns that women must be restrained and regulated by religious observance according to ecclesiastical discipline—women who can excuse their adornments by their husbands—how much more fitting is it for a virgin to observe this, for whom no pardon for her adornment is appropriate, nor can the false excuse for her fault be shifted to another; she alone remains guilty of the offence? Therefore, since your outward person is corruptible and you have ceased to possess the blessedness of integrity, which properly belongs to virgins, imitate the incorruptibility of spirit through abstinence; and what you cannot do [Col. 0231D] in body, hold fast in mind. For Christ seeks these riches and these ornaments of your union.”

Among the Pythagoreans, under the guidance of the law of natural knowledge, the same opinion is found: the true ornaments of married women are chastity, not clothes.

It follows: “For thus also holy women, hoping in God, adorned themselves, being subject to their own husbands; as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, whose daughters you are if you do good and do not fear any disturbance.”

As though he said: Thus also in former times holy women, through incorruptibility of spirit and hoping in God, adorned themselves even before the time of grace, being subject to their own husbands—not in adornment of clothing but spiritually; as Sarah obeyed Abraham, even in things which seemed grievous, calling him lord [Col. 0232A] out of reverence (Gen. 18). You are her daughters if you do good, namely by honouring your husbands, and do not fear any disturbance: even if some evil happens to your husbands, do not be disturbed by it.

“Likewise husbands, living with them according to knowledge, granting honour to the womanly vessel as the weaker, and as also co-heirs of grace and life, that your prayers may not be hindered.”

If we abstain from intercourse, we grant honour; if we do not abstain, it is clear that intercourse is contrary to honour. As though he said: Therefore conduct yourselves so modestly with your wives that your prayers may not be hindered; for if you are at discord, your prayers will not please God.

Alternatively: “That your prayers may not be hindered.” He says prayers are hindered by the marital act [Col. 0232B], because whenever the conjugal debt is rendered to a wife, prayer is hindered. But if, according to the Apostle’s saying, one must pray without ceasing (1 Thess. 5), I should never serve marriage, lest at any hour I be hindered from prayer, to which I am commanded always to attend.

Let blessed Peter therefore say: As I commanded wives through their holy conduct to gain their husbands and serve them, so likewise I command you, O husbands, through your conduct to gain women. Guard them—namely, you who live with them by rendering the conjugal debt—and do this according to knowledge, not in passions of desire, but as you understand God wills: namely, that you may beget children for the worship of the one God, granting honour to the womanly vessel as the weaker. Provide for them in clothing [Col. 0232C] and other necessities; at times also, if it pleases them, abstain from intercourse. Grant them honour because they are weaker; grant it also because they are co-heirs of grace now given by God, and of life to be given in the future, or of life given through grace.

As though he spoke plainly, saying: I have instructed different persons, different conditions, and different sexes; now I admonish all in common that in the cause of the Lord’s faith you may have one heart and one soul. Therefore he adds, saying: “But in faith be all of one mind in prayer, compassionate, lovers of the brotherhood, merciful, modest, humble.”

As though he said: Be of one mind in faith and prayer, namely that you may not despair even in thought, lest you destroy [Col. 0232D] the brotherhood and thereby more freely depart from the faith; merciful, forgiving sins and giving alms; modest, doing all things with moderation; humble, lest you be proud of these things.

It follows: “Not rendering evil for evil, nor curse for curse, but on the contrary blessing; because to this you were called, that you may possess a blessing as an inheritance.”

As though it were said more plainly: Do not render evil for evil, which might appear, according to the justice of the world, to be done justly in action; nor curse for curse in words; but on the contrary bless: that is, not only cease to return a curse, but even give a blessing in return for a curse. For you were called to this, that you may possess a blessing as an inheritance, as the Judge says: [Col. 0233A] “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). Or, the blessing by which the saints shall bless God in the future life. Therefore let each person strive now to meditate upon and do what he desires to find in the future: let him bless the Creator and his brother, and make himself worthy of divine and brotherly blessing.

Again he says: “For whoever wishes to love life and see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil, and his lips from speaking guile.” As though he said: Whoever wishes to love life—that is, whoever wishes to show that he has love—and to see good days, since in this age days are evil, let him restrain his tongue inwardly, lest it murmur evil, and his lips outwardly, lest they speak guile—that is, lest they utter anything deceitful.

“Let him turn aside [Col. 0233B] from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it.” As though he said: Even if an external occasion for sin is given, nevertheless let him turn aside from evil and do good; let him seek peace as something hidden with God and his brother, and pursue it as something fleeing.

“For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are in their prayers; but the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil”: namely judgment, or manifestation, or first place, or the repayment of evils to them. Because he had forbidden rendering evil for evil and instead commanded that those who curse be blessed, he rightly confirms by prophetic testimony that the heavenly gaze always sees both the wicked and the good, so that we may remember that both our patience, by which we endure the wicked, and our goodwill, by which we wish good to persecutors, will be rewarded with eternal reward, [Col. 0233C] while persecutors will be punished with deserved penalty. If, however, they repent, we too shall receive a crown for the salvation which we pray for on their behalf.

It follows: “And who is he who will harm you, if you are imitators of the good?” As though he said: Therefore you ought to turn aside from evil and do good, because no one can draw you away from good or from the crown, if you wish to persevere; indeed, those who wish to harm you benefit you. “But even if you suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed”: that is, not only does what the wicked inflict not harm you, but it also benefits you because it exercises patience. If they inflict insulting words, loss of possessions, or torments, they do not harm you but exercise your patience. But if someone, overcome by these things, fails, the one who harmed him is not the person who inflicted the [Col. 0233D] evil, but the person who did not endure the evil.

Every house is tested, both that which is founded upon rock and that which is founded upon sand; but to one the firmness of its foundation grants the crown of perseverance, while the frail structure lays the other low.

Again he adds, saying: “But do not fear their fear, nor be troubled.” As though he said: In the future you shall be blessed; but in the present do not fear their fear—that is, things which may appear fearful in them, such as royal power and the like. Therefore do not fear them, “and do not be troubled,” namely by departing from faith and love of God.

“But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts.” As though he said: [Col. 0234A] Contemplate with the innermost affection of your heart how incomprehensible Christ’s holiness is, and thus sanctify Christ himself in yourselves, so that you may not depart from remembrance or from love. Whoever does not consider this holiness falls into the snares of the enemy.

It follows: “Always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you.”

We must give an account of our hope and faith in two ways: by making known the sound grounds of hope and faith to those who inquire faithfully or unbelievingly; and by preserving faith and hope unblemished amid pressures, showing through patience how reasonably we have learned to keep them, for love of which we do not fear either to suffer adversities or to undergo death.

We therefore ought always to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason—that is, to one wishing in return to receive rational money, we ought not refuse it. Hence Paul: “Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, knowing how you ought to answer each person” (Col. 4). For those who are outside, that is, not yet believers, wish to know something concerning the hope that is in you. Therefore whoever exercises ecclesiastical teaching should instruct the receptive and silence those who resist.

Again he says: “With modesty and fear, having a good conscience, so that in the matter in which they speak against you, those who slander your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame.”

In the very knowledge of teaching he warns that the manner of teaching should be observed, so that humility may be displayed both in speech and conduct. As though he said: Give an answer to those who ask with modesty and fear; that is, have not only teaching, but also modesty in teaching, which is the mother of all virtues.
