Or, according to modesty and fear, let that which you outwardly show be possessed inwardly, so that those who mock in you the faith and hope of heavenly things which they cannot see may be put to shame by your good works, which they cannot deny are good.

Or, take care to do good, so that those who slander your good conduct, when the time of recompense comes, may be put to shame, seeing you crowned with Christ and themselves condemned with the devil. Let them be put to shame, as it were, for the very thing in which they slander you.

It follows: “For it is better, if the will of God should so will it, to suffer while doing good than while doing evil; because Christ also [Col. 0234D] died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God, having indeed been put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.” Here he rebukes those who, when they are reproved by their brethren for faults, or even restrained by punishments, bear it patiently. But if something is inflicted on them by their brethren without their being at fault, they immediately collapse into anger; and those who until then were considered innocent make themselves guilty by impatience and murmuring. It was more profitable for Tobias to be struck with blindness without fault, so that his patience might be tested (Tob. II), than for Elymas

> [Note: [Col. 0233D] Ms. *Ermias*, 415.]

the magician, who, struck because of his treachery, is removed from the fellowship of believers and prepared for eternal punishment (Acts XIII). “It is better,” he says, “to suffer while doing good [Col. 0235A]—if the will of God should so will it—than while doing evil.” As though he said: You ought thus to endure and confound your slanderers, because it is safer for you to suffer for good deeds than for evil deeds—I say this if God’s will so wills, which prepares a greater reward. For Christ too died once for our sins. Thus we too die once, that is, by a temporal death, for which an eternal reward will be given. Therefore the righteous person who suffers imitates Christ; the one chastised by scourges is likened to the thief who, recognizing Christ on the cross, entered paradise with him (Luke XXIII). The one who is not corrected even by scourges imitates the thief on the left, who ascended the cross because of sins and, after the cross, fell into Tartarus. “The just,” he says, “died for the unjust, that he might offer us to God, having indeed been put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.” [Col. 0235B] Christ offers us to the Father and displays our praiseworthy life before the Father’s sight when, through the mortification of the flesh, we rejoice to be sacrificed for him. Or he offers us to God when, released from the flesh, he introduces us into the eternal kingdom. It follows:

“In which spirit he also came and preached to those who were in prison, who had formerly been unbelieving, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built; in it a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water.” Those whose understanding is darkened by darkness are rightly said to be shut up in prison even in this life; and in this inner prison of the mind they are burdened by unjust deeds, until, released from the flesh, they are cast into the outer darkness of eternal condemnation. The righteous too have a prison here, but [Col. 0235C] one of tribulations; the reprobate, one of vices. For he says: “In which spirit he also came and preached to those who were in prison.” As though he said: He who, coming in the flesh in our times, then preached life to the world, also came in spirit before the Flood and preached to those who were then unbelieving and had lived carnally; for he was in Noah and in other good people through the Holy Spirit, and through their good conduct preached to other, wicked people, that they might turn to good.

Let it be stated again more plainly: “In which,” that is, in which spirit, “he also came and preached to those who were in prison”—namely, the prison of darkness and unbelief—or

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] Bede and several others read thus, as may be seen in Sabbatier; therefore the other manuscript and the interlinear gloss plainly err when they correct here to “or prison.” For the exposition “in [Col. 0236D] carnal desires” will not be sufficiently fitting if the reading “or flesh” is removed. Nevertheless, Calmet says on this passage that both this reading and the preceding one, “spirit,” in place of “spirits,” clearly lie in error.]

“flesh,” that is, in carnal desires. He came and preached, namely in order to offer them to God, because if any then had wished to believe the Lord’s preaching, which he set before them through the life of the faithful, he rejoiced to offer them also to God the Father; but if any disparaged the good as evildoers, they were confounded by the coming Flood. “Who had formerly been unbelieving,” that is, who had not believed God threatening through Noah, “when God’s patience waited”: namely, when God’s patience invited them to repentance, sparing them for the hundred years during which Noah built the ark, by which it was shown what would happen to the world. They did not use God’s patience for [Col. 0236A] repentance, but waited for it as though it would last forever. “In which ark a few, who had believed God—that is, eight souls, who possessed hope in the eighth day—were saved through water.” As the ark was constructed of smoothed timber, so the Church consists of an assembly of faithful souls; and as, when the world perished, few were saved through water, so, in comparison with those who perish, the number of the elect is small: “Narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are they who find it” (Matt. VII). That the Flood-water saved no one outside the ark but killed them signifies that every heretic, even though possessing the sacrament of baptism, is to be plunged into hell not by other waters but by the very waters by which the ark is raised heavenward.

It follows: “And now baptism, corresponding in form to this, saves—not the removal of the filth of the flesh, [Col. 0236B] but the inquiry of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is at God’s right hand, swallowing up death, so that we might become heirs of eternal life; having gone into heaven, with angels, authorities, and powers subjected to him.” By those who were submerged in the Flood is signified the mortification of the flesh; by those who were saved is signified the enlivening of the spirit. Noah, whose name means “rest,” signifies Christ, who gives his faithful the rest of their souls.

Let it therefore be stated more plainly: “And now baptism corresponding in form to this saves”: namely, baptism now also saves; I mean baptism corresponding in form, that is, altogether analogous to that ark, because whatever occurred there carnally occurs here [Col. 0236C] spiritually. “Not the removal of the filth of the flesh”: that is, I do not say that the baptism saves in which there is only removal of the filth of the flesh, in which the flesh alone is washed outwardly—such as heretics too have possessed—but that baptism in which there is the inquiry of a pure conscience; that is, in which a good conscience is sought and required of the person being baptized. Such baptism saves; the other kills. The inquiry is made and directed toward God, so that through a good conscience one may be made one in God. “The inquiry of a good conscience toward God”: that is, it is not enough for the baptized person to have a good conscience, unless at the Church’s questioning he displays his faith; and this occurs through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of [Col. 0236D] the Father, so we, purified from vices through the water of regeneration, may walk in newness of life (Rom. VI). This was also signified by the eight souls saved in the ark.

“Through him,” he says, “who is at God’s right hand, swallowing up death.” What we swallow, we cause to be taken into the interior of our body so that it appears nowhere. Thus the Lord consumed death utterly, so that it had no power against him; and although the appearance of a real body remained, the defect of former frailty was absent—a state which is also promised to us. Hence he added: “That we also might become heirs of eternal life.” “Having gone,” he says, “into heaven, with angels [Col. 0237A] and authorities and powers subjected to him.” Angels are the first order, authorities the second, powers the third. We do not doubt that angels have always been subject to the Son of God; but he mentions subjection here in order to show that the assumed humanity was so exalted in the resurrection that it is set above the powers of angelic dignity. Hence that saying: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen; moreover, also the beasts of the field” (Ps. VIII).

Augustine: As though the Prophet said to God the Father: “You have subjected all things beneath the feet of Jesus Christ, your Son: namely, sheep—that is, innocent beings, both human beings and angels; and oxen, namely those who plough and thresh, who in the Lord’s vineyard tear up the fields of sin with a spiritual ploughshare. I say all oxen.” He uses the feminine gender [Col. 0237B] in order to denote those who bear fruit, who cause human hearts to bear fruit through the seed of God’s word; and these are human beings and angels. It follows: “Moreover, also the beasts of the field.” As though he said: You have subjected to him not only the good, but moreover also the beasts of the field. By saying “moreover,” he distinguishes these from the saints mentioned above; for these are grapes, whereas those mentioned above are wine. He calls the wicked also subject to Christ, a point which seems less obvious; this he signifies when he says, “also the beasts of the field,” that is, carnal persons dwelling amid the expanse of pleasures, as though in the breadth of fields, not upon the mountains of virtues. Therefore the beasts of the field are people who live in the flesh, where nothing laborious is undertaken and nothing steep is climbed, but they cling to the broad road that leads [Col. 0237C] to death (Matt. VII). Hence Abel too is killed by his brother in the field (Gen. IV). Again he adds: “You have subjected to him also the birds of heaven” (Ps. VIII), that is, the proud. The proud are suitably signified by the birds of heaven, concerning whom it is said: “They have set their mouth in heaven” (Ps. LXXII). Their head says: “I will ascend into heaven and exalt my throne” (Isa. XIV), etc. It follows: “And the fishes of the sea,” that is, the curious, who traverse the paths of the sea—that is, who stubbornly investigate the temporal things of this age in its depths, things that, like paths in the sea, quickly vanish. Thus he rightly does not say “walk,” but “traverse,” thereby showing the most obstinate pursuit of what is empty and passing away.

These three kinds of vice—pleasure of the flesh, curiosity, and pride [Col. 0237D]—include all vices, which, as blessed John says, are the lust of the flesh, worldly ambition—that is, pride—and the lust of the eyes (I John II). For curiosity is especially powerful through the eyes. The Savior was tempted by these three and overcame them; the first man, defeated by them, succumbed. Therefore all things, as stated above, created in heaven, on earth, and in the sea are subject beneath the feet of Jesus Christ, Son of God and man, who deigned to suffer not for his own sins but for those of the entire human race; and, as Christ in rising ascended into heaven,

> [Note: [Col. 0237D] Supplied from the *Gloss*: “and.”]

and sits at the right hand of God the Father, so [Col. 0238A] through baptism he also opened for us the way of salvation and the entrance into the heavenly kingdom, our homeland.

After blessed Peter established, from the mystery of the ark and the Flood, the example of the Lord’s resurrection and of our washing, he returns to what he had begun: that, in imitation of the Savior, amid the good which we do, we should patiently endure the wickedness of evil persons. He says:

“Therefore, since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought: for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins, so that for the time remaining in the flesh he may live no longer according to human desires but according to God’s will.” Whoever among the righteous subjects his body to martyrdom, having nothing in the world in which to sin, is compelled to desire only this: that, when the contest is ended, he may receive the crown of life. Peter always wishes [Col. 0238B] to imitate the mind of such persons; for, by setting before us the example of the Lord’s passion, he commands us to arm ourselves with the same thought against the wickedness of the depraved and against the delights of vices. He intends us to understand that even when we rest in the Church’s peace, if we put on the disposition of one who suffers, with the Lord’s help we easily avoid falls into sin.

Therefore let Peter, prince of the apostles, state it more plainly: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh,” not in his divinity, “arm yourselves also with the same thought”: that is, as he willingly suffered, so let us suffer willingly; as he endured all things, so let us endure. And there results this benefit: “for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins,” because the person who, through fear of heavenly judgments, extinguishes carnal desires in his mind, now, made like Christ crucified, [Col. 0238C] and as though dead to sins, lives only for God’s service, so that “for the time remaining in the flesh he may live no longer according to human desires but according to God’s will,” strengthening himself in good works. It is fitting that every faithful person, for the sake of eternal recompense, should courageously gird himself to endure the temptations and sufferings of the body, and should be an imitator of his Redeemer, who said to his disciples—indeed, to all who believe in him: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI).

For the strengthening of the mind amid the adversities of this age, let him recall the words of blessed Job, who, while under scourges, said:

“As the stag longs for shade, and as a hired laborer [Col. 0238D] awaits the end of his work, so I too have had empty months, and have counted out laborious nights for myself” (Job VII).

Gregory:

> [Note: [Col. 0237D] *Morals*, Book VIII, ch. 4.]

For the stag to long for shade is to seek the rest of eternal refreshment after the heat of temptation and the sweat of labor. That stag desired this shade when he said: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” (Ps. XLI).

Augustine: Here he defines his desire, since one might understand the stag to desire the spring for drinking or washing; and he shows that it desires the spring especially for drinking.

> [Note: [Col. 0238D] The manuscript wrongly has *desiderate*.]

As though he said: “My [Col. 0239A] soul longs for you.”

Cassiodorus: “My soul has thirsted,” I say, formerly as well, not only now, “for God strong,” or “for the fountain,” that is, Christ, who is the flowing fountain from which all good things flow; “living”

> [Note: [Col. 0239D] Perhaps *living*, to agree with the substantive “fountain.”]

not for the dead images of the Gentiles. And for what has it thirsted? Namely, to come and appear before the face of God; and this is “when shall I come?” As though he said: I desire to be dissolved, because I thirst in exile, I thirst in the course; I shall be satisfied at my arrival—but when shall I come? He says this because what is soon for God is late to one who longs. “And I shall appear,” he says, because we too, who are now hidden, shall then appear before the face of God, because then we shall see him as he is (I John III).

Therefore let David the prophet say: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” He who, as though fleeing the heat of labor in the field and seeking a covering in order to gain the rest of refreshment, [Col. 0239B] says again:

“I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God” (Ps. IV).

Augustine: The tabernacle on earth is the faithful, in whom this person already marvels: namely, that sin does not reign in the body, but it is an instrument of righteousness; that the soul obeys God, endures hardships, reaches upward, and so forth. He passes beyond even these and reaches in mind as far as the heavenly house of God, and marvels. This is why he says, “I poured out my soul, because in this manner I shall pass over,” or, “I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle,” that is, into the present Church, which is a kind of image and likeness of the future Jerusalem. When it is seen, that other city is desired more keenly, and in this Church one groans more deeply. [Col. 0239C] Therefore he says, “I shall enter into the place of the tabernacle,” because whoever seeks God outside the place of this tabernacle goes astray. I say that he reaches in mind as far as God’s house, not captured by the desires of the age. How do you reach the inner chamber of the house? “In the voice,” namely, “of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting.” For something melodious and sweet sounds to his heart from the eternal festival; by this he is drawn away, like a stag to fountains of water, and is delighted. It follows: “And of confession,” that is, of eternal praise, which is sung to God by angels; from this a wondrous sweetness sounds to him. Therefore let blessed Job say:

“As the stag longs for shade, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work,” etc.

> [Note: [Col. 0239D] Gregory, as above.]

Paul panted to attain this [Col. 0239D] shade, “having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). Those who said, “We have borne the burden and heat of the day” (Matt. XX), had already arrived at this shade through the perfection of desire. The one said to long for shade is aptly called a stag, because every elect person, so long as he is bound by the condition of weakness, is held beneath the yoke of ruling corruption, as though beneath the distress of heat. But when he has been stripped of corruption, he is then revealed to himself as free and at peace. Hence Paul rightly says: “Creation itself shall be freed from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII). The elect [Col. 0240A] are now weighed down by the punishment of corruption, but then glory will exalt them; and as nothing of freedom is now displayed in God’s children because of the burdens of present necessity, so then nothing of bondage will appear in God’s servants because of the glory of freedom that follows. Therefore creation, stripped of the bondage of corruption and granted the freedom of dignity, is transformed into the glory of God’s children, because, united to God in spirit, it is shown to have passed beyond and overcome, as it were, its very status as creature. But because it still longs for shade, it is a stag; because so long as it endures the heat of temptations and sufferings, it bears the yoke of its wretched condition. He aptly adds: “And as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work.”

> [Note: [Col. 0240D] Gregory, ch. 5.]

For when a hired laborer looks upon the work he is doing, he immediately draws his mind away from the remoteness [Col. 0240B] and weight of the labor. But when he recalls his weary spirit to desire the reward of his work, he at once restores the strength of his soul for labor’s exertion; and what he considers heavy because of the work, he considers light because of the reward. So all the elect, when they suffer the adversities of this world—when they endure insults to their honor, losses of possessions, and bodily tortures—consider the things by which they are tried to be grievous; but when they direct the eye of their mind to contemplating the eternal homeland, from contemplating the reward they discover how light is what they suffer. What is shown by pain to be wholly unbearable is lightened by provident consideration of the recompense. Hence Paul is always raised up, stronger than himself, against adversities, because, like a hired laborer, [Col. 0240C] he awaits the end of his work.

He reckons the thing he endures to be grievous, but judges it light by considering the reward. For he himself indicates how grievous is what he suffers: he testifies that he was more abundantly in prisons, beyond measure in beatings, often in deaths; that five times he received from the Jews forty lashes less one; that he was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, and spent a night and day in the deep sea (II Cor. II); that he endured perils from rivers, robbers, his own race, Gentiles, the city, solitude, the sea, and false brethren; that he labored in toil and hardship, in many fasts, hunger and thirst, many vigils, cold and nakedness; [Col. 0240D] that he endured conflicts without and fears within (II Cor. VII); and that he declares himself burdened beyond his strength, saying: “We were weighed down beyond measure, so that we were weary even of life” (II Cor. I). But he himself declares how he wipes away the sweat of so great a labor with the linen cloth of recompense, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). Thus, like a hired laborer, he awaits the end of his work, because while he considers the profit of the recompense, he counts as insignificant what he labors at almost to exhaustion.

He aptly adds: “So I too have had empty months, and have counted out laborious nights for myself.” The elect indeed serve the Creator of all things and [Col. 0241A] are often hemmed in by want of material things. They cling to God in love and yet need the support of this present life. Therefore those who do not seek present things through their actions pass empty months without the world’s gains. They also endure laborious nights, because they bear the darkness of adversities not only to the point of want but often to bodily suffering. For people of good mind, to endure contempt and poverty is not laborious; but when adversity turns into bodily affliction, labor is unquestionably felt through pain.

It may also fittingly be understood that every holy person passes empty months like a hired laborer, because he now endures labor but does not yet possess the reward: he bears this and awaits that. He counts laborious nights because, by exercising himself in virtues, he heaps up for himself the adversities [Col. 0241B] of the present time. For if he does not desire to advance in mind, he perhaps feels less keenly the harsh things that belong to the world.

But if this statement is referred to the voice of holy Church, its meaning is examined a little more closely. Holy Church herself has empty months in that she endures, in her weak members, earthly activities that pass away without life’s reward. She herself counts laborious nights in that she bears manifold tribulations in her strong members. For in this life some things are laborious, some empty, and some both empty and laborious. To be tried by the tribulations of this present life out of love for the Creator is indeed laborious, but it is not empty. To give oneself up to pleasures out of love for the age is empty indeed, but not laborious. But to suffer adversities out of love for the same age is both empty and laborious, because the mind is afflicted by adversity and is not filled with the reward of recompense.

Therefore, in those within holy Church who still give themselves up to pleasures and consequently are not enriched by the fruit of their work, she passes empty months, because she expends the times of life without the gift of recompense. But in those who, devoted to eternal desires, suffer the adversities of this world, holy Church counts laborious nights, because she bears the darkness of tribulations as though in the gloom of the present life. In those, however, who both love the passing world and are nevertheless wearied by its adversity, she endures both empty months and laborious nights; because no future recompense rewards [Col. 0241D] their life, while present tribulation constricts it.

Rightly, moreover, she declares that she has not empty days but empty months in them; for by the name of months is signified the collection and sum of days. Thus each action can be expressed by a day, but by months is indicated the end of actions. Often, when we do something in this world, suspended in eager hope, we do not think what we are doing empty. But after we come to the end of our actions and do not obtain what we seek, we grieve that we have labored in vain. We therefore spend not only empty days but empty months, when we judge that we have labored fruitlessly in earthly actions, not from the beginning of our actions but from their end. When adversity follows our labors, the empty months of our life are, as it were, exposed, because it is known from the completion of our actions [Col. 0242A] how vainly we labor.

Night, however, is used for ignorance, as Paul testifies. Teaching his disciples, who knew of the life to come, he says: “All of you are children of light and children of day; we are not of night or darkness” (I Thess. V). Before this he said: “But you, brethren, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief” (ibid.). In this place the voice of holy Church may be understood as spoken on behalf of those who return to the love of righteousness after the darkness of their ignorance and, illumined by the rays of truth, wash away by tears the errors they committed. For every person who has been enlightened looks back and sees how shameful it was to have labored out of love for this present life. Therefore, in those in whom she returns to life, holy Church compares her labor to a servant oppressed by heat and a hired worker desiring the end, saying: “As the stag longs for shade, and as a hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so I too have had empty months, and have counted laborious nights for myself.” For in the comparison he first set forth two things; and in expressing weariness he likewise added two. At once he assigned empty months to the heat-oppressed person, because the more eternal refreshment is sought, the more clearly one sees how vainly one labors for this life. But he added laborious nights to the person waiting, because the more we behold the reward which we shall obtain at the end of our work, [Col. 0242C] the more we groan that we did not know the good which we ought to have pursued. Hence the care of the penitent is itself expressed watchfully, in saying that he had counted laborious nights: because the more truly we return to God, the more carefully, in sorrow, we reckon the labors we endured in this world through ignorance. For the sweeter that what one desires of eternal things becomes to anyone, the more grievous is shown to be what he endured for love of present things.

> [Note: [Col. 0241D] *Etymologies*, Book XII, ch. 1.]

“According to blessed Isidore, a stag (*cervus*) is called so from the Greek ἀπὸ τῶν κεράτων, ‘from the horns’; for *kerata* (κέρατα) is the Greek word for ‘horns.’ Stags are enemies of serpents. When they perceive themselves burdened by sickness, they draw the serpents from their holes by the breath of their nostrils; and, once the destruction caused by their venom has been overcome, they are restored by food. They themselves revealed the herb dittany; for when they eat it, they shake out arrows that they have received. They are delighted by the sound of pipes; with ears raised they hear sharply, but with ears lowered they hear nothing. Whenever they swim across vast rivers or seas, they place their heads upon the haunches of those preceding them; succeeding one another in turn, they feel no burden of weight.”

Having briefly set forth these remarks of blessed Isidore on the nature of stags, it is necessary to return to those matters which we omitted above. Therefore let every faithful person, through the desire of seeing Christ, who is the fountain of all good things, [Col. 0243A] become a stag; and by patiently bearing adversities for the sake of heavenly gifts, let him be like a hired laborer, so that, as blessed Peter says, no longer conforming himself to human desires but to God’s will, he may live the time remaining in the flesh in good works: namely, so that he may die to the world and live to God, gladly enduring sufferings for love of him.

Again let blessed Peter say: “The time past is sufficient for fulfilling the will of the Gentiles, who walked in luxuries, desires, drunkenness, revelries, drinking bouts, and unlawful worships of idols, in which they now are astonished.” As though he said: Truly the one dead in the flesh now ceases from sins, because, considering the enormity of crimes, it is enough to have spent the past time in fulfilling the will of the Gentiles. I say “fulfilling,” because, like the Gentiles, they walked from vice to vice, not remaining fixed in a single vice. “In this they are astonished that you do not run with them into the same confusion of dissipation, blaspheming; they shall render an account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.” As though he said more plainly: They are astonished that you do not run with them into the same confusion of dissipation in which you formerly ran, because you have now crucified your flesh with its vices and desires. And although they blaspheme you, now separated from their treachery, still, when they see works of righteousness and piety in your manner of life, they marvel and in some manner revere the faith. As though he said: Care less, therefore, if, while doing good, you are blasphemed by [Col. 0243C] the reprobate; for even if you keep silent, the just Judge will not be silent, and he will repay them the punishment of blasphemy and you the rewards of patience.

It follows: “For this reason the gospel was also preached to the dead, that they might indeed be judged according to men in the flesh and live according to God in the spirit.” God is so concerned that we be dead in the flesh and alive in the spirit that he commanded even those enmeshed in the greater crimes, who were to be numbered among the dead, to be evangelized with words of faith: “That they might indeed be judged,” that is, condemned by themselves, “according to men,” that is, according to their life after the manner of sinners

> [Note: [Col. 0243D] Another manuscript has *peacorum*; and perhaps an unlearned hand unsuccessfully wished to correct the reading of our manuscript, which has *peccorum*, that is, “of sinners,” as does the *Gloss*.]

in the flesh—that is, in carnal desires—and, rejecting vices, might live in the spirit, that is, spiritually according to God’s will. Or: “that they might be judged according to men,” that is, according to the reason God gave human beings, so that their reason may condemn evil in themselves.

He says: “But the end of all things will draw near.” Since he had said that he is ready to judge the living and the dead, lest anyone flatter himself because the future judgment is distant, he prudently warns that, although the coming of the final decision is uncertain, it is nevertheless certain for all that we cannot remain long in this life.

It follows: “Therefore be prudent, and watch in prayers.” As though he said: Since the hour of death is uncertain, be prudent—that is, do not fall away [Col. 0244A] from faith—and watch in prayers, lest the mind think of anything other than what it prays. When we stand to pray, let every carnal thought depart. He adds again, saying: “But above all have continual mutual charity among yourselves, for charity covers a multitude of sins.” Because of the frailty of the flesh, we cannot always persist in prayer, hospitality, or other virtues which must be exercised through bodily services and at appropriate times. But charity itself, by whose prompting these outward acts are done and which presides over the inner person, can always be possessed there, although it cannot always be shown publicly.

Therefore let it be stated more plainly: “Above all have continual mutual charity among yourselves”: that is, in order that you may understand the manner [Col. 0244B] of praying and obtain what you have prayed for, have charity among yourselves, not because of your outward possessions but in yourselves—that is, let you yourselves be the cause of love. “Charity covers a multitude of sins”: this means that, although faults are washed away through other virtues, they are especially washed away through charity, by which we forgive our neighbors what is owed to us, so that God may forgive us. Whoever through charity admonishes, rebukes, or corrects his neighbor, through charity covers a multitude of sins; because “he who causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way shall save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.”

“Be hospitable to one another without murmuring,” that is, so that one may not murmur because of the long practice of hospitality. [Col. 0244C] “Each one, as he has received a gift, administering it to one another as good stewards of God’s manifold grace,” that is, grace shaped according to each person’s desire, as manna tasted according to the foods they desired. Again he says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God”: that is, if anyone has the knowledge of speaking, let him attribute it not to himself but to God, and fear lest he teach contrary to God’s will, or contrary to the authority of the holy Scriptures, or

> [Note: [Col. 0243D] The *Gloss*: “beyond the benefit, teach his brother”; and another manuscript has, incorrectly, “beyond the brethren’s benefit,” arising from a mistaken understanding of an abbreviated note which, according to the construction, admits both senses.]

contrary to the benefit of the brethren; lest he also keep silent about what ought to be taught. “If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be honored through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.” As though it were said: If anyone ministers—namely by almsgiving [Col. 0244D] or by some good work—let him do so humbly, because he has nothing from himself to give, but only from God; so that in all your deeds God may be honored: when you do all things well and according to his will, attribute them not to your own merits but to his grace, so that others, seeing your good works, may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. V), through Jesus Christ, helper and mediator, to whom belong glory—that is, good repute—and dominion—that is, power—for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0245A] Beloved, do not regard as strange the fiery ordeal that is taking place among you for your testing, as though something strange were happening to you; but rejoice insofar as you share in Christ’s sufferings, so that also [Col. 0245B] at the revelation of his glory—when every veil, that is, shall be removed—you may rejoice in spirit and exult in body.

As though he said: If you endure the heat of tribulations which are brought upon you for the certain purpose of your testing and glory, do not therefore suppose that you have been cut off from Christ’s members. Do not be astonished at the evils inflicted upon you, through which God tests and proves you; for it is ancient and common for God’s elect to suffer present adversities for the sake of eternal salvation. “Do not regard as strange,” he says, “the fiery ordeal”: that is, do the good things mentioned above, and cease from them because of no tribulation, lest you [Note: [Col. 0245D] More explicitly, the interlinear gloss: “Do not regard as strange,” or wonder; do not depart from God’s love, lest you grow faint by failing in faith.] grow faint or change by falling away from faith. Rather, rejoice as those who share in Christ’s sufferings by representing them, so that also at the revelation of his glory you may rejoice in spirit and exult in body.

Whoever suffers for Christ’s name is blessed. For you must not suppose that you suffer without recompense, like those who suffer for their crimes and are punished unwillingly. Or: let no one be ashamed to commit crimes for which he is justly punished. But if he suffers as a Christian, for faith and confession of Christ’s name, let him not be ashamed; rather, let him glorify God by remaining in this name, so that it may be said: “Good is this Lord, who has such faithful servants.” It follows: “If you are reproached for Christ’s name, you will be blessed, because the Spirit of honor, glory, and God’s power, who is his Spirit, will rest upon you.”

As though he said: Because he will rest upon you who endure—[Col. 0245C] in the present, partially, to enable good works; and in the future, perfectly, to reward—you possess that which belongs to honor, so that in the present you may be honorable in good works and in the future sharers in Christ’s honor; that which belongs to glory, namely a pure conscience in the present and, in the future, freedom from every corruption both in soul and body; and that which belongs to power, both now and in the future, over the devil and his members. He then adds the source of all these things: “And the Holy Spirit, who is Christ’s, will rest upon you,” because Christ himself received him fully, gave him to his members, and will give him most fully in the future.

Again he says: “For let none of you suffer as a murderer, or thief, or slanderer, or one who covets another’s possessions.” Where someone suffers as a thief, [Col. 0245D] absolutely no recompense is expected. He suffers as a slanderer who, at the time of his suffering, gives free rein to abuse of his persecutor, to the injury of his own salvation. But if he suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; rather, let him glorify God in this name, for it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God.

As though he said: One must suffer for Christ’s name because, since no evil can pass without punishment, and God [Note: [Col. 0246D] Gloss: God, who will judge the wicked, severely chastises them in the present.] will judge the wicked severely at the last, he chastises and corrects in the present all whom he wishes to receive into salvation in the future. Hence Solomon says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” [Col. 0246A] (Ecclesiasticus 2).

There are two judgments. One is hidden: namely, the punishment by which each person is now either exercised for purification, warned toward conversion, or, if he despises the one calling him, exercised for condemnation. The other judgment is manifest, by which he who is coming will judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire. Now is the time for the Church to be prepared for glory through the trials of the world. But now the reprobate spend their days in prosperity and descend in a moment to hell (Job 21). “But if,” he says, “judgment begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel?” As though he said more plainly: If judgment begins with us—if here he afflicts those whom he loves, if he scourges the sons whom he receives (Hebrews 12)—what should utterly wicked servants hope for?

[Col. 0246B] It follows: “And if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?” This is taken from Proverbs according to the old translation. But in ours, which follows the Hebrew truth, it reads thus: “If the righteous receives on earth”—understand, scourges—“how much more the ungodly and the sinner?” (Proverbs 12). That is: if the frailty of mortal life is so great that not even the righteous, who are to be crowned in heaven, pass through it without tribulations because of the countless stains of corrupted nature, how much more do those excluded from heavenly grace await the certain outcome of their everlasting condemnation?

Let it therefore be said more plainly: If the righteous person—namely, one who receives and embraces the words of God, conscious of no evil in himself—is scarcely saved, that is, amid great struggle, laboring fiercely [Col. 0246C] and contending, where will the ungodly and sinner appear? Entirely outside God, in a foul and dreadful place. He is one who, even if he receives God’s words, does not faithfully believe in him, but despises him and afflicts his members.

Adding again, he says: “Let those who suffer according to God’s will commend their souls to their faithful Creator.” As though he said: Since judgment begins from the Lord’s house, and we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations (Acts 14), this alone remains for those who suffer: when they suffer as God wills, that is, for righteousness’ sake, let them commend their souls to God, presuming nothing concerning themselves, so that he may purify them here according to his will and make them blessed in the future; for he is faithful, [Col. 0246D] rendering good things to those whom he created (1 John 1). I say, they suffer in doing good, not because of sins. It is not difficult for God to deliver the righteous; but, in order to show that the whole human race was deservedly condemned, not even the Almighty wishes easily to deliver it from so great an evil. Therefore sins are easy and righteousness laborious, except for those who love God; but the charity that makes them lovers comes from God (1 John 4). It follows:

“Therefore I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings, and also a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed.” After he had [Col. 0247A] separately admonished children, servants, men, and women above, and inserted a general exhortation, he here addresses old and young, saying: “I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings.” As though he said: Since one must suffer, and those who suffer commend their souls to God, then endure and labor for him. Or, more plainly: Elders, whether by age or by office, I, a fellow elder—that is, one favored with like age—exhort you. I am a witness of Christ’s sufferings, because I stood present while Christ suffered, endured prison and chains for his name, and wrote what I saw concerning him. “I am,” he says, “a witness of Christ’s sufferings and also a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed.”

Certainly Peter became a sharer in Christ’s glory [Col. 0247B] when, with James and John on the holy mountain, he saw the heavenly glory of Christ’s face, in which he also hopes to share; or when, together with the other apostles present, he saw the power of Christ’s resurrection and ascension (Matthew 17).

Again he says: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, according to God.” Just as the Lord commanded Peter to take charge of the whole flock, so Peter rightly directs the pastors of the Church who follow him that each should diligently safeguard by governance that flock of God which is with him. “Feed,” he says, “the flock of God which is among you”: that is, the flock is among you, or you yourselves are God’s flock, providing your subjects with all things necessary, not under compulsion—that is, do not preach the Gospel because of a lack of temporal goods, so that you may live from the Gospel [Col. 0247C]—but willingly according to God, that is, with the sole regard of heavenly reward.

It follows: “Not for shameful gain, but willingly; nor as lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart an example to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.” As though he said: Let no gain impel you, for all works of religion ought to be voluntary. Thus, in the construction of the tabernacle, which signifies the present building up of the Church, the entire multitude of Israel’s children, with devout mind, offered firstfruits to the Lord for the work of the tabernacle, and the craftsmen themselves offered themselves freely (Exodus 35). “Not for shameful gain,” he says, “nor as lording it over those allotted to your care (*clerīs*).” Or more plainly: First demonstrate in deed and preserve with an undivided heart the humility which you [Col. 0247D] wish your subjects to possess, so that, becoming from the heart an example to the flock, the flock may be formed through you toward humility. Then, when the chief Shepherd appears—he who was the first to be humbled—you will obtain this reward: you will receive the unfading crown of glory.

It follows: “Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders.” After teaching the elders how they ought to preside, he also instructs the younger to obey their guidance; he urges nothing else than that they should be subject to the elders whom he had more fully instructed, look to their examples, and imitate them. But lest prelates, on hearing this, should suppose that the obligations of humility were to be observed by their subjects and not by themselves, he immediately adds a general admonition: [Col. 0248A] “All of you”—that is, elders in governing and younger people in obeying—“show humility toward one another, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.” By Solomon’s authority he frightens all his hearers away from the pride that cast down the devil (Proverbs 3). God resists the proud, first the devil and then humankind, but gives grace to the humble, as to all penitents.

He adds what grace God gives the humble: the more they have been humbled for his sake in the time of struggle, the more gloriously they may be exalted in the time of recompense. By humility we mean either when someone begins beneficially to be worn down for the washing away of sins; or when, with spontaneous devotion of mind, the more perfect humble themselves before God and neighbor; or [Col. 0248B] when, against persecutors, the mind is armed unconquered by the strength of patience. To every kind of humility there follows a fitting reward of exaltation.

Again he says: “Humble yourselves therefore under God’s mighty hand, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation.” As though he said: You who are in this pilgrimage, humble yourselves under God’s mighty hand, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation—that is, on the day of judgment. “Casting,” he says, “all your care upon him, because he cares for you.” As though he said: Cast all your care, of body and soul, upon him as an anchor into the sea, because he cares for you. Cast your care upon God in such a way that you also cooperate with assisting grace.

Again he adds: “Be sober and watchful, because [Col. 0248C] your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour. Resist him, steadfast in faith, knowing that the same suffering is being brought upon your brotherhood which is in the world.” As though he said: Be sober, not intent upon worldly pleasures, and watchful in good works, because your adversary the devil goes about seeking someone to devour. As a lion’s roar obstructs the ears so that they receive no other sound, so the devil, by frightening believers’ minds or suggesting unlawful things, turns them away from the way of truth lest they hear Christ’s voice. “He goes about,” he says, “seeking someone to devour,” just as an enemy besieging enclosed walls examines whether any part of the walls is less secure.

To gain entry and penetrate within, [Col. 0248D] he presents unlawful forms to the eyes and easy desires, so as to destroy strength through sight; he provokes the tongue by insult; he incites the hand to violence by provoking injuries; he promises earthly honors in order to take away heavenly ones; and when he cannot deceive secretly, he adds open terrors. Deceitful in peace, violent in persecution: against him the mind ought to be as prepared to resist as he is prepared to attack.

It follows: “But the God of all grace, who has called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will perfect, strengthen, and establish you.” As though he said: Do what lies within you; but God, the giver of every grace—of faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues—who has called us into his eternal glory, as we exist as members in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will perfect you: he will add to those virtues which you already possess others necessary for you; he will strengthen you to endure tribulations; and he will establish members dissolved by fear or error, that is, restore them to the unity of the Church. [Col. 0249A] “To him be glory and dominion for ages of ages.”

“Through Silvanus, a faithful brother to you, as I suppose, I have written briefly, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God in which you stand.” As though he said: I have written to you, not commanding but exhorting you to persist steadfastly in faith; or exhorting and testifying by the authority of the Scriptures that this grace which I proclaim in writing is true, because salvation is in no other in whom you must be saved (Acts 4); and exhorting you to practice this grace in which you have been instructed, [Col. 0249B] because this is the true grace that benefits you. Whoever despises grace does not find grace, but makes it not his own—that is, not beneficial to himself.

“The Church which is in Babylon and Mark my son greet you.” He calls Rome Babylon because of the confusion of its manifold idolatry, in the midst of which the holy Church, still undeveloped, dwelt. It shone forth as small indeed, just as the people of Israel, small in number and sitting captive by Babylon’s rivers, bewailed the absence of the holy land and did not sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land (Psalm 136). Appropriately, while encouraging his hearers to endure present adversities, he calls the Church which is with him established in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of tribulations—because God’s holy city cannot be immune from the mixture and oppression [Col. 0249C] caused by the devil.

“Mark also”—the evangelist—“my son,” that is, baptized and instructed by me, greets you. “Greet one another with a holy kiss,” namely, as a sign of the common faith and with a peaceful, dovelike kiss, not a deceitful or feigned one. “Grace be with all of you who are in Christ Jesus. Amen.” This epistle began with grace and ends in grace. As though he said: What I write to the churches named above, I write to all churches throughout the world.

Therefore, dearest brothers, together with blessed Peter and all the saints, we must humbly give thanks to almighty God, who, in order to redeem us from the enemy’s power, did not spare his own Son but mercifully handed him over to death for us, so that [Col. 0249D] in him we might share eternal life (Romans 8). Therefore we ought to be all the more devoted to him and readier to serve him, the greater the gifts that we have received from him.

With the utmost application of mind, let us love purity of body; with the utmost vigilance let us seek what is pleasing in his sight; let us drive from ourselves the stains of evil thought together with evil deed; and let us not suppose that any vice can lie hidden in the heart, because all things are naked and exposed to the eyes of his majesty (Hebrews 4). Just as open action does not escape him, neither does hidden thought: he sees hidden things, he who made things concealed. For he himself perfectly knows what we do not know in ourselves. Hence we read that blessed Job [Col. 0250A] said: “There are no darknesses and no shadow of death in which those who work iniquity may hide” (Job 34).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0249D] *Morals*, book 25, chapter 4.]: “What did he seek to signify by ‘darkness,’ if not ignorance, and by ‘the shadow of death,’ if not forgetfulness? For concerning the ignorance of certain people it is said: ‘Having the heart, or understanding, darkened in darkness’ (Ephesians 4); and again concerning forgetfulness, which occurs in death, it is written: ‘On that day all their thoughts shall perish’ (Psalm 145), namely, when his spirit goes forth and he returns to his earth.”

Augustine: “His spirit shall go forth,” that is, his soul shall suddenly go forth when he neither wishes nor knows it; and when the spirit goes forth, he shall return to his earth, from which he took his beginning; and on that day—namely, the day of death—all [Col. 0250B] his thoughts which were directed toward the various circuits of the world shall perish, that is, be frustrated.

Since, therefore, we cannot adequately speak of the soul and its faculties, let us question blessed Isidore, teacher of the Spains, whom God enriched with the great gift of wisdom, and listen attentively to whatever he tells us about its nature.

[Note: [Col. 0250D] *Etymologies*, book 11, chapter 1.] “Man,” he says, “is twofold, namely, inner and outer. The inner human being is the soul; the outer is the body. The soul (*anima*) received its name from the pagans, because they believed it to be wind. Thus in Greek wind is called ἄνεμος (*anemos*), because we seem to live by drawing air through the mouth. But this is plainly false, because the soul is generated much earlier than air can be drawn in through the mouth, since it already lives in the mother’s womb.

“The Evangelist declares that spirit is the same as soul, saying of Christ: ‘I have power,’ he says, ‘to lay down my soul; and again I have power to take it up’ (John 10). Concerning this same soul of the Lord, at the time of his passion, the Evangelist similarly stated: ‘Bowing his head, he gave up the spirit’ (John 19). For what is it to send forth the spirit except to lay down the soul? It is called soul because it lives; but spirit either because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes in the body.

“Likewise, mind (*animus*) is the same as soul; but soul is life, while mind is deliberation. Thus philosophers say that life remains even without soul, and soul endures without mind. Hence people are called ‘out of their minds’ (*amentes*). For *mens* is so called because it knows, and *animus* because it wills. Mind is called so either because it stands out within the soul or because it remembers; hence the forgetful are also called *amentes*. Therefore it is not the soul, but that which excels in the soul, that is called mind, as its head or eye. Thus the human being himself is called the image of God according to the mind.

“All these are attached to the soul and become one thing. For the soul has acquired diverse names according to the operations of its causes. Memory too is mind; hence the forgetful are called *amentes*. Thus, when it gives life to the body, it is soul; when it wills, it is *animus*; when it knows, it is mind; when it recollects, it is memory; when it judges rightly, it is reason; when it breathes, it is spirit; when it perceives something, it is sensation. [Col. 0251A] Indeed, *animus* is called sensation (*sensus*) from its perceiving; whence the word *sententia* [judgment, opinion] also derives.”

Having briefly set out these points of blessed Isidore concerning the soul’s faculties, we must return to those matters which we omitted above.

Therefore, as blessed Gregory says, by darkness we understand ignorance, and by the shadow of death the forgetfulness that commonly occurs in death: while some persons’ understanding is darkened by the darkness of ignorance, and, when the shadow of death intervenes, whatever was thought in life is consigned to forgetfulness. “The shadow of death, then, is a kind of forgetfulness. For just as intervening death causes what existed in life no longer to be, so intervening forgetfulness causes what existed in memory no longer to be. Therefore it is rightly called the shadow of death, because it is as though expressed from death itself, [Col. 0251B] when, by putting its power to sleep, the faculty of perception is altered.

“But because God neither fails to know the evil things that all people think nor forgets those they have perpetrated, unless they are blotted out from his sight through repentance, it is fittingly said: ‘There are no darknesses and no shadow of death in which those who work iniquity may hide.’ As though he said: No one is hidden from his judgment because he can neither fail to see what we do nor forget what he sees.

“Yet darkness and the shadow of death may also be understood otherwise. Every change is a kind of imitation of death. For what changes, as it were, kills what it was, so that it ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. True light, therefore, is our Creator, [Col. 0251C] who is not darkened by any alternation of change and is not shadowed by any defects of his nature; rather, his being shines without change. It is said that darkness or the shadow of death has no place in him. Hence elsewhere it is written: ‘With whom there is no change nor shadow of variation’ (James 1). And Paul again says: ‘Who alone has immortality and inhabits unapproachable light’ (1 Timothy 6).

“But since we all know that both the human soul and angelic spirits were created immortal, why does the Apostle declare that God alone possesses immortality, unless because he alone truly does not die who alone is never changed? The human soul would not have fallen if it had not been mutable. Likewise, if, when expelled from the joys of paradise, it had not been mutable, it would never return to life. Yet in striving to return to life it is compelled always to endure its defects through alternating change.

“Therefore, because it was created from nothing, it nonetheless tends downwards by itself unless it is held in the state of good desire by the hand of its Maker. Thus, from being a creature, it has a tendency to descend. It recognizes that by its own power it can plunge headlong, but it holds itself back by the hand of love toward its Creator, lest it fall, until it passes into immutability; and then it will truly live immortally, [Col. 0252A] because it lives immutably.

“The angelic spirits themselves were created mutable by nature, so that they might either fall of their own will or stand by choice. But because they humbly chose to cling to him by whom they were created, they have now overcome this mutability in themselves by the immutability of standing, so that by merit they might transcend that very condition by which, under the order of their nature, they could have been subject to mutability.

“Therefore, because it belongs to the divine nature alone not to suffer the shadows of ignorance and change, it is rightly said: ‘There are no darknesses and no shadow of death in which those who work iniquity may hide.’ For the eternal light, which is God, sees all the more penetratingly because it shines all the more immutably: it does not fail to know hidden things because it penetrates all things, and does not forget what it has penetrated because it remains unchangeable.

“Accordingly, as often as we conceive something unworthy in our heart, we sin in the light, because that light is present to us—not we to it—and, walking perversely in it, we stumble against that from which we are far by our merit. But when we do not believe ourselves seen, we keep our eyes shut in the sun: that is, we hide him from ourselves, not ourselves from him.

“We therefore, while we are able, should blot out from the sight of the eternal Judge our evil thoughts and still worse deeds. Let us recall before the eyes of our heart whatever we have perversely done through the wickedness of presumption. Let our weakness flatter itself in nothing, nor gently caress itself in the things it recalls; but the more it knows itself guilty of evil, the more kindly severe it should be against itself. Let it set God’s judgment against itself; and whatever it perceives within itself must be struck sternly by the Judge’s sentence, let it itself strike piously by the repentance of conversion.” [Col. 0252C]

Therefore, dearest brothers, as we said above, it is fitting that we guard the heart from impure thoughts and the hands from evil actions, since in the sight of almighty God we can conceal nothing even if we wish to do so. Let us purify ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit; let us follow Christ’s footsteps, according to the counsel of blessed Peter the apostle, as far as possible; and, if necessary, let us shed our own blood for him, so that we may be counted among his elect. For this purpose he suffered for us: he left us an example of suffering, so that, suffering for him, we too may deserve to attain to him.

[Col. 0252D] Let us then wipe away the stains of mind and body by diligent contrition of tears; and, after his example, willingly endure this world’s adversities. For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him (2 Timothy 2). Let us therefore take up our cross, as he himself commands; let us serve him unceasingly by doing good works, so that where he is, we too may be, by his aid—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity, through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0253]

## EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST EPISTLE OF BLESSED JOHN, BY SAINT MARTIN, PRIEST OF LEÓN

[Col. 0253A] John the apostle and evangelist, son of Zebedee, was chosen by the Lord while a virgin and loved more than the others. Reclining also upon his Master’s breast, he drank the streams of the Gospel from that sacred fountain of the Lord’s breast; and, like one of the rivers of paradise, he spread the grace of God’s word throughout the whole world. At Christ’s command he also succeeded to Christ’s place, when the disciple, receiving his Master’s mother, was in a sense left as another son in Christ’s stead.

While he preached Christ’s Gospel in Asia, he was banished by the emperor Domitian to the mines on the island of Patmos, where he also wrote the Apocalypse with his own hand. [Domitian was the son of Vespasian and the brother of Titus, namely, the one who destroyed Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 0253C] Apart from the passages we enclose in brackets, the author transcribes the remainder concerning Blessed John from Isidore’s *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, chapter 72. Since several things adduced here are not of sufficiently established credibility, we shall note briefly that Domitian was killed by Stephen, Domitilla’s steward, in the manner related by Baronius for the year of Christ 98, no. 9. In no. 19 he also rejects as apocryphal the miracles reported to have been performed by the Evangelist, except for restoring a dead man to life. He likewise rejects the prodigies said to have occurred at the translation of the most blessed apostle, under the year 101, nos. 11 and following, relying especially on the testimony of Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 114, which must certainly be consulted. All more recent critics support the most illustrious cardinal; above all others Tillemont, vol. 1 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, should be read.]] But after Caesar Domitian was killed by the Roman [Col. 0253B] senate, Saint John was released from exile, returned to Ephesus, and there, at the request of the bishops of Asia, published the Gospel last of all, in order to refute the deceits of heretics.

Among his other virtues, this was the greatness of his miracles: he changed wild rods into gold and stones from the shore into gems. He also restored fragments of gems to their original nature. At the people’s prayer he raised a widow, and, restoring the soul, renewed a young man’s body to life. Drinking a deadly draught, he not only escaped danger but restored to life those struck down by that same cup.

In the ninety-ninth year of his age [Note: [Col. 0254C] Isidore more correctly says in the sixty-seventh year—or rather the sixty-eighth with Jerome—after the Lord’s Passion. For Usuard was the first to write that the Evangelist died in the ninety-ninth year of his life, says the aforesaid cardinal under the same year 101, no. 8, without any certain assertion of the ancients. It is more probable that he died at the age of ninety-three, as Baronius seems to hold, or ninety-four, as others think.], under the emperor Trajan, worn out by the long burden of age, [Col. 0253C] when he sensed that the day of his departure was near, he is said to have ordered a grave to be dug for himself. Then, after bidding farewell to the brothers and praying, he entered the tomb alive and rested in it as in a bed. Hence some maintain that he lives and contend that he lies not dead in the tomb but sleeping, especially because the earth there gradually wells up from below and rises to the surface of the grave, while dust bubbles upward as though from the breath of one resting beneath. He rested at Ephesus on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

This most blessed evangelist and apostle John wrote the Gospel, as stated above, against the teachings of heretics who thought and taught wrongly concerning the eternity of the Word. He also wrote an Epistle against the folly of those same and other heretics, in which he treats the perfection of faith and charity, so that we may understand what we ought to love and what we ought to believe. For many, led astray by corrupt doctrines, did not rightly understand the sincerity of faith and charity. They said that works of charity were frequent feasting, luxurious living, and consenting to others’ vices, while opposing participation in Christ’s sufferings [Col. 0254B] and the other things fulfilled through love of God and neighbor.

“Heresy,” as Isidore, teacher of the Spains, says [Note: [Col. 0254D] *Etymologies*, book 8, chapter 3.], “is called in Greek from ‘choice,’ because each person chooses for himself what seems better to him, as do the Peripatetic, Academic, Epicurean, and Stoic philosophers, or as others who, devising a perverse doctrine, departed from the Church by their own judgment. Therefore heresy is so called by a Greek word interpreted as ‘choice,’ because [perhaps *qua*, ‘by which’] each person by his own judgment chooses for himself what doctrines or beliefs to establish or embrace. But we are permitted to introduce nothing from our own judgment, nor to choose what anyone has introduced by his own judgment. We have God’s apostles as authorities, and they themselves chose nothing by their own judgment to introduce; rather, they faithfully assigned—that is, handed down—to the nations the teaching received from Christ.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, it is fitting that we too choose or add nothing on our own judgment, but faithfully hold what we have received from Christ and his apostles. Blessed John, therefore, at the beginning of this epistle, in commendation of his message, sets forth Christ’s divinity [Col. 0255A] and humanity, and thereby indicates God’s charity toward humankind and his own charity toward those to whom he writes, saying: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have observed, and what our hands have handled concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested, and we have seen and testify and announce to you the eternal life which was with the Father and appeared to us” (1 John 1).

As though he said: What was in the true being of deity; what we heard through the Law and the prophets; what we saw, namely, a human being coming visibly and perceptibly; what we observed, perceiving divinity in the human being; and what our hands handled concerning the Word of life—not by fortuitously assenting to him who was seen in flesh, but, through much handling, by searching the Scriptures [Col. 0255B] which bear witness concerning that Word.

What anyone has seen can report to others; what he perceives perfectly he is sometimes unable to explain in words. Let it therefore be said more plainly: “That which was from the beginning” means the Son of God in the beginning; yet the disciples saw and heard this same one in the flesh, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). “What we heard,” namely with the ears of mind and body; “what we saw with our eyes,” namely a man living among men. For we also saw “the glory of his appearance, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (ibid.). “What we beheld closely,” namely his life and conduct; and with spiritual eyes we also recognized his divine power on the mountain (Matt. 17). “And our hands handled concerning the Word of life” [Col. 0255C]: that is, being joined to him in great familiarity, we proved by touching that he had true flesh, both before and after his resurrection—he to whom it is said: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me to have” (Luke 24). “Our hands,” he says, “handled concerning the Word of life,” that is, the life-giving Word. “And the life was manifested”: the bread of angels, by assuming flesh, became known to human beings; it shone forth in miracles, rose again, and caused others to rise with itself. “And we have seen, and bear witness, and announce to you eternal life”: through the things just mentioned life was manifested, to be with the faithful—life which was with the Father in eternal divinity and appeared to us in time in humanity. As though he said: We saw manifest life [Col. 0255D], that is, Christ, whom the unbelieving did not see; and we are witnesses. We saw, I say, and, by proclaiming him to unbelievers, became martyrs.

It follows: “What we have seen and heard, we announce to you, that you also may have fellowship with us, and that your fellowship may be with the Father and his Son Jesus Christ.” As though it were said more plainly: What we saw, namely Christ in the flesh, and heard, namely words from his mouth, we announce to you; and you ought to believe those who heard and saw, so that you too, who did not see, may have fellowship with us by believing well, living well, and patiently enduring all things; and that our fellowship may be with the Father and his Son Jesus Christ. That is, through our fellowship you may pass into fellowship with God, so that we may be heirs of God and fellow-heirs with Christ (Rom. 8). Whoever wishes to be joined to God must first be united to the fellowship of the Church. Nor do those who believed through the apostles have less than those who believed through Christ himself. Hence it is said: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20). And again: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John 17).

[Note: [Col. 0255D] The gloss incorrectly reads: “These.”]

Again he adds: “We write these things to you that you may rejoice, and that your joy may be full.” As though he said: We write these things to you—that is, we do not announce them only fleetingly, but commit them to memory—so that we may lead many into the same fellowship with us, and that our joy may be full in this age, namely in the unity of the Church, and in the future in the fellowship of angels [Col. 0256B].

It follows: “This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you: that God is light, and there are no darknesses in him.” As though he said: We drew near to the light, and the light shone upon us; we were darkness, but now through the light we are light and enlighten others, while we announce that sins are forgiven and darkness expelled. God is light. Therefore whoever wishes to have fellowship with light must drive out the darkness of sins, because darkness cannot have fellowship with light. “God,” he says, “is light”: that is, he drives out the darkness of sins; “and there are no darknesses in him,” that is, those who persist in sins and darken others are not counted among his members. Perhaps someone says: Why was the Word made flesh? What new thing did Christ bring to the world? Why did he come to suffer? [Col. 0256C] It was not without purpose. See what he wished to teach: namely, that God is light. By this statement he shows the excellence of divine purity, which we are commanded to imitate. Here the Manichaeans are refuted, who say that God’s nature was conquered and corrupted in warfare by the prince of darkness.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, ch. 5.]

“The Manichaeans arose from a certain Persian called Manet [perhaps *Manes*]. He introduced two natures and substances, namely a good and an evil one; and he asserted that souls flow forth from God as though from some fountain. They reject the Old Testament and receive the New only in part.”

Thus far, the commendation of the Epistle. Here the Evangelist shows how charity must be held. “If, therefore,” he says, “we say that we have fellowship with him” [Col. 0256D], “and walk in darkness, we lie and do not do the truth.” As though he said: Since the Word was made flesh in order to announce this to the world, if we say that we have fellowship with him through faith and charity, which join us to God, and yet walk in darkness—that is, in sins of ignorance or wickedness, adding sin to sin—we lie within ourselves and do not do the truth, while by our example we lead others into the same falsehood. Hence blessed Paul says: “What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” But “if we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from every sin” (2 Cor. 6 [Col. 0257A]). God is said to be in the light because he is supreme goodness, in which he finds no possibility of further progress. A human being dwells in light because through works of virtue he advances toward better things.

Let it therefore be said more plainly: If we walk in the light—that is, if we are guided by the same cause for which Christ is called light—as he himself is in the light, that is, enlightening others by his example, we have fellowship with one another through charity; and this deservedly, because the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from every sin. Namely, the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion releases all original and actual sins. If we walk in light, we are thus clean; yet we should not think that, so long as we live, we can be wholly cleansed from sins. Nor do those have charity [Col. 0257B] who, proud of their own merits, say that they are clean.

It follows: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” He does not say, “We have not had sin,” lest it perhaps appear to be said concerning past life. Let it therefore be said more plainly: if, puffed up by some righteousness of our own, we say that we have no sin, we lead ourselves into greater sins; and truth—that is, God—is not in us, because he withdraws himself from the proud. Again he adds: “If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, so as to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.” Because in this life we cannot be without sin, the first hope of salvation is confession, more from humility than necessity [Col. 0257C]; then love, because we love him before whom we humble ourselves, and “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4). Pride extinguishes charity, but charity extinguishes sin. Therefore let humility strengthen charity; let humility lead a human being to confession. As though it were said more plainly: If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, he who promised grace to the humble. He is faithful in fulfilling his promise, and just because he justly forgives true confession: so that in this life he may forgive us our sins, without which life is not lived; and after death may cleanse us from all iniquity, so that we may neither wish nor be able to sin, namely in eternal life.

It follows: “If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.” God alone is true [Col. 0257D]; but a human being is true from God and a liar from himself. It is impossible for any saint not sometimes to fall into minor sins; yet he does not cease to be righteous, because, with God’s help, he rises again more quickly. Let it therefore be said more plainly: If we confess our sins, we are cleansed from sins; but if we say that we have not sinned—that is, if we wish to excuse ourselves as though we did not need absolution—we make him a liar who says that not even an infant of one day is without sin (Job 14); and his word is not in us, namely Christ, through whom forgiveness is given, who does not remain in the proud. Or: the word which he spoke, “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3).

It follows: “My little children, I write these things to you, that you may not sin” [Col. 0258A]. As though he said: If through human frailty you cannot avoid all vices, take pains at least to avoid the greater and more evident ones, so that no temptation may seize you except what is human (1 Cor. 10). “That you may not sin,” he says—that is, lest, hearing that we are cleansed by God, you assume a harmful security; rather, have a salutary fear. As though he plainly said: My little children, for whom I ought to provide and who ought to obey me, I write these things to you, namely that you may retain them in memory and not sin by saying, “We have not sinned.”

Again he adds, saying: “But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world.” As though he said: If anyone even after my admonition [Col. 0258B] falls, let him not despair. The Son of God is advocate only for those who call upon him purely. Therefore let your sins displease you; cry out, and he hears and delivers you. John, a righteous man accommodating himself to the weak, did not say, “He has an advocate,” but “We have,” placing himself among or in the number of sinners, that he might have Christ as advocate. A righteous advocate does not undertake unjust causes. Yet he will defend us as righteous at judgment if we do not accuse the unrighteous in this age. “He himself,” he says, “is propitiation for our sins,” that is, reconciling us to God the Father by preaching and intercession, not only for ours, who now live in the flesh, but also for those of the whole world, that is, for the whole Church. Therefore let no one say, “Look, Christ is here” [Col. 0258C], “or there is Christ” (Mark 13). Why? Because Christ is everywhere, and everywhere makes propitiation.

“And by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments.” To know or recognize is not always said of information, but of experience and union with another thing. We know God when we are united to him; for one who knows in this way keeps the commandments. As though he said: By this we know—that is, have knowledge—that we know the one God by cleaving to him, if we keep his commandments, that is, charity, as he says elsewhere: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15). Therefore we ought to consider our frailty; in sins we ought to seek an advocate. In order to obtain this, let us labour to keep the commandments, through which one comes to knowledge [Col. 0258D] of him.

It follows: “He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and truth is not in him.” It is no great matter to know the one God, since even demons believe and tremble (Jas. 2).
