Thus to know God is to love him. As though he said: He who says that he knows God—that is, he who keeps his commandments—knows God. For he who does not keep the commandments does not know him, and truth is not in him, namely Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). But whoever keeps his word—truly in him the charity of God is perfected; that is, he knows him. “By this we know that we are in him,” that is, if we keep his commandments, we live in him with true life and do not die.

It follows: “He who says that he remains in him ought himself also to walk as he walked” [Col. 0259A]. As though he plainly said: God’s commandments must truly be kept, because after baptism we say that we remain in him; and whoever says that he remains in him ought, as he walked—he who prayed for his enemies—to walk also, according to his measure, in the way of righteousness, charity, and patience, advancing from virtue to virtue. Hence it is said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16). Again he adds:

“Beloved, I do not write to you a new commandment, but an old commandment which you have had from the beginning.” The same charity is an old commandment, because from the beginning the same commandment was commended; and it is a new commandment because, darkness having been cast out, it infuses a desire for new light. As though he said more plainly: I do not write to you a new commandment [Col. 0259B], but an old commandment—that is, one practised by righteous Abel and the holy Fathers—not one belonging only to the old human being, but also to the new, which you have had from the beginning of your faith. The old commandment is the word which you heard. As though he said more plainly: this word which you heard from me and from other preachers is that old commandment; and it is old because you heard it from the beginning of your faith.

It follows: “Again I write to you a new commandment, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness has now passed, and the true light now shines.” As though he said: You ought to keep this commandment; for I do not preach and commend it only once, but because I see it to be very useful to you, I repeat it again and again as though new. “Which is true,” he says, “both in him and in you”: that is [Col. 0259C], according as I promised that through keeping God’s commandments one comes to knowledge and love of him; and it is fulfilled in Christ himself, because he obeyed the Father unto death and was therefore glorified (Phil. 2). This commandment is true also in you, some of whom already glory with God through it. And it is truly new, because darkness has now passed and true light now shines. Darkness belongs to the old human being, but light to the new. Darkness—that is, the passible body and the miseries of the flesh—have passed away in Christ, and the true light of immortality now shines in him who also enlightens others, who were the old human being and darkness but are now light in the Lord (Eph. 5).

Again he adds: “He who says that he is in the light” [Col. 0259D] “and hates his brother is still in darkness.” Here he defines what commandment he means, namely charity, and how that charity must be held: namely love of neighbour. As though he said: He who says that he is in the light of Christian faith or good works, yet hates his brother, whom God commands him to love, is still in darkness, namely in the sins in which he was born; or he is assigned to the darkness of hell. Again he says: “He who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him.” Whoever loves his brother endures all things for the unity of charity; even when he corrects his brother, he is not angry and does not inflict disgrace.

[Col. 0260A] Hence the Psalmist speaks to God, saying: “Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. 118). As though the Prophet spoke more plainly to the Lord, saying: Great peace is in the mind of those who love your law, even if not in every respect; or great peace will be in the future, where charity will truly be perfect, for those who love you. For charity drives out all disturbances. “And there is no stumbling-block for them”: that is, those who love God’s law are not offended by the rock of stumbling, as the Jews and heretics are.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] Another manuscript incorrectly reads: “is shown.”]

Those who love are not scandalized because they are not little ones, of whom the Lord says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble” (Matt. 18), etc. It belongs to the little ones to be scandalized, not to the perfect. Or the law itself is not a stumbling-block to them; for whoever loves the law, if he does not understand something [Col. 0260B] in it, honours it; what seems absurd in sound he judges to be great, and judges himself not to know it; and therefore the law is not a stumbling-block to him. Or there is no stumbling-block for them from any source [perhaps “for him”], because his faith depends upon the law itself and not upon the conduct of human beings, lest, when some highly esteemed persons fall, he himself perish through scandal. He who is about to follow the law loves it and has both peace and no stumbling-block; though many sin in that law, it itself does not sin and does not know how to sin.

[Note: [Col. 0260D] The gloss reads “secure” instead of “about to follow the law.”]

Therefore great peace belongs to those who love the law of God, that is, charity, and there is no stumbling-block for them. As though the most blessed Evangelist John said more plainly: Whoever loves his brother, after he has drawn near to God through baptism, remains in the light of good works [Col. 0260C], because then good works and the light of faith benefit him.

It follows: “But he who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes.” As though he said: Whoever loves his brother is in the light of knowledge and action; but whoever hates is in the darkness of ignorance, and through that ignorance walks from vice to vice. He does not know—that is, he does not foresee—where he goes, or to what punishment he is to be carried away. He does not know where he goes, namely the way by which he may turn to better things; and this is not because the way is not open, but because darkness has blinded his eyes: departing from Christ’s light, he is so hindered by sins and carnal pleasure that, even if he sees the good, he nevertheless does not carry it out.

Again he says: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” [Col. 0260D]. As though he said: Charity may also be had in this way, if you love God and despise the world with everything that belongs to it; and I write this to you as a useful matter.

As though he said more plainly: I write to you, fathers—not by age but by wisdom, whose task it is to remember ancient things and disclose them to those younger—because you have known him who is from the beginning, namely Christ with the Father and the Holy Spirit, whom you know always to have existed, and whom you announce to others. Or the fathers are venerable old men, whose love for the world ought by now to grow cold. As though he said: I write to all; to some indeed as fathers, to some [Col. 0261A] as children, and to others as young men.

It follows: “I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name’s sake.” Therefore they are fathers because they have known ancient things; children because their sins are forgiven; young men because they are strong and have conquered. He calls all children whom he himself preceded in faith. “Little children” are little not in age but in knowledge. As though he plainly said: I write to you, little children, obedient, namely to the Father, or newly born, because your sins are forgiven you. He sets forth a reason by which he may draw them away from love of the world: because sins are forgiven to those baptized in Christ’s name and invoking his name; therefore one must cling more closely to Christ than to the world.

Again he says: “I write to you, young people, because you have conquered the evil one.” The period of adolescence [Col. 0261B], because of the incentives of the flesh, is slippery; but because of the strength of age, it is capable and suited to struggle. These young people whom he praises overcame the temptations of pleasures through love of God’s word and despised persecutions. It follows: “I write to you, children, because you have known the Father.” Here he calls “children” those humble in spirit, who, the more they humble themselves under the mighty hand of God, know the mysteries of eternity all the more sublimely. Hence it is said: “You have revealed these things to little ones” (Matt. 11). “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning.” He commends and repeats it. As though he said: Remember that you are fathers; for if you forget him who is from the beginning, you have lost fatherhood.

It follows: “I write to you, young people, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have conquered the evil one” [Col. 0261C]. As though he said: I write to you young people, who by strength of mind and love of God’s word have conquered the incentives of the flesh and have manfully resisted the devil when he tempted you. At that time they were drawn by custom to the brothel, but these conquered by resisting manfully. As though he plainly said: Consider also that you are young; fight, that you may conquer; conquer, that you may be crowned; be humble, lest you fall in the battle; and because you have already conquered the evil one, it would be shameful to be conquered by him whom you have already conquered.

Since, therefore, while the most blessed Evangelist John has been preaching about the ages of human beings, this reading has presented itself to us, it is fitting, beloved, that we hear somewhat more fully about the distinctions of these same ages, as holy Isidore, teacher of Spain, discusses them [Col. 0261D].

[Note: [Col. 0261D] *Etymologies*, book XI, ch. 2.]

“The stages of human life,” he says, “are six: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity, and old age. The first age is infancy, extending through seven years. The second is childhood, that is, pure and not yet fit for generation, extending to the fourteenth year. The third age is adolescence, mature for begetting, extending to the twenty-eighth year. The fourth is youth, the strongest of all ages, ending in the fiftieth year. The fifth is the age of older persons, that is, maturity, which is the decline from youth into old age: not yet old age, but no longer youth [Col. 0262A], because it is the age of the *senior*, which the Greeks call πρεσβύτης (*presbytēs*, ‘elder’); for an old man among the Greeks is called *presbyter*, but γέρων (*gerōn*, ‘old man’). This age begins in the fiftieth year and ends in the seventieth. The sixth age is old age, which is limited by no fixed number of years; after those five ages, whatever life remains is assigned to old age. Senility, moreover, is the last part of old age, so called because it is the terminus of the sixth age. In these six periods philosophers have described human life, in which it changes, runs its course, and reaches the boundary of death.”

It is necessary for us to return again to the matters we omitted above. Saint John the Evangelist also says: “Beloved, do not love the world or the things that are in the world.” As though he said: Use the world [Col. 0262B] for necessity, but do not love it for superfluity; and “make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13). As though he said: I write this to all of you: Do not love the world, that is, the world’s abundance or beauty, nor the things that are in the world, such as gold, silver, and every fleeting flow of riches.

It follows: “If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him.” As though it were said: Since the heart does not contain two mutually hostile loves, being rooted in charity, build upon this root nothing except what accords with charity, because “you cannot serve two masters” (Matt. 6). As love of God is the source of all virtues, so love of the world is the source of all vices. Hence follows: “Everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes [Col. 0262C], and the pride of life; this is not from the Father, but is from the world. And the world will pass away, and its lust.” Such lust and pride are not from the Father. The warfare of vices also is not from God the Father and Creator, but from the love of the world which we prefer to God. God made human beings upright, but they have entangled themselves in endless questions (Eccles. 7). God does not tempt toward evils, but each person is tempted by his own lust (Jas. 1). All lovers of the world have nothing except these three things, under which every kind of vice is comprehended.

The lust of the flesh is desire for everything pertaining to bodily pleasures and delights, such as food, drink, sexual intercourse, and the like. The lust of the eyes [Col. 0262D] is every curiosity exercised in investigating magical arts, in viewing shameful spectacles, in acquiring superfluous temporal possessions, in detecting and criticizing the faults of neighbours. The pride of life is when someone boasts in honours and seeks large households. Adam was overcome through these three things, because he desired the forbidden food and wished to know good and evil—that is, wished to be like God (Gen. 3). Christ conquered these three, because, not captured by desire for bodily bread, he did not descend from the pinnacle nor consent to be raised over the kingdoms of the world (Matt. 4).

Let it therefore be said more plainly: Everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, when the flesh is delighted by touch [Col. 0263A] or taste; and the lust of the eyes, when sight is delighted, as by beautiful garments, gold, and such things; and the pride of life, namely every worldly ambition. This is not from the Father—that is, not from God, who creates and provides for us as a father—but from the world, that is, from our attaching ourselves to the world. Let us therefore cling to God the Father in this world, because the world will pass into a new form, and its lust with it, when on that day all the thoughts of the wicked perish (Ps. 145). But whoever does God’s will remains forever, because while living he sought eternal things.

“Little children, it is the last hour.” As though he said: Each person’s end is near, and therefore it is fitting that you press on with good works. “And as you have heard,” he says, “that Antichrist is coming, many antichrists have now arisen; from which we know that it is the last hour” [Col. 0263B]. We are in the eleventh hour. The Saviour came in the flesh, and the plague of Antichrist will follow, attacking the proclamations of salvation and uprooting the vineyard cultivated by Christ. Many members of that utterly wicked head have already been sent ahead, against whom one must be on guard, because the end of the age is now at hand. Or “the last hour” means one like the last, namely that this persecution is like the future one. As though he said: Charity may also be had in this way, if by no prompting of heretics you depart from the faith and the other things that belong to God; and, in order that you may retain it, let what you heard from the beginning remain in you. He offers the reasons: because you are little children, and because it is the last hour.

All heretics are antichrists: namely all who destroy by their actions the faith they profess; all who are opposed to Christ and bear witness to their coming head, because “the ministry of iniquity is already at work” (2 Thess. 2). Those baptized and anointed with chrism are antichrists in the sense that they may more aptly be understood as persons opposed to Christ and his Church. As though he said more plainly: For this reason you ought to persist in faith and good works, because there are many antichrists who wish to deceive you; and just as you heard long ago with what force and error Antichrist will come, so these too come with great violence. From this we know that it is the last hour: because there are many antichrists, the day of judgment will come without delay.

Again he says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” [Col. 0263D]. As though he plainly said: There are many antichrists, yet do not let them frighten you if they have returned to Judaism or paganism. Nor should you think that the Church suffers any harm through this, because although they went out from us, they were not truly of us and could not have gone out unless they were opposed to Christ. Whoever is not opposed to Christ remains in Christ’s body.

Let what blessed Isidore thinks concerning Antichrist and his members be shown for our instruction.

[Note: [Col. 0263D] *Etymologies*, book VIII, ch. 11.]

“Antichrist,” he says, “is called thus because he will come against Christ. Therefore, contrary to the understanding of certain simple persons [Col. 0264A], Antichrist is not so called because he will come before Christ—that is, because Christ will come after him—but because *Antichrist* in Greek means in Latin ‘one opposed to Christ’: for ἀντί (*anti*) in Greek means ‘against’ in Latin. When he comes, he will falsely claim to be Christ; he will fight against him and oppose his sacraments, in order to destroy the Gospel of his truth. For he will attempt to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem and restore all the ceremonies of the old Law. Indeed, that person too is Antichrist who denies that Christ is God, who is opposed to Christ; and all who leave the Church and sever themselves from the unity of faith are likewise antichrists.

Again blessed John adds, saying: “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us; but [Col. 0264B] in order that they might be made manifest that they are not of us, they went out from us.” False Christians in the Church are like harmful humours in the body; and as the body is relieved when they are vomited out, so the Church is relieved when the wicked depart. Many who are not of us receive Christ’s sacraments with us; but temptation proves those who are not of us. When temptation comes upon them, they fly out as if at the occasion of a wind, because they were not grains. But unquestionably all the wicked will fly away then, when the Lord’s threshing-floor begins its work on the day of judgment.

Let it again be said more plainly: “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” That is, this proves that they were not of us by the predestination and election of the Lord. But in order that they may be made manifest, by God’s permission some depart from the Church in the final sifting [Col. 0264C], showing that they were not of Christ’s body, so that it may thereby plainly appear that not all are of us who, set within with us, receive Christ’s sacraments; and therefore their separation ought not to distress you.

Again he adds: “But you have an anointing from the Holy One and know all things.” Although he was speaking about heretics, he suddenly turns to his own people and says that they have an anointing from the Holy One, that is, from Christ, in order by contrast to show that heretics and all antichrists are deprived of the gift of spiritual grace and do not belong to him who is called Holy by the prophets. As though it were said more plainly: You ought to remain in faith and good works because you have [Col. 0264D] an anointing from the Holy One, Christ—namely baptism or the Holy Spirit—by which every pain of sin and ignorance is driven out. “And you know all things,” namely which are good and which evil; nor is it necessary that you be taught, because the anointing teaches you. As though he said: You know the truth of faith, taught through the anointing of the Spirit; you have no need to be taught except to persist in what you have begun. As though he said: I did not write to you as persons ignorant of truth but as persons knowing it. As though he plainly said: You truly know all things; for if you did not know what must be held concerning the faith, I could give you milk as to little children; but because you are perfect in knowledge, I have written to you as to the perfect.

Again he says: “And because no lie is from the truth; who is a liar except he who denies that Jesus is the Christ?” [Col. 0265A] As though he said: No lie is from truth, because whoever lies is not from Christ. But spiritually, who is a liar except one who denies that Jesus is the Christ—that is, the Messiah promised in the Law? This is Antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. In vain does one confess God the Father who denies the Son who proceeds from him. Lest anyone say, “I do not worship Christ, but I worship God the Father,” he adds: “Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either”; that is, whoever denies that Jesus is the Son of God has neither the Son nor the Father himself propitious. But “whoever confesses the Son has the Father also”: that is, whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God has the Father favourable.

See, we have been instructed how to recognize Antichrist: namely, anyone at all who denies Christ. He had said that no lie is from truth; but because there are many mutually differing kinds of lies, he now sets forward the particular lie of denying Christ, in comparison with which the rest seem small or nothing. This is characteristic of the Jews, who falsely say that Jesus is not Christ; but it also characterizes all who disdain to obey Christ’s commandments.

It follows: “Let what you heard from the beginning remain in you.” As though he were plainly saying: What you heard through the preachers from the beginning of your conversion, let it remain in you; that is, retain it in memory through observance. As though he said: If anyone should say to you, “Behold, here is Christ, or there” (Matt. 24), do not believe it; but hold only to what you learned from the apostles. Again he says: “But if what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father.” He puts the Son first, because no one comes to the Father except through the Son (John 14). As though this were said more plainly: If the things you have heard remain in you, you will be members of the Father and the Son, so that you do not fall away from the remembrance and protection of the Father and the Son. And you ought especially to desire this: to be in the Father and the Son, because from this you will obtain your reward. “And this is the promise which he himself promised us, namely eternal life.” As though he said: Let the remembrance of the promised reward make you persevering in good work.

As though he said plainly: This is the promise which he who does not lie promised us through himself and through his preachers—not gold, not silver, nor anything earthly, but eternal life. “These things,” he says, “I write to you concerning those who deceive you.” As though he said: I warn you to attend to these things which I say, because I wrote these things to you in order that you might avoid the wicked. “Concerning those,” he says, “who deceive you”: those who draw you back from eternal life either through perverse doctrines, through certain enticements, or through the adversities of this age.

It follows: “And let the anointing which you received from him remain in you.” As though he said clearly: In order that you may faithfully retain the teaching which I teach you outwardly, take care to preserve whole in heart and body the grace of the Holy Spirit which you received in baptism.

Again he says: “You have no need that anyone should teach you; but as his anointing teaches you concerning all things, and is true and is not a lie—and as it taught you—remain in him; so that, when he appears, we may have confidence and not be put to shame by him at his coming.” As though he said: You have no need that anyone teach you, because, when the Holy Spirit teaches you inwardly, you have less need to be taught outwardly by human instruction. But as his anointing—that is, the Holy Spirit, whose sacrament is in the visible anointing—teaches you concerning all things that must be retained; or, his anointing is the charity which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us [Col. 0266B], the charity which, filling the heart, inflames it to observe God’s commandments.

> [Note: Col. 0265D, Homily 30 on the Gospels.] Therefore, as blessed Gregory says, let no one attribute to the teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth; for unless the Holy Spirit is within to teach, the teacher’s tongue labours outwardly in vain.

Yet the teacher should not be silent, but should do the good that he can. “It is true,” he says, “and is not a lie”—understand, what I preach—because those who teach otherwise are false. Nor will you find eternal life otherwise, unless you follow the chaste way of faith which you heard through me. It is true and is not mutable like the old law. Another translation is: “And the anointing is true and is not deceitful; and as it taught you, remain in him.”

As though he said: Therefore, because it is truthful, as his anointing [Col. 0266C] taught you, remain in him. “And now, little children, remain in him.” By frequent repetition he impresses these words so that they may be more firmly fixed in their minds. “Remain in him,” he says; and if you possess any good, ascribe all of it to him and none to yourselves; but attribute evils to yourselves and to the devil. Thus, when he appears for the reward of the good and the condemnation of the wicked, we may have confidence, enjoying this advantage, and may not be put to shame by him, because we neglected or denied him, at his coming. Whoever remains in the Lord amid persecutions is not ashamed and has hope at his coming; but he who is ashamed here will be put to shame at his coming, whose commandments he neglects.

“If you know that he is righteous, know also that everyone who does righteousness is born of him.” Therefore, if we are born of the Righteous One, we ought to follow the righteousness of our righteous Father. Perfect righteousness is scarcely found even in angels or holy men who always remain in contemplation of God. But in us righteousness begins from faith. The beginning of righteousness is the confession of sins; righteousness will be perfected when there is no longer struggle with the flesh, but triumph over the enemy.

Let this be said again more plainly: If you know—that is, if it is certain to you—that he is righteous, that is, in the primary sense the author and nature of all righteousness, know also this: that everyone who does righteousness is born of him, with his assistance, passing from evil to good.

It follows: “See what manner of charity the Father has given us, that we should be called and should be sons of God” [Col. 0267A]. God the Father gave us charity, so that, when we know and are able to love him, we may love him not only as servants love a Lord, but also as children love a Father. Hence it is said: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1). “See,” he says, “what manner of charity the Father has given us.” That is: even if you do not understand that all righteousness is from God, prove it from this—by how great and what kind of gifts God has shown his fatherly charity toward us. For he gave us that in this age we should be called sons of God both in name and in fact, and that in the future we should be sons of God by possessing our inheritance in eternal blessedness.

Again he says: “For this reason the world does not know us, because it did not know him,” namely, the Father. As though he said: Because we are called sons of God, the world—that is, lovers of the world—does not love us, that is, does not perceive our dignity. They do not honour us, but afflict us.

Again he adds: “Beloved, now we are sons of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be.” As though he said: What dignity is it to be and to be called sons of God? He answers: Now, through the miracles we perform and through purity of life, it appears that we are sons of God; but whatever belongs to the present age is little in comparison with the future.

> [Note: Col. 0267D. “In comparison,” or, with the Gloss: “for comparison with.”]

“It has not yet appeared what we shall be,” because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2).

It follows: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” When we enjoy the contemplation of unchangeable and eternal divinity [Col. 0267C], we too shall be immortal and eternal in him—not the same as he, but like him, because we are creatures. Insofar as “the Word became flesh” (John 1), the wicked saw Christ and will see him at the judgment; but as the Word was in the beginning with the Father (ibid.), only the righteous shall see him. “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26).

As though he said plainly: We know that when he appears in his coming according to the body, we shall be like him, namely immortal and impassible, because we shall see him as he is; for we shall contemplate him in the very substance of his divinity, something granted to no one in this life.

Again he adds: “Everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy” [Col. 0267D]. Not only have we been made sons of God through God’s grace, and hope that we shall be like him; we are also freed from iniquity, because he appeared in order to take away sins. No one should excuse himself from this iniquity, because “everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity. And you know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.”

Therefore everyone, as stated above, who has this hope—namely, that he will attain likeness to God—sanctifies himself; that is, in the present life he imitates God’s holiness, not wholly but according to his measure, by living piously and renouncing worldly things, just as he is holy. Let no one therefore say: “I am a sinful man, but I am not iniquitous,” because he who commits sin also commits iniquity [Col. 0268A].

He does not take away free will when he says that a person sanctifies himself; nor, however, does he agree with the Pelagians, who say that man does not need God’s grace. Rather, just as we are commanded to hope for the glory of divine likeness according to our measure, so we are commanded to imitate the purity of divine holiness according to our capacity, so that, grace going before us, we may labour to avoid evils, saying to God:

> “Be my helper, O Lord; do not forsake me, nor despise me, O God my Saviour” (Ps. 26).

As though the Prophet were praying to God more plainly, saying: Be my helper, O Lord, because although I am free and have been set upon the way, I am nevertheless not sufficient for myself. For when shall I find you unless you help me? Without you I shall fail, and therefore be a sinner. In this—that is, on this way—do not forsake me, as though I had set out on a journey. You have already placed me upon the way, but I shall wander if you forsake me. You have given me free will, but without you my effort is nothing. “Nor despise me,” that is, do not scorn me, because I, a mortal, dare to seek you, the eternal one. For you are the God who created me, and my Saviour, who heals the wound of my sin.

As though he said: You created and re-created me in vain if you despise a mortal; and you ought not do so, because it is not my own fault but the inherited fault through which I fell into this mortality. Therefore man needs divine grace, by which he can do good and avoid evil—a need which the Pelagians assert he has no need of at all. The Pelagians arose from Pelagius, an African monk. They set free will above divine grace, saying that the will is sufficient to fulfil the divine commands [Col. 0268C].

Therefore everyone, as has been said, who commits sin is opposed to the divine law. In Greek, νόμος (*nomos*) is called *lex* in Latin, “law.” From this comes *anomia*, that is, “iniquity,” which is against the law or without law. Hence he says, “Sin is iniquity,” because when we sin, we act against God’s law. Thus the Psalmist says: “I accounted all the sinners of the earth transgressors; therefore I loved your testimonies” (Ps. 118).

As though he said plainly: Those are transgressors whom I accounted, or judged, or reckoned to be all the sinners of the earth. For although there is no transgression where there is no law, and not all have the written law, namely that given through Moses, nevertheless they have the natural law, which says: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another” (Matt. 7), against which all act [Col. 0268D]. Even little children are transgressors, just as they are sinners in their father. Therefore every sinner is a transgressor; and he rightly says, “sinners of the earth,” because there are also sinners against heaven, such as he who said: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15). For whoever diminishes anything of the grace received from heaven, which the Holy Spirit gives or pours in, sins against heaven. Thus he sins against heaven who, being a citizen of heaven, leaves heaven; he is a sinner of earth who is entangled in earthly sins.

It follows: “Therefore I loved your testimonies.” As though he said: And because the law—whether given in paradise, naturally implanted, or written in letters—has made all people transgressors, therefore I loved your testimonies, which are in the law concerning your grace, so that righteousness in me may not be mine but yours [Col. 0269A]. For the law was given in order to send men to grace, not merely by testifying to it but by the fear of the transgression which it produces. Therefore he says, “I loved your testimonies,” because the law leads to grace, which alone frees. Therefore not only those who despise the written law are transgressors, but also those who corrupt the innocence of the natural law.

Again blessed John adds, saying: “You know that he appeared in order to take away the sins of the world.” Lest we, who cannot be without sins and iniquities, should despair, he adds that through Christ we are released from sins. Hence it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). The Son of God takes away sins by forgiving those already committed; by helping so that similar sins are not committed; and by leading us to eternal life, where they cannot occur at all. “And in him there is no sin”; for if sin were in him, it would have to be taken away from him, not taken away by him.

As though he said: And what advantage is it to us if he came without sin? He answers: “Everyone who remains in God does not sin; and everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him.” As though he said more plainly: He who sins does not see him, and he who remains in him does not sin. As though he said: He truly is free from every sin who remains in God, because even he who clings to God, insofar as he remains in him, does not sin; and by clinging to him he avoids sins. For everyone who sins does not see him by faith in his humanity [Col. 0269C], nor has known him by tasting his sweetness. For if he tasted his sweetness—that is, how sweet the Lord is—he would not, by sinning, remove himself from beholding his glory.

It follows: “Little children, let no one deceive you,” by saying either that righteousness is from man or that anyone can remain in God together with sin; for all righteousness is from God and every sin is from the devil.

Again it is said: “He who does righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous.” “Just as” is not always said in the sense of equality. For example, there is a great difference between a human face and its image in a mirror: here there is a body; there there is only an image. Yet here are eyes and there are eyes; here are ears and there are ears. So also we have the image of God, namely God’s righteousness and holiness; but not the image by which the Son is equal to the Father; not God’s righteousness, by which he is righteous in unchangeable perpetuity. We are righteous by believing in him whom we do not see; nor do we possess the holiness by which he is holy through his own eternity, while we are holy by faith alone.

As though he said more plainly: He who does righteousness is righteous—that is, whoever has the act and intention of righteousness is indeed righteous, but not from himself; rather, as he is righteous. That is, righteousness proceeds from the same root, but in him it exists primarily and in the other secondarily; in him naturally and in the other by adoption, because whoever is righteous is righteous from him [Col. 0269D].

Again he adds: “He who commits sin is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning.” He who commits sin is of the devil, not by deriving the origin of his flesh from him, as Manichaeus wished concerning all human beings, but by taking from him the imitation and suggestion of sinning. Thus the children of Abraham are so called by imitating his faith, while Jews who abandon Abraham’s faith become not sons of Abraham but sons of the devil. “From the beginning,” he says, “the devil sins”; that is, he began to sin from the beginning of his creation and sins daily until the present time.

It follows: “For this purpose the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil.” As though he said: For this purpose the Son of God appeared in the flesh, that he might destroy—that is, overthrow—the works of the devil, namely that birth which we derived from the devil. Adam was made by God, but through sinning was born of the devil. The devil begot children such as he himself was.

[Col. 0270B] We are born with concupiscence; before we add our own offences, we are born and die under that condemnation. But Christ, God and man, was born in order to release human sins and bring us back to life.

Again he says: “Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.” As though he said: Christ thus destroys sins, because everyone who is born of God in baptism does not commit sin, because his seed—that is, the Word through which he is begotten—remains in him. And not only does he not sin, but he cannot sin as long as he retains the Word, because he is born of God, in whom there is no sin.

> [Note: Col. 0269. This clause is absent from the Gloss and appears superfluous.]

He does not speak of every sin. For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us” [Col. 0270C]. Therefore he speaks of violation of charity, which [perhaps read: *quam*, “which”] he who has in himself the seed of God—that is, the Word of God by which he has been reborn—cannot commit; and what follows pertains to this. Or it may be understood of any grave sin. “In this,” he says, “the sons of God and the sons of the devil are made manifest.” A true son cannot abandon his Father’s law. The Father’s law is: “I command you that you love one another, as I have loved you” (John 15).

As though he said: In this the sons of God are made manifest, because they do not sin; and the sons of the devil, because they do sin. Hence it is said: “By their fruits you will know them” (Matt. 7).

It follows: “Everyone who is not righteous is not of God, and neither is he who does not love his brother, because this is the message which you heard from the beginning: that you should love one another” [Col. 0270D]. Love is the sure sign by which the sons of God and the sons of the devil are distinguished. Other commandments are common to good and bad people, but an outsider has no share in this spring. Have whatever else you wish; if you lack this one thing, nothing profits you. You may lack other virtues; if you possess this, you have fulfilled the law, because “charity is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13).

As though he said more plainly: Everyone who is not righteous—that is, who does not render to God what he owes—is not of God. And he who does not love his brother is not of God, because the love which you heard from the beginning must truly be possessed. Hence it is said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15). It is good, therefore, that we love one another, but not like Cain, who was of the evil one and killed his brother. “And why did he kill him? Because his works were evil.”

> [Note: Col. 0271D. Here are lacking the words read in the Vulgate: “but his brother’s were righteous.”]

Where envy is, brotherly love is not. By Cain’s evil works he means nothing but envy and hatred of his brother; by Abel’s righteous works, nothing but charity. People are distinguished in this way: let no one attend to words, but to deeds. If the heart does not do good for its brothers, it shows what it has within itself, namely hatred. Cain rightly offered the creature to the Creator, but did not divide rightly when he thought that gifts offered together with hatred of his brother could please God. Abel offered gifts to God with love, and pleased the Creator.

As though he said: Not like Cain, who was of the evil one, that is, of the devil, who envied God and fell from heaven; envied man and cast him out of paradise. For Cain’s works were evil—that is, he envied his brother—whereas Abel’s works were good, pleasing to God through charity. It is no wonder if a lover of the world hates his brother, by “brother” meaning one separated from love of the world and intent upon heavenly desires.

It follows:

“Do not wonder, brothers, if the world hates you,” that is, the lovers of the world. As though he said more plainly: Have love, and do not abandon love because of the world’s hatred or persecutions, for you are tested by temptations. “We know,” he says, “that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers.” Let no one exalt himself because of virtues; let no one fear the poverty of his own powers; because whoever loves his brother gives clear evidence that he belongs to the lot of the righteous [Col. 0271C].

As though he said plainly: We know that love ought not be diminished because of the world, because we have passed from death to life, namely eternal life, because through this we love the brothers. But “he who does not love remains in death”; that is, not only will he come into eternal death, but even now he remains in the death of the soul.

“Everyone,” he says, “who hates his brother is a murderer.” He who pursues his brother in hatred provokes him to anger and discord and thus, so far as he is concerned, kills him in soul. Hence it follows: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.” The life of the flesh is the soul; the life of the soul is God. Death of the body is the loss of the spirit; death of the soul is the loss of God. Therefore he who loses God through hatred of his brother loses life [Col. 0271D]. We must therefore love, not hate, because he who hates is a murderer. “And you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.”

A murderer is one who either strikes with iron or pursues with hatred. If anyone regards hatred of his brother as a slight thing, he will not regard murder in his heart as a slight thing: he does not move his hand to kill, yet he is already held to be a murderer. The other lives, yet this man is judged a killer.

Let this be said again more plainly: You know that every murderer—even though he may seem here to live among the saints through faith—will nevertheless be condemned forever with Cain, because he is guilty of this kind of murder, in that he is at discord with his brothers.

Often, when God strikes with the scourge of correction the one whom we claim to love, and touches him with adversities of this world, we despise him; and the more we see him humbled by divine correction, the more we disdain to count him among our friends. And thereby, while we disdain to aid him in his necessities, we offend God, who mercifully scourged him. Hence we read that blessed Job said:

> “He who takes mercy away from his friend abandons the fear of the Lord” (Job 6).

Gregory [Note: Col. 0272D. Book VII of the *Etymologies*, ch. 10]:

> “Who is designated in this place by the name of ‘friend,’ if not any neighbour, who is joined faithfully to us insofar as, through the good work now received from us, he truly helps us to attain the eternal homeland hereafter?”

Since there are two commandments of charity, namely love of God and of neighbour, love of neighbour is generated through love of God, and love of God is nourished through love of neighbour. For he who neglects to love God certainly does not know how to love his neighbour; and then we make fuller progress in the love of God when we are first nourished with charity for our neighbour in the bosom of that same love.

> “For because love of God generates love of neighbour, the Lord, about to say through the law, ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself’ (Lev. 19), first said, ‘You shall love the Lord your God’ (Deut. 6), so that he might first plant the root of his love in the soil of our breast, and afterward brotherly love might sprout forth through its branches. And again, because love of God grows together with love of neighbour, John bears witness, rebuking in this Epistle when he says: ‘He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?’ Yet this divine love is born through fear, but as it grows in affection it is transformed.

> Often, indeed, almighty God, in order to show how far each person is from love of him or of his neighbour, disposes all things in a wonderful order: he oppresses some with scourges and supports others with success; and when he temporarily abandons some, he reveals in the hearts of others the evil that lay hidden. For those very persons often pursue us in misery whom they honoured beyond comparison when we were prosperous. Everyone placed in prosperity is loved, but when he falls into poverty he is despised, because the loss of prosperity tests the strength of love. Hence one wise man rightly said: ‘A friend is not known in prosperity, and an enemy is not hidden in adversity’ (Ecclus. 12). For prosperity does not reveal a friend, nor does adversity conceal an enemy, because the one is often covered by reverence for our prosperity, while the other is disclosed by the confidence given by adversity.

> Therefore a just man placed under scourges should say: ‘He who takes mercy away from his friend abandons the fear of the Lord.’ For indeed, whoever despises his neighbour because of adversity is openly convicted of not having loved him in prosperity. And since almighty God strikes some people in order both to instruct those struck and to offer those not struck an occasion for good work, whoever despises one who has been struck drives away from himself an opportunity for virtue. He sets himself more wickedly against his Maker insofar as he recognises neither his mercy in his own salvation nor his justice in another’s wound.

> It must also be considered [Col. 0273A] that blessed Job speaks his own words in such a way that through him the life of the whole chosen people is also signified. Since he is a member of that people, when he tells what he himself suffers, he also declares what that people endures: ‘My brothers have passed me by, like a torrent which swiftly passes through the valleys.’ Because the mind of the reprobate loves only present things, it is now as far removed from the scourge as it will later remain estranged from the inheritance. Thus, in pride, it despises the righteous whom fatherly severity mercifully afflicts. Often, however, the reprobate retain the same faith by which we live, receive the same sacraments of faith, and are held within the unity of the same religion; yet they know nothing of the bowels of compassion and do not recognise the power of charity by which we burn toward God and neighbour.

> Thus they are rightly called both brothers and passers-by: through faith they come forth with us from the single womb of their mother, but they are not established in the single devotion of charity toward God and neighbour. Hence they are aptly compared also to the torrent that swiftly passes through the valleys. For a torrent flows down from the mountains to low places; gathered from winter rains, it dries up in the summer sun. Those who love earthly things and abandon hope of the heavenly homeland, as it were, seek valleys from the mountains. Winter, that is, the present life, multiplies them; but the season of the coming judgment dries them up, because when the sun of heavenly strictness grows hot, it will turn the joy of the reprobate into dryness.

> It is well said that it ‘swiftly passes through the valleys.’ For a torrent swiftly passing to the valleys means the minds of the wicked descending to low desires without any obstacle or difficulty. Every ascent involves labour, but descent involves pleasure: by effort a step is directed upward, but by relaxation it declines downward. To haul a stone to a mountain summit requires great labour; to release it from the heights to the depths requires no labour. It rushes down without delay, but reaches the heights only through great exertion. A crop is sown by long labour and nourished by prolonged sun and rain, yet a single great spark consumes it. Tall buildings rise gradually for a little while, yet by sudden collapses they seek the earth. A sturdy tree raises itself through slow growth, yet whatever it has long produced on high falls once and all at once. Therefore, because descent is pleasurable, it is rightly said: ‘My brothers have passed me by like a torrent which swiftly passes through the valleys.’

> This may, however, be understood differently. If we understand valleys as the low places of punishment, all the unjust swiftly pass like a torrent to the valleys, because in this life, which they seek with all their desires, they cannot remain long. For as many days of life as they receive, they proceed toward their end as though by that many daily steps. They desire their time to be increased; but because the time granted cannot endure, as many additions of life as they receive, so many portions of their lifespan they lose. Thus the moments of time which [ed. *quo*] they pursue flee; what they receive, they lose. They swiftly pass to the valleys: drawn out indeed toward long desires of pleasure, but suddenly brought to the gates of hell.

> For even that which is extended by however great longevity is not long if it is enclosed by an end. From the end, the miserable learn that what they held while losing it was short. Hence Solomon rightly says: ‘If a man lives many years and is glad in them all, he should remember the dark time and the many days which, when they come, prove the past to have been vanity’ (Eccles. 11). For when a foolish mind suddenly encounters an evil that does not pass away, by enduring its eternity it will understand that what could pass away was vain.”

Therefore, as we said above, whoever despises a brother struck by some adversity offends God, who afflicted him for the salvation of his soul, because he is both impious toward his brother and proud toward God. It is fitting, therefore, that as God loved us, we also love one another in word and deed [Col. 0274B], lest through hatred we be found guilty of murder at his judgment.

Blessed John says again:

“In this we have known the charity of God: that he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” Having set forth many reasons why charity must be possessed, he finally adds the perfection of charity under the example of the Lord’s passion. Peter is urged to possess this when, in answer to the Lord’s question, he professes that he loves him; to whom it is said: “When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you” (John 21). By these words he was taught to lay down his life for the sheep. For “no one has greater charity than that he lay down his life for his sheep” (John 15).

As though he said: I have shown in many ways that charity must be possessed; but, to come to the conclusion, we must through charity lay down our lives for the brothers, just as Christ laid down his life for all of us.

Again he says: “Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, and closes his bowels against him—how does the charity of God remain in him?” If, either because of an occasion of time or because of human weakness, one does not happen to lay down his life, we ought at least to lay down our possessions for the brothers, because this is the nourishment of charity. Whoever has learned to give his property to one in need will consequently be able to spend himself for his brother’s salvation.

As though he said plainly: Whoever sees his brother in need, namely of clothing or food [Col. 0274D], and closes his bowels against him, so as not to have compassion on his misery—or gives him nothing, even if he does have compassion—how does the charity of God remain in him? That is, if you do not wish to give what is superfluous to your brother, how will you give your life for your brother?

It follows: “My little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.” As though he said: Because charity is not perfect in one who does not lay down his life for the brothers, or who at least does not give them money, therefore, in order that you may have perfect charity, little children of the same Father, do not love in word—that is, in word alone—nor in tongue, that is, in merely polished speech, but in deed and truth, that is, in works of mercy without pretence. By “tongue” elaborate speech is understood, as when some people seek to commend their desire through frequently repeated words [Col. 0275A].

Again he says: “In this we know that we are of the truth, and before him we persuade our hearts, because if our heart reproves us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things.” As though he said: In this, that we love in truth, we know that we are of the truth—that is, we know that we possess this true love from God, who is truth—and from this love we know that we are before him, that is, worthy to obtain his sight. And through this love we also persuade our hearts to devise better works.

As though this were said more plainly: In this, namely that we confer benefits upon the brothers with a simple intention, not for boasting nor for any temporal advantage, but with regard to God alone, we know that we are of the truth. That is, when we perform works of piety in truth, it is evident that we are from God, who is unity, when we imitate his perfection according to our measure. And “before him” means that we persuade our hearts to entertain such thoughts as are worthy of divine sight. For everyone who plans to do something persuades his heart to turn itself to meditate upon the intended deed.

But he who thinks evil would hide it from God if he could; whereas he who thinks good readily persuades his heart to desire that what it thinks should be made manifest before God. This is the beginning of great perfection: when a person rejoices that God sees his works or thoughts, because “he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because they are done in God” (John 3).

This too is great: through love we have thoughts so pure [Col. 0275C] that we wish to show them to God. For even if conscience accused us inwardly, and we wished to hide from God because we did not perform our good deeds with a good intention, we could not remain hidden from God, because he is greater than the heart and knows all things. Therefore charity is powerful, because it commends us to him from whom we cannot hide.

As though he said plainly: Let us love in deed, not in word; because even if, through human weakness, we are mistaken in love, we are not mistaken concerning the reward, because God is greater than our heart and knows with what zeal all things are done.

Again he adds:

Beloved, if our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing in his sight. [Col. 0275D] As though he said: If our heart does not reproach us—namely, in love—we are certain that we possess pure love, seeking the salvation of our brethren without any other gain. Or again: If our heart does not reproach us, namely in prayer, when we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6), and so forth. Therefore, if our heart does not reproach us in love, we have confidence before God—not in the sight of human beings, but where God sees, namely in the heart. And whatever we ask from the root of love, even if it is sometimes not granted according to our will, it will always be granted for our salvation; because we keep his commandments—that is, love—in our minds [Col. 0276A], and perform the works of love that are pleasing before him, in secret, where he himself sees.

This is a great promise, desirable to the faithful. But if anyone is so perverse as not to delight in heavenly promises, let him at least fear what Wisdom thunders forth, in the contrary sense: “He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, even his prayer shall be abominable” (Prov. 28). It follows: “And this is God’s commandment: that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he gave commandment to us. And he who keeps his commandments abides in him, and he in him.”

He gives “commandment” in the singular and adds two things, because these cannot be separated. As though someone asked, “What is that commandment?” He answers: Faith and love—namely, that we should believe in the name [Col. 0276B] of his Son Jesus Christ, because “there is no other name in which we must be saved” (Acts 4); and that we should love one another with so pure a love—not as robbers or any other criminals love one another, but as he gave commandment to us. Hence it is said: “Love for that end for which I loved you” [Note: [Col. 0275D] Interlinear gloss: namely.], “and so that you may attain blessedness.”

He then explains by what reward these commandments of faith and love are kept, when he says: “And he who keeps his commandments abides in him,” that is, in God as in a house, a secure refuge; and he—namely God—abides in that person in the present and in the future, as in a clean vessel. “And by this we know that he abides in us: from the Holy Spirit whom he gave us.” As though he said: If we keep love, God abides in us; and if we doubt whether he dwells in us, we can demonstrate this by manifest [Col. 0276C] signs: because he gave us kinds of tongues, the grace of healings, and the other charisms. It follows:

Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God. In the earliest times of the growing Church, the Spirit fell upon believers, and they spoke in tongues and performed miracles. But now the Church does not require outward signs, because everyone who has faith and love testifies that the Holy Spirit abides in him. This is that necessary grace called the discernment of spirits, for distinguishing them.

As though he said more plainly: Do not believe every spirit—that is, every person speaking spiritually—so as to choose him for imitation; for certain gifts of the Holy [Col. 0276D] Spirit are shared alike by good people and bad, except love. But test the spirits, whether they are from God: that is, whether they are spiritual according to God, whether they rest upon love. And therefore I warn you, because many false prophets have gone out into the world, who under the pretext of faith preach error and corrupt the morals of the good by evil examples, having no love.

Because many who lack love and the unity of the Church, and who rend it by false doctrine, nevertheless insist that the Holy Spirit is within them, he adds that they are to be tested by their fruits, whether they are false or true prophets; for “grapes are not gathered from thorns, nor figs from thistles” (Matt. 7). Again he says: “By this the Spirit of God is known.” Someone asks [Col. 0277A], “How can we test the Spirit of God?” It is known by this sign: “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is Antichrist, of whom you have heard that he is coming, and now already is in the world.” Many heretics and many schismatics confess that Jesus came in the flesh, but deny it by their deeds, since they do not possess love.

[Note: [Col. 0277D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 8, chapter 3.] “Heresy, as has already been said, is so called in Greek from choosing, because each person chooses for himself what seems better to him. Schismatics are called from the splitting of minds. For they believe with the same worship and the same rite as the rest; but they delight only in dissension from the congregation. A schism arises [Col. 0277B] when people say: ‘We are righteous; we sanctify the unclean,’ and other such things.”

Love is therefore necessary to us, dearest brethren, because through love the Word became flesh. Whoever does not possess love denies that he came in the flesh, and thus is convicted of not possessing the Spirit of God. For the Spirit of God declares that Jesus came in the flesh, not by the sound of the tongue, but by loving and acting. Jesus came in order to gather together; the heretic comes in order to scatter. Therefore he does not possess the Spirit of God.

“And every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God,” that is, whoever denies his divinity, or soul, or flesh, or neglects his commandments. He dissolves Jesus who separates God from the man; who divides the members from God; who interprets God’s words wrongly; and who, by living badly, [Col. 0277C] departs from God. And this is Antichrist, of whom you have heard that he will come when the Day of Judgment is near, and who is now already in the world, dwelling in the minds of those who oppose Christ in word or deed; for the ministry of iniquity is already at work.

Indeed, Bildad the Shuhite seems to speak in the book of blessed Job about this son of perdition himself, when he says:

“May the memory of the wicked perish from the earth, and may his name not be celebrated in the streets of the city” (Job 18).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0278D] *Morals*, book 14, chapter 11.] says: “We must observe that Bildad the Shuhite speaks of every wicked person in such a way that his words are secretly directed toward the head of all wicked people. Certainly the devil is the head of the wicked. He himself, having entered that vessel of perdition in the last times, will be called Antichrist, because he will strive to spread his name far [Col. 0277D] and wide. Each person now imitates him when he seeks to extend the glory of his praise from the memory of an earthly name, and rejoices in transient renown.

“Thus let these words be understood of each individual, while also being referred especially to the head of the wicked himself. Let it therefore be said: ‘May the memory of the wicked perish from the earth, and may his name not be celebrated in the streets of the city.’ The term *platea*, ‘street,’ is named from the Greek word for breadth. Antichrist seeks to establish his memory upon earth when he desires, if possible, to remain forever in earthly glory. He delights to have his name celebrated in the streets when he spreads the operation of his iniquity far and wide [Col. 0278A].

“But because his wickedness is not permitted to be exalted for long, let it be said: ‘May his memory perish from the earth, and may his name not be celebrated in the streets’; that is, may he quickly lose the praise of earthly power and lose all joy in his name, which he had spread far and wide in the brief prosperity of time. It follows: ‘God will drive him from light into darkness.’ He will be led from light to darkness when he is condemned from the honour of the present life to eternal punishments. Hence it is added more plainly: ‘And he will remove him from the world.’ He is removed from the world when, at the appearance of the Judge from above, he is taken from this world in which he wickedly gloried.

“Since he will be condemned along with all his followers when the end of the world intervenes, it is rightly added: ‘There shall be no seed of his, nor offspring among his people, nor any remnant in his regions’ [Col. 0278B]. For it is written of him: ‘Whom the Lord Jesus will kill by the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming’ (2 Thess. 2). Therefore, when his wickedness comes to an end with the world’s present order, no offspring will remain among his people; for both he himself and his people will together be driven to punishment. All the wicked also, who have been born into evil actions through his perverse persuasion, will be struck with eternal destruction at the brightness of the Lord’s coming, together with that same head of theirs. None of his offspring will remain in the world, because the strict Judge will bring his wickedness to a conclusion with the end of the world itself.

“That these things must plainly be understood of Antichrist is shown when it is added: ‘In his days those who come last shall be amazed, and horror shall seize those who came first’ [Col. 0278C]. For he will then be so unrestrained in wickedness against the righteous that even the hearts of the elect will be struck with no small fear. Hence it is written: ‘They shall be so astonished that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error’ (Matt. 24). This is said not because the elect will fall, but because they will tremble amid great terrors.

“Then both the elect who come last and the first are said to wage the contest of righteousness against him. Those who are found elect at the end of the world are to be laid low in the death of the flesh; and those also who proceeded from the earlier ages of the world—namely Enoch and Elijah—will be called back into the midst, and will suffer the violence of his cruelty in their still mortal flesh. Those who come last will be astonished at his powers, unleashed in [Col. 0278D] such great authority, and the first will be afraid. For although, perhaps insofar as he is raised up by the spirit of pride, they so despise all his temporal power, nevertheless, in respect of the fact that they themselves still possess mortal flesh, in which they can temporarily be tortured, they dread those very punishments that they steadfastly endure. Thus at one and the same time there is in them both constancy from virtue and fear from flesh: because, though they are elect and cannot be overcome by torments, yet insofar as they are human they themselves fear the torments which they conquer.

“Let it therefore be said: ‘In his days those who come last shall be amazed, and horror shall seize those who came first’; because he will display such great signs [Col. 0279A] and commit deeds so cruel and harsh that he will bring to astonishment those whom he finds at the end of the world, and pierce with the pain of bodily death the earlier Fathers preserved for his defeat—namely Enoch and Elijah.

“Therefore, because Bildad has said much concerning all the wicked and concerning the head of the wicked himself, he immediately adds a general definition: ‘These, then, are the tents of the wicked man, and this is the place of him who does not know God.’ Earlier he had said: ‘He will drive him from light into darkness and remove him from the world.’ When he proceeded to add that person’s evils, he joined: ‘These are the tents of the wicked man, and this is the place of him who does not know God,’ clearly indicating that he who now exalts himself through ignorance of God will then come to his own tents, when his malice or wickedness plunges him into punishments. At last he finds his own place—namely darkness—who, while here he rejoiced in the false light of righteousness, occupied an alien place. Thus the wicked person comes then to his own place when he is tormented in fire by the desert of his wickedness.”

Let blessed John speak again, whose holiness God enriched with the privilege of chastity. “Every spirit,” he says, “that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is Antichrist, of whom you have heard that he is coming.” Many heretics, wishing to separate the unity of the Church by false doctrine, erased this verse from the Epistle lest their errors be refuted by it.

Again he adds: “You are from God, little children, and have overcome him, because he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.” As though he said [Col. 0279C]: They are not from God, but you are from God. By confessing that Jesus came in the flesh and by possessing love, you have overcome him, namely the devil—not by the power of free will, because he who is in you, namely God protecting you, is greater than the devil who is in the world to attack you.

It follows: “They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.” As though he said: These spirits are neither to be loved nor heard, because, although they invoke Christ’s name and mark themselves with Christ’s sign, they belong nevertheless to the number of those who desire worldly things and are ignorant of heavenly things. Therefore, he says, they speak from the world: that is, by the reasoning of worldly wisdom, arguing that God cannot become human, that the dead cannot be raised, that a mortal human being cannot have a dwelling in heaven [Col. 0279D], and other such things. And the world listens to them—that is, those devoted to the desires of the world—because they cannot turn the hearts of spiritual people away from truth.

Again he says: “We are from God, and he who knows God listens to us; he who is not from God does not listen to us.” As though he said: Because we possess love, we are from God; and whoever knows God through love listens to us—to us, I mean, the preachers of truth. And whoever is not from God—that is, whoever does not possess love—does not listen to us, because “the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). “By this,” he says, “we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error.” As though he said more plainly: Whoever listens to us possesses the spirit of truth; whoever does not listen to us possesses the spirit of error.

[Col. 0280A] Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God. And everyone who loves God is born from God and knows God. With God it makes no difference whether he is called righteous and righteousness, loving and love. For he is not called righteous derivatively from righteousness, or loving derivatively from love, as though he possessed righteousness or love; rather, because he is righteousness and love. The Son is God from God; the Holy Spirit [supply: is God] is from God; and there are not three gods, but one God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And that person loves in whom the Holy Spirit dwells. Therefore love is God, but God who is from God; and thus it is truly said both that love is from God and that God is love.

When “from God” is said, either the Son or the Holy Spirit is understood. Since the Apostle says, “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5) [Col. 0280B], we understand that the Holy Spirit is present in love. This is the fountain in which no stranger shares, although he shares in all the other sacraments of the Church. The evangelist urges us to drink from this fountain, saying: “Let us love one another, because love is from God.” As though he said: Because we are from God and not from the world, let us therefore love one another in word and deed.

Again he says: “He who does not love does not know God, because God is love.” He has commended love in many ways, but now he comes to its distinctive praise, in which we must especially listen to him: namely, that the one who loves is born from God and knows God, because God is love. Above he said, “Love is from God”; here he adds, “God is love.” Whoever, therefore, acts against love acts against God. And if it may seem easy to anyone to act against a human being, who would not fear to act against God?

Let it be said again more plainly: “He who does not love does not know God, because God is love”; that is, one does not come to knowledge of the love which is God except through love, because “wisdom shall not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1). In proving that God is love and that he loves us, he wishes to lead us by his example to love one another; and, that we may come to know him, he adds, saying: “In this the love of God appeared among us: that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him.” As though he said: God sent his only-begotten Son—who was invisible in himself, visible in the flesh—into the world, that is, to die for the world, so that we who were formerly dead might live through him who has risen [Col. 0280D].

Again he says: “In this is love: not as though we had loved God, but because he first loved us and sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins.” The Father’s love was proved because he sent the Son; the Son’s love, because he died for us. As though he said: In this is love, that is, in this manifest sending by which God the Father sent his Son for our salvation. “Not as though we had loved God,” that is, we did not love first, as though he loved us by the merit of our love; but rather because he first loved us, so that, with his grace going before, we might love him. And he sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins, as the demonstration of his love. He loved the wicked, but not wickedness.

It is therefore fitting, beloved brethren, that just as God did not wait for us first to love him, so we should not wait for our neighbours to love us, but should love them first. Another translation: “God sent his Son as an offerer of sacrifice,” that is, a sacrificer, “for the destruction of our sins.”

Again he adds: “Beloved, if God loved us, we too ought to love one another.” Love, and do what you will. Whether you keep silence, keep silence in love; whether you cry out, cry out in love. As though he said: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ also loved us” (Eph. 5).

[Col. 0281B] It follows: “No one has ever seen God.” Therefore we ought to love, because, although God is invisible, we see him through love in a manner almost contrary to nature, as these visible things known to the bodily senses are seen. Yet even if at some time he has been seen in this way, he is not seen as these natures are seen; rather, he has been seen by his will, in the form in which he willed, appearing while his nature remained hidden and unchanged in itself.

In the manner in which he is seen as he is, perhaps he is now seen by angels; and we shall see him then, when we are equal to angels (Luke 20). But even then he will not be seen as these visible things are seen by bodily sight; rather, the Only-Begotten who is in the bosom of the Father will himself declare him (John 1), which belongs not to the eyes but to the vision [Col. 0281C] of minds. Therefore, just as, if we wished to see this sun, we would cleanse the eye of the body, so, wishing to see God, let us cleanse the eye of the heart.

But since this vision is hoped for in the future, what must be done, what consolation is to be used, while people are still pilgrims in the body? This, namely: that we should love one another; and thus God abides in us, and his love is made perfect in us. As though he said: If we love one another with sincere and disciplined love—not with lax and idle mildness—God abides in us, inspiring good things, and his love is perfected in us. As though it were said: Begin to love, and God begins to be in you; grow in love, and God, dwelling more fully in you, will make you perfect, so that you may love even an enemy, as he himself loved his enemies.

[Col. 0281D] Again he adds: “By this we know that we abide in him and he in us: because he has given us from the Holy Spirit.” God abides in us and we in God; and let no one despair of salvation. For even if the diseases of crimes weigh us down, the physician is omnipotent and can save. Let us rejoice in hope, so that we may come to the reality.

Let it be said again more plainly: “By this we know that we abide in him,” that is, if we love, he abides in us. We prove this by such evidence: “because he has given us from the Holy Spirit,” that is, he causes us to know and speak subtly of his divinity. “And we,” he says, “have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son, the Saviour of the world.” As though he said: We prove that he gave us from the Holy Spirit because we have seen—that is, through the inspiring Spirit we have known by faith [Col. 0282A]—and through the strengthening Spirit we testify, something which those who have not received the Holy Spirit do not do: that the Father sent his Son for human knowledge, now as Saviour of the world, in the future as Judge.

How do you know whether you possess the Spirit of God? Question your inward parts; and if they are full of love, you possess the Spirit of God within you, because “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. 5). It follows: “Whoever has confessed that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.” As though he said: We believe and testify through the Spirit given; and, following our example, whoever through that same Spirit has confessed with a true confession of heart, so as not to waver either under the frauds of heretics, the torments of persecutors, the example of carnal brethren, or his own frailty.

“And we,” he says, “have known and believed the love which God has in us.” As though he said: We have seen and testify that God sent his Son, and we have known why he did this—not because he had need, not because he owed anything, but through love alone. Though he had an only Son, he did not wish him to remain alone; rather, so that he might have brethren, he adopted for him those who would possess eternal life with him. Above he said, “If we love, God abides in us”; here he says, “Whoever has confessed that Jesus is the Son of God abides in God, and God in him,” indicating that whoever has love among the brethren truly testifies that Jesus is the Son of God. For when the effects of causes agree, the causes themselves [Col. 0282C] agree.

While he commends love, he neither wholly passes over God’s love in silence nor names it frequently; he entirely passes over love for an enemy in silence, while very frequently recalling brotherly love. Why, when he says that it is no great thing if we love those who love us, unless love extends even to enemies? But the person who has reached love for enemies will not pass beyond the brethren. Therefore, after the manner of fire, love must first take hold of what is near and then spread to what is farther away.
