One who desires that an enemy should become a brother loves the brother; for he loves in that person not what he is, but what he wishes him to become. Just as a craftsman loves timber cut from the forest, from which he is going to make something: he does not love what it is, but what he is going to make. He has therefore not given less instruction concerning [Col. 0282D] love, because the perfection of divine love is found in mutual love.

Again he says: “God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him.” He said the same thing above; and see, he says it again, to commend it more fully and to add another effect of love. Above he said that love brought about the first coming of the Son of God into the world for the salvation of the world; here, through that same love, he announces the salvation of the faithful at the second coming, on the Day of Judgment.

“God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him.” The one who contains and the one who is contained dwell reciprocally in each other. You dwell in God, but so as to be contained; God dwells in you, but so as to hold you up lest you fall. How can the one whom God holds up fall? Not at all.

Again he says: “In this the love of God is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the Day of Judgment, because as he is, so also are we in this world.” [Col. 0283A] As though he said: By this sign it can be tested how much each person has advanced in love. Ask your heart, and it will answer you. Someone believes in the Day of Judgment, but because he is not perfect in love, begins to fear. If he were perfect, however, he would have confidence, and would thus desire that day rather than fear it. When someone turns to repentance, he begins to fear; but through progress in good conduct he learns not to fear but to desire the coming of the Day of Judgment. Hence it is said: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1).

Let it be said again more plainly: “In this the love of God is perfected with us,” that is, we show that we love God perfectly if we do not fear the coming of the Judge, since he who fears is not perfect in love; “so that we may have confidence on the Day of Judgment,” not fearing to appear before the Judge; “because as he is, so also are we in this world.” That is, we have confidence because we imitate the perfection of his love in the world, loving even enemies, just as he rains from heaven upon the righteous and the unrighteous.

Again he adds: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment” (Matt. 5). As though he said: Perfect love is understood by this: in such love, which does good even to enemies in imitation of divine love, there is no fear. As has now been explained, “as” is said not always of equality, but of a certain likeness—as when I say, “I have ears, and so does an image” [Col. 0283C]. If, therefore, we have been made in God’s image, why are we not as God is?

Fear prepares a place for love; but perfect love, which has confidence because of the merit of righteousness, casts out the fear of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). It also causes present tribulations not to be feared, because fear has punishment: it torments the conscience of sinners. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110): by this fear everyone beginning works of righteousness fears lest the strict Judge come and condemn him as insufficiently chastened. Perfect love makes perfect righteousness and has no reason to fear; rather, it desires to see its judgment.

It is one thing to fear God lest he send you into Gehenna; that fear, not yet pure, will cease. It is another thing to fear God lest he abandon you; that fear is pure, endures for ever and ever, and desires the coming of the Bridegroom, that is, Christ. But whoever fears is not perfect in love. Why? Because he does not love God as a son loves a most tender father, but fears him as a slave fears a most cruel master.

It follows: “Let us therefore love God, because he first loved us.” As though he said: Because the one who fears is not perfect, let us therefore love God, so that we may be perfect, because he first loved us without any necessity, in order to make friends out of enemies [Col. 0284A]. But because many say only in words, “I love God,” it is added: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar.” Whoever loves a brother necessarily loves God, because he loves love itself, by which he loves his brother. And God is love; and if he loves love—that is, God—he cannot hate the brother whom God loves and commands to be loved. Love enabled us to love him. Hence it is said: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15).

Again he says: “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” By this he is proved a liar: that is, he does not see God because he does not possess love; and therefore he does not possess love because he does not love his brother. If he possessed it, he would without doubt see God. Therefore, with the eye of the mind cleansed by love, let us strive to behold God’s unchangeable substance.

A different and contrary outcome occurs: at times flattery is gentle, and love is fierce. Therefore, lest anyone should dare say, “I can love God even if I do not love my brother,” he adds [Col. 0284B]: “And we have this commandment from God: that whoever loves God should love his brother also.” As though he said: How do you love him whose commandment you neglect? Whoever loves God should love his brother also; for if he does not love his brother, neither does he love God, whose children he hates. It follows:

“Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born from God. And everyone who loves him who begot [Col. 0284C] loves him who has been born from him.” Everyone who believes—that is, who lives as Christ commanded—is born from God. But if he believes otherwise, demons also believe (Jas. 2). Works done before faith are either nothing, or, even if they appear good, are empty, because they are done apart from Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14).

Truly, whoever loves God loves his brother also. For whoever loves God the Father loves God the Son, begotten from the Father; and whoever loves God the Son also loves God’s children, who are the members of that head. Therefore let us love the children of God, so that we may be able to love the Son of God, whose members they are; and, loving the Son whole—that is, together with his members—let us also love the Father. Love joins together Christ’s body so that there may be one Christ [Col. 0284D]. Likewise, whoever loves his brother loves himself; for with him he is one.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] An excessively scrupulous hand corrected *unus*, “one,” to *unum* at this point in the manuscript, perhaps thinking that the Gloss was speaking of *unum*, “one,” in the unity of the divine nature. But since it is discussing the mutual bond of friends, it makes no difference whether we read *unus* or *unum*. For the person whom I love is equally called either another self or the same as myself.]

Nor can one who loves Christ’s members fail to love Christ. Just as whoever loves the Son, who is the same as [Note: [Col. 0284D] That is, the same as the Father.] the Father, necessarily loves the Father also. “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born from God.” Truly, whoever loves God loves his brother also; and whoever loves him who begot loves him who was begotten, insofar as he was begotten from him.

And who is born from God? Namely, the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God. And who is the one who begot? God the Father. Therefore [Col. 0285A] whoever loves God, who begets in faith, loves the one begotten in faith. And, appropriately speaking of love, he mentions faith: for if anyone is so hard-hearted as to neglect loving a human being because he is human and shares the same exile, he should be urged at least to love that person because he is born from God and shares in the same grace.

But because many love their neighbours because of kinship or temporal advantage, he defines who is a true lover of the neighbour, when he adds: “By this we know that we love God’s children: when we love God and keep his commandments.” As though he said: He is rightly proved to love his neighbour who also loves God. And lest anyone deceive himself about love of God and say merely in words that he loves God, he adds: “And we keep his commandments.”

Again he adds:

“This is the love of God: that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not burdensome.” As though he said: This is why I join loving God with keeping his commandments, because otherwise there is no love. He does not love the king who hates his law; therefore, out of love for the king, his law must be fulfilled. “This,” he says, “is the love of God,” that is, by this it is proved that God’s love is in us: if we keep his commandments, which should be kept gladly. For his commandments are not burdensome in loving God’s children: that is, they do not drag one downward like a talent of lead; rather, the keeping of God’s commandments carries one upward and makes one exalted. And his commandments are not burdensome, because “God’s yoke is sweet and his burden light” [Col. 0285C] (Matt. 11). What are by their nature hard and harsh to human beings are made light by God’s love and hope of reward. If anyone says that they are burdensome, he accuses his own weakness, because what is light to the strong is burdensome to the weak.

And truly God’s commandments are not burdensome, because “everything born of God overcomes the world.” The one who loves God and neighbour is born from God; he so trains himself by God’s commandments that he brings them into action. Such a person overcomes the world and scorns the pleasures and adversities of the age, even the sufferings of the body itself. He seeks what is above, not what is upon the earth (Col. 3). And lest anyone trust in his own strength to be able to overcome the world, he adds: “And this is the victory that overcomes the world: our faith.” Namely, the faith that works through love and also seeks God’s help. Demonstratively, as though with a finger, he points to faith as confessing and persevering.

Again he says: “Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” He defines what faith overcomes the world: namely, faith in Christ. As though he said: Truly, the world is overcome through faith, because it is not overcome through anything else. Or, more plainly: Who overcomes the world—that is, who can despise the world—except the one who believes that Jesus is the Christ who was prophesied, and who joins works worthy of faith to that belief? And because faith alone and confession of Christ’s divinity do not suffice for salvation or for overcoming the world, he adds concerning his humanity: “This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ.” As though he said: He who was eternal came for salvation and remission of sins through [Col. 0286A] the water of baptism and the blood of his Passion. He not only deigned to be baptized for our cleansing and in order to consecrate for us the sacrament of baptism, but also gave his own blood for our redemption.

Again he says: “Not by water only, but by water and blood.” Behold what faith conquers: namely, that which believes Jesus Christ to be true man and true God. “And the Spirit is he who bears witness that Christ is truth.” As though he said: Although Christ suffered according to his humanity, nevertheless the Holy Spirit was seen above him when baptized, in the form of a dove (Matt. 3). Or “spirit,” that is, every spiritual teacher, bears witness to this: that Christ is truth, that is, the true Son of God, not a phantom; the true mediator and reconciler, [Col. 0286B] free from sin and sufficient to take away the sins of the world.

Again he adds, saying: “For there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit.” The Father gave testimony to his divinity when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (ibid.). The Son of God himself likewise gave testimony: when transfigured on the mountain, he displayed the power of his divinity and the appearance of eternal blessedness (Mark 9). The Holy Spirit too gave testimony, resting upon the baptized one in the form of a dove, or when he filled the hearts of believers at the invocation of Christ’s name. Thus it appears most plainly that Jesus is truth, that is, true God and true man, because we have certain testimony concerning each: concerning his divinity [Col. 0286C] through the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but concerning his humanity through the soul, water, and blood. “And these three are one.” As though he said: These three, testifying to the same thing, are one God.

“And there are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit,” that is, the human soul which he gave up in his Passion; “the water and the blood,” which flowed from his side (John 19). This could not have happened if he had not possessed the true nature of flesh. But before the Passion, his sweat becoming like drops of blood (Luke 22) showed the reality of his flesh; while the fact that water and blood flowed vigorously, contrary to nature, from the side of one already dead testifies that the Lord’s body would live more gloriously after death, and that his death would give us life. The fact that [Col. 0286D] his sweat flowed down to the ground like blood signified that by his blood he would wash the Church throughout the whole world.

Again he says: “If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater.” As though he said: If we receive human testimony—that is, since we have such certain testimonies, we ought to receive them—then the testimony of God is greater, that is, more worthy of acceptance; for we are accustomed to accept even the testimony of men, who can lie. Great is the testimony of the man David, who bears witness concerning the Son of God, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 119), and so forth. He also introduces the Son speaking of the Father when he says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). Great is the testimony of the forerunner, who says: “I baptize [Col. 0287A] you in water, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 3). But greater is the testimony of the Father, who visibly sent upon him the Spirit with whom he was always filled. As though he said: If you believe men who foretold his coming, you ought still more to believe God the Father, who testifies that Christ has come.

“For this is the testimony of God,” which is greater, because he has borne witness concerning his Son. As though he said: By this testimony I prove that God’s testimony is greater—that is, more worthy of acceptance—than human testimonies, because he has testified of his Son, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). It follows: “He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself.” Since the Father bears witness concerning the Son, let us believe in the Son; for [Col. 0287B] he who believes in the Son, and thus by good works advances toward that Son, has the testimony of God in himself. God, as it were, also testifies concerning him that he is a believer and will be among the number of God’s children, according to the Son’s own promise: “If anyone serves me, my Father who is in heaven will honour him” (John 12). Therefore, if you have God as the witness of your faith, how can human disgrace or persecution harm you? Hence it is said: “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8). Truly, one who believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself, because he understands the Father to be truthful in his testimony concerning the Son. But one who does not believe calls the Father a liar.

It follows: “He who does not believe the Son makes him a liar,” namely because he does not believe the testimony [Col. 0287C] which God has borne concerning his Son. “And this is the testimony: that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.” As though he plainly said: He who does not believe the Son when he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), makes a liar of him who says that the Son is not less than the Father. In what does he make him a liar? Namely in this: that he does not believe the testimony which God bore concerning his Son, saying: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17). And again in the Passion: “I have glorified,” he says, “and I will glorify again” (John 12). This is the testimony which God the Father bore concerning his Son. For he has also borne witness concerning us, his adopted children: that through his only Son [Col. 0287D] he has already given us eternal life in figure, but in the future in reality. “And this,” he says, “is in his Son,” that is, in faith and confession of his name and in reception of his sacraments; for no one comes to the Father except through him (John 14), nor is there any other name in which we must be saved (Acts 4).

And lest he seem to have said too little in saying that eternal life is in the Son, he adds that the Son himself is that life. For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself (John 5), and he gives his own eternal life, as he says: “He who has the Son of God in himself has eternal life; he who does not have the Son does not have life.” That is: he who does not have the Son by believing and imitating him does not have life—that is, he cannot be saved. It follows: “These things I write to you, that you may know that [Col. 0288A] you who believe in the name of the Son of God have eternal life.” As though he said: I write these things to you—that is, you ought to give faith to these words—so that you may know that you have eternal life, that is, may be assured of your future blessedness, you who believe in the name of the Son of God; lest you be deceived by the frauds of those who deny that Christ is the Son of God, for by the merit of faith you will have life.

“And this,” he says, “is the confidence which we have toward him: that whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us.” As though he said: From faith in Christ you ought not only to hope for heavenly goods in the future; in this life also there is confidence, because we shall obtain whatever we ask beneficially. As though he said: Whatever we ask, not according to our carnal desires; for “we do not know what we ought to pray for” [Col. 0288B] (Rom. 8), unless he himself shows us his will, he who understands our advantage better than we ourselves do. Let us therefore ask according to the will of him who said: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. 6); and he will hear us by bringing our petition to effect.

Alternatively: “What we ask according to his will”—or, perhaps, *that we ask what he wills*, or that we come to prayer as persons such as he desires us to be. If we desire our own salvation or that of our neighbour, let us not disagree with God’s will. But if our will departs from God’s will through ignorance, may God’s good will correct our foolish will, as happened to the apostle Paul. In many ways blessed John here impresses what he has previously set forth, so as to stir us more eagerly to prayer, saying: “And we know that [Col. 0288C] God hears us, and whatever we ask he will give us.” As though he said: He will not only hear us in the future, but we also know that he hears us daily; and because we are already heard, we are certain concerning the future.

Again he says: “We know that we have the petitions which we ask of him.” As though it were said more plainly: Because we know that we have from him the petitions we ask, we ask nothing contrary to him; we ask nothing except what he has taught us, what he has inspired in us; and if we err in anything, we immediately correct our errors. Here he speaks of daily and light sins, which, as they are difficult to avoid, so are easily healed. If you have sinned by word, thought, forgetfulness, [Col. 0288D] or ignorance, confess to a brother, as James teaches, and ask him to intercede for you; and if he in turn confesses to you, then you too should in turn intercede for him (James 5). Here the Lord’s Prayer, mutual confession, and a light penance suffice. But if the sin is grave, summon the presbyters of the Church and submit to correction upon their examination.

It follows: “He who knows his brother to be committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life will be given to the one sinning not unto death.” As though he said: He who knows through confession, or also in some other way, that his brother is committing a sin not unto death—that is, not criminally, or not until the end of his life—let him pray for him, and through his prayer life will be given him by God: to him, I say, who sins not unto death, that is, not until the end of his life. If we ask according to [Col. 0289A] God’s will, we obtain, as when we ask for a brother for whom prayer ought to be made. David sinned grievously; but because, born of God, he belonged to the fellowship of God’s elect, he did not sin unto death, but deserved pardon through repentance. As sin unto death separates a person from God, so death separates the soul from the body. He then expressly adds, saying: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.” Why? Because pardon for what is not corrected in this life is sought in vain after death. This may also be understood of every criminal sin. The Lord commands prayer for persecutors (Matt. 5). John says that one should not pray for certain persons, because among brothers there are sins more grave than the persecution of enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] This exposition, like all the rest, is taken from the *Glossa ordinaria*; but Augustine explains this passage more fully in Book I of *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 22.]

A brother’s sin is unto death when, [Col. 0289B] after knowledge of God has been given through Christ’s grace, someone attacks brotherhood and is stirred by the firebrands of envy against the grace by which he has been reconciled. There is sin not unto death if someone has not estranged himself from his brother in love, but, through some weakness of mind, has failed to render the duties of brotherhood. Hence Christ is read to have cried so mercifully from the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). For, not yet made sharers by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they had not entered into the fellowship of holy brotherhood. Thus Stephen also prays for those who had not received grace (Acts 7); Paul does not pray for Alexander because he was already a brother [Note: [Col. 0289D] Alexander was a brother, if he is the same man—as is believed—as the one whom the Apostle handed over to Satan with Hymenaeus (1 Tim. 1), and if he belonged to the number of those who suffered shipwreck concerning the faith.] and was attacking brotherhood. For those who had yielded through fear he prays, saying: “All deserted me; may it not be charged against them” (2 Tim. 4).

Again adding, he says: “All iniquity is sin, and there is sin unto death.” As though he said: Truly, prayer should be made for those sinning not unto death, because all are occupied with many sins and no one can be without sin (Job 14), since all iniquity is sin. But above other sins there is sin unto death, committed not from human frailty but from envy and hatred; and therefore it is not cleansed by the prayer of the righteous, since those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God (Gal. 5). As though it were plainly said: All iniquity is sin—that is, whatever departs from the rule of equity is counted among sins—but the least sins do not harm the righteous. Yet certain sins disagree so utterly with all righteousness that, unless corrected, they plunge a person into punishment.

It follows: “We know that he who is born of God does not sin; but the generation of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him.” As though he said: He who has God’s seed in himself cannot sin unto death; that is, he cannot at the same time practise righteousness and sin. But God’s generation preserves him: that is, the grace by which those who are called saints according to his purpose have been regenerated preserves him from committing sin unto [Col. 0290A] death; and if he should offend in anything through human frailty, it defends him so that he cannot be touched by the evil enemy. Those who persevere in God’s generation cannot sin or be touched by the evil enemy. Just as day and night cannot be mingled, so righteousness and iniquity, the evil one and God’s generation, cannot be combined. The evil one does touch some people, harming and afflicting them, but not for their evil. He who is born of God does not sin unto death; he who is not born sins.

Again he says: “We know that we are born of God, and the whole world lies in the evil one.” As though he said: We are born of God, that is, reborn in baptism; and the whole world lies in the evil one, that is, not only lovers of the world but also newly born children, who have no discernment of good and evil, belong through the first transgression to the devil’s kingdom unless God’s grace rescues them from darkness. Again he adds: “And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son.” As though he said: The Son of God came in the flesh only for our salvation, and he gave us who believe understanding, so that, by believing in the true Son of God, we may know the true God and, as members, may be in his true Son by loving him. Through him we shall be gods in God, living without end in the Living One, who has neither beginning nor end. “This is the true God and eternal life.” No one can attain eternal life without knowledge of divine grace; no one can know God without God’s grace, because [Col. 0290C] “no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11). The same Son reveals both the Father and himself: appearing visibly in the flesh, he opened to the world through the Gospel the hidden mysteries of divinity.

It follows: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.” As though he said: You who know the true God and await eternal life, keep yourselves from the teachings of heretics, who assume for themselves an appearance of holiness and who exchange the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible things through perverse doctrines. The service of idols is also avarice. For those who put the world before God are idolaters (Eph. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0290D] Book VIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 11.]

“There were,” says blessed Isidore, “certain brave men or founders of cities. When they died, those who loved them fashioned images, that they might have some consolation in contemplating their likenesses. But gradually, through demons’ persuasion, this error is said to have crept into and increased among later generations, so that those whom the former honoured merely for remembrance of their name their successors established as gods for themselves and worshipped. Thus the use of images arose when images or effigies were set up from longing for the dead, as though they had been received into heaven; in their place demons set themselves up on earth to be worshipped, [Col. 0291A] and persuaded the deceived and ruined to sacrifice to them.

“*Simulacra* [images] are so called from likeness, because by the hand of an artisan their faces are imitated in stone or another material, those in whose honour they are fashioned. Therefore they are called *simulacra*, either because they are similar or because they are feigned and fabricated; hence they are also false. And it should be noted that the Latin word exists among the Hebrews: among them an idol or image is called *Semel* [probably *Selum*]. The Jews say that Ishmael was the first to make an image from clay. The Gentiles, however, maintain that Prometheus first fashioned images of human beings from clay, and that from him arose the art of shaping images and statues. Hence poets also pretend that human beings were first made by him, figuratively, because of the effigies.

“Among the Greeks, however, Cecrops—under whom an olive first sprang up on the citadel, and the city of the Athenians received its name from Minerva—first of all called upon Jupiter, invented images, established altars, and sacrificed victims; things of this kind had never before been seen in Greece.”

Blessed John again admonishes his disciples, saying: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.” Although he has borne much testimony to their perfection, nevertheless it may be feared that some recent convert retained in his mind remnants of idolatrous superstition. Therefore, as stated above, those who place the world before God are idolaters.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] In the same place.]

“Idolatry is interpreted as the service or worship of idols. For Greek *latreia* (λατρεία) is called *servitus*, ‘service,’ in Latin. So far as true religion is concerned, it is owed only to the one and only God. Just as impious pride, whether of human beings or demons, commands or desires that it be rendered to itself, so the devout humility of angels, saints, and human beings refuses it when offered to itself, and indicates him to whom it is owed. An idol, moreover, is an image made and consecrated in human form, according to the meaning of the word; for Greek *eidos* (εἶδος) means ‘form,’ and from it, by diminution, the word *idolum* [idol] is derived.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, since those who place the world before God are idolaters, it is necessary, according to the counsel of most blessed John, that we despise the world—that is, the world’s desire—through the love of God; and that we place God before every creature in heaven and on earth [Col. 0291D] and before all carnal desires, so that we may not become idolaters but may deserve to be worthy servants of God. For by the word of his preaching he begot us for this purpose: that we may love him in all things and above all things as our most sweet Father; that we may cling to him with all our mind as to the highest good; and that, according to our strength, we may serve him as the Lord who provides and governs, because “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17).

For it is fitting that we love him above all things, because he first deigned to love us through his love. He loved us so greatly that he mercifully sent to us the Son of his love and [Col. 0292A] instructed us through him in heavenly disciplines; washed us from the flood of sin in baptism; redeemed us from the hand of the ancient enemy; adopted us as sons; opened heaven to us; granted us fellowship with the angels; and, what is far more blessed and happier, promised that we should behold himself in his glory. Therefore, since we have been born from him—that is, begotten by his word—it is fitting that we love him above all things and love our neighbours as ourselves, because we do not truly love God the Father if we hate our neighbour, who has the same Father with us.

Let us therefore love God with an undivided mind, and, according to our ability, provide good things for his children—that is, our neighbours. Let us serve almighty God with fear and reverence, and assist our neighbours with a full heart if need requires. Let us offer God the affection of pure devotion, and extend to our neighbours the affection of compassionate pity. Let our mind be humble and devout toward God, useful and kind toward our neighbours; let conscience always be pure in God’s sight and the hand generous toward our neighbours. In prayer let the mind contemplate God with its inward eyes, and through love have compassion on its neighbour in his needs; at the time of prayer let it rise devoutly in contemplation of the Creator, and at the time of need let it carefully share in the miseries of neighbours. But if the mind willingly desires earthly things outwardly, greedily acquires what it desires, and avariciously possesses what it has acquired, it will be unable either perfectly to contemplate God with inward eyes or to be useful in its neighbours’ needs; for, entangled in the desires of passing things, [Col. 0292C] it is hindered from every work of perfection. Hence blessed Job is read to have said:

> “The paths of their steps are entangled” (Job 6).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0292D] Book VII of the *Morals*, chapter 12.]:

“Everything that is wrapped up is folded back upon itself. There are some who, in the face of deceiving vices, deliberate as though with their whole intention to resist them; but when the moment of temptation comes upon them, they do not persist in the purpose of their deliberation. One person, puffed up by the perverse habit of pride, considers how great are the rewards of humility. He rises against himself and, as it were, lays aside the swelling of inflated arrogance; he promises to show himself humble under any insults whatever. But when suddenly the injury of a single word strikes him, he immediately returns to his accustomed exaltation, and is so carried away into swelling pride [Col. 0292D] that he no longer remembers the good of humility which he had desired.

“Another burns with avarice, panting to increase his possessions. Seeing that all things pass quickly away, he fixes his mind, which wanders through desires. He decides now to desire nothing, but only to possess under the rein of strict self-restraint what he has acquired. Yet when things pleasing to the eyes are suddenly presented, his mind at once pants in ambition; it cannot contain itself, seeks an opportunity to obtain them, and, forgetting the continence to which it had bound itself, agitates itself with the goads of thought through desire for acquisition.

“Another is defiled by the contagion of lust and held captive by long habit. He sees how great is the purity of chastity and recognizes it as shameful to be conquered by the flesh. Therefore he resolves to restrain the excesses of pleasures and prepares, as though with all his strength, to resist habit. But when an appearance is presented to his eyes, or recalled to memory, and he is shaken by sudden temptation, he is immediately scattered from his former preparation; and he who had raised against it the shield of resolution lies pierced by the dart of pleasure. Thus lust overcomes him unarmed, as though he had prepared no weapons of purpose against it.

“Another is kindled with the flames of anger and becomes unrestrained even to the point of inflicting insults on neighbours. But when no occasion of fury assails his mind, he considers how great is the virtue of gentleness and how lofty the excellence of patience, and he restrains himself patiently even against insults. But when some slight occasion of disturbance arises, he is suddenly inflamed to the marrow with insulting speech [Col. 0293B], so that not only does his promised patience fail to return to memory, but the mind does not recognize itself or the abusive words it utters. When it has fully satisfied its fury, it returns, as though after exertion, to tranquillity; and then it gathers itself again within the restraints of silence, when not patience but satisfaction of its own insolence puts a bridle on the tongue. Thus only late, after insults have been hurled, does it scarcely restrain itself, because racing horses, foaming from their course, are often checked not by the rider’s hand but by the boundary of the field.

“Therefore it is well said of the reprobate: ‘The paths of their steps are entangled’; for in deliberation they desire what is right, but always fold back into their customary evils and, stretched as it were beyond themselves, return to themselves by a circuit. They desire good things indeed, but never depart from evil. They wish to be humble, yet without contempt; content with their own possessions, yet without want; chaste, yet without mortification of the body; patient, yet without insults. And while they seek to attain virtues but flee the labours of virtue, what else do they do but fail to know the contests of war in the field while desiring to triumph from war in the cities? Yet the statement that their paths are entangled may also be understood in another way.

“Often some neglect to subdue certain vices to themselves. Since they do not rise up against these, the vices which they have already subdued rise up against them again. One person has already tamed his flesh from lust, [Col. 0293D] but has not yet restrained his mind from avarice. Since he remains in the world in order to practise avarice and does not withdraw from earthly affairs, when an occasion arises he falls even into the lust which he seemed already to have subdued. Another has overcome the heat of avarice but has not subjected the force of lust; as he prepares the price for satisfying lust, he also places his neck of heart beneath the yoke of avarice which he had long ago tamed. Another has laid low rebellious impatience but has not yet overcome vainglory. Since he entangles himself in worldly honours through it, pierced by the goads of disputes, he returns as a captive to impatience; and when [Col. 0294A] vainglory lifts his mind to defend itself, he endures as conquered the vice that he had overcome. Another has already subdued vainglory, but has not yet laid low impatience. When, through impatience, he threatens many things against those who resist him, ashamed not to carry out what he says, he is recalled beneath the yoke of vainglory; and, conquered by one vice, he suffers again what he rejoiced to have wholly conquered through another. Thus vices retain their fugitive by mutual assistance and, as it were, receive back under the right of mastery one already lost; they hand him over to one another as a captive.

“Therefore the paths of the perverse are entangled; for even if, after conquering one wickedness, they lift their foot, another remaining wickedness ensnares that foot even in the vice they conquered. But sometimes, with the paths of their steps entangled, one fault is not overcome and another is committed. Often the deceit of denial is joined to theft, and often the fault of deceit is increased by the guilt of perjury. Some vice is often committed with shameless presumption; and often—what makes every sin more serious—one is even proud of the vice committed. For although arrogance is usually born from virtue, sometimes a foolish mind exalts itself over wickedness it has committed. But when fault is added to fault, what else happens except that the steps of the perverse are bound by entangled paths and knotted chains? Hence Isaiah fittingly says of the perverse mind under the figure of Judaea: ‘It shall be a lair of dragons and a pasture of ostriches; demons shall meet onocentaurs, and the hairy one shall cry to the other’ (Isa. 34).”

Let us ask Isidore, teacher of the Spaniards, and hear together what he has said to us concerning the natures of these animals: [Col. 0294C]

“[Note: [Col. 0293D] Book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4.] The dragon,” he says, “is greater than all serpents, indeed than all living creatures upon the earth. It has a crest, a small mouth, and narrow tubes through which it draws breath and puts forth its tongue. It has its force not in its teeth but in its tail, and does harm more by its lash than by its teeth. It is called *struthio* [ostrich] by a Greek name because, although this animal appears to have feathers in the likeness of a bird, it is not raised high above the ground. It neglects to brood over its eggs; but once cast away, they are quickened merely by the warmth of dust.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] Book VIII, chapter 11.] They say that demons are called by the Greeks, as it were, *daimones* (δαίμονες), that is, ‘knowing’ and ‘skilled in matters.’ For they foresee many future things, and hence are accustomed to give certain answers, though deceptive ones. They possess knowledge of things beyond human weakness, partly through a subtler acuteness, partly through the experience of a very long life, and partly through angelic revelation by God’s command. They are vigorous by the nature of aerial bodies. Before transgression they indeed bore heavenly bodies; but after their fall they were changed into an aerial condition, and were permitted to occupy not the purer spaces of that air but these gloomy regions [the printed reading is *justa*, perhaps *ista*], which are like a prison to them until the time of judgment. These are the transgressing angels, of whom the devil is prince.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] Book XI, chapter 3.] The *onocentaur*, they say, is so called because one half is said to have the form of a human being and the other half that of an ass, as also the hippocentaurs, in whom the natures of horse and human being [Col. 0295A] are thought to have been joined. Their appearance gave the Centaurs their name: that is, a human being mixed with a horse. Some say that they were Thessalian horsemen, but assert that centaurs were invented because, as they rode about in war, horses and humans seemed to be one body. Further, the monocentaur is said to have received its name from bull and man, the sort of beast fabulously said to have been confined in the Labyrinth. Of it Ovid says:

> “The half-bovine man, and the half-human bull.”  
> (Ovid, *Ars Amatoria* 2.23)

[Note: [Col. 0295D] Book VIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 11.] “The hairy ones are called *Panitae* in Greek, *Incubi* in Latin, or *Invi* from entering indiscriminately among animals; hence they are also called *Incubi* from lying upon, that is, committing sexual violation. For they are often wanton toward women and have intercourse with them. The Gauls call these demons *Dusii*, who continually practise this uncleanness. The being commonly called an *incubo* is called by the Romans *Faunus Timerius* [perhaps *Ficarius*], to whom Horace says:

> Faunus, lover of the fleeing Nymphs,  
> pass gently through my boundaries  
> and sunny fields.  
> (Horace, *Odes* 3.18.1)

Therefore let Isaiah the prophet say of the perverse mind under the figure of Judaea: “It shall be a lair of dragons and a pasture of ostriches; demons shall meet onocentaurs, and the hairy one shall cry to the other” (Isa. 34).

[Note: [Col. 0296D] Gregory, cited above.] “For what is signified by dragons except malice? And what by the name of ostriches except hypocrisy? [Col. 0295C] The ostrich has the appearance of flying but not the use of flight, because hypocrisy presents to all who look upon it an image of holiness, but does not know how to maintain a holy life. Therefore in the perverse mind the dragon lies down and the ostrich grazes, because hidden malice is cunningly concealed and an appearance of goodness is placed before the eyes of beholders.

“What, however, are figured by the name of onocentaurs except the lustful and proud? In Greek speech *onos* (ὄνος) means ‘ass,’ and by the designation of the ass lust is signified, as the prophet testifies when he says: ‘Their flesh is as the flesh of asses’ (Ezek. 23). By the word ‘bull,’ however, the neck of pride is indicated, as is said by the Lord’s voice concerning the proud Jews through the Psalmist: [Col. 0295D] ‘Fat bulls have surrounded me’ (Ps. 21). Thus onocentaurs are those who, subjected to the vices of lust, raise their neck from that from which they ought to be humbled. Serving the pleasures of their flesh, having utterly put shame far away, they not only do not grieve that they have lost rectitude, but even rejoice in the work of shame. Demons meet onocentaurs because evil spirits zealously serve them as they wish, when they see them rejoicing in what they ought to mourn.

“It is openly added: ‘And the hairy one shall cry to the other.’ Who else are figured by the term ‘hairy ones’ except those whom the Greeks call *Panes* [printed: *Panas*], but the Latins *incubi*? Their form indeed begins with a human appearance [Col. 0296A] but ends in a beastly extremity. Thus by the name ‘hairy one’ the roughness of any sin is signified: even if it begins under what seems a covering of reason, it nevertheless always tends toward irrational impulses. It is as though a human being ends in a beast: beginning a fault under the guise of reason, he carries it on to an irrational result. Often the pleasure of eating serves gluttony, pretending to serve the necessity of nature; and when it expands the belly into gluttonous excess, it plunges the members into lust.

“But the hairy one cries to the other when a perpetrated wickedness summons wickedness still to be perpetrated; and, as though by some voice of kinship, a fault already committed invites the fault that is yet to be committed. For often, as we have said, gluttony says: ‘Unless you refresh your body with abundant food or nourishment, you will persist in no useful labour.’ And after it has inflamed the mind with fleshly desires, lust immediately makes its own suggestion in these words: ‘If God had not wished human beings to unite bodily, he would not have made the bodily members themselves suitable for the uses of intercourse.’ By suggesting this as though on rational grounds, it draws the mind into unrestrained lusts. Once detected, that mind immediately seeks the protection of deceit and denial, and does not reckon itself guilty if it preserves life by lying.

“Thus the hairy one cries to the other when, under some appearance of reasoning, a subsequent fault ensnares the perverse mind through the occasion of the preceding fault. And when the harsh and rough [Col. 0296C] sins [printed: *peccata*] press it down, the hairy ones, as if summoned, rule in it together in agreement. Thus the paths of its steps are always more grievously entangled, while fault binds the reprobate mind through fault.

“But amid these things it must be known that sometimes the eye of understanding is first dulled, and afterwards the captured mind wanders through vain desires, so that the blinded mind does not know where it is being led and willingly submits itself to the enticements of its flesh. At other times, however, the desires of the flesh first boil over, and after long practice of unlawful action they close the eye of the heart. For often the mind sees rightly, yet does not boldly rise up against what is perverse; and, though resisting, it is conquered, while, judging the very thing it does, it is overcome by the pleasure of its flesh. For that the eye of contemplation is commonly first lost [Col. 0296D], and afterwards the mind is wearied by the labours of this world, Samson, captured by the Philistines, bears witness: after he lost his eyes, he was assigned to the millstone (Judges 16). For evil spirits, once they have gouged out within the sharp sight of contemplation by the goads of temptations, send a person outside into the round of labours. However sin may arise, or from whatever occasions it may break forth, the paths of the reprobate are always tangled, so that, given over to depraved desires, they either desire no good things at all, or, though desiring them, do not direct toward them the free steps of the mind with a strong desire. For they either do not begin what is right, or, broken on the very journey, [Col. 0297A] do not reach it at all. Hence it often happens that, wearied, they abandon heavenly love, cast themselves down from the mind’s intention into pleasures of the flesh, think only of the things that pass away, and take no care for those that remain with them. Hence it is openly added: ‘They will walk in emptiness and perish.’ For those walk in emptiness who carry with them no fruit from their labour. One sweats to obtain honours; another burns with eagerness to multiply wealth; another pants to win praise. But because, when each dies, he leaves all these things here, he loses his labours in emptiness, because he brings nothing with him before the Judge. On the contrary, the Law rightly says: ‘You shall not appear empty before the presence of the Lord’ (Exod. 23). Whoever does not provide, by doing good, for the reward of the life to be gained appears empty before God. Thus the Psalmist says of the righteous: ‘They shall indeed come with exultation, carrying their sheaves’ (Ps. 125). For those come to the testing of judgment carrying sheaves who show, from themselves, righteous works by which they may merit eternal life.”

Cassiodorus: “Those coming to the judgment which will be common to all shall come with exultation; and this belongs only to the good, since none but the good come to joy.” Augustine: “They shall come carrying their sheaves,” that is, the fruit of the seed—namely, crowns of joys and exultation. Then will be the triumph of those rejoicing and taunting death, in which they had groaned. Therefore, whoever, as was said, while living in this world does not persist in good works loses [Col. 0297C] his labours in emptiness, because he takes nothing from good work with him before the eyes of God.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Gregory again.] “Thus it is again said by the Psalmist of each of the elect: ‘Who has not received his soul in vain’ (Ps. 23). For one receives one’s soul in vain who, thinking only of present things, pays no attention to what follows eternally. One receives one’s soul in vain who, neglecting its life, puts the care of the flesh before it. But the righteous do not receive their souls in vain, because with continual intention they refer to its benefit whatever they do bodily, so that, even when the work passes away, the cause of the work may not pass away—the cause which prepares rewards of life after life. But the reprobate neglect to care for these things, because assuredly [Col. 0297D], walking in emptiness, they flee the life they pursue and lose it when they find it. ‘Who has not received,’ he says, ‘his soul in vain’: that is, who has not assigned his soul to things impermanent and transitory, but, recognizing it as immortal, desired eternal things.”

Again, dearest brothers, after what has been said I urge you more carefully: store up with the utmost diligence in the treasury of your breast the words of the holy Fathers which you receive through the ear of the body, and strive to fulfil them by good works, so that, like good soil, you may be able to render a hundredfold fruit to the Creator. [Col. 0298A] Take the greatest care, therefore, to receive your souls—that is, lest by loving earthly things without restraint you lose them in this world; rather, by devoutly cleaving to spiritual pursuits, may you be able to find them unto eternal life. Therefore despise present goods with the whole intention of your mind, but desire eternal things with undivided devotion; and strive rather that before the presence of the eternal Judge you may deserve to be presented happily, not empty or naked, but filled with the fruits of good works and clothed with the incorruptible garments of innocence and of the other virtues—garments which you lost, indeed, in the transgression of the first parent. Let the mind, then, be full of love for God and neighbour, while the hand applies itself to religious work. Let the mind appear at the final examination filled with the fruits of devotion, [Col. 0298B] and let the hand offer sheaves of righteousness in good works.

Furthermore, attend diligently lest the delights of this world entangle the paths of your steps, hinder you as you press toward the eternal homeland, and make you strangers—God forbid!—to the fellowship of God’s elect. Beware also lest the dragon lie in the dwelling-place of your mind—that is, lest malice reign there, and, ceasing to be God’s habitation, it become the devil’s chamber; for the Holy Spirit undoubtedly withdraws far from that mind in which malice reigns. Thus Paul says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6).

Again, most beloved brothers, I urge you not to permit the ostrich—that is, the unclean bird—to feed in your mind: remove hypocrisy far [Col. 0298C] from yourselves, so that you may not display one thing inwardly and another outwardly before human eyes; rather, adorn with good morals the habit which you outwardly put forward in appearance. Truly the ostrich, that is, hypocrisy, devours the mind it possesses like a certain plague, because under an appearance of holiness it makes that mind empty of virtues. Let onocentaurs also be far from the mind of your holiness—that is, pride and lust—for where these two chief vices come together, no perfection of good work can be there. Take heed again lest demons encounter centaurs there: that is, lest they rejoice in the loss of your holiness, favour you toward unlawful action, and, urging unlawful things, move you to commit vices. [Col. 0298D] Take care also lest the shaggy ones dwell in your mind, which ought to be the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, and one cry to another: that is, lest sins be multiplied, sins arise from sin, and sins already committed invite those still to be committed. Rather, once the filth of vices has been expelled, let there be in it compunction of tears, diligence in prayers, emulation of virtues, compassion for neighbours, hatred of vices, the temple of God, an example of good works, contemplation of the Creator, and all heavenly virtues. May he grant this, who lives and reigns as perfect God in the Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0299]

EXPOSITION OF THE BOOK OF THE APOCALYPSE BY SAINT MARTIN, PRIEST OF LEÓN.

[Col. 0299A] Jeremiah the prophet, dearest brothers, among the other miseries of the human race which he laments with devout compassion, also mentions the hunger for spiritual bread, saying: “Little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4). For before Christ’s coming, Jews and Gentiles were little children and untrained in their knowledge of the divine dispensation, because they did not understand the mysteries of Christ and the Church. They sought bread, who desired to have knowledge of the divine will; but there was no one to break it, because there was no one to expound the mystical and hidden marriage of Christ and the Church. But after the Son of God was born through the womb of the undefiled Virgin, suffered, died, rose again, and ascended to the right hand of God the Father, he broke bread for the little children: that is, for Jews and Gentiles [Col. 0299B] he opened the seven seals of the sealed book, namely, he revealed the sacraments of hidden mysteries. Thus Jesus Christ himself, true God and true man, now standing in heaven, sent the Apocalypse through his most faithful servant John to the seven Churches, in order openly to make known to his servants his own and God the Father’s hidden dispensation concerning things which were, are, and will shortly be.

This Apocalypse—that is, revelation—is called prophecy among the other books of the New Testament; yet it is more excellent than other prophecies, because it announces mysteries concerning Christ and the Church which have for the most part been fulfilled. And as the Gospel expels the observances of the Law, so this prophecy sets aside the ancient prophecies which foresaw from afar things to come. To strengthen [Col. 0299C] this prophecy, moreover, the authority of sender, bearer, and recipient also comes to its aid. For God—that is, the whole holy Trinity—sent it. Of the Father it is said: “Sending through his angel” (Rev. 1). But near the end of this book the Son says: “I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify to you” (Rev. 22). And this also is written concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Lord God Almighty” (Rev. 4). It should therefore be known that when “Spirit” is placed without qualification, the whole Trinity is more commonly understood. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel to the Samaritan woman: “God is spirit, and therefore he must be worshipped in spirit and truth” (John 4). Although, therefore, the angel bore the person of the incarnate Word alone, the whole Trinity nevertheless acted in the angel. That John saw these things while in exile shows that Christ’s faith claims heaven for itself amid earthly afflictions. By the fact that blessed John, deprived of every human utterance and aid, [Col. 0299D] was divinely visited, it is also indicated to us that the more we withdraw from worldly tumult, [Col. 0300A] the more worthy we shall be judged of divine visitation.

It must therefore be considered in what manner John saw such things in vision. There are three kinds of vision. One is when we see heaven, earth, and similar things with bodily eyes. Another is when, sleeping or even awake, we see something by which we signify something else, as Pharaoh saw fat and lean cows (Gen. 41). The third kind is intellectual, when we conceive something in the mind, not through images, as David did in the Psalms. John, however, saw images and understood truth in them.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we wish briefly to write for you the obscurities of the words and the figures of the visions in the book of the Apocalypse, as they have been expounded by [Col. 0300B] the holy Fathers, so that in reading them you may understand more easily and, should it be necessary to suffer adversities for Christ’s name and love, may not flee. “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). God the Father, therefore, foreseeing the tribulations which the Church would suffer after it had been founded in faith by the apostles, determined together with the Son and Holy Spirit to reveal those tribulations and their rewards. Christ fittingly disclosed this revelation to John, who surpasses all others in the privilege of virginity and whose name is interpreted “the grace of God.” For John himself invites us to read, hear, and keep the words of this book, because if we do so we shall attain eternal blessedness. This book must therefore be read, because it is the Apocalypse of Jesus Christ—that is, the revelation not of just anyone, but of Jesus Christ—of which it is said:

## CHAPTER ONE

**VERSE 1.**—“The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known to his servants what must shortly come to pass.” In this place “God” is understood as the whole Trinity. It is as if he openly said: The Apocalypse, that is, the revelation, of Jesus Christ, which God the Father gave to him according to his humanity, to make known by word and example to his servants the things which must shortly come to pass—that is, in the present time. For all the time of this present life, compared with eternity, is like the tiniest moment of a single hour. Two things are contained in these words: [Col. 0300D] that things which are to be finished may quickly receive their end, and things which are to be begun may quickly take their beginning. It follows:

[Col. 0301A] **VERSE 2.**—“And he signified it, sending through his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever he saw.” It is as if he said: Jesus Christ, Son of God and of man, signified it by sending through his angel, who bore his person, to his servant John, a man most approved, who bore witness to the Word of God—that is, who testified to the words of Christ himself, both concerning his divinity and concerning his humanity—and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever he saw: namely, those things which he saw either bodily, such as Christ suffering, or by the mind alone, such as his being with the Father before all ages. The Son of God the Father is called the Word because through him God the Father is made known to humankind.

[Col. 0301B] **VERSE 3.**—“Blessed is he who reads and he who hears the words of this prophecy, and keeps those things which are written in it.” It is as if blessed John the Evangelist openly said: Because Christ sent me this revelation or prophecy, blessed will be the person who receives it from me, reads its words, and keeps what is written in it—that is, does not violate Christ’s faith, fears the threats, and hopes for the promises. Truly blessed, because the delay of labour will not be long, nor will the time of recompense be prolonged. For the time is near, namely, that of judgment or recompense.

**VERSE 4.**—“John, to the seven Churches which are in Asia.” As was said above, God the Father gave this Apocalypse to Christ, Christ to John, and John [Col. 0301C] to the seven Churches which are in Asia: principally, that is, those over which he had been appointed teacher; and, by likeness, to other Churches. Or he makes this revelation known to the universal Church through the seven Churches, because universality is represented by seven; or because it is illuminated by the sevenfold Spirit. “Grace,” he says, “and peace to you, from him who is, and who was, and who is to come.” Grace is called a freely given gift, not a reward rendered but pardon bestowed. “Grace to you and peace,” that is, remission of sins and rest from vices, from him—namely, Christ—formerly passible according to his humanity, who now is immutable, who was eternally, though born in time, and who will come such as he is, although he does not now appear. The Evangelist is silent about the person of the Father, because no one had understood wrongly concerning God the Creator; [Col. 0301D] therefore he sets forth the persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit, concerning whom all heresies arise in the Churches. It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“And from the seven spirits who are before his throne; and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.” “Spirit” often means the same as charity; hence remission of sins and other gifts, which belong to the whole Trinity, are attributed to the Spirit, so that [Note: [Col. 0301D] The manuscripts wrongly read: “so that we may not understand.”] we may understand that the Trinity works through love alone. Let it then be stated more plainly: “from the seven spirits,” that is, from the sevenfold Spirit, who is one in nature [Col. 0302A] and manifold in the distribution of graces; or from spiritual men enlightened by the Holy Spirit, who are before his throne, in whom God sits as an example or for protection. Thrones are angels and holy men, in whom God now judges so that he may not judge in the future. “And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness”: namely, he who did not deny that he was God even on account of impending death; or he will be witness of our works on the day of judgment, when he will say to the righteous: “You saw me hungry and gave me food; come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). “The firstborn of the dead,” because he rose from the dead now incapable of suffering; or the first of those who mortify themselves, because he committed no sin. “And ruler of the kings of the earth,” that is, of earthly [Col. 0302B] powers, able to remove them and permitting them to rage for the benefit of his own. He is rightly called the firstborn of the dead, because he rose from the dead in such a way as never again to die. It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father—to him be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.” It is as if he openly said: Truly, he who loved us will give grace and peace, because through love alone he washed us from original or actual sins—of Adam, [Note: [Col. 0301D] It is absent from the Gloss; what we enclose in parentheses [Col. 0302D] seems to be superfluous.] or even our own—in the blood not of calf or ram, as in the old Law, but in his own blood. He made us a kingdom and priests: that is, able to resist vices and to offer ourselves to God the Father for ourselves and our brothers [Col. 0302C], and to himself and to the Holy Spirit. To him, from our priesthood, be glory, and from our kingdom dominion, for ages of ages. Amen.

**VERSE 7.**—And this dominion will not delay, “for behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, and those who pierced him.” It is as if he said: Every eye, good and evil alike, will see him, including also the Jews who pierced him on the cross, so that they may be tortured the more. It is as if he openly says to the Churches: You ought indeed to glorify him, because he is the one who will come to reward with clouds—that is, with the saints who were clouds, raining upon others and working miracles; or, as he ascended in a cloud, he will come in a cloud, by which the clemency of God is understood. For to the good it is refreshment [Col. 0302D] and illumination, but to the evil terror and blinding; this was signified by the cloud through which the children of Israel were led out of Egypt. It follows: “And all the tribes of the earth shall mourn themselves over him. Even so. Amen.” It is as if he said: They will mourn themselves and dash themselves against him, unable to resist his rule, like a stone and earthenware vessels. Or, “they will mourn themselves,” that is, they will grieve as they look upon those who were founded upon him, because they will grieve not so much at the torment itself as because they will be excluded from such fellowship and from the Lord himself. “All the tribes of the earth,” he says: that is, all earthly persons. This is to be confirmed in every tongue: “Even so. Amen.” It is as if [Col. 0303A] he said: They will not doubtfully mourn themselves over him in judgment, but “even so. Amen,” that is, truly. It is as if he openly said: This can well be so, because he who is God and Lord says this:

**VERSE 8.**—“I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.” It is as if he said: I am Alpha—that is, the beginning, before which there is none, or from which all things began—and the end, after which there is none, or in which all things will be completed. No letter precedes Alpha, for it is the first of all letters. So also is the Son of God. He himself answered the Jews who questioned him that he was the beginning (John 8). He is also the last, because he himself undertook the final judgment. Here it is plainly shown that the angel who showed John these things bore in himself the person of God. “I am,” he says, “Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty”—namely, to judge the living and the dead. It follows:

**VERSE 9.**—“Behold, I John, your brother and fellow-partaker in tribulation, kingdom, and patience in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ.” Having completed the greeting, he proceeds to the narrative, setting forth four things—namely, person, place, cause, and the time of the place—which serve to confirm the revelation itself. It is as if he openly said: I, John, am your brother in the unity of faith and a fellow-partaker in tribulation, because I was scourged, put into a vessel, and separated from people; I am also to be a fellow-partaker in the kingdom of God and in patience in Jesus, that is, for the sake of the patience held in imitation of Jesus. I was on the island called Patmos, that is, a strait [OCR: *fretu* for *fretum*]. Or: in tribulation, in which heavenly things are more fully disclosed to believers, because of the word of God and the testimony rendered to divinity and humanity. Blessed be almighty God, who opened heaven to his most approved servant John, when earth was denied him, and revealed secrets to him for the instruction of the whole Church. For the more holy people are afflicted for Christ in this present life, the more heavenly secrets are disclosed to them. Hence it appears that punishment does not make a martyr, but righteousness does. Thus the Psalmist says: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy people” [Col. 0303D] (Ps. 42). “I was,” he says, “on the island called Patmos.” The Church is compared to an island because, just as an island is battered by storms of the sea, so the Church is afflicted by persecutions of the wicked. He adds again, saying:

**VERSE 10.**—“I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.” He has set forth four things to confirm the revelation: person, place, cause, and the time of the place. He indicated the person when he says, “I John, your brother”; the place when he says, “I was on the island of Patmos”; the cause when he says, “Because of the word of God”; and the time when he adds, “I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet saying: ‘What you see, write in a book.’” It is as if he said: I was in the Spirit, that is, in an ecstasy of mind, on the Lord’s [Col. 0304A] day—that is, established in hope of resurrection through Christ’s resurrection—and I heard behind me, that is, in a clear knowledge of the resurrection, I recognized a loud voice, that is, a disclosure, because it concerned future things or great mysteries; “like a trumpet,” because [OCR: *qua*] one is stirred to spiritual battle by it. Behold, a bodily image teaching that Christian soldiers must be exhorted to spiritual warfare, in which patience is necessary. Here it is plainly shown that blessed John saw this vision not bodily but in the Spirit. Yet he did not see it in sleep; rather, he was caught up in ecstasy, as Ezekiel was, and his mind cleaved to the Spirit of eternity. “I heard,” he says, “behind me a loud voice.” He heard behind himself because, when drawn out from the tumults of present life and stretching the force of contemplation toward things before him, he was instructed to look back at others; or he heard behind himself because he understood that this same thing had been foretold by the Law and the prophets. The character of events is customarily indicated by time: Abraham, fervent in faith, saw the angels at noon (Gen. 18); Lot, at the destruction of Sodom, in the evening (Gen. 19); Adam, after noon (Gen. 3); Solomon, who would not preserve wisdom, received it at night (3 Kings 3). Whether he saw this vision at once and in a single gaze, or over different times on that Lord’s day, the angel could have imparted either to him. It follows:

**VERSE 11.**—“What you see, write in a book, and send it to the seven Churches which are in Asia: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Sardis, Thyatira, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.” It is as if he openly said: What you see—that is, what you will see—write in a book, that is, store it in your mind. Or literally: Do not hide the talent in a napkin, but send it to the seven Churches. Ephesus was the metropolitan see of all Asia, over which John presided. Ephesus, therefore, is interpreted “will” or “counsel”; Smyrna, “their song”; Pergamum, “division of horns”; Thyatira, “illuminated” or “living sacrifice”; Sardis, “beginning of beauty”; Philadelphia, “love of a brother,” or “saving an inheritance”; Laodicea, “a people beloved by the Lord.” A common admonition is given to blessed John, directing him generally to send to the Churches of Asia, because all other Churches are to be understood through them. Why then, if the Church is one, does John write to seven, except that the one catholic Church, full of the sevenfold Spirit, may be indicated? Thus we know Solomon said: “Wisdom,” that is, the Son of God, “built herself a house; she cut out seven pillars” (Prov. 9). Yet these seven are undoubtedly one, as the Apostle says: “The Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Tim. 3). It follows:

**VERSE 12.**—“And I turned to see the voice which was speaking with me.” It is as if he said: Having heard that voice, I turned away from ignorance in order to see—that is, understand—the voice of the angel bearing Christ’s person under the image of a trumpet, which spoke with me because it did not differ from my will. God speaks to the saints in the heart without sound of voice; but they speak by forming words with the tongue of flesh. Adding again, he says: “And having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands” [Col. 0305A]. It is as if he said: Because I turned from carnal understanding, I saw—that is, recognized—why the Church is comprehended under this number seven and under the bodily figure of golden lampstands. “I saw,” he says, “seven golden lampstands”: that is, Churches burning and illuminated with the wisdom of the divine Word. As gold, tested by fire and extended by blows, becomes a lampstand, so the Church, purified by tribulations and stretched in long-suffering by the blows of temptations, is perfected. It follows:

**VERSE 13.**—“And in the midst of the seven golden lampstands, one like a son of man, clothed with a garment reaching to the feet and girded at the breasts with a golden belt.” It is as if he plainly said: I saw in the midst of the seven golden lampstands—that is, in the midst of the Church—one like a son of man: namely, the angel in Christ’s person, who is as though no longer a son of man but “like” one, because he no longer dies; or like a son of man because he appeared not in sinful flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh. “Clothed,” he says, “with a garment reaching to the feet,” that is, with the priestly garment—namely, flesh—in which he offered himself and daily offers himself, presenting himself to God the Father. Or the garment reaching to the feet is the Church with which God is clothed; it is ankle-length because it extends to the end of the world. “Girded at the breasts,” because he, the head of the whole Church, first showed in himself what he now requires from his own. “Girded with a golden belt,” that is, with the girdle of charity, because he ministers to his saints in love. Thus he says of himself in the Gospel: “He will pass by and minister to them” (Luke 12), namely, after judgment he will prepare—that is, appoint—for [Col. 0305C] them eternal dwelling places. Daniel saw him girded at the loins in the Old Testament, because there carnal deeds were restrained (Dan. 10); John, at the breasts, because in the New Testament even thoughts are judged. It follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“But his head and hair were white as white wool and as snow.” It is as if he said: Christ’s head was white, in whom are all things necessary for the governance of the Church; and his hair was white with the whiteness of righteousness: namely, holy persons, imitators of his innocence and simplicity, made thin by disciplines and cleaving to that head. It was “as white wool,” that is, a garment against cold, namely, against vices; and “as snow,” namely, whiter than every creature, by which the brightness of immortality is indicated. Thus the Lord expressed on Mount Tabor before the disciples the brightness of the future resurrection by snowy whiteness (Matt. 17). [Col. 0305D] The saints also have wool’s whiteness because they imitate the simplicity and innocence of their head, who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). This wool, that is, true innocence, belongs to him of whom Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before the one shearing him he shall be silent” (Isa. 53), etc. Adding again, he says: “And his eyes were like a flame of fire”: namely, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which belong to Christ who possesses and gives them to believers, and also to the Church which receives them; they illuminate and make people burn in God’s love. Or Christ’s eyes are spiritual people in the Church, of whom [Col. 0306A] Solomon, speaking in the voice of the bride—that is, the same holy Church—says in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like doves beside streams of water” (Song 5). Or the eyes are divine commandments shown under such a bodily figure.

**VERSE 15.**—“And his feet were like bronze, as though glowing in a furnace.” It is as if he openly said: His feet, that is, the final believers who will be found near the end of the world, in the times of Antichrist, tested as if by many beatings because of the greatness of their sufferings and various tribulations, will not retain the oldness of the old human being, but through Christ will be transformed into a better colour—that is, into the newness of spiritual life—like bronze, which is seen more brightly the more it is burned and hammered. The Lord’s feet sometimes signify the stability of eternity; sometimes his humanity, through which knowledge of divinity came to us; sometimes preachers, of whom it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace and proclaim good things” (Isa. 52). As Antichrist will be more cruel than all persecutors, so the saints of that time, we believe, will be stronger than all preceding martyrs. In another translation it reads: “His feet like the bronze of Lebanon,” by which it is shown that in the region where the Lord was crucified the tribulation of the faithful under Antichrist will be especially powerful. Adding again, he says: “And his voice was like the voice of many waters.” Above, the angel’s voice was compared to a trumpet; now it is compared to many waters, because what at first few preachers proclaimed [Col. 0306C], the whole world afterwards cries out.

**VERSE 16.**—“And he had seven stars in his right hand.” It is as if he said: Under another figure he had in his right hand—that is, in his predestination or power—seven stars: namely, the prelates of the Churches, who shine upon the faithful sailing in this sea. Above he set forth lampstands without lights; here he sets forth stars, thereby indicating that some have the office of preaching, while others have knowledge alone. The stars are bishops, who ought to shine for others in word and example of life. Even if they sin, they are still called stars, according to what they were appointed to be; he has them in his right hand, that is, among the greater gifts signified by the right hand. “And from his mouth,” [Col. 0306D] he says, “went a sharp two-edged sword.” It is as if he said: From his mouth—that is, from his preachers, through whom God reveals his secrets—went a sharp sword with two edges: namely, preaching, which cuts off both carnal works in the Old Testament and sinful desires in the New. “And his face,” he says, “was as the sun shines in its strength.” It is as if he openly said: His face—that is, the holy Church after the day of judgment, seeing him face to face (1 Cor. 13)—will shine through the power of the same Jesus Christ, her bridegroom, like the sun in its strength: that is, like Christ himself, because she is his body. Thus the Apostle says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3). And the true sun of righteousness himself says: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. [Col. 0307A] 13). “His face was as the sun shines in its strength,” that is, at midday without clouds, or when, after judgment, it shall be fixed eternally. Thus Isidore, teacher of the Spains, says: “This material sun which we see will not suffer setting after the day of judgment, lest the ungodly enjoy the brightness of its light.” The Lord showed this brightness of the future resurrection on the mountain before three disciples, when his face shone like the sun (Matt. 9). “For he shone,” says blessed Hilary, “a hundred times as brightly; but the Evangelist had no more splendid creature with which he could compare that brightness, and therefore says that his face shone like the sun.
