And such as the Lord then appeared, such indeed will he come to judgment, except that he will show the marks of the nails and lance.” It follows:

**VERSE 17.**—“And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead.” It is as if he said: I fell at his feet—that is, I cast away concern for humanity, namely, temporal matters, after the likeness of the final believers. “I fell,” he says, “at his feet”: that is, I humbled myself so as to be one of his feet, reckoning myself to have been dead in understanding. John falls at the feet of the angel bearing Christ’s person when the holy Church imitates the footsteps of Christ’s passion. It falls at his feet when, considering its Redeemer dead, it immediately dies to the world and humbly prostrates itself in order to imitate his footsteps. “And he placed,” he says, “his right hand upon me, saying: ‘Do not fear.’” It is as if he said: Because I fell [Col. 0307C] at his feet as though dead, he therefore placed his right hand—that is, his help, namely, the strengthening Spirit, or his favour or power through a preacher or through the Scriptures—upon me, that is, above the powers of humanity. It should be noted that John, in this prophecy, bears the person of the Church.

VERS. 18. — “Do not be afraid,” he says, and adds: “I am the First and the Last, and the Living One; I was dead, and behold, I am living for ages of ages, and I have the keys of death and hell.” As though he were plainly saying to the whole Church: Since you have risen from sins and vices, as I did, do not fear to suffer tribulation for me; for I, who had no need on my own account [Col. 0307D]—being the First and the Last—nevertheless died for your sake. As though he said: I am the First according to divinity, and the Last, “as a worm and not a man”; and I died for your salvation, and behold, I live eternally for ages of ages. Therefore do not be frightened to suffer for me, because it is manifest that I shall not die again. For the victim is both sacrificed and alive, because the saints, although for love of Christ they put themselves to death with their vices and lusts, nevertheless do not die utterly. “And I have,” he says, “the keys of death and hell.” As though he said: Therefore do not fear, because I have the keys of death and hell, and because wicked people can do you no harm unless permitted. Nor shall I allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, because I have the keys—that is, power over [Col. 0308A] the devil and over his members. The devil is death, because he is the cause of death; his servants are hell, in whom he has a place. Here it appears most plainly that the angel who appeared to blessed John bore the figure of Christ. For these words suit no one but Christ, who was born, suffered, was buried, and rose again.

VERS. 19. — “Write therefore, O John, what you have seen, and what is, and what must shortly come to pass after these things.” As though he plainly said: Write what you have seen, such as the Passion and Resurrection; and what is, namely present tribulations and the present help of God; and what must shortly come to pass after these things, namely in the last faithful, by whose example these persons ought greatly to be encouraged. Again he adds:

[Col. 0308B] VERS. 20. — “The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands.” A mystery is where one thing is seen and another understood, as in the Lord’s body, where bread is seen but the true flesh is present. Hence the priests themselves say: “The sacraments which we have received, O Lord,” etc. As though he said more plainly: O John, write for the faithful those things which you saw, but conceal from heretics those things which I show you under a sacrament. “The seven stars are the angels of the seven Churches.” As though he said: By the seven stars are signified all rulers of all Churches; “and the seven lampstands are the seven Churches.” By the seven lampstands are understood those who possess knowledge of preaching but do not possess office, because they are not prelates. [Col. 0308C] He discloses the allegory in part, in order to teach that it must everywhere be sought out.

## CHAPTER II

He begins the particular admonitions, each of which may be universal according to the different members of any Church, saying:

VERS. 1. — “Write to the angel of the Church of Ephesus.” As though he plainly said: Although I said, “Send to the seven Churches,” nevertheless write first to this one in particular. Therefore he writes to the angel—that is, the bishop—of the Church of Ephesus, from whose hand he requires the sins of those subject to him, and without whose consent he does not presume to judge those subject to him. Ephesus is interpreted “will,” or “counsel,” or “a deep fall.” Therefore Ephesus, according to the part of those who persevere well, is interpreted “will,” [Col. 0308D] whose works delight God; he places these first, so that through their example those who have fallen may be corrected. According to the latter, Ephesus is interpreted “counsel,” that is, needing counsel. It follows: “These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.” As though he said more plainly: He says these things whose words must not be despised, and who holds the seven stars—that is, all the Church’s prelates—in his right hand so that they may not fall; who walks, as one distributing gifts, or as one not yet at rest, in the midst of the seven lampstands, providing for all and assisting all. “Who has,” he says, “the seven stars in his right hand.” It should be noted that in this right hand both good and evil persons are contained. The good are restrained, lest they either exceed the measure of received [Col. 0309A] virtue through vain glory or plunge into the enticements of vices; the evil are restrained by the power of this right hand, lest they be able to do as much as they wish. Yet, like servants under the Lord’s authority, they may strike his children with scourges in due measure. He walks in the midst of the seven lampstands because he moves among the elect and the reprobate by the word of exhortation until he finds one in whom, through works of virtue, he may make his dwelling. The Lord walks in the midst of the lampstands—that is, among his elect—when he pours into them the gifts of his grace. He sits when he judges each person’s merits. But what does he who holds the seven stars in his right hand say to the angel of the Church of Ephesus?

VERS. 2. — “I know,” he says, “your works, and labor, and [Col. 0309B] patience, and that you cannot endure evil people; and you tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them liars.” As though he said: I know—that is, I approve and choose—your works; and your labor, that is, tribulation; and your patience, because you do not complain of the delayed reward; and because you cannot endure—that is, tolerate—evil people without correcting them or expelling them from the Church. And you tested them—that is, you examined their teaching—who call themselves apostles, that is, persons sent by God, but are not, in order to deceive more easily; and you found them liars by their wicked life and perverse preaching. “You tested them,” he says, to determine whether they were true or false; or, wishing gradually to recall them from their error. In the time of blessed John false apostles arose—that is, heretics: Marcion, namely, Ebion, [Col. 0309C] Cerinthus, and many others in Asia—wishing to corrupt the right faith and preaching Christ as less than the Father. These indeed were false apostles. Again he adds, saying:

VERS. 3. — “And you have patience and endured for my name’s sake, and have not failed.” As though he plainly said: You have patience and endured the evils which these false apostles, already convicted by earthly arguments, inflicted upon you; and you did this not for human praise but for the glorification of my name, and you did not fail, but persevered in the true teaching. Again he continues:

VERS. 4. — “But I have a few things against you, because you have forsaken your first love.” He notes that [Col. 0309D] human failings would indeed have been opposed to the crown, unless God’s help had gone before this same bishop. As though he said: I rebuke you for avarice, because you have abandoned your first love. Perhaps the bishop, wearied by the vices of his subjects, abandoned his first love in his own person; or his subjects did so through love of earthly things. The chief and first love is for a person to give himself to God; the second, his possessions. Or he abandoned the first love which he first possessed in preaching. In the good works mentioned above there was the will of God; but in those which follow, because they require correction, counsel is effective. There he said, “I know your works,” that is, “I praise them”; here he says, “I have against you,” that is, “I see in you certain things needing counsel,” that is, correction—things which are against [Col. 0310A] you, that is, contrary to your salvation, or which make me turn away from you. Yet do not despair because of the severity of the correction, because these things are few and therefore need an easy amendment. It follows:

VERS. 5. — “Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works.” As though he plainly said: Since, therefore, what you do is against you, remember from where—that is, from the fellowship of the faithful, or from what grace—you have fallen; and repent, that is, bear worthy fruits of repentance, so that you may recover my grace, because you abandoned me and took up earthly love, like an adulterous woman. “Remember,” he says, “from where you have fallen”: that is, from how great a virtue or from friendship with me. “And do the first works”: that is, return to love for your former husband, namely me. “But if not, I will come [Col. 0310B] to you quickly, and I will move your lampstand from its place unless you repent.” As though he plainly said: If you do not do the first works, I shall come quickly to your harm, namely to destroy soul and body; and I shall move your lampstand from its place, that is, take away the virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit, through whom lampstands are established, because another will receive your episcopal office, or the reward which you expected from it. But if you repent, you can be saved. Although Peter denied Christ, because he repented he did not lose his apostolic rank. “Will not one who falls add [something], so as to rise again?” (Ps. XL).

VERS. 6. — “But this you have: you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.” As though he said: Although this is against you, nevertheless do not despair, because [Col. 0310C] you have this good thing: namely, that you hate the practices of the Nicolaitans—the common use of women and the eating of things sacrificed to idols—which I also hate; and you hate them because you have learned that I hate them. Nicholas was one of the seven deacons who were chosen and ordained by the apostles; but while the others remained in the faith and holy ministry, he withdrew from their faith and teaching. Nicholas is interpreted “foolish people,” that is, all false persons from whatever law. Therefore Nicholas is the foolish people—that is, Gentiles ignorant of God, who use wives publicly and eat things sacrificed to idols. Heretics too are foolish before God: the error of idolatrous worship is imputed to them, and they commit fornication by serving the uncleanness of the flesh. [Col. 0310D] The Jews also are foolish; likewise false Christians, who, devoted to lusts, worship the world.

VERS. 7. — “He who has an ear,” he says, “let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches: To the one who conquers I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” As though he plainly said: What I say to one, I say to all. I forbid avarice not only to the Ephesian bishop but also to the bishops of the other Churches. As though he said: Let the one who has an ear—that is, spiritual understanding—hear what the Spirit, namely the holy Trinity, because “God is Spirit” (John IV), says to the Churches: namely, that they should hate avarice, not only in giving but also in advising and preaching. As though he said: Truly, everyone ought to hate avarice and the other vices, because to the one who conquers—that is, perseveres in this—[Col. 0311A] I will give to eat of the tree of life. Why must one hear what the Spirit says to the Churches? Because, for the conqueror—that is, the persevering one—Christ is the tree, strength, and shelter, giving fruit, namely his body and blood here and especially in the future. As though he plainly said: To the one who perseveres in love of God and neighbor, I will give to eat of the tree of life, that is, of my body, which is in paradise—that is, in the garden of delights, namely in the Church of my God, according to my humanity. The tree of life is the wisdom of God the Father, of which it is said: “It is a tree of life to those who lay hold of it, and blessed is the one who holds it” (Prov. III). It follows:

VERS. 8. — “And write to the angel of the Church of Smyrna.” Smyrna is interpreted “song,” or “as though myrrh.” [Col. 0311B] As though he plainly said: Make this known also to the other Churches, who dwell and persevere in the song of Moses, or in the songs of the other holy Fathers, or in mortification of the flesh.

VERS. 9. — “These things says the First and the Last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and your poverty—but you are rich—and you are blasphemed by those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.” As though he said: Do not fail in tribulations, because I, so great—the First, existing before all things, through whom all things subsist; and the Last, through whom all things shall be brought to completion—suffered death for your sake and rose from it; and you too ought to await and suffer it for me. And I was dead [Col. 0311C] for you, through whom you will live, because I live. He describes Christ in such a way as can console those upon whom tribulations are inflicted. “I know,” he says, “your tribulation,” because “blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V), “and your poverty,” because “blessed are the poor in spirit” (ibid.); “but you are rich” in soul, namely in the hope of reward; “and you are blasphemed by those who say that they are Jews,” that is, confessors, “and are not,” because, if they were children of Abraham, they would do the works of Abraham (John VIII), “but are the synagogue of Satan,” that is, the assembly of the adversary. As though he said: When you are praised by me, you need not care about the blasphemy of blasphemers. No plague is more effective than an enemy within one’s own household. Misery is heaped upon the afflicted if they are defamed by their adversaries. [Col. 0311D] Again he adds, saying:

VERS. 10. — “Fear none of the things which you are about to suffer.” Having first given praise, he adds a warning. As though he said: You will still suffer many things; but fear none of them, because they can kill only the body. Again he continues: “Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested; and you will have tribulation for ten days.” As though he plainly said: Fear none of these things, because even if in the present time the devil, through his members—such as Nero, Domitian, and the other persecutors—is about to cast some of you into prison, nevertheless he will not cast all of you, but only some of you, so that you may be tested, that is, proved; or that you may be held in contempt by the devil and his members. For prison is put for every tribulation. [Col. 0312A] Or, he will cast some of you into the prison of vices, that is, into the pleasure of the flesh; and you will have tribulation for ten days, that is, for the time of warfare. For God, sending his servants to battles, arms them with the Decalogue. Or “ten days” means the whole time in which, through seven days, the Church fights against the three principal vices—namely avarice, vain glory, and covetousness. Or, “for ten days you will have tribulation” on account of the love expressed in the ten commandments. Or throughout this whole life, which is considered through the five zones of heaven and the five zones of earth, you will have tribulation; or through the five senses of men and the five senses of women. Or the ten days signify the ten emperors who were between Nero and Diocletian and inflicted many torments upon Christians.

[Col. 0312B] Thus the first persecution of Christians was carried out by Nero; the second by Domitian; the third by Trajan; the fourth by Antoninus; the fifth by Severus; the sixth by Maximian [Maximinus]; the seventh by Decius; the eighth by Aurelian; the ninth by Valerian; and the tenth by Diocletian and Maximian, his colleagues. Through these ten kings the Church suffered from Christ’s Ascension until the Council of Nicaea—that is, until the emperor Constantine—for two hundred and fifty years. Therefore the holy Church had tribulation for ten days, namely in the aforesaid periods of the ten kings. It follows: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” As though he said: Although the enemies of truth bring adversity upon you, nevertheless be faithful—that is, persevering in good works with right [Col. 0312C] faith—and I will give you the crown of life, namely the prize of eternal reward.

VERS. 11. — “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches: The one who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death, which is in Gehenna.” The first death of the soul is in sins; the second is in punishments. The first is also the death of the body, when the soul is separated from it; the second is when it is condemned at judgment. Again he adds, saying:

VERS. 12. — “And write to the angel of the Church of Pergamum.” Pergamum is interpreted “division of horns.” As though he said: Write to the angel of the Church of Pergamum, that is, to one discerning between the defenders of the Church and heretics.

[Col. 0312D] VERS. 13. — “These things says he who has the sharp two-edged sword: I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast my name and have not denied my faith. And in the days of Antipas, my faithful witness, who was slain among you, where Satan dwells.” As though he plainly said: These things says he whose words must not be neglected, who has the sword—that is, the divine Scripture, sharp on both sides, cutting off vices through love of God and neighbor. By these words he requires that these persons should have this degree of discernment in choosing the good and rejecting the evil: that the horns of sinners may be broken and the horns of the righteous exalted (Ps. LXXIV). “I know,” he says, “where you dwell,” namely, in the midst of a perverse nation, where Satan’s throne is. As though he said: I praise this, namely that among evil people you are good; and because against disputants you hold [Col. 0313A] my name—namely, that I am the Son of God—and the name of Christianity; or because what you preach in word you fulfill in deed. Or, “you hold my name,” that is, you worship with whole faith, even in the time of tribulation, and you have not denied my faith for any tribulation. And you did this in those days in which Antipas, my faithful witness, was among you and was slain—“I grieve,” as it were, “because they killed him”—where Satan dwells. As though he said more plainly to the bishop of the Church of Pergamum: You too were my faithful witness, testifying that I am the Son of God and equal to him, in those days in which Antipas was slain.

VERS. 14. — “But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to eat and [Col. 0313B] commit fornication.” As though he said: Although you stand firm in this and distinguish well who are heretics and who Catholics, yet you do not fight strongly against them; and therefore I have a few things against you—that is, on account of a few things I am your adversary unless you are corrected—because you have there, that is, under your jurisdiction, persons holding the teaching of Balaam, whom you do not expel but tolerate. Balaam means “vain people,” from whom God took away the spirit of prophecy because of their wickedness; he taught Balak to place a scandal before the children of Israel, to eat and commit fornication—that is, to take delight in vain things with the devil. Balaam signifies heretics, who teach earthly princes how to overthrow those who see God, that is, the Christian people. Or Balaam signifies demons, who try through carnal pleasure and impurity to deceive souls that see God. [Col. 0313C] When heretics set forth persuasive and sweet words in their false doctrines, they desire, as it were through beautiful women, to seduce people so that they may eat things sacrificed to idols—that is, follow the doctrine of idols, full of every impurity—and there commit fornication, that is, abandon the teaching of truth and cling to the lies of perverse persons. Again he continues:

VERS. 15. — “So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.” As though he plainly said: Just as you have there persons holding Balaam’s teaching, and do not exclude them but tolerate them, so you have persons holding the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Therefore repent concerning these in the same way as concerning those. He repeats the matter of the Nicolaitans in order to invite repentance, [Col. 0313D] which he did not do above. From this it appears that the person who teaches perversity and the person who silently permits perversity to be taught are bound by an equal guilt. It follows:

VERS. 16. — “If cominus [perhaps: *si quo minus*, ‘if not’], I will come to you quickly and fight against them with the sword of my mouth.” As though he said: Unless you repent and rebuke those teaching perversity, I will come to you quickly and fight against them, that is, convict them of having sinned as fornicators, with the sword of my mouth: namely, by saying, “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

VERS. 17. — “He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches: To the one who conquers I will give hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone; [Col. 0314A] and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” As though he said: To the conqueror—namely, of his own desires and the temptations of demons—I will give manna, namely myself, or the holy Eucharist, and the contemplation of me, hidden for the present; and I will give him a white stone, namely myself, or knowledge of the Gospel, which will make them white by the twofold robe. Or, I will give him hidden manna, that is, eternal glory, concerning which all will say in amazement, “What is this?” This is the glory which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the human heart (Isa. LXIV). And I will give him a white stone, that is, a body solid and bright with virtues, and immortal. The white stone signifies a body whitened in baptism and destined to be immortal. And on the stone—that is, in such a body—a new name [Col. 0314B] written: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I), namely Christ the Son of God, in whom nothing of old Adam remains. No one knows this name—that is, no one knows, by experience, its power or what will be found through this name—except the one who receives it, that is, except the one who has first conquered sins and fulfilled in deed the good things which he preaches or hears. For the one who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar (1 John II). A *calculus* is a precious stone, also called a carbuncle, because when placed in darkness it is said to shine like a burning coal. By this stone Christ himself is understood, who shone amid the darkness of this age when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). It is therefore rightly called white, because he appeared among human beings [Col. 0314C] undefiled by any darkening of sin and illuminated the darkness of our mortality with the light of his divinity. “And on the stone,” he says, “my name is written.” Isaiah says of this name: “You shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name” (Isa. LXII). Again he adds, saying:

VERS. 18. — “And write to the angel of the Church of Thyatira.” Thyatira, as stated above, is interpreted “illuminated” or “living sacrifice.” Let us then hear what Jesus Christ says to the angel of the Church of Thyatira.

VERS. 19. — “These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire and whose feet are like bronze: I know your works, and faith, and love, and ministry, and your patience, and your latter works [Col. 0314D] more numerous than the former.” As though he plainly said: These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, that is, who possesses gifts of the Holy Spirit and gives or takes them away as he wills; and whose feet are like bronze, which must altogether be imitated. Therefore let those who have already received those gifts take heed lest they lose them by consenting to evils. Or, the Lord’s eyes are understood as the teachers who enlighten us by teaching and example and provide the light of knowledge. The Lord’s feet are either the holy preachers through whom he goes around the world—namely, the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors tested by the fire of tribulation—or certainly his last and final members, glowing in the final persecution. “I know,” he says, that is, I have received, your works—namely faith and love and the other good works—and your ministry [Col. 0315A] in almsgiving, and your patience in every adversity; and your latter works more numerous than the former, because the inexperienced Church begins with lighter things and reaches perfection. Again he continues:

VERS. 20. — “But I have against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet, to teach and seduce my servants into committing fornication and eating things sacrificed to idols.” As though he plainly said: I have against you because you permit—that is, do not excommunicate—the woman Jezebel, namely the soft and lascivious woman, “a flow [Note: [Col. 0315D] The words which we enclose in brackets are extant.] of blood or a dung-heap,” who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants into committing fornication. Jezebel is indeed interpreted “dung-heap” or “flow of blood.” For just as women suffer a flow of blood at the time of [Col. 0315B] menstruation, so the reprobate person, whatever he conceives wickedly, promptly carries out when the time comes; and when afterward the flame increases, he is said to be wholly flowing. But when he brings sin into habit, he spreads its stench far and wide. When he says, “You permit the woman Jezebel,” he signifies the rulers of the Church, that is, bishops, who have authority to permit and to forbid. Therefore a bishop permits the woman Jezebel to seduce God’s servants and commit fornication when he does not oppose subjects who act perversely. Thus the bishop makes himself guilty if he does not resist those subject to him when they sin. Fornication is said to be fourfold: in the mind, if you look upon a woman in order to desire her (Matt. V); in the act itself; in love of earthly things; and in the worship of an idol. It follows:

[Col. 0315C] VERS. 21. — “And I gave her time to repent, and she does not wish to repent of her fornication.” Jezebel, as has been said, means people in Christ’s Church who live wickedly and teach perversely. God gives them time for repentance, that they may recover from their perversity. Because bishops neglect to correct them, while they themselves, though they have time, do not wish to depart from their perversity, the Lord threatens them terribly, saying:

VERS. 22. — “Behold, I cast her upon a bed, and those who commit adultery with her shall be in great tribulation, unless they repent of their works.” As though he said: Behold, I cast her, namely Jezebel—that is, all who live wickedly and teach perversely in the Church [Col. 0315D]—upon a bed, that is, into a reprobate mind and blindness, and into security in sinning; or upon a bed of pain, that is, into despair of healing, as a physician who despairs of a sick person. And those who commit adultery with her, namely her imitators and those conformed to her, shall be in great tribulation, that is, enduring through the ages. This I say unless they repent of their works. Or in this place he used “bed” for mourning, by which he signified eternal misery. By God’s just judgment it often happens that, because of past sins, people fall into greater crimes.

VERS. 23. — Again he adds, saying: “And I will kill her children with death, and all the Churches shall know [Col. 0316A] that I am he who searches the reins and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works.” The wicked indeed prosper for a time, in order to be punished with eternal death; the elect are afflicted briefly, in order to be consoled with everlasting goods. As though he said more plainly: Her children—that is, all their followers—I shall kill, leading them into perpetual death; and thus all the Churches, that is, the entire order of believers on the day of judgment, shall know that I search the reins and hearts, punishing carnal desires and evil thoughts. Or, “the reins” means the lust of evil people, and “hearts” the pure thoughts of good people. “And I will give,” he says, “to each of you according to your works.” As though he plainly said: Then they shall know that in the present I see good and evil, and in the future I shall reward [Col. 0316B] good things to the good and repay evil things to the evil. Again he continues:

VERS. 24. — “But to you I say, the rest who are in Thyatira: Whoever do not have this teaching, who have not known the depths of Satan, as they say, I will put upon you no other burden.” As though he said: I shall punish Jezebel and her followers, but I say to you who are in Thyatira, that is, illuminated and living sacrifices, who are separated from them, that I shall not punish you. Here there is a change of person and an interposition of a statement. “Whoever do not have,” that is, those who do not follow this teaching of Jezebel, “and who have not known,” that is, have not approved by any consent, “the depths of Satan,” that is, his pride and cunning, or the carnal observance [Col. 0316C] of the law, in which he glories and which he regards as the highest depth, as certain persons who came out of Judea say—that I shall again subject you to the yoke of the law. But I shall put upon you no other burden, namely observance of the old law, although they say this; that is, I shall not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear. Or, I shall put upon you no other burden of the law, that is, I shall not again enslave you to carnal observances, as certain persons say, because you must again become Judaizers. Hence blessed Peter says: “Why do you wish again to impose a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts XV). It follows:

VERS. 25. — “Nevertheless, hold fast what you have until [Col. 0316D] I come.” As though he said: Although you are among such people, nevertheless hold fast, by acting, persevering, and defending, what you have—namely faith—until I come to repay you your reward, or to teach you greater things. Again he adds, saying:

VERS. 26–27. — “The one who conquers and keeps my works to the end, I will give him authority over the nations, and he shall rule them with an iron rod, and they shall be broken as a potter’s vessel.” As though he said more plainly: Hold fast the right faith and conquer heretics and carnal affections, because to the one who conquers and keeps my works—not merely for a time, but until the end of his life, or until perfection—I will give in this age authority [Col. 0317A] over the nations living as Gentiles who are committed to him, as to Peter over the Romans, or authority over the companies of vices. And he shall rule them with an iron rod, namely unbending justice, and they shall be broken as a potter’s vessel. That is, their vices shall be broken irrecoverably, so that they are sinners no longer. Or some of them shall be broken so swiftly that they perish utterly, while others are broken so as to be changed for the better.

VERS. 28. — “I will give him,” I say, “authority over the nations, just as I myself received it from my Father according to my humanity.” Hence in the Psalm God the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II), etc. “And [I will give] him the morning star,” that is, myself rising in the morning. The morning star and Lucifer, which when risen announces the day, is Christ, who in rising [Col. 0317B] brought to the world the light of faith and immortality. Therefore he will give the one conquering sins and keeping his commandments—that is, his whole Church—the morning star, namely himself, and the glory of the resurrection. Or the morning star is the first resurrection.

VERS. 29. — “He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches”: namely, let him flee perverse teaching and keep the right faith together with good works. Again he continues:

## CHAPTER III

VERS. 1. — “And write to the angel of the Church of Sardis.” Sardis, which is interpreted “the beginning of beauty,” is understood as “fitted out and adorned”: “These things says he who has the seven spirits and the seven stars in his right hand,” that is, in his power: “I know your works, that you have a name [Col. 0317C] that you live, and you are dead.” As though he plainly said: These things says he from whose eyes nothing is hidden, who has the seven spirits, because the Spirit of the Lord rests upon him, and the seven stars, that is, the sevenfold Church subject to him. “I know,” he says, that is, I know your works, and I know that in those works you seek human praise, because you have a name for holiness and for living, like hypocrites. Or you have some people subject to you who consider themselves holy, but because you do not correct them, you are dead. Or you are dead in love of neighbor, whom you do not correct, because “whoever has sinned in one thing has become guilty of all” (Jas. II). “You have a name,” he says, “that you live, but you are dead.” He shows that in part a person is dead through crimes and in part alive through good works. As though he said: You think you live because you are active in certain good works, [Col. 0317D] but consider that you cannot live if vices prevail over the virtues by which you seemed to live. For there are some who devote themselves to almsgiving and care for the poor, but do not themselves withdraw their hands from robbery. While persons doing these and similar things think that they live by certain good works, they die many times over through any single crime. This kindly exhortation is directed to such persons.

[Col. 0318A] VERS. 2. — “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest, which were about to die.” As though he said: Therefore be watchful, that is, solicitous for salvation, and by this strengthen the other good things you possess, which were about to die unless you correct yourself and your neighbor. All the good things you do also die within you if you seek human praise from them. Therefore, if you wish to live in those things which you have done well, wake through repentance from those things which you do wickedly. For if you remain dead in the latter, you shall by no means live in the former. Hence it is shown that if anyone perfectly awakes from sin through repentance, he shall not lose even those works which he did well while dead; rather, he gives life to them, being himself awakened from the sleep of sin. As though he said more plainly to the whole order of bishops: Be watchful, because although you may be solicitous concerning yourself, you are nevertheless not perfect if you do not rouse others to act well. Or it is not enough to confess Christ with the mouth unless you also do Christ’s works. Be watchful, I say, for I do not find your works complete before my God. As though he plainly said: [Col. 0318B] Your works are not perfect, because they are done without love or for human praise, and therefore are not pleasing to God. If, therefore, you come to life again in that respect in which you are dead, you strengthen the other things which still remain alive in you, lest they die.

VERS. 3.—Therefore keep in mind how you have received and heard, and keep it, O bishop of Sardis, and repent. As if he said: Because your works are not complete, that is, not perfect before God, keep in mind how you received from the apostles and heard from the holy Fathers—namely, that whoever has sinned in one point has become guilty of all (Jas. 2); and that those who do good works for human praise lose the eternal reward. Keep it, and repent: that is, complete by action the good which through negligence you had left undone. Therefore, if you do not keep watch, I shall come upon you like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I shall come upon you. As if he said: Because your works are not complete before God, if you do not keep watch in good works, I shall come upon you, blinding you, like a thief, that I may despoil and kill you; and you will not know—that is, you will be unable to guard against—the hour at which I shall come upon you. For that person rightly keeps watch who both eagerly looks ahead to good things and diligently avoids evil things.

VERS. 4.—Again he says next: But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy. As if he said openly: You have a few names in Sardis—that is, persons known to me by name—who, in comparison with the rest, serving crimes and the uncleanness of the flesh, have not defiled their garments—namely, the garment of immortality and innocence which they received in baptism—with a criminal stain, or have wiped away with tears a stain they had incurred. And therefore they shall walk with me from virtue to virtue in white; that is, advancing themselves, they shall always be changed for the better and shall ascend to conformity with me, because they are worthy—that is, clean.

VERS. 5.—He says: He who conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments, and I shall not blot out his name from the book of life, and I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels. As if he said plainly: Likewise, among the imitators of these, whoever conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments, as these also are; and I shall not blot out—that is, I shall not deprive—his name from the book of life, that is, from God’s eternal knowledge. The book of life is also the foreknowledge of God, in which all things stand. For the Lord knows those who are his. The Lord knows not only the number but also the names of the elect, as he himself says to Moses: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33). And he says, “I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels”: that is, in the sight of all the heavenly powers, saying: “I was naked, and this man clothed me; I was hungry, and he gave me food; I was thirsty, and he gave me drink,” etc. (Matt. 25).

VERS. 6.—He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches. As if he said: What I say to one, I say to all. It follows:

VERS. 7.—And write to the angel of the Church of Philadelphia. Philadelphia is interpreted “love of a brother,” or “saving an inheritance.” These things says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David; who opens and no one shuts; who shuts and no one opens. I know your works, etc. As if he said: These things says the Holy One, that is, the steadfast One; and the True One, in his promises; who has the key of David, namely flesh from David’s seed; who opens the sayings of the prophets, or human hearts to faith, or the obscurity of the Scriptures, or the gate of eternal life. And no one—namely, among persecutors—shuts it. He shuts it to swine and dogs by withdrawing grace; and no one opens it before swine, lest they trample underfoot the pearls of faith (Matt. 7). Moreover, Christ’s humanity and divinity opened for us the gates of paradise and defeated the strong man armed. As if he said openly: He has the key—that is, royal power—as one born, as it were, from David’s stock; or because he received flesh from David’s seed, through which the gate of life, closed to us in Adam, was opened; or because by his dispensation David’s prophecy was laid open, as he himself says: “It is necessary that all things written concerning me in the prophets and the psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

VERS. 8.—“I know,” he says, “your works,” that is, I approve them as good. And again: “Behold, I have set before you an open door which no one can shut, because you have little strength, and have kept my word, and have not denied my name.” As if he said more plainly to the bishop of the Church of Philadelphia: I have set before you an open door: namely, human hearts formerly hard, or the obscure Scriptures, which are the door of the sheep unto life, and which no one can shut. Hence the disciples, when forbidden and beaten for speaking, said: “We cannot but speak the things which we have seen” (Acts 4). And because you have little strength—that is, strength not proud but humble; or little in comparison with the strength to come, where there shall be no labor—and have kept my word, that is, my preaching; and have not denied my name amid afflictions. And because you are such,

VERS. 9.—Behold, I shall give you some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews, and are not, and lie. As if he said plainly: I shall give you some from the synagogue of Satan, who call themselves Jews and are not, because they lost that name when they said of Christ, “We do not know where he is from” (John 9). But they lie, because they are said to believe in words and in certain pretenses, but deny him in deeds. As frequently in the sixth sequence that follows, so here also in the sixth angel the last persecution is signified, in which some Jews are to be deceived, while others, fulfilling the Law spiritually through Elijah’s admonitions, are believed to be about to conquer the enemy, that is, Antichrist. Again he adds, saying: “Behold, I shall make them come and worship before your feet.” As if he said: I shall do this for those who falsely say that they are Jews, namely, so that they may not lie, by producing virtues and works: that they may come—that is, may approach the faith with the steps of virtues, though they had withdrawn far from God—and may worship, that is, may reverence before your feet, humbled through likeness to the example of feet, as Joseph’s brothers worshipped him (Gen. 42). Faithful persons are called feet, either because they bear God or because by good works they bear others with themselves toward God. As if he said to the bishop of the Church of Philadelphia: Labor, as you have begun, for the conversion of your brethren, because I, who promised that whatever you ask the Father in my name he will give you (John 15), am true in my promises. From this you may know that I shall gather many to you, as you desire. Again he adds:

VERS. 10.—Knowing that I loved you because you kept the word of my patience. As if he said plainly: Unbelievers, who did not believe that God loved the Church which he allowed to be afflicted, shall know that I loved you—that is, I shall now make the proof of my love—because for this reason I loved you: because you kept the word of my patience, namely, the command concerning patience which I displayed in myself, praying for persecutors; or the command of which I am the giver. As if he said more plainly: When I have brought to the faith the Jews who formerly persecuted the Church, then they shall know—that is, believe—that I love her whom I formerly did not seem to love, while I allowed her to be afflicted. This shall happen near the end of the world, when the remnant of Israel shall be saved (Isa. 10). Again he says next: And I shall keep you from the hour of trial which is to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell upon the earth. As if he said plainly: As you kept the word of my patience, so I shall keep you from being conquered by the hour of trial—that is, testing—which is to come upon the whole world, that is, upon the universal Church, which always returns to its proper condition, to test, that is, to prove as gold, those dwelling on earth: namely, those who cultivate well their inheritance, that is, their body and their works. “I shall keep you from the hour,” he says: that is, from the examination of the hour which shall take place in the time of Antichrist, or on the day of judgment; or from the hour beginning when Antichrist’s temptation begins, which has already begun through his ministers. Hence Saint Jerome says in his commentary on the prophet Nahum: “Just as Christ had his forerunners—namely David, Solomon, and the other holy kings and prophets—so Antichrist had the most impious king Antiochus and the other kings who persecuted the Church.” It follows:

VERS. 11.—Behold, I come quickly. As if he said: The trial shall indeed come; but lest you succumb, behold, I come quickly to reward or to help. Again he adds, saying: Hold fast what you have, that no one may take your crown. As if he said: Because I come quickly, meanwhile hold fast what you have—namely faith and good works—so that, since the number of God’s elect is fixed, if anyone falls back, another is introduced through his mercy; and let no one take your crown, that is, your reward. Here it is shown that the reward which is sometimes taken from the proud by the just judgment of God is mercifully assigned to others. Again he adds:

VERS. 12.—He who conquers, I shall make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go out no more; and I shall write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from heaven from my God, and my new name. As if he said: Hold fast what you have, and conquer; for whoever conquers, I shall make him an unbreakable pillar: steadfast in himself and supporting others by word and example, in the temple of my God, namely in the heavenly Jerusalem. And he shall go out no more: namely, I shall not allow him ever again to depart from it. The younger son—that is, the people of the Gentiles—had gone out from his father’s house; but, reconciled by the death of the fattened calf (Luke 15), that is, by Christ’s blood, he shall go out no more. “And I shall write upon him,” he says, “the name of my God”: beyond what the human mind can comprehend and understand, he shall in some fashion be called God, according to the saying: “I said, You are gods” (Ps. 81). And I shall write the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem: he shall be called the city of God, that is, fortified with virtues, where there shall be nothing old, but a full vision of peace; which comes down from heaven, that is, from conformity with heavenly creatures, from my God, because God sent it the virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit by which it was made such. And I shall write my new name: namely, he shall be called Christian, that is, anointed with grace, so that he has nothing of the old man.

VERS. 13.—He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.

VERS. 14.—And write to the angel of the Church of Laodicea. Laodicea is interpreted “a beloved tribe.” These things says: Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation. As if he said: These things says Amen, that is, “truly”; the faithful witness, namely, of the things he heard from the Father, or the witness before the Father of our works. He is indeed true, because through him the Father’s promises are fulfilled; or because he is to be believed in all his words. He is the beginning of God’s creation, namely of the first creation or of re-creation: that is, Jesus Christ, whose kingdom shall have no end, who is without defect.

VERS. 15.—“I know,” he says, “your works, that you are neither cold nor hot.” As if he said to the bishop of the Church of Laodicea: I know—that is, your works do not escape me. You are unwilling to be corrected from your perversity, because you are neither cold—that is, you do not wholly lack faith—nor hot, that is, you do not openly deny what you have received. Cold is the person who has neither knowledge of God nor practices works of charity; hot is the person who, having knowledge of God, has the fervor of charity. Would that you were cold or hot, because there is greater hope for the cold than for the lukewarm.

VERS. 16.—But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth. It should be noted that he does not therefore wish him to become cold, as though he should possess no good thing; but because it is a lesser sin, according to the judgment of the blessed apostle James: “To one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (Jas. 4). For coldness signifies ignorance. Thus the cold person will not be punished for transgressing what he understands, but only for ignorance. Or he wishes him to be cold rather than lukewarm because such unlearned and simple persons are more quickly converted to a better life and advanced to greater things than proud wise persons. Hence Saint Paul says: “Knowledge puffs up; charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8). We call lukewarm the person who has knowledge of God but lacks the fervor of charity, or who holds faith without works. As if he said openly: But because you are lukewarm, that is, sluggish, and neither cold nor hot, I shall begin, by excommunicating you, to vomit you out of my mouth: that is, to remove you from the fellowship of the saints through my preachers, in whom I speak.

VERS. 17.—Because you say, “I am rich or have become wealthy, and need nothing,” and do not know that you are wretched and pitiable and poor and blind and naked. As if he said more plainly: Therefore I shall again vomit you out, because you say—that is, you deliberate within yourself, saying this: “I need no longer labor as sinners do, because I am rich,” that is, cleansed in baptism; or rich in divine and secular knowledge, and wealthy, namely filled with virtues. “And I need nothing”: and, for my part, I have added certain other good things. And you who say this do not know—that is, do not understand—that you are wretched, since such works will not benefit you unto salvation; and pitiable, so much so that you perish through ignorance; and poor in works of virtue; and blind, lacking the light of knowledge because you do not recognize vices; and naked in your soul of virtues. Yet, although you are such, I do not deny mercy; rather:

VERS. 18.—I counsel you to buy from me gold tried in the fire, that you may become rich and be clothed in white garments, and that the shame of your nakedness may not appear. As if he said plainly: I counsel you—that is, exhort you—to buy from me, by the fruit of repentance, namely fasting and prayer, gold: that is, myself, or charity; gold fiery, that is, splendid and tested, in which there shall be no uncleanness, and which will make you fervent in love of God and neighbor. Or gold means divine wisdom, which will purify you and kindle you for good works, so that you may become rich in works of virtue and be clothed in white garments, that is, in the virtues themselves; and so that the shame of your nakedness may not appear, as it appeared in the first parents when they sought to cover their fault with certain excuses, when it was said: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3).

It should be noted that there are especially five ways in which people are scourged by the Lord. Sometimes it is to increase merits, as with Job and Tobias; sometimes to preserve virtues, as with Paul; sometimes so that past sins may be corrected, as with the paralytic to whom it was said: “Behold, you have been made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5). Sometimes, however, it is not that they may be corrected, but that they may perish by a double destruction, as Antiochus and Herod; sometimes so that God’s glory may thereby be made manifest, as with Lazarus and the man born blind (John 9, 11). But whichever way the elect are scourged, they are made better by the scourging. Again he says next: And anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see. As if he said: Anoint with the gift of the Holy Spirit the mind which earthly things had closed. Or anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that is, with compunction and tears of repentance. Hence the Psalmist says: “The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18). It follows:

VERS. 19.—Those whom I love, I rebuke and chasten. As if he said: You ought to yield to this exhortation of mine, because, for the reason already stated, those whom I love I rebuke with words—I make them recognize their sins—and chasten with scourges, and render chaste. Therefore be zealous, and repent. An *aemulus* is called zealous, or envious, or an imitator. As if he said: Imitate those whom you see suffering adversities, and repent of your lukewarmness.

VERS. 20.—“Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock.” As if he said: Because you are lukewarm, behold, I stand at the door, namely the closed heart, and knock, that is, rebuke. I stand, that is, I wait, or inspire, or call through preachers. “If anyone,” he says, “hears my voice and opens the door to me, I shall enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me.” As if he said openly: If anyone hears, by understanding, my voice, and opens the door, in order to do my work, I shall enter into the secret places of his heart, and dine with him, because I delight in his faith and work; and he with me, because he shall rejoice in my visitation and aid. A dinner is a common meal, because *coenon* means “common.” Again he adds:

VERS. 21.—He who conquers, I shall grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne. As if he said openly: Whoever conquers all these things mentioned above, I shall grant him to sit with me—that is, to judge—on my throne, namely in those in whom I sit and judge; as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne, because his victory and his session are the cause of their victory and their session. This may be understood concerning prelates and, through prelates, concerning subjects. Therefore it should be known that what such persons and the other subjects do not have in themselves, they shall have in their prelates. Those, therefore, who shall not judge in their own persons shall certainly judge through their rulers. For there shall be such great charity in them that whatever each person sees in another, he will count as his own. Therefore what he does not have in himself, he will have in another. Thus all the elect shall have the power of judging in their prelates, just as the whole human body has the power to speak through the mouth, see through the eyes, hear through the ears, smell through the nostrils, and work through the hands, although the individual members have distinct functions: because what one member does not have in itself, it has in another. But in order that the Church may attain this dignity, in this present pilgrimage she groans in humiliation. Nor does she seek the summit of loftiness, since the whole life of the saints bears the name of humility.

VERS. 22.—He who has ears, he says, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.

## CHAPTER IV

Having finished the first vision, he enters upon the second, saying:

VERS. 1.—After these things I saw, and behold, a door opened in heaven. This vision is set down not as the first but as the second, because, when he invites his own to tribulations, they are unable to endure unless the neglected matters are first corrected; and that was done in the first vision. Nearly all this second vision deals with the last faithful, which greatly serves to encourage those now living; it also introduces a few things about those who suffered before Christ’s Incarnation, which serves the same purpose. In this second vision he treats of the one seated on the throne and his adornment; of the Lamb opening the book, that is, the divine dispensation; of the restoration of the human race; and of the one loosening the seven seals: so that, seeing God to have bestowed such understanding of the Scriptures upon the faithful, we may be grateful to him and not fear to suffer for him. Let us then hear what the blessed John saw in the second vision.

“After these things,” he says, “I saw; and behold, a door opened in heaven.” This is not to be referred to a succession of times but to the order of the visions. As if he said plainly: After these things I saw—not in time, but in order—and I was able to see because, behold, a door was opened in heaven: namely, in the Church, that is, Scripture, which is the way leading to life; or Christ, who is truly the door, whose mysteries were formerly closed but are now opened to those who are heaven by faith and works. Indeed Christ is a door in the Church, closed to none of the faithful but open, except to thieves—that is, heretics—and to those who reject his commands. Again he adds: And the first voice which I heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, said: “Come up here, and I shall show you what must shortly happen after these things.” As if he said: And the first voice which I heard—that is, the prophetic voice, because it precedes the New Testament—was like a trumpet, exhorting to battle, speaking with me: namely, not at variance with my reason, providing a reason why suffering is fitting; saying, “Come up here, and I shall show you what must shortly happen after these things.” As if it were said: You, having been corrected, enlarge your mind to understand these other things, and ascend from the surface of the letter to this place, that is, to spiritual understanding; and I shall show you the tribulations and miracles which must happen after these things. Things already past, he says, must still happen, because they are to remain in the same state in which they began, and after these things are to happen in another state. Or “after these things” means among the last faithful. As if he said openly: After you have corrected your Churches for their sins, you ought to see the secrets of heaven, by which the faithful may be encouraged for battles. Again he says next:

VERS. 2.—Immediately I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne. It should not be understood that his spirit was taken from his body and that he thus immediately saw the vision; rather, as has already been said above, he saw all this in his mind. For the power of the Holy Spirit raised his mind to contemplate the heavenly mysteries, and he neither heard nor saw anything through the body; but, caught up in ecstasy by the Holy Spirit, he was led forth so as to see and hear spiritually, retaining what he heard, so that he could write these things and transmit them to posterity. But if we wish to refer this to the elect, their spiritual manner of life is declared, to whom Paul says: “You are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. 8). And again: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5). “Immediately,” he says, “I was in the Spirit.” As if he said more plainly: Immediately—that is, I did not resist, but without delay cast off concern for all earthly things; and because I so desired, behold, a throne was set in heaven: namely, the greater persons in the Church, in whom God sits and judges; and one seated above the throne, so that, surpassing them, he sits in other persons subject to him. Christ, formerly walking among the lampstands, now sits: that is, he judges the merits of individuals. He fittingly calls them to mind for those whom he is about to exhort to battle.

VERS. 3.—And he who sat, he says, was like in appearance to a jasper and sardius stone. As if he said plainly: He who sat, prepared to judge, formerly unknown, was like in appearance to a jasper stone: that is, he appeared through the flesh to the world, crushing enemies like a stone, furnishing strength and pasture to his own, and flourishing in his divinity. He was also like sardius: namely, his flesh was red in the Passion. By the color of these two stones he indicates God and man. Christ has greenness in the brightness of divinity; he also has redness in humanity, through which he recalled to heavenly things Adam, whose name is interpreted “red earth.” Therefore, what is green in him belongs to power; what is red, to mercy. And by that which is green, namely because he is God, he created us; by that which is red, he redeemed us. Jasper, being somewhat dark, signifies through its greenness the divinity hidden in humanity; sardius, being red, signifies the Passion. And there was a rainbow around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald. *Iris* [Ἶρις] in Greek is called *arcus*, “a bow,” in Latin. The bow appears on a rainy day and is a sign of propitiation, as the Lord said to Noah at the time of the flood (Gen. 9): “I shall set my bow in the clouds of heaven,” etc. The emerald stone is green and red. Therefore baptism is understood through the green color, which is watery; while through red are signified the gifts of the Holy Spirit received in baptism, by which sins are burned away. Through the blue-green color, which lies between red and green, the justice of redness and the propitiation of greenness are tempered. Or in these colors are indicated the past judgment of water and the future judgment of fire, in which God shall save his own. It follows:

VERS. 4.—And around the throne were twenty-four seats. As if he said: From all sides of the principal throne I saw twenty-four attendant seats, consenting to his judgment. The twenty-four seats are said to be the books of the twelve apostles and the twelve prophets. Again he adds: And upon the twenty-four thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed round about in white garments, with golden crowns upon their heads. All teachers of the Old or New Testament are called twelve, on account of the faith in the Trinity which they proclaim to the four parts of the world. Or twenty-four is made from six and four: six refers to the works which God made in six days; four to the Gospels, that is, to the Church, which honors God’s works through the Old and New Testament. As six times four or four times six make twenty-four, so four times three or three times four make twelve. For twenty-four contains twice twelve. “Upon the twenty-four thrones,” he says, “sat twenty-four elders”: namely, the perfect in the Church, possessing aged morals, gathered from the four parts of the world, fulfilling the ten commandments through the twofold love of God and neighbor. They sit, that is, rest from other concerns, dwelling upon and delighting in knowledge of the twenty-four books. They are clothed round about in white garments, which they put on in baptism, by which sins are covered; and they become white outwardly in good works and inwardly in virtues of the soul. And upon their heads—that is, in their minds—were crowns: namely, victories through wisdom or through charity extending even to enemies, golden crowns. Again he adds:

VERS. 5.—And from the throne proceed lightnings and voices and thunders. As if he said: From the throne, that is, from the Church which rains spiritual teaching, proceed lightnings, namely miracles which terrify and enlighten; and voices, namely exhortations to blessedness; and thunders, that is, threats of eternal death. And, he says, seven lamps burning before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God: that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which kindle and enlighten human hearts, which are God’s thrones. *Lampas* [Λαμπάς] in Greek is called *flamma*, “flame,” in Latin. Again he says next:

VERS. 6.—And before the throne, as it were, a glassy sea like crystal. As if he said openly: Before the throne—that is, in the Church’s plain sight—the prophetic Law is, for those first approaching faith in Christ, like a sea: that is, deep, whose understanding is called literal. For those somewhat more advanced, it is like pure glass, through which one sees somewhat more clearly; their understanding is called moral. But for the most perfect it is like crystal, through which one sees most clearly; their understanding is called spiritual. As crystal hardens into stone through excessive cold, so the faithful, through the excess of tribulations inflicted upon them by the impious precisely so that they may grow cold in charity, pass into conformity with the cornerstone, that is, Christ. Or because crystal has this nature, that water made moist and exposed to a ray of the sun sends out sparks of fire from itself, so the faithful in the Church, moistened by the water of baptism or by the rain of the Holy Spirit, when exposed to a ray of the sun—that is, to Christ’s example—send out sparks of fire from themselves, kindling others to good works. Hence Saint Paul says: “By doing this, you shall heap coals of fire upon his head” (Rom. 12). It follows: And in the middle of the throne and around the throne, four living creatures full of eyes before and behind. As if he said openly: I saw in the middle of the throne—that is, in the middle of the world, namely in Jerusalem, where God’s throne first began to be established—and around the throne, that is, throughout the whole world, where God’s throne was enlarged, four living creatures: namely, the order of preachers of the New and Old Testament, full of eyes in order that they may defend the four Gospels from heretics; before and behind, remembering past sins and guarding themselves for the future; or possessing knowledge of what God did in the beginning and will do at the end of the world. “I saw,” he says, “four living creatures”: that is, all teachers of the Old and New Testament in the middle, as it were sustaining the throne, that is, the Church; and around it, everywhere as guards of the throne, dealing with present things, which lie between past and future things, and dealing with past and future things. Again he adds, saying:

VERS. 7.—And the first living creature was like a lion, namely Mark, who under the likeness of a lion recounts Christ’s royal lineage; and he is therefore called like a lion because, as a lion, he uttered a great voice, saying: “The word of the Lord came upon John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness.”

> [Note: [Col. 0327D] Mark nowhere reads thus; the words are those of Luke, chapter 3, verse 2. Interpreters generally follow Jerome here, *Against Jovinian*, book 1, [Col. 0328D] saying: “Mark … has … the face of a lion because of the voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight’” (chapter 1).]

And the second living creature was like a calf, namely Luke, who speaks of the sacrifices of the fathers of the Old Testament, in which Christ is prefigured. For thus he speaks at the beginning of his Gospel, saying: “In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zacharias” (Luke 1). And the third living creature had a face like a man, namely Matthew, who speaks thus concerning the humanity of the Son of God and of the Virgin: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). And the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle, namely John, who, transcending every human and angelic creature, contemplated divinity itself with unblinded eyes, saying: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1).

These living creatures typologically signify Christ, who for the salvation of the human race deigned to be born, die, and rise again; and, ascending into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father. God’s living creatures are also the faithful, rational and gentle like a human being; bearing adversities without terror like a lion; mortifying themselves like a calf in sacrifice; and seeking heavenly things like an eagle. The lion, it is said, is born dead and on the third day is made alive by its father’s voice. So also Christ rose on the third day. And he had to rise because he was dead; and he could die because he was human. And since he was human and dead, he could rise, because he was an eagle: that is, not merely human, but God and human. Ezekiel, foreseeing what was to be, set the human first and then the lion (Ezek. 1), because Christ was human in being born, but became a lion in preaching. Then he set the calf, because he was sacrificed to God the Father upon the altar of the cross; finally the eagle, because he ascended to heaven. But John, seeing all these things fulfilled, set the lion first, as the foundation of the whole faith. Again he adds:

VERS. 8.—And the four living creatures, each of them, had six wings. As if he said more plainly: They were well instructed in order to preach these things concerning Christ. The first wing is the natural law; the second, the Mosaic law; the third, the prophetic law; the fourth, the evangelical law; the fifth, the institutions of the apostles; the sixth, those of whomever else, such as Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, Ambrose, Benedict, and Isidore. By these the holy Church seeks lofty things, and from them preachers receive the foundation of all preaching. Or the six wings are knowledge of the works which God completed in six days; those who work well in them are greatly raised by this knowledge. “And around,” he says, “and within, they are full of eyes.” Indeed, because teachers of the Church keep themselves clean and form others by examples, they instruct the simple through the letter and the more perfect through allegory. Or because they enlighten both the center and the boundaries of the earth, they are full of eyes around and within; or they are full of eyes within, that is, in a clean conscience, and around, that is, irreproachable in the sight of human beings; or because they manifest outwardly with their mouth the faith which they have in their heart. Again he says next: And they had no rest day or night, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, who is, and who is to come.” He says “holy” three times, because God is three in persons; and once “Lord God Almighty,” because he is one in majesty: he who was without beginning, and who is unchangeable, and who is to come. Namely, the Son shall appear bodily; indeed, divinity itself shall manifest itself to the faithful. It follows:

VERS. 9–10.—And when those living creatures gave glory and honor and blessing to him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages, the twenty-four elders fell down before him who sits upon the throne and worshipped him who lives for ages of ages, casting their crowns before the throne and saying: “You are worthy, Lord,” etc. As if he said plainly: When those living creatures—that is, all teachers of the Church—gave, attributed, preached, and professed their faith, or glory in the resurrection, honor in the ascension’s working, and blessing in the exaltation of heavenly recompense, to him who sits upon the throne and lives for ages of ages, the twenty-four elders fell down: that is, all preachers of the Old and New Testament humbled themselves before him who sits upon the throne, that is, in accordance with his good pleasure; and they referred all their good to him, saying: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us; but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113). And they worshipped him who lives for ages of ages: what they did not have from themselves, they sought from him by voice, work, and in the secrecy of the heart, casting their crowns before the throne—that is, attributing to God victory over vices or tribulations, and giving to others an example of praise—saying:

VERS. 11.—“You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power; for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.” As though they were saying: You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive from us glory, honor, and power, because you bestowed all these good things upon us, and therefore they must be attributed to you, not to us. Therefore too [Col. 0329B] all things must be referred to you, because you created all things; and they did not exist suddenly, but were in the art—that is, according to your will—before they were formed in actuality. And they were created by coming visibly into existence; or some things already existed, according to spiritual creation, in the predestination of almighty God, and were created in visible actuality. This was indeed prefigured when, as the Lord came to Jerusalem, the crowd that went out to meet him spread before the feet of the ass on which he sat palm branches, by which victory is signified (Matt. XXI). For what is signified by palm branches strewn in the way is signified here by crowns placed before the throne.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0329C] VERS. 1.—And I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals. As though he said: I saw in the right hand of God the Father, who sits upon the throne—that is, in the Son, through whom he made all things and to whom the intention of the whole book is directed—a book written within and without: namely, the two Testaments, which are the same externally according to the Old, which signifies, or because it promises outward things; internally according to the New, which is signified, or because it sometimes promises blessedness. Or “within,” that is, in its more hidden matters, according to the more perfect; “without,” in simpler words, according to the less perfect: sealed, that is, closed, with seven seals, namely with all mysteries and obscurities concerning the seven ages of the world. Or the book was closed by the sevenfold Spirit, through whom faith is opened. Or the book is the divine plan for the restoration of humankind; it is written—that is, disclosed—within, namely obscurely in the Old Testament, as Moses says to the children of Israel: “At evening you shall sacrifice the lamb” (Exod. XII), there revealing our future restoration in the last age through Christ’s sacrifice; and without, that is, clearly, in the New Testament. He adds again:

VERS. 2.—And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice: that is, any one of the ancient Fathers, searching and announcing to others, and, from excessive longing, lamenting that the matter was delayed so long, and saying: “Who is worthy to open the book and loose its seals?” As though it were said more plainly: “Do you suppose that I shall see it? Do you suppose that I shall endure?” Who is worthy to open the book—that is, to fulfill the divine plan for the restoration of humankind—and to loose, namely to disclose and expound, the seven seals—that is, the riddles and obscurities of the book? No one except the Son of God and the Virgin. The opening of this book, therefore, is the redemption of humankind.

VERS. 3.—And no one was able, in heaven or on earth or beneath the earth, to open the book or to look upon it. As though he said plainly: None of those who were in heaven, namely an angel; nor on earth, a human being; nor beneath the earth, a soul stripped of flesh, was able to open the book—that is, to fulfill the divine plan [f. *divinam disposition.*], or perfectly to understand the mysteries of either Testament—nor [Col. 0330B] to look upon it. Hence it is said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII).

VERS. 4.—And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to see it. As though he said more plainly: I, John, wept greatly in the person of the ancient Fathers, who grieved at the long captivity of humankind and did not fully understand its restoration. Concerning them, the Son of God and the Virgin himself says in the Gospel to his disciples: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X). Therefore, he says, I wept greatly, because not only was no one worthy to open the book, but neither could anyone look upon it; that is, no one could perfectly understand the plan [Col. 0330C] of human redemption.

VERS. 5.—And one of the elders said to me: “Do not weep.” That is, any prophet who, by announcing Christ’s coming to others, offers consolation. Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, the Lord, prince of the kings of the earth, will come, and he himself removes the yoke of our captivity” (Isa. XIV). But let us hear what the elder said: “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and loose its seven seals.” He uses the past for the future. As though Moses or David, or some prophet, were speaking for consolation to the ancient people, saying: “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah”—that is, he will conquer the devil, the world, death, and hell—“the root of David,” namely proceeding from the seed [Col. 0330D] of David, or David’s support, through whom David endures; he will conquer, I say, in order to open the book and loose—that is, expound—its seven seals, namely the riddles and obscurities of human restoration. This lion, who conquered the world and the strong armed man—that is, the devil—spares the humble and resists the proud. When a lion is pursued, he flees through the mountains; with the knot which he has in his tail, he erases his tracks. Thus Christ fled through the mountains, that is, ascended into heaven; his divinity was hidden from the Jews, and, by assuming flesh, he veiled his divinity so that he could not be recognized. As a lion is accustomed to sleep with open eyes, so Christ breathed his last while his divinity remained alive. It follows:

VERS. 6.—And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a lamb [Col. 0331A] standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent into all the earth. He explains how and where the lion conquered. As though he said: As one of the elders, namely one of the holy prophets, had foretold to me, I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne—that is, in the common benefit of the Church—and of the four living creatures, namely the preachers of the New Testament, and in the midst of the elders, that is, the prophets, a lamb standing: namely, simple and innocent, helping his soldiers as they fight; as though slain, because, though he died through the weakness of the flesh, he nevertheless lives through the power of God (II Cor. XIII); or, among his own, as though slain, in whom he is daily put to death; having seven horns, namely holy persons in the seven ages of the world, and seven eyes, [Col. 0331B] which are the seven Spirits of God sent into all the earth. He adds again, saying:

VERS. 7.—And he came and took the book from the right hand of him who sat on the throne. As though he said: The Son of God came in the flesh to human knowledge and took the book—that is, the plan of human restoration—from the right hand, namely from the Word united to himself: I mean, the Word of God the Father who sits upon the throne.
