VERS. 8.—And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb, each having harps and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. As though it were said more plainly: When he had opened the book, that is, when he had disclosed all that had been foretold concerning himself, the four living creatures—namely all preachers—and the twenty-four elders, that is, all judges in the Church, fell before the Lamb, thinking humbly of themselves and imitating him, so that they too might suffer after his likeness; and, both for themselves and for those subject to them, they gave thanks to God the Father, to the same Lamb, and to the Holy Spirit for the redemption of humankind. Each had harps: that is, by mortifying and chastening their flesh they rendered to the Trinity a sweet sound, namely grateful praises. A harp consists of wood and strings; therefore the wood is Christ’s cross, and the string is the flesh of the saints, which is stretched upon the wood when, through diverse torments, they render the same sound and imitate Christ’s cross. And they had golden bowls—that is, broad hearts filled with divine wisdom and charity, [Col. 0331D] even unto the love of enemies—full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints, sweetly fragrant to God. This is what the Psalmist prays: “Let my prayer, O Lord, be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL).

VERS. 9.—And they sang a new song, saying: “You are worthy, O Lord,” etc. For the holy Church sings the new song with exultation: that is, it confesses the New Testament in deed when it is baptized into Christ’s death; and with joy it proclaims Christ’s commandment, namely: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XIII). But let us hear what the elders of the Old and New Testaments say:

[Col. 0332A] VERS. 10.—“You are worthy, O Lord, to take the book and open its seals, because you were slain, and redeemed us to God in your blood out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation; and you have made us a kingdom and priests to our God, and we shall reign upon the earth.” As though they said more plainly: You are worthy, O Lord Jesus Christ, because you are free from sin, to take, insofar as you are human, from the hand of the Father the book—that is, the office of human restoration—and by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending, to open its seals. And you are truly worthy because you were slain; for in obedience you redeemed us to God in your blood from every tribe of Jews, and tongue of gentiles, and from every gentile people and nation, both slaves and free persons; and you made us, thus gathered together, a kingdom to our God, [Col. 0332B] namely reigning spiritually, and priests, offering ourselves and praying for others. And we shall reign, freed from every servitude, like kings over the land of the living, or over all earthly things, despising them. All the elect are called kings because they do not allow the tyranny of vices to rise up within themselves. “You redeemed us,” he says, “from every tribe and tongue.” A tribe is so called from the three orders, in which there are seventy-two tongues; in each of these are many peoples, and within a people, nations. For with God there is no distinction of persons; but in every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him (Acts X). He then says:

VERS. 11–12.—And I saw and heard the voice of many angels [Col. 0332C] around the throne and the living creatures and the elders; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing.” As though he said more plainly: Not only did I see the living creatures and elders testifying to the same thing in accordance with their office, but all the angels too rejoiced with them. “I saw,” he says, “and heard the voice of many angels,” namely the elect heavenly spirits, who fortify and guard the Church; who rejoice over the restored fellowship of holy human beings; who bear witness to Christ in his announcement, birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension, and have testified that he will come as judge. Or the lesser angels are human beings—that is, subjects in the Church who lead an angelic life—who surround and honor their prelates and judges, assenting to and confirming their testimony. And the number of all the aforesaid was thousands of thousands, that is, infinite and unknown to us; for what is infinite to human beings is finite to God. The more witnesses there are, the greater the testimony and the greater the joy. For as many holy human beings will ascend to heaven as angels remained there after the devil fell, because holy human beings will have a place in all the orders of angels. Blessed Gregory testifies to this, saying [Note: [Col. 0331D] Homily 34 on the Gospels]:

> “That heavenly city consists of angels and human beings. We believe that as many human beings [Col. 0333A] ascend to it as angels remained there, as it is written: ‘He established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the sons of God’ (Deut. XXXII),”

that is, of the angels. Hence Isidore, teacher of Spain, says [Note: [Col. 0333D] Book I of the *Sentences*, ch. 10]:

> “The number of good angels, diminished after the fall of the evil angels, will be made complete from the number of elect human beings; this number is known to God alone.”

But let us hear what the multitude of angels and all the saints says: O hearers, worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, that is, freedom from sin; and divinity, because God was seen dead; and wisdom, of all things through the Word united to himself; and strength, by which he conquered the devil through steadfastness in his passion; and honor in the resurrection; and glory, that is, impassibility [Col. 0333B] and immortality; and blessing in the exaltation of his ascension: “That at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). He who is called a lion because of strength is also called a lamb because of innocence and simplicity, and because he was offered as a sacrifice to God the Father. Let it be explained again more plainly, so that it may be impressed more firmly upon the minds of the hearers: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, that is, the Spirit of counsel; and divinity, namely the Spirit of godliness; and wisdom, namely the Spirit of wisdom; and strength, that is, the Spirit of strength; and honor, namely the Spirit of knowledge; glory and blessing, that is, the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. It follows:

[Col. 0333C] VERS. 13.—And every creature that is in heaven and on earth and beneath the earth, and the sea and all that is in it, I heard all saying: “To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and power for ages of ages.” As though he said plainly: Every creature—that is, every rank of the faithful—which is in heaven, namely the host of angels; and which is upon earth, namely contemplatives; and beneath the earth, that is, the elect dead, or active persons, who are signified by the sea or, literally, the world; and those who are in it, who are, that is, remain unmoved: all these I heard—that is, the living creatures and elders, giving assent through the testimony of the angels—saying all together, that is, confessing: To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb, namely to God the Father and the Son—that is, to God the Trinity, [Col. 0333D] because the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son—be blessing in miracles, honor in operation, glory in confession, and power for ages of ages, rightly so, because he is almighty in resisting vices. As though he said more plainly: The blessing, that is, the increase which we have in good works; and the honor which follows from it [Note: [Col. 0333] “We obtain,” or, as the Gloss has it: “which follows from it.”]; and the glory from the virtues which we received in baptism; and the power by which we resist desires—all this should be attributed not to us but to God the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, who lives for ages of ages.

VERS. 14.—And the four living creatures said: “Amen”; [Col. 0334A] that is, others who had already become the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders through the preaching of the aforesaid living creatures and elders, confirming what they had said, said: “Amen”—namely, “The testimony which you have rendered to God is true.” And the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces and worshipped. As though he said: The twenty-four elders, that is, all the judges of the Church, of both the old and the new law, did not become proud because they judged others, but fell—that is, humbled themselves upon their faces, that is, in their hearts—and worshipped in mind, speech, and deed; namely, they venerated God because their consciences were good.

## CHAPTER VI

VERS. 1.—And I saw that the Lamb had opened one [Col. 0334B] of the seven seals. Above it was said: “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, to open the book and loose its seven seals”; and then I saw that the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals, namely that which was to occur in the first state of the seven states of the Church. The opening of the seal is the revelation of the mystery. But by the seven seals, as was said above, is signified the fullness of hidden mysteries that lay concealed before the Lord’s coming. And I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with the voice of thunder: “Come and see.” As though he said: I heard one of the four living creatures—that is, one of the four orders that preach the four Gospels—speaking as with the voice of thunder, because the Gospel terrifies like thunder. The living creatures invite John, that is, the primitive Church following him. As though they said plainly: Come, pass on from the mystery, and see the complete truth.

VERS. 2.—And behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he went forth conquering so that he might conquer. As though he said plainly: Behold, a white horse, that is, the first state, namely the Church made white in baptism; or especially the preachers who bear God everywhere; or the flesh of Christ, free from sin. And he who sat upon it had a bow: namely Christ, possessing Scripture, who enlightens his own and slays his enemies. And a crown was given to him, that is, divine Scripture, which wounds the hearts of hearers and resists heretics. And he went forth conquering, so that he might conquer in himself or in his members the nations, [Col. 0334D] because what preachers do we attribute to God. Or he went forth from the bosom of the Father or from the Virgin’s womb, conquering so that he might conquer in himself and in his members the devil and all the proud. The first state of the Church is signified by the white horse, that is, by the Church innocent, whitened with virtues, and strong against heretics. Of the seven states, therefore, the first is the state of preachers, understood by the white horse; the second by the red horse; the third by the black horse; the fourth by the pale horse, when those converted from Jews and gentiles suffered persecution from heretics; the fifth, in which we are [Col. 0335A] now, in which the rage of heretics is not so great; the sixth, in the time of Antichrist; the seventh, the day of judgment. Therefore, after the Lamb fulfilled what had been foretold of himself and established his Church in faith through the testimony of prophets and angels, he opens its understanding so that it may understand the Scriptures; and through preachers he outwardly declares what it must suffer for this faith, and what aids or what crowns he sets before his soldiers. For, if he had recalled its restoration but remained silent about tribulations, they might more quickly fail when tribulation unexpectedly arose against them. He adds again:

VERS. 3.—And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying: “Come and see.” As though he said: When he had opened the second seal, that is, [Col. 0335B] when the apostles and their disciples began to preach to unbelieving Jews, in the order of vision and of time, I heard the second living creature of the aforesaid four orders preaching the Gospel [f. *Evangelium*], saying: “Come and see.” As though it said plainly: O John, beware of the red horse, for what it has in its heart it carries out in deed.

VERS. 4.—And another, red horse went forth; and to him who sat upon it it was given to take peace from the earth, so that people might kill one another; and a great sword was given to him. As though he said plainly: Another red horse, unbelieving and opposed to the former horse, went forth from friendship with God: namely, open and bloodthirsty persecutors. And to him who sat upon it—that is, [Col. 0335C] the devil—it was given, that is, permitted, to take peace, namely outward peace, from the land, that is, from Judea, through Titus and Vespasian; or it was permitted him by God to remove all tranquility of mind from those who are devoted to earthly things. And people might kill one another with a material or spiritual sword, by urging one another to evil action and by giving each other a perverse example. And a great sword was given to him, that is, great power to kill, because not only lesser persons but also greater ones, such as Peter and Paul, were slain. Seeing that the Church was being established to fill the place from which he himself had fallen, the devil strives to overthrow everything, first openly and then secretly [Note: [Col. 0335D] The conjunction “and” is superfluous; the Gloss has it in place of “everything.”].

VERS. 5.—And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: “Come and see.” As though he said: When the Lamb had opened the third seal—that is, when the disciples of the apostles passed from the Jews to the gentiles—I heard the third living creature, namely the third order of preachers, saying: “Come and see, and beware of the black horse.” And behold, a black horse, and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand. As though he said: Behold, a black horse, that is, the gentile people or heretics, obscuring their vices by certain good works. And he who sat upon it—namely, we attribute to the devil what his followers do through him—had a balance in his hand, [Col. 0336A] because he was not permitted to harm except insofar as it was allowed him. Or he had a balance in his hand because heretics say that they possess true discernment in the Scriptures, and boast that they fulfill in deed what they preach. Seeing that he had not succeeded through open persecutors, the devil sends heretics to contend against the Church with false arguments, so that they may deceive it more easily. He adds again:

VERS. 6.—And I heard as it were a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying: “A bilibris of wheat for one denarius, and three bilibres of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and oil.” As though he said plainly: Because a greater danger is presented here, I heard help, as it were the voice of an angel standing in the midst of the four living creatures—that is, in the common benefit of the preachers—saying: [Col. 0336B] “Do not fear, O faithful, for they will not be able to harm you; and you devils, do not harm them, for you will not prevail. For a bilibris of wheat for a denarius”—namely, a vessel holding two full sextarii of wheat, that is, the Church possessing faith and works—is purchased for a single denarius, namely Christ’s blood. “And three full bilibres of barley, purchased for a denarius,” that is, those who, with faith in the Holy Trinity, fulfill the two commandments of charity; and “do not harm the wine and oil,” namely those refreshed with wine, that is, Christ’s blood, and anointed with oil, that is, the Holy Spirit. A pound consists of twelve ounces, and twelve is composed of two sixes; by this are understood those who, through twofold love, fulfill the commandments of the twelve apostles. Or, do not harm those [Col. 0336C] who fulfill the four Gospels with faith in the Holy Trinity and with love of God and neighbor, full of wheat—that is, abounding in nourishing doctrine—because they have been redeemed by one, that is, the sole denarius, namely the unique blood of Christ. Here wheat denotes the more perfect, who, ground by tribulation and baked by fire, are sweet food to God [Note: [Col. 0336D] From Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVI, ch. 26.]. A hemina weighs one pound; when doubled, it yields a sextarius. A sextarius is of two pounds; when taken twice it is called a *bilibris*; when taken four times, it becomes, by the Greek name, a *conix* [f. *choenix*]; when multiplied fivefold, it makes a *quinarius* or *gomor*. Therefore, seeing that he could succeed neither through open tribulations nor through open heresies, the devil sends ahead false brothers who, under the habit of religion, possess the nature of the red and black horse. He then says:

VERS. 7.—And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying: “Come and see.” As though he said plainly: I heard the voice of the fourth living creature warning me thus: “Come to the faith and see,” that is, beware; and this is necessary because:

VERS. 8.—Behold, a pale horse: namely, those dead in spirit or those who afflict themselves like hypocrites, who fast and keep vigils in order to appear pale. And he who sat upon it, namely the devil, had the name Death, because through [Col. 0337A] him death entered the world (Rom. V); or literally, because he kills some in body and others in soul. And hell followed him, that is, those insatiable in earthly vices imitate him; or those who are to be placed in hell obey him. And power was given to him over the four parts of the earth, to kill with sword, famine, death, and the beasts of the earth. As though he said: Power was given—that is, permitted—to that horse, namely to heretics, over the four parts of the earth, that is, over all wicked people dwelling everywhere, or over Jews and gentiles, heretics and false Christians, to kill the faithful with a material sword or the sword of persuasion, with famine of the divine word, with spiritual death, and with beasts of the earth, namely beastly agents. Here it is openly shown that almighty God appointed angels over individual nations according to their merit. And as he set a good angel, that is Michael, over the good, so he set an evil angel over the evil. Hence comes this statement: “There is no helper for me in all these things except Michael, your prince” (Dan. X). The four angels who were set over the four chief kingdoms were likewise not good, but evil. If God sends this famine, in what respect does the devil sin? This question is easily resolved: what God does by just judgment, the devil does by assault, deception, and evil will. It follows:

VERS. 9.—And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held. In this fifth state he adds consolation for those upon whom such things are inflicted, so that they may endure them patiently and await two robes, one in the present and the other in the future. As though he said: I saw beneath the altar souls humbling themselves to Jesus Christ their head; or beneath, that is, hidden, because in this life no one fully perceives how they are there. I mean the souls of those slain by certain tribulations or by open martyrdom for the word of God, that is, the commandment which they fulfilled, and for the testimony which they bore before kings and governors. As though it were said more plainly: I saw beneath the altar of God, that is, beneath the divine power which is effected through spiritual sacrifice, namely through the contrite and humble heart which is upon the altar—that is, upon Christ, who is our foundation—and [Col. 0337D] beneath him, because he preserves for us, as if in secret, the recompense of that sacrifice: the souls of those slain for God’s testimony, which they bore before others. In the tabernacle of Moses there were two altars: first, one covered with bronze and open to the sky, where sacrifices were burned; and another within, before the veil, on which only blood and incense were placed, and which was overlaid with gold (Exod. XXVI; XXX). These two altars signify two peoples. By the outward altar is signified the carnal, that is, Jewish people, which thinks that it can be saved and justified solely through works and sacrifices of the law; by the golden altar within, however, are signified the spiritual persons of both Testaments, who think that they can be saved not merely through the law or through sacrificial works, but rather through [Col. 0338A] faith in Christ. Hence the patriarch David says: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit, a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L).

VERS. 10.—And the souls of those slain cried with a loud voice, that is, with great longing, saying: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell upon the earth?” As though they said plainly: How long, O Lord, holy—namely loving holiness in works—and true in promises, why do you not judge, by making a distinction between good and evil, and avenge, by inflicting punishments, our blood upon those who dwell in love upon the earth, that is, in earthly pleasures? Christ is understood as the altar, upon whom the faithful offer and whom they have as their defense. [Col. 0338B] Or the souls themselves are the altar, from which smoke pleasing to God proceeds, and which were smeared with blood, now being beneath, that is, in a dignity lower than that which they will have. The saints seek vengeance from their enemies in charity in two ways: namely, that those predestined to eternal life may be converted from evil to good; or that those whom God foreknows are to be damned may die and cease to sin, so that through this they may suffer a lesser punishment in hell. Therefore the souls of those slain cry to God because they desire greater joy and the fellowship of the saints, and agree with divine justice in the condemnation of the ungodly.

VERS. 11.—And a white robe was given to each of them; and it was said to them that they should rest yet [Col. 0338C] a little while, until their fellow servants and their brothers, who were to be killed as they were, should be completed. As though he said plainly: A white robe, that is, the blessedness of the soul, was given to each of them; and it was said to them by God, namely inspired, that they should rest—that is, patiently await—a little while, until their fellow servants, servants indeed for the sake of the Lord himself, and their brothers who were to be killed as they were, whom they ought to await in love, should be completed.

VERS. 12.—And I saw, when he had opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as a sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood. As though he said: There was a great earthquake, namely the persecution of Antichrist; for, as the Lord says, there will then be such tribulation as has not been and will not be from the beginning of humankind (Matt. XXIV). And the sun became black: those in whom God shines will be reckoned guilty and sinners, like a sackcloth of hair, retaining their brightness within themselves. Or some will fall into darkness. Or Christ, the true sun, now bright, will be dark in the time of Antichrist—that is, shining with no miracles. And the moon, that is, the holy Church, became wholly like blood, because it will suffer everywhere.

VERS. 13.—And the stars of heaven, that is, saints once bright, fell, leaning upon the earth, as a fig tree casts its unripe figs, namely useless and empty fruits that will never come to maturity: persons who appeared good but were not, when it is shaken by a great wind [Col. 0339A]—that is, when the Church has been shaken by the great wind of Antichrist’s persecution. Then this will occur.

VERS. 14.—And heaven, that is, the Church, withdrew like a rolled-up book, namely concealing its preaching from the ungodly, like a closed book. And every mountain, namely those eminent in virtue, and the islands were moved from their places: that is, all the faithful who are amid the fluctuations and buffeting of those who embitter will be moved from their places, that is, from their offices; namely, they will be separated in faith and deed from wicked people, as it is written: “Come out from her,” that is, Babylon, “my people, and do not touch what is unclean” (Isa. LII).

VERS. 15.—And all the kings of the earth and princes and tribunes—those greater and lesser persons resisting the vices of the flesh—[Col. 0339B] and the rich in good works, and the strong against the devil’s temptations, and every slave, that is, a married person or a servant of God, and every free person, free from sin or marriage, hid themselves in caves, namely seeking the aid of angels, who are lofty mountains, and among the rocks of the mountains, which are strong and indissoluble: that is, they will implore help from the apostles, evangelists, and other saints, so that through their prayers they may obtain the judge’s mercy.

VERS. 16, 17.—And they say to the mountains and rocks: “Fall upon us and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, because the great day of their wrath has come.” As though they said: O mountains and hills, that is, all you saints, descend to us with great affection and compassion, and by your [Col. 0339C] prayers hide us from the face—that is, from the wrath and presence—of him who sits upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, namely Jesus Christ, God and man. Therefore it is necessary that you fall upon us, that is, assist us by your prayers, because the great day of their wrath has come. For who will be able to stand unless helped by your prayers?

## CHAPTER VII
VERS. 1.—“After these things,” he says, “I saw four angels standing upon the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, so that no wind might blow upon the earth, or upon the sea, or upon any tree.” As though he said plainly: I saw four angels—that is, four demons—standing, that is, remaining, upon the four corners of the earth, even in its remotest regions. They are called four for the four parts of the world. The devil is called an angel, that is, one sent by God for the testing of the good and the deception of the wicked. Thus in the Book of Kings the prophet Micaiah says to King Ahab of Israel when he inquired: “I saw the Lord sitting upon His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him, at His right hand and at His left. And the Lord said: ‘Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ Then a spirit came forth and stood before the Lord and said: ‘I will deceive him.’ And the Lord said to him: ‘How?’ And he said: ‘I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ [Col. 0340A] And the Lord said: ‘You shall deceive him and prevail; go forth therefore and do so’” (III Kings 22).

Moreover, an evil spirit is sent by the prince, the devil, for the overthrow of all. “Holding,” he says, “the four winds of the earth”: that is, hindering spiritual men who temper the earth of the Church, so that the wind may not blow upon the earth—that is, upon those dwelling on earth or given over to earthly vices—nor upon the sea, that is, upon the nations, or those flowing with diverse vices.

[Note: [Col. 0339] More correctly, the collateral gloss: “Upon those dwelling in the islands, or those abounding in diverse vices.”]

Hence it is said: “Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song of Songs 4). As the wind raises clouds, waters the earth, makes it fruitful, and renders its face cheerful, so preaching [does the same to] the minds of men. In a time of tribulation nothing is more necessary than preaching; but the devil strives to hold it back in every place [Col. 0340B]. The four good angels are justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance. Conversely, the four evil ones are injustice, imprudence, weakness, and intemperance. Having described the Church’s manifold warfare, he adds that during this warfare the devil stands ready to harm, yet is restrained by God, lest His own grow faint in any respect. He adds again, saying:

VERS. 2.—“And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God.” As though he said plainly: In opposition to those four evil angels, I saw another angel, namely, the Angel of Great Counsel, ascending—that is, causing His own to ascend—from the rising of the sun, namely from God the Father; and thereby having the seal of the living God, that is, the cross by which He would seal His own, or power equal to God the Father; or else freedom [Col. 0340C] from sin, through which God is manifest, because apart from Him every human being is a sinner.

This angel is that stone cut out without hands, which shattered the statue made of four metals; and He loosed these four winds (Dan. 2). From the time when Christ expired on the cross, He ascended and conquered the devil; gradually, through His preachers, He illuminated the world with faith, as the sun does with light. Or He ascends from the rising of the sun, that is, from the Father, increasing in wisdom and age insofar as He is man (Luke 2). Or, according to His humanity, He ascends from Himself, because He did not assume flesh through intercourse with a man, but Himself created it—He who is the rising of the sun.

VERS. 3.—“And he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: [Col. 0340D] ‘Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we seal the servants of our God upon their foreheads.’” This angel, that is, the Son of God and of the Virgin, cried with a loud voice to the four evil angels, to whom it was given to harm the earth and sea—that is, the Jews and the embittered Gentiles—when in His Passion He restrained the demons by great authority, saying: Do not harm, beyond what is permitted you, the earth and sea, namely the Jews and Gentiles; nor the trees, namely those who, having already surpassed an earthly manner of life, have grown in the knowledge of God; until—that is, until I inwardly in the heart, and the priests of the Church outwardly—seal the servants of our God upon [Col. 0341A] their foreheads, that is, distinguish by the sign of the cross those predestined to life.

The sign of the cross is borne upon the forehead so that it may not be concealed in tribulation; for the signing of the breast is the confession of the heart. By this sign, if not in actuality, yet in faith, the ancient Fathers were sealed. The faithful bear the sign of the holy cross in body and soul. In the body, because they are outwardly signed on the forehead in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. In the soul, because they imitate Christ’s Passion, crucifying themselves with their vices and desires. Hence in the Old Testament it was commanded that they put some of the lamb’s blood upon both thresholds (Exod. 12). For it does not profit anyone to bear the outward sign unless one also receives it inwardly; for faith, if it does not have works, avails nothing (James 2). Therefore children are signed upon their foreheads—that is, openly—so that before kings and governors they may not be ashamed or hesitate to preach the cross of Christ. They are also signed upon the breast, that they may keep this very thing in memory. He adds again:

VERS. 4.—“And I heard the number of those who were sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed, from every tribe of the sons of Israel.” As though he said: I understood what manner of persons were to be sealed in the book of life, and I heard the number of the sealed: namely, one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed, perfect in works, from every tribe of the sons of Israel—that is, from all nations imitating the faith of Jacob. He gives a finite number because God comprehends all under a definite number. For the faithful labor in order that they may be one hundred, that is, perfect [Col. 0341C] in works; and that they may be thousands, that is, perfect in virtues.

He does not say that one hundred and forty-four thousand are sealed from every race of those who see God because there are no more; but he chose this number rather than another because the whole Church is signified by one hundred and forty-four thousand, and as perfect, because the number twelve multiplied four times makes forty-eight. This fourfold multiplication signifies the universal Church spread through the four regions of the world. Moreover, the number forty-four multiplied three times signifies the Holy Trinity, whom the Church worships. He then says:

VERS. 5.—“From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed.” [Col. 0341D] Judah is interpreted “confessing.” This is sufficient for those who are not reserved for performing works, but die immediately after they confess God in baptism, their confession having been made. These confessors are undoubtedly sealed, that is, predestined to eternal life. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). Judah, who is first in order, was fourth by birth; thereby it is indicated that spiritual lineage must be considered.

Antichrist will be born from the tribe of Dan; and therefore it is omitted here, in order that he may be shown as one to be cast out from every number of the saints. Of him the patriarch Jacob, when blessing his sons, said: “Dan shall be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path,” etc. (Gen. [Col. 0342A] 49).

(He does not say that twelve thousand are sealed from the tribe of Judah—that is, from confessors—because no more are sealed from the same class; but by twelve, which is multiplied through three and four, he signifies the Church spread through the four regions of the world and worshipping the Holy Trinity.)

[Note: [Col. 0341] The words enclosed in brackets are absent in another manuscript and are altogether superfluous.]

“From the tribe of Reuben,” that is, “one who sees sons”: from those, namely, who, having been preserved after making confession in baptism, see their sons—that is, their good works which they perform after baptism—twelve thousand are sealed. “From the tribe of Gad,” that is, “of temptation,” or “girded”: from those, namely, who, by doing good, are tempted by the devil and thus are found girded, ready for battle and resistance, and strong so that they cannot be overcome by him; likewise twelve thousand are [Col. 0342B] sealed. To them Paul says: “Be strong in battle, and fight against the ancient serpent” (Heb. 4).

VERS. 6.—“From the tribe of Asher,” that is, “the blessed”: from those, namely, who attain this name, being called blessed, by enduring temptations, twelve thousand are sealed. Hence it is said: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation; for when he has been tested, he shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love Him” (James 1). “From the tribe of Naphtali,” that is, “of breadth”: from those, namely, who after overcoming temptations widen and enlarge their hearts in love of God and neighbor, so that they even love their enemies, twelve thousand are sealed. “From the tribe of Manasseh,” that is, “forgetful”: from those, namely, who after their love [Col. 0342C] of God and neighbor has been enlarged forget all things belonging to this world, twelve thousand are sealed.

VERS. 7.—“From the tribe of Simeon,” that is, “the hearing of sorrow”: from those, namely, who, after they rise to such perfection that they consign all things of this world to forgetfulness, continually remember the sins in which they were formerly involved and grieve over them, having sorrow—twelve thousand are sealed. “From the tribe of Levi,” that is, “of addition”: namely, those who perform what is enjoined upon them and also add to themselves precepts which are not commanded, such as virginity, and those who give away part of even their plain clothing; twelve thousand are sealed. “From the tribe of Issachar,” that is, “of reward”: from those, namely, who continually add to the penance which they undertake for their past [Col. 0342D] sorrow over sins, in which they remember that they once were, and do this so as thereby to obtain the reward of eternal blessedness—twelve thousand are sealed.

VERS. 8.—“From the tribe of Zebulun,” that is, “the dwelling of strength”: from those, namely, who do not refuse labor but sometimes, for the need of their brethren, descend from Mary to Martha; twelve thousand are sealed. “From the tribe of Joseph,” that is, “increase”: from those, namely, who persevere in Christ’s warfare and always ascend from virtue to virtue, twelve thousand are sealed. “And from the tribe of Benjamin,” that is, “son of the right hand”: from those, namely, who are [Col. 0343A] sons of propitiation and attribute nothing to themselves but everything to divine goodness; they labor to be placed not among the goats but at God’s right hand; twelve thousand are sealed.

VERS. 9.—“After these things,” he says, “I saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from all nations and tribes and peoples and tongues, standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands.” Up to this point he has shown that those foreseen for life are with God under a definite number; now he shows that, as regards us, they are innumerable, saying: I saw a great multitude which no one living in the flesh could count by a certain number, not only from the twelve tribes of Jacob but from all nations, even barbarians and Scythians, and [Col. 0343B] from all the tribes and peoples of the Jews; for one people is contained in a city; and from tongues, because in many places there are diverse languages within one people; standing before the throne, ready to obey God the judge, and so as to be seen in the sight of the Lamb—that is, in the good pleasure of Jesus Christ, God and man—clothed, that is, adorned, with white robes signifying God’s yoke, first in baptism and afterwards in tears. These things are in the present; and palms, that is, the sign of victory, are in their hands—that is, in their works in the present, and especially in the future.

He added this as though he wished to say: Although I set down a definite number, namely one hundred and forty-four thousand, nevertheless I saw many more, innumerable, and not only from the twelve tribes of Israel but also from all nations. Therefore, although he had seen those to be designated figuratively under a definite number and only from the sons of Israel, he now openly teaches that by that number all the faithful are meant, and by the twelve tribes all nations are to be understood. And all those innumerable peoples are not slack in their conduct.

VERS. 10.—They “cried with a loud voice,” that is, with great desire, addressing their greeting to God: “Salvation belongs to our God,” that is, God the Father—not through ourselves, but through the Lamb, who has salvation, remission, good works, and eternal glory in His power; and God the Father sits upon the throne—that is, upon ourselves, in whom He judges—in order to save us; and salvation belongs to the Lamb, His Son. And when that innumerable [Col. 0343D] multitude rendered glory and honor to the God of the Trinity:

VERS. 11.—“All the angels stood around the throne, and the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell before the throne upon their faces and worshipped God, saying: Amen.” As though he said plainly: All the angels—that is, the preachers of the faithful mentioned above—stood as helpers around the throne, and the elders, and the four living creatures: that is, around the greater and lesser persons whom they had already begotten in the faith by their preaching; they stood in the guardianship of the whole Church. And they fell before the throne, that is, humbled themselves before God so that they might be seen by Him and give others an example of humility, upon their faces, reasonably, like the [Col. 0344A] elect. The reprobate fall backwards, because they neglect to foresee the evils that will follow them in the future; but the elect fall upon their faces, because they provide for themselves in the future. Those former angels, that is, preachers, instructed their subjects to ascribe to God the seven blessings which follow.

VERS. 12.—They “worshipped God, saying: ‘Amen’: that is, truly and faithfully, let blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and strength be to our God for ages of ages. Amen.” It is fitting that Amen, that is, truth, be ascribed to God in His promises; and blessing, that is, the exaltation He possesses above every creature. The sequence is: Amen, that is, truly and faithfully, is always to be ascribed to God; blessing, that is, the Spirit of the fear of the Lord, because He gave us the Spirit so that we might fear Him; and glory, that is, the Spirit of understanding, through whom we know how to discern the mysteries of the law; and wisdom, that is, the Spirit of wisdom, through whom we experience some savor of the knowledge of Divinity; and thanksgiving, that is, the Spirit of piety, through whom we know how to give Him thanks for benefits bestowed; and power, that is, the Spirit of counsel; and strength, namely the Spirit of fortitude, for ages of ages. Amen.

When blessed John had seen the multitude in such dignity, he is instructed to attend to the way by which it could ascend there, that he might teach others likewise to consider it. Hence follows:

VERS. 13.—“And one of the elders answered, saying to me: ‘Who are these clothed in white robes, and whence have they come?’” As though he said plainly: As I was pondering [Col. 0344C] their great blessedness, one of the elders, satisfying and increasing my desire, answered, that is, explained to me: Those clothed in robes—that is, adorned with the twofold yoke of the two Testaments, namely with the law, in the law, and under the law, as regards the unwilling—how worthy they are, how they are to be imitated; who are they, and whence have they come to this dignity? Or, more plainly: These who are clothed in white robes, that is, immortality and impassibility—who are they? Tell me, and from where have they come here?

VERS. 14.—“And I said to him: ‘My lord, you know.’” I do not know, but teach me. As though he said plainly: I, being subject to you, ought to learn from you, not resolve this question. And he said to me: “These are those who have come [Col. 0344D] out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” As though he said: These are those who came, come, and will come out of great tribulation to the great dignity which you see; and because no one is without sin, they washed their robes—that is, the innocence received in baptism, or their bodies—and made them white in the blood of the Lamb, through faith in His Passion. They make their robes—that is, their bodies—white in Christ’s blood when they imitate the example of Jesus Christ, their Head: either by suffering for Him, by patiently enduring insults inflicted by others, or by mortifying themselves with vices and desires for Christ’s love.

VERS. 15.—“Therefore,” he says, “they are before the throne of God, and serve Him day and night in His temple.” As though [Col. 0345A] he said: Because they came out of great tribulation and made their robes white in the Lamb’s blood, they are therefore before God’s throne—that is, before God the Judge in the fellowship of angels—and serve Him day and night by continually praising Him, in His temple, namely in the present Church or in heaven. And they have this perseverance from God, who sits upon the throne and dwells over them, that is, guards them; and therefore:

VERS. 16.—“They shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more,” because they shall enjoy the living bread and the fountain of life; “nor shall the sun fall upon them,” namely a greater or outward tribulation, “nor any heat,” namely a lesser, inward tribulation.

VERS. 17.—“For the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, shall rule them,” namely from virtue to virtue in the present life, and thereby in the future shall lead them to fountains of the waters of life: that is, to God the Father, who is the inexhaustible fountain of life. “And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes,” by removing the will to sin, which is the cause of groaning and tears—that is, every sorrow, whether for their sins, adversity, exile, or other such things.

## CHAPTER VIII

VERS. 1.—“And when He had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” As though he said plainly: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, namely the things that were to happen after the death of Antichrist in the conversion of the remnant, there was silence in heaven, because after Antichrist’s death [Col. 0345C] there will be peace in the Church, as it were for half an hour, because the day of judgment will come quickly. Therefore, after the persecution of Antichrist, holy Church will devote itself to prayer and divine contemplation, but as it were for half an hour, because the mind of the elect in this mortal life both perceives something of the heavenly rest and yet cannot remain long in what it has perceived. He adds again, saying:

VERS. 2.—“And I saw seven angels standing in the sight of God, and seven trumpets were given to them.” They are called seven angels because they proclaim the four Gospels to be held and the faith of the Holy Trinity; for seven consists of four and three. They are said to stand in God’s sight because, having trampled down all earthly pleasures, they cleave to God in contemplation, always consider the will of Him who is absent nowhere, [Col. 0345D] and accomplish in deed what they know pleases Him.

“I saw,” he says, “seven angels,” that is, all preachers of this present life, which runs through seven days, namely imitators of the holy apostles, standing in God’s sight, that is, opening the sealed writings of the prophets; and seven trumpets were given to them, that is, the office of preaching. In this third vision, the subject is the seven angels sounding trumpets for the destruction of the Church’s enemies, in likeness of those priests who, sounding trumpets, destroyed the walls of the city of Jericho. The intention of this vision is sufficiently clear. As though he said: When I understood the salvation of the righteous, I understood from another side the condemnation of the wicked through the office of preaching enjoined upon God’s servants.

[Col. 0346A] VERS. 3.—“And another angel came and stood beside the altar, having a golden censer.” The other angel is understood to be Christ, who came—that is, united humanity to Himself—and stood before the altar, ready to offer Himself upon the altar of the cross, having a golden censer, that is, a body full of divinity. Or the golden censer is the apostles, who are vessels of fire, that is, of the Holy Spirit, and from whom prayers go forth and rise before God. And much incense was given to Him: from the saints, prayers acceptable to God the Father are offered to Christ, or through Christ, in order that He might give—that is, present—them to the Father, not all prayers, but those prayers of the saints that please God; for they sometimes ask for what ought not to be asked: upon the golden altar, that is, God the Father, who [Col. 0346B] is above Him, which is before the throne, namely in the good pleasure of God the Father sitting upon the throne.

VERS. 4.—“And the smoke of the incense rose from the prayers of the saints, from the hand of the angel, before God.” As though he said plainly: Since much incense was given to Him, with God’s fire kindled inwardly, the smoke of the incense rose—that is, compunction produced by the zeal of prayer—proceeding from the prayers of the saints through the hand of the angel, namely through the hand of Christ, and this before God the Father. And this angel is Christ.

VERS. 5.—“And he took the golden censer,” namely the apostles and evangelists and their imitators, “and filled it with fire from the altar,” namely with the same Spirit with which He Himself was full, for the illumination of the nations, [Col. 0346C] “and cast it upon the earth,” namely upon those who were fit to bear fruit. And from these heralds of Christ there came thunders, that is, preachings threatening eternal punishments. Hence it is said: “Every tree which does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3). And voices, namely their sweet persuasions leading into faith; hence it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). And lightnings, that is, miracles, by which the faithful and those predestined to life are enlightened, while unbelievers are blinded, attributing them rather to the devil than to God; and a great earthquake: that is, earthly people were greatly moved by their preaching, some coming to faith, others to persecute Him and His own.

[Col. 0346D] VERS. 6.—“And the seven angels,” that is, all preachers imitating the apostles, “who had the seven trumpets, prepared themselves”: first they fulfilled in deed what they were to preach by word, in order that they might sound the trumpet; first they corrected themselves, so that afterwards they might correct others; or they foresaw what was suitable for each person. These angels, that is, the preachers who will exist after the death of Antichrist, will so recall that persecution which occurred in the first state of the Church that the remnant to be saved may thereby have an example of patience. As though they said: O remnant of Israel, believe and preach as the apostles and their imitators believed and preached concerning Christ’s incarnation, birth, Passion, resurrection, and so forth.

[Col. 0347A] VERS. 7.—“And the first angel sounded the trumpet, and hail and fire mingled with blood came to be, and it was cast upon the earth.” As though he said: And the first angel, namely he who was previously the white horse, in the order of the narrative—or because the blinding of the Jews happened first while the apostles preached—sounded the trumpet, that is, preached; and in his preaching hail and fire mingled with blood came to be, namely these two things. This figure signified that the first preachers proclaimed hail, that is, wrath striking and crushing: that is, slaying unbelievers in this age; and fire, that is, eternal damnation in the other; and it was cast upon the earth, namely upon the Jews who had been cultivated by the Law and the Prophets. And a third part of the earth, that is, of earthly people, [Col. 0347B] was burned—namely blinded by God and condemned by His ministers. The two parts signify the righteous, the perfect and the less perfect; but all the reprobate are to be understood by the third part. And a third part of the trees, that is, of philosophers—whose two parts are the wiser and the less wise—was burned, here and in the future, by God’s wrath. And every green grass was burned. All those resting in the bloom of the world are compared with grass and will quickly burn. In contrast, those refreshed by the Lord’s loaves recline upon grass, because they suppress within themselves all carnal pleasures (Matt. 14).

VERS. 8.—“And the second angel,” namely after the apostles, that is, the red horse, “sounded the trumpet; and as it were [Col. 0347C] a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea.” And the second angel, he says, in the order of the narrative, sounded the trumpet, that is, preached; and as it were a great mountain, namely the devil, who is called a mountain because of his pride, burning with the fire of envy, was sent to harm into the sea, namely the Gentile people tossing in carnal vices. Although he was there before, he is now said to be sent because, as some withdraw, he strives to hold others fast. Therefore, after this was fulfilled—when the Jews were blinded and the apostles turned to the Gentiles—the two parts, namely the perfect and imperfect, believed; the third, that is, all the reprobate, were given over to a reprobate mind.

VERS. 9.—“And a third part of the sea became blood,” that is, sinners; “and a third part of their creatures died,” that is, were blinded—namely those Gentiles who were considered worthier than others because of certain good works, and who had souls, that is, discernment; and a third part of the ships, namely those governing others, [Col. 0347D] died. Therefore, because the devil could not blind all Jews and Gentiles, he introduced heretics.

VERS. 10.—“And the third angel sounded the trumpet: and a great star, burning like a torch, fell from heaven; and it fell upon a third part of the rivers and upon the springs of waters.” The third angel, in the order of the narrative, sounded the trumpet, and his preaching contained this: A great star fell from heaven, namely the envious devil—not because he shines, but because he transforms himself into an angel of light—burning like a torch: that is, he sets on fire, destroys, and consumes himself [Col. 0348A] and others; and he fell upon a third part of the rivers and springs of waters, corrupting through heretics the Gospels and the reasons of our faith. Springs are called those places in which the summary and, as it were, the origin of the whole faith is contained, such as the Gospel. The rivers drawn from them are the expositions of the saints, in which there are two senses belonging to the faithful, namely the historical and the allegorical; the third is that of heretics, when they confirm their heresies by corrupt expositions of Scripture.

VERS. 11.—And the name of the star, that is, of the heretics, is called wormwood because of its bitterness. “And a third part of the waters,” that is, of the Scriptures, “became wormwood,” that is, bitterness—the error of the heretics; “and many irrational people died [Col. 0348B] in their souls from the waters,” that is, through the teaching of heretics, because they became bitter, namely without the savor of charity. By wormwood is expressed the perverted doctrine of heretics, because by their falsehood they turn the sweetness of faith into the bitterness of unbelief, error, and evil action; for all their action and doctrine is turned into bitterness.

VERS. 12.—“And the fourth angel,” in the order of the narrative, namely the pale horse of hypocrites, “sounded the trumpet; and a third part of the sun was struck,” namely blinded by the withdrawal of grace, that is, all the greater and more learned persons; “and a third part of the moon,” namely the lesser persons; “and a third part of the stars,” that is, the simpler persons, “so that a third part of them was darkened,” namely so that it lost [Col. 0348C] knowledge and good action. For the part of the New or Old Law which the heretics themselves preached, by interpreting it badly they made a third part; and a third part of the day did not shine, namely those enlightened by the greater persons of the New Law; and likewise of the night, namely those enlightened by the lesser persons of the Old Law.

For when the devil had blinded some of the Jews and Gentiles and converted some to heresy, he finally set about attacking the very children of the Church and carried off some both among the greater and among the lesser. “A third part of the sun, and a third part of the moon, and a third part of the stars was struck,” he says. In the sun the open error of heretics is shown; in the moon or stars, the hidden error, because some of them deceive those whom they can by open, others by secret, persuasions in hidden places (Exod. 7). “So that a third part of them might be darkened,” he says. Heretics are first wounded secretly in mind, but afterwards they are darkened when they are openly expelled and anathematized by the Church.

He has narrated these four condemnations as though past, since they are seen daily in the Churches; but he causes the other three to be foretold as future, so that he may teach that they will occur in the last times and be graver than the former; this may also be applied to the consolation of those in the present. But lest the destruction of such people be ascribed to God, the statement about the aforesaid luminaries, “A third part of them was struck, so that it might be darkened,” should be understood as Pharaoh’s heart is said to be hardened by God, whose hardness He does not mercifully soften [Col. 0349A] (Exod. 7). For it is not the sun’s fault that, by its rays, it brings blindness to bleary eyes; rather, the fault must be attributed to the eyes, which grow dark from light. Almighty God, however, who makes good use even of our evils, is accustomed to work many good things from them. For the error of schismatics stirred up the doctors of the Church to defend the truth of the faithful; undoubtedly, they would never have devoted themselves with such zeal to expounding the Scriptures if the falsehood of error, resisting truth, had not grown. He then says:

VERS. 13.—“And I saw and heard the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice: ‘Woe, woe, woe to those dwelling on earth!’” As though he said plainly: I saw and heard, that is, I firmly understood, the voice of one eagle—namely the preaching of one order of preachers—flying subtly, that is, spiritually contemplating the marrow of the Law, which conceals, that is, contains, God’s mysteries, through the midst of heaven: that is, through the Church, which conceals divine sacraments within itself; saying with a loud voice throughout the world, or with great constancy, or because it sounded through all the earth and was to be feared by all.

The eagle signifies all preachers who perceive distant things with their minds and, going around the Churches in preaching, fortify them against future things. All are one because they tend to the same end. Holy Church is aptly called an eagle because, having spurned the desires of earthly pleasures, it is lifted up by inward contemplation to heavenly things. The Church flies through the midst of heaven on the wings of contemplation, because on either side it possesses the whole world in its elect. But let us hear what the eagle’s voice announces: “Woe, woe, woe to those dwelling on earth!” As though he said plainly: Woe to Gentiles, woe to Jews, woe to heretics dwelling upon the earth, not to the children of the Church, on account of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound trumpets. For of the seven angels, four have already been said to have completed their office; three still remain to expound three woes.

## CHAPTER IX

VERS. 1.—“And the fifth angel,” in the order both of the narrative and of time, “sounded the trumpet.” This angel proclaims that the devil fell; here, therefore, is the condemnation of those whom the devil sends to prepare the ways of Antichrist. “And I saw,” he says, “a star,” that is, the devil, who was called Lucifer because of the great brightness God had given him, “falling from heaven,” that is, from the fellowship of good angels, “to earth,” namely ruling over earthly persons and striving with all his strength that no mortal may ascend to his place.

He explains from what source [fomite; printed *fonte*, “source”] the flame of the heretics, of which he had said a little above, grew, saying: “And the key was given to him,” namely the power and eloquence of obscure doctrine, “of the pit of the abyss,” namely leading to hell. The pit of the dark abyss is the more profound heretics, because they drown others in perverse opinions. Therefore he is said to receive the key, that is, power, over them, because then he will not be restrained by God as he is now [Col. 0350A]. Or the key is the rulers of the world, through whom heretics work many evils; for they would not dare to say things so great and such as these unless supported by temporal power.

VERS. 2.—“And he opened the pit of the abyss; and smoke ascended from the pit like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.” As though he said: The devil opened the pit of the abyss, namely the heresies hidden in the hearts of perverse men; that is, he openly displayed the teaching of the heresiarch and thus overthrew many. And the blinding smoke of the pit ascended: namely their teaching was made manifest, a teaching lacking the light of truth, like the smoke of a great furnace—that is, like the teaching of Antichrist, who is smoke purifying the good and reducing the wicked to ashes. And through this the sun, namely the Law, was held cheap by heretics; and the air, that is, the Church, was darkened by the smoke of the pit, namely by the darkening doctrine of heretics [Col. 0350B].

The great furnace is the final affliction which will occur in the time of Antichrist. “The sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit,” he says, because just as the air is neither on earth nor in heaven but in between, so the Church of the faithful is not on earth, because it despises earthly things; nor is it bodily in heaven, but is, as it were, in the middle, so that it is raised from earth and lifted toward the heights of heaven.

### Verse 3

And from the smoke there went out over the whole world locusts—that is, the disciples of heretics, leaping from heresy to heresy and gnawing away the crop of the Church. Heretics’ disciples are rightly compared with locusts, because they neither fly upward through knowledge, [Col. 0350C] nor walk firmly through good conduct; but they leap through pride and fall into worse things, because they are destroyers of good people. And power was given to the locusts, as the scorpions of the earth have power: they appear harmless in appearance, but grievously injure with their tail. The scorpion is pleasant in face, but secretly strikes with its tail. Therefore he compares heretics to the scorpion, because, just as the scorpion’s sting is not felt at the moment it strikes, but afterward the poison gradually spreads, so those deceived by heretics do not perceive it, but are at last destroyed. And God restrains the deceits of heretics, although they themselves do not understand it.

### Verse 4

They were commanded not to injure unto the death of the soul the grass of the earth—that is, the untrained and [Col. 0350D] readily deceived—nor any green thing, that is, persons already advanced, nor any tree, namely those already bearing fruit in good works; but only human beings—that is, absolutely no one except those who do not have upon their foreheads, in truth, the sign of the living God, which is charity, by which the children of God are marked: namely, those who do not dare openly to confess that they are Christians.

### Verse 5

And it was given to them not to kill them, but that they should be tormented for five months. As though he said: God will not grant them power openly to kill bodies, nor secretly to deceive souls, but to torment them for five months—that is, throughout the whole time of this present life, in which people use the five bodily senses. And their torment is like the torment [Col. 0351A] of a scorpion when it strikes a person; for although power is given them to torment the children of the Church, they do not openly inflict tortures, but accuse them before the rulers of the world, because they do not dare act by themselves.

### Verse 6

And in those days, fearing a fall, people will seek death—that is, they will desire martyrdom—and will not find it, so that they may be rendered more approved; and they will desire to die and to be with Christ (Phil. 1), and death will flee from them, because care for the flock will bind them to labor, and therefore they will be preserved for suffering. Having shown how they harm—namely, through deceits and hidden assault—and God’s restraint in both respects, he now shows what they themselves are and by what means they are able to act. Let blessed John therefore say under what likeness they [Col. 0351B] will show themselves, so that they may be recognized more readily and avoided more carefully.

### Verse 7

And the appearances of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle. As though he said openly: They were not truly locusts, but like locusts, like horses prepared for battle, because they are swift to range about and fierce in attacking, and do not foresee whom they rush upon, whether fellow citizens or enemies. And upon the heads of the locusts—that is, in their minds, where they are proud both in themselves and before others—were things like crowns resembling gold: that is, victory acquired by their false opinions and disputations. Or, crowns like gold upon the heads of the locusts—that is, upon the teachers, masters, and rulers of heretics, upon the earlier heretics—were acquired [Col. 0351C] not by true wisdom but by fabrications of falsehood. And their faces—that is, their countenances—were like human faces. As though he said plainly: By this false resemblance they do harm, because they show themselves to be human and devout, whereas inwardly they are rather savage and beastly. They call themselves rational; for although they are teachers of error, they nevertheless mingle in certain true things in order to deceive more effectively. Another true likeness is also set forth.

### Verse 8

And they had hair like women’s hair, and their teeth were like lions’ teeth. As though he said: They had hair—that is, fallen and effeminate habits—which cling inseparably to them and hang from them for the deception of others, like [Col. 0351D] women’s hair; that is, habits like those of women, soft and pliant toward every vice; or disciples attached to them and inclined toward every vice. And their teeth—that is, they themselves, tearing others to pieces—were like lions’: they had the tearing and the stench of lions. By human faces and women’s hair both sexes are denoted, because they deceived not only men but women also. Thus women themselves defended them, as Constantine’s sister recalled Arius from exile, and Justina defended Arius’s teaching.

### Verse 9

And they had iron breastplates—that is, obstinate hearts, which the arrow of truth cannot penetrate; or judgments fortified with deceptions, which truth breaks apart. And the sound of their wings—that is, the tumult of their opinions, which they create once reason fails them—was like the sound of many horses’ chariots running to battle. Just as different chariots are drawn along different roads by different horses toward the same battle, so heretics, although adhering to different heresies, attack the Church with one mind. For heretics wish to liken their false doctrine to the preaching of the faithful, who run throughout the whole Church upon the four wheels of the four Gospels toward the spiritual reward.

### Verse 10

And they had tails like scorpions; for although they likened themselves to good preachers, yet in the tail—that is, at the end of their speeches—they had stings by which they harmed. Or, when neither their argument nor their tumult prevails, they seek the aid of rulers, who are called tails [Col. 0352B] because, in order to bind people, they terrify and flatter, and sting secretly. And the stings—that is, sin, because they cause people to sin—are in their tails, namely at the end of their words. Their power is to harm wicked people for five months, that is, according to the five bodily senses, throughout all the days of their life. Yet they will not have this power from themselves, except by God’s permission. Having shown what they are in themselves, he also shows through whom they can do these things, saying:

### Verse 11

And they had over them as king the angel of the abyss—that is, the devil ruling over earthly things—whose name in Hebrew is Labadon, in Greek Apollyon, and in Latin he has the name Exterminator. As though he said: Beware of this evil angel, O Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, because Christ’s Gospel was written and received in these three [Col. 0352C] languages. What is found written in some manuscripts as *Abadon*, where the first letter is A, is written falsely through copyists’ error; rather L must be placed first there, and it must be called *Labadon*, as blessed Jerome says in the Hebrew interpretations. This same malignant angel of the abyss has in Latin the name Exterminator, namely, one who drives from the homeland of life; for just as the name “Gatherer” is fitting for Christ, so the name “Exterminator” is fitting for the devil. Hence: “He who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11).

### Verse 12

One woe has passed, and behold, two woes—that is, two persecutions—still come after these things. “Woe” sometimes signifies temporal misery and affliction, but sometimes eternal condemnation. Concerning temporal affliction the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18). And again: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Matt. 24). And blessed Job says: “If I am wicked, woe is me; but if righteous, I shall not lift up my head, filled with affliction and misery” (Job 10). Again, “woe” signifies eternal condemnation where it is written: “Woe to the wicked in evil; the recompense of his hands shall be rendered to him” (Isa. 3). Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who now laugh, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6). Likewise he says: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Mark 9). And again: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire,” etc. (Matt. 25). But the eagle flying through the midst [Col. 0353A] of heaven foretold three coming woes, one of which is said to have passed in the preceding narrative, or in the tribulation which occurred in the times of the holy apostles and martyrs. Thus two woes are said still to remain, either to be narrated or to be fulfilled at a later time under Antichrist. It follows:

### Verse 13

And the sixth angel sounded the trumpet, namely in the order of narrative and of time: the order of preachers in the sixth state, or Christ. For this is the condemnation of the wicked who shall exist in the time of Antichrist. And he heard one voice from the four horns—that is, because of the four Gospels, which preach Christ’s divinity and humanity—of the golden altar, where blood was placed, upon which whatever is offered is most gladly received by God the Father; this altar is before the Lord’s eyes, from whom it is always illuminated by a most radiant gaze. Hence the Psalmist says: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Ps. 33).

### Verse 14

“One voice,” he says, “speaking to the sixth angel”: namely, heralds of an earlier time forewarn those who shall exist in the time of Antichrist what they are to do; to the angel, I say, who had the trumpet, namely existing in the preachers of the sixth state. Christ is called the altar; the horns of the altar are preachers who uphold Christ and are ready to die for him, just as blood was placed upon the horns of the altar. Or the altar is the Church sacrificing itself to God, in which are horns—that is, defenders of others—all tending toward the same end [Col. 0353C] (Lev. 4). Or the four horns of the altar are the four Gospels, which teach people to expose Antichrist’s deceptions. The altar is rightly called golden, because the Church of the righteous is indeed illuminated by the everlasting wisdom of God. Of this Solomon says: “Receive wisdom as gold” (Prov. 16). In the blood poured upon the horns of the altar were signified the holy martyrs to be washed for Christ by their own blood. But let us hear what the voice going out from the four horns of the altar says: “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” It is as though the altar’s voice said to the sixth angel: “Release,” that is, preach that all those devils are released who, having power to harm the inhabitants of the four parts of the world, [Col. 0353D] are still bound by the Lord in the great river Euphrates—that is, in the powerful and wealthy persons of this age, flowing from vice to vice—so that, being as it were bound in them, they may work more openly through those handed over to them. For those unclean spirits, reigning in the four parts of the world, will be released in the time of Antichrist; they had been restrained at the coming of Jesus Christ, God and man. Or “release” means “preach them to be released,” so that the elect may beware, just as the Gospel says concerning the fig tree, “Cut it down” (Luke 13), that is, preach that it is to be cut down. Since the Euphrates is a great and most deep river, descending from the pleasant dwelling places of paradise, through it is understood the great and most profound power of God. Or because it runs through Babylon, it signifies the confused and most profound [Col. 0354A] doctrine of heretics, or that they themselves are in the depth of vices.

### Verse 15

And the four angels were released, who had been prepared to kill the children of God in an hour—that is, in childhood—and a day, namely in “dolestia” [probably *adolescentia*, adolescence], and a month, that is, in youth, and a year, namely in decrepit old age. Or they were prepared in an hour—that is, continuously through half a year—and a day, namely through a year; and a month, namely through the second year; and a year, that is, through the third year. For Antichrist’s persecution will last three and a half years. They were therefore prepared in an hour, as stated, and a day, and a month, and a year, to kill the third part of humankind—that is, all the reprobate.

### Verse 16

[Col. 0354B] And the number of that cavalry army was twenty thousand times—that is, through twenty thousand iterations—destroying ten-thousands. “I heard,” that is, I understood, their number: that they were more numerous than the good. Ten thousands signify holy men made perfect by the commandments of the Law and the Gospel; against them is set the double number of the wicked, because the wicked are more numerous than the good. Or it is double because it consists of malignant spirits and reprobate human beings. Thus the array of the heretics’ army was destroying ten-thousands—that is, the perfection of the ten commandments—through twenty, that is, twice ten, and through twice a thousand, because the army of the wicked is multiplied from malignant spirits and reprobate people. These numbers, namely “twenty [Col. 0354C] thousand times,” are an irregular construction, as also “seventy times seven,” because it consists of two adverbs; it ought to consist of a noun and an adverb, thus: “twenty thousand times,” or “a thousand times twenty,” just as “seventy times seven,” or conversely “seven times seventy.”

### Verse 17

And thus I saw the horses in the vision, and those who sat upon them, having breastplates fiery, hyacinth-colored, and sulphurous. As though he said openly: Just as I understood that they rode in order to destroy others, so I understood that they did these things through the devil, whom they carried as horses. Or the devils are horses upon which the wicked are founded; and those who sat upon them—that is, devils, or impious persons founded upon the devil—had fiery breastplates, namely opinions leading to hell; hyacinth-colored ones, that is, of the color [Col. 0354D] of a smoky stone; and sulphurous ones, foul with blasphemies against God. “They sat,” he says, “upon them,” that is, they towered over them by opinions from which follows eternal punishment, where there are fire, smoke, and stench. Or the breastplates are eternal punishments, which never release those whom they seize. Hyacinth is clouded in color, and by it is understood the smoke of idolatry, which appears brighter from a distance; for the life of the wicked does not wish to be seen in light, because, according to the Lord’s saying, “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3). Therefore idolatry is denoted by the color of smoke, which commonly comes forth from sacrifices to idols. And the heads of the horses—that is, the chief ministers of demons—were like lions’ heads, because they tear, stink, and compel people by punishments to confess. And from their mouth—that is, from their openly evil preaching—proceeds the fire of envy, sulphur, namely the stench of blasphemy, and the smoke of idolatry. Otherwise: fire is covetousness, smoke pride, sulphur the stench of evil works. Above, in the plague of the locusts, he saw human faces; here, lions’ faces, because heretics display something of humanity, whereas the ministers of Antichrist compel people by punishments to confess what they teach by words and signs.

### Verse 18

By these three plagues the third part of humankind was killed—that is, made wicked—namely by the fire, smoke, and sulphur that proceeded from their mouth, that is, from their evil and open persuasion. He repeats these things so that we may retain them in memory and thus guard ourselves against them more effectively.

### Verse 19

[Col. 0355B] For the power of the horses—that is, of the heretics—is in their mouth, namely in evil preaching, and in their tails, because if they cannot harm openly, they do so by hidden deceits. Truly the power of heretics is in their mouth, because those whom they cannot deceive by the perversity of error, they deceive through the rulers of this world. And truly they have power in their tails: for their tails are like serpents, because they flatter to one’s face and secretly inject poison; having heads, namely other leaders who bite severely and do harm in these things.

### Verse 20

And the rest of humankind, who are wholly without Christian faith, who were not killed—that is, although they were not killed by these plagues—did not repent of the works of their hands, namely of the other sins not previously mentioned, which they wickedly conceived and carried out; so that, after repentance had been performed, they might no longer worship demons and images of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which ought not to be worshiped because they can neither see nor hear nor walk.

### Verse 21

And truly they did not repent of their works—that is, of open murders—nor of their sorceries (*veneficiis*, evidently corrupted in the printed text), namely hidden murders, nor of their twofold fornication, namely uncleanness and idolatry, nor of their thefts; yet they are dead to God in the soul. Therefore the third part—that is, all the reprobate from the Church—as likewise all Jews and pagans who were never baptized, [Col. 0355D] although they were not dead in these aforementioned plagues, are nevertheless dead in their souls and alienated from the kingdom of God.

## Chapter 10

### Verse 1

And I saw another mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow upon his head. As though he said plainly: I saw another mighty angel, namely the messenger of the Father’s will, opposed to the devil and his members through the mighty remembrance and faith in the hearts of believers.
