[Col. 0405D] VERSE 8.—But as for the fearful and unbelieving—namely, those who through fear of punishments avoid receiving the faith, or abandon it after receiving it, despairing of this renewal—and the accursed, that is, the excommunicated; and poisoners, for them there shall be the greater eternal pain. Or we may understand them as those who lord it over others by human power. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called poisoners” (Luke 22), that is, evildoers. There are also fearful persons within the peace of the Church, who fear to do good works because of dread of secular rulers. Of them it is said: “There they trembled with fear, where there was no fear” (Ps. [Col. 0406A] 13). Therefore murderers, fornicators, poisoners, idolaters, and all liars—namely, those for whom lying is habitual—their portion shall be, that is, they shall participate more or less, in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.

Blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0405D] *On Lying*, no. 25.] that there are eight kinds of lies; yet there is no lie that is free from sin. Hence it is written: “A mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1); and, “You will destroy those who speak a lie” (Ps. 5). Some, nevertheless, attempt to maintain that it is not a sin if a lie is uttered for righteousness’ sake, as we read happened in Egypt with the midwives (Exod. 1). In the case of Rahab it was indeed a sin, but it was cleansed by a work of mercy. For it would have been worse had she betrayed them to [Col. 0406B] death than that she denied them and lied (Josh. 2, 6). One thing, however, we must firmly maintain: no kind of lie remains unpunished unless it has here been remitted through repentance or some work of mercy. Having described the glory which the saints will possess, he says by what merit or with what aid they will receive it.

VERSE 9.—And one of the seven angels came to the hearts of the righteous, namely Christ, having bowls full of the seven last plagues; and he spoke with me, saying: “Come,” that is, enlarge your understanding, “and I will show you the bride, the Lamb’s wife”; namely, by what merit the faithful ought to attain this aforesaid renewal, and why the Church is the bride and why she is the Lamb’s wife. And that it might be believed more fully [Col. 0406C] by me,

VERSE 10.—He carried me away in the Spirit, through an understanding of the Old and New Law, onto a great and high mountain. Christ is the mountain, because he is the defense of his own; great, because he fills the whole world; high, because he is unconquerable. And he showed me upon that mountain the city, that is, the Church gathered for righteous living and fortified with holy virtues; holy, namely firm and stable in its purpose; and great, namely powerful to overcome adversaries: Jerusalem, that is, seeing and contemplating eternal peace, descending from heaven from God, namely from God’s hidden counsel.

VERSE 11.—Having the glory of God, namely [Col. 0406D] knowledge of God; because, dwelling in heaven by the Spirit, it possesses the same glory of God as the angels. And truly that city, that is, the holy Church, is glorious, because its light is like a precious stone: according to its measure, it has light like Christ, who was and is firm in purpose, radiant in virtues, and providing pasture for his faithful. Hence the saying: “The Lord guides me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has placed me” (Ps. 22). Therefore the Church’s light is like that of a jasper stone because of the greenness and steadfastness of faith; like crystal, because its faith is transparent to all. For as jasper is hard and green, so the Church flourishes in faith and is steadfast in it.

[Col. 0407A] VERSE 12.—And it was truly holy and steadfast because it had a wall, that is, Christ the defender, who is great in Zion and high with the Father: great according to his humanity, high according to his divinity. Or the wall of this city, that is, of the Church, consists of defenders, who are great through good living and high—that is, unconquerable—and powerful to overcome persecutors. This city is shown to be great not only by its wall, but also by its gates, that is, by the twelve patriarchs, through whose example others are brought into the faith. It is likewise shown to be great because at the gates, that is, in the faith and in the footsteps of the patriarchs and prophets, it had twelve corners, that is, the apostles, who are corners—that is, defenders of others. And the names [Col. 0407B] written, that is, all the faithful who hold the four Gospels and faith in the Holy Trinity, are held in remembrance: these are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel. For all the faithful are founded and, as it were, inscribed in the prophets and patriarchs, and stand firm in love for the earlier Fathers. I mean the names written upon the gates, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel: that is, of all those who spiritually, in both the old and the new Church, are sons and imitators of those who see God, following the examples of the holy patriarchs, prophets, and apostles who contemplated God.

The number of the twelve gates, which by their threefold number are distributed through the four regions of the world, pertains to the ministry of the twelve [Col. 0407C] apostles, through whom faith in the Trinity is spread throughout the fourfold world. Therefore, as was said, that city had twelve such gates:

VERSE 13.—On the east there were three gates, through which the Jews entered, from whom the Lord arose; or they signify those coming to the worship of God from childhood. In this place the east signifies the Jews, from whom the Sun of Righteousness arose. Thus they have three gates, because faith in the Holy Trinity came first to them. And on the north three gates, through which the Gentiles entered, who were cold and barren, coming to this city in old age. The north, therefore, signifies the cold nations which believed after the Jews. And on the south—that is, for those coming in youth—[Col. 0407D] three gates, through which the faithful were to enter from the coming of the Lord until the west, that is, until the last age of the world, in which Elijah and Enoch will preach the four Gospels and faith in the Trinity. Thus on the south are three gates, that is, from the brightness of faith which comes from Christ’s advent. And on the west three gates, for those coming in decrepit old age. Thus on the west are three gates, that is, from the last age of the world, which through Elijah and Enoch will receive faith in the Trinity.

VERSE 14.—And the wall of the city, that is, the faith of Christ which fortifies the city itself, had twelve foundations, namely the twelve patriarchs through whom it is founded; for they first held this faith, and all who come to faith rely upon them. [Col. 0408A] And upon those twelve foundations, that is, upon the patriarchs and prophets—in their memory and preaching—were the names of the twelve apostles and of the Lamb: that is, the remembrance of Christ whom they foretold would come, and the remembrance of the apostles and of all who hold the four Gospels and faith in the Trinity. For the faith which these hold, those understood as future and foretold. Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7).

VERSE 15.—And he who spoke with me, namely the angel in the person of Christ, according to my good pleasure, had a golden measuring reed, that is, Holy Scripture composed by divine wisdom, which touches and enlightens the hearts of the faithful, in order to measure [Col. 0408B] the city; for not all were of equal merit, whom he measured by divine wisdom. He therefore measured the city in order to give superiors and subjects, according to their measure, an understanding of the Scriptures themselves according to the capacity of those using them; and its gates, that is, those who bring others into the faith; and its wall, namely the defenders of others.

VERSE 16.—And the city is laid out as a square, and its length is as great as its breadth. The four sides of the city are faith, hope, charity, and action. These are equal, because as much as one believes, so much one hopes and loves; and as much as one loves, so much one acts. It is therefore laid out as a square, because it is strong in faith, patient in hope, broad in charity, and effective in work. Or the four sides are the four [Col. 0408C] principal virtues, of which one ought not to exceed another in a person: prudence in seeking good and avoiding evil, followed by temperance, so that a person withdraws from pleasures; then fortitude, so that one performs what one understands; and afterwards justice, so that one so moderates one’s actions as not to seem overly righteous or wise. Again he continues: “And he measured the city,” that is, the present Church, “with the golden reed,” that is, through divine Scripture, “for twelve thousand stadia”: namely, those who are perfect in faith in the Holy Trinity and who, as if by stadia, hasten to the heavenly homeland from the four quarters of the world. A stadium is a place for running, and denotes those striving for the prize. The number forty is considered perfect in Sacred Scripture for many reasons: because of the Lord’s fast completed over forty days, or because of the Decalogue of the Law and the four Gospels, in which the perfection of the Decalogue is contained. Likewise the number four is sacred because of the four rivers of Paradise or the four books of the Gospel, also because of the four regions of the world or the four principal virtues. Therefore, in the higher sense, the measure of a man, which is that of an angel, rightly measures the Church, because the glory of angels and human beings in heavenly blessedness will be equal. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22). Or it is called the measure of a man, which is that of an angel, because [Col. 0409A] as many angels remained in heaven after the fall of the archangel, so many human beings will ascend from earth to heaven. It follows: its length, that is, faith or long-suffering; its breadth, namely charity; and its height, that is, hope or contemplation, are equal.

VERSE 17.—And he measured its wall, that is, the defenders of others, as they labor both for themselves and for others in the commandments of the Law, at one hundred and forty-four cubits, the measure of a man, which is that of an angel. The cubit, in which the hand is found, signifies action. In the literal sense, this shows that an angel appeared to him in the form of a man, in order openly to teach [Note: [Col. 0409D] Edition: “Deo notet” (meaning uncertain).] that he who was signified was the true angel, that is, the Son of God, and true man.

VERSE 18.—And the construction of its wall was of [Col. 0409B] jasper stone, that is, of steadfast faith. For if anyone is trained to be a defender of others, he has this from the faith which he holds and preaches firmly, as the green stone signifies. But the city itself, that is, the Church, was pure gold like clear glass. Gold signifies wisdom; glass, purity of faith, because the holy Church professes with its mouth what it believes in its heart. These words cannot refer to the present Church, in which each person’s conscience is hidden, but to the time when the Lord comes, “who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4), and the consciences of all individuals will be made manifest to everyone. For whatever is thought by anyone will be wholly seen by another. Thus each person will then be visible to another as he now cannot be visible [Col. 0409C] to himself. He had said that in this city there were walls, gates, and foundations, and that among these some were greater and some lesser. Here, however, he explains what the wall itself is like, and what the city itself is like, and its foundations and gates.

VERSE 19.—The foundations of the wall of the city are adorned with every precious stone, that is, with patriarchs and prophets whom the defenders of the Church have as their foundation. They were decorated and adorned with every precious and steadfast virtue, and among them the first foundation was jasper, that is, strong and steadfast faith. The first foundation is green jasper, which signifies the unfading greenness of faith. The second is sapphire, like the clear sky, which when struck by the rays of the sun emits a burning brilliance. It signifies the loftiness of the saints’ hope, whose citizenship is in heaven; renewed by the true sun, they seek the eternal homeland more ardently and teach others to seek it. The third is chalcedony. Like the pale fire of a lamp it shines and gleams under the open sky, not in a house. It signifies the flame of inward charity, which does good in secret; but when it is commanded to benefit others, it immediately reveals what brightness it has within. It resists engravers; glowing at the sun’s stroke or at the rubbing of fingers, it draws straws to itself. So the saints, when they are sorely afflicted, become more ardent and cannot be overcome by anyone; indeed, they draw to themselves straws, that is, the more fragile. The fourth [Col. 0410A] is emerald, of extraordinary greenness, surpassing grasses and leaves. This stone is found in the cold of Scythia, that is, it signifies a strong confession of the same faith amid adversities, which are denoted by cold. Because this faith has been made known so greatly to the world through the Gospel, it is called the fourth on account of the four Gospels.

VERSE 20.—The fifth is sardonyx, black below, white in the middle, red above; it signifies the holy martyrs, who are red through suffering, inwardly white in conscience, yet despised in their own eyes through humility. Since this humility descends from bodily weakness, and the body is governed by five senses, it is fifth. The sixth is sard, blood-red in color; it signifies the glory of martyrs, and is therefore placed sixth, because Christ was crucified on the sixth day and [Col. 0410B] at the sixth hour. The seventh is chrysolite, which shines like gold and sends forth fiery sparks: that is, spiritual preaching amid miracles. For gold signifies heavenly wisdom, and sparks exhortation or miracles. Because this comes about through the Holy Spirit, it is placed seventh. The eighth is beryl, by which the perfect activity of preachers is denoted; for water shines when struck by the sun. This does not occur unless it is polished into a hexagonal shape, because brilliance is sharpened by the reflection from its angles. Water signifies human understanding; the brightness of the sun, divine wisdom through which it shines more fully. But neither human nor divine wisdom shines perfectly unless it is brought to completion through works. The perfection of works is understood through six, since the work of the world was made in this number. This [Col. 0410C] stone burns the hand of its holder, because one joined to a holy man is kindled by his way of life. The ninth is topaz, which is the more precious the rarer it is. It is two-colored, shining most brightly with gold and heavenly radiance; when touched by the sun’s brilliance, surpassing the brightness of all gems, it uniquely draws viewers’ eyes to itself. If you polish it, you dull it; if you leave it in its natural state, it is brighter. Nothing among royal treasures is more costly. It signifies the contemplative life, which holy kings prefer to every wealth of works and jewels of virtues, and toward which they direct their minds especially; and they do so the more fully the more often they are enlightened by divine grace. Its golden color comes from inward charity, and its heavenly hue from the sweetness of contemplation; this contemplation is cheapened by the attrition of the world or by worldly business. For scarcely can anyone at once be afflicted by bodily pains and with a tranquil mind contemplate the joys of heaven. And as the active life is in the eighth place, so the contemplative life is in the ninth, which is that of the angels, whose orders are nine; or because it is one degree short of the tenfold number of reward, namely death. The tenth is chrysoprase, green, with a certain admixture of gold, purple with golden drops. It is also found in India; and it signifies those who merit through charity the greenness of the eternal homeland, who display to others the purple of martyrdom, and who merit to follow the example [Col. 0411A] of the Lord; they are in India, namely near the rising of the sun. And because they await reigning with Christ, they are in the number ten, and the Decalogue will be fulfilled through the charity which was ninth [Note: [Col. 0411] More correctly, the marginal gloss: “which does not end.”]. Thus in chrysoprase the work and reward of martyrdom are indicated. The eleventh foundation is hyacinth, which changes with the air: in clear weather it is transparent; in cloudy weather it withers. It indicates teachers raised to lofty things, yet condescending through charity for their neighbors’ benefit. The twelfth foundation is amethyst, purple, emitting gentle flames in a mingled color of violet and rose. Purple splendor bears the appearance of the heavenly kingdom; violet signifies the modesty of the saints, and the rose the precious death of the saints, who amid adversities [Col. 0411B] are in mind on high; and who pour back flames of charity not only upon one another but also upon enemies. Thus amethyst signifies the continual remembrance of the heavenly kingdom in the mind of God’s humble servants. Such, as stated above, are the foundations of this city.

VERSE 21.—And the twelve gates are twelve pearls: that is, each of the twelve apostles possessed together all the aforesaid stones, each gate being one pearl. He explains this by considering them individually. As though he plainly said: “I said there are twelve gates; and since this is so, those twelve gates—that is, the apostles and their imitators, preaching faith in the Holy Trinity [Col. 0411C] through the four regions of the world and bringing others into the Church—are pearls, each through the instruction of individual teachers; namely, those called from whatever part of the world to faith in the Trinity are resplendent in virtues. And the individual gates, that is, the individual apostles—indeed all such persons—are from each of the aforesaid pearls or stones; namely, they rest and are founded upon the patriarchs and prophets, who among all were adorned with all the aforesaid stones.” Such are the walls and gates of the city, as I have said. But the street of the city—that is, the simpler members of the Church, who make freer use of the world, such as married persons—is pure gold, namely full of wisdom and charity, and free from the mortal stain of the world, like transparent [Col. 0411D] glass, concealing no defilements within themselves. The streets of the city, therefore, are the humblest members of the Church, whose life is less strict, not possessing these aforesaid stones; nevertheless, they are pure gold, having charity without hypocrisy and purity of faith, denoted by clear glass; or because evil persons can recognize their own wickedness in these persons’ works as in a mirror.

VERSE 22.—And I saw no temple in it, that is, no place of prayer and supplication, which will have no place there. Where there will be no sin, undoubtedly there will also be no temporal sacrifices. For the Lord God the almighty Father is its temple, namely its complete [Col. 0412A] rest, and the Lamb, that is, his Son, upon whom they will offer a sacrifice of praise.

VERSE 23.—And that city has no need of the sun of the New Testament, nor of the moon of the Old Testament, to shine in it. Here the holy Church needs sun and moon for the service of day and night; there, however, it does not, because almighty God will fully enlighten it. For the long-promised glory of God the Father has enlightened it; and its lamp, that is, its light—namely the humanity containing within itself divinity for the illumination of many—is the Lamb, the Son namely of God and of the Virgin.

VERSE 24.—And the nations shall walk in its light, that is, they shall remain eternally in that brightness, namely in hope of its light, or through the rays of its knowledge which they already possess. And that light will be so great [Col. 0412B] in the future that, until the end of the world, the nations shall walk: namely, those who lived as Gentiles, having abandoned gentile ways, shall always walk, that is, advance from good to better. And the kings of the earth—that is, rulers of the Church, who govern themselves and others—shall bring their glory, that is, those acquired for God, on whose account they will be crowned, and their honor into that city, namely the purity of their conscience, in order to obtain it, after the manner of victors who transfer spoils into their cities. These words are to be referred not to the reward of the future but to the labor of the present time, because the saints will not then labor in walking, but after labor will rest, living blessedly. Thus they now walk by its light, namely [Col. 0412C] through faith in Christ and the other virtues, so that afterwards, having reached their homeland, they may rest in that light itself, that is, in the contemplation of God himself.

VERSE 25.—And its gates shall not be shut by day. These things concerning the future are expressed in the present. At times preaching is withheld, lest thieves enter and trample when it is night, that is, a time for ambushes. But because there will be perpetual day there, all fear is removed. For there will be no night there, namely in the future.

VERSE 26.—And the holy apostles and other teachers shall bring, that is, present to God the Father, the glory—that is, the purity of the consciences of the faithful—and the honor of the nations into it, that is, the nations themselves, honored for their good works. Having spoken of the city’s excellence, [Col. 0412D] lest any false brother presume to belong to one of these ranks, he determines who will enter and who will not. Therefore, although the gates are not shut,

VERSE 27.—Nothing defiled shall enter it, that is, defiled with others through consent; nor one doing abomination, namely some mortal sin; nor falsehood, namely one who delights in inventing lies. Why should I enumerate each case? No one shall enter it except those written in the book of life, that is, in the foreknowledge of the divinity and of the Lamb, namely God and the man Jesus Christ, through whom that life shall be given to those written in God’s remembrance.

## CHAPTER 22

[Col. 0413A]

After describing the location of the city, its dignity, walls, and foundations, he also shows the refreshment which God grants to the city itself, both in the present and especially in the future, saying:

VERSE 1.—And he showed me a river of the water of life, shining: that is, the abundant refreshment of the saints both in the present and in the future. I mean refreshment, namely flowing water, that is, eternal blessedness, like crystal, because the saints shall shine eternally; proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, namely from those in whom God principally sits, because especially in them, and through their instruction, the lesser shall be crowned—that is, in confessors, who unite lesser persons to God.

[Col. 0413B] VERSE 2.—In the midst of its street, namely of those who have lived a less strict life. In the image of water it is indicated that they attained this blessedness through the cleansing of baptism. And on either side of the river was the tree of life: that is, according to both natures of Christ, Christ himself is for his own the tree of life. Its first fruits were the apostles, bearing twelve fruits through each month, namely prophets and apostles who bear fruit in faith in the Trinity through the four regions of the world, in every age or continually—that is, at all times. I mean the tree yielding its fruit, namely the refreshment of souls. Christ, therefore, is the tree of life yielding its fruit through twelve months, that is, through the twelve apostles; for Christ is the day or year, while the apostles are the hours or months, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11). As though he said: “Because you are subject to me, I must [Note: [Col. 0413D] The marginal gloss states more clearly: “I must be served, not you.”] provide for you.” There are also other trees there yielding their fruit, that is, saints who render rewards according to merits to those subject to them. And the leaves of the tree—that is, Christ’s commandments, which cover and adorn the fruit, namely the words of his preaching—are for the healing of the nations, namely Gentiles who have been converted, if they fulfill them. Therefore Christ will yield fruit, and the apostles and their successors after them, by preaching, will scatter throughout the whole world the leaves, that is, Christ’s commandments. Or on this side of the river, that is, in this life, we have the tree of life, namely Christ’s body and blood, by which we are refreshed; [Col. 0413D] beyond the river, namely in the future, we shall have him present himself. Or by “on this side of the river” we understand the time before baptism, and by “beyond” that which was after baptism, so that we may show that the faithful under both the Old and the New Law are saved through Christ. This was prefigured by Moses, who led the children of Israel as far as the river Jordan, and by Joshua son of Nun, who led them from the river Jordan into the land of promise. It follows:

VERSE 3.—And there shall be no more curse, that is, no more withdrawal of grace. This is the curse of the Law: “Cursed is he who does not perform all the words of the Law” (Deut. 27). But the throne of God and [Col. 0414A] of the Lamb shall be in that city: that is, God the Father, Christ God and man, and the Holy Spirit—namely the Trinity, one God—shall rest eternally in them; and his servants shall serve him, not from fear but from love, with eternal praise.

VERSE 4.—And they shall see his face, not in an enigma as now, but as he is.

VERSE 5.—And night, that is, transgression or ignorance, shall be no more. And they shall not need the light of a lamp, that is, the teaching of the Old Law or of some mediocre preacher, nor the light of the sun, namely the teaching of the New Law or of some outstanding doctor. This is inconsistent with needing others’ light, because God will enlighten them, and they shall reign with him for ages of ages. As at the beginning he set forth a commendation of the vision, so also at the end he sets it forth. He continues again, saying:

VERSE 6.—And he said to me, namely the same angel: “These words,” that is, whatever is shown in words and figures, “are most trustworthy,” namely fit to receive belief, “and true,” because they shall be fulfilled. And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants the things which must soon happen. As though he said: “O John, you ought therefore rightly to believe what you have heard and seen, because he who has in his power the gifts of the Holy Spirit, through whom the prophets spoke, sent his angel [Note: [Col. 0414D] Supply here: “to show.”] not to kings or philosophers, but to his servants, the things which must soon occur”; that is, the reward of the saints, because it cannot remain unfulfilled, namely beyond the very brief moment of this present life. And truly they shall occur soon, because he himself says:

[Col. 0414C] VERSE 7.—“Behold, I come quickly.” And he also said this to me: “Blessed is he who keeps,” that is, fulfills in deed, “the words of this book.” As though he said more plainly: “Because I shall come swiftly to render to each according to his works, blessed is he who keeps the words of this book, that he may be judged worthy of everlasting reward.” As the angel commends these things to John, so John commends them to his disciples. As though he said: “These things were shown to me not for my own sake, but for the salvation of the whole Church and that you might believe me.” Therefore the angel spoke to me.

VERSE 8.—And I, John, who am accustomed to announce to you nothing false, heard the voices and saw these things indicated by figures. And after I had heard and seen, I fell down, that is, humbled myself, in order to worship before the feet of the angel who showed me these things, that is, for this reason.

[Col. 0414D] VERSE 9.—And he said to me: “See that you do not do this; for I am your fellow servant, and of your brethren, namely the prophets—that is, preachers—and of those, namely those obedient to preachers, who keep in faith and deed the words of this book. Worship God, because he alone is to be worshiped.”

VERSE 10.—And he says to me: “Do not seal,” that is, [Col. 0415A] do not keep under seal, but make public to all the words of the prophecy of this book.” Since it could be said that it would be evil to prophesy to evil persons, because they would be punished more severely, he is told not to refrain for that reason, because it is good. Therefore the time is near in which all things shall be examined. Accordingly,

VERSE 11.—Let him who harms, harm still: namely, after the revelation of the book, let the evils which the wicked inflict be inflicted upon the good; and let him who is in filth, namely in his own wickedness, become filthy still; and let him who is righteous, giving good things to others, do righteousness, that is, give more abundantly still; and let him who is holy be sanctified still, advancing toward better things. This is a permissive mode, not an optative or imperative one. For almighty God often permits a person, because of past sins, to fall into graver ones. Hence the Lord also says through the Psalmist: [Col. 0415B] “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me. And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart; they shall go in their own devices” (Ps. 80). In this sentence it is plainly shown that the fault of disobedience preceded, through which they were permitted by God to go after their pleasures. And truly, he says, the time is short, because

VERSE 12.—“Behold, I come quickly, and my reward,” that is, the reward of my own, “is with me,” namely in my consideration, “to render to each, to one more and to another less, according to his works.” And I shall be able rightly to do this because

VERSE 13.—“I am Alpha and Omega,” that is, the first, in whom all things had their beginning, and the last, in whom all things shall be consummated—the beginning, namely, and the end.

[Col. 0415C] VERSE 14.—Blessed are those who wash their robes, namely their bodies and lives, in baptism and in the tears of repentance, so that they may have power over the tree of life, that is, so that they may be able to eat from the tree of life and, through the gates—namely through the faith of teachers—enter the holy city Jerusalem; for “this is the gate of the Lord, and the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. 117). Since he had said, “Let him who harms, harm still; let him who is filthy, become filthy still,” lest any evil person should say, “Since I am evil, why should I repent?” he says: Not only are those blessed who possess greater perfection; but even those who have defiled the robes they received in baptism, if they wash them again and repent of having sinned, shall be blessed. But,

VERSE 15.—Outside are dogs, namely barkers and [Col. 0415D] babblers; and poisoners, that is, the unclean and heretics; the shameless, murderers, idol-worshipers, and everyone who loves falsehood by listening to it and does it by inventing it.

VERSE 16.—“I, Jesus, sent my angel,” that is, my messenger, “to testify these things to you in the churches.” And I am therefore to be believed, because I, Jesus, am the root according to divinity, that is, the support, and the offspring of David according to humanity; the bright morning star, namely the great brightness announcing the day, that is, future blessedness, through my resurrection accomplished in the morning.

VERSE 17.—And the Spirit and the bride, that is, the holy Church, say: “Come.” But the Spirit says it through hidden inspiration, and the Church through open preaching, to every person outside the Church: [Col. 0416A] “Come,” namely to knowledge of this book. And he who hears, that is, understands, should say not only to believers but also to every unbelieving person: “Come.” And not everyone indiscriminately should come, but only the one who thirsts, that is, desires to believe. And no one should come under compulsion, but only the one who wills should receive the water of life through baptism, freely, without the price of merits, through which baptism one goes to eternal life. After blessed John commended this book through God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; through the angel, through himself, and through the faithful, because he knew that some in Asia, to foster their own errors, would add or subtract something, he adds an excommunication, saying: “And I, John,

VERSE 18.—Testify,” that is, with the testimony of God [Col. 0416B] the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I say to everyone hearing the words of the prophecy of this book: “If anyone adds to these things what ought not to be added, God shall add upon him,” that is, to his punishment, “the plagues written,” that is, mentioned, “in this book.”

VERSE 19.—And if anyone takes away anything from the words of this prophecy, God shall take away his portion from the tree of life, that is, from Christ the giver of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book. This I say, that is, I excommunicate; and that same Christ

VERSE 20.—Who bears witness to these things says: that is, he excommunicates with me the one who has changed anything. Christ also says: “Amen,” that is, all the aforesaid things are true. “I come quickly.” As though he said: “Beware, for I am coming quickly to judge [Col. 0416C] the world.” “Amen,” that is, what I say is true. “Come, Lord”: we pray that you may come to reward. The whole Church speaks this in John, desiring that Christ come to judgment. Hence it daily asks in the Lord’s Prayer: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6).

### Verse 21

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, the forgiveness of sins, “be with you all,” from that same Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

In this place blessed John bears the type of preachers, who, knowing that a human being cannot be justified by the Law but by grace, desires that this same grace [Col. 0416D] may always remain with the Church. Note that here blessed John took his beginning from grace and set his conclusion in grace, because we are saved by the prevenient grace of God and justified by grace following after.

It is fitting, dearest brothers, that we jointly render thanksgivings to almighty God. By his grace preceding, accompanying, and following us, we have set forth for your instruction the obscurities of the words and the hidden mysteries of this most truthful revelation, insofar as they have been explained by the holy Fathers; so that you may hold firmly in heart, speech, and deed the Catholic faith which at baptism you confessed to God and to the priests of the Church through your godparents, and, if necessary, may not flee from suffering adversities for love of God and love of neighbor. I also exhort [Col. 0417A] all you faithful of the Church who will see the times of Antichrist: cleave with devout mind to Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin; offer him a pure and incorrupt faith; and do not depart from the integrity of faith in this same Jesus Christ either because of promises of temporal things or because of the terrors of Antichrist or his ministers. He was ineffably born of God the Father before all ages; he deigned, for our redemption, to be born in time of the Virgin Mother. Conceived by the Holy Spirit, he united our humanity to himself without sin in the Virgin’s womb; and, born according to that humanity and obedient to the Law, he presented himself in the Temple on the fortieth day after his birth, with lamps divinely kindled and with crowds coming to meet him singing praise. By divine inspiration he led the Magi from the regions of the East, a star going before, to worship himself. Before Herod—the earthly king, that is—he went down into Egypt, not by resisting but by humbly avoiding persecution, at the angel’s warning. And though he had absolutely no sin, he wished to be baptized, in order to wash his bride, the Church, from original sin; and, in order to give the children of that Church an example of abstinence, he fasted for forty days. Teaching us to overcome temptations, he endured temptation; and, conquering the tempter himself, he delivered us from his power. By his preaching he enlightened us miserable persons sitting in darkness and the shadow of death (Luke I [or IV, as printed]); according to his humanity—not for himself, but for the restoration of the human race—he endured the Passion; he mercifully mounted the cross [Col. 0417C] (Luke XXIII), and upon it, as the good Shepherd, laid down his life for his sheep (John XI). Descending thereby into hell, he shattered its gates; he bound in the depths of hell the enemy of the human race itself, namely the devil; he recaptured the captivity which that inventor of all wickedness had taken captive; and, returning from there, on the third day he raised his body from the tomb. For forty days he manifested himself to his disciples by many proofs; on the fortieth day, ascending into heaven, he placed in heaven that same captivity which he had drawn forth from hell. He sits at the right hand of God the Father, from whom he came forth; from there also he will come at the end of the world, to render to each according to his works, to judge the living and the dead, [Col. 0417D] and the world by fire (Eph. IV).

I testify to you, O children of the Church who will see Antichrist or his false apostles, that this is the true and Catholic faith; unless you preserve it whole and inviolate, you cannot be saved. Therefore he who is, as we have said above, born without sin of God the Father and of the Virgin Mother, is one and true God with the same Father and the Holy Spirit. He is true God and true man, without whom no one can come to the Father. Ineffably begotten of God the Father before all ages, he received in time from the Virgin Mother a true substance, with which he possesses the third person in the Trinity. Therefore Christ is the most firm foundation of the true [Col. 0418A] faith, having testimony from the Law and the Prophets. Hence the apostle Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. III). We have him on earth as a most loving and mighty shepherd; through him we believe that we shall attain the everlasting and most sweet vision of his Father. He is the straight way, the truest truth, and eternal life (John XIV), through whom the children of the Church run and attain eternal rewards.

Again I warn you, O Christian peoples who will be found alive in the body at the time of Antichrist, that you hold firmly this faith in Jesus Christ, God and man, against the persecution or deceitful disputation of that Antichrist. For, as the blessed apostle Peter says, “There is salvation in no one else; for neither is there any other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV), except Jesus Christ the Son of God, who redeemed the world from the hand of the ancient enemy. Therefore do not fear Antichrist’s threats, do not yield to his promises, and do not place faith in his miracles, because he will not come to redeem the world, but to drag the human race with himself into destruction. Therefore Scripture calls him the son of destruction, because by his false miracles and deceitful words he will hurl many with himself into the lake of burning fire; and at last he himself will be killed by the spiritual sword, sharp on both sides, which proceeds from the mouth of Jesus Christ seated at the right hand of God the Father (2 Thess. II). Hence the prophet Isaiah, having enumerated [Col. 0418C] the powers of this same Son of God and of the Virgin, speaks thus: “With the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked one” (Isa. II). Truly he is wicked and cruel, sparing neither himself nor others. The prophet therefore fittingly called him wicked, because when he comes he will condemn both himself and many others with himself. The apostle Paul also says of him: “When that man of sin, the son of destruction, is revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called or worshipped as God, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. II). He is rightly called a man of sin because, as Master Anselm says—namely, a wise and Catholic man:

> “In Babylon he will be born of a prostitute of the tribe of Dan; in his mother’s womb he will be filled with a diabolical spirit, [Col. 0418D] and he will be nourished by sorcerers.”

[Note: [Col. 0417D] *Elucidarium*, book III, chapter 10.]

He will sit in God’s temple, showing himself as though he were God, because he will restore ancient Jerusalem, in which he will command that he himself be worshipped as if God.

Therefore he, O faithful Christians, who is called the man of sin and son of destruction, is by no means to be worshipped as God, but is in every way to be abhorred and cursed by the children of the Church. He will feign holiness, but will be full of every deceit and fraud. He will perform miracles—not true ones, but ones deceitfully contrived by himself and his father the devil. He will be trained in every magical art, worldly learning, and incredible eloquence, by which he will deceive and subjugate the human race. [Col. 0419A] See therefore, dearest brothers, when that man of sin, the son of destruction, is revealed, that you are not quickly moved from your understanding—that is, from the right and true state of the Catholic faith—by his signs and portents, his utterly false powers. See that you do not worship the son of destruction in place of the Redeemer. It is madness and folly to worship the son of iniquity and to despise Jesus Christ, Son of almighty God, who redeemed the world by his precious blood. Therefore, without doubt, if you worship Antichrist or receive his mark on your hand—that is, in your conduct—or on your forehead—that is, in your confession—you will perish with him. Place, then, the anchor of your hope in Christ, the Son of God and [Col. 0420A] of the Virgin; approach him by the steps of good works; endure for his sake, if necessary, persecutions, wounds, beatings, and other adversities; embrace him with the arms of true faith and sincere love; raise to him, seated at the right hand of God the Father, the eyes of your mind with the utmost devotion; worship him, reigning in heaven with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, as one true God, so that with his elect you may reign without end in his presence. May he grant this—he who with the same Father and Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1202: Walter of Châtillon

[Col. 0419]

## Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, II, 112)

[Col. 0419B] Master Philip Walter of Châtillon, a native of Lille [Note: [Col. 0419C] A one-line verse in Henry of Ghent, chapter 20:

> Lille gave me birth; Châtillon took away my name.

But in the brief Life of Walter prefixed by Sebastian Linck to the *Alexandreis*, the couplet is read as follows:

> Lille gave me birth; Châtillon took away my name;  
> All Gaul resounded with my melodies.],

provost of the canons of Tournai, wrote, following in the footsteps of Quintus Curtius, the *Alexandreis*, or heroic poem on the deeds of Alexander the Great. It is elegant for its age, and consists of ten books, whose initial letters spell the name *Guillermus* [Note: [Col. 0419C] Pagi, under the year 1102, no. XIII.]; for he dedicated them to William II, who was archbishop of Reims from 1176 to 1201. Around the year 1280, when Henry of Ghent was writing, this poem held such distinction in grammar schools that, compared with it, the reading of ancient poets was neglected. Yet Alain of Lille is not so much Walter’s superior that, unless envy had dictated this judgment to him, he ought to have attacked these *Deeds of the Macedonian Leader* with the reproach of a shadowy poem.

After the Strasbourg edition of 1513, in octavo, Oswald Eck published these books and dedicated them to Albert, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, at Ingolstadt in 1541, in octavo, from the press of Alexander Weissenborn. The distinguished Christopher Augustus Heumann testifies in his *Survey of the Republic of Letters*, p. 65, and in the *Acts of Philosophers*, part XV, p. 371, that he possessed this edition with variant readings handwritten by Christian [Col. 0419C] Daumius, “of blessed memory” (*τοῦ μακαρίτου*), who was contemplating an edition of this writer. Finally, Walter’s *Alexandreis* [Col. 0420B] appeared at Lyon in 1558, in quarto, in a distinctive and neat typeface more closely resembling the running script which we use in writing [Note: [Col. 0419C] In French, *caractères de civilité*.—There is a fourth edition of the *Alexandreis*, a whole century later than the Lyon edition (1659, duodecimo), printed from two manuscripts of St Gall and Mont-des-Anges at the same monastery of St Gall and “in its own type,” as the title-page says, under the care of Athanasius Gugger, a monk of St Gall, who believed Walter’s work had not previously been published. “Here, candid reader,” he says, “you have a new work, though ancient: so far as I know, nowhere published; eagerly examined and desired by many; venerable no less for its antiquity than for its learning.” EDITION OF THE FATHERS.].

We expect from another learned man the old Icelandic translation, which Arnas Magnæus, a man most skilled in those letters, had been preparing to publish. He may also be able to make use of two Latin manuscript codices of this writer, acquired at the Gudius auction and sent by me to the aforesaid Magnæus.

The various rhythmic little works which Oudin notes as extant in manuscript 5333 of the King of France’s library [Note: [Col. 0420C] In the Life prefixed to the treatises against the Jews and in vol. II of *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, p. 1668.] are not by Walter of Châtillon, but by Walter Map, of whom below. Yet Oudin himself was the first to publish, under Walter of Châtillon’s name, three dialogic treatises written against the Jews, from a manuscript of the Abbey of St Evodius at Brana; he also prefixed an engraved portrait of the author. They appeared among several sacred little works of writers from Gaul and Belgium, Leiden, 1692, octavo. Finally, Bernard Pez, in vol. II of the *Anecdota*, [Col. 0420C] part II, p. 51, published from a Salzburg manuscript the treatise *On the Holy Trinity* by Master Galter, whom he persuades himself is this Walter of Lille, at Augsburg, 1721, folio. See the introductory dissertation of the aforementioned Pez, p. XXII.

[Col. 0421]

## Second Notice

(Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings*, II, 1666.)

[Col. 0421A] Walter of Lille, called of Châtillon, flourished from about 1160 until 1200, or even later. John of Salisbury mentions him in Letter 134, to John Geoffrey of St Edmund, indicating that Walter had been asked by him to approach the king of England on behalf of St Thomas, archbishop and martyr of Canterbury:

> Earlier on this matter I had approached that most excellent man and, for his merits, one whom I reverence, Master Walter of Lille, and through him other fathers, whose faith seemed to me more sincere.

And at the end:

> I hear that Master Walter is bound by oath not to receive either letters or messengers from the exiles.

And in Letter 159:

> But Master Walter of Lille sent word to England from the conference at Chinon, so that he might forewarn the people of Lille concerning the appeal made, ensure that the gates of passage were more carefully guarded, and suspend the clergy from obedience, although an appeal has been made and the archbishop can easily be found. Nor do I doubt that this intrigue [Col. 0421B] displeases the said Walter, together with all the measures advanced against God’s Church, because he fears the Lord.

Letter 189 is addressed to the same man. From these passages it is clear that Walter flourished somewhat after the middle of the twelfth century, from about 1160 to 1200, and that he was not bishop of Maguelone, as some write, since during these years John of Montlaur governed the Church of Maguelone.

Henry of Ghent mentions him in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 20, p. 165 of Aubertus Miraeus’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, in these words:

> Walter, called of Châtillon, was born at Lille, whence comes his one-line verse:
>
> > Lille gave me birth; Châtillon took away my name.
>
> He wrote the *Deeds of Alexander the Great* in elegant verse. This book has today such standing in grammar schools that, in comparison with it, the reading of the ancient poets is neglected.

There survive ten books of the *Alexandreis*, or *On the Deeds of Alexander the Great*, written in fairly successful heroic verse by Walter of Châtillon [Col. 0421C] and dedicated to William, archbishop of Reims, around 1180. They were printed at Strasbourg in 1531, and at Ingolstadt and Lyon in 1558. Manuscripts are held in the royal library of France, codices 5644 and 5645. The prologue begins, “It is customary,” etc.; Book I begins:

> First [he] imbued Aristotle with sacred nectar, etc.

They are also held in the library of Saint-Germain in Paris, codices 536 and 537, of the best quality; and repeatedly in the Colbertine and Victorine libraries. They are also among the manuscripts of Cambridge University, no. 344; in the manuscript codices of Trinity College, in the southern part of the library, first series, codex 3; among the manuscripts of the Bodleian Library, no. 1269; among the manuscripts of William Laud, letter II, codex 6; and there also, no. 1515, among the same manuscripts, letter K, codex 89. Finally, among the manuscripts of Cambridge University, no. 1346, in the manuscripts [Col. 0421D] of St Benedict’s College, codex 69, no. 6.

No. 5 is also believed to be his: *The Art of Speaking Well in Verse*, beginning, “Behold the laws of the pope,” which more correctly is attributed by others to Geoffrey of Vinsauf, the English poet. This poet Walter is mentioned by William the Breton at the beginning of his *Philippid*, composed in twelve books:

> If it was permitted to you, Walter, to describe in celebrated verse  
> The deeds of the Macedonian leader, which the wide-ranging report of Fame  
> Alone taught you to recount;
>
> If each Gentile poet was permitted  
> To embellish his falsehoods with loudly booming sound;
>
> If you, Peter Riga, did not think it a fault  
> To draw the hidden senses of the Law from its abundant breast,
>
> [Col. 0422A] Though you make elegy sing in light words  
> The mighty deeds of men, compressed into a shorter measure,  
> Which should rather have been told in the metre of Maevius—
>
> Why should I not dare to write the great deeds of the great king,  
> Things which I know and have seen in their own light?

And at the end of the seventh book he indicates how much inferior to Walter he recognizes himself to be in poetic art:

> Since you know yourself lesser than Walter in voice,  
> Let at least the number of books make you his equal.

Yet there were some among the ancients who disparaged Walter, perhaps envying him the glory which they saw spread abroad by the trumpet of fame. For Alain of Lille, his fellow townsman and compatriot, calls him Maevius—that is, a bad poet, after Virgil’s Maevius:

> There Maevius thunders forth Priam’s fortunes,  
> Daring to set his mute mouth in the heavens;  
> While he attempts to fashion the deeds of the Macedonian leader  
> In the shadow of a dark poem, he falters at the very threshold  
> And complains that his sluggish Muse grows numb.

Various little works of his are in the Royal Library of France, codex 5333: namely Walter of Lille’s rhythmic work, *On the Estates of the World*: “I was sent into the vineyard,” etc., fol. 36; similar works *On the Estates of Ecclesiastical Persons*: “The manifold fraud of men,” etc., fol. 36; *Against Ecclesiastical Prelates*: “Deceitful is,” etc., fol. 37; *Against Churchmen according to the Vision of the Apocalypse*: “From the scorching Bull,” etc., fol. 37; *That the Pope Is Supreme and the Emperor beneath Him*: “The whole order of this age,” etc., fol. 40; *Against the Corrupted State of the Church*: “By the stream of Helicon,” etc., fol. 41; [Col. 0422C] *On the Coming of Antichrist*: “While the despiser,” etc., fol. 41; *To the Lord Pope*: “Being about to speak to so great a man,” etc., fol. 42; *To Good Scholars on Their Return from the Roman Curia*: “Let the members cleave together,” fol. 43; a rhythmic paraphrase on the Psalm, “Have mercy upon me, O God,” etc.; “While Walter was sick,” etc., fol. 44.

However, William Cave—himself an Englishman—in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1210, p. 706, attributes a large part of these little works, for they are slight, to Walter Map, an Englishman, chaplain of King Henry II and eventually archdeacon of Oxford. Those able to consult manuscripts should investigate which of the two Walters, both flourishing in the same age—one in Belgian Flanders, the other in England—these works belong to.

He also wrote three treatises against the Jews, which I saw in manuscript in the library at Brana, of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Soissons, bound in one volume with other treatises against the Jews. [Col. 0422D] They take the form of a dialogue between Walter, who calls himself of Châtillon, and Baldwin of Valenciennes, a canon of the Abbey of Brana and particularly dear to Walter because of their common country. Under my supervision this little work was published in octavo in 1692, at Leiden, by Pieter van der Meerche, together with other twelfth-century works.

Valerius Andreas, in his *Belgian Manuscript Library*, confused two men surnamed Walter of Lille, [Col. 0423A] whom he wrongly says flourished around 1255. One of them became bishop of Maguelone in 1108 and died in 1128 on a pilgrimage undertaken to the Holy Land, as the Sammarthan brothers correctly report in vol. III of *Gallia Christiana*, fol. 567, under the bishops of Maguelone. The other flourished from 1160 to 1200, as stated above.

The following treat of this Walter of Lille: John Trithemius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Antonio Possevino, vol. I of the *Apparatus Sacrus*, p. 692 in my copy; Gerard Johann Vossius, book III of *On Latin Historians*, part II, *On Historians of Uncertain Date*, letter P, who calls him Philip Walter of Châtillon and correctly judges that he flourished around 1200; the fourth century [i.e. volume] of the *History of the University of Paris*, p. 740, in the catalogue of the distinguished academics of that century, from which we have drawn much; Aubertus Miraeus, in his scholia on Henry of Ghent’s little book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he discusses the two Walters of Lille; and Valerius Andreas in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 773, where he calls him Philip Walter of Châtillon, in the final 1643 Louvain quarto edition.

[Col. 0423]

## Treatise, or Dialogue, of Master Walter of Tournai and Baldwin of Valenciennes against the Jews

(Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, XIV, 505.—Oudin had already published Walter’s little work in the collection entitled: *Previously Unpublished Sacred Little Works of Certain Ancient Writers of Gaul and Belgium*, Leiden, 1692, octavo.)

## Prologue

[Col. 0423B] Since it is agreed that there were three causes of the first perdition—namely avarice, *kenodoxia* (*κενοδοξία*, “vain glory”), and gluttony—the whole succession of posterity, as from corrupt seed, took from these three the beginning of sinning. Thus, from them as efficient causes, there sprang forth, as something propagated originally, the source of all human frailty. And, like water always tending downward, with the rein of free choice allowed free course, the calamity of our captivity came to this: that a human being, not remembering in whose image he had been made, subjected himself to the worship of idols and worshipped what had been made rather than him who made it.

Therefore the divine Judge, weighing the merits of the good and examining the faults of the reprobate, destroyed by the overflowing flood of waters that which was to perish. Keeping to the practice of a good surgeon, he cut away dead flesh lest the sound portion be carried off with it, and preserved what was alive. But as a long course of time passed, very many, savoring the fat of their former iniquity, incurred the danger of apostasy through long-established wickedness; while few remained in the worship of the one God. From these came the patriarchs and the sons of patriarchs, the holy root, the chosen people. To them the Law was given for a time, until the Holy of Holies should come, who, making the two one, would both absolve the transgression of the first-formed human being and open the entrance of the heavenly kingdom to believers.

The Church, partaker of his mercy, awaits the Bridegroom who is to come for the universal wedding; but the Synagogue, still having a veil before its eyes, awaits his first coming just as the Britons await Arthur. Hence I greatly marvel at the shameless hardness and stubborn obstinacy of the Jews, who, by some hidden judgment of God unknown to me, are so persistent in their old perfidy that, even if someone were to drive their unbelief away as it were with a fork, he would still incur anger—as though unbelief, their inseparable accident, could find no seat elsewhere. O wondrous dispensation of the Creator! O severe vengeance of the Judge, who thus rejected the tabernacle, thus excluded Israel his firstborn; who thus destroyed those whom he had built, thus uprooted those whom he had planted! They not only refuse to yield to the truth of new grace, but even, like retrograde planets, try to oppose the firmament of our faith and dispute against Christ’s worshippers by adducing the authority of the Pentateuch.

In response to their ignorance, I, Walter, of the diocese of Tournai, native of the town called [Col. 0425A] Lille, and Baldwin of Valenciennes, canon of the Church of Brana, have written a little book against the Jews in dialogue form. In it, gathering certain flowers from the books of the prophets, we have woven various kinds of defense by which we restrain the lying tongue. For the prophets’ oracles almost proclaim nothing other than Christ’s coming, passion, and resurrection; but because some speak less clearly and somewhat enigmatically, we have assembled from them certain very plain prophecies against which that yoked she-ass cannot argue, even if she wishes.

**Baldwin.** But before we turn to the text, let us distinguish under headings the matters on which they disagree with us.

**Walter.** What you say pleases me. I think the first point should be that they assert that the Messiah has not yet come and that, when he comes, he will be born not of a virgin but of a woman who has had intercourse.

**B.** That is so. They also maintain that he will not be God but a mere human being, and they assert that he will neither suffer nor rise again. [Col. 0426A] Moreover, I remember arguing, three days ago, with one of them whom they had appointed as their representative and advocate against me; and I compelled him to admit that there will be two Messiahs, one already come and the other still to come.

**G.** Good heavens! What new kind of absurdity is this? It resembles the assertion that the sin of transgressing Adam inflicted no harm upon his descendants except the necessity of dying, and that because of this guilt none have gone down to hell to be condemned there—especially none from Judaism.

**B.** Add this too to what has been said: they boast that they alone are God’s people, excluding the calling of the Gentiles.

**G.** Indeed; and I shall set down by the service of my pen both their rejection and whatever else your smallness may suggest to me.

**B.** And I, taking in some places the role of the Jews, shall raise the objections which I see can be made.

**G.** You have spoken wisely; but now let us do what lies before us, and first turn over the oracles of Isaiah, who proclaimed Christ’s coming more plainly than the rest.

## Book One

[Col. 0425]

[Col. 0425B] **I. Walter.** Isaiah, at the beginning of his book, plainly suggests both the blinding of the Jews and the illumination of the Gentiles. For he says: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. I, 2). But because this may be understood of both Gentiles and Jews, hear what follows: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood” (ibid., 3).

**B.** I do not see what they can object to in these words; proceed, therefore.

**G.** He also shows that their burnt offerings are not pleasing to God, where it is said: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord? I am full of them” (ibid., 11). And, after inserting certain matters concerning the rite of sacrifices, he adds: “Do not continue to bring sacrifice in vain. Incense is an abomination to me. The new moon, Sabbath, and other feasts I will not endure. [Col. 0425D] Your assemblies are iniquitous; my soul has hated your calends and solemnities. They have become burdensome to me; I am weary of bearing them. When you stretch out your hands, I shall turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I shall not hear” (ibid., 13, 15).

**B.** In all these things, as I see, nothing other than their rejection can be understood.

**G.** And a little later he plainly indicates their rejection, saying: “You have cast away, O Lord, your people, the house of Jacob” (Isa. II, 6). A little afterward he turns to the conversion of the Gentiles, saying: “The Lord alone shall be exalted on that day, and idols shall be utterly destroyed” (ibid., 17–18).

**B.** I do not see how you could argue from these that the Messiah has come, since we too possess crucifixes and images of saints, which they themselves call idols.

**G.** Baldwin, no room remains for this sort of objection if you carefully attend to what follows. For Isaiah says of the same matter: “On that day a man will cast away his idols of silver and images of gold, which he had made for himself to worship moles and bats” (ibid., 20). For in the whole world there is no people so devoid of reason that it does not bend beneath the yoke of the one Creator; none affirms that idols are gods; none worships moles and bats.

**B.** That is so.

**G.** What then have they, that they may boast above others of worshipping the one God? Rather, they have reason to be called unhappy. For Isaiah wrote in the person of the Lord speaking: “My people, those who call you blessed themselves deceive you” (Isa. III, 12).

**II. Baldwin.** I ask you, if you find anywhere in the entire page of the Old Testament something that can convict them of needing to receive the Trinity in the Godhead, explain it.

**G.** Indeed, there are many things; but first, having dealt with the rest as comparatively easy matters, at the end of this work—ascending as it were from earthly matters to heavenly—we shall speak at greater length about the Trinity in unity. But for now let us pursue our purpose. It follows: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. VI, 10). For their heart is made heavy and the eyes of their heart are closed when they lie that Christ has not yet come and that he will be born of a woman who has had intercourse, although Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14).

They say that the Hebrew reads differently. Where we read *virgo*, “virgin,” they say that they have the word *alma*, which is equivalent in Latin to *puella*, “girl,” so that *alma* signifies age within the female sex, not integrity of chastity. They therefore read the foretold verse thus: *Hinne ahalma haara vatielezebeir (Vejoladib Ben)*—as though in Latin it were said, “Behold, a girl shall conceive.” O marvelous cunning of wretched people! They not only do not believe the good things which they possess, but, lest they believe them, distort them in reading. You can easily observe this distortion if you are willing to understand what precedes. He says: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depths of hell or in the heights above” (Isa. VII, 11). And a little later: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (ibid., 14). O transgressors of the Law! O stiff-necked rebels! O unbelievers! What sign does he show you if a girl conceives? What wonder would it demonstrate if a young woman gave birth—a thing which we see happen every day? Truly, transgressing Judaea, you are rejected by the Lord. For it follows: “I shall wait for the Lord, who hides his face from the house of Jacob” (Isa. VIII, 17). He hides his face from the one whom he does not love.

But we have heard what Isaiah thought concerning the illumination of the Gentiles and Christ’s birth and divinity. He says: “The people of the Gentiles who walked in darkness saw a great light; upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light arose” (Isa. IX, 2). Explaining, as it were, how this came about, he adds: “For a little child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us; and his name shall be called Wonderful, [Col. 0427C] Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (ibid., 6). What do you think, Baldwin? Will the Messiah be God when he comes?

**B.** Indeed, he is God, he has already come, and we await his second coming.

**III. G.** That is so; and those who do not believe this will deservedly be scattered. Hence it follows: “The Lord shall destroy from Israel head and tail” (ibid., 14). But let those who deny that Christ was full of the Holy Spirit hear what follows: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him,” etc. (Isa. XI, 1–2). Likewise: “On that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which stands as a sign to the peoples; the Gentiles shall entreat him, [Col. 0427D] and his tomb shall be glorious” (ibid., 10). For whose tomb is as famous, whose pyramid as glorious, as the burial-place of our Redeemer?

**B.** No one’s.

**G.** It follows: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. XVI, 1).

**B.** Who is this Lamb, promised to be sent from the rock of the desert?

**G.** Who else is designated by the name Lamb except our immaculate Lamb, who underwent death for us, who, carried by his mother into Egypt, ascended the mountain of the daughter of Zion to be crucified? Of him it is also added: “On that day man shall bow toward his Maker, and his eyes shall look toward the Holy One of Israel; and he shall not bow toward the altars which his hands have made” (Isa. XVII, 7). Again: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend [Col. 0428A] upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt, and Egypt’s images shall be shaken at his presence” (Isa. XIX, 1). Again he says: “Behold, I shall lay in Zion’s foundation a stone: a tested, precious cornerstone, established in the foundation; whoever believes shall not hasten” (Isa. XXVIII, 16). And a little later: “Your covenant with death shall be destroyed, and your pact with hell shall not stand” (ibid., 18); and he adds: “That he may perform his strange work, his work” (ibid., 21).

**IV. Baldwin.** All these things sound somewhat obscure; nevertheless, I think they should be raised against them.

**G.** You judge rightly. But hear what follows: “On that day this song shall be sung in the land of Judah: Zion, the city of our strength; a saviour shall be placed in it as wall and outwork. Open the gates, and let the righteous nation that keeps truth enter; and the old error has departed” (Isa. XXVI, 1–3).

**B.** Behold, now he speaks openly.

**G.** Attend to what follows. He says: “God himself shall come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the ears of the deaf shall be unsealed” (Isa. XXXV, 4–5). We see these things already done and done daily. For when the Church from among the Gentiles, having beheld the truth of the Gospel with the eye of the heart, has offered believing hearing to apostolic preaching—though previously blind—what else has it done but receive sight and hearing? Yet the foregoing may also be referred to the Saviour’s miracles: for when our Redeemer came in the flesh, he restored hearing to the deaf and sight to the blind and, what is greater, [Col. 0428C] raised the dead.

**B.** Nothing is truer.

V. G. Let us now refute, as we proceed, their error which maintains that the transgression of the first-created man inflicted no punishment of hell upon anyone. For Isaiah says: “I said in the midst of my days: I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. XXXVIII, 10). B. Alas, wretches that we are! How good it would be for us if truth agreed with your opinion, if none of us went down to hell! G. It follows: “I have given my spirit upon him. He shall bring forth judgment to the nations; he shall not cry out nor show partiality, nor shall his voice be heard abroad” (Isa. XLII, 1–2). And shortly afterward: “He shall bring forth judgment in truth. He shall not be sad nor troubled, until he establishes judgment in the earth; and the islands shall await his law” (ibid., 3–4). And again: “I have kept you and given you as a covenant of the people, [Col. 0428D] as a light of the nations, that you might open the eyes of the blind and bring forth from confinement the bound man, from the prison-house those sitting in darkness” (ibid., 6–7). B. Almost all these things have been explained above. G. Let us proceed, then: “Behold, the former things have come to pass; I also declare new things; before they arise, I will make them heard by you. Sing to the Lord a new song, his praise from the ends of the earth” (ibid., 9–10). And a little later: “I shall lead the blind by a way which they did not know; I shall cause them to walk in paths which they have not known” (ibid., 16). Explaining this, he adds: “Who is blind but my servant, and deaf but he to whom I sent messengers?” (ibid., 19.) And again, shortly afterward: “Behold, I shall make new things” (Isa. XLIII, 19). And, after inserting certain matters, he explains what new things he will do, adding: [Col. 0429A] “Drop down dew from above, O heavens, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” (Isa. XLV, 8). For then our earth brought forth its germ; then it gave its fruit, when the Word of the Father, made flesh, impregnated the Virgin’s womb by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. But let us hear what more he says of him: “This man shall sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths before him, because those to whom he was not announced shall see concerning him” (Isa. LII, 15). And after inserting certain matters, he plainly adds concerning the Saviour’s passion: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our sorrows; and we thought him, as it were, a leper, struck by God and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was bruised for our crimes. The chastisement [Col. 0429B] of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we are healed. All we, like sheep, have gone astray; each one has turned aside into his own way; and the Lord placed upon him the iniquities of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth. Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before one shearing it he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 4–7). For we read that many prophets underwent martyrdom, and that many kings in Israel were killed; yet it cannot be attributed to any of them that he bore our sorrows and was bruised for our crimes, except to the King of kings alone, God and man, of whom it is added: “He was taken away from distress and judgment. Who shall recount his generation?” (ibid., 8.) As though he said: [Col. 0429C] No one. Again: “He, the just one, shall justify many of my servants, and he himself shall bear their iniquities; therefore I shall distribute very many to him, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he delivered his soul unto death and was reckoned with the wicked. And he himself bore the sin of many and prayed for transgressors, that they might not perish” (ibid., 11–12). B. All these things seem to me so plain that they need no exposition. G. What is plainer than what he says: “I shall glorify the place of my feet”? (Isa. LX, 13.) Again: “You shall suck the milk of the nations, and shall nurse at the breasts of kings” (ibid., 16). And again, concerning Christ’s passion: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra? This one beautiful in his robe, advancing in the multitude of his strength” (Isa. LXIII). He then replies, as though questioned: [Col. 0429D] “I who speak righteousness and am a champion able to save” (ibid.). And there is added, as though the voice of one questioning: “Why, then, is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread in the winepress?” (ibid., 2.) And he gives the reason: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and there was no man of the nations with me. I trod them in my fury and trampled them in my wrath. Their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I defiled all my clothing” (ibid., 3). And he shows what he will do concerning this, saying: “The day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my recompense has come” (ibid., 4). Likewise, concerning the calling of the nations: “Those who formerly did not ask for me seek me; those who did not seek me have found me” (Isa. LXV, 1). And again: “To a nation that did not call upon my name, I stretched out [Col. 0430A] my hands all day long, to an unbelieving people” (ibid., 2). Likewise, concerning the same matter: “I shall set a sign among them and send from them those who have been saved to the nations upon the sea, in Africa, in Lydia, those drawing the bow, into Italy and Greece, to distant islands, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. And they shall proclaim my glory to the nations, and shall bring all our brethren from all nations to the Lord” (ibid., 18, 20). We have set forth these matters from Isaiah briefly, according to our ability; now let us turn the course of our pen to Jeremiah.

VI. Jeremiah, who was sanctified before he was formed in the womb and came forth from the belly, plainly indicates the passion of the Lord and Saviour, the calling of the nations, and the rejection of Judaism. For he says: [Col. 0430B] “Therefore do not pray for this people; do not offer praise and prayer for them, and do not oppose me, because I shall not hear you” (Jer. VII, 16). And elsewhere: “The kite in heaven knew its season; the turtledove, swallow, and stork observed the time of their coming; but the people did not know the judgment of the Lord. How do you say, ‘We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us’? Truly, the lying pen of the scribes has wrought a lie” (Jer. VIII, 7–8). And shortly afterward: “I shall abandon my people and depart from them” (Jer. IX, 2). B. These things are all bare and plain, and I have nothing which may be objected against them. G. But what is clearer than what follows? “Behold,” he says, “I shall feed this people with wormwood and give them gall-water to drink; and [Col. 0430C] I shall scatter them among nations which neither they nor their fathers have known; and I shall send the sword after them until they are consumed, says the Lord of hosts” (ibid., 15–17). And further: “I shall bring evils upon them from which they will not be able to escape; and they shall cry to me, and I shall not hear” (Jer. XI, 11). Again, the same prophet concerning the same matter: “Therefore do not pray for this people, and do not offer praise and prayer for it, because I shall not hear them in the time of their affliction.” B. Is there anything in all this that needs exposition? G. Not at all.

VII. B. But let us hasten to what he says concerning the rise of the new grace. G. I embrace nothing more readily than this very point. He says, therefore: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I shall make with the house of Israel and the house of Judah a [Col. 0430D] new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with your fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—a covenant which they made void; but I ruled over them, says the Lord. But this shall be the covenant which I shall make with the house of Israel: After those days, says the Lord, I shall give my law in their inward parts, and I shall write it upon their hearts; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. And a man shall no longer teach his neighbor, nor a man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jer. XXXI, 31–34). And elsewhere: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up the good word which I spoke concerning the house of Judah. In those days and at that time I shall cause David [Col. 0431A] a shoot of righteousness to spring forth, and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth; and this is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord our righteousness.’ There shall not fail David a man to sit upon the throne of the house of Israel, nor shall there fail before me a man from the priests and Levites to offer burnt offerings, burn sacrifice, and slaughter victims all days” (Jer. XXXIII, 14–19). Likewise, concerning the same matter: “If my covenant with day and my covenant with night can be made void, so that day and night do not occur in their proper time, then my covenant also with David my servant can be made void, so that he has no son to reign upon his throne, and no ministers who are my priests” (ibid., 20). B. By these and similar passages it seems possible to prove either that this was said concerning us, or that they themselves—which is false—even now have a king, Levites, [Col. 0431B] and priests offering burnt offerings and slaughtering victims. G. It is so, I say; otherwise the prophet would seem to have lied.
