No indeed, I say: rather, they are liars and false worshippers of God, concerning whom it follows: “Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the Lord, that my name shall never again be called from the mouth of any Jew” (Jer. XLIV, 26). And shortly afterward: “Behold, I destroy those whom I built, and I uproot those whom I planted” (Jer. XLV, 4). And again: “My people have become a lost flock; their shepherds have led them astray” (Jer. L, 6). And a little later: “All who found them devoured them; and their enemies said, ‘We have not sinned,’ because they sinned against the Lord, the beauty of righteousness and the Lord, the expectation of their fathers” (ibid., 7).

[Col. 0431C] VIII. Now let us state, if you please, what Jeremiah in the Lamentations plainly intimated concerning the Saviour’s passion and the rejection of the Synagogue. B. Yes, provided that the things we compile from them are made clear to the eye of understanding. G. Indeed, I think it necessary also to write down certain things said figuratively, so that believers may gather grain for themselves from the very place from which unbelievers gather chaff. For what else is it to discern Christ’s passion under the person of destroyed Jerusalem than to find grain beneath chaff? He says, therefore: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is a sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. IV, 8)! Likewise: “The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah” (Lam. I, 15). And concerning the rejection of the Jews: “The Lord rejected his altar; [Col. 0431D] he cursed his sanctuary” (Lam. II, 7). Again, in the person of the Lord: “I have become a mockery to my people” (Lam. III, 14). Likewise, concerning the Synagogue: “My end and my hope from the Lord have perished” (ibid., 18). He also says: “He shall give his cheek to the one striking him; he shall be filled with reproaches” (ibid., 30). And their explicit rejection follows, where it is said: “Their faces have become blacker than coals” (Lam. IV, 8). And shortly afterward: “He shall not continue any longer to dwell among them; the face of the Lord has divided them; he shall no longer look upon them” (ibid., 15–16). This indeed is said plainly enough, but far clearer is what follows: “Christ the Lord, the spirit of our mouth, was taken in our sins” (ibid., 20). Baruch also, Jeremiah’s secretary, speaks of him, as though expounding this verse of his master: [Col. 0432A] “This is our God, and none other shall be accounted in comparison with him. He found out every way of instruction and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen on earth and conversed with men” (Baruch III, 36).

IX. We have said these things concerning Jeremiah according to our measure. Let us now turn our pen to Ezekiel; yet in Ezekiel we find few things not enveloped in enigmas. We have therefore passed them over, because through them we despair of being able to refute the Jews literally. But let us pursue those things that speak plainly. He says: “Behold, I am against you, and I myself shall execute judgments in your midst before the eyes of the nations; and I shall do in you things which I have not done and the like of which I shall never again do” (Ezek. V, 8). B. Let them therefore be asked what these things are, the like of which he will not—or has not—done again. G. Good. This also follows shortly afterward: “Trouble upon trouble shall come, and report upon report; they shall seek a vision from the prophet, and the law shall perish from the priest and counsel from the elders” (Ezek. VII, 26). Again: “I shall leave from among them a few men from sword, famine, and pestilence, that they may recount all their abominations among the nations to which they shall enter” (Ezek. XII, 16). And shortly afterward, he plainly indicates their rejection and the calling of the nations when he says: “And all the trees of the countryside shall know that I, the Lord, have humbled the lofty tree and exalted the lowly tree; I have dried up the green tree and made the dry tree put forth leaves, says the Lord” (Ezek. XVIII, 24). B. I beg you, explain why from these words you maintain that they were rejected and the nations exalted. [Col. 0432C] G. What do you understand by the lofty tree humbled, formerly green and now dried up, except the rejection of the Synagogue? For she who was formerly lofty and green has now, cast down in unbelief, wholly withered away; and the nation which was formerly dry now flourishes, exalted in the faith of Christ. Of it he further says: “And I shall set my glory among the nations” (Ezek. XXXIX, 21). But the passages following in Ezekiel are so obscure that not even they understand them literally, much less figuratively. Yet when mystically understood by believers, they taste sweet and offer spiritual manna. Hence it has been said by a certain wise man that they are imbued with heavenly nectar: to the palate of faith the honey of God tastes sweet.

[Col. 0432D] X. B. It is so, I say; but now, if you please, let us turn over Daniel’s oracles. G. Gladly; for who expressed the Saviour’s advent and passion more clearly? For he says: “I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before his presence; and he gave him power and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power is an eternal power which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII, 10). And again: “But the kingdom and power and greatness of the kingdom which is under all heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is everlasting, and all kings shall serve and obey him” (Dan. VII, 13–14). And after inserting certain matters, [Col. 0433A] he adds: “Seventy weeks,” he says, “are shortened upon your people and upon your holy city, so that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may receive its end, iniquity may be wiped out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. IX, 24). By these words, Baldwin, the followers of Moses must necessarily admit either that these things were not foretold concerning the Messiah, or that, when he comes, he will be God. B. In what way, I ask? Since God is certainly holy, if the Messiah is the Holy of Holies, then either he himself will be God, or someone holier than God will be shown to exist. G. You reason plausibly, I think; attend to what follows: “And after seventy-two weeks Christ shall be killed, and the people who are to deny him shall not be his” (ibid., 26). Whoever searches the following words inwardly will find them full of heavenly savor. But because we ought not give what is holy to dogs (Matt. VII, 6), let it suffice to have read Daniel thus far, and let us prepare to consider the prophecies of the book of the Twelve Prophets.

XI. And because Hosea occurs first to be read, let us hear what he says concerning the rejection of the Jews and the despoiling of hell: “Because,” he says, “you have forgotten the law of your God, I too shall forget your children; according to their multitude, as they sinned against me, I shall change their glory into shame. They shall eat the sins of my people” (Hos. IV, 7–8). And elsewhere: “Come, let us return to the Lord, because he himself has seized us and will save us; he will strike and heal us. He will revive [Col. 0433C] us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. VI, 2). And a little later he adds more evident words concerning the Saviour’s passion: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. XIII, 14). For he bit hell when he wrested from it part of those whom it held, while leaving another part behind.

XII. Joel also says: “Wail, ministers of the altar; enter in; lie down in sackcloth, ministers of my God, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God” (Joel I, 13). Again: “The sun and moon have been darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their brightness” (Joel II, 10). Likewise: “The Lord shall roar from Zion and give forth his voice from Jerusalem; heaven and earth shall be shaken; and a fountain shall go forth from the house of the Lord [Col. 0433D] and shall water the torrent of thorns” (Joel III, 16, 18).

XIII. Amos also, a shepherd of sheep, foresaw that the true Shepherd would die. Of him he says: “For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I shall not turn him back, because he sold the just man for silver, and the poor man for sandals” (Amos II, 6). Again, concerning the Lord’s advent: “After I have done these things to you, prepare to meet your God” (Amos IV, 12). There follows concerning the rejection of the Synagogue: “The virgin Israel has fallen; she shall not rise again. Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! What is it to you?” (Amos V, 1, 18). This can be understood of both the second advent and the first. For woe was to the Synagogue at the first advent, because she did not recognize him whom she had desired! Hence: “Woe [Col. 0434A] shall be to her at the second!” Concerning this it is also added: “I hate and reject your festivals, and I shall not accept the smell of your assemblies” (ibid., 21). And shortly afterward: “The end has come upon my people Israel. And there shall be iniquity on that day, says the Lord. The sun shall set at midday, and I shall cause the earth to grow dark on a day of light; and I shall turn your festivals into mourning and your song into lamentation” (Amos VIII, 8–10). For when the Sun of righteousness underwent death, the material sun hid its rays of light. These things Amos foretold concerning Christ.

XIV. Obadiah likewise plainly disclosed the calling of the nations: “As,” says the Lord, “you drank upon my holy mountain, all nations shall drink continually; and upon Mount Zion there shall be salvation, and there shall be holiness” (Obad., vv. 16–17). B. As we proceed through these passages in order, we ought likewise to explain each one in order. G. It would be long and difficult if we wished fully to unravel everything. For the length of a work often produces weariness in the ears of the hearer. Therefore, what the voice of prophecy means mystically must be left to the reader’s diligence. We have passed over Jonah because nothing in him speaks literally that we might set before the Jews.

XV. Micah, however, says: “Behold, the Lord shall go forth from his holy place, and he shall descend and tread upon the high places of the earth” (Mic. I, 3). Likewise: “Then they shall cry to the Lord, and he shall not hear them; he shall hide his face from them” (Mic. III, 4). Likewise: “In the last days the mountain of the house [Col. 0434C] of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains and shall be raised above all hills; peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall hasten and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways and we shall walk in his paths; for from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem’” (Mic. IV, 1–2). What law is this, which the prophet foretold would go forth, if not those precepts of grace which, seated upon the mountain, he disclosed to his disciples? It follows: “They shall strike the Judge of Israel upon the cheek with a rod; and you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are little among the thousands of Judah: from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. V, 1–2). What do you think, dearest friend, that the Jews can answer to this? Do they suppose that these things were said concerning their Messiah? B. By no means can they do so; for since they confess him to be a mere man, how can his going forth be from the beginning and from the days of eternity? G. You have answered well, I say. It follows: “On that day the law shall be removed far away” (Mic. VII, 11).

XVI. Nahum also said: “Behold upon the mountains the feet of one evangelizing and announcing peace” (Nah. I, 15).

XVII. Habakkuk, a most vigorous wrestler, says: “Look,” he says, “among the nations, and see, marvel, and be astonished, because a work has been done in our days which no one will believe when it is recounted” (Hab. I, 5). Likewise, concerning the Saviour’s advent: “It shall appear at the end and shall not lie; if it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and shall not be late” (Hab. II, 3). The following also may be understood concerning him: “All those who remain of the peoples shall despoil you, because of the blood of man and the iniquity of the land, of the city, and of all who dwell in it” (ibid., 8). But what follows ought to be embraced by believers with the greatest devotion, because it declares the mysteries of our redemption: “His brightness shall be as light; horns are in his hands. There his strength is hidden; death shall go before his face” (Hab. III, 4). Thus far the words of Habakkuk.

XVIII. Zephaniah also says: “All men shall worship, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. II, 11). Again, concerning the rejection of the Jews: “Her priests [Col. 0435B] have defiled the holy thing; they have acted unjustly against the law” (Zeph. III, 4); and elsewhere: “Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection to come, because it is my judgment to gather the nations and assemble the kingdoms” (ibid., 8).

XIX. Haggai also says concerning him: “Yet one little while, and I shall move heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land; and the Desired One of all nations shall come, and I shall fill this house with glory. Mine is the silver and mine is the gold, says the Lord of hosts. The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former” (Hag. II, 8–10).

XX. Zechariah likewise: “Praise,” he says, “and rejoice, daughter Zion, for behold, I come and shall dwell [Col. 0435C] in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations shall be joined to the Lord on that day, and they shall be my people, and I shall dwell in your midst” (Zech. II, 10–11). Likewise, the same prophet on the same subject: “Many peoples and strong nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem and to proclaim the face of the Lord [Vulgate: ‘entreat the face of the Lord’]” (Zech. VIII, 22). And shortly afterward, beholding Christ coming in the flesh, he says: “Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; shout for joy, daughter Jerusalem: behold, your king comes to you, just and a saviour, humble and riding upon a she-ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass” (Zech. IX, 9). He immediately adds: “He shall speak peace to the nations, and his power shall be from sea to sea and from the rivers [Col. 0435D] to the ends of the earth” (ibid., 10). Turning to him, he says: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there was no water” (ibid., 11). In this, indeed, the prophet indicates the faithful whom Christ brought out in his own blood from the pit of the lower regions. It follows: “And our God shall be seen over them, and his dart shall go forth like lightning” (ibid., 14). After this he figures the Saviour, sold by a disciple, saying: “And I took my staff, which is called Beauty, and cut it off, in order to make void my covenant which I made with all peoples. And it was made void on that day; and thus the poor of the flock who keep watch for me knew that it was the word of the Lord. And I said to them: ‘If it is good in your eyes, bring me my wages; but if not, refrain.’ And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: ‘Throw it to the sculptor, at whose price I was valued by them [Vulgate: “the handsome price at which I was valued by them”].’ And I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them in the temple to the potter” (Zech. XI, 10–13). Likewise, concerning the passion and the advent of the Holy Spirit: [Col. 0436A] “I shall pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and prayers; and they shall look upon me whom they pierced. And they shall mourn for him with mourning as for an only-begotten son” (Zech. XII, 10). Again, to confirm the same point: “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands? And he shall say: ‘I was wounded with these in the midst of those who loved me’” (Zech. XIII, 6). It follows: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered; and I shall turn [Col. 0436B] my hand upon the little ones” (ibid., 7). And elsewhere: “The Lord shall go forth and fight against those nations, and on that day his feet shall stand upon the Mount of Olives” (Zech. XIV, 3–4). He also plainly adds the calling of the nations: “And all,” he says, “who remain from all the nations that came against Jerusalem shall go up year by year to worship the Lord of hosts” (ibid., 16). He adds also something which we know has already been fulfilled, saying: “On that day, what is upon the horse’s bridle shall be holy to the Lord” (ibid., 20). Do you understand what he says? B. I understand. For it is read that Constantine, Helena’s son, added to the upper part of a bridle—that is, the part over a horse’s head—the nails by which the Lord had been fastened to the cross, acting on his mother’s advice, so that, thus fortified by the Lord’s sacred token (sancto Domini), he might proceed securely from the enemy into the hazards of war. G. It is so, I say; now let us return to our subject.

XXI. Malachi sums up both the faith of the nations and the blinding of Judaism in one verse, speaking in the person of the Lord: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I shall not accept a gift from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place a clean offering is sacrificed and offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations” (Mal. I, 10–11). And he adds again: “I am a great king, says the Lord of hosts, and my name is dreadful among the nations” (ibid., 14). Likewise, in the person of the Lord speaking: [Col. 0436D] “Priests, if you are unwilling to listen, and if you are unwilling to lay it upon your heart to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I shall send want upon you and shall curse your blessings” (Mal. II, 2). And after inserting certain matters he adds: “But you have departed from the way and caused many to stumble in the law, says the Lord. You have made my covenant void; on account of this I too have made you contemptible and lowly among all peoples” (ibid., 8–9). He also says: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, and he shall prepare your way before you; and immediately the Ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to your holy temple. Behold, he comes, says the Lord” (Mal. III, 1). But no believer doubts that all these things have been fulfilled, together with what follows: [Col. 0437A] “And for you who fear my name the Sun of righteousness shall arise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Mal. IV, 2).

XXII. We have briefly set forth these passages from the book of the Twelve Prophets, as far as we knew them to be capable of being set against the Jews. Now let us give ourselves for a short time to rest before we unfold Moses’ Pentateuch. [Col. 0438A] Therefore, while devoting a brief interval to refreshment, let us humbly implore him to whom nothing is impossible, that we may strive to please him in such a way as to deserve to attain him who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 8), our Lord Jesus Christ, whose dominion remains without end unto ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0437]

[Col. 0437B] I. Since yesterday and the day before yesterday we have been at leisure, Baldwin, I fear that the torpor of a long rest may shake off the powers of intellect which divine grace invisibly supplies to us; for an interruption of work is commonly the cause of dullness. Since leisure blunts even keen and subtle men, what wonder if the softness of rest dulls our intellect? Moreover, habitual labor is usually the guardian of virtue. For the instability of the human mind is often restrained while the body is afflicted by the concern of work. Thus it happens that the visible human being in us is worn down precisely where the resting invisible human being is increased in virtues. Let us therefore return to the labor of writing, so that grace may be added to our mind.

II. And first, I judge that this evangelical passage of the book of Genesis ought to be set before the Jews: what Moses writes in affirming the Trinity when speaking of the works of the six days, using these words: “The earth,” he says, “was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. I, 2). Secondly, they should be asked why the second day and its works lacked a blessing, whereas in the other days Moses says: “And God saw that it was good” (ibid., 10), but not on the second. Thirdly, put this question to them: why did God say, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (ibid., 26)? But we shall discuss all these matters, which we now skim over in preliminary fashion, more fully in the treatise *On the Trinity*; for the present, let us touch briefly on what follows.

[Col. 0437D] III. Attend, O Jews, to what Moses records after the expulsion of the first-created man from paradise, when he says: “And he placed before the paradise of delight cherubim, and a flaming and turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life” (Gen. III, 24). What do you think? Was not the entrance to paradise blocked through the transgression of the first father? For just as the transgressor transmitted death to his descendants, so he closed the gate of life to all. Hence they must either admit that the threshold of paradise is still barred, or proclaim with us that it was opened through the passion of the Redeemer. B. Since you have mentioned our redemption, one thing now comes to mind which they frequently object to us. “Tell us,” they say, [Col. 0438B] “O worshippers of Christ, where have you found that life ought to be restored through a woman and the kingdom of the devil destroyed?” G. You will find this plainly enough if you attend carefully to what has gone before. For the Lord says to the serpent: “I shall put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; and she herself shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (ibid., 15). Whoever investigates all this more closely will know both that sin came to an end through the woman and that through her the head of the crafty serpent—that is, the devil—was crushed. Moreover, something must be gathered from what follows which especially rebukes the Jews’ pride and indicates some mystery to those who concede it. For we read three times that the Lord blessed Abraham before he was circumcised, as it is written: “Go forth from your land, from your kindred, and from the house of your father; and I shall make you into a great nation, and I shall magnify your name. I shall bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XII, 1, 3). God also said to Abraham, after Lot had separated from him: “Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, northward and southward, eastward and westward. All the land which you see I shall give to you and to your seed forever; and I shall make your seed like the dust of the earth. If any man can number the dust of the earth, he will also be able to number your seed” (ibid., 14–16). And elsewhere: “After these things the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying: ‘Do not fear, Abram; I am your protector and your exceedingly great reward.’ And Abram said: ‘Lord God, what will you give me? I shall go childless, and the son of the steward of my house is this Damascene Eliezer. But you have not given me seed, and behold, my home-born servant shall be my heir.’ And immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘This man shall not be your heir, but he who shall come forth from your womb—him you shall have as your heir.’ And he brought him outside and said: ‘Look at the heaven and number the stars, if you can’; and he said to him: ‘So shall your seed be.’ Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV, 1–7).

IV. It is therefore clear that the Lord blessed Abraham before circumcision; and he promised that not only the Jews, as they themselves maintain, but also the Church from the nations would be blessed in his seed, which is Christ. For if they wish to be included alone under this blessing, how did God make Abraham’s seed innumerable like the dust of the earth and like the stars of heaven? Never from the day of the promise until the period of the Jewish dispersion—described as having occurred under Titus and Vespasian—was Israel so numerous that it could not be included within a definite number; this you can establish even from their own testimony. For when the most mighty King David reigned, Israel was most abundant and numerous; nevertheless, a definite number of it was reported to the king by Joab, commander of his army. For it is written: “David said to Joab, commander of his army: ‘Go through all the tribes of Israel from Dan to Beersheba, and number the people, that I may know their number’” (II Sam. XXIV, 2). And shortly afterward it adds: “Having surveyed the whole land, they came to Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days. Joab therefore gave the king the number of the census of the people, and there were found from Israel eight hundred thousand strong men who could draw the sword, and from Judah five hundred thousand fighting men” (ibid., 8–9). The promises were also spoken not only to Abraham but to Isaac, when the Lord said: “Do not go down into Egypt, but remain in the land which I shall tell you; for to you and to your seed I shall give all these regions, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXVI, 2–4).

V. But lest they perhaps think that we are Ishmaelites or sons of Esau, and not Israel, it is fitting to review the very words of the promise made to Israel. For when Jacob saw the ladder and the angels ascending and descending upon it, he saw the Lord saying to him: “I am the Lord of Abraham your father; the land on which you sleep I shall give to you and to your seed after you, and your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth. You shall spread abroad to east and west, north and south, and in you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 28:13–14). Let the unbelievers therefore say whether that blessing has been fulfilled, and in whom, or whether it still remains to be fulfilled. [Col. 0439D] But, to confess the truth, it has already been fulfilled in part and is fulfilled daily, since the number of believers increases every day. Yet the universal blessing remains to be fulfilled, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:23), so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). But enough concerning these matters.

VI. Let us now pass to the end of Genesis, where Jacob, blessing each of his sons according to the order of birth, turns to Judah and prophesies, saying: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness. Who shall rouse him? [Col. 0440A] The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations. Binding his colt to the vine, and, O my son, his ass to the vine-stock. He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of grapes. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Gen. 49:8–12). From this they must either show—what they cannot—the sceptre of the kingdom and the ruler in Judah, or voluntarily concede that he who was to be sent has come.

Why then, O Jews, do you glory in the observance of the Sabbath, which you see was broken from the beginning? For blessed Jerome says thus in his book *Hebrew Questions*: “We shall press the Jews, who glory in Sabbath rest, with the fact that the Sabbath was already dissolved at the beginning, when God worked on the Sabbath, completing his works on it and blessing that day itself, because on it he had completed all things.”

VII. Exodus also, which in Hebrew is called *Beelezemoth*, supplies many arguments to Christ’s worshippers for breaking the horn of the Synagogue. Since they especially glory in legal observance of the commandments, they must be asked whether they observe the things commanded by Moses, who says: “You shall not harass a stranger. For six years you shall sow your land and gather its produce; but in the seventh year you shall let it go and cause it to rest, so that the poor of your people may eat” (Exod. 23:9–11).

B. Perhaps they will answer that they possess no fields or such things with which to fulfil what is commanded.

G. Do you not know some people—for example Isaac and his brother—who, although they have fields or vineyards, nevertheless do not observe such things?

B. I do.

G. Furthermore, one must ask what was meant by that threat of the Lord speaking to Moses after they had worshipped the golden calf: “You are a stiff-necked people; I shall go up once in your midst and destroy you” (Exod. 33:5). But what is this, tell me, O Jews, which follows: “The Lord spoke face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend” (ibid., 11)? And shortly afterward Moses says to him: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me your face” (ibid., 13). For if he spoke face to face, why does he ask, “Show me your face?” [Col. 0440D] Will you say: “The Lord,” that is, an angel, spoke face to face? You cannot, because it is written there *Adonai*, which is interpreted “Lord God.” What too are the signs which the Lord promises that he will perform, speaking to Moses and saying: “I shall make a covenant; before all men I shall perform signs such as have nowhere been seen upon the earth” (Exod. 34:10)?

VIII. In Leviticus, however, which in Hebrew is called *Vaicra*, everything in the sea and in rivers that has neither fins nor scales is shown to be abominable and unclean. And concerning a menstruating woman it is written: “A woman who, at the return of her monthly period, suffers a flow of blood shall be separated for seven days. Everyone who touches her shall be unclean until evening; and whatever she has lain or sat upon during the days [Col. 0441A] of her separation shall be defiled. Whoever touches her bed shall wash his garments and, after washing himself with water, shall be unclean until evening. Whoever touches any vessel upon which she has sat shall wash his garments and, after washing himself with water, shall be defiled until evening” (Lev. 15:19–33). Either all these things must be understood mystically, or they must confess themselves transgressors of all of them: “You shall not wear a garment woven from two materials” (Lev. 19:19). So much for Leviticus.

IX. From the book of Numbers, also called *Vajedaber* in Hebrew, we first set down the following, which agrees with what has been said, in the person of the Lord speaking concerning Moses to Aaron and Miriam his sister: “I speak with him mouth to mouth, openly and not through riddles [Col. 0441B] and figures; he sees the Lord” (Num. 12:8). If, therefore, it was not through riddles and figures, how does this stand with: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20)? Let them also display the fringes at the corners of their cloaks, concerning which the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel and tell them to make fringes for themselves at the corners of their cloaks, placing blue bands upon them; when they wear them, they shall remember all the commandments of the Lord and shall not follow their own thoughts and eyes, committing fornication through diverse things” (Num. 15:38–39).

Nor should Balaam’s prophecy be omitted. For he says: “I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near. A star shall rise from Jacob and a staff shall arise from Israel” (Num. 24:17). And shortly afterward he adds: [Col. 0441C] “Alas! Who shall live when God does these things?” (ibid., 23). Nor should it be passed over in silence that the daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Joseph, said to Moses: “Our father died in the wilderness, and he was not in the rebellion stirred up against the Lord under Korah, but he died in his own sin” (Num. 27:3). Let the Jews therefore say: since he is described above as righteous, in what sin did he die, unless in original sin?

X. From here let us consult Deuteronomy, which they call *Elle hadebarerim*, from which they especially claim to derive the conclusion that they ought rightly, compelled by the Law, to have killed our Saviour Jesus. Let us therefore bring forward the authority from which they draw this conclusion, [Col. 0441D] so that they may be proved defeated precisely where they seem to have triumphed. There are two chapters upon which they rely. This is the first:

“If a prophet arises in your midst, or one who says that he has seen the God of all, and predicts a sign and wonder, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Let us go and follow foreign gods, and serve them,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer” (Deut. 13:1–3).

And a little later: “But that prophet or fabricator of dreams shall be put to death” (ibid., 5).

This is the first. Behold the second chapter:

“The Lord your God shall raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him, as you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb when the assembly was gathered and you said: [Col. 0442A] ‘I shall no longer hear the voice of the Lord my God, nor see this great fire again, lest I die.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘All that they have spoken is good. I shall raise up for them a prophet from among your brothers, like you, and shall put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak to them everything that I command him. But whoever refuses to hear his words, which he shall speak in my name, I shall exact vengeance. But the prophet who, corrupted by arrogance, wishes to speak in my name things which I did not command him to say, or in the name of foreign gods, shall be put to death.’ But if you reply in silent thought, ‘How can I understand a word which the Lord has not spoken?’ you shall have this sign: whatever that prophet has foretold in the name of the Lord and does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; [Col. 0442B] rather, the prophet has invented it through the swelling pride of his own mind, and therefore you shall not fear him” (Deut. 18:15–22).

XI. What occasion, then, did they find in all this for destroying their Messiah? He neither urged them to follow foreign gods, “nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22); his works bore testimony concerning him, so that if they did not believe his very words, they ought at least to have believed his works. You who are uncircumcised in heart: was it perhaps of you that what follows was spoken? “Circumcise, therefore, the foreskin of your hearts, and do not harden your neck” (Deut. 10:16).

But lest some should transfer what was said above to something else, he adds as though by repetition: “You shall make cords in the fringes at the four corners of your cloak with which you are covered” (Deut. 22:12). Then, as though bringing this to a summary, he says: “Keep yourself from every evil thing” (Deut. 23:9)—as if to say: Do you wish me to gather in a brief epitome what you must do? Hear: “Keep yourself from every evil thing.” It follows: “You shall have a place outside the camp to which you may go for the needs of nature, carrying a peg on your belt; and when you sit down, you shall dig around it and cover with the excavated earth that from which you have relieved yourself” (ibid., 12–14).

XII. B. Perhaps they will answer that, because they are not in their own land, these things need not be observed.

G. Because they are exiles and strangers, will they therefore think themselves able to transgress these and other commands? Hence they exact debts from us with interest, although it was said earlier: “You shall not lend at interest to your brother, but to a stranger” [Col. 0442D] (Deut. 23:19). Yet in this same book it is said: “And you therefore love strangers, because you too were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Deut. 10:19). How do they reconcile these things? For since, in their view, all who have foreskins are strangers and foreigners, how are they said to love those from whom they violently extort usury and plunder? We pass over for the moment the fact that they buy whatever goods have been stolen, because they are purchased cheaply from thieves. But why say more? “You shall know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16).

XIII. There follows also that glorious proof of the Lord’s Passion, which, because they do not give it credence, they wholly fail to understand: “And your life,” he says, “shall be as though hanging before you; you shall fear by night and by day, and shall not believe in your life” (Deut. 28:66). What is clearer than this Gospel [Col. 0443A] passage? What is sweeter than this prophecy? Our Saviour—the way, truth, and life—who was the light of men before the eyes of the Jews, hung upon the wood of the cross; and yet the unhappy Synagogue did not believe in her life as it hung there.

Moses too, in his blessings of the children of Israel, puts forward such riddles as seem to promise the rising of the Saviour and the calling of the nations. For he says: “The Lord came from Sinai, and rose for us from Seir; he appeared from Mount Paran, and with him were thousands of saints. In his right hand was a fiery law; he loved the peoples; all the saints are in his hand” (Deut. 33:2–3).

Let it suffice, to avoid weariness, to have read thus far the questions drawn from the Pentateuch of Moses, by which Jewish cunning or wickedness is refuted. We have omitted the book of Joshua, which the Jews call *Josue Jehosua*, [Col. 0443B] and *Sphetim*, that is, Judges, because we have seen in them little which, according to the letter, breaks the horn of the Jews. Henceforth, if it pleases you, let us carefully search the volumes of *Malachim*, that is, Kings, perhaps in the sequence of events we may find the cake baked under ashes by which Elijah was fed.

XIV. Let us now first inquire what the verse in the song of Hannah means: “The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth, and shall give power to his king, and shall exalt the horn of his Christ” (1 Sam. 2:10). There was not yet a king in Israel; what then does “He shall give power to his king” mean?

B. He undoubtedly speaks of that king who, “while he was at his table, the nard of” the bride “gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1:12; cited here as Cant. 2:11).

G. Blessed be the utterance [Col. 0443C] of your mouth, dearest brother, for you have answered well. For he is the king and priest according to the order of Melchizedek, concerning whom it is also added: “I shall raise up your seed after you, who shall come forth from your womb, and I shall establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I shall establish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I shall be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2 Sam. 7:12–14). This cannot be understood of Solomon. For if his throne was to be established literally for ever, let them show, I pray, someone now sitting on the throne of the kingdom from the house of David.

Furthermore, tell me, I beseech you: what is meant by David’s saying before the Lord, after the words of Nathan the prophet: “Who am I, Lord [Col. 0443D] God, that you have brought me thus far? Yet even this appeared too little in your sight, Lord my God, unless you were to speak concerning the house of your servant for a long way off. For this is the law of Adam” (ibid., 18–19). What, I ask, is “this law of Adam”? The meaning is this: You speak concerning the house of your servant for a long way off because you have determined that your Son shall be incarnate from his seed. Why? “For this is the law of Adam”: “as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:22).

For David himself was not speaking, but the Holy Spirit was upon him, as the following history declares: “David son of Jesse said: The man said, he to whom it was ordained concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob, the excellent psalmist of Israel: the Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was upon my tongue” (2 Sam. [Col. 0444A] 23:1–2). Do you see how in three expressions he has comprehended the whole Trinity? “The Spirit of the Lord, concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob.”

B. “Truly this place is holy,” and “it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4; Gen. 28:17).

XV. G. There is another matter with which we shall press the Jews, who reproach us with images of saints, calling Christians idolaters. For if we are to be rebuked for these, why do we find that Moses made the bronze serpent in the wilderness, and Solomon twelve oxen and other such things in the construction of the Temple? Indeed, it was forbidden in the Law: “You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on earth below, or of those things which are in the waters beneath the earth” (Exod. 20:4). Why then does the Lord forbid through his servant, “You shall not make [Col. 0444B] a graven image,” and afterward command him to make a serpent of bronze? Therefore, O miserable people, we are not forbidden to make images, but to make and worship them. Hence he immediately added: “You shall not worship them nor serve them” (ibid., 5).

Someone might perhaps find other such matters in the books of Kings by which Jewish unbelief could be disproved. But because the book of Psalms, in which the purpose of our project is especially strengthened, remains to be expounded, Solomon’s books are not to be explained. Since the length of a work is customarily the mother of weariness, it is enough to have passed briefly through *Malachim*. Let us now hear what the Psalmist foretold concerning the restoration of the human race.

XVI. In the second Psalm he says: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.” Likewise: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

B. What, I ask, is “Today I have begotten you”?

G. The utterances of the Psalmist have been explained by men of such great and numerous renown that they do not need our exposition. Yet it will not be unsuitable to relate what we have received from them. What else, then, is “Today I have begotten you” than “eternally” or “from eternity”?

Psalm VII: “Arise, Lord God, in the command which you have ordained; the synagogue of the peoples shall surround you. And because of this return on high.”

Psalm IX: “Let sinners be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God.” If by “hell” they meant the pit or cavern of the grave, as they themselves falsely claim, [Col. 0444D] why would he desire sinners to be turned into hell, since all flesh makes its way there? And again: “Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them.”

Psalm XV: “You shall not abandon my soul in hell, nor shall you give your Holy One to see corruption,” concerning which there has been fuller discussion in the Acts of the Apostles.

Psalm XVIII: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.”

Psalm XXI: “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones.”

Psalm XLVI: “God ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord at the sound of a trumpet.”

Psalm XLVIII: “Like sheep they are placed in hell; death shall feed upon them.” In the same Psalm: “Yet God shall redeem your soul from the hand of hell, when he receives me.”

Psalm LIV: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell.”

Psalm LX: “You shall add days [Col. 0445A] upon days to the king; his years unto the day of generation and generation.” If they presume to understand this of anyone other than Christ Jesus, God and king, how does what follows stand: “He remains for ever before the sight of God; who shall seek his mercy and truth?”

Psalm LXVII: “You ascended on high; you took captivity captive.”

Psalm LXVIII: “Let not those who wait for you, Lord, be ashamed.” Speaking of how many instances of waiting: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord”; “Wait for the Lord; act manfully”; “I was waiting for him who saved me”; “I shall wait for the Lord my Saviour.” Do you think I shall endure? Shall I see? “Wait, wait again; wait, wait again” (Isa. 28:10).

In the same Psalm: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst gave me vinegar to drink. Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their backs always.”

Psalm LXXI: “He shall come down like rain upon fleece. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts. From usury and injustice he shall redeem their souls. And he shall live, and gold of Arabia shall be given to him.”

XVII. But lest they think this was said concerning their own Messiah, since they say he will be a mere human being and affirm that no one except God is to be worshipped—which is true—he added and said: “And they shall worship him continually.” And again: “Before the sun his name endures.” Do you see how greatly the entire sequence of this Psalm is filled with the heavenly dew of balm?

Psalm LXXIX: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us; God of hosts, restore us, and show us your face, and we shall be saved.” As though he openly said: If you wish us to be saved, show us your face—that is, make visible the form of your substance through the assumption of flesh—and we shall be saved.

Again in the same Psalm: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved.” In this threefold repetition nothing else is to be signified than: “He who sees me sees also the Father” (John 14:9); and he who sees the Father and the Son sees the Paraclete proceeding from both.

B. “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance” (1 Tim. 1:15).

G. Psalm LXXXVIII: “The lawgiver shall give blessings; they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.” O perverse generation and unbelieving children! Today Moses, your lawgiver, will strike you with a horned syllogism: whichever alternative you choose, confusion will follow you. For since Moses says in the person of the Lord, “No man shall see me” (Exod. 33:20), while the Psalmist says, “The God of gods shall be seen in Zion,” one of them must necessarily be lying. Rather, you are liars, because you are of your father the devil, and your father is a liar. Put, miserable people, put wood into Marah so that the waters may be sweetened, and you shall see the God of gods in Zion.

Psalm LXXXIV: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.”

Psalm LXXXVI: “Will not Zion say: A man—and a man—was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her?”

Psalm LXXXVIII: “He himself called upon me: You are my Father”; and almost every verse of this Psalm breathes the incarnation of Christ God and his other mysteries. In the same Psalm: “Who is the man who shall live and not see death? Who shall rescue his soul from the hand of hell?” Will they say that here “hell” means an earthly pit or cavern? But can a soul be said to be confined in an earthly cave, when it is itself spirit?

In Psalm CVIII, that is, “O God, do not be silent concerning my praise,” it must be asked of them against whom, precisely, he utters the curses.

XVIII. Psalm CIX follows: “The Lord said to my Lord,” concerning which Truth sufficiently disputed with the adversaries of truth in the Gospel. Not only this Psalm, but all its verses are watered with the dripping of heavenly rain: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power,” etc. Likewise, “You are a priest for ever,” not according to the order of priests who offer sacrifices carnally, but “according to the order of Melchizedek,” who, as we read, offered bread and wine to your faithful Abraham as a mystery of your life-giving body and blood.

Psalm CX: “The Lord sent redemption to his people; he commanded his covenant for ever.”

Psalm CXI: “A light has arisen in darkness for the upright.”

Psalm CXVII: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.”

There is one thing further on which I would wish you to give me an explanation. Since he was governed by the law of nature and was also bound by the commandments of the written Law, why did he so earnestly establish another law for himself, saying: “Set before me a law, O Lord, the way of your justifications” (Ps. 118:33)? I believe that the excellent psalmist of Israel said this because he saw, according to the Apostle, that no one could be justified by works of the Law (Rom. 3:20); and therefore he earnestly prayed that a law might be set before him in which, grace going before, he might be justified.

We have thus touched briefly upon the Psalms, in which, taught by the Holy Spirit, we have noted certain interpretations that are novel but not unbelievable. But if anyone thinks it unbelievable that the Holy Spirit speaks through the mouth of a sinner, let him consider that the poet, the Cumaean prophetess, and Caiaphas prophesied. But enough of this. Let us now proceed in order to *Malloth*, that is, Solomon’s Proverbs, where we shall show both that hell exists—which some Jews deny—and that at that time no one was freed from original sin. We have also thought it fitting first to set down the words of Wisdom, who is Christ, so that we may at least ask them in what sense they judge those words to be expounded concerning him.

XIX. He says, therefore: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. I was established from eternity” (Prov. 8:22). And after inserting many matters pertinent to this, he adds: “And my delights were to be with the children of men” (ibid., 31). If, then, Christ the Lord delights to be with the children of men, “how long, you sons of men, are you heavy of heart?” You are children of men, not sons of God, adherents of Moses: “Why do you love vanity” by following the carnal things of the Law “and seek falsehood” (Ps. 4:3), denying him whom the Law and prophets foretold would come?

Again: “Hell and destruction are before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of men?” (Prov. 15:11). Likewise, concerning the same: “The path of life is above for the wise, that he may turn aside [Col. 0447A] from hell on the last day” (ibid., 24). Again: “Hell and destruction shall not be filled” (Prov. 27:20). Likewise in the same book: “There are three insatiable things, and a fourth which never says, ‘Enough’: hell, the mouth of the womb, and earth not satisfied with water; and fire never says, ‘Enough’” (Prov. 30:15–16).

It is clear, therefore, from what has been set forth that hell is a place of punishments, to which all who died under the Law departed from life. For all who were born were held by original sin; hence it is written in the same book: “Who can say: My heart is clean; I am pure from sin?” (Prov. 20:9). There is another evident testimony in this same volume concerning the Son of God against the Jews, which we reserve for the following book.

XX. From the book of Wisdom, also called Solomon’s, we have drawn a testimony to the Lord’s Passion which not even Apella the Jew can oppose. For they said: “Let us surround the righteous man, because he is useless to us and opposed to our works; he reproaches us for sins against the Law and defames us for sins against our discipline. He promises that he has knowledge of God and calls himself the Son of God. He has become to us a reproach for our thoughts. Even to see him is burdensome to us, because his life is unlike that of others and his ways are changed. We have been regarded by him as triflers, and he abstains from our ways as from uncleannesses; he declares the latter end of the righteous and glories that he has God for his Father. Let us therefore see whether his words are true; let us test what will happen to him and discover what his latter end will be. For if he is the true Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hand of his enemies. Let us examine him by insult and torture, that we may know his reverence and test his patience; let us condemn him to a most shameful death, for there shall be regard for him according to his words. They thought these things and went astray; for their wickedness blinded them, and they did not know the mystery of God” (Wis. 2:12–22).

B. All these things plainly express the Lord’s Passion and their blindness. It is therefore remarkable that, although they are literalists—that is, although they seek a literal rather than spiritual understanding—they disdain to acknowledge agreement with this text.

XXI. G. Indeed, in Ecclesiasticus, also entitled the book of Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, you will plainly find that by which you may subdue the necks of the rebellious Synagogue. For they say that confession of sins is useless and was invented by priests for profit. But Scripture says: “Do not be ashamed to confess your sins to a man” (Ecclus. 4:31).

You also have in the same book an evident argument concerning the curse of paternal ruin. For it is written: “Woe to you, ungodly men who have forsaken the law of the Most High Lord! Even if you are born, you shall be born in a curse; and if you die, your portion shall be in a curse” (Ecclus. 41:11–12). If they answer that this was said of transgression of the written Law, how are its forsakers born under a curse? Can anyone be accused of transgressing the Law before being born? Far be it from us to think this, we who believe in him of whom it follows: “At his word the wind was still; by his thought he calmed the deep, and he planted the islands [in it] [the Lord Jesus]” (Ecclus. 43:25).

XXII. Because they do not believe in him, the book of Paralipomenon also writes concerning them, not without reason: “Many days shall pass in Israel without the true God, without a priest who teaches, and without the Law” (2 Chron. 15:3). A long discussion could be extended upon this, if the strength of our intellect were sufficient.

XXIII. But since our purpose was to show from different places of Scripture that hell is a place of punishments, to which not only unbelievers now descend, but also believers before the Incarnation of the Redeemer were tending, let us also establish the certainty of the disputed matter from the words of Job. For he said: “Leave me therefore a little, that I may lament my sorrow before I go and do not return, to a land dark and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death dwells and there is no order, but everlasting horror” (Job 10:20–22).

The man of God was certainly convinced that, as soon as he was released from the mass of earthly dregs, he would descend to the land of misery and darkness, led there by original sin. Hence shortly afterward he adds: “All that is mine shall descend into the deepest hell” (Job 17:16). As though he used these words openly: I shall descend not only into the hell which they call the cavern of the grave, but “into the deepest hell”; not only with my body, but “all that is mine”—that is, my entire self, body and soul, shall descend—either to be held there only by original sin, or to be punished for some actual offence.

Hence, as though in doubt, he adds: “Do you think that there will at least be rest there for me?” (ibid.). As if he said: Do you think that the flame of Gehenna will find some actual sin in me there to punish? Or shall I be held there only because of original sin and thus ought to rest? For it must not be believed that the holy fathers, predecessors of the Lord’s coming, suffered in hell any torments other than darkness. Blessed Augustine also affirms this concerning infants one day old who, overtaken by death, did not obtain the grace of baptism. For the punishment of those who added no sin to original sin will be most mild.

XXIV. A diligent reader could indeed draw many other testimonies to the Lord’s birth, Passion, and Resurrection from the volumes of the Old Testament. But since our purpose is to investigate the Trinity, who is God, amid the ancient ceremonies of the Synagogue, let us bring the work of this second little book to an end and prepare the devotion of our heart for the expenditure required by so great a subject.

B. Let it be so, provided that, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*, we first invoke divine help, without which nothing at all is strong, fruitful, or perfect.

G. Your counsel, man of God, is good; what you have said is both good and fitting. And although “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9), nevertheless, because [Col. 0449A] we are going to speak concerning the Trinity, let us burst forth into praise of the threefold God at the beginning—that is, at the head of the third book—so that what is again said may thus be fulfilled: “At the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. 39:8).

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0449]

[Col. 0449A] I. “How good is God to Israel!” (Ps. 72:1). How good are your ancient works which you showed to our fathers, leading them out from the land of servitude; but how good—indeed, how excellent—are your latter works, which you wrought in the midst of the earth (Ps. 73:12), rescuing us from the prison of death, not with the rod of Moses but with your outstretched arm, so that, as this redemption was greater than the former one, so its minister of redemption might be greater!

There God, through a man, freed from slavery not the human being but the human being’s body; here God delivered body and soul, that is, the whole human being, from the bond of perpetual death. There, through wood and water; here, through wood, water, and blood. There, a servant liberates a fellow servant; here, the Lord liberates a servant. There, a servant is raised up as a leader; here, the leader and Lord is humbled into a servant.

O wondrous condescension, worthy of wonder! The righteous is condemned so that the unrighteous may be saved; the Lord is punished and the servant acquitted. He has mercy on the servant who does not spare the Son. O gentle cruelty! O cruel mercy! He imprisons the one more dearly loved in order to release the one less dearly loved—or rather, one almost equally dear. What love can be greater than this love? Although Truth says: “No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13), there is yet greater love: that one lay down his life for his enemies. But while we were enemies of God, he laid down his life for us. With what depths of mercy, therefore, did he love us, who, in order to love us, hated his own life?

II. O highest good, one source, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one loving him who is from himself, one loving him from whom he is, and love itself; and yet one—lover, beloved, love! Not three essences, but three persons, whom personal property differentiates, while the equality of one and the same essence unites: one unbegotten, one begotten, one proceeding; one Godhead, one blessedness, one eternity: “From whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things.”

Grant us, we beseech you, to find what we seek and attain what we investigate. Grant that, once light has been found, we may fix the clear eyes of our mind upon you. Grant us to contemplate the fountain of good. Open the treasures of your wisdom; fill the vessels of our hearts, which, though empty of good works, are nevertheless refreshed with the wine and oil of faith. Establish the course of our pen, so that we may bring to light what the holiest Fathers thought concerning the Trinity, who is God, before the time of revealed grace, without falling into error; and so that we may blunt the darts of the arrogant Synagogue without, nevertheless, falling into heresy: through him who, born of a Virgin, destroyed heretical depravity. Amen.

III. There is among us a Jew at Châtillon, whom the Hebrews of all the neighbouring cities and towns call, by antonomasia, “the Master.” The day before yesterday, therefore, when I had armed myself with the sign of the cross to dispute with him, I confidently went down into the assembly of the wicked, [Col. 0450B] and discussed much with them concerning the observance of the legal commandments. After a great part of the day had already been consumed by lengthy debate, conversation finally arose concerning their Messiah. Having argued long concerning him, we eventually mentioned the creation of the first man. Seizing the opportunity, I immediately turned the subject of discussion to the Trinity and began with this point: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

“Who,” I asked, “is speaking, and to whom?”

“God,” he said, “to the angels, wishing to make man by their counsel.”

On hearing this, I burst out laughing, and, before raising a second question, added with a laugh: “Tell me, I pray, was man made in the image of the Creator or of the angels?”

“Of the Creator,” he said.

“What, then,” I said, “is the meaning of what follows: ‘In our image’? Since man was made in the image of God alone, even if God had said to the angels, ‘Let us make,’ he nevertheless ought, considering the singularity of his own person, to have said, ‘In my image,’ not ‘in our image.’ For ‘our’ is a pronoun designating not one but several persons: it is internally of the first person, but externally of the third.”

IV. B. I ask you to dwell a little longer on this passage and briefly settle what judgment should be made concerning it. G. We cannot at all be discharged from these matters except insofar as the Holy Spirit grants us utterance. [Col. 0450D] Besides, I fear that, if I undertake so great a burden, crushed by the weight of the work I may succumb to the labour and leave my attempts vainly unfinished. But because it is written, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11), although we distrust our own powers, yet following the footsteps of those who have written on this matter, we shall briefly explain the aforesaid verse: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” The Father speaks to the Son, saying, “Let us make man.” Therefore he says “Let us make” to the Son, because “all things were made through him” (John 1:2). For the Father wrought all things through the Son, and the Son is co-worker in all things, because, when “he prepared the mountains, I was present with him, ordering all things” (Prov. 8:27).

He says “Let us make” [Col. 0451A] to the Son; but does he also speak to the Holy Spirit? Truly, he speaks also to the Holy Spirit. For if he spoke only to the Son—“Let us make man in our image”—man would have been made in the image only of Father and Son. But it is established that man was made in the image of the Trinity; therefore the Father spoke to his Son and to the Holy Spirit: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” In this, certainly, one must note that he said both “Let us make” and “our” in the plural: both “Let us make” and “our” are plurals; and they ought not to be understood except relatively. For it was not, as Augustine says, that gods should make, or that man should be made in the image of gods; but that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit should make him.

Furthermore, [Col. 0451B] if he had said to the angels, “Let us make,” it would indeed seem plausible that man was also made in the image of angels, and that not God the Creator alone, but angels too, were makers of man and, as it were, co-creators. For example: if you, being a priest and sufficiently learned, were speaking to a certain layman wholly without learning and like a brute animal, saying, “Come, brother, let us celebrate Mass; let us sing Vespers,” or something similar—when it was clear that you alone, and not he, were capable in this matter—would you not signify that the person to whom you said these things could become your helper and a participant in your ministry or office?

V. B. Certainly it would be so; but now let us proceed to what follows, for a long road remains to us. Yet [Col. 0451C] we must not pass over in silence the point which you thought should be raised against them above. G. What is that, pray? Why were the works of the second day deprived of a blessing? G. When, the day before yesterday, I consulted a theologian of considerable authority about this question, he sent me a solution in writing [Note: [Col. 0451D] Reply of Master Peter the Chanter of Paris.]; although it satisfied the question, it did not suffice for the questioner. This is a copy of the letter which he sent me:

“To Master Walter, his friend, Master Peter: greeting and sincere affection. Since I am unable to supply from my own resources what may satisfy a hungry palate, the Holy Spirit answers in my stead, he who communicated the solution of this scrupulous question to the orthodox Fathers. From [Col. 0451D] their tradition I have learned that the second day takes its name from the number two, and two is an ill-omened number. Since it admits division, it signifies the discord of schism. But God is a lover of peace and unity; in mystery of this matter, the work of the second day is denied a blessing. Or, what is more probable,” he says, “the second and third days have water as their common material. On the second day God divided the upper waters from the lower by interposing the firmament; on the third he gathered the waters beneath the firmament, so that they might flow away through underground channels and conduits. Therefore, as the material was common, so the blessing ought to have been common; hence [Col. 0452A] the blessing of the second day was reserved for the third, as though it were to be received from their common character. Farewell.”

VI. But since those who have thus thought and expounded well were themselves human beings, and since we too are human, though not their equals, let us hunt a little longer in the thicket of this question, so that, as is read of Jonathan, if we find honey, we may at least touch it with the tip of the rod (1 Sam. 14:29). The number two, then, as has already been mentioned, receives the cutting of division, and is, as it were, a boundary separating unity from unity. But what is more accursed, what more worthy of condemnation, than to divide the Trinity from unity in such a way that either three gods are believed to exist in the Trinity, or only one person in the Godhead? Was not Arius of the household of the number two, since he divided the Trinity from [Col. 0452B] unity in such a way as to affirm that there are three persons in the Trinity while refusing unity of substance in that Trinity? But did not Sabellius likewise lack blessing together with the number two, since he believed in unity of essence in the Godhead in such a way that he divided the Trinity of persons from unity? Therefore the number two lacked blessing because it exceeds unity and separates the Trinity from it.

Thus three persons are to be believed in the Trinity, in such a way that the three—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are believed to be one essence in the Godhead. But whoever believes otherwise than this, or otherwise than this faith, and has not entered the sheepfold—that is, the holy Church—through the door, which is Christ (John 10:9), is a thief and a robber (ibid., v. 1), and worthy to be struck with an anathema together with the number two. [Col. 0452C] “For this is the Catholic faith: unless everyone faithfully and firmly believes it, he cannot be saved” (Athanasian Creed). This is the threefold cord that is not easily broken (Eccl. 4:12). This is the number of which I believe the poet dreamed when he said:

> First I bind about you these three threads,  
> Diverse in threefold colour; and three times around these altars  
> I lead the image.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* 8.73–75)

And, as though explaining the unity of the number three and why he ordered these things to be done three times, he adds:

> . . . . . God delights in an odd number.  
> (Id., ibid., 75)

[Col. 0452D] And again:

> Bind the three colours in three knots, Amaryllis.  
> (Id., ibid., 77)

B. “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28:16). Truly this is the honeycomb which you proposed to hunt, which you found in the thicket of the letter through Jonathan—that is, “the dove’s dwelling,” namely through the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. Although you did not drink it fully, you nevertheless tasted it, as it were, with your mouth from the very tip of the rod.

VII. G. Let us further consider concerning the Trinity, which is God, how Abraham, the faithful elder and first path of believing, father of the blessed seed, understood it. “When he was sitting at the entrance of his tent, the Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre, in the very heat of the day. And when he lifted up his eyes, three men appeared standing near him. When he saw them, he ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them, and bowed to the earth and said: ‘Lord, if I have found favour in your eyes, do not pass by your servant; but let me bring a little water, and let your feet be washed, and rest beneath the tree. I will set out a morsel of bread, and strengthen your hearts; afterwards you shall pass on, for this is why you have turned aside to your servant.’ They said: ‘Do as you have said.’ Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah and said to her: ‘Make haste; mix three measures of fine flour and make cakes baked under the ashes.’ Then [Col. 0453B] he ran to the herd, took from it a very tender and excellent calf, and gave it to a servant, who hurried and cooked it. He also took butter and milk, and the calf which he had cooked, and set them before them; while he himself stood near them beneath the tree. And when they had eaten, they said to him: ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’ He answered: ‘Behold, she is in the tent.’ To him he said: ‘I shall return to you, life accompanying me, and Sarah your wife shall have a son’” (Gen. 18:1–10).

You see, therefore, dearest friend, how Abraham sometimes speaks in the plural to the three, while at other times one speaks to Abraham, and at other times three speak. Nor is this strange, because these three are one. But because blessed Augustine dwells at length on this chapter in his book *On the Trinity*, we do not dare add anything to his disputation. [Col. 0453C] Let it suffice to have said this alone about it: from what precedes, it should be understood that the Trinity consists of persons and that the essence of the Trinity is one.

This too is intimated in what follows, when the Lord speaks to Moses, saying: “I am who am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14–16). Behold, “I,” a pronoun signifying substance, is placed first; and the substantive verb is repeated three times: “I am who am,” and “he who is.” By these words nothing other than unity of essence and trinity of persons is, one must believe, signified. This is certainly confirmed by the subsequent words of the holy Gospel according to Moses, to whom the Lord again spoke, saying: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: The Lord, God of your fathers, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob, [Col. 0453D] has sent me to you” (ibid., v. 15). Observe carefully: “the Lord, God of your fathers.” Behold, unity of essence is designated. “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob”: behold, the Trinity of persons. “God of Abraham”: God the Father, who in many places of Scripture bears the figure of God the Father. “God of Isaac”: God the Son, in whose type Isaac was led out to be sacrificed. “God of Jacob”: God the Holy Spirit, in whose mystery Jacob anointed the stone, in accordance with the saying of Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61:1). Thus the meaning is, “God of Abraham and God of Isaac and God of Jacob”—that is, God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit. Otherwise, why should he be called the God of these three alone and so often, [Col. 0454A] and not also the God of Moses, the God of Samuel, and the God of David, unless so that he might be shown to be threefold and so that a quaternity might not be admitted into the Trinity?

VIII. Let us stand here a little against useless servants, against enemies of the faith. Come then, O Jews,

> Ready alike to sing and to answer.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* 7.5)

If the mystery of the Trinity had been wholly unknown to the holy forerunners of the Lord’s birth, why did the Old Scripture embrace the number three with such reverence? For the Lord commands Abraham: “Take,” he says, “a heifer of three years, a she-goat of three years, and a ram of three years” (Gen. 15:9). Isaiah hears the seraphim crying one to another: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isa. [Col. 0454B] 6:3). He also says: “The Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king” (Isa. 33:22). Note the order of the words. The Psalmist says something similar: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us” (Ps. 66:8). May God the Father bless us, our Lord and judge; but now “he has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). May God our God bless us, our lawgiver, who redeemed us and gave us the law of grace. May God the Holy Spirit, our king, bless us.

Hear also Jeremiah saying: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord it is” (Jer. 7:4). Likewise: “I, I am; I saw, says the Lord; and: Alas, alas, alas!” (Jer. 34:17). And in Ezekiel: “Alas, alas, alas: Lord God!” (Ezek. 9:8). But why say more? If you still unbelievers [Col. 0454C] refuse to believe in the Trinity, consult Elijah: why did he stretch himself out and measure himself over the boy three times (3 Kings 17:21), and why did he order jars of water to be poured three times over the holocaust and the wood? For it is written: “Fill four jars with water and pour them over the holocaust and the wood. And again he said: Do this a second time also. When they had done it a second time, he said: Do the same thing a third time also. They did it a third time, and the waters ran around the altar, and the trench of the watercourse was filled” (3 Kings 18:34–35). You see how, in the threefold pouring, the man of God completed his sacrifice.

IX. Moreover, the second book of Maccabees invites us to the same conclusion. It writes thus about Heliodorus and his attendants: “There appeared to him a certain horse with a terrible rider, adorned with the finest trappings; and, charging upon Heliodorus, it crushed him with its forehooves. He who sat upon it seemed to have golden armour. There also appeared two young men, handsome in strength, most glorious, and splendidly clothed” (2 Macc. 3:25–26). But what shall I say of blessed Job, whom perhaps you will not receive because you say that he was uncircumcised? For in his book it is written: “Behold, God works all these things three times with each person, that he may call back their souls from corruption and enlighten them with the light of the living” (Job 33:29–30). Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, what will you answer to this? Are these testimonies enough for you? Certainly not. For how will a wall be built where its foundation [Col. 0455A] is lacking? If you savoured the things above and not those upon earth (Col. 3:2), you would at least believe the oracle of Isaiah, who introduces the Son of God speaking so openly that no Gentile, still less a Jew, would dare contradict anything.

For in it is written: “Hear me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call: I myself, I am the first and I am the last. My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens. I shall call them, and they shall stand together. Gather yourselves, all of you, and hear: Who among them will announce these things? The Lord has loved him; he will do his will in Babylon, and his arm among the Chaldeans. I, I have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and his way has prospered. Draw near to me and hear this: from the beginning [Col. 0455B] I have not spoken in secret; from the time before they came to be, I was there; and now the Lord God has sent me and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:12–16).

Who, then, is this person of such sovereign authority, who speaks in this way? It is established that he is God and not man, who says: “I myself, I am the first and I am the last,” and “from the time before they came to be, I was there.” But is it God the Father who speaks, or God the Holy Spirit, who says, “I am the first and I am the last”? He is undoubtedly God, and “before they came to be, I was there.” But who says, “Now the Lord God has sent me and his Spirit”? Since the Father is never read to have been sent, he certainly is not the Father, but his Son.

X. B. Since you have mentioned the Son of God, something happened to me some time ago which I do not wish to conceal from you. For the day before yesterday, as I was disputing with one of the sons of Belial about their superstition, the Ishmaelite asked me: “Where, brother,” he said, “have you, who believe in the Son of God, found that God had a Son? Unless perhaps you wish to call human beings sons of God by adoption?” Compelled by the necessity of this question, we must cast the net on the right side of the boat and probe the waters of Scripture with the fishing-spear of reason, in case, fishing in them, we may come upon the Son of God. B. “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked” (Luke 11:27), because your request is not worthy of rejection; but, as you have advised, let your will be done.

Let us therefore see what Solomon, that most wise king, said concerning the Son of God. Although he is known to have been an idolater, it is nevertheless certain that he said nothing heretical about him. In *Qoheleth*, that is, the book of Proverbs, he speaks thus of the Son of God: “I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me; I have not learned wisdom, nor have I known the knowledge of the holy ones. Who has ascended to heaven and descended? Who has held the wind in his hands? Who has bound the waters as in a garment? Who has raised up all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his Son, if you know?” (Prov. 30:2–4).

Consider, then, these utterances, and receive the words of this king with your ears, that you may see and know of whom he speaks here: whether of some son of God according to adoption, or of the only-begotten Son, substantial and coeternal with him, whose name he so earnestly seeks [Col. 0456A] and investigates. B. He asks concerning that one and his name, “whose name is wonderful in all the earth” (Ps. 8:2), and whose name is above every name (Phil. 2:9). G. It is indeed as you think. For not only here, but also in the Book of Wisdom, he writes the same concerning the Son equal to God the Father, in these words: “Let us see, the Jews say, whether his words are true; let us test what shall happen to him, and we shall know what his end will be.
