For if he is the true Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hand of his adversaries” (Wis. 2:17–18).

Behold, now he speaks openly and uses no parable (John 16:29). For he said “the true Son of God,” to distinguish him from those who are called sons of God not by nature but by designation. Of these the Psalmist says: “I [Col. 0456B] said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 21:6 [citation as printed]). More plainly, Truth says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12:50). If, therefore, they are Christ’s brothers, they are also sons of God.

XI. We therefore have two suitable testimonies in Solomon concerning the Son of God. If these do not suffice for the sons of perdition, we must return to Daniel, in whom Nebuchadnezzar, beholding the Son of God in the furnace, says: “Behold, I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no corruption in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3:92). Hear, Israel; hear an idolater; hear a foreigner. Submit to the Gentile, you who refuse to believe Solomon. Who is this Son of God? This, indeed, is the Son of God who much later wondrously deigned to become the Son of Man. Shall we say “wondrously,” or “miserably”? But, to confess more truly, let us say both wondrously and miserably: wondrously, because “O wonderful exchange! The Creator of the human race, taking an animate body, deigned to be born of a Virgin” (*Office of Blessed Mary on Saturday*). Miserably in us, because “truly he bore our infirmities” (Isa. 53:4). Likewise wondrously in himself, because a wonderful mystery is declared: “God was made man” (John 1:14); and because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7). But miserably in us, because the true Samaritan, travelling on his way, [Col. 0456D] came beside the wounded man and, seeing him, was moved with compassion.

“This, therefore, is wonderful in our eyes” (Matt. 21:42). This is the new thing which the Lord declares through Jeremiah the prophet that he created upon earth, saying: “Return, virgin Israel, return to these cities. How long will you dissolve yourself in delights, wandering daughter? For the Lord has created a new thing upon earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31). And it should be noted that he more properly said “shall encompass” than if he had said “shall beget”; for generation is properly spoken of when a woman is made pregnant after receiving a man’s seed. But because that generation of the Saviour came from the pure flesh of the Virgin without any antecedent material of male seed, “shall encompass” is beautifully said rather than “shall beget,” [Col. 0457A] though either may rightly be said. We have therefore what we sought: namely, clear testimonies concerning the Son of God.

XII. But now let us turn the pen to the third person in the Trinity, the Holy Spirit, whom some falsely allege to be wind or the whistling of a breeze. On this subject blessed Jerome writes in his *Hebrew Questions*: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1). In place of what is written in our codices, *was borne*, the Hebrew has *marahahephet* [*merachephet*], which we may render “was brooding” or “was fostering,” after the likeness of a bird giving life to eggs by its warmth. From this we understand that it is not said of the spirit of the world, as some suppose, but of the Holy Spirit, who is himself said from the beginning to be the giver of life to all things.

Let those who assert falsehood, who insist that the Holy Spirit is to be understood as wind, say how it can be established that “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). For something happened recently which I shall relate to you.

XIII. The day before yesterday, as is my custom, when I was at leisure, I went down on the solemn Lord’s Day to the house of a certain Hebrew, as though I were going to hear something new. When I asked him what the Holy Spirit was, he replied that it was wind. “What, then,” I said, “is meant by David’s saying: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inmost parts. Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit [Col. 0457C] from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit’” (Ps. 50)?

“Furthermore,” I said, “the book of blessed Job does not seem to wish the Holy Spirit to be anything other than God himself. For there Elihu son of Barachel writes thus concerning the Spirit of the Lord: ‘The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life’” (Job 33). “Tell me, then,” I likewise said, “who is this Spirit by whom David desires to be renewed, concerning whom he entreats that he not be taken away from him, and by whom he longs to be strengthened? But who is this Spirit of God, by whom Elihu testifies that he was made? Is he not the Spirit of whom the eminent Psalmist of Israel says: ‘You shall send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth’?” (Ps. 103).

[Col. 0458A] By these and other authorities I drove this adversary of truth to confess that the Holy Spirit is God, and that this same Spirit is wind. Then I said: “By your judgment, the Holy Spirit is wind, and the Holy Spirit is God; therefore God is wind.” B. Certainly you have argued truly and syllogistically. Now let us continue concerning the Holy Spirit, so that, by the completion of him at whose prompting we began this work, we may carry it through.

XIV. G. Let it be as you ask. Let us gather together the testimonies of the prophets concerning the Holy Spirit, whom they bring forth under his same inspiration. Solomon therefore says in the Book of Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit and withdraws from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1). In the same book: “The Spirit [Col. 0458B] of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (ibid.). It is also written in Isaiah: “The joy of wild asses, the pasture of flocks, until the Spirit be poured out upon us from on high” (Isa. 32). Likewise: “I shall pour out my Spirit upon your seed” (Isa. 44). In the same prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61). Micah too says: “I am filled with the power of the Spirit of God” (Mic. 3). Zechariah likewise has: “Not by an army nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord God” (Zech. 4).

But why proceed through each one? Even if I spoke with the tongues of men and angels, I could not explain the Spirit of whom we are speaking. Therefore, bringing our work to an end and setting a limit to our course, we seek the prize—not gold or silver, nor the favour of worldly applause and secular praise. Rather, we ask to be rewarded by him for whom to serve is to reign, concerning whom and from whom we have said whatever we have said well. Henceforth, from those who shall read this work—if anyone captivated by its love reads it—we ask pardon for things omitted or not rightly said; and we ask that, for what has been well said, they render thanks to God and pray to him for us, so that, when we are about to enter the way of all flesh, we may have ready our merciful and gracious defender, the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honour and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0459]

# THE *ALEXANDREIS*, OR DEEDS OF ALEXANDER THE GREAT, COMPRISED IN TEN BOOKS, BY WALTER OF CHÂTILLON

Brought to light from old manuscripts in the libraries of St Gall and Engelberg by the labour of the Reverend Father Athanasius Gugger, monk of St Gall, with his superiors’ permission; printed at the monastery of St Gall by its own press, in the year of salvation 1659.—Duodecimo. (According to the copy preserved in the library at Strasbourg, graciously sent to us by Mr JUNG, librarian of that same library.)

# GREETING TO THE KIND READER

Here for you, kind Reader, is a new work, though ancient, nowhere, so far as I know, published [Note: [Col. 0459]

He is mistaken, as we have already observed above. We have thought it worthwhile to append here the preliminaries of the Lyons edition of 1558, which was printed in italic type (*caractères de civilité*):

*The ten books of the* Alexandreid *of Philip Galtherus, poet, now for the first time published in France and in French handwritten-style characters.*—Lyons: sold by Robert Granjon, printed at his own press, 1558. By royal authority.

## Extract from the King’s Privilege

It has pleased the King, our lord, to grant privilege and permission to Robert Granjon to print this present book, entitled *Alexandreidos*, in his French handwritten-art typeface. And, as recompense for his invention, the said lord wills that no other person whatsoever in this kingdom may cut punches, counterfeit the said French handwritten-art typeface, sell or distribute any impression made with it, except that printed by the said Granjon, under the specified severe penalties contained in the letters and privileges granted to the said Granjon. This is for the successive period and term of ten years, reckoned from the day and date hereof with respect to imitation of the said handwritten-style characters, and with respect to printing of the said book, from the day and date on which it shall have been completed in print. Furthermore, for this work and for the others contained and mentioned in his said letters, the said Granjon wills and intends that, by the extract and notice thereof to be made in every book, the prohibitions and injunctions stated in the privileges, often held to be sufficiently notified to all printers and others concerned, shall be sufficiently made known—as is more fully contained in the letters patent of the said Granjon, granted at Saint-Germain-en-Laye on the twenty-sixth day of December in the year of grace 1557, thus signed:

By the King,

Master Jehan NICOT, Master of Requests of the Household, present. FIZES.

## Epigram of R. Constantinus

> Alexander the Great, who once envied Achilles’ poet  
> Maeonian, now fears envy,  
> Since he has perceived that Galtherus, the lofty-speaking poet,  
> Has thus sung his deeds on the Ausonian trumpet.  
> Homer need not resent this poet’s being preferred to himself,  
> For, even sightless, he could not yet have had his equal.  
> Yet against envy’s sharp goads  
> The Macedonian, who was a monarch, sets forth  
> An allusion to the saying of Zeuxis, and to the king and poet:  
> “You may be envious; you cannot be a rival.”

## From the Latin, into Alexandrine verse

> Alexander the Great, stung by the honour  
> Achilles received, possessing as his beloved Muse  
> The most eloquent of the Greeks, raged with envy;  
> And now he fears that anyone may repeat his error,  
> Since he has heard Galther, lofty sounder,  
> Thus sing his deeds with the Ausonian trumpet;  
> And that blind Homer may not deny him precedence—  
> Homer, who until now has had no equal in his greatness.  
> Yet the Macedonian, who with the arm of victory  
> Made his glory resound through the circuit of the universe,  
> Prepares against the envious man’s pointed missiles  
> The apophthegm drawn from the picture that gives life to  
> The good painter Zeuxis: “Of the poet and king  
> You may be envious, but you cannot equal them.”

## R. Constantinus to the Reader

I do not doubt that, in proportion as the novelty and unusual character of these typefaces have turned the reader toward admiration, their usefulness and elegance will delight him. Robert Granjon has not only ingeniously formed their printed types, but also, like another Dibutades of Sicyon, made and cast their prototypes and impressions. First, as to the beauty of the characters and ease in reading, their form is certainly no less commendable than others, but more familiar to us, since it reproduces as closely as possible the hand of one writing. Thus the printing simulates handwriting, and one may afterwards doubt whether a text is handwritten or printed from type.

Its usefulness will be by no means slight both for our countrymen and for foreigners; I leave its exposition to men of letters. Even without their assistance, the very “wordless practice” (*alogos tribē*, ἄλογος τριβή) will sufficiently reveal its usefulness and will make this script, which was not new, but most familiar to all, familiar above all to the entire European people, whose hand it now especially wears down. Unless, perhaps, someone despises his own things and admires foreign ones; for this very reason he deserves, as among the Romans of old, to be accused and punished for foreign-mindedness, or, in Ulpian’s words, to be reduced to foreign status through the punishment of deportation. For a bad citizen is one who is more captivated by barbarian institutions than by his native ones, and to whom another state is more pleasing than his own. Farewell.

[Col. 0463] (The Engelberg manuscript has the following:

## EPITAPH

Walter, the author of this book, wrote or composed this before beginning the poem, because he feared that death might forestall him:

> An island gave me birth; Châtillon took my name;  
> All Gaul trembled at my songs.  
> I wrote the deeds of the Macedonian leader, but fate’s sudden stroke  
> Closed my work, begun, with death’s barrier.

], a work eagerly examined and desired by many, venerable no less for its antiquity than for its learning. Its author is a certain Walter of Châtillon. He wrote about three hundred years ago; a man most richly equipped both in poetry and in every kind of learning, especially in knowledge of sacred literature. He pursues the deeds of Alexander the Great in such a manner that, through keenness of intellect and sharpness of judgment, he may seem able to enter into competition with those ancient writers whom he admirably emulates: wholly graceful and florid, full of vigour, dense with sententiae, often, as it were, surpassing himself; he has not merely imitated but attained that golden brevity of Quintus Curtius.

In publishing this work I obtained two ancient manuscript copies: one was communicated to me by the most reverend and learned abbot of the celebrated Benedictine monastery of Engelberg; the other was taken from our own old treasury, that is, that of St Gall. The latter is explained by an interlinear gloss, which the former manuscript also has, though more sparingly; this fully persuades me that this author was once publicly lectured upon in the schools. Thus I conjecture that what is reported of Aristotle’s philosophy, combined with the afternoon rhetorical exercise, was also done in the humanities by alternate exposition of Quintus Curtius and this author. This seems capable of being inferred quite clearly from the epitaph which the author composed for himself.

Yet, as nothing in human affairs is blessed in every respect, there are things in this work that may displease more polished readers. To pass over matters forced by necessity, such as *topographus*, *Mesopotamia*, *Jerusalem*, and so forth, so great an author perhaps employs the licence of caesura too frequently. Moreover, he was rather careless with Greek words. Since most of these are names of military commanders and must be taken from the histories of Curtius, Plutarch, and others, and could not be changed without confusing the narrative of events, [Col. 0461] they are marked, lest the reader be troubled, by a change of type and an asterisk. Only proper names that carry error with them, and which Curtius himself does not use, have been altered.

And, not to mention the name *Darius*, whose first two syllables he nearly always makes short, there are many Greek words which cannot be saved even by dialect, such as *Symmachus*, *Nicanor*, and so forth—although what is not permitted to Greeks, when even Virgil varies *Orion* as he pleases? There were also some unusual and obsolete Latin words, though few; in their place, lest these blemishes, as it were, darken the splendid garment, I substituted others, generally recording the former in the margin—except the ablative *mediante*, a word which, since he uses it often, he seems to have liked.

The copies also differed not merely in transposition of words, which is a slight matter, but in their readings. In order that both might be preserved, I consigned most variants to the margins, while omitting errors. More serious scribal errors were corrected in such a way that they would not be plainly apparent; the reader will easily infer them from the changed type, for it is not likely that the author committed such errors, unless perhaps some were made by the author himself, since otherwise he would be overturning himself by self-contradiction. Certain doubtful forms, supported even by the authority of ancient writers—such as *temulentus*, and *Clytus*, which is found written equally with *y*—will offend no one. These are the matters of which I wished to warn you, benevolent reader. Farewell, and enjoy this work while other things follow; take kindly this labour of mine in bringing antiquity into the light.

# THE AUTHOR’S EPISTLE [Note: [Col. 0463B] Absent from the Lyons edition.]

[Col. 0463]

[Col. 0463A] It is customary, when something new is recited before the ears of a crowd, for the multitude to divide into opposing factions: one person applauds and declares what he hears worthy of praise; another, whether led by ignorance or warped by the sting of envy or the fuel of hatred, disparages even well-spoken things and judges finely polished verses fit to be returned to the anvil. And it is remarkable that the human race, from its first nature—according to which all things made by God were created very good—has been so corrupted that it is readier to condemn than to pardon, and finds it easier to distort doubtful matters than to interpret them in the better sense.

Fearing this, my *Alexandreis*, I long intended always to suppress you in my mind, and either wholly to destroy a work laboured over for five years or at least, for as long as I lived, to bury it in concealment. At last I resolved to bring you into the light, so that you might finally dare to enter the public records. For I do not think myself better than the Mantuan poet [Virgil], whose works, loftier than mortal talent, were assailed by the tongues of detracting poets; and men presumed to disparage him after his death whom no mortal could equal while he lived.

And our Jerome too, a man as eloquent as he was thoroughly Christian, who habitually replies to his rivals in each of his prefaces, clearly shows that among authors no place of safety remains, since the spur of rivals pierced a man of such celebrated authority. Yet I wish readers of this little work—if anyone, captured by love of it, reads it—to be entreated that, should they find anything blameworthy or deserving of satire in this volume, they consider the shortness of the time in which I wrote and the loftiness of the subject, which, Servius testifies, none of the ancient poets dared undertake to set forth in writing. With this consideration in mind, let them learn at least from dispensation that many things ought to be tolerated which, if anyone proceeded by strict law, might be condemned by the rigour of justice. But enough of this. Now let us address what is at hand; and, so that anyone may more easily find what he seeks, let us divide the whole work into chapters.

## Argument of the First Book

The first book tells how Alexander, imbued with Aristotle’s sacred nectar, was distinguished by sceptre and arms; how he again allied the Cecropids [Athenians] to the king; destroyed the Aonian strongholds; entered the deep with a numerous fleet; and, coming ashore in Asia, shot an arrow from his ship.

Thinking mercy proper, he triumphs over his enemy without battle; and, exalted in spirit, already deems the kingdoms lying beneath the sun to be his own. From a mountain-top he surveys Asia, apportions the cities of his native land among his citizens, marvels at Pergamum, and recalls his dreams.

## Book One

[Col. 0463C] Tell, Muse, of the deeds of the Macedonian leader, spread throughout the whole world; how lavishly he scattered wealth; with what soldiery he conquered Porus and Darius; under what ruler victorious Greece rejoiced; and how tribute returned from the Persians to Corinth.

[Col. 0464C] Had he not, worn down by old age, fallen beneath the unarmed thumb of the Fates, Fame would never speak in our age of Caesar’s triumphs, and all the glory of the Roman race would lie neglected.  
[Note: [Col. 0463] *longum*: “long”; *stratus*: “laid low,” for *fractus*, “broken.”]

[Col. 0465A] For the furnace would outshine its little sparks with the brilliance of his merit; Lucifer himself would pale at his rising, and the wagons of slow Bootes would languish.

But you, whom greater Britain rejoices to have begotten from kings as ancestors; under whose episcopal rule the city of the Senones [Sens] entered upon honour no less great than when Brennus shattered Rome with Senonian arms, about to seize the Tarpeian citadel had the silver goose not awakened the guards; you, upon obtaining at last the government of the see of Rheims, caused a land famous for warlike hardness to lose its name for harshness; you whom Philosophy received into her own lap when you were born, to rear you, and, offering you all Helicon to drink, opened the sacred hall of learning to your heart; whom, long refined in the furnace of study, she granted, once the cloud of things had been dispersed,

[Col. 0465B] to penetrate hidden causes: come hither, run with me across the open sea, pour forth the sacred springs, press the laurel upon your hair, and allow my Muse to be inscribed to you.

The full down of nature had not yet appeared, flourishing in soft hairs and preparing to set forth cheeks unlike those of his mother, when the boy, thirsting with all his heart for arms, heard that Darius imposed laws upon Pelasgian cities and pressed the fields of his fatherland beneath the yoke of empire; indignantly he gave utterance to his anger in these words:

“Alas, how long a rest is imposed upon boys! Shall it never be permitted me, amid funeral battle-lines, with flashing sword to condemn the Persian yoke, to outrun in swift course the sluggish steed of the fugitive tyrant, to throw the confused commanders into disorder, and at least in war to play the man beneath a crested helmet, marked by the banner of the lion’s cub? Is it true that Alcides [Hercules], as a boy, once strangled two serpents by the throat in his cradle? Then, unless the great name of Aristotle terrifies my boyish years, I should not hesitate boldly to begin like exploits.

“Add that greater courage is usually present in a small body at the flowering age, and the lofty force of green youth makes up for delays. Shall I always be thought the offspring of Nectanebus? Or shall I be accused as degenerate? Far be it!”

[Note: [Col. 0465] “nations,” for “cities”; “half-ruined,” for “funereal”; “leader,” for “man”; *Neptanabi* for *Nectanebi*; “or,” for “and”; “as he dictated,” for “he said”; “twelve-year-old,” for “flowering.”]

So he spoke; thus he reasoned within himself with a doubting heart:

As when, perhaps, in Hyrcanian fields a lion-cub sees antlered stags going to pasture, though strength has not yet descended fully into his shoulders,

[Col. 0465D] nor is he yet firm of foot or fierce with hooked teeth: he pants, strikes his empty palate with his eager tongue, spills blood first in spirit before he spills it with his teeth, and mature resolve redeems the slowness of his feet.

So the unbridled boy rages wholly for arms; weak in hand, he bears a lion in his high heart; headlong daring outstrips his tender years. By chance his teacher, lean, pale, and with unkempt hair—nor did his countenance ill correspond to his study—had come forth from open chambers, where he had recently armed wrestlers, fully equipped with the art of logic, for refutations.

[Verse 72.] O how difficult it is for study not to reveal itself in one’s face! His pallid countenance savoured of the nightly lamp; skin married itself to bones in a thin partition upon his face, and fasting leanness, spread through every joint of his hands, pressed upon him. No parenthesis of flesh drove back the bones from the skin: for the fierce labour of study wastes the limbs with leanness, and the inward man takes for himself, as fuel for his labour, the mass of flesh and what food produces outwardly.

Therefore, when he saw the youth threatening with an inflamed face—for fiery redness betrayed his hidden anger—he demanded whence his spirit had caught fire, whence he had drawn the material of grief, and what anger had boiled up so fiercely.

[Col. 0466B] The boy, reverencing the presence of his instructor, lowered his eyes with suppliant countenance; and, prostrate at the knees of the seated man, lamented with tears the old age of his father, oppressed by Darius’s rule, and his fallen fatherland; with tears he intensified his wrath. His teacher drank in these words with attentive ear:

“Clothe your mind with manhood, Macedonian boy; take up arms. You possess matter for courage: bring it into action. Listen here, and I shall teach you how you may do this.

“Despise the double-tongued and worthless servants who are commanded by nature to lie low; do not exalt them. For the torrent swollen by rainwater flows more violently than a perennial river. So a slave, raised by acquired riches and the height of honour into mastery, is more savage than a deaf asp: he closes his ears to prayers and does not know how to become gentle.

[Col. 0466C] “Yet reason’s reckoning does not forbid you to wish to exalt those distinguished by honour, those raised high by excellence of character, even though they lack ample resources, ancestral country, and the glory of lofty birth. For, if I speak the truth, money commonly takes away good character; it does not bring it. Indeed, among the other monsters of night, nothing is more corrupt than this monster that brings forth monsters.

“But the man whom character, not abundance of possessions, enriches; whom virtue raises up—he possesses something to prefer to gold, something to redeem the defect of his native land and to confer upon it both lineage and beauty. Virtue is not sought outside: one who abounds inwardly in character needs no external things. Nobility alone is that which adorns the spirit with character.

“If a dispute arises, hold the scales of judgment straight when you are judge. Let neither affection bend you nor gifts flatter you, nor regard for a person move your steadfast mind.

[Col. 0466D] “The unjust judge is convicted by the gift he has received: for a gift twists the keenness of the judge from the rule of right and wraps his mind in foul darkness. Once the plague of greed—the mother of vices, which alone imprisons every form of virtue—has gained possession of the court, the restraint of law being despised, men run to crime and the council disregards laws.

“Spare the humble; be ready to grant the petitioner’s request; crush the proud. If you have it in your heart to will something great, you will have power to accomplish it. Move the camp, marshal the squadrons, carry war against the enemy.

[Verse 127.] “If, while the hazard of Mars is being played, weak and not-yet-mature age should shrink from hand-to-hand combat, yet let your troops see you armed and cheerful, fighting with prayers, exhortation, and thundering threats. It has sometimes profited commanders to fight by giving orders.

“For while fear treads down the camp, while terror prostrates the languid ranks, while hearts and hands falter, if a stern instructor intoxicates their ears with exhortation, fear withdraws; and, once dread is submerged, unbridled youth rushes into the sword at his counsels. Above all, press upon fleeing enemies first.

“If, however, your soldier should by chance retreat toward his tents, fleeing the hostile ranks with backward step, flee last at the rear; let them see you delaying, and let them be ashamed to return dishonourably from flight without their king.

[Col. 0467B] “Meanwhile measure with your eyes how many thousands threaten, how many troops of infantry are present, how many horsemen, with helmets and shields, strike back the sun. Let not their number frighten you. If you see them advancing weakly, be first to rush into the weapons of those who follow; be first to turn your horse and fall back with bridle drawn tight. Let your vigour stand out here, and the zeal of your men, their burning spirit and experience of harsh war. Here let horse confront horse, sword sword, shield shield, and helmet helmet, buried beneath the helmet of the foe. Scarcely may the conquered offer a trophy to the conqueror.  
[Note: [Col. 0467] “returns,” for “should return”; “by pressing on,” for “at the rear”; “triumph,” for “trophy.”]

“When you either enter a city as its defeated inhabitants surrender it, or, if they resist, break down its gates, open the treasuries and rain largesses upon the companies.

[Col. 0467C] “Pour the oil of gifts upon fresh wounds and hearts swollen with grievous distress; when the treasure-houses are opened, anoint their spirits with presents and apply the liquid of gold. This medicine can heal the sick mind. Thus the rich man heals the poor, and the generous man the greedy.

“But if circumstances should not answer your high spirit, if resources fail or the heap is diminished, let love not be diminished and let no abundance of spirit be lacking. Entice them with promises, and fulfil what you have promised at the appointed time. For a gift shapes dispositions, ensnares the greedy, conceals vice, augments lineage, and subdues the enemy.

“Those whom a lavish right hand embraces need no rampart. Whether peace prevails, or, with the treaty of peace broken, discord rules and rages throughout the whole world, while rulers are uncertain and fear a sudden enemy,

[Col. 0467D] giving is like a wall and a solid fortification. Neither wall nor arms protect a greedy leader.

“What more should I advise? Let not prodigal luxury soften you within; let not love, the sickness of the mind, delighting in hiding-places and murmuring, break your strong heart. If you give yourself to Bacchus and Venus, you who have subjected all else beneath the yoke have come beneath the yoke yourselves: the mad freedom of the idle mind has perished in Venus’s blazing furnace.

[Verse 180.] “The mind grows dull within and commands and urges quarrels and wars to arise—the vile tomb of reason. These two, drunkenness and lust, enervate firm characters. Let a sparing will suffice to satisfy pleasures for those who govern human laws and hold the reins of the world.

“Therefore let Justice, celebrated by the pursuit of those before you, direct your actions; and through you let Astraea, last of the immortals to leave the earth, be recalled from on high. Let piety, modesty, and reverence for right not be absent. Search out divine mysteries; be gentle when entreated; labour over laws; reprove criminals in a civic spirit. Defer vengeance until anger has passed; do not wish to remember hatred after punishment. If you live thus, you will extend your name through everlasting ages.”

Thus the instructor, forming the pupil of virtue by such counsels, soaked his receptive ear in fruitful showers

[Col. 0468B] and impressed honourable character upon the chamber of his heart. The boy gladly fitted his thirsty ears to these sacred words, committing every point to the innermost cell of memory.

His mind, trusting in itself under the spurs of glory, burns. Within, love of war and desire for a kingdom sprout. Now all fear is absent; now hope judges in advance of his years; now he enjoys his wish; now in thought he rushes fiercely upon his enemies; now he rules; now the four-cornered world is subject to him.

Therefore, when the age arrived which frees boys from the rod, the Macedonian assumed arms in a civic cause: he lived not for himself but for his fatherland, and in its ruler he was a citizen. A recruit indeed, but a giant in mind; a soldier in heart already discharged from service: then you might see untamed Neoptolemus aspiring to deeds which Achilles himself could scarcely accomplish. Nor did he prepare to rage only against the Persians, against whom he had just cause for complaint,

[Col. 0468C] but he conspired against the world itself and all of it, if the Fates allowed.

There was a city named Corinth, deriving its name from its founder. The situation of the place itself, its greater abundance of resources, the firm resolve of fathers, people, and kings had established it as the head and foremost city of the kingdom. Paul, driving idols away with evangelical speech, converted it to the pastures of eternal spring. Here, therefore, the Macedonian, lest he blunt the rights of the city, after his father’s death reverently placed the sacred diadem upon his head and shone with ivory sceptre.

[Note: [Col. 0467] MS: “that it should be a metropolis”; “Aeolicly,” for “with evangelical [speech]”; “receiving upon his head,” for “placing upon his head.”]

He stands amid the nobles; the venerable grey hair and gentle old age of the fathers crowd either side of him,

[Col. 0468D] men whose right it was to order the whole kingdom; through whom plots are resisted by the barrier and rampart of counsel; men stronger in conducting the affairs of war by interpretive speech than by fighting hand, and in managing military concerns than in being girded with arms. At a distance stand those of unbridled spirit, under whose breast strength commands intellect and Nestor yields to Achilles. Before the ruler, surrounded by the unarmed band of poets, sits Aristotle, clothed in a soft garment, already given the staff of retirement, bent under the weight of advancing years; a laurel corrects his uncombed hair.

[Col. 0469A] The Macedonian, then, surveying every individual strength, feeds upon the sight of the nobles. His vehement daring, which for long had been unable to grow further, grew at the sight of the king; the applause of the people enlarges the feeling he had conceived before and echoes in the ears of his heart, and he ventures upon things greater than his powers.

His countenance matches his spirit; his eyes answer his profound mind, and his whole face is kindled. Thus it was easy to recognize that he was ready to be king. Although the royal ornaments were lacking—the bright circlet for the hair of pure gold, and the purple which burns with flame-bearing gems—yet the majesty of his countenance alone proclaimed him king.

It was the month whose name comes from young men, by which the vine receives its flowering, the grape its ripening, autumn its drinking, and winter its store; when the lofty crop swells into fruit and Phoebus was already preparing with his rays to set Cancer aflame in retrograde motion. Then, with the assent alike of people and leaders, the Macedonian was raised to kingship. He divided selected citizens for war into squadrons: their cavalry numbered two thousand five hundred, all alike in military ardour, though age distinguished them.

[Col. 0469B] Alexander chose not only the young but also those whose white old age bore witness to military service and whose excellence had been proved under his father. There was no commander or leader of a cohort who was not sixty years old.

[Col. 0469C] So much so that if anyone, laying aside arms, had viewed the headquarters of the camp or the officers of the citizens at close quarters, he would have thought them not horsemen but rather a senate.

Besides, he equipped thirty-two thousand infantry for war. Their weapons were stakes, the Dacian battle-axe, sling-cast missiles whirled in deadly flight, sword, life-spending bow, crescent-shaped shields, and the dart that precedes death; they strike with spears and threaten with sharp javelins. Their breasts are protected by breastplates and their necks securely by helmets. Although courage, superior to every weapon, armed them, I marvel equally that Alexander wished, and that he could, subject the world to himself with so few thousands; this course of events, by which so many kingdoms submit to one small company, is most like a prodigy of fate.

[Col. 0469D] Amid such tumult of affairs and crashing of the world, when the whole earth trembled with various rumours, the Cecropids [Athenians] themselves, at Demosthenes’ prompting, dared withdraw their assistance, challenge doubtful war, disparage one who was absent, and oppose force to force.

The Macedonian boils on hearing this; he therefore orders the camp moved more quickly. Thus he comes unexpectedly near to his Greek enemy and applies ladders to the walls.

[Note: [Col. 0469] “with Demosthenes first urging”; “the Greeks,” for “to the Greeks”; “perhaps fits ladders to the walls with his hands,” for “applies wings [i.e. ladders] to the walls”; Curtius supplies “Aeschines”; “and begun,” for “and Aeschines began.”]

Meanwhile, when the old men had withdrawn into Pallas’s citadel, Aeschines speaks, accuses Demosthenes of having begun the strife, and demonstrates that nothing is safer than peace.

[Verse 288.] While each embassy carries out the duties entrusted to it, the king, touched by love for his nursing motherland, renews the treaty and restores peace to the city. With serene countenance he grants them leave to devote themselves to liberal arts and studies, and dismisses Mars from action.

[Col. 0470A] Then, when he had once again joined Athens, lately divided against itself, he flies with swift force to ancient Thebes. The Aonians, with a band of young men surrounding the walls, stand armed and oppose the man seeking to enter the gates. If they had wished patiently to accept him as master; if they had chosen to meet him with entreaty rather than arms; if, as was fitting, they had regretted their begun treachery and crime, perhaps they might have restrained the torrent of fury and deserved an unharmed condition of life and pardon.

But because they presumed to despise both the king’s age and the king himself,

[Col. 0470B] they justly experienced him as a tyrant. While the Macedonian deliberates upon the city’s destruction, and the people are already afflicted by various calamities, satraps gathered from neighbouring cities arrive. They accuse the entire race and recall that from its origin the people had been bent on crime and drenched in Greek slaughter: fathers born from a serpent, who had always kept in their hearts the hereditary venom instilled into their descendants.

Who does not know Niobe’s pride? Who does not know Agave, spattered with her son’s blood, howling through the female throng? Who does not know Semele’s flames, or the king bereft of sight, shamefully turned back upon his own birth? Or, besides, that twins born of unspeakable seed fought one another to the ruin of all Europe?

[Col. 0470C] These accusations inflame the ruler’s anger to a hotter blaze, and he orders his men to gird themselves for battle. Then, a wedge of a thousand horsemen prepared, he circles the swollen city. The citizens strive to keep them from the walls, and a vast shower of missiles envelops them at close range.

No less meanwhile do the infantry burn to tear down the walls with driven levers and powerful mattocks. So that the enemy may not frighten them from above with missiles, others, to lie safely concealed, press forward after joining their shield-bosses in the likeness of a tortoise, to ward off deadly blows.

Now, with footing removed and a mass threatening ruin, whatever Aonians happen to remain alive flee with headlong leap and retreat into hidden places. But the Greeks, as the stones give way and the enemy withdraws, made a way through the wall. The whole multitude rushes into the city.

[Col. 0470D] Every sex and age alike perishes without distinction. The Pellaean leader himself too is present, entering Thebes surrounded by arms. Faithful Cloades joined him and sang a sweet melody to the great king, adding these verses in lyric measure:

“Renowned offspring of the gods, Macedonian, bravest of kings, whom the course of the stars favours, to whom the Sisters [the Fates], as the thread hastens on, promise the four regions of the world: Aristotle has so often armed your eager heart with divine counsels, that, invincible over the conquered, you might know how to spare suppliants when victorious and subdue rebels. And now, king, do you intend utterly to destroy this city?

[Col. 0471A] “Was this the land that bore gods and nurtured Alcides, the author of your lineage—he whose glory, derived from his repeated conquest of the world, surpasses all others? Behold the walls and citadels built to Amphion’s measures. Learn to be merciful to the conquered and bloody toward those still to be conquered. A kingdom which clemency does not establish is unstable. But if so great is your desire to torment the citizens, spare at least the soil itself, and pardon the gods of the place.”

Cloades had finished, but the king’s decision stands. Clinging to his purpose, he gives his anger free rein; first he orders towers and walls levelled with the ground, then strikes the remaining city with the thunderbolt of Vulcan.

[Note: [Col. 0471] “destruction,” for “ruin.”]

[Col. 0471B] After vengeance had sufficiently checked Dirce, and Boeotia had now learned to serve a new king, the Macedonian, having arranged alike his homeland and household, prepares to rage against Darius. Therefore he separates those less experienced in arms, less bold, and of lesser reputation, and assigns them the protection of their native Argos. Then he heaps ships with various kinds of supplies. He did not choose to employ only a few in so great an undertaking: the number of vessels amounts to fifty times four, unless thrice six is an obstacle [i.e. 182].

When the free fleet had gained the sail-bearing sea and begun its flight, and no anchor now bit the sand as its inhabitants departed from their native harbour, the shrill air rang with wondrous harmonies: the voices of men foretelling ill were mingled with the roar of trumpets,

[Col. 0471C] and the whole sea bellowed in answer.

“O native land, such is the love in which you draw all things! O how great is your sweetness! While the fleet, fleeing over the deep, swiftly steals the fatherland’s sons away, though they hasten willingly to invade the Persian borders and their leader does not drag unwilling men toward the prizes of plunder, still the sweetness of their homeland alone calls back those who are willing. It does not allow the mind’s keen sight to be torn away from its country, but turns their sweet eyes and hearts back toward Argos, until the distant summit of Europe fails from sight and the harbour recedes.

“So great was the desire for war beneath their unconquered hearts, so great their forgetfulness of parent and sisters. The unbridled Macedonian alone turns his eyes away from the Inachian land.

[Col. 0471D] When, rising over the hills, he first saw the Cilician fields and Asia emerging, he rejoices; the narrow lodging of his breast scarcely holds such joys. He orders the sailors to bend to the oars and to entrust themselves beyond the sails alone when they are stretched tight; joy condemns delay. At their ruler’s word, they promptly rise through the benches, far from sluggish, and lash the sea with many a stroke.

The fleet was distant from its harbour station by only as much as a sling can send a stone in a swift cast.

[Verse 398.] From afar the Pellaean wounds the hostile land with a loosed arrow; the whole troop proclaims it a favourable omen and raises joyful applause to the stars. Without delay the grappling hook is sunk in the sands of the shore. First they unload the ships, leap out in swift flight, and set their camp upon the green shore.

[Col. 0472A] Then they give themselves to feasting and, while they pass the ceremonial cups, prolong their banquets into late night.

The third part of the world, which was said of old to be held under its dominion, has received its name from it: this is Asia. Ocean bounds it by its vast flood at the sun’s rising; from the south it extends northward, while the Tanais, together with the waters of Maeotis, encloses it on the north; our sea separates it from Europe.

[Col. 0472B] To this land fell an equal portion of the world; and though it is one of three, geographers declare that this one alone divides the world. Thus, with the other two content with shorter extent, the central region does not begrudge it this distinction.

Such is Asia’s position; but its gentle canopy of forests shades it, courses of rivers flood it, and it boasts the abundant renown of noble regions. Here gem-rich India trumpets with elephants, sows twice and reaps crops as often; Caucasus rises in the north; Paradise breathes from its watered east. It contains Assyrians, Medes, and Persia, now called Parthia, bounded by Mesopotamia. It contains the wealth of Babylon and the Chaldaean kingdoms; the lands of the Arabs, fragrant with Sabaean frankincense, in which that marvel of natural philosophers is born—the Phoenix, ever one bird only—and cinnamon neighbouring myrrh.

[Col. 0472C] On this side Euphrates touches Syria; on that, the Armenian nation, mindful of the Flood, threatens heaven and the gods above. Beyond, Palestine is pre-eminent among all lands: Judaea, Jerusalem, the land of one God. It is placed at the centre, where Life, brought forth in a Virgin’s childbirth, died; and the reborn world could not stand fast while God died, but, terrified, trembled.

There are so many regions of Asia that, if my pen should plough them all, either it will break the sequence or produce weariness.

Already toward dawn the birds were accustomed to chirp and precede the light with the soft whisper of their tongues. Lucifer drove forward the boundary of exhausted night and, precursor of the sun, hastened the flight of the stars with panting horse, when Alexander relaxed his limbs from easy sleep. Then, with the first sun, he looked out upon the dulled sea and its swimming rays.

[Col. 0472D] He springs from the temple into the camp and, climbing to the mountain-height, measures Asia’s boundaries with his eyes. When from there he sees so many plains flowering with grain, so many wooded glades, so many meadows green with grass, so many cities encircled by walls, so many shoots of Bacchus, so many elms married to vines, he says: “Companions, this one region is enough for me; I leave Europe and your homeland to you.”

[Verse 452.] Thus he spoke and divided his native world among his leaders.

[Col. 0473A] For that terror of commanders—so great is his confidence in destiny—already considers his own all kingdoms lying beneath the fourfold pole. Thus he frees fields from ravagers and turns away the seizure of livestock from the enemy.

Setting out now, he claims for himself the Cilician citadels and wins cities by the clemency of a pious ruler. This skill was of greater value to Alexander than if he waged Mars at the cost of blood: by sparing and overwhelming the foe, he performs the offices of war through peace.

Then he hastens onward and makes for Ilium through the towns of Phrygia and surveys the walls built after a violated treaty and the groves of Ida, where Jupiter’s winged bearer [the eagle] seized in hooked feet the boy remarkable for beautiful face and bore the welcome gift above the sky.

[Col. 0473B] While he diligently seeks at least traces of antiquity, he comes upon a poplar planted beside a flowing stream, where the writings of adulterous Paris, marked by Oenone’s sickle, lie hidden and tender loves are read; where below is the dense valley in which the cause of the playful dispute was handled, when the adulterer rashly gave judgment—whence came the contagion of evil and the first origin of the Trojan disaster, and fire overwhelmed Pergamum.

These things are indeed now to be reckoned small; but how great they were is inferred, for that ancient ruin bears witness how immense was the extent of fallen Troy.

While the Macedonian wanders among so many tombs of warriors, amid Argive ashes and buried shades—whom inscriptions, nevertheless, identify by sure epitaphs—behold, he happens to see Achilles’ tomb, smaller in site than his fame, distinguished by this inscription:

> I, the Aeacid, tamer of Hector, fell secretly, unwary and unarmed,  
> struck in the foot by Paris’s arrow.

[Col. 0473C] The brevity of this inscription moved the king to behold the monument of so great a leader. He satiated the barren sand with sweet wine and hastened to burn incense for the place from the censer he had taken up:

“O fortune surpassing that of all men! Your praises breathe of the Maeonian poet [Homer]. Though he sang how you tore lifeless Hector apart, mighty man, I judge it the greatest addition to your honour, father of your country, that after death you deserved so great a herald of praise as Homer. Would that, when my body is dissolved, not-envious Fame might raise my triumphs to such praises!

[Col. 0473D] “For when a broad field has received my laws; when Ganges is subdued, Atlas cast down, Boreas has felt the might of Macedon, and Hammon too; when the world is content with one ruler, as with one sun—this alone I shall fear: that, after death, fame may fail my buried ashes. I would prefer this single thing even to the Elysian fields.

“And do not, provident Argive people, let Fortune shake you from the war you have begun, although she may at times threaten harshly; she never persists with the same countenance.

[Verse 506.] “He is unworthy to possess flattering and gentle Fortune who refuses to endure hard or bitter things. For I have seen things once hard grow soft. And lest ignorance of the truth trouble you anxiously as to whence such great confidence rises in my mind, I shall impart this one secret to your ears.

[Col. 0474A] “When grieving Greece tottered at my father’s death, and Pausanias’s crime had atoned murder with murder, I was alone, about midnight, pressing the royal couch in the inner chambers while the sloth of sleep relaxed my companions. But wakeful cares burned in my heart. As the condition of the kingdom was shaken by its newness, I was uncertain whether to pursue enemies or defend my homeland. Steady in neither course, I seemed destined to undertake both.

“Behold: I sensed the place made radiant by a sudden lamp; I saw heavenly brightness break into the doors through night’s pressing darkness, and the shadows turn to day. As fear oppressed my mind, and sweat wandered tremblingly through my limbs as witness to my terror, there appeared a man—if it is permitted to call him a man—of noble gravity, whose barbarian garment, varied and marked with many colours, covered him down to the feet.

[Col. 0474B] As a priest commonly goes forth in shining linen, a jewelled fringe touched his flaming feet. A golden plate confined his dewy-flowing curled hair. In the centre of his breast twelve stones burned in wondrous arrangement, proud in the light of gems. A plate bearing the tetragrammaton seemed to inscribe some name across the middle of his forehead; but because the language of those foreign letters was unknown to me, I confess I was unable to read it.

“A tiara embraced the concealed head of the high priest, and his modest foot lay hidden in an ankle-length garment. Had he not addressed me first, I had what I might briefly ask: who he was, what he was, and whence he came.

“‘Go forth from your native borders, bravest of Macedonians,’ he said, ‘and I shall utterly destroy every nation for you. But if you happen to see me coming to meet you in this guise, spare my people.’

“He spoke, departed into the upper air, and as he left filled the house with a wondrous fragrance. ‘Under this leader and this commander,’ he said, ‘you will wage hard wars’; and he turned swift steps back toward the camp.

[Col. 0474C] “Yet he taught the truth. For when, after Tyre’s overthrow, I was preparing in victory, with many a legion, to approach Jerusalem, and was thought to wish to violate the temple and houses of God, the high priest came forth before the city, anticipating the anger of the invincible ruler, accompanied by the city’s sacred senate and dressed exactly as the king had previously seen the priest in the starry vision.

[Col. 0474D] Recognizing him as it were, I dismounted from my horse and bowed in worship before him—to the astonishment of all—bestowing upon a man the honour which he alone had long before ordered should be bestowed upon him. Then, having excluded the following legion, the king enters the city with a few companions.

[Verse 560.] Warned there by the Hebrews, he offered peace-offerings and enriched the temple with abundant gifts.

[Col. 0476A] And now, taking leave, having remitted war against the blessed city, he granted its citizens a perpetual benefaction.

## Argument of the Second Book

The second book prepares Darius and the Persians for battle; Darius writes to Alexander and reviews his people. But the Macedonian breaks the fateful yoke with the sword and recovers himself, while Philip heals his sickness. Battle-lines stand on either side, hemmed in by the mountain passes of Cilicia; the hazard of unjust fate presses Sisines. Though the Persians’ commanders despise it, the useful counsel of learned Thymodes is approved; it is decided to entrust matters to the Fates. Each keen leader alike urges all his strength and allies to arms, and the air resounds to answering applause.  
[Note: [Col. 0475] “air,” for “ether.”]

## Book Two

[Col. 0475B] Swift-running Fame, messenger of the Persians, announcing the great avenger of his homeland, now threatened by the Fates, had shaken the ears of Darius with dreadful noise amid the cities—Darius heavy with the torpor of idleness and dissolved in luxury.

Though greater in empire, more fortified in arms, richer in the obedience of kings and precious money, surpassing the new warrior in forces and more mature in age, nevertheless his inexperience in war, from which he had long been estranged, and long peace had driven the king’s wavering spirit to be inferior in every respect to the leader whom he might have surpassed, had his spirit for fighting been as great as his resources.

Yet, lest royal majesty, caught in error and deficient in firmness, should appear diminished, Darius thunders proud threats and gathers the subdued nations into camp.

[Col. 0475C] As his edict flies through the kingdoms, all the youth rushes more swiftly to arms.

Meanwhile, lest he seem to have done nothing, Darius sends Alexander a letter of this kind:

“Darius, king of kings and kinsman of the gods, writes to Alexander his servant. Though you are distinguished by natural ability, spare yourself, boy, in your tender and still-growing years. A tree which has not matured is not fit for the yoke. Rash one, put off the equipment of arms which you have assumed, return yourself to the bosom of your chaste mother, and the things more suited to your age, I have sent—

[Textual variants omitted from the draft: [Col. 0465] *Hyrcanus* for *Hyrcanis* (“Hyrcanian”); *effrenis* (“unbridled”) for *effrenus*; *Philippida vultu* (“with a Philip-like countenance,” uncertain) for “with threatening, inflamed face”; *iram* (“wrath,” singular) for *iras* (“wraths”). [Col. 0467] *vincis* (“you conquer”) for *subdis* (“you subject”); *monitis* (“by counsels”) for *monitor* (“the instructor”); *cupido* (“desire”) for *libido* (“desire/lust”); *corde* (“heart”) for *mente* (“mind”); *non expleret* (“would not accomplish”) for *vix expleret* (“would scarcely accomplish”); *non solum* (“not only”) for *nec solum* (“nor only”). [Col. 0469] *flagrascit* (“burns fiercely”) for *supercandescit* (“blazes more hotly”); *excussos* (“dislodged”) for *incussis* (“driven/struck”); *eoque* (“and him”) for *eique* (“and to him”). [Col. 0471] *famaque minores* (“and lesser in reputation”) for *famae minoris* (“of lesser reputation”); *onustat* (“loads”) for *acervat* (“heaps”); *aethera* (“the ether/sky”) for *aera* (“the air”); *voluntas* (“will”) for *voluptas* (“pleasure”); *recepit* (“received”) for *receptat* (“contains”). [Col. 0471] *inumbra t* (“shades”) for *obumbrat* (“overshadows”); *contremuit* (“shuddered”) for *pertremuit* (“was greatly terrified”); *parabat* (“was preparing”) for *solebat* (“was accustomed”). [Col. 0473] *armiger* (“arm-bearing”) for *aliger* (“winged”); *placitumque* (“pleasing”) for *gratumque* (“welcome”); *objicitur* (“is encountered/comes before him”) for *occurrit* (“he encounters”); *quam fuit immensa* (“how immense was”) for *quam fuerit* (“how great it was”); *occubuit* (“he fell”) for *occubui* (“I fell”); *consistit* (“remains fixed”) for *persistit* (“persists”). [Col. 0473] *exire* (“to come forth”) for *errare* (“to wander”); *lambebat* (“licked”) for *tangebat* (“touched”); *potuisse* (“to have been able”) for *valuisse* (“to have had the strength/been able”); *superasque recessit* (“withdrew into the upper air”) for *superas decessit in auras* (“departed into the upper breezes”). [Col. 0475] *obsequio* (“obedience,” singular) for *obsequiis* (“obediences/services”); *deprensa* (“caught/discovered”) for *depressa* (“weighed down”); *vigoris* (“vigour”) for *rigoris* (“firmness/strictness”).]”

Leather reins for you, a smooth ball, and capacious cases

For the expenses of attendants, provisions, and the comforts of travel;

But if such madness vexes your breast [Note: [Col. 0475] “such madness [vexes] your mind.”]

[Col. 0475D] That you contend against peace and prefer an enemy to a friend:

I shall send out, not horsemen, but servants driven mad,

Who, having seized you with the lash, may afflict you

With harsh punishments and consign you to everlasting darkness [Note: [Col. 0475] “add [you].”].

[Vers. 608.] Alexander, moderately disturbed, ground his teeth and replied

[Col. 0476B] To those who had brought him the commands of the Median tyrant:

“I interpret,” he said, “the little gifts of your king better,

And more admirably. The rounded form of the ball clearly indicates

The sphere and shape of the round world

Which I shall subject to myself.

With these reins I shall govern the Persians subject to me,

When as victor I have shattered Darius’ ancient treasures.”

So he spoke; and, with his royal likeness impressed upon wax,

He presented the envoys with various gifts.

But Darius, although his heart wavered, shaken

By the news, brought through report, of Memnon’s death,

Still, turning the harshness of fortune to its opposite [Note: [Col. 0475] “changing.”],

Surrounded by a train of nobles and masses of infantry,

Marched toward the Euphrates. There he deployed, among so many nations

Glittering with gold and spread across the broad plain,

[Col. 0476C] The strength of so many peoples for all to see.

Elated in spirit, he enclosed a camp; and there, when the first sun

Struck the place, he counted them all over,

In imitation of Xerxes, until Hesperus preceded

The rising of night-wandering Phoebe [Note: [Col. 0475] “mountain-wandering.”].

The innumerable phalanx poured forth from the camp over the green fields;

When counted, it surpassed its reckoning,

Scattered abroad, and its multitude filled out the appearance of a greater host [Note: [Col. 0475] “presented [it].”].

Thus, when bleating sheep are to go to the pastures of spring,

So that the shepherd may return as many as the fold sent out

At dawn, the sheep are counted; diligent Baucis, anxious

Lest a wolf diminish their number under an ill-omened shepherd,

Entrusts them to goat-footed Faunus.

But the first encounter with great Darius, and the fierce

[Col. 0476D] Battle under the distinguished leader of the opposing side, Memnon,

Had detained six hundred thousand noble men;

Though inferior in number, Alexander, stronger in arms,

Routed them, and entered the conquered hall

[Vers. 642.] Of exceedingly wealthy Midas, which the ancients called Gordium,

[Col. 0477A] But later men called Sardis [Note: [Col. 0477] “modern [men].”].

Here the twin Pontic seas confine Asia with narrow

Straits and the ebbing currents of their waters;

Here the Sangarius, equally distant from either sea,

Nevertheless communicates its waters to alternate shores.

Here, in Jupiter’s temple, gleam the lofty wagons of Midas’ father,

And the ancient yoke, fateful for Asia. By hidden art

Its cords ran together [Note: [Col. 0477] “came together.”] and were again interwoven;

For a long time no one could either find their end

Or untie the knots. There was a firm belief that the stubborn sequence

Of fates had so ordained that whoever loosed the bonds

Must obtain the kingdom of all Asia.

The desire to fulfil fate stirred Alexander; lifting the yoke,

He tried to undo the knots.

[Col. 0477B] And, after struggling briefly, when he saw that he strove in vain,

Lest he repel a gloomy omen for the bystanders [Note: [Col. 0477] “reflect it back.”]:

“What matters it,” he said, “nobles [Note: [Col. 0477] “companions.”], by what art

Or in what way the riddles of silent destiny are laid open?”

He spoke, and, drawing his sword, cut the knots apart.

Thus he either evaded fate or, by fate, disclosed it [Note: [Col. 0477] “unloosed [it].”].

From there he came to Ancyra, having sent forces to subdue by war

The peoples of Cappadocia. Having reduced them to his authority,

The Macedonian hastened his march at dawn and, in the course

Of a single day, covered five hundred stadia with swift

Steps [Note: [Col. 0477] “Virgil: ‘and thresholds and laurels.’”], hastening to forestall the frightened king.

For, fearing the difficult approaches to Asia and the narrow

Passes of the region, Darius, who now held the Cilician plain,

Prepared to meet him. At the first eastern light,

[Col. 0477C] When the sun dripped with dewy lamp, he moved his camp

From the Euphrates [Note: [Col. 0477] “The short preceding vowel is lengthened by the Greeks.”]. Hollow rocks resound with trumpets,

The valleys answer; and the air, struck by the blasts,

Doubles its roar, while the trumpets shake the clouds like thunder.

Such was the din in the camp; but this also was the order of the host.

An altar of silver, mounted upon golden axles, bore before it

The fire which the Persians called sacred and eternal.

A line of white horses drew Jupiter’s chariot;

Twelve nations, as varied in dress

As in language and customs, accompanied in one procession

Ten chariots embossed with gems and gold.

Those whom popular belief falsely calls immortal

Were borne, some ten thousand, in wagons of gold.

But the king’s kinsmen, all dressed effeminately,

Fifteen thousand were carried in bordered garments.

[Col. 0477D] Darius himself rode in the middle in a heavy chariot, sparkling

With golden rays; innumerable images of gods attended him on either side;

The glitter of gems proclaimed him, and the barbaric splendour

And wealth of kings [Note: [Col. 0477] “the king.”].

Above him, a clay image of Jupiter’s winged armour-bearer,

Hanging from a gilded wing, tempered the heat of the burning sun [Note: [Col. 0477] “winged.”].

Ten thousand spearmen preceded him; their spearheads were gold,

Their shafts shone silver-white.

Moreover, Darius had ordered two hundred kings, illustrious by birth,

[Vers. 696.] To march close beside him.

[Col. 0478A] And lest it be easy for the Danaans to penetrate the king’s tribunal,

The rear of the army was enclosed by thirty thousand infantrymen

Outstanding in their weapons.

There followed a chariot full of the Median tyrant’s mother;

His wife, children, and the whole royal household were there,

With as many concubines. Nearly fifty wagons groaned

Under so great a burden of passengers.

It was the custom of Persian leaders at that time to lead

Their whole household to war whenever they ordered the standards raised.

Money was carried on six hundred mules,

And loaded the humped backs of three hundred camels.

A very great host of slingers, a hundred thousand strong,

Surrounded the column, throwing with the light thongs of their slings.

Last marched the lightly armed men, beyond number; and, trampled

By feet and wheels, a dusty whirlwind wrapped the golden stars.

[Col. 0478B] Meanwhile the Macedonian commander, seeing the deserted Cilician fields

Devastated by fugitives, hurried his troops

To the place which earlier men called Cyrus’ Camp.

Accordingly, having sent forces ahead under Parmenio’s command,

He saved Tarsus, half-dead, from Persian fire.

Here, as writings report, one illustrious by birth shone forth,

Through whom especially, error overcome, a ray

And lamp of faith emerged for the nations in darkness.

The Cydnus, pure and unstained, flows through the middle of the city,

Drawing its cold waters from springs.

It is content with itself and admits no waters

Of any rushing torrent from elsewhere; but its pebble plays in the eddy,

And the sand frolics in the backward-moving flow.

Here the Great Man first learned that safety is granted

[Col. 0478C] To no one without interruption, but adversity is mingled with prosperity [Note: [Col. 0477] “in another manuscript, the following two verses are omitted.”].

Here presumptuous force drove the proud king onward,

Which might rather have been called boastful vaunting of glory.

Therefore, when you saw fate struggling against chance,

And favourable fortune supporting your enterprises, it paused

A little and compelled Macedon’s hope to despair.

It was summer: July burned while the sun held the middle of Leo,

And fiery heat split [Note: [Col. 0477] “splits.”] the dry fields of Cilicia

Under the mid-point of the day’s axis.

The Macedonian, drenched in sweat and dust, his limbs

Enticed by the river’s temperature and the appearance of its water,

Leapt into the stream while his body was still hot.

At once the whole mass of the man shuddered, drenched by the cold liquid;

When here the breath found no open channels,

[Col. 0478D] It left the body empty through cold, the vital heat being shut out

By the waters. The afflicted king falters and, almost lifeless,

Is drawn out by the hands of his companions. A mournful tumult rises

Through the camp, and the youth of Greece break out into lamentation:

“O Macedonian, flower of young men, what impulse among friends,

What chance, compelled you naked to an unforeseen death?

Fortune, more fickle than a falling leaf,

[Vers. 749.] More savage than tigers, harsher [Note: [Col. 0477] “more hostile.”] than dreadful hydras,

[Col. 0479A] More horrible than Tisiphone, bloodier than every monster—

Why do you cut off before its day the prince’s flourishing years?

Until now you had been a mother: who compelled you

To become his stepmother, when the world was adopting as its promised king

Him whom it claimed for itself? But what end awaits those

Who followed your camp from their native land, best of kings,

And are not permitted to return through deserted places to their homeland?

Shall we be sent without you into the midst of enemies?

But who will be worthy to succeed so great a king?”

Fortune heard this; as she happened to sit, exhausted, upon the ground,

Turning her wheel, she recovered breath, rose,

And, smiling serenely, rebuked the Argolic fears

Without ceasing, and murmured a few words to herself:

“How great is the darkness in which the ignorant human mind

Lies oppressed! How often it attacks me as unjust,

[Col. 0479B] Though it permits the other goddesses to exercise their own prerogative,

Yet singles out me alone. While I bestow good things, I am exalted

With great praises [Note: [Col. 0479] “raised.”]; whenever I withdraw my commanding hand

From affairs, I am accused as guilty of a crime—as though

I could be held under the condition of a stable nature;

if I always remained one and the same among all persons,

I should no longer rightly be called Fortune.

By nature’s ordinance, my law is to move without law;

mobility alone makes me constant.” Having spoken thus,

A freer breath revisited the king’s sickly limbs

And began for a while to follow its accustomed passages;

but excessive sickness still burned his inward parts.

Yet, raising his face with uplifted gaze, he said:

“Then shall a bloodstained victor capture Alexander, defeated in camp without war

[Col. 0479C] [Note: [Col. 0479] “carry him off.”]? For the enemy is near,

And allows neither idle doctors nor the critical stages of illness

To be awaited. The hostile barbarians will howl over spoils taken away,

While their inglorious king, an exile, naked and without praise,

Will lie upon an enemy’s sand.

But if physicians have it in their power to restore health

By medical art, let medicine assist; and let them know

That I seek not so much a span of life as war.

It is not death that concerns me so much as the delay of battle.

For, though I am still sick, if only I can stand before the line

Of my men, the Persians will turn their backs in swift flight,

And the Danaans will pursue in triumph.”

This ardour of the king and headlong desire had stirred

The hesitant troops; but, lest eagerness for treatment

Increase the illness, while Philip, his companion from his father and guardian

[Col. 0479D] Of his health, promised recovery, Alexander waited anxiously

For three bright returns of Phoebus, and for the disease’s departure

And health’s return.

A letter sent in advance by the commander disturbed the king:

it denounced the physician as bribed by Darius with gold

And by the marriage of his sister. Already the third dawn had scattered

Its bright fires through the world, darkness having fled.

The commander, about to drink the innocent man’s draught, was compelled

To doubt the physician’s loyalty; but after the potion had been drained,

He offered the letter, to be read by his trembling right hand, to Archigenes.

While the latter read it, no signs of fear could be observed

[Vers. 805.] On the reader’s face.

[Col. 0480A] Then, smiling, he said: “Good king, banish fear;

Release your mind from cares; allow [Note: [Col. 0479] “from cares.”] the power of this medicine

To enter your veins. He who brought this to you—listen—

Either zealously desires that you should perish in this manner more than all others,

Or is consumed with envy of my skill,

Or, to speak more truly, is reckless in seeking your harm.

He who brands the innocent with crime, who accuses the guiltless

Of treason, is deservedly not believed innocent himself.

For how would a guilty man know another guilty man? He will bitterly

Object this; thus the just man is sometimes unjustly bound,

And the lying court absolves the unjust.”

Having said this, he ordered the king’s fear to vanish.

Therefore, when the administered medicine had soaked the inner veins,

The seeds of the exhausted disease perished.

Colour brightened his face, and, pallor destroyed,

[Col. 0480B] His countenance emerged, suffused with snowy blush.

His mind returned, and living courage was born anew within.

The nobles rushed together, eager to see Philip;

They threw their arms around the beloved man’s neck

And hailed him as Father of the Country and saviour.

When next day’s sun shone from its glowing axis,

The king, mounted [Note: [Col. 0479] “ridden forward.”] upon a notable horse, showed himself

For viewing through the camp; he shook all sluggishness from fearful minds

And renewed his men by countenance and voice.

Then, after his army had overwhelmed the neighbouring cities

And paid to the gods the sacred vows which he had made

For his uncertain safety, he brought iron wedges against the walls of Issus.

There Parmenio, meeting him as he approached, led him into the city

Deserted by its inhabitants.

[Col. 0480C] Here the nobles debated whether the battle-line should be extended farther

For war, or whether the enemy should rather be awaited there.

At length this opinion seemed preferable to the commanders:

that amid the mountain passes with their ridges, there each force

Should commit its strength to fate [Note: [Col. 0479] “on both sides.”].

For Parmenio judged that the lines of the two rulers would there be equal

In the narrow valley.

But Sisenes, because he had secretly concealed the matter,

Was believed to have been covertly bribed with Darius’ gold,

And unjust death struck him, not without the tyrant’s knowledge.

And now cavalry arriving from the Greek shores,

Accompanied in their flight by exile, under the commander *Thymodes,

Entered Darius’ camp and offered the king salutary advice:

while there was still time, he should swiftly turn his oblique route backward

And, in winged flight through dust,

[Col. 0480D] Recover the wide plains of the level country.

Or, if shame forbade the degenerate king to retreat,

Lest a reversed step perhaps become a grievous omen for his men,

At least he should divide the treasure and resources of war into parts,

So that, if fortune—may it not be so!—should favour

The Argolics in the first battle, reserves might remain,

And fresh youth might plunge into danger.

For it is no small madness to expose everything at once

To fortune under a single blow of war.”

He had offered useful advice, but it seemed useless

To the Persian chiefs, whose purpose was to forestall the king

[Vers. 861.] So that he might destroy [Note: [Col. 0479] “condemn.”] the hired Romans by a deserved death.

For they think that the Greeks wish to scatter the treasure,

So that, loaded with spoils and wealth, they may return

To the Macedonian king and renew peace.

The king, being mild and sufficiently receptive, stopped his ears

Against these counsels; wounded at heart, he said: “Far be it,

O nobles, that this disgrace should rule in my lifetime!

Shall I betray the men who followed my camp [Note: [Col. 0481] “following.”],

My camp and my pledged word? Never shall such savage infamy

Pollute my stern and now ageing years.”

So he spoke; and, giving thanks, dismissed the Achaeans.

But he counted it dishonour for a king to return,

Lest he perhaps be thought a fugitive. He burned to join battle at once

And decide matters among the narrow mountains. He first arranged the treasure,

And at his order the greater part was conveyed in detachments to Damascus.

[Col. 0481B] Yet the ancient custom was maintained: the royal wife,

Sister, children, followed the fates of the camp.

Thereafter Darius, resolved that, when on the next day

The light-bearing Titan revealed the world, the forces of the kings should meet,

Climbed a mound swelling with a modest hill,

In the middle of the camp. There a fragrant laurel, spreading its leafy branches,

Covered the sweet-smelling grasses with its hair.

They often report that beneath it they have seen choirs of nymphs

Singing woodland songs, and wanton satyrs.

A spring falls on the left, shaded by grass with purple turf;

Beneath the garment of spring a little stream hides and plays,

Watering the lower ground [Note: [Col. 0481] “the inner ground.”] with slow course,

Babbling, and making the mountains deaf with its sound.

[Col. 0481C] Here Mother Cybele springs up; Flora weds Zephyrus,

And the spring’s charm favours the valley,

As the Rhone descends from Alpine rocks with foaming crest,

Where Maximian destroyed eastern battalions,

When the wave of blood from the slaughtered legion aided

The river’s course, and mingled blood burst into the air,

Scorning the earth-bank, and watered all Agaunum.

Then Darius turned the orb of his peaceful gaze toward the troops

Of commons and nobles stationed below. Having first summoned the commanders,

He divided into groups those who were going into danger, and finally began thus.

Mature prayers breathed from his pious mouth;

his mature countenance deserved favour by its appearance alone:

“Heirs of the gods, Persians, nation unique in war,

[Col. 0481D] Whose lineage descends from the origin of ancient Belus,

Who first deserved, venerable in divine image,

To be placed among the dwellers in heaven upon a starry throne—

Free your hearts from fear [Note: [Col. 0481] “free fear from [your] heart.”]. It is madness, and shameful to call it battle,

When a slave abuses weapons against his master.

It is vengeance, not war, when sceptres seize rebellious slaves,

Subdue them when captured, and defend their native land.

That spurious boy, having gained control of the kingdom

And supposing everything would yield to him, is carried away

By youthful heat and rushes unprepared into every danger.

[Vers. 914.] He prefers to die fighting rather than yield defeated;

[Col. 0482A] And now, devoid of hope, he weakens in empty spirit,

Mindful of the losses which the Granicus river inflicted.

He begins partly to distrust his shattered fortunes.

Shame! Against the masters of the world, whom every metal serves,

Poor slaves, few and without strength, dare to rise.

I should like to know, Macedonian, by what arts,

Megaera inspiring you, you boast that you can possess

The empire of that Cyrus, before whom Lydia, Croesus, and every tyrant

Under whatever sky bent the knee.

Though he has died, he lives on, with me as successor;

and the fortune of the buried man lives in the living king.

If the monuments of the ancients remain; if I remember in my mind

The writings of the fathers, who does not know that we trace our race from the stock of Giants?

[Col. 0482B] Who does not know the wars of the gods,

The baked brick and the tower built with bitumen by our ancestors?

Who is forgetful of the great city

To which the confusion of speech gave an everlasting name?

Come then, nobles: recall ancestral vigour;

Stand for your country, and watch over your country’s titles

And honour, as is fitting. Let not the poor foreign victor

Trample beneath his feet the monuments of ancient forefathers [Note: [Col. 0481] “the land and.”].

But if, which I abhor, the wicked enemy should strike down any of you

On the field and harass him as he flees over the plains;

If you refuse arms to me, to your country, to your fellow citizens,

[Col. 0482C] Let at least your wives and children, whom hostile slaughter

Will crush [Note: [Col. 0481] “bury.”] in the camp, urge you to return to the camp [Note: [Col. 0481] “to the wars.”].

Yet I do not fear that victory will now applaud the Persian leaders;

for in a playing spark [Note: [Col. 0481] “applauding.”] I saw the Macedonians’ tents

Burning in a dream, and their frenzied leader, dressed in Babylonian fashion,

Entering the city’s walls in purple splendour,

Brought before me, then snatched away and vanishing.

Why delay? I call as witness the eternal radiance, the golden

Lights of the sun, whose rising we granted within our borders:

Whoever loosens the reins for flight shall be an enemy.”

As he was about to say more, a messenger with swift foot brought word

That the Greeks had abandoned their position and that their fearful troops

Had sought escape, already hastening by short cuts through the wooded passes

Toward the sea and hurling their route over steep rocks.

[Col. 0482D] Thus the flatterer feeds the prince’s yielding ear; struck by empty

Joy he is elated and condemns delay. Therefore the army,

Having crossed the river, seeks a route rapidly through rocks

And trackless places [Note: [Col. 0481] “pathless places.”], preparing to overtake the fugitive king.

Where are you rushing, doomed band [Note: [Col. 0481] “force.”]? Do you suppose
