That this unconquered young man is fleeing—he who believes

Nothing more disgraceful than flight, whatever the charge?

To keep you from fleeing sluggishly, this alone he fears:

indeed, if such a choice were given him—whether he would prefer to flee

[Vers. 964.] Or to conquer, rather than be conquered by fugitives and resist the enemy defeated—

[Col. 0483A] Perhaps he would hesitate over which course were less dishonourable.

The Chaldaean force, hastening near Issus, was now revealed by scouts.

The line of arms gleams with the brilliance of gold and stones,

And marches in a swift whirlwind, stealing the sun

Within its dusty cloud.

A watchman runs in foresight from the brazen tower

And announces that the Argolics, the tyrant of Babylon,

And every race of men are present. The man who is moved only by delay in war

Can scarcely endure to believe it. Therefore before the companies he thunders:

“Arms, arms, Danaans!” Leaving the city first,

He charges like lightning upon the Persians, and helmeted youth follow.

So Lycaon, with hungry throat, rushes upon prey;

The cry of his offspring, hanging at a dry udder, begs his aid,

And hunger, conceived beneath empty caves and friendly to slaughter,

At last falls upon the fields.

[Col. 0483B] The flock stands astonished: it does not dare flee, and, if it flees,

Will encounter other openings of the wood.

The leash is torn away by the dogs, whom the shepherd, from the embankment,

Urges with ringing voice, staff, and clapping hands.

No differently does the Macedonian king rage through that barbarian host,

Which had just begun to fear him as a fugitive,

When it sees the opposing line, in divided forces,

Suddenly come forth in a swift attack for battle.

Fearing that its hope has lied, it rushes bewildered to battle;

but the cries and onset of men rushing to arms throw the army’s ranks into disorder.

For the soldiers were suited rather to flight [Note: [Col. 0483] “flight.”]

Than to war and the crushing of an enemy. Yet Darius, once more setting his battle-line

In order, cautiously considered how, with a carefully arranged force,

[Col. 0483C] To surround the enemy by the strength of a great multitude.

What he judged a useful plan [Note: [Col. 0483] “counsel.”] and wholesome for king and men,

Reckless Fortune, stronger than every calculation, dispersed.

She alone safeguards what is safe, raises what is burdened,

Shakes what is settled, breaks compacts,

Weakens the strong, moves the fixed, and breaks the lofty.

Now the Macedonian line, firmly established in fixed formation

And divided into its proper battle ranks, occupied the mountains.

The king placed the phalanx of infantry in the first line before the Persians,

Like an insuperable rampart.

Nicanor, prefect of the right wing under Parmenio, held command there;

Ptolemy, Amyntas, Perdiccas, Coenus, Clytus, and Meleager stood beside him,

Each commander of his own division. But to you, Parmenio—

Second to no one in war—the left wing had been entrusted.

[Col. 0483D] Noble Craterus followed; Antigonus joined them,

As did Philotas, turbulent with his sword.

Hospitus, mounted before all his standards and urging on his war-horse,

The Macedonian, mighty in arms, glittered in battle on the right in flaming helmet,

Terrible with sword and spear. Closest at his side stood

Hephaestion, equal to the king in devotion and age, privy to his secret counsels [Note: [Col. 0483] “secrets.”],

But far surpassing him in rosy beauty.

Going before the Roman standards cheerfully, he solicited the commanders with appeal,

Persuaded them as a friend, strengthened the wavering,

Increased the courage of the bold,

[Vers. 1020.] Checked those straying, and gathered the scattered wings.

[Col. 0484A] He invited slaves by the hope of freedom, the poor and the greedy by payment;

He signalled with his spear to the slowly advancing men to hasten,

Now circling these, now those.

Now he urged them to handle [Note: [Col. 0483] “attempt.”] their bows; now to cast sling-bullets

If enemy ranks stood far off; now, when the enemy was near,

To settle the matter by the sword [Note: [Col. 0483] “to conduct [it], now to seek.”];

now to seek their destiny with the battle-axe.

And while they checked their advance, he spoke these few words to them:

“Offspring of Mars, whom the whole world desires to be held

Under dominion and bound by laws,

Behold the day we have longed for, on which provident Fortune prepares

To fulfil for us the triumph so often promised.

I felt its prelude long ago in Europe,

When you destroyed the race of the Aonians and the whole city from its seat,

And subdued Athens by fear alone.

[Col. 0484B] Do you see the unwarlike ranks glittering with gold?

Do you see how the womanish host gleams with gems?

They display more plunder than peril. Gold

Must be conquered by steel. Soft luxury [Note: [Col. 0483] “wealth.”] has learned only to threaten;

they shrink from swords and wounds.

When your deadly blade has searched their vital parts

And once spattered the fields with hostile blood,

They will seek pathways of flight through woods and rocks.

How great your care for me is, you will be able to prove

When I see dull, broken swords and shields battered

By blows. The right hand that strikes will express the feeling of the mind:

Alexander will be as dear to you in your hearts

As your sword permits.

Conquer men already conquered. He who spares an enemy with his sword

[Col. 0484C] Is himself his own enemy. He who prolongs an enemy’s life

Diminishes his own. It is no mercy in war

To be gentle toward enemies. The hand that is sparing of slaughter

Is burdensome to itself and worthy of slaughter. Cowards encounter death:

while they are afraid, they dare, but do not meet death.

Whenever the injuries, battles, and massacres inflicted upon Pelasgian peoples

By Persian leaders recur to your minds,

Do you think that this very great people suffices

To atone for the deeds of your fathers upon their descendants?

I shall balance Europe’s slaughter by Asia’s ruin:

Media, joined with Darius, shall atone for Xerxes’ crimes.

With me as leader, commanders, bring forth the standards; with me as leader,

Level the rampart; advance amid crowded enemies with slaughter.

Distinguish battles, not spoils, with me. Let rewards and plunder yield to my men;

Glory alone is sufficient for me.

[Col. 0484D] I love the deed for you, the name for myself.” Thus he spoke, and behold,

The battle-lines clash. The Persians, raising their cry,

Assail the thin air with ear-splitting howls;

Trumpets stretch the fields with terrifying bellowing;

Sound arises on both sides, and the air is struck by trumpets;

Mountain peaks return harsh calls;

Echo, which repeats sounds—a pure name without a body—

Was never to answer so many voices.

Yet Darius’ arms, produced by much toil of craftsmen, gleam

And display memorials of men of old. Rival to the sun’s ray,

[Vers. 1072.] A shield, cast in seven circles, challenges its unconquerable light.

[Col. 0485A] The origin of Darius’ fathers gleams forth, and the profane succession

Of the Giant race. Under their leader Memrot,

You may see earth-born brothers assembling upon the plain of Shinar,

Where, while they repeat the events of the Flood,

A brick-built work rises; speech, formerly one for all,

Is divided—marvellous to say—into various languages.

In another part the Chaldaean king directs his course against the holy city;

The ancestral emblems and battles shine, and triumphs famous

Over the Hebrew people. The captive tribe follows the victor’s chariot

With downcast eyes [Note: [Col. 0485] “captured.”]; after its walls and Temple have been leveled

To the ground, the dispossessed tyrant is brought within the walls of the enemy city,

In the double light of day.

But lest the blemishes of certain men obscure the praises of ancient kings,

The sculptor’s hand passed over a great series

[Col. 0485B] Which it judged should be omitted.

Among so many memorable triumphs of commanders and kings,

It would have been shameful to portray a king, fed with rustic food

And river water, lowing in a transformed shape,

Then restored to his former appearance when sense returned.

It passed over the life of a father whom his mad son,

Lest he should ever reign alone in his native city,

At Joachim’s counsel—shame!—is said to have torn limb from limb

And scattered through trackless places by a dreadful bird.

[Col. 0486A] The final portion of the shield begins the noble Persian kingdom:

you may see Belshazzar drinking from sacred gold,

The writing hand, and the fates being changed as it records them;

a Man of Desire resolves its hidden riddle.

But Cyrus’ most famous history travels over the whole circumference

And surrounds the edges of the shield. Lydia rejoices to be conquered

By so great a prince, and Croesus, deceived by ambiguous Apollo.

Yet Tomyris dared to test the tumult of war,

Set strength against strength, and repulsed him in battle;

She broke one unbroken by wars and sank, under an adverse star,

That head illustrious with so many titles. Alas for the deceptive glory

Of empire! Alas, how vast are the mockeries of human fortune!

Cyrus, lord of land and sea, delight of the world, whom virtue

Had lifted to the highest summit of affairs,

[Col. 0486B] Whom fame had set among the stars,

Who was ruler and master of himself, who was the whole world’s one hammer—

An unwarlike woman broke him.

Mortals, cease to raise [Note: [Col. 0485] “exalt.”] your hearts in pride

Because of amassed wealth, and to despise those beneath you.

Victors, cease ungratefully to live contrary to the highest Victor:

He who was able to give strength, sceptre, diadem, triumphs,

And riches, is able to take them away.

## ARGUMENT OF THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0485]

The third book sings of arms and peoples rushing upon their fate.

The Persians are defeated; Darius’ precious household goods

Are plundered; his sister, mother, wife,

And seven-year-old son are captured. Sidon is taken and Tyre

Wholly overthrown; Gaza is conquered with great difficulty,

And Libyan Hammon is conquered by a few.

Moreover Darius, his strength restored, again rushes to arms in greater force;

The cause of mutiny arises in the Macedonian camp;

There is an eclipse of the moon; and behold,

The consulted seers discuss the grim time.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0485]

[Col. 0485C] Now the crash of arms and carnage of war overwhelms

The blare of trumpets; arrows weave beneath the stars,

And a thick storm of missiles darkens the air.

First against the opposing Persians, with spear extended,

The Macedonian swiftly spurs his horse, launching a stone

In the whirling course of its missile-engine, where shields of kings,

Thickly crowded and golden, shine; where many a gem

Sparkles on proud helmets; where, terrible to behold,

The fiery form of a dragon, swallowing the open air with gold-spewing jaws,

Is borne before Darius.

As he seeks a leader worthy to be overwhelmed by his first wound,

[Vers. 1143.] Arettas, governor of Syria, is set before him.

[Col. 0486C] From his golden spear, flying and pendent,

A lion claims the stars; a carbuncle blazes upon his helmet.

The Chaldaean first pierces Alexander’s shield with a trembling blow;

but the ash-wood, unable to endure the close approach of the shaft

[Note: [Col. 0485] “fearing.”], cracks dryly as the wood breaks.

The man of Pella, bravely answering Arettas with steel,

Shatters the boss where the barbarian ornament gleams

On the prince’s shield. Nor content with this, it breaks apart [Note: [Col. 0485] “tears apart.”]

The work of the triple-woven cuirass, wanders through the hidden places

Of the heart, and the deadly point drinks his life.

He falls, himself slain; blood flowing from a great wound

[Vers. 1155.] Makes the fields purple. With a loud cry he declares

[Col. 0487A] That his king has conquered and has taken the first

First-fruits of the war. The Greek phalanx calls it a favourable omen

For itself and bears joyful applause to the stars.

The divisions thicken; Clytus and Ptolemy, conspicuous in arms,

Are carried upon the enemy with as much swiftness

As lions’ rage drives [Note: [Col. 0487] “presses.”] them against twin bulls,

Whom hungry famine spurs, while the heavy swishing of the shaken tail

Assists the cause of their fury.

Here Ptolemy, from horseback, pierces Dodantas through the temples,

And he groans with his brain flowing; Clytus tries with his spear

To overthrow Artophilus. They strike each other in turn,

And, blunted by the shields, each lance shattered against dull iron.

Horse confronts horse, shoulder shoulder,

Breast breast, shield-boss is battered by shield-boss,

[Col. 0487B] Cuirass by cuirass; helmet groans, overwhelmed beneath helmet.

Without delay both riders, their hamstrings slackened, fell;

Their mounts fell too, and, resembling the dead,

They lay lifeless for a long time. But when their bodies regained strength,

Clytus first, strength renewed, rose upright [Note: [Col. 0487] “straight.”]

And got himself back on his feet. As Artophilus tried to rise,

He furiously cut off his head with a single stroke of his sword

And committed it to the earth for burial.

In the left wing Mazaeus, distinguished in speech, war, and appearance,

Had overthrown the Greek Iollas. Swift Philotas, avenger, comes with drawn sword;

and because Othim had driven Mazaeus’ war-horse away [Note: [Col. 0487] “removed.”],

He attacks him at close quarters and cleaves his side with the sword.

Meanwhile Hyrcanian horsemen surround Philotas, sweating with much slaughter;

[Col. 0487C] Energetic Antigonus, Coenus, Craterus, and furious

Parmenio break their ranks. Without him Alexander never performed

Anything worthy of song; but what requital came to him

For his services, I think should rather be left unspoken.

Phylax lies by Antigonus’ sword, Midas by Coenus’ spear;

Craterus strikes down Amphilochus, whom, his helmet broken,

He drags lifeless from his chariot and joins to his own falling charioteer,

Already dragging his ruptured entrails.

According to his custom, Parmenio, condemned by an unjust star,

Rushes upon the Persians. Isannes, of royal descent, and Dimus

Strike spears into his side. He remains unmoved and steadies

The courage [Note: [Col. 0487] “flight.”] of frightened Orestes,

Who on foot was making for the heights of the worn cliff.

As soon as he sees him, he throws Isannes, pierced through the breast,

From his horse, and restores the fleeing rider to arms.

He crushes advancing Dimus, with sword drawn, beneath the hoof

Of his war-horse, leaving him helpless.

To these he adds Agilon, Elan, and the Arab Cherampus.

Elsewhere an Eumenid rages and assails the Persians,

Now with sword, now with missiles. With his sword he casts down Diaspes;

his weapon bloodies Endochius’ lung.

[Col. 0487D] He scatters men’s bones and tramples heaps of nobles.

[Vers. 1208.] Nor, while Nicanor fights no less on the right wing,

[Col. 0488A] Does he fail to spatter the fields with blood and moisten the plain with slaughter.

Eclimus meets him: rich in youthful beauty, but richer in lineage,

For he traced his race from the famous blood of Cyrus.

With a blow he challenges Nicanor’s shield,

As wandering hail at spring’s beginning commonly strikes the roof-tile;

but the secure house repels bronze’s fury. Yet Nicanor, his heart hardened,

Rushes into the deed of pitiful slaughter [Note: [Col. 0487] “fate.”], striking him

Where the shining cuirass opens a window for the eyes,

With his spear, and depriving him of both lights.

While the ash spear, venturing through the entrance of one eye,

Ran its course, it extinguished the use of the other light.

In the opposing line of harsh conflict stood

The illustrious offspring of Ninus, the Ninevite chief Negusar,

Skilled in raging upon opponents with the uncertain axe,

[Col. 0488B] And skilled in assailing fate from behind with missiles.

Now he rages [Note: [Col. 0487] “strikes.”] with missiles, now sword, now battle-axe,

Tearing out brains. With a javelin he had pierced Helim,

Son of Actor; he had deprived Dorylus of his right shoulder;

He had brought down Hermogenes, his neck struck by the axe.

When Philotas saw him devastating the Pelasgians with manifold slaughter,

He swiftly flew at him with drawn sword. Where a fire-coloured gem

Above the helmet’s cone emits light, he pierced the helmet;

but its slippery surface deflected the blow.

Yet the sword did not descend without effect: it cut off his left hand,

Which he had by chance held before his forehead.

Behold, the right hand prepares to avenge its sister

Exposed to slaughter and, fearless of death, raises the axe,

[Col. 0488C] Balancing it and threatening the standing foe with a fall about to come.

Philotas might perhaps have lamented his life taken before its day,

But Amyntas, raised above him on horseback,

Interposed his shield. The dreadful weapon passed through it with a marvellous blow [Note: [Col. 0487] “pierces [it].”]

And lodged in the middle of the shield-boss. While he was eager to withdraw it,

The hand where forearm joins upper arm was cut off

By the sword of the attacking man, withdrawn from his breast.

Pain sometimes awakens strength. Seeing himself in battle,

His hands cut off, an useless body,

He did what he could and threw himself before Iollas’ horse,
Three fell at once; Iollas perished, pierced through,

And the horse beneath the missiles; yet neither the harsh Negusar,

Nor the hailstorm of darts [Note: [Col. 0487] “cloud.”], nor so great a destruction spared you.

Now the drenched grass lies hidden, and corpses cover the ground;

[Col. 0488D] the fields float in gore; the valleys are filled [Note: [Col. 0487] “completely filled.”] with blood.

Blood flows freely on both sides, but the greater slaughter of Persians

Intoxicates the fields; the barbarian enemy grows thin

And melts away in spirit, though innumerable; and a small band

Of Macedonians does not cease to cut them down, their excessive lack

Of numbers [Note: [Col. 0487] “of number.”] being supplied by burning courage.

Therefore, as they now offered their backs to flight [Note: [Col. 0487] “presented.”], the Macedonian pressed them,

Like lightning [Note: [Col. 0487] “lightning-like.”], through impassable missiles, through swords,

And through masses of horsemen, amid a surrounding circle of infantry;

He directs his course towards Darius, but Oxathres gathers the troop—

[Vers. 1261.] none nearer to Darius by birth than he.

[Col. 0489A] Here is grief, here groaning; vigorous youth dies on both sides;

The death of commanders sweeps the crowd into one whirlwind

And scatters every form of death among the Persians, as Bellona,

Shaking her bloody hands, rages. One groans with throat laid open;

Another lies with his side transfixed by iron.

This man a spear kills [Note: [Col. 0489] “dashes out his brains.”], that man a sling strikes;

One vomits gore through limbs and broken neck; another’s

Entrails fall out; the sword claims another for itself.

This man dies; that man [Note: [Col. 0489] “that one.”] has died; this one throbs, that one is still.

Clad in splendid [Note: [Col. 0489] “beautiful.”] snowy armour, there stood, opposite,

Zoloas of Memphis, than whom none was more skilled in the stars:

In foreknowing the changes of the world; under what star the field

Would suffer failure of its crop; what year would be fruitful;

[Col. 0489B] whence winter brings forth snows; what mildness at spring’s arising

Makes the soil rich; why summer burns;

And with what autumn clothes itself—in ripe grapes;

Whether a circle can be squared; whether music produces

Heavenly harmonies; or what proportion obtains

Among the four elements. He knew what contrary impulses carry

The seven planets through the oblique world;

How many degrees apart they stand; what star prevents the baleful

Old man from raging; under what star he becomes

Propitious when obstructed; what fire moderates Mars;

What house each seeks for itself; what star rules in this

Hemicycle. He investigates their motions and computes their hours;

He weighs human events by the stars.

I speak too little: he enclosed the whole heaven within his breast.

[Col. 0489C] Therefore, having discerned in these stars that the Fates threatened him with death,

Yet because he could not alter the sequence of fate,

He dared to make his way to the Macedonian ruler himself,

Striving with all his strength to fall by so great a man,

Hating life and bringing death to birth upon the very face of battle-fury.

He met him and, from his high chariot, assailed

The prince’s shield, pierced by a hailstorm of missiles;

Nor did he provoke him only with darts, but with voice and insults,

Speaking thus: “Undeniable offspring of Nectanebus

[Note: [Col. 0489] “Neptanabus.”],

Eternal disgrace of your mother, why do you waste wounds

On cowards in flight? Turn your fury upon me.

If any courage yet remains in you, crush me—I whose

Military service is contained within the sevenfold chest of Wisdom,

And whose star-bearing head each of the two laurels claims.”

[Col. 0489D] Moved, Alexander pitied one wishing to die,

And gently replied: “What a marvel! Whoever you are, live, I pray;

And in dying do not destroy, with so great

Skills, their dwelling-place. Never may my right hand sweat,

Nor my sword grow red with the brain of one who knows so much.

You are useful to the world. What error impelled you to wish

To make for the river Styx, where no learning flourishes?”

He spoke, but Zoloas [Note: [Col. 0489] “He had spoken.”] committed his feet to the ground; and there,

[Vers. 1312.] where the breastplate, separating itself, leaves [Note: [Col. 0489] “left.”] the greave,

[Col. 0490A] he wounded his thigh with the sword and consecrated the field with blood.

The Macedonian roared; and so that he might spare Zoloas,

He drove his admitted horse away to a distance. Thus removed,

He restrained his anger; but Meleager rushed upon him

And struck both knees of Zoloas where the shin joins the thigh.

Then the rest of the crowd shattered the fallen man into fragments

And restored him to the stars.

Then indeed the whole weight of the crisis turned upon Darius.

What should he do? He sees fields enriched with the blood of his men;

Around him he sees the lifeless bodies

Of so many nobles lying—[and those in whom he had formerly placed

His chief trust were fleeing [Note: [Col. 0489] “Both these hemistichs are enclosed; in another manuscript they are omitted.”]]—while, dragging out his spilled entrails

Among the horses, his charioteer lies with severed neck.

While he wonders whether to flee on foot or strive to destroy himself,

[Col. 0490B] Perdiccas hurls a javelin; it strikes against his head,

But the bones protect his brain.

Darius is thrown from his chariot; he can no longer endure

The battle-line, but on foot withdraws from the throng, and among

The craven fugitives finds the shortcuts through the passes,

Until a horse brought to him by an Italian carried him over the great

Euphrates, and he withdrew to Babylon.

When Mazaeus perceived that he had escaped by flight the fortune

[Note: [Col. 0489] “secret.”] of war and the ruin of death, and saw those

Whom the excellence of the conqueror’s spirit had not yet allowed

To be torn from the field and the fury of Mars,

Straightway, shaken by disasters, courage abandoning such great

Undertakings, he learned to be a slave to fear.

Loyalty turned to fear: in ordered ranks the crowd of commanders fled,

[Col. 0490C] factions collapse when the summit is shaken [Note: [Col. 0489] “are shaken.”];

And when the head nods, the limbs must be thrown into disorder.

The people are cut down from behind; a second slaughter rages.

Though they might have died honourably for lord and fatherland,

By fleeing they incur the contagion of disgrace and death.

Now the sword, sated with slaughter, returns to its scabbard; and the conqueror himself,

Ordering the Pelasgian victors to withdraw from killing,

Commands them to hasten to the treasures and seize the gifts of the treasure-store

[Note: [Col. 0489] “booty.”],

Which lie shut away in the hiding places of the pass.

He goes swiftly and, victorious, divides the acquired wealth in equal shares.

The horses are laden; the greedy axle groans.

The sack is already full and vomits gold up to its very mouth;

It escapes its bonds and spurns being tied;

[Col. 0490D] the hand weary from gathering [Note: [Col. 0489] “tying.”] is not sated with gathering.

Indeed, even boots and wide folds of clothing are taught to swell.

They proceed against the defenceless, the bands of women;

When they have torn necklaces from their marble necks,

They wrench off torcs, and the ear loses its earrings [Note: [Col. 0489] “torn off.”].

They proceed to the embraces of married women, and virginity

Suffers violence. Intercourse occurs openly, and a bloodstained hand

Handles private parts. One party in intercourse contracts

The stain of incest; but the other party laments

[Vers. 1363.] and receives pardon, since violence inflicted lightens guilt

[Col. 0491A] and compulsion diminishes fault.

Yet, with her majesty and modesty preserved,

The whole household of Darius—his mother, royal wife,

Sister, and son (so great was the king’s clemency)—

Is conveyed in gilded chariots to the Dorian camp.

He treats Darius’s mother [Note: [Col. 0491] “Thus he restrains himself towards his own mother.”] in such a way that he chooses her as his own mother;

He grants his wife the name of sister.

The gentle man adopts the seven-year-old boy as his own son [Note: [Col. 0491] “adopts.”].

For so great a love of virtue then reigned

In that breast. Had that disposition remained [Note: [Col. 0491] “endured.”] in him,

No infamy could have blackened with accusation

A reputation bright with honours.

But when royal luxuries, after Persian affairs had been gained,

Set no limit, and the mother of extravagance—wealth—persuaded him

That the unlawful was lawful,

[Col. 0491B] fortune seized his nature, and, with its course reversed,

The former stream halted, clinging to the rocks of vices.

Thus he who had first been pious towards enemies became an enemy to friends;

Impious in slaughter, and finally turned to civil wars,

Thinking nothing unlawful to a tyrant.

Moreover, who could pass over his having claimed Jupiter as his supreme father

[Note: [Col. 0491] “to claim.”]? For he commands men to believe that he was begotten by Jupiter;

And power, having overstepped humanity, believes it.

As a man, he disdains being a man, and it seems too little

For him to be supreme among mortals.

Meanwhile soldiers are sent with Parmenio to Damascus,

To wrest from the conquered city the reserves of treasure stored there.

But its governor now thought that the wealth ought to belong to the victor;

A faithless traitor to his former lord, he had cautiously drawn his own people

Out of the city, intending to hand them over to the enemy.

[Col. 0491C] For, fortune’s course having changed, he too had changed.

Thus, by the single crime of one Persian, he himself,

With the rest, fell, after so many thousands had been slain;

And this was Darius’s one consolation for his losses and grief,

When a messenger reported that the very contriver of the crime

Had perished in the foremost rank by his own contrivance.

Nor did Darius thereafter endure to call fortune unjust,

Since it sometimes repays the guilty with an even balance,

As cowardly treachery deserves.

This was Darius’s remedy for evil: thus almost all adversities

Bring with them some fruit of consolation.

The seventh day, having kindled Phoebus’s lamp over the world,

Had pressed upon the stars, when, the customary funeral rite performed,

The king made for Sidon, that ancient

[Col. 0491D] nation of the Phoenicians. Having brought them under his authority,

He turned his march toward the Tyrians, whom he rejoiced

To find wholly ready for the test of Mars and defended by precipitous walls,

The city being formidable at close quarters.

So many battlements rose high from its walls;

Towers stood arranged in a long line,

Able to frustrate the cast of stones hurled from afar.

But wherever the stony mass sought an entrance,

Defenders stood there behind an interposed [Note: [Col. 0491] “opposed.”] latticework of shields.

[Vers. 1417.] Here many a slinger looses his sling and bow;

[Col. 0492A] many a ballista, set beneath them, threatens death.

But when the long day had broken the city, its citizens exhausted,

Now by naval engagement, now by warfare on foot,

And when engines, brought against the walls on both sides by Greek ships,

Had broken through [Note: [Col. 0491] “struck against.”] the hostile walls,

Every sex and age perished without any distinction;

No sword, judging guilt by any equitable standard, abstained.

For before the siege had yet encircled the walls, the citizens,

Within a short time and in violation of both peace

And the law of the intervening treaty, had involved in death

Envoys sent by the king to negotiate peace. Therefore they were hateful to the tyrant;

Nor indeed did they deserve to obtain forgiveness,

They in whom the embassy of both pardon and peace

Found no pardon. The Macedonian commands all swiftly

[Col. 0492B] to be involved in destruction, except those protected by the temples.

There is a crash and lamentation; the plaintive murmur grows frequent;

A woman’s cry strikes the golden stars.

And while, in the precipitous crisis of affairs, they waver,

Wherever the force of the winds bears most heavily upon the city,

They set fire; flame flies to the rooftops.

The kindled hunger grows ever more hungry,

The more floors furnish it with food and fuel.

Fathers perish mingled with the populace; death is one in kind for all,

But the manner of dying is not one.

One, to escape the pyre [Note: [Col. 0491] “fearing.”], runs upon swords; another,

To escape swords, casts himself into the midst of flames.

Some, while seeking to avert death by another death, fell of their own accord

From the half-ruined walls of the city; them the violent opening

[Col. 0492C] of the sea swallowed.

Others, seeking hidden retreats and vacant homes,

Prepared to fit nooses to their throats,

And inflicted death on themselves lest they should perish by death

Inflicted by the Greeks. Others, ashamed to seek the alternatives of death

[Note: [Col. 0491] “of war.”],

For the rights and laws of their city, defending

The face of their fatherland and liberty, chose to die:

That kind of death was honourable.

To fall without disgrace meant not to yield, but to be cut down,

To cut down and be cut down [Note: [Col. 0491] “To cut down rather than be cut down.”], provided that they were not cut down unavenged.

They rush forward [Note: [Col. 0491] “They rush together.”], a people devoted to death,

And furnish material to their assailants. They strike and are themselves struck;

While suffering slaughter, they inflict it, ready for either fate.

Nor does the spouse of Cytherea inflict less destruction.

[Col. 0492D] That noble Tyre, first founded by Agenor, is dissolved into ashes—

Tyre which, if the illustrious utterances of poets deserve belief,

If one may credit tradition, alone either first learned

Or taught the signs of sounds and the figures of things.

Thus, after so many years, the untamed fury of the Macedonians subdued

A city that had been untamed.

But true faith and divine peace, under Christ of the Christians,

Restored the city, its walls rebuilt [Note: [Col. 0491] “The poet alludes to the time when Tyre was subject to the Franks.”],

Where a people devoted to truth and burning with the censer of the mind

[Vers. 1470.] worships the name of the Crucified One,

[Col. 0493A] whose are the other cities of the sevenfold clime,

Which his native dominion possesses and will long possess.

Overthrown Tyre could have warned other nations

Not thereafter, in the eastern region of the world,

To presume upon the name [Note: [Col. 0493] “name.”] of the Pellaean

And provoke the strength of the Macedonians.

Yet Gaza, following Darius and the earlier cause,

Dares the like; with her walls she attempts to exclude the gods (superos) [Note: [Col. 0493] “for/against the gods” (superis)],

If perhaps loyalty might overturn fortune.

While Mars performs his work, while with bloody killing

And loss on either side he lays both sides low,

A barbarian, coming as a deserter to the king, concealing a sword

In his shield, attacks the head of the Great One with his blade.

But because the order of the Fates stands inevitable,

And the immovable sequence of human events constrains all,

His drunken hand missed; Lachesis does not permit him to perish by the sword—

[Col. 0493B] Lachesis, who already considers that she will offer the leader, after ten years,

To drink the destined poison, prepared long ago

And shut in a deadly casket, through the intervening assistance of his friends.

Here the king orders the Arab’s right hand to be cut off by the very sword

Which he had wrongly aimed [Note: [Col. 0493] “brandished.”].

And Mars’s fury, which had previously been lulled

By recent treachery, now awakens; anger grows anew beneath his heated breast.

As he presses furiously upon the enemy who dared the crime,

An ash-wood spear grazes his left arm,

And a stone mass crushed the middle of his leg.

Yet though he had received two wounds, the Macedonian did not abandon

His fierce undertaking; lavish of vital breath,

He breaks the wedges, overwhelms [Note: [Col. 0493] “tramples.”] the tyrant himself,

And enters the city as the defeated surrender it.

[Col. 0493C] Then, having arranged the kingdom by the discrimination of nobles,

He proceeds to Egypt. Once it had been reduced under his power,

The king burns to visit the Libyan seat of Hammon:

Difficult approaches, a journey unbearable even

For the strong and few. The dry land thirsts for dew

And begs water from the sky; the region withers

In perpetual heat [Note: [Col. 0493] “increases.”], and barren sands die.

When the tenacious sand has received the sun [Note: [Col. 0493] “received.”] and the fields [Note: [Col. 0493] “the air.”],

And the whirlwind has thickened under the tread of feet,

Here the Syrtes had their storms; here another Scylla barks in a dry sea;

Here is a dusty Charybdis.

One place spews dusty globes; another lies buried

In sand. Perhaps Neptune’s sea would have punished them

With a gentler storm than this sea of dust.

[Col. 0493D] Nowhere do cultivated things grow green; nowhere are there human footprints;

Nowhere does the earth meet the eye; nowhere does a tree present itself.

Already four times Dawn, shedding Memnon’s tears upon his tomb,

Had raised her dewy chariots through the air,

When the Macedonians’ leader and the surviving multitude

Entered Hammon’s grove and drank from the spring,

Which it would be quite unworthy to leave unmentioned among memorable things.

When the sun reins in his horses, the water runs warm;

It is colder than ice when Titan, burning more fiercely,

Scorches the fields with the heat of midday;

When beneath the western axle the hostess Thetis,

[Vers. 1526.] cleansing the horses’ stalls, prepares to stable the Sun’s horses in the sea,

[Col. 0494A] sets out ambrosia and frees their mouths from the bits,

Jupiter’s spring, its numbness of cold somewhat expelled, grows warm;

And the same spring burns hotter than Phoebus

When midmost sleep waters the world with moist wings.

And the more swiftly Phoebus hastens toward firm sunrise,

The more the water remembers its customary warmth;

Nightly cold compels it to lessen its heat,

Until it again becomes languid at Phoebus’s rising.

When the king, rejoicing after consulting Jupiter, had paid his offerings,

He returns to Memphis, although he desired to approach

The scorched peoples of Ethiopia, Memnon’s inhospitable lands,

The seat of Dawn, and the sun’s impassable path.

But a hard and unconquerable [Note: [Col. 0493] “inevitable.”] season of Mars,

And the appointed day that was to see the world’s tumult

And the slaughter of a battle which the enemy had hastened,

[Col. 0494B] pressed near and compelled the ruler’s mind, fixed upon its purpose,

To desist from the intended undertaking.

Greater business constrained his resolute mind.

Meanwhile Darius, his strength restored, is wholly present for battle;

The whole world has conspired. Shame at the past and hope,

Spurs to the future, summon him once more to arms.

Citizens, mingled with farmers, come together in the camp;

The deeply rooted field complains that its mattocks are idle,

And earth overgrown with brambles; oxen sigh for their wagons.

The backs of camels, the barbarian war-machine,

Burden elephants marching in towered formation;

Nor is the buffalo absent. Xerxes, attacking Argos,

Never dried up rivers with so many thousands of men.

Nor did the avenger of adultery gather so many peoples at Aulis,

[Col. 0494C] when the sea failed the fleet,

And virgin blood, at the prompting of unjust Calchas,

Wiped away the offence and released the winds.

The Macedonian marvels that, after so many thousands had previously been reduced

To nothing, more peoples should be reborn for death, as though by renewed death,

And summoned again to war—just as Jupiter’s son Antaeus,

On Libyan sands, marvelled after a fall to rise stronger,

Until, snatching him up, his opponent said: “Here, Antaeus, you shall fall.”

Or as the Tirynthian subdued the Hydra, fertile in heads,

By slaughtering so many of its own.

And now, utterly heedless of danger and scorning numbers,

The conqueror of lands had led his swift force over the Euphrates.

[Col. 0494D] He found cities which he was approaching burned with fire,

And fields smoking, which Darius had ordered to be burned

Under the command of Mazaeus, so that at such a turning-point of fortune

He might be able to alter its course, and force the Greeks,

Stripped of crops, Ceres’ gift, to abandon their bold attempt,

To despair of a passage through rocks stiff with flames,

And to plan flight, while they saw everything burnt—

Places fruitful with fire and hills deprived of grass;

While furrows lamented their idleness and Ceres, reduced to ashes,

Denied sustenance.

But Alexander, enjoying favourable fortune and always aspiring

[Vers. 1581.] to the summit of highest honour,

[Col. 0495A] swifter than the Tigris itself—the Tigris, which takes its name from swift motion—

Crosses the waters of the Tigris, which, rolling great stones in its torrent,

Rushes fiercely into marble waters.

Without delay, lest Darius be able to penetrate the interior

Of his kingdom, just as a hunting dog tracks hidden Actaeon

In the deep woods by his keen nose, or as a Gallic hunter

Pursues a boar in rage, brandishing hunting-spears of iron,

So he hunts Darius, and pitches camp beyond Arbela—

Where he was to make him infamous by his slaughter and the treachery of his own men,

And was himself to perish. Already then he had pitched his tents

In that ill-omened settlement.

It was the time compelling the uncertain light to pale;

Yet neither light nor night gives it a name: it is both,

[Col. 0495B] and neither, separated by a slight distinction. Therefore our Greeks more truly

Called it “Twilight,” because it is ambiguous [Note: [Col. 0495] “the Greeks” (rather than “our people”)].

Hesperus had now hastened on the dewy rising;

And now, with darkness threatening their eyes, the stars,

Through the moon’s intervention, were preparing to fulfil the sun’s office.

When Phoebe, made manifest to the world by her brother’s withdrawal,

Cheering the regions of humankind as she rose in her circuit,

Grew pale, suffering first a failure of brightness,

Then at last, wholly suffused with blood-red colour,

Defiled her light and terrified even the Macedonians

[Note: [Col. 0495] “all of them.”],

The nobles together with the common people; while the enemy ground its teeth [Note: [Col. 0495] “the earth ground its teeth.”],

And while the day of battle, appointed by unwilling divinity,

[Col. 0495C] fatal to both sides, pressed upon them,

And they beheld threatening stars in heaven,

They shuddered greatly at the portent and at what it signified.

No wonder that their spirits wavered and hands full of weapons

Slumbered; hearts shaken by fresh fear trembled,

And the camp grew fierce with hoarse murmuring.

The Macedonian is blamed; the mutinous host casts the fault upon him.

They are already weary of being dragged unwillingly by their king

To the uttermost bounds of the world. They complain of inaccessible mountains,

Lands deserted by avenging Vulcan;

Of cities and rivers refusing to admit criminals;

That he wishes, though the gods are indignant, to be lord of men;

That the stars are hostile to them and deny their customary light;

That he oversteps the bounds assigned to humankind, transcends the kingly condition,

Aspires to heaven, and despises his native home;

[Col. 0495D] that for the glory of one man they enter upon so many dangers

And undergo such changing turns of fortune.

Already the crowd had burst into these complaints; already it had begun

To be stirred to mutiny, when the undismayed king calls the entire council

[Vers. 1628.] and consults the seers to whom skill in the stars had given the name

[Col. 0496A] and power [Note: [Col. 0495] “power.”] of diviners:

What cause has stained the orb of the moon?

What do the gods warn concerning these things [Note: [Col. 0495] “this matter.”]?

What riddles of fate do they intend to signify? He orders their views to be reported publicly.

Among the prophetic diviners and followers of the stars was

the foremost Aristander [Note: [Col. 0495] “stood” (stabat), in place of “foremost” (major)], already withered by barren old age:

“Cease,” he says, “to assail the fates with empty complaints.

The Fates govern the stars; and the courses, places, motions,

And whatever the great creator of things gave them from the beginning

To portend, they keep in a fixed order.

They cannot change anything of that profound mind:

Whatever it foresaw from eternity will come to pass.

Whether Thetis, pressing against the earth, extends the shores

[Col. 0496B] by an increase of her flood; whether the earth overthrows cities

By the collision [Note: [Col. 0495] “shock.”] of their sides; whether diseased air flows in;

Whether it wishes to darken the day with shadows; whether the moon’s horns

Grow dim; whether a helmet (galerum) [Note: [Col. 0495] “a planet” (planetam)] moves more slowly—

All things descend from the supreme counsellor of affairs.

Unless he has so decreed, there is nothing the stars can do.

Thus the moon’s pale orb grows wan

When, as it is said, she is about to go beneath the earth

And hide her face, preparing to vanish from human sight.

Or when Diana is oppressed by her brother’s splendour,

Just as the greater flame of a blazing hearth

Out of envy [Note: [Col. 0495] “bright.”] obscures the gleam and little flame of a lamp.

Yet, following the not unworthy doctrine of the ancients and of the fathers

Of Memphis, I should not hesitate to call the sun the Greeks

And the moon the Persians: when the former suffers eclipse, the ruin

[Col. 0496C] of the Greeks is marked; when the latter suffers eclipse, that of the Persians.”

He spoke and, using [Note: [Col. 0495] “using.”] ancient examples as evidence, explained

The deeds of Persian leaders, when, as fortune’s scourge bore down,

Mournful Cynthia had grown pale with her horn obscured.

Thus the judgment which white-haired old age had pronounced stood confirmed,

And the seer’s opinion won belief.

When it was publicly put forth, superstition bent the fearful hearts

Of the people; nothing draws a crowd more tightly [Note: [Col. 0495] “more tightly bound.”] to itself,

Seizes their speech, and restrains their hands.

When the crowd, fierce, powerful, and changeable, boils with the heat

Of a wandering mind, if it is stirred by the empty religion of leaders,

Despising the guidance of seers, it assumes [Note: [Col. 0495] “rules.”] authority

And scorns the reins of kings.

Therefore, when hope and trust in fate had raised their numbed

[Col. 0496D] minds, the Macedonian judged that arms must be used while their hearts were warm,

Lest their ardent impetus grow cold. At once he commands the tents

To be struck about the middle course of night, and himself leads the rejoicing bands

[Vers. 1675.] in the foremost rank, content with no small body of soldiers.

## ARGUMENT OF BOOK FOUR.

[Col. 0495]

The fourth book turns to the lamentable funeral of Darius’s wife;

Lamentations weary Darius, and false suspicion.

Envoys bring Darius definite replies; battle formations stand ready

On either side; the Macedonian is frightened by the appearance of war,

Calls a council, rejects the answers of his followers,

And postpones sleep until daylight.

Roused from sleep [Note: [Col. 0497] “dreams.”], he swiftly puts on his arms

And strengthens his men with words and deeds. Behold, the battle-lines clash

And the cry penetrates to the stars.

## BOOK FOUR.

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497A] Pale and with his lights suffused by pitch-black smoke,

The fourth Lucifer, before the fatal tumult, rode on his panting horse;

and the imperious phalanx of Pelasgians, led by hope, hurried along a desert road,

spread over barren [Note: [Col. 0497] “green.”] fields between

the channel of a sandy torrent below

and a mountain producing clouds from its summit

[Note: [Col. 0497] “And forests producing from the summit.”];

when the royal wife fell, collapsing among the soft ranks

of captive women. Grief for her absent husband and fallen country,

And the unceasing toil of the journey, compelled her to expire.

The bravest of kings, that pious destroyer, grieved no less

Than if a messenger had reported that his sisters had fallen and been slain

Together with their mother. Tears such as Darius would have shed arose,

And the young man’s age, already grey, broke into lamentation.

[Col. 0497B] He sat beside the bier, and noble affection—ever a rare thing in tyrants—

Broke the sternness of that unconquered prince

And drew tears from the enemy.

Since her capture he had looked upon her only once; but the queen’s precious beauty

Had not been a cause or incentive of passion for him.

He preferred to be the guardian of her chastity and beauty;

To violate neither was greater glory to him

Than if he violated both.

An eunuch from Tyre, escaping through the midst of the Greeks,

Goes as messenger to Darius. When Darius saw him with garment torn,

With bloody nails, hair lying dishevelled over his face,

And countenance submerged beneath a great stream of tears,

He said: “Do not delay in troubling me. If anything of salvation

[Col. 0497C] remains for me, release my fear into grief.

I have learned to be miserable and battered by disasters.

This is the consolation, this the remedy for a wretched man’s evils:

To know one’s fate. You bring cruel mockeries of my own people,

And things more grievous than every affliction itself—

What nevertheless I fear to say aloud.”

Then the other replied: “As much honour and reverence as can be rendered

By those who obey to queens has been rendered to yours by the conqueror

[Note: [Col. 0497] “so great.”]. But that noble woman, your

Sister and wife—what I scarcely dare utter—

Has departed from among us and left her body empty.”

Then indeed you could have seen the camp turn to groaning and lament;

The old man lies unconscious and, unhappy, defiles his venerable

[Vers. 1727] grey hair with dust, affirming in ignorance that his wife had therefore been killed

[Col. 0498A] because she would not consent to suffer unchaste outrage.

Having kept back only the eunuch and dismissed all others,

The eunuch swears that she suffered no injury to her chastity,

That her captor inflicted nothing harsh upon his captive;

Rather, that with tears he performed a husband’s office

And paid funeral rites worthy of so great a character.

Thereupon suspicion mingled with anxiety deeply pierced

The lover’s heart. The sick lover seethes, inferring from habitual adultery

A love arising between captive woman and captor:

“This woman was captive and radiant in beauty and bloodline;

He was her lord and young; that he wished it is proved

By the fact that he was able.” Darius’s weakened mind seethes in these anxious cares,

Until, with household gods and gods above as witnesses, the servant attested

That his wife had lived chastely.

[Col. 0498B] Faith was scarcely won by Darius. Raising to the stars his palms

And a face wet with an overflowing fountain of tears:

“Supreme Father of gods,” he says, “and single power of things,

Gods of my fathers, by whose nod the Persian [Note: [Col. 0497] “spherical.”] world stands:

First, I pray, establish the kingdom for me and mine.

But if you have decreed that it be taken from me, and fate’s imperious will

Commands the empire of Asia to be transferred from me,

Then after me let this enemy, so pious and so merciful a conqueror, possess it.”

He spoke and, with pouring tears, invokes the gods

That the Fates may follow his prayer.

And although it was in vain, peace having already twice been sought,

He turned his counsels to war. Conquered by love for his enemy and by his example,

He orders ten commanders of horse, protected by Pallas’s tree,

To go as envoys entrusted with a mission of peace. One of them was Achillas,

[Col. 0498C] who surpassed the rest in age as much as in eloquence.

He began thus: “Most merciful king, no force compelled Darius

To seek peace from you so often [Note: [Col. 0497] “forced.”];

Rather, your compassion—so abundantly exercised for our benefit—drew it from him.

We have experienced mother, dear pledges, and children as absent only,

Not as captives. You, the pious guardian and protector of their chastity,

Care for those who remain as though their father.

With favourable omen you call them queens; forgetting hostile anger,

You allow them to retain the appearance of their former fortune.

The pallor of their faces and eyes bruised by weeping prove

[Note: [Col. 0497] “suggest.”] how much more merciful an enemy you are than the enemy;

[Vers. 1770] and the face strips veils away from the mind.

Such was Darius when we were sent from him as envoys

As Alexander plainly is. Yet he mourns your wife, though she is an enemy.

Already his left hand would hold the shield;

Already you would stand in battle-line; already thundering Bucephalus

Would bear you against the enemy; already Darius would feel you,

Terrible in arms—unless concern for the burial of his wife delayed him.

Let concord be ratified. Darius offers you his daughter not without a dowry:

All the land everywhere between the shore of Phryxus

And the Euphrates he begs you, through his daughter, to accept as dowry.

Let his son be held as hostage both for fidelity and peace.

Let the mother return attended by two

Virgins, whose price is thirty thousand talents,

Refined from yellow metal.

[Col. 0499B] Unless the gods had supported you with a greater heart

And blessed human limbs with a divine mind,

This was the time when you should not merely grant peace,

But seek it and enter into a treaty. Do you not see

How great a Darius rushes to arms? How many peoples he has summoned

From the remotest world? With how many fleets he shadows the sea?

Neither sea for navigation nor land for pitching camps is sufficient;

The ships set in the way close off the sea’s mouths.

Why delay? One enclosure possesses forces which no other enclosure possesses.”

When the Great One received Darius’s reply, he quickly summoned

His commanders into council and asked what should be done about it.

You might have seen the senate whisper uncertainly;

The council is said to have remained silent for a long time, until

Parmenio—whose prudent eloquence was not so great as his steadfast spirit,

And for whom speaking brave deeds was not as easy as doing them—said:

[Col. 0499C] “Long ago I thought they ought to be restored to those redeeming them,

Since the greatest sum might be paid from those among them

Who either died on the journey or, slipping free of close

Fetters, escaped. I likewise now advise

That the helpless old woman, together with the twin offspring, be exchanged

For so great a weight of gold. They hinder rather

The Greek army and its march. By this condition you can acquire

So broad and noble a kingdom without spending

The blood of your own men. Nor do I think that anyone has hitherto possessed

So much land lying between the Danube and Euphrates;

Yet graver matters remain.

Consider how much of the world you seek, and how much you will leave

[Col. 0499D] behind your back already subdued. Keep your native country, not Bactra or India,

In mindful heart. After brave achievements it is safer

To return home than to live always under arms.”

The Great One took the counsellor’s judgment badly: “If I were Parmenio,”

He said, “I should prefer the money offered to the palm,

And should rather go [Note: [Col. 0499] “be.”] without glory

Than win a palm with glory but without wealth.

But Alexander now reigns secure beneath poverty’s garment;

I pride myself on being a king, not a merchant.

Away with the seller of fortune!

[Vers. 1823.] Nothing is for sale to me. If it is agreed that they ought to be restored,

[Col. 0500A] I judge it more agreeable that they be restored freely and released as a gift

Than for payment: if gifts follow a price [Note: [Col. 0499] “follow.”],

Gratitude does not follow; transactions possess no gratitude.

When he had said this in response to the counsellor, he commands

The envoys to be admitted and this reported to Darius:

‘What I have done mercifully, and what was worthy of my character,

Let him know I have attributed to my nature, not to his honour.

The enemy shall not find me womanish; those alone may safely despise Alexander

Who are despised. I do not bring arms against such persons

As cannot use arms, to whom nature’s sluggish softness has denied weapons.

He whom I shall have made worthy of hatred or anger must be armed.

But if perhaps he kept faith and sought peace from me,

And withdrew from the whole world,

[Col. 0500B] I might perhaps hesitate whether I would wish him to fall.

But since Darius now entices my friends, though only recently pledged to me, into treason,

Now flatters them with gifts, so that they may hasten my fate with fatal poison,

I shall pursue him to the death. For he prepares battle against me not as a just enemy,

But as an assassin—indeed, to confess the truth, as a brigand and poisoner.

The peace terms which you hold out to him, if I accepted them,

Would seem to concede the victory. You bring us as dowry

Everything lying beyond the Euphrates; hence I judge that you too have forgotten

Where we are speaking: my winged force has crossed the Euphrates;

My camp leaves behind the boundary of the dowry.

[Col. 0500C] Drive the Macedonian king hence, so that what you give me may be known as yours.

It does me great honour if he seeks to set me before Mazaeus as his son-in-law.

Go and report these my words to your tyrant:

Whatever Darius possesses, whatever he has lost, and he himself,

Are mine by right, and the prizes of Greek warfare [Note: [Col. 0499] “for the Greeks.”].’”

So he speaks and swiftly sends the Persians back to camp.

Mazaeus is sent by Darius to occupy the hills and plains of the roads

Which the enemy was to approach.

Meanwhile the Macedonian embalmed the body of Darius’s wife with spices

And ordered a tomb to be carved on a mountain summit. Famous Apelles,

A Hebrew skilled with his hands, raised it in a wondrous design,

[Col. 0500D] depicting not only kings and the names of the Achaean race,

But also the narratives of Genesis, beginning from the world’s creation.

There was matter, *hyle*, with its parts confused;

A shapeless globe, distinguished by varied colour,

Giving birth to the four elements, marked with equal seals

[Note: [Col. 0499] “figures.”].

Here was the sequence of works which the Godhead accomplished in six days.

Among them, with gold breathing forth brilliance,

And ruddy gems licking the air,

You could see the first light emerge from darkness.

Here man, more worthy among creatures lacking reason,

Is formed from clay; his own rib deceived him,

Led astray by the death-bearing poison of the serpent.

[Vers. 1876.] With the parents expelled and received by the first mother,

[Col. 0501A] the fiery sword guards [Note: [Col. 0501] “the sword guards the threshold of the grove.”] the threshold of the grove.

Then Cain, an exile, did not escape the bow of the bigamist.

The human race multiplies, and its polluted stock;

Virtue departs, vice succeeds; they cling

To unlawful marriage, while piety and uprightness withdraw.

If you note the sorrowful sign in the image, the Creator—
You might think that He regretted having made man. The Master-Craftsman labours; every kind of living creature is shut within the ark.

After the waters have withdrawn, the number eight replenishes the world; a vine is planted, and the grape makes the father drunk.

Here gold depicts, with special detail, the succession of the patriarchs; you may see the aged fathers smile, Esau hunting and returning with his two companies, and Jacob wrestling. Joseph’s sale follows, with deceit, imprisonment, and the first migration.

[Col. 0501B] Here Egypt suffers, struck by ten plagues; the royal cavalry and arms are overwhelmed as it conveys the Hebrews across, and the sea gleams darkly amid pure gold.

Here manna feeds the people in the desert fields; the Law is given, and the rock offers drink to the thirsty. Ben-Nun succeeds Moses, buried after his wars; the nation is subdued, and Jordan draws back its streams. After Jericho’s ashes, Achan, guilty of theft, expiates his crime; Joshua pays nature’s due after dividing the ancestral land among his brethren by lot, and at last Apelles brings the people down to the Judges.

Among these is Samson, the strongest of men; yet Dalilah, stronger still, blinds him when his hair is cut.

[Col. 0501C] And Ruth the Moabitess, widowed by her first husband, enters the Hebrew race by a happy marriage-bond.

A second division of the painting follows, treating of the kings: from the beginning, Samuel mourns the death of Eli; the people murmur at Shiloh; from Benjamin comes one to rule the Hebrews. But because his end accords ill with his beginning, a prince of Jesse’s seed is set over the people—he who shattered Goliath’s arms and, when the tyrant fell with his offspring in battle, condemned the abandoned mountains by a royal curse.

Here Asahel and Abner fall; Uriah meets the death he had brought upon another; a tree holds fast the parricide, whom a man’s spear pierces—you would think the image itself mourned for its native land. But after this had happened to him in human fashion, the Temple is built; while the peaceful son reigns, the father’s ordinances live on after he is buried. Nor does the sacred altar protect Joab, and the greedy sword cuts down Shimei. By the counsel of young men, the perpetual schism endures among the kings and people; there is contention over the wealthy kingdom.

Whatever either kingdom accomplished gloriously, the learned hand portrays in the same marble both deeds and names. Yet, lest it disgrace the nation and its lineage, it passes over the kings’ idols, the shame of brotherly Samaria, the deities of the kingdom; it passes over Jezebel’s death as she falls from the tower, Ahab’s death is unmentioned, and so is the vineyard acquired by blood.

[Col. 0502A] There no captain of fifty burns together with his companion. But Baal’s sacred people are struck down by Elijah’s sword, and the disciple grieves that his master does not appear.

The higher order contains those kings whom the page declares illustrious: Hezekiah cleanses away idols and restores laws long dormant; here you may see the sick man, the sun’s reversal, and Josiah gloriously celebrating the Passover, renowned in inscriptions. Apart from these, no one reigned altogether free from the stain of apostasy, and none was wholly pure from guilt.

Behold: the higher row contains the images of the prophets, showing under what king and at what time each wrote. Here Isaiah, son of Amos, gives Ahaz a sign: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive.” Here Jeremiah, under Jehoiakim, mourns the setting of the sun and says that the Lord has created new wonders

[Col. 0502B] on earth: “A woman shall encompass a man.” Ezekiel, standing after the city’s capture by the nations, reports that he saw the gate closed for ages—plainly signifying the womb of the untouched Virgin.

“Christ shall be killed,” says Daniel, “after those seventy weeks of time.” The names of the twelve prophets follow, together with their headings and their mutually harmonious utterances. The final part contains Cyrus’s kingdom and the people’s return under Zerubbabel as leader; here the rebuilding of the Temple is painted. Esther’s history is not passed over, nor Haman’s cause of death, nor Vashti’s foolish pride. Here Tobit sits in darkness, deprived of light; and manly Judith kills Holofernes in the camp. The whole sequence of the painting ends with Ezra.

[Col. 0502C] When Alexander had performed the customary funeral rites at the tomb, he paid the offerings to the dead, then hastily ordered the camp moved and rushed swiftly against the enemy. He orders Menidas, content with few soldiers, to reconnoitre the plains and discover where the Persian king and his forces lay concealed. When Mazaeus saw him from afar, he gathered his troops and withdrew at rapid flight into camp.

But Darius, eager to fight on open plains, renews his battle-lines; moving through the formations, he equips their hearts with exhortations as much as he arms them with weapons. Already the Pellaean had selected a place for his camp from which the Persians’ golden tents could be seen; already the commanders’ standards stood at a short distance; already the battle-lines were deployed. On either side you could see dragons flying through the void at the easy onset of the winds.

[Col. 0502D] Then the fury of the Macedonians roared, and, when the sound was loosed, drove the air against the Persians with hoarse shrieks. No less did the opposing Persians strive to strike the heavens with terrible trumpet-blasts. At the sound the world and its axis tremble; Atlas scarcely sustains the eternal weight on quaking knee. Echo, thinking that new wars of the giants have arisen, springs back with returning voices; broad valleys answer with hoarse throat.

Alexander could scarcely restrain the armed hands and the people’s frenzy, lest, their formation broken, they should rush forward and be swept into the enemy at their first impetuous movement.

[Col. 0503A] But because the Sun, weary after traversing his orbit, was darkening his face lest he should see so many deaths, and strove to plunge his spent chariot into the sea, Alexander himself throws up a rampart and commands the Greeks to establish camp in that same place. They obey; and, once the earthwork is made, he hastens to a mound from which he can survey the whole enemy at close range and recall the scattered phalanxes to view.

The entire aspect of the coming crisis is set before him. He sees the armour-clanging cohorts gleam, their ordered battle-lines proud in trappings and gold; he hears the barbarian multitude and the confused murmur of voices, while the dreadful neighing of horses strikes his ears. All this, if it is permissible to believe it, inspired fear in the man; I suppose that terror rose readily into that noble, giant heart.

[Col. 0503B] Typhis is no otherwise tossed upon a sea of anxieties when the mild governance of the west winds has long borne his contented vessel under breeze alone, with no oarsman, and the choir of Nereids has feasted upon the quiet waves—if he sees, far away, storms boiling up in their approach, while the South Wind, sending swift seals forth from their deepest homes, now lashes the air with dripping wings. He calls to his companions and himself flies to the helm, fastening the stern-ornament to the ship’s side.

So likewise, when Alexander saw the barbarian masses pressing upon the fields in so many thousands, it is permissible to believe that the great-hearted leader was afraid. Therefore he calls the Romans—or rather, perhaps, summons his men, either uncertain what he should do or, more plausibly, to test them by asking what course should be followed.

[Col. 0503C] At length he receives the long-awaited opinion of learned Parmenion: they need the aid of night, and he judges that they should act by stealth rather than by battle. The enemy, he says, may easily be driven back, killed by swords, or compelled to yield defeated—taken unawares by sudden attack, oppressed by night’s darkness, benumbed by the stupor of peaceful sleep, inert, and divided in customs and languages.

For if the issue is to be decided in daylight, the terrible bodies of the Scythians, the Indians hateful for their uncut hair, and the giant stature of those whom Bactra produces will confront their eyes; their fearful shapes may throw their hearts into empty panic. He adds that so many thousands of the nation cannot be surrounded or moved in war by a few men.

[Col. 0503D] Moreover, he demonstrates that Darius has chosen fields lying in open flatland, rather than, as happened before, engaging amid the narrow passes of Cilicia. Nearly the whole Macedonian force approves this, and agrees as one; among them Polypercon declares that they should make use of the night, and that the Greeks’ triumph lies in the night.

The king looked upon him; for he could no longer bear to rebuke Parmenion or offend him with swollen words, though he had recently struck the counsellor with sharp satire:

“This,” he says, “is the practice of a robber and the craft of thieves that you suggest to me—men whose sole hope and highest aim is to harm by tricks and deceive by concealed fraud.

[Col. 0504A] Our glory does not campaign by deceit. Let there be nothing able to blacken the brightness of my reputation with the soot of disgrace. No longer do the narrowness of the pass, the Cilician gorge, Darius’s sluggish absence, or the furtive support of timid night please me.

“I shall attack the men in daylight. The victory which we seek by swords must either be none at all, or honourable. I would rather that the king repent of fortune and an unjust lot than that I be ashamed of a triumph gained in part by night. Victory is not worth so much that posterity should read that I won by deceit and that cunning should diminish the palm of victory.

“Moreover, lest they be deceived, lest they be detected by the enemy: it is known that the Persian sentries and companies are standing under arms. Therefore attend to your bodies and restore, by sleep, the work of the day,

[Col. 0504B] remembering that the movement of the approaching day is at hand, a day which must overthrow the world’s middle for you.”

When he had finished speaking, the soldiers return to their tents.

Darius, on the other hand, arms the Persians no less vigorously and fortifies his men. He supposes the enemy will do what he himself would have done had Parmenion’s advice possessed force: they prepare food for their fury; horses are bridled, and their adorned backs shine. With fires lit, the battle-lines seem to blaze; helmets rival the stars, and high heaven marvels that battered shields have found flames their equals, fearing that earth may become sky and sky earth. Nor does night take the least pleasure in resembling day.

[Col. 0504C] For, in place of the sun, Darius’s helmet—rival of Phoebus—is granted to him; a fiery lamp stands upon its summit, obscuring the stars of night and, alone among lights, refusing to yield to the sun’s rays. By as much as it surpasses them in brightness, by so much does it detract from them. A thousand stones glitter in a circle, none of which does not dispute the fiery radiance’s claim to be a carbuncle.

Sudden alarm seizes the shaken host on both sides. Already the golden couch dared to cherish its second Jupiter, but could not promise him sleep: royal body, entangled in anxieties, held him fast.

Now he plans to send the Greeks against the right-hand wedge from the mountain’s crest; now to break the left wing; now to meet the enemy face-to-face with opposing fronts; now he devises means of evading the scythed chariots.

[Col. 0504D] Thus, while he turns such things over, the sleepless night drags on; a breast too narrow cannot contain the thousands of anxieties.

An island enclosed by the channel of many-branched Tiber is held sacred by its very site. The world claims it as the capital of empire. There, set beneath the slope of the moon’s aerial course, stands a palace firm upon four-square columns, whose royal mistress is named Victory. It lies open through a thousand doors; resonant it quivers at the touch of trembling stones. Once its hinge is turned, it murmurs through the whole world and whispers at the first thresholds. At the entrance stands watchful Ambition, mother of anxieties,

[Col. 0505A] wakeful through the night. Within, on an ivory throne, sits the goddess, her triumphal laurel-crowned hair governed by her generous, armed hand. Her sisters encircle each side and crown the royal dwelling as her everlasting companions: Glory, singing an immortal song to the lyre’s measure and living through all ages; Majesty, pressing down the ages with wrinkled pride; Reverence, readily winning the people’s obedience; and the goddess who arms laws and guards rights, Justice, not inclining by her office to either side.

Mercy also sits beside them and strengthens the realm: she alone is fittingly compassionate toward the wretched and spares the conquered. Among these stands wealthy Money, barbarous in character, nurse of vice and mother of luxury, taking the first kisses from the rest with a peaceful face.

[Col. 0505B] Concord, forgetful of hatred and the end of war, and Peace, cultivating the fields, and Plenty with full horn sit applauding before her. Ambiguous Favour, the crafty, lisping-mouthed smile of the flatterer, and invented games, each delight the goddess by diverse entertainment; musical instruments sound around her as the Muse fits their rhythms.

When Victory saw Alexander turning over so many anxieties in his heart—he to whom from the cradle she had granted an unbroken succession of triumphs—she feared lest a possible shipwreck of the coming war should overwhelm his sleepless limbs. At once she rises, veiled in a mantle of cloud, and goes to the caverns of rest and the halls of sluggish sleep.

[Col. 0505C] And she says: “Rise, Father, and steal into the Macedonian king while he lies asleep and loosens his mind and body from cares.”

She had spoken. He, scarcely shaking himself free from heavy drowsiness, beat his dripping wings through the air; wherever he carries himself, stars touched by Lethean liquor sleep, forgetting their customary courses.

Thus, when in drowsy flight he reached the Greek camp and banished the swarm of cares, he settled upon the whole camp of the prince and soaked his very marrowy bones with poppy dew.

So deep sleep, with his body relaxed, overcame the king’s mind, previously burdened by anxiety, and held him long, until, with night’s darkness sunk away, the stars of the Hyperborean Wain grew faint and Lucifer swiftly spurred the fires of heaven.

[Col. 0505D] And now Titan, bringing the presages of deadly light, had appeared, wan amid Nabataean waters. At the rising of day the Pelasgian nobles assemble before the king, amazed to find him lying in his chamber contrary to his customary practice. At other times he used to rouse the watchful, spur the sluggish, and hasten the laggards; but now, when the hour of supreme crisis was pressing, when the fatal storm threatened to crush one or the other host, they marvel at the young man free of cares and inert in sleepy torpor. Some fear that he is hiding, concealing his terror in darkness; nor can they bring themselves to believe that he yields to sleep.

[Col. 0506A] None of his bodyguards dares enter or come nearer; none ventures, without his command, to arm his side; no soldier dares go among the troops without his commander. Parmenion, judging that no means should delay the war, decides usefully that the men should attend to themselves and take food; accordingly he proclaims to the tribunes:

Since it was necessary for them now to march out from the opposite side, Parmenion at last approached the king’s bed. Calling him repeatedly, and unable to rouse him by voice, he awakened him with a gentler hand. “Day has risen,” he says. “Now I urge you to put away soft sleep. What such great repose has held you? The Median ranks are already near; the enemy has already brought his formations close; Bellona now rages, but your unarmed army still waits for your command.

[Col. 0506B] Where now is that vigour’s firmness and that strength of spirit which has never sunk defeated? You yourself normally rouse the hearts of sentries sluggish with sleep.”

“Believe me,” says the martial hero, “sleep could not have been admitted to me until my heart, released, had laid down its grievous cares.”

The commander marvels without end that the Macedonian has said his heart is free from care, but does not dare ask the reason. “When,” Alexander says, “the enemy was burning villages, devastating fields, razing cities, and fleeing because he despaired and entrusted himself to fate—then I had just cause for fear, and my mind was burdened with cares and could not receive alternating rest. But now, when Darius is wholly before me, and all his force presents itself to me under arms,

[Col. 0506C] and cannot flee to seek the partings of war, there is nothing for me to fear. But why do I delay? Go, ready yourselves; as is customary, I shall more freely repeat these matters another time.”

He spoke and commands the Pelasgians to arm at the herald’s trumpet. He himself fits armour to his limbs: bronze scale-armour, descending serpentine to the ankles, covers the feet with the sharpness of its biting tooth; a spur is fixed to the sole, to rebuke delay and lend wings to his feet, so that when he attempts in flight to overtake fugitives, if voice or trumpet does not rouse the slow horse, at least his side may feel the sharp goads.

A threefold iron garment, hanging from the crown in linked knots, protects his broad shoulders and lordly breast; it encircles his rounded arms with hooked meshes,

[Col. 0506D] yet spares the eyes, allowing the enemy to be seen. That the nobler part of the human body may lie safer beneath double protection, a bronze helmet is fitted to his head, fiery with blazing crests.

At his side is placed the dreadful destroyer, the sword that will make streams of blood, by which the spirits await the dead to fill the vacant halls of black Jupiter.

Bucephalus is summoned. When the king has mounted him with a swift leap and tamed the fierce creature—he who tames the fierce world—his left hand joins in happy alliance with the shield, yet so that it is united in equal affection with the reins.

[Col. 0507A] In his right is an ash spear, whose point gleams with a blazing banner and strikes the stars with its lion. Never, in the first hard crisis of war, had his men seen him more eager. When their great leader came among them, sound hope revived the sickened host, and victory seemed to sit upon his face.

He himself assigns the army to its divisions and deploys the battle-line in proper order. He commands them to receive Darius’s scythed chariots—the sole hope of triumph—in loose ranks and open formation; to avoid them, but not allow their drivers and horses to roam unpunished, rather entangling them with missiles.

While he advises and fortifies his men, while he strengthens their hearts by words, a Mede who had deserted from the Medes crosses to the Macedonian king and reports the iron instruments concealed in the earth by secret contrivance.

[Col. 0507B] They are called “murices” [spikes]: by them Darius hopes, even if he cannot conquer the enemy by force, to hold them in tenacious hooks and swallow the Greeks in hidden ruin. As soon as Alexander hears this, lest the Mede be speaking falsely or tricking his men by his account, he commands that he be kept under guard. Yet he himself has the place marked and shown to his own troops, where the Babylonian king, relying on Ulyssean craft, had planted hooks in the ground.

Lest their lofty courage succumb to the trick once it had been exposed, he orders the suspect place to be shown to everyone and, once shown, avoided. Then, going before the advancing line and rousing them to battle by eloquent word and gesture:

“Comrades, the last labour is in your hands. What glory, what honour have the war witnessed by the Granicus and victory in the narrow Cilician pass,

[Col. 0507C] unless God and fortune crown the final triumph with a happy ending?

“But Fortune is a goddess, and she, standing ever by Alexander according to his powers, delights as much that sceptres should be held under me as that other mighty men should reign under me. When Greece saw me holding the Macedonians’ reins, she has henceforth advanced my cause; men may wish, and may be permitted to wish, to harm mine, but they will not be permitted to dare it.

“This most populous host contributes nothing except the number of the danger. Yet Fortune strives for this—that I may be ashamed to number such scanty triumphs so often—that she may bring me the world to conquer once and all at once.

[Col. 0508A] The more a victory is gained by few against many, the more valuable it will be to us. Go against the unwarlike ranks with the sword as your leader. Do you see how shields glittering with gems and gold obscure the sun, how the splendour of jewels occupies blazing crests, how purple clothes the fields? Who would not wish to conquer when men come to war so? Who, unless bereft of mind, would reject gold offered to him?

“The amassed wealth of the East and the produce of Arabia lie ready to be seized, if the sword obeys the mind, if the sword’s desired blow answers the heart, if your spirit is as fond of slaughter and thirsty for blood as it is thirsty for gold. Whatever you see is yours. I claim none of it for myself: only win for me; divide the spoil among yourselves. You who decide to conquer with me have me as your partner in glory; take all the rest for yourselves.

[Col. 0508B] Have Alexander as an example of courage and model of conducting war. Unless the king himself appears first in the foremost rank, unless he turns his back to the enemy, you will be excused, and he who flees will deserve pardon, if I act slowly; but if I undertake nothing with energy, if I never say to the brave man, ‘Go before; go—but come into battle commanded to lead,’ then only am I worthy to have comrades who follow me. Let whoever rules move the brave by example and display proofs of valour.”

So he speaks, and behold the battle-lines clash. So great a shout rises to heaven, and such the people’s din, as if the discordant fabric of the world, falling back through renewed conflict into its ancient chaos, should collapse with the structure of things dissolved, and the shaken elements give out a dreadful crash.
