## Argument of Book V

[Col. 0507]

The fifth book contains diverse slaughter and deaths lamented by those dear to the fallen; the Persians are defeated at Arbela. Arsacides, considering the harsh situation, takes counsel whether, with strength restored, he should again engage fate in the broad realms of the Medes. But the nobles hesitate. Aeacides summons the companies for largesses and heals wounds with gifts. Behold Mazaeus, a distinguished man and not inglorious in the preceding battle, surrounded by his manly sons, brings the king within Babylon’s walls.

## Book V

[Col. 0507]

[Col. 0507D] By the law of King Numa, long ago established concerning the months, the fifth month, descending from double-faced Janus in the sequence, was distinguishing the year by rosy divisions.

[Vers. 2290–2292] The Ledaean brothers rejoiced in double applause at Phoebus as guest. At the first part of day the leaders joined battle; Daniel is believed to have foreseen, after the allotted time had passed, the destruction to come upon the Medes and Persians and to have committed it to hidden writing.

[Col. 0509A] From the cold north came the Hyrcanian, divine vengeance, Philip’s offspring, Alexander the Great. When the Indian Aristomenes saw him from afar, glittering in a flaming helmet, he lavishly drove an elephant with ten lashes and plunged a steel-tipped, treated spear into Alexander’s shield; but the blunted blow is stopped by the corselet protecting his body.

Alexander confronts the monster with a reed-shaft; where the trunk joins its side, he opens its vital recesses with the intervening steel. A tremendous crash follows as the monster falls; but when the beast has fallen in its headlong plunge,

[Col. 0509B] the vengeful sword, sparing not Aristomenes, makes him headless.

“The victory is ours, ours!” the Greeks repeat. The Persians crowd together as one, and a dense rain of missiles flies about the king. But neither javelins nor the fiercer double-axe move him; unbroken valour, under Fortune’s leadership, protects him. Invincible and tireless, he flies through interposed swords and bursts through missiles, ignorant of retreat.

Like an iron hammer crushing armoured limbs, he strikes down Elephaz, born of Pharaoh, and Pharos, son of Orchanes—Elephaz by sword, Pharos by spear; the one mounted, the other on foot; one Egyptian, the other Syrian.

The earth, previously dry and sterile for long, moistens with the stream of poured blood; now a flood of gore inundates the earth’s veins. An innumerable force of Persians and Macedonians falls in turn. Henos and Caman lie slain by Philotas’s sword: Henos because he had cut down Euryphilus with his sword, Caman because he had struck Laomedon with an axe.

[Col. 0509C] Geon, dweller by the Red Sea, was going to inflict a fatal wound upon Alexander, if Fortune had allowed it: ugly of face, he is believed to have been born of a giant mother and an Ethiopian husband, drawing his origin from giant brothers. Resembling his mother in immense body and his father in black colour, he terrifies with his physique those whom he cannot frighten by blackness.

He had therefore struck down fifteen men with a three-knotted club while, breaking the Greek ranks in a winding whirl, he forced a path toward Alexander—as the Nemean boar scatters dogs with sharp tusk, foam sweating from open jaws, bristles rigid upon his back like a threatening sharp fence, towering above all the dogs at the shoulder; now he strikes these on the left, now blasts those on the right, now twists his head toward his haunches, then from them to the opposite side, guarding either flank, not ignorant how to defend himself in swift rotation.

He had reached the king. The martial hero marvels at the sight of the man’s bulk; and while the giant raises his bloody club high,

[Col. 0510A] he thunders to the king in a shouting throat: “Ho! Great one, what madness has driven you against a giant enemy—one whom you read to have aspired to Jupiter’s starry citadels, and from whom Saturn’s son scarcely remained safe at last in his heavenly fortress by means of thunderbolt?”

He had not yet finished when Alexander’s pine spear, hurled by his nimble arm, stood in the middle of the speaker’s mouth, pinning his tongue in his throat so that he might blaspheme the gods no further. Yet the giant still stood, clutching the bloodied weapon; then at last the Macedonian, admitted by his horse’s breast’s impetus, strikes and sends the creature sprawling over the ground. Mother Earth mourns her fallen offspring and, struck, gives a crash as great as when Boreas’s violence uproots from the mountains an ancient oak still proud in its root.

[Col. 0510B] The Argive phalanx rushes together and pierces fallen Geon with javelins, plunging swords into his entrails. At last, mangled in face and chest by a thousand wounds, they send him back to Acheron’s caverns.

In another quarter the famous Cleitus tramples the Persian army. His sister had nursed Alexander at her own breast, but what recompense came to him for his merits is, I think, better left unspoken.

When Sanga of Damascus saw Cleitus spattered with his brother’s blood, stirred by fraternal love, he groaned three times; sighs drawn again from deep in his breast return a confused voice. Unable to satisfy his heart’s passion with three javelins, he drew his flashing sword,

[Col. 0510C] leapt from his chariot, and struck a bright blow at Cleitus’s head, where his helmet burned with blazing carbuncle. Had Cleitus’s head not been safely hidden beneath the helmet’s protection, the pierced casque would have made his brain lament.

But although Sanga was stunned and bleeding, Cleitus, not unaware, answers with his sword and plunges into the other’s heart the steel which had just passed through the wounds of the first brother.

Their father Metha froze at the first sight of his sons’ slaughter and could find no tears to shed: grief within had swallowed the tears that arose, and the rain due to his withered face watered the dry recesses of his heart; his lamenting breast supplied the office of his eyes.

[Col. 0510D] Lifeless, the old man turned pale, his right hand weak, his heart frozen; death seemed to sit upon his face. But when his mind returned at last, with his blood revived, a sob interrupted his midst of lamentations:

“Then, most savage tormentor, you have devoured two brothers by the sword before their father’s eyes? You did not fear to precipitate the days of an aged father and wretched parent? But lest any crime remain open to you, join the father to his sons with the same sword, fierce tiger, with which you tore my children’s entrails before my eyes, and send back three corpses,

[Col. 0511A] of husband and brothers, for a mother bereft, to mourn. Yet if you have any wife, any son and heir, or sister or mother, may they, by the avenging thread of the Fates, grieve what I grieve and mourn what I mourn.”

He spoke, and, hurling a missile with his feeble right hand, he sent it at Cleitus’s face. Cleitus scarcely stopped it upon his shield, swiftly tore it away, and where the sacred woodland-like grey hair, curling back in shaggy locks, fell upon his shoulders, pierced the old man’s throat with deadly steel.

He fell headlong—a pitiable sight—among his half-dead sons. Embracing both offspring, he goes toward the infernal city accompanied by his children.

Now Darius’s line itself, marked out by royal splendour, had drawn near; the king shone from his lofty chariot, his royal rank betrayed by the countless brilliance of jewels.

[Col. 0511B] Nicanor was stunned by so great a blaze. Since he was commander of the force on the right wing, he turned his battle wedge there, entrusted to his command by lot. At first Fortune smiled craftily upon Parmenion’s son’s undertaking and gently received him as he rushed forward. The wave of retainers scarcely withstood the first encounter and only weakly sustained Nicanor’s steadfast wing, until Rhemnon the Arabian chief, raging, rushed into their midst, covered by a storm of Romans, steadied the fugitives, and restored their dispirited minds.

They stand firm and plant their feet unmoving. At a distance they fall beneath javelins and the sling’s whirling; at close quarters infantry fight with sword and axe thirsty for brain, sometimes with bruising club and bloodied spits. The dwellings of greedy Pluto and the insatiable house of his shadowy cavern are filled;

[Col. 0511C] one of the sisters is insufficient to break the threads by hand. Clotho and Lachesis, their distaff cast aside, reap the fates of men; the two sisters assist the one.

Commanders perish mixed with the common crowd on either side. But amid so many thousands of nobles, Nicanor, distinguished by especial glory and illustrious for much slaughter, shines out. Through all the Persians opposing him he tracks Rhemnon, believing nothing accomplished by the slaughter of so many thousands while he sees the commander himself, lord of the cohort, still alive.

Without delay, as the crowd of his men gives way, the two conspicuous warriors meet. A terrible crash strikes the heavens, and the people’s din shakes the fields; the iron-shod hoof of the horses, pressed together, crushes the loose clods.

[Col. 0511D] They engage at close range. Each, with spear held out, recognized the gods as favourable in the blow. Though the riders were cruelly struck by the maple-wood shaft, they remained mounted; then each bronze hand turns toward the nearby hilt. Blood bursts from a broken helmet and drenches the field; no shield withstands the sword’s rage. Horses and riders fall together, their knees collapsing.

[Col. 0512A] Parmenides first rises with drawn sword and fiercely pins Rhemnon’s breast with both knees, until his sword, up to the hilt, enters the Parthian’s vital parts and entrails.

At once the alarmed Arabs, abandoning the fight, prepare to turn their backs. But a Hyrcanian-born division of Romans, conspicuous in battle and exceeding their number, comes up; having formed a station, they surround Nicanor, enclosed by a wall of clanging weapons.

He is overwhelmed at first by javelins; his bronze helmet rings with leaden bullets and stones, and, torn as he is, he marvels that a forest should grow upon him with veteran strength. His feet and arms already falter; sweat mingled with blood washes his limbs. Yet his mind, unbroken valour, and commanding spirit rule beneath his battered body.

[Col. 0512B] Assailed by so many javelins and blows, that wall of Alexander nevertheless at last falls—not without distinction—and by the ruin of one man draws with him a destructive mass and great slaughter of Persians.

Just as when a tower falls in Romulus’s city, it buries neighbouring houses beneath a thunderous crash.

Meanwhile Alexander, violently stirred by the bitter lament of the Macedonians, flies in more savage than a bear bereft of cubs—the Macedonian a flood of the world. The crowd before him fears the prince’s coming; they flee headlong through trackless places, taught to prefer life to triumph.

One man alone presses Alexander as all others flee: Sthenelus, son of Memnon, whose too-rival beauty, in first down, marked his rosy cheeks. He was noble, recalling Cyrus through his father’s blood;

[Col. 0512C] Darius’s sister was to marry him if the glory of war yielded to him. From this pride arose, and he prepares to confront Alexander. But neither reverence for his forebears, nor the favour of his age, nor abundance of resources shakes off death. Hephaestion meets the young man, equal in form but unequal in fate, with loose reins. Where a golden tiger gleams with fire-breathing jaws, he shatters the shield-boss; through a wide opening in the loosened iron garment, the deadly shaft enters the hidden recesses of his breast and passes into his shoulders through the sloping snowy neck. Sthenelus is borne away covered in the darkness of perpetual night, and his eyes are closed in eternal sleep.

[Col. 0512D] But on the left wing, which Parmenion, second to none in war, commanded, discordant Bellona raged, stained with bloody gore and her hair smeared with fresh corruption. Her brother comes rushing with deadly whirl, his foaming eyes like thunder and lightning in the hurled chariot.

Fury itself clears paths for him; cowardly spirits yield before his rage. Anger, the inseparable companion of fury, carries his headlong steps, rolling eyes of gall;

[Col. 0513A] impatient of delay, light-minded and a bad manager of everything, he drives his chariot in slanting courses through the dust. Successes and disasters alike fly confusedly about him, and from Mars’s summit a thousand deaths, each with its pallor, waver through the air.

Such was he as he came to embrace his sister round the neck.

Apparatus (source notes; readings retained with concise English glosses): [Col. 0501] “Archifaber,” a variant spelling of Arcifaber, “Master-Craftsman”; “speculatius,” “more observantly/in greater detail,” for specialibus; agris, “fields,” for arvis; et tamen, “and yet,” for attamen; pretioso, “precious,” for praeciso; pharizaeat, an uncertain reading, for perdurat; Et populi, et regum, “both of the people and of the kings,” for Cum populo regum; Aeolice, “in Aeolic fashion,” for idola; terris, “lands,” for terra; septuaginta, “seventy,” qualifying the weeks; contemptum, “despised,” for contentum; bellis, “wars,” for bellorum; armat, “arms,” for onerat; impulsu facili per …, “by the easy impulse through [lacuna],” for the wind passage.

[Col. 0503] moderantia, “moderation,” for moderatio; epulatur, “feasts,” for epulatus; adest, “is present,” for habet; occurrunt, “confront,” for Occurrent; obscurare, “darken,” for Offuscare; famam, “reputation,” for palmam; nobis, “us,” for vobis; Quod, “what,” for Quae; elidere, “crush,” for eludere; causarum, “causes,” for curarum (also at the entrance of Victory’s palace).

[Col. 0505] mordente, “biting,” for moderante; estque, “and is,” for est; Vibravit, “beat/flapped,” for libravit; stratis, “the prostrate,” for totus; dormire, “to sleep,” and jacentem, “lying,” for vacantem; tribunis, “to the tribunes,” for tribunus; in armis, “under arms,” for inermis; Jussit et, “and he ordered,” for Imperat; ad, “to,” for in; latos, “broad,” for laeves; Et, “and,” for Quae.

[Col. 0507] a, “from,” for in; Disponensque, “and arranging,” for Disponens; Transvolat, “flies across,” for Transmeat; mandasse, “had ordered,” for mandata; ut si, “as if,” for etsi; semel, “once,” for simul; praecipit, “orders,” for imperat; habent, “have,” for habet; se, “himself,” for me; et, “and,” for sed; coruscum, “glittering,” for corusci; rapere, “seize,” for capere; curas, “cares,” for certas; habe, “have,” for habes; qui, “who,” for si; agit, “acts,” for agam; moneat, “urge,” for moveat; Arsamides, a variant form of Arsacides; committere, “join/engage,” for concurrere.

[Col. 0509] siccis, “dry,” for gelidis; immisit, “sent/aimed,” for Immersit; tela, “weapons,” for gesa; prorumpens, “bursting forth,” for perrumpens; ense, “by sword,” for hasta; imbuit unda cruoris, “a wave of blood drenches,” for the transmitted wording; aliumque, “and another,” for nigroque; affigens, “fastening/pinning,” for astringens; Parthorum, “of the Parthians,” for Persarum; reprimunt, “check/suppress,” for repetunt; Mecha, a variant form of Metha; ubi, “when,” for Mox ut.

[Col. 0511] recurvis, “curving back,” for retortis; perfodit, “pierces through,” for pertundit; propinquabat, “was drawing near,” for propinquarat; furentem, “raging,” for ruentem; Arabarches, “Arabian chief,” for Arabites; sedesque, “and the seats,” for sedes; auri, “of gold,” for antri; enituit, “shone forth,” for emicuit; adversos, “opposing,” for objectos; ensifer, “sword-bearing,” for horrifer; subactas, “subdued,” for coactis; vicinantur, “come close,” for congrediuntur; profluidus, “flowing forth,” for Erumpens; retento, “held back,” for retecto; morte, “death,” for Marte; veterano, “veteran,” for veterato; lavit, “washed,” for lavat; regnant, “rule,” for regnat; Occubuit, “fell/died,” for Procubuit; Romana, “Roman,” for Romulea; truculentior, “more savage,” for violentior; area, “open space,” for aurea; in cornu, “on the wing,” for laevo cornu; jubis, “manes,” for fibris; cruento, “blood-stained,” for citato; Consternit, “throws into panic,” for Cui sternit.

The note “Ille responderit ms. Vict. 13. ille responderet” is not present in this supplied source and is therefore not supplied here.

The dreadful God spread wide his arms: “Quickly,” he said,

“Glide away, dear sister, and go, announce to the king of the Macedonians:

‘Are you being carried away by vain hope? Unwittingly, do you seek to destroy Darius—or, in the variant, the king—through yourself? May the gods remove this crime from so great a prince; nor is it right that the hand holding the sceptres of the world should be stained with the blood of an aged throat.

“Another fortune is owed to Darius: he will fall through the treachery of his own men. Therefore hasten through arms and enemies; meet Mazaeus at once, for he is ravaging the Greeks with varied slaughter. He hungers after plunder and Macedonian spoils; he loosens the Persians from their shackles and, with the roles reversed, consigns the Argives to chains. Parmenio, with a few companies, is no longer sufficient to attack so many thousands.’”

He spoke; and Bellona, swifter than the shadow-bearing South Wind, hastened away. She crossed toward the right wing, whirring, and assumed the cheeks and dreadful face of Pallas, presenting the serpent-haired countenance of the Gorgon upon her aegis—or, in the variant, her weapons. Recalling the god’s commands briefly, she departed, darkening the day as she withdrew in a deadly cloud.

The Macedonian sprang up and pursued the fleeing goddess with his voice:

“Wherever you come from, goddess, from whatever quarter, we scorn the vain omen,” he said. “Nor shall it tear me away from arms and from Darius’ chariot, even if the winged son of Atlas himself, sent from on high as a truthful messenger, should bring me word that my sisters, seized from the Persians, had been carried off with my mother. My single hope rests upon Darius. If I lose him, everything else is of little account to me, and what has been lost is of little consequence. If I alone conquer him, he alone will restore what was lost. What can be recovered is not such a great loss that I should not prefer also to conquer.

“Nor, if a sevenfold wall enclosed Darius in a tower, though Acheron, flowing around it in burning waters, defended the walls with sulphurous banks, would Fortune snatch him from me.”

Having spoken thus, he took his place in arms and, with his raised arm striking the shield’s star-bearing circle, set it before his breast like a wall and rampart. Raising his head and thrusting his spear toward the stars, he rushed into the midst of the enemy. Hurling flaming missiles—or, in the variant, smoking missiles—he made the dust proclaim that Alexander was present.

The African Aristides was borne along with the pole of his chariot raised; Pelias was crushed beneath horses’ hooves and died. The African had come from the Libyan Syrtes; Pelias, a tetrarch, from the Scythian frosts. Here Craterus struck down the African; Amyntas, Pelias. Pelias lies by the sword; the African fell by the spear.

Amilon joined them, his throat pierced and breathing out his crimson life; Antigonus added Baradas to the fallen, while Ptolemy held back the mass of Persian cavalry. Eumenes’ slaughter was no less, nor was Coenus’ glory inferior, Meleager; Perdiccas pressed on more savagely than usual.

With all looking on, Polypercon, directly before Darius’ battle line—the man who had earlier maintained that the night should be used—openly withdrew in daylight the counsel he had given for the night. The Attic youth raged with a new spirit and equal resolve. The same fury possessed everyone, and all had equal courage in war, each resembling his lord himself. Had great Alexander observed his companions face to face, raging in battle, he would have rejoiced that he possessed so many Alexanders.

Already the victor’s tumult struck Darius’ ears; already the whirlwind of the deadly storm was bursting upon his closest companions.

The spirit of the wise man is troubled by adversity and scarcely counsels itself when, in difficult circumstances, it loses confidence in its first resources and defenceless hope grows faint. For what should Darius do? By what plan should the distracted man direct himself? Flight was not safe; nor, if he wished to remain, would he find allies. Of the many thousands whom he had formerly trusted, scarcely a thousand remained in the war to stand for their country. Shame and regard for reputation prevented them from fleeing; anxious fear, on the other hand, drove them toward flight.

While he stood stunned and wavering in his troubled heart, hesitating whether to flee or, weary of life, to let himself be captured, the Persians formed into a column, turned their backs to flight, and hurried across the fields, abandoning their king. At last Darius, unwillingly loosening the reins and mounting a horse, fled backward over the fields wet with the slaughter of his men.

“Where are you fleeing, doomed king? Toward what place are you directing this helpless flight? Alas, ruined man, do you not know whom you flee? As you flee the enemy, you rush upon enemies; seeking to avoid Charybdis, you fall into Scylla. Bessus and Narbazanes—Curtius gives *Nabarzanes*—a great part of your power, whom you had raised from humble birth into the ranks of your nobles, did not fear to violate their loyalty and destroy the grey hair of their revered ruler. Casting aside the restraint of law—shame upon it!—the lord’s retainers conspire against their master’s fate.”

When Alexander learned that Darius had been snatched from the very threshold of death, he rushed blood-stained over the bones of kings and, leaping greatly over the very corpses, pursued the fugitive, almost unattended by the Greeks, forgetful of himself—as the force of a star’s fire carries off flames and marks the clouds with bright—or, in the variant, rare—fires.

But the son of Belus, with a few companions, had already crossed the Lycus in a headlong leap over rocks and trackless ground. Uncertain whether he should hasten to break the bridge spread across the raging water, thereby closing the way to the man of Pella, he feared that, if the bridge were cut, he would expose his own men to dreadful slaughter by the enemy pressing upon them. The honourable consideration prevailed over the useful plan: Darius preferred his men to himself. He chose to undertake a just flight and to offer the victor an open road rather than close it against the defeated.

The Persians fled, running everywhere toward the bridge in confused disorder. Intolerable heat and thirst, doubled by running, consumed their weakening entrails; sweat claimed their exhausted limbs, and sighs agitated the wandering chambers of their lungs.

Deprived of water, they were led through the trackless parts of the woods and sought hidden springs, leaping wherever they found veins of concealed water. They crowded upon every stream; having greedily swallowed the muddy torrent, their inward organs, stretched by mud, grew rigid, and their belly, forced to imitate a pregnant womb, produced a miserable death by conceiving the river.

For some, while they gulped the river with thirsty throats, the onrushing water blocked the passages of life and cut off the breath enclosed within its dark caverns.

Yet the narrowness of one bridge could not accommodate so many ranks of nobles and common soldiers, rushing without order toward death under the leadership of fear. The swollen water scarcely held the heaps of falling men, and the river’s whirlpool swallowed them. They slipped everywhere; the river’s gulf engulfed those who had fallen, and the green Nymphs stared in astonishment at the corpses.

When the Macedonian looked upon their languid swords—or, in the variant, their languid spirits—and the weapons bearing the marks of their masters, while sloping Olympus was being traversed by Phoebus’ horses above the smoking fields of the Ethiopians, and the sun’s neighbourhood was burning the Herculean Gades with its customary fire, though somewhat more mildly, he used the approaching night as an excuse and turned his way toward those whom he believed still stood on the left wing.

He had already turned his arms toward the left when a horseman sent ahead by Parmenio announced the triumph and the enemies afflicted by varied slaughter. While the cavalry were being led back to camp, a Persian force suddenly appeared emerging from the valleys, setting the fields ablaze with shields and glittering helmets. At first they checked their advance and fixed their steps; but when they saw so few Macedonians, they turned their bloodstained battle line against Alexander the Great.

The king advanced before the Roman standards in his usual manner, concealing rather than despising the dangers of war. Against the Persians he opposed the unconquerable fortress of his breast, which the enemy had so often shaken. Nor did his enduring Fortune fail him in doubtful circumstances: he received the commander of the troop, raging with a love of death and war, and searched his entrails with swift steel.

Then Lysimachus and the glory of the Achaean race attacked the Arabs everywhere; that martial fury spared neither side, where no one fell unavenged.

But when the star of Atlas’ daughter already dared to set its face against Phoebus’ rays, the Persians judged flight safer than battle. Their ranks broken, they resolved upon flight and, freely loosening their reins, crossed the river about midnight—having crossed it, or, in the variant, having been carried across—and reached Arbela.

There the Babylonian king, grieving and distraught, conferred with those whom flight had brought with him and deliberated with them alike upon the difficult crisis. Having restrained the sighs of his complaining heart, he looked with tearful eyes upon the remnants of the Macedonians:

“To endure now adversity, now to exult in prosperity; now to bow one’s head beneath evils, now to raise it again—this is the condition of human fortune. Thus Lydia saw Croesus humbled; thus, yes thus, in changed fortune, a woman defeated a conqueror. Thus Thermopylae also saw Xerxes lying low; and he who had just covered the whole sea with a ship—or, in the variant, ships—was scarcely permitted to return defeated with a single vessel.

“No novelty of circumstances should overthrow brave hearts, since Fortune is bound by no law to remain faithful to a man for long. The one hope of the defeated is to hope again for triumph against the conqueror.

“Nor do I doubt that the victor will enter fields and cities drained of their citizens, but filled with rich possessions and gold. There, where a most greedy people, with its whole heart—or, in the variant, its whole throat—and with dry entrails, thirsts for the deadly metal, he will try to quench his thirst and satisfy the hunger conceived from fresh booty. I think this will not be useless to us.

“Meanwhile, as he seeks the borders and untouched kingdoms of the Medes, I shall readily restore my strength. Powerful men have learned through long experience how burdensome are precious furnishings, camps filled with eunuchs, and many concubines, and how greatly they impede those waging war. The Macedonian, formerly greater when these things had been removed, will be defeated when burdened with spoils—he who conquered while unencumbered.

“Wars are not waged with gold but with iron; neither bronze nor cities protect kingdoms, but the courage and strength of men. Let us penetrate to the very borders of the Medes. In difficult circumstances, opportunity itself teaches us to pursue what is useful, not what is splendid merely in speech.

“Thus we know that our ancient fathers, tested by the utmost crisis of affairs, granted several days to both enemy and themselves, restored their fortune, and afterward carried triumph from the opposing side over their defeated enemies.”

Darius had finished. His voice, full of fear—or, in the variant, grief—and without hope, had seemed so to his followers, while Alexander was about to destroy first in the East proud Babylon, rich in such great wealth, and the other cities left without a defender.

No opportunity for restoring their fortune seemed to exist, nor even, as a last resort, any means of preserving the kingdom. Nevertheless, whether they had strengthened their battle line or were following authority rather than the commander’s counsel, they hastened with one mind to visit the borders of the Medes.

Without delay, the generous Macedonian distributed the celebrated treasures at Arbela. His soldiers, eagerly burdened with such riches and satisfied with the booty they had found, crossed Syria—or, in the variant, Assyria—more swiftly than the rainy South Wind. Having overcome its inhabitants by force or friendship, he burned to enter the palaces enclosed by walls of baked brick, the city once renowned in the praises of so many kings.

The confusion of tongues gave it its everlasting name. And since Semiramis was as far from the city as Dionysius is from the waters of the Sequana, behold, the illustrious Mazaeus, attended by his blessed children, eagerly met the king as a deserter. He surrendered himself and Babylon to the authority of Alexander the Great. The king embraced him eagerly and received him with a kindly expression, silently stifling the joy of his hopes.

For it would have required great labour and long preparation to capture by siege a city fortified by so many peoples and towers, unless a machine, through the power of the gods, could shatter its baked masonry by repeated blows, and unless a man skilled—or ready—with his hands, distinguished in the preceding battle and repeatedly tested in war, could invite others to a treaty of peace by his own example.

Then, with his cohorts carefully—or, in the variant, closely—arranged and the Persians ordered to follow and withdraw, he entered the astonished city in a square formation.

Babylon shines to meet so great a king. The treasures gathered by the ingenuity of ancient kings are displayed; the altars blaze with gems; ancestral statues are uncovered in sacred porticoes. Through forums, streets, and crossroads, silk garments gleam, and temples blaze with crowns of gold. Matrons weighed down by years and grave citizens are scorched by silk coverings worked with engraved figures of monsters.

The slave and the maidservant, ordered to glitter in barbarian luxury, cannot endure their unfamiliar finery. Forgetting themselves while they contemplate their clothing, they already imagine themselves—and confess themselves—not to be slaves.

Those who lacked deceptive wealth he ordered to shine among the honoured in borrowed garments. Already wantonness had scattered flowers over—or, in the variant, covered—the entire path of the victor, and the tree stood green but stripped of its branches.

Wherever he enters, balsams compete with nard—or, in the variant, incense with frankincense. The sacred fires feed upon the divine perfumes of the Arabs, and nostrils are filled with morning spices. The savage tiger, indignant to be confined in an enclosure, is led forth, along with panthers shut in an iron prison. Lions enclosed in cages roar terribly, as does every beast inhabiting the Hyrcanian forests.

And lest the dense crowd obstruct the eyes of those following, many people, carried by steps to the roofs, eagerly desiring to recognize their king, crown the heights of the walls in a long line.

Mimes meet him, singing odes in lyric song with citharas; cymbals agree with sistrums, drums yield to harmonies, and the responsive tortoise-shell lyre did not fail to move—or, in the variant, lull—the human ears.

The Memphis prophets, whom the false tales of the Nile-born people report to be seers and skilled in foreknowing the movements of the stars from the signs of heaven and unavoidable fate, worship the victor’s chariot.

Never did boastful Rome, marvelling at her own conqueror, receive a victor in such rich luxury at so celebrated a triumph: whether when Caesar, after Antony had been defeated beneath Leucas, changed the name of the sixth month and Cleopatra gave her breasts to be suckled by serpents—or, in the variant, her nipples; or when Julius, already sated with the blood of Pompey after the battles of Emathia, burst into the Tarpeian citadel.

And deservedly. For if, recalling the remarkable deeds of kings, you take care to raise them with their rightful praises and titles; if you remember how rarely, with so few soldiers, against the conquerors of the world, in the tender flower of youth, the Macedonian undertook so great an enterprise; if you consider how, in so short a time, the whole world cast itself at Alexander’s knees, then the entire succession of commanders—whether those whom Spanish poetry has celebrated in grandiloquent style or those whom Claudius has distinguished in lofty verse—will be mere commoners in comparison with this prince.

One may regret that Lucan sang the Caesarean melody and Rome’s ruin in so great a light; and glorious Honorius will yield to Macedonian arms.

If divine mercy, moved by pious groaning and the tearful prayers of his people, granted the Franks such a king, true faith would without delay shine throughout the whole world. Parthia, broken beneath our arms, would voluntarily seek renewal through baptism. Carthage, long lying fallen with her walls thrown down, would rise again at the name of Christ; and Spain, which under Charles deserved to pay its penalties, would raise the banners of the Cross. Every nation and every tongue would sing God’s praise and willingly enter the sacred font beneath the sacred bishop of Rheims.

## Argument of Book Six

The sixth book shows Alexander corrupted by the luxury and gold of Babylon. He distributes military rewards according to fixed numerical categories—or, in the variant, gifts. With armed soldiers he enters the land of the Uxians. Sisigambis frees the city and Medates—or, in Curtius, Madathes—through her entreaties. Renowned Persepolis, razed, smokes; the transmitted readings *inclyta* (“renowned”) and *eruta* (“razed”) are interchanged in the variant. The meeting with the wretched moves the troubled king. Darius prepares to undertake the hazards of war again. Here a mutiny separates the parricides from Darius, but their innate rivalry restores them after they have been received and caresses—or, in the variant, appeases—their credulous hearts. Yet the decrees of the Fates cannot be changed by their patrons.

## Book Six

Behold the world’s plague, the final—or only—terror of kings! Behold the man whom, Babylon, you could so often have read would be Asia’s destroyer, whom the sacred page had foretold as the goat (*Hircus*), who would break the horns of the twin kingdom. Look upon the man now present, and do not despise him because he is enclosed by baked-brick barriers: he whose embrace encompasses the wide world and whose name makes kings tremble.

“He will be your king, the king by whom every land would seek to be ruled, if his power endured in the character of virtues in which it began. See how gently he governs the conquered with yielding reins; see how merciful the conqueror is amid so much prosperity. See how mildly he dictates law to nations: those whom he had as enemies in war, he recognizes as citizens in the city, and those whom he conquered in war he conquers by love.

“Yet the wealth of Babylon and the luxurious idleness of its people broke the adornments of spirit that schooling had impressed upon him from tender youth: the principles for shaping life, the work of inborn virtue, and his customary severity. For nothing is more corrupt than the morals of that city, and nothing is more richly equipped for Venus’ purchasable vice. When hearts have grown warm with much unmixed wine, provided only that the price of such bitter crime be offered, parents compel not merely wives but their own offspring to prostitute themselves to guests. At night they witness the solemn banquets and games that tyrants customarily celebrate according to ancestral practice.”

Amid Babylon’s luxuries and leisure, thirty-four days held Alexander the Great. The army destined to conquer the world would have been weaker had it sluggishly rushed against an unbridled enemy after the banquets of an idle table.

Therefore, after the warrior hero had departed from the territory of Semiramis and stood in the satrapal fields, judging that certain instructions handed down by his fathers from earlier military discipline ought to be changed, he reduced military rewards to carefully calculated numerical categories. He established commanders—*chiliarchs*—for each thousand of his Roman soldiers, so that the courage of the cavalry might be tested beyond doubt by judges, honour worthy of the approved might be displayed, no one who had served lukewarmly might falsely claim rewards, wickedness might not shine beneath the cloak of virtue, and a brave man who had performed brave deeds might not lose his title because his reward was withheld.

Among the ancient Macedonians and under his father Philip there had hitherto been this custom: when they ordered the standards to be raised, the trumpet summoned the camp, but amid obstructing tumult and the sound of weapons it did not reach everyone. A provision was therefore made that, when the Parthian standards were to move, smoke should serve as the signal by day and fire by night.

And lest anyone dare to usurp another man’s service or brave deeds, or attribute them to his own strength, he ordered each man to be content with the rank in which he was rewarded and with his own achievements. He exhorted, attracted, and constrained the brave, the mercenaries, and the citizens by entreaty, gift, and written order.

We read that the Roman kings, after the world had been subdued, imposed laws and judicial causes upon peoples, when almighty God—or, in the variant, Theodosius—kept the avenging Furies from the earth. But it was a greater thing to bind armed men by laws than to establish laws for the conquered, and greater that armed men should accept strict decrees in war than agree upon law in peace.

When these measures had been promptly considered, everyone accepted them gladly. As the citizens surrendered Susa and the soldiers had been cheered with many treasures, he turned his active column toward the Uxian heights.

Medates, prefect and chief authority of the Uxian region, was truly a brave man and a great example of loyalty. For that loyalty he was not afraid to endure the utmost, and he preserved—or, in the variant, had preserved—his friendship with Darius.

Having learned from the natives that there was a hidden and covered route, unknown to the citizens, which led the Greeks into the city, the Macedonian placed Tauron, whose merit had been proved, over the selected cavalry who alone were to undertake the danger.

He himself moved around the first beginnings of tender daylight. He crossed the narrow gorges and approaches of the place; timber was cut for the construction of hurdles, and a mantlet rose in a curved tortoise formation against the citadel, so that armed youth, protected by such a defence, might utterly tear down the walls through skill and effort.

But the approach was difficult, since a harsh land threatened with sharp crags and rocks, and the ground could not be cut down. The Macedonian was not contending only with a hard enemy: the place itself had to be fought, a living cliff fortified by its natural position. Nevertheless, under their leader preceding them, the light-armed cohorts climbed the narrow and precipitous routes.

Though he was attacked from above at a distance by a hail of missiles, the man protected by the opposing testudo could not be torn from the barbarian walls either by force or by entreaty.

For, first among the foremost, with his helmeted head he thundered against the walls: now rolling down huge stones, now undermining them with a stake, now breaking the gates with a battering ram, now turning siege engines—the world’s lamentable engines—and urging on his men.

“Shame now—shame indeed!” he said. “Shame upon you, conquerors of Asia, comrades before whom so many cities have yielded, to lie idle before the walls of a tiny fortress! What place, what structure that stands, what rampart will not collapse before Macedonian hands? What walls or citadels can remain standing? What foundations supported by solid columns can endure once the lofty wall has felt that Alexander is present? Though it is equal to Olympus, it will fall, and the towers will learn to submit themselves—or, in the variant, to bend down—to me.”

He spoke, and Tauron appeared on the summit of the citadel. At the sight of him Greek courage increased, while fear and despair seized the citizens. Some resolved in their hearts to suffer the last extremity and lay down their lives for their country; others desired flight, if only it could be free. A very great crowd withdrew into the cloud-bearing citadel.

Without delay, thirty envoys were sent to bend the victor, asking permission for the defeated to depart with their lives safe. A grim answer was brought back from the prince: there was no place for pardon; only brief delays of pain and punishment remained. The citizens, struck and weakened by the torpor of fear, became ready to dread the worst.

Therefore Medates sent prayers by a hidden path through the shadows to Darius’ mother, asking that she soften the prince’s anger and that the unconquered king spare the conquered and their city. He knew that she was honoured by the victor and revered in the dignity of a mother. Medates had married her niece and was related to Darius by blood.

For a long time she refused to comply with his entreaties, although he was asking what was just.

“It does not accord with the fortune that I now endure—or, in the variant, by which I am now afflicted,” she said, “to admit such great presumption. With what face should I, a captive woman, petition the conqueror? He who asks for more than he has earned deservedly suffers refusal. Hope that does not precede merit departs from hope, and presumption gives it its true name. It is fitting that I contemplate rather that I am a captive than remember that I was a queen.

“After so many petitions have been made, I fear that the king’s indulgence may be exhausted, or that his clemency may be unable to endure further fatigue.”

Thus Sisigambis. Yet Medates, struck by grief, wrote to Alexander: if he did not wish to spare the conquered, let Medates, now conquered and now confessing that he had sinned, at least enjoy the light of day.

How great Alexander’s moderation, piety, and constancy were is shown by this one fact: he pardoned not Medates alone but everyone. Having first granted freedom, he restored the captured city to its captives; he restored the captured fields to their former cultivators and ordered them to be cultivated free of taxes.

Had fickle Fortune given Darius the city in his hands, the mother would not have obtained more from him than the enemy gave to conquered enemies.

Without delay, after dividing the troops with Parmenio, he ordered him carefully to track Darius and directed him to proceed by the plain road. Alexander himself, retaining three hundred chosen cavalrymen, headed toward the rugged heights whose continuous ridge extends downward toward Persia.

Never had the Macedonian endured more serious dangers. Through experience he learned that Fortune is always changeable, unlike herself, and permanently faithful to no one. Advancing through so many narrow passages, trackless gorges, and winding routes that nowhere admitted human footprints, the man of Pella was overwhelmed by the enemy from above. He was often compelled to retreat—not without paying dearly in the blood of his men. Yet after so many dangers he at last, by concentrated strength, broke the enemy standards. The defeated weapons settled beneath the victorious arms.

Scarcely had the darkness of night been cleared from the sky when the Macedonian, constructing a substantial bridge, crossed the Araxes. He hastened to Persepolis and reduced to ashes the famous city that had belonged to so many ancient kings.

Although he had previously captured so many cities swollen with wealth, the barbarian riches of this one far surpassed the others. The kings had brought there the luxury of all Persia: sacred gold from the inner chambers, an unworked mass of ancient silver, and from the shrines not merely the wealth accumulated for practical use. Greedy antiquity had not amassed so much even to provide material for use, but to draw the wondering gaze of spectators.

They rushed more eagerly to the booty and competed even among the plunderers. A friend was cut down as though he were an enemy when the plunder he had seized or discovered was more precious. The costly furnishings became both the cause and the price of murder. Whatever each man snatched, the wicked man could no longer contain; hence it happened that he valued what he could no longer seize—or, in the variant, occupy.

Purple garments were torn apart; royal clothing, produced by the sweating hands of craftsmen, was ripped to pieces; golden vessels bristling with designs yielded to axes. Greed, satisfied by nothing, left nothing untouched. No statues remained whole, their limbs torn away; mutilated, they possessed more terror and less beauty.

Such was the end of the city that had once flourished under so many royal titles and had once alone given laws to so many peoples: that distinctive and unique terror of Europe, when, with ten thousand ships, it blocked the entire deep with its numerous fleet, daring to let Neptune pass through hills cut open and daring to spread sails upon mountain ridges.

The kings who followed Alexander held the remaining cities of Persia. Nowhere will you find traces of this city, unless the rapacious Araxes displays its walls lying low, a little distance from its marble banks.

Whether one should call the city undeserving or deserving of these disasters is disputed. For as Alexander was about to attack its walls, three thousand Macedonian captives met him—a pitiable sight: bodies of men who had been mutilated, deprived of their ears, with hands and feet cut off, their lips completely severed, or their eyes destroyed, or some other part of their limbs cut away by the Persians. Moreover, a barbarian mark had been impressed—or, in the variant, placed—upon their rough foreheads in letters that preserved their long-standing mockery.

When the king judged that they seemed not human beings but images, tears finally rose in his eyes and warmed him. The victorious army also wept, and victory was suddenly turned into mourning.

The king ordered the wretched men to be brave in spirit. He promised to give them whatever they requested: they would see the pleasant fields of wealthy Europe, their wives and dear relatives, and would sleep upon their native soil.

The pitiable crowd withdrew behind the rampart until an impartial balance might deliberate what it should seek as more important. Some chose to remain in the borders of Asia; for others, native soil was sweeter than a foreign clod.

Eutition—whom the eloquence of his skilled tongue had made famous; Curtius gives *Euctemon*—is believed to have spoken thus:

“We who have only now been brought forth from darkness and the enclosed cavern of prison, that we might seek help: how will you be able to display to your fatherland the ruin of your mutilated body? With what face will you offer it a pleasing spectacle?

“It is indeed uncertain whether one should regret more or be more ashamed to have endured such great hardships. An unhappy condition is borne well when it remains hidden; a bitter condition is borne well if you know how to conceal a wretched life. No place is so familiar to the wretched, no homeland so sweet, as an alien dwelling or house without a witness to their former fortune. Solitary places make the wretched happy when they bring forgetfulness of happier things.

“Those who place everything in hope or love of their own people do not know how quickly the stream of tears grows dry. Tears come lightly and depart lightly; they readily flatter those willing to be moved. Only relatives bestow tears upon the wretched, and when tears dry up, the love and affection of your people—or, in the variant, their people—dry up with them.

“The lot of the wretched is full of complaint; the condition of the fortunate is proud, and there is no compassion in a swollen mind. The man who despises another does not truly love him. True love is that which does not despise an unhappy friend.

“While each man considers another’s fortune, he returns to his own and perhaps examines his own circumstances. He judges others outwardly as he knows himself inwardly. Fortune commonly seeks a similar lot. We might have despised one another and become a mutual reproach, had not our shared fate given all three thousand of us equal misfortunes.

“O tender wives whom we married in the ardour of youth and abandoned when we took up arms: with what solemn expression will you admit these worthless mutilated bodies into the bonds of marriage? Will you wish to share the marriage covenant of the bridal bed? So completely unknown to us is that sex.

“A woman’s heart is more changeable than the spring breeze. The diamond is softer than the woman who is accustomed to be hard toward a fortunate man. Will she be able to look upon an unhappy husband?

“I beseech you, youth long since finished with life: seek dwellings for half-eaten corpses. Let us seek, with a common desire, a place suited to mourners and the outcast; let us hide in unknown lands, among people by whom we wretched men have now begun to be recognized—indeed, among whom the hated corpse has already ceased to be hated.”

Thus far Eutition.

To him Theseus, an Athenian by birth—Curtius gives *Theatetus*—replied:

“No one judges a friend by the condition of his body; no one first weighs the mockeries of harsh Fortune. It was not nature our creator that made us so, but the violence of a contemptible enemy.

“In my judgment, a man deserves every evil if he is ashamed of his circumstances and his own fortune is a disgrace to him. Those who would not wish to pity others if the Fates gave them contrary threads commonly despair that others will pity them in difficult times. A man of cruel disposition wrongly reasons from himself that mercy rarely dwells in the human heart.

“You see that God—or, in the variant, the gods—offers beyond hope and desire wives, fatherland, children, and ancestral hearths. Come! Let us burst from the prison in which we have been shut up, regain the light, the air, and our ancient customs.

“Why should you be wretched here and a slave if your fatherland is granted as you desire—that fatherland in which alone you are destined to be wretched? For exiles and those who have endured Fortune’s final extremity, it is something to be able to return themselves to their native grave. Bones lie more softly when buried by the hands of their own people.

“Let others remain in Persia and breathe Median air, fortunate men whom distrust of their fathers and wives can tear away from their sweet fields. But I am determined to use the king’s gift, to follow Europe and my fatherland, provided the gods grant me the freedom to see my birthplace and its fields.”

Theseus had finished, but he found few participants in this desire. Powerful habit, stronger than nature itself, overcame the hearts of the others.

Agreeing with their decision, Alexander distributed not only rich fields but also, generously, money, various herds, and heaps of fertile grain, so that grain should not fail from the soil, nor money the cultivators; the variants read *nec* for *ne* and *desunt* for *desint*.

When the warrior hero had prudently provided for them, he entered the borders of the Medes with his army restored, following Darius’ tracks in headlong pursuit, lest flight should steal away the greater part of the triumph, the only part that remained. He pressed on more relentlessly than upon panthers—or, in the variant, Parthians.

But the son of Belus had already reached Ecbatana, the first city of the Medes, and had resolved from there to enter the borders of the Bactrians. When rumour announced that Alexander was near, against whose forces and winged steps the long distances between places seemed no distance at all, he changed his mind, changing his heart, and prepared everything for war. He decided that it was more honourable to die fighting than to prolong a life so often defeated by the Fates.

Therefore, looking upon his travelling companions, whom he had ordered to halt briefly, he said:

“If equal Fortune had joined me to men lazy in effort, who considered death honourable whatever its form, I would prefer to remain silent rather than consume time with empty speech.

“But having tested the strength of your courage with greater proof than I wished or than was fitting, I have now learned how venerable is the name of friend and how sincere faith is among sincere friends. Warned by so many events, I ought to presume myself worthy of such great companions. Of all the Persian army that once existed, you alone remain its glory: you who, though defeated, twice followed me in flight and twice followed the arms of your prince.”

[Verse anchors: 2515, Amilon is joined to the slain; 2569, Darius prefers his men to himself; 2622, the fugitives cross the river about midnight; 2677, Alexander overcomes the inhabitants by force or friendship; 2720, the beasts of the Hyrcanian woods; 2762, the sacred font under the bishop of Rheims; 2823, smoke by day and fire by night signal the movement of the standards; 2872, the walls learn that Alexander is present; 2925, Fortune remains faithful to no one; 2979, the king recognizes the mutilated captives; 3032, the captives seek a place for mourners and outcasts; 3086, Darius begins his address to his companions.]

[Omitted apparatus restored. In the preceding battle narrative: *neque/nec* both mean “nor”; *at/et*, “but/and”; *non/nec*, “not/nor”; *verax/verus*, “truthful/true”; *ipse/ipsas*, “himself/themselves”; *Afferat/Nuntiet*, “bring/announce”; *patenter/patenti*, “openly/in open daylight”; *Attica/Inacha*, “Attic/Inachian”; *qualis/qualem*, “such as/which”; *pontem/pacem*, “bridge/peace”; and *Demum/Verum*, “finally/but.”

[In Darius’ speech and the Babylon narrative: *abactos* means “driven away” (for the printed *ipsos*, “very”); *summo/primo*, “utmost/first”; *affectos/afflictos*, “having sought/afflicted”; *fortes/sortis*, “brave men/of fate”; *superatis/superandis*, “having overcome/to be overcome”; *bestia/bellua*, “beast/wild beast”; *transvecti/evecti*, “carried across/carried up”; *ineluctabile/inevitabile*, “inescapable/unavoidable”; and *Memphitae/Memphites*, respectively the Latin nominative and Greek-form designation “Memphite prophets.” The exchanged readings *victorem/excepit* and *Excepit/victorem* mean “the conqueror/received”: they alter the word order, not the sense. The corrupt note *synaer.* after *Antonio* is retained as corrupt and is not an additional name or claim. *quae/quas* are the paired relative forms “which/whom”; *Erigeret/Exigeret* means “would raise/would exact.”]

[In Book Six: *victos/victor*, “the conquered/the conqueror”; *astitit/constitit*, “stood by/came to a halt”; *factum/cautum*, “done/provided”; *usurpasse/usurpare*, “to have usurped/to usurp”; and *arctat/aptat*, “constrains/adapts.” The route “leads *ad/in urbem*,” “to/into the city”; *Ipse/Ille* is “he/him”; *cautibus/cotibus* is “crags/whetstones”; and *discedere/abscedere* is “depart/withdraw.”]

[Medates’ petition has the alternative reading: “that she soften the anger of the *prince*”; alternatively, “of the *king*, and that the unconquered king spare the conquered and the city” (*Principis*; *Regis, et ut victis invictus parcat et urbi*). *Ei deferri/eam venerari* means “that honour be paid to her/to revere her.” The fields are *captos/patrios agros*, “captured/native fields”; the troops are *divisis/diversis catervis*, “divided/different companies”; and Alexander retains *retentis/trecentis* horsemen, “having held back [chosen men]/three hundred.”]

[In the Persepolis and captives episode: *nusquam/nunquam*, “nowhere/never”; *gradus/pedem*, “steps/a foot”; the isolated *in* after *citius* is corrupt and is retained without invented sense; *praedantes/praedones*, “those plundering/plunderers”; *occurrunt/occurrit*, “they meet/he meets”; *docilis celebrem/celebrem docilis* reverses the order of “skilled” and “famous”; *consuescat/sustineat*, “becomes accustomed/endures”; *miseratio/compassio*, “pity/compassion”; *genialia/genialis*, the neuter/plural and adjectival forms concerning the marriage-bed; *nobis/vobis*, “us/you”; and *desinit/desiit*, “ceases/has ceased.”]

[In Theseus’ reply and the pursuit: *aeraque antiquum* is “the air and the ancient [custom]”; the variant *Aeraque et linquam* is corrupt and is retained as such. *Mollius/Molliter* means “more softly/softly”; *usurum/visurum*, “to use/to see”; *facultas* means “capacity or opportunity,” not a separate divine grant; and the crossed sequence *longa/nulla … Nulla/Longa* reads “long/no … no/long,” preserving the exchanged adjectives rather than smoothing them away.]

[Other supplied variants already represented above retain their paired Latin readings and their English associations, including *lyricis* (“lyric”), never “Lydian.”]

Your loyalty—[variant: *true*]—and the steadfastness that proves your firm resolve make me unafraid to entrust myself as king; they make me dare to declare that I still reign over the Persians. You chose rather to remain with the defeated king in his camp than to follow the victor’s standards; in my judgment you are worthy—if it is not permitted me myself—to receive from that ruler of heaven the thanks due you. For no posterity, so ignorant of what is right, so free from the claims of justice, so deaf, shall exist as not to exalt you with fair praises to heaven, not to speak of deeds worthy of remembrance, not to keep silent concerning you and the encomium your merit deserves.

After death, it shall be granted you, though buried, to live through fame. Virtue alone does not know how to die; it knows no eclipse. Therefore, although I have always abhorred the hiding-places of flight, yet, relying on courage of heart and on the counsel of such companions, I would go out to meet the enemy. Darius is an exile within his own kingdom; but how long, citizens, will you endure that a foreigner should rule as king in your ancestral realm?

[Col. 0525C] Either an honourable end of life will befall me, or I shall recover my cities from the afflicted enemy and swiftly restore what we have lost. Do you judge it honourable that I should await the victor’s pleasure, and that, by the precedent of Mazaeus, authority over only one district should be granted to Darius on sufferance? I who lately held the reins of all Asia—shall I be preserved for such disgrace, to be the victor’s glory, admitted into a portion of my own kingdom? It shall not be that anyone ought to strip me of this honour of my head, or, having stripped it away, boast that he has restored it to me. While alive I shall lose my empire; I shall be deprived both of empire and of life; may death, more precious to Darius than life and diadem alike, deprive me of both.

[Col. 0525D] If this is your resolve, comrades, if this is your mind, none shall be compelled after death to endure Macedonian arrogance and accursed pride: each man’s right hand shall decide. Either there will now be an end, or worthy vengeance for our wrongs. Therefore, if the gods are absent from those who undertake righteous wars, if they judge the defence of justice a crime, at least the end will be honourable, and brave men may die in the honourable fashion of death—[variant: *love*]—I entreat you by the deeds of your ancient fathers, by the once precious praises of your forefathers,

[Vers. 3137; Col. 0526A] and by the illustrious men to whom this nation of Macedonians has so often paid tribute and taxes. I beseech you, soldiers, to conceive spirits worthy of so great a lineage, so that, with Olympus as witness, it may be your lot either to be conquered in a glorious battle or to conquer.

Thus spoke the Arsacid. But the cohort did not receive his words with the same spirit; even the applause due to such speech was lacking, that applause which an emboldened crowd is wont to give to those who persuade it. Genuine fear had sealed every mouth, until Artabasus [variant: Curtius, *Artabazus*], foremost among the king’s friends [variant: conspicuous], said: “We shall follow the king unanimously to arms; our end shall be the same as yours and as our country’s.” The rest received the speaker with hesitant [variant: slowly] assent and raised a hoarse uproar.

[Col. 0526B] As, upon the Aegean sea, a sailor in despair—when the storm-wallowing South Wind seems, now that his ship is broken, to have conspired against him—comforts his helpless companions, conceals his fear, strengthens their wavering hearts, and prepares to go across the waves against an unconquered wind, so Bessus, having already premeditated his dreadful crime, and his associate Narbazanes, surrounded [variant: supported] by a numerous soldiery, had resolved to seize Darius alive. If the Great King followed them, they could more readily win the victor’s favour by so great a gift. But if fortune allowed them to escape the swift wings of the prince, they would dare, once Darius was killed, to reign and to restore their strength and provoke a new war.

Narbazanes therefore, having found a time suitable for his crime, said: “King, I know that what I shall say will displease you, and that this counsel of mine will not please your heart. But a very grave wound is cured by bitter steel; harsh is the remedy for one in pain; a stronger potion heals graver diseases. Often a sailor, fearing shipwreck, has redeemed himself by a sacrifice of cargo, and lessened losses by loss, insofar as he could.

[Col. 0526C] You know that you are waging bitter wars beneath an adverse divine power; harsh fortune does not cease to press upon your Persians. Fortune has been tried [variant: must be tried] by every means, and new omens are needed. Lay aside the insignia of kingship for a time, good king; entrust the administration of supreme power to another, one who may possess the kingly name and auspice, until, when the storm of war has ceased and the enemy has been expelled, Asia restores the kingdom to you, its rightful king.

[Col. 0526D] The wait for this act will be brief: Bactra will supply so many, and so will the peoples of India [variant: India will supply], that there will remain a larger force for war, greater strength than was exhausted in the earlier war. Why do we rush to destruction, bleating like sheep? It is the mark of a brave spirit to despise death; yet it is the mark of men not to hate life, but to love it. Degenerates, those whom we know are weary of labour,

[Vers. 3189; Col. 0527A] are driven to consider life worthless—what wonder? For the coward, life is death. On the contrary, strong and lofty virtue leaves nothing untried: it sets all in motion and attempts all things; it reaches toward death only when nothing seems left over; death is the final recourse after every other fate. Therefore come, king: entrust the governance of your kingdom for the present to Bessus, as the favour of the occasion offers, so that in due time he may restore to you the sceptre received [variant: when received].

When this had been said, the gentle and patient ruler scarcely restrained his anger. “Now,” he said, “bloody slave, I perceive that you have found the hour of fatal opportunity in which you intend to perpetrate a dreadful crime against your master and unweave the threads of the Fates.”

[Col. 0527B] He spoke, and, with drawn sword, seemed about to attack him [variant: kill him], had not Bessus, wearing a suppliant expression, seeming indignant, and attended by a great host of his own men, prevailed upon the king; and without delay he would have bound him, had he not sheathed his naked sword. Then the others ordered their own men to pitch camp apart; but Artabasus counselled the king, in his anger, to spare them and grant time to the occasion. “Bear,” he said, “the error or folly of your men calmly. Alexander presses hard and prematurely in arms; the soldier must be held by winning affection, lest discord disturb sound judgment, or the citizens of Bactra estrange themselves from their king.”

The Arsacid assented [variant: obeyed], following the gods and fate, and pitched camp. Grief and despair, inseparable companions of the defeated, darkened his spirit.

[Col. 0527C] Thus in the camp, which now lacked a ruler, men’s minds were variously stirred; the king’s fatal day was near, and he no longer, as before, held the supreme rule, guarding the royal tent alone and weighing [variant: brandishing] wakeful anxieties in his breast. But the two men, already conceiving in their minds [variant: hearts], through desire of kingship, their contemplated crime, considered [variant: were considering] inwardly that the king could be seized only with great difficulty. For no small fear and reverence for kings reign among the Persians; royal majesty usually has great weight. Even a barbarian people shudders at the name of king, and the barbarian reveres as pressed down by divine power those whom it fears in a more prosperous fortune.

[Col. 0527D] In adversity there survives reverence [variant: moderation] for a former condition: one who has once rendered honour continues always to render it. Since there was such loyalty and favour toward the king among that people, the agents of crime could not bind Darius openly or by force without great slaughter among their own men. They therefore resolved to employ deceit and excuse their madness: with feigned speech they would pretend, as was proper, that they had returned and repented of so great an offence, and would represent themselves as ready to suffer the uttermost for their king.

[Vers. 3241; Col. 0528A] The next day Titan had restored the world which night’s darkness had taken away, and Darius had already given the signal to move camp, when the partners in the crime, skilled in cautiously displaying outwardly the customary service and an appearance of obeying their prince’s command, arrived with many soldiers. Yet deep [variant: narrow] in their minds lay hidden crime and the insolence of so great a wickedness.

Darius still bore the gleaming sceptre and the insignia of royalty, shining from his high [variant: in] chariot. The mutinous cohort lay prostrate on the ground, begging [variant: requesting] pardon, and waited to do reverence to the commander whom a parricidal servant would afterward thrust into chains. With tears rising, it compelled Belides to believe, and to wet his aged face with flowing tears. Yet even then the friends of fraud did not repent of their crime, though each clearly saw how gentle a man and king he deceived. Darius, indeed, secure and forgetful of the imminent hour which fate and his servant together were preparing, eager to escape the hands of the Pellaean and the Macedonians—the only hands he feared—hurried, with loosened reins, to accelerate his flight and enter remote [variant: hidden] regions.

[Col. 0528B] But Patron, leader of the Greek contingent, a man sound in age and steadfast in loyalty, a genuine friend of Darius, had learned of the parricides’ plot. Surrounded nobly by thousands of his armed men, he went beside the king, and when opportunity to speak was given, said: “Narbazanes and Bessus, greatest of kings, are preparing to pour out upon you plots conceived with the bloody sword. This daylight will be the end of your life—or theirs. Therefore allow us to be guards of your person. Give the command, while the matter permits, for the tents to be pitched among our camp.

[Col. 0528C] We have left Europe; neither Bactra nor India is ours. We have heaped fields, home, and all our hopes upon you. Nowhere [variant: never] would I seek, as an outsider and foreigner, to be your guardian or to become the defender of your safety, if I saw anyone else willing [variant: able] to render you this service. The glorious renown of the king’s having been saved [variant: of saving the king] had made Patron illustrious; yet if anyone should read [variant: reads] these poems too, Gallic posterity shall never be silent about Patron. The glory of Patron shall survive with the poet, never to die through any age.

[Col. 0528D] I judge that the ages are not rolled on rashly by an eternal chain [variant: flux] of causes; let no one believe that worldly affairs are conducted by chance. All things proceed according to the law which that Creator of things established from eternity. Though Darius could live by the counsel of the Greeks, he follows the decrees of fate.”

“Although,” he said, “your loyalty has been sufficiently known and tested often, yet I shall never withdraw from my own people or seek separation from those whom I have so often favoured. It is enough, and easier for me, to be deceived than to condemn my own. Whatever fortune commands, I prefer to suffer it among them rather than be thought a deserter.

[Vers. 3292; Col. 0529A] If my own people do not now wish me safe or alive, I perish too late; I now desire death of my own accord.”

Astonished and compelled to despair of the king’s decision, Patron returned distraught to the Greek troops, ready to suffer all things for uprightness [variant: truth], the strictness of justice, and loyalty. Bessus, the parricide, ignorant of the Pelasgian language, yet himself aware of so great a madness, seized [variant: understood] a secret word through an interpreter. He would already have killed Darius, had he not believed it safer to deliver the living enemy to the Pellaean. By this more advantageous means the assembly friendly to murder hoped [variant: believed] to win the victor’s favour.

[Col. 0529B] He therefore postponed the crime until a suitable hour of night—night, when shameful deeds are commonly done; night, when what is shameful in daylight [variant: in the light] pleases without punishment, when fear grows bold and the brow knows no shame [variant: blush].

Then Bessus strove with feigned mind to thank and honour Darius, because he had avoided the treacherous words of the deceitful and witty, handsome-speaking Roman [*Quiris*], who, while awaiting [variant: looking upon] riches, intended to please the Macedonian tyrant with this king’s neck, giving fatal gifts. Nor is it surprising: Romans are known to hold everything for sale, and the Roman himself to be venal and led by payment. A man without children, home, or wife, poor and exiled by the price of buyers, he is carried about like a reed.

The Arsacid assented, nevertheless sure that everything reported by the Greeks [variant: Graians] was true. But matters had already reached such a point that it was equally hard, full of fear, and hopeless either not to obey his own people or not to wish to entrust himself to them and so expose his head to their swords.

## Argument of Book Seven

[Col. 0529] The seventh book arms slaves against their master, displays his justice, and at last thrusts him into chains. Meanwhile Magnus, pursuing the defeated [variant: Darius], destroys the agents of the crime in a confused battle. At length Darius, pierced by spears, while in death Polystratius seeks living waters, entrusts his final words and last utterances to him. The Macedonian wets the discovered body with abundant tears and buries it. Again he suppresses the tumult of nobles and common people, and rushes with rapid course in fury against the enemy.

## Book Seven

[Col. 0529C] Phoebus halted sorrowfully upon the western shore; his horses stood fixed, and, sadly relaxing the light, he delayed the reins of the approaching night. The daughter of Latona, to behold so great a crime, lingered before revealing her rosy face to the earth. But the law that has bound [variant: gathers] all things in an eternal knot, and the sacred love of the universe by which all things are governed, seized both and commanded them to complete their appointed alternations. Already the steaming wave of Tethys smoked, about to enclose the day in its whirlpools; human toil, together with the sun, sought rest. But punishment awaited grieving Darius, and, placed at life’s evening, he was to make his setting together with the world’s evening.

[Col. 0529D] The unhappy man had shut himself in his tent, alone consulting with himself concerning himself; but the counsel of the wretched and of one dragging life through straits is always weak and hopeless.

[Vers. 3351; Col. 0530C] At last he said within himself: “Into what disasters, impious father of the gods, do you drag [variant: pull down] me? For what offence does the lot of fate prepare to destroy me? Gods above, by what crime have I earned such punishments? No place remains for me among friends or acquaintances; for I am safe among none of those with whom, as their master, I ought to have laid down my life in security. But a domestic enemy, more savage than a manifest foe, thirsts for this life and prepares arms against an old man’s throat.

“If it was unworthy that I should be girded with so great a diadem and rule all Asia; if I governed my subjects badly; if, as a tyrant, I attempted to dissolve public laws or ancestral statutes; if I oppressed citizens with arms and the people with tyranny; if, when sitting in judgment, as an unjust censor,

[Col. 0530D] I turned deaf ears from the poor man’s case; if, corrupted by a bribe, I favoured the unjust side;

[Vers. 3367; Col. 0531A] if fatal money persuaded me to sell a just judgment; if through me a disinherited son wept that his ancestral estate and his father’s vines had been taken away; if, hating law and good faith, I ran in the stadium of the world with an unclean mind—then I have deserved death, and I do not deprecate the appointed hour. It is now enough, gods above, that by your gift I have lived. Let the Furies rage more cruelly in Bessus [variant: in war]; let Narbazanes vent his rage upon me; and let the whole house, drenched in an old man’s cold blood, appease the sad [variant: just] wrath of the deity.

“But if I have been a worshipper of justice, if I have followed law and done nothing except what the letter of reason commands—so far as nature permits and the wanton condition of harmful flesh—remove the swords of dependants from their master’s throat. Let it profit Darius to have lived innocently throughout his age; let death turn upon those who have deserved to die. Let me live; let simplicity profit the righteous; let his own offence harm the guilty [variant: and let guilt harm the criminal].

[Col. 0531B] But if the fixed and imperious will of the gods remains, if the unchangeable sequence of fates prepares to take away my vital air, and Atropos, shortening life, hastens to break the cut thread, why may another do more concerning me than I myself? Or why shall I be preserved for Narbazanes, taken away from the Greeks? Do I still have blood, a right hand, a sword, that I should hesitate to release this life from fate?”

So he spoke and would have pierced his breast [variant: entrails] with cold steel, but the eunuch who alone was present stirred the tent and camp with lamentation. Then others rushed in hastily with tears [variant: shouting], groaning that the king had fallen. A barbarian wailing arose in the camp; the countryside thundered with the dreadful sound, and the trembling air echoed it back. His men did not dare take up arms, lest their retainers [variant: the retainers] should perhaps rush upon the swords. Yet loyalty, joined to duty, urged the Persians to take up arms lest they seem shamefully to have deserted their leader; but terror overcame them both, and powerful reverence for death excluded honour.

[Col. 0531C] Behold: as the stunned Persians hurried in troops, the sacrilegious companions arrived with drawn swords, burst through the entrance, scattered the bystanders with the sword, and caused the king—whom they had thought already dead—to be bound. Alas, how great is fate’s licence! How wandering is the chance that turns human fortunes!

[Col. 0531D] Him whom they had formerly seen seated in a gilded chariot, and before whom his own men trembled, now no longer his own, they overcame by the hands of his own people and placed in a narrow [variant: now] enclosure. The confinement of the chariot carried the king captive. Yet, lest he receive no honour even in the name of king, a slave more cruel than an asp ordered his master to be bound with golden fetters. The royal property was plundered as though by right of war; and when the discovered money had burdened the greedy chariots, loaded with their share of goods through utmost crime,

[Vers. 3420; Col. 0532A] they prepared for flight. Whither do you go, agents of an eastern crime, of wickedness [variant: wickednesses] and deceit, formed into a troop? What land will bear you? Where will such a monstrous evil be safely hidden [variant: remain]? Who can safely live under a slave thirsting for his master’s blood?

Meanwhile the conqueror of lands, having called [variant: girded] his soldiers to urgent action, pursuing Darius’ tracks with rapid [variant: seized] course, prepared to surround Ecbatana with a siege, seize the fugitive king, destroy the utterly ruined city by arms, and put the final hand to the long wars. But when he heard [variant: had heard] that Darius had fled [variant: moved], intent upon swift flight and had left Ecbatana, he immediately changed [variant: abandoned] his begun route and, leaving Persian fields,

[Col. 0532B] pursued the fugitives, driven by the spurs of his spirit. Because the sure rumour of fame had proclaimed that Darius, wishing first to enter Media and then Bactra, was hastening [variant: crossing] into Media, he prepared to pursue him there. But more trustworthy news turned him aside, affirming that the king had been thrust into chains and unfolding the sequence of events in fair order.

The Macedonian shuddered at what he heard and, summoning his commanders, said: “This labour is short, and its reward great. The men who remain, comrades, have abandoned Darius not far from here and reserve him, bound, for final evils—the end and goal of his fortunes [variant: misfortunes]. Either he has already yielded to fate, or he unwillingly enjoys the gift of life. Therefore the sluggish horse must be urged more quickly than is fair,

[Col. 0532C] and our pace must be precipitated against the enemy, so that we may give life to our afflicted foe. Once he has become pitiable, it is no less great to spare one already broken [variant: now broken] than to be able to break a rebel.”

The nobles applaud the king’s command [variant: reply] and press on, promising to follow him through the greatest dangers. Thus, once the charge was begun, the Macedonian host, the fateful scourge of the world, advances; nor does nocturnal rest, though sleep gives healing, relieve the weary of their day’s labour.
