So Jupiter’s wrath rushed upon the hostile Giants—a wrath which poets imagine armed in its right hand with thunderbolt—when hundred-handed Typhoeus already stretched his knotty arms toward heaven. You might have seen Mars flaming, Pallas thrusting forward with her shield its viperine face, and Delian Apollo scattering arrows from his fateful bow.

[Col. 0532D] At the rising of the stars they had reached a village in which Bessus, in frenzied heart, had bound the Arsacid. Two men met them, who, loathing Bessus’ monstrous crime, thought it safer to join the Macedonian camp than to remain in the company of parricides. With these as guides the Macedonian took a shorter route, now that Phoebus was sluggish; proceeding in a square formation, he so moderated his march that the rear line could join the front. Delian Apollo was now at an equal distance from each house by two stades [variant: perhaps “by dissensions”]; and behold,

[Vers. 3472; Col. 0533A] Brocubelus [variant: Curtius, *Broculus*], a deserter, affirmed that the king [variant: Darius] still lived and was only two hundred stades away. “But take care,” he said, “lest this army march in disorder or rush unarmed against armed lines. Their crime more fiercely inflames [variant: arms] the parricides to slaughter, now that despair cries in their hearts that no place for pardon remains.”

At this the nobles were fired up, and their desire to follow Alexander rather than the servile camp grew stronger. Therefore, though weary, the horses were pricked with loosened reins and commanded to heed the goads more heavily than usual; taking wings, they fly through the empty air. Already the sound, clamour, and crash of wheels had begun to be heard by the Greeks, so that either side could be seen by the other, had not a dreadful cloud of dust

[Col. 0533B] taken away their sight. Alexander ordered the Greeks to halt briefly until, when the storm of dust had ceased, they could recognize the enemy troops.

When the dust had settled, Bessus turned his gaze sideways and, from the summit of a lofty mountain, saw men coming up panting; he saw Romans flashing with the brilliance of arms and companies of infantry gleaming [variant: darkening] with steel. He shuddered at the sight, and hearts conscious of monstrous guilt, shaken by cold fear [variant: blood], trembled [variant: held fast].

Conversely, the fierce nation of Macedonians, seeing Bessus, hastened their step, and pouring their run over steep ground burned to engage the enemy with unequal forces. For if Bessus had possessed as much spirit and vigour for war and the offices of Mars as he had for crime, and had been as powerful in battle-line as in committing wickedness and betrayal,

[Col. 0533C] he could have repelled [variant: and beaten back] the Pellaean’s and the Macedonians’ strength, and avenged Asia. For those following Bessus’ camp equalled the Greeks in barbarian strength and in number; refreshed by sleep and food [variant: and food], they were about to give great proof of battle [variant: memorials of war], and rest contributes much in turn to strength for the weary.

But terror of the Macedonians and Alexander’s name, formidable to the world, turned aside [variant: war] the frightened men and compelled them to despair that the warriors could be conquered. The mutinous cohort fled, angry at its weapons, turning its backs toward its breasts; the degenerate men took flight. Then the accomplices in the abominable crime [variant: deed], wholly girded in spirit

[Col. 0533D] for the final crime, urged Darius to descend from the chariot, mount a horse briskly, and strive to preserve his life by flight. He rejected their poisonous [variant: venomous] counsels and words, called the avenging gods to witness, and, with tears rising, invoked the faithfulness of stern Alexander. He declared that he would not accompany the attendants of crimes. “No fear of death,” he said, “nor violence of fate

[Vers. 3525; Col. 0534A] shall compel Darius to join the camp of criminals. Fortune’s sword has nothing further to add to our disasters; death, with which the parricide threatens me, shall be an antidote to grief. I shall take death’s poison as medicine and cure for suffering.”

Thereupon the parricides, inflamed and conceiving anger deep in their hearts, pierced their master and father with bloody javelins; like hail they hurled darts at him, and at last left him, his breast pierced by many wounds and scattered with blood. And so that the pursuing forces could not follow farther, they struck with missiles and swords the royal team, trained to draw the yoke-bearing chariots; and they ordered the two attendants [variant: “they afflict [them] with wings”], whom he had had as companions in life, to be partners also in death, and overwhelmed them in the same destruction.

[Col. 0534B] When this was done, so that the traces of so great a monstrosity might be hidden, they divided their flight: Bessus hurried to enter Bactra; Narbazanes to visit the Hyrcanian woods. Others fled scattered [variant: others dispersed separately], wherever fear drove them, or hope—the ever-best companion in uncertain circumstances.

Only five hundred Romans gathered themselves, who, for the honour of justice and their fallen country, chose to die and resist the Macedonian troops, whether because they hoped to prolong life by arms or because it was shameful to survive their murdered king. While, however, the barbarian legion debated in the twofold motion of its counsels whether it were better, with the enemy near, to turn its back in flight or oppose its breast to the Greeks, behold the Macedonian force, borne upon the swift wings of triumphant spirit, came upon them, all possessing strength, all martial ardour.

[Col. 0534C] Now crash and a new horror of war again arose [variant: was brought on]. Flight does not profit the timid, nor boldness the brave; the brave are cut down, the timid captured. And behold, a thing unworthy of belief, marvellous to tell: the captives were more numerous than those who took them, and the abundance of plunder outweighed the number of captors and robbers.

Yet the rebels of the opposing side fell not without great glory: three thousand distinguished Romans fell [variant: a thousand fell]. Nor did the wrath of slaughter or fury of death cease until Alexander’s sword recalled their frenzy, and the young men devoted to slaughter abstained from killing.

Then indeed the surviving troop was driven like untouched cattle [variant: cattle], and in the whole host there were no traces of men able to show Darius to the Greeks. They search each Persian wagon one by one, but nowhere find the royal corpse, the disgrace of fate.

[Col. 0534D] For the royal team, having left the beaten road, stood in a remote valley, their breasts pierced by darts, mourning their own death and Darius’s. Not far from there a murmuring stream glides in playful babble and alone rules amid the spring grasses.

[Vers. 3577; Col. 0535A] The stream has a fountain as father; pouring from a rock, pure and released in drops through the stony entrails, it flows [variant: flows] and moistens the dry clods with nectar. To it a Macedonian, Polystratius, led after battle, his panting mouth assailed by the storm of thirst in order to refresh his parched throat with water, saw Darius, exhaling life and covered with discarded [variant: added] hides, in his chariot, and saw the wounded beasts of burden. Drawing near, he found Darius pierced by many wounds, his eyes troubled by death [variant: “eyes [by] death, inter— and of the final [moment]”: uncertain], lying upon the boundary between life and a scant remnant of it.

When he was asked in the Indian language who he was, he rejoiced, insofar as could be understood, at the sound of the voice: “This one and only consolation remains to Darius amid present fortune and approaching death: that I have no need of an interpreter’s tongue with you; that I speak my last words to ears that understand, and that I shall not utter my final words in vain.

[Col. 0535B] O how welcome to me, a king, would have been the presence of the Macedonian! How gladly would I have been heard by so pious an enemy and enjoyed his conversation, that by exchanging words a brief hour might have assuaged the old complaints of war [variant: ‘might have assuaged our old …’: uncertain]! Since fate denies me him, whoever you are, receive this and carry it to Alexander:

“After so many contests I die debtor to Magnus [variant: the Great One] and deeply obligated to him, because with a merciful heart, forgetting hostile anger, he sheltered Darius’ mother and children; because as victor he showed the conquered, not a hostile spirit such as befits a tyrant, but a royal heart and a serene countenance;

[Col. 0535C] because he was a more faithful enemy to his foe than my acquaintances and fellow-citizens were. Through him life was granted to my people; my kinsmen also took life away. To those to whom I gave kingdom and life—miserable to say—those through whose protection Darius ought to have been safe even from enemies, I was killed by them; safe among enemies, I fall among friends.

“I pray that such retaliation, as a just prince may render according to their deserts, be returned to these men [variant: first]; such as a parricide deserves, and such as I would have repaid had fortune granted me triumph. For my lot is not at stake in this crisis alone [variant: only], but theirs also, the lot of those who command the crowd [variant: troop] and hold the reins of the people. My cause is being tried: let Magnus decide with just weight

[Col. 0535D] what vengeance is due to so great a crime, what unprecedented punishment may expiate the wickedness of so great a deed. If he postpones it, or perhaps acts more leniently than is just, the illustrious reputation of the king will diminish, tarnished and greatly unlike its former fame. Add that a pious king ought to protect himself from a like plague and avoid the dangers of sudden disaster. Since the stability of justice is at issue on one side and advantage on the other,

[Vers. 3628; Col. 0536A] let him preserve [variant: let each be held] both by a single strictness.

“This one thing I pray of the gods above, with urgent [variant: dying] vows, and of infernal Chaos: that, as fates proceed in their order, the whole world may serve Alexander in subjection; that the Great One may rule supremely in a great world; and that, when the right of a just burial has been granted me, the final honours may not be begrudged me by the king.”

Thus he spoke, extended to the Greek his right hand as though it were a special pledge to be borne [variant: to be borne] to Alexander, and death-bringing sleep stole through his stiffening limbs. At last the sacred spirit, bursting from its muddy prison, abhorring the wretched lodging of flesh, went forth and escaped [variant: vanished] free into the thin air.

Happy souls! While vital warmth animates the limbs steeped in it, if we were allowed to taste beforehand what rewards, what rest await the spirits at the decreed and just time, and what contrary fate awaits the wicked as against the righteous,

[Col. 0536B] the fatal love of possession would not entangle us, nor would flesh’s friendly desire scorch our inward parts. Nor would a vile belly swallow ancestral [variant: fathers’] acres at an excessively rich table; nor, detained in an iron prison, would Bacchus rage horribly, about to break the casks, nor would Liber lament himself confined without breathing-space.

The old Simon would not so eagerly seek the honour of a purchasable chair; fatal money, the incentive of evils, would not defile sacred sees. One still beardless, though distinguished by the innate quality of ancestral blood, would not aspire to the pontifical summit until character, the fruit of studies, and age chose him, rather than the undeserved influence of parents.

[Col. 0536C] Men led by envy would not create twin fathers and set them over the world, deriving their title from the cardinal point. Nor would love [variant: scent] of gain rule; a judge corrupted by a gift would not wish to pervert the forms of judgment. Nor would sacred pontiffs today fall indiscriminately, such as neighbouring lands, separated by a narrow sea, lament to have recently fallen: Flanders grieves for Robert slain; England for Thomas.

But because, seduced by desire for fleeting [variant: unstable] things, the soul follows the rushing, momentary [variant: precipitous] goods of the fugitive world, flesh entices it with delights and does not allow it to remember its origin, in whose image it was made, or whither, when the flesh is dissolved, it ought to return. Hence comes ignorance of the true good.

[Col. 0536D] Hence it is that, rejecting the rein of reason, we desire what nature forbids; and man, ready for every crime, does not fear what divine and human law command him to fear. Hence it is that Bessus, servant inflamed by love of kingship, reverencing neither men nor gods, unravels the fateful threads both of his father and of his master.

Yet you, Darius, if what we now write shall someday receive credence, France shall justly match you with Pompey in praises.

[Vers. 3681; Col. 0537A] The glory of the dead man shall live on with the poet, never to die through any age.

When Magnus learned that Darius had breathed his last, troubled, he hastened his rapid pace; he bathed the discovered corpse in tears and drenched it with abundant weeping. He sat with clasped hands and, laying aside the sternness [variant: vigour] of a ruler, lamented and groaned over him as he lay outstretched—him whom, while he stood, he had so often attacked [variant: struck] in order to bring him down.

Then, when he had dried his tears with his purple cloak and cleansed his cheeks, he said: “For wretched mortals this alone is relief [variant: this is the sole consolation]: glory does not know death, and fame that survives does not feel destruction. If glory in reputation corresponds to the merits of a life, no antiquity can erase your deeds. Nor shall posterity forget you, illustrious Darius, king of Persia, nor shall the saw of ancient days consume you.

[Col. 0537B] You shall shine in titles and be read throughout the whole world because you dared resist Alexander and the Macedonians’ fates. If only fate had preserved you alive under a favourable omen, you would have proved that under the Macedonians’ yoke nothing is burdensome: lesser only by one king, second only to Magnus, you would have given laws to others, admitted into a portion of your kingdom.

But because the slavish bands who cut short with the sword your father’s earned old age did not permit me to be praised as a merciful victor over a conquered enemy, you leave me—dead man—the only thing permitted: an avenger against the unspeakable enemies, one whom you formerly had as an enemy.

So may it be granted me, once the East has been subdued in war, to enter the western gulfs, carry a threatening fleet upon the western seas, and, turning my course,

[Col. 0537C] subject the Gallic necks to Greek dominion. So may the gods grant me, once the Alps have been crossed, one …

And with the peoples of the Ligurians, to break the Roman strength.

He spoke; and, when the funeral rites had been duly discharged according to custom, he buried the royal body with kingly magnificence. He ordered the limbs to be embalmed and, once embalmed, laid among the monuments of his ancestors. When they had been placed there, a lofty pyramid was raised, built of snow-white marble and further adorned by the art of learned Apelles. Molten metal, poured into the fissures, bound the joined stones together inwardly with alternating union; wherever the exterior lay open, gleaming gold, engraved with diverse figures, flashed from the joinery.

The weight was supported by four columns, set at equal distances by art; their golden base [Note: [Col. 0537] court/space.] gleamed. [Col. 0537D] A silver shaft rose up; capitals, brought out from double furnaces, were wrought in refined gold.

Above these was built—so great was Apelles’ skill—a hollow dome, brighter than gold [Note: [Col. 0537] brighter than glass.], purer than a peaceful stream, like crystal and the revolving heaven, of balanced weight. Upon it was beautifully depicted the form of the threefold world. Here the realm of Asia spreads widely; there, within a narrower space, lie its two sister regions. Here were marked with definite signs places, rivers, peoples,

[Vers. 3735.] [Col. 0538A] cities and woods, lands, towns, mountains, and every island enclosed by the wandering sea; what each land lacks, and in what things it abounds. Libya is rich in crops; Hammon, neighboring the Syrtes, begs for rain; the Nile enriches Egypt; ivory makes India wealthy, and shores clothed in gems.

Africa displays the citadels of mighty Carthage; Greece, Athens rich [Note: [Col. 0537] wealthy.] in divine renown and immortal fame. The house of Pallas, Rome as it grows, is proud. France boasts of its soldiers; Campania of renowned Bacchus [Note: [Col. 0537] vice.]; Spain of Herculean Gades; Saba of incense; the Britons of Arcturus; Normandy of its customary pride; England of gentleness. Love of possession burns the Ligurians, and the German retains his accustomed fury.

The slippery Ocean runs around the outermost borders of so great a dome; the Pontus, lying between Asia and the tracts of the two sisters, separates them by an opposing barrier [Note: [Col. 0537] distinguishes them.]. Into this Pontus all wandering rivers descend from their distinct [Note: [Col. 0537] distorted.] banks, and, led by it, after winding through curved channels, glide into the great sea.

And because Daniel’s meaning had not escaped Apelles, he inscribed the golden marble with this epigram:

> Here lies the symbolic ram, whose two horns  
> Alexander, hammer of the whole world, broke.

Moreover, following the Hebrews and their writings, he recorded the succession of past, recurring [Note: [Col. 0537] the succession having been unfolded.] time—the years of humankind from its creation down to the warlike times of triumphant Alexander the Great. In all, there are reckoned twice two thousand years, twice four hundred, sixty, and twice four: 4,868 years.

Meanwhile the Macedonian invited the deserving companies [Note: [Col. 0537] many companies.] to receive gifts. With lavish rewards he treated their groans and wounds; and, having found a suitable occasion, he renewed solemn feasts and Bacchic joys throughout the entire camp. While the soldiers handled their cups and, given over to pleasures, enjoyed leisure, behold: a sudden report—the customary vice of an army at leisure—struck the ranks with abrupt agitation.

It was said that Alexander, swollen after successful wars, his enemies crushed and Persia won, wished to return to the borders of his fatherland [Note: [Col. 0537] his ancestral borders.] and its beloved realms. Therefore, eager for return, though the rumor lacked an author, they ran everywhere through the camp’s streets like waters; they fitted tents onto wagons,

[Col. 0538D] gathered baggage and camp equipment as though the march were to be prepared for the morning. Joyful commotion rose throughout the camp, and they carried happy [Note: [Col. 0537] mingled.] applause to the stars.

When the rumor struck the astonished ears of the unconquered prince, a hidden dread terrified his mind [Note: [Col. 0537] spirit.], and rage tightened the loose reins of reason. But soon, when his mind returned and was recalled after rage had been subdued, he ordered the commanders summoned; and, with tears poured forth, he complained that his fellow citizens were taking the world away from him at the midpoint of the earth, that at the very threshold of valor the dominion of the entire world, opened to Alexander, was being shut against him; that he would carry back to Argos nothing but disgrace, the fortune of a defeated man rather than of a victor. He complained of the envy of the gods, which always entices strong hearts and draws them by love of their native country, making men wish to return dishonorably and without renown to their own birthplaces; though, if time were granted, they would return with great glory.

The council applauded the king, promising its strength in every danger, and that nobles and fickle populace alike would obey his commands—provided only that he soothed their harsh ears with persuasion [Note: [Col. 0539] first soothe them.].

Therefore, when the tribunal had been set up and the leaders summoned, before the nobles and the crowd [Note: [Col. 0539] throng.] of common people standing by, Alexander began:

“Friends, as you recall the titles and names of deeds accomplished by you [Note: [Col. 0539] by us.], it is no wonder that the seats of your homeland come to mind—places in which fame may sing of your illustrious labors and celebrated glory exalt your battles [Note: [Col. 0539] praises.].

“Through you the fatherland, now free, has been released [Note: [Col. 0539] snatched away.] from the ancient Persian yoke. Your arms have subdued Phoenicia, Persia, the Medes, Armenia, and Syria. Lydia, Cappadocia, the Parthians, and the Cilician ranges have yielded to your yoke. Your courage has subdued for me more lands than slippery Fortune has granted cities to other kings. Therefore, if the possession of the lands which I have subdued with such swift valor were assured to me forever, with fixed treaties, then, citizens, while you still held them, I should gladly hasten of my own accord

[Col. 0539C] to the cities of my homeland and my beloved country; I should wish to see my mother and my two sisters, and to enjoy the glory won together with you.

“But the condition of the empire is new and has not yet taken firm root; and, while barbarian necks do not yet bear the yoke evenly, victory wavers. We need, then, a brief period of habituation, until barbarian hearts soften with time allowed them and foreign breasts lay aside their native customs. For delay ripens crops, and new wine softens at its appointed time, though it lacks sensation. What nature cannot do, long time calms: it tames minds and the rage of wild beasts; the hand and gentle voice of a human trainer soften the savage, untamed lion.

“You have conquered the Persians, but you have not yourselves subdued them. They are held in check by arms, not by the law of customs; those whom they now fear when present will become enemies when absent. And although the Persian king has been killed, many an enemy still remains. Bessus, murderer of his father, and his own Narbazanes, retaining the kingdom, are joining battle. Shame! Though born to serve forever as dependents, through the utmost crime, having gained power, they stretch bloody hands toward the scepter.

“But just as physicians cut away from sick bodies everything that will do harm [Note: [Col. 0539] cut back.], so I judge that nothing should be left behind to impede us as we depart; whatever may harm us after the kingdom has been left behind must be cut off by the sword [Note: [Col. 0539] with a sword.]. A small thing often furnishes the cause of great ruin, when the little spark of a lamp has been neglected.

“To remain safer from an enemy, there is nothing which you may safely despise in him. The man whom you neglect becomes for that very reason a stronger and much more powerful enemy. Did we conquer Darius so that the murderer Bessus should inherit the empire? Keep this madness far away, lords of the earth. The road is short: scarcely four days lie between us and the place where Bessus the parricide cannot seek an escape from death. You have crossed so many rivers, so many mountain ridges [Note: [Col. 0539] places.], traversed so many far-off chasms, dreadful lakes, rocks, and trackless places; you have made them passable. No sea with restless swell [Note: [Col. 0539] wave-vomiting.] divides you; all lies flat and full of triumph. The prize is near, at the very threshold. Few remain to be conquered: glory memorable for all ages,

[Col. 0540C] when credulous posterity hears that, through your [Note: [Col. 0539] our.] labor, slaves paid the penalty after killing their master. A labor worthy of Hercules: that none condemned by public judgment for killing his father escaped your hands. Soldier, by this one deed you can make your honor everlasting and win the favor of the Persians and of Asia.”

So spoke [Note: [Col. 0539] having spoken—and behold, ready…] the leader; and all [Note: [Col. 0539] the horsemen.] raised their right hands, ready for battle, and unanimously promised to follow him through the greatest [Note: [Col. 0539] every.] dangers—old men joyful and youth cheerful alike. Eager for battle, the Great One ordered the tents struck [Note: [Col. 0539] turned.] and rushed with swift course in fury against the enemy.

## Argument of Book Eight

The eighth book subdues the Hyrcanians; and an Amazon, bearing no hostile vows, presents herself to the king with her quiver. The Macedonians’ treasures are burned—a marvelous deed. Dymnus’ crime is uncovered, and there follows in the camp an accursed lament, a speech, and the death of Philotas. Impious Bessus, an implacable monster, is dragged in; hung up, the parricide atones for his father's shades. He makes war upon the Scythians. When their embassy accomplishes nothing, and warnings [Note: [Col. 0539] warnings, nominative.] do not bend the prince’s anger, a people previously unconquered is subjected to the conqueror of the world.

## Book Eight

[Col. 0541]

Mourning Memnon’s death in everlasting grief, Dawn for the third time scattered her light-bearing rays across all lands, when that brave and tireless [Note: [Col. 0541] this.] conqueror of lands, headlong toward every danger, entered the Hyrcanian borders with armed soldiers. After he had thoroughly subdued them, Narbazanes, bloody in deed, won life from him by writing in soft language.

Without delay, inflamed by the desire to see the king, Thalestris, queen of the Amazonian people, came, attended by two hundred maidens, and entered the camp. This woman gave laws to all the peoples whom Caucasus encloses on one side and the swift river Phasis surrounds on the other. As soon as access to the king was granted her, she swiftly dismounted from her horse, carrying two javelins in her right hand, with a quiver suspended from her left arm.

[Col. 0541B] The Amazons’ garment does not cover their whole body. The left side of the breast is exposed; the rest the clothing occupies and conceals what should be concealed. Yet beneath the joining of the knees the soft garment does not descend. The left breast remains intact, so that a female infant may be nourished by its milk; the other is not left untouched, but is burned, so that they may more readily draw their flexible bows and hurl their javelins.

Examining the king with attentive gaze, Thalestris wondered that his body, so slight, did not answer to his fame, and silently considered where such great valor could lie in an unconquered prince. Barbarian simplicity reveres and estimates all persons of great deeds by the majesty and bearing of a handsome body; it believes that none are capable of great achievements except those upon whom nature has deigned to confer a comely [Note: [Col. 0541] to offer whom nature a comely.] body and to bless with beautiful appearance.

Yet sometimes a greater, mighty spirit excels in a small body, and illustrious power, passing beyond the limbs of the body, rules in obscure members. Asked at last why the queen had come, whether she wished to seek some great boon from the prince, she declared that she had come so that, returning with her womb full, she might bear a shared offspring by so great a prince. She deemed herself worthy to bear the king an heir to his realm: if a girl should be produced in childbirth, the daughter should possess her mother’s kingdom; if a male should result, he should be returned to his father to be raised.

Alexander asked whether Thalestris wished to remain free from military service for that purpose. She pleaded that her kingdom could not be without its guardian; at last she stayed as a favor for thirty nights. Having gained what she sought, she returned to the throne of her realm and the cities of her homeland.

Meanwhile Bessus, having put on a diadem, had come to Bactra [Note: [Col. 0541] had vowed.], daring to assume a new name; and, having summoned the Scythians, he was rising to arms with every preparation. The Macedonian boiled on hearing this, but the ranks, burdened by luxury and war with so many acquired possessions, could scarcely be moved. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0541] therefore.]—a marvelous deed!—judging that everything which normally burdens men in arms during movement ought to be burned, he ordered first his own things, then those of his men, to be brought into the middle.

There lay an expansive plain, where were displayed riches won with much blood, the products of Arabs and the labors of the Seres, and wagons laden with diverse kinds of goods. Once these had been piled together, the martial hero seized a torch, set fire beneath them, and mingled everything with flames. All their possessions burned while their owners watched in astonishment—possessions which, lest they burn,

[Col. 0542B] had so often resisted fire when cities were set aflame [Note: [Col. 0541] burned.]; which, when shoulders undertook the labor, had endured greedy flames at great risk. Yet neither citizens nor common soldiers dared lament the price of blood shed, things won by such labor, when the king’s wealth was burned by the same fire.

When this grief had subsided, they are said to have declared that, by the king’s wise plan, the companies had been freed from heavy cares and great anxiety; and that those whom royal money had made slaves, now, by the prince’s example, had been made free men through fire.

Already he was choosing his route, already preparing to enter Bactra with unburdened troops, when the unconquered king—safe from the foreign enemy—was almost killed by the Macedonians themselves, his own advisers. Yet, with the Fates sparing him, he had so far avoided his people’s internal arms [Note: [Col. 0541] had turned aside from.] and civil crime.

Among the king’s friends Philotas, son of Parmenion, was foremost, greater than an entire legion. Without him Alexander had accomplished nothing worthy of song. When the grave crime reported to him by the informer Cebalinus had been kept silent by Philotas for three days, until Metron discovered the bloody plot, Dymnus fell by his own sword with his accomplices bound. Philotas himself was convicted [Note: [Col. 0541] bound again.], believed to have wished the tyrant slain for this one reason: that for three whole days he had suppressed notice of that crime.

Therefore he was brought into the court with his hands bound behind his back and his face veiled. By the prince’s command the people had assembled girded with weapons, and the palace was pale with dreadful iron. The whole company murmured, ignorant why it had been summoned amid such great disturbance, and waited with ears pricked, until Alexander, breaking the silence with a speech, revealed the crime. When Dymnus’ corpse had been brought in, at first he was silent; then at last he said:

“Citizens, I live, almost taken from you, by Fortune’s gift.”

At the king’s words the hall resounded with the clamorous roar of crowds, all demanding that he reveal [Note: [Col. 0543] destroy.] the authors [Note: [Col. 0543] actors.] of this crime. He said:

“What? Parmenion—my father’s and my own special friend, preferred above others by such honor [Note: [Col. 0543] affection.]—was the author of so great an outrage; and Philotas himself, with his father conceiving a deed so detestable to earth and heaven, chose Lycolaus [Note: [Col. 0543] Curtius: Peucolaus.] and Demetrius, and Dymnus, whose wretched body you see before you, as his companions, and enlisted them as agents of my destruction.”

Again the wild assembly thundered with a terrible cry. Metron, Cebalinus, and the informer Nicomachus were brought forward as witnesses and related in public the origin of the charge. The martial hero added:

“By what service, by what affection, did the man seem to love the master and father who, when he learned this crime of crimes, remained silent? Yet it is clear that Dymnus’ murder must not be governed [Note: [Col. 0543] kept silent.] by silence. As soon as Cebalinus received this bitter crime, he did not delay even one hour. Parmenides alone did not fear; he alone did not believe it—Parmenides, indeed, swollen with the rule of his native country. Since I set him over the Medes, in pride he hopes for greater things and aspires to the summit [Note: [Col. 0543] highest summit.] of honor.

“Perhaps Philotas was given this intention [Note: [Col. 0543] mind.] against my life because I have no relatives, no free offspring, and no father left. You are mistaken, ruinous Philotas: with so many Macedonian leaders alive, whose ranks you see standing around me, do not call Alexander bereft. Behold my brothers whom I see; behold my fathers [Note: [Col. 0543] my own.]!

“The fact that Dymnus conceals him and does not name him among the partners and accomplices of the plot does not make him less guilty. It is evidence against the leader, and of terror at betraying those who are in command [Note: [Col. 0543] able.]: while they confess their own part, they dare not, terror-stricken, confess concerning their leader. Philotas has often been accustomed both to sow suspicions about me and to lend willing ears to those sowing them. He said that he rejoiced for me, whom Jupiter, he affirmed, had begotten from himself; yet that those who must live beneath the pride of so great a prince ought to be pitied,

[Col. 0543D] pride exceeding measure and the course of mortal life [Note: [Col. 0543] rein.].

“I knew it and was silent. For I did not wish to make cheap and contemptible to others those upon whom I had previously conferred so many benefits. But now his reckless tongue turns to swords: his hand gives birth by the sword to what his mouth conceived. Where may I betake myself? To whom may I entrust this head? I put one man over many, one to whom I entrusted the rights over my life and head; yet from where I sought protection came an unforeseen destruction of safety. Better had I fallen in war, destined to become the enemy’s prey rather than a citizen’s victim.

“Now saved from those whom the Macedonian alone feared, he has fallen [Note: [Col. 0543] fallen down.] among companions at my side and among troops whose hands he neither could nor ought to have feared. Therefore, my citizens, I flee to the defenses and arms of you, my fellow citizens. Let it be lawful for you to be the authors of my safety. I neither wish nor can remain safe against your will. If you wish to save [Note: [Col. 0543] be safe.] me, undertake the office of avenger; avenge me by punishment.”

When, prompted by anger, he had persuaded them of this, he left the council and ordered Philotas, bound, to be brought forward to state his case, lest the judicial order be said to have lost its powers in the court of so great a ruler. Philotas stood with hands tied, pale, his limbs veiled in cheap covering [Note: [Col. 0543] his face veiled in a cheap garment.], mournful in expression, greatly changed from the man who lately, chief of the cavalry and second to the Great One, had gone more noble and magnificent than the commanders, arranging battle lines and conducting the business of war.

Flanders once saw Burchard in this guise pay the deserved penalty for killing the prince [Note: [Col. 0543] consul.]. A punitive wheel tortured him for such a crime and broke all his limbs, with Ludwig acting as avenger.

The company wavered in pity, and love for Parmenion moved their hearts: the bitter plight of so famous a citizen, who, bereft already of his two sons, Hector long before and great Nicanor recently, was administering justice to the Medes. His third son, the sole surviving consolation of his father, with his parent absent, pleaded his case before an unfair judge in barbarian lands.

The minds of the nobles were hesitant, and the rigor of cruelty [Note: [Col. 0543] slowness.] might seem to have yielded [Note: [Col. 0543] fallen.] when Amyntas, the royal magistrate, seeing their minds soften through pity [Note: [Col. 0543] relaxed.], began, after raising many accusations, to condemn Philotas. By speaking he revived the commanders’ dormant anger and made the wound, once soothed, grow cruel again.

Then Philotas, truly stunned and mentally shaken, turned his eyes away from the surrounding crowd; he neither raised his head nor moved his gaze—whether because his mind, conscious of so great a crime [Note: [Col. 0543] deed.], had collapsed, or because it wavered, pressed by fear of punishment. Without delay, out of his mind, he fell upon the man by whom he was held [Note: [Col. 0543] he.]. At last, when he recovered his senses, wiping his face [Note: [Col. 0543] tears.] with a cloth and his countenance wet

[Col. 0544D] with weeping, he said:

“It is easy for an innocent man, citizens, to find words and keep his composure; it is no light thing for one in misery. Since, on this side, my mind is in harbor, free from this accusation and conscious of no guilt, while on the other a stormy south wind lashes me with the swollen wave of Fortune, I am set between both and hemmed in by the straits of each. I do not see by what law I can obey either this critical moment or a mind clean of crime. [Vers. 4084.] I perish if I obey powerful Fortune; Fortune, stronger, does not permit an innocent mind to be stronger than itself.

“This mind [Note: [Col. 0545] the mind.] remains secure; that one prepares the axe for me. Here is hope, there fear; here I am safe, there shipwrecked. Moreover, I enter upon my case without the judge whose interest it was to recognize the merit of a just cause. Nor do I see why he is absent, when he alone may condemn the guilty and he alone may acquit. I cannot be acquitted unless the investigator and judge of the case himself sits here; yet it will scarcely happen that I am freed in the absence of him by whom I was bound in his presence.

“But although the defense of a bound man is weak—a man who does not instruct his censor and indeed seems to accuse him of injustice—still, so far as may be allowed, at the point of death I shall plead this for myself and shall not desert myself. Yet I do not see for what crime the court condemns me. No one declares that I was among the conspirators or accomplices. Nicomachus extracted nothing about me; Cebalinus could know no more than Nicomachus, from whom he heard this crime. Yet the king accuses me of being the author of this plot. But how does it appear that the head of the murder, the master of the crime, was kept silent? Whom did Dymnus follow in so great a danger? It is not likely that anyone spares another who does not spare himself. Rather, one must believe that he shields himself under a greater name: that Dymnus would have named Philotas before the other participants.

“Writings tell how the Ithacan, when Ajax charged him with the theft of Pallas and the nighttime abduction of Minerva, properly excused the act [Note: [Col. 0545] theft.] as done with Diomedes as his companion, or veiled his own fault under Diomedes’ name. And when he charged the son of Laertes in turn with feigning madness and seeking concealment from fear of war, he answered: ‘If I sought concealment, let it be shameful for me only if Achilles too, by the same reasoning, is judged guilty for hiding timidly among women’s companies. I do not reject a crime shared with so great a man.’

“So, where a shared case of two persons is treated, the greater sometimes excuses the lesser. Tell me, learned jurists and experts in law [Note: [Col. 0545] laws.], by what reasoning does a man perish, by what law does he deserve death, whom no one accuses, against whom not even rumor weighs, whom his own confession does not condemn? If Cebalinus, the messenger of this accusation [Note: [Col. 0545] disclosure.], had not first approached me, I should not be dragged into court today, no one accusing my name.

“Yet you are charged with having suppressed the crime reported to you, and with having closed your ears to these reports. Why not [Note: [Col. 0545] for why.]? Is faith to be given to boys’ complaints? A serious statement is less valuable and lacks weight when no serious authority utters it; the frivolity of its author makes rumors empty. If I had been Dymnus’ companion in guilt or confidant,

[Col. 0546A] I certainly would not have allowed myself or the partners in this crime to be exposed. While the affair could have been carried out during that interval, secretly or openly, I could have removed Cebalinus, lest he carry to the king news of the conceived crime, once intelligence of this undertaking had been brought to me. After the treachery by which I was to perish [Note: [Col. 0545] he was.] had been disclosed to me, I went alone, sword accompanying me, to the private dwelling and bedchamber of the king. I do not see why I delayed the crime. Or was I not bold without Dymnus? Was he the chief and leader of the bloody counsel, while Philotas is believed to have lurked beneath him? And was he to seek kingship after killing the Great One?

“Which one of you, citizens, however, did I corrupt by a gift? Which did I court more zealously than one man among all of you? But the king charges that I wrote to him that I rejoiced in his honor, whom he declared Jupiter had begotten from himself, but that those who must live beneath the pride of so great a prince were to be pitied.

“It was true faith, love, trust, and freedom of candid counsel—harmful to some—and sound correction with which I addressed the king. You have deceived me. And I confess that Philotas wrote this: I wrote this to the king, but not about the king. I knew that it was more fitting to recognize Jupiter and the offspring of the gods in silent prayers [Note: [Col. 0545] acknowledge.] than, by boasting of himself, to stir envy against himself and provoke the anger of the nobles.

“What good has it done me, king, to sweat so often for you under arms, to spend my youth with you and for you, and to endure uninterrupted labor in war? What good has it done me to lose two brothers [Note: [Col. 0545] my brothers.] in the ranks? I cannot show my father present or bring him to my troubles; nor dare I invoke my father’s name, because he too is believed [Note: [Col. 0545] is said.] guilty of this crime. It is apparently not enough that a father be bereft of two sons unless he is bereft also of the one who remains, and an innocent son is laid upon the pyre.

“Therefore, dear father, you too will die—and because of me [Note: [Col. 0545] and because of me.]? You were the cause of life to me, and shall I be the cause of death to you? Shall I break your thread and, as your son, extinguish your old age? Why, then, did you beget this body for your own ruin? Ought you not to have destroyed it once begotten? Or was it so that you might receive these fruits from an evil stock [Note: [Col. 0545] reap.]? Whether the father’s old age is more pitiable or the son’s youth more to be lamented is uncertain. I am taken from the midst in the still-coming years of spring, while from my father, exhausted in blood,

[Col. 0546D] life is snatched away—a life which, if Fortune had permitted it to remain even a little while in its well-fed body, Nature rightly claimed for herself.”

So he spoke; and behold, the king returned to the council surrounded by a company armed with grim iron. Then Philotas, terrified by fear of punishment and death, again fell to the ground, his body [Note: [Col. 0545] breast.] chilled, fainting with the face of one dying.

Dissenting opinion had begun to spread among the nobles, and the factions of the commanders wavered in divided murmuring. [Vers. 4191.] Some judged that Parmenides should be killed by the ancient method, by stones; others prepared [Note: [Col. 0547] wished.] to extract the truth by torture. Following their words, the king ordered instruments of torture prepared. As the executioners stretched out their hands and made ready every kind of cruelty before the eyes of miserable Philotas, he said: “There is no need, nobles, for a harsher scourge. I confess: I wished it.”

But when they inflicted harsher punishments on him, when his body had been torn and the blows struck bare bones, and no place remained upon him for wounds, he finally disclosed the deadly plot, the sequence of events, and the crime. Yet it was a doubtful inference whether he had confessed such monstrous matters concerning himself in order to escape those tortures [Note: [Col. 0547] a long torment.] and end his pain by swift death.

Oh, by what difficult effort slippery Fortune raises mortal deeds

[Col. 0547B] and how easily she overturns those whom she has made ascend! Fortune, with great labor, had raised Philotas, born of the common people [Note: [Col. 0547] race.], to high estate: made commander of the army and leader of a cohort, son of Parmenion. Soon thereafter, as he sought to rise, condemned by fate [Note: [Col. 0547] is condemned.] and exiled, he was crushed by stones. Every hand competed to hurl stones at the one whose hand had formerly given [Note: [Col. 0547] gave.] the signal to move camp. How frivolous is worldly glory! How fleeting the world’s honor! How empty a name! One set above others who wishes to rule, refusing to be of service [Note: [Col. 0547] One set above, who desires to rule, refuses to be of service.]!

When six days had passed after the sad death of Philotas [Note: [Col. 0547] after Philotas had perished.], the Macedonian hurried his ranks against Bessus. Lavish and enduring in toil, the fated hammer of the world did not cease until Bessus, that implacable monster, was dragged captive from the eastern region and presented to enraged Alexander, wholly stripped of his covering, naked, with a chain fixed about his neck and feet.

When the king saw him, his eyes blazing, he said: “Bessus, what madness of a beast, or what Fury, suggested so great a crime to you that you dared to bind a king who had deserved well of you, and, through desire of the throne, violently to close with the sword the life of both your father and your lord?”

He spoke thus and summoned Darius’ brother, whom the destroyer of kingdoms held first among the guardians of his person; he handed Bessus over with feet and arms bound. Taking his sacred life through long torments, Darius’ brother summoned [Note: [Col. 0547] summoned together.] him to the rites of the Stygian sisters, appeased his brother’s spirit with blood, and ordered Bessus, fastened to a cross, to go down to Tartarus.

Such was Bessus’ end. While he tried to climb, he fell; while he sought dominion, it returned [Note: [Col. 0547] rules.] against himself. A slave, he put on his master’s insignia.

But the Macedonian, long desiring with thirsty heart the kingdom of Scythia, transferred his army to the Tanais more swiftly than leopards. With its vast channel that river separates Bactra from the kingdom of Scythia; [Vers. 4245.] it is likewise the boundary between Europe and Asia, flowing between them in its waters.

[Col. 0548A] That people is a part of Sarmatia, if ancient report deserves belief. They inhabit mountains and inhospitable haunts of wild beasts as homes and marriage chambers. Hating gain and content with the food which nature gives, they refuse to corrupt their happy life by sacred ambition.

And while the Macedonian, encamped by the Tanais, was preparing a vessel in which on the following day he would cross the river as a warrior to the Scythian lands, behold: twenty men, their rough backs pressing upon strange, horn-hoofed horses, entered the Macedonian camp, bearing the king’s [Note: [Col. 0547] king.] message. The eldest of them, looking upon the king, said:

“If you had a body equal to your ambition, and a body as great as the mind that seeks boundless things, the greatest world would not suffice for your grasp; your measure would exceed the limits of the earth. Your right hand would hold the east, your left the west; and, not content even with that, you would dare to search and seek with every desire where the wondrous light hides itself. You would dare to climb the sun’s chariot and, Phoebus driven away, govern the wandering lights.

“Even so, you seek many things which you cannot grasp. Once you have subdued the world and overcome humankind, bloody as you are, you will move your arms against trees, wild beasts, and stones. You will leave neither mountain snows nor monsters hidden in cliffs untouched; even the elements themselves, though devoid of feeling, will be compelled to feel your rage.

“Do you not know that the strength of a tree, proudly lifting itself toward heaven with a long branch and firm root, which has grown for a long time, may be uprooted in a single hour? He is foolish who, while he receives the fruit, refuses to measure the tree’s height. You may see, while striving to seize the lofty top, that after you have grasped it you perhaps fall with the branches. A lion, once king of beasts, has become food for small birds. Rust, devouring all things, consumes iron that subdues everything and is harder than every bronze. Beneath Phoebus’ sphere, nothing is so firm that it cannot fear ruin. Who, while sailing the world, ought not to fear sunset and the storm of death from a feeble source?

“What have we to do with you? We have not harassed you with arms or touched your land in order to make war. Let the Scythians, fleeing weapons and the noise of men and dwelling in forest caves, be permitted not to know who you are, from what stock you derive, for what purpose you have been sent, or whence you come.

“The free people of Scythia seeks nothing beyond what first-parent Nature gave; by her gift it can neither serve anyone nor desires to rule. [Vers. 4295.] To be one’s own master, to defend one’s property and oneself,

[Col. 0549A] to be content with one’s own, and not desire another’s, makes a man happy. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0549] therefore.], if you seek anything further, your desires exceed the measure and limit of happiness.

“Yet do not [Note: [Col. 0549] do not.] remain ignorant of the customs and peoples of the Scythians. The Scythians have herds, a plowshare, a cup, a spear, and an arrow; we use these things among both friends and enemies. To the gods we pour wine in a sacred bowl; to friends we give grain won by the labor of oxen; from afar we overwhelm enemies with the arrow, at close quarters with the spear.

“What land can hold you? What will be sufficient for you? You have subdued Lydia, Cappadocia, Syria, Persia, and the Medes; you have subjected Bactra; now, conqueror, you stretch toward India. Shame! You extend greedy

[Col. 0549B] and restless hands to our cattle; and though all kingdoms furnish you riches, you think yourself poor and needy.

“What need have you of wealth? It always produces hunger in the greedy [Note: [Col. 0549] greedy man.]. The more you acquire, the more you seek, and the more fiercely you burn to possess; thus abundance, by creating hunger, nourishes want.

“Does it occur to you how long Bactra will keep you? While you subdue this people, that one revolts. Victory arises from war, and wars rise anew for you from victory. You will cross the Tanais in order to find enemies and subject Scythia, which has always been free. But our poverty is swifter than your wings. Your army carries the wealth and booty of the whole world; we carry little, and with that lighter burden we flee and pursue enemies more swiftly. When you believe the Scythians far removed from you, you will see them within your camp. When you think enemies easy to capture and captured [Note: [Col. 0549] or captured.], they will slip away, swifter than the rapid east wind.

“No wealth and no desire attracts the impoverished Scythians. This race of men despises towns and cities and inhabits wildernesses ignorant of human refinement. Therefore remember to hold your Fortune with a pressed hand and fingers bent back, because she is always slippery and light; she can never [Note: [Col. 0549] and never can.] be held against her will.

“Therefore follow the salutary counsel which the favor of the present moment offers, while prosperous chance plays into your hands, while the divine powers of Fortune have not yet…”

You accuse: “Set a limit to your successful arms,

Lest the wheel, once turned, overthrow your achievements.

Your own people have said that Fortune has no feet,

And they paint her with winged hands and arms.

[Vers. 4341.] Therefore, if she should stretch out her hand to you,

[Col. 0550A] Seize her wings, lest, when she wishes, she fly away on swift wings.

Finally, if you are a god, you ought to be kind to mortals,

And give what is yours; you should never take away what is theirs.” [Note: [Col. 0549] “not what is.”]

“If you are a man like ourselves, you ought always to remember

That you are what you are. It is foolish to remember those things

From which you yourself have forgotten that you derive. You will have friends

Upon whom you have not made war. The strongest [Note: [Col. 0549] “most secure.”] bond

Among equals and peers is love;

Those are equals or peers who neither yield to you

Nor surpass themselves. They are those who have made no dangers

Of bloody [Note: [Col. 0549] “blood-stained.”] warfare [Note: [Col. 0549] “death.”] against one another by force.

Do you think that those friends whom you conquer are dear to you? [Note: [Col. 0549] “Take care not to believe as friends those whom …”]

Sooner shall the earth bear the stars, and Ocean

[Col. 0550B] Wash the seven Bears, and fish love dry land,

Than there be a true bond [Note: [Col. 0549] “connection.”] of love from slaves toward their master.

There is no harmony among them; for though peace is displayed outwardly,

Within, they contend in hatred.

The face has peace; the heart stirs up war.” [Note: [Col. 0549] “wars.”]

So he spoke; yet the Macedonian nevertheless, having drawn up his line,

Prepares to carry war against the Scythians. After crossing the river

With much labour, and joining battle, he routs the enemy [Note: [Col. 0549] “enemies.”]

And at last, though not without slaughter among his own men,

Compelled Scythia to serve the Macedonian empire.

As a fir-tree in Alpine crags, with age-old strength,

Reaching toward the stars, and bent through many years

By blasts of the East Wind, has scorned the West Wind and the South Wind—

Yet if perhaps the breath of Boreas, according to its custom, should assail it,

[Col. 0550C] And beat the air with all its force,

Neither its old branches nor its trunks rough with moss

Will avail it [Note: [Col. 0549] “avail.”] against being overwhelmed by the wind,

Falling, and striking the ground with its downward-pointing top—

So, although they had broken the arms of Assyrians, Medes, and Persians,

When he swooped down swifter than Boreas with icy wings—

That cruel, bloody sword of fate, the common plague of the world,

Great Alexander—the Scythians, their strength broken,

Yielded to him. [Note: [Col. 0549] “Men, and Fortune …”] The gods and fates follow. . .

When rumour, chattering, scattered his neighbouring triumphs

Among the nations, at once their hearts drank in sudden fear;

The whole world shuddered, as did the lands subject to the rising Phoebus.

For they had lately heard that the Scythians, formerly unbroken by force,

[Col. 0550D] Were held under Macedonian rule [Note: [Col. 0549] “subdued.”]

They thought that no powers remained in the world

Equal in courage or strength,

When they saw the Scythians fall, previously unconquered.

Consequently many willingly took on the Macedonian yoke.

Not more did the commander’s arms move men

And subject them to his yoke than did his merciful conduct

Toward the conquered. For those whom the Great One conquered by force,

[Vers. 4391.] He bound [Note: [Col. 0549] “joined.”] to himself by love; neither harsh nor greedy

[Col. 0551A] As an exactor, he released captives at their entreaties and without payment,

And acquitted the accused, in order by this deed to show

That, when he went against a people, he entered the contest not under the goads of anger,

But from the impulse of virtues.

## Argument of Book Nine

[Col. 0551]

In the ninth book the Great One, having mustered his forces,

In turbulent fury attacks India; but warlike Porus delays fate and the gods.

The particularly lamentable death of two young men, mourned by both sides,

Troubled each army, when the Great One occupied the hostile [Note: [Col. 0551] “hostile—banks.”] bank with his soldiers.

The battle-lines clash [Note: [Col. 0551] “come to the aid.”]; but Porus at last being broken,

The remaining tyrants are broken, together with the entire East.

Alexander’s leap is remarkable; mutiny moves the Greek ranks;

And more remarkable still is the purpose of his astonishing mind:

he sends fresh cohorts into new wars.

## Book Nine

[Col. 0551B] India remained, destined to feel the last terrible tumults of the Macedonians,

To be subdued with much sweat and grievous wars. While that rival

Of the gods on earth sought it, Clytus, *Hermolaus, and his

Teacher—second to none except Aristotle—

Met their final day, leaving sure proofs

For future generations. For their end testifies

That the friendships of kings are not everlasting.

Almost all India lies beneath the rising Phoebus

And looks toward the East, stretched out with bold headland;

But on the side toward Libya and the South Wind,

The land rises higher and reaches into the sky.

The rest lies flat, where Caucasus, famous in its own right,

Sends forth rivers rushing in rapid courses.

But colder than the others is the Indus, from which India took its name.

[Col. 0551C] On the southern side, through mountainous country,

The Ganges flows in a straight channel, greater than all rivers

Of the East; both, muddy rivers, lash the Red Sea with their spreading waters.

It swallows many trunks torn up by the roots, with a great portion of earth.

If it finds soft ground under its powerful waters, it stagnates,

And the land, made into an island, drinks up the stream. Here it intercepts

The Acesines flowing into the sea; each meets the other

With great force, and they clash between themselves in swift current. [Note: [Col. 0551] “impact.”]

Moreover, if one believes swift-flying rumour, those streams carry gold,

Gems, and other things more precious than usual

To our age among Eastern peoples. Hence comes the wealth

Of the Eastern nations. For when talkative Fame had spread abroad

That the Indians had been enriched by these wares,

[Col. 0551D] The swift nation runs [Note: [Col. 0551] “runs down.”] from the whole world,

[Vers. 4437.] To buy glittering gems, the refuse of the red [Note: [Col. 0551] “gleaming.”]

[Col. 0552B] Sea, things which human desire alone has made precious to itself,

Though they are of small weight. [Note: [Col. 0551] “lust.”]

Therefore, when the Indian leaders heard with astonished ears

That the son of Jupiter from Pella, scourging all the kingdoms of the world

By Macedonian valour, had reached their borders,

They assembled, overwhelmed with fear, [Note: [Col. 0551] “mingled.”]

To appease the leader with gifts [Note: [Col. 0551] “god.”] and surrendered cities full of riches.

But alone among the greatest rulers of those lands, Porus,

With great exertion, prepares to go forth against Alexander;

Just as, when part of an Alpine mountainside has been torn away,

It rushes down steep [Note: [Col. 0551] “trackless.”] cliffs,

Breaking the rocks before it in twisting eddying force;

But if a rocky mass, penetrating with its root to Stygian depths,

Like a mountain confronts it, there is a crash, and the two contend with great force.

[Col. 0552C] Alexander hears that Porus, with armed soldiers,

Is guarding the borders and extremities of the Indian kingdom

And displaying a show of arms with all his power.

Gladly seizing the opportunity for triumph offered to him through Porus,

He carries his army headlong and swiftly seeks the rushing Hydaspes.

Porus, having arrayed his battle-lines, stood with assembled strength

On the farther bank of this river.

A terrible beast, larger and more dreadful than the other elephants,

Carried Porus himself with its immense bulk,

Surpassing the measure of a human body.

Arms, distinguished with gleaming metal, cover the king.

His spirit is equal to his limbs; and by as much as he surpasses all

In bodily size, so much does he excel the other Indians. [Note: [Col. 0551] “is more prudent.”]

Not only the turbulent enemy had frightened the Greeks,

[Col. 0552D] But also the violent abyss of the river which had to be crossed by boat.

[Vers. 4469.] It was like the wave-sounding sea, with the appearance of a deep,

[Col. 0553A] The Hydaspes spread four stadia in width.

Its channel was deep, nowhere shallow; passage therefore

Had to be sought by ship. But the barbarian enemy

Stood opposite and, showering missiles like a storm-cloud

Into the middle, after taking up a desired station,

Could easily have turned the ships away from shore.

In the middle of the river was a vast [Note: [Col. 0553] “great.”] island firmly rooted in the earth.

Thither, borne by swimming arms, went armed young men from both companies,

To test their strength in a small contest.

For the impending great crisis rehearsed its preliminaries

In the hazard of a modest encounter.

In the Macedonian camp occurred an event not unworthy of narration. [Note: [Col. 0553] “of being told.”]

*Nicanor and *Symachus [Note: [Col. 0553] “Symmachus.”] were alike in body and spirit;

One day, as was believed, had brought both of them into the world.

Equal labour in warfare and equal love bound them;

They entered into the hazards of war

As equals in gain [Note: [Col. 0553] “in.”] and loss. Whether ordered [Note: [Col. 0553] “sent.”] to roll rocks by artillery,

To hem in an enemy with ramparts, or break walls,

They advanced with shields joined. [Note: [Col. 0553] “press forward.”]

If sent to forage, to confine besieged men with trenches, to deceive

The enemy by night, to serve on watches, or to reconnoitre ambushes

Hidden in valleys—whatever dangers warfare might have set before them,

The enterprises [Note: [Col. 0553] “instabilities.”] of uncertain fortune

They bore in the companionable equality of body and spirit.

Therefore, with green spirits animated by youth,

They at last prepare to utter some great design conceived in their hearts.

And first *Symachus, keen in spirit, said: “Do you see, *Nicanor,

[Col. 0553C] How the glory of our unconquered king is held fast and totters

At this slight [Note: [Col. 0553] “slight.”] barrier of a river?

We must dare something which, having driven the enemy from the riverbank,

May crown us with the victorious laurel of our own valour;

Or, if the Fates threaten something, clothe us—our bodies stripped away—

In everlasting fame.” [Note: [Col. 0553] “bereft.”]

Hardly had he spoken when *Nicanor, snatching up the speech, himself said:

“This I have long conceived in silent thought, with the gods as witnesses.

But now there is no delay: let us be borne against the enemy,

Content with light arms.” Saying no more,

They gird themselves with swords and cast themselves into the rapid waters.

A lance floats behind them. A large band commits itself to the river under these two leaders.

When the neighbouring island received them, the sky resounded with confused shouts,

For the numerous enemy had already occupied the place described.

[Col. 0553D] The Indians meet them in a fierce encounter. Missiles fly like hail,

And sow [Note: [Col. 0553] “bear.”] many deaths through the empty air.

But *Symachus, who happened to have crossed over to the enemy first,

Attacks with sword drawn, and his companion *Nicanor

Strives hard to clothe the ground with many corpses.

Enough had now been done with missiles; the martial weapons were now red,

The river being marked with crimson drops.

The young men could now return with deserved [Note: [Col. 0553] “remarkable.”] praise,

[Vers. 4522.] But reckless valour is content with no measure.

[Col. 0554A] And while they exult over their defeated enemies, behold,

More Indians stealthily come upon the dying men.

Here was grief; here lamentation; the ruin of Greeks and Macedonians.

Androgeos falls, noble offspring of kings;

Fifteen renowned citizens perish,

Whom Greece mourned as taken away with prolonged grief. [Note: [Col. 0553] “chosen.”]

Only the brothers in spirit, not blood, remained—

Companions in life and soon to be in death, born in Greece.

When the surrounding shower of missiles pressed them,

They stood stunned in mind: what was to be done?

For the men had neither missiles nor lance, since both lay shattered bit by bit [Note: [Col. 0553] “therefore lie scattered.”]

Therefore, taking up the only weapons that remained, their swords,

They rush headlong against the enemy.

[Col. 0554B] But darts lodged in their tender limbs check their steps,

Nor were they permitted to perform the work of Mars at close quarters.

Therefore, because they see that the ultimate Fates now threaten them,

Each prays to die first

And fall before the other, for to behold his companion’s funeral

Would be crueler than every death.

So they throw themselves before one another, competing in turn

To postpone the other’s death, while each exposes himself.

Yet while this one protects that one and that one protects this one, [Note: [Col. 0553] “the other.”]

Behold, a fir-shaft launched by gigantic arms

Flies toward them and, in the midst of their efforts, [Note: [Col. 0553] “embraces.”] binds both fast

And pins them to the ground. Thus their undivided youth lies joined by one spear;

Yet love itself lasted no longer [Note: [Col. 0553] “lasting in it.”] than death.

[Col. 0554C] Amid embraces and kisses it departs; dying through both

Its own death and that of its companion, its body at last dissolving,

It passes [Note: [Col. 0553] “tends.”] by a narrow path to the Elysian fields.

The sight of his men’s victory raised the unconquered spirit of Porus

And did not compel Alexander, destroyer of kings [Note: [Col. 0553] “of kings.”] and despiser

Of every peril, to despair. Yet he ponders in his silent heart

By what art a crossing to Porus may be opened.

Among so many thousands, Attalus alone resembled the king,

Reproducing the Great One in face and body.

The king orders him to be dressed in royal garments,

To hold the bank and offer Porus the appearance

That the king remains there and is not further concerned

With the means by which a crossing is to be made.

[Col. 0554D] But the king, leaving the Macedonian station across the water,

Withdraws farther away, content with a few companions in order to deceive the enemy.

The gods aided the great commander’s bold plan. For a cloud spread [Note: [Col. 0553] “dark.”]

Over the world wrapped the elements in blind darkness,

And such gloom covered [Note: [Col. 0553] “held.”] the troops below

That one scarcely recognized the face of another speaking.

This cloud would have been a source of terror to others,

[Vers. 4572.] Since it was unknown how the fleet should be led across the water;

[Col. 0555A] But while the darker air frightened others,

The Macedonian, confident as though night had come by his own contrivance,

Orders the first ship, in which he was borne upon the waters,

To be pushed off [Note: [Col. 0555] “driven on.”] with its rowers embarked.

Without delay, the crowd of soldiers, launched upon the river in rivalry,

Follows its commander; arriving at a bank without enemies,

It takes up arms and rushes armed against the enemy.

Porus was still watching the other bank which he had first begun to guard,

Where Attalus, shining in royal dress, stood. [Note: [Col. 0555] “was standing.”] Then a messenger brings Porus word

That the ruler of the Macedonians and the crisis of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0555] “of affairs.”] are at hand.

Soon, after the brightened world had shaken off the clouds

And the opposing phalanx shone, struck by Phoebus,

Porus immediately sent against the enemy four thousand cavalry

And a hundred wagons crowded with bloodthirsty men,

[Col. 0555B] Who, scattering missiles widely like a storm-cloud, rained groans [Note: [Col. 0555] “groans.”] and death.

But because the violence of the rainstorm, having soaked the earth, had softened it,

And the plain was not ground fit for cavalry,

The heavy chariots by reason of their bulk [Note: [Col. 0555] “heavy.”] stuck in the soft ground and mud,

And the use of horses was less effective.

Conversely, the Macedonian, with his accustomed swiftness, vigorously charges among the Indians.

The light-wing follows the rushing force, and the hand is unsheathed.

A confusion of voices arises, and the blare of trumpets;

But on the other side beaten drums resound.

Wedges rushing to death rage on either side;

The two Sisters can scarcely spin sufficient mortal threads—the third cuts them. [Note: [Col. 0555] “cuts.”]

First to dare meet Alexander with loosened reins,

[Col. 0555C] Wearing out a panting [Note: [Col. 0555] “hesitating.”] elephant with spurs,

Enachides falls, pierced by the spear of Hiulton [Note: [Col. 0555] “Inachides”; “Hyulcon.”]

Through so many enemies set before him, invincible and tireless,

The martial hero forces a path toward Porus.

When Alexander saw him from afar, pressing the backs of elephants,

Like a citadel rising above subject walls, he said:

“At last I have found a contest worthy of wonder and equal to my own spirit.

Behold, I must deal with monsters, and with illustrious men besides.”

He spoke and turned [Note: [Col. 0555] “twists.”] his steps toward the left wing,

Where the heavier turmoil of war, as Porus fought, vexed the air.

The warrior Ariston follows; Polydamas rushes on;

Rubrius falls, struck by Ariston’s sword, and reddens the earth with his own blood.

Candaceus, thinking to overthrow Polydamas with a long spear,

[Col. 0555D] Is forestalled [Note: [Col. 0555] “girded.”] by the swift shaft of Glaucus,

Falls, and dying murmurs to the wet earth.

The Argive phalanx had now broken through the centre of the Indian host;

Their foremost strength being shaken, the Indian ranks wavered.

Then Porus ordered elephants, equal to great towers, driven against the cavalry force.

But this animal was slow, almost motionless in its gait,

And could not match the fleet courses of horses.

Therefore the light Macedonian force confronted it; after striking the enemy,

It escaped the blow with retreating reins.

[Vers. 4626.] [Col. 0556A] Nor was it possible to wage war with barbarian arrows,

For their bows were heavy and huge: unless first set against the ground,

Unless bent from below, they could not be drawn.

Now the Indians were rejecting Porus’s command;

as happens when ranks are wavering, fear, sharper than the commander’s orders, issues commands.

Some order the line thinned out, others the squadrons joined together,

Others again order a stand. Among the thousands there was not one

Who offered counsel in their midst. Yet Porus, having drawn up his line again,

Reassembles his scattered arms and sets the terrifying elephants before the enemy’s eyes.

The monsters struck no small terror [Note: [Col. 0555] “fear.”] into the Greeks;

Not only their trumpeting moved the horses, but the dreadful sound moved human ears,

And the trembling air was alarmed.

[Col. 0556B] And [Note: [Col. 0555] “but.”] now the terrible noise had thrown the ranks into disorder,

Their formation loosened; those lately victorious were preparing to turn their backs in flight,

When the Great One, seizing the sluggish Macedonian divisions,

Orders the Agrianian cavalry and Thracians to turn at once against the monsters.

Their courage immediately returns; fear of death laid aside,

Their valour grows in the opposing contest.

Hands empty their quivers, and the fatal arrow flying

Not without death [Note: [Col. 0555] “slaughter.”] makes men and monsters bloody.

While some, too eager and too incautious, [Note: [Col. 0555] “and incautiously.”] pursue,

Crushed beneath elephants’ feet, they leave their own

Certain warning to their comrades, that they should press on at once.

[Col. 0556C] For a long time the Macedonians’ battle was doubtful, and not without a great outlay

Of blood, until they began in unison to brandish axes

And cut with hooked iron the elephants’ solid feet

And shapeless limbs. [Note: [Col. 0555] “hands.”]

Wearied by javelins and at last oppressed by bloody wounds,

They charge in one simultaneous onset, and their riders tumble down.

Then indeed the frantic army flees, fear accompanying its retreat,

And abandons Porus, who scatters storm-clouds of missiles

And discharges darts from the high summit of his monster,

Alone as if in the middle of the sea.

But when he was pressed, assailed from every side,

Torn and failing from nine wounds, his charioteer, seeing the tyrant

Weak in limb, spurs the weary elephant

And turns it toward flight. Equal to a thunderbolt, the Macedonian wrath of God pursues the fugitive;

[Col. 0556D] But while he flees, Bucephal falls dead, pierced by a bloody rain

Of missiles; collapsing on failing knees, he fell more beneath the king than thrown down—

That noble *Bucephalus, alone worthy of so great a prince.

Soon afterwards the man of Pella founded a city called from his name.

Therefore, while the king changes horses and follows Porus and his men more slowly,

Taxiles’ brother—the ruler of the Indians, himself a king, but subject to him

[Vers. 4676.] Whom Fortune had made king of the world—

[Col. 0557A] Earnestly urges Porus to yield to Fortune

And entrust himself to so swift and favourable an enemy. [Note: [Col. 0557] “give himself.”]

But Porus, although his whole body was wasting away

And blood was failing him, nevertheless, under a favourable omen,

Roused at a familiar voice, said: “Are you not [Note: [Col. 0557] “are you.”] Taxiles’ brother—shame upon you!—

You who, a deserter, have betrayed me and your own dominion?”

He spoke, and hurled at the enemy the one weapon

Which had not yet fallen from his hands.

Caught in the young man’s breast, it burst through his back

And lulled his eyes in eternal sleep.

Porus again committed himself to flight, but the beast, wounded by many

Wounds [Note: [Col. 0557] “missiles.”], utterly failed and delivered him up on foot to the enemy.

The Great One, following him, thought the noble body [Note: [Col. 0557] “breast.”] dead and ordered it stripped;

[Col. 0557B] But the elephant began bitterly to attack [Note: [Col. 0557] “harass.”] those stripping him,

And again to set the half-dead man on its back. [Note: [Col. 0557] “back.”]

Until its vital organs, swollen within by many missiles, drove life forth.

But when the king saw Porus, whom he had thought delivered

To the peoples of Avernus, raise his eyes with lifted gaze,

Mercy conquered hatred.

“What madness, Porus,” he said, “drunk with frenzy, has perverted your senses?

When the fame of my achievements was known to you,

How did you dare, in such ruinous pride,

To meet me with standards drawn up?”

Porus replied: “Since you ask, I answer you

With as much freedom, Great One, as you granted me

By asking first. Before the evil of this contest,

[Col. 0557C] There was no man on earth whom I judged able to resist me,

Or equal to me in war or in mind. I knew my strength and my merit;

I had not yet experienced your fate and your power.

But the outcome of war taught me how much stronger you are.

Yet I seem to myself fortunate in being second to you, not in the least degree.

But do not on that account lift up your spirit because you have conquered.

I am an example to you: though I had been most brave, I found one braver.

Do not call him blessed who has that by which he may increase [Note: [Col. 0557] “increases.”]

Unless he has nothing by which he may decline.

It is better not to rise than to retreat after rising;

Better not to grow than to be diminished after increase.

The avaricious are more grievously tortured by remembering what they have lost

Than delighted by possessing it.

Therefore restrain your course with a bridle, [Note: [Col. 0557] “restrain your courses with a bridle.”]

For Fortune’s goods are perishable; she is ignorant of stable [Note: [Col. 0557] “and stable.”] favour.”

[Col. 0557D] The Macedonian marvels at a king unbroken by Fortune’s storm,

Whose conquered spirit possessed the spirit of a conqueror.

Therefore, restraining the anger of his altered heart,

Contrary to his nobles’ expectation, he generously cared for the sick man,

Cherished him when cured, and kindly admitted him

To the gatherings and number of his friends.

He bestowed more liberally and enlarged the boundaries of his former empire.

[Vers. 4729.] The enemy was received with such honour

[Col. 0558A] As he could scarcely have hoped for himself as a friend.

After magnanimous Porus, who had previously not known how to yield,

Had yielded to the Macedonians’ victorious arms,

The Macedonian rose in pride, to whom scarcely, with the stars yielding,

Had lavish Fortune granted so celebrated a triumph.

With Porus serving [Note: [Col. 0557] “intervening.”] him, he judged that the borders of the East stood open,

And hastened with loosened reins

To turn warfare against the remotest peoples of the world

And attach Ocean’s peoples to his camps.

Swifter therefore than the South Winds, he roams among Indian peoples and kings,

Subduing the farthest climates of the world.

He brings no less prodigy into human minds,

Nor less terror than the fire of nocturnal lightning, [Note: [Col. 0557] “flash of lightning.”]

Which is followed by crash and the collision of a shattered cloud,

[Col. 0558B] And wandering thunder, which moves the pallid mind of the world,

Terrifying it by remembrance of past guilt.

Nevertheless, the nation of the Sadracae [Note: [Col. 0557] Q. Curtius: “Oxytracae.”] dared resist fate

And the fame of the Macedonians, enclosing itself within the strong [Note: [Col. 0557] “strong.”] walls of a city,

Fearful of entrusting itself to uncertain Mars.

He orders ladders fitted, and, while the others hesitate, [Note: [Col. 0557] “those men.”]

The Macedonian is first to attack [Note: [Col. 0557] “escaped.”] the opposing wall, his head helmeted.

But the place was so narrow that the wall could scarcely contain him.

Thus he held the summit in such a way

That he clung more than stood, though he alone

Was assailed from towers by a thousand missiles. [Note: [Col. 0557] “from.”]

No Macedonian could come up the steps,

For a storm of missiles drove those climbing back from the mound.

At last shame and embarrassment overcame danger and the force

[Col. 0558C] Of missiles. [Note: [Col. 0557] “overcomes.”]

For delay in aid could compel the lingering man

To surrender himself perhaps either to death or to the enemy.

Therefore they hasten to climb in rivalry, life’s pledge laid aside,

But by hurrying they delay the assistance.

For while they compete to get up [Note: [Col. 0557] “attack.”], they overload the ladders;

When these break, the whole force, falling from above, collapses upon itself.

This compelled the Great One to despair of Macedonian hope,
