For he saw himself standing alone,

As though abandoned by them in a wilderness.

Already the hand which wielded his shield against blows,

Wearied, threatened to fail. His shouting companions now urged him

To leap back swiftly so that they might catch him. [Note: [Col. 0557] “and.”]

Then the king dared—marvellous to tell,

More than belief—to hurl himself in a winged leap headlong into the city,

[Col. 0558D] Full of savage barbarians.

The prince judged it unworthy of his divine design,

So renowned in titles, to show his back to the enemy.

One may ask whether in this deed he was brave or reckless.

But if you wish to join contraries:

He was both brave and reckless in this deed.

Though he could have been captured alive or slain before he arose,

Fortune powerfully shook off either outcome,

[Vers. 4781.] And [Note: [Col. 0557] “but.”] protected her foster-child in a wonderful manner.

[Col. 0559A] For the Macedonian had so balanced his body that he landed on his feet.

Standing, therefore, he began to provoke battle; and powerful Fortune

Had beforehand provided for the commander that he could not be killed [Note: [Col. 0559] “moved.”] by the enemy from behind.

For a laurel stood there with an age-old trunk,

As though born to defend the Macedonian leader with its ancient branches.

When his unconquerable body reached its trunk,

Heavenly vengeance held a shield around him, receiving the missiles’ blows.

Although all attacked this one man from a distance,

No one dared approach nearer or engage hand-to-hand.

The wide-spread fame of his fearsome name, already extended through the conquered world,

Fought for the leader; so did the great spur of despairing valour

And the opportunity for an honourable death.

But the shower of missiles had already pierced his shield,

[Col. 0559B] And his helmet lamented, broken by the storm [Note: [Col. 0559] “hail of missiles.”] of stones.

His slipping knees had given way, [Note: [Col. 0559] “had fallen.”] and, shaken by the burden

Of continual labour, could scarcely support

His noble body. When those standing nearer prepared to strip it,

The Great One met them with his sword so that two lay before him,

Their life fled, lifeless. Their deaths so frightened all

The Sadracae that thereafter no one dared attack the Great One

At close quarters with force joined.

Yet, holding his body up upon his knees, [Note: [Col. 0559] “held.”] exposed to every blow,

He defended himself without difficulty, like a tiger, with his sword,

Until an arrow flying through the air, daring its crime,

Ran into his right side.

At its entrance so much blood burst from the raw wound

That the king, shaken and distraught,

[Col. 0559C] Could not pull out the weapon with his trembling right hand.

Therefore, dying, he leaned the bloodless limbs of his afflicted body

Against the laurel and lowered his arms.

The Indian who had thrown the javelin ran up [Note: [Col. 0559] “ran down.”] eagerly,

Thinking the king lifeless and preparing to strip him.

When the Macedonian perceived him touching the royal body

With profane hand, he said: “Shame! Do you not know [Note: [Col. 0559] “me.”]

The leader of the Macedonians?” Saying no more, and recalling his failing spirit,

He stabbed [Note: [Col. 0559] “struck.”] the exposed side of the enemy with his raised sword

And joined him lifeless [Note: [Col. 0559] “bloodless.”] to his two companions.

“Such a one ought to go beneath the shades,” Alexander said;

“Be such a messenger to me.”

He spoke, and so that he might fight unconquered before

His sacred spirit burst forth into the thin air,

He tries to lift himself with his shield and the laurel’s branches.

[Col. 0559D] But unable even thus to carry forward his venerable body,

His knee failing, he falls again and challenges the enemy,

If anyone dares to fight with naked weapon [Note: [Col. 0559] “sword.”]

And carry away for himself the spoil of so great a victory. [Note: [Col. 0559] “thus.”]

At last Peucestes, following a different route along the wall,

Having driven off the city’s defenders, vigorously burst through

The opened entrances and barriers, arriving with sword drawn.

[Vers. 4834.] When the Macedonian beheld him with trembling gaze,

[Col. 0560A] Thinking that not life’s consolation but death’s companion had come,

He received his body upon his weakening shield. Then *Timaeus came up,

Then *Leonatus, and Ariston [Note: [Col. 0559] Q. Curtius: “Aristonus.”]

All these, set against [Note: [Col. 0559] “exposed to.”] the Indians, burn [Note: [Col. 0559] “were burning.”] with all their strength

To defend the king. But while alone they repelled so many thousands,

*Timaeus, illustrious in battle, fell; [Note: [Col. 0559] “illustrious.”]

Peucestes was wounded by a grave injury to the head;

Then *Leonatus, their weapons cast aside, lay

Before the king’s feet. All hope now rested solely in Ariston,

But he too, wounded by the onrushing Indians,

Could not restrain such great fury.

Meanwhile rumour carried to the Greeks that their commander had fallen within the walls.

Such a hard report would have broken others with fear,

But it roused them; forgetful of all peril,

[Col. 0560B] They broke down the wall with axes and made an entrance.

Despising danger of death, they made a path through the wall.

The crowd before them perishes everywhere; without distinction of sex or age,

All fall. Whoever meets them is deemed responsible for Alexander’s death or wound;

Nor did the pitiless sword lay down its anger

Until nothing was left surviving from the destruction

And the striking hand lacked an enemy.

Without delay the eager nobles run to care for the fallen man of Pella

And bring him back to camp, blaming the gods’ envy.

When his wound had been uncovered, Critobulus, great among physicians

In medical skill [Note: [Col. 0559] Q. Curtius: “Chritobolus.”], discovered that the king had been struck by a barbed spearpoint.

It could not be drawn out unless a skilful hand enlarged the wound by cutting;

And, lest the withdrawn iron cause an excessive flow

[Col. 0560C] Of blood, he feared with trembling mind.

Therefore, when he saw that fate threatened him with a dreadful consequence,

If he treated the king badly, and that disaster would recoil upon his own head,

He stood stunned at heart. When the king perceived him trembling in his clothing,

Drying [Note: [Col. 0559] “concealing.”] his tears and overcome in mind, he said:

“What are you waiting for? Since this wound is incurable,

Will you at least release me, who am to die, [Note: [Col. 0559] “perish.”] from slow death?

When you can help me by a swift death,

Do you fear being held guilty of this fate?”

At last, whether himself fearing nothing or concealing fear,

The physician humbly requested that Alexander offer his body to be held

While he pulled out the barbs of the weapon.

[Col. 0560D] For at the slightest movement, however small, there would be no small danger to life.

“No,” he said, “it is not fitting for a king to be bound;

It is not fitting, Critolaus, for him to be held.

Let the king’s power be free and always inviolate.”

So he spoke and, what one would scarcely dare believe, offered

His body unmoving; nor [Note: [Col. 0559] “not.”] did his face contract into signs

Or wrinkles of pain. But after the point had been driven out,

A greater flow of blood burst forth [Note: [Col. 0559] “flashed forth.”] from the opened wound.

[Vers. 4886.] Darkness spread [Note: [Col. 0559] “poured over.”] across his eyes, and such pain held his failing spirit suspended

[Col. 0561A] That, as though dying, he was scarcely caught by the friends [Note: [Col. 0561] “those very men.”]

Standing around him.

As soon as this was learned, tearful tumult arose throughout the camp,

And the Macedonian youth burst into lamentation,

All confessing that they lived by the life of one man.

The outcry did not cease until the physician, with skilled thumb

And healing herbs, checked the flow.

Only then was the Great One permitted to yield to sleep. [Note: [Col. 0561] “the Great One.”]

Only then, when the king’s recovery had been received throughout the camp,

Grief banished, lavish joy set feasts throughout all the troops,

Tables having been laid. [Note: [Col. 0561] “solemn observances.”]

As in the Aegean deep, while Boreas rages, a cry arises

When the master, his ship broken, rolls amid the waves,

His head submerged;

[Col. 0561B] There is a crash, and each man fears a like disaster,

And all confess that they have perished in one life.

Yet if they can draw him back safe with gripping hooks

To [Note: [Col. 0561] “and.”] the helm and restore [Note: [Col. 0561] “draw back.”] him,

The air resounds with joyful uproar, and new joys first conquer grief.

After a few days had passed since the Pellaean’s wound was treated [Note: [Col. 0561] “being treated.”]

While the scar had not yet formed and seemed able to produce a more grievous illness,

Yet impatient of delay, he prepares arms against the peoples beyond Ocean

And to bring swift sarissas against them.

Having subdued for himself the region where Phoebus rises,

He seeks the source of the Nile, unknown to mortals.

Porus and Abisaris [Note: [Col. 0561] Q. Curtius: “Abiasares.”], kings of the Indians, with Taxiles assisting,

[Col. 0561C] Are entrusted with preparing the fleet.

When this report filled the astonished ears of the soldiers,

And the nobles, weary, considered the king’s safety and their own,

All assemble at once as though drawn up in formation.

Noble Craterus brings prayers and entreaties to the king himself:

“Greatest of kings,” he says, “what limit or measure can there be

To your valour and hunger of mind, for which this vast world

Is not enough? If your own safety is worthless to you,

As now it is, or less dear, let the safety of your people

At least be precious to you, Great One. Every nation conspires against these throats;

Let the sea lie hidden beneath fleets;

Let every creature sharpen poisoned teeth,

Let every beast we meet have an unknown appearance;

Expose us to every danger of land and sea,

[Col. 0561D] Provided only that you preserve yourself, provided you take care to spare yourself.

As we always press toward new dangers, what god can keep us

Unconquered so often?

Things stand thus: no one is permitted always to remain

At one fixed degree. But which god would dare promise

That you, Macedonians’ star, will endure long?

Who can keep you safe for long, rushing over the world’s slippery paths?

[Vers. 4936.] Why do you expose yourself to evident

[Col. 0562A] Dangers in order to take an ignoble fortress?

When labour and reward are joined in an equal balance,

In equal causes rewards correspond to losses.

The fruit is usually sweeter and greater [Note: [Col. 0561] “better.”] in prosperity,

And consolation greater in adversity.

Henceforth be more sparing of yourself, for your own sake and ours.

Expose us to any monster, to ignoble war,

To base battles, to life’s obscure dangers.

Glory, however great, is cheapened by a contemptible enemy.

It is altogether unworthy that glory or valour should be spent [variant: *consumantur*, “should be spent”] upon them, where achievements won by much labour cannot be displayed. Ptolemy likewise, and the whole assembly [variant: *caetus*, “gathering”], with tears and broken voice, pleaded.

The piety of the son of Aeacus was not unwelcome to his followers; and thus he spoke: “I shall not prove in the least ungrateful to you, not merely because I know, nobles, that today you prefer my safety to your own; but because, from the beginning of my reign, or from the outbreak of the war, you have omitted no work of devotion toward me, no token of love. Yet my purpose is not wholly yours: for I do not wish to abandon what I have begun, or to end the war. My age does not contain me; nor do I measure myself by the span of age or the laws of life: my glory surpasses the bounds of a lifetime. This alone is the measure by which I wish your king to be measured.

“Men of base spirit and ignoble heart think the supreme good to be a long life; but I, sole king of the world, if I rightly reckon Fortune’s gifts or review my famous deeds well, have lived long—not by the number of my years, but by a thousand triumphs. I subdued Thrace [variant: Crete] and Asia. The world’s limit is close at hand; and, to speak without offending the gods, this globe is far too narrow, this expanse of earth does not suffice for one lord. Yet, after I have subjected this world, I have already resolved to open before you who follow me another world beyond it. Nothing is unconquerable for the brave. I hasten to penetrate the regions of the Antipodes and to behold another nature. Yet if you deny me arms, hands cannot fail me wherever I go. I believe myself to stand upon the stage of the whole world; unknown places and a populace ignoble in war I shall make famous by my wars; and, under such a leader, you shall tread lands hidden from nations and removed by nature. To these enterprises I have dedicated myself, nor do I reject the glory of ending my life in them, if Fortune so wills.”

He spoke, and summoned his companions to the ships; but they urged him to lead them wherever he wished. And behold, a sailors’ cry rises from the mouths of the river.

## Argument of the Tenth Book

In the tenth book, with a daring fleet, he troubles Ocean, a chaos infernal by nature; and he moves the citizens of Gehenna by their complaint and warning [variant: tears]. Great Alexander returns when Ocean has been conquered and, revolving wonders in his mind, proposes to break the western world by war. He prepares a voyage; but the terrified world flows together as one and worships Alexander with gifts sent to him. Though unconquered by the sword, he is overcome by poison acting as its servant [variant: by means of poison]; and, released from his clay-built body, his spirit at last, set free, vanishes into the airs of heaven.

## Book Ten

The west wind had offered starry countenances [variant: waves] and a river friendly to ships; and now, after leaving its anchorage, the sailor had driven his rising fleet farther onward, ignorant whither the course was tending, or how far the river, hitherto unknown to the peoples of Ocean, lay from Ocean.

Meanwhile Nature, recalling with enduring grief the prince’s insult, an insult common to the world and to herself—he who had called the circuit of the lands far too narrow—was preparing to reveal her secret regions to armed peoples. Suddenly disturbed, angry Hyle, her countenance made venerable by grey hair, breaks off her new work; and, troubled, she abandons the figures which she had begun to form and the various souls [variant: souls into various limbs] which she had begun to breathe into their bodies. Veiled in a cloud’s garment, she turns [variant: directs] her journey toward the Styx and the mysteries of the second world.

Wherever she bears herself, the elements give way; they rise before their maker, and the hovering air worships the entrance of her divinity. The earth’s luxuriance meets her with spring flowers; she makes the sea command its waves more gently than usual, and the swollen billows kept silence. All things worthily worship Nature and pray that she may multiply their crops, offspring, and seeds of things, increasing their heat with moisture poured in and mingled with it. Returning thanks to her followers, she commanded them to preserve their appointed limits and nowhere to exceed Nature’s bounds.

“I depart for the Styx [variant: descend],” she said, “to provide for myself and my own against Alexander, whose head earth and sea dread [variant: dreads] as the destroyer of us—the common scourge for you [variant: us].” So saying, she opens the dark clefts of the earth and enters Tartarus by a descending path.

Before the gates of Erebus, beneath the walls of the Stygian city, dwell the livid sisters, monsters of the earth. Among them their mother, in the dark caves of the others, hides her coffers and gulps down gold, melted in a thousand furnaces and poured into her parched jaws [variant: gulps it down]; nor can the blazing thirst of her insatiable ardour be filled.

Mocking the rest, Pride alone towers above all, scorning an equal, with blazing face. Lust lies submerged in burning mud; drained to the marrow, she twists and burns as far as her groin. Drunkenness is nauseated; dainty Gluttony licks greedily; and Beggary consumes her own limbs with bites. Wrath is forgetful of herself and, drunk, rushes wherever her impulse carries her, scourging herself and her companions. Treachery is the companion of Deceit; and Detraction, thin daughter of Envy, though unable to deny good deeds, tries by every means to distort them and diminishes praises which it is not lawful to conceal [variant: which it is not lawful to distort].

Here sits the plague of Hypocrisy, livid of face with wasting decay, and supreme Advancement in the court today—the plague of flattery, intent on instilling the soul’s deadly poison into the receptive ears of the powerful. So great a power has been granted to this fault of the court that it takes human ears away from the masters of affairs.

When the first mother of things, passing by, had seen these with a sidelong glance [variant: fixed her gaze upon them], she entered the city walls where she saw souls burning in eternal furnaces. There is a place sloping down into the furthest cavern of the abyss, hot with a perpetual furnace, where the avenging flame of Gehenna punishes crimes and guilty souls. Although one and the same fire scorches [variant: terrifies] them, its flames do not inflict equal punishments on all: these are tortured more lightly, those more fiercely. Thus Gehenna conforms itself to each person’s deserts, so that one who sinned more lightly [variant: in lighter matters] is subject to lighter penalties, while one who transgressed with graver guilt feels a more grievous fire.

There are some whose life, apart from the original parent’s slight transgression, suffered no stain, even a venial one. Upon these the fiery heat of punishment inflicts nothing, or little. Just as, in summer weather, harmful Sirius burns the fields, while beneath the same light of the sun the healthy person sports about, but the sick person is tormented and fevered.

There Leviathan, mingling the fires of everlasting death, stood in the furnace [variant: heat] at the middle of the abyss. When he saw the Divinity at a distance, he left the furnace and came toward her; but, lest he frighten her, he assumes the serpent’s face and returns to the first form which creating Nature had given him, when he swelled more brightly than the sun’s star and Pride raised his mind so high that he wished to share the highest Olympus.

When the goddess saw him, she said: “Father and avenger of crimes, you whose face, surpassing the light of morning Lucifer, Lucifer’s pride cast down from the citadel of heaven, I flee at last to you in my misery—to you whom I received, lest, when you had lost the stars, no dwelling at all should remain to you, at least in this night of the earth. To you I bring the common complaints of men and gods. For you know with what upheavals the warlike Macedonian harasses the elements: after subduing Pamphylian Ocean with his fleet, he conquered Darius three times, crushed [variant: shattered] all Asia, and compelled Porus, unconquered in war, to serve. Not content with that, he searches the eastern hiding places, and now, madman that he is, makes war even upon Ocean itself. If fate guides his sails with favourable winds, he prepares to trace the Nile’s source, remote from the world, and to surround Paradise with a completed siege. Unless you take precautions, he will not leave this chaos untouched, nor the retreats of the Antipodes; he wishes to behold the sun of another nature. Come then: avenge this common plague upon us. What is your glory, Serpent? What your renown? That you first drove man out, if so venerable a garden yields to Alexander?” Having said no more, she departed.

Following her with words, he promised his aid in every outcome and vowed not to desist until the public enemy had been joined [variant: plunged] to the darkness of Hell.

Without delay, he shook the shadowy city with a roar [variant: shadow] and called an assembly. There lies an ancient plain of evils, hardened by frost and wounded by snow, whose stubborn rigour neither sun nor softening breeze alleviates. Here guilty souls, scattered across the level ground, lie writhing in the agony of an unheard-of death. Their death is the inability to die: for those whose life was dead here in sin shall there have their death live forever in punishments. As one who lives here does not cease from sinning, so there he shall know no end of dying.

Afflicted [variants: bound; worn away] by ice, he passes from the cold of snows to burning coals—alas, a miserable punishment!—and the one tortured by the prison of Avernus always suffers and never dies.

When the satraps of Styx and the commanders of darkness had gathered and taken their seats, the ancient serpent uttered three hisses from his hoarse throat. By these he stilled every murmur and imposed silence upon infernal punishments, commanding the grievous lamentations of the shades to be mute. When he had suppressed their groans, he rose from his breast into their midst, set forth the goddess’s commands, and added:

“What limit, companions, will there be, what end to this scourge by which all things tremble, if a longer delay grants him leave to break the world at his pleasure? Behold—though I say it reluctantly—he prepares, once earth’s barrier has been broken, to penetrate Tartarean chaos; and, after conquering in war the lords of the shades, to lead the captive spirits away. Yet it is in the fates, what I abhor, that a time shall come when a new man, born upon earth with some strange novelty of birth—I know not who—will shatter this prison’s iron bars after its pillars have been overthrown. Plundering its vessels and its strong armour, a stronger man will ravage our halls with triumphant wood. Therefore, commanders of death, meet death as it is born [variant: disease], and bar life with death to the king of the Macedonians, lest he perhaps become the future conqueror of Hell.”

He had scarcely belched forth these words when Treachery arose with a flattering, deceitful expression. “This task,” she said, “is very easy for me. I possess a deadly poison surpassing all poisons, which neither earthenware nor a cast-metal pot nor glass nor any other vessel can contain, except the hoof of a horn-footed animal alone. This liquid, mixed with Falernian wine, will be given to Alexander; the opportunity is at hand. For my Antipater, governor of the Macedonians, skilled from his cradle’s tears in feigning affection with his voice while concealing [variant: displaying] hatred in his inmost heart, is preparing to go to Babylon to the king, summoned by the king himself, that under him he may spend his old age and, though a veteran, again endure the harsh burdens of military life [variant: of a female veteran]. I, if I am a goddess more powerful than any among the children of Night, if you know me well as your foster-child, will rise to the upper world, poison in attendance [variant: through poison’s agency], to give the deadly draught to the leader.”

So she spoke. The entire shadowy host shouted as one; every member of the provident council praised her because [variant: since] she so zealously prepared to break, by an armed draught, one unconquered [variant: unbroken] in war.

Without delay Treachery, changing her ancient appearance, emerged from the darkness and, borne through Sicilian air upon poisoned wings, at last entered her foster-child’s chamber. Leaving him well furnished with seductive speech, she returned to eternal chaos and her accustomed cities [variant: shades].

For the Pellaean had broken resistant Ocean with his threatening fleet and, now victorious over Ocean despite its indignant waves, was preparing to return to Babylon. Wretched and ignorant of the future, he intended, after arranging the affairs of Asia, to transfer his sarissas to the borders of the Carthaginians; then, after subduing the Libyan territories, to advance beyond the Spanish bounds where report said Hercules’ pillars stood, and to bring the western sun beneath his rule by war.

After these nations had been subdued, he dared to conceive, in the citadel of his thirsty mind, the desire thereafter to cross the Pyrenees, conquer by arms the rebellious peoples of Gaul, and add the Rhine to the conquered. Then at last he planned, after casting aside the Alps, to revisit his native land and Macedonia’s borders, and to make Italy and, within it, Rome serve him—to teach Rome to bear the Greek yoke. Therefore he ordered the governors to seek timber for a fleet to be built in Syria. Lebanon grieves as its lofty cedars fall, and its green ash trees are drawn down to the waves [variant: driven by force].

Every forest falls for the fleet. The earth, stripped of its tree-like locks and everlasting shade, marvels at the sky [variant: bronze], and at its summits, laid bare, marvels at the new sun.

Where does your hunger lead, Alexander? What is the end of possessing? What end will there be to seeking, what limit to toil? [Variant: “what measure or what …”] You accomplish nothing, madman: even if you enclosed all kingdoms beneath one rule and subjugated the whole world, you would always be needy. Things do not make the mind free of want, but sufficiency does; however little one has, if it is enough, one will lack nothing.

O man easily deceived! While he prepares arms, poison is prepared [variant: “while he prepares arms, poison is being prepared”] for his destruction, poison that shall check his arms [variant: “that shall check them”]. The young man’s greedy thirst grows, but one draught will overwhelm so great a thirst [variant: poison]. For that wicked traitor [variant: wicked men], Antipater, instructed by these counsels and carried by adverse winds, had come to Babylon, where he plotted the bitter crime with patricides and his accomplices.

What madness, gods above? What are you doing, Fortune? Will you allow your foster-child, protected so often, to perish? If you cannot change fate’s decrees that the Macedonian should die, at least reveal the secrets of his executioners. You can turn the agents of death and change the kind of fate [variant: death]: turn poison into a sword. He who offended more than all others ought more fittingly and honourably to die by arms. Yet perhaps the gods could not openly conquer by weapons the man whom deadly poison could conquer in secret. Therefore it was more fitting that he should experience hidden crime than yield to the sword.

Still, in order that before the last day which the fates prepared he might see all kingdoms subject to him, the sound of fame and Fortune made him monarch.

For such terror and consternation seized the remaining nations that, after all the peoples of the East had been subdued, every nation trembled to its marrow and every distant island enclosed by the wave-tossed tide was afraid. Therefore embassies from the whole world, bringing gifts intended to turn the tyrant from his course, hastened to the sea under full sail.

The citadels of Carthage do not disdain to be subjected to Alexander’s rule; all Africa too, setting aside resistance, writes that it is ready to serve him. Spain, though secure in position and mighty in many wars, writes the same, constrained by fear alone. All Gaul worships the terrible king by sending a diadem—a thing I can scarcely bear to believe. The Rhine’s fury grows mild and, abandoning its harshness [variant: fury], the German advances upon Babylon, mingled with the Sicambrian.

No lesser fear seized the peoples of Italy and compelled them to serve. Although Nature sets snowy cliffs in the way on one side, and the barrier of the continuous sea protects it on the other, Italy believes nothing impossible for Alexander and anticipates the king’s anger of her own accord. Sicily commands its mountains and lakes of the underworld to serve Philip’s son, writes to him, and seeks by gifts to appease him. But why delay? Every nation hastens together and, carried over the sea, seeks illustrious Babylon and its citadels [variant: “the illustrious citadels of Babylon, and …”]. There one might see ambassadors streaming in, ships laden with objects of value, and herds of four-footed beasts—so many that one could scarcely believe the swift breath of rumour had reached them.

When Alexander learned that the frightened world had assembled as one [variant: because] and was awaiting [variant: watching for] his arrival, he burned to approach the place of death and, swiftly rowing, hastened with his fleet toward Semiramis’ city. Not otherwise does a tiger, on seeing a herd of horses from afar, whose fierce thirst parches [variant: burns] its lightning-swift jaws, spring forth when hunger urges it; mercilessly it drinks living blood and absorbs the torn limbs. If then a hunter following it along a secret path pierces it with his spear point, it cries out and, thirsty and not yet sated with blood, dies stretched over the grass.

Now, alas, the Pellaean, surrounded by a square formation of troops, entered the fateful citadel. Behold, a throng shining in wondrous splendour met him. The nobles came forward; accompanied by them, he entered the lofty city, assumed the insignia of kingship, and ordered the ambassadors admitted. Ascending the throne as an established monarch, conqueror over a conquered world, he received the gifts sent to him: the shield which Gaul had sent, embroidered with gems; the helmet, burning above with red gold, which Carthage had sent; the German sword that seemed to thirst for blood; the horse sent by Spain, foam-flecked at the lips, its limbs marked in varied colours, champing its golden bit with worn wolf’s-teeth.

A Sicilian tyrant presents a cuirass, interwoven with twisted silver rings by the fingers of the Cyclopes. Yet, beyond these gifts, as many crowns of kings as there are kingdoms in the world proclaimed him king. Here were garments of diverse peoples; here purple woven in countless marvellous patterns; here whatever anywhere could be found to attract the mind or delight mortal eyes by its appearance—all metals and the brilliance of stones. In short [variant: “in few words”], the riches of the whole world were joined [variant: added] to these.

Receiving them, he said: “Thanks be to the gods, through whose favour kingdoms have been won for me and cities which we have not yet seen are already being triumphed over [variant: have been triumphed over]. No lesser gratitude is owed to heaven by you [variants: by us; glory] because, without the clash of wars and without expenditure of our [variant: your] blood, before you have experienced Macedonian combat at close quarters, you have yielded to our rein. Had Darius, after laying down his diadem, entrusted himself to me as a suppliant when he received his portion of the kingdoms, he would have discovered that nothing is gentler than this yoke. Porus is an example of the gentleness with which I, the conqueror, govern the conquered. I wish those mortals subject to me—those who voluntarily obey, whom no force compelled to bear our yoke—to live with liberty preserved, so that service to me is no longer servitude but liberty. There will be no distinction of freedom among those of whom none is rebellious.”

Having spoken briefly to the ambassadors, he turned to those by whose outstanding valour he had subdued the world:

“You too, conquerors, whose arduous labour has brought it about that earth is silent in our sight, have worthy rewards awaiting you. The soldier is most worthy of Hercules, mine under this king; but this king is also worthy of such a soldier [variant: this soldier], whom neither winter broke with icy regions nor the heat at Libya’s centre rendered numb. Macedonian companies conquered [variant: saw] the Indian deserts, subdued by these our [variant: your] hands, their monsters lamenting. Why recount the triple triumph while Darius lived? Memnon cast down, and the arms of Porus and Taxiles? Why say that shapeless giants yielded to us [variant: you]?

“Now, since nothing remains to be done in this world, lest our use of arms, long accustomed to war, should languish, come [variant: I pray], let us seek the peoples of the Antipodes lying beneath another sun, lest our [variant: your] glory or valour leave anything untried by which it may grow, or by which it may deserve the songs of everlasting poetry. With me as leader, no land will be inaccessible to my men. Labour conquers all; nothing is beyond the brave person’s exploration. The teaching of the ancients reports that there are several worlds. Woe is me, who have not yet subdued one out of many.

“For you know, companions, that when Rome once sent me a royal diadem through Aemilius and wrote to me as to a king, it now exceeds the agreement of the treaty, standing against me with its horns restored. Therefore, lest any part remain untouched by our triumphs and lest completeness be lacking to my titles, I have decided first of all to destroy Rome.”

When he had said this, he dissolved the council, as Phoebus’ chariot was now sloping downward in its weary course.

Already the wheel of the fiery sun had plunged into the wave-resounding waters of the sea, and precipitous night had confounded all the elements in its dark mass. A gloom more mournful than usual, together with rising clouds, held back the stars that wished to come forth into the light, the moon, and the stars appointed to rule the night [variant: *nocti praeesse*, “to rule the night”].

That night the sailor, seeking Cynosura, now Helice, and the Wain forbidden to sink beneath the sea—since nowhere did he dare turn his course without a star—lay hidden in the midst of the deep while his prow drifted. All things mourned Alexander’s funeral, foretelling his coming death; Olympus wept for one who would die, though it had recently foretold his birth by such signs.

True stones fell from heaven; in Egypt a lamb spoke; a hen bore a dragon. And, unless popular report lies falsely in an opinion worthy of belief, on the day the queen gave birth to twins, eagles fought in formation above her father’s house and roof. Thus was the Macedonian marked from birth by so many prodigies. Gods above, by what crime did he earn your favour for so brief a life?

But had he been content with mortal honour; had he conducted himself humbly amid prosperity; had he borne Fortune’s sweet gifts as he bore her bitter ones: perhaps, by fate’s disposition, he would have avoided both the sword and poison more cruel than every sword.

Now, when the night was ended, sluggish Boötes turned his weary chariot, and the infancy of tender light had lulled the darkness. Yet even at light’s rising the dewy moisture of dawn did not fall upon the grass; birds under the trembling branches did not precede the day with song. Philomela, foreknowing the coming grief, held back the lyre of her love-bearing voice. They say that Lucifer was the first to yield to the coming day; while the other stars had not yet yielded, he first turned, in a reversal, toward the shores of the western sea, bent low and faint in dullness [variant: grew faint again].

Then at last [variant: but at last], though reluctant—because Titan could not delay the fates—he raised his ray-armed head from Nabataean waters. Unless the provident sequence of fate had prevented him, he threatened with all his might to turn his chariot round and return [variants: with the yoke turned; return journey].

“Stay your step, venerable father of light and fire; stay your step. Unless you turn back the day-bearing globe, the lamp of Macedon will extinguish your lamp, Phoebus.”

But the fated hour had now come to plunge the head of the great-hearted ruler into death; fate would not allow the crime, and the world’s ruin, to be delayed any longer.

The palace was fragrant with eastern scents [variant: shone], where the people and sacred order of nobles had assembled. Much of the day was spent with them in conversation; then at last, when he was honoured [variant: when they were honoured] by the leader with rich gifts, he ordered wines to be carried round by servants enriched [variant: servants]. He who had so often, secure from the enemy, scattered hostile weapons in wars [variant: battle], father and lord alike, falls and dies among his friends.

His whole body stiffened with sudden paralysis; scarcely master of himself, he was restored to the bed with bent knee. Immediately the entire palace was shaken by deadly tumult. Yet they did not dare publicly to express their grief, because they hoped that Fortune’s remedy would be at hand—a remedy which had always been accustomed to attend those falling into every calamity.

Therefore, when the poison had infected his veins and his pulse gave sure signs of approaching death, he ordered a bed prepared for himself in the midst of the hall. When the distraught army gathered there, along with the illustrious company of commanders mingled with the common crowd, he looked upon them as they surged with tears and tore their faces with their nails.

“When I have departed from the earth,” he said, “who will find one worthy of such men? It is now enough for me to have ruled the world. Under this sky Fortune’s favourable cast has attended those who obey in war. It may now weary me that this soul is enclosed in mortal limbs. I have spent time and age enough; devoted to human affairs, I have clung long enough among mortals. Thus far, these things. Henceforth I shall rule the highest Olympus; I am called to greater things. The lofty heaven calls me, that, having received a royal throne and seat among the stars, I may arrange with Jupiter the hidden workings of affairs and the brief outcomes of men, and transact the business of the gods in heaven’s citadels and among the host of heaven.

“Perhaps presumption arms the brothers of Etna, and rugged Pelorus has loosened Enceladus’ limbs [variant: Typhoeus has loosened them]. Under decrepit Jupiter, they believe that the gods and stars can be easily seized, and they try again to assail them. Since Mars abhors the hazards of war without me, by the counsel of Jupiter and the gods, though I myself resist, I am dragged unwillingly to kingship.”

Thus he spoke; and with lamentation and flowing tears they urgently asked whom he wished to leave as heir and king of the world. “Let the best and most worthy of rule,” he said, “be your king.” But after his voice failed him, he gave Perdiccas the ring removed from his finger. From this the commanders inferred that he wished Perdiccas to succeed him as supreme king in the full sovereignty of the kingdom [variant: “in the kingdom’s supreme power”].

Without delay vital warmth abandoned his body, released by death’s chill; and at last his spirit, breaking out from its clay prison, passed into the thin air. Then grief was loosed in bitter mourning; then lamentations recovered their force, and the agitated crowd no longer suppressed their dreadful uproar. Not so great a crash stirs the stars when the four brothers shake the star-bearing axis by hurling thunderbolts.

O happy mortal race, if it always held eternal good in mind and feared the end, which comes unexpectedly to noble and common alike, amid great peril to the soul—while wealth is sought, while the deceptive glory of things flutters about mortal eyes on vain wings; while we seek fleeting honours which are now sold; while we sweep the sea’s waves and, weary of life, commit both our lives and our wealth [variant: “that wealth”] to swollen waters.

And when, anxious to see the Roman citadels, the walls of greedy Rome, through Alpine winters and bands of robbers, we perhaps return by a fortunate course to our native soil and our fatherland’s city [variant: “return to our native world”], behold: the onset of sudden and slight fever destroys everything which we have prepared through a whole lifetime.

Alexander is an example. For him the world had not sufficed; yet the earth suffices, a house of five feet made from marble cut from the quarry, where his noble body rested in little soil until Ptolemy—into whose portion Egypt is said by law to have passed [variant: fallen]—transferred that deposit of dreaded fate, venerable throughout the world, to the city named after its ruler.

But now Phoebus, about to plunge the day into night with headlong light, turns his panting course toward the waters. Enough of play: it is time to break off the game, Pierian Muses. Henceforth let your songs attract other minds; I seek another spring, which, once thirst has been exhausted, may be the medicine of a second thirst.

But you, great bishop, whose abundance from a full horn has poured out help for me, so that I might despise hostile tongues, receive Walter’s devoted labour. Do not disdain that this poet’s ivy should be joined about your sacred mitre.

For although the poem is unworthy of so great a bishop, yet when the spirit has put off its mortal limbs, we shall live together; and with the poet the glory of William shall live on, never to die through any age.

The Engelberg manuscript concludes the work thus: “Here ends the *Alexandreis* of Master Walter of Châtillon. This book was written in the year of the Lord 1277.”

## Appendix to Walter of Châtillon

### A Treatise on the Trinity, by Galtherus, an Ancient Theologian

(D. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, II, II, 51, from a manuscript of the monastery of St Peter at Salzburg.) (G)*

## Notice
This distinguished treatise, *On the Trinity*, by Galtherus was brought to our attention by the library of Saint Peter’s at Salzburg, exceedingly rich in ancient books, in a quarto parchment manuscript about five hundred years old. For our benefit it was copied from that manuscript by the Reverend Father Michael Bockn, the learned librarian of the place and brother of Placidus. We cannot determine anything certain concerning the author, since a great number of learned men distinguished by the names Gualterus, Galtherus, and Waltherus lived in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries of Christ, about which time he can scarcely be doubted to have flourished.

Yet, to offer at least a conjecture, Galtherus, the author of the present treatise *On the Trinity*, seems not to be distinct from Gualterus of Châtillon, provost of the canons of Tournai, whose three little books of dialogues against the Jews Casimir Oudin published from a manuscript of the abbey of Saint Evodius at Brana, in his *Sacred Minor Works of Certain Ancient Writers of France and Belgium*, at Leiden in 1692. For nothing occurs in our treatise incompatible with the period, learning, style, or rank of Gualterus of Châtillon.

Our conjecture is in some measure confirmed by the Saint Peter manuscript, in which the work is entitled only as follows: “Treatise of Master Galtherus on the Trinity.” And at the end: “Here ends the treatise on the most holy Trinity, indeed composed by Master Galtherus.” In nearly the same way Oudin has: “Here begins the Treatise, or Dialogue, of Master Gualterus of Tournai against the Jews.” John of Salisbury, moreover, throughout his letters calls Gualterus of Châtillon simply “Master Gualterus of Lille” and “Master Gualterus,” as may be seen in the Oudin cited above. Thus the title *Master* appears to have adhered to Gualterus of Châtillon by some special usage and prerogative distinguishing him from other Gualteri of the same name.

Accordingly, if this conjecture has any truth, the date of our Galtherus can readily be determined from those who write that Gualterus of Châtillon died in 1201. Yet, because we ourselves clearly perceive the weakness of our arguments, we think it preferable to leave the entire matter undecided.

Whoever our Galtherus may finally have been, he seems to have composed his little work chiefly against those who maintained that in God there are certain properties or relations which are not identical with God, but are realities other than the divine substance. In Chapter IV he refutes them by authority and reason. In the following chapter he was unwilling to pass over the profane innovations of certain persons:

> Their folly supposes that the divine power, wisdom, and goodness must be distinguished, assigning omnipotence to the Father alone, wisdom to the Son alone, and goodness to the Holy Spirit alone. It is evident that this was devised by men unlearned and almost wholly ignorant of the truth.

Then, after certain further remarks, he adds:

> Therefore omnipotence belongs to all three, wisdom to all three, and goodness to all three. It is astonishing how those senseless men dare, against so many authorities agreeing in this truth, to introduce their errors. It is not enough for them to lie with impunity against the truth of the Catholic faith; among an unlettered populace they even glory in making their name notorious through their fabrications, further adding that they fully know that, in the unity of the divine substance, there is the begetting of the Son by the Father and the procession of the Holy Spirit from both, etc.

Finally, Galtherus concludes and repeatedly insists—as he does elsewhere—that no one ought to possess such madness as to attempt to comprehend this incomprehensible secret of the divine nature by the acuteness of his own intellect, and, as though he had comprehended it, presumptuously to expound it to others with boastfulness. Conversely, no one should be so obstinate as to refuse belief because he does not fully understand the unfathomable mysteries of the holy Trinity. Rather, he says:

> Whoever begins to doubt because he does not understand should have recourse to the authorities mentioned above, which affirm that no one in this life possesses perfect knowledge of God. Instructed by them, let him begin to believe concerning God what Peter believed. Peter’s shadow healed the sick, as did other martyrs and confessors, whose holiness became known not only in life but also after death through incomparable miracles.

If it should happen that a Jew or heretic attacks Catholic truth concerning the divine substance—which transcends all things ineffably—by dialectical arguments devised according to the ordinary course of nature and customary uses of words, then, although Catholics cannot refute him by human reasoning, he should nevertheless remain steadfast in the faith fortified by such great authorities, remembering that a faith to which human reason supplies proof has no merit.

These are Galtherus’s words, than which nothing more salutary could have been prescribed in so difficult a question.

We further inform the learned reader that, only after this portion had already been printed, we discovered two manuscript copies of the same little work in the library of Melk; in both of them, however, the name Galtherus is absent. The first is in a fifteenth-century quarto paper manuscript, marked Q, 4. It begins: “Here begins a useful treatise on the Trinity of persons and unity of essence in the Godhead: *I believe that there is one God*, etc.” It ends: “Here ends a most useful and Catholic treatise on the most blessed Trinity.” The other is in a twelvemo paper manuscript, marked II, 44. Its scribe, John of Wailhaim of Melk, an exact and learned man, adds that the author of this most useful and Catholic treatise is unknown, and that the exemplar from which he copied it in 1469 bore no prefixed title. Had these facts been known to us earlier, we would not have omitted to collect variant readings from both manuscripts. But now that the matter is no longer open to revision, we note only this: in Chapter VIII, after the beginning, where the printed text has *sunt essentialia* (“they are essential”), we correctly suspected that the reading should be *sunt enuntiabilia* (“they are predicable”), a reading retained by both Melk manuscripts.

# HERE BEGINS THE TREATISE OF MASTER GALTHERUS ON THE TRINITY

[Col. 0575]

## CHAPTER I. God is one, incorporeal, almighty, eternal, creator of all things, immutable, immeasurable, simple, wise, and just; and he is so essentially, not by some accidental quality.

[Col. 0575A]

I believe without doubt that there is one God and not many, [Col. 0576A] according to Moses: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord God is one” (Deut. VI). I believe him incorporeal, according to that evangelical saying of John: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John IV).

I believe also that he is almighty, [Col. 0577A] according to the Psalmist: “Whatever he willed, he did” (Ps. CXIII). And according to the Apostle: “Who resists his will?” (Rom. IX). I believe him also eternal and the creator of all things, according to: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I); and: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. XVIII).

I believe him immutable, according to the Psalmist: “You will change them and they shall be changed; but you are the same” (Ps. CI); and according to James the Apostle: “With him there is no change or shadow of turning” (Jas. I). I believe him everywhere present, wholly present essentially everywhere, according to: “If I descend into hell, you are there; if I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Ps. CXXXVIII); and the prophet’s words: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII).

I believe him also simple, [Col. 0577B] incapable of receiving anything extrinsic, and containing within himself nothing divided from his own substance. For although he is wise and just and is designated by other names which, when we speak of a human being, state distinct properties, nevertheless by these names we affirm of God nothing other than the divine essence. In God wisdom or justice is nothing other than the divine substance. Thus God is called not merely wise, but Wisdom itself.

When we hear, “God is wise; God is wisdom,” we understand the same thing by the differing expressions. Yet when it is said, “God is wise; God is just; God is merciful,” we seem to conceive differing meanings, not because there are distinct properties in God—for there are none—but because of the differing effects [Col. 0577C] which God works in creatures. For when we hear that God is wise, we infer that he has never done anything except with the highest reason. When we hear that God is just, we observe that he judges justly and not laxly. When we hear that God is merciful, we perceive that he grants pardon mercifully.

## CHAPTER II. In the unity of the divine substance there are three persons, or hypostases: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Moreover, I confess that in the unity of that divine substance there are three persons, or, as the Greeks say, three subsisting *hypostases*, of whom one is called Father, another Son, and another Holy Spirit. Many testimonies concerning the existence [Col. 0577D] and plurality of these persons are found in the sacred Scriptures of both the New and Old Testaments.

Of the Father and Son the Psalmist says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; this day I have begotten you” (Ps. II). Of the Son—that is, the wisdom of the Father—the Proverbs of Solomon say: “I was already conceived, and the fountains of waters had not yet broken forth; before the hills I was brought forth; he had not yet made the earth” (Prov. VIII). Of the Holy Spirit Genesis says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. I).

Of the Father and Son, John’s Gospel says: “For the Father loves the Son and shows him all things” (John V). Of the Holy Spirit, the same Gospel says: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John XIV).

This Trinity is [Col. 0578A] one God, the same God, and the same substance, though Arius contradicts this. The Lord shows it in the Gospel when he says: “I and the Father are one” (John X). John says in his Epistle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one” (I John V).

Yet it must be believed most firmly that there are three persons, of whom one is not another. Although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same in substance, the Father is not the Son, nor is he the Holy Spirit; nor is the Son the Holy Spirit. Rather, the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. This opposes the Sabellian heresy, which asserts three names and one sole person, and that the same person is Father, Son, and [Col. 0578B] Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER III. The Father is from no one; the Son is begotten by the Father and proceeds from him; the Holy Spirit proceeds—not by generation—from the Father and the Son.

From the authorities cited above it is therefore unquestionably clear that the whole Godhead has one substance and that there are three persons of one substance; or, as the Greeks say, three *homoousion* hypostases—hypostases “of the same substance.”

Concerning the nature of these persons, one should know that the Father is from no one, but the Son and Holy Spirit are from the Father. The Son is from the Father by being born and by proceeding. The Psalmist bears witness to the Son’s begetting by the Father: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CIX). That he proceeds from the Father is shown by his own words: “I proceeded from God and came” (John VIII).

But the Holy Spirit is from the Father [Col. 0578C] not by being born, but by proceeding; for both proceed from the Father, though in ineffable and dissimilar ways. That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father is shown by the Lord’s words: “The Paraclete, whom I shall send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV).

Nor does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father alone, but also from the Son, according to the Gospel: “Power went forth from him and healed them all” (Luke VI). For that power was none other than the Holy Spirit, who proceeded from him and bestowed healing upon all. Thus the Holy Spirit is from both, not by being born but by proceeding; therefore he is neither the Father’s nor the Son’s Son, but is the Spirit of both.

That the Holy Spirit [Col. 0578D] belongs to both is confirmed by these other testimonies. The Lord says in Matthew’s Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X). The Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII). And elsewhere: “The Lord sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV).

## CHAPTER IV. The Father has from no one what he has. The Son has all that is his from the Father. Whatever the Holy Spirit has, he has from the Father and the Son, not by grace but naturally; yet it does not follow that there is any inferiority among the divine persons.

Just as the Father is from no one, so he has from no one whatever he has. But whatever the Son has, [Col. 0579A] he has from the Father, and likewise the Holy Spirit. For from the Father—from whom he has his being—he also has all that he has. The Son says in Matthew’s Gospel: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. XI). And in John’s Gospel: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John V).

The Holy Spirit has from the Father not only what he has, but also from the Son, from whom, like the Father, he has being. That the Holy Spirit has from another what he has is read in John’s Gospel in this way: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John XVI).

Whatever the Son and Holy Spirit have, they have naturally, [Col. 0579B] and not by grace. For if they had it by grace, they would already be inferior to the Father, by whose grace and benefit they possessed it. But although the Son says, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV)—which must be referred to his human nature—nevertheless, according to his divine nature, the Son is equal to the Father. The Apostle says: “Being in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Phil. II). Therefore, insofar as he is God, the Son is equal to the Father.

There is such equality in the most holy Trinity that no person in it is greater than another, nor are all three together greater than one alone. Anyone may observe this who, accepting the foregoing on faith, believes each of those three persons to be the simple substance of God, and [Col. 0579C] believes the three together to be one and the same simple substance.

The Son is also coeternal with the Father. Though he is from the Father, just as brightness is from fire, he is nevertheless coeval with the fire. He is also God and Creator, as is the Father, according to John the Evangelist: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). And shortly afterward: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (ibid.). Solomon’s Proverbs say of the Father’s Wisdom, that is, of the Son: “When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when he established the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things” (Prov. VIII).

Likewise, the Holy Spirit is equal and coeternal with the Father and Son; he is God and Creator. Of him it is written in Job: [Col. 0579D] “The Spirit of the Lord made me” (Job XXXIII); and elsewhere: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job XXVI). It is therefore clear that the Son, although from the Father, is true and perfect God: God from God the Father, light from light, principle from principle, wisdom from wisdom. All these things may truly be said also of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER V. The whole Trinity, and its operation outwardly, is entirely inseparable; whatever one person works, the others work also. Objections to this doctrine are resolved.

Moreover, every believer must firmly believe the foregoing statements concerning the most holy Trinity: because the Trinity is of one [Col. 0580A] substance, it is wholly inseparable. This is attested by the Lord’s words to Philip: “Do you not know that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John XIV). From these words we recognize not only that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot be separated from one another by any distance whatever, but also that the Father is in the Son and each person is in the other.

As the whole Trinity is inseparable, so its every operation is inseparable. Whatever the Father works, the Son and Holy Spirit entirely work as well. This is declared concerning Father and Son in John’s Gospel: “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John V). The Psalmist testifies that the Son and Holy Spirit worked inseparably with the Father, who created all things, in making [Col. 0580B] creatures: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXXII). Thus whatever one works, another works also.

But someone wishing to undermine this unity objects: “If the Trinity works inseparably, then the Son begot himself, because the Father begot the Son; and the Father proceeds from another, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from another.”

The answer to this objection is that God is said to work only in relation to a creature. Therefore, the begetting of the Son and the proceeding of a divine person from another are not operations. For if the Father’s begetting of the Son were an operation, it would follow that the Son worked it as well, or it would be false that the Son works all that the Father works.

[Col. 0580C]

Again it is objected: “If the Trinity is inseparable and works inseparably, then the Father and Holy Spirit assumed flesh and were incarnate, because the Son assumed flesh and was incarnate.”

The answer is that although the Trinity is inseparable and works inseparably, something belongs to one of the persons which does not at all belong to the others. This may be recognized from a likeness found in creatures themselves. In a sunbeam brightness and heat are inseparably joined; heat expands and brightness illuminates. Likewise, in producing sound on a lyre, the hand works inseparably while striking, and the string while being struck; yet one thing belongs to the hand and another to the string. The hand alone strikes, [Col. 0580D] and the string alone resounds.

Thus in the holy Trinity each person worked the incarnation of the Son, yet that operation and the assumption of flesh belong to the Son alone. Someone may, however, be troubled because Scripture also says that Christ was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit, as though assigning the work of incarnation—worked by the whole Trinity—to the Holy Spirit alone.

But one should know that, although the Holy Spirit is God and consubstantial with the Father and Son, he is nevertheless the gift of both. Therefore, so that it might be evident that the Son of God assumed flesh by the grace and gift of God, not on account of human merits, divine Scripture provided instruction for us by saying that Christ was born of the Holy Spirit as the incarnate gift of God.

It is sufficiently evident from the preceding comparison [Col. 0581A] that, although the Trinity works inseparably, the Son alone assumed flesh; just as the Holy Spirit alone appeared in the form of a dove, and the voice of the Father alone was heard saying to the Son: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII).

## CHAPTER VI. Whatever is said of God substantially is affirmed alike of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. May one say that in the Trinity there are three individual substances of rational nature?

To the preceding points must be added that whatever is said of God substantially—that is, whatever belongs to the divine substance from eternity without relation—is affirmed alike of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Just as the Father is almighty, wise, eternal, just, and merciful, so the Son is [Col. 0581B] almighty, wise, eternal, just, and merciful, and likewise the Holy Spirit.

Yet one must not in any way say that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three gods or three almighty beings. In order that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit should not be thought to be three divine substances—which would oppose sound faith and the Godhead saying, “I and the Father are one” (John X)—almost no noun is permitted to be predicated of them in the plural.

For the Latins say that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, while the Greeks say three *hypostases*, in order to indicate the plurality of persons; that is, to show that the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor the Son the Father or the Holy Spirit, nor the Holy Spirit [Col. 0581C] the Father or the Son, but that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

Thus we say three persons, not three gods and not three almighty beings. Yet, as Augustine testifies in his book *On the Trinity*, *person* is a substantial term and is used without relation; and when we say “person,” we name nothing other than a rational essence. Although this is so, the custom of the Latin Church confesses, in order to indicate the plurality mentioned above, that the Father is one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Yet no one dares confess that the essence of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, lest several gods and essences be understood.

It is therefore clear that just as three gods are not posited, neither would three persons be spoken of if more suitable words were available [Col. 0581D] by which the plurality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit could be expressed more appropriately. This is not said in order that *person* may be understood as a substantial term and an essential diversity asserted, but so that the plurality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may not be left unspoken.

Although we say three persons, and the definition of person is “an individual substance of rational nature,” we nevertheless do not dare say that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three individual substances of rational nature. For in that way we would seem to assert three divine substances and three gods. Just as, in order to confirm unity of essence, we say one God and not three gods, [lacuna] lest the plurality of persons seem to be denied.

It is also read somewhere, in order to assert the plurality and equality of these same persons, [Col. 0582A] that they are coeternal, just as they are coequal. By analogy with this expression, they seem capable of being called consubstantial and co-almighty. But because no authority is found to have used these words, one should not rashly presume concerning them. For since the Apostle commands that profane novelties of words be avoided, this must be observed especially when we speak of the essence of the Godhead and the distinction of persons, a matter in which one cannot err without danger.

By “profane novelties” we mean not only those which profess heresy, but also those which, although they can be expounded in accordance with sound faith, nevertheless seem, because they are unusual, to assert some novelty contrary to faith. Therefore, whenever unfamiliar formulations of words are proposed and devised for novelty’s sake or display, I consider it better [Col. 0582B] to remain piously ignorant of their meaning than rashly to determine anything concerning them. From what has been said it is now sufficiently clear how the substantial names of God are to be affirmed of each person.

## CHAPTER VII. Things that belong to God from eternity in relation to nature are also predicated of each person, as are things that belong to God temporally in relation to creatures. The Son alone assumed flesh in time. God is affected by no accident; remaining unchangeable, he has acquired differing names from the variety of things which he made.

Just as substantial names are affirmed separately of each person, so also are those names which belong to God eternally in relation to his nature, such as *foreknowing*, *provident*, and [Col. 0582C] similar names. These belong to God from eternity because he foreknew and provided for all things from eternity, before they came to be.

Likewise, names which belong to God temporally in relation to creatures are affirmed separately of each person, such as *Lord*, *Creator*, and *Merciful One*. For, as Augustine testifies in *On the Trinity*, God was not Lord before he had a servant. Thus he began to be Lord temporally, when the creature made in time began to serve him. Similarly, God began to be Creator in time, when he made creatures. He did not create them from eternity, nor are they coeternal with the Creator, as some suppose because of the words, “All things in him were life.” These words should be expounded as follows: in his foreknowledge—which is life living from itself and [Col. 0582D] giving life to others—all things existed as ordered and known, as though personally existing.

Therefore, it is true that God is Lord and Creator in time. Although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are Lord and Creator, they are not three lords or three creators, but one and the same Lord and Creator. Yet they are spoken of in the plural: “The three of them created the world.” That they may be designated in the plural by a nominal expression and a verbal one is evident from the words set above of John the Apostle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: Father, Word, and Spirit” (I John V).

Here one must observe that the Son alone assumed flesh in time. Thus being incarnate in time belongs to him alone, because the incarnate man [Col. 0583A] is called Christ. For although it is true that he always existed, as he himself indicates in saying: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John VIII), nevertheless this name belongs to him from the assumption of flesh temporally and not eternally. This can be illustrated by the following comparison.

On the last day of Abraham’s life, it was true to say: “This old man Abraham lived in Ur of the Chaldeans.” Yet those two names—*old man* and *Abraham*—did not belong to him when he lived in Ur. Thus the aforesaid names are affirmed of the Son alone and do not appear to be relative, although the preceding names belonging to God in relation to creatures are affirmed of each person and are relative.

From what has been said above, one might infer that something accrues to God and that God is mutable [Col. 0583B] because he possesses certain names in time. But one should know that God governs all things which he made without labour or motion on his part, and changes them according to his will, without departing from the state of pure and perfect simplicity and immutability. For he is not said to be angry at the wicked or glad at the good because he experiences, in any respect, an emotional movement of anger or joy in the manner of a human mind. Rather, he appears as though angry when punishing sinners, and as though glad when bestowing rewards upon the righteous. Thus he is affected by no accident at all; remaining unchangeable, he has acquired diverse names from the variety of things which he made.

## CHAPTER VIII. What is to be predicated of the individual persons in the Trinity concerning relative predicates? Although all three persons are one God, and one God is the Trinity, God is not therefore to be called triple.

[Col. 0583C]

To what has been said must therefore be added that there are certain other names which are not predicable commonly of all, but are predicable distinctly and relatively of certain persons from eternity. For the Father alone is called Father, begetting and generating, relatively to the Son, and whatever similar terms are found. These names are not predicated of the other persons.

The whole Trinity and each person may indeed figuratively be called Father as Creator and ruler of the whole creation. Likewise, the Father alone is *unbegotten*, which, as to the word, appears to mean nothing other than “not begotten.” But since the Holy Spirit, who is not begotten, is nevertheless not called unbegotten, it is clear [Col. 0583D] that the Father is called unbegotten because he is neither begotten nor from another.

*Unbegotten* is not, however, a substantial name. It is said of the Father by negation of the relative term *begotten*, which does not belong to the Father. But to the Son belong these other names: Word, Son, born, begotten, generated, and other names signifying birth. Substantial terms, with a qualification of begetting added, are made proper to the person of the Son, such as “begotten God” and “born Wisdom”; and by all these names the Son is spoken of relatively to the Father.

At times the Son is also designated by the name *Wisdom* without an added qualification, as frequently occurs in Solomon’s Proverbs. Yet this is a substantial name of all three persons: the Father is Wisdom, the Son is Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0584A] is Wisdom.

The following appear to be proper to the person of the Holy Spirit: Holy Spirit, gift, proceeding—when *proceeding* denotes the procession proper to the Holy Spirit. For it belongs to the Son to proceed from the Father in a certain different way, and yet he too seems capable of being called “proceeding.” Therefore *spirit*, *love*, *charity*, *affection*, and similar terms are customarily spoken distinctly and relatively of the Holy Spirit, especially when qualifications are added, as when one says “the charity of the Father” or “of the Son.”

When such terms are uttered without qualifications, they may be predicated not only relatively of the Holy Spirit but also substantially of the other persons. For the Father is charity, the Son is charity, and the Holy Spirit is charity. Augustine’s words suggest that the designation *Holy [Col. 0584B] Spirit*, in its common meaning, is spoken of each individual person. For he said that the Holy Spirit, because he is the Spirit of both, is called by the common designation of both: for each—that is, Father and Son—is spirit and holy.

By the preceding names the Holy Spirit is spoken of relatively to Father and Son. For he is said to proceed from Father and Son. Although no name belonging to the persons of Father and Son seems to be constructed relatively with that name of the Holy Spirit which is *proceeding* or *Spirit*, it is nonetheless no less proper for the Holy Spirit to be called relatively proceeding or Holy Spirit. This may be clearer by such an example: if by no name a master were said in relation to a servant, it would nonetheless still belong to the servant to be called a servant relatively.

Moreover, [Col. 0584C] there is one name, namely *Trinity*, which is not predicated separately of any of the persons. For neither the Father nor the Son nor the Holy Spirit is the Trinity; rather, the three persons together—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are the Trinity, and the Trinity is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

It is also true that the Trinity—that is, the three persons together—is one God, and that one God is the Trinity—that is, the three persons—but God is not therefore to be called triple. The name *Trinity* may be termed collective, since it is not predicated of any person separately but of all simultaneously; it is not a substantial name, but indicates the plurality of persons.

## CHAPTER IX. The mystery of the Trinity is explained by an analogy with the human soul.

[Col. 0584D]

It has been demonstrated above by many authorities that the whole Godhead has one substance and three persons of one substance. Although it is impossible for human intelligence fully to comprehend the depth of this matter, we may nevertheless, as far as possible, seek some analogy of the divine and ineffable Trinity in the nature of creatures, though they are very unlike it. The Apostle says: “His invisible things are understood and seen through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world” (Rom. I).

Leaving aside other things for the present, let us consider the nature of the rational soul, which Scripture testifies to have been made in God’s image. The soul, then, is an incorporeal substance [the printed text has *corporea*, “bodily,” but it should read *incorporea*], simple in comparison with bodies, and not occupying different spaces by its parts. Since it remembers itself, it sometimes considers and knows itself, and loves itself when known.

Thus, in the same simple substance of the soul there are three things: memory, knowledge, and love. Although it may most truly be said that memory is not knowledge or love, and those three are distinct from one another, they are not three substances, nor are they anything other than the soul and its substance.

In these three one must observe that knowledge proceeds from memory, and love or will from both. Nor should anyone be troubled that knowledge is said to proceed from memory, when memory seems first to proceed from knowledge. For thought is not aroused from knowledge in the same manner as memory proceeds from knowledge; rather, secondly, through memory, thought is aroused from the knowledge proceeding in the soul. This thought, when formed and adhering to the thing thought, is called knowledge, or the word of the mind. [Col. 0585B]

This conception of the mind is called the person’s word; and the term *word* was transferred from it to the outwardly sounding voice. Thus through memory knowledge or word is aroused, bearing an express likeness of the knowledge that proceeds through memory, from which the word itself arises and is, as it were, begotten. For the word contains within itself exactly the same thing which memory knew through knowledge; hence it may be called the image of knowledge.

But when knowledge—that is, the word—has been aroused through memory, love or will follows. For when the soul arrives in thought at a thing which it knew in memory, it wills and loves to know [Col. 0585C] what it discovers by thinking. By such an analogy of the soul, though it is very unlike the divine nature, let us attempt, as far as we are able, to set forth the divine and ineffable Trinity.

One is God’s substance, simple and incorporeal; and there are three subsistences, three persons, of one substance, of whom one is not another—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. These three are nothing other than God himself and the one substance of God, just as in the same substance of the soul there are three things—memory, knowledge, and love—which three are nothing other than the soul.

But just as knowledge or the word proceeds from memory in the substance of the soul, so from God the Father, who is from no one and is supreme wisdom, the Son was begotten from eternity: that is, the Word, containing by most certain knowledge [Col. 0585D] whatever the Father knows. He is fittingly called the Father’s wisdom and the Father’s image, since in every respect he is expressly like the Father. Since, moreover, the Father loves the Son, consubstantial with himself and like him in every respect, and the Son loves the Father, who begot him perfect and supremely blessed from his own substance, love and benevolence proceed from both—that is, the Holy Spirit—just as love or will proceeds from memory and knowledge.

And although these three persons are of the same substance, they are nonetheless so distinct that, just as memory alone is memory, knowledge alone is knowledge, and love alone is love, so the Father alone is Father, because the Father alone begot the Son; the Son alone is Son, because the Son alone was begotten; but the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0586A] who neither begot nor was begotten, is neither Father nor Son, but is only the Holy Spirit, and is the Spirit of both.

For it must be noted that, although it is true that the Father begot the Son and that the Father and Son are one God, God nevertheless did not beget himself. The divine substance did not beget itself, nor did it beget another divine substance; rather, the person of the Father begot the person of the Son. Likewise, although the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, God nevertheless does not proceed from himself.

## Chapter X. Only the blessed in heaven will possess perfect knowledge of the supreme Trinity

We have discoursed sufficiently concerning the holy Trinity, which is incomprehensible, insofar as God has permitted our smallness to behold it through a mirror [Col. 0586B] in an enigma—that is, through the likeness of the rational creature, though very unlike it. But if anyone desires to be shown by clearer reasoning how, in the one substance of God, there can be a plurality of persons without diversity of forms and substances, let him remember this: no one, however subtle and trained, can attain perfect knowledge of this matter as long as flesh troubles the soul in this life.

For that knowledge belongs only to the blessed who already enjoy eternal life, as the Lord testifies when he says: “Eternal life [is] to know you, the one God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). Of this same knowledge the Lord says to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exodus 33).

## Chapter XI. By authority and reason it is shown that in God there are no properties or relations which are not identical with God, but are things other than the divine substance

[Col. 0586C]
