After these matters, it seems necessary to inquire whether there are in God any properties that are not identical with God, but are things other than the divine substance. Here we judge that the common usage of the Church ought to be followed, and it ought without any hesitation to be declared that neither quantity, nor quality, nor relation, nor indeed anything whatsoever exists in God that differs from his substance.

For the Lord is not called great because there is quantity in him, nor just or good because there is in him a quality distinct from him. Rather, as Augustine testifies, he is understood to be great without quantity, [Col. 0586D] good without quality. And although there are three persons in the divine substance, of whom one is not another, they nevertheless differ from one another by no relations or other forms. Rather, because God begot a Son consubstantial with himself, and because, as the Father loves the Son and the Son the Father, love or benevolence proceeds from both—that is, the Holy Spirit—there is a plurality of persons in God. It is not because persons are distinguished from one another by relations or things distinct from God.

That there is no admixture in God of anything different from him is demonstrated not only by arguments, but also by authorities. Isidore says: “God is called simple because he does not lose what he has, and because he is not one thing while that which is in him is another.” Boethius, affirming the same [Col. 0587A] simplicity of God in his book *On the Trinity*, says: “Therefore this is truly one, in which there is no number, and nothing else in it besides what it is.” And shortly afterward: “Therefore there is no diversity in him, no plurality arising from diversity, no multiplicity arising from accidents.”

Augustine, after setting forth many things in the seventh book of *On the Trinity*, adds these words: “And there will not be there the highest simplicity.” But far be it that this should be so; for there truly is the supremely simple essence. Therefore, there to exist is the same thing as to be wise.” And in the same book he says: “When human poverty strove, by speaking, to bring before human understanding what it held, according to its capacity, in the secret chamber of the mind concerning its Lord and Creator—whether through devout faith or through understanding—it feared to say ‘three essences,’ lest some diversity be understood in that supreme [Col. 0587B] equality.” And shortly afterward: “By all these [expressions] he did not intend diversity, but he did not wish [to deny] singularity.”

By these authorities it has been shown that there is nothing in God which is other than God himself. The same may also be proved by arguments. For if, as some assert, in that supreme Trinity which is God, the Father could not be other than the Son and the Holy Spirit unless there were certain relations in them by which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit differed from one another, it is plainly apparent that that supreme Trinity which created all things without admixture or assistance from things different from itself could not exist at all.

It is likewise evident that in the essence of God, without the intervention and assistance of those things, there would not be supreme sufficiency [Col. 0587C] and supreme blessedness, if, as they assert, the Father could not without those relations beget the supremely good Son, or the supremely good Holy Spirit proceed from both. For without them that incorporeal beauty of the Trinity could not exist, without which God could in no way be supremely good.

Again, if there are three relations in God, then besides God there are three things without beginning and coeternal with God, which are neither Creator nor creature, neither substances nor accidents; for there can be no accident in God. Again, if there are three relations in God, and they are things other than the divine substance, it is apparent that from eternity there was not only the holy Trinity which is God, but together with it another Trinity of relations. Thus it is manifest [Col. 0587D] that there are two coeternal Trinities in God: one which is God and another distinct from him. Yet concerning that other Trinity nothing is found revealed or stated in any creed, any synod, or any canonical Scripture.

## Chapter XII. It is shown that the opinion of Saint Jerome in no way supports the contrary view, nor do the words of the preface in the Mass of the Holy Trinity

Nor are we unaware that some wish to affirm the existence of the aforesaid relations from certain words used by blessed Jerome in his exposition of the faith. But so that Jerome’s words themselves may clearly show that he thinks differently, and that those who assert relations think differently, we have taken care to set down Jerome’s own words. They are as follows:

“The whole Godhead is equal in the perfection of itself, so that, except for the terms which indicate the property of the persons, whatever is said of one person could most worthily be understood of all three. Thus, confounding Arius, we say that the substance of the Trinity is one and the same, and we confess one God in three persons; thus, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons expressly by their property, not saying that he himself is Father to himself, Son to himself, and Holy Spirit to himself, but that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons—or, as the Greeks express it, three *hypostases*, that is, subsistences.”

These are Jerome’s words, which some, [Col. 0588B] interpreting badly, endeavor to use in support of the existence of relations, especially insisting on the earlier words: “So that, except for the terms which indicate the property of the persons, whatever is said of one of the persons can most worthily be understood of all three.” They say, however, that Jerome signified by these words no property of the persons other than relations distinct in essence from the persons themselves.

Desiring to exclude this error, Jerome himself explained in what follows what he meant in the earlier part, when he said: “Not merely the names, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons—or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases, that is, subsistences, we confess.” In saying this he plainly indicates that he calls the properties [Col. 0588C] of the persons nothing other than the several persons themselves, distinct from one another; nor does he understand the properties of the names to be other than the persons denoted by the names. For, wishing clearly to express his meaning, he says: “the properties of the names, that is, persons.”

In a similar way the words of a certain preface, expressed as follows, are to be understood: “That in the confession of the true and everlasting Godhead, distinction of persons, unity of essence, and equality in majesty may be adored.” For “property” in the persons means nothing other than their distinction, and their distinction is nothing other than the persons themselves, who are distinct from one another. I think enough has been said against those who posit relations, or other properties distinct from God, in God.

## Chapter XIII. The error is refuted of those who madly claim that omnipotence must be attributed to the Father alone, wisdom to the Son alone, and goodness to the Holy Spirit alone—and who think and boast that they have comprehended the mystery of the most sacred Trinity

At this point I did not wish to pass over the profane novelties of certain people, whose folly thinks that the persons are to be distinguished by God’s power, wisdom, and goodness, assigning omnipotence to the Father alone, wisdom to the Son alone, and goodness to the Holy Spirit alone. It is clear that this has been invented by people unlearned and almost entirely ignorant of the truth.

For who, unless wholly devoid of all truth, fails to know that God the Father is wise—he who arranged all things in fitting [Col. 0589A] order before they existed? Or who denies that he is good—he who by his goodness alone created rational natures out of nothing, in order to make them participants in his blessedness? Likewise, no one ought to doubt that the Son is omnipotent and good, he through whom all things were made and who is consubstantial with the good Father. Likewise, let no one doubt that the Holy Spirit is omnipotent and wise, because he adorned the heavens (Job 26).

Therefore omnipotence belongs to all three, wisdom to all three, and benevolence to all three. It is astonishing how those senseless people dare, against so many authorities agreeing upon this truth, to introduce their errors. It does not suffice them to lie with impunity against the truth of the Catholic faith; among the unlettered populace [Col. 0589B] they even glory in spreading their name by their inventions. They further add that they fully know, in the unity of the divine substance, the Son’s begetting by the Father and the Holy Spirit’s procession from both.

But their stubborn presumption is refuted by blessed Clement, who says: “Let it not be asked how he begot the Son—a thing unknown to the angels and hidden from the prophets. Hence it was said: ‘Who shall recount his generation?’ (Isaiah 52). For he alone who begot knows the hidden origin together with his own Son; God is not to be scrutinized by us, but believed.” By this testimony of Saint Clement the folly of these people, who boast that they fully know the deep mystery of the Trinity’s knowledge, is most plainly refuted.

Therefore no one ought to be so mad as to attempt to comprehend by the acuteness of his own intellect this incomprehensible secret of the divine nature, and, as though he had comprehended it, presumptuously to explain it to others in boastful fashion. Conversely, no one should be so obstinate as to refuse belief because he does not fully understand the unsearchable mysteries of the holy Trinity. Rather, whoever begins to doubt because he does not understand should have recourse to the authorities mentioned above, which affirm that no one in this life has perfect knowledge of God. Instructed by them, let him begin to believe concerning God what Peter believed. Peter’s shadow healed the sick, and so did the other martyrs and confessors, whose holiness became known through incomparable miracles not only during life [Col. 0590B] but also after death.

But if it happens that a Jew or a heretic attacks Catholic truth concerning the nature of the divine substance, which ineffably transcends all things, by dialectical arguments devised according to the ordinary course of nature and customary uses of words, then, even though Catholics cannot refute him by human reason, he should nonetheless remain steadfast in the faith fortified by so many authorities, remembering that a faith to which human reason supplies proof has no merit.

# In the Year of the Lord 1203: Saint William, Abbot of Saint Thomas of the Paraclete in Denmark

[Col. 0589]

# Life of Saint William the Abbot, by an Anonymous Author, His Disciple

(*Writers on Danish Affairs of the Middle Ages, partly hitherto unpublished and partly published in more corrected editions, collected and edited by Jacob Langebek, Councillor of State and Keeper of the Privy Archives to His Sacred Royal Majesty; after the death of that eminent man, revised, annotated, and published by Peter Frederick Suhm. Vols. I–VIII, folio—Vol. V, Copenhagen, 1786, p. 458.*)

## Preliminary Observations

This Life was copied by B. Langebek from the great work of the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. I for the month of April, pp. 625–645, with the learned annotations of Henschenius and Papebrochius. Yet these men, being foreigners, sometimes err in matters concerning our Denmark. See especially note e, p. 632, where they think that Eschiloe and Iselfiort—thus they write incorrectly for Isefiord—designate the same thing, and that the name is distorted from Eschil. Yet *Isefiord* in our language means “icy inlet,” whereas *Eschilsoe*, a word meaning “Eschil’s island,” unquestionably derives its name from the personal name Eschil.

Those two learned men indeed prefixed to this saint’s Life a learned introduction, pp. 630–674, whose summary is as follows: the house of Saint Victor at Paris was founded in 1129 and was the first house in that royal city of the Regular Canons of Saint Augustine; from that house Odo, prior of Saint Geneviève, came forth in 1140, and this Saint William was trained in his discipline; William died on 6 April and was canonized by Pope Honorius III in 1224, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January]. In the bull the pope testifies that he caused inquiry to be made into the life, reputation, and miracles of the aforesaid servant of God by Thomas, formerly Archbishop of Lund; by Peter, Bishop of Roskilde; and by the abbot of Herivad of the Cistercian Order.

The same learned pair continue: “In the same year in which the bull was issued—namely, 1224—the solemn ceremony was also performed. Peter, son of Jacob (Sunonis), Bishop of Roskilde, performed it; and under Bishop Nicholas Stig, the translation took place at Ebelholt in 1238. At the end of the Victorine manuscript, from which this Life was published, are found certain short prayers in honor of Saint William, which Papebrochius and Henschenius inserted in their introduction. Since, however, as the frequently mentioned pair write, the day of this holy man’s death fell upon Easter Day, his feast was transferred to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June], lest the annual veneration appointed for him should repeatedly be impeded. Yet afterward William’s name so fell into oblivion among the brethren of his order that he was neither mentioned by the Regular Canons in their proper offices nor counted among the saints of his order in the calendar before 1613. But then, through Pennotto’s efforts, after his Life had been read in Surius, his name appeared among the proper offices of the order—first at Rome, then at Mons in 1625, then at Venice in 1643, and afterward in other regions.”

This Life was published by Surius in the *Lives of the Saints*, vol. II, p. 98, but, by his own testimony, he abridged it in several places and for the most part also changed its phrasing, according to his custom. The authors of the *Acts of the Saints*, however, subsequently published it, as I said above, from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Victor at Paris. These most learned men think the author was a Frank, and infer this from his calling *Percas* “Perticas” (undoubtedly formed from the French word *Perche*); but they think that he lived with William in Denmark in the latter years of the saint’s life. From this, they say, stem his inaccurate accounts of Saint William’s acts in France. For it is credible that the saint was not accustomed to speak of his own praises; hence the writer had to borrow them from others, who related at third hand events done fifty years before their own time in a foreign land.

We may learn the truth of the things done in France from the letters of Abbot Suger—some of which are published in Martène’s *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. I, col. 414 ff., though nothing relevant to this matter is found there—and from those published by Duchesne in *Writers of the History of the Franks*, vol. IV, pp. 493–546 [Note: [Col. 0591] Suger’s letters are found in the *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI.]. There, especially at p. 506, we learn that the change in the church of Saint Geneviève did not occur in response to the most earnest pleas of the abbot of Saint Victor, but at the request of the secular canons themselves, although, as we have seen from another letter of Suger to Pope Eugenius, some of them strongly opposed it. Claude du Molinet, in a letter to the editors of the *Acts of the Saints*, observed that the necrology of Saint Victor contains the names of ten brethren of Saint Geneviève, among them William the subprior, who is unquestionably our William.

Our Stephanius, in the *Prolegomena* to Saxo, chapter 11, p. 10, says that an ancient manuscript had existed in the library of the University of Copenhagen, and that these words were found in it: “In the year of the Lord 1161, Absalon, Bishop of Roskilde, sent Saxo, provost of Roskilde, to Paris, to the church of Saint Geneviève; and he brought Brother William, with three other brethren, into Denmark. Saint William was made abbot at Eschilsø, where there were Regular Canons possessing nothing beyond the name and habit, and who had previously had a prior as their superior. Saint William died in the fortieth year after undertaking pastoral care, and was buried in the monastery of Saint Thomas, in a small town of Zealand called Ebelholt, in the year 1202.” Thus far the manuscript.

It is clear to me that this parchment contained the Life of Saint William, though in certain respects differing from the Life which we publish here, as the mention of Saxo proves. But that parchment perished in the Copenhagen fire of 1728. My late friend Langebek collected much from breviaries and the like—for example, from the Breviary of Roskilde and Fascicle no. 670 among the Magnæan manuscripts, entitled “Historical Lessons concerning the Saints,” the Breviary of Schleswig, and the Copenhagen Missal—but I have decided to omit all of it for the reasons stated above.

In the Bartholinian collections, volume I, or B, there is a privilege of Absalon, then Bishop of Roskilde, granted to the monastery of Saint Thomas of Eschildsø in 1171, together with two confirmations by him, one issued as bishop and the other as archbishop. There are also several other letters, full of confirmations and favors, from popes, our kings, and the archbishops of Lund, down to Christian II and the year 1517, concerning the monastery at Ebelholt. There also occurs, at p. 581, “The ordinance of Lord Abbot William concerning his anniversary day, and how it should be observed after his death.” Among other things, it tells us that his father was called Radulf and his mother Emelina. It does not name his birthplace; however, in Saussay’s *Gallican Martyrology*, p. 193, it is given as Paris.

After his death Saint William’s fame became renowned abroad. Thus Alberic’s Chronicle, part II, p. 528, writes of him: “In the year 1228, in Denmark, Saint William, an abbot canonized by the pope, worked many miracles day by day.” And the Colmar Annals in Urstisius, vol. II, p. 6, state: “In the year 1232 Saint William shone by miracles.”

Among us also the reputation of Saint William has always been great. Therefore our forefathers ardently maintained that certain relics of his sacred body were preserved among them: the canons of the church of Saint Mary at Copenhagen claimed one of his fingers; the Franciscan friars of Copenhagen, part of his tunic, shoes, and girdle; and the Franciscans at Roskilde, a joint of a finger, as well as parts of his shoes, earth, staff, chest, and bones—as the relic-books to be published later in this work inform us.

Not far from Ringsted, near Vigersted in Zealand, there is still a spring called Saint William’s, visited by the sick on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist. Yet he left the greatest memorial of himself among us in his letters, which still survive, although some have perished; they will follow this Life. Moreover, he left a *Genealogy of the Danish Kings*, published by Langebek, vol. II, pp. 154–163. It was written for the benefit of Queen Ingeborg, in order that Saint William might show that no blood relationship existed between her and her husband Philip Augustus, King of France; the king wished to dissolve their marriage on that pretext. In this matter Saint William devoted much labor and great diligence to our King Canute VI, Ingeborg’s brother.

That the translation of Saint William took place in 1238 we learn from the Annals in Langebek, vol. IV, p. 24; from the *Chronology*, vol. II, p. 168; and from the *Chronicle of Zealand*, p. 629.

As for the monastery of Ebelholt, its surviving ruins show that it was great in former times. Traces of its garden are also visible. This epitaph is still preserved there: “Here is buried the noble man Sir Ake Andreas, knight, with his wife Anna Dorothea, who died at Dronningholm; pray God for them. 1520,” with two coats of arms; and below: “1511, the Virgin Anne Bild’s daughter.” In Langebek, vol. IV, p. 624, the *Chronicle of Zealand* contains the following epitaph of this holy man:

[Col. 0593]

Born at Paris, blessed in word and deed,  
Removed from the world, William lies buried here.

The following abbots at Ebelholt after William are found in charters: Richard, 1218; William, 1258; Ascer, 1385; Benedict Esberni, 1403 and 1417; Matthew, 1423; John Andreae, 1435 and 1449; Thomas Budh, 1457 and 1464; Jeip Nicolai, 1477 and 1498; Claudius Martini, 1505 and 1512; Nicholas Juni, 1503, 1512, and 1515. When the Evangelical religion was introduced into these regions, this monastery, with the others, was secularized; in 1548 it was possessed as a fief by Christopher Thrandi. Finally, it was destroyed along with the town when Frederiksborg Castle was built. See Sperling, *Testament of Absalon*, note 40. According to letters of King Frederick II dated 29 May 1561, the church of Ebelholt was still then standing, large and spacious. In the Lund book of anniversaries in Langebek, vol. III, p. 500, this monastery is called that of Saint Thomas and Saint William of the Paraclete.

# The Life Begins

[Col. 0593]

## Chapter One. The dissolute colleagues persecute Saint Geneviève’s secular canon; Regular Canons are introduced there

[Col. 0593A]

Blessed William, born of noble lineage [Note: [Col. 0593C] Born about the year 1105, since he died in the year of Christ 1203 at the age of ninety-eight. LANGEBEKIUS.], was entrusted by his parents for education to the venerable Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés [Note: [Col. 0593C] This Hugh became abbot in 1116 and died [Col. 0594C] in 1145.]. Hugh kindly received him as his nephew and had him carefully trained in literary studies.

While still a little child he was brought up in the cloister at Saint-Germain and instructed in the first elements of letters. He carefully observed how the monks sat, read, sang, and prayed in the cloister. Thus, like a most prudent bee finding diverse flowers, he received from them the gifts of honey and stored them in the honeycomb of his heart. For in his boyish mind he then meditated upon what he would devoutly fulfill in old age.

Accordingly, through God’s grace working with him, surpassing many of his contemporaries in quickness of intellect, he excelled in the study of the liberal arts. He was esteemed as renowned even among the masters conspicuous for knowledge and learning in the arts. Therefore Abbot Hugh rejoiced greatly at the advancement and uprightness of his nephew’s character, and gave thanks to God. Wishing to provide for William’s future advantage, when he had been promoted to the subdiaconate he procured for him a prebend in the Parisian church of the Apostles Peter and Paul and of Blessed Geneviève, where secular canons were then established.

Having thus become a secular canon, William prudently performed everything pertaining to him. Moreover, remembering what he had observed the monks among whom he had been raised doing in quietness in his tender years, he would often take a book and sit alone in the cloister, reading and applying himself to sacred reading.

When his fellow canons saw this, they became greatly indignant. Envying his good habits, from which they ought to have profited, they began instead to deteriorate. Their thoughts against him were evil, inflamed by hell. They gnashed their teeth at him and could say nothing peacefully to him; for “their throat was an open grave; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully; the venom of asps was beneath their lips” (Psalm 13).

Therefore they assembled together against [Psalm 2] the innocent man, saying: “Men and brethren, what shall we do? Behold, this man does many things against us and our customs; for he opposes our works, wishing to impose the monastic life upon us. Let us recall what the philosopher says [Note: [Col. 0594C] Ovid, *Remedy for Love*, verses 91–92.]:

> Resist beginnings: medicine is prepared too late,  
> When evils have grown strong through long delay.

“Let us therefore oppose his evil schemes and uproot them completely. For if we leave him thus, not only the Romans but also the supreme pontiff and the King of the Franks will come, take away our place, expel us, install men of another habit to rule in our dwellings, and we shall become a proverb among all people.”

They exchanged these and similar words among themselves as though by a spirit of prophecy, unaware that something of this sort would befall them a few years later.

From that day, therefore, they considered how they might afflict him and, by entangling him in deceit, quickly remove him from his canonry; and in their thoughts they became accomplices in the deed. One of them, who seemed more familiar with him than the rest—whether by his own design or at the urging of the others is unknown—approached him secretly under a show of affection which he did not bear in his heart, saying:

“O dearest man and most worthy of every affection, there is a secret which I wish to tell you, if, when put under oath, you promise not to disclose it to anyone until I have accomplished in deed what I am considering in my mind.”

[Col. 0594C] To this the man of God replied that he could very well keep hidden what the other wished to be secret. Then he said:

“For a long time, dearest brother, I have resolved, from a desire for heavenly life, to exchange this life which we have for another. For although it is called life, it ought rather to be called death than life, because it is known to lead its lovers to eternal death. For the world lies in wickedness and is full of every impurity by which it incessantly ensnares its own. Let us therefore heed what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Watch, because you know neither the day nor the hour’ (Matthew 24). And again: ‘Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple’ (Luke 14). And the Apostle: ‘It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep’ (Romans 13). Let us therefore rise from the sleep of sin, trim our lamps, and keep watch with the prudent, so that, when the master of the household comes, we may enter with him into the wedding feast without rejection.”

As William listened intently to his words, the other added: “If we are two, we shall be sustained by mutual service.”

The man of God replied: “What you have said is salutary, and more desirable to a wise man than gold and precious stone. But what shall we do?”

The other said: “If we truly wish to leave the perishable and transitory things of the world, let us faithfully offer ourselves to God, with what is ours, in the habit of religious life.”

At this William smiled and said: “I do not yet have the desire to become a monk. But for the salvation of my soul and yours, if you match your words with deeds, I shall do what you urge—provided that I shall more safely follow what I first see you undertake.”

The other, rejoicing, answered: “You have spoken well; let it be so.”

As they often held familiar conversations with one another about contempt for the world and their resolution, it pleased them both to go as soon as possible to the monastery of monks called Charity [Note: [Col. 0595D] In the *Acts of the Saints*, April, vol. I, p. 627, note C, it is thought to have been the monastery of Charity in the diocese of [Col. 0596D] Besançon, founded in 1133.]. When they arrived there, the proposer of this plan summoned the father of the monastery and humbly disclosed the reason for their coming. The latter rejoiced at their arrival as he had wished, embraced them with the arms of charity, and replied thus:

“Our Lord says: ‘Whoever comes to me I will not cast out’ (John 6). Relying on this saying, I will gladly share with you the temporal and spiritual goods of this house, and shall see to it that you are joined to this holy congregation, if you do not abandon your purpose.”

After they had offered him many thanks for this sweet answer and for deciding to accept their request, the abbot ordered that they be received into the guesthouse and that necessities be supplied to them.

When they had sat down, the other addressed William in this manner: “Now, with the Lord’s favor, we have begun a good work profitable for the salvation of our souls. It remains that, with his aid, we should by no means withdraw from what we have begun. How fortunate you are, beloved brother, that you are subject to no temporal impediment! Free from all things, you can at once receive the habit with these holy men. But I must return home briefly, to provide a guardian for my mother and sister; for it would be a wicked and most grievous sin to leave them without protection, since the Apostle says: ‘If anyone does not care for his own, especially those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever’ (1 Timothy 5). But be patient, and do not take my temporary absence ill. Rather, ‘what you have to do, do quickly’ (John 13). Once the term of truce which you have granted me has elapsed, I promise before God and his saints that I shall return to you with all speed.”

Then William, perceiving that these things were not being done by the Spirit of God but in order that, separated from him, he might be bound by the chains of the cloister, answered: “Your more mature age calls you to lead the way. Since I am younger, it is fitting that I should not precede you but rather follow you. I remember that I promised you this at the beginning of your exhortation.”

Then the inventor of this deceit, seeing that the contrivances of his fraud were frustrated, drew deep sighs from the bottom of his breast and said: “Let us defer it to another time.” Thus leaving the cloister, they returned by the way they had come; and, having recoiled upon itself, iniquity lied to itself (Psalm 26).

Lord Abbot Hugh, always steadfastly fervent with the same zeal of affection for his nephew’s advancement, wished William to be promoted to the rank of deacon. When his enemies learned this, wounded inwardly with grief of heart, they feared that, if he were ordained in their church, he would be advanced to a higher dignity. Therefore, devising comfort for their fear, they besieged the Bishop of Paris with many entreaties, asking that he should by no means receive William for promotion, or should entirely refrain from conferring holy orders at that time.

The bishop, overcome by their prayers and too ready to believe their words because they accused William of many things, postponed conferring holy orders. But almighty God, who “takes the crafty in their own craftiness,” destroys the wisdom of the wise, and rejects the understanding of the understanding, did not wish what they had devised against his nephew to remain unknown to Abbot Hugh. Therefore the abbot sent William with his letters to be ordained by the Bishop of Senlis [Note: [Col. 0596D] Today Senlis.]; [Col. 0596C] and that devout bishop carried out what Hugh desired.

Having thus obtained the office of deacon, he returned home, with none of his fellow canons knowing where he had gone or for what purpose. On the following Saturday he was appointed to read the homily, because, owing to their harassment, he could not have a substitute. They did this so that, since he had no one to perform for him the Levitical office which the foundation of his prebend required, he might be put to shame and they might have material for maligning him. On Sunday night, when the seventh lesson was to be read, he came forward to read it; and, opening the book, he rang out in a loud voice, “Bid, Lord, a blessing.” The Gospel was (Luke 11): “Jesus was casting out [Col. 0596D] a demon, and it was dumb.” At the sound of this command, filled with great astonishment and ecstasy at what had happened to them, they were struck dumb and kept silence instead of responding with the blessing. And because their pain was renewed, abandoning Matins and choir, they went out one after another, beginning with the elders; and William alone remained at the lectern, and Master Alberic in the middle of the choir, a good and righteous man. He had not consented to their plan and deeds, but was awaiting the kingdom of God.

When morning came and the canons had assembled together and were discussing among themselves what had been done, Master Alberic came in and began to speak thus: “Truly we may say that this night [Col. 0597A] we have seen wonders. And who would not marvel? It is not surprising that the only-begotten Son of almighty God could cast out a demon that was dumb, and that, when the dumb man spoke, the crowds marvelled. But to me this is more wonderful: while Lord William was reading the homily, ‘Jesus was casting out a demon,’ his fellow canons—rational men, indeed—were cast out of the church; and while he spoke, they became dumb; and his brethren were removed far from him, and his acquaintances withdrew as though strangers.”

When he had finished speaking, the persecutors of the servant of God became a byword to all who heard these things.

But blessed William, strengthened by continual meditation upon God’s word, governed himself prudently in all things, so that with the Psalmist he could say: “The Lord is my [Col. 0597B] helper; I shall not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. 117). And again: “But for me it is good to cleave to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72). And, armed with patience by the help of God—whose judgment is a great abyss, and against whose scrutiny human counsel has no standing—he rendered powerless his adversaries, who persisted in their begun malice; and he was raised to the dignity of a certain provostship. O mercy of Christ, worthy of every praise! You know how to exalt Your servant at the time of Your good pleasure, though before the time the sons of envy were striving to crush him.

His fellow canons, meanwhile, rotting in shameful idleness, ate and drank in royal display unto luxury, in pride and excess, until the day when Pope Eugenius [Col. 0597C] entered Gaul, bearing, besides those concerns that were outward, the daily burden of care for all the churches entrusted to him by God. He shattered their pride and brought it to nothing. For when he came to Paris, what they feared came to pass, and what they dreaded befell them (Job 3): not by chance, nor through a course of action devised or premeditated by William, but by the just judgment of divine Wisdom disposing all things.

Accordingly, wishing to know whether the vineyard had flourished and whether its flowers had yielded fruit, the lord pope withdrew into the regions of Gaul. As he approached Paris, King Louis and the bishop of that city, with a multitude of clergy and laity, met him; and, receiving him with honor, [Col. 0597D] they conducted him with great rejoicing to the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary. After a few days he desired to visit the church of St. Geneviève and there celebrate the divine offices, because it was called apostolic.

When he had arrived, the ministers of the church spread a silk pallium before the altar, upon which the lord pope prostrated himself in prayer. When the prayer was completed, he entered the sanctuary and was vested in sacred garments for celebrating Mass. Meanwhile the servants of the lord pope took up the silk pallium, asserting that it belonged to them according to ancient custom. The servants of the canons, indignant at this, tried to pull the pallium from their hands; the Romans, on the other hand, with all their strength did not cease pulling it toward themselves. Why linger over this? They did not cease pulling against one another until, [Col. 0598A] when the pallium had been torn into pieces, they began striking one another with their fists, and the church’s attendants, using clubs, left the servants of the lord pope bloodied. When the cry of the disputants rose in the church, King Louis came up, wishing to restrain them; but they, because their foolish heart had been darkened (Rom. 1), did not fear the king as he came in his splendor, but struck him, like the others, with heavy blows.

While these things were happening, certain members of the lord pope’s household, with their garments torn and faces scratched by their fingernails, threw themselves at their lord’s feet and tearfully laid their injuries before him, saying: “See how those are honored whom the lord pope wishes to honor. Is such a reward due to us, who have left Rome and our own possessions and followed you? Let Rome now be ashamed: [Col. 0598B] nowhere have we been without honor except in this church, in which evils have happened to us that we did not deserve. Thus: ‘We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those who are around us’ (Ps. 78); but, if you can do anything, remove our reproach” (Isa. 4).

When the apostolic lord had learned all that had been done, greatly inflamed with indignation, he replied: “‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay’” (Rom. 12). Summoning King Louis, he spoke thus: “Out of reverence for the Apostles Peter and Paul and for blessed Geneviève, I came here to handle the divine mysteries; and the canons of this church, wicked and foolish men, casting off the fear of the Lord, struck my servants with fists and whips in order to provoke me to anger. [Col. 0598C] But lest they glory long in their malice, do not delay, you who uphold the cause of this church, to render me justice against the aforesaid offenders.”

But King Louis said to the lord pope, who sought justice from him: “Holy Father, to whom shall I set forth complaints of the injury done to me, or who will do justice for me? For I too, like your people, while I was trying to separate them, received heavy blows from raging men. But since the power of binding and loosing has been granted to you by the Lord in just judgment, behold, they are in your hand: render their recompense upon themselves.” Having said this, they departed together from that place.

As they went together, discussion again arose between them as to how they might destroy the pride of those canons and let out that vineyard to other husbandmen [Col. 0598D] who would render its fruit in its season. Yet they did not wish to inflict violence upon any of them by depriving them of their prebends before God had removed them from their midst, because many of them were noble and learned. Rather, wishing without sin to avenge the injury done to them through religious men, they resolved to entrust to such men the church of St. Geneviève. They therefore decreed that Black Monks should be established there; but they were especially troubled because, apart from one prebend which happened then to be vacant, they had nothing for those men’s support.

The abbot of St. Victor, having learned of their plan to change the order, earnestly besought the lord pope and King Louis that the Order of St. Augustine might be established in the church, under their patronage, to the honor of God, the Apostles [Col. 0599A] Peter and Paul, and the virgin St. Geneviève. He supported this with many arguments, asserting that it would be easier to convert those obstinate men to the regular life of the canons themselves than to the habit and customs of monks.

The apostolic lord and King Louis, knowing the good reputation of this abbot and his brethren, that their religious life was praised throughout all the neighboring country, and that the house of St. Victor gave forth the fragrance of great charity, willingly assented to the petition of the abbot, who burned with righteous desire. On the following day Odo, the prior, a man of holy conduct, complete prudence, and tireless love of religious life, was chosen abbot. Twelve canons, honorable men of good reputation, were sent with him to the church [Col. 0599B] of St. Geneviève, as befitted the purity of that virgin. Thus the Order of St. Augustine in the church of St. Geneviève, immutably confirmed by the privilege of Pope Eugenius and the most Christian King Louis, is preserved there to the present day. Behold, as was recalled at the beginning, the former canons, possessing Caiaphas’s prophecy, lost their place, and that place was given to an alien people: namely, to a religious people cultivating the Lord’s vineyard religiously.

## Chapter II. St. William, becoming a regular canon from the secular estate, gives great examples of zeal.

While these things were taking place, William had withdrawn to his provostship, discussing and arranging domestic affairs with his friends. On the following day, as he reclined with his companions at a table laden with various dishes, suddenly a man entered and addressed him thus: “Lord Abbot Odo of St. Geneviève greets you and sends you this letter.”

Astonished beyond belief by the words of the greeting, he said: “Who is this abbot, or when has there been an abbot in the church of St. Geneviève?” The messenger replied: “Odo, prior of St. Victor, is abbot of the church of St. Geneviève; yesterday he was established there by the supreme pontiff and the lord king.” At this William said: “Do I hear this in a dream? Or do you report the truth to me?” “It is true,” he said.

Then, examining the tenor of the letter, he saw that Abbot Odo commanded him [Col. 0599D] not to delay in coming as soon as possible to his chapter. Therefore, putting aside concern for his meal, he rose; and, taking leave of all, said: “I shall go and see whether this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” When he entered the cloister of St. Geneviève, he saw there men clothed in the garb of religious life. He therefore believed what the messenger had told him; yet he was greatly perplexed within himself as to why this had happened and what had been the cause of this change. The arrival of Lord William was immediately announced to the abbot, who hurried to meet him and, receiving him with the kiss of peace, embraced him most devoutly.

As they sat down and exchanged conversation, the abbot disclosed to William the manner of his own and his brethren’s arrival, and the other things that had befallen them in those days. Having related these matters, he began to warn him to despise [Col. 0600A] the world, saying: “My son, if you wish to be rich, seek true riches; if you love the glory of rank, hasten to be enrolled in that heavenly court of angels. Consider what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘He who loves father or mother and fields or houses and other things more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matt. 10). And again: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of God; blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be filled’ (Matt. 5). And St. John the Evangelist says: ‘Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him’ (1 John 2). St. James the Apostle agrees well with this, saying: ‘Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God’ (Jas. 4).

“Therefore do not delay in turning [Col. 0600B] to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day, lest the wrath of God suddenly come upon you and destroy you in the time of vengeance. He is exceedingly foolish who, because he serves luxury for a short time and feeds his wretched desire with corrupt pleasures, loses heavenly delight and incurs eternal damnation. Therefore renounce all that you possess and bear Christ’s cross daily. Though he was rich and all-powerful, king of heaven and earth, he freely became poor for our sake, that he might make us rich with himself in the kingdom of heaven.”

After ending these exhortations, he took William by the hand and led him to a glass window in which the image of the Crucified One was painted. Renewing his speech, he said: “Do you see, my lord, this image, and do you consider it?” William replied: “I indeed see it and consider it carefully. For though this mystery is old to me, through use it is nevertheless always new to me, because of him who reformed us and conformed us to the body of his glory, and renews our inner person from day to day.”

Understanding that his heart was kindled by the Holy Spirit, the abbot said again: “Do you see with what sweetness of love he desires to bind you to himself and, with arms outstretched, to receive and embrace you—he who allowed himself to be crucified for you?” Immediately the man of God, his face drenched in a shower of tears and scarcely able to utter words because of excessive sobbing, answered fearfully: “Would that I might know that he would deign to have me as his servant and forgive the errors of my past iniquity and [Col. 0600D] frailty!” The abbot replied: “I will be your surety, if you are willing to obey sound counsels, that he will not only forgive your sins but, after the end of this life, will crown you with eternal glory among his saints.”

Without delay William fell at his feet, believed his words, graciously entrusted himself and his possessions to God, and thus escaped naked from the shipwreck of this world.

Christ’s household rejoices at the conversion of so great a young man, and no less rejoices at the unexpected help sent to it so suddenly from heaven. O good Jesus, how magnified are your works! (Ps. 91); for, as the prophet says, “You have wrought all our works in us” (Isa. 26). We now see fulfilled what we read that you said: “It is easier for a camel to pass through a needle’s [Col. 0601A] eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). But when men whose thoughts were only earthly asked, “Who then can be saved?” you answered: “What is impossible with men is possible with God” (Luke 18). Behold: because you predestined this man to grace, you could easily make the proud humble and the rich poor.

Let each person say what he thinks concerning what is written in praise of the brother Apostles Peter and Andrew: that at the single command of the preaching Lord, leaving their nets and boat, they followed the Redeemer. This man, however, at the admonition not only of the Lord but of his servant, left not only nets and a boat, but estates and possessions, houses and households, riches and honors, and even himself as well. Yet we do not say this [Col. 0601B] in order “to compare him with the highest Apostles; rather, we approve lesser works in such a way that we do not disparage the great deeds of the greater ones.”

Having therefore received the regular habit, William was placed among the other brethren and numbered with those twelve. With his habit changed, he was changed into another man; and, by the cooperation of divine grace, which had foreseen him as a vessel of election, he advanced from strength to strength, so that he might be counted worthy to see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83). For he was endowed with the virtue of charity, outstanding in humility, strong in patience, tractable in obedience, and ready for every other kind of virtue. He devoted himself to reading, prayer, and divine contemplation; by vigils and fasts he subdued the limbs [Col. 0601C] of his body. He who had been accustomed to go clothed in silk thereafter, in lowly garments, served as a poor man among the poor. Forgetting the riches of his former life, he ate bran bread like the others and took with thanksgiving wild herbs prepared for food. For the two prebends, which at the beginning alone were available to the brethren and their household, could provide them with no other luxuries. Hence this strong athlete of Christ, steadfast in the religious life and order he had undertaken, became so ardent a champion that, when he discharged the office of superior, he permitted none of the ordinances of the order to be transgressed.

While he exercised himself unceasingly in these and other like pursuits of virtue and had already proved himself before God and men, our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0601D] according to the Gospel saying, “He who loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14), appeared to him one night in a vision, after he had given his limbs to sleep, in the form of a most beautiful young man. Calling him by name, he said: “Know that you will go with me to a certain island, where you will endure many kinds of temptations and troubles; but, having overcome these with my help, you will lay aside the burden of flesh and will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). What such a vision and admonition meant for him, he could not at all conjecture until he was summoned to Denmark, to the island called Zealand, where he now rests.

[Col. 0602A] After not many years had passed, Abbot Odo departed to the Lord in a good old age. After his death, Lord Garin, prior of the same monastery, because he was regarded as an honorable, learned, and prudent man in practical affairs, was chosen abbot. After he had been consecrated and confirmed in his seat, discussion was held with the brethren in chapter concerning the appointment of a prior. There was one man there to whom the abbot was in every way eager to give the priorate, all agreeing and consenting to the abbot. But that brother resisted, saying: “It is right that, in a royal abbey, officers should be installed in their offices by the king.”

On hearing this, the brethren were deeply troubled and said: “If you wish to receive the office of prior according to the rule of the order, we consent [Col. 0602B] to your election; but if you attempt to transgress the boundaries set by our Fathers, you shall never obtain it.” But he persisted in his purpose. Therefore the abbot, in order to achieve what he had begun, took that brother with him to the king’s palace; and because the order’s institution was unknown to the king, the man was made prior by him in the palace.

Having thus obtained his desired result, at the hour of the meal he went to the cymbal and, striking it, summoned the community. Seeing this, what could the brethren do or say? They could not speak, but by nods and signs they showed the inward bitterness of their hearts. Yet because “the righteous is bold as a lion” (Prov. 28), William, encouraged by zeal for the order and love of justice, after entering [Col. 0602C] the refectory removed that presumptuous man from the bell and put the subprior in his place.

The man who had been removed went out in shame and with great groaning reported to the abbot the dishonor inflicted upon him. The abbot gently consoled him, saying: “If I do not repay this to William of St. Germanus, I shall never be abbot.” When the brethren assembled in chapter in the morning, William was charged with having laid violent hands on the prior. He denied that he had ever inflicted any injury upon the prior. But after some exchange of words, he said: “If I have sinned in any respect by driving from the prior’s office not a prior but a transgressor against the order, I am ready to undergo corrective punishment.” Having asked leave, he was immediately sentenced to silence; and he was ordered, every week, to fast three days on bread and water and to sit on the ground without a table-cloth [Col. 0602D] while eating. He did not recoil from such a sentence; but, observing that a pastor’s sentence, whether just or unjust, is to be feared, he humbly endured what had been imposed upon him.

Then word spread among the brethren that this disciple had been unjustly condemned in office. Therefore one of them hastened to the apostolic lord, who was then staying at Sens, and reported to that great Father everything as it had occurred.

> **Note [Col. 0601D].** This took place in 1163, according to the authors of the *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I, p. 624.

The supreme pontiff, not taking lightly the violation of the order and the severe sentence passed upon an innocent man, immediately ordered the abbot of St. Geneviève to present himself without delay, and to make William his companion on the journey. He obeyed the command and, taking William with him, came to Sens. Appearing before the supreme pontiff, he was rebuked for rashness and lack of discernment; William was freed from the sentence; and it was most strictly commanded that henceforth officers should not be elected or instituted contrary to the ordinances of the order.

While all things kept the silence of midnight, and every storm of disturbance seemed calmed in that church, a rumor arose among the people that the head of St. Geneviève had been removed from its holy place. At last the spirit of this blasphemy struck the royal ears. Thus, from the reports made to him, King Louis was inflamed with immense wrath and swore by the Holy One of Bethlehem that, if this were true, he would have all the canons whipped and expelled from that church. [Col. 0603B] Having posted guards to watch over the treasure and relics of that monastery, he sent letters to the archbishop of Sens and his suffragans, and to the abbots and priors of that diocese, commanding all to meet at Paris on a day fixed by him, to investigate the truth of the matter.

When the brethren heard the king’s oath, they were troubled and shaken; trembling seized them. Although they feared the prince’s wrath, they grieved more over the treasure more precious than gold and a costly pearl, which they feared had been taken from them. Above all, William’s spirit was distressed, for he had long had in his custody all the reliquary chests and the treasure of the church.

The appointed day dawned. The king came with his retinue; bishops and abbots came; a considerable multitude also came, desiring to know the outcome. At last, when those who were to ascend with the archbishop and the other bishops to the holy place of the holy Virgin had been named and designated, William wished to ascend with them, but was not permitted. Therefore, taking—I know not whether a candlestick or a censer—he said to himself: “If it is not otherwise granted to me, at least I shall go up as a minister”; and he began to go.

When the shrine was opened, behold: the head of St. Geneviève, the jewel of France, was found with the other relics of her limbs. When her faithful servant, the great William, saw this, the joy conceived in his heart could not be contained within him, so that he did not pour it forth in a cry of exultation. Forgetting those [Col. 0603D] who were of greater authority, he boldly began the *Te Deum laudamus*, so that the whole church resounded with his voice; and the entire people who had assembled for the feast, with no less eagerness, sang what he had begun through [Col. 0604A] to the end. When it had been sung, the archbishop proceeded with the collect of that virgin.

> **Note [Col. 0603D].** This happened in 1162; concerning it there is also extant, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, January, vol. III, p. 152, a treatise of St. William on the discovery of the head and body of St. Geneviève. See *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I, p. 624; it was not thought desirable to publish it, however, because it contains nothing concerning our matters.

When he had finished, the bishop of Orléans cried out with the greatest indignation: “Who is this flatterer, who, against the authority of the lord archbishop and the other bishops, has dared so rashly to begin the *Te Deum* on account of the head of some little old woman, which these men have deceitfully placed here?” William replied: “If you ask who I am, I want you to know that you have slanderously insulted me. I am not a flatterer, but the servant of St. Geneviève. As for the presumption with which you charge me, it was not reckless presumption but my whole-hearted love for the holy virgin, which I have always had, that compelled me to act.

“I do not deny that the head which you saw was that of an old woman—one who always retained the flower of virginity. St. Geneviève lived seventy years and more, always a virgin, pure and immaculate, until she rendered her soul to heaven and the material of her body to earth. But lest any scruple of doubt concerning this head cling to your hearts, have a furnace heated intensely; and I, taking the head with me, shall safely enter the flames, to demonstrate the merits of the blessed virgin.”

The bishop replied mockingly: “I certainly would not enter a cup of hot water with him, and you would enter a burning furnace?” But the archbishop, unable longer to endure the bishop’s superstitious verbosity, signaled him to be silent. He approved the faith of the devout brother and his sincere devotion toward the holy virgin. [Col. 0604C] Yet the foolish speech which the bishop had uttered against the blessed virgin with defiled mouth could by no means go unpunished; for “God will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5). Accordingly, afterwards entangled in many crimes, he was expelled from his see and miserably ended an unworthy life by a fitting death.

> **Note [Col. 0603D].** Although, according to the authors of the *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I, p. 630, this occurred in 1164, it is clear from note E that the writer believed it happened to Bishop Manasses, who occupied the see from 1146 to 1185. But since he died in good peace, whereas his predecessor Elias was removed from office in 1146, see *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, cols. 1450–1455, it is evident that the author erred here. [Col. 0604D]

## Chapter III. Summoned to Denmark, William becomes abbot of Roskilde and bravely endures many adversities.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1161—

> **Note [Col. 0604D].** Henschenius and Papebrochius, *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I, p. 624, likewise believe that St. William was summoned to Denmark not in 1161 but rather in 1171; therefore the reading here should be: “1171.” **Langeb.** [I myself, with Bartholín in the manuscript *History of the Church of Denmark*, under the year 1165, believe that he came to Denmark in 1165. For in 1201 he himself writes that he had then lived thirty-six years in Denmark; and in 1164 he was still in France, as is evident from documents in Papebrochius, *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I, p. 624.]

—Valdemar, king in Denmark, reigned. He was the son of King Canute and martyr. He drove the Slavs from the borders of his kingdom; they had often been accustomed to invade, carrying off captive men and women and plundering everything they could reach. [Col. 0604D] Since he was the son of a martyr, through his father’s intercession he emerged a glorious victor in all the battles he fought against the Slavs, who were then pagans. Thus, having shown them the way of eternal salvation, [Col. 0605A] he compelled them to submit their necks to Christ’s yoke.

This man was wise and discerning, powerful in deed and word, and acceptable to all the people. At the same time Absalon, bishop, governed the priesthood in the church of Roskilde: a man of great counsel, an ornament of the clergy, a comforter of the sorrowful and afflicted, a loving patron of all religious persons, and a moderate governor of all the people; a merciful supporter of strangers and the poor, a most vigorous persecutor of the Slavs, an ornament of the faith, an example of sobriety, a model of chastity, an eminent mirror of nobility and uprightness, a shining lamp in God’s temple, and its strong and immovable pillar.

In his diocese was a monastery of canons on the island called Eschil—

> **Note [Col. 0605D].** Eskilsø, which now belongs to Selsø, the noble seat of the de Pless family.

—not far from the settlement of Roskilde, surrounded on every side by the sea. [Col. 0605B] The place, adorned with green meadows and diverse forest trees, was pleasant and agreeable to those dwelling in it. Yet at that time the number of brethren living there was small; they were called Regulars to no purpose, since they were adorned with no disciplines of religious life. How could those be called Regulars who submitted their heads to no regular rule? How could those be cloistered who lacked cloistered enclosure? They possessed the written ordinances of the order, but observed none of them.

On the greatest feasts of the year secular friends of theirs came to their house with their wives to celebrate the feasts with them. Men and women feasted and became drunk together in the refectory, [Col. 0605C] and held dances. Thus the house was brought to disorder by their conduct and its resources were squandered. Alas! What then became of divine service, when they devoted more of the night to drinking than to psalmody and divine contemplation? Who then could worthily intercede with God for the people? At the morning assembly, burning with excessive drink, they preferred to sleep rather than sing. Living thus shamelessly, they filled the ears of all religious persons with a detestable infamy.

The venerable bishop of Roskilde, Absalon, seeing and considering that their life differed from all religion, was inwardly moved with grief. He detested the souls of such men, darkened by diabolical deceit [Col. 0605D] and too strongly inclined toward the flux of the world. He therefore often pondered silently how he might provide for that church, changing its form of order and religious life for the better, God granting it. At length he remembered the familiarity and friendship he had formerly formed with William, a religious man, while he was living in Paris for the sake of study. Considering him to be an honorable man—indeed prudent and discerning, adorned with holy conduct—his heart was pleased with him, and he determined, once William had been summoned, to give him the place mentioned above.

Accordingly, he sent a messenger, namely the provost Saxon, an honorable man, to the church of St. Geneviève, urgently and earnestly requesting in his letters that the often-named man, Lord William, [Col. 0606A] be sent to him with three other brethren. He declared that he had a place suitable for their religious life and promised to grant it to those brethren for the honor of God and the advancement of the Order of St. Augustine.

The abbot, considering the request of so great a prelate just and honorable, with the chapter’s consent granted his petition. Brother William was therefore sent with three brethren whom he took with him, and with Provost Saxon, to Denmark. Travelling prosperously, after the Assumption of Blessed Mary they entered Zealand and on the third day arrived at Ringsted, which is made illustrious by the merits of St. Canute the martyr, whose glorious life shone with the greatest light of justice.

It was God’s will that what they desired should meet them there: namely, the presence of King Valdemar and Bishop Absalon. Rejoicing at the arrival of those brethren, they embraced them with joyful arms, received them with the kiss of peace, and, after congratulating them somewhat upon their arrival in gracious conversation, promised that they would cherish them as sons, love them as brethren, and counsel them as friends. Rejoicing in what had been said to them, they returned with joy to their lodging. After spending three days there, they went on to Roskilde. Certain members of the bishop’s household followed their steps in order to provide for them there; for this accorded with the honorable custom of the land and the integrity of the man who had summoned them.

After they had spent several days in the city, they landed by boat on the island [Col. 0606C] of Eschil. There they found six men who were canons only in name. At the newcomers’ arrival their faces turned pale and bloodless, and speech dried up in their mouths, because they saw that the loss of their evil custom was now imminent. Therefore, to the injury of the arriving brethren, they held meetings that night after supper and decided to seek the presence of the lord bishop, so that they might report to him, as though he were unaware, what had occurred and wring from him a feeling of pity, lest he destroy their people and place.

But the lord bishop, having long known the whole sequence of the matter and censured their wickedness, pretended not to have heard, lest, while he delayed in coming there, the resources of the house should be destroyed even more than before. [Col. 0606D] Nevertheless, he appointed them a day on which he would appear in person and, as if unaware, carefully investigate the cause of the arriving brethren’s coming.

Accordingly, on the first day after the feast of St. Bartholomew, he arrived as promised. After holding discussion with them concerning the pastor to be appointed for them, Brother William was chosen abbot and placed in the abbot’s seat, although previously they had customarily had not an abbot but a provost and prior. On that same day two of the former canons received and obtained permission to depart and return whence they had come; the lord bishop judged that they ought to be dismissed, lest, if they remained in malice, a tumult should arise among the people. Four remained, very old and almost useless for every task. One of them, who had held the office of prior, was an honorable man and was found righteous in his days; therefore he began to be one of the brethren and, instructed in the regular way, brought his former life to a better end.

Accordingly, after Lord Abbot William had assumed care of the house, the lord bishop, at the abbot’s request, wished to know what and how great the substance of that house was, and what provisions it possessed. Seeing that their storehouses were nearly empty, with only six cheeses, one ham, and half another ham found there, he knew that “they had devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling-place.” Filled with worthy shame and astonishment, the bishop began to strengthen the spirits of the brethren and the abbot himself. He ordered five pounds of denarii [Col. 0607B] to be given them to buy necessary provisions, promising them in future assistance sufficient for their expenses.

After some time had passed, the brethren who had come with the abbot, unable to bear the unfamiliar poverty and recoiling from the excessive severity of the cold, received permission from the bishop to return home. This greatly troubled the lord bishop, but he did not wish violence to be inflicted upon anyone.

The abbot, however, could not bear well the departure of his men, who were frightened by the customs of a foreign land and an unknown language. He himself asked for the same leave which they had received from the bishop, maintaining that the task to which he had been called was beyond his strength, and that it would be safer for him to return freely with the others. At these words of the abbot, the bishop’s face and heart fell; yet at last he broke out into this speech:

“We have earnestly desired your coming for the advancement of this church; but, as we perceive, the enemy greatly envies its prosperous success and growth. For he is exceedingly afraid that he will lose the ancient right which he has hitherto possessed through the monstrous conduct of those dwelling in that place. But if the more gracious counsel of the Lord were willing to change the purpose of your hearts, we would entreat you with deep affection of charity not to attempt to abandon the office of governance once undertaken. Do not be afraid to undertake this work alone; for victory in war does not rest in the power of man, but strength comes from heaven; and the Lord saves by few as by many. What you believed would be accomplished through the help of your brethren, the Lord is able to accomplish through the service of us alone.” [Col. 0607C–D]

Strengthened by these and other admonitions of the venerable bishop, seasoned with the salt of wisdom, the abbot recalled inwardly what the Lord says through the prophet Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. 17). He changed his purpose and consented to remain, in order to see the end.

In that same year a decree went forth from the Lord, and behold, there was famine in the land because the grain supply failed; and nearly all the animals died, namely sheep and cattle. Therefore the remaining brethren could obtain neither butter nor cheese, save a little, to eat. Hence they turned to mutiny. They did not assess all things by the judgment of God, but attributed the entire weight of their adversity to their abbot, saying: “Woe to us! Why in our days has this ragged man, this contemptible little fellow, come here? He drinks nothing, eats nothing, but converts all the best property of the house into silver and gold and puts it away in his coffers; he torments us with hunger for food, supplying us, instead of food, with leaves of trees and wild herbs.” [Col. 0608A]

This seedbed of falsehood, broadcast by them, spread through the ears of very many. Since men’s perverse minds are always inclined to disparage the good, truth was obscured among the malicious. But the man of God was not disturbed by the accusations; he endured everything patiently, becoming like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth.

[Col. 0608B] One night, while the brethren had given themselves to sleep, Satan came among them. He overturned the lamp which customarily burned in the middle of the dormitory, and set it beside the abbot’s bed, where there was a great heap of straw, intending to burn the abbot. But heavenly protection did not abandon its soldier in this contest. The straw around the bed burned in the form of a crown, and the board placed beneath the straw endured scorching; yet the fire did not touch the abbot’s bed at all. Report of this event reached the bishop, who, after not many days, came to the cloister and found that what was reported agreed with the truth.

The following night, the ancient enemy, grieved that his devices had failed of effect, turned to another kind of temptation. He came to the bed of a sleeping brother and said: “Know that I was lord of this place and ruler over all drinkers and fornicators; but at the coming of your abbot I am subjected to force, and it will not turn out well for him.” When the brother asked who he was and by what name he was known, he confessed that he was called Salmanasar and had been king of the Babylonians in ancient times. [Col. 0608C]

And he added: “Advise the abbot to desist from what he has begun and not receive from the bishop the blessing due to abbots; for he will not be able to remain in this cloister against my will.”

The brother replied: “What you urge me to do, urge upon him yourself. Do you not also know him?”

“I do,” he said, “but less now than formerly. Therefore report to him what I have commanded, adding this sign: in the crypt of Blessed Geneviève of Paris he wrote out with his own hand seven Psalms with the Litany for a certain cleric. Report also that, on another night, because of the injury done me, I wished to burn him; but I was frustrated in my desire, because one stronger than I came upon me, and I could not bring about the accomplishment of what I wished.” [Col. 0608D]

When morning came, the brother reported to the abbot what he had heard; but the abbot made light of it and gave no heed to the devil’s suggestion. A little later, the servant of Provost Thocon, returning to Denmark from the city of Paris, addressed Abbot William in these words: “My lord greets you; commending himself wholly to your friendship, he earnestly asks that you entreat the lord bishop for him, so that he may extend a helping hand of his customary generosity to one devoted to study. And this is the token that he has sent me: that at Paris you wrote for him seven Psalms with the Litany.” [Col. 0609A]

The abbot marvelled at what was reported, but remembered the truth of what the devil had insinuated to the brother in a dream—namely, that he had written the seven Psalms for Provost Thocon.

At another time Abbot William, accompanied by the priest Thrumo, a man learned and discerning, went to lodge at the village called Thorstanthorp [Note: [Col. 0609D] Undoubtedly the parish of Thaastrup in the district of Holbek.]. There, when night was halfway through its course, the ancient enemy, raging against the saint of God, devised new incitements of his wickedness. Wearing an appearance of sanctity under the guise of a very old and most vile monk, he approached the abbot’s bed, which had first been fortified with the sign of the saving cross, and sought by an obscene act to arouse in the sleeping man a spark of lust. [Col. 0609B]

But although he had given his eyes to sleep, the abbot remained watchful in mind and said to his adversary: “Get behind me, most filthy of all beings. By God’s grace you will obtain no result of your desire in me.”

Hearing this, the devil was driven by the goads of fiercer cruelty. Coming nearer, he breathed a cloud of stench into the abbot’s face, and with his foul mouth unfolded again sins long ago abolished by confession and washed away in a shower of many tears. While the abbot was so grievously harassed by him in sleep, he thrust the enemy away from himself with a powerful kick of his somewhat raised foot. [Col. 0609C]

Seeing himself mocked by the man of God, the devil began to rage like a most cruel lion. He turned his steps toward the bed of the priest Trumo, who lay awake on the other side, and struck him a most violent blow in the side, so that the priest thought some of his ribs had been broken.

In the morning, when dawn brought the night to an end, after the praises of God had been sung, both men—the abbot and the priest—went into the warming-room, for the weather was cold. While they sat there, the priest addressed the abbot thus: “O my lord abbot, may almighty God protect and help you.”

The abbot answered: “Amen.”

When the priest had said this twice or three times, the abbot asked why he repeated it so often. The priest replied: “I know that you have endured many barbs of temptation and will endure more; but may God deliver you from them all. This night I saw how great a distress you suffered from Satan, how he poured a cloud of the foulest stench into your mouth, and I heard the insults and reproaches he hurled at you. When he left you in confusion, he rushed violently upon me, and, striking my side, as I think, broke one of my ribs. Therefore I judge that you must resist that same enemy manfully, lest, if he triumphs after defeating you, he send you to Gehenna.” [Col. 0609D]

At these words the abbot began to be troubled and afraid, recalling the assaults of the adversary which he had endured on the preceding night.

## Chapter IV. The virtues of St William, and certain miracles during his life

[Col. 0610A]

The ancient enemy still raged because none of his temptations against the Lord’s anointed had produced an effect. He therefore planned to accomplish through his satellites what he had been unable to do by himself. He inspired the hearts of certain brethren to assail the man of God with various insults and many injuries, and thus force him shamefully to return to his own home. But he was not afraid of the words of the wicked, because he was founded upon the firm rock. He frequently recalled to himself that apostolic saying: “Tribulation produces patience, patience testing, and testing hope; and hope does not put to shame” (Rom. 5).

When these degenerate sons made no progress by such means, they took counsel together to deliver him to death. At times they planned to put him in a sack and drown him in the sea; at times to pierce him with weapons; at times to sell him to the Slavs. More often they attempted to destroy his brain with axes bound together. But God, whose providence is not deceived in its ordering, scattered their counsels and gave His beloved, together with temptation, a way of escape. [Col. 0610B]

But why did they dare to do this? Because his spirit was with God in maintaining the strictness of the Rule and every observance of religious life; nor did he allow them to run headlong into the precipices of vice. He was an unfailing imitator of holy religion, an admirable keeper of the Rule and holy institution, a strong uprooter of vices, a true lover of virtues, investigating and teaching whatever was honourable and full of holiness. He was stern in rebuke, diligent in correction, gentle and humble in exhortation, restrained in giving an account; truthful in speech, just in judgment, faithful in what was entrusted to him. [Col. 0610C]

He consoled the sick and was a most kindly provider for the poor and pilgrims. He devoted himself to vigils, fasts, and continual prayers, tirelessly caring for his flock; and, that as a faithful servant he might make gain from the talent entrusted to him, he continually commended it to his Lord in prayer. While the brethren rested at night, he anticipated the morning hours with vigils and begged the Lord’s mercy for them with devout groanings. In his sermons, through which he instructed the brethren to do good, he was ready for tears and lamentations, so that he often moved his hearers to repentance and contrition of heart; and it was plain to all that divine grace was always present with him. [Col. 0610D]

Moved by zeal for the Rule, he was sometimes severe toward the proud and haughty, and compelled transgressors of the Rule to undergo corrective punishment and bear sentence. For he knew that he would have to render an account to God for as many as he permitted, by his example or silence, to stray from the paths of righteousness. Finally, toward those of obstinate mind who were not inclined to ask pardon for their offences, he himself showed a pattern of humility, asking pardon from them—contrary to the rule of his rank.

In persecutions inflicted upon him by his disciples and others, he was steadfast and patient, and by the power of patience overcame them all. The virtue of piety and mercy abounded in him so greatly that he received with all cheerfulness and gentleness those who sinned against him and, after sinning, returned for pardon. He wept most abundantly over their offences and gave manifold thanks to the Lord for their conversion. [Col. 0611A]

He always pursued charity, detested envy and slander, and neither uttered nor wished to hear from anyone an indecent word, idle talk, or foolish laughter. His speech was continually of peace and concord, humility and gentleness, and of the honour with which brethren ought to prefer one another. He was frequent in prayer, assiduous in reading, and eminent in devotion. Except in a grave emergency, he never wished to be absent from the day and night offices. His mind was diligently occupied with the devotion of those chanting in choir and with the service of the sacred altar, and he most tenderly loved those more devout in these matters. [Col. 0611B]

He subdued his flesh with a hair-shirt until the day of death and compelled it to serve the spirit. He wished to maintain a frugal table, not for the refreshment of his own body, since he was remarkably abstinent, but for the restoration of the poor and sick, whom he cherished with fatherly affection. On his bed he had nothing but woollen bedding laid over straw, or bearskins to drive away the cold when winter raged more fiercely, unless the suffering of excessive illness compelled him to indulge his body with softer things. As his food was modest, so too was his clothing. [Col. 0611C]

He was the first to build the monastery of St Thomas the Apostle in the place called Paraclete [Note: [Col. 0611D] In our language the place is called Ebelbolt, in the parish of Tierebye and the district of Frederiksborg.
