According to Pontoppidan, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 443, the transfer took place in 1176.]. He transferred the Order of St Augustine there, ordained that it be observed there after the transfer, and caused its perpetual observance there to be confirmed by the privilege of Pope Alexander.

But now, since in praising the man of God we have somewhat departed from our purpose, let us return to the matters we began to relate. A man suffering from dysentery, in the village called by the natives Methelhuse, was instructed in a vision to taste Abbot William’s food and be healed of his illness. The man believed the message he had heard, sent a messenger promptly to the cloister, and asked for and received what he desired. When he had eaten the food brought to him, the flow of his sickness ceased, and he immediately deserved to be restored inwardly by it. [Col. 0611D]

A certain girl from the village named Nadweth, near the cloister, was held in the torment of a severe illness. For three days she lay as if an inanimate body, with only vital warmth seeming to remain in her limbs; and her friends and relatives stood around her mourning her as dead. But her mother, named Brigida, having spent many days and nights sleepless over her in vigils, was overcome by a light sleep on the fourth day. As she slept, she saw in a dream a woman clothed in snowy garments standing beside the sick girl’s bed and saying to her: “Woman, you are greatly troubled for your daughter.”

She replied: “What wonder is it? For three days we have endured her as one about to depart at any moment; and behold, little time remains.”

The other answered: “Know that your daughter can recover health and receive an extension of life if she tastes food or leftovers of Abbot William of Paraclete.” [Col. 0612A]

Having said this, she disappeared. The girl’s mother awoke and described to everyone present all that she had heard and seen in her dream. They advised her to obey the command of the one who had warned her, for the said abbot was regarded as holy by many—and he truly was so, divine grace shining in him.

Therefore the woman, strengthened by the hope of the good vision and by the consolation of her people, hastened with quicker steps to the cloister. To the officials whom she found outside the enclosure she set forth in order the vision which she had seen. The woman’s request was accordingly reported to the abbot by the brethren, and the heaven-sent vision concerning the remedy for her daughter was recounted. [Col. 0612B]

The man of God, always bearing compassionate feelings toward the afflicted and sympathizing with both mother and daughter, ordered that the woman be given, in the Lord’s name, fish which we call *perticae*—more correctly, perches—and broth prepared for him, that it might be health and remedy for the girl struggling at the point of death. [Note: [Col. 0611D–0612D] *Percae* is the more correct reading. *Pertica* derives from the French word *perche*. We Danes call these fish *Aborre*.] Rejoicing in the gift, she quickly returned home and promptly poured into her daughter’s mouth the liquid food which she had brought. [Col. 0612C]

When this had been done a third time and it descended to her interior with a wondrous gurgling sound, the girl revived, drew breath, and after a little while sat up, though she had been as if dead. When her own people came to her, she opened her mouth, blessed God, and said: “I shall not die but live, and shall declare the works of the Lord. For I trust in the Lord that, through the prayers and merits of Abbot William, I have been restored to health.” Those who had gathered round her bore witness to the truth of these matters, and we know that their testimony is true.

[Col. 0612D] A certain man was ill in the village of Anese [Note: [Col. 0612D] Today the parish and village of Annise, in the provostship of Holboe, district of Cronborg.] and desired to drink water from the spring which the abbot had caused to be cleaned and secured with strong locks. But since no one could gain access to that spring except with the permission of the man who kept it locked, he caused his desire to be communicated to the abbot. Brother Eric, keeper of the aforesaid spring, was summoned and commanded to offer the sick man a cup of its water. When the sufferer tasted the water brought to him, he immediately learned how health-giving was its taste; for it not only quenched his thirst but also bestowed the grace of the health he had desired. [Col. 0613A]

A Cistercian monk named Haquinus, of the monastery of Esrom, had suffered for many years from such hoarseness of his constricted chest that those standing near could scarcely make out what he said. Since he had found no remedy for his illness in any medicinal drink or other treatment, a good counsel occurred to him: to turn aside to the sanctuary of St Thomas at Paraclete. He came, approached the Father of the monastery, and explained in a plaintive murmur what he suffered. Then he began humbly to beg him, for the grace of recovering health, to lay his hand upon his throat. [Col. 0613A–B]

The man of God, somewhat pleased by the petitioner, first made the sign of the cross and touched his throat, saying: “May the Son of God heal you.” The man of God was heard because of his reverence. For the monk felt divine help present with him: the passages of his laboured chest gradually opened, and the instrument of his voice, long lost, was restored day by day. He therefore returned to the house from which he had come and strengthened his brethren, declaring to all that there was an elder at Paraclete who knew how to heal people, and affirming that he was Abbot William.

At one time, as William was returning from the Roman curia [Note: [Col. 0613D] In the year 1195.], his servant’s horse injured its foot among the rocks of the Alps and was unable to proceed at all. Troubled in mind by this misfortune, he prayed the Most High that, through the merits of the saints whose relics he was carrying back with him, that horse might be healed. When the prayer was ended, he felt with his hands the horse’s pain-filled foot; by feeling it, he relieved the pain. From that hour the horse was healed and completed the journey it had begun. [Col. 0613C]

One day, when he was going out on the affairs of the house, he rode a certain nag [Note: [Col. 0613D] A *roncinus* is a lowly horse.]. The brother travelling with him, observing the horse’s beauty and the arrangement of its limbs, said: “Alas, that such a horse does not pace!” [Note: [Col. 0614D] That is, it does not make paces or steps; hence we call such a horse a *Pasganger*, a pacing horse.]

The abbot said to him: “Do you believe that it will be able to pace?”

He replied: “I do not believe it at all, because it is old and will not alter its natural gait.”

The abbot said again: “O you of little faith, why do you doubt? (Matt. 14.) God is able to make it pace as much as you please.”

Saying this, he began to urge it with his spurs. The horse, forgetting its usual gait, made even paces and moved well for as long as the man of God sat upon its back. The brother, filled with wonder at the miracle he had seen, returned home and told the brethren what had happened on the road: how the Father of the monastery had made the nag pace. And they all marvelled. [Col. 0613D]

At one time he took to a sickbed, held in the torment of grave illness. Doubting how long his life might last, on a Sunday night, harassed by a more severe attack of illness, he invoked his lady Blessed Geneviève, whom he loved with the whole desire of his mind, asking that she remember him and approach the Lord to pray for him. [Col. 0614A]

Taking pity on her devout servant, when he had fallen into a light sleep she appeared to him, standing at the foot of the bed in which he lay. With a cheerful face and sweet speech she consoled him, saying: “Do not be afraid, for we have a good Lord.”

Recognizing her by the joy of her countenance, he began to give thanks to her who had come and asked who that Lord was.

She replied: “Jesus, the Son of God.”

Hearing the Son of God named, the man of God rejoiced exceedingly, as far as sleep permitted. Soon afterward he awoke and, sensing that through the prayers of St Geneviève the Virgin he had been restored to health, blessed God, “who does not abandon those who hope in Him” (Ps. 33), but “is always wonderful in His saints” (Ps. 67). Many other miracles indeed the Lord deigned to work through him, which are not written in this book, either because through negligence they were consigned to oblivion and are not remembered, or because they seemed unbelievable to those detracting from his holiness. [Col. 0614A–B]

But now the pen must turn back to his glorious passing, and it ought briefly to be related at what time and in what manner he departed from this world to the Lord.

## Chapter V. The blessed death of the saint, and signs of his future glory preceding and following it

Seven years before his passage from this world to the Father, on a certain night, a man of handsome appearance, venerable grey hair, and comely face stood before him in a vision and said: “You will live seven days.” Deeply troubled by this vision, but filled with the Spirit of the Lord, he passed seven days unharmed and interpreted the seven days as signifying seven weeks, or seven months, or—what was truer—seven years, as the outcome proved. [Col. 0614B–C]

Therefore, chastening his body and bringing it into servitude (2 Cor. 11), although he had previously loved the Lord God with all devotion of mind and adhered to His commandments through continual observance, yet from that time to the end of his life he so crucified his flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5) that his former life, compared with the life that followed, would have seemed luxurious and pleasure-loving. Who saw him praying, his cheeks bathed in tears, without weeping? When he celebrated divine worship at the altar, offering the sacred mystery to God, he was so inflamed and so tearful as though he saw before him the Lord’s sufferings in the flesh. [Col. 0614D]

It would take too long to express in words with how many vigils, fasts, and continual prayers he afflicted himself and prepared himself as a burnt offering to the Lord. The Lord further chose to test the patience of His servant and prove him as gold in a furnace: He so filled his body with ulcers that from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no soundness in him (Isa. 1). Knowing that power is perfected in weakness, he endured all things patiently and said: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

[Col. 0615A] Meanwhile, after nearly seven years had passed in remarkable abstinence and mortification of the flesh, Lent approached, to be observed by all the faithful with sacred devotion. The man of God, diligently meditating upon his last things and the struggle of his end, although still ignorant of the day and hour of his dissolution, knew that the inescapable limit was drawing near. Every day, with the utmost contrition of heart, an outpouring of tears, and great reverence, he celebrated the sacrifices of our Lord Jesus Christ and fortified himself by receiving His most holy body and blood.

On the Wednesday preceding the Lord’s Supper, while he rested in his chamber with certain brethren who had come to speak with him, the prior complained to him and to the other brethren that he had never endured a more grievous night. But the man of God replied, on the contrary: “I do not remember ever having had a better or more delightful night, because I saw my Lord Jesus Christ. Two others were with Him, and I was the third; with them I was delighted beyond expression.” [Col. 0615B]

The prior said: “Perhaps, holy Father, in this visitation the Lord came to call you to Himself, as He promised you before you entered the regions of Denmark.”

Sighing at the prior’s response and bathing his face in tears, he said: “Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1).

The next day, called the Lord’s Supper, he approached the altar to celebrate the divine mysteries. After giving absolution to his disciples in the customary manner, communicating them from his own hands, and celebrating Mass, he went with the other brethren to receive Christ in the poor and performed the *mandatum*—the washing of feet—with great devotion alongside them. When this was done, he entered to take his last supper with his disciples, imitating in this the Lord’s example. [Col. 0615C]

O blessed supper, made more illustrious by the presence of so great a Father than enriched by the delicacies of its meal! Who could express in words how cheerful a countenance, how joyful a face, the holy man showed to all who attended that feast? Already his face wonderfully displayed a presage of future joy, discernible from the abundance of gladness seen in him beyond his usual manner. Already divine mercy had entered the dwelling-place prepared for it to dine; already the Holy Spirit had wholly filled his inner person and, like a bridegroom in his chamber (Ps. 18), rested in the chamber of his heart. Already his flesh, visible to bodily eyes, showed how great was the joyful exultation with which his soul rejoiced in the Lord his God because of the glory of the future reward which the Lord had determined to give him. [Col. 0615D]

The Lord had deigned to reveal this more than twelve years earlier in a vision to one of his disciples, a man of honourable conduct named Gerard.

One night, as the aforesaid canon rested in his bed, a man mature in age spoke thunderously: “Rise; follow me.” Following him, he was led through unknown places and at last came to a very beautiful plain, delightful with flowers. They entered a house of marvellous size, built of marble stones. The tongue of the beholder could not express how great its brightness, sweetness of fragrance, and marvellous delight were. Within it stood a throne adorned with precious gems and the purest gold; in the midst of the throne was placed a golden crown, decorated with the most precious stones but not yet complete. Around the throne sat four men in white, fitting golden plates with precious stones together to complete the crown. [Col. 0616A]

As the aforesaid brother, full of amazement and as though caught up in ecstasy, silently considered what had been shown to him, his guide addressed him in these words: “Do you know whose throne or crown this is?”

When he denied knowing, the guide said: “Your abbot merited this throne when he was converted from the world to the Lord, when for Christ he left houses, riches, and the glory of this world, denied himself, took up his cross, and followed the Redeemer. But when the crown is completed, he will be crowned through the many tribulations and grievous persecutions which he has bravely endured and will yet endure for the observance of the Rule; and in him will be fulfilled what the Apostle James says: ‘Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love Him’” (Jas. 1). [Col. 0616B]

After he had risen from supper, he wished to wash the feet of his disciples, but was prevented by an extremely severe pain in his side. Sitting down, therefore, he prayed: “Lord God, in all things and through all things (Eph. 4), let Your will be done (Matt. 6), You who are blessed for ages (Rom. 4). Make Your face shine upon Your servant (Ps. 118) and save me; do not disappoint me in my expectation. Do not cast me away in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not forsake me” (Ps. 70). [Col. 0616C]

As the illness continued and worsened, he was led to bed, enduring the rest of the day and half of the following night in great suffering. Afterwards, since divine grace was not idle in him, that pain was soothed and he was seized by a mild fever. When his bodily strength began to fail, on the vigil of Easter the brethren who had come to visit him urged him to provide for himself and be anointed with holy unction.

As they thus urged him, he said: “It is not as you think with me. I feel no pain and absolutely no weakness in my body. I should like a bed to be made for me in the choir, so that I might be present at the service of the Lord’s Resurrection on the coming night.”

When they replied that he would be unable to endure the voices of those singing, he added: “Let us then do what is better.” O the venerable and unchanging devotion of so great a man toward divine worship—a devotion which could not be diminished either by any event or by the distress of so great a bodily decline! [Col. 0616D]

As he suffered thus, brethren were appointed to keep watch over him in vigils. On the holy night of the Lord’s Resurrection, the man of God, concerned for his passing, summoned one of those standing by him and said: “You know, son, that a new solemnity has come, to be revered by all the people; therefore we must be clothed in new garments. Bring me the garment which you have, that I may put it on.”

Understanding what garment he meant, the brother brought him a new hair-shirt, removed the old one, and clothed him in the new. [Col. 0617A]

Although he was in great weakness, his attendants again urged him to receive the liquid of holy oil. As they pressed this upon him, he answered: “By the favour of our Lord Jesus Christ, I shall await the light.”

Meanwhile, while the convent persisted in the vigils and praises of the glorious night, when the third reading had ended and the third responsory had begun, after the Sabbath had passed, one of the attendants hastened in and announced that he would soon depart. The darkness of night having been driven away, the dawn of sacred light now glowed—the light which the man of God had promised to await. [Col. 0617B]

As the responsory was sung, “that those coming might anoint Jesus,” the prior summoned some brethren and left the choir, carrying with him the liquid of holy oil, with which he might anoint the venerable Father, now at the point of death. When they arrived, the saint of God did nothing but repeat frequently: “Quickly, quickly.”

After the anointing was completed, he was laid upon ashes and hair-cloth, so that, according to Martin’s teaching, he might die in ashes and hair-cloth as a Christian and a true Catholic. This done, released into precious death, he breathed forth his spirit on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1202 [Note: [Col. 0617D] St William died on 6 April, very early on Easter morning, in the year 1202 according to the old French reckoning then ending, but according to our reckoning in 1203. For in this year Easter fell on 6 April, whereas in 1202 it fell on 14 April. L.], in the ninety-eighth year of his age, and in the fortieth year after he had undertaken the care of the Lord’s flock [Note: [Col. 0617D] Henschenius and Papebrochius, *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I, p. 624, think that “thirtieth” should be restored here, since they do not believe that St William came to Denmark before 1171. LANGEB. [But see above, col. 604, note 9. I believe, however, that this author used a round number, since William was actually in Denmark only thirty-eight years.]]. [Col. 0617C]

Thus that soul, released from the prison-house of the flesh, passed from sorrow to joy, from labour to rest, and from the world to the Lord. The spiritual sons of the venerable Father bore his body with hymns and songs, groanings and tears, into the holy church, laying it in the middle of the choir. When they had returned to their places, they began the *Te Deum laudamus*, and completed the Easter-morning Lauds with the tearful voices of those singing, yet with due veneration.

Reader, observe how wonderful God is in His saints: for neither was this man’s life without glory nor his death without grace, but it was most precious in the sight of God. On the very day on which the Lord Himself rose victorious from the underworld, the Lord received him into paradise. He who had often celebrated the solemnities of the Lord’s Resurrection on earth with great rejoicing was, on that same day, joined with fitting honour to the choirs of angels. [Col. 0617D]

On the second day of Easter he was buried before the altar of St Thomas the Apostle, which he himself had built. Lord Abbot Turchillus of the church of Blessed Mary of Esrom, with his monks, rendered the rites of his funeral; priests, clerics, and many others also came running with great devotion to take part in his obsequies. In that place our Lord Jesus Christ, to the praise and glory of His name, through the intercessions of His glorious confessor, grants innumerable benefits to this present day to those who seek Him with their whole heart—to whom be honour and glory through endless ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 0618A]

O how great was the mourning of all, and especially the lamentation of the disciples! Although we were certain of the glorification of so great a Father, nevertheless, deprived of his presence, we grieved in the human manner. “The days of our festival have been turned into mourning, and our sabbaths into lamentation.” Although we ought to have rejoiced that he whom we had had as teacher on earth we should have as intercessor in heaven—if the mind were capable of admitting reason in grief. [Col. 0618B]

But blessed be God, who “turns our sorrow into joy” (John 16). For after the passing of our Father, our young men saw visions and our old men dreamed dreams, through which we were certain that the Lord would shortly make His saint glorious.

Two young men of this saint’s household, living in different regions, at the very hour of his passing from this world saw in a vision how he passed to the joy of the angels. Although their visions differ somewhat, both deserve to be related and remembered in full faith. One of them, named Nicholas, was pursuing literary studies at Hildesheim, a city in the German lands [Col. 0618C]. At the same hour when the man of God, about to enter heaven, laid aside the clay of his body, he saw in a vision a person unknown to him, clothed in a white robe, ascending into heaven. As is commonly shown in paintings commemorating the Lord’s Ascension—where he is depicted as received wholly beneath the clouds and only his feet appear—so this saint too was received beneath white clouds, and only his feet and the hems of his garments could be seen. As he marvelled at the sight, gazing fixedly into heaven, a man stood beside him and said: “Why do you marvel as you look into heaven? This man taken up into heaven is your abbot, who overcame the persecutions of the world through patience; now he is crowned because [Col. 0618D] he lived faithfully according to the Lord’s commandments.” When he awoke, he was led by the way to the monastery from which he had departed in apostasy. He returned there, offered himself for correction, and made the aforesaid vision known to all.

To the other of those mentioned above, named Godmund, who was living in the cloister called Sora, the following vision of the glorified man was shown. As dawn approached on the Sunday of the Resurrection, he saw in a vision, while almost awake, a multitude of angels singing with most sweet [Col. 0619A] melody. Among them two angels, shining with inexpressible brightness, supported on their right and left a mature man adorned in priestly vestments; his arms rested upon their shoulders, which they held up, and they proceeded even to heaven. The devil followed them, accompanied by no small throng of raging and shrieking demons. But once the holy angels had been received into heaven, that ancient enemy, like one in grief, returned by the way he had come with his company; some of the demons followed at a slow pace, walking lame. The man who saw this vision, becoming bolder, said to one of those who came more slowly than the others: “I adjure you by the Son of God to tell me what these things are that I have seen.” Looking at his questioner with a grim face and sidelong eye [Col. 0619B], he answered: “If you wish to know: your Abbot William has been taken from the world and carried into heaven with so great an angelic escort. We came in order to claim some right over him; but, suffering violence from the angels, we were disappointed of our purpose.” Rising at first light on the first day of the week, the aforesaid young man explained his vision to his master and to all who were with him. They answered: “We truly believe that he has now fallen asleep, and that his place has become one of peace.” At length he returned to our house, carefully related these matters to us in order, and, receiving the habit of religion there, began to serve God.

## CHAPTER VI. Miracles after the passing of St. William

[Col. 0619C]

Our Saviour Jesus Christ, wishing to reveal before the sons of men the outstanding miracles of his most beloved confessor William—whom after death he clothed in heaven with the robe of immortality—gave him power to perform upon those sick with various ailments the works that he himself did, and greater than these: so that many might praise his wisdom, that it might not be blotted out for ever, that his memory might not depart, and that his name might be sought from generation to generation. Therefore the servant of God, after he slept with his fathers, began first among his unbelievers and enemies to shine gradually in miracles, like the morning star in the midst of a cloud, in order to show as liars [Col. 0619D] those who had stained him and slandered his holiness, blaspheming his name. But after he had been glorified among those near him, he began, for the praise and glory of the name of him who made all saints, to flash far and wide with greater and more frequent wonders, like the sun shining at noon. Hence, from the four quarters of the earth, people gathered, desiring to see the marvels performed through him. He drove demons from possessed bodies; healed paralytics; restored sight to the blind, walking to the lame, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute; raised to their proper state those who were contracted and crawled upon their own knees; cleansed lepers; raised the dead; and recalled the half-dead from the very jaws of death to life. [Col. 0620A] He healed not only people but also animals, as God multiplied his mercy with him. Winds checked their storms at the invocation of his name, and seas rested from their bitterness. But, having briefly recalled these things, let us come to the miracles which we either heard or saw in the city of our God, that is, at Paraclete, where the glorious confessor of God, William, rests.

While Abbot William was still in his corruptible body, worn down by old age, two teeth were pulled from his head. Entrusting them to Brother Saxo, he said: “Keep these teeth in your care, and do not lose them.” Saxo did as he had been asked, wondering within himself why this charge had been entrusted to him. But after the Lord took William from their midst [Col. 0620B], his disciples who survived wished, in memory of so great a father, to receive for themselves some article of his possessions or clothing. Among them was a sacristan named Brixius, who complained that he had received nothing belonging to him except the fur mitre which William had been accustomed to wear upon his head. To him, while he so complained, the brother entrusted with the teeth answered: “I shall give you no small gift, indeed a great one: a precious pearl, namely, a tooth of our Father, who loved you in his lifetime not merely singularly but especially.” Saying this, he handed him the tooth. Giving abundant thanks for the gift bestowed upon him, Brixius held the tooth he had received in great veneration, as was fitting. O how great were the benefits which God afterward bestowed upon mortals [Col. 0620C] through this tooth—benefits which, if written down, a weak mind would by no means consent to believe.

At that time there was in the cloister a schoolboy named Grimolf, about fifteen years old, afflicted with falling sickness. One day, when he had been thrown to the ground by that disease and was rolling about foaming, Abbot Richard, successor of the man of God, came upon him. Moved by compassion for him, he said to the secretary who had come with him: “Do you see how wretchedly this cleric is tormented? Go quickly; wash the Father’s tooth in water, and pour that water into his mouth, so that we may test what power that tooth possesses.” Obeying the abbot’s command, the man fulfilled what had been enjoined upon him. But when he wished to pour the health-giving liquid [Col. 0620D] into the sufferer’s mouth, he could not, because his teeth were clenched together. He therefore took a knife and forced open his jaws, pouring the brought water into his mouth. When Grimolf swallowed it as he tasted it, he began to roar and groan as though he had taken a boiling liquid of oil. Yet shortly afterward he became still, as though caught up in ecstasy. After some hours of the day had passed, his spirit revived and he rose healthy. Thereafter that illness neither touched nor distressed him, nor caused him any trouble. This was the beginning of the signs which the servant of God performed after his passing, before his disciples, and by which he made his glory known. Sueno son of Tolph, afflicted by a similar illness, received the same mercy.

[Col. 0621A] St. William again made known the glory of his holiness in the village of Frisleven.

> [Note: [Col. 0621D] Perhaps the parish and village of Ferslev in Horn provostship and Frederiksborg district; or perhaps [Col. 0622D] the village of Froerslev in Herlov parish, Lyunge-Frederiksborg provostship, and Frederiksborg district.]

He made it known in this way. There was there a woman possessed by a most evil demon. To everyone who came to her to offer consolation, she disclosed the secrets of the heart and reproached them with sins, as the enemy suggested to her. The deacon of that village came to invoke the name of his God over her and cast out the demon. The woman saw the deacon entering to her, and, aroused to insults, cried: “Deacon, why do you come? Stand outside. You are not worthy to enter beneath my roof. I know very well who you are and what you have done, having knowledge of your ways. You are the one who used to steal and pluck the hen of a poor woman, hiding the feathers and down under a hedge, and eating that same hen for supper, thinking that your theft was hidden from me. Depart from me, most wicked man, depart! Let your blessing be far from me.” Confounded by the accusations made against him, the deacon returned home sadder than he had come, conscious of the crime charged against him. A certain lay brother of the household and house of this saint, who was serving as a resident at the same village, detested the madness of the aforesaid woman. He came to the cloister and asked for water in which the holy man’s tooth had been washed. He asked and received it; returning, he offered it to the woman to drink. She drank, and, once the unclean spirit had been expelled, was made well of her illness. Not long afterward, another woman in the same village was seized by a demon and cured by the same remedy.

As Brother Saxo travelled and was passing through Metheluse [Col. 0621C], the people of that village cried out to him: “Lord, if you can do anything, help us; take pity on us.” When he asked them what was wrong and what they wanted done, they replied: “There is here a woman named Hestrith who, having an excessive desire to eat vegetable roots, entered her garden and began to dig them up from the earth and gnaw greedily at those she had dug up. As soon as she had done this, an evil spirit leapt into her and violently tore at her. Behold, we keep her bound so that she may not kill herself or strangle her children. We beat her with rods and threaten more severe lashes, but gain nothing by it; indeed, we pile punishment upon punishment.” Moved by the woman’s misfortune, he ordered [Col. 0621D] water to be brought. Marking it with the tooth of St. William which he had kept for himself, and dipping the tooth in it, he invoked the name of the Holy Trinity and of the saint himself. He gave it to them to carry away and offer to the raging woman. When she drank the water offered, the wicked guest, unable to endure the force of the sacred liquid, unwillingly left the dwelling he had occupied, and the woman recovered her former senses. A little later, the aforesaid brother returned and turned aside to the woman’s house to see how she was. He found her sound of mind and praising God in his saint, who had shown her his mercy.

In the same village, Wider’s wife was pregnant. The time [Col. 0622A] for her childbirth had been fulfilled, but because of the difficulty of labour she could not give birth. She was miserably tormented: labouring, yet not delivering; languishing, yet not dying. Afflicted by such tortures, she became a cause of grief to all her household. Meanwhile the child was deprived of life within the enclosure of its mother, and the womb of the unhappy mother became the tomb of her wretched offspring. A corpse lay within a corpse, the dead within the dying: taken away before it was seen, buried before it was born. Her husband, anxious about his wife’s death, ran here and there and sought out everyone to discover whether any remedy might be found for the dying woman. At last he came to the cloister, found the sacristan, and asked him whether he knew any counsel, written charm, or medicine against so miserable a case. The latter answered: “There is no [Col. 0622B] need of medicine or a written charm in such a crisis, but of the aid of God and the saints. If you bring faith to it, I believe that I can provide her with an antidote of salvation. I shall wash St. William’s tooth in water, which you shall take to her to drink. If she believes that she can be delivered through his merits, after tasting it she will escape the danger of death.” He did what he had promised, sent the man back home with the saving drink, well instructed in faith. When he had returned home, he poured into the woman’s mouth what he had brought, though she was already near death from pain, and then went out. Scarcely had he gone outside when the holy liquid ran down into the woman’s innermost parts and she gave birth to a putrid foetus. Seeing this, and recovering her breath, she cried: “If this was to be my lot, what need had I to conceive? Look, O Lord, and see whether there is [Col. 0622C] a sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1); “yet I give you thanks, for through the merits of your holy confessor William you have delivered me from the danger of death.” When the neighbours heard that such a miracle had been performed for her, they rejoiced with her, giving praise to God and St. William no less for the second miracle than for the first.

Once, when the frequently mentioned Brother Saxo came to Willike and lodged there, a demoniac entered, raging and gnashing his teeth. Such madness tormented him that he often abandoned human habitation and lived among beasts like a beast. At his entrance the entire household was thrown into turmoil, fearing his attack. Looking at the madman, the brother said: “Do you wish to eat?” He mockingly and abusively replied: [Col. 0622D] “You eat.” The brother again said: “Do you wish to drink?” and ordered water to be brought to him. When there was delay in bringing the water, he took whey, which was at hand, dipped St. William’s tooth in it, and offered it to the madman. When he drank it, it became sweet as honey in his mouth. He therefore said to the giver: “What you gave me is good; I ask that you give me more.” When he drank a second and third time, the phantasmal spirit was expelled and he came to himself. The next day he followed the same brother to the cloister, magnifying God and rendering thanks to William, his deliverer, teaching all by his own experience that he is mighty and his name is holy [Col. 0623A] (Luke 1).

Once, when Lord Peter, bishop of Roskilde, our brother, was staying with us and had reclined at supper in the evening, his servants, who were bringing what was needed for the meal, announced to him: “Blessed be God, because we have now seen with our own eyes a burning candle, like a torch from heaven, descend above the tomb of St. William and, as it descended, make a passage through the roof of the church.” One after another entered to report the same vision. Then the venerable priest, raising his eyes to heaven and blessing God, began to speak as follows: “Unless it were that the Lord is mighty to magnify and glorify whomsoever he wills, to whatever extent he wills, and in whatever manner he wills, I could scarcely give credence to miracles reported [Col. 0623B] as performed at the tombs of certain persons whose life and conduct while in the flesh I knew. But no scruple of doubt clings to my heart concerning the miracles performed by this saint. I have considered his life proven in every respect, so that one can scarcely admire sufficiently the contrition and compunction of his heart, the humility of his mind, the purity of his conscience, his great charity toward friends and enemies, and his exceptional generosity toward the poor despite extreme poverty. Therefore I shall praise his name continually and celebrate it in thanksgiving, because his goods are established in the Lord, and the Lord himself will be his eternal reward.”

> [Note: [Col. 0623D] On him Claude du Molinet says thus in his notes on Stephen of Tournai’s letters, p. 119: He was Absalon’s nephew and succeeded him. He had made canonical profession at Paris into the hands of Stephen, abbot of St. Geneviève, later bishop of Tournai, who addressed to him two of his letters, namely Letters 157 and 163. His death [Col. 0624D] is recorded in the necrology of St. Geneviève on 18 October as follows: “The anniversary of the pious memory of Peter, bishop of Roskilde, chancellor of the kingdom of Denmark, and professed canon of our house.” LANGEBEK. He died in 1214, having become bishop of Roskilde in 1192 after Absalon’s resignation.]

A certain woman, poor in possessions but rich in faith, presented herself at St. William’s tomb to seek from him the grace of health. Her belly, as we saw, was so swollen by the magnitude of its tumour that it could scarcely be encircled by a girdle three cubits long. While the brethren went to their meal, she obtained permission and persisted at the tomb of the man of God in tears and prayer. While they took bodily food, she was refreshed by spiritual food: within that hour she was healed of her illness, as if the Lord’s confessor had answered her prayer, “Woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you desire” (Matt. 15). O how steadfast was the faith of that weak woman—how meritorious, how swiftly rewarded! When the brethren returned to the church to give thanks, she was found so slender and thin that she could scarcely be believed to be the same woman, retaining no trace of swelling or distension. Asked whether she had suffered any rupture, inward [Col. 0623D] or outward, through which harmful fluid or pus had flowed away, she denied that in her cure she had felt any rupture or pain; rather, the swelling had subsided, as pleased him who made her well. In memory of this event and to increase the faith of others, the girdle which she had used, of the length stated above, was hung up. Thus bells are rung, praises are given to God, and he is glorified by all in the miracle which he performed through the merit of his servant [Col. 0624A]. Wonders multiply day by day. The cruse of oil in the house of God does not fail but increases; the alabaster jar of ointment exudes; the heavenly fragrance of balsam fills the air; crowds of the sick assemble and receive the rewards of benefactions.

How great was the holiness of our memorable Father St. William in his life will be declared by the wonders of the following miracles as well as the preceding. For he frequently bestowed the many benefits of his compassion publicly upon the needy. He often complained in visions to the brethren and others that he was confined in a cramped place, because he had been buried in the middle of the choir of a small church made of timber, capable of receiving few besides the brethren. Therefore, he said, he could neither benefit them nor grant to others the grace of the desired health, [Col. 0624B] as long as he was confined there and people’s access was prevented. Thus, in the seventh year after he rested from his labours, when the sanctuary of a new and broader church built of tiles was completed, and the brethren’s choir was arranged in it, far removed from the mausoleum of the man of God, while the wooden church was left to pilgrims and sick people coming from every direction to pray, such a multitude of people gathered on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension that, when the church itself was filled, scarcely the whole courtyard could contain the rest. Then from evening until Mass on the following day fourteen miracles occurred; on the next Sunday, four; and on every day of the feast of Pentecost, four or five.

[Col. 0624C] When the feast of Blessed Abbot Botulf followed—celebrated eight days before the feast of St. John the Baptist—and the high altar in honour of Blessed Thomas the Apostle was dedicated by the venerable Peter, bishop of Roskilde, so many and such great marvels occurred that no one can recount them except him from whom nothing is hidden. For the sick were healed on the road by which they came, and in the wood far from the monastery where the servant of God had sat or walked. O what joy and exultation then filled all the people, seeing the mighty acts and wonders of God which he worked through his saint. The church resounded, the courtyard resounded, and the wood resounded with the voices of those praising and saying: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117). We too rendered the service due from us [Col. 0624D], singing and making melody to the Lord in heart and voice (Eph. 5), because he is good, because his mercy endures for ever (Ps. 106), and because the Dayspring from on high has visited us and raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant (Luke 1). Then we remembered his own words, by which in his lifetime he comforted us when we complained of our poverty. He said to us: “Be patient” (1 Thess. 5), “for God will yet visit you with his salvation [Col. 0625A]” (Ps. 105), “and your barns shall be filled with abundance” (Prov. 3), “and this place shall be very glorious.”

## CHAPTER VII. Other miracles of St. William

A certain woman from Kopmanhaven, named Olava, had suffered from sore eyes since infancy, and for that reason became blind. Hearing the everywhere-famous report of the holy man, she came to his tomb, seeking in tears and prayers to be worthy to receive light. She sought and obtained what she desired: while she persisted in prayer, her eyes were opened so that she saw everything clearly.

> [Note: [Col. 0625D] In charters of 1186, 1193, and 1198 this town is called *Hafn*. Saxo, book XIV, Ascensius edition, fol. 164, calls it, about the year 1167, “a village of Zealand which is named the Merchants’ Harbour”; on fol. 179b he mentions a castle founded by Absalon in the public [Col. 0626D] harbour of merchants, and on fol. 180 calls it “Absalon’s city.” In a charter of 1253 it is called *Koopmannoehafn*. The most ancient mention of this place is in *Knytlinga Saga*, ch. 22, p. 38, under the name *Hofn*, for the year 1044.]

On the vigil of Pentecost, a young man of twenty, paralysed and deprived of all use of his limbs, was brought in others’ hands to the tomb of St. William [Col. 0625B] and laid down. The keeper of the tomb was asked to give the paralytic the saving liquid, namely water in which St. William’s tooth had been washed. Granting the petition of those who asked, he gave him the healing water. When he tasted it, the sick man recovered the use of his limbs, all his joints being strengthened for their proper function.

A woman from Bardeleve, named Reginalda, had been born blind from her mother’s womb. Her darkness was as her light: she lacked the light of her eyes, but flourished in the light of her heart. Therefore, rooted and founded in faith, and knowing that the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth (Ps. 144), she set out as a pilgrim for St. William, guided by her brother. When she arrived, she began to keep vigils in that cemetery at night. While [Col. 0625C] she sat and rested from her labour, a heavy horror came upon her, and fear and trembling seized her. Thus, as though in ecstasy, she was raised above her feet and made strange clappings with her hands; soon afterward she fell back to the ground and was raised again. Since she was thus repeatedly moved, her brother, knowing that she was pregnant, became greatly afraid that she might miscarry or suffocate in her womb what she carried through the violence of such exertion. He therefore turned to the Lord and his saint and began humbly to pray for her. But because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous and his ears attend to their prayers (Ps. 33), the child was preserved in the womb and the woman was enlightened through the merit of the man of God. For her night [Col. 0625D] was turned into light, and amid that very time of darkness she lost the darkness of her eyes.

Andrew, a priest of Zunthe, was endangered by a long affliction of the eyes and feared that he would lose their light and be subjected to the darkness of unending night. With a contrite heart and humbled spirit, therefore, so that he might escape this darkness, he vowed that he would go to St. William. Hoping to recover health and knowing that a foolish and faithless promise displeases God, he set out to fulfil his vow. [Col. 0626A] Since the saint’s power was available to heal him, the dimness was removed along the road by which he travelled, and his eyes began to grow clear and recover their lost sight. Arriving at the tomb of the man of God, he disclosed this miracle to all, blessing God, who had given them such a protector for the salvation of his people.

Five days before the feast of Blessed John the Baptist, citizens of Roskilde left their city and came to St. William. A mute man accompanied them, a good hired labourer named Ketillus, Norwegian by birth. Satan had bound his tongue for eleven years, and he could say nothing. After entering the church, the spirit disturbed him and he was dashed down to the ground. He often rose again but could not stand with steady step; he turned [Col. 0626B] onto his sides and rolled from place to place, fell upon his face, and was thrown against a stone wherever the impulse carried him. Injured by repeated falls and badly torn, he cast off his clothes. He seemed to have come to his harm, since he was thought mad, though divine power was thus preparing to heal him. On Sunday night, when Matins had nearly been sung, the bond of his tongue was loosed and he spoke properly, glorifying God. People ran together to this kindly and glorious spectacle, so full of joy and worthy of wonder. The people of Roskilde ran to see Ketillus speaking, whom they had long known to be mute. At length he was presented to the brethren and brought before the prior. Asked where he was from and how he had lost his speech, he replied: “I am [Col. 0626C] from Norway. Eleven years ago, while sleeping in a field, I lost my speech: I fell asleep healthy and woke mute.” As he related these things, a noble matron with whom he had lodged for two years bore witness to his words, together with many others who had gathered for the feast day.

On the day of St. Nicholas, a peasant from Lucethorp came to us with his twelve-year-old son, deaf and mute. The father had assigned him as keeper of his livestock. While lying upon a little hill, as is the custom of shepherds, he fell asleep; but when he rose from deep sleep, he had become deaf and mute. The father asked us to admit his son to the saint’s tomb, and we granted his request. The keeper [Col. 0626D] of the tomb took St. William’s tooth, put it into water, and poured the same water into the boy’s ears and mouth, saying: “I command you, in the name of the Lord and through the power of St. William, to tell us what your name is.” At the exorcist’s voice the boy’s mouth was opened and his hearing was restored at the same time. He answered: “Peter.” Thereafter, asked many further questions, he freely answered each one. Seeing these things, we rejoiced greatly, praising God in his saint, who made the deaf hear and the mute speak.

[Col. 0627A] At another time a seven-year-old boy was brought forward, whom his mother’s womb had brought into this light deaf and mute. A considerable crowd was then present in the church, drawn by the report of this new event. The brother therefore took that effective common remedy for the sick and infirm and put it into the boy’s mouth and ears, saying: “By the power of St. William I command you to repeat after me the words which you hear me utter.” Adjured through the power of the holy confessor, he immediately acquired the two senses denied him from the beginning of his birth, namely hearing and speech. As the brother began the Lord’s Prayer, he spoke word after word in an articulated and intelligible voice, although he stammered in forming [Col. 0627B] and pronouncing the words. Those who had brought him stood astonished, marvelling at what proceeded from his mouth.

At a certain feast, when countless men and women were flocking to our saint, a woman brought in her arms a little girl in whose eye an immense ulcer had grown, a very horrible sight. Approaching the brother responsible for the care of the sick with her daughter, she begged him to pour a drop of the sacred liquid into the unhappy child’s eye. He listened to the woman’s petition and did as requested; moreover, he applied the holy tooth to the swelling. Wonderful to tell: immediately the skin below the eye burst, as though pierced by iron, and the swelling subsided, yielding to the presence of the relic. The discharge did not cease flowing [Col. 0627C] until the eye opened and became like the sound eye in clarity of vision; and, seeing this, all the people gave praise to God.

As the miracles increased and the confessor’s fame grew, a woman afflicted by many pains fled to his aid. She humbly entreated the saint to commend her to the Lord by his prayers, so that he might free her from her sufferings in whatever way he knew to be expedient for her. Spending night vigils in the church, she was overtaken by a light sleep and rested her head upon the *forma*—the seat against which the saint had customarily leaned during his life—while remaining intent on prayer.

> [Note: [Col. 0627D] By *formae*, Henschenius and Papebrochius, p. 641, note e, understand choir benches.]

She saw the Lord’s confessor standing beside her and saying: “Woman, return to your home, because you cannot be healed [Col. 0627D] at present. Yet your salvation is in the Lord’s hand. After you have spent a little time in your sufferings, you will be placed like a living stone in the heavenly building.” Awaking at these words, the woman became happier because of the promises than if she had lost her bodily pains. Reporting what had been said to her to those present, and recognizing that God’s decree is unchangeable, she returned home and, with the utmost devotion, awaited the end of her life.

Nor do I think the following should be passed over in silence, since it is not greatly unlike the earlier account. There was a man weak in his limbs and almost mad in the village of Anese, which is near the cloister. Seeking to obtain from the saint relief for his illness [Col. 0628A] and weakness, he came to William’s sarcophagus. After continuing there for five days in prayers and tears, that he might see divine aid come upon him, he fell asleep. While he slept, God’s confessor appeared and said: “Why do you lie here? You will not have health in this place; but when you return home you will recover health, though it will not endure long.” At this news the man’s heart was troubled and his bones trembled (Jer. 23), and sleep departed from his eyes. When he awoke, mindful of his vision, he reported to us what he had heard, not without great contrition of heart. Instructed, then, that divine Providence does not fail in its ordering of him, he returned to his own home. Not long afterward [Col. 0628B] he became stronger, seized an axe, and went into the forest to cut wood. While he worked more intently, the tree on which he was working fell upon him; his limbs were broken, and he died. It is not for me, however, to investigate why he met such a death, because “the judgments of God are a great abyss” (Ps. 37).

In the same village lived two women afflicted with different infirmities. One had lost the light of her eyes; the other was being consumed in some part of her body by the sacred fire. They diligently offered prayers to God for their deliverance and bound themselves by a vow to St. William, that through the aid of his merits they might deserve to be delivered from so great a calamity. As they persisted thus in prayer, she whose eyes had grown dim [Col. 0628C] saw in a vision that she was going, as though on pilgrimage, to the monastery of St. Thomas. She met St. William on the way, clothed in a surplice and carrying a sprinkler with holy water in his hand. Greatly frightened at seeing him, she scarcely dared ask who he was. Nevertheless she asked, “Who are you, lord?” He replied: “Take heart, daughter. I am Abbot William, whom you have often invoked. I am now going to the woman in your village who is afflicted by the biting fire, because she cries out to me all day. But meanwhile go to the place of my rest and await my arrival there.” At that same hour she awoke well, with the light of her eyes restored; and in the other woman the fire was extinguished—not a fire that gave light, but one that [Col. 0628D] consumed. In short: just as both were cured together by divine mercy, so they came together to the tomb of God’s confessor, fell to the ground together, rose together, and, after giving thanks, together proclaimed to all the glorious miracles worked upon them. Nor did they alone do this: their fellow villagers also bore witness to their cures with great joy.

A certain priest from Scania, named Reinerus, of Hazdelzar [Note: [Col. 0628D] A place unknown to me, and perhaps corruptly read.], afflicted by the holy fire in his tongue, lay almost at the point of death, for the illness was exceedingly severe. He had formerly been a disciple of St. William, but, having apostatized, lived a worldly life among secular people. When death was already at the door and the end of his life was hastening on, [Col. 0629A] he sent his son to the monks of the Church of All Saints [Note: [Col. 0629D] Near the city of Lund; incorrectly called the church of St. Helena by Lord Tunel in his introduction to the geography of Sweden, p. 235.], to bring him some brother who might administer to him confession and anointing, and clothe him in the habit of their order. Meanwhile, coming to himself and reflecting on the glory of miracles with which the Lord had glorified his holy man William, he was pierced with contrition of heart because he had made no satisfaction to him either while he lived in the flesh or after he had been glorified by laying aside the flesh. He said within himself: “Holy Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15). “But spare my sins; and if, before the messenger returns, some grace of salvation visits me, I shall return to your house and endeavor to amend what I have done amiss.”

In his heart he vowed righteousness; and behold, the divine [Col. 0629B] mercy, which is always at hand for penitents, was present to him and delivered him as he invoked his saint. The biting fire was suddenly extinguished; the swelling in his mouth burst; and matter mingled with blood flowed out, as though someone were squeezing his tongue with his fingers. Having been made well, he went to the saint, telling us how greatly the Lord had dealt with his soul. Yet he delayed renouncing his apostasy; for he was among those who cry to the Lord in their time of distress and, once delivered, return to iniquity—and that error is worse than the former one.

A certain girl in the village of Gherlufe [Note: [Col. 0629D] Today Gierlose, between Slangerop and Frederiksborg. [Col. 0630D] L.], was tormented by the same illness. She had already ceased to speak and awaited her final hour. There was in the same village a [Col. 0629C] cleric named Lawrence, who cherished her tenderly. More distressed than the rest at the death of the woman beloved to his soul, he hurried to the cloister and, having obtained medicinal water, returned swiftly. With particular care he poured into his beloved’s mouth the healing liquid which he had brought, and anointed with it the growing swelling. When this was done, the substance of the disease was extinguished and the woman recovered from her infirmity.

But what is easier: to grant health of mind or of body? He who healed many in body healed in mind a woman from the city of Ribe. For many weeks after childbirth she had been mad, and had inflicted upon her husband, mother, sister, and other friends an unexpected wound of grief. They brought her to the saint with her hands bound behind her back; although she resisted and cried out, [Col. 0629D] she was presented to the saint. Led into the church, she filled the church with shouting, multiplying blasphemous words. There, raging all day and all night, she deserved, with the coming of the sunlight, to receive the light of reason. Released from her bonds, she parted her hair; clothed in her own garments, she brought joy to her kinsfolk. At the morning Mass she received the Eucharist from the priest’s hand; and she who had been brought in grief returned, now in possession of herself, with joy.

A man named Bernard was travelling by ship to the Scanian fair. While he was sailing at sea, [Col. 0630A] a hawk which he held in his hand escaped and flew away. The next day, when he had put into harbor and reclined for dinner, he heard those reclining with him say that in their days unheard-of miracles were being wrought through St. William. Astonished by this, and with his heart still wounded by the loss of his hawk, he burst out in these words: “St. William, restore my hawk to me, and I will give you a mark of wax.” When these words were finished, the hawk came by divine command and settled before him. Astonished at the novelty of so great a miracle, he did not delay to pay what he had vowed to the saint, giving praise to the Most High, who gave such power to men. Great is our confessor, and great is his power, and there is no number to his miracles.

A certain woman was brought to his tomb, [Col. 0630B] named Caelia, from the village of Ekebe [Note: [Col. 0630D] Perhaps Egbye, a village in the parish of Glostrup, in the provostship of Smörum, Copenhagen prefecture.]. All her limbs were utterly disabled by excessive paralysis; she lay completely powerless in hands, feet, and all her body. She seemed to have no sign of life except movement in her eyes. Whenever bodily necessity called her, she was carried with the help of two or three people; for she could neither turn herself from side to side, nor close her outspread hands or extend them when closed, nor draw back her stretched-out feet or extend those drawn up to herself. From the ninth hour until evening she lay awaiting God’s mercy. Then she first began to tremble, then to move her head a little; finally she felt her legs and feet recalled from insensibility, her sinews grow warm, and her whole body, [Col. 0630C] except the right arm, renewed into a certain grace of agility. Thus she felt and experienced that, by the manifest power of God, she had been made well except for the right arm, which remained withered for her correction. At once, rejoicing, she sat up; and, with tears arising from joy, she approached the saint’s tomb to offer thanksgiving.

A cry arose among the people; God was praised on high, who bestowed upon his William so great a grace of healing. Yet the woman wondered, and the brother who guarded the tomb marvelled, why the arm remained withered and why she had not received complete healing. Accordingly, on the following Sunday he asked her to return and earnestly seek the mercy of the Lord and of the saint himself for the restoration of her arm. The woman kept in her heart the words of him who asked her, and on the following Sunday [Col. 0630D] returned; but she departed as she had come.

Again she returned on the holy day of Pentecost, but then too she did not deserve to be heard. The guardian of the tomb marvelled that the woman came and went so often with fruitless labor, and said to her: “Woman, search your conscience; carefully inquire whether there is any way of iniquity in you; confess it, and you shall be cleansed.” She obeyed this sound counsel, and in her house set before the eyes of her heart the hidden things of her conscience, diligently investigating by what offense she was still held guilty. At last she remembered a certain deed which she had committed and had never confessed to anyone. [Col. 0631A] Then, groaning and giving herself more abundantly to prayers and tears, she returned to God’s saint. Finding the brother who had charge of the tomb, she prostrated herself in worship before him, saying: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner. I have indeed sinned greatly and have not sought to amend my life; but hear me, though late in repenting: pray for my sins.”

Having confessed to the aforesaid priest the crime which she had concealed, and having pledged herself to a more reformed life, she suddenly received health in her withered arm. Seeing that she had recovered the health of her whole body, the woman cried out in joy: “Return to the Lord our God, for he is gracious and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy, and ready to relent concerning evil” (Joel 2). On that day there was also the feast of St. John the Baptist, and [Col. 0631B] a very great crowd of both sexes had assembled. Hearing what had occurred, they glorified God, who had until then afflicted the woman’s body in order that he might cleanse her soul from crime. O man of great compassion, through whose prayers the woman was delivered from every calamity, both of soul and body! O notable wonder! For inasmuch as the soul is the nobler part of a human being, its healing is evidently the more glorious miracle. Truly this was done through our confessor, and it is wonderful in our eyes (Psalm 117).

There was in Gotland a certain young man named Lignerus, very rich but leprous. He was willing to give much to physicians—sons of men in whom there is no salvation (Psalm 145)—for the cleansing of his body, but there was no one to help him. At last perceiving that human salvation is vain [Col. 0631C] (Psalm 59), and that it is good to cling to God and place one’s hope in the Lord God (Psalm 72), he came to us after crossing the sea, hoping to obtain bodily health. His hands, arms, feet, legs, and whole body had been infected with foul leprosy. For some time, according to his request, he remained with us, devoting himself to vigils and prayer, and frequently washing and cooling himself with the medicinal water. When this was done, according to the merit of his faith, he improved day by day as the contagion of leprosy disappeared. Returning to his homeland, he was completely healed; and he who had formerly been avoided by everyone because of his stench thereafter had fellowship with people and lived among them. We had as witnesses to his cure [Col. 0631D] his parishioners and priest, who testified that, his flesh having been restored and blossoming anew, no sign of leprosy remained in him.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Remaining Miracles of St. William

Truly the Lord is glorious in his saint and praiseworthy in his works. He mercifully helped a girl named Inghefrit of Nordenberghe [Note: [Col. 0631D] Perhaps the parish and village of Lundbye in the provostship of Hammer, Vordingborg prefecture.], from the village of Luagbe [Note: [Col. 0631D] Perhaps corruptly for Wordingborgh.], who was infected by the most grievous contagion of leprosy and blinded in her left eye. In the house of his confessor William, he partly restored her sight and partly cleansed her of leprosy. Having received this gift of so great a benefit, [Col. 0632A] she brought unexpected occasion for joy to her parents, to whom she had been a cause of immense grief, as she returned home, becoming wholly cleansed along the way. The next year she returned with her mother, her leprosy entirely banished, to thank St. William for so great a benefit, since he had delivered her body from ruin. At her return those who had previously seen her were astonished, for her appearance was so changed, the leprosy so annihilated, and the flesh so flourishing. The priest John and her mother gave testimony that she had been cleansed from her leprosy through the merits of St. William.

The hand of the Lord weighed heavily upon a woman from Halland, named Tonna [Note: [Col. 0632D] Hallandic, from Halland, not from Laland as Henschenius supposed, p. 643, note b.], spreading leprosy throughout her body and wounding her flesh with a grievous ulcer. All who saw her despised [Col. 0632B] her, because from the sole of her foot to the crown of her head there was no soundness in her (Isaiah 1). The woman heard the fame of the confessor and learned many things concerning his miracles. Therefore she hastened to visit him, that he might grant her according to her heart, fulfill her desire, and let it be done according to her faith. When she reached the place, she prostrated herself in prayer beside his tomb and cried to the Lord with all her heart that he would have mercy on her. The Lord heard and pitied her; he became her helper. For, as she rose from prayer, in the sight of all present, the leprosy fell from her body like scales from a fish; and all who saw it blessed the Lord, saying, “Today we have seen marvellous things” (Luke 5).

A certain crippled woman from Norway was brought to us, [Col. 0632C] twenty-six years of age. With the assistance of her own people, she had sought the thresholds of many saints, so that the Author of nature, to whom all nature is subject, might through the saints’ intercession grant her the use of walking which nature had denied her. But God delayed granting her health through others, so that it might become a cause of praise and glory to his saint William. The woman arrived at the harbor of salvation, namely at the tomb of the man of God, and resolved in her heart not to relax her spirit from prayer or depart elsewhere until he should strengthen the bases and soles of her feet. After fifteen days, with her sinews stretched and the ankles of her feet extended away from her buttocks, our confessor set her feet upon the rock and directed her steps. All the people saw the crippled woman walking [Col. 0632D] and praising God; they saw and rejoiced.

When a very great crowd assembled at St. William and people hurried to him from the towns, a woman named Olava, crippled from birth and from the town of Copenhagen, heard the report of the preceding miracle and was brought to the saint on the vigil of St. John the Baptist. But because of the press of people she could not enter the church. Therefore, on the following night, as she sat south of the church and most devoutly pleaded, with tears streaming forth, for the saint’s grace to deliver her, a man of venerable white hair appeared to her and said: “Woman, enter the church.” But she said: “Lord, [Col. 0633A] lacking the power of walking, I cannot enter because of the crowd, nor have I anyone to carry me into the church.” “Crawl,” the old man said to her, “to the church door which faces north; there you will meet a man in a gray cloak and white cap, who will bring you in.” Comforted by these words, she crawled quickly; and when she came to the door, she found a man dressed as the old man had described. At her request, he carried her into the church.

There, received among the sick, trembling and falling about in every direction, she herself began to tremble. When this occurred, she knew that the days of her healing were near. Yet she was anxious because she did not have a long garment, but only the short clothes in which she was accustomed to crawl. Therefore she addressed the saint in this manner: “Gracious [Col. 0633B] confessor of Christ, William, if you are willing to grant me the grace of health, I beg you: do not permit me, half-clothed as I am, to roll on the pavement, lest my shame be uncovered and I become an object of ridicule to all the people.” She prayed, and it happened to her according to her prayer. For when the first nocturn had ended and she rested, she felt the sinews of her right leg, contracted from birth, loosen and, in loosening, stretch out; and about an hour later, in the same way, the sinews of her left leg. When after a little while the soles and bottoms of her feet had been strengthened, she rose upon her feet; and what nature had not given, she acquired by practice, walking here and there. By this deed he put a new song into the people’s mouth, a hymn to our God; for many [Col. 0633C] saw, rejoiced, and hoped in the Lord.

The witnesses of this woman were Dean Absalon of the church of Blessed Mary at Copenhagen [Note: [Col. 0633D] This is the earliest mention of the church of Blessed Mary at Copenhagen. On this basis I infer that this church was founded by Absalon together with the castle or fortress, and that it was then the only church in that city. This is also confirmed by a diploma of this archbishop, without place or year, in which he confirms certain donations made [Col. 0634D] to this church by the citizens of Copenhagen.], together with his brethren and all the citizens of that fortress.

Memorable and worthy of remembrance among the faithful is the fact that the grace of our most merciful Father forestalls the vow of some and compels them to fulfill the obligation of the vow; it immediately follows the promise of others with health; it meets some on the road; receives others at their entrance into the cemetery; waits for others either in the church or at the very tomb; accompanies others as they depart; and, suspending some from help for a longer time, finally restores them to health.

For a woman from the city of Lund, named Gutha, whose sinews were contracted and constricted, the power of walking had been taken away for twenty-five years. She came to the saint twice, yet returned without obtaining her wish and without being healed. On the second day after the Ascension of the Lord, she came a third time and, until the vigil of Pentecost, devoted herself constantly beside the tomb to vigils and prayers, waiting more devoutly for the mercy of God and of the saint himself. The Lord regarded the lowliness of his handmaid, adding to her what she sought in prayer. For, on the holy vigil of Pentecost, after the prophecies and the doxologies had been completed, while the deacon was proclaiming the Gospel, [Col. 0634A] a very sweet sleep stole over her, and she heard a voice saying to her: “Woman, rise; it is not fitting for Christians to sit during the Gospel, but to stand reverently and listen to what is read.” Awakened, she looked at the woman standing behind her and asked what she had said to her. Realizing that this voice had come from above, she rejoiced exceedingly and immediately felt her sinews stretch, though not without pain, her shins become vigorous, her flesh be warmed, and marrow grow warm in her bones. Having therefore found the drachma which she had lost, she rose joyful and praising; and before the Gospel reading was completed, she walked firmly around the confessor’s tomb three times, uttering more earnest thanks. The people, meanwhile, in hymns and confessions blessed the Lord, [Col. 0634B] who chose to anticipate with the glory of so great a miracle the following day, on which Mount Sinai shone with heavenly fire and the Holy Spirit descended in tongues of fire upon Christ’s disciples (Acts 2).

Paul, son of Entinghus, an eight-year-old boy from the village of Tortorpuyt, was staying with his parents near the mill belonging to the house of the monks of Aswarbode [Note: [Col. 0634D] Also written Aswardebothe, today Asserboe near Esrom. Carthusian monks were introduced there by Archbishop Absalon in 1169.]. When they went into the meadows to gather hay, the boy remained at home. Entering the millhouse in order to lead the horse that drove the mill, he was struck by the force of the mill wheel and fell between a certain pillar and the wheel itself, so that the horse could not draw the mill. Thus, caught between [Col. 0634C] the wheel and the pillar, with his back broken and other limbs crushed, he remained from sunrise until the third hour. At that hour eight men came and, pulling back the wheel with great difficulty, drew out the boy dead.

The mistress of the house, named Ingerth, ran up and, wishing to test whether he was still alive, turned him this way and that and raised him into the air. But it was in vain, for there was neither voice nor sensation in him; rather, he lay without the breath of life, so that all said, “He is dead.” At last his unhappy parents arrived, wailing and crying: “Lord, have mercy! Alas, what has happened to us?” And, bending their knees, they cried: “Glorious confessor of God, William, restore our son to us.” But the boy did not rise. He remained dead throughout that day and through the night until cockcrow. At cockcrow, however, when they vowed that, if he were raised, they would present him to God and blessed William, his spirit revived and he began to move; but he did not recover speech until daylight. When morning dawned, he said to his mother: “When shall we go to St. William?” The woman rejoiced and marvelled that he named the saint, whose name he had never before heard, and replied: “Son, after eight days, on the day of St. Lawrence, if you live.”

When the feast of the glorious martyr Lawrence came, the boy’s father and mother came together, carrying him in their arms. His limbs were now healthy except for his back, which was still wounded and diminished at the place where it had been broken. [Col. 0635A] We investigated the truth of this miracle more carefully and learned from the testimony of them and of others who had been present that our confessor truly raised him from the dead and restored him to his parents.

The four-year-old son of a certain widow at Oreberghem [Note: [Col. 0635B] Perhaps Ortingborgh or Wordingborg.], while playing with other boys near a stream, slipped on a stone below the bank of the channel and was drowned in the water itself. The boys who had played with him returned home and told his mother that her son had fallen into the stream. Hearing this, [Col. 0635B] she tore the garments from her breast and ripped the hair from her head, crying and wailing: “Woe is me, miserable woman!” At her cry the neighbors gathered together; running to the place where the boys said he had fallen, they did not find him at all. Descending along the stream-bank, they found him in a bend of the river, where the force of the whirlpool had wrapped him about. They pulled him out when found and carried him home with mourning and lamentation.

They hung the boy up by his feet, pale in color, and opened his mouth by putting in a piece of wood so that the water with which he was swollen might flow out. But this only brought further labor and grief, because his spirit had departed. Then they rolled him in a trough and strove by fruitless effort to bring him back to life. Meanwhile, the boy’s mother—now a mother no longer, bereaved of her son—[Col. 0636A] poured out continual tears, gave frequent sighs, and directed loud cries to God, never ceasing to invoke St. William that he might restore her son to her. She was shaken by such pain and afflicted by such grief that she moved all to weeping and lamentation, and all cried out with her: “Holy confessor of God, show the power of your aid over our dead one, although we are unworthy to believe your wonders, which have so often sounded in our ears.”

The mother, however, made a vow, saying: “Holy man of God, if I deserve to receive my son raised through your merits, I will offer you half of his share, whatever may come to him in movable goods, and I will bring him to you.” The compassionate confessor restored the boy to life. First a sign of redness appeared in his face, and afterward he moved his eyes about. Great joy arose in the house, and joy took the place of deepest mourning. The woman obtained joy and gladness; grief and groaning fled from her; and all cried out: “We will praise you, holy man of God, because you have been fearfully magnified: your works are wonderful (Psalm 138), and we know them exceedingly.” In the following year she visited St. William with her son, and before all the brothers and a multitude of people, having produced witnesses, confessed that her son had been dead and recalled from the dead through the merits of St. William.

[Col. 0635]

# LETTERS OF ST. WILLIAM, ABBOT

*(Scriptores rerum Danicarum, VI, 1.)*

## NOTICE TO THE READER

It is sufficiently established that Abbot William—whose Life we gave in volume V, pp. 458–495, and whose *Genealogy of the Kings of Denmark* in volume II, pp. 154–163—left letters divided into three books, or only two, as Magnæus thinks. These letters both corroborate and illuminate one or another chapter of our history, and make known not a few customs and institutions of the age in which he lived.

In the index prefixed to the first volume of this work, Langebek counted these letters among works lost or sought after. Certainly, so far as we know, no parchment codex survives. Yet not a few paper copies, transcribed at different times, have come into our hands; comparison has taught us, however, that they all derived from a single parchment manuscript. That parchment was undoubtedly the one preserved in the University Library, Copenhagen, in Cyprian’s case, order 3, octavo; it was destroyed in the Copenhagen fire of 1728. In that fire there was also consumed volume A, or I, of the Bartholinian Collections, in which these letters had been transcribed on pp. 132–210, 346–356, 359, and 360.

Among the manuscripts which we used, we assign first place to a certain quarto, written in various old hands, as the character of the letters indicates. Purchased at a public auction, it was given to Grammius by Arnas Magnæus on 19 February 1726. In a letter written on this matter, Magnæus conjectures that this copy had been written for the benefit of Andreas Welleius. The following title—whose errors are not ours—is inscribed on it:

> One book of letters abridged from three books of letters of Lord William, who six hundred years ago was summoned from the Parisian monastery of St. Geneviève to Denmark through the agency of Saxo Grammaticus, in order to perform the office of abbot in the monastery of Ebelholt among the Zealanders, etc. Now for the first time made public for the benefit of lovers of antiquity by N. N. N.
