The following note is added on the preceding page: “The codex is mutilated in various places, as may be seen from this edition of it.” We call this manuscript, which lacks beginning and end, **MAGNÆANUS I**.

The second manuscript which we possess was transcribed in folio from the said parchment of the University of Copenhagen—or rather excerpted from it, as is evident partly from the preface to the letters and partly because many letters found in the other copies are omitted. On the final leaves of this manuscript are transcribed [Col. 0637] from the parchment of the said library certain scholia on Adam of Bremen. This copy is for us **GRAMMIANUS I**.

The third manuscript, or **GRAMMIANUS II**, was likewise transcribed in folio and has appended to it legends of St. William and certain other native saints, which we omit for the reasons set out in the preface to William’s Life.

We judge that these three copies are those which Grammius says in his notes on Meursius, p. 356, that he had at hand.

The fourth manuscript was transcribed in octavo by a certain Master Georg Claussen, who was afterwards living at Leiden in 1717. Arnas Magnæus purchased at public auction the book, which had been owned by one Lyegaard, who was departing for the Indies. In a note appended to it, Magnæus relates, besides the matters already mentioned, that Lyegaard told him Claussen had written it not at home but abroad, perhaps at Rome. That this was not so, however, will readily be clear to anyone examining it and comparing it with the other copies, especially the Welleian copy, of which later. This copy, which ends with Letter XXXI of the second book and which we call **LYEGAARDIANUS**, contains, inserted in their proper places, headings of certain letters transcribed from a sheet attached to the codex; these headings are not found in the other copies.

The fifth manuscript, which we call **MAGNÆANUS II**, was collected, arranged, caused to be transcribed, and corrected by Magnæus himself. We made it the basis of our edition in such a way that we never depart from it without grave necessity, while supplying and enriching it from the other copies.

The first and last of these manuscripts are preserved in the University Library of Copenhagen; the others are in the greater royal library.

Besides the manuscripts mentioned, we had at hand three less valuable quartos found among Langebek’s Collections. One is written in Welleius’s hand; another has a chronology attached to most of the letter-headings in Langebek’s hand; the third may be dispensed with without loss.

Among Langebek’s Collections we further found a chronology of William’s life and letters, compiled by Thomas Bartholin the Younger from his father’s annals. But because this chronology differs from Langebek’s in almost every place, we have appended both, so that the discrepancy may be judged by others who have leisure for it.

Some of these letters have previously been printed: by Bartholin in the *Danish Antiquities*, by Grammius in the *Notes on Meursius*, by Pontoppidan in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, and by Holberg in the *Danish History*, as we shall note in the appropriate places.

No one acquainted with the age in which William flourished will be offended by his style, which abounds in the stench of barbarisms and the awkwardness of expression. At least this admits of no doubt: the Latin of Stephen of Tournai, a writer of letters of the same age and a friend of Ingeborg, Absalon, and William, is not to be esteemed more highly.

# PREFACE OF WILLIAM, ABBOT OF ST. THOMAS OF THE PARACLETE, TO THE BOOKS OF HIS LETTERS

**WILLIAM**, servant of the servants of God who are at the Paraclete [Note: [Col. 0637] Thus he called the monastery of Eskildsø, afterward transferred to Ebelholt.], to the reader of these compositions: greeting, and the wish that, in reading, he may entertain no envy tending to malicious words.

To apply diligence to the common benefit of humankind is as worthy of approval before God and men as it ought not to be condemned by any hostile attacks, lest judgment seem absent from a good work and envy or hatred be present. If anyone’s mind inclines to that side, it is most rightly proved that he does not love equity. But since we take especial delight in the benefit of our neighbors, we have resolved, without pretense, to share with them whatever we know or believe ourselves able to accomplish; for the advancement of those to whom we are joined by the bond of charity concerns us.

For this reason, we have gathered into one volume, for the information and instruction of those unable to attain higher things, the matters which we have briefly set down according to the modest measure of our understanding: namely, the letters which we have sent to various persons or written in the names of others, so that humble things may serve their small—or slender—advancement.

Therefore, reader, whoever you are who examine this work of ours, if you cannot find rhetorical elegance or ornament of expression, we ask you to remember our intention. For, as we have said, we have resolved to direct these compositions not to the learned but to those who desire to make progress through what is written. Thus, if anything occurs in them that exercises their thought and understanding, let them give thanks with us to divine grace and commend it to memory. Let the rest remain untouched, so that they may not gnaw at our goodwill with a dog’s tooth.

For certain humble dishes are customarily brought to royal tables, and may rightly be mixed without fault even with costly feasts, since such feasts often become wearisome; and they are commonly sought more eagerly by those who eat. Nor should anyone wonder that we place the names of popes or bishops before our salutations, since we have done this so that greater authority, derived from their names, may attend the openings of our letters to which they are prefixed. But in those letters in which knots of questions are resolved, let no one consider anything to have been introduced into their solution except what flows from holy ordinance.

The preface ends.

The chapter-headings of the following letters of Lord William, Abbot of the Paraclete, begin.

[Col. 0639]

# BOOK ONE
## Letter I

To a bishop, asking whether anyone may marry a woman whom he had previously defiled through adultery. [Note: [Col. 0639] Missing.]

## II

To the Bishop of Paris [Note: [Col. 0639] The word *of Paris* has been erased and can be read only conjecturally.], asking whether a condition can invalidate a marriage.

## III

Likewise to the same person, asking for information concerning degrees of consanguinity and affinity: namely, in what degree a marriage may or may not be contracted; and whether persons who have been separated may subsequently be reconciled.

## IV

Sent to the lord pope, asking whether there is a marriage between a man and a woman who were united in the presence of the Church, where the husband went away to a distant region and, unable to remain continent, took another wife.

## V

An answer is given to the foregoing inquiry, stating that there is no marriage there; that the woman is excused by ignorance; and that the man has committed adultery.

## VI

It is asked whether a husband may, without his wife's permission, make a vow of chastity; or whether a wife may, without her husband's consent, undertake the monastic life.

## VII

To the lord pope, asking whether a man may marry the wife of his kinsman, to whom that kinsman had been betrothed.

## VIII

To the lord pope, stating that neither his brother nor anyone of his kindred may ever marry her. [Note: [Col. 0639] This title is wholly false, for the entire letter shows that it is an answer to the pope.]

## IX

To the lord pope, asking whether consent concerning the future, with an oath added, constitutes marriage.

## X

Answer to the questions asked.

## XI

To the pope, asking whether someone not known to have been baptized ought to be baptized, since no sacrament ought to be subjected to an affront; also, whether any material other than water ought to be sought for performing baptism; and whether the person baptized, if immersed once or twice, ought to be called baptized.

## XII

To the lord pope on behalf of a certain man who had cast off the religious habit and transferred himself to the Hospitallers, for which reason the lord of Lund had pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him.

## XIII

To the pope on behalf of the man who had carnally known a female relative of his wife, asking by what penance he ought to make atonement.

## XIV

The lord pope's answer to the questions.

## XV

It is asked whether a virgin who did not consent, but resisted and was forcibly violated, ought to be counted among other virgins.

## XVI

Concerning one who defiled the marriage bed by carnally knowing his wife's sister.

## XVII

This letter establishes from the authorities of the saints that a wife may bring an action against her husband on account of fornication, just as a husband may against his wife.

## XVIII

Here it is asked whether the offering of one who sought a priest but was overtaken by death ought to be considered.

## XIX

Here it is asked whether confession made at the point of death is valid for a sick person whose power to repent has been removed by the force of pain; and whether one upon whom a penance was imposed but who did not complete it—although it was not an adequate penance—will be saved when he dies.

## XX

In this letter the pope is urged that his vigour be more sharply aroused against heretics.

## XXI

Whether baptism administered by a better person is more efficacious than baptism administered by a worse.

## XXII

The Bishop of Paris asks whether the church of Saint-Germain had been withdrawn from the obedience and jurisdiction of the Church of Paris. There is also another question in the same letter: namely, whether someone can be baptized in the womb of his mother.

## XXIII

The lord pope's answer to both questions.

## XXIV

To the lord pope: the Archbishop of Norway acting on behalf of himself and his church against the tyrant of that kingdom and his coronators.

## XXV

To the lord of Lund, acting on behalf of the Abbot of Paraclete against a cardinal.

## XXVI

An admonition toward improvement for the consecrated virgin daughters of the king.

## XXVII

To the convent of nuns in the city of Roskilde, that they restore to the church of Paraclete something secretly taken away from a certain fugitive and entrusted to them.

## XXVIII

To the convent of Slangethorp concerning certain gifts received by them.

## XXIX

An exhortation to good addressed to the same women.

## XXX

To the lord pope, in the person of the king, on behalf of his sister who had been separated from the King of France.

## XXXI

To the pope, in the person of the Queen of France, complaining that she had unjustly been separated from the King of France.

## XXXII

To the lord pope concerning the same matter.

## XXXIII

To the cardinals concerning the same matter.

## XXXIV

A consolatory letter, in the person of Abbot William, to the Queen of France.

## XXXV

The same abbot, likewise consolatory, to the same woman.

## XXXVI

To the Abbot of Esrum, applauding his return from the Cistercian chapter.

## XXXVII

The same person, petitioning him that his return may bring peace to both parties.

## XXXVIII

Likewise to the same person, in which Abbot William puts forward a defence against the accusation which enemies had sown between them.

## XXXIX

A letter to Lord Ebbo containing his abundant praises.

# Chapters of the Second Book Begin

## I

To the brothers of Blessed Geneviève of Paris, concerning the preservation of that same abbot from the danger of death through that virgin. [Col. 0641]

## II

To the lord pope against the excommunicated Norwegian tyrant and his bishops, who crowned him.

## III

To Andrew, chancellor of the King of the Danes, concerning a promise made to him—namely, that Mass was to be celebrated every day for one year. Loving and consolatory words are also prefaced.

## IV

Sent to the Abbot of Blessed Geneviève, concerning the kindly reception of Abbot William. [Note: [Col. 0641] Perhaps Walbert of Esrum.]

## V

An exhortation is sent to the chancellor concerning his return from Clairvaux or from the Roman journey.

## VI

Sent to the princes of France in the person of the lord Archbishop of Lund, concerning the divorce of the King of France and the queen, sister of the King of the Danes.

## VII

Sent to Brother Bernard of Vincennes concerning the aforementioned divorce, containing tender and loving discourse in the person of Lord Abbot William.

## VIII

Sent to the lord archbishop concerning the same divorce and the delay in the return of himself and his companions, in the person of the chancellor.

## IX

Sent by Abbot William to the Abbot of Saint Geneviève, concerning his own capture and detention and that of his companions.

## X

Sent by Abbot William to the monks of Saint Michael, in which the same monks are summoned to the appointed [lacuna].

## XI

Concerning the assignment of the goods of that church to the Grey monks.

## XII

To the lord pope concerning the same matter.

## XIII

Sent to the lord pope by the Bishop of Roskilde, concerning the benefices of priests who die, to be held for one year.

## XIV

The lord archbishop to the parishioners of Lingby, concerning the transport of stones for building a monastery at Paraclete.

## XV

Abbot W. to Count B.: at first concerning friendship; near the end, exhorting him to build the aforesaid cloister.

## XVI

The same man to a certain bishop of Sweden, using more flattering language to urge the bishop to complete the undertaking.

## XVII

The same abbot to Cardinal Ceufred concerning a man who had seized church land by robbery and held it by force.

## XVIII

Sent by the same W. to the lord archbishop in plaintive and devout words, seeking justice against a man who had appropriated his land and taken it back for his own uses.

## XIX

Sent by the abbot to Lord Ebbo, wholly full of sweet and friendly words, stirring his affection toward the advancement of the entire cloister.

## XX

Sent by Abbot W. to a certain abbot and archdeacon: a reproving letter concerning simony, since they intended to purchase something for a certain cleric.

## XXI

Sent to the lord archbishop by the aforesaid abbot, lamenting barns consumed by fire and a lack of grain; it gives a long account and, at the end, seeks leave to return home. [Note: [Col. 0641] Between this and the following letter, the Lyegaard manuscript inserts under no. XXII this title: “Sent to the Abbot of Saint Geneviève.” Manuscript Mag. II, which we follow, assigns this letter the last place.]

## XXII

Sent by the lord archbishop to the princes of France concerning the divorce of the king and queen, setting forth at length the queen’s lineage and, at the end, requesting that through the aforesaid prayers they bring the said king back from error to truth. [Note: [Col. 0641] This title is false, for this letter was sent to Pope Celestine.]

## XXIII

Sent by Abbot W. to Canute, King of the Danes, warning and, as far as possible by reasoning, persuading the king not to allow the marriage agreement between the King of France and his sister to be dissolved for lack of money.

## XXIV

To the same king, in the person of the aforesaid abbot, concerning the foregoing. It may seem inglorious that he should be written to by such a person. The praise and glory of the Archbishop of Lund are set out abundantly, and a brief supplication is added that he should not believe detractors against him.

## XXV

Sent to the King of France in the person of the aforesaid abbot, pleading that he receive the dismissed queen again in marital love, and order the chancellor, himself, and their companions to be released from the captivity in which they were held.

## XXVI

Sent to the cardinals by the King of the Danes: first softening them with gentler words, and near the end setting forth his complaint about the divorce made between the King of France and his sister, and seeking justice from them concerning it.

## XXVII

Sent by Abbot W. to the lord Abbot of Esrum, briefly relating what they had accomplished at Rome in the affair of the Queen of France, and sending him a transcript.

## XXVIII

Sent by the same man to the lord archbishop, a rather plaintive letter in which the abbot, weaving a long sequence of words concerning the change in his paternal countenance toward him, charges him with lack of bread and seeks leave to return home.

## XXIX

Sent by the same man to Geoffrey, canon of Saint Geneviève of Paris, wholly composed in love.

## XXX

Likewise, in his person, sent to Peter, son of Lord Suno: an exhortation that he may advance in virtues and literary learning, and ought not to doubt his help and counsel. It reports that his father has been reconciled to the abbot.

## XXXI

Likewise, in the same person, sent to the lord of Lund, full of complaints: both over the death of Master Peter, over the burned barns, and over hunger.

## XXXII

Sent by the same man to the Abbot of Saint-Victor, containing in its first part a page full of the sweetness of love and, at the end, a kind recommendation that his prior be received by him for a time.

## XXXIII

Sent by the chancellor to the lord of Ostia, putting forward an excuse and seeking pardon because he had departed from the city without his permission.

## XXXIV

Sent by Abbot W. to the lord of Lund, containing a sealed request to be explained orally by the bearer in his hearing. [Col. 0643]

## XXXV

Written by the same man to the Abbot of Esrum, containing in its first part an appeal for goodwill and, in the remainder, a request that Brother Stephen remain with him for four days in order to repair the watercourse.

## XXXVI

Likewise, sent by the same man to the Abbot of Nostved, briefly praising him for improving the state of his monastery.

## XXXVII

Sent by the same man to the King of the Danes, briefly referring to the honour of his sister, the queen.

## XXXVIII

Likewise, sent by the same man to a certain friend, wholly composed concerning love.

## XXXIX

Sent by the same man to the prior of Kuningahälla, concerning the dispatch of a ship to them with malt.

## XL

Sent by the aforesaid man to a friend suffering illness: a consolatory letter.

## XLI

Sent by the aforesaid man to Lord Thurgot, briefly referring first to his promotion and, at the end, to his support of the error of canons at variance with their provost.

## XLII

Sent by the aforesaid man to the provost of Saint Theudegarius, urging him to patience and endurance of sufferings.

## XLIII

Sent by the aforesaid man to the lord pope, concerning the poverty of the house, begging him to induce the lord of Roskilde by his letters to provide aid.

## XLIV

Sent to the lord pope in the person of the King of the Danes, complaining that the justice requested concerning Bishop Waldemar had not been rendered to him, and seeking it again at the end.

## XLV

Sent to the lord of Lund in the person of the chancellor of the King of the Danes, concerning all that had happened to him and his companions on their Roman journey, how they lost the lord pope’s letters, and many other matters.

## XLVI

Sent by Abbot W. to the lord pope, complaining that Grey monks had been beaten by Black monks.

## XLVII

Likewise to the same person, asking in which order it would be safer for him to remain.

## XLVIII

Likewise against the Black monks.

## XLIX

Likewise to the Bishop of Roskilde: an intercession on behalf of a certain dependent.

## L

To the Abbot of Prémontré, putting forward an excuse in the accusation of Abbot John.

## LI

To Lord Sincius [Note: [Col. 0643] Read here, and in no. LIV, undoubtedly “Cincius.”], cardinal.

## LII

To Seufred, concerning a certain dependent sent to him for assistance.

## LIII

To Lord Sincius, cardinal: an intercession on behalf of a certain person.

## LIV

To a certain provost.

## LV

To a certain bishop, concerning a certain goodwill shown to him.

## LVI

To Gozwin the monk, urging him in words full of love to maintain honourable conduct.

## LVII

To the Abbot of Saint Geneviève, in the person of the same man, putting forward an excuse because he had not sent him a horse sooner.

## LVIII

For the recall of the expelled Daniel.

## LIX

To the chancellor, wholly concerning kindness and love.

## LX

To a friend: first an admonition and an appeal to love; and at the end, seeking help and a kindly hearing.

## LXI

To Canute, King of the Danes, petitioning for favour and exhorting him not to be miserly in giving to the King of France on behalf of his sister.

## LXII

A plaintive letter to the lord Archbishop of Lund because he does not hear the abbot’s prayers sooner.

## LXIII

To Geoffrey: first wholly concerning love; at the end, indicating that he has arrived in Paris.

## LXIV

To the lord Archbishop of Lund, commending and urging his compassionate goodwill toward a monk sent to him.

## LXV

To Master Melior, cardinal and legate, in the person of the chancellor, complaining that he and his companions are held in captivity at Dijon.

## LXVI

To Bishop Thurgot on behalf of the church of Saint Theudegarius, in the person of Abbot William.

## LXVII

To the lord of Lund, complaining that his countenance has changed against the brethren.

## LXVIII

A letter of commendation to all on behalf of anyone travelling.

## LXIX

To the Bishop of Odense, for the restoration of a certain fugitive.

## LXX

To John, subprior of Esrum, concerning a confidential matter.

## LXXI

To King Canute: the beginning of a certain letter concerning a confidential matter.

## LXXII

To the Abbot of Esrum: the beginning of a certain letter similar to the preceding one.

## LXXIII

To Lord Ebbo, requesting concerning a certain [lacuna].

The remaining letter-headings that were formerly prefixed to the work are now lacking. After these, the following occur in the Lyegaard copy:

Here the parchment fails. We add the following headings from paper attached to the parchment and marked in a hand not especially recent, so that they may serve as evidence that the parchment had not suffered loss merely yesterday or today, and thus that it comes closer to the abbot’s own age, although the paper seems to have been written after the Reformation.

## LXXIV

To a certain cardinal. [Note: [Col. 0643] Barth. 1197.]

## LXXV

To John the monk. [Note: [Col. 0643] Barth. 1192.]

## LXXVI

Inserted from the papers up to this point.

# Letters of Abbot William

## Book One

### Letter I

Missing. [Note: [Col. 0645C] Langebek assigns the year 1200 to this letter.]

[Col. 0645A]

### Letter II

The beginning of this letter is missing. [Note: [Col. 0645C] Bartholinus, nephew of Thomas, and Langebek assign this letter to the year 1200.]

…having been discovered, according to that passage in Numerianus [Note: [Col. 0645C] The Lyegaard copy reads “Vermariam.” Read “Gratian.” This article occurs in the same words in Gratian’s *Decrees*, Fontanni edition, Rome, 1727, vol. 2, title 2, rubric 2, IV, p. 631.]:

> If a freeborn man has taken another’s female slave as wife and believes her to be freeborn, but that woman is afterwards reduced to slavery [Note: [Col. 0646C] Read *detecta*, “discovered.”], he should redeem her from slavery if he can; if he cannot, he may, if he wishes, take another. But if he knew that she was a slave and approved her, let him have her as his lawful wife. And if a freeborn woman has taken a slave, knowing him to be a slave, let her have him, because we all have one Father (John VIII). If anyone has presumed otherwise, let him be subjected to a strict examination [Col. 0645B] until he acknowledges that he has acted wickedly.

Concerning what you add at the end of your letter—whether there is marriage if the slave of one master has taken the female slave of another—know that this was decreed at the Council of Chalon. [Note: [Col. 0646C] In the year 813. Ibid., VI, p. 652.]

> We have been told that certain persons, by the arbitrary exercise of authority, dissolve lawful marriages of slaves, without considering that the Lord says: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX). Therefore it has seemed good to us that marriages of slaves should not be dissolved, even if they have different masters, but that, remaining in one marriage, they should serve their masters.

This must be observed where there has been a lawful union; and you should understand that this is firmly established by the will of the masters. If anyone attempts to oppose it, apply the canonical sentence against him. [Col. 0645C]

### Letter III

[Note: [Col. 0646C] Barth. and Lang., year 1200.]

Your fraternal letter, sent to us, has made known how greatly you are occupied with spiritual pursuits, unceasingly seeking the means by which you may please God [Col. 0646A] and what is fitting for a bishop’s honour. We gladly welcome such concern, especially since few are those who wish in this time to occupy themselves with such matters.

In the first part of your request, you seem to ask that we instruct your diligence concerning the degrees of consanguinity and affinity: namely, in what degree marriage may or may not be contracted according to the canons or the authority of the decretals. At the end you added the further question whether those whom the judgment of the Church has separated may subsequently obtain the benefit of reconciliation.

Now kinship is one thing by blood and another spiritual. Let us first consider kinship by blood and affinity. Therefore persons related by blood or affinity ought not to be joined in the seventh degree or within it. Hence Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 0646C] Gratian, *Decrees*, vol. II, p. 654, title IV, rubric 2, III, where it is attributed to Nicholas.]

> We decree that every person shall observe his offspring to the seventh generation, and, so long as they recognize themselves as close by affinity, we deny them the right to contract a marital union. If they do so, they shall be separated.

Likewise Pope Nicholas: [Note: [Col. 0646C] Ibid., IV, p. 655, although there it is not attributed to Nicholas.]

> No one shall take a wife from among his blood relatives before the seventh generation, or for as long as the kinship can be known. Likewise, no one shall take a wife from among those related by his own blood within the seventh degree.

By these and many other authorities, unions of blood relatives are prohibited to the seventh degree. Isidore shows how degrees of consanguinity are to be counted as follows: [Note: [Col. 0646C] Ibid., VIII, p. 655, though in different words.]

> The series of consanguinity is divided into six degrees in this way: the son and daughter are the first stock; the great-grandson and great-granddaughter the second; the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter the third; the third great-grandson and third great-granddaughter the fourth; the fourth great-grandson and fourth great-granddaughter the fifth; the grandson of the fourth great-grandson and the granddaughter of the fourth great-granddaughter the sixth.

Observe that Isidore gives only six degrees because he does not count the stock among the degrees. [Col. 0646C] Others, however, who give seven degrees, count the stock as well. For degrees of consanguinity are counted in various ways. Some place the father in the first degree and his children in the second. Others call the children the first degree, denying that there is a degree of consanguinity between father and son, since father and son are one flesh.

Therefore, the authorities which prescribe the restriction concerning consanguinity to the seventh degree put the father in the first position, which is called the first degree. Pope Zacharias counts in this manner, saying: [Note: [Col. 0647D] This does not occur in Gratian, unless perhaps at p. 657, rubric 3, III.]

> The degrees of kinship are counted thus. My brother and I are one generation and make the first degree. Again, my son and my brother’s son are the second generation and make the second degree; and so the remaining successions in this manner.

Yet between those who count six degrees and those who count seven there is no difference in sense, although there seems to be a variation in the number of degrees. For the last generation, if counting begins from the fathers, is found to be the seventh. [Col. 0647B]

Isidore himself explains why he counts six degrees:

> When consanguinity, gradually distinguishing itself through the ranks of descendants, has extended to the final degree and has ceased to be kinship, then for the first time the law admits it into the bond of marriage and in a sense begins to call back the one fleeing away. Consanguinity is therefore established to the sixth degree of descent so that, just as the generation and condition of humankind ends in the six ages of the world, so the nearness of kinship may be bounded by the same number of degrees.

Within these degrees all names of relationship are contained; beyond them neither affinity can be found nor succession further extended. [Col. 0647C] According to others, seven degrees are counted so that, after seven degrees, bridegroom may be joined to bride just as, after this life which revolves through seven days, the Church will be joined to Christ.

This raises the point that Gregory, in answer to Augustine, bishop of the English, who had asked whether persons in the fourth generation ought to be joined, wrote: [Note: [Col. 0647D] Gregory the Great, book XII, letter 32.]

> A certain Roman law permits a son and daughter, whether of a brother and sister, of two full brothers, or of two sisters, to unite. But we have learned by experience that offspring cannot arise from such a marriage. Therefore it is necessary that the fourth or fifth generation of the faithful may lawfully be joined to one another.

But much later, when the same Gregory was asked by Felix, bishop of Messina in Sicily, whether he had written to Augustine that marriages contracted in the fourth generation among the English should not be dissolved, he gave, among other things, this explanation: [Note: [Col. 0647D] In Gratian, VII, p. 635.]

> What I wrote to Augustine concerning the English people, who had recently come to the faith, you should understand to have been written specially, not generally, lest through fear of justice they should turn back from the good which they had begun. Nor did I write this to them so that, after they had been established [Col. 0648A] in the faith, if they were found within their own consanguinity, they should not be separated, or should be joined within the first line of affinity up to the seventh generation.

We must now consider affinity. Gregory says concerning it: [Note: [Col. 0647D] In Gratian, vol. II, p. 680, rubric 5, I.]

> Moreover, concerning affinity, which you call kinship—namely, that which belongs to a husband on his wife’s side or to a wife on her husband’s side—the reason is evident: because, according to the divine declaration, my wife and I are one flesh. Assuredly, therefore, for me and for her, her kinship and mine become one and the same closeness. Accordingly, my wife’s sister and I are in one and the first degree; her son is in the second degree from me; her granddaughter in the third; and this must be done on both sides in their remaining descendants. The wife of one’s relative belongs to his degree. Thus I ought to consider how a woman of my own kinship belongs to her degree. This, plainly, my wife must observe concerning the kindred of her husband in every degree of her kinship. Whoever thinks otherwise are antichrists.

Likewise Pope Julius: [Note: [Col. 0647D] Also, unless perhaps it refers to the passage in Gratian, vol. II, p. 656, rubric 3, I.]

> A man is joined equally to his own blood relatives and to his wife’s blood relatives.

Likewise Isidore: [Note: [Col. 0648D] Gratian, vol. II, p. 679, rubric 3, II.]

> Certainly, the consanguinity which must be observed in relation to one’s own husband must also, by the law of marriage, be observed in the wife’s kinship; for it is established that the two were one flesh, and therefore each kinship is common to them.

Likewise Pope Julius: [Note: [Col. 0648D] Gratian, vol. II, p. 654, rubric 2, I.]

> We permit no person of either sex to take a wife from among those related by his own blood to the seventh degree of generation, or to be joined in the stain of incest; and, just as no Christian may take a spouse from his own consanguinity, so neither may he take a spouse from his wife’s consanguinity, because of the unity of the flesh.

Likewise Gregory: [Note: [Col. 0648D] Perhaps found in Gratian, vol. II, p. 654, rubric 2, II.]

> Concerning the affinity of kinship, it has been decreed that it should be observed according to the degree of consanguinity to the seventh generation. For inheritance of property also, by the legal definitions of instruments, establishes succession of heirs to the seventh degree. For they would not succeed unless this were due to them from the line of kinship.

These authorities make clear both what affinity is and to what degree it must be observed—namely, to the seventh degree. Let your fraternity be content with these, and preach that these things also must be maintained. If any persons should attempt to act against them, do not delay in pronouncing canonical judgment against them unless they repent. [Col. 0648D]

### Letter IV. To the Lord Pope

[Note: [Col. 0648D] Barth. and Lang., year 1198.]

Since all churches have the Roman pontiff as patron and judge, it is all the safer to have recourse to him in doubtful matters because the interests of Christian religion must be safeguarded, and no one ought of his own accord [Col. 0649A] to establish as custom what the authority of the holy Fathers unambiguously declares should be disapproved.

For this reason we often have recourse to the Apostolic See when we do not know matters which, by the duty imposed upon us, it is fitting that we should not fail to know; since, as we have said, danger threatens us if we presume to overstep the boundaries of the ancients.

A certain man in our diocese, having received a wife in the nuptial bond in the presence of the Church, went away into a distant region intending to remain a long time. But, unable to remain continent, he took another woman as wife, whom he considered suitable for himself. At last, returning to himself, he repented of what he had done and wished to dismiss her, declaring that he had married another woman. The Church subject to whose obedience he was, being ignorant of this, opposed the possibility of doing so. We are therefore asked [Col. 0649B] what should be thought on this matter: namely, whether a firm marriage is to be held to exist between them, and whether the husband ought to render the marital debt to such a wife, when his conscience reproves him for transgression and the Church does not permit him to return to his lawful wife.

It is therefore for you, Father, to give counsel on this matter that will be useful in perpetuity not only to us but also to the prelates of other churches.

### Letter V. Resolution of the Matters Asked

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Barth., year 1198.]

Since the Church of God has been entrusted to us, we must provide with every vigilance lest any adversity arise that may oppose ecclesiastical institutions [Col. 0649C] and, because of sins, endeavour to overthrow the foundation of the Christian faith.

You have therefore proposed to us the case of a man who, having received a wife in the presence of the Church, went to another region and joined another woman to himself in the presence of the Church. Moved by repentance, he wished to dismiss her, but the Church opposed this because it was ignorant of his earlier marriage contract. You ask, therefore, whether he ought to dismiss the first woman and retain the second, and whether there is to be held a marriage between them—that is, between him and the second woman.

To this we answer your fraternity briefly. It may indeed be said that there is no marriage, that the woman is excused from guilt by ignorance, and that the man has committed adultery. But since, wishing to return to the first woman yet unable to do so, he is compelled by the discipline of the Church to retain this woman, he begins to be excused, through obedience and fear [Col. 0649D] of God, for rendering the marital debt to the woman who asks it of him—though he himself must never ask it of her.

### Letter VI

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Bart. and Lang., year 1198.] The same person as above.

As blessed Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 0649D] I cannot find this either in Gregory or in Gratian.]

> “The governance of souls is the art of arts.”

Since the Church of Rome is mother and teacher of all churches, and by the Lord’s authority we preside over it, the office laid upon us requires us to show more attentive compassionate concern for their tribulations and straits, [Col. 0650A] lest perhaps, through our silence, the torpor of negligence creep in and injury be done to the divine sacraments if they perceive a failure, in these matters, of the Apostolic See’s defence and protection.

Therefore, because we intend with especially earnest care to assist the Church against dangers and assaults, we command your fatherhood, once you have assembled together, briefly to resolve people’s doubts concerning the many questions proposed to us. We are asked whether a husband may lawfully make a vow of chastity without his wife’s permission; whether a wife may do so without her husband’s consent; and whether, in order to serve the Lord more freely, either of them may undertake monastic life without the consent of both. [Col. 0650B]

To these questions is added a point of another question: whether a kinsman may take another man’s betrothed into marriage. Relying upon the authorities of the saints, we have judged that an answer should be given to all these matters, and that what we answer should be held throughout the whole Church without doubt and firmly.

There are those who say that marriages may or ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion. Gregory says, writing to the patrician Theotista: [Note: [Col. 0649D] This classic passage occurs in the works of Gregory the Great, Antwerp edition, 1572, folio, vol. II, fol. 251, part 1, [Col. 0650D] col. 2; book IX, letter 39, indiction IV. Note: the Lyegaard copy has “Theutici patriciae”; read “Theotistae patriciae.”]

> There are those who say that, for the sake of religion, marriages can or ought to be dissolved. But it must be known that, although human law has allowed this, divine law has forbidden it. If, therefore, both agree to remain continent, who would dare condemn this? For we know that many saints lived a continent life with their spouses and afterwards passed to the governance of holy Church. But if the wife does not follow the continence desired by her husband, or the husband refuses that desired by his wife, the marriage cannot be divided; for it is written: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Cor. VII).

Agathosa, a dancer, complained in the presence of the pope that her husband had become a convert against her will: [Note: [Col. 0650D] In Gratian, vol. II, p. 644, title II, rubric 13, X.]

> Therefore we command your experience to investigate diligently whether perhaps he became a convert with her consent; nor may he keep continence except by mutual consent, nor seek a monastery unless both together profess continence.

### Letter VII. To the Lord Pope

[Note: [Col. 0650D] Barth. and Lang., year 1198.]

What is debated among us even by learned persons, and whose knot remains unresolved, we judge ought to be referred to the Apostolic See, lest we rush into danger if we presume to determine for ourselves what we cannot show has been resolved by the authority of any saint.

It seems to some, who have confidence only in themselves, that after the death of his kinsman, one of the kinsmen may marry the wife whom that kinsman had betrothed [Col. 0651A] and given earnest money for, especially when intercourse had not taken place but only present permission or consent. Therefore, dearest Father, since we do not yet know what ought to be maintained in a question of this kind, we ask that your authority declare to us what ought to be promulgated and maintained in the Church on this matter.

### Letter VIII

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Barth. and Lang., year 1198.]

It may be well understood that you have acted most wisely for the honor of God and for your own reputation and glory in judging that the counsel of the apostolic see should be sought in doubtful matters, lest, as your letter expresses it, you might fall into error over an uncertain matter. Since, then, your inquiry concerned whether a kinsman of another kinsman [Col. 0651B] who had betrothed a wife might, after his death, take her as his own wife: we wish to make known to you, and bring to light, what we find written by the saints on this subject, lest God’s people be led astray by the perverse assertion of anyone, if they are not instructed by the understanding of their elders. First, therefore, let it not escape your notice that a kinsman’s kinsman ought not to take his betrothed woman, since the authority of the saints forbids this.

Hence Gregory [Note: [Col. 0651D] I cannot find this passage.]: “If anyone has betrothed or given earnest-money for a wife, although afterward, death intervening beforehand, he has been unable to take her as his wife, nevertheless no one of his blood-kindred may take her in marriage; and if this is found to have been done, they shall be entirely separated.”

Likewise Pope Julius [Note: [Col. 0651D] Likewise.]: “If anyone [Col. 0651C] has betrothed a wife or given earnest-money for her, and has not known her either because death intervened beforehand or because certain circumstances arose, neither his brother nor anyone of his blood-kindred may ever take that same woman as wife.”

Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 0651D] This agrees with that decree of Gregory in Gratian, vol. II, p. 633, rubric 5, I.]: “He who takes in marriage the maiden betrothed to his neighbor shall be anathema, he and all who consent with him, because according to the law of God they are decreed to die.”

## LETTER IX [Note: [Col. 0652D] Barth. and Lang., year 1198.]

To the lord pope.

In a matter which causes us doubt, most loving Father, it is neither surprising nor contrary to fitting discipline if we refer the entire business to the successor of the blessed apostle Peter, through whom the condition of the whole [Col. 0651D] Church is confirmed in faith and receives the discipline of good morals. It is sometimes asked among us whether consent concerning the future, with an oath added, can effect a marriage: if someone promises, or even swears, that he will take a certain woman as wife, and she likewise humbly promises and swears that she will marry him, does such a betrothal make a marriage? But if, changing intention, either man or woman transfers himself or herself to another union, is the agreement of the second [Col. 0652A] alliance to be broken because of the earlier betrothal supported by an oath? We desire to be taught by your prudence and wisdom what we ought to answer to these questions, lest we be mocked if we appear ignorant.

## LETTER X [Note: [Col. 0652D] Barth. and Lang., year 1198.]

The lord pope’s answer to the questions.

We have assumed the care of governing the whole Church of God in order that things shattered by the sinister assaults of evils may be restored to a better condition and that the ignorant may be truthfully instructed in their doubts. Your inquiries, therefore, must be answered by us, and suitable counsel given concerning your uncertainty, lest in matters which we ought to know you hold an opinion contrary to the truth.

It must therefore be considered that promising is far different from doing. [Col. 0652B] He who promises a thing does not yet do it. Therefore he who promises that he will take some woman as wife has not yet taken her as wife; and she who has promised that she will marry has not yet married. How, then, can those be called spouses who have not yet contracted marriage, but promise under oath that they will contract it in the future? Likewise, if by force of an oath concerning the future they immediately become spouses, then they bring about this thing when they swear that they will do it. Accordingly it must be said that there was then no marriage, but a future marriage was being promised.

But if he subsequently takes a wife and she marries a husband, there certainly is a marriage, and it cannot be dissolved. The preceding lie or perjury must therefore be corrected by penance; but the subsequent marriage is not to be dissolved. It is otherwise, however, when an oath is confirmed by the attestation of present marital [Col. 0652C] consent. For after such consent, if either party joins himself or herself to another, even if children have been begotten, that union must be made void and the person restored to the former union. Whatever you determine ought to be done in these matters, nevertheless we do not doubt that you will not delay in the least to meet so many evils, so that the members may adhere to the head and Christ’s enemies may everywhere perish.

## LETTER XI a [Note: [Col. 0652D] Lang., under the year 1199.]

We must return to you, Father, so that in the matters about which we are uncertain we may be more diligently instructed by you and may not stray from the faith and Catholic teaching. We recently found a boy for whom we could establish by no testimony that he had been baptized. We wished therefore to immerse him in the water of baptism, had we not been hindered by this consideration: that no wrong should be done to a sacrament, lest perhaps the sacrament be repeated in him; yet, if he lacks baptism, lest he perish, or, if he is baptized, lest the sacrament be repeated. We judged that the grace of your fatherhood should be consulted.

We should also like to know whether we must use only water, and no other element, for administering baptism; and whether one who receives baptism, if immersed once or twice, can be called and believed baptized. For there are those who appear to hold differing opinions on this. We have judged that the counsel of the divine and apostolic see should be sought as to [Col. 0653A] which position ought to be believed. And whether baptism administered by an evil man is as valid as that administered by a good man.

## LETTER XI b [Note: [Col. 0653D] This letter is omitted in the list prefixed to the work. It was therefore necessary to append the letters a and b to number XI, lest the numbering of the letters be confused. (Note of Árni Magnússon.) Perhaps for the year 1199 and addressed to a certain bishop, namely the bishop of Capua.]

In the person of the lord pope.

When the duty we must perform comes before us, if we should be found negligent, we fear the judgment of the heavenly Judge to our own ruin. Since, therefore, you have urgently encouraged us by letter to defend the Christian faith, although a labor rests upon us that does not spare old age, with the Lord’s help—weak in strength, yet not fearing to undertake the journey—we intend shortly to meet the aforesaid heretics and engage them vigorously.

But lest we appear to undertake so great [Col. 0653B] a business without deliberation, we judge it fitting first to summon the Church of God into our presence in order to celebrate a council on this matter, so that whatever is decided by the counsel of the greater and religious men may obtain an effect that is timely, desired, and irrevocable. To summon the council and carry out this act of convocation, we appoint you to be invested with a legation of the apostolic see; we hope that in all things, because of the uprightness and good will natural to you, you will win an excellent name for the honor of God.

Concerning the matters which you wished to have explained to you, by the favor of divine mercy and fortified by the authorities of the saints, we answer each point. Of the person who is said by no testimony to have been baptized, Pope Leo says [Note: [Col. 0653D] Gratian, vol. I, p. 240, rubric 13, XVI, where this is attributed to Augustine.]:

“It must be understood that concerning those for whom no evidence exists among relatives, clerics, or neighbors by which they may be shown to have been baptized, it should be done that they be born again, lest they perish. In cases in which what was done is not shown, reason does not allow it to appear to have been repeated. What is unknown to have been conferred seems to be conferred upon them, because there is no rash presumption where there is the diligence of piety.”

Concerning the second article of your question, blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0654D] I cannot find this passage.]:

“For this reason it is commanded that this be done uniformly in water: that it may be understood that, just as water washes bodily dirt and garments, so baptism wipes away the stains of the soul and the defilements of vices.”

Again Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0654D] Likewise.]:

“For this reason it is in water: so that no lack might excuse anyone from doing what could be done if it were done in wine or oil; and so that a common material for baptizing might be found among all people. Water signified this, water which flowed from Christ’s side, just as blood was the sign of the other sacrament. Therefore baptism cannot be administered in any other liquid than water.”

Concerning the third article—namely, whether one who is immersed in water once or twice is baptized—Gregory answers [Note: [Col. 0654D] Gratian, vol. I, rubric 6, III, p. 230.]:

“Nothing truer can be answered concerning the threefold immersion of baptism than what you yourselves have thought: namely, that in one faith a differing custom does no harm to the holy Church. For since there is one substance in three substances, it can in no way be reprehensible to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once, because in three immersions the Trinity, and in one the unity of the Godhead, can be denoted. We, however, who immerse three times signify the sacrament of the three-day burial. Accordingly, it is permissible in this respect to immerse not only three times but also once only. Yet it is permissible to immerse once only where the custom of the Church is such.”

## LETTER XII [Note: [Col. 0654D] Barth. and Lang., under the year 1198.]

To the lord pope.

Although no merits of ours [Col. 0654B] commend us to apostolic eminence, nevertheless, because it is indebted to wise and foolish alike in matters on which salvation or the peril of souls depends, we have judged that it should be sought and consulted by this letter. The bearer of this letter assumed the religious habit in our house and remained with us for four years in the Order of Saint Victor of Paris. But afterward, deceived by the devil, abandoning the way of holiness and living luxuriously in the world, squandering his substance, he fed swine; and, despising the Order of Saint Victor, seeking no permission from us, breaking the vow of his first profession, he sought, at his pleasure, the way of life of the Hospitaller brothers [Note: [Col. 0654D] Of the Order of Saint John, later the Knights of Rhodes, now of Malta.], sweetly in the land of the living.

At last, when those good men learned that he had rendered his profession [Col. 0654C] void, they decided to reject him from their fellowship. When he perceived this, he obtained from us personally—not from our chapter—after many entreaties, permission to remain longer with them. But the bishop of London, not tolerating this, bound him with the bonds of excommunication, maintaining that no one can be absolved from a solemn vow without the cognizance of the supreme pontiff, especially when he had disdained to pass to a higher life. Therefore, reverend Father, we send him, now finally absolved from the bonds of excommunication, into the presence of your holiness, that we may be instructed by apostolic letters concerning what we ought to maintain in this matter and that provision may be made for the salvation of the sinner’s soul.

## LETTER XIII [Note: [Col. 0654D] Barth. and Lang., year 1198.]

To the lord pope.

[Col. 0654D]

The more the apostolic see surpasses all others in authority of holiness, the more fitting and safe it is to seek its judgment in doubtful matters, lest, if we should perhaps wish by our own authority to determine what we do not know, we incur the mark of presumption and danger to our office. The bearer of this letter, having acquired a wife by the bond of marriage, as he reflected at one time upon his years in bitterness of soul, remembered that before the time of his marriage [Col. 0655A] he had fallen into carnal intercourse with a kinswoman of his wife. Since the guilt of his own conscience accused him more sharply, led by repentance he sought our presence, drenched with the dew of tears; nor was he ashamed to confess his sin, which he committed with a kinswoman of his wife, and he submitted his neck to our judgment in order to lament his sin.

We, however, greatly appalled by so grave an offense and yielding to his misery, judged that he should be sent, with compassionate feeling, to the bosom of the apostolic see, to be instructed by apostolic admonitions and absolved from the bonds of his sins. Yet we, most loving Father, because we glory greatly in the abundance of your grace, earnestly ask to be more diligently instructed by your mercy and learning [Col. 0655B] in offenses of this kind, so that, should such a case arise again, we may be fit to answer those who seek us.

## LETTER XIV [Note: [Col. 0655D] Perhaps for the year 1198.]

The lord pope’s answer to the questions.

That the apostolic see ought to provide counsel to those who ask and flee to it in doubts and difficulties shines forth all the more clearly, both to the wise and the foolish, inasmuch as, in order to impart instruction to all and imprint knowledge upon weak minds, it strives to summon to itself from all parts of the world diligent men eminent in the light of learning. The power granted by the Lord to blessed Peter to render judgments, together with the authority of canons and decrees, supports them [Col. 0655C] in making judgments. Having therefore shared their counsel, we answer your inquiry briefly, brother, all the more confidently because we know them to excel in learning and good conduct.

As has become known to us from your letter, a certain man in your diocese took a certain woman as his wife according to the law of marriage, although he had previously known her kinswoman or relative by marriage; he confesses, however, that this had then slipped from his mind, but later, by the Lord’s inspiration, he recognized that he had been deceived in this error. Your brotherhood therefore asks whether, when he wishes to render it, he ought to render the marital debt to his wife, or dismiss her because of the aforesaid blood relationship or relationship by marriage.

Let your brotherhood know, however, that our Lord permits marriage to be dissolved in the Gospel for no cause except fornication; for he says: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19). Since, therefore, both entered marriage in the face of the Church, while the Church was unaware of what had been committed before, we absolutely forbid and, under anathema, prohibit the marriage between them from being dissolved. Adding this: that the marital debt is in no way to be rendered to the wife unless he is requested by the wife; nor should he render it except with trembling, fear, and an outpouring of tears, provided only that he has been forestalled in this grace by the Lord. Nor should what we say in such cases concerning not dissolving the marriage [Col. 0656A] seem to anyone to exceed the bounds of justice, because if provision were otherwise made, many lying men would be given an occasion by which they might dismiss their wives.

But the man who previously knew his wife’s kinswoman should persist in fasting and prayers, proclaim himself an unworthy sinner, and with fitting tears lament the deeds of his perversity, so that he may someday deserve pardon for his offenses.

## LETTER XV [Note: [Col. 0655D] Barth. and Lang., year 1198.]

In the person of the lord pope.

We send to your brotherhood writings of the apostolic see, in which the substance of your inquiry is fully set forth, so that, instructed by them, your understanding and intellect may extend themselves to higher matters [Col. 0656B] and determine the doubts of others by fitting examination. Your inquiry has reached our hearing through the letter sent to us, asking us to instruct you in writing what we thought concerning a virgin violated not willingly but by force—namely, whether she could thereafter be joined to the number of other virgins. That she can be is proved by the following testimonies of the saints.

For blessed Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0655D] Gratian, vol. II, p. 557, title II, rubric 2, I.]:

“It is more tolerable to have a virgin mind than virgin flesh. A virgin may be prostituted; she cannot be made an adulteress. Brothels do not disgrace chastity; rather, chastity abolishes even the infamy of the place. Nor can the flesh first be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted. For while the soul is clean from contagion, the flesh does not sin.”

Relying upon these and very many other testimonies, [Col. 0656C] we grant that a virgin corrupted in flesh without consent is to be counted among virgins. We admonish your diligence to preach throughout the province entrusted to you this question, which we have resolved for you by the testimonies of the saints, lest the people, led astray by error, be deprived of the benefit of divine grace.

## LETTER XVI [Note: [Col. 0655D] Barth. and Lang., year 1198.]

Likewise, on the same matter.

You should know that it has come to our hearing that in your diocese a certain man, at the devil’s instigation, has defiled the marriage-bed by knowing his wife’s sister; and although you learned that this very wicked act had been committed, you did not exercise the judgment of punishment due to such wickedness. Rather, the desire to receive money imposed silence upon you in this matter, as though you did not know of it, so that you would not even speak of it. If this is established as true, you have made yourself worthy not only of correction but most worthy of deposition from your office.

For you ought to have known, since you hold episcopal office [Note: [Col. 0656D] Therefore this letter was not written to William, but to some bishop—perhaps in Denmark—on the occasion of William’s letter to the pope, now lost.], that he who has presumed to sleep with two sisters, if one of them was previously his wife, may retain neither of them. Nor may he render the marital debt to his own wife, since he made her unlawful to himself by knowing her sister. Proclaim to the people the truth of this judgment, lest they [Col. 0657A] someday fall into error in such a case and incur the punishment of eternal condemnation.

## LETTER XVII [Note: [Col. 0657D] Lang., year 1199.]

Just as all must rejoice if an increase of Christian religion occurs, so also grief is increased if what the authority of the holy Fathers decrees is altered by enemies of the Christian faith. You should know that, through the report of many people, something has been brought to our ears by which the ecclesiastical sacraments are injured. [lacuna] The rest is missing.

Letters XVIII [Note: [Col. 0657D] Barth., year 1198.], XIX [Note: [Col. 0657D] Lang., year 1199.], XX [Note: [Col. 0657D] Lang., year 1199.], XXI [Note: [Col. 0657D] Lang., year 1199.], XXII [Note: [Col. 0657D] Lang., year 1200.], and XXIII [Note: [Col. 0657D] Perhaps year 1200.] are missing.—In the copy which I call Magnússon I, there appears at this point the following fragment of an uncertain letter [Note: [Col. 0657D] In the Lyegaard copy it is called the end of Letter 23, but undoubtedly less correctly, as is proved by inspection of the heading of Letter 23 in the old index.]:

“[lacuna] the sevenfold grace of the same one comes into a human being with every [Col. 0657B] fullness of holiness and virtue. This sacrament, like baptism, is administered by persons who are fasting and to persons who are fasting, unless necessity compels otherwise. Nor should it be repeated, just as baptism should not be repeated. For no injury ought to be done to any sacrament, which is thought to happen when what ought not to be repeated is repeated.”

## LETTER XXIV [Note: [Col. 0657D] Barth., year 1191; Lang, more correctly 1193.]

In the person of E. [Note: [Col. 0657D] Erik of Nidaros, who held office from 1189 [Col. 0658D] to 1206. See Peter Claussøn Friis’s Danish Snorri, pp. 520–560.], Archbishop of Norway.

To the most holy Father and lord C. [Note: [Col. 0658D] Celestine.], supreme pontiff by God’s grace, E., Archbishop of the Norwegians: greeting in the Lord and due reverence to so great a Father.

It is believed and said that, just as the Roman Church surpasses all churches in dignity, so likewise [Col. 0657C] it compassionately aids and relieves their burdens and oppressions with paternal mercy. In our burdens and oppressions, therefore, most loving Father, we must seek the clemency of the apostolic see, so that in time of need paternal compassion may aid the son and the tinder of wickedness may be crushed by the hammer of severity and justice. Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your holiness, we lay our complaint before your ears, humbly entreating that a kindly hearing be granted to those who relate it.

Last year, after receiving the pallium from your holiness and returning to our country, he [Note: [Col. 0658D] Sverrir, king of Norway, who reigned from 1177 to 1202 amid great tribulation.] who boasts in the royal title and in the usurped fullness of royal power had us summoned into his presence and requested that we place a royal crown upon his head. Since we saw that his request was contrary to your reverence [Col. 0657D] and the salvation of our soul, we judged that it must not be accepted until, after envoys sent by us had returned from the apostolic see, we had learned fully what your holiness’s judgment decided we ought to maintain in the matter [Col. 0658A]. The prince therefore was angered against us, and all his army with him. He maintained that apostolic favor ought not be consulted in such a matter, since other kings have freedom to receive the sacrament of anointing wherever, whenever, and from whomever they wish [Note: [Col. 0658D] Thus far this diploma has been published by Bartholin in *Antiquitates Danicae*, pp. 241–242.].

Again, when we were making an appointed visitation through the church [Note: [Col. 0658D] Of Stavanger. See Peter Claussøn Friis’s Danish Snorri, p. 520.] over which we presided, clergy and people alike came together in one vote and one consent for a person worthy in life and learning to preside over them in the episcopal office. But because the aforesaid prince had not been present at this election and had not cast the first vote in it, he judged it should be annulled. Yet we know that this custom had been renounced by his predecessors, the Norwegian kings, under oaths given [Col. 0658B] [Note: [Col. 0658D] By the agreement made between Augustine, Archbishop of Nidaros, and King Magnus, son of Erling, of Norway—whom, however, Sverrir regarded as a usurper and persecutor of the royal house.], and had been granted to our Church through instruments sealed with the characters of their names, confirmed by the privileges of Pope Adrian of blessed memory and of your holiness.

Since he cried out that we had thereby done injury to royal majesty, without consulting us and despite our protest, he compelled clergy and people to consent to another person, who was living with a bigamous wife in that very, if it may be called such, election, and he presented him to us for consecration. But since the aforesaid Pope Adrian of holy memory had condemned bigamy among the clergy in our region by apostolic authority, we did not presume to proceed to the deed, lest we appear to render void what that holy man had commanded to be observed among the clergy.

Now, by the common law of the secular court, he has the clergy dragged into his court and judged by his retainers, as though in lawsuits, contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers and every custom of the Church of God. He calls parish or baptismal churches adjoining his little estates “royal chapels,” and wishes to retain in his own power, without our leave, the right to give them to whomever and whenever he pleases. How far this departs from ecclesiastical custom we leave to your holiness to consider.

We humbly ask that your holiness set forth by letter what we ought to do in all these matters. Nor, most loving Father, may we conceal in silence that in all these things, because we do not obey his commands, inflamed with wrath and indignation, he ordered our goods and all our revenues to be confiscated to the last [Col. 0658D] farthing; and, after taking everything from us, summoned us into your presence, seeing and reflecting that, when our resources failed, we too would fail to undertake the journey and would thus seem [Col. 0659A] to incur contempt of the apostolic see. But he did not know that your prudence knows how to apprehend malice in its cunning and that paternal clemency shows compassionate affection toward the needy who are oppressed.

But lest impossibility perhaps seem to furnish an excuse for contempt if we did not come to you by the appointed date of appeal, we sent from our side representatives, men of good repute. We humbly ask that they be kindly received by your holiness and, as they bear witness to the truth, be cherished in the bosom of your fatherhood, so that the malice conceived may be uprooted from our lands and the liberty of our Church, confirmed by the privileges of the apostolic see, may be preserved unharmed. Meanwhile, having left our kingdom because resources failed, we have been received with every reverence and honor, and most humanely supported, in Denmark by our fellow brother, the lord [Col. 0659B] Archbishop of Lund, a special and most devoted son of the holy Roman Church.

## LETTER XXV [Note: [Col. 0659D] Barth. and Lang., year 1197. Partly already published by Bartholin the son in *Antiquitates Danicae*, pp. 244–247.]

To the lord archbishop.

To his most loving Father and lord, his devoted son and unprofitable servant: fear together with love.

Necessity compels us to write to your holiness. For a thousand times we have experienced through your grace both counsel in doubtful matters and aid of relief in need. Nor can or ought this be ascribed to merits, which are none, unless the favor of divine grace is added, where the affection of piety finds room for compassion, so that temporal goods bestowed upon the poor for the Lord may be followed by eternal gifts and joys. Nor do we say this because we suppose your prudence ignorant of such things, since we do not in the least doubt that for these and similar deeds the Lord has exalted you above all who dwell in this land in his Church [Note: [Col. 0659D] Part of this letter, from the words “Furthermore, my Father” to “which is offered to you by us without the oil of flattery” [Col. 0660D], was published by Pontoppidan in *Annales Danici*, vol. I, pp. 489–491, and by him assigned to the year 1197.].

Furthermore, my Father and lord, we have judged it fitting to inform you that Lord Cardinal Fidentius [Note: [Col. 0660D] He came and died in Denmark in 1197.] has summoned us and our fellow abbots by letter and by the admonitions of Lord Bishop Peter, commanding that, to pay his expenses, we must pour the patrimony of Christ into his purses or coffers. We judge that doing this is nothing other than committing sacrilege, especially since this year we possess less grain than in another [Col. 0659D] year. As is said, intolerable threats are added: namely, that we shall not be able to escape the penalty of suspension from our offices if we should resist his commands.

The matter is difficult, and pressures beset us on every side. If we do this, death is ours, because it is against God. If we do not do it, we shall by no means escape the violence of his hands, for he has come in order to seize and devour, like a lion seizing and devouring. What then shall we do? Is it a counsel to take from the poor in a time of famine and put the little they possess into the lion’s mouth? May God do this to me, and add this besides, if I do anything other than what I know pleases God.

Behold, the wickedness of the ancients is brought again before our eyes. In the time of persecution the holy martyrs were told: “Worship the idols and you shall live; otherwise you shall be killed.” We are told: “Fill the cardinal’s bags, or you shall lose your offices.” O perverse greed! O blind ambition! As the Lord lives and as your soul lives, my Father and lord, even if all poor abbots and monks sacrifice to his purse in order not to be suspended from their office—yet I shall not. He also sets forth another edict: that whoever refuses to sacrifice to his purse must appear before him and bend the knee before Baal. Shall I purchase an office of prelacy with poverty, and place my feet in the fetters [Col. 0660B] of simoniacal wickedness, which I have always hated? Let him therefore stretch forth his hand and cut me down, if he pleases, for no flattering person’s assertion will change me.

Bread will not fail me in my country, because the Lord cares for me and will not abandon me in evil days and in the time of the proud. May the Lord grant concerning our little ones, whom he has given into my bosom, that they do not perhaps perish through lack of grain. For no less danger threatens them than last year, when through almost the whole summer we drank water and ate bearded bread—bread, I say, not of angels, but fodder for beasts. Indeed, we should not even have had that had the mercy which excels in you withheld its hand from giving.

Nevertheless, out of fear of God, honor for religion, and particular love for your holiness, we have resolved to endure, certainly without murmuring, but setting the shield of patience against adversity. For he is greatly avaricious to whom God does not suffice. You know—and know well—to whom you then lent, and that you will receive eternal things for transient ones. Know, moreover, that our boys daily, without interruption, offer to the Lord God at the altar a sacrifice of praise for your salvation: at every hour of day and night, a psalm and the Lord’s Prayer with the collect assigned to them. Even among the more secret tears offered to the divine gaze, the sweet and celebrated memory of you is commended, especially there where the Son is sacrificed to the Father for the redemption of the world. We say this so that the charity conceived and enkindled [Col. 0660D] may not grow cold in their affection if we depart from the place.

We think—indeed, we are certain—that he called cardinal and legate contributes little additional provision to their needs. But was blessed Peter’s legation to the Romans such a legation? Far be it! He did not seek silver or gold, but met the afflictions of the sick with signs and wonders, and restored to God those whom he took away from the devil. Did he not say to a certain man suffering bodily infirmity: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you. In the name,” he said, “of Jesus the Nazarene, rise and [Col. 0661A] walk” (Acts 3)? Did not the dead rise from death through the staff of so great a legate, namely the apostle Peter, sent here and there? But let us leave the staff and speak of the cardinal’s presence and deeds.

Where are the power and strength of him who boasts of the office of legation? Whom has he brought back from unbelief to faith? Whose lost function of sight has he restored? Which sick persons has he cured? Which lepers has he cleansed? Which dead persons has he raised? If he who is called our cardinal were such a cardinal, who would not come to meet him? Who would deny him temporal goods? But behold: he seeks what it is not expedient for us to give, because there is neither material substance available nor can our will be induced to it. It has not been heard from time immemorial that the Order of Saint Victor of Paris has been subject in tribute to any cardinal. Shall I then, alone and first, weaken the immunity and granted privilege of the whole order? It is better for me that a millstone be hung around my neck and that I be drowned in the sea.

O senseless bishops of Denmark—if indeed it is lawful to say it! O, I say, senseless men! Who has so bewitched you, overthrown your prudence into imprudence—I dare not say folly—and blinded the eyes of your discernment? Are you not those who used to say, “We abound in provisions, but we have no abundance of gold and silver”? If the assertion you put forward was true, why do you so eagerly stretch out your hands in gifts to ravening wolves coming from afar? One man strives with all his strength to restrain the rage and quench the thirst of the aforesaid wolves at the price of one hundred marks, another at fifty, [Col. 0661C] another at thirty. To what end such waste? Amen, I say to you: whoever drinks of this water will thirst again and forever (John 4). Should not all these things be given to the poor, not to wolves, whose ravenous maw could not be filled by the treasure of the whole world? Would that it might happen to them, and be said to them, as it was said to Crassus when molten gold was poured out: “You thirst for gold; drink gold”—and not unjustly either. For all who have come are thieves and robbers, hirelings and not shepherds.

Alas for sorrow! Christ is dying of hunger at the door for bread: which of you has compassion on Christ? These things, to tell the truth, are spent for vain glory, so that one man may seem more outstanding and lavish than another in giving gifts. Amen, I say to you: you have received your reward (Matt. 6). In this way you most certainly invite, both to drain what remains to you, the greed of those who disembowel you, and their return to you, together with others whom you have not yet seen. It ought to have been sufficient not to refuse them merely a table, with four horses and four silver marks.

Most loving Father, do not take this path, you who have always generously bestowed upon the poor what God has granted you. This is offered to you by us without the oil of flattery. May your holiness live and prosper here, in eternity, and beyond. Finally, most merciful Father, we beseech the bowels of [Col. 0662A] your mercy that, in this matter which the prayers of religious men and of our fellow brothers, namely the abbots—who love you and embrace you with all the tenderness of charity as Father and Lord—seek, they may not be left undefended by your protection against a man whose breath is in his nostrils and who intends to harass them, lest, while they already suffer scarcity of grain, they be burdened with grave and unprecedented exactions.

May the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead save you and strengthen you in every good work; and, for the gifts which you have so often bestowed upon our poor brethren, may eternal glory crown you with the recompense of the righteous. Amen. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVI [Note: [Col. 0661D] Barth., year 1188; Lang, year 1187.]

To the daughters of the king
[Col. 0662B] To the holy virgins of royal lineage, M. [Note: [Col. 0661D] In the Magnaeus transcript I it appears as *Margaritae*; in the Lyegaard manuscript, *Margaretae*.] and M. [Note: [Col. 0662D] Perhaps Maria or Magdalena, although it is not established that Waldemar I had a daughter bearing either of these names.], brother WILLIAM, servant of the servants of God at the Paraclete: may you enjoy the embraces of the eternal King.

What was formerly foretold by the prophets through the Lord’s inspiration, we now see fulfilled in God’s Church: daughters of kings submit their necks to Christ’s most sweet yoke and entreat his countenance. Happy, then, are you both: royal blood brought you forth, but lest the world entice you by deceitful blandishments, Christ enrolled you in the heavenly host and consecrated you as brides devoted to himself by his blood. Happy are you, I say, who have given to other virgins and to people entangled in sins an example of conversion worthy of imitation, by which the world [Col. 0662C] ought to return to its beginning, and the devil should grieve at the loss inflicted upon him.

Let that most cruel robber now rage, since those whom he had resolved to swallow into the belly of his malice become vessels of honour and glory. Let him groan and lament that he has been conquered even in the weaker sex, when he sees delicate daughters of kings, reared in saffron-coloured garments, made servants of divine worship and entering upon the way of humility—a way which he despised, being excessively exalted through pride. Through love he refused to be subject to his Creator, but, wickedly deceived, wished to be like God. For although, in beauty, excellence, and splendour, he was more eminent than the other creatures which the Creator of the whole world had made for his own praise and glory, he wished, as we have said, to make himself equal to God; and, despising what he was, unless [Col. 0662D] he should be like the Most High, he fell irreparably from heaven with his companions, becoming the dragon and the devil: more shameful than all others, inventor of all iniquity, instigator of vices, inventor and author of death.

Therefore, seeing himself cast down from the glory of paradise and having no refuge outside the darkness—though he was at first a spirit glorious in appearance and established amid delights—he groans more heavily and envies more fiercely that humankind, formed from mud, should ascend to heaven and possess through the grace of humility what he himself lost through malice and pride. Thus what he lost through pride becomes for humankind an honour and [Col. 0663A] everlasting glory.

But, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0663D] I cannot find this passage.], “the fall of the greater ought to be a warning to the lesser.” For if God did not spare angels, who possessed greater dignity and glory, should one suppose that he will spare a human being, who is wholly dust and ashes, if that person sins? Therefore, holy virgins, you must take more careful thought, so that you may in no way love anything you see to be contrary to virtue, nor incline either the consent of your minds or the gaze of your eyes toward obtaining it, lest you lose the honour granted you by the Lord and the crown appointed for you according to your merits. For it is more pleasant never to have possessed the honour of pre-eminence than to have gained it and then lost it through one’s deserts.

It is necessary that all our works be seasoned with the grace of humility, because whoever gathers virtues without the grace of humility [Col. 0663B] resembles one carrying dust in the wind.
