Rejoice, moreover, that you are companions not of the rich but of the poor, because God communes with the simple and the poor. For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such people. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4). Virginity without humility cannot advance toward life, however fortified it may be by the supports of virtues. For “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10).

We read that the Lord spoke thus when, in his school, he taught his disciples about the progress of virtues: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). What he taught in word, he demonstrated by example. He humbled himself, [Col. 0663C] becoming obedient to God unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2). We trust in the Lord that you will think nothing otherwise (Gal. 5), for with you is the Bridegroom, the Lord of knowledge, “who teaches mankind knowledge” (Ps. 93).

We have written these few words to you, dearest friends and ladies, so that the page of our writing may be to you a pledge of affection and a sign of love; and so that the fragrance of your manner of life, diffused far and wide, may receive an increase of still more sincere esteem, so that, as we have said, nothing may hinder you from being set forth as an example for others, but the inextinguishable fire of charity may kindle your neighbours. Although we do not know the appearance of your outward persons, nevertheless from the joyful report of our brethren and the growth of your excellent reputation we earnestly [Col. 0663D] embrace your inner persons. Present with you in spirit though absent in body, we most earnestly desire that things pious, just, chaste, and peaceable may come to you.

We do not think it necessary to remind your holiness and purpose not to make drunkenness a familiar refuge at your tables. Although this vice may belong to the custom of the land, it ought to be abhorrent to you, since through it even the strongest man falls into ruin and guilt. When drunkenness intervenes, honour yields up its weapons to unchastity; the fruit of a holier purpose degenerates; and the fragrant glory of one’s reputation [Col. 0664A] damnably vanishes.

Moreover, we rejoice that we are joined to your friendship, and we give thanks that this is granted us, without merits, by grace alone; and in many ways we glory in the Lord. Yet see how carefully you walk (Eph. 5), lest perhaps that prophetic curse come upon you: “Woe to those who call good evil” (Isa. 5). As we have heard, you esteem us highly, though we are altogether small or nothing. Why do you judge us greater among you than common opinion among people does? Weigh us more secretly in yourselves, and do not think us greater than the balance of truth weighs us. It is the word of the Lord: “Weight and weight are an abomination” (Prov. 20). There is one in heaven who searches hearts and reins (Ps. 7). See that you mingle in no deceit, but weigh us equally before God and people [Col. 0664B].

As for the favour of grace that smiles upon certain of our sons, namely S. and T. [Note: [Col. 0663D] Perhaps Thomas, named in Letter 29.], we render you solemn thanks; and this will be repaid by our services when either opportunity, time, or place presents itself. We commend all the more devotedly to your generosity our most intimate friends K. and J. [Note: [Col. 0663D] See above, Book I, Letters 28 and 29.], whom we venerate in the Lord and to whom we too are bound by the arms of the sincerest charity, because we have greater confidence in your good will. Finally, we ask that remembrance of us may be present in your prayers, because remembrance of you is implanted in our hearts, where the Son is sacrificed to the Father. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVII

[Note: [Col. 0663D] Lang, year 1187.] To the community of virgins at Roskilde.

[Col. 0664C] To the venerable and beloved in the Lord prioress of blessed Mary [Note: [Col. 0664D] This monastery was founded at Roskilde not long after 1156. See *Atlas Danicus*, vol. II, p. 341; vol. VI, p. 134; and Saxo, pp. 215–16.], and to all the sisters, holy virgins: W., unworthy minister of blessed Thomas at the Paraclete, affection of sincere love.

You know, dearest sisters, that the offences of subjects are by no means corrected if, through willfulness, negligence, or the rashness of presumption, they act beastlike against the ordinances of their order. Therefore, if a pastor neglects to oppose all these things, or, frightened by fear, does not dare to utter a word, although he bears the office of pastor he loses its merit, since by his silence he permits those whom he ought to correct to sin.

We, therefore, whom the Lord has determined to raise to pastoral honour in his Church, shall receive a similar judgment for betraying the flock entrusted to us if we permit it to proceed [Col. 0664D] into the precipices of vices, though by our word and example it ought to have advanced in the increase of virtues. Hence, by the Lord’s gift, we have endeavoured to apply sufficiently watchful and diligent care to those entrusted to us, that we might plough up their errors with the ploughshare of discipline [sic] and set virtues before vices, so that on the day of judgment we may render an account of the talent entrusted to us in security.

We trust that your holiness is not unaware what kind of person we received in Nicholas, the son of your prior, and how far we advanced him in teaching and discipline. Since we have sometimes rebuked him for his offences more severely than he wished, he is distressed by repeated grievances and threatens to abandon the purpose of his pledged faith. Therefore, rebellious and contumacious, he has disposed of his garments—namely his cope and surplice—without consulting us, and, as we have learned from the report of others, has deposited them with you, to our great astonishment. For we cannot suppose that wisdom accompanies malice or that sincerity of faith supports those who act wickedly. We therefore ask and advise your charity that, setting every excuse aside, you send us the deposit, lest your religious house, which has always been a lover of truth, become a hiding-place and refuge for malice and wickedness by sharing in evil works.

## LETTER XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0665D] Lang, year 1187.] To the community of virgins at Slangathorp [Note: [Col. 0665D] Slangerup, today a small town in Zealand.].

[Col. 0665B]

To the beloved holy virgins in the Lord, A., prioress by the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0665D] I know nothing concerning the antiquity of this monastery. King Erik the Good caused a church to be built there in 1100 [Col. 0666D].], K., and J.: brother W., servant of the servants of God at the Paraclete—may you so run as to attain the prize of the heavenly reward.

We received the letters of your holiness and read through them with devout eagerness. If we have taken care to bring into effect anything that accords with honour and redounds to the glory of your holiness, we rejoice the more for that reason and render the thanksgiving due to God, always desiring to stretch forward, so that benefits may respond more abundantly to benefits received.

Recently we received from charity the gifts of charity, through which we have without doubt proved that charity is present in charity. Yet because we frequently receive blessings of your sweetness, our conscience is reproved by sluggishness, since in repaying the benefit we are found less provident than we would wish. Yet one thing brings us the remedy of consolation: namely, the sincere affection of love, which, once arisen among friends, never grows old with time; rather, if anything is lacking, it is nourished by mutual conversation and grows warmer still through more recent letters.

Among all things known to hold a place of privilege with us, we embrace most dearly and closely that affection of which we speak, especially when it is clothed with the radiance of honour. Therefore we offer it also to you, and we receive it, once offered, into ourselves—not that you may lack it, but that you may possess it [Col. 0665D] more abundantly. We believe that this will likewise occur in us when we have put off our bodies: what each possesses through merit and grace will be common to all through love. We have judged that your request should in no way be opposed, but that the person whom you requested should be sent as soon as we can. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 0666D] Lang, year 1187.] To the same persons.

WILLIAM, by the grace of God servant of the servants of God at the Paraclete, to the holy virgins K. and J.: may you cleave happily to Christ the Bridegroom [Col. 0666A] and shine with the glory of virtues.

Just as a fire grows greater when oil is poured upon the flames, so the virtue of love grows stronger and warmer through good works. From the report of our dearest son Thomas, who reveres and loves you in the Lord, holy virgins, we have learned that you bear a devout concern for our needs. This astonishes us, since we know of neither work nor merit of ours that has attained to this. But since it is a fuller grace that you have shown yourselves to possess from the Lord the desire to benefit not one person but many—for he came by his Passion to benefit not one but all—you also offer an exemplary instance of good will in doing good to many. Thus you may attain greater grace, spread everywhere [Col. 0666B] the sweet fragrance of your reputation, and, as we have said, awaken by your services our love, now as it were asleep and reduced to ashes, so that we may love you in the Lord and commend one another to the Lord in mutual prayers.

For our adversary is like a lion ready for prey, going about and seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5). Let us resist him, strong in faith and armed with the weapons of righteousness. Therefore, my happy ladies, holy virgins—not ladies from any other source than because you are brides of my Lord—let neither the deceitful glory of this world nor the desire for temporal things lead you even a little into the gulf of vices, nor let it boast miserably that it was able to overthrow the glory of your continence.

We know that you have renounced the world and consecrated yourselves to the Lord; and we do not believe that it has yet been erased from your memory that “greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6): the mother of transgression, teacher of harm, seedbed of iniquity, charioteer of malice, murderess of virtues, origin of sedition, and pit of scandals. Do you not know? Indeed, I know that you know that “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44). Since, therefore, you too are daughters of a king and brides, let your glory be inward, not in outward things, lest, when the Bridegroom comes, he find you foolish [Col. 0666C] virgins, without the oil of a good conscience in your lamps (Matt. 25).

Moreover, may the Lord of graces, who recompenses us, himself repay you for the grace shown to us. Farewell.

## LETTER XXX

[Note: [Col. 0666D] Barth. and Lang, year 1196.] To the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0666D] Already published by Holberg in *History of Denmark*, vol. I, pp. 261–62.].

[Col. 0666D]

The more the Apostolic See surpasses others in dignity, the more carefully it ought to provide in rendering judgment, so that in conducting affairs and handling cases it does not abandon the law of justice, or the way of truth and equity, through love for anyone or through indolence. For if any one of these things, as has become known to the grace of your fatherhood, is lacking from the praises of a judge’s virtues—especially those of the supreme pontiff—it will bring harm, and at the final examination of the heavenly Judge he will suffer punishment for so [Col. 0667A] grave an offence.

But far be it, my Father, that your conscience should suffer from this disease. In the matter of our sister, the queen of the French, your conscience remains favourable and unchanging, and still abhors false assertion as a detestable enemy. We have heard and learned from the truth of the matter that your piety has struck fear of your threat into the king of that land; the force of justice on your part has not yet grown lukewarm, and this delights us. Under threat of anathema, you commanded him not to join himself to another woman as long as our sister remained alive.

Now therefore, Father, since in contempt of God and for everlasting disgrace he has, as a rebel and contumacious man, despised the decree of your holiness, what remains except [Col. 0667B] that the madness of this despiser of your command be so punished that the celebration of the heavenly sacraments is forbidden throughout his kingdom? Thus, my Father, let zeal for justice now shine forth in you, and if he has not understood until now how rash it is to oppose apostolic commands, let him at least now perceive it by enduring this disgrace. We therefore ask, Father, and entreat the heart of your mercy, that our petition may not lack its effect, since your affection of love toward us is great. For it has always pleased us to submit our necks to the yoke of obedience to the Roman Church; and unless the Roman Church first fails us, we shall have no will to depart from it.

## LETTER XXXI

[Note: [Col. 0667D] Barth. and Lang, year 1194.] To Lord Pope Celestine, from the queen of the French [Note: [Col. 0667D] Published by Holberg in *History of Denmark*, vol. I, pp. 262–63. Without doubt written by William at the king’s command to the pope, after news had been received of Ingeborg’s divorce.].

[Col. 0667C]

One must have recourse to the seat of mercy as often as necessary, until mercy looks down from heaven and God accomplishes the wishes of those who hope in him. Therefore, most loving Father, I too—whose heart is pierced day and night by the stings of grief—do not cease to cry out, first to God and then to the clemency of the Apostolic See. Perhaps the Lord may look upon the prayer of his humble handmaid and remove from me his arrows that wage war against me, whose indignation drinks up my spirit; and perhaps the successor of the apostle Peter may benignly pour the dew of his blessing upon the dryness of my heart and grant me, amid my tribulation, the healing remedy of consolation for the injury inflicted upon me.

For who, Father, would not be distressed by grief if he did not compassionately share in the groans of his daughter? Far be that from you! Cast down from the height of glory and prostrate on the earth, I seek a comforter and find none. I lament the loss of my former eminence, since [Col. 0668A] “there is none to redeem, nor one to save” (Ps. 7) [Note: [Col. 0667D] Perhaps: “to bring salvation”; in the Magnaeus transcript I appears “his daughter,” which makes no sense.]. I am ashamed of my misery; my spirit is distressed within me, and my heart is troubled within me (Ps. 142).

One thing, my Father, refreshes and consoles me among the straits of my tribulations with the benefit of hoped-for consolation, and apart from it there is nothing else. If one asks what it is, it gives no answer other than what I am about to say: the clemency of the Apostolic See. Therefore, most merciful Father, I beg you: restore your daughter to the full measure of your glory; through justice, cast down the man by whom I am afflicted, so that I may again be reconciled to him and ascribe the joys of reconciliation to God and to the grace of your fatherhood.

For it concerns God’s honour and human salvation that truth should always be brought [Col. 0668B] into the light in judicial proceedings. For this purpose you also, Fathers and lord Cardinals [Note: [Col. 0667D] This whole clause, from “For this purpose you also” to the end, seems suspect to me, and perhaps taken from another letter. In manuscript Arnae I the passage is restored thus, although in a later hand: “You have been established and especially appointed by him. Farewell.” And in the Lyegaard manuscript: “The manuscript is defective; it is supplied in this manner: ‘You are able to grant [it].’”].

## LETTER XXXII

[Note: [Col. 0668D] Barth. and Lang, year 1194.] To the lord pope, as above [Note: [Col. 0668D] Published by Holberg in *History of Denmark*, vol. I, p. 263. Also written by William at royal command.].

Since it is the belief and desire of all that the successor of the Prince of the Apostles possesses in all matters the authority to govern God’s Church, matters corrupted by wicked people ought all the more securely to be referred to him, because those who obtain grace and are supported by his patronage are more often rescued from impious actions.

Therefore I, led out from my father’s house and brought into the kingdom of the Franks, raised by the Lord’s ordering to the royal throne, have been cast down to the ground like dry and useless wood through the envy of the enemy of humankind against my happier fortunes. I am deprived of every consolation [Col. 0668C] and counsel. My bridegroom, Philip king of the French, has abandoned me, finding in me nothing to condemn except what malice had forged upon the anvil of falsehood. That matter ought to be pursued in your presence, if I did not know that it has already been spread among all the people by flying rumour. Therefore, miserable as I am, I flee to the seat of mercy, so that, having obtained mercy, I may henceforth profess myself your daughter, should a happier and kinder fortune attend me, and devote myself as your handmaid to your service all my days.

## LETTER XXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0668D] Barth. and Lang, year 1196.] From the king [Note: [Col. 0668D] Canute. In the Lyegaard manuscript, very erroneously: “the queen.”] to the cardinals.

It concerns God’s honour and human salvation [Col. 0668D] that truth be brought into the light in the conduct of affairs and judgments. For this purpose the apostolic primacy has exalted you also, Fathers and lord Cardinals, as judges of the world: that in the causes of all poor and oppressed persons who flee to the Apostolic See, truth may not be suppressed through love or hatred of any person. This reputation, [Col. 0669A] diffused everywhere from your sacred actions, calls very many from far away to seek the help of grace in their tribulations.

Accordingly, this same reputation, reaching our ears, stirred us greatly to prove in deed what we had learned by report. Long ago we committed our cause—or rather, that of our sister, the queen of the French—to your grace; and from it we have received, if not complete consolation, at least some consolation, for which we render you thanks. Since there remains something for which we ought to rejoice more fully, if it receives its due effect, we have judged that our prayers should again be laid before your eyes, although neither work nor merit gives us confidence in this matter. Yet among lovers of justice, compassion commonly draws forth an affection of pity, especially [Col. 0669B] in matters supported by the protection of justice.

Your holiness knows that the lord pope commanded the king of France to take back in marriage our sister, whom he had maliciously separated from himself; and, if he refused to take her back, he was not to presume to marry another. Behold what the person does who neither fears God nor respects people: in marrying another—not a wife but an adulteress—he did not fear to oppose apostolic commands. For such a deed we ask that you render us justice. At present we seek no other justice than that the ecclesiastical sacraments celebrated throughout his kingdom be withheld, until his mind is reformed for the better: that is, until he repudiates the woman whom he has taken [Col. 0669C] and takes back the woman whom he dismissed.

## LETTER XXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Barth. and Lang, year 1194.] Abbot W. to the queen of the French.

We are compelled by the debt of charity and the law of nature to put hand to pen and, if not by bodily presence—since it is weak—yet by the spirit, which is willing, to visit our lady, the queen of the French, whether the devil wishes it or not. Yet, if it could be done, we would more gladly enter into familiar conversation mouth to mouth, especially since we should delight in seeing you present and be cherished by sweeter speech. By such speech the mind wounded by the arrows of charity bears more powerfully the wound of divine love, and glories that its whole self is consumed as a sacrifice of praise.

He who knows secrets is aware that we earnestly embrace your honour [Col. 0669D] and glory. By honour we mean this: that you tread underfoot the pressure of the world with the foot of virtues, and that in your tribulation strength increases through divine dispensation, since you endure hostile wickedness courageously, not as a woman but as a strong-hearted man, and entrust your cause and judgment to divine grace. You know—and know well—because you have often read in the book of experience, that it is the part of virtue not to be conquered by evil but to conquer evil with good. This will be to your glory and an example for imitation to all who suffer injury.

It must be believed that you have been instructed by God to rise vigorously to greater praise of virtues, keeping before your eyes what the Apostle says—indeed, what Christ says through the Apostle: “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). What patience contributes is by no means foreign to your thought, since Truth says: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21). Therefore, dearest lady and glorious queen, do not depart from the path of uprightness which you have begun; for soon, as we truly hope and trust, unless he who troubles you comes to his senses, he will bear judgment, and what has been granted you by the Lord as a dowry will by no means be made void through justice.

Pay no attention to the threats of those who hate and afflict you, nor to the blandishments of their promises. For even if the king’s severity at times frightens you, let the judgment of divine justice [Col. 0670B] strengthen and confirm you: it never abandons those who hope in it; it disperses the evil counsels of princes and establishes its own counsel forever.

## LETTER XXXV

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Barth., year 1195, and Lang., year 1194. Without doubt written at Rome.] The abbot to the queen.

Whenever the presence of travellers offers itself to us, we have determined that it would be unworthy if our smallness failed to send even the least writing to our lady, whom we truly love and revere in the Lord. For you know, lady, and we know as well, that the force of love has this property: it grows warmer through more recent letters and does not permit itself to grow old through any turn of events. The knot of love is also bestowed upon the bonds of friendship as a healing comfort to the desolate, especially those in whom the bowels of compassion abound and in whom there is no … [Note: [Col. 0670D] In the Magnaeus transcript I, *Domini* is absent, although the lacuna remains. Perhaps the correct reading is *Dominum colentium*, “of those worshipping the Lord.” In the Lyegaard manuscript: *dominion*.] corruption in good morals.

Therefore we offer your excellence the service of our greeting, so that on receiving it you may also receive a saving remedy from tribulation, and may suffer no detriment to Christian faith—the sort of detriment that commonly brings contempt upon the unfaithful and negligent. We know that, while the devil rages but the Lord provides better things for you, a temporal paternal scourge has been sent upon you, so that the strength of patience, tested in the contest, may make gold wholly purified from leaden dross; and that the means through which the devil thinks he gains victory may cause you [Col. 0670D] to obtain the crown of eternal glory, while he himself bears the punishment due to his malice for the injury inflicted upon you.

Let not the empty glory of this world, taken away for a time, deceive you, my lady; for the Lord is able to restore you to the fullness of power, so that your highness may rule peoples as head of nations and hold the throne of glory. You know—and know well—that he “who covers heaven with clouds” (Ps. 146) also, when they have been removed, pours the light of heavenly brightness upon the stars when he wills. So too he will surely exalt you when he wills, because he “looks upon the prayer of the humble and does not despise their petitions” (Ps. [Col. 0671A] 101), whose groans come to him; and the Most High will not take delight in them. He himself kills and makes alive, leads down to the underworld and brings back. “The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and raises up” [Note: [Col. 0671D] In Magnaeus I: “He can make and give humble and exalted things.”] (1 Sam. 2). These are the words of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore do not lose confidence, which will have great recompense. God will give an end to these matters also; your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you (John 16). “The heart of the king,” as Scripture says, “is in the hand of God,” and he will turn it wherever he wills (Prov. 21). Furthermore, we rejoice greatly because we learn that you fear the Lord and his commandments, and because the sweetest fragrance of your most holy conduct is everywhere spread abroad, so that no enemy can gnaw at you, since he finds nothing [Col. 0671B] opposed to honour and good morals.

Let your highness know that forgetfulness will never make old the love we have for you. We shall never be able to cease from prayer until we perceive that the Lord will hear us—a thing we trust will happen soon. Furthermore, we complain greatly that we receive nothing from your side, even in writing. We say this with your reverence and peace preserved, since behold, we have written to you twice and, for your love and honour, we have never feared to expose our body to the greatest labour against the lord king, your husband. We therefore ask that what we find has been done less fittingly in this respect may be kindly remedied, because we glory greatly in the fullness of your grace, lest we seem to have been consigned to oblivion [Col. 0671C].

## LETTER XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Barth. and Lang, year 1194.] To Abbot Walbert of Esrum.

To the venerable father and lord W., by God’s grace abbot of Esrum: W., servant of the servants of God at the Paraclete—may fullness of joys attend the fullness of your days.

A report sweet to our ears, dearest Father, has sounded forth: it has gladdened the city of God and stirred us greatly to praise God. For who, even if foolish, would not rejoice that you have made your long-desired arrival in these parts, to benefit many by counsel and help, through the Lord’s gift? I say “even if foolish”: although not everyone thereby attains the glory of this joy, nevertheless we no less devoutly render solemn thanksgivings and praises before God’s sight for the newness of this happiness, because we are joined to you by bonds of the most sincere love—not according to outward appearance, but according to purity of conscience.

And not without cause. Whom would not the services, so often bestowed upon us under the title of sincere and true love, bind indissolubly to you? Who could fully comprehend the affection of compassion in our needs, a compassion that pursues the fulfilment of our desired things? These, Father, are what make us rejoice at your arrival and render us inattentive [Col. 0672A] to considering and repaying so many and such great gifts. If, through unequal efforts, less cautious provision should perhaps result, kindly friendship will not take that amiss. For “charity is kind, is patient, does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13).

Moreover, my Father, since love cannot bear delay, we are compelled by an affection of concern to inquire what our most friendly chancellor [Note: [Col. 0671D] That celebrated Andrew, son of Suno.] is doing and what plan is under consideration with him. Therefore, if it does not oppose your wishes, we ask that you set this down for us in your letter, because amid the changing events of affairs we hang in great longing. For just as a lover’s mind is wounded by the stings of sorrow when sad news of a friend is reported, so [Col. 0672B] it is made joyful if it obtains the gifts of a more favourable fortune bringing well-being.

## LETTER XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0672D] Barth., year 1178; Lang, more correctly, year 1194.] Likewise, upon his return from the chapter.

To the abbot of Esrum: greeting in the salvation of God.

That an opportunity for conversation is sometimes withheld from you and us is neither pleasing to us nor consistent with love. For familiar conversation is usually among friends a relief in love and a remedy in sorrow. We do not know whose evasion is at work in this matter, and we think that you are entirely unaware of it. But if some falsifier, perhaps infected by the pest of lying, is responsible, he will receive the reward of the iniquity he has conceived—he who has resolved to sow tares over a well-cultivated field instead of wheat.

Let the charity of brotherhood remain unharmed between us, lest the child of dissension and worker of iniquity at some time rejoice in his wickedness. You should know that our heart toward your holiness has not been disturbed in the least, since in this matter no annoyance has come upon us by which our smallness ought to be injured. Rather, the benefits granted us by you testify to your love and favour. They cannot and will not be torn from our memory unless, which may God avert, we should be alienated from our senses.

Therefore, if any opposition should arise from our works, words, or even yours—though we do not suppose it will—let forgetfulness make all of it old, erase it, and wipe it away, lest anything diminish the grace of our conduct. We ought always to devote ourselves to divine service in innocence and simplicity of heart, [Col. 0672D] and by this means even enemies, on account of the Lord’s command, ought to be moved by greater benefits to the love of God, so that in all things and through all things God may be praised and glorified by our works—he who is blessed for ever.

## LETTER XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0672D] Barth., year 1178; Lang. also, but doubtfully; I assign it to 1194.] To the abbot of Esrum.

When the vigor of faith has grown too lukewarm, it is no wonder that, as evils rush in, truth becomes doubtful to those who stand far off and are less discerning [Col. 0673A]. Hence it is that we, who are less able to distinguish liars, sometimes accept falsehoods as true, making darkness light and light darkness, calling good evil and evil good (Isa. V). What then? Are we subject to the curse of the presiding Judge, from whom no iniquity is hidden, who neither knows how to be deceived nor to deceive? Far from it! For he knows that the enemies of truth lie maliciously in order to deceive innocence. But if simple people are sometimes deceived and give credence to the assertions of the deceitful, just as inward malice does not blacken them, so neither does the sentence of the supreme Judge condemn them. Although they believe the lying words of such men, they do not lose the steadfastness of the faith which is in Christ.

Therefore, venerable Father, if perhaps we have been compelled to stray [Col. 0673B], if perhaps we are found to have strayed from the path of uprightness, and if sight or hearing has stolen anything from fraternal charity, let the integrity of that love by which we formerly loved one another be restored, with goodwill taking the lead; and, once the light of truth has been received, let the darkness of error be scattered. For we have learned—and it does not become us to deny it—that we were deceived by a false report and assailed by the goads of envy and the wicked shafts of malicious men, while our heart was departing far from the path of truth and was by no means turning aside from the oil of flatterers. We therefore wish it to come to your knowledge that, on the occasion of this controversy, we were so disturbed that we fixed not the gaze of our eyes upon services of advantage or honour, abandoning our regard for virtue.

O envy, how destructive you are! [Col. 0673C] You do not cease to persecute those whom you see involved even in good works; you cast down from heaven the devil, the purveyor of all wickedness; and you did not fear to assail the Author of human salvation. But now let that which took its beginning in us be brought to light, so that, its origin being known, wickedness may be rejected and justice may remain unharmed in its proper degree. It was said, beloved Father—though this be far from the honour of your holiness—that we sat in ambush like lions, in order that, while men wished to adhere to your religious house, we might endeavour to turn them away from you and unite them to our fellowship through desire for their possessions. This, you said, was sufficiently evident from our reception of our boy Philip, whom we had received for no other reason [Col. 0673D] than because we wished to invest in our own habit the money bestowed upon him by his father.

It was also said of us, as we truly learned, that we had fallen into such wickedness that it was our practice to call you devourers of men and, if the superiors should in any respect depart from the commands of the elders, to fasten cruel teeth upon them like beasts. If you have chosen to give credit to these things, know that you too have been deceived, and that we, if we did such things, have lied and exceeded the cruelty characteristic of beasts [Col. 0674A]. This was what spread the seed-bed of discord between us and infected the concord of fraternity with perversity. Since, therefore, all these things supplied fuel for hatred between us, we ask and humbly entreat that we may return to concord in peace and pursue, though late, whatever is pious, just, and honourable. For friendships after enmities are indeed sweeter than they were before, when we suffered no distresses of dissension.

## LETTER XXXIX

[Note: Bartholin places this in the year 1194, and Langebek in 1195. This letter is entitled in the Lyegaard manuscript, in Danish words: “To Ebbe Sunesson.”]

To his dearest lord and heartfelt friend Ebbo [Note: Killed in 1208 in the Swedish war at Lena. See above, vol. V, table IV.], brother W., by the grace of God servant of the servants of God at Paraclete: may you receive a portion of eternal glory.

[Col. 0674B] There is, as you know better, my lord, a certain sweet and wonderful delight in love; indeed, to confess more truly, in conversation there is a pleasant, honey-sweet intoxication. When friends converse together, it so intoxicates the minds of those speaking that it introduces playful matters before serious ones and excludes the word which ought to have come first concerning necessary affairs. For, as our Solomon says: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII). Only those taste this sweetness in love who, bound more tightly by the bonds of affection, are in no way constrained by unlawful desires. We experienced this most certainly very recently, while we refreshed one another with mutual conversation and delighted in the sight of you: though we ought to have entered upon discussion of necessary matters, forgetfulness wiped it from our minds, brought on by the abundance of love’s sweetness [Col. 0674C].

Yet whatever has been omitted for love’s sake cannot bring us lasting loss. And let it not seem burdensome to you if what had been omitted by us is brought forward by us [Note: In Magnaeus I, all that follows is missing until “Concerning your steward.” In the Lyegaard manuscript, rightly: “And let it not seem burdensome to you if what had been omitted by us is brought forward by us.”], since from it we hope, through your inborn goodness and kindness, to obtain a remedy in our affliction. Know, therefore, that among the evils by which we are afflicted, this is added to complete the sum of evils: royal power, which by right ought to protect poor religious persons, attacks us harshly, while “there is none to redeem, nor any to save” (Ps. 7).

We have sometimes stirred up a dog—yet not just any dog, but one that would give a confident bark and, by the sentence of royal severity, keep raging wolves from biting the sheep [Col. 0674D]. The matter concerns your steward B. [Note: In Magnaeus I and the Lyegaard manuscript: Be, perhaps Bernard, of Alisander Thorp.] of Alexander Thorp and a certain smith, his tenant, who destroy and kill animals. On this matter we have thought it right to seek justice from you: once in person ourselves, and twice, unless we are mistaken, through our messengers. We hope—indeed, we are confident—that, had not the press of cares obscured your mind, the injury inflicted on us by both of them would have received the due execution of justice [Col. 0675A].

Again we ask your affection, in which we place very great confidence, not to suffer the wrong done to the poor brothers to remain unavenged any longer, after summoning us and the aforesaid men before your presence by a fixed date. Moreover, we have gratefully received and keep in mindful remembrance the word which you uttered—or rather, which the Lord through you [Col. 0676A] did and showed to us. It is surely worthy of remembrance, such that no forgetfulness can erase it. If you ask briefly what it was, we answer: … The remainder of this letter is missing.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0675]

## LETTER I

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek assign it to the year 1196.]

Missing.

[Col. 0675B]

## LETTER II

[Note: Bartholin: 1196; Langebek: 1193.]

The beginning of this letter is missing.

[lacuna] …may they feel themselves struck by the goads of [wickedness?], who have conspired together as one against the Lord and against his Christ. Let them feel, I say, my lord, how great is the rashness of opposing apostolic commands. Your Holiness knows that, in the church of the Prince of the Apostles, before an innumerable multitude of people, on the octave of Saint Martin last year, you bound in the bonds of excommunication those bishops who did not fear, contrary to your command, to place the crown of royal dignity upon the aforesaid tyrant [Note: Sverre, king of Norway.], as you know better.

But these lying and wicked men [Col. 0675C], wholly given over to fraud, fashioned cavils and unjust schemes against the aforesaid righteous man, namely the archbishop, upon the anvil of falsehood, so that they might catch you in speech—which is far from you. For since the beginning of the world it has not been heard that, in the Christian religion, an excommunicated priest has been anointed king. We therefore ask and entreat—and with us the multitude of saints asks—that in the present affair the zeal of your Holiness may shine forth; that, justice prevailing, falsehood may succumb in its assertion; and that the wicked may be caught in their own pride, so that there may be peace for people of good will (Luke II), but for the ill-disposed and those who hate peace, a rock of stumbling and a stone of offence (1 Pet. II). May your Holiness live and prosper for ever and beyond.

## LETTER III

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1196.]

To the chancellor [Note: Andrew, son of Suno, later archbishop of Lund from 1201.] of the king of the Danes.

[Col. 0675D]

To his most heartfelt friend and lord A., by the grace of God chancellor of the king of the Danes, W., a little friend among his great friends: the fullness of love and the joy of eternal blessedness.

We consider it necessary to write, if only a little; but to whom? Surely to my beloved, whom my soul loves, [Col. 0676B] without whom to live is no longer life, but pain and groaning. Yet this may seem doubtful to those who have not experienced in themselves the power of love. But far be it that you should hear with trembling, lest perhaps pride creep in, the ardour of your charity—in the ordering of your conduct and in a manner of life conscious of purity—as we say without flattery: unstable constancy in faith, affability in refinement, in the accomplishment of affairs … The remainder of this letter is missing.

(LETTERS IV [Note: Bartholin: 1195; Langebek: 1194.], V [Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1195.], VI [Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1194.], VII [Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1194.], VIII [Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1195.], IX [Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1195.], X [Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1192.] are missing.)

## LETTER XI

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1192.]

The beginning of this letter is missing.

[lacuna] …and at some time consented, or consents, to the transfer; [Col. 0676C] or, if he does not consent, and the Grey monks have retained in their monastery the right of patronage which they held, then, relying upon our authority, you shall confirm—setting aside the process of appeal—that what has been piously and reasonably done by the aforesaid bishop concerning that transfer; so that there may always be some persons in that monastery of Saint Michael who, according to the observance of the White monks [Note: That is, the Cistercians.], ought to serve the Lord there, provided that the aforesaid monastery remains with them.

Since, therefore, the White monks, in our presence and hearing, offered to the illustrious man, namely the aforesaid duke [Note: Waldemar of Jutland, brother of King Canute VI and son of Waldemar I.], the right of patronage in their monastery, we awarded to the White monks the possessions of the aforesaid church of Saint Michael, assigned to them by the gift of Lord W., bishop [Note: Waldemar I, son of King Canute V.], and strengthened by his seal and by the protection of the privilege of the lord archbishop of Lund. And lest anyone in the future should maliciously oppose this our constitution, we confirmed it by the impression of our seal, with the names of the witnesses present written below.

I, Homerus, called bishop of Ribe [Note: He held office from 1186 to 1203.], and W., abbot of Paraclete, exercising apostolic delegation [Col. 0677A] between the monks of Guldholm [Note: This monastery was founded in 1190. Above, vol. V, p. 379.] and those of Saint Michael [Note: A monastery formerly near Schleswig.], since concerning the three articles proposed to us in the letters of the apostolic lord—namely, whether the duke is patron or not; whether he once consented, or consents, to the transfer, or does not consent; and whether the White monks are willing to preserve for him the right of patronage—it is most truly established for us that the aforesaid White monks promise, of their own good will, to render to the lord duke and his successors for ever every honour belonging to the right of patronage; we pronounce in favour of the White monks that whatever has been bestowed upon them by the lord bishop of Schleswig and confirmed by the lord metropolitan, they shall possess quietly and without disturbance by our authority.

## LETTER XII

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1192. Published by Pontoppidan, *Annales Danici*, vol. I, p. 482, who assigns it to 1194.]

To the lord pope in the case of the monks.

[Col. 0677B]

To the most beloved father and lord C. [Note: Celestine.], by the grace of God supreme pontiff, brother W., servant of Christ’s poor at Paraclete: the reverence due to so great a Father.

It was the paternal pleasure of your Holiness that the case of the Black monks [Note: Monks of the Cluniac order, so called from the colour of their clothing.] of the church of Saint Michael and of the White monks should be remitted to the lord bishop of Ribe and to us for investigation and settlement. We carried out your command the more willingly because we perceive more certainly that your will is directed toward that which accords with divine service. For your Holiness had commanded us to be diligent in investigating the truth of the case, after summoning both parties [Col. 0677C] before us; and, if we found that the noble man Waldemar, duke of the Jutes, was patron of the Black monks, had not consented to the aforesaid transfer of the church of Saint Michael, did not yet consent, and could not have the right of patronage in the monastery of the White monks, then the Black monks were to rejoice in the fullness of their restoration and possess what had been offered without any disturbance. But if the White monks were willing to preserve this in their monastery, then we were to assign to the White monks the entirety of all the property which the church of Saint Michael possessed.

But while we were labouring in this inquiry, the White monks most willingly offered the aforesaid noble duke the right of patronage in their monastery, in our presence [Col. 0677D]. Therefore, relying upon the protection of your authority, we have judged that the aforesaid church, with all its movable and immovable goods, should be bestowed upon the White monks. We therefore entreat that what, by the command of your majesty, has been assigned to them by us may, with the favour of your grace attending them, be confirmed by a privilege of your authority.

## LETTER XIII

[Note: Bartholin: 1192; Langebek, more correctly, 1194.]

To the lord Pope Celestine.

[Col. 0678A]

To the most holy father and lord C., by the grace of God supreme pontiff, PETER [Note: He held office from 1192 to 1214.], by the same grace of God bishop of Roskilde: greeting, and the reverence and obedience due to so great a Father.

The petitions of the Apostolic See, the holier they are, are, with the Lord’s inspiration, the more worthy of fulfilment. We therefore gratefully received those petitions which you recently chose to present to us by your letters on behalf of the church of Saint Thomas at Paraclete and its abbot William, your most devoted son. For we perceive without doubt that whatever is bestowed, from regard for divine love, upon religious and honourable men suffering hunger, redounds to the salvation of those who bestow it. We have therefore decreed to grant to the aforesaid church the annual revenues of priests dying in our bishopric [Col. 0678B], both at your request and out of regard for divine grace: namely, on this condition, that it shall hold the aforesaid revenues from the Easter following their death until the next Easter. In those churches which, as stated, it has held for a year and then happens to restore to us, it shall pay without dispute the right due to us and our successors.

For the accomplishment of this, we request letters from your Fatherhood, so that we may rise more effectively to carry it out and the mouth of malicious and iniquitous speakers may be stopped. May your Holiness live and prosper.

## LETTER XIV

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1175.]

To the parishioners of Lyngby [Note: In Zealand, in the prefecture of Frederiksborg.]

[Col. 0678C]

ABSALON, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Roskilde, to his beloved sons, all parishioners of the churches of Lyngby and Helsingø [Note: In Zealand, in the prefecture of Kronborg.]: greeting and paternal blessing.

We wish you, dearest sons, to know that the founding or building of God’s church concerns the salvation of you and of all Christians. For just as it is unquestionably true what the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims—or rather, what the Holy Spirit speaks through the mouth of Paul—“The temple of God is holy, and whoever violates the temple of God, him will God destroy” (1 Cor. III), so it must likewise be considered that whoever founds or builds God’s temple [Col. 0678D] will receive from the Lord the recompense of eternal reward.

For when divine mysteries are celebrated in the temple of God—when, that is, Christ’s body is made by God’s words uttered through the mouths of priests [Note: In manuscript Magnaeus I this word was deleted and “is offered” (*porrigitur*) written above it, doubtless by a Lutheran.]—things below are joined to things above, the choir of angels stands by, and pardon is granted to sinners returning to the Lord. Since, therefore, we have learned that our sons, the brothers of Paraclete, whom we embrace with the arms of ampler charity and whose advancement occupies our concern, intend to construct and build a church to the Lord and the blessed apostle Thomas, we wish you to become their willing helpers, that you too may share with them in eternal recompense [Col. 0679A].

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish your whole community, more devoutly entreat you, and enjoin upon you for the remission of your sins [Note: In place of these words, “for the remission of your sins,” manuscript Magnaeus I has: “By virtue of our office,” deleting the words cited, though adding no reason for the alteration.], that before you set your ploughs to casting the foundation of the aforesaid church, you bring suitable stones in your carts, for reverence for the aforesaid apostle, for his merits, and for regard for our affection. Thus you will be more pleasing to us, and, as we have said, a greater reward will accrue to the fruits of your righteousness [Col. 0679B]. Farewell.

## LETTER XV

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1175.]

To Count Bernard [Note: He is unknown to me.]

The place of love and favour which we are said to hold with your clemency is both a greater cause of joy to us and a confidence of progressing toward better things. Strengthened, then, by this gift of favour, we carefully cherish the remembrance of you inwardly and are continually moved by the desire to see your face. We hope and truly trust that he who fulfils the vows of those hoping in him will someday fulfil our desire. But if, because the absence of our bodies stands in the way of our wishes, we are not granted the enjoyment of each other’s countenances, your face is not withheld from our inward eye [Col. 0679C]. What is less granted to us in the present will be completed in the future with happier success.

Meanwhile, because we received your letters very gratefully and read them through with devout eagerness, we send in return letters from our lowliness to your excellency. For as often as we send absent friends anything in writing out of goodwill, so often is a manifold benefit of consolation bestowed upon them. Devout correspondence does not allow friendship to grow old; rather, as it promotes longing, the affection of pious devotion grows strong, lest through torpor or sloth of mind a detestable failure of love should arise. Thus our mind blossomed anew at the writing of your greatness, and the love which perhaps could have grown old through silence regained strength and grew green again through your friendly letter [Col. 0679D].

Know, moreover, that we hold these same letters of yours as a great gift and are bound to answer your favour with more solemn services at a suitable place and time. Furthermore, at your command we send two of our brothers, one a canon and one a lay brother, highly trained in regular discipline and endowed with honourable conduct [Col. 0680A]. We trust and ask that you will receive them with a more kindly eye, for the sake of honour and out of regard for our affection, and hear them more carefully. What befits the Order of Saint Victor, what strictness belongs to its way of life, and how great is the abundance of charity among them, you will hear fully—not from us speaking, but from them relating it. And concerning your good pleasure, for which you sent us your letters, you may and ought confidently to entrust them with reporting to us, because they will be faithful in reporting and we, in more devout obedience, devoted to your request. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI

[Note: Doubtless between 1197 and 1202.]

To the bishop of Skara [Note: Read “of Skara,” in Sweden; so in Magnaeus I.]

To the most reverend father and lord I. [Note: Jerp-Ulf, who held office from 1190 to 1201. See Rhyzelius, *Episcoposcopia Svio-Gothica*, p. 168.], by the grace of God bishop of Skara [Col. 0680B], brother W., unworthy minister of Blessed Thomas at Paraclete: fullness of joys in the fullness of days.

Father and lord, we praise in many ways the fact that, though separated from us not in spirit but in body, you grant us the favour of your holy friendship and love, as your letters informed us last year and as their bearer, present among us, explained to our ears by his account. Would that either work or merit answered such condescension, so that the blush of shame might not contort our countenance, nor grief afflict our wretched mind for not having rendered the service due to such great favour and love. For we know that even among good and more honourable manners it is not easy to find [Col. 0680C] that a ragged and humble man may now enjoy favour from one who is eminent in blessings. The remainder of this letter is missing.

## LETTER XVII

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1197.]

To the lord Cardinal Seufred.

Although the perils of a long stretch of land and sea prevent your presence from being with us, may the kindness of your redemption and the sweetness of the favour you have bestowed ensure that no adversities exclude us from the bosom of your Holiness. It is the mark of exceptional virtue that, once persons have been received into the love of your favour, no adversity can arise such that you do not always deign to cherish their affairs in the bosom of charity and advance them as the advantage of petitioners requires [Col. 0680D].

Strengthened by this hope, therefore, and confirmed by the protection of your love, we have judged our affair worthy to be entrusted to you on this occasion also, especially since, as you can ascertain, both utility and reason support it, and it is upheld by the testimony of truth. We therefore ask that a gracious hearing from your highness be granted to its prosecution, so that a judgment of equity may proceed from the countenance of your favour. A certain man … The remainder of this letter is missing.

## LETTER XVIII

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1198.]

(The beginning of this letter is missing.)

[Col. 0681A]

[lacuna] “…may your faith make [you whole]” [Note: From Magnaeus I.]. Among the other evils which we suffer, another son of wickedness has arisen, armed with lies and ready for crime. He asserts that his father, who had been bound for the third time in the bonds of excommunication, in order to be released from that sentence, did not transfer his land to our predecessor, who held our place, in the king’s castle, while we stood by and Lord Ebbo held a part of the cope, according to custom; and thus he strives to obtain that same land [Note: In Magnaeus I the following is also found after these words: “And now, after his father’s death, he has received the fruit of the land. By these and similar injuries we are worn down, while there is none to bring help. If you have any bowels of compassion, we beseech you, impose a due end upon so many evils, lest the wicked continue to exult—for how long?—while there is no helper for the orphans.”].

## LETTER XIX

[Note: Bartholin: 1194; Langebek: 1195.]

To the lord Ebbo.

To the illustrious man and dearest friend E., his W.: so [Col. 0681B] to pass through temporal goods as not to lose eternal ones.

In presenting requests we may perhaps seem importunate too often; and unless compassion conceals its indignation, the judgment of equity will more quickly condemn the rashness of presumption. We therefore ask that judgment be tempered with mercy, upon which, according to our usual custom, we now also rely, so that the severity of indignation may neither oppose our requests nor cloud the countenance of clemency so often experienced. For we know that, when cheerfulness has been driven away and the countenance cast down, indignation discolours the beauty of goodwill and mars the grace of honourable manners.

But far be this from one whose heart the ray of wisdom illumines, whom the favour of heavenly grace attends, whom the prerogative of birth commends, and whom the renown of his name has made lovable [Col. 0681C]. For who does not love Ebbo? Who does not venerate in him both faith and purity of faith? Who does not extol before God and men, in our Ebbo, prudence in all temporal matters and earnest devotion toward religious persons? Who does not approve prayer and reading in Ebbo? May the Lord of hosts grant Ebbo such honour and grace that what he has well begun he may conclude with a better end.

## LETTER XX

(The beginning is missing.)

[lacuna] …of the soul, but a carnal affection seems to be present. Yet far be it, my fathers and lords, that you should think otherwise than the will of God and the divine sentence [Col. 0681D] have prescribed—you who have care of souls. From the tenor of your aforesaid letters, however, we have understood that he is summoned to obtain in his lifetime a certain parish church personally, on the condition that he first assume the religious habit, and, having assumed it, obtain the aforesaid church. This indeed opposes the salvation of souls, because neither the divine law nor the authority of the saints has ordained this. For the promise of heavenly—not earthly—goods alone imposes the religious habit, lest perhaps, if the motive of the person assuming it be otherwise, he hear not me but the Lord speaking and threatening in Scripture: “Woe to the man who enters the land by two ways” (Ecclus. II).

Finally, your letters declare that, if the aforesaid Hugh does not assume the religious habit, he will by no means be able to obtain the aforesaid church without offering a great gift [Col. 0682A]. But, to speak more truly in your ear, this is heretical and ruinous, if blind ambition should bring such a thing to pass; and he will hear with Simon Magus: “May your money perish with you” (Acts VIII). Yet far be this from our friend, whom we embrace with the arms of ampler charity! Far be it, I say, from him thus to mar the grace of his conduct and to cause the good odour which he has spread in the nostrils of those around him by virtuous living to stink, and, burdened with sins, to descend to hell after living but a short time!

He is a simple man, far removed from malice; cunning has made a covenant with peace, so that he may desire to live in peace and not exceed the boundary of justice—unless perhaps sheep-like simplicity is defrauded by wolfish cunning. Yet because he has long intended to return home, not compelled by necessity nor suffering want of bread or clothing, he will undertake the journey to you at the coming feast of Easter, with life and bodily health accompanying him. He would already have brought this to effect, had he put his church and household in order. But to do this he needs much care and time, lest too hasty haste result in the dispersal of his goods [Col. 0682C], and it be said of him: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV).

## LETTER XXI

[Note: Bartholin and Langebek: 1178.]

To the lord archbishop of Lund.

We are compelled by necessity, most loving Father, to write: “We waited for good, and it came not; for peace, and behold trouble” (Jer. XIV).

You know, Father—for we speak to one who knows—that our coming to Denmark was on account of you, whom we loved and whom we thirsted to see as an angel of God. It was not, I say, need—God is witness—that compelled us to leave our own borders, visit the regions of Denmark, and be afflicted by many hardships beyond our strength; rather, it was the intensity of love which we had conceived in our heart upon knowing Lord Absalon, bishop [Col. 0682D]. If, therefore, we acted as friends, such an action should not be attributed to the lack arising from necessity.

And surely, above all men who could come within your acquaintance, you determined to respond as friend and lord to the favour of love. Your cheerful face [Note: We have supplied this word from Magnaeus I and the Lyegaard manuscript.], liberality of hand, and paternal countenance, afterwards not changed in another direction, gave certain proof of this and confirmed our coming to you, so that we might be firmly established in what we had begun and might render diligent service of love according to our powers—indeed, beyond our powers, as God knows—not merely for appearance, but for the aid of salvation [Col. 0683A].

God and the heavenly court are witnesses that we have always embraced your remembrance in the embraces of love—not falsely, but truly and sweetly—whether prosperity or adversity attended us. And now, what is this, my Father and lord? What in us has so displeased your fatherhood that you left a friend among enemies, without help, without counsel, a stranger and pilgrim in foreign parts? What, I ask, was lacking for you to abandon an orphan and fatherless man among the mouths of lions, while there is none to redeem or save? (Ps. VII.) Among … [A large portion of this letter is missing.]

[Note: In Magnaeus I; however, elsewhere the following fragment of this letter occurs: “We cannot bear to see you offended, for such is the disposition of one who loves. May the King of glory, who will crown his own, place upon the crown of your head the love for us conceived by divine grace, the honour shown, and the manifold benefit bestowed upon us, for whose love and honour you have thought fit to expend your possessions upon his poor.” In the Lyegaard manuscript, after “Among” occurs: “Six letters are missing,” which is undoubtedly false.]

## LETTER XXII

[Note: Bartholin: 1195; Langebek: 1194.]

(…sent by the lord archbishop of Lund.)

[Col. 0683B]

To the most beloved lord and father C., by the grace of God supreme pontiff, A., by the same grace archbishop of Lund, legate of the Apostolic See, and primate of Sweden [Note: “Svetia,” or “Svecia,” as in Magnaeus I.]: the reverence and obedience due to so great a Father.

As the perfection of good pursuits accords with honour and justice, so their detestable deformity disfigures the face of the Church. What divine authority has therefore sanctioned and the sincerity of the Christian religion has approved must not be violated; it is a decree to be inviolably observed by kings and princes alike, lest an injury to holiness furnish those below them with an example for imitation. But if, through the demands of sins, such obstinacy should arise that kings or princes become authors or supporters of so great a crime, it is for you, most loving Father, to provide a remedy and to correct it with the strictest correction—you whom the Lord has set in the higher place—so that the apostolic blessing may attend those who make progress, while upon the ill-disposed, and upon those who hate peace (Psalm 119), the stone of stumbling and rock of offence (1 Peter 2) may follow in judgment.  

[Note: In Magnaeus I, *obstinatia* has been deleted and *contumacia* written above it.]

We have therefore considered it necessary to bring to your sacred ears the act of Philip, king of the Franks, by which the Christian religion is injured, so that the bowels of your compassion may grieve with her, who complains that she has grievously borne a wound inflicted upon her integrity by the aforesaid king. Certainly, we do not doubt that reports from many persons have reached the ears of your Holiness: that the aforesaid king of the Franks took as wife and consort in his kingdom the noble sister of the king of the Danes, with the solemnities appropriate to the rite of the Gallican Church; but that certain malicious persons, displeased by their marriage, turned sacrilegious arts and schemes to deception and wrongdoing, swearing that a degree of affinity existed between them; and that, under this pretext of an impediment, with no procedure of law observed, a divorce between those aforesaid and so eminent persons was hastily and rashly pronounced.

How absurd and contrary to truth this is will readily be perceived by anyone who examines this lady’s genealogy, which we have thought fit to set forth for Your Dignity, testifying before God and His saints that we shall say nothing contrary to the truth.  

[Note: From the words “There was in Denmark” to the end, this letter was published by Holberg in *History of Denmark*, vol. I, pp. 260–261.]

There was in Denmark a king of outstanding renown named Sweyn. Though he had several sons, two of them must here necessarily be mentioned. One was called Canute, king and martyr of the Danes, whose holiness is commended even today by miracles. He had as wife the daughter of the count of Flanders, by whom he fathered a son, Charles by name, count of Flanders. Yet this queen, joined in marriage to the aforesaid king, does not descend from him or from his mother, but from the brother of the aforesaid King Canute, who was called Erik the Good. Erik fathered Canute, who became duke of the Danes and king of the Slavs, whom he held powerfully not by hereditary right but by arms. His mother was Queen Botildis, born of a most noble Danish stock. He himself later became a martyr, and frequent miracles testify what merit he possesses before God.

This martyr Canute fathered King Valdemar, whose mother was Ingiburgh, daughter of Rizlav, a most powerful king of the Ruthenians, and of Queen Christina, who was the daughter of Inge, king of the Swedes, and Queen Helena.  

[Note: *Virzlavi* in Magnaeus I; *Zizlavi* in the Lyegaard manuscript; *Izizlavi* in the Vellej manuscript. Perhaps Iziaslav, who died in 1155, son of Mstislav and grandson of Valdemar: Nestor, pp. 180, 183, 184. Perhaps Mstislav himself, who died in 1132, is intended by this Iziaslav.]

Moreover, the sister of the aforesaid Ingiburgh was the mother of Béla, king of Hungary, who had the sister of Philip, king of the Franks, as his wife. Valdemar fathered this lady, our queen of France, by Sophia, whose father was Valdemar, himself also king of the Ruthenians—for there are many kings there.  

[Note: In the Lyegaard manuscript: *Waledar*; likewise perhaps in the Bartholinian and Vellej manuscripts. Possibly Volodar, brother of Vasilko, who was captured by the Poles in 1122: Nestor, p. 177.]

Her mother was the daughter of the duke of Poland named Bolesław.  

[Note: Namely Bolesław III, who died in 1139. Perhaps Volodar, on account of his captivity with Bolesław, married his daughter and thereby obtained his freedom.]

Upon carefully examining these matters, it is clearer than light that this branch has no connection with the kindred of Flanders, and that no blood relationship exists between the former queen of France and this lady. For the former descends neither from Erik’s line, nor does the latter derive her carnal origin from Canute’s descendants. Behold: we have faithfully set forth the whole truth of the matter, with Truth Himself as witness.

We therefore beseech you, Father, bowed at the feet of your Holiness, that from the countenance of your favour there may issue a judgment of equity, by which our lady, queen of the Franks, may be restored to the king’s favour and returned to the honour from which she was removed through the error of wicked men. Thus she will glory in being a devoted daughter of the holy Roman Church, and so long as she lives will retain in her heart the memory of the benefit bestowed upon her. May your Holiness prosper greatly.

## LETTER XXIII

[Note: Barth. year 1193; Lang. year 1192. On this letter see Gramm in Meursius, p. 361, note c.]

To the lord C., king of the Danes, concerning his sister’s affair.

To the most excellent lord CANUTE, by God’s grace the glorious king of the Danes, Brother WILLIAM, unworthy minister of the poor brethren of Saint Thomas at Paraclete, due reverence and devoted service to so great a lord.

It contributes to the splendour of the royal crown that, just as the king’s temporal glory makes the princes of the realm glad and cheerful, so likewise the lowering of his majesty casts them down. Those, therefore, who stand at the king’s side and preside over royal affairs must preserve rights and the order of things: rights, namely, must remain whole and unimpaired, and the goods allotted to human use must increase; but above all the king’s honour must be preserved and increased without injury.

My lord, we say this because, if the honour offered by the king of France finds no place with Your Excellency, we greatly fear that such a resolution will be followed by long-lasting repentance, and that the sweet repute of your fame, already fragrant through nearly the whole world in its renown, will suffer loss. Alas! Who then would not groan? Alas! Who then would not hasten to tears? Honest money does not rule its lord, but serves in obedience to its lord. Silver and gold come and go; but whoever has obtained honour’s glory and has not abused it will remain with it for age upon age.

Now, I pray, let Your Royal Highness attend to what its humble little servant says to his lord. Let my lord the king consider the difference between what perishes and what does not perish, and with a purer eye he will see that money ought not to prevail over honour. If sufficient funds are not presently at hand, let Your Sublimity seek a delay until, through the help of your princes and friends, the hand of your power is strengthened for payment. Though we are constrained by the hardships of poverty, because we desire your honour, we shall gladly devote to your service—if it meets your approval—that with which royal generosity has most recently bound us to itself.

The honour offered to your favour is not small. Yet we say this privately in your ear: if you have the king of France joined to your friendship, thereafter the greed and avarice of the Romans will not be a cause of fear to you. But enough on these matters.

We further beseech, bowing before the bowels of your mercy, that you do not allow the little plot of land which your piety granted us, situated in your castle at Methulese, to be taken from us.

[Note: Vellejus wrote in the margin of his manuscript: “Mersulose.” Undoubtedly Maerlose in Zealand, in the district of Holbæk.]

For your honour requires this, and it suits the poverty of our Church. There is one who troubles us concerning it, namely Bjørn, and threatens to kill ours with the sword. If it please you, let our lord command him to desist from his undertaking. Farewell. May the Lord crush Satan beneath your feet.

## LETTER XXIV

[Note: Barth. and Lang. year 1193.]

To the illustrious Canute, king of the Danes.

To the most excellent lord C., illustrious king of the Danes by God’s grace, Brother WILLIAM, unworthy minister of Blessed Thomas at Paraclete: after receiving the temporal crown from the Lord’s hand, may you receive the eternal crown.

My lord king, we approach the throne of your glory with greater confidence because we find more certainly that the king’s heart is in God’s hand; for grace always attends your fortunate undertakings, and heavenly greatness increasingly enlarges the boundaries of your realm after subjecting your enemies to you. If therefore anything we have presumed to write to Your Highness should be offensive, may divine mercy incline the summit of royal serenity to pardon at the voice of a poor man.

[Note: The remainder of this letter, apart from the words “Sons” to the end, is taken from Magnaeus I.]

For who are we, and who are you? Your servants through Christ. First, therefore, we render thanks to God, author of all good things, through whom we have sometimes received the gift of so great a favour that the ear of royal sublimity has been inclined to our prayers, and a desired outcome has attended our petition, though we are strangers and poor men unworthy of the royal gaze.

Yet, lord, God in heaven and the court bear witness that it was no need of food or clothing that brought us, wandering within your dominion, to your shores, but love of religion: the steadfastness of that faith and the gracious affection whose celebrated name has now become known through almost the entire world—the name of Archbishop Absalon. With him, love for friends never grows old, because the man’s liberality and generosity never know how to exceed the bounds of love, and strength of mind never permits its possessor to degenerate from the uprightness of good men. For he is of tenacious and steadfast faith, whom not even fortune, which often envies human affairs, can prevail upon to turn in another direction.

Therefore, my lord, we cannot leave him who pursues us with kindly favour against his will, lest we seem to wrong love itself, since love for our native soil often compels us to visit our paternal homes. Yet, my Father and lord, we are bound to cling all the more devoutly to you before the Lord in love and devotion, and to offer the tribute of most devoted prayers, because we have so often experienced the help of your magnificence in our need. May He grant you, in the recompense of the just, the glorious vision in its splendour of the eternal King, whom none of the reprobate is believed to see.

We say this to you in the word of the Lord: before the King of glory and Lord of hosts, we never cease day by day to double prayer upon prayer for your safety. Let others say what they wish and smear us with the mark of infamy; their office is to estrange a friend from his neighbour. But if God is for us, who is against us? (Romans 8). They pour out upon us the poison of their malice, but they do not confound us so long as the Lord of hosts is with us.

We would gladly have customary and frequent access to Your Excellency, so that in beholding your face we might have manifold cause for rejoicing, if we did not fear that our own faces would be smeared with the reproaches of those who speak wickedly. But what then? If we do not come, if we do not see you, shall we cease to venerate and love you? Far be it! Even if—may it never happen—we felt ourselves injured by you, we would nevertheless continue to commend before the Lord, with no less fitting praise, the renown of your virtues.

Finally, we beseech you not to give a royal hearing to ill-wishers and detractors because we cannot provide for everyone, having suffered for four continuous years the devastation of fire and been deprived of the abundance of crops, as sons chastened by the Lord. May Your Highness live and prosper here and eternally, and may your hand be upon the head of your enemies.

## LETTER XXV

[Note: Lang. year 1195.]

To Philip, king of the Franks.

To the dearest and most excellent lord PH., by God’s grace king of the Franks, W., called abbot in Denmark, his servant and the least of his friends: may you receive the everlasting crown of the heavenly kingdom.

Although no merits of ours advance us to the throne of your glory, the greatness of our love and our unceasing concern for your soul compel the writings of our littleness to make their way to Your Excellency. We approach your feet because we assuredly love you, your honour, and the advancement of your realm ever more. There is no surer proof in matters of affection than the wish that an increase of virtues should join itself to good character.

We therefore desire that the memorable renown of your name may remain unblemished and be bitten by no one’s dog-tooth. We know that the king’s heart is in His hand, and that He will incline it wherever He wills (Proverbs 21). But far be it that He who is the author of salvation, through whom kings reign and princes decree what is just (Proverbs 8), should incline it toward what opposes salvation. Divine providence has brought you to birth through the prayers of the poor and tears of widows, and has raised you by nature’s gifts to the royal throne, so that in everything you do and ordain after deliberation you may always keep the author of salvation before your eyes, lest you, insufficiently conscious of God’s truth yet presuming upon your own justice, should turn the excellence of so great a majesty to lower things.

Since the king’s honour loves judgment, and judgments advance the honour of the highest King, let no heedless presumption arising from others’ counsel disfigure the grace of excellent character. We ask, indeed we beseech, bowed at the feet of Your Majesty, that, with conscience as witness, you reconsider for the better what was done concerning the queen separated from you; and that, through justice and with God as judge, you alter it and remove the opportunity from those who malign this act.

Having departed from the city, we brought you letters of admonition from the lord pope—not letters of severity, but of love, fatherly concern, and compassion—not as despisers of royal greatness, but as diligent guardians of your honour and of your soul’s salvation. For we do not truly love you if we desire only your bodily presence and not your soul’s salvation.

Moreover, let Royal Highness consider whether it brings you glory that your friend is held captive—a ragged man, a priest of the Lord. If it does bring you glory, we ought not resist, since servants are bound to follow their lord’s will. Yet, lord king, we know of no fault for which we are held in captivity, unless—may it never be—your wisdom should judge it a fault to wish to preserve royal majesty without injury of sin. But suppose it is so. Is an innocent person condemned with the wicked?

Behold, the chancellor of the illustrious king of the Danes and the envoy of the supreme pontiff is held captive, just as we are: a simple and innocent man, turning away from evil, whose life is set before us all as an example to imitate. What evil has he done? Because he, like us, is the bearer of the lord pope’s letters, these men of little goodness do not hesitate to lay hands upon the Lord’s anointed. Yet certainly the letters contain nothing by which the countenance of royal majesty ought to be offended even in the least. Therefore, while I am kept in captivity, command him to be released, if it please you, for we firmly believe that heaven is disturbed because of him. Farewell. May the Lord send you the spirit of wisdom and compassion, that there may be peace for people of good will (Luke 2), and not a rock of scandal and stone of stumbling (1 Peter 2).

## LETTER XXVI

[Note: Barth. and Lang. year 1194.]

To the cardinals in the person of the king of the Danes.

K., by God’s grace king of the Danes and Slavs, to his venerable friends and lords, the bishops, priests, and deacons, cardinals of the holy Roman Church: fullness of days and joys.

[Note: Read perhaps “joy”; in Magnaeus I and the Lyegaard manuscript: “and of joys.”]

The Apostolic See, the more it excels all others in dignity, is believed to abound in a correspondingly greater abundance of compassionate feeling when rendering judgments, while more carefully preserving equity. Far be it that men of mercy should wish to incline judgment to one side, or depart from the path of truth, when to them are directed the cry of the poor and the groaning of the afflicted—those whom the Lord has appointed defenders of orphans and judges of widows.

Blessed are those to whom truth does not become hateful, nor falsehood flatter so greatly that they transgress, or permit others to transgress, the bounds established in the Church by the holiness of the ancient Fathers. We therefore entreat that you kindly receive and hear our present envoys, and, after hearing them, pursue the completion of our entire affair with kindly favour, that from the breast of compassion we may draw the milk of consolation.

The substance of our affair is this: Philip, king of the Franks, took our sister as wife a year ago; after raising her to the royal throne and carnally knowing her, he dismissed her, almost entirely deprived of all consolation, at the prompting of sons of iniquity and friends of falsehood, who fashioned a word of deceit upon the anvil of lying.

[Note: This shows the falsity of the report according to which the king of France is said to have contemplated repudiating the queen immediately after the nuptial blessing.]
