For they swore that a degree of consanguinity existed between them. This is as far from truth as falsehood is from truth, as will plainly appear to you when our envoys furnish proof. We therefore ask that your Holiness and the justice of your holiness not lie inactive in a matter of compassion, so that, through your efforts, what was done contrary to what divine law requires and contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers may without doubt be wholly brought to nothing. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVII

[Note: Barth. and Lang. year 1195.]

To the lord abbot of Esrom.

To the venerable Father and dearest friend WILLIAM, abbot of Esrom, WILLIAM, least of his friends and servant of Christ’s servants at Paraclete: may you happily complete the present life.

The love by which we are bound to one another in stronger bonds impels and urges us greatly to write something to you concerning our condition. For there is no true love without concern, nor concern without fear. Let Your Holiness know that, by God’s favour, the safety of our bodies is secure; and that, insofar as equity and reason presently dictate, judicial authority serves the cause entrusted to us.

Yet the end has not come: labour is joined to labour until the affair receives the fullness of justice and the injured integrity of the sacraments is restored—the integrity disfigured by the perversity of wicked men in the divorce celebrated between the king of the Franks and the queen contrary to law and ecclesiastical sacraments. Thus, thus does wisdom reject the cunning of iniquity, but gives grace to the humble (James 4). Although justice does not yet fully secure what belongs to it, we nevertheless confidently hope in Him that He who began will Himself bring to completion, He through whom monstrous things are reduced to measure.

Divine mercy must therefore be implored concerning this affair, that the judgment of the heavenly Judge may accomplish and graciously fulfil what Christian devotion demands; so that both the merits of Your Holiness and of your brethren may aid us, and we may bring more fully into the lands of the Danes the glory of joy at the conclusion of the affair.

We would have judged it fitting to send you a copy of the lord pope’s letters that are sent to the king of the Franks, unless we had been certain that you could obtain the copy dispatched to our brethren. We trust that you will receive it from them and will more diligently ensure that our labour is not useless. May Your Holiness live and prosper, and pray that we may be restored to you as speedily as possible. But far be it that fear—which has punishment—should bring torment to you on our account, while until now you have not known that a happier outcome has arisen from our labours and that stronger progress has been made in the affair entrusted to us.

## LETTER XXVIII

[Note: Barth. and Lang. year 1178.]

To the archbishop of Lund.

To his most loving Father and lord, his devoted son and useless servant: fear together with love.

No great abundance of verbal elegance is required where truth itself proceeds plainly into the open, especially before Your Excellency, which tirelessly feels compassion for the poverty of the poor and the groans of the afflicted. Far be it that we should think otherwise of you, whom we embrace especially in the arms of charity and whose memory we continually commend before the Lord of glory in prayers, though unworthy.

Most dear Father, the rashness of presumption does not attempt to intrude where the business is one of compassion. How exceedingly great has hitherto been the outpouring over us of paternal blessing, we can neither express in words nor follow out in writing. That day the sun smiled more brightly than usual upon the world, when the Lord, lover of the poor and merciful comforter, instilled into the bowels of your compassion remembrance of us—or rather care, concern, and direction of our life.

Since no merits of ours advance us to so great a condescension, let the distinction of your nobility and liberality alone act and shine forth for us in the rendering of thanks. If we so often stir your paternal affections and rather too frequently and shamelessly seek your help, we are not surprised if you are surprised, unless it be because, under the reckoning of giving and receiving, we bind you more closely by a greater return, you who bear care for the poor. For what is bestowed by His grace upon the poor, as you know best, is rewarded with many proclamations of praise, with honour, and with glory.

Yet, most loving Father, while we frequently seek your aid, as we said, after putting shame aside, we greatly fear that this may be cast at us: “You have the brow of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed” (Jeremiah 3), especially since we already fear and suspect that your paternal countenance toward us has been altered more than usual in another direction. We therefore bear heavily a fault of which we are ignorant; and with tears poured out we turn with our whole heart to God, humbly beseeching Him to restore to you what has been bestowed upon us and not abandon us in an evil time.

But suppose, my Father, that an unfavourable opinion of your little servant disfigures his face in your favour. Will you condemn the just with the wicked? Far be it from you to do this, you who judge with equity. If the shepherd has sinned, strike the shepherd, lest the sheep be scattered. Let the wicked man be removed: let him not stand with firm root, flourish in advancement, or be strengthened by use. Why should he even occupy the ground? Let him therefore be removed and crucified. Or at least, I beg, let the axe be laid to the root of the tree, and let the useless tree be cut down.

But what have the sheep deserved, who have hitherto been preserved from the bites of wolves by your care and labour, and glory in the gift of safety granted under the shade of your protection? Let this iniquity, I pray, fall upon me and upon my father’s house. But if, by our merits, not favour but punishment is owed, then let not paternal diligence fail the aforesaid sheep.

Alas, my Father, who will be the helper of the fatherless and orphans? Who will stand in opposition for the house of Israel? But far be it, my Father, that an exercise of severity should turn judgment in another direction or that anything of this kind should disfigure the elegance or grace of your character. It would greatly detract, God forbid, from your glory and reputation if your concern allowed your sons, our brethren, to perish of hunger. For it would be better to have been slain by the sword than killed by hunger.

Indeed, when we were recently with you, we twice brought to your ears the need of those same poor brethren for bread; yet we have not received a friendly or pleasant answer, because the deficiency of grace, disfigured and withdrawn, had closed the bosom of mercy and hardened it against us. It is enough, therefore, that your wisdom has been informed that bread will scarcely suffice them until Easter. Nor this time do we offer prayers concerning this to your fatherhood, since we have fallen into your displeasure. For a judge is offended more quickly if one entangled in wrongful deeds is sent to appease him. We know that wisdom is pre-eminent in you and foresees what needs to be done even while we are silent.

Moreover, the brethren have learned that you are in a land of animals, and they trust that you will look upon these matters in answer to the prayer of the humble.

[Note: These words undoubtedly refer to the multitude of livestock in Denmark.]

You understand what I say. Finally, know that we receive most grievously among our complaints the fact that, in a foreign nation, the days of our old age have at length fallen into contempt. Enough has been said to the wise. May the Lord preserve your person and strength—namely, your zeal for uprightness and your kindly affection toward religious persons—for ever. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX

To Geoffrey, canon.

To his G., his W.: that which belongs to himself.

Just as one is truly proved to love who never strives to oppose the laws of love, so whoever either refuses or neglects, in writing or speech, to comfort the minds of those who love him is convicted of not loving. For when love penetrates inwardly, it does not permit lovers’ tongues to be idle. He rejoices, then, in feasts both given and received, who is always nourished by mutual conversation; and experience shows that nothing is sweeter in human affairs, nor is anything more pleasant than the reciprocal return of benefits and kind offices.

Therefore, dearest friend, because you have not yet sent a reply after receiving our feast, we wonder that you are unwilling to provide us in return for the benefit some comfort. Your service and cheerful countenance have hitherto made us certain of your affection. If some fault of ours has preceded, you will find us readier to correct and make satisfaction than to excuse ourselves—provided you uncover, in speech or writing, the fault of which we are ignorant. For we have chosen, so as not to incur the mark of presumption, not “to think high things,” but “to associate with the lowly” (Romans 12), in order that whatever vice wrongdoing may bring into discipline may be restrained by the censure of instruction. But if perhaps—God forbid—when stirred this time by our letter, you persist in your obstinacy, you may indeed be called a friend, but you will not be proved to be one. Farewell.

## LETTER XXX

[Note: Barth. and Lang. year 1185.]

To Peter, son of Suno.

[Note: He was later bishop of Roskilde from 1192 to 1215.]

To his inmost friend—indeed, to another self; indeed, not another, but more truly himself—P., WILLIAM: the same health he wishes himself, and fullness of love and favour.

Love has this particular property: it does not wish lethargy or idleness to attend the affairs of friends. We do not suppose, dearest friend, that you can in any way doubt our love for you. Yet in loving you, we obey the laws of love. When, I say, we love our Peter, a young man of good hope, we desire him to be occupied in worthy studies and distinguished by more honourable conduct. For it is not fitting that you should do anything that disfigures the favour bestowed upon you, you whom both the prerogative of birth adorns and a fair natural ability in literary studies, granted by the divine gift.

These are things that ought to bring you glory, provided that arrogance does not creep in—arrogance which in the case of those negligent in good works is usually an occasion of destruction. But far be it that what you once consecrated to the Lord and to virtue in your heart should admit what brings you neither honour nor a cause of salvation. If divine mercy finds a mind conscious of purity, it heaps happier outcomes upon good beginnings.

Moreover, having received and read the letter of your affection last year, we could not but rejoice at the things said to us. But because we were occupied with many affairs and until now could not find at a suitable time or place anyone to carry back our letter, we have been unable to reply to you, dearest friend. We would long ago have gladly committed to effect, with pious concern, your requests addressed to our humility; but your father has altogether forbidden us to make even mention of the matter—now, behold, for the second or third time. Since it is safer to act without counsel than against counsel, we have not thought fit to bring your requests to effect.

But know, and never let it come into doubt for you, that we shall not cease earnestly and constantly to seek your honour and advancement. It is not our merits but the affection of the sincere love by which we love one another that makes us look to the height of the honour and fullness of advancement bestowed upon you. Nor do we wish, nor is it consistent with reason, that it should be judged contempt or negligence that devoted care has not yet supported your requests according to your desires. For a ready and devoted will has not been lacking to our love at the urging of your prayers; but, as we have said, we could not oppose your father’s will and sound counsels.

For he is a man of counsel, powerful in deed and word, whom nature compels you to love and who provides what is more beneficial for you, lest some envious and ill-disposed person gnaw at your desire with a dog’s tooth. But as soon as that same father judges that time or place is suitable and expedient for your advantages and honour, he will find us not unprepared. So far as our knowledge instructs us and health permits, our littleness will not cease to bring a welcome remembrance of you before our lord the archbishop and all who know and love us, and to commend the divine favour bestowed upon you in every uprightness and honourableness of character.

We nevertheless wish it to come to your knowledge that our humility has so gained the favor of your aforesaid father that, in every need concerning royal right, we experience his clemency and steadfastness in the Christian faith. Indeed, the favor of your father’s grace smiles upon us so warmly that he strives with all his desires toward our friendship; and whatever opposition presumptuous rashness had formerly introduced between us, [Col. 0693C] forgetfulness has wholly antiquated, since, as a religious and God-fearing man, he wishes nothing to be present in his actions that might mar the grace of his character. Moreover, we heartily rejoice that by your services you establish among our brethren so full a place of affection, honor, reverence, and favor; for thereby you pour into the nostrils of those around you a great fragrance of sweetness. And to whom would it not seem sweet that literary learning so adorns you that honor does not make you illustrious, but you are able to make honor itself illustrious? Yet we refrain from praises, lest, if we repeat what we have heard, we appear to flatter rather than to speak truth. It is enough to have said a few things to the wise person, who knows and can infer more from a few things. This we beseech, [Col. 0693D] this we admonish—if indeed it be not presumptuous for the wise to be admonished by the foolish, the exalted by the lowly. This, I say, we admonish: that you always stretch yourself toward what lies before you and set a better end upon good beginnings. Also attend carefully to this—which you should not doubt is in accordance with the counsel and agreement of your father—that, when your acquaintances and friends flock to you, you do not burden the Church either in expenses or in the institutions of the order. You too, as no ordinary but a special member of that body to which we also belong, should render thanks to your venerable father for the proven goodwill and favor which, by God’s gift, we have received from him, so that he may know [Col. 0694A] that we are not unmindful of the favor and benefit conferred upon us, but may also, impelled by this encouragement, rise to still greater acts of favor toward you.

Moreover, if you should ask anything worth knowing about our condition, we enjoy good health; the brethren are most diligently devoted to divine service and most perfectly observe the institutions of the order. Their number is about twenty-five; and our material resources have increased so greatly that, where formerly scarcely eight or ten men could be fed, now more than one hundred are fed every day. These things, dearest one, had been entrusted to this little letter to be sent to your affection before your most recent writings arrived and were placed in our hands. They brought us joy concerning your health, but also, in part, sorrow and astonishment.

[Col. 0694B] For we are astonished, deeply grieved within, if you have any complaint against us which justice dictates; for among us a grateful remembrance of you continually flourishes, and our lowliness embraces it, as is fitting, with all our heart. Each day we make that remembrance celebrated in chapter and unceasingly present it before worthy eyes. Far be it from us, having passed you over, to stand before the Lord of glory—we who once undertook, with devoted will, to love you in the Lord. It would indeed be fitting for us to answer in our defense regarding those matters which are calumniously alleged against us in your letters, were we not of the opinion that what has been said above is sufficient. Let what has been said therefore suffice for you, and do not let the left-hand party draw you [Col. 0694C] in different directions, since we love you in truth and wish prosperous success in your advancement—as in our own, indeed certainly more than in our own. You understand what we say.

Therefore, moved by a desire to see you, we sought permission from the lord archbishop to return home.

> [Note: [Col. 0693D] Peter was then studying at Paris.]

But because we learned that he took ill the permission we had sought during the week of Pentecost, sorrowing indeed and groaning, we abandoned our purpose. Thus, dearest one, you have been brought into our remembrance—not as one dead, but as one living. Let complaint therefore cease where all is sound, where your advancement and honor alone are attended to, desired, expected, and will be bestowed by God’s gift. This also your sons—namely, your fellow brethren—strive to obtain from the Lord by their desires, vows, and prayers.

[Col. 0694D] Moreover, although this letter may seem long, as you know better, there is nothing sweeter in human affairs than familiar conversation with a friend; nor does discourse extended at length seem sufficient to a friend. It will be for your prudence to answer us by letter through the bearer of this present letter, as you please. Greet on our behalf Master Andrew, whom we love truly and most affectionately, and Master Jocelin,

> [Note: [Col. 0693D] He is unknown to me.]

whose memory is blessed among us. May you live and prosper.

## LETTER XXXI

> [Note: [Col. 0694D] Barth., year 1179; Lang., year 1178.]

To the lord Archbishop of Lund.

To his most beloved Father and lord, his least son and useless servant: fear together with love.

[Col. 0695A] Just as it is not without danger to wish to make progress against the violent current of a river, so it is the disposition of a fool to wish to oppose the counsels of the wise. Yet this cannot readily be perceived clearly until affliction gives understanding to the hearing. Hence it is that the human mind is sometimes so oppressed by carnal desires that it chooses to seek nothing except whatever it happens to desire, because it is shut out from the light of truth. But divine wisdom, taking the wise in their own craftiness, knows how to mingle bitter things with pleasant, so that a person, as though rising from deep sleep, may now despise that for which he had previously, without judgment, sighed with all his desire. Father, we feel this fulfilled in ourselves, while divine mercy instructs us through chastisements, [Col. 0695B] while it withdraws friends and allows possessions to be destroyed,

> [Note: [Col. 0695D] Here the Lyegaard copy ends; the rest has undoubtedly been torn away by a violent hand.]

and reduces to nothing things granted for human use.

Thus it happened recently when—alas, alas!—it took Master Peter from us,

> [Note: [Col. 0695D] Unknown to me.]

and again burned our granaries, so that nothing of our grain supply remained to us. Yet in all these things we overcome both ourselves and the devil through him who loved us: patience does not accuse the sentence of the Judge who strikes, and the insight of reason confidently affirms that this comes about for the cleansing of offenders and the increase of the crown. For the Lord corrects every son whom he receives; and he himself says through John: “Those whom I love, I rebuke” (Rev. 3).

But what, my Father, was passing [Col. 0695C] in the mind of your son when he saw both the granaries burned and the livelihood of his poor brethren wholly taken from him? O merciful, O good Father! Where were you then, when distresses and pains were wringing your son as a woman in labor? It was he—yes, he—who sighed with unutterable groanings for the abundance of paternal sweetness and the goodwill so often experienced in necessities. And because then no helper was found in his troubles, he certainly bewailed your paternal absence in tears—you who had so often drawn forth the milk of consolation from the breast of compassion. “Woe to one alone, for when he falls he has no one to raise him up” (Eccles. 4). The child of your holiness was already thinking of undertaking flight, certainly sorrowing, certainly inwardly pierced with pain of heart, because he intended to abandon the poor of Christ in tribulation, [Col. 0695D] who had no helper, and because he would have to depart without our leave.

Then Jesus and paternal affection came into my mind, and what had formerly seemed to me a judgment of equity was turned for me into the bitterness of gall, as both the many benefits freely bestowed upon us presented themselves to our sight, and likewise nature, degenerating at the same time from good conduct, and the love of the sons whom, under the guidance of your mercy, [Col. 0696A] we had undertaken to govern. We therefore resolved to remain again and await him who consoles the desolate both in word and deed, who is not accustomed to abandon friends in tribulation.

Meanwhile, when the Lord saw us standing firm, the Dayspring from on high visited us: through Master John,

> [Note: [Col. 0695D] Unknown to me, unless perhaps he is the man who became bishop of Othine about 1187 and was a master of arts.]

through the lord abbot of Esrom, and through Lord Peter,

> [Note: [Col. 0695D] There were many Peters at that time, all kinsmen of Archbishop Absalon.]

he somewhat relieved our want with a mark’s worth of grain

> [Note: [Col. 0696D] Undoubtedly “of grain.”]

and five *horis*.

> [Note: [Col. 0696D] “Five horis,” a kind of coinage.]

Thus, thus divine providence knows how to meet human desires, so that what people propose they are sometimes unable to bring to effect, as we said above. Therefore we leave to your judgment the intention of purchasing Master Peter’s house—both because the resources now necessary for this are not available and because the wishes of our brethren object. Yet we most earnestly request that your providence so arrange the matter [Col. 0696B] that the convenience of hospitality which we have hitherto had in that house may not be wholly taken from us, but that something suitable may be arranged for us. We do not doubt that this will happen if your munificence graciously deigns to assist and provide for your most faithful Master John,

> [Note: [Col. 0696D] Undoubtedly John.]

in acquiring and retaining the aforesaid house. He often labors faithfully and wholly in carrying out your affairs and does not refuse, for your honor, to expose himself as it were to certain dangers. But your providence should not pass over untouched what both you and we ought to do concerning Master Peter’s disposition of the property, since he assigned its price to the poor of Christ. We pray that you receive kindly the bearer of this letter, our prior, and, once received, hear him more graciously in matters supported by the protection of mercy and justice. May your holiness live and prosper.

## LETTER XXXII

> [Note: [Col. 0696D] Barth. and Lang., year 1179.]

To the Abbot of Saint Victor.

To the most beloved Father and lord G.,

> [Note: [Col. 0696D] Guarinus, who held office from 1170 until 19 November 1174, when he died. See Bulaeus, *Historia Universitatis Parisiensis*, vol. II, pp. 384 and 742.]

by God’s grace abbot of Saint Victor at Paris, and to all his brethren: Brother WILLIAM, unworthy minister of Saint Thomas of the Paraclete, greetings and the reverence and obedience due to so great a Father and lord.

Because the presence of a traveler affords us the opportunity, dearest Father, we have thought it fitting, having received signs of your well-being, to refresh the breast of virtues, the breast of love and favor, with sweeter consolations. For, as you know, [Col. 0696D] this law is established in love: adverse report wounds the minds of lovers, while happier success furnishes a more abundant matter for joy. Since we rejoice both in the health of our bodies and in the sound condition of the possessions entrusted to us, we should think that we offended your holiness if we did not commit this news to writing and send it to you. We therefore judge it fitting for love that we write often, [Col. 0697A] because whenever we do so, we refresh your paternal heart by a kind of representation of ourselves. For to good minds the well-being of absent persons impressed in letters, and the worthy sweetness of holy love, taste sweetly.

If you consider anything further concerning our state worth knowing, you will learn it more fully from travelers. A little book recently composed by us and sent to our lord abbot will also speak more fully and truthfully of the circumstances in which we live. We therefore ask you to have it sought from that same Father and lord of ours and shown to you. Furthermore, our dearest son and prior, drawn by the report of your religious life and honorable conduct and inflamed with zeal for the order, has obtained from us permission to remain for a time both in our house and in yours. [Col. 0697B] Therefore, falling at the feet of your fatherhood, we beseech you that, with your customary regard for brotherly charity and through the intervention of our affection, if he should decide to stay with you for a while, your paternal countenance may smile upon him and receive his pilgrimage joyfully by nourishing it, so that when he returns to us he may shine in learning, character, and the adornment of holy conduct. We believe that his way of life and the pattern of conduct which he received from us will be no burden to you, but an honor. Without any long digression of our own speech, his conduct itself will provide you, if we are not mistaken, with the surer proof of this. Whatever honor and favor you bestow upon him will without doubt be repaid by our services.

[Col. 0697C] It would count as a great gift to us, Father, if your exalted station would send to our lowliness the Passion and History of blessed Victor, since every year we commemorate him on two feast days.

## LETTER XXXIII

> [Note: [Col. 0697D] Barth. and Lang., year 1195.]

To the Chancellor of Ostia,

> [Note: [Col. 0697D] Cardinal Octavian. He possessed the right to consecrate the pope-elect. Baronius, *Annales*, vol. XII, year 1160, no. 44.]

I draw confidence for presenting myself to your sight from no other source than the favor of your kindness. I trust that whatever the assertion of truth brings to your ears cannot be unwelcome to you. For a lover of truth should love nothing that opposes truth. I therefore wish it to come to your knowledge that I revere and love in you what I have seen and heard from the account of honorable men concerning [Col. 0697D] the praises of your virtues, by which the name of your excellence has become famous throughout the world in many ways. I pray him who never abandons those who trust in him that he may preserve for you, to the end, the gifts of your virtues.

But one thing adds to the fullness of my sorrow: namely, that I departed from the city without your permission. If your charity deigns to consider the matter, there will be nothing in this deed that ought or can offend respect. [Col. 0698A] For I shall speak the truth. Many believed, and the assertion was gaining force, that snares were being laid for my capture in many places and that I could not escape them unless I committed myself to the danger of the sea. Having communicated this plan only to the lord pope, I rose by night and boarded a ship coming from the emperor’s army and bound for Pisa. Thus, without pause, I reached Pisa on the second day. I therefore ask, my lord, that your kindness not be angered at this: that I departed the city without taking leave of you, as of everyone else; for, truth being witness, the urgency of the aforesaid necessity excluded taking leave.

## LETTER XXXIV

> [Note: [Col. 0697D] Barth. and Lang., year 1178.]

To the lord of Lund.

[Col. 0698B] We seem importunate in presenting petitions; and unless mercy conceals its indignation, the audacity of presumption will be restrained by the judgment of equity. We therefore ask that judgment be tempered by mercy, so that, with the aid of grace, upon which according to custom we rely in devout prayers, the severity of indignation may neither oppose our requests nor cloud the countenance of paternal clemency toward a son. You know, Father—for we speak to one who knows—that an abundance of paternal sweetness not granted to sons seriously wounds filial affection and mars the grace of the ruler’s good character. We therefore beseech that the ears of paternal mercy be inclined to the prayers of suppliants and that pious desires obtain their due effect. But lest we burden you, occupied with many and very great affairs, with the weariness of reading, [Col. 0698C] we restrict this present page within narrower limits and have entrusted our desires to the bearer of this letter, to be explained to you orally.

## LETTER XXXV

> [Note: [Col. 0697D] Lang., year 1175.]

To the Abbot of Esrom.

To the most beloved Father and lord WALBERT, by God’s grace abbot of Esrom: Brother WILLIAM, ever bound in charity as the servant in the Lord of his holiness.

A manifold benefit of favor and goodwill should always be pursued by manifold acts of thanksgiving. Hence we rise willingly to render praises to your fatherhood, because in our petitions with Sirium

> [Note: [Col. 0698D] In Magnaeus I: “Sinum.” The passage is undoubtedly corrupt. Perhaps one should read “Sunium,” and understand Suno, counselor of Waldemar I and Canute VI, who died in 1186 and was the father of Andrew, Archbishop of Lund, the intimate friend of Abbot William.]

we are heard more frequently and more kindly through your clemency. Moreover, my [Col. 0698D] Father, we gladly received Brother Stephen, whom you sent to us. We would already have enjoyed more abundantly the fruit of his arrival among us, had not the watercourse, for which we have often petitioned, afflicted us in many ways and now again deceived us by many frauds. It therefore seems to us that iniquity lies hidden in the water and ought to be discovered by more prudent ingenuity, lest we be wearied longer. But who is fit for this except Brother Stephen? Yet alas, my [Col. 0699A] Father, we cannot retain him—though we wish to keep him with us for a few days—unless your permission and the authority of your command urgently require it. We therefore ask that, on this occasion also, a kinder hearing not be denied us, so that he may remain more securely for three or four days and our lowliness may not offend your reverence. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI

> [Note: [Col. 0699D] Lang., year 1193.]

To the Abbot of Nestveht.

Just as the decline of religious life in the Church of God brings sorrow to devout minds, so happy progress in its restoration gladdens the City of God. Hence, most beloved Father, we diligently embrace your zeal and solicitude for the restoration and conversion of the entire order in the church committed to you, [Col. 0699B] and pursue it with manifold praise before God and all people, as is fitting. Therefore the foul stench of the monastery [lacuna]

> [Note: [Col. 0699D] Here the name of the monastery mentioned has fallen out.]

having been spread in the nostrils of those around it, infected many with evil conduct; and, because of one person’s offense, scandals rushing in to condemnation, as it is said, cast many down from their purpose—a miserable thing to relate. But now, through God’s grace and your diligence, the axe has been laid to the root of the tree (Luke 3).

## LETTER XXXVII

> [Note: [Col. 0699D] Barth. and Lang., year 1200.]

To the lord King of the Danes.

Where the grace of consolation comes, it is fitting that the languor of desolation depart, lest, if the harshness of languor grows strong, the strength of the soul, weakened, succumb. [Col. 0699C] Therefore, lest the wound inflicted upon your spirit for so long should continue to ulcerate it, here is sweet, pleasant, joy-bearing news, at whose glad report you may rejoice. Justice looking down from heaven, long cast down by the cloud of sin, resumes its customary honor, because wisdom conquers malice (Wisdom 7). For the Lord has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid (Luke 1), our daughter F. R.,

> [Note: [Col. 0699D] Queen of the Franks.]

whom

> [Note: [Col. 0699D] “Quae” in Magnaeus I and the Bartholin manuscript.]

now R. S. S.,

> [Note: [Col. 0699D] In the Vellejus manuscript: “whom now to her kingly bridegroom.”]

with Christ’s assent, R. G.

> [Note: [Col. 0699D] “V. C. I.” in Magnaeus I and the Vellejus manuscript; “v. c. o. i.” in the Bartholin manuscript; perhaps: “reconciled again.”]

J. Heaven rejoices and earth exults (Psalm 95), and all their adornment (Genesis 2) is summoned to praise, and all the sons of God shout for joy. For who would not rejoice? To whom would this word not be sweet: “The Lord has made this, and has shown it to us”? Thus boys, thus young men, old men with the younger; thus rich and poor alike: for the cause of rejoicing is common, since [Col. 0699D] among you there is no one for whom sadness has any permitted place.

## LETTER XXXVIII

> [Note: [Col. 0700D] Barth. and Lang., year 1190.]

To an intimate friend.

> [Note: [Col. 0700D] To Peter Suno, according to Bartholin.]

Love does not know how to conceal love’s affection, because it suspects that the cloak of concealment is a failing among those who love. Since therefore we write, we comply with love’s custom, so that through the tenor of our letter you may experience the sweet outpourings of [Col. 0700A] our heart plainly expressed. For what is loving greatness except sweetness flowing from purity of heart? Yet vicious love does not possess this characteristic, for that cannot be called love which heart-corruption enslaves to vice.

Know, therefore, that we have judged you to be so deeply impressed upon the heart of our sincerest affection that from our love there may come to you an increase in virtues, and that, by regard for a more sincere life, you may set yourself before others as an example for imitation. In order that you may more certainly attain this, it suits both you and the honor of your name to abstain and strive with every care to abstain from desires of the flesh, and to cling inviolably to things of the spirit. Thus you will obtain praise and glory from the Lord and spread [Col. 0700B] everywhere throughout the world the fragrance of sweetness in your conduct. We would say more, but we fear wearying you by length, and therefore confine this present page within narrower bounds. Although every hungry person desires to swallow more, what is scanty is consumed more eagerly when more is unavailable.

## LETTER XXXIX

> [Note: [Col. 0700D] Barth., year 1183; Lang., year 1182.]

To the Prior of Cunungelle.

> [Note: [Col. 0700D] Today Kongehelle, near the fortress of Bahus in the province of Viken or Bahus, formerly belonging to Norway, now to the kingdom of Sweden. In Magnaeus I: Kongelle.]

To the beloved in Christ, LAURENTIUS, prior, and HENRY and the other professed followers of the canonical life at Coninguhelle: Brother WILLIAM, unworthy minister of Saint Thomas of the Paraclete, wishes that you may so run toward the prize of the heavenly calling that you may attain it.

You know, dearest ones—for we speak to those who know—[Col. 0700C] that hearts truly bound by the laws of love are not separated by any danger of the sea or any expanse of lands. Nor do we deny, but rather affirm more truly, that as fire burns more strongly when oil is poured upon it, so love, if bodily presence is sometimes withdrawn and thus is not nourished by mutual conversation, is nevertheless warmed by more recent letters. Hence, absent in body but present in spirit, we offer ourselves in our presence to you, lest the affection conceived among you either grow old or the force of love perhaps weaken through the occasion of bodily distance.

We recently wrote to you, desiring to know more certainly your condition: if happier fortune smiles upon you through the favor of the Godhead, we rejoice; but if a sadder necessity harms your affairs, we mourn the misfortune of a common loss. For [Col. 0700D] it accords with reason that what is given in common should be borne in common. Moreover, we wish it to come to your knowledge that we intend soon to send our ship with malt to your region, so that we may receive its due profit. Yet regarding this we wish to have the advice of your brotherhood: namely, whether we ought to fear an encounter with your kings or with any others of yours. Let it therefore be your diligence to indicate to us, by word or writing, the safer course, [Col. 0701A] lest we lose both expense and labor. We wish and ask that all this be carried out through the bearer of this letter.

## LETTER XL

> [Note: [Col. 0701D] Barth. and Land, year 1190.]

To a friend suffering impatiently in illness.

> [Note: [Col. 0701D] To Peter Suno, according to Bartholin.]

When familiar conversation sometimes fails between friends, does it wound the minds of those who love? At times they take from consolation offered a healing remedy. Therefore we have thought fit to send this letter, because we have learned that you suffer from sickness of spirit. You grieve because you are deprived of the gifts of happier fortune, while it cherishes certain others with the same, sweeter services and nurses them at more fruitful breasts. But if [Col. 0701B] you knew that you possessed a strong heart, adverse fortune would not easily incline you in the opposite direction. For a Christian, whose expectation is not temporal but eternal, ought not to be broken by any misfortunes; because temporal prosperity, as you know, and failing to love heavenly things, are more a burden than a help. The more you perceive yourself occupied by concerns of household property, the less you will know yourself to be kindled by heavenly desires. Do you not know that there is little difference between being able to deceive and being able to be deceived? You are wholly deceived if you decide to exchange heavenly things for earthly. But who of sound judgment would maintain this to be true? Therefore, if sadder fortune withholds its hand from you, let it come into your mind that God intends, having removed you from human goods, [Col. 0701C] to crown you in heavenly things.

## LETTER XLI

> [Note: [Col. 0701D] Lang., year 1187.]

To Bishop Thurgot.

> [Note: [Col. 0701D] In the province and diocese of Vendel, now Aalborg. Moreover, this letter was published by Pontoppidan in *Annals of the Danish Church*, vol. I, pp. 475–476, who assigns it to the year 1188. He was already bishop in 1187. The date of his death is unknown.]

Where the rigor of religious life and discipline suffers loss, the Church’s sons must not remain silent, lest concealment of the offense accumulate the guilt of a graver punishment. Hence, my Father, we confidently offer this letter to your sight—you whom we know in person, indeed have truly loved in Christ—both on account of the obligation of Christian faith and the sweet fragrance of your reputation. If perhaps we are accused of presumption in this, zeal for uprightness and brotherly compassion will excuse us, to whom we render the duty of humanity.

Know then, Father, that we rejoiced on hearing the happier news of your promotion, [Col. 0701D] and all the more devoutly because we hoped that through your efforts the Church of God would advance with more abundant fruit. But those especially rejoiced in your glory whom your fatherhood had previously undertaken to govern and advance in more honorable pursuits. But behold, Father: “the finest color has changed” (Lamentations 4); harp and choir have been turned to mourning, and, as we hear, the organ into the voice of weeping (Job 30), because former things have passed away. Baldness has succeeded hair, stench has succeeded sweet fragrance (Isaiah 3), [Col. 0702A] while the rigor of the order perishes and reproach is brought upon its more sacred and ancient institutions. Yet it is lawful to alter the boundaries established by the Fathers and commanded by them to be observed by their children only for the better.

Does it not seem to you, Father, that the iniquity of the elders resists commands, refuses obedience to superiors, and reduces to nothing the Rule of our Father Augustine? Is it not a kind of divination to refuse acquiescence? To let and watch the feet of foolish young men range about at will outside the cloister, to seek to be seen, and to defame the chamber of chastity—is this not weaponry of iniquity? When virtues are suppressed, liberty is granted to vices; and it is deemed blameworthy if a superior dares to grumble, because the shield of defense is raised and the face is suffused with shame at harsher words of correction being addressed.

But, that I may freely submit a few matters to your ear, who is at fault except the lord bishop, whose authority among them can restrain swelling waves and bring enormities back within measure? But if you can act and remain silent, are you not shown to consent? You know the proverb: “He who is silent when he can rebuke, consents.” Those who consent and those who act, according to the Apostle, will be punished with equal punishment. And would that, Father, you merely kept silent and did not give horns to sinners! We beseech you therefore, for Christ’s sake, to show yourself a lover of religion in defense of justice, and, when an honorable superior and man of holy life reports to you the failure of discipline in the Church committed to him, grant him a kindly [Col. 0702C] hearing. For it is shameful to wish to appear to foster justice and to permit the perverse to overthrow discipline by their corrupt conduct. May almighty God grant that henceforth those among you who are perverse may have no refuge, but may feel zeal for uprightness burn within you once error has been removed; for this suits both your reputation and salvation.

## LETTER XLII

> [Note: [Col. 0702D] Lang., year 1187.]

To the Provost of Saint Theodegarius.

> [Note: [Col. 0702D] At Vester Vig in Jutland, in the diocese of Vendel, now Aalborg.]

Moved by brotherly love, we write a few words to your affection because we have heard of the sufferings, afflictions, and injuries which you endure for the Lord. Know that we cannot fail to grieve when we perceive that you grieve, because from the time when we came to know you we have never ceased to love you. We would indeed more willingly enter into conversation with you face to face, because you would more fully recognize the nature and extent of our affection toward you—an affection which, God willing, can never suffer diminution on account of tribulation. Therefore, if distresses of tribulation rise against you, since Christ is the issue at stake, let the Christian spirit not abandon the virtue of patience, but with the Lord and for the Lord expose its very body to the goads of tribulations.

[Col. 0703A] For you know him who said to his members: “In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage, I have overcome the world” (John 16). Therefore, if we are members of Christ, let the labor undertaken for the Lord not frighten us, because Christ, as you know better, rewards his athletes with a worthy and incomparable recompense. Moreover, if, wearied by tribulation, you determine in any way to yield to ill-wishers by changing your place, let your heart not be weakened from its strength. Whatever we are, whatever we can do, which does not conflict with your honor and the integrity of your reputation, we gladly offer for your honor and benefit: our house and the whole of its external administration, to be managed with your assistance. But if perhaps you say that you reject this, we advise you to seek fellowship with the religious brethren of Esrom. [Col. 0703B] Whichever of these you judge should be chosen, know with certainty that it is advised for your salvation, because each place is suited to the salvation of souls.

## LETTER XLIII

> [Note: [Col. 0703D] Barth. and Lang., year 1192.]

To the lord Pope.

May your holiness know, holy Father, that I, your servant, was summoned into Denmark by Lord Absalon, then bishop of Roskilde and now Archbishop of Lund, in order to perform there the office of abbot in a certain very poor church. At that time I found there for the support of the brethren only seven cheeses and half a bacon-side.

> [Note: [Col. 0703D] That is, pork.]

But Lord Absalon, who is now, as I have said, Archbishop of Lund, being devout, a lover of religious life, and a supporter [Col. 0703C] of the love of God—and out of regard for his affection toward me—added generously from his own resources and increased that same church in many ways for the brethren’s food, though not enough to provide them with clothing. Thus those who serve the Lord there suffer the greatest want.

In that province, the episcopal office is held by Peter,

> [Note: [Col. 0703D] Mentioned above as bishop of Roskilde.]

a canon of our order, who succeeded Lord Absalon: a man endowed with honorable character and thoroughly educated in literary studies. I therefore beseech the bowels of your mercy that you may deign to write to him, requesting that, since he is a canon of our order, some benefice may be assigned to our poor brethren, for the honor of God and out of regard for your affection, by which they might be relieved in some measure.

## LETTER XLIV

> [Note: [Col. 0703D] Barth. and Lang., year 1193.]

In the person of the King of the Danes.

[Col. 0703D]

The Apostolic See must be sought by us as often as scandals arise in our kingdom through the demands of sin—scandals which receive no fitting end through the counsel or judgment either of ourselves or of our princes. Therefore we brought to the ears of your fatherhood the deed of Waldemar, formerly bishop of Schleswig: a dreadful deed, by which the majesty of royal eminence is injured. But perhaps a cloud of sin stood in the way, so that our prayer did not pass through; for we have not yet received an answer providing for the execution of justice, although this matter is well known among us and there are almost as many witnesses as there are people. [Note: [Col. 0703D] Bishop Waldemar wished to make himself king, and insisted that at least a third part of the kingdom was due to him; and, in order to obtain this, he drew foreign princes to his side. [Col. 0704D]]

It would be fitting for us to repeat this again to your reverence, if we did not fear to offend your hearing by the importunity of frequent reports. We do not doubt, however, that letters from the lord of Lund, legate of the Apostolic See, and from his suffragans have reached your hearing and, with the testimony of truth to support them, have fully presented or explained the entire matter. We therefore wonder, reverend Father, that the bowels of paternal tenderness have been so hardened toward your son—who has hitherto displeased you in nothing, but in all things and throughout has been a willing executor of obedience to your Apostolic See—that, to speak in your ear with due respect for your reverence, in this affair justice, as we have said, gives us no answer whatever.

The fact that we keep the aforesaid former bishop in custody is a measure for the peace, tranquillity, and stability of our kingdom; it is not because he himself is an object of fear to us in his own person, but because we cannot oppose the deceitful schemes of his accomplices and supporters without danger to ourselves. Again and again, therefore, we entreat that a fatherly affection may soften at a son’s prayers, and that the bitterness conceived because justice has not been rendered to us may at last receive the sweetness of your blessing, through the remedy of that same justice. We ask, therefore, that your clemency be inclined to our petition; and, with prayers offered, we beseech the happy memory of our father—who, for as long as he lived, stood in your favor—to aid us. [Note: [Col. 0704D] Waldemar I, father of Canute VI, in the dispute between Alexander III and Victor, and the subsequent antipopes, always stood on Alexander’s side against Emperor Frederick I.] Thus, as we have been devoted in carrying out apostolic commands, may we henceforth be found still readier and more devoted in the same.

## LETTER XLV

[Note: [Col. 0704D] Barth. and Lang., year 1195.]

To the lord of Lund, in the person of the chancellor.

To the most beloved Father ABSALON, by God’s grace archbishop of Lund, ANDREAS, chancellor of the king of the Danes, and those who are with him: greeting and the service of devoted piety.

Because parents and friends who are travelling and making for distant places are commonly uncertain how succeeding events will turn out, we have thought it right to inform your fatherhood of our situation. Once it is known, should there be any grief that wounds the heart of your fatherhood, the newness of this report may remove it, so that joy received from it may, by the ray of its brightness, calm all troubled things.

Although we have been stretched out under many afflictions and burdens, both the king’s honor and advantage, and the great difficulty of the business entrusted to us, have compelled us to oppose to them the shield of patience. For progress in love or labor is lessened if, through the idleness or negligence of agents, a useful and honorable undertaking has a less successful outcome. Therefore, lest disgrace come upon us and failure upon our labor, we are kept longer away from your presence, for which we sigh with all our heart’s desires. For we have undertaken not the work of one day but of many, until divine grace brings its completion to a joyful conclusion.

You should know that, when we departed from the city, fickle fortune did not run prosperously for us. It very treacherously mixed bitter things with sweeter ones: while we were held captive for six weeks at Dijon and Châtillon, the duke of Burgundy took from us sixteen pairs of letters of the lord pope. At last, through the efforts and labors of the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux, after royal favor had been obtained for us, we arrived at Paris, the Lord guiding us. There we await the arrival of the aforesaid king, because—as has now been more privately made known to us through a messenger sent to us—he wishes to have a familiar conference with us.

How great the affection of the aforesaid abbots toward us has been is demonstrated by the manifold result of deeds worthy of approval. Nor should the loss of the letters give us cause for sadness, since nothing is lacking to us for carrying out the business: we possess other letters differing in parchment, but not in tenor. The lord pope also—whose memory be blessed—providing for the welfare of the whole kingdom and maintaining a devoted feeling of compassionate concern for the queen’s honor, sent after us his notary, namely the prior of Saint Praxedes, a man excellently learned in letters, furnished with apostolic letters to the king and to all the prelates of France. Even if we had no other letters, these would suffice for completing the whole business.

Accordingly, on the Sunday on which is sung, “These are the days,” the archbishop of Sens [Note: [Col. 0705D] Michael de Contul, from 1194 to 1199. *Gallia Christiana* of the Sammarthani, ed. 1656, vol. I, p. 635.] and the bishop of Arras [Note: [Col. 0705D] Today Arras, in the province of Artois. At that time Peter I presided, from 1184 to 1194. Ibid., vol. II, pp. 215–216.], the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux, together with Master Peter, Parisian precentor [Note: [Col. 0705D] That is, the first of the singers.], as judges delegated by the supreme pontiff, must diligently investigate the procedure of the separation made between the king and queen and induce the king, by whatever means they can, to take back the same queen. And if, God forbid, they can make no progress, then on the Tuesday of the week in which is read, “I am the good shepherd” [Note: [Col. 0705D] The second Sunday after Easter.], the lord Melior, legate of the Roman Church, by command of the lord pope, has most strictly ordered the archbishop of Reims with all his suffragans, and the archbishops of Sens, Tours, and Bourges with their suffragans, to be present, so that the legate himself and the pope’s notary, with the aforesaid archbishops and bishops and the other faithful of the Church, may deliberate upon the aforesaid affair and with all their strength induce the king’s mind to receive back the aforesaid queen.

The delay that detains us is sufficiently burdensome, because the cost is considerable; but God is witness that in this matter we are providing both for the king’s honor and for the avoidance of the vice of greed and infamy, lest those who know us should hold us in contempt.

## LETTER XLVI

[Note: [Col. 0706D] Barth. and Lang., year 1192.]

To the lord pope.

When scandals arise among the children of the Church through the demands of sin, then, as the wind of malice blows, chaff is lifted up and grains are crushed beneath the chaff. Accordingly the Apostle cries out and says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11).

We too burn, holy Father—we burn from the affliction of evils and sorrow—when we see those who seemed to bear the world succumbing, and Cain once more rising up against Abel in the field. Blacks rise against Greys [Note: [Col. 0706D] That is, Cistercians.], monks against monks, with clubs, as they say, and swords prepared for war; so that days of tribulation are now believed to be at hand, days of which the Lord spoke: “Days will come in which they will say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us’” (Luke 23).

These matters ought to be explained to you more fully, if they had not been more certainly set forth to you in the letters of other persons. Yet, lest this crime seem unpunished, may our Lord stretch out the arm of his power and break the necks of those who neither keep the order nor are held by the order, so that there may be peace for people of good will (Luke 2), but for the ill-disposed and those who hate peace (Ps. 119), a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence (1 Pet. 2).

## LETTER XLVII

[Note: [Col. 0706D] Barth. and Lang., year 1197.]

To the lord pope.

There were two men who eagerly desired to come in order to obtain my benefices. Because they saw that I wished to embrace the religious habit, they surrounded me with fraud and deceit, saying that they wished to embrace the same course. Therefore an oath was sworn by us upon the Gospel. A monastery was provided—namely Pontigny [Note: [Col. 0706D] Today Pons-sur-Yonne, in the district of Perthes, France.]—and a day appointed, on which I stood before the abbot, together with one of them. . . . [Note: [Col. 0706D] In Velleianus this lacuna is supplied thus: “The third and the other.”] Yet he refused to surrender himself.

After a year had passed, we ought to have returned to the monastery, but we did not do so, because I had experienced their wickedness. Meanwhile the Order of Saint Victor came to our church; receiving it, I bound myself to its institutions, and have now completed almost fifty years in it. I therefore ask, my lord, of your holiness: please indicate by your letters to your servant in which order I may remain more securely. I ask also, my lord Father, that by your letters, whenever I wish, my liberty to return to my church at Paris may be confirmed, especially since, before I left, I retained both my order and my seat in choir and everywhere in the common chapter. I ask that these letters be made so consolatory to me that all who see and read them may perceive how sincerely you have loved me, and that I may glory in them amid the straits of my tribulations.

## LETTER XLVIII a

[Note: [Col. 0707D] Barth. and Lang., year 1192.]

To the lord pope.

We would have thought it fitting to report to your reverence, holy Father, the dispute carried on between the Black monks and the monks of the Cistercian Order, had we not known it to have been more carefully written out for your ears in the letters of many who write to you. Therefore, lest we cause weariness of hearing to ears occupied with the affairs of the whole world, we have thought it enough, in presenting prayers, to ask that the offence committed by the Black monks against the Grey monks—an offence known to have been referred to your hearing both before and after the appeal—may be punished more severely.

For, as we have learned from the report of other religious persons, after the Cistercians had placed both themselves and their possessions under your protection and believed that they rested upon the benefit of security, the Blacks came upon them and cruelly afflicted them with injuries, insults, and wounds, and plundered their goods. Our country mourns lamentably for the madness of these men. They deform the grace of good conduct; by their shameful manner of life, discrediting their ministry, they infect the nostrils of the surrounding monks with a cloud of stench, making honey bitter and darkness light.

Behold, they come into your presence as men who have wrought judgment and justice, armed with the darts of impiety, in order to attack the citadel of piety. But they shall not take it, for wisdom will always conquer malice (Eccles. 7). “By their fruits you will know them” (Matt. 7). But far be it, my Father, that those whose mouth is full of cursing (Ps. 10) and whose tongue is a sharp sword (Ps. 56) should catch you in speech. Far be it, I say, that those should catch you in speech who judge the world, who have always loved justice and hated iniquity, whose praise is in the Church of the saints (Ps. 149) and whose memory is in everlasting blessing (Ecclus. 45). Let the sons of confusion therefore be confounded, and let them find no place of refuge with you—those who have trained their hands for battle (Ps. 17) and glory that their tongues speak falsehood (Jer. 9).

## LETTER XLVIII b

[Note: [Col. 0707D] This letter does not occur in the index, and is perhaps the beginning of Letter 47.]

To the lord Peter. [Note: [Col. 0707D] Correct: “the pope.”]

I am that William who was first a secular canon of Blessed Geneviève and then a regular canon; I was sent to Denmark, where, having become an abbot, I was sent twice to you at Venice by the lord archbishop of Lund, and on another occasion to Tusculum. I am the nephew of Abbot H. of Saint-Germain [Note: [Col. 0707D] Hugh.], whom you greatly loved; I received you and Lord Bernard, bishop of Porto, in a certain house of Blessed Geneviève near the city of Senlis [Note: [Col. 0707D] Now Senlis.], when you were going to meet the lord of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0707D] Perhaps “of Magdeburg,” though all these matters are obscure.] as far as Compiègne [Note: [Col. 0708D] Now Compiègne.]. Therefore, because you have always loved me for the sake of my lord, the aforesaid abbot of Saint-Germain, I seek your counsel concerning a certain deed of mine. I was a boy of fifteen or sixteen years.

## LETTER XLIX

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Barth. and Lang., year 1192.]

To the lord Peter. [Note: [Col. 0708D] Bishop of Roskilde.]

To his intimate friend PETER, his own WILLIAM: what he is, what he can do.

As often as a disease, more severe than usual, grows stronger in a sick person, so often is a physician’s help urgently sought for relief. In like manner, since a critical necessity presses upon us, we ask that our importunate recourse to you may not occasion indignation or surprise in you. Especially because, in this evil time, we have no one to answer for us, “while the wicked is proud and the poor is set on fire” (Ps. 10).

In the bearer of this letter we suffer injury to our peace. Because he is united to us by the bond of brotherhood, he is frequently summoned before a judge’s tribunal concerning a matter that should turn to his good, having once before been rescued from the hands of the wicked through the help of your favor. To avoid burdening you with reading, we refrain from explaining his cause to you, but leave it for him to present more carefully to your ears and for you to hear more kindly. We therefore entreat that the compassionate concern of your mercy may not be far from us in his cause, so that through it the result we desire may come to us. May it not happen—God forbid—that we who confidently rely upon your favor should perish more miserably before our enemies. Farewell.

## LETTER L

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Barth, year 1180; Lang, doubtfully, year 1192.]

To the abbot of Prémontré.

To the most loving Father and Lord HUGH [Note: [Col. 0708D] Hugh died in August 1192, according to Langebek’s manuscript diplomatic collection.], by God’s grace abbot of Prémontré, Brother WILLIAM, unworthy minister of Blessed Thomas of the Paraclete: the deepest affection of love.

The love by which we are proved once to have loved one another constantly urges us to write—a love that cannot be renewed by later services, because, unless we are mistaken, it grows old at no time. For it is not right that devotion should grow slack when equal kindness is rewarded by a return of favor. We have undertaken, however, to speak to your clemency on behalf of our venerable brother and fellow abbot John, of the house of Holy Trinity at Lund [Note: [Col. 0708D] In Scania.]. We cherish him in the bosom of a more kindly familiarity, and therefore neither wish nor ought to fail him in his prayers or necessities, especially since his reputation has not departed from the path of justice.

For he is a simple and upright man, departing from evil. Nor do we commend him to your fatherhood as though unknown, since he glories in the fullness of your testimony. If perhaps someone has brought to your ears anything with a blasphemous mouth that ought to injure his reputation, let it come to your mind what blessed Jerome says: “Liars bring it about that truth-speakers are not believed.” [Note: [Col. 0709D] I cannot find this passage.] If he has been deficient in works and in the display of virtues, you should not ascribe this to his negligence or fault, but to the vice and ill will of those who ought to have borne his burdens, both for love of you and for the honor of religion.

But what does the Apostle say? “Faith is not for all” (2 Thess. 3). Yet God is faithful, who does not allow his own to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear (1 Cor. 10). We have indeed heard these things from religious men who grieve over the affliction of Joseph. There is therefore one thing, dearest Father, which we ask and beseech: provide for the honor of your order by removing from the midst the wicked men through whom the house is defamed, through whom, as we have heard, the house’s substance is wasted and the order is put to shame.

We know, dearest Father—provided you do not wish to charge what we say with the mark of presumption—that certain persons who seem to be pillars of your order or Church do not cease to persecute and gnaw with canine tooth the person of the aforesaid man, so eminent and so great, indeed his whole house together with him, as we ourselves have sometimes learned from them. Even if there were any weakness in them, they certainly ought not to have brought it publicly forward, especially since the injury of one member concerns the whole body. But if—God forbid—the examination of your discernment does not restrain the fierce spirit of the contradictors and rebels in that house, know that the lord archbishop, whose care for religious houses is frequent and watchful, will lay on the avenging hands of justice and, through judicial process, correct with fatherly solicitude the enormities of the aforesaid house. Woe, therefore, to those through whom scandal comes (Matt. 18). And who are they? You will learn more fully from the traveller, without any lengthy exposition from us.

## LETTER LI

[Note: [Col. 0709D] To Cardinal Cencius. Barth. and Lang assign it to 1197.]

Although a pitiable necessity presses us at present, your kindness, so often tested, nevertheless raises us in hope. For we trust, both in your favor and in our service, that whenever you are present, nothing will hinder our affairs. We have therefore thought it right to commit to you those matters which, we trust, will be put into execution through your efforts and labor. We ask that, with grace accompanying, we may obtain what we hope from you. We ask that the bearer of this letter be kindly heard by you and cherished in the bosom of your mercy, so that we may be more devoted to you and more ready in your service.

## LETTER LII

[Note: [Col. 0709D] Barth. and Lang., year 1197.]

To Lord Suffredus, cardinal. [Note: [Col. 0710D] Read: Seufredus.]

We trust that to flee to your help is a saving remedy for us and our affairs. Therefore, because we trust in you, we flee confidently to you and entrust our business to your advancement. It does not depart from the path of equity, since reason does not at all oppose what is sought. But because we did not judge it fitting to commit the matter to this letter, we have entrusted it to the bearer, who will more safely set forth by word of mouth what the letter does not express. We therefore ask that he may have familiar access to the heart of your mercy and a kind hearing, with the execution of the business. And lest labor be imposed upon you without recompense, know that we have instructed him that, when the business is completed, he is to provide you from our charity with five marks of silver.

## LETTER LIII

[Note: [Col. 0710D] Barth. and Lang., year 1197.]

To Lord Cencius, cardinal.

We do not commend the bearer of this letter to your affection, because he does not need our commendation to attend him: he glories in the testimony of his own conscience and in the fullness of your favor. Yet, lest we seem to have withheld from him either counsel or help in his need, we commend his business more earnestly to your charity, so that he may be bound to you by a closer union of affection and may be found readier and more devoted in your service.

How great a weight it has before God to extend a helping hand to the poor is not within our power to unfold. For one who has experienced a thing has a greater and more certain knowledge of it than one whom ignorance does not advance toward those things whose knowledge makes a person blessed. As your experience knows more surely, true love grows old at no time; yet it is cherished by more recent letters, so that its power may be more truly proved in a friend’s affairs. We do not suppose that it can be in any way doubtful to you that we love your honor and advancement.

We therefore commend to you all the more earnestly Master John, who serves our instructions and the carrying out of our affairs in going to Rome, because we have proved him unfailingly more devoted to us. The desired progress of our affairs will be evidence of the affection on both sides; for these we humbly entreat that sloth or idleness may not intervene.

## LETTER LIV

[Note: [Col. 0710D] Lang, year 1187.]

To a certain provost.

As often as benefits received are brought back to mind, so often praises are uttered in proclamation of the benefactors. Otherwise, if a benefaction is met with ingratitude, the hand of the giver is rightly withheld from giving. But this is deserved not by goodwill, but by idleness. Far be it, however, that ingratitude should follow the things which your favor has bestowed upon us, for which thanksgiving serves us so long as we live. Yet sometimes, in view of later things—when, that is, they are supported by a greater favor—earlier benefits are nevertheless surpassed. We therefore remind and beseech you with humble prayers that in this matter we may experience how great your affection for us still is.

## LETTER LV

[Note: [Col. 0711D] Barth, year 1183; Lang, year 1182.]

To the venerable Father and Lord B., bishop of Zven [Note: [Col. 0711D] Read “Zverinensis,” as in Magnaeus I. His name was Benno.], by God’s grace, Brother WILLIAM: that little thing which he is.

Desires supported by the patronage of reason obtain their due result among lovers of truth. Therefore, most holy Father, we have received with open hands the tenor of your holiness’s letter; and, following its directions, we consider ourselves bound, life accompanying us, to seek the place assigned to us at the fixed time. Whether the labor undertaken by so insignificant a little man, or his slight presence, may benefit you, you yourselves will see; for nothing else occurs to us to think than that you are bringing a shadow from the cloister into public view. Yet what then? Certainly the affection of our smallness will not be withdrawn, even though no result, or only a slight one, follows; for the debt of charity presses us.

## LETTER LVI

[Note: [Col. 0712D] Lang, year 1187.]

To Gozsvinus, monk.

To his intimate friend G., his own WILLIAM: greeting and the deepest affection of love.

Because, dearest friend, with God’s favor, charity has bound us together by an indissoluble bond, just as it often inserts itself into our affairs, so it sometimes binds us by a certain law of goodwill to offer the service of greeting to those whom we embrace in the arms of ampler favor—especially when the present presence of travellers presents itself before our eyes. Therefore we greet you also and join you to our friendship under the title of special love.

For, just as we judge it fitting to pursue honorable conduct and to keep slippery and shameless persons away from our boundaries, so likewise we judge it favorable to justice to receive into our hearts as friends men of honor and sobriety. It is indeed no small remedy in our exile, amid so many delusions of phantoms and vain shadows of pretence, to have someone whom you may love, whom you may trust, through whom you may rise from faint-heartedness of spirit and storm, and by whom you may repel the injuries of tribulations rushing upon you. Thus the soundness of a broken heart is restored, since oil cast upon flames heightens the fire into larger and more burning flames.

One remedy, then, must be established and maintained in love: that, through the exchange of letters from both sides, discourse concerning divine things may strengthen wounded hearts, so that the love of the absent may never grow old and zeal for a holy purpose may always rise to greater things. For there is no doubt that at every hour, if you do not advance, you decline.

But what are we doing? Are we teaching Minerva? We seem, indeed, to offer an insult to those who feast and banquet splendidly every day if we wish to set upon their tables barley bread, the food of beasts of burden. Clearly it is absurd if a servant judges himself to be set above his lord, when it belongs to the lord’s power to decide what he wishes to do with his servant. So indeed we take on the office of presumption if we give you admonition, who seem to dwell wholly in heaven, while we, by reason of the occasion of pastoral office, appear to be occupied only with transient matters. Yet you will pardon our presumption, since we do not at all deny the fault as well. We would say more, but our own folly reproves us, because this is conversation with a wise man. Besides, we ask that the little sheets or booklet of our trifles be sent back to us.

## LETTER LVII

[Note: [Col. 0712D] Barth, year 1185; Lang, more correctly, year 1179.]

To the abbot of Saint Geneviève.

To the most loving Father and Lord STEPHEN [Note: [Col. 0712D] Stephen, later bishop of Tournai.], by God’s grace abbot of Saint Geneviève at Paris, Brother WILLIAM, unworthy servant of his holiness: fear and love and his whole self, even to his feet.

We are urged, even though late, to write by the gracious command of love. We judge it an injury either to begrudge the claims of love or to refuse to comply with them, since it is holy among the saints; and, shame cast aside, we write to him who has long occupied our whole heart. For we were ashamed—truly ashamed—not to offer first the service of greeting to so great a Father, of such reverence and majesty, and, as though truth had fallen asleep, not to fulfill our promise, as if the shadow of falsehood might obscure truth.

But what does blessed Jerome say? “Liars,” he says, “bring it about that truth-speakers are not believed.” If the delay in fulfilling our promise has seemed tedious to you—which we sufficiently suppose and fear—no evasive breach of faith has intervened. Rather, at one time the weakness of horses hindered our payment of the debt; at another, difficulty of travel because of wars; sometimes a great shortage of fodder, which grievously afflicted Denmark this year; and at other times the absence of a trustworthy traveller.

Now, however, since a happier and more favorable outcome has smiled upon our affairs—since the road is safer, a more abundant yield of provisions is expected, and the presence of a more reliable traveller has offered itself to us—no further occasion for delaying what was promised could remain. We therefore send not just any horse, but the one among our horses which we considered worthy to be sent to your dignity. If it should please you, our glory will greatly increase thereby, and, once the harm of the delay has been repaired, it will win us favor with your clemency. But if, God forbid, it should bring you any cause of displeasure that clouds the serenity of your fatherly countenance, it will give us also matter for grief.

Know, moreover, that we have instructed the faithful bearer of this letter to spare the horse as much as possible when riding and to provide it most abundantly with necessities. Whether he has done so or not, let your letter inform us. Furthermore, my Father, we request that you make known to us by letter the state of yourself and your brothers: if happy things smile upon you, let us rejoice; if, God forbid, sad things occur, let us mourn together.

We earnestly commend to you our beloved Peter [Note: [Col. 0713D] Peter, later bishop of Roskilde, mentioned above.], the very heart of us, so that through you he may increase day by day more and more in conduct, discipline, and literary learning. Though he establishes for himself with your fatherhood a place of favor through good conduct and an even better reputation, we nevertheless commend him to you. May your holiness live and fare well.

## LETTER LVIII

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Barth. and Lang., year 1196.]

For recalling Daniel.

Brother WILLIAM, by God’s grace unworthy minister of Blessed Thomas of the Paraclete, to his beloved son DANIEL: greeting and fatherly love.

As the Apostle says: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Therefore, dearest son, in our absence your spirit has been troubled by the injuries of tribulations, and you have been compelled to leave spiritual studies. But because you had of your own will entrusted to us the care of your soul, moved by mercy we have thought it fitting mercifully to call you back and, by word and example, summon you to your former duties.

The battle is still at hand: Amalek has been attacked, but not yet conquered. Israel indeed fights, but victory has not yet come to Israel—perhaps because Moses has ceased from prayer. Come, therefore, and do not delay your coming while battle is still being fought against the adversaries, for no one will be crowned unless he has contended lawfully. If you have done anything that caused offense to brotherly charity, know that it has been moved to forgiveness by the same mercy. But if you scorn to return when your father calls you back with his customary kindness, consider earnestly with yourself what answer you will give concerning this before the tribunal of Christ, since with him neither contempt nor malice excuses anyone.

## LETTER LIX

[Note: [Col. 0714D] Barth. and Lang., year 1194.]

To the chancellor. [Note: [Col. 0714D] Andreas Sunonis.]

A friend more surely learns a friend’s goodwill by deeds than by words. Therefore, if a friend is to gain experience of love, we judge that a friend must take care, in a necessary matter, that favoring grace cannot refrain from producing an advantageous result, especially when reason does not oppose the request. We do not believe that it has escaped your memory that we have thought it necessary to remind your excellency often concerning our affairs, sparing no labor. Yet we have not received the consolation of the fulfillment of the promised benefit, perhaps because the cloud of our sins has prevailed, so that prayer did not pass through.

If this judgment of equity is proper among friends, we have judged that nothing should be advanced as a complaint. But if it conflicts with law and honorable conduct, we leave even this to be corrected by the laws of love, lest injured charity, God forbid, incur reproach, while there are no lack of those who call good evil and evil good (Isa. 5). Far be it, however, that either deceitful talkativeness or the detestable perversity of feigned affection should disfigure the grace of your character. For both are an abomination before God and people.

This, then, is our counsel to our friend, provided it does not incur the appearance of presumption: that devoted favor may meet the obligations of friends, and that it may not depart from the paths of truth through the evasions of wicked persons. But alas, where are we going? Do we teach the unlearned? Do we instruct Minerva? Far be it! Yet the affection of love could not contain itself, but had to bring forward, whether justly or unjustly, what it feels, and what is not at variance with good morals.

But if in this extensive testing of words we have exceeded due measure: “I have become foolish; you compelled me,” since you have esteemed me so highly that I hold so intimate a place in your favor that I may say whatever comes into my mouth. And you know me better, because, as someone has said and written, “love nurtures confidence.” If we have therefore gone too far, love will kindly bear it. It also belongs to true friends not to speak merely for appearance’s sake, but, whether it pleases or displeases, never to turn their course away from the path of truth. To speak otherwise is not to serve virtue but to be enslaved to one’s own vice.

## LETTER LX

[Note: [Col. 0714D] Barth. and Lang., year 1178.]

To a friend.

Whenever a time of need comes on, if a friend’s help is called for, no semblance of evasion ought to intervene to prevent friend from aiding friend. Otherwise, one is proved not to be a friend who previously appeared to be so by the gifts of more favorable fortune. Far be it from you that your affection should suffer from such a disease or that the judgment of equity, whose goodwill has never wished to exclude from itself the heart of mercy, should incline to the opposite side! Far be it, I say, that we should think otherwise of you than that a friend’s just request, with goodwill accompanying it, will obtain its effect.

Know, then, that we are harassed by the straits of rising tribulations, and there is no one to grieve over the affliction of Joseph. He who was accustomed to provide iron protection for the afflicted, though he longs from afar toward the prayers of suppliants, nevertheless cannot bring help.
