For this reason we cry to the Lord, in the hope that he may regard the prayer of the humble and not despise their petitions, “while there is none to redeem or to save” (Ps. 7). Would that our cry too might incline your merciful hearing to our prayers, so that there may no longer be one to seize and devour the poor! (Ps. 10)

## LETTER LXI

[Note: [Col. 0715D] Barth. and Lang., year 1196.]

To the lord king of the Danes.

Although it may seem beneath royal majesty for a poor man to approach the throne of glory, the clemency of royal gentleness is accustomed kindly to embrace or raise up those whom rank does not advance. We therefore, my lord, although no merits raise us so that we may have access to your excellence, whether justice wishes it or not, when a matter of mercy is at issue, its rigor will be tempered by mercy’s administration of judgment. We therefore beg—and add prayers to prayers—that on this occasion too the compassion of your royal highness may incline its ear to our petition; and that, if anything in us be worthy of correction, forgetfulness may consign it all to the past, lest we perhaps incur the king’s hatred and our affairs consequently suffer loss. It is true, lord, nor can we deny, that we were sent by your excellence to the king of France, and that we spoke—as this day proves—what tended to your honor, what the peace of the kingdom required, and what brought glory in the king’s ears. This is certainly your—[Note: [Col. 0715D] Read: “Without doubt, our.”]—greatest sin: that your sister is delivered into the embraces of the king of France in a marriage confirmed by ecclesiastical law. Behold, this blood is required at our hands. We beseech you, my lord, not to regard as slight what is known to be most grave; nor let the payment of money trouble you, for it is greater to acquire honor than to possess money. Though that money be withdrawn, the greatness of honor remains. Praiseworthy is money that does not rule its master, but yields to its master’s glory.

## LETTER LXII  
[Note: [Col. 0715D] Barth. 1179; Lang. 1178.]  
To the lord of Lund.

Because we are often assailed by various tribulations, we cry out more frequently for the help of one who raises us up. Yet, because we have not yet deserved to be heard, we fear either that our voices have not reached you or that you have—far be it!—held them in contempt. But the cry will not cease until the usurper is laid to rest; and this, indeed, we do not believe will happen except by a strong hand and an outstretched arm (Deut. 5). Therefore, that we may learn that it is not your will for us to be afflicted longer, we ask to be cherished in the bosom of your protection, so that all—both human beings and the Lord—may know that through your consolation we breathe again in such a way that, once our troubles have been removed, we may be set free. This will be to your glory, lord, and to our security and peace.

## LETTER LXIII  
[Note: [Col. 0716D] Barth. and Lang. 1195.]  
To Geoffrey.

The solicitude of love urges us to place this letter before you. For love cannot endure sickness; it rejoices in the novelty of those present and is impatient of delaying its writing. Know therefore that the magnitude of the honor and love which you have shown us, and the great remembrance of these things, draw us so wholly to themselves that to live without you should rather be called death than life. Do you not know? Rather, you do know—for we speak to one who knows—that when friends see one another and delight in each other’s sight, their mutual gaze is an indescribable cause of joy; and, as when oil is poured upon flames, the affection of the heart grows stronger and gathers strength. Therefore, because we do not doubt in the least that you eagerly desire our coming to you, we announce to your holiness, now that we have arrived in Paris, that tomorrow, the Lord granting it, we shall be worthy to receive the longed-for joys of your presence, which we greatly seek. What the cause was of the delay would have been worth committing to paper, had we not intended to convey that very matter mouth to mouth into the ears of your holiness.

## LETTER LXIV  
[Note: [Col. 0716D] Lang. 1178.]  
To the archbishop of Lund.

To his most beloved Father and lord, his devoted son and unprofitable servant: fear together with love.

We are urgently bound by the obligation of charity to take the concern of men before your clemency: men whom long monastic association has worn down beneath the yoke of discipline, whom the good report of virtuous people commends, and whom the ugliness of vices does not in the least stain—lest iniquity boast before the Judge of equity that it has found a place of refuge. We therefore commend the bearer of this letter, though he has no need of our commendation, since he confidently rests upon the testimony of his own conscience, together with the good opinion held of him; and we ask that the favor of your grace may smile upon him, that falsehood may fall vanquished before your eyes with its head crushed, and that the mouths of those who speak iniquity may be stopped—for their purpose is to estrange a friend from his neighbor. We should have judged it fitting to set down in writing the reason for his coming to you, had we not known it to be fully expressed in the letters of the masters Peter and Osmar; so that, through your consolations, the bitterness in his heart arising from the wrong done to him may be driven out—the bitterness that is immediately inflicted more sharply upon his inmost being because he has not received the fruit of his labor.

## LETTER LXV  
[Note: [Col. 0716D] Barth. and Lang. 1195.]  
To Master Melior, cardinal.

To the venerable lord M., cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church of the title of Saints John and Paul, and legate of the apostolic see: ANDREW, styled chancellor of the lord king of the Danes, with his companions, due reverence and love for so great a lord.

As you know, it is a great remedy for the tribulations of the afflicted to resort to the proven support of prelates; for they rejoice all the more abundantly in the gift of freedom as they perceive that greater remedies of mercy are being applied to them. Let your holiness therefore know that, sent to Rome by the illustrious king of the Danes, we carefully presented to the ears of the supreme pontiff the affair of that same king, our lord; and, as time required, we received letters of the lord pope setting forth the execution of that affair, to be brought before the eyes of your holiness. The king’s affair is the divorce effected between the king and queen. But if you ask why we do not carry out in person what we received in command, we answer briefly. Having left Rome—or rather the city—we came as far as Dijon; but there, setting aside reverence for the apostolic see and invocation of your name, and indeed despising the office of the apostolic legation, the servants of the duke of Burgundy detained us for seven days and committed us to close custody. At last, through the prayers of the lord of Cîteaux, we were brought out and came, under the Lord’s guidance, to Clairvaux, subject to an agreement and an oath: that, if our release should displease the lord king, we must again be taken to Dijon or to another place. Since, therefore, as we have said, we could not come in person into your presence, we send you the lord pope’s letters, asking and earnestly beseeching you to obtain from the lord king permission for us to come to you and speak with you. Concerning the wrongs unjustly inflicted upon us—when he found that we had undertaken nothing contrary to the honor or peace of the king or kingdom—we judged it proper to leave to your authority what should be done. That we greet you through such a messenger and send the lord pope’s letters is not contempt for your person, but the deficiency of a person higher and worthier.

## LETTER LXVI  
[Note: [Col. 0717D] Barth. 1188; Lang. 1187.]  
To Bishop Thurgot.

[Col. 0717C] To the venerable Father and lord T., by God’s grace bishop: Brother WILLIAM of Saint Thomas of the Paraclete, that he may happily bring evil days to their end.

When the rigor of religious life and discipline suffers harm from malignant perverse persons, it is not fitting, my Father, for the sons of the Church who are zealous for God’s law to keep silent, lest concealment of the offense accumulate the guilt of a more grievous punishment. Therefore we confidently offer this letter to your sight, because we know you by face and have truly loved you in Christ, both from the duty of Christian faith and from the fragrant scent of your good reputation. If, however, we are accused of presumption because we write, zeal for righteousness and compassion for brotherhood will excuse us, to whom we render this service of humanity. First, then, know, beloved Father, that we rejoiced with a gladder hearing at your promotion—indeed all the more devotedly because we hoped that through your efforts the Church of God would advance with more abundant fruit. Yet those who especially rejoiced in your glory were those whom, as you know, your fatherhood had formerly undertaken to govern and to advance by more honorable pursuits to the heights of virtue. For your celebrated name conveyed nothing else to us than that you wished those subject to you to excel in the gracefulness of noble character and, by the example of a holier life, to pour light upon those who wander. Nor do we infer anything else from your past works, whether by our own perception or the report of others, than what we knew while you lived among them for a long time.

[Col. 0718A] But alas, my Father, “the finest color has changed” (Lam. 4), and gold has become dross. The vineyard which ought to have yielded grapes has produced wild grapes (Isa. 5). “Their harp has been turned to mourning, and their organ to the voice of those who weep” (Job 30), as we have learned from the report of others: for former things have passed away, and what is heard pollutes the nostrils of those around them. Baldness has increased in place of curling hair, and stench in place of sweet fragrance (Isa. 3), while the rigor of the order is lost and calumny is inflicted upon holier and more ancient institutions—although it is lawful only to change for the better the boundaries which the Fathers established and commanded their children to preserve. Does it not seem to you, Father, that iniquity opposes sounder commands: that subjects are unwilling to obey their superiors, and that the Rule of our Father Augustine is being brought to nothing?

[Col. 0718B] Certainly, as Scripture says, unwillingness to comply is a kind of divination (1 Sam. 15). What observance of religion is there where the discipline of silence is abandoned and people devote themselves to tales and frivolity? To leave the cloister at will, to look at prostitutes and wish to be looked at by them, and to disgrace the chamber of chastity—are these not weapons of iniquity? Once virtues are suppressed, liberty is granted to vices; and if, in rebuke, a superior presumes to utter a complaint, laughter is immediately raised against him, insults are spoken, and harsher threats are made. Grant us, therefore, leave to speak in your ear. I beg you, my Father, let what follows be said with your permission. Who, I ask, is at fault except the lord himself, whose authority among them is greatest, who can restrain the swelling waves and reduce enormities to measure?

[Col. 0718C] But if you can act and remain silent, are you not proved to consent? The proverb is well known: “He who is silent consents.” But what does Scripture say? “Those who consent and those who do shall be punished with equal punishment.” And would that, Father, you merely kept silent and did not give horns to sinners. We therefore beseech you, most merciful Father, to prove yourself, in defense of justice, a lover of religious life as you have been; and, when the honorable superior—a man of holy conduct—has brought to the ears of your holiness the failing of order in the church committed to him, to give him a kindly hearing. For it is shameful to wish to seem to foster justice, yet to allow perverse persons to overthrow discipline. May almighty God grant

[Col. 0718D] that henceforth the perverse may find no refuge with you, but may feel in you, error removed, zeal for righteousness burning hot: so that there may be “peace for people of good will” (Luke 2), but for ill-wishers and those “who hate peace” (Ps. 119), “a rock of stumbling and a stone of offense” (1 Pet. 2).

## LETTER LXVII  
[Note: [Col. 0717D] Lang. 1175. Perhaps erroneous, for Absalon was not yet archbishop then, unless perhaps he is so called by anticipation.]  
To the lord archbishop of Lund.

To his most beloved Father and lord, his devoted son and unprofitable servant: fear together with love.

As blessed Jerome says: “Liars bring it about that truthful speakers are not believed.” Therefore, most reverend Father, darkened by the mist of falsehood, we could fear that your fatherly countenance had been changed against us for the worse, and that a cloud of iniquity had been set in the way so that prayer might not pass through. But this was in vain: for wisdom conquered malice (Eccl. 7), and mercy looked upon the prayer of the humble and did not despise their petitions (Ps. 101). At the cry of the poor, your fatherly compassion could not contain itself, but showed itself ready to help them—though not fully—and they became “as those who have been comforted” (Ps. 125). We approve this in your deeds, dearest Father; it is considered wholly glorious and deserves to obtain the preeminence among your virtues: that, in raising up the poor, your compassion beholds the King of Glory and Lord of Hosts. May he himself therefore answer for us and restore to you a reward in the future.

Moreover, my Father, for the adornment of God’s house and the crown of your head, that “the rush of the river may make glad the city of God” (Ps. 45), we labor exceedingly to introduce fountains. But since we began, in hope of the assistance of your favor, that which you have already begun by providing pipes, we ask that it may be brought to fuller and more magnificent completion.

## LETTER LXVIII  
[Note: [Col. 0719D] Lang. 1178.]  
To all, commending a certain person.

When faithful people perform good works by which the frailty of humankind may grow toward better things, greater care must be taken lest the detestable malice of perverse people rise up to their destruction. For this reason, therefore, we furnish our brother G., bearer of this letter, with our letters, so that all may know that he enjoys the liberty of your permission to make his journey. Whoever, therefore, places an obstacle or a calumny in the way along which he travels, may bear the punishment due to his malice. But whoever renders him the service of humanity may receive an eternal reward from the recompender of all good things.

## LETTER LXIX  
[Note: [Col. 0719D] Barth. 1198.]  
To the bishop of Odense.

To the venerable Father and lord John [Note: [Col. 0719D] John, son of Jani. He was already in office in 1187. He was a master of arts.], by God’s grace bishop of Odense: Brother WILLIAM of Blessed Thomas of the Paraclete, sinful minister, due reverence and love for so great a Father.

In writing, we may perhaps incur the charge of presumption if the favor and kindness of the recipient are lacking. [Col. 0719D] We believe—indeed, we are certain—that although merits do not raise our humility to the excellence of your majesty, your zeal for justice and your compassion for the afflicted will nevertheless be unable to restrain themselves in matters that belong to God and that the honor of religion demands. Far be it from us to think otherwise of you, whom both nobility of blood ennobles and the repute of virtues commends! Know therefore that our fugitive has fed swine in a far country; and, when scarcity of bread came upon him and the substance he took from us had been squandered in evil living, he has returned to his father—yet he wishes to remain forgetful of his purpose and of the profession he made, if he should wish to hide longer beneath the cover of his malice.

[Col. 0720A] Yet your nobility knows with how much goodwill and how urgent a pleading the lord archbishop, when we were at Roskilde, addressed you at table: that, if the man could be found, he should be brought before the archbishop’s eyes. We ask therefore, for the sake of your love for so great a lord, for the honor of religion, and for our sake—if indeed you think we have any weight with you—that you have him seized and presented to the lord archbishop. Farewell.

## LETTER LXX  
[Note: [Col. 0720D] Barth. and Lang. 1178.]  
To John [Note: [Col. 0720D] Perhaps John.] subprior of Esrum.

To his dearest friend John, subprior of Esrum: Brother WILLIAM, unworthy minister of Blessed Thomas of the Paraclete, the inmost affection of love.

We offer this letter to you with greater confidence because we are more certain of your religious devotion, integrity of faith, and sincere affection. Yet true love, as you know more truly, never denies its affection to the needs of friends when asked. Since we have often found this to be true, we ask nothing from your charity which it would not befit either your nature or the gracefulness of your character to grant, and which could ever cover the petitioner’s face with shame. But lest we weary you by reading, we have entrusted the whole matter, to be explained to you, to the bearer of this letter; and we ask that it be carried out with devotion, so that we may know more truly that love is neither lukewarm nor weak in the affairs of friends. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI  
[Note: [Col. 0720D] Barth. and Lang. 1194.]  
To the lord king.

[Col. 0720C]

For a poor person to gain access to a rich one, a lowly person to an exalted one, a servant to a free lord, is not a debt of nature but a gift of privileged grace. Therefore we are not surprised if you are surprised; but if you are not surprised, we are amazed that we are so brazen as to dare to disturb royal ears, though we have little or nothing to commend us by merit. But, if it is permitted for the assertion of truth to come into public view, we seem to have this one remedy to aid the excuse of our presumption: that the graciousness of royal gentleness has often anticipated us with blessings of sweetness. Encouraged by this, love, forgetful of fear,

[Col. 0720D] approaches the throne of your glory under the guidance of confidence; and we follow it, as those familiar with your affairs, step by step, beseeching with it that your compassionate ear may not be closed to its and our prayers, lest—far be it!—malice boast that it prevails against justice. We have thought it proper briefly to set before you the sum of the matter, lest you be wearied by a longer delay.

## LETTER LXXII  
[Note: [Col. 0720D] Barth. and Lang. 1178.]  
To the abbot of Esrum.

Because, most beloved Father, justice accompanies the urgency of our prayers, as we believe, we do not at all fear to send them into the bosom of your clemency. We therefore ask that a gracious result attend our petitions, so that, having received it, we may receive a remedy for our tribulation. Know, moreover, that the kindness shown to us will by no means lack blessing; rather, whatever benefit comes to us through you will be rewarded by our services.

## LETTER LXXIII  
[Note: [Col. 0721D] Lang. 1185.]  
To the lord Ebbo.

Although no merits raise us to your excellence, we nevertheless trust that in our cause your charity will not exclude the feelings of compassion. This is proclaimed among all people by famous report, which everywhere announces the praises of your virtues as a sweet fragrance. Happy is the man whom, in evil days and in the time of the proud, the merits of his life do not accuse, but whose virtue grows through the mouths of those who praise him, while his deeds proclaim and commend that virtue. We ask that, for our sake, this poor man’s want may be relieved, so that we may prove by the outcome that what is proclaimed about you is true.

## LETTER LXXIV  
[Note: [Col. 0721D] Barth. 1197.]  
To a certain cardinal.

Because your kindness has always shown itself ready in our affairs, our hand could not refrain from writing to you. First, therefore, because the favor of your grace has smiled upon us, we ask that your counsel also assist these affairs of ours,

[Col. 0721C] whose execution will bear witness through our works that they are good. We ask that we may find you present to our prayers as none other than him whose praises are proclaimed everywhere. We would say more, but we have entrusted to the bearer of this letter a fuller explanation of those matters not committed to this little page. We are worn down by many scourges and subjected to tyrannical laws; therefore it will be your mercy’s duty to bring the petitions to their proper conclusion. We commend the bearer of this letter to your compassion, all the more confidently because we have repeatedly experienced his praiseworthy conduct. . . . . [Note: [Col. 0721D] Perhaps a fragment of a letter to Chancellor Andrew Sunesen.] We also offer this letter to you so that, through more recent writings, love may burn more strongly; and if anything of uncouthness or irritation has ever arisen in you toward us or our acts through sluggishness or negligence, we ask that the integrity of love may repair it, the sweetness of kindness may consign it to the past, and proven goodwill may wholly erase and wipe it away—so that iniquity may not rule where the sweetness of a more sincere life has occupied all.

[Col. 0721D] And just as, when oil is added to flames, a greater fire rises, so familiar conversation sometimes supplies strength to love. Therefore, as stated above, after first offering the duty of greeting to your love, we send this letter for reading, so that the present page may testify how great is the love conceived in our heart toward you. What we have learned by personal observation, worthy to be recalled, concerning your condition, and what the famous report now spread abroad among you recounts through many people, are sweetly enclosed in the inmost parts of our heart and considered more sweetly—indeed, all the more sweetly as they are heard more frequently. Therefore, stretching our hands to the Lord with the inmost affection of our heart, we pray unceasingly and humbly beseech him that, through the greater gifts granted by the Lord, an ever happier grace may increase for you.

[Col. 0722A] You know, my lord, that when prosperity accompanies success, one must fear and take the greatest care lest a mind softened by sweeter enticements slip too easily, God forbid, into vain things. For abundance of possessions is accustomed to change people’s mind and purpose, unless the firm discipline of the fear of God labors, unbent by the temptations of prosperous things, to keep them out. But where are we tending? Why this excursion of words? Are we instructing Minerva? Far be it! Rather, borne onward by the desire of good will, we pray that a spirit smothered by too many delights may never wish to be conformed to this world. But in all your deeds may you continually keep before your eyes reverence and fear of God, as you have begun to do, and always strive to extend yourself toward the things before you. For although, through the more fruitful gifts of fortune, lovers . . . . . .

## LETTER LXXV  
[Note: [Col. 0722D] Barth. 1192.]  
To John the monk.

To his JOHN, WILLIAM: may you be able to attain, and imitate in deed, what you receive in your name.

But your love, dearest one, knows that where the outcry of a tumultuous people arises, neither decency in conduct nor the equity of justice is preserved. Therefore, because we see discord brought upon peace and wickedness upon equity in your house, we fear that before long we shall be excluded from the affections of your charity. Yet when evils rush in, you will display a great proof of your probity or innocence if you resolve to remain at your post. It is no badge of virtue to profess that you wish to harm no one when no one attacks you; rather, it is to wish to benefit all. But this is most noble in a person, and should often be considered: to be assailed by enemies and yet not wish, when one can, to inflict harm on those assailing one. Nor is love sincere when it smiles only upon the prosperity [Col. 0722D] of affairs, but is overcast by the cloud of adversity. O deceitful, unhappy, and unstable course of times! O faithless minds of human beings, in which constancy of faith is found rarely, if at all! But what shall I say, except that love passes away with time? One poet cries out among many [Note: [Col. 0722D] Ovid, *Tristia*, book I, elegy VIII, verse 5; and there more correctly: “So long as you are prosperous.”]:

> If you are rich, you will count many friends;  
> If times become cloudy, you will be alone.

But far be it that we should wish you to be numbered among those in whom no constancy of faith is found!

## LETTER LXXVI  
To Brother Stephen, monk.

[Col. 0723A]

Although in our affairs we suffer wrong from some of your people, we nevertheless sweetly embrace with all our inmost feelings the grateful remembrance of you. For there is a law established in love: whoever transgresses it, though called a friend, is nevertheless shown not to love. Do you wish to know? Where there is a firm union of souls, there too, without doubt, is communion of the Holy Spirit. And if this is true—indeed, because it is true—true lovers are joined by an equal bond, so that they do not allow any losses of separation to break into the boundaries of love. Thus we necessarily conclude that you can be separated from us by no circumstance of necessity or adversity.

It is good and pleasant for us to be here.

[Col. 0723B] Yet the outsider does not share in that good; nor can the merely natural person do so, since he does not perceive the things of God. To return to what has gone before: we rejoice so in your presence that we judge our own existence without yours to be either nothing or of little account. Therefore we do not at all suppose that you think otherwise. For like persons make the same judgment. Moreover, we leave it to your prudence to provide us with seeds of vegetables, various herbs and roots, and shoots of trees. In a friend’s necessities, however, true affection never feels the sluggishness of indolence, but offers itself wholly ready for the services requested. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXVII  
[Note: [Col. 0723D] Perhaps about 1194; Barth. 1195. This letter should perhaps be the seventh of this second book, according to J. Grammius’s written annotation.]  
To Brother Bernard of Vicennes.

[Col. 0723C] Where love is believed to contain a remedy, it is fitting that an afflicted friend should experience the compassion owed him. Therefore we confidently flee to the protection of your love, since we endure the straits of tribulations in defense of justice. Although we have been bound in the chains of close custody, love, which freely serves among us, has not been bound—as indeed it ought not to have been. Thus, knowing no rebuff and impatient of delay, it swiftly flies to your sight, so that the greatness of affection between us may be proved. We trust—indeed, we are certain—that, sent out by us, it will be received by you in more joyful embraces, and that the blessed merits of your holiness will attend the things upon which it rests and which it serves through justice.

[Col. 0723D] For far be it that love should be excluded from the feelings of charity in a time of need, when it boasts of the fullness of your grace! You know, lord, that we too, together with you, recognized how much labor and solicitude we expended in bringing about the marriage between the king and queen whom he is shown to have dismissed by a wicked and miserable counsel. This would have turned to our glory, had malice not happened to prevail against justice. We confidently call it malice, because through it the sacraments of the Church are injured and an example is offered to the people for attempting similar acts. Alas, who would not grieve over such a deed? Who would not groan? Who would not weep that the king’s fortunate beginnings have been changed into madness?

[Col. 0724A] Although, according to the Lord’s saying, scandals must come (Matt. 18), yet when they arise they are neither sweet nor pleasant, but are endured in bitterness. Therefore we have been sent by the lord and illustrious king of the Danes—who loves and reveres us in the Lord—to the apostolic see, so that by our report the king’s less fitting and sacred-law-abominable action might become known to the supreme pontiff. The same pontiff, moved beyond words by anger and astonishment, and inclined by the petitions of the aforesaid king of the Danes, judged it fitting to write to the lord king; he exhorts him fatherly and quite humbly to restore the queen to his favor and to show her, as is fitting, marital affection. We too therefore beseech you: since that king relies upon your counsels, may your efforts be added to complete the same work, so that more joyful and better things may, by God’s gift, succeed evil deeds.

## LETTER LXXVIII  
[Note: [Col. 0724D] Barth. 1190.]  
To a certain sick man.

Because, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0724D] I cannot find this passage.], weapons that are foreseen strike less severely, although we are hemmed in by many stings of tribulation, we must never despair of God’s mercy. Human foresight must therefore so provide for the power of its own virtue that it always retains the firmness of Christian faith. For the virtue of faith soon dries up unless it is continually put into action through good works and advances in holy observances. For the apostle says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2).

[Col. 0724C] Therefore, while we have time, as the Apostle says, “let us do good to all” (Gal. 6). Know, however, that through the report of many people word has reached us that you have taken on such sorrow that no reasoning can turn you to anything else, so that you may receive even the slightest healing remedy from tribulation. But neither reason admits this in a Christian nor should it be supported by any aid, since heavenly things should attend him more than he should crave earthly gains and delight in worldly enticements. But if you had carefully considered the matters stated above, so as to foresee evils coming, you would have been dealt with more gently, and your heart would not have been turned to such madness. We ask you, after so many stings of tribulations, to recover again the strength of a Christian breast,

[Col. 0724D] lest you utterly plunge into the abyss of despair and “your latter state become worse than the former” (Luke 11). If you have lost much, give thanks that you are without those things whose possession placed a great burden upon you, turned your whole mind toward earth, and made you neglect to attend to heavenly things. Dearest one, we have taken care to offer you these things out of love, so that you might recognize not lukewarmness but the love conceived toward you in us, and that by love’s counsels we might draw you away from sorrow. If you listen to us, you will know that we have not labored uselessly; if not, you will both waste away here in pain to no purpose and, God forbid, fail to escape the losses of eternal death.

## LETTER LXXIX  
[Note: [Col. 0725D] Barth. 1191.]  
To the lord pope, in the person of the king of the Danes.

[Col. 0725A]

To the most reverend Father and lord CELESTINE, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: KNUD, king of the Danes, that he may so govern the Church committed to him, justice acting as mediator, as to be able to receive eternal recompense from the author of all things.

Dearest Father, with what feeling of pious devotion we are delighted by the famous report spread abroad concerning your glory cannot be expressed either in the strokes of letters or in the course of our speech. For who would not gratefully receive the news that your fatherhood presides over kings and princes, before whom, as they say, malice complains that it has no place, while justice does not fail those oppressed by tribulations? From this, Father, the splendor of your glory will grow still further: famous report of your holy actions, spread throughout the world, will diffuse everywhere the fragrance of sweetness. May divine providence so deal in human affairs that, in our days, the force of malice may be weakened and fall, zeal for justice may arise, and truth not be lacking in rendering judgments that reduce enormities to measure.

[Col. 0725B] You know, Father—for we speak to one who knows—that our father, while he lived, was bound to you by friendship. We trust that through your efforts our kingdom received an increase of honor and glory; and we trust that, through your compassion, our kingdom is cherished by pursuits no less earnest, nor excluded from the affections of your fatherhood by any outcome of events.

[Col. 0725C] Moreover, we do not doubt that it has come to your attention that Philip, king of France, sought our sister in marriage; that she was joined to him according to God’s law and ecclesiastical ordinance; and that she was crowned with the royal diadem, her dowry having been arranged and the matter confirmed by the faith and oaths of many. But because the enemy lies in wait for good works so that they may perish, certain enemies of truth arose, asserting that there was a degree of affinity between the former queen and our sister, and that execrable oaths had been made concerning this. Let those who have read the document see: we protest, at the peril of our soul and with us the whole Church of the Danes, that they swore rashly, as will be clear to you upon inspection of this present instrument. We therefore set the matter forth so that the concern of your fatherhood may be vigilant over it, and so that what falsehood boasts it has wickedly done may, through a judgment of truth and justice, be condemned

[Col. 0725D] and rendered void—lest something of this kind, without precedent, redound to your disgrace and that of the Church “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5). It will be ascribed to your merits and praises, Father, if so detestable a crime is driven from the midst.

## LETTER LXXX  
[Note: [Col. 0725D] Many years after 1177; Barth. 1199.]  
In the person of the lord of Lund.

The apostolic see, the farther it seems removed from us, the more urgently, amid rushing evils and oppressed by many injuries, are we compelled, most holy Father, to seek counsel and help from your grace. For the proven grace of past things gives us confidence for things to come. We believe—indeed, we know, Father—that it has not escaped your notice that we were endowed by your predecessors with favor and honor in the privileges of the apostolic see in the kingdom of Denmark and Sweden, and that our Church has from ancient times held the primacy of that same Sweden.

[Col. 0726A] Yet because the people of that kingdom are less subject to divine observances, the honor owed to us is scarcely, if ever, rendered. Hence its archbishop and his suffragans neglect to assemble; and at times they allege, in excuse against our summons, that they are held back by royal edicts. Therefore, if anything there should ever require correction,

[Col. 0726B] let your holiness know that everything remains unpunished, because the freedom to correct it is denied even to us. We have therefore judged it fitting to consult your fatherhood on this matter, asking that, because they avoid our citations, they may feel the rigor of apostolic severity, lest they presume to attempt anything of this kind further.

## LETTER LXXXI  
[Note: [Col. 0725D] Not extant in the table of contents.]  
To the abbot of Saint Geneviève.  
[Note: [Col. 0726D] Barth. 1191.]

Although we were held not with iron chains but under close guard, yet, with the Lord’s help, we are not abandoned, because we contend bravely for justice, ready not only to be bound but, for love of justice, to submit our necks to swords. For we know him who said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake” (Matt. V). What the cause of our suffering is, we have not thought worthy to commit to writing, since we do not doubt that the divine law has impressed it upon your minds. Therefore it must be obtained from the Lord by your prayers that he may soften the hard heart of the royal highness, which, at the counsel of wicked men, has shamefully strayed from the path of justice; or that the rigor of the justice of the Roman Church may appear—as it has not yet appeared, nor have we wished it to appear, as is fitting—so that all the people may know that there is a priest in Israel to execute judgment and justice in the land. Nor do we wish your knowledge to understand otherwise than this: if we are subjected to the swords of persecution, there will nevertheless not be lacking those who grieve over the ruin of Joseph, who will not bend their knees before Baal, and who will neither cease nor tire of going and returning to the supreme pontiff, to urge him to cut off from their midst the counsel of Ahithophel and to let the house of David reign in Jerusalem.

## LETTER LXXXII

[Note: [Col. 0726D] Barth., year 1195.] To the abbot of Saint Geneviève.

Most loving Father, a report of great renown has lately sounded in our ears: namely, that the Shepherd of all has appointed you shepherd over His household. Happy is that day, to be remembered with every joy, on which the Lord raised upon the lampstand the light that lay hidden in darkness, that it might shine upon all who are in the house; so that strict order may be joined to discipline of conduct. This is the Lord’s doing, and it is wonderful—indeed sweet and praiseworthy—in our eyes (Ps. CXVII).

In this also the power of our virgin has become known: that one whom no deformity of conduct discolors should preside over her household, and that, by the Lord’s ordering, he should succeed as legitimate heir to Lord Stephen, a man of happy memory [Note: [Col. 0727] Stephen was not dead, but had become bishop of Tournai.] and worthy of all praise—one who would rule vices and, by praiseworthy conduct, heap virtue upon virtue. This, I say, has virgin purity obtained: that her church, through its conduct and its better—indeed more noble—institutions, should surpass other churches in the pursuit of virtues; and, correcting wandering steps and those living less religiously, should henceforth set before them a rule for living more honorably.

This, my Father and lord, is what we desire to hear of you: that by your efforts irregularities may be reduced to measure; that nothing may come before the divine gaze by which the Lord of glory may be offended. It is no slight burden, Father, beneath which you have placed your shoulders; for, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0727] See above.], “The government of souls is the art of arts.” He who must perform the office of a physician in healing souls ought to have in his hands both cautery and ointment, so as to pierce, burn, and anoint the unruly. Yet let those struck by a worthy paternal rebuke be first met with sweetness, for the days are evil. But if anyone is found to whom such grace is granted, as you know better, this gift belongs not to nature but to grace, which neither man nor angel instills, but God, distributor of graces and infuser of every blessing.

And insofar as we are believed to be of any consequence with you, may He repay you grace for grace who gives abundantly to all and reproaches no one. For our part, if occasion, place, or time presented itself, we should count among our services whatever we have heard has been poured out upon our affection through your favor and paternal loving concern. Moreover, my Father, you have informed us by letter that Henry’s son wishes to send us six ounces of silver for his father’s inheritance, which he possesses, and that he is not otherwise bound to us in many respects. We therefore ask your paternal care that what he acknowledges may be sent through the bearer of this letter to our brethren. May your holiness live and prosper in Christ Jesus.

After Letter LXXXII, the following fragment of a letter “To Lord Canute, king of the Danes,” occurs in the first Magnaeus transcript:

To the illustrious king of the Danes, CANUTE, by God’s grace king of the Danes, WILLIAM, servant of the servants of Christ in the Paraclete: may you administer the government of the earthly kingdom in such a manner as to deserve to receive the everlasting crown.

We are compelled by the obligation of charity to grant our presence to the hearing of your royal excellence; and the departure of our most dear—indeed, rather your—bearer of this letter, H., urges us to do so.

[Col. 0727]

## GENEALOGY OF THE KINGS OF THE DANES

(*Script. Rer. Dan.*, VI, 154.)

[Col. 0727]

## NOTICE

I call this little book by its genuine and simple title. Henry Ernst, who formerly published it at Sorø in octavo in 1646, entitled it thus: *Genealogy and Succession of Certain Kings of Denmark, by an Anonymous Author*. Ludewig inserted that edition, reproduced word for word, with only the dedicatory epistle removed, in his *Reliquiae Manuscriptorum*, vol. IX, pp. 591–650.

Ernst not only indicates on the title page of the book whence he obtained this ancient writing—namely, from an old manuscript codex of a certain chronicle of the Church of Laon, ending in the year of Christ 1218—but also, in the prefatory letter, attributes it to the gracious permission of the most distinguished André du Chesne, geographer to the king of France. At the same time he gives the following reason for his opinion concerning the anonymous writer:

> Although I know nothing certain about the author, I nevertheless suspect, because of the dispute which Canute VI, son of Valdemar I, had with Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, concerning the dissolution of the marriage which Philip had contracted with Canute’s sister Ingeborg, that this little book was written by him. For the Anonymous Author seems to have this object: to investigate the descent of Canute’s sister Ingeborg. This is why, in this succession of Danish kings, he does not even name Magnus, son of Olaf, king of Norway, or other kings of Denmark, but inserts Duke Canute, Ingeborg’s grandfather, in the catalogue of kings.

How much this author was ignorant of in our history, and how often he departed from the truth, has been indicated in the notes in its proper place. Thus far Ernst, who rightly suspects that the little book was written because of the controversy that arose between Philip and Ingeborg concerning their marriage. It is therefore clear that it deserves the title *Genealogical Demonstration* rather than *Succession of Kings*.

If, however, Ernst had read Hvitfeld more attentively, he could easily have known the author as well. For that distinguished historian, excellently informed upon the matter, tells us that, because of this dispute, King Canute sent to Rome and to France his chancellor Andrew Sunesen and William, abbot of Æbelholt; and that the latter wrote a *Little Book on the True Genealogy of Ingeborg*, in opposition to that false and absurd Hungarian and Flemish genealogy, fabricated by the French, concerning the consanguinity of Philip and Ingeborg. [Col. 0729] [Note: [Col. 0729] On this false genealogy, invented and sworn to by certain bishops and knights of France, see Gram’s notes on Meursius, pp. 363–364.] Hvitfeld, pp. 160–161, recounts the contents of this book, and they agree exactly with what the book published by Ernst relates. Therefore anyone must conclude with me that the book published by Ernst is the same one which Saint William wrote to set out and establish the true genealogy of Ingeborg.

Now that its author, about whom I have no doubt, has been discovered, it seems probable that the copy preserved in the Chronicle of Laon derived from William’s own authentic writing, which he took with him to France; while the errors and interpolations with which it teems, I believe, entered through the fault of copyists. Besides the copy preserved in the Laon codex and published by Ernst, another also survived in our own country until the catastrophic fire of the metropolitan city in 1728: namely, in a parchment codex of the library of the University of Copenhagen, in the same volume as Adam’s *History of the Archbishops of Hamburg*, Solinus’s *Polyhistor*, the *Image of the World*, and other works.

Although that codex has now perished, together with the rest of the treasure of books and manuscripts, in the fury of the fire, the care and foresight of Árni Magnússon preserved a transcript of Saint William’s little book. A copy written in his own hand before the fire came into my possession. Since it is in some respects fuller, in others more correct, and in a few places shorter than Ernst’s edition—and since it contains its original prologue, lacking in the Laon copy—it is the text which I present here. At the same time, I retain Ernst’s text, printed in italics in the left-hand column, so that, by comparing them, the proper value of each may be preserved. The divisions into chapters and the numbers of years in Ernst’s edition appear to be of later date and perhaps to have been added by the editor himself. Of Ernst’s notes, in which he often comments on trifles, on a name badly read, or on a place corrupted through a copyist’s ignorance, I have omitted most, substituting my own brief annotations wherever necessary.

## GENEALOGY OF THE KINGS OF THE DANES

[Col. 0729]

In this catalogue of Danish kings, we have judged it worthwhile, in accordance with the trustworthiness of histories and the recollection of persons still living, carefully to record from how ancient a royal stock this lady, Ingeborg by name, queen of the Franks, derived her bodily descent; so that whoever sees and reads it may ascertain by direct evidence that she had no line of consanguinity with the Flemings. Nor is it to be supposed that this Harald, who is placed first in the order of this genealogy, was the first king of the Danes; but for the present business it was unnecessary to trace more. For many came before him, of whom we shall enumerate a few.

The first king of the Danes was called Dan; hence the Danes received their name. Afterwards came Gorm, Frothi, Gothorm, Frothi, Sweyn, Cuthlac [Note: [Col. 0729A] The author undoubtedly has in view that king of the Danes who invaded Gaul about the year 515 and whose name is monstrously written by certain Frankish writers as *Chochilaicus* or *Clochilaicus*, but more correctly by Gregory of Tours as *Gothilacus*. See Gram’s *Meursius*, p. 87; Huitfeld, p. 16. He was perhaps the same king whom Saxo, p. 66, calls Huglethus, but whom our ancient annals more correctly call *Huglekaer*, *Hughleker*, *Hughlek*, or *Huhlek*. See *Script. Rer. Dan.*, vol. I, pp. 15, 19, 21, 27, 32.], Eskil [Note: [Col. 0729B] Among the most ancient Danish kings, whether real or fictitious, listed by Saxo and in our annals, I do not recall finding an Eskil named anywhere except here. Saint William borrowed him from Geoffrey of Monmouth, an early English writer. For in the *History of the Kings of Britain*, X.6, 9, and XI.2, Geoffrey mentions Aschillius, king of Dacia, or Aschil, king of the Danes, who fought against the Romans for Arthur, the celebrated sixth-century king of Britain.], Warmund, Godfrey, Hemming. The aforesaid Eskil fought with King Arthur of the Britons against the Romans.

## TEXT OF THE COPENHAGEN MANUSCRIPT

[Note: [Col. 0730] The following sections of the “Textus Codicis Hafniensis” and the “Textus Editionis Ernstii” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

This HARALD, surnamed Bluetooth—that is, “blue” or “black tooth”—was a pagan; but although afterwards baptized, he did not remain in the faith, but apostatized. [Note: [Col. 0730A] From what our author relates concerning Harald and his son Sweyn, he appears to confuse father and son. For Harald is said to have retained Christianity steadfastly to the end, while Sweyn, rebellious against God, carried out a great persecution of Christians in Denmark, as Adam of Bremen testifies, II.15, 21. Saint William nevertheless had a contemporary Danish historian, Sweyn Aggesen, who supported this assertion about Harald; I infer that William was misled by him. See *Scriptor. Rer. Dan.*, vol. I, p. 52.] For this he was expelled from the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0730B] Saxo, ed. Steph., p. 185, reveals the true causes of his expulsion from the kingdom. Compare Sweyn Aggesen, cited passage, p. 51, and the *Encomium Emmae*, in *Script. Norm.*, p. 164.], fled to the Slavs, then devoted to pagan rites, and harassed the Danish kingdom with repeated incursions; but he did not prevail.

### On Sweyn Forkbeard, king of the Danes

[Col. 0731A]

This SWEYN, surnamed Forkbeard [Note: [Col. 0731A] Our forefathers called him *Tiugos-cegg* or *Tiuguskegg*. See Snorri Sturluson, vol. I, p. 243; *Knýtlinga Saga*, p. 6. Others translated this by the Latin *Admorsae Barbae*, “of the cloven beard.”], Harald’s son, accepted the Christian faith together with his people and faithfully persevered in it. [Note: [Col. 0731B] Read the preceding note (20).] He also invaded England and wore it down by repeated incursions of war; but he did not altogether subdue it.

### On Canute the Great, son of King Sweyn

This CANUTE [Note: [Col. 0731B] On the name *Kanutus*, *Canutus*, or *Cnuto*, arising from Danish *Knude*, “knot,” see Perill. Suhm, *Forbedr. til D. og N. Hist.*, p. 1. On coins of King Canute the Great, of which I possess several, his name is read *Cnut*; but in his charters occur indiscriminately *Knut*, *Cnut*, *Chnut*, *Knuth*, *Cnud*, *Cnudus*, *Cnutus*, *Cnute*, *Cnuto*, and *Knuto*. Latinizing writers inserted the letter *a* for euphony, producing *Kanutus* or *Canutus*.], surnamed the Great [Note: [Col. 0731C] Here our twelfth-century author shows that Canute was called “the Great” even in ancient times, although other ancient writers also address him by other bynames. See *Script. Rer. Dan.*, vol. I, p. 54.], Sweyn’s son, after his father’s death entirely subdued England and made it subject to himself. His magnificence and power were so great that he held the monarchy of three kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0731C] Our author rightly says that Canute held the monarchy of three kingdoms: England, Denmark, and Norway. On this count he agrees well with Adam of Bremen, II.47, who says that King Cnut, through the power of three kingdoms, was greatly feared by barbarian peoples. The contemporary poet Halvard sang of the three kingdoms subject to Canute, in Snorri Sturluson, vol. I, p. 715. It is certain that he conquered and occupied further realms—Scotland, part of Sweden, of which our author was unaware, Sambia, and Slav provinces. Hence Saxo Grammaticus, not altogether inappropriately, calls him possessor of six mighty kingdoms. Sweyn Aggesen plainly invents when he extends Canute’s dominion as far as the Irish, Franks, Italians, Lombards, Teutons, even Thule-dwellers and Greeks; to these he adds Finns in the Military Laws.]: England, Denmark, and Norway.

He also made tributary to himself the Rani [Note: [Col. 0731D] The Sorø edition corruptly reads *Bojanos*, concerning which unknown people Ernst comments vainly and unsuccessfully. But if, following our copy, we correctly read *Roanos*, or *Rojanos* in Absalon’s will, we recognize the Rugians among the Slav peoples subdued by Canute the Great in 1019. It is uncertain whether the Rugians were tributary to the Danes in the time of Harald Bluetooth, perhaps even earlier. Our people formerly called the island of Rügen *Roo* and *Ro*; hence its inhabitants were called *Roani* by Adam, ed. Lindenbrog, pp. 19, 59; *Rhuni*, *Rani*, and *Runi* by Helmold, ed. Bang, pp. 6, 21; *Rani* or *Rugiani*, or, as my old codex has it, *Ruiani*; *Raenger* by the Icelanders; and *Robo* by our people. Hence the evident reasons emerge which moved not only Erik Ejegod—who entrusted Skjalm the White with the administration of tributary Rügen, Saxo, p. 227—and Erik Emune, Saxo, p. 248; *Knýtlinga Saga*, p. 202, but also Valdemar I and other Danish kings, so often to wage war against the Rugians, besides other Slavs: namely, because they had repeatedly revolted from the ancient Danish dominion. In the time of King Niels, between 1120 and 1130, when Bishop Otto of Bamberg was performing the apostolic office among the Pomeranians, the bond between the Danish kingdom and Rügen is evident from the fact that the Rugians told the bishop not only that they ought to be subject to the archbishop of the Danes, but that Otto did not undertake to preach to the Rugians unless he had obtained the Danish archbishop’s consent; and the archbishop could not give it until he had first consulted the Danish princes and magnates. See the *Life of Otto of Bamberg* in Canisius, vol. III, part II, pp. 88–89.], the Pomeranians [Note: [Col. 0732B] Our author teaches that Canute the Great conquered, besides the Rugians, many peoples of the Slavs and Pomeranians; this is also evident from other circumstances. In particular, it is clear that he asserted his rightful claim to the province and city of Jumne or Jomsborg, conquered by his grandfather Harald and defended by his father Sweyn, because he had placed his son Sweyn—afterwards king of Norway—over Jomsborg and his Wendish lands. Snorri Sturluson explicitly testifies to this, vol. I, p. 811. Thus Slavia, or rather that part of Slavia, is counted among the regions subject to the dominion of Harthacnut, son of Canute the Great, in the Chronicle of Erik, above, vol. I, p. 159. On Jomsborg and the territory of Jumne, see what I noted above in *Script. Rer. Dan.*, vol. I, p. 51 ff. Saxo and all the corrupt editions of Adam of Bremen read *Julinum*, but in my view wrongly.

Marcus Skeggi, a poet contemporary with Erik the Good, who sang this king’s deeds in verse, and, following him, the author of the *Knýtlinga Saga*, call the Danish kings’ claims regarding Slav lands just and ancient, deriving them from King Sweyn Forkbeard, but vigorously vindicated by Erik, who had earlier been appointed viceroy there by his father Sweyn and his brother Saint Canute. See *Knýtlinga Saga*, pp. 150, 152, 154, and 156:

> “Konungr lagdi a pa stor fegiolld, oc taldi pat arftekna eign sina, er Dana Konungar hofdu att i Vindlandi, sidan SVEIN Konungr Tiuguskegg lagdi unndir sik. Sva segir Markus.”

That is: “The king imposed a heavy fine upon them and declared his hereditary ancestral possession to be the kingdom which the kings of Denmark had held in Wendland ever since King Sweyn Forkbeard had subjected it to his dominion.” Marcus explains the matter in this manner:

> Eirikr vad med uppreist harri,  
> Undan Hydu Vindr af stundu.  
> Giolld felldu pa grimmir holldar,  
> Gumnar urdu sigri numnir.  
> Yngvi taldi erfdir pangad.  
> Alpyda vard stilli hlyda.  
> Velldi red pvi astvinr alldar,  
> Emart la pat fyrr und Sveini.

Erik gained a splendid victory;  
the Wends immediately turned their backs.  
Then cruel men paid the penalty,  
men deprived of victory.  
The king claimed dominion there by hereditary right.  
The people were compelled to obey their ruler.  
The king, beloved by the people, had formerly ruled this realm,  
for it had once lain under Sweyn.

> “Eptir petta setti EIRIKR Konungr menn til Landzgaezlu a Vindlandi, oc helidu peir Riki pat undir EIRIK Konung.”

That is: “Thereupon Erik, after stations had been established throughout all Wendland to keep that realm in loyalty and obedience to him, made for his ships.” After Canute, the most powerful kings of the Danes—Magnus the Good, Sweyn Estridsson, Saint Canute, Erik the Good, Niels, Erik Emune, Valdemar I, and Canute VI—bravely defended their rights over the Slavs, whom some call Wends or Vandals. See Saxo Grammaticus, pp. 204, 225, 236, and frequently thereafter; Snorri Sturluson, vol. II, pp. 30–31; *Knýtlinga Saga*, besides the places cited, pp. 36, 42, 86, 142, 146, 202; and throughout the history of Valdemar I and Canute VI. Not to mention the unsuccessful expeditions against the Slavs of Erik Lam and Sweyn Grathe, who waged war against not only Rügen but all Slavia more frequently than successfully: Saxo Grammaticus, pp. 253–254, 258, 268.], the Slavs, the Hermines [Note: [Col. 0733B] It is uncertain what people Abbot William understood by “Hermines.” He scarcely had in view the ancient people of Germany neighboring the Cimbri and Teutons, whom Pliny calls *Hermiones* and Tacitus *Herminones*; rather, perhaps the Heruli, whom he considered a Slav people, or the Prussians, since he names them among the Slavs and Sambians.], and the Sambians [Note: [Col. 0733C] By the *Samos*, which Ernst’s edition incorrectly reads as *Savios*, are meant those otherwise called *Sembi*; the region they inhabit is called Sembia or Samland. In a diploma of 1253 it is *Zambia*, and in 1258 *Sambia*; in Adam, ed. Lindenbrog, pp. 19, 58–59, *Semland* and *Sembi*; in Saxo, *Sembia*, *Sembi*, *Sembici*; in the *Knýtlinga Saga*, *Samland*. Even today the Samland district is that part of the kingdom of Prussia in which the capital Königsberg is situated. Whether the Sembian people have anything in common etymologically with Tacitus’s Semnones, I leave for others to investigate. It is enough for me to say that our forefathers had many dealings with the Sembians.

Leaving aside the oldest and more obscure reports of our history, one finds that the great King Harald Bluetooth sent his son Haquin to subdue the Sambians. Saxo, p. 184, describes the outcome of that expedition thus:

> “Having gained possession of Sambia, the Danes killed the men and compelled the women to marry them. They broke the bond of marriage with their own people and, clinging more eagerly to foreigners, shared their fortune with the enemy through the common bond of marriage. Nor without reason do the Sambians reckon the weaving of their bloodline among the stock of the Danish people; so completely did love of the captives capture the minds of the victors that, abandoning their desire to return, the barbarians cultivated barbarism as their homeland and held themselves closer to alien wives than to their own.”

It is therefore not surprising that Canute the Great wished, when occasion offered, to vindicate the right to Sambia acquired by his grandfather. For Sambia, subdued by Haquin, after his death acted rebelliously against the Danes, as Saxo, p. 192, relates. Yet whether he conquered the Sambians in the same year, 1019, in which he overcame the Slavs, is not sufficiently certain. Saxo, p. 192, plausibly believes that Canute subdued Slavia and Sambia before undertaking the invasion of England; and, if conjecture is permitted, this happened either in the summer of 1014 or the spring of 1015, during the same Slav expedition in which the two royal brothers Canute and Harald brought back their mother: *Encomium Emmae*, p. 167. Whatever the case, Sweyn Aggesen, above, vol. I, p. 54, lists Sambia among the regions subdued by Canute the Great.

This may relate to the statement of the Chronicle of Erik, ibid., p. 159, that Canute also subdued the Estonian people; compare the Chronicle of Peter Olai, ibid., p. 117. For it is well known that among ancient writers—Tacitus, Cassiodorus, Jordanes, Einhard, Wulfstan, and the Chronicle of Dijon—*Aestii*, *Esti*, *Haesti*, *Aisti*, *Eosti*, and *Agisti* denote those peoples who formerly inhabited the Prussian and Livonian coasts. Among the titles by which Canute is addressed in his Military Laws, published in Old Danish by Resen, p. 568, occurs also *Konungii Semland*, “king of Sambia.” [For *Sembia* in Sweyn Aggesen, ed. Stephan., p. 148, *Finlandia* is incorrectly printed; and *Smalandia*, found in Resen, p. 546, is a typographical error.]

At this passage I am surprised that Resen, p. 579, comments among other things as follows:

> “Livonia is divided among four peoples: the Aestii, Letts, Curonians, and Semigallians. To soften the names, Saxo called the last two Curetes and Sembians, with that audacious self-confidence which he continually indulged in his writings; for one scarcely finds the name of the Sembians anywhere except in this author.”

But Resen, better informed later, acknowledges on p. 724 that Sembia is Prussia. Since Sambia was conquered by Danish arms under Harald and Canute, it becomes comprehensible why, in later centuries, the most powerful kings—Sweyn Estridsson through his son Canute, then King Saint Canute himself, and even Valdemar II—undertook wars against Sambia or Samland. On the last, see the Chronicle of Erik, *Script. Rer. Dan.*, vol. I, p. 165; the Annals of Esrum, ibid., p. 343; the Annals of Visby, ibid., p. 254.

Of Canute, whom his father Sweyn sent out, Saxo, p. 212, declares that he spent his youth gloriously in victories over the Sambians and Estonians; and later, p. 214, says of the same man, under the rule of his brother Harald, that he vigorously pursued the war against the eastern peoples, begun while his father was alive; and shortly afterward, that after obtaining the throne he sought to renew the eastern war, which he had begun in youth and undertaken in exile, more for the sake of extending religion than of satisfying ambition. “Nor did he withdraw his hand from the enterprise until he had utterly destroyed the kingdoms of the Curonians, Sambians, and Estonians.” Ibid., p. 217, Canute’s eastern victories are still celebrated.

The *Knýtlinga Saga*, p. 46, confirms the same point from the testimony of Kalf Mana’s son, a contemporary poet:

> “Knutr son Sveins Konungs hafdi adr verid i hernadi i Austrveg.---Sva segir Kalfr Manason i Kvaedi sinu, at Knutr hafi sigrad X. Konunga, pater hann var i hernadi i Austrveg.”

That is: “Canute, son of King Sweyn, had previously campaigned in the East. … Kalf Mana’s son relates in his poem that Canute defeated ten kings while he was engaged in warfare in the East.”], all devoted to pagan rites. He made them tributary to himself. The emperor of the Romans also joined this king’s daughter to himself in marriage. [Note: [Col. 0734D] That is, Henry III, then king of Germany, afterwards Roman emperor in 1039.]

### On Canute the Hard, son of Canute the Great

This Canute, son of the preceding Canute, surnamed the Hard [Note: [Col. 0734D] On the byname *Harde*, *Harthe*, *Horde*, or *Haurde* of this Canute, son of Canute the Great, called Harthacnut, see Gram’s excellent discussion in his notes on Meursius, pp. 132, 194. On one of his coins, which I possess, one reads *Hardecnut* and *Hardacnut*. Compare Ernst’s note at this passage.], yielded the kingdom of England to his brother, being content with the kingdoms of Denmark and Norway. He lived only a short time and died without offspring; whereupon the reins of government were assumed after him by Sweyn [Note: [Col. 0735C] The author perhaps omitted Magnus, king of Norway, who succeeded Harthacnut, and then Sweyn immediately succeeded Magnus on the Danish throne. But Magnus was not to be inserted, since he does not pertain to this genealogy.], the son of his paternal aunt.

### On Sweyn the Great, nephew [Note: [Col. 0735C] Sweyn was not Harthacnut’s nephew, but his cousin, or his paternal aunt’s son.] of Canute the Hard, who succeeded the same Canute powerfully and gloriously in the Danish kingdom

This SWEYN, surnamed the Great [Note: [Col. 0735D] Here, among other evidence, we have ancient testimony that Sweyn Estridsson was called “the Great.” Compare *Script. Rer. Dan.*, vol. I, p. 245.], who succeeded Canute the Hard in the kingdom, was very powerful and glorious in his days, feared by all the surrounding nations, and greatly devout in the Christian religion. Although he had very many sons [Note: [Col. 0735D] Five of them became kings; hence Sweyn was called the Father of Kings. See Sweyn Aggesen, above, vol. I, p. 56.], mention need be made of only two who concern the present matter: Canute and Erik.

### On Erik, son of Sweyn the Great

This ERIK, son of Sweyn the Great and brother of Canute the Martyr, received, because of his great goodness, the surname “the Good.” When he went to the Lord’s Sepulchre, he performed many distinguished deeds on that journey; while returning, he died at Cyprus, where he was buried with royal burial. Hence he was also called “the Cypriot.”

### Again, on Erik, son of Sweyn and brother of Canute the Martyr

This ERIK, by Queen Botild, descended from a most noble Danish stock [Note: [Col. 0735D] Gram carefully investigates the descent of Queen Botild in his notes on Meursius, p. 229 ff.], begot Canute the Martyr, who rests at Ringsted [Note: [Col. 0735D] In Ernst’s edition *Kinostadium* is incorrectly printed in place of *Ringstadiam*, through a copyist’s error.], a royal abbey, where to this day he is made illustrious by frequent and glorious miracles. For, as the Gospel says, “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed” (Matt. XI); and, through his merits, the Lord deigns to perform many other outstanding works.

### On Blessed Canute, father of Valdemar, king of the Danes

[Col. 0735C] This CANUTE was duke of the Danes and king of the Slavs, whom he held powerfully not by hereditary right but by arms. He had a wife named Ingeborg [Note: [Col. 0735D] Saxo Grammaticus, p. 230, likewise teaches that this Ingeborg bore that name.], daughter of Iziaslav [Note: [Col. 0735D] Icelandic historians call this Iziaslav, king of Rus’, or ruler reigning over some part of Rus’, Harald, so called from the name of his maternal grandfather or great-grandfather, Harald Godwinson, king of the English, who fell in 1066. See Snorri Sturluson, vol. II, pp. 178, 254, 402; *Knýtlinga Saga*, p. 178. At the beginning of the twelfth century there were very many rulers in Rus’, whose names foreign writers confused remarkably, and whom even the Russian annals did not distinguish with sufficient accuracy. Thus it is not easy to determine who were the two kings of Rus’ named by our author—Iziaslav, father of Duchess Ingeborg, and Valadar, father of Queen Sophia. [Northern writers formerly assigned the title “king” to every Russian prince.] Certainly Saxo Grammaticus, p. 207, seems to err in the name of Ingeborg’s father when he calls him Valdemar, called Jaroslav by his own people, and assigns him as wife a daughter of Harald Godwinson, king of England; she was rather Ingeborg’s paternal grandmother than her mother. Setting aside every discrepancy in names—for, in their usual manner, our northern writers frequently named foreign rulers differently—the following genealogy is, I think, probably constructed from Snorri Sturluson, vol. II, p. 179, and the author of the *History of the Knytlingar*, pp. 178, 200, when compared with our author:], a most powerful king of the Rus’, and of Queen Christina. By her he begot Valdemar, the glorious king of the Danes, who became father of King Canute, now reigning in Denmark [Note: [Col. 0736D] Here we have the period in which the author of this little work lived: namely, the reign of Canute VI, who ruled about and after the year 1190.], and of Ingeborg, queen of the Franks.

The aforesaid Christina, grandmother of King Valdemar, was daughter of Inge, king of the Swedes, and Queen Helena. [Note: [Col. 0736D] Saxo, p. 230, likewise reports that King Inge’s wife was called Helena.] The sister of the aforesaid Ingeborg, Valdemar’s mother—and another daughter of King Iziaslav—married the king of Hungary, who had as wife the sister of the king of the Franks. It is thus plainly shown that Valdemar, king of the Danes, father of Ingeborg queen of the Franks, and King Béla of Hungary [Note: [Col. 0737C] Hence Saxo Grammaticus, p. 371, says that the king of Hungary was connected with Valdemar by close kinship. From the genealogical table just presented, it appears that King Géza of Hungary had married Valdemar I’s maternal aunt, not his sister, as Torfæus, vol. III, p. 377, and others maintain. Catherine, Valdemar’s sister, whom the *Knýtlinga Saga*, p. 190, says was married “in the East” (*i Austurveg*), I believe to have been the wife of Prislav, prince of the Slavs, whose son Canute was brought up and died in Denmark with his maternal uncle Valdemar I.], were first cousins.

But King Canute of Sweden and King Sigvard of Norway are related to him in the second degree of consanguinity. [Note: [Col. 0737C] From the genealogical scheme set out above, it is clear that King Canute of Sweden was related to Valdemar I in the third degree of consanguinity. But as regards Sigvard, or Sigurd Jorsalafar, king of Norway, son of King Magnus Barefoot, our author is mistaken in believing that Margaret, maternal aunt of Duchess Ingeborg, was the mother of the aforesaid Sigvard. His mother was Thora, as Snorri Sturluson testifies, vol. II, p. 221.] The brothers of Queen Sophia, mother of Ingeborg, still gloriously administer the government of the kingdom in Rus’ today. [Note: [Col. 0737D] About 1196. But who were those Russian rulers, brothers of Queen Sophia?]

### On the glorious King Valdemar and his children, King Canute and Queen Ingeborg
Waldemar, this glorious and mighty king in his day, begot by Sophia the pious and glorious King Canute, who now reigns in Denmark, and his sister Ingeburg, who married the most excellent King Philip of the Franks. The aforesaid Queen Sophia was [Col. 0737B] the daughter of Waledar, king of the Ruthenians—for there are many kings there. Sophia’s mother was the daughter of Boleslav, duke of Poland.

> [Note: [Col. 0737D] Our author rightly calls Waledar, Sophia’s father, king or prince of the Ruthenians. [Col. 0738C] This is affirmed by Saxo, a contemporary witness, p. 266, who declares that Sophia was born of a Ruthenian father. His name, Valadar, also occurs in Snorri Sturluson, vol. II, p. 179, and in the author of the *History of the Knytlingar*, p. 218. These writers, however, are mistaken in calling Valadar king of the Poles. The old Russian annals in *Sammlung Russischer Geschichte*, vol. I, p. 398, do indeed name among the princes of Russia a Wolodar, brother of Wasilko, who was carried off captive by the Poles in 1122. Whether he was the same man who afterwards married the Polish Richeza, widow of Magnus, and by her became father of Queen Sophia, I leave for others to investigate.]

> [Note: [Col. 0738C] The name of Sophia’s mother, Richeza, has been preserved not only by our Icelanders Snorri Sturluson, vol. II, p. 179, and the author of the *Knytlinga Saga*, pp. 182, 206, but also by Alberic, vol. II, p. 290. Długosz, and after him Kromer and Messemus, call her Świętosława, not altogether correctly, unless one wishes to prove that she had two names in her native Poland. That she was called [Col. 0738D] Richeza is also clear from the fact that one of the daughters of Sophia and Waldemar I received the name Richeza from her. Nor had the name previously been unknown in Poland: see Richeza, queen of Poland and wife of Mieszko II, in Mabillon, *Acta SS. Bened.*, vol. IX, pp. 676, 682. Richeza, mother of our Sophia, was daughter of Boleslav III, duke of Poland, whom Saxo [Col. 0739C] Grammaticus, p. 235, calls Bogislav, governor of the Poles, while the author of the *History of the Knytlingar*, pp. 182, 206, calls him Burislav, *Vinda Konung* [king of the Slavs], less correctly. The Polish Richeza was married three times: first, to Magnus, son of Nicholas, king of Denmark, king of the Goths, slain in 1134, to whom she bore Canute V; second, to Valadar, prince of the Ruthenians, to whom about or after 1140 she bore Queen Sophia, wife of Waldemar I; third, to Sverker, king of Sweden, slain in 1151, to whom she bore Boleslav, mentioned in the catalogue of Waldemar II as Sophia’s [Col. 0740C] brother. When Queen Sophia is called Sverker’s daughter in the Ringsted table and elsewhere, this must certainly be understood as meaning his stepdaughter. On Richeza read Gramm’s extensive discussion in his notes on Meursius, pp. 237, 239, 273, 282; compare Eckard, *Genealogia Principum Saxonicorum*, pp. 654, 659.]

## On the holy martyr Canute, most sacred king of the Danes

[Col. 0739A]

Canute, king of the Danes and innocent martyr, slain by evildoers for righteousness’ sake, rests in the church at Odense. How great his merit is before the Lord is testified by frequent miracles even to this day. While he lived, he had as wife Adela, daughter of Robert, count of Flanders, surnamed the Frisian; by her he begot a son named Charles, afterwards count of Flanders. After Canute had passed through martyrdom to the heavenly kingdoms, his wife returned with her little son Charles to her father in Flanders.

## On Charles, count of Flanders, son of the martyr Canute

Charles, afterwards made count of Flanders and slain by traitors for righteousness’ sake, died without children and left the government of Flanders to his cousin Theodoric. This Theodoric, count of Flanders, begot Count Philip and Margaret, countess of Hainaut; from her sprang [Col. 0739B] Isabella, queen of France, who has departed this life.

When these matters have been carefully examined, it is clearer than daylight that Lady Ingeburg, queen of the Franks, has nothing to do with the kinship of the Flemings, and that there is no blood relationship between the aforesaid Queen Isabella and this lady. For the former descends neither from Eric’s lineage, nor does the latter derive her carnal origin from Canute’s descendants.

## Text of Ernst’s edition

[Col. 0730A]

### Chapter I. A.D. 931

HARALD, surnamed Blachtent, that is, “bluish” or “black tooth,” who, fourth after Gorm, was converted from paganism to Christianity; but he apostatized. Consequently he was expelled from the kingdom, fled to the Slavs, who were then pagans, and harassed the kingdom of the Danes with frequent incursions; but he did not prevail.

> [Note: [Col. 0730B] “Who, fourth after,” etc. These words are absent from the Copenhagen manuscript.]

### Chapter II. A.D. 981

[Col. 0732A]

SWEIN, surnamed Forkbeard, received the Christian faith with all his people and persevered faithfully in it. He invaded England and wore it down by repeated attacks in war, but did not completely conquer it everywhere.

> [Note: [Col. 0731B] The copyist of the Laon manuscript wrongly read *Suevo* for *Sveno*. In our native tongue this king was called Sven and Svein. On his runic coins, *Snen*; but by the encomiast of Emma, Svein and Sveinus; by Adam, Svein and Svenotto; by Saxo and Sven Aggesen, Sveno; by Snorri and the Icelanders, Svein and Sveirn. In some old English writers he is called Swain and Swanus.]

### Chapter III. A.D. 1015

CANUTE, surnamed the Great, after his father’s death completely subdued England. His courage and magnificence were so great that he held the monarchy of three kingdoms: England, Denmark, and Norway. He also subdued the Bohemians, Pomeranians, Slavs, Savii, Hermini, [Col. 0734A] all devoted to pagan rites. He gave his daughter in marriage to the emperor of the Romans.

### Chapter IV. A.D. 1037

CANUTE, son of the preceding king, surnamed the Hard, content with Denmark and Norway, yielded England to his brother. [Col. 0736A] He died without offspring; his aunt’s son Sweyn succeeded him in the kingdom.

### Chapter V. A.D. 1051

SWEIN, surnamed the Great, was very powerful and glorious, feared by all surrounding nations, and greatly devoted to the Christian religion. Although he had several sons, mention is made of only two: Eric and Canute.

> [Note: [Col. 0735D] Here, as above, *Suevo* is wrongly read for *Sueno*.]

### Chapter VI. A.D. 1095

ERIC, son of the preceding king, surnamed the Good, [Col. 0736B] visited the Lord’s sepulchre, performed many illustrious deeds on his journey, and on his return died in Cyprus, where he was buried with royal burial. Hence he was called the Cyprian. By Batilda, the noblest woman in all Denmark, he begot Canute the Martyr, who rests at the royal abbey of Ringsted, where he is renowned for miracles even to this day.

### Chapter VII. A.D. 1110

[Col. 0736C] CANUTE, brother of the preceding king, was not king of Denmark but duke, later king of the Slavs, whom he gained powerfully not by inheritance but by arms. He married Engelburges, daughter of Juzillan, king of the Ruthenians, and of Queen Christina; by her he begot Waldemar. The aforesaid Christina, Waldemar’s grandmother, was daughter of Inge, king of the Swedes, and Queen Helena. [Col. 0738A] Christina’s sister Ingelburg married the king of the Hungarians and bore Bela, their glorious king. It follows that Waldemar, king of the Danes, and Bela, king of Hungary, were cousins. Moreover, Canute, king of Sweden, and Livard, king of Norway, were related to them in the second degree of kinship. The brothers of Queen Sophia, who was sister of Ingelburg, [Col. 0737D] Waldemar’s mother, reign gloriously in Russia even to this day.

> [Note: [Col. 0735D] “Brother of the preceding king”: these words have been ineptly interpolated in the Laon manuscript; for Duke Canute was not brother but son of King Eric the Good, and they do not occur in the Copenhagen manuscript.]

> [Note: [Col. 0737D] Sivardus should be read for Livardus; the printer’s error is readily apparent in this name.]

> [Note: [Col. 0737D] Ernst’s edition here gives a false statement.]

### Chapter VIII. A.D. 1153

WALDEMAR, glorious and mighty in his day, begot by Sophia, daughter of Walerda, king of the Ruthenians, Canute, king of the Danes, a religious man. He also begot Canute’s sister Ingelburg, who married Philip, king of France. Nor should the statement concerning Walerda’s daughter, whom Waldemar married, cause concern, since there are many kings in Russia. Canute, [Col. 0740A] brother of Eric, father of Waldemar, an innocent man slain by evildoers for righteousness’ sake, rests as king and martyr in the church at Odense. How great his merits are before God is shown by the frequent miracles occurring there. This Canute took as wife Adela, daughter of Robert, count of Flanders, surnamed the Frisian; by her he begot Charles, afterwards count of Flanders. For when Canute was killed, Adela returned to her father with Charles, still a little boy. Charles, afterwards made count of Flanders, was slain by traitors for righteousness’ sake and died without children. His cousin Theodoric of Alsace succeeded him. He begot Philip, afterwards count of Flanders, and Margaret, countess of Hainaut, by whom was born Isabella, who married Philip, king of France. Isabella’s brothers, [Col. 0740B] Baldwin and Henry, were emperors at Constantinople.

> [Note: [Col. 0740C] “Father of Waldemar”: these words have been wrongly interpolated and are absent from the Copenhagen manuscript; Canute [Col. 0741] the king was by no means Waldemar’s father, but his father’s paternal uncle. Had Ernst observed this, he might have spared his annotations on this passage.]

### Chapter IX. A.D. 1180

Canute, Waldemar’s son, a devout man, gave his sister in marriage to Philip, king of France. Because, on the advice of certain wicked men, he repudiated her and brought in another woman from Germany, the whole kingdom of France lay under an interdict for some time.

*(Thus far the text of Ernst’s edition.)*

[Col. 0739] In the parchment are added connected circles intended to represent the generations; but they adhere badly together and are insufficiently shaped to correspond to the course of the genealogy, and so I have omitted to copy them.
