> [Note: [Col. 0740C] These are the words of Árni Magnússon.]

In these circles certain human heads, crudely executed, have begun to be painted; in the last circle slight traces of two faces appear. The circles, however, should, according to the writer’s intention, stand as displayed in this diagram.

[Col. 0741] The two seated together below are Canute, the pious, mighty, and glorious king of the Danes, and his sister, the venerable and devout queen of the Franks, the noble Lady Ingeburg.

[Col. 0741]

## Revelation of the relics of Saint Genevieve

*(This small work, which Bollandus published anonymously from a Brussels manuscript in the* Acta Sanctorum, *January, vol. I, 3 January, p. 152, is entitled thus in a manuscript preserved in the Royal Library at Paris: “Treatise of Saint William, abbot, on the revelation of the head of Saint Genevieve.” See* Histoire littéraire de la France, *by Benedictine religious, vol. XVI, Paris, 1824, quarto, p. 454.)*

[Col. 0741A] 1. In the year 1161 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, while the most pious King Louis, son of Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, was reigning, a royal edict was issued throughout the realm requiring all prelates of churches, with all the nobles, to hold a council at Paris concerning the welfare of the kingdom. On the appointed day all who had been summoned assembled in the city and began privately to deliberate upon the honorable advantage of the realm. Since malignant men are always spurred on toward worse malice, certain enemies of religion and honesty came forward, and, like a sharpened sword against God’s saints, armed their tongue.

What more need be said? A false accusation reached the royal ears: namely, that the head of the most blessed virgin Genevieve was not in [Col. 0741B] our church. The king’s mind, stained by rumors of this matter, was greatly disturbed and his countenance darkened. Both clergy and people were consulted; after sharing their counsel, they came without delay to our church. So that no other head might that very night be placed by the brothers in the shrine in which the venerable virginal body rested, the shrine itself was secured with the royal seal. On the following day, at the beginning of the first hour, venerable lords were sent by the king’s command to our church, namely the bishops of Sens and Auxerre. There also came the bishop of Orléans, named Manasses, worthy rather of oblivion than remembrance, an enemy of truth and a most ready persecutor of religion and honesty, with a great multitude of people.

At last discussion arose among them [Col. 0742A] concerning the opening of the shrine. The aforesaid most cunning changer of crimes, in order to cloak with an appearance of virtue the wickedness conceived in his heart, poured forth floods of tears and was the first to begin singing the antiphon of the most holy virgin. Without delay our Lady was removed from her holy place; the seal of royal authority was removed, the shrine was opened, and the body of the most holy virgin, its wrappings taken away, was exposed before our eyes. Examining the whole virginal body carefully with our eyes, we burst forth in praise of God with inexpressible exultation, singing *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God.” The tears of the people flowed more abundantly: they had first expected our ruin, but now congratulated us in our rejoicing.

[Col. 0742B] 2. “There is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isaiah 48:22). Thus, where the righteous rejoice and praise, the sinner is confounded and blasphemes. For it is written: “When the sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3). Therefore, the bishop of Orléans, carried away by the whole spirit of his malice, falsely asserted that the head of the venerable virgin had been removed and that another head had been substituted by the deceit of some wretched old woman. Unable to conceal the evil he had conceived in his heart, wholly turned to fraud, he came to the king, leaving the aforesaid bishops behind. With insolent talk he repeated the same account he had begun above and falsely asserted that the aforesaid bishops, having failed to find the virgin’s head, had departed in anger. Yet that which [Col. 0743A] wickedness fabricated after the manner of lying . . . did not succeed.

3. The venerable bishop of Sens had gone out before the people as a witness to the truth. He explained in detail how some had come to doubt whether the head of the most holy virgin was in her church, and how then the body had been found whole with all its limbs. “We rejoice,” he said, “that we have found the head of this most holy virgin, who is the glory of all Gaul, together with her body in its entirety. And lest this matter ever become doubtful to you or to posterity, we have thought it proper to declare it to you.” The aforesaid prelate had spoken these and very many other things in the hearing of the people which might have restrained the excessive and shameless boldness of our enemy, had that been granted from above.

But [Col. 0743B] because it was then the hour and power of darkness, so that his wickedness might be found worthy of hatred, he tried by every means possible to turn the king’s mind against us to evil. Since reason or counsel was now of no use—for royal majesty had already been stirred against us—it occurred to them to send after the oft-mentioned bishops, so that truth, subsequently confirmed by their testimony, might shine out before the king’s eyes. Certain brothers were therefore sent with great haste to Melun. They set before the hearing of the aforesaid venerable fathers the detestable perversity of the bishop of Orléans, and earnestly explained that they should not refuse to make the truth of the matter known to royal clemency through the tenor of their letters. Therefore those men of peace and lovers of truth, [Col. 0743C] moved by the prayers of our brothers and graciously granting assent to their just petitions, wrote back to royal majesty, declaring the truth of the matter in this fashion:

4. By command of royal serenity, we came to the church of the holy virgin Genevieve and caused the shrine in which that virgin rests to be opened in our presence. Carefully inspecting its interior with eyes and hands, we found beyond doubt the most holy body complete with its head and all its limbs, whole and . . . . We therefore burst forth with great rejoicing in praise of God upon finding this, and immediately took care to proclaim it to the people standing around. This, and nothing else, we report to our lord. Behold, by this letter we inform you a second time, that malicious men, whose study it is to corrupt good things so that truth may be obscured by detraction . . . . Farewell in the Lord.

[Col. 0744A] 5. The mild king’s mind, soothed by the testimony of such great men, drove far from himself all darkness of the aforesaid doubt, and loved and protected our church, as before—indeed, more earnestly than before. Thus, after truth came to light, impiety grieved that it had been deceived. From that time onwards the lion of Orléans became a dragon from a lion, no longer openly vomiting forth the poison of his wickedness, but doing so in secret. And because, when the head has been crushed, the remaining limbs retain no strength, when the Lord had turned back the jaws of the lions into their own mouths, his accomplices, ministers [Col. 0744B] of confusion, sons of perdition, and our enemies were confounded because God rejected them. Therefore, since we have been rescued from power and from the snare of hunters, let us all say, let each of us sing: “The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Psalm 124 [123]).

6. Our Lady was revealed in the year 1161 of the Incarnate Word, in the month of January, on the tenth day of the month, within the octave of that most holy virgin; and she was sweetly celebrated before God by the brothers. On the third day following she was raised with hymns and spiritual songs to her holy place from which she had been removed. In memory of so great a joy following our previous grief, after taking counsel with our brothers and receiving their common agreement, we have decreed that this same day be solemnly venerated by us and our successors, [Col. 0744C] so that this solemnity shall always possess no less devotion and every observance than is offered on the feast-day of her nativity. We have also arranged that every year the text of this event should be read on that same day, so that the righteous may have cause for rejoicing and the sinner’s conscience find what may pierce it; so that it may be a grace of blessing to the well-disposed, but to the ill-disposed and those who hate peace, a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.

On the octave of John the Evangelist there is Genevieve’s celebrated feast; on the day after Simon and Jude, her Translation; on the day after Catherine, the Excellence, called the Feast of her Miracles.

[Col. 0743]

## Fragment of the instrument by which Saint William founded the anniversary observance of Absalon, archbishop of Lund, who died in 1201

*(Scriptores Rerum Danicarum, VI, 79, from the Bartholin manuscript B or T 2, after the first Copenhagen fire.)*

[Col. 0743D] . . . . .tus of the same church had formerly been in danger at sea, it pleased him that it should be transferred to the cloister elsewhere where it now stands, which the Latins call, from the [Col. 0744D] name Paraclete, and Danish laymen Ebblaeholt. But lest we should be too greatly burdened if the lands possessed by the church remained too far from us, in exchange for the land which the church held at Gudenso,

> [Note: [Col. 0745A] Today Gundsømagle, in the prefecture of Roskilde and the district of Somme.]

and for that which was ours at Julighe, while retaining for ourselves the mill,

> [Note: [Col. 0745A] Today Jyllinge, in the same prefecture.]

and also for that which it possessed at Synderby, we received that at Frideslovae, that at Geretorpp,

> [Note: [Col. 0745A] Today Gierdrup, in the same place.]

that at Hals, and that at Tyereby,

> [Note: [Col. 0745A] Perhaps Tiereby, in the same place.]

namely half a *boll*, and that at Valby towards Roskilde,

> [Note: [Col. 0745A] Perhaps Valdbybille, or Little Valdby, in the same place.]

its own lands, namely Frideslovae, Thaerby, Naedeveth with its fishery, which belongs to it alone; and these are indeed wooded lands. Nor should this be omitted: over thirty-six years, because it must be brought to light how much we received from his benefices. [Col. 0746A] Therefore let all who wish to know recognize that in one of the aforesaid years we received from his money twenty marks of silver; in one year eight marks of silver, in another six, in a certain one four, in another twelve, in another sixteen; and there was no year among the aforesaid in which we received less than six marks, except one, as we remember. Therefore every year, on the day of his anniversary, we have decreed that twelve poor persons be fed with bread, ale, and meat or fish, so that his soul may obtain with the Lord the place of the blessed in the life to come. Amen.

> [Note: [Col. 0746A] Namely of Archbishop Absalon, who gave all the aforesaid things to the monks at Eskilsø; and since Absalon died in 1201 and bestowed his benefices on them for thirty-six years, namely from the time of Saint William’s arrival in Denmark, it follows that William came to Denmark in 1165.]

[Col. 0745]

## Charters of Saint William and others relating to the church and monastery of Saint Thomas of the Paraclete and to the abbey of Saints Thomas and William at Ebbelholt

### Notice

These charters have been transcribed from an old parchment codex once possessed by Otto, count of Rantzau, and afterwards given, among other books, to the Library of the University of Copenhagen by Christian, count of Rantzau. Part of this codex—namely, the privileges—was also copied in the hand of Árni Magnússon into the Bartholin manuscripts, vol. B or I, formerly before the second Copenhagen fire, and is found there on pp. 533–593. It seemed proper also to add these charters because they concern the monastery whose founder and first abbot was Saint William. The entire codex, containing both privileges and donations, was copied by Langebek in 1736; following it, we provide this edition, since the codex itself, though anxiously sought, has not yet been found. Certain charters taken from other sources, from Raynald, Stephen of Tournai, and others, have also been added.

> [Note: [Col. 0745C] We give only those documents which do not extend beyond Saint William’s lifetime. Patristic Edition.]

### I. [1171.]

Absalon, bishop of Roskilde, receives the church of Blessed Thomas at Eskilsø under his protection; confirms its possessions; and confers many benefices and privileges upon it.

> [Note: [Col. 0745C] Bartholin, manuscript *Annals*, under the year 1171: “From these letters of Absalon it may probably be concluded that Saint [Col. 0746C] William and the brothers were still at Eskilsø in this year; they were transferred to the Paraclete (Saint Ebelholt) at some time between this year and 1178.”]

[Col. 0745B]

ABSALON, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Roskilde, to his dearest son WILLIAM, abbot of Saint Thomas at Eskilsø, and to his brothers, present and future: greeting and paternal blessing.

It was long ago proclaimed by the mouth of Isaiah, who says: “I will make rivers into islands, and I will dry up pools; and I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, and make them walk in paths which they have not known” (Isaiah 42). This promise is continually fulfilled in the Church of God, [Col. 0745C] when those who long sat in darkness and the shadow of death, enlightened by the light of heavenly brightness, return to the way [Col. 0746B] of truth, and when a holy nation, a people for possession (1 Peter 2), is brought into that Church for divine service—in which certain persons who had assumed the religious habit but did not love the power of religion, dishonoring the ministry of clerics by their shameful manner of life, had formerly seemed to live.

We see that this has occurred through divine mercy in the church of Blessed Thomas at Eskilsø. Although certain canons once lived there quite dishonorably and outrageously, through our effort and diligence you have been introduced to perform divine services; and the church itself, sprinkled with heavenly dew, has received a faithful planting and a shoot pleasing to God, though formerly, because of sins, it produced thorns and briars. Since we see this occurring in our own time, we render thanks to the Lord, Creator of all; and we wish that those religious institutions which we see should be kept inviolate [Col. 0746C] and immovably preserved in their condition. We receive the aforesaid church, with the whole island upon which it is situated, under God’s protection and ours, and confirm it by the protection of this present document.

First, we decree that the canonical order which is recognized as established there according to the Rule of God and of blessed Augustine, and according to the institution and observance of the brethren of Saint Victor at Paris, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future be able, God willing, to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm, unimpaired, and perpetual to you and your successors. [Col. 0747B] Of these we have thought certain ones should be named expressly:

The village of Terby, with all its possessions, and the church of the same village—which, for the salvation of our soul, we have bestowed upon you as a benefice, free and absolved from every disturbance and exaction of all our successors—together with the fields and woods of that village, whether those which you previously possessed or those which you later received there from our hand in exchange for the land of Hals. We also confirm by this present charter that you shall possess the third part of the tithe which accrued to us throughout that parish, and that it shall be conveyed to your barn situated within that parish by all who cultivate the lands of the same parish, in their own carts. [Col. 0747C]

For the discharge of the office of the church of the aforesaid village, you shall always appoint whichever one of your brethren you prefer; and whenever it pleases you, you may recall him to your cloister for any need or advantage, provided that the church itself is not deprived of its service. But if it should happen that you prefer the service of the same church to be performed not by one of your canons but rather by another priest, we nevertheless wish this to remain within our discretion. If necessity should arise for us or for any of our successors that another neighboring church must be built, because that parish may seem to some to extend too far in length, neither we nor any of our successors may take from the tithes of your aforesaid church more than a fourth part [Col. 0747D] and assign it to the new church.

The land at Hathaelosae, both fields and meadows; the holding which you have at Juleghe, with its fields, meadows, and nearby mill; and the church of the same village with the tithes and offerings belonging to it, which likewise we have granted you to possess in perpetuity on the terms set forth above. We also confirm by this present charter that you shall possess the third part of the tithe which accrued to us in the same parish, and that it shall be conveyed to your barn situated within that parish by all who cultivate the lands of the same parish in their own carts.

The holding which you have at Guthenso, [Col. 0748A] with the fields and meadows pertaining to it. We also confirm by this present charter that you shall possess the third part of the tithe which accrued to us throughout the same parish, and that it shall be conveyed to your barn situated within that parish by all who cultivate the lands of the same parish in their own carts. We also confirm by this present charter that you shall possess the third part of the tithe which accrued to us throughout the parish of Kyrkethorp, and that it shall be conveyed to your barn situated within that parish by all who cultivate the lands of that parish in their own carts.

The holding which you have at Gaerethorp, with the fields and meadows of the same holding; the holding which you have at Synderby, with fields and meadows [Col. 0748B] and the share which you have hitherto possessed in the wood of that village; the land at Thureslovae; and the land at Aranachae.

When you, now abbot of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it through any trickery or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, have provided should be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. We also decree and forbid that any of your canons, after making profession in your monastery, may transfer to another cloister; nor may anyone dare retain one who has been received without your permission.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly [Col. 0748C] disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things are to be preserved whole for the use and support of those for whose governance and sustenance they have been granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to oppose it, and after a second or third warning does not correct his presumption by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power or office; let him know that he is answerable before divine judgment for the wickedness committed; let him be alienated and anathematized from the most sacred body and blood of God our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. [Col. 0748D] Amen.

I, Absalon, bishop of Roskilde, have subscribed, in the year of the Lord 1171.

Given by the hand of Absalon, bishop of Roskilde.

I, Walter, chaplain, have subscribed.

### II. [Between 1171 and 1178.]

Absalon, bishop of Roskilde, confirms to William, abbot of Saint Thomas of the Paraclete, and the brothers of the same church those things which they obtained from him by exchange or gift.

ABSALON, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Roskilde, to all the faithful in Christ, future as well as present, forever.

[Col. 0749A] The authority of our office urges us not to be found sluggish or negligent in those matters demanded by the advantage of religious persons, but ready, devout, and eager. For thus we shall be able to offer God service pleasing to him, if he finds our aid ready in his need. Therefore let future and present persons know that we have been so moved by the petitions of our venerable and dearest son William, abbot of Saint Thomas of the Paraclete, and of the brethren of the same church, that we have resolved to fortify with a special privilege those things which they have obtained from us by just exchange or voluntary gift. Since we do not wish that this matter should ever expose either the aforesaid church or its brethren to the assaults or any calumnies of wicked men, we have taken care to commit it to this present [Col. 0749B] charter.

For the entire village of Naeveth with its wood, meadows, fields, and fisheries, and those of Clonae; for Therby and Fretersloff with their woods, meadows, and fields, we received many lands in various places. In exchange for the third part of the tithes which they had previously held in the four churches of Thorstenstorp, Akaetorp, Kyrkaetorp, and Guthenso, we compensated them with it in four other churches, namely Craekym, Helsinghe, Annessae, and Alsaentorp.

> [Note: [Col. 0749] In a later marginal hand: Kregome, Helsinge, Annesse, Alsyndrop.]

We bestowed upon them, for the remedy of our soul, the two churches of Therby and Fretersloff with their tithes. We granted freedom to their possessions, so that no one might presume to demand tithes from lands which they cultivate by their own labor and expense, or to harass their peasants on account of the brethren themselves under pretext of our justice. [Col. 0749C] Whoever attempts to invalidate this charter . . . .

### III. [About 1175.] Confirmation of Alexander

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons William, abbot of the church of Saint Thomas of the Paraclete, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: forever.

“The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things,” etc. It is printed in *Patrologia*, vol. CC, col. 1039, under Alexander III.

### IV. [1178.]

William, abbot, under sentence of excommunication, forbids Eskilsø to be sold or exchanged by the monastery of Blessed Thomas of the Paraclete. Undated. Bartholin assigns it to the year 1178.

[Col. 0749D]

It belongs to the office of all prelates not only to proclaim to their subjects the joys of the heavenly homeland which are to be sought, but also to provide for their temporal livelihood, lest, if they lack either of these, divine severity rebuke the prelates for the fault of negligence. Therefore I, William, called abbot by the grace of God, guarding against the snares of wicked men and wishing to ward off the bites of wolves from the sheepfolds, do not wish so to devote effort to external affairs that any temporal care can turn their minds [Col. 0750A] away from divine offices.

Accordingly, considering and weighing the good things which divine grace has conferred upon us, we have turned our attention to the island of Eskil. We have recognized it to be very useful both for gathering the fruit of its trees and for feeding animals on its pastures. Therefore, by the common counsel and consent of our brethren, we have resolved that it is to be retained by us in perpetuity without any exchange of lands. And whoever dissents from this constitution and wishes to violate it should know himself to be bound by the bonds of anathema through the mouths of all the priests then present. Let it be done, let it be done. Amen, amen.

V. [About 1178.] Confirmation by Abbot William of the settlement between the monasteries of Ebelholt and Esrom concerning certain tithes and other disputed matters. Undated. I suspect it belongs to the year 1178 or thereabouts.

[Col. 0750B]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God unworthy minister of Blessed Thomas of Paraclete, to all whom these letters shall reach, greeting.

The more worthily the observance of most holy religion is raised in the beauty of virtues by the prerogative of merits, the more completely the devil—enemy of charity, assailant of justice, fuel of discord, instigator of vices, son of perdition—is excluded from the sacred folds of the sheep. Therefore we, who, though unworthy, have received a place of governance in the Church of God, must take greater care that the Lord’s flock entrusted to us, advancing through our words and examples, may always rise to better things and rejoice in the tranquillity of peace; [Col. 0750C] lest, if perhaps the poison of discord infects simple hearts, the whole fabric of virtues collapse, and, while it disfigures the grace of honourable conduct, our ministry be reproached among the professors of the Christian faith.

Accordingly, that peace and affection between ourselves and our venerable brethren of Esrom may remain uninjured, we wish it to come to the knowledge of all that, now that every discord has ceased which, through intervening sins, appeared to have arisen between us and them: concerning certain tithes of the parish church of Tyereby, which they had diverted to their own use, to our loss; concerning the enticement away of one of our canons, whom they had received into their order contrary to the tenor of the lord pope’s privilege; and concerning a certain road leading to Sponholt, which had been closed against our passage—[Col. 0750D] peace and concord now reign, on this condition: henceforth they shall not acquire land to be held in the aforesaid parish except through colonists; they shall not receive our brethren without the security of reciprocal letters; and they shall provide for us a suitable and convenient road from Towekop to Sponholt through the territory of their grange.

In return for the tithe of the lands which they now possess in the parish of Tyereby—namely, at Sponholt, Skwroth, Stry, and Towekopp—they have obtained from Lord Archbishop Absalon, to hold in perpetuity, the tithe at Lutztorpp, which belonged to that same bishop. And that [Col. 0751A] these provisions may not hereafter be invalidated by any evasions, by the assent of both parties, namely ourselves and them, we have caused them to be authenticated by the impression of our seal and by our name-sign, with the names of our brethren written below.

I, William, abbot of Saint Thomas of Paraclete. I, Hesbert, prior. I, Richard, subprior.

[lacuna] The remaining names are missing, for here a leaf of the parchment is lacking.

VI. [About 1178. [Note: [Col. 0751D] Thus the Bartholin Annals, or somewhat later.]] Absalon, Archbishop of Lund, confirms to the brethren of the church of Blessed Thomas of Paraclete all their possessions. Undated. Bartholin assigns it to the year 1178.

[Col. 0751B]

ABSALON, by the grace of God Archbishop of the holy Church of Lund, primate of Denmark and Sweden, to all the faithful in Christ, both future and present, for ever.

Divine providence has appointed some persons to be set over others in the Church so that those whom piety would not invite to rewards might be more sternly compelled, even unwillingly, by judicial censure. Hence the Lord has raised even us, though unworthy, to the episcopal throne, so that we may love religious men with paternal affection and advance them by material assistance; and so that unbelievers, corrupters, and oppressors of the poor, if we cannot correct them by word, may be condemned by ecclesiastical judgment and example, in order that, delivered to Satan for the destruction [Col. 0751C] of the flesh, they may at last recover from the devil’s snare and their spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Since, therefore, we know that the religious brethren in the church of Blessed Thomas of Paraclete are devoted to divine offices, we wish to assist those brethren with the patronage of our favour whenever they need and request it, lest either they or their goods should in any way be attacked by hostile incursions. We have also decreed that the order which is known to have been established there, through our care and labour, according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of Saint Victor at Paris, shall be observed inviolably in that same church for all time and shall not be altered in any respect.

We therefore receive the aforesaid church with all its goods under our protection [Col. 0751D] and command that it be perpetually secured by this present charter, marked with the impression of our seal, the names of the possessions of the aforesaid church being written below.

The island of Eschilli, on which they are known first to have dwelt, together with the church situated on it; and we decree that this island with that church belongs to the cloister of Paraclete as a member of that house. The church of Julighe, with the land and tithe belonging to it; likewise the dwelling in that same village belonging to the same house with all its appurtenances; and the mill situated near Vaerebro. The church of Thaeraeby and the dwelling situated there [Col. 0752A] with fields, meadows, and woods; the dwelling at Wlueroth with fields, meadows, and woods; the dwelling at Hathelosae with fields, meadows, and woods; the whole village called Naeueth, with all its land, meadows, and woods, free from every claim and legal challenge; and the fisheries of the Clona and others which they hold in common with the other people. A court-house in the city of Roskilde, with its houses and enclosure.

One third of the tithes in the churches of Anessae, Haelsinghe, Craekhom, and Alsentorp, and the entire tithe in the church of Thaerby, which the aforesaid brethren possess partly for the service of that church, partly hold from us, and partly have obtained as benefices from the parishioners for the service of such a church—excepting the repair of the bells and walls of that church, should they happen to fall. The village called Frethersloff, with fields, woods, meadows, and mills, and the church of that village with its tithes.

And that this charter of our enactment may remain whole and ratified, and may not be weakened in any way either by a legal challenge or by the cunning of anyone’s deceit, we decree that whoever attempts to violate it, whether an ecclesiastical or secular person, shall be bound by the bonds of excommunication and shall be deprived of the body and blood of God and our Redeemer at the last judgment, unless the offence of such rashness has been corrected by fitting satisfaction.

VII. [About 1178. [Note: [Col. 0752D] Or later.]]

WALBERT, by the grace of God abbot of Esrom, to all [Col. 0752C] whom these letters shall reach, greeting.

How good it is for men who fear God to be bound by the bonds of peace is shown by the fall of the angels. Though they could have lived in concord, endowed with perpetual blessedness, they became discordant from the highest good and fell through pride. The fall of elders ought to serve as a warning to their juniors. Therefore, lest the same gulf of wickedness should likewise enclose us and our brethren and neighbours of Paraclete—whom on some occasion, for certain reasons, we perceived to be stirred against us by the gall of discord—now that every complaint has ceased, we love them, bound by the laws of affection toward us, and rejoice that they are well-disposed.

For the restoration of concord, then, bound by a covenant of peace, we leave them no ground for complaints to bring against us; and by the tenor of the present document we have thought fit to record the following: the tithe which belonged to the lord archbishop at Lunztorp is, by the concession and gift of that bishop, left to them to possess in perpetuity, in exchange for the tithes of our granges which our brethren cultivate in the parish of Tyeraeby, namely at Swenstorp, Skwroth, Sponholt, and Thoaekopp, lands assessed at four solidi. We may neither receive nor retain their canons without the security of reciprocal letters. We have promised that we shall by no means enter their parish or their lands except lands held through their own colonists. We shall open for them a suitable and entirely unobstructed road from Towekopp to Sponholt through [Col. 0753A] the territory of our grange.

And that all these provisions may remain whole and inviolate, we have thought fit to strengthen this present charter by the impression of our seal and to validate it by our hands and those of our brethren as well.

I, Brother Walbert, abbot of Esrom. I, Brother Torbern, prior. I, Brother Helgo, subprior. I, Brother Peter, cellarer. I, Brother Peter. I, Brother Ebbo. I, Brother Jocep.

VIII. [1178.] Confirmation of Pope Alexander.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [Col. 0753B] WILLIAM, abbot of Blessed Thomas of Paraclete, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

“The pious request of willing devotion,” etc. See Alexander III, no. 1361, *Patrologia*, vol. CC.

IX. [1179.] Concerning a mill and wood near Graesae.

In the year of the Lord 1179, the prudent man Tosthae, living at Graesae, of his own free will granted us a mill, with a portion of woodland situated eastward beside Graesae, because of the disputes and insults he had previously inflicted upon our Father William.

X. [About 1184.] Stephen of Sainte-Geneviève to William, abbot of Paraclete.—He requests lead from him.

[Col. 0753C]

To his venerable brother and friend William, abbot of Paraclete, Stephen of Sainte-Geneviève, growing old in old age: fullness of joys in the fullness of days.

“We praise the ancients, yet use our own years,” etc. See *Patrologia*, vol. CCXI, under Stephen of Tournai, epistle 148.

XI. [1185, 28 June.]

To all who behold this present writing, GRIMOLPHUS Wlffsson, greeting in the Lord.

By these presents I make known to those born and yet to be born that I have entirely granted to the prudent and religious men, Abbot Vilhelm and the whole convent of the monastery of Saint Thomas of Paraclete at [Col. 0753D] Ebbleholt, for the remedy and salvation of my soul and those of my forebears, to possess by perpetual right, my goods situated at Mynghe: namely, one dwelling with all its appurtenances, near or distant, with none excepted. This is on the condition that the said lords shall yearly devoutly perform for me and my parents a Mass with vigils, and that after my death I shall have free burial there.

In testimony of this matter and for firmer security, my seal has been appended to the present document.

Given at Mynghe in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1185, on the Vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul.

Rent from Mynghe: 5 pounds of provisions.

XII. [About 1193.] Confirmation of Pope Celestine.

[Col. 0754A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of the church of Saint Thomas of Paraclete, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

“The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, provider of all good things,” etc. See *Patrologia*, vol. CCVI, under Celestine III, no. 206.

XIII. Confirmation by King Canute of the settlement, made through Chancellor Andrew and others, between the canons of Paraclete and the king’s colonists concerning the Clona fishery. [Bartholin, in his manuscript Annals, assigns it to the year 1195.]

[Col. 0754B]

CANUTE, by the grace of God king of the Danes and Slavs, to all the faithful, both present and future, for ever.

For this purpose divine mercy has granted us lordship over peoples: that whatever discord may have been introduced among them through error at the devil’s persuasion may, through our care, be purged by means of the sickle of judgment. Thus we shall render service pleasing and due to God, and a more excellent glory of good merits shall accrue to the royal crown. For we know, and cannot deny, that the more worthily the observance of most holy religion is raised in the beauty of virtues by the prerogative of merits, the more completely the devil—enemy of charity, assailant of justice, fuel of discord, instigator of vices, son of perdition—is excluded from the sacred folds of the sheep.

Therefore we, as said above, who have received the helm of the kingdom, must take greater care that the Lord’s flock, subject to cloistered discipline, may always rise to better things under our protection and rejoice in the tranquillity of peace; lest, if perhaps the poison of discord infects simple hearts, the whole fabric of virtues collapse, and, while it disfigures the grace of honourable conduct, their ministry be brought into reproach among the professors of the Christian faith.

Accordingly, because the abbot of Saint Thomas of Paraclete and the brethren of that church, and our colonists, were in dispute concerning a certain fishery called Clona, which each side claimed as its own [Note: [Col. 0753D] Correct: “each side” (*utrique*).], they came before [Col. 0754D] us, and each party vigorously laid out its complaint. Our men indeed said that they had suffered no slight injury because [Note: [Col. 0753D] Read: “because” (*quia).] the aforesaid brethren had forcibly and violently carried off the fish which they had caught. On the other hand, the brethren said that they possessed those same fish by right, asserting that the water from which they had been taken belonged by right to the church.

Since we could not obtain full knowledge of the matter, wishing to settle their dispute, we sent from our side our chancellor A[ndrew], [Note: [Col. 0754D] Andrew, son of Suno, provost of Roskilde.] provost of Saint Lucius, and his brother Ebbo, together with our faithful man Torbern, to investigate the truth; and we command by royal authority that the settlement [Col. 0755A] which they made between the two parties shall remain acceptable [Note: [Col. 0755D] Perhaps “ratified” (*ratam*). *Gratam* frequently occurs for *ratam*, or *gratam ratam* occurs.] and inviolate in the future.

The settlement is as follows. If our steward wishes to fish with his men in that water which the brethren claim as their right, and which they obtained from the archbishop in an exchange of lands, they may do so; but from the catch that accrues to them, the cloistered brethren shall receive the share which would fall to each individual. If the cloistered brethren wish to fish in the water which they say is ours, this too shall be permitted to them without opposition; and our men shall likewise receive the portion which would fall to one of them. From the place called in Danish Yadehr as far as the hedges, neither the cloistered brethren shall enter our portion nor our men [Col. 0755B] theirs without the permission of both parties.

So that this may not be erased by forgetfulness, we have caused this present charter to be secured by our name-sign and the impression of our seal, with the names of the witnesses who were present written below: Lord A., chancellor, and Ebbo his brother; Nicholas, provost; Torbern, our faithful man; Thurgot, priest of Stro; Swnnae of Wlveroth; Awti, steward of Ramlosae; and many others.

XIV. [About 1196.] Ordinance of Lord Abbot William concerning the manner in which his anniversary shall be observed after his death.

Just as, in giving counsel and conducting affairs, the perversity of wicked men must always be guarded against and restrained, so, once counsel has been given and affairs disposed, whatever the authority of elders ordains with justice must be approved and observed. For the horns of sinners will not be broken more effectively than if what elders have decreed with goodwill and reverence for God enjoys the freedom of integrity and is secured by the root of perpetuity.

I therefore, William, by the grace of God called abbot of Blessed Thomas of Paraclete, wish all to know what I have pondered in my heart and devoutly carried out in deed. Seeing that the duty of pastoral care frequently separates me from the repose and sweetness of contemplation that I have sometimes tasted, and compels me to concern myself with secular affairs, while spiritual pursuits are interrupted, [Col. 0755D] I thought it fitting to provide some remedy for myself, [Col. 0756A] by which fraternal charity, when the days of my life have run their course, may obtain for me through prayers a place among the companies of angels.

Therefore, so that every year, on the day of my death, they may perform a festal office throughout for me, I have assigned to those brethren, on the day of my death, one mark of silver for a full refectory meal for the brethren—of wheaten bread, fish, and mead—from the two churches acquired by my labour, namely Tyereby and Frithersloff. Twelve poor persons must also be supported on that day with bread, beer, and meat if it is the season, or with fish.

As long as I survive, the same provision shall be made on the anniversary of the death of my lord, the abbot of Saint-Germain of Paris; after his collect, the remembrance of my father Rodulf and my mother Emelina shall always be observed, and both collects shall conclude with one *Per Dominum* [“Through the Lord”]. And lest any claim or deceit might violate this charter of our ordinance, with the assent of the entire chapter, while stoles hung around the priests’ necks, we caused a sentence of excommunication to be publicly pronounced. Whoever, therefore, breaks this decree, after a first or second warning, if he does not make full satisfaction, shall be excluded from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. So be it, so be it. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0756D] Written in the margin beside these two lines: “It scarcely still holds.”] Episcopal tithes at Craekom.

Rent from tithes at Craekom: 6 pounds of provisions.

XV. Newlinghe.

[Col. 0756C] To all Christ’s faithful to whom this present document shall come, GWNIL BOOSDOTHER, greeting and charity in the Son of the Virgin.

I make known to present and future persons that I acknowledge that I have entirely granted and conveyed to the religious men, the canons of Saint William of Paraclete, all my goods situated at Newlinghe, namely one small holding with everything adjoining it—meadows, fields, and woods—with none removed, for the remedy and salvation of the souls of my most beloved parents and of myself, by the assent and counsel of my brothers Peter Boosson and Agghae Boosson, to be possessed in perpetuity. In testimony of this matter, the seal of my beloved brother Peter Boosson, together with [Col. 0756D] the seal of Sigmund Aggaeson, has been appended to the present document.

## Appendix to Saint William

[Col. 0755]

# Testament of Absalon, Archbishop of Lund

(Langebeck, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, vol. V, p. 422.)

## Preface

This testament was published by the most distinguished and learned Otto Sperling under the title: *Testament of Lord Absolon, Archbishop of Lund, recovered from the best manuscripts and illustrated with notes by Otto Sperling, Doctor of Both Laws, royal counsellor, and public professor of history and eloquence at the Royal Equestrian Academy in Copenhagen*. Copenhagen: printed by Johann Jacob Bornheinrich, 1696, in octavo.

The manuscript used by Sperling was formerly owned by the great Harald Hvitfeld, a man made greater and more illustrious by his history than by the office of chancellor which he held. Permission to publish it was granted by the celebrated Johannes Laurentii, great-grandson of Andreas Velleius. There was formerly a paper manuscript in the public library at Copenhagen, in Cyprian’s case, third order, quarto; it perished in the fatal fire of 1728. A copy nevertheless still survives in volume III or D of the Bartholinian manuscripts, and agrees with Sperling’s edition both in words and syllables.

We have therefore arranged for Sperling’s edition to be printed in its entirety, retaining both the dedication and the learned notes of that most erudite man, though they are more extensive and fuller than ours, lest we appear to have cut away anything useful, and so that those wishing to read Sperling’s work unabridged may have the opportunity. What we have judged fit to add is enclosed in brackets, so that it may be distinguished from Sperling’s material.

## Letter

To the most illustrious and noble lord, Lord John RANTZOVIUS, distinguished commander of the army, formerly called brigadier, and commander of the cavalry squadrons of His Royal Majesty of Denmark and Norway, etc.; hereditary lord of Frydendal, Brammingen, Orslefcloster, Strandoe, and Bistrup; my patron, never not to be venerated: thanks, good wishes, and greeting.

What is yours ought rightly, most illustrious lord, to return to you. You made it yours when by your persuasion you urged the publication of this modest work; it is yours also because you chose that it should appear at your own expense and through your great generosity. For a long time now presses have ceased to be burdened or heated except by certain necessary works which time brings forward and presses upon us, rather than learning; and if printers were now permitted to concern themselves only with necessities, not so many trifles and scraps would be sold throughout the world for reading everywhere.

Patrons indeed are few who either encourage or support writers; for we see that composing or devoting oneself to nightly studies, while at the same time bearing the expense, is scarcely the task of one man. That several patrons have come alive again in you, best of patrons, is not something I need declare in this little preface alone; for you have not deserved so poorly that it should be necessary for your praises to be poured forth from their confines toward such very narrow limits. Whatever I might say, all already know: though raised amid military affairs and distinguished in them, you labour in letters in such a way that by your new example you teach once more that military service needs learning—you who have joined those arts so successfully.

Here, therefore, soldiers have their patron; learned men also have theirs; and citizens of every rank who strive for virtue have theirs—men whom, so far as you can, you desire not merely to help emerge, but who in very great numbers testify and boast that they have been honoured and assisted. The same is true in your household, which seems no less an academy: into it, for your most noble children and grandchildren, you have wished so many teachers and mistresses of every kind of conduct and learning to gather that you maintain an army no less at home than abroad.

Hence nothing can be expected from you except what the ancient RANTZOVS, your ancestors, ardently sought with their highest wishes and vigorously accomplished. Their glory you have now most happily equalled by your merits, or will some day surpass more happily. May God preserve you and yours; and may both the living and posterity know to whom I owe such great thanks, and know that I

remain, most illustrious lord,

devoted to you in humble respect and obedience.

Given at Copenhagen, 30 June.

O. SPERLING.

Testament which our pious father Absalon, archbishop, made before his death.

[Col. 0757A] The venerable [Notes 1, 2] Lord Absalon, Archbishop of the Church of Lund, primate of Sweden, summoned and had present for this purpose his brother Lord Esbern; [Note 3] Lord Geoffrey, abbot of Sorø; [Note 4] Tocho and Acho, provosts; [Note 5] Master John; [Note 6] Thordon, [Note 7] his chaplain, canons of the Church of Lund; Anfrid, priest; Håkon, [Note 8] his chamberlain; Paul and Simon, [Note 9] his boys; and Henry, [Note 10] lay brother of Sorø. In the testament he bequeathed and gave his entire patrimony, except Fialensleve, which he granted to his brother, to the monastery of Sorø.

To the monastery [Note 12] of Aas in Halland, he gave and legally conveyed (*scotavit*) Vathby with all its appurtenances, except the mill. [Col. 0757B] [Note 13]

To the canons’ table of the Church of Lund, he gave and legally conveyed [Note 14] Esbiruth, with the mill at Rogen and all its other appurtenances, all woods and lands. [Note 15]

Likewise he gave and legally conveyed [Note 16] Saxulstorp in Ruma, with the church and all its other appurtenances, to the same brethren [Note 17] for their table.

[Col. 0758A] For wax candles [Note 18] for both crowns and for the night candle [Note 19] in the monastery of Blessed Lawrence, [Note 20] he gave four marks of silver each year from the city rent commonly called [Note 21] *Midsommers Gylde* [Midsummer Guild].

To the venerable Lord Eric, archbishop of Nidaros, [Note 22] in exile for justice’s sake: one hundred marks of silver.

To Martin, bishop of Bergen: fifty marks of silver.

To [Note 23] Nigel, bishop of Stavanger: fifty marks of silver.

To [Note 24] Ivar, bishop of Hamar: fifty marks of silver.

To [Note 25] Nicholas, bishop of Aslo: a silver cup, [Col. 0758B] [Note 26] and the silver bowls which that bishop had formerly given him. [Note 27]

To [Note 28] the lord king he gave a wonderfully fashioned silver cup, [Note 29] which the lord of Nidaros had formerly given him, and a little gold vessel containing musk.

Lord Suno owed him 130 marks of silver; he left that debt to Lord Peter, bishop of Roskilde, and his brethren. [Note 30]

[Col. 0759A] He had granted the bishop of Roskilde fifty marks of silver, less two, for buying Alstofta; he remitted this sum to that bishop and gave him the silver cup which he had formerly given Absalon. [Note 31]

To his brother, [Note 32] the lord chancellor, he bequeathed the silver cup which Lord Suno had formerly given him.

To [Note 33] Lord Esbern he gave a silver cup made by [Note 34] Hildebrand, a small cup from which his father used to take drinks, and to each of Esbern’s sons silver cups from the larger cups.

To [Note 35] Lord Alexander he gave one of the better silver cups, [Note 36] and the coats of mail which he possessed; [Note 37] and to Alexander’s two sons, two modest silver cups.

[Col. 0759B] To [Note 38] Lady Margaret, two cups from the [Note 39] idols of Rügen.

To [Note 40] the canons of Paraclete, a silver cup [Note 41] of plain workmanship, weighing approximately [Note 42] ten marks of silver.

He gave the larger silver cup which Sorø possessed to the chapel of Sorø, [Note 43] to make a chalice.

From his silver bowls he ordered stout and adequate chalices to be made in the monastery of Blessed Lawrence; whatever remained from the aforesaid silver cups and bowls he ordered to be kept for completing [Note 44] the crowns in the church.

[Note 45] Lord Alexander had [Note 46] eight and a half marks of gold for the making of [Note 47] a chasuble and crowns; [Col. 0759C] from this gold I have already caused a large part of the chasuble to be applied.

The priest Eschillus has several gold pieces to be reserved for the same purpose. He ordered all the silver which Liuthger owed him to be distributed to the poor.

The lord archdeacon shall pay the archbishop of Nidaros and the bishops named above from the silver he received for tithes and from the silver held by Lord Alexander; and he ordered that what remained should be faithfully distributed among the monasteries of Scania and Zealand.

Lord Alexander, however, has no silver of his own except what can be established from seven hundred marks [Note 48] of old Danish coinage; and from that silver he ordered Lord Alexander to send sixteen marks to Sorø, to pay certain persons.

The silver which Eric, son of [Col. 0759D] Harina, and his brother Sweyn, and Conrad of Tumethorp owe him—whose total debt is known by the archdeacon—he ordered to be reserved. [Note 49]

He entirely remitted, [Note 50] for the sake of his soul, to Bondo’s heirs the debt which Bondo, son of Gamaliel, owed him for the grant of exactions.

To Eric Batti he gave [Note 51] a fur-lined cloak [Note 52] of marten skins.

To Master Peter, chaplain of the archbishop of Nidaros, he gave a fur-lined cloak of [Note 53] grey squirrel skins.

[Col. 0760A] To the dean of Lund he gave [Note 54] a marten-skin mantle.

To his chaplain Thordon he gave [Note 55] a surplice with marten fur, a cloak [Note 56] lined with vair, and [Note 57] a tunic lined with vair.

To Simon, a smaller tunic lined with grey squirrel fur; to Peter Stamma, an everyday grey mantle.

To Marsilius Coco [Note 58] he gave a fox-fur coverlet.

To Peter [Note 59] the Stableman he gave the horse which Bjorn’s son had given him.

To his brother Wlff he granted the coat of mail which [Note 60] Esbern Mule had given him.

To [Note 61] his chamberlain Håkon he had given the horse which Bondo had given him.

[Col. 0760B] He gave the brown-coloured [Note 62] horse to Håkon the Norwegian.

He left the black horse which he had at Sorø to that same monastery.

He ordered [Note 63] the dappled horse to be given to the lord archbishop of Nidaros.

He granted [Note 64] Eschillus Bathsven his freedom.

The women whom [Note 65] Nicholas the Stableman had taken from freedom into servitude, wherever they may be found, shall be granted freedom together with their children.

He granted freedom to a woman taken from Biargaherred in Scania, together with her children.

To [Note 66] Saxo, his clerk, he granted two and a half marks of silver, which he had given him.

[Col. 0760C] Saxo must return to the monastery of Sorø the two books which the archbishop had granted him.

To [Note 67] Master John he gave [Note 68] a silver drinking-cup.

To [Note 69] Master Walther he gave [Note 70] the grey mantle which he wore at Christmas.

He gave fifteen gold rings with stones, and a sixteenth without a stone, to the monastery of Blessed Lawrence for making [Note 71] a *plenarium* [a book containing the full Gospel readings].

To [Note 72] Provost Acho he gave the smaller silver cup which he had at Sorø.

He gave half the silver which [Note 73] he had at Cluny to that monastery; he ordered the other half to be sent to [Note 74] Clairvaux.

He owed the church of [Note 75] Wellinge silver [Col. 0760D] repayment, the amount of which the archdeacon knows.

He owed the church of Stangby [Note 76] one hide of land, which he had given in exchange for a hide at Kopingh; he ordered that the church at Stangby should have a hide at Kopingh until the debt is repaid from the bishopric.

To a certain prebend he owed half a hide at Huphackre, and he ordered that it should have half a hide at Arleff until the debt is repaid from the bishopric.

To the prebend of Nicholas the nun he owed half a hide at Asmundathorp, and he ordered that it should have half a hide at Nybyle in the parish of Saxulstorp until payment is made from the bishopric.

[Note 77] Master Hugh shall retain the property of his prebend until payment is made from the bishopric.

To the archdeacon he gave a large mantle [Note 78] of Laekatt, if it is there; if it is not there, he gave him a bed-covering lined with marten skins. [Col. 0761A]

To Jofrid Coco, two copes, one of them lined.

He especially charged the archdeacon to complete the bell which he had intended to have made.

To Master Hugh, a bed-covering lined with vair.

To Nicholas, [Note 79] son of the archdeacon, a surplice lined with vair.

[Col. 0762A] To the priest Eschillus, a fur-lined cloak which is [Note 80] in the castle of Copenhagen.

He granted freedom to Christian Coco, who had unjustly been taken into servitude.

He ordered that the archdeacon should treat Acho, master of brickmakers, [Note 81] and Acho the stonemason well.

He gave a silver reliquary-box containing relics to the monastery of Sorø.

May the Lord repay him with a reward in eternal life. Amen.

# Notes on the Preceding Testament

[Col. 0761]

[Col. 0761B] The distinguished manuscript of this testament was shared with me by the most accomplished man and most devoted lover of our antiquities, Lord Johannes Laurentii, great-grandson of that eminent historian Andreas Velleius. He had obtained this manuscript of Harald Hvitfeld, that historian of excellent memory, and it is from this copy that you now see it published here.

In meeting the costs, the distinguished Copenhagen citizen Lord Georgius Mollengracht deserves praise. Although he has not himself been cultivated in more learned letters, he nevertheless loves learning and favours learned men. If many followed his example, the writings of scholars would not be compelled to struggle with cockroaches and moths. I ought to have said this by way of preface in praise of those who helped by counsel, means, or labour.

[Col. 0761C] (1) **Venerable.** This title, after the time of Bede, to whom it was first of all given, pleased ecclesiastical writers; and so they continued to address bishops, emperors, and Roman popes in this manner. Archbishops too were accustomed thus to address emperors and kings, while popes in many of their letters called them “most reverend” and “most holy.” Nor did this title remain confined to churchmen: it passed also to secular princes who were liberal toward the clergy.

Thus, in Pope Gregory IV’s letters concerning the archbishopric of Hamburg, Emperor Louis the Pious is called not merely a venerable prince in the words, “Moreover, all things assigned by the venerable prince to this office worthy of God, we too confirm his pious wishes by our authority”; the emperor’s envoys are likewise called venerable in the same letters, although they were not bishops. For we read: “The venerable bishops Ratolf and Vernold, and also Count Gerold, or the venerable envoy, are reported as requiring confirmation.” [Col. 0761D]

Indeed, women and matrons distinguished by piety also repeatedly received this title from ecclesiastics themselves. In Adam of Bremen, first that Ikia who gave Ramsola in the diocese of Verden is called venerable, book I, p. 22: “Whence it happened that he received the estate called Ramsola from a certain venerable matron named Ikia.” Then, in the same way, he honoured Emma, wife of Count Ludger, with this title on account of the same generosity, book II, p. 64: “Benno, duke of the Saxons, died, and his brother Ludger, who, with his wife [Col. 0762B] the venerable Emma, bestowed many goods upon the Church of Bremen.” Today it is fitting to address any priest as *venerable*, *worthy of veneration*, or *reverend*.

(2) Lord Absalon of Lund. This archbishop deserves frequent commemoration because of his many outstanding achievements and the distinction he brought to his family. The son of Asser Rig, he became bishop of Roskilde in A.D. 1157, rose to the archbishopric of Lund in A.D. 1178, and finally died in A.D. 1201 on St Benedict’s Day, that is, 21 March, as Arnold indicates in Book IV of the *Slavonic Chronicle*, chapter 18. There, too, are certain words suggesting that this testament, called the Sorø Testament, was oral, since he writes that Absalon, toward the end of his days, had been brought to Sorø by bodily illness and lay sick there, having reached his seventy-third year. He was born [Col. 0762C] in 1128, as Hvitfeld observed; thus he began to govern the bishopric of Roskilde at the age of thirty and the archbishopric at fifty. He made this testament in 1200, or even later, sick toward the end of his days, as Arnold says. And since he mentions the canons of Paraclete, to whom he left a notable legacy, it seems that their abbot William, so greatly beloved by Absalon, had already passed from this life when Absalon dictated his testament, and that the canons were without an abbot, since he took care to write only to them. Thus this Testament must be said to have been drawn up shortly before his death in 1201; for Abbot William and Archbishop Absalon died in the same year, but William first.

[Col. 0762D] That it was an oral testament taken down from the archbishop’s lips is indicated by wording written not by the archbishop but by another person about the archbishop, and by the frequent repetition of “he gave” and “he endowed,” not “I gave” and “I endowed.” Hence it also lacks subscriptions and seals, while only eleven witnesses are named and recorded as present. This too confirms that, near the end of his life, Absalon—feeling his strength fail and illnesses press upon him—dictated and orally declared these provisions, since many things were bequeathed and given there which had entered his possession only in his very last years. Although other testaments could not be valid in Denmark unless confirmed by the king, we must nevertheless consider that bishops and clerics, who did not believe themselves subject to Danish [Col. 0763A] laws and customs except insofar as they themselves wished, or insofar as the laws were beneficial, lived by Roman law. From this they claimed for themselves a free right of making wills; and, lest their written testaments might easily be overturned by kings, they preferred to declare them orally rather than write them down.

Andreas Sunesen, Absalon’s successor in the archbishopric of Lund, likewise declared his final will by testament, as Saxo teaches in the dedication of his historical work. Whether he declared it orally or wrote and sealed it formally, I cannot say, because I have not yet seen it. Yet many other donations of the same Archbishop Andreas are read as having been committed to writing, and he took care to have them confirmed by King Valdemar II.

[Col. 0763B] I shall now also offer a warning concerning Absalon’s name, by which this archbishop is now better known to everyone than by his own. For it is certain that from the beginning he did not use the name Absalon, at least not in Danish; rather, clerics and churchmen, not understanding the force of the Danish name, fashioned “Absalon” from *Axel*, as though the man called *Axel* in Danish ought to be called *Absalon* in Latin. The slightest resemblance of names once gave clerics occasion to substitute a Latin name: thus from *Kield* they made *Kilian*, and from *Orm*, *Homer*. Therefore no one should be surprised that Absalon was made from Axel.

All Absalon’s ancestors bore Danish names customary and accepted among that people: his brother Esbern; his father Asser; his grandfather Skjalm; his great-grandfather Toke, the first Christian [Col. 0763C] in this family; and his great-great-grandfather Slag. There is no reason whatever to believe that Absalon alone, with a Hebrew name added, grew up among the Danes. The name Axel indeed remains among Danish names to the present day; nothing is more common than this name, especially among noblemen. Nor did this happen to Absalon alone: all who wrote in Latin called other men named Axel “Absalons” as well.

There survive letters of Christopher of Bavaria, dated 1443 and printed by Hvitfeld, in which the man who elsewhere a hundred times is written and listed as Oluf Axelson—the exceedingly noble and celebrated senator of the realm, one of the sons of Axel (“of the Ulfsson sons”), most renowned in Danish history and ancestors of all the present lords Tot—is, I say, expressly written in these Latin letters as *Olaus Absolonis*. The same judgment must be made concerning the other names Absalon in Denmark.

Indeed, the archbishop himself believed that the name Axel had been distorted from Absalon, since the ancient opinion long prevailed that the entire Danish language had flowed either from Latin or from Greek and that the origins of names and words should therefore be referred to those languages. Saxo too followed this opinion. He always called him Absalon, although he lived with him and had heard the name Axel pronounced among common people a thousand times. The archbishop’s own letters addressed to others likewise everywhere give precedence to the name Absalon.

To these should be added the runic inscription at Åsum, carved in runic letters, found [Col. 0764A] in the wall and doorway of the church, and transcribed by the most eminent Master Worm in his *Monuments*, p. 171. There Absalon and Asbjørn Mule are plainly recorded as benefactors of that church:

> KRIST MARIV SVN HIALPI THEM ER KIRCKIV THINO GVTHI ABSILON ARKIBISKVP OK ASBIORN MULI.

That is:

> Christ, Son of Mary, help those who benefit thy Church (or this church): Archbishop Absalon and Asbjørn Mule.

Here too he is called Absalon, not Axel. The cause of all this is that they were persuaded that the names Absalon and Axel were one and the same, and that unlearned clerics had taught them that Axel was derived and contracted from the Hebrew Absalon. Yet in this they were mistaken, since Axel and Absalon differ as widely as heaven and earth. *Absalon* is interpreted “father of peace”; *Axel* means “magnificent and great.”

We still call *Axeltorg* a very spacious and crowded market-place. *Axelhus* is either a large house shared by many persons, or a house built by an Axel. Hence Hvitfeld quite rightly wrote in his *Chronicle*, under the year 1201, p. 67 of the latest edition, speaking of Absalon, that the Copenhagen castle was called Axelhuss in his time:

> Hand stistte Risbenhaffns Slot oc By, med Amager Land til Rostilde Stifft.

“He founded Copenhagen Castle and town, with the land of Amager, for the bishopric of Roskilde.”

And why was this castle called Axel’s house? Surely for no other reason than that its lord and founder was commonly called Axel—he who became Absalon in Latin. For in 1168, while he was bishop of Roskilde, [Col. 0764C] he built this fortress against pirates; from that time it began to be called Axelhus, until he transferred the whole site to the Church of Roskilde. After his death, when its boundaries had been enlarged and its settlement had spread somewhat more extensively into a town, they gave the fortress the name Stegelburg; or rather, it seems to have acquired the name Stegelburg when Germans and foreigners arriving there repeatedly called it so. Thus it continued to be called Axelhuss by natives and Stegelborg by foreigners. In this way those differing names, given to one place by different peoples—as often happens—are readily reconciled.

Yet they led Svaning, in his *Danish Chronology*, to reverse the whole matter; for on p. 78 he wished to state it thus:

> In the year 1168, to drive pirates from the borders of Zealand, Copenhagen Castle was built by Absalon, bishop of Roskilde; it was formerly called Stegelburg, and later Axelhus.

But the name Axelhus came first; we find Stegelburg added later.

The castle Axelvold in East Gothia, founded by Canute Porse, duke of Halland, about 1326, seems to me not to have taken its name from some Axel or Absalon, but from the immense forest which contained the castle. Thus *Axelvold* is a spacious, dense, long forest, nurturing every kind of tree; in the same way, I have said that northern peoples use the word *Axel* to intensify a conspicuous or extraordinarily great size of things. So *Axel* is, as it were, contracted from *Allsaell*: so blessed that he can supply everything. Thus *Aarsoell* is one rich in crops and provisions and able to procure them abundantly; [Col. 0765A] *Vinsaell*, one attended by friends and welcome to all; *Seyersaell*, one blessed with victories and able excellently to gain them. We call the latter more explicitly *Seyersalig*, just as *Lycksalig*—in German *glückselig*—means one favoured by fortune. All derive from the one word *saelge* (for this is a better spelling than *sellie*), meaning “to deliver” or “to sell”; so that *Saell* and *Salig* are said of one to whom fortune willingly and generously delivers its riches. Likewise *Axell* is one whom fortune has favoured in all things, who is truly great.

For this reason the village of Axelstad by the river Suså in Zealand, lying not far west of Ringsted, is still called in contracted form Allsted. Saxo thought it worthy of mention. Since clerics did not understand these matters, they persuaded themselves and others that Danish *Alex* was the same as Latin *Absalon*. And thus all those err who derive the Danish language from Hebrew, Greek, or Latin, since the ancient Danes in proper names regarded no language but their own. Because they believed Danish to be the last of all languages, and that nothing could proceed from it which had not first existed in other languages, they greatly deceived themselves in so holding; for innumerable ancient matters of no slight importance remain which can be explained from no language other than Danish.

Another error concerning this same Archbishop Absalon has so possessed many minds that scarcely any hope remains to me that it can ever be uprooted. They think that not only Absalon bore the surname Hvid, but that the whole [Col. 0765C] family of the Hvids descends from this source. This is altogether false. For we find that surnames then borne by Danish nobles were variable, neither permanent nor hereditary nor transmitted into a family; rather, they died with those who had received them and were not passed down to posterity. This has hitherto caused countless persons to err in establishing the most noble families and tracing their origins.

It is further false that Archbishop Absalon ever bore the surname Hvid or Albus (“White”). No ancient monuments of his age say this—not Saxo, not Sven Aggesen, nor other chronicles written in his age or shortly afterward. Certain more recent writers began to foster this opinion and to make a great controversy from it, as though the safety of the entire Danish nobility were endangered unless we immediately gave them our credence. Yet when I inquire on what grounds they rely for the family of the Hvids, I find absolutely nothing except that they had read that Absalon’s grandfather Skjalm was surnamed Candidus, or Hvid. From this they reason thus: if the grandfather bore Hvid as a surname, then his sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons will all be Hvids; and therefore Skjalm’s grandson Absalon must be surnamed Hvid.

But I deny—indeed emphatically deny—that this follows, since surnames had not yet become hereditary for any family throughout Denmark. It is true enough, and clear from Saxo, that Skjalm was Absalon’s grandfather; it is also established that the surname Candidus was given to Skjalm. [Col. 0766A] Yet the surname did not arise from his family, but from common usage and contingent circumstances; therefore it could not descend to his posterity. Indeed it did not descend, and no monuments will prove this to me. The contrary at once becomes clear from this very family of Absalon, where no surname outlasts the individual surnamed or descends to his family.

Toke, Skjalm’s father, was celebrated by more than one surname: he was called both *Tryller*, “magician,” and *Sfytter*, “archer,” both because he had been devoted to magic while pagan and until he professed Christianity—being recorded as the first Christian in that family—and because he excelled with the bow. But he was far removed from the surname of the Hvids. Skjalm’s son Asser, Absalon’s father, is often celebrated by his own surname, *Ryg* or *Rog*, “hairy,” not Hvid [rather, perhaps the same as *Rig*, namely “rich” or “powerful”]. Absalon’s brother Esbern likewise had his own surname, being called *Snare*, because he was most prompt both in counsel and in action. Then Esbern’s son Absalon was surnamed *Belg*, as if “pot-bellied” and all belly; Esbern’s other son was called John, but surnamed *Marskalk*, apparently from the office he held; and his third son Nicholas was again given a different surname, *Mule*. Thus none of them was called Candidus, Albus, or Hvid. One may add Esbern, son of Nicholas Mule, called *Snerling*. Thus in those days no one took the surnames of his ancestors, but each bore his own while he lived. Whoever wishes to make such names hereditary and attach them to families [Col. 0766C] will entangle both himself and all of us in many errors. Several persons have hitherto boldly attempted and undertaken this, whenever they read of a surname that had appeared, or merely judged it capable of alluding to the present surnames of noble families: immediately they wished to summon forth or construct an entire family from it.

Surnames by which families are now distinguished hereditarily were adopted late among the Danish nobility—later than among almost all others. We find that scarcely before the fourteenth century did a few Danes approve the practice of marking whole families with hereditary surnames, after northern peoples wished to imitate German customs in this matter too. Moreover, the surnames of which I have spoken then had this condition: they were not adopted by those so surnamed, but were imposed by courtiers and common people, so that all were compelled to hear such things said of them. Such surnames commonly had something ludicrous mixed into them, as *Belg*, *Mule*, and the like.

Consequently, when speaking of themselves, they did not use these surnames. This is also why in this testament we see Esbern’s bare name, without the added surname Snare; nor did Saxo anywhere introduce Esbern in his history under that surname. He had already learned that it was unpleasant to be mocked by such surnames, whether they tended to excessive praise—the feeder of envy—or to provoke laughter, since it was altogether grievous for illustrious men to be exposed [Col. 0767A] to be devoured by the jeers of the common people.

Yet these observations concerning hereditary surnames of nobles, which may be called new, do not imply that Danish nobility or families most ancient and laden with honours are themselves new and to be counted only from the fourteenth century—nothing could be further from the truth. Nobility does not depend on these surnames, but on continuous and long-lasting succession, which men of the highest rank have preserved from antiquity and transmitted down to us. Such succession has given us very ancient families under many surnames.

In antiquity it sufficed, for indicating nobility, that all descendants should be called from the name of the first founder: from Ingo, Inglingar; from Skjold, Skjoldungar; from Folke, Folkungar; from Charlemagne, Carolingians; from Merovech, Merovingians; from Immeding, Immedingians; from Sturla, Sturlungar; and innumerable other families of most ancient nobility, adorned with no other surname. When these designations later ceased, because such surnames seemed to spread too broadly and nobles and non-nobles alike were included and confused in the same family—for many branches of noble lines could not always maintain the same degree of nobility, but some were reduced to dire straits, which seemed to the remaining nobility, for whom nothing is so characteristic as splendour, not merely lamentable but deeply dishonourable, to have among their own persons whom they did not wish to see sunk so low—nobles began to resort to their fathers’ names and for a long time called themselves by them, making their nobility conspicuous: Erik Otteson, Axel Olufson, Tycho Nielson, and so forth. [Col. 0767C]

But since even thus they were not safe from, or sufficiently distinguished from, the common people—for the common people always creep beneath and into the insignia of nobility—they came at last to this method of naming, by which they left hereditary surnames to families and lineages. For a time this admirably distinguished nobles; but now it too has spread so widely among common people that, unless nobles shine forth by their own light while living, their descendants can scarcely distinguish nobles from commoners any longer. Other remedies must again be sought if nobles wish henceforth to provide for their posterity.

Therefore nothing is detracted, because of names or surnames, from the antiquity of noble families, which among the Danes [Col. 0767D] are certainly most ancient—so ancient that they may contend with any nation, indeed surpass many. I have undertaken to demonstrate this elsewhere, should strength and resources be supplied to me. Whether they are Urnes, Banner, Gøye, Tott, and so on, all these families may be found to possess an antiquity beyond what one can believe, even though they adopted the surname Urnes, Banner, and so forth only late. In such names, in truth, no nobility resides, since names often change even for the most trifling causes. But nobility, once it has struck root, like an ancient oak growing through hidden time, does not cease so long as breath and marrow remain.

For the present I have wished only to demonstrate that the family of the Hvids does not properly belong to, or descend from, Skjalm Candidus; and that it is not very long since the Hvids made this surname hereditary in their family. By the same reasoning it follows that Saxo Grammaticus, who lived with Archbishop Absalon, is not to be considered a member of the most noble family of the Langs merely because he acquired the surname Longus somewhere; for in those times surnames were neither hereditary nor familial, not among nobles and much less among common people.

(3) Lord Esbern, his brother. This is the man who bore the surname Snare, because he dispatched his affairs very swiftly; thus he was distinguished from other Esberns. That Esbern was the elder brother is first shown by his condition, since he was devoted to producing offspring and to other secular pursuits at court, at home, abroad, and in warfare. Such concerns belonged [Col. 0768B] to firstborn sons, so much so that histories often tell us that, when the firstborn died without children, the younger brother was recalled to the secular world and obtained permission to leave holy orders in order to support house and family.

So it was with the brothers Hartung and Adolf of Schauenburg. Hartung had been destined for government and warfare, Adolf for ecclesiastical affairs. Yet when Hartung had been consumed by the wars in which he served, the succession reverted to Adolf, who, leaving the monasteries, devoted himself to the secular world and marriage. Thus this first teaches that Esbern preceded Absalon in age. Then the speech of Dambor of Rügen in Saxo, Book XIV, p. 296, quite expressly indicates this, when he explains his reasons for wishing to use Absalon, rather than Esbern the elder, in seeking peace from the king of Denmark:

> “Nor, in passing over your brother, although he surpasses you in age, is it agreed that we have employed unequal diligence. For to you”—he speaks to Absalon—“the prerogatives of authority and honour give precedence: not privileges of character or age, but the adornments of rank.”

No one will readily believe that these words of Saxo, who lived with Esbern and Absalon, depart from the truth. Yet there was found Martin Petersen, abbot of Sorø—for he presided there until 1571—who in his Danish booklet *On the Genealogy of Archbishop Absalon*, published at Copenhagen in 1589, both on the title-page and later on p. 29, dared to write and maintain against Saxo that Absalon and Esbern were twin brothers, born in one delivery.
