[Col. 0768D] He relied upon certain old wives’ tales, with which that book is full, and did not hesitate to prefer them to so great a historian, allowing their falsehoods, so far as lay in him, to do violence to so great a light and to truth itself.

There is no need to refute such trifles, but only to condemn them. For he has provided no reasons why Saxo should be believed less, but he himself—heaven preserve us—more; nor can what he tried to oppose avail more than a final wave against the Marpesian rock. Esbern, son of Asser, was therefore the elder, and for that reason destined for secular affairs; Absalon was the younger and therefore trained in ecclesiastical discipline, as was then customary in the upbringing of sons.

That this Esbern had two wives is taught by the manuscript concerning those buried at Sorø, which gives their names as Hulmesfreth and Ingeburg. It says:

> Beside them are buried the two wives of Esbern Snare, Hulmesfreth and Ingburg; lower down, before the step, is buried Lady Gundil, mother of the aforesaid Hulmesfreth.

The same manuscript notes that these bodies lay in the southern part of the choir, in the presbytery of St John the Evangelist, while Esbern Snare’s bones lay before the step of Absalon’s presbytery, thus separated from his wives’ bones by a considerable space. This is not what usually happens to husbands and wives, who desire to be joined in one tomb. Indeed they formerly lay together. But when the church of Sorø was destroyed by flames and fire in A.D. 1247, the bones of these patrons were transferred in A.D. 1285 into the new and larger church, and in this manner, having formerly lain together, were separated from one another and buried again in three places in the new church. [Col. 0769B] On this matter the author of the same manuscript should be heard in a notable and excellent passage:

> Yet the bones of all these persons—he is speaking of Absalon’s bones and those of his family—together with many others whose names are written in the book of life, were transferred from the old church by Lord Abbot Nicholas the Third into the larger church, and deposited in three places: one part in the presbytery of the high altar, at the right hand of Lord Archbishop Absalon, as has now appeared; a second part in the presbytery of Blessed John the Evangelist, where the wives of Lord Esbern Snare received their place from that time together with Gunilda; and a third part in the presbytery of Blessed John the Baptist, in the year of the Lord 1285, on the day after the Commemoration of All Souls.

The remaining matters worth saying about Esbern are found in Saxo, from whom information concerning him and his outstanding deeds may be sought.

(4) Lord Geoffrey, abbot. He governed the monastery of Sorø in this office from 1189 to 1213, being English by nationality. For the Danes employed many monks and churchmen from England as long as the Danish kingdoms themselves could not provide so great an abundance of clerics; accordingly Geoffrey’s predecessor Simon too is written to have been English.

(5) And Toke and Aage. Both were provosts, but Toke was provost of the Church of Roskilde, as becomes evident from the catalogue of those buried at Sorø. For its words are as follows:

> Before the church door lies Lord Tucho, provost of Roskilde; for he was among the benefactors of the monastery of Sorø.

Since he lived and was present when Absalon orally declared his testament, we readily see that Saxo the provost—whom several letters published by Stephanius in his notes on Saxo mention around 1180 and 1184—had already died and made way for Toke as his successor in that office. [Col. 0770A] I have not yet encountered when Saxo, provost of Roskilde, died and Toke succeeded him; but Stephanius’s opinion is quite clearly overthrown by these indications. In the Prolegomena to Saxo, chapter XI, he made many efforts to assert that Saxo Grammaticus and the Saxo who was provost of Roskilde were one and the same person.

The name Saxo alone, borne by the provost, does not make our Saxo Grammaticus or historian a provost. Several Saxos lived in those same times, only one of whom was provost of Roskilde. He certainly was not Saxo Grammaticus, as Stephanius contends. For Saxo Grammaticus remained a cleric of Archbishop Absalon until the archbishop’s very death, and remained alive for a long time afterward, as I shall someday demonstrate more clearly; whereas Saxo the provost died before Absalon and received as successor this Toke, who stood with the others when Absalon’s testament was orally declared. It is therefore established from this Testament too that Saxo Grammaticus was not provost of Roskilde. Nor do many other proofs fail by which I could establish this, were they not foreign to this place and requiring us to extend ourselves too far, since we have undertaken an inquiry into Provost Toke, not Saxo Grammaticus.

This provost, as we have heard, is called both Tocho and Tucho. But care must be taken not to confuse this with the name Tycho. They are different Danish names, *Tocke* and *Tyge*; we must attend not to corrupt Latin inflections or spellings, but to the Danish language itself, which always has been and is most precise in expressing and distinguishing its names. The same must be said of the name Aage, joined here with Toke. Latin clerics have mistreated this name in many ways: some write Aggo, Ako, Hako, Hacho, Haquinus, and other distortions of the name besides, [Col. 0770C] whereas the true Danish name is *Aage*, and the Norwegian is *Haagen* [among Icelanders, *Hakon*].

(6) Master John. See below, note 67.

(7) Thordon, chaplain. Archbishops had chaplains, notaries, and clerics of their own, who attended to writing in the household or chapel—that is, in the archbishop’s retinue. The chaplain was head of the entire chancery, analogous to the chancellor in princely courts; whatever chancellors provided for princes, chaplains provided for archbishops. Moreover, chaplains and archchaplains are older in this office than chancellors, and first occupied the courts of kings and bishops throughout Germany for purposes of writing, because, at the beginning, scarcely any laymen apart from clerics had learned to write. But after the title chancellor gained prevalence from Roman law and the imperial court, that of chaplain began to disappear even among bishops. Thus those called archchaplains in the time of Charlemagne began shortly afterward to be called archchancellors, down to the present day.

But no one should suppose this chaplain Thordon to be Thordon, commonly surnamed Degn, who illustrated the Jutland Law of Valdemar II with very brief notes. It is of no help that chaplains were sometimes called *Degne* by the Danes. First, the dates do not agree: Thordo, Absalon’s chaplain, lived under King Canute VI; Thordo Degn under Valdemar II, and indeed at a late period, after the promulgation of the Jutland Law in 1240, a date to which Thordo the chaplain could scarcely have lived. Secondly, [Col. 0771A] Thordo, chaplain of Archbishop Absalon, belonged to Roskilde, as Hvitfeld’s *Chronicle*, p. 134, suggests. Thirdly, *Degn*, or deacon, and chaplain were by no means the same. The Degn or deacon of an archbishop was not ordinarily employed in chancery business, but assisted the archbishop in the services of the Church; the chaplain, however, lived in the archbishop’s chapel, as a chancellor in the prince’s retinue, directing writings and written documents.

(8) His chamberlain. Bishops borrowed this title also from secular persons.

(9) His *pueri*. These *pueri* were not children. The expression had become established for the younger attendants of a courtier, those in the flower of life. In England they were commonly called *thegni*, whether they were of mature or vigorous age, and whether they were appointed to the most distinguished offices or lower ones. The designation had passed into long use from the old Danish and Saxon word *tienne*, *deenen*. In pagan times and at the beginning of Christianity it was a sufficiently familiar word among the Danes, who had nothing more often on their lips than *Herda Gudan Thiagn*, that is, “minister or servant of God’s Church.” But the word eventually disappeared completely from the Danish court, while the Church retains its *Degne*, who are subordinate ministers, as it were, of the Church. Nor should we derive it from the Greeks’ διακονεῖν, “to minister,” as most do; rather, *Degn* was made from the old *Thiagn*, and *Thiagn* from *thionne*, “to serve.”

Therefore all who served in the courts of kings and princes were called *Thiagni* and *Thegni*. Clerics wishing to speak Latin made from these, when conspicuous in early youth, *Pueri*; Germans made *Knaben*, *Edelknaben*. The term occurs not only here, but in many writers, in this sense of attendants and servants of no mean status. Thus the short *Zealand Chronicle*, recently published by the Icelander Árni Magnússon, says of Canute, duke of Schleswig, p. 17:

> When his *pueri* wished to follow him, he forbade them. But when they said that it was shameful for a duke to proceed not only without *pueri* but even without a sword, etc.

Thus they were not children who could offer advice and make suggestions to a duke. So too it says of Nicholas, king of Denmark, p. 19:

> When he had come near Hedeby, his counts and *pueri* advised him not to enter there.

These *pueri* are what the ancient Danes and northerners called *Drenge*, whom we know to have been sturdy, noble young men, resembling adult men, although today the name is restricted only to younger persons and those of lower standing. Hence the soldiers called *Drungarii* among the Greeks of Constantinople retained the name: they were the same as *Drenge*. Likewise the Danish expression *goden Dreng*, “good man,” corresponds to Swedish *karle*. In English writers they are called *Tyrones*, that is, men not yet made knights but next in line to become so. For those at court were called knights who, because of the offices and services they rendered, had been granted a benefice or fief. Hence *milites feudati*, “enfeoffed knights,” occur frequently. But those *Tyrones* and *Pueri* were nobles who served indeed, yet had not obtained a fief, living, serving, and fighting in hope of obtaining one.

[Col. 0772A] There is no doubt whatever that the *pueri* of whom we speak here were nobles, and also young men of suitable age, since they are recorded as witnesses to the testament of so great an archbishop; such a role is not for underage children or common persons. The ancient Romans also sometimes used the word *pueri* in this sense. Plautus frequently does so. In *Curculio*, Act I, scene I, verse 9, concerning the young Phaedromus, indulging in nocturnal love-affairs and going

> Where Venus and Cupid command, and Love persuades,

he says:

> You yourself are a fine young fellow; you shine like a wax candle.

In the *Mostellaria*, Act IV, scene II, verse 30, the old man Theuropides addresses the slave and Phaniscus:

> Hey, you young fellows, what are you doing there? Why are you smashing up those houses?

Varro, in the *Eumenides*, says:

> Hardly does a crowd gather—not of Furies, but of young fellows and maidservants.

The Germans say *Knechte und Mägde*, “menservants and maidservants.” Likewise women who were already wives or widows were called *puellae*, “girls.” Horace, *Odes* III.22:

> . . . girls labouring in childbirth.

Ovid, *Fasti* II, bids

> . . . widowed girls refrain.

Penelope herself is called a *puella*, though she had long before borne Telemachus to Ulysses. Scaevola the jurist calls a woman a *puella* though she was a widow and later married another man; Aulus Gellius, Book XII, chapter 1, calls a woman a *puella* though she had already borne children twice. Thus they were *puellae* so long as they were young women. Why then should men not likewise be called *pueri* so long as their youth is green and their “knee is green” (γόνυ χλωρόν)? Thus *pueri* here are those whom in our language we are accustomed to call *junge Herren* or *Junckeren*, “young gentlemen”; [Col. 0772C] in ancient Danish *Scalcke*, and properly in German also, while that word was taken in a better sense. Such *pueri* were therefore not called servants simply, but *Scalke*, serving a more honourable kind of service.

Hence in Burgundian Law, title 49, §4:

> We had ordered [persons] to be brought before our *pueri*, who exact the fine throughout the districts.

These *pueri* were called *Whytescalke* by the Danes and Germans. Thus title 76 of the same law begins concerning *Wittiscalci*:

> Our *pueri*, who execute judgments and whom we order to exact the fine.

These *pueri*, therefore, bore that name; they were certainly not children, but sufficiently mature and equal to the duty entrusted to them. Only the name *marescalci*—marshals—has retained its ancient form; and the word itself shows what they originally were: namely, that they appeared among the king’s *pueri*, until time rendered their dignity more illustrious and raised marshals to their present splendour at courts.

In Salic Law, title 14, one reads:

> If a *puer* of the king, or a *litus* [dependent], carries off a freeborn woman—that is, commits abduction—he shall make composition with his life.

And in Ripuarian Law, title 53, §2:

> If a royal *puer*, or one from a *tabularius* [register-keeper], has risen to that rank.

The capitularies of the emperors Charles and Louis, Book VI, chapter 319, similarly say:

> The *puer* shall be guilty before his lord of that punishment, if he has violated his lord’s wife by adultery.

Gregory of Tours likewise, *History*, Book III, title V:

> A strap was placed under his neck and tied beneath his chin; two *pueri* pulled it toward themselves from opposite sides, and he was suffocated.

From these passages we sufficiently understand how *pueri* are to be understood: namely, as the more noble young men called *scalci* by the ancient Danes and Germans. [Col. 0773A] In this way *Whytescalcki* can also be excellently distinguished from the *Whytetheovnes* occurring in King Athelstan’s laws, chapter 3, in Bromton, p. 841. For, as we have heard, *Whytescalcki* are servants of the king who exact fines; but *Whytetheownes* are penal slaves, or, as the law explains, “a forfeited slave,” one reduced to servitude because of his crime.

Nor should one read *Whytethegnes*, as Bromton wished, because *thegni* is a title of honour among the English; rather, *Theovnes* must be retained, although both *Thegni* and *Theovnes* have proceeded from the same root: Danish *tienne*, German *dienen*, “to serve.”

(10) Concerning Henry, a monastic convert of Sorø. In almost all monastic writings mention is made of *conversi* brothers, [Col. 0773B] who lived together with the monks; yet no one has explained what they were, why they were so called, or how they differed from the rest—whether they were those now called lay brothers (*Lagbruder*), or others. Among the Carthusians and Bernardines there are certainly persons called *conversi*, because they leave the world and commit themselves to monasteries, converted from the turbulent affairs of secular life to things better and more tranquil. They serve the fathers and brothers of these orders, and are distinguished from the other brothers whom they serve also by their habit and colour. They are, as I have said, like those called *Lagenbruder* in other monasteries. They are uneducated in letters pertaining to theology and sacred matters. Sorø and its monastery were from the beginning dedicated to Bernardine brothers and fathers; hence *conversi* are also recorded as having been there, and, because they were servants of the monks, they are even placed after Absalon’s boys.

(11) Fialensleve. I think this is the same estate called *Fienneslof lille* in the manuscript catalogue of those buried at Sorø. There it is said that Absalon transferred thence the bones of his grandfather Lord Skialmon Hvide, and of Skialmon’s son Tuko, from the church of Fiennesloflille to “our church,” that is, Sorø. Thus that estate, Fialensleve or Fienneslof, seems to have been hereditary paternal property in Absalon’s family, and was therefore left to his brother Esbern. These estates still survive and are called Fienneslof Magle and Fienneslof Lille, in Zealand not far from Sorø. For *magle* in these regions means “greater,” just as *lille* means “small,” [Col. 0773C] and it is joined to several estates which wish to distinguish themselves, such as Agli Magle, Steen Magle, and so forth. Thus we see what Roskilde’s *Magle Kilde* means: namely, “the greater spring,” in comparison with which the other springs of the same place are smaller. For Roskilde acquired its name from the springs gushing forth there, famous for greater and lesser springs. Thus the etymology hitherto accepted—that *Magle Kilde* means “the spring of Magdalene”—has been derived from a corrupt source, by those who did not understand what *magle* meant among the ancient Danes.

(12) To the monastery of Aas. The monastery of Aas, situated in Halland, is recorded as founded by Eskil, Archbishop of Lund, and endowed by Valdemar, Bishop of Schleswig. Eskil held office from 1138 to 1178. [Col. 0774A] I conjecture that it was founded around the year 1165, that the monks of Sorø led the first colony there in that year, and that the Sorø monks sent a second colony in 1195. Hvitfeld should therefore be read thus on p. 148: “Then Sorø sent a swarm of monks from itself to Aas in Halland, in the year 1165” (instead of 1195). For on p. 162, under the year 1195, he states that Sorø monks went to the monastery of Aas a second time: “In the year 1195 the monastery of Sorø again sent a swarm of monks of the Order of St Bernard to the monastery of Aas in Halland.” This was the reason why Absalon benefited the monastery of Aas and left it important legacies: the church of Sorø was, as it were, its mother, and through it the monastery of Aas had received its growth. From this monastery arose the common name *Hallands Aasz* in these kingdoms; [Col. 0774B] I recall several places so named even outside Halland.

(13) “He gave and *scotavit*.” Here you see the Danish word *skisde* rendered in Latin. For it occurs frequently in ancient writers. *Scotare* and *skisde* mean the same thing: to hand over, and to transfer a thing into another’s power and ownership. This is clear from letters of Christian, Bishop of Ribe, issued about 1298 and cited by Hvitfeld, where he says that he “conferred and *scotavit*,” and handed over under actual possession, goods to be possessed by perpetual right.

But whence this delivery came to be called *scotatio* and *scotare*, “to hand over,” must be explained. It is no insignificant matter, but embraces ancient rites of conveyance among the northerners and Germans—indeed, among all Celts. Since the Celts [Col. 0774C] did not cultivate writing and letters, but judged this *paideia*—“education”—to be something utterly alien to them, they nevertheless always ensured that contracts should be secure and in good faith. For that purpose they used certain signs in place of writing, to testify that contracts had been duly completed and perfected: things to be handed over had been handed over, things to be done had been done, and promises had been discharged.

Among these signs were straws, from which the stipulations of Roman law retained their name; and hands were said to be “stipulated” which gave or received the straw. We say that those promise “with stipulated hand” whose promises we believe will be fulfilled with the utmost good faith, joining hands—*einander die Hand darauf geben* (“to give one another one’s hand upon it”)—although today the straw is absent, which formerly [Col. 0774D] had to be present if they wished to be said to have done something “with stipulated hand.” So likewise there were twigs and acts of “un-twigging” (*exfestucationes*).

For the Romans also had times when they conducted transactions without any writing, content with verbal obligations and accompanying signs which preserved the memory of the act. Likewise the northerners completed contracts by the most readily available signs, whatever was thrown into the lap or bosom of the contracting parties: whether straws, little rods and sticks, a handful of earth or a turf, keys, gloves, or other things. All such tokens placed in someone’s lap signified that the preceding contract had now been duly brought to completion; consequently, when these signs were produced in court, their credibility could not customarily be denied, nor could it be.

This is what [Col. 0775A] the Danes called *at skisde*. Although those rites of throwing something into the lap have perished, and other rites are now observed by contracting parties, the old word has remained to the present day. For even now those making a contract are said *at skisde*, or *scotare*, when a contract is duly concluded. *Skisd* is known to mean the lap or bosom which receives something: *Scoot* among Germans, Saxons, and Netherlanders; *Schoosz* among Upper Germans. Hence *skisde* and *scotare*: to throw something into someone’s lap for the purpose of completing a contract. *At skisde sit Barn* means “to receive one’s infant into one’s lap.” *At skisde hannem Huus, Ager, og Eng* means “to hand over to someone a house, field, and meadows in ownership.”

The Saxons and Franks expressed this rite of *scotatio* by another term as well: they called it *laisowerpum*, [Col. 0775B] which nevertheless comes to the same thing as *scotatio*. For it is a compound word: *Lisze*, an old Danish word still in current use, denotes a lap—specifically, the lower lap by the belly, that part of the body naturally fitted for collecting and receiving everything while persons are seated. It thus retains its name from *laese* and *lese*, because all things are gathered into that lap; and it is accordingly written both *Laisum* and *Lesum*. The added *werpum* is likewise a word of German origin: *werpe*, “to throw, cast”; *een Werp* and *Worp*, “a throw.” Hence *werpum* in a Latin inflection, and *laiso werpum*, “a throw into the lap”; in Danish *skisde*, *scotatio*.

The whole title XLVIII of the Salic Law in Lindenbrog belongs here; since it explains the entire matter and is noteworthy, it must be quoted. Its words are as follows:

> This ought to be observed: that the *tunginus* or centenary official shall appoint the court, and shall have a shield in that court itself; and three men must commit three causes in that court itself. Afterwards the man who does not belong to him shall be summoned, and so he shall throw a twig into the *laisum*; and he into whose *laisum* he has thrown the twig shall state a word concerning his property, how much he wishes to give him.

This law speaks of the *exfestucatio*, or “un-twigging,” of goods and property which one wishes to give to another by instituting him as heir. It continues:

> Afterwards, he into whose *laisum* he has thrown the twig must remain in that man’s house, receive three guests, and hold in his own power, from that man’s property, as much as is given him. Afterwards, he to whom it has been entrusted must perform all these things with witnesses assembled. Then, either before the king or in a lawful court, he ought to restore them to the person to whom he assigned his property; and afterwards, within twelve months, he whom he appointed heir shall take the twig in that court itself and throw it into his own *laisum*, neither less nor more than what was entrusted to him.

> And if anyone should wish to say anything against this, three sworn witnesses must declare that they were present in the court appointed by the *tunginus* or centenary official, and that they saw the man who gave his property throw the twig into the *laisum* of the person whom he had chosen; and they must name the man who threw his property into the lap of the chosen person, and likewise name him into whose *laisum* he threw the twig and whom he called heir. And three other sworn witnesses must declare that, in the house [Col. 0776A] of the man who gave his property, the person into whose *laisum* he threw the twig had remained there, had gathered and fed three or more guests, and that they had there given him thanks, and had gathered porridge and witnesses in his *heudus* [uncertain technical term]. All these things three other sworn witnesses must declare: that in a lawful court, or before the king, he who had received the property into his *laisum* in the public court—that is, before the *theada* or *tunginus*—had publicly, in the presence of all, thrown the twig into the *laisum* of the person whom he had called heir; and all these things the nine witnesses must affirm.

Here we see all the rites customarily observed in *scotationes* when someone wished to choose and institute an heir to his property. So too *skisde* and *scotatio*, or *laisowerpum*, had a place in other alienations, such as the legacies in this passage. So long as they concerned estates and fields, the words “he gave and *scotavit*” are added. Our Absalon is recorded merely as giving and donating the other movable goods, without *scotatio*.

Marculf’s formulas also speak of these *laisowerpa*, as Formula 43, “On *laisowerpum* through the king’s hand”; and in that formula itself: “He appeared to us to have *lesowerpised* or bestowed by means of a twig”; and shortly afterwards: “He appeared voluntarily and in due form to have *leisowerpised* or bestowed.” That is, witnesses were present who saw him place a twig in the royal lap and thereby complete his donation. Nothing could be firmer or more stable than to make *laisowerpum* or *scotatio* in the presence of the king, or through the king’s hand. Hence the opening of the formula runs as follows: [Col. 0776C]

> Whatever is done in our presence, or appears to have been transferred through our hand, we will and command to remain hereafter most firmly established by the strongest right.

(14) “To the canons’ table.” In former times particular villages and estates were customarily assigned in monasteries and collegiate churches for the maintenance of monks and clerics. Since they were cenobites, living from a common table and board, wherever a great number of brothers lived at the same table and in the same community, many estates had necessarily to serve for the nourishment of that number. Hence the German *Taffelgutter*, properties assigned to the tables of kings and princes. This practice is believed first to have come from the Persians; for they are recorded as having assigned some estates to the table, others to clothing, and others [Col. 0776D] to hunting.

(15) Esbiruth. I think it is the same village called Esperod, in which, around 1329, Archbishop Charles of Lund still granted one farm to the chapter of Lund, according to Hvitfeld’s episcopal chronicle.

(16) Saxulstorp. The addition “in Ruma” does not seem pointless: it distinguishes it, evidently, from another church of Saxeldorp, which Archbishop Isarn granted to the same chapter of Lund in the year of Christ 1305. They must have been different churches, although of the same name; for those brothers and canons could not recognize as a new gift what they had already received once by gift.

(17) “To the brothers.” Nowadays canons have ceased to be called brothers.

[Col. 0777A] (18) “Of each crown.” He means the hanging lamps and those candelabra whose arms are encircled and spread out in the form of a crown, customarily suspended in our churches. He indicates that there were two of them in the church of Lund, for which he provides wax and candles by this legacy. In Danish and German they are called simply *Kroner*, *Kronerne i Kirken* (“crowns,” “the crowns in the church”); or, to distinguish them more clearly from other crowns, *Liusekroner*, *Lieth-Kronen* (“light-crowns”). They are generally cast in brass, and, for greater ornament and splendour, sometimes also in silver—a thing which, as we shall hear below, Archbishop Absalon likewise attempted in his church.

(19) “To the monastery of Blessed Lawrence.” The monastery of Lund adjoining the cathedral church is indicated. For the whole establishment at Lund—the church together with the monastery—was dedicated to St Lawrence the martyr and bore his name. Small bronze coins survive, frequently dug up, bearing Lawrence’s gridiron and showing themselves to have come from the episcopal mint of Lund. For we know that martyrologies record the peculiar and carefully devised martyrdom of Blessed Lawrence: laid upon a gridiron with fire beneath it, he was roasted, and the steadfast holy man so despised those torments that, amid the flames, he cried out and ordered himself to be turned onto the other side, because the first seemed to him sufficiently roasted. This is why those little coins bear the gridiron. [Col. 0777B]

(20) “Four marks of silver.” I shall now say nothing about marks, except that their name is Danish and first came from the North to all who either used marks or use them still. A silver mark is a silver weight of sixteen half-ounces; in our currency it yields eight ounce-thalers. Thus four silver marks make thirty-two ounce-thalers; and the following one hundred marks make eight hundred ounce-thalers, while fifty make four hundred. These are silver marks, *Mark Eslf*.

There were other marks, marks of pennies, *Mark Penge*. Among our marks there remain marks of pennies in Scanian coinage, others Zealandic, and others Jutish. In the time of this Absalon, and for a long time thereafter, Scanian pennies and marks were worth twice as much as Zealandic ones. Four marks of Scanian pennies, but eight marks of Zealandic pennies, were required to make one silver mark. Thus among the Zealanders an ounce-thaler at that time was a mark of pennies; among the Scanians, however, two ounce-thalers made a Scanian mark of pennies. Since sixteen pennies make a mark of pennies, we see that each Scanian silver penny was worth six Lübeck *asses* in current money, and so was equal to a Roman denarius; while Zealandic pennies were worth three Lübeck *asses*, or a Roman quinarius. Such at that time was the size and weight of Scanian and Zealandic pennies. [Col. 0777C]

I have more than once seen pennies of Valdemar I, each weighing half a drachm, or three Lübeck *asses*; but I have seen none of Scanian drachm-weight. It does not immediately follow from this that they were never struck at that weight, merely because none survives anywhere today—in Germany, France, England, Denmark, or Sweden—though Roman denarii survive and old three-*as* pennies frequently occur in the regions mentioned. Otherwise there would be no reason why drachm-weight pennies of these peoples should not also have been preserved.

I admit that this reasoning bears heavily against Scanian and Slavic pennies; for the latter also had the same weight, so that four Slavic marks made a silver mark. Yet we know that old pennies, especially silver ones, were eagerly sought out whenever new pennies were coined, and were required by severe public edicts to return to the mint. I need not add the workshops of silversmiths, which melt down and destroy all silver coins from which they can hope for profit. From those men flows the principal calamity of coinage: they consume every coin of any usefulness or value and force kings and princes to debase so many currencies, since there is no other way to resist these harpies. No golden harvests, no Gargara, nor mountains of gold or silver converted into coin, will be safe from—or suffice for—these profit-hunters. [Col. 0778B]

Thus I do not find it surprising that so few little coins of the old Danes survive, and that those which do are of the baser sort, since the avarice of the said silversmiths has long since seized the superior ones with hooked hands. Yet no one should suppose, when he reads here of silver marks and marks of pennies, that there was at that time some coin struck which represented a silver mark and a mark’s weight in silver. Nothing could be further from the truth. No coins above pennies were then minted; the other monetary names were weights and nothing more.

Thus sixteen Scanian pennies made a mark of pennies, and sixty-four pennies a silver mark. Sixteen Zealandic pennies made a mark of pennies, while one hundred and twenty-eight made a silver mark; for, as I have said, the Zealandic penny was half the Scanian. The Hanseatic cities of Lübeck, Hamburg, Wismar, and Lüneburg were the first to issue a coin called a mark, in the year of Christ 1506, and not earlier. This was a mark of Lübeck or Slavic pennies, not a silver mark; [Col. 0778C] for sixteen Lübeck *asses* then went into that coin, though much smaller ones than formerly. Indeed, this mark of pennies contained only thirty-two present-day Lübeck *asses*, so that Lübeck pennies at that time were worth two present-day *asses*, and in 1506 pennies had declined and fallen short of their ancient standard by two-thirds. This coin was called a *Markstuck*; twelve of them make a silver mark.

Those coins still survive, but scarcely escape those predatory silversmiths, especially the first issue, because it was purer than the second and third issues which followed it. At that time those cities reduced the mark of pennies to a fixed standard. In place of pennies they assigned sixteen shillings to the mark of pennies, and twelve pennies to each shilling. Thereafter they established the shilling such that 2,304 pennies, or 192 shillings, made twelve marks of pennies, and twelve marks of pennies made one silver mark. This was the condition of the Lübeck mark in the preceding century, to which it was reduced by the said cities; they therefore caused this inscription to be placed upon the coin: *Status marcae Lubicensis 1506*—“Standard of the Lübeck mark, 1506.” [Col. 0779A]

They themselves gradually departed from this standard, for no other reason than the old one: those silversmiths carried off all the silver, while luxury in household furnishings increased with the wealth of the citizens. At last even that mark fell to half its value, and today twenty-four marks of pennies, 384 shillings, or 1,608 pennies in Lübeck currency, are required to make up a silver mark.

(21) Midsummer Guild. Midsummer is the time of mid-summer in June and around the feast of St John. *Gylde* derives from *Gielde*, the payment or due which they are obliged to pay. The Germans call it in the same way *die Gulten*.

(22) “To the exile for justice’s sake.” That archbishop was called Eric the Blind because he suffered from a defect of the eyes. He went voluntarily into exile in Denmark, compelled by no one. Sverre the Great, king of Norway, was willing to offer equitable terms; but since neither the archbishop nor the bishops would accept them, they did not cease trying to incite the kings of Denmark and Sweden against him, hoping that, once exile had been undertaken, the kings would be moved more swiftly. This is why Absalon here appoints legacies to the archbishop and bishops of Norway: all were then in Denmark. Sverre began to acquire the kingdom in 1178. Archbishop Eric is placed as elected in the catalogue of bishops of Nidaros under the year 1184.

Soon afterward Hvitfeld writes that Sverre died in 1195. If that were true, the whole chronology of Absalon’s testament would collapse, and it would have been made before 1195, since the bishops returned immediately to Norway and their churches upon Sverre’s death. Thus some less trustworthy history deceived Hvitfeld, one which tends to seize upon one thing in place of another. Yet the Norwegian Chronicle, p. 524, testifies that in 1195, on the feast day of Saints Peter and Paul, Sverre was first publicly crowned and proclaimed king at Bergen—unless the marginal year 1194 has been incorrectly added. For the words themselves, *Om Buaren derefter*—“about the spring thereafter”—refer to Sverre’s victory over Sigurd Magnusson; that victory indeed befell Sverre in 1194. Therefore the spring which follows is that of 1195, when Sverre summoned an assembly for his coronation on the feast of Peter and Paul. [Col. 0779C]

The Norwegian Chronicle’s account is therefore more correct: Sverre died in the year of Christ 1202, on 8 March, at Bergen; he was crowned in 1195 on the day of Peter and Paul; and he began to reign in 1178. With Sverre’s dates thus established, let us also set forth certain facts about the bishops’ dates, in order to elucidate these words of the testament.

I said that Eric was elected in 1184 while Archbishop Øystein was still alive, because Øystein, his strength failing, could no longer attend to his office. After Øystein’s death around the year of Christ 1186, while disturbances and factions still continued, Eric remained archbishop-elect until 1188, when he sought and obtained the pallium from Rome. Thus established as archbishop, he began to oppose Sverre in various ways. Sverre received this with considerable moderation and gentleness and sought to pacify the man; but Eric, as though oil had been poured on the flames, added flames to flames and fires to fires. Necessity therefore compelled Sverre to resist more sharply and curb those claims of authority. Unable to endure this, the archbishop departed, escaped, and broke out into Denmark around 1191. This is the “justice” for which he is said here to be an exile, and by reason of which he is found greatly relieved by Absalon’s legacies to the archbishop. [Col. 0780A]

The other Norwegian bishops named here, however, did not go into exile with the archbishop. Rather, after Sverre had been crowned in 1195 or 1196, they too went to Denmark to the archbishop. By their persuasions they accomplished so much that Canute, king of Denmark, sent an army against Sverre into Norway. Having gained victory, it ravaged Norway with great calamities, until in 1201 it was so thoroughly defeated by Sverre that it could not recover. The Norwegian Chronicle teaches this and adds on p. 530 that the archbishop and bishops did not return to their sees in Norway until after Sverre’s death in 1203, when his son Håkon was reigning and came to terms with the bishops. Thus it is again demonstrated that this testament of Absalon was composed only around the end of his life.

[Col. 0780C] (23) Concerning Bishop Nigellus. In 1190 he had obtained the bishopric of Stavanger, and in 1196, together with Nicholas of Oslo, was making for Denmark. He is called Nield in the Norwegian Chronicle; but in Hvitfeld’s catalogue of the bishops of Stavanger both the name is wrong and the added year 1183 is wrong. For he is called Nicolaus, who is Niellus, Nigellus, and Nialus—a name not unknown among Norwegians. An error also occurs in the Norwegian Chronicle when it reports his return on p. 530, where it prints *Nioefsz* for *Nioeld*.

(24) Concerning Ivar of Hamar. From this we learn that in that age the principal town of the diocese of Hamar was called not Hamar but Hammerkisbing. The common people, however, to whom all words would be monosyllables if possible [Col. 0780D]—for they contract everything—called it Hamar rather than Hammerkisbing.

(25) Concerning Nicholas of Oslo. It should be read “of Oslo.” In Norwegian, *Opsloe*; today it is Christiania, after Christian IV moved it and caused it to be built more elegantly. May it flourish for the longest possible time; for it is my native city, which I left when I was not yet two years old and was still at the breast, and which I have not afterward had occasion to see. Bishop Nicholas was plainly then the leading bishop. He had assumed the bishopric in 1190 and presided over the ceremonies of Sverre’s coronation in 1195. In the Norwegian Chronicle he is called Nicholas Arneson. The archbishop therefore bestowed a richer legacy upon him, because he was more experienced and more esteemed than the others in conducting affairs, although he is placed last among the bishops because he obtained the bishopric after the others. [Col. 0781A]

(26) “A silver *ciffus*.” Here *ciffus* stands for *scyphus*, “cup”; in Danish it is properly called *een Skaal*. No one among us is unaware what form of vessel it is, although it is more easily shown to the eyes than described by the pen. Some cups are understood to be shallow, in the form of a dish, without a sufficiently distinct bulge; others are larger, deeper, and more convex; most are round and broad. By this shape they differ especially from other drinking-vessels, which are taller and narrower than cups.

The word is of Greek origin and very ancient, well known to Homer. This itself sufficiently refutes those who believed that *scyphus* was formed from and derived from the Scythians; among them the Greeks themselves were mistaken, especially Athenaeus, Book XI. For the Scythians were neither known nor named by Homer or Hesiod, whereas *skyphoi* (“cups”) were; the name of the cup is thus older even than that of the Scythians. Those who, in the same Athenaeus, conjectured that *scyphus* was named from *skaphis* (“little boat”), because such cups commonly imitated a boat’s form, perhaps did better. Yet, since these vessels were specifically called *scaphia*, even this source cannot be assigned to the origin of *scyphi*. Indeed, cups are older than *scaphia*, as I have said; therefore older things cannot derive their origin from later additions.

Eustathius seems to me most rightly to have derived the word from *kyphos*, “a hump” or “convexity.” For nearly all cups are *opithokyphoi*—“curved at the back”—and display a conspicuous convex bulge corresponding to their hollow, with a low foot beneath upon which the bulge rests. In Homer *skyphos* is neuter, as also in Phaedimus and Theocritus:

> “A broad wooden cup for the sweet wine’s drink.”

Thus in the wooden cup we see the antiquity of the earliest age shining forth, when silver, gold, bronze, and tin were not yet available in such abundance, but almost all household equipment was of wood. Tibullus too mentions a cup of beechwood, Book I, Elegy 10, verse 2. [Col. 0781C]

Among the various forms of cups belongs Stesichorus’ *skyphien depas*, “a cup-like drinking vessel,” which partakes of both a drinking-cup and a *skyphus*; and Athenaeus’ *ōoskyphia*, “egg-shaped cups,” which represented the form of eggs, such cups as we still preserve today.

Why *ciffi* rather than *scyphi* occur here arises from differing pronunciation and spelling. Some pronounce *sci* as *zi* and *ci*—thus *scire*, *nescire*, with softened pronunciation—whereas it seems too harsh to pronounce *skythropon* as *skire* and *neskire*. Meanwhile they make many words Greek-like and pronounce them in Greek fashion, such as *scyphus*, *Scythae*, and *sceptici*. Many also Latinize them, so that we hear rather *cyphos* and *ciffos*, *Cythas* and *Cepticos*, lest the pronunciation be too harsh and so that it may fall more softly on the ear. They extended this to spelling as well, especially in *ciffus*, where they also represented the Greek phi, φ, by doubled Latin *f*. For Hesiod too has *skypphos* in Greek:

> “Having filled a silver cup, he brought it and gave it to the lord.”

Hence *ciffi* are written in this testament. [Col. 0782A]

(27) “Silver dishes.” Cicero used the word *scutella*, but in a meaning different from that appropriate to this passage. For Cicero uses it for a cup from which one drinks, in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book III:

> “Let us remove grief from this man. How? Let us place him upon a feather bed; bring in a girl playing the psaltery; burn fragrant perfume; give him a little dish of sweetish drink; let us provide some food as well.”

He gives very dainty words to a delicate fellow; hence Cicero’s *scutella* and *dulcicula*, “sweetish.” For to place food upon, he requires not a *scutella* but another vessel. Therefore Cicero’s *scutella* differs from ours.

Martial, however, used *scutella* for a plate and serving-dish upon which foods are placed; for he compares it with platters and bowls, Book XI:

> “Thus he fills bowls and serving-dishes,  
> And light little dishes and hollow platters.”

And likewise in Book VIII:

> “We reached a little dish of one-sixth measure in the sixth year.”

Thus it means plates like shields. That *scutula* and *scutella* derive from *scutum*, “shield,” is beyond doubt; Cicero too, in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, called a small shield a *scutulum*. Today most little dishes and dishes are round; formerly they were oblong, in the form of the Roman shield, whence they received their name. [Col. 0782B]

Thus Pliny calls a spider’s web *scutulata*, “patterned with little shields,” in Book XI, chapter 23, where oblong openings appear in the nets—not wholly round, as some wish. “With what artistry,” he says, “they conceal their snares as they move across their shield-patterned web.” For just as we see in nets openings separated by their meshes, which Germans and Danes usually call *Masken*, connected with one another in an oblong roundness, so they elegantly called them the *scutulae* of the net and spider’s web.

Pliny likewise calls a piece of bark a *scutula*, for the same reason, in Book XVII, chapter 16, where he describes the art of grafting in very elegant words:

> “When all branches have been cut away, lest they draw off the sap, in the brightest part, where the greatest vigour is seen, after a little shield-shaped piece has been removed, so that the blade does not go deeper, bark from another tree, with the small bud of its own shoot, is inserted into the bark.”

Thus the form in which this is removed teaches us that it is precisely the form of a *scutula* most suited to the purpose: not wholly round, but oblong. The ancients accordingly applied the word to smaller things resembling the ordinary shield in shape. Garments and horses are also called *scutulatae*, scattered with such net-like figures; the French call them *pommelez*, the Germans *Apffelgrave Pferde*. [Col. 0782C]

Hence also *scutrum*, a kind of vessel extending in the manner of a shield—such as today especially many basins which we call *Spulkessel*, containing water for washing glass and drinking-vessels. These may properly be called *scutra*. The word occurs in Varro and Plautus, in the *Persa*, Act I, scene 3:

> “How well they trample in the *scutra*—and throw in a reed!”

From this it is clear that it was bronze, since it could be placed upon the fire, and shield-shaped; likewise the little vessel *scutriscum*, of the same form, in Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 10. All these things were derived by the Romans from the shield and its form and introduced into their language, although the very word *scutum* is Greek and reveals to the Latins its origin from *skytos*, “hide.”

But when that oblong form of the little dishes began to be inconvenient for plates and saucers, they were reduced to a round form and nevertheless continued to be called *scutulae*. For if plates had been round from the beginning, they should have been called not *scutulae* but *clypea*, since *clypei* were round, not oblong like shields. The name *patina* rightly expresses the shallowness of little dishes: they are wholly open, have almost no depth, and are flat and low—*flach und plat*. Hence the French call plates *des plats* and dishes *des escuelles*. Italians and Spaniards also admitted the word into their languages. Nor can I wonder that the Germans too wished to retain it, calling plates *Skottel*, in Netherlandish *Schootel*, and in Upper Germany *Schussel*, like the round and square dishes called among us *Telle* and *Tellerken*, from *telle*, “to cut,” either because they were wooden and fashioned from wood with a knife, or because we cut food upon them. [Col. 0783A]

The Danes and northerners scarcely adopted the word *Skottel*. Yet one may observe times when that name entered Icelandic or Old Danish. They knew the *Scutilsvein*, and we read that this was the man at court to whom the custody of all this household equipment was entrusted. This display of courtly offices, with its new names, pleased even the farthest North around the time of Olaf Kyrre, king of Norway. For old customs and names still survive in Denmark, where dishes are called only *Fade*, because they hold food; where *Fadebur* is the place in which such vessels are kept; and where a *Fadeburs Pige* is the maidservant entrusted as storekeeper of such things.

It was more splendid, however, to have in one’s retinue particular servants placed over silver and gold, whom we commonly call *Sølv Poppe*, or those who serve kings with dishes brought on platters—*Credentzer*, *Vorschneider*, *Dugsvenne*—just as those who carried and held candles before kings sitting at table were called *Kertisveini*. Thus *scutellae* spread so widely through all languages, and the name was admitted into use from this origin. [Col. 0783C]

(28) “To the lord king.” Here the archbishop and bishops of Norway precede the king, although they are exiles.

(29) “Wonderfully wrought”: that is, made with great and remarkable skill, an art in which goldsmiths then applied themselves with no little care, producing splendid works. The golden horn, which is among the Danish kings’ *keimēlia*—treasured possessions—and is a work of astonishing craftsmanship, especially commends these ancient arts. It is singular both in art and ingenuity, and scarcely anything comparable can be produced by the rest of the world from that age. Since writers everywhere praise Mexican pagan goldwork as most worthy of admiration, and since we are taught that the Mexicans, like our northerners, first crossed over from Scythia, we must acknowledge that our forefathers were men of great genius and skill, easily surpassing all others. For the workmanship which many of today’s ordinary, uncouth, and impoverished peasants in Norway produce in ivory, walrus tooth, and wood with a single knife [Col. 0784A] I prefer to pass over rather than compare with these ancient works.

(30) Lord Suno. He was the son of Ebbo, son of Skialmo the Fair, Absalon’s paternal cousin. He had several sons: Peter Sunonis, bishop of Roskilde, and Andreas Sunonis, here called chancellor, but by Saxo Grammaticus the royal secretary; he succeeded Absalon in the archbishopric. This Suno Ebbonis died A.D. 1186. His father Ebbo, appointed prefect of Roskilde by Sweyn Grathe, died in 1150. The meaning is that Suno owed Absalon 130 marks of silver; Peter and his brothers, Suno’s sons and heirs, were bound to repay that debt to Absalon. But he now remitted it to them [Col. 0784B] and never wished it to be demanded thereafter. It amounts to 1,040 silver thalers of our currency.

(31) To the bishop of Roskilde. This is the same Peter Sunonis, to whose father Archbishop Absalon had granted 130 marks, and to Peter himself forty-eight—that is, had lent them. When Absalon became archbishop of Lund, he did not immediately relinquish the bishopric of Roskilde, but retained it until he could hand it over to this Peter Sunonis, his paternal cousin’s son, down to the year 1192. He held it until 1214, dying on the day after Simon and Jude.

The episcopal chronicle published by Huitfeld is mistaken in calling him King Valdemar’s chancellor, and thus he would necessarily have succeeded his brother Andreas in that office after Andreas assumed the archbishopric of Lund [Col. 0784C]. Yet no records teach us this. Indeed, immediately afterward the same words contain another error: they wished to make Peter the son of Absalon’s brother—*hvis Broderssøn hand var*, “whose brother’s son he was”—whereas Peter was Absalon’s great-nephew through his paternal uncle Ebbo. These points must therefore be noted and corrected.

(32) To the lord chancellor. This is Andreas Sunonis, brother of Peter, bishop of Roskilde. At that time he was King Canute’s chancellor and, in Saxo, *epistolaris*, “secretary,” because the common title *cancellarius* seemed to Saxo insufficiently Latin.

(33) To Lord Esbern. Is this Absalon’s brother Esbern Snare, or another Esbern related to Absalon—perhaps a brother of Peter and Andreas Sunonis? Either may be understood; but it is incongruous for Esbern, the archbishop’s brother [Col. 0784D], to be postponed to more distant persons, since his legacy ought especially to have been placed before those of other relatives.

Nor do I judge that Esbern Snerling is intended, the son of Nicholas Mule, son of Esbern Snare. Absalon can scarcely have seen him born; or, if he did, he could not have seen the sons whom this text here brings forward. Another Esbern must therefore be indicated here, but who he really was is by no means clear. That he belonged to Suno’s family together with Peter and Andreas, who immediately precede in this Testament, is not improbable.

Below Esbern Mule is named, who gave Absalon a coat of mail, which Absalon in turn bequeathed to Ulf, the brother of his steward Peter. I think this is the Esbjørn intended here, and the one who occurs together with Absalon himself in the Aasum stone of Scania, cited by Wormius, p. 171 [Col. 0785A]. For I do not agree with those who make him the son of Nicholas Mule. As I have already said, Esbern, son of Nicholas Mule, neither bore that surname nor was of an age, when Absalon died, for it to be said that he stood with him and performed deeds with him. Saxo too seems to attest this when Archbishop Absalon and Asbjørn Mule are joined together as though equal in age.

The son of Nicholas Mule was called Esbjørn Snerling, for whom Wormius reads Suerting from the genealogy of Martin Petreus. Therefore, whether that Esbern, son of Nicholas Mule, was surnamed Snerling or Suerting, he is certainly not the Esbern who here in Absalon’s Testament and on the Aasum stone bore the surname Mule, but another, older Esbern, Absalon’s contemporary, perhaps son of Suno’s, Ebbo’s, or Toko’s paternal uncle [Col. 0785B].

Many Esberns are indeed mentioned in Absalon’s family, but none suits Absalon’s age except his brother Esbern Snare and this Esbern Mule, whom I also consider older than Nicholas Mule and his predecessor in age. It seems to me that nothing prevents Esbern, Absalon’s brother, from being understood. Moreover, the Esbern Mule named below is not called “lord,” a title which this Esbern nevertheless bears.

(34) Hildebrand had made it. Among the ancients it was customary for gifts to be commended, and considered more valuable, by naming their maker. Thus Pliny, *Natural History* XXXIII.11, writes that L. Crassus possessed cups chased by the hand of the craftsman Mentor, valued at one hundred thousand sesterces. So Martial, VI.92:

> Since, Ammianus, a serpent is chased upon your dish  
> by Myron’s art;

and III.35:

> … the famous embossed work  
> of Phidian art which he held—  
> you see fishes; add water, and they will swim.

But Virgil says it best, *Eclogues* III:

> … I shall set out cups  
> of beechwood, a carved work of divine Alcimedon;  
> upon them a supple vine, added by the easy lathe,  
> clothes its spreading clusters with pale ivy.  
> In the midst are two figures: Conon—and who was the other,  
> who marked out with his rod the whole heaven for the nations,  
> the seasons which the reaper and which the bent ploughman should observe?  
>   
> [Col. 0785D] I have not yet put my lips to them, but keep them stored away.  
>   
> DAMOETAS. And the same Alcimedon made two cups for us,  
> and clasped their handles round with soft acanthus;  
> he placed Orpheus in their midst, and the woods following him.

In the same way the northerners had outstanding craftsmen of their own. Hildebrand was not among the least of these; by his skill he made this silver cup especially renowned, and Absalon gave it to Esbern.

(35) To Lord Alexander. This Alexander was Absalon’s nephew through his sister Ingefrith, as I learned from the manuscript catalogue of those buried at Sorø. For there he is said to be buried near the entrance of the choir: “Lord Alexander, nephew of Lord Absalon, archbishop, through his sister Ingifrith.” The same occurs in the manuscript genealogy of Absalon in my possession [Col. 0786A], in these words: “Moreover, the aforesaid Lord Ascerus Ryg begot a daughter, Ingifrid, by whom [came] Alexander; from him [came] Absalon, Alexander, and Nicholas.”

This genealogy of Absalon is uniquely useful for elucidating this Testament of Absalon and ought to have been published alongside it. But I spare expenses which no one supplies; therefore I must preserve and suppress this and other matters for another time, when I shall be better provided for.

(36) And the coats of mail which he had. That is, Archbishop Absalon’s. They indicate that Alexander, his sister’s son, was a distinguished soldier, worthy to receive so great a legacy of the archbishop’s coats of mail; for in those days coats of mail were exchanged for gold and were “worth many other things in exchange” (*ἄλλων ἀντάξιαι πολλῶν*).

[Col. 0786B] (37) And to his two sons. Alexander had three sons—Absalon, Alexander, and Nicholas—as is clear from the preceding observation. Therefore either one of them was born after the Testament was made, or one had died before it.

(38) To Lady Margaret. There are many Margarets in Lord Absalon’s family. Skialmo the Fair had a daughter Margaret who entered the convent at Roskilde; but she is too remote from Absalon and his legacies. He also had another daughter, Cecilia, married to Peter Torst of Pedersborg; she bore Ingerda, who, after being married to Vagn, bore among other children a daughter Margaret. From her came Vogn Gallen, and from Vogn again [Col. 0786C] Margaret, who became the wife of Juri Stigson, a very famous man.

This Margaret, Ingerda’s daughter, seems to be intended, to whom Absalon wished to leave this legacy, as his great-grandniece through his paternal aunt Cecilia. There was also another Margaret, daughter of Suno, son of Ebbo, son of Skialmo the Fair, and therefore likewise Absalon’s great-niece through his paternal uncle Ebbo. This legacy could apply to her: she was sister of Archbishop Andreas and Peter of Roskilde, to whom legacies are also found written here. I confess that I might vote for this latter Margaret, since throughout this entire Testament Absalon appears especially inclined toward Suno’s family.

(39) The idols of the Rugians. The Rugians of the island of Rügen are meant here. We know that King Valdemar I [Col. 0786D] not only conquered the Rugians but made them Christians, and that Absalon was the chief commander in that campaign. That these idols had their own priests, a great household, and equipment of many kinds in gold and silver is too plain to require lengthy repetition here. It is enough to know that Absalon retained these cups from that booty, and that they were excellent enough to deserve preservation.

(40) To the canons of the Paraclete. The canons intended are those of Ebelholt, of the monastery of St Thomas. Their abbot at that time was William, whom Absalon had summoned from Paris through Saxo, provost of Roskilde—not through Saxo Grammaticus—and appointed there. This monastery was called that of the Holy Paraclete, *zum heiligen Geist*, “of the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0787A].

The place where it was situated and founded was not far from Roskilde, on an island called and known as Eskildsø, or Estildtune. The author of the Life of St William the Abbot notes that the whole island was surrounded on every side by the sea, and describes the place as exceedingly pleasant, delighting the eyes and minds of those dwelling there with green meadows and diverse woodland trees.

Huitfeld says, under the year 1201, that this island lay near Selsø, p. 168; that the monastery was subsequently transferred in 1238 to the small town of Ebelholt, where a church was built in honour of St Thomas; but when Frederiksborg was built by King Frederick II, both the town and the monastery nearby were demolished.

Before Abbot William, these canons [Col. 0787B] were governed by a prior. When William arrived and was appointed abbot, they adopted the Rule of St Augustine according to the precepts of St Victor customarily observed at Paris, and thus seem to have become Canons Regular, having previously been monks of the Benedictine order.

I see that this monastery too was first founded by Archbishop Eskil; hence the names Eskildsø and Eskildstune. Yet I do not find recorded when Eskil established it. He founded Hervad monastery in Scania in 1144 and Esrum in Zealand in 1150, for he was bound by a vow to establish five. But in the manuscript *On the Origin of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 3, chapter 25—now published and excerpted through the kindness of Arne Magnæus in the anonymous *Chronicle of the Danes*, which he made public—it is expressly said [Col. 0787C] that, after becoming archbishop from 1138, Eskil immediately recognized that the time had come to fulfil his vow:

> Having obtained an opportunity, he took care to summon from the remote regions of Gaul, where he had learned that the fountainhead of religion was found, not only five but even more communities of spiritual profession.

And shortly afterward:

> In order perfectly to redeem himself and to render to his most merciful deliverer, as he had promised, a good and overflowing measure, he was unwilling to be satisfied with the foundation of five monasteries, but endeavoured to build others upon others, both from his own resources and from the gifts of other faithful persons.

Among these, therefore, Eskildstune on Eskil’s island can no longer be doubted to have been founded by him. Thus those are mistaken [Col. 0787D] who maintain that Absalon was its first founder. He embellished, corrected, and remedied faults which had arisen; he did not lay the first foundations.

If Huitfeld’s opinion is true—that Abbot William died in 1201 and the monastery was transferred from Eskil’s island to Ebelholt in 1238—as I believe it is, I do not know how Stephanius’s statement in the prologue to Saxo, chapter XI, taken from a manuscript codex, can be true:

> St William died in the fortieth year after undertaking pastoral care, and was buried in the monastery of St Thomas in the town called Ebelholt, in the year 1202.

For, whatever may be said of the town of Ebelholt, the monastery of St Thomas was not yet there when William died and therefore could not have been the place of his burial. Otherwise two monasteries would have to be assumed, one in Eskildsø and another at Ebelholt, under one abbot, which is unsuitable.

The very words of the legacy also seem to indicate that Abbot William had already died before Absalon in the same year, 1201; for the gift is made to the canons of the Paraclete, not to the abbot. William was very dear to Absalon, whom he certainly would not have passed over had he still been alive. [See the Life of St William, published below in this volume.]

(41) Of plain workmanship. Everyone knows the distinction between these types of silverwork. The Germans call it *flecht Arbeit*, when the craftsman displays silver without emblems, carved images, or chased ornament. Medieval writers call vessels bearing figures *imaginata*; ancient Latin calls them *pustulata* [Col. 0788B], “embossed”; the Germans, *getriebene und verhobene Arbeit*, work wrought into various raised forms.

(42) Ten marks of silver. One may therefore observe the weight of these cups: this was 160 half-ounces, equal in value to eighty silver thalers.

(43) For making a chalice. The names of drinking vessels differ because the forms they indicate differ. Cups (*scyphi*) have already been said to be called *Skale* by the Danes: it is a bowl on a low foot, whence remains the phrase *at dritkke Skaale*, “to drink bowls.” The *caucium* and *caucia* mentioned in Justinian’s Code and elsewhere are called *Kousken* by the Danes and have the shape of a bowl without a foot. Chalices are not so broad, but rise deeper and narrower upon a conspicuous foot [Col. 0788C]. What distinguishes *biccaria* will be said below.

Among Christians, however, *calices* generally began to mean those cups, or *ποτήρια* (“drinking vessels”), that were used only at the sacred supper; so much so that Germans and Danes considered it a matter of religion to name that holy cup differently: *Den ny Testamentis Kalf et nam er den Kelch*, “the cup of the New Testament is called the chalice.” Among the Latins, the word *calix* was not so restricted.

Thus substantial and adequate chalices belonging to the monastery of St Lawrence also belong to the sacred uses and to the altars of that church and monastery. Chalices should therefore today be understood either in their sacred use—indeed, their Eucharistic use alone, marked by their distinct form—or in their non-sacred use in ordinary life, which was the more ancient. Here only a chalice intended for the Lord’s Supper [Col. 0788D], to be fashioned of silver, is indicated.

When the name *calix* first began to be applied to these sacred cups is not hard to see: namely, after Jerome’s Latin translation of the sacred books began to prevail in the fifth century. Before that, the Latin and Roman churches called such vessels by any name for a cup, using *scyphi*, *calices*, and *cuppae* indiscriminately. Tertullian already mentions sacred chalices engraved with the Lamb of God upon the shepherd’s shoulders, *On Modesty* I.7:

> Let the very pictures on your chalices come forward, if in them the interpretation of that sheep will shine through;

and shortly afterward, chapter 10:

> But I draw from Scripture concerning that shepherd whom you paint on the chalice—a Scripture which cannot be broken.

Yet use in the sacred supper was not then confined to the name *calix* alone, as it was later [Col. 0789A], when Jerome had rendered the sacred writings into Latin. At that point they seemed to speak in the words of Holy Scripture when they spoke with Jerome. Many names for cups, not *calix* alone, may be found among the ancients by anyone willing to consult and collect them.

In the Greek text there is everywhere only *ποτήριον*, both in the Evangelists and in St Paul: “a cup,” a small vessel from which we take drink. At first, then, names for these sacred vessels were interchangeable, just as their materials in churches were interchangeable: wood, earthenware, glass, horn, silver, gold, stone, even precious stone, and also tin, according to the condition and resources of each church.

In ordinary life, cups are still commonly made of various woods [Col. 0789B]; formerly beechwood cups were especially common. Hence many have wished the name *calix* to derive from *καλόν*, “wood.” But they quickly perceived that wood was unsuitable for these venerable sacred uses, because it necessarily absorbed some particles of the consecrated wine, which seemed exceedingly *ἀνόσιον*, “profane” or “impious.”

Therefore, although reason itself counsels abstaining from wooden and copper vessels, necessity sometimes compelled the admission even of wooden cups for such great mysteries. Pope Zephyrinus, wishing to correct this, judged that no necessity or poverty could be so great that persons lacking silver or stone vessels could not at least administer in a glass cup, since glass at that time did not greatly exceed wood in price; thus those divine [Col. 0789C] draughts could be kept and presented more cleanly.

Some pontiffs have ventured to deny that matters ever came to the point that sacred mysteries were administered anywhere in wooden cups. I am unwilling simply to agree with them, for the matter is not incredible: very many canons exist prohibiting the use of wooden cups for this purpose.

Canon VI of the Council of Rheims expressly decreed that no one should presume to sing Mass in a wooden or glass chalice; Gratian included this in *On Consecration*, distinction I, chapter “That the Chalice.” The Council of Tribur, held in 895, canon XVIII, reads:

> We decree that henceforth no priest shall presume in any manner to celebrate the sacred mystery of the body and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord in wooden vessels, lest God be angered by that whereby He ought to be appeased.

It was well enough that they completely prohibited them when no such necessity arose as would reduce them to wooden cups. But because wooden cups were common in ordinary use, the earliest bishops did not condemn their use even in sacred rites; rather, they always regarded it as a matter left to free judgment.

I do not, however, wish to defend the opinion of Honorius of Autun, that the Apostles celebrated Masses in wooden chalices, *On the Ancient Rite of Masses* I.89. I contend only that celebrations were once held even in wooden chalices; otherwise canons prohibiting them could not have been issued.

For the Council of Tribur by no means prohibits the other chalices—glass, horn, or stone—but wooden ones alone. Around 787 in England, however, at the Council of Calchuth under Pope Adrian I, chapter 10, the Fathers forbade the making of a chalice or paten from ox-horn for use in sacrifice.

The Church retained glass vessels longer, for we still read of them in the fourth and fifth centuries. Jerome, in letter 4, reports that Exuperius of Toulouse, living toward the end of the fourth century, administered the sacrament in glass vessels:

> None is richer than he who carries Christ’s body in a wicker basket and his blood in glass.

Cyprian, biographer of St Caesarius of Arles, eminent at the close of the fifth century, wrote: “Is not Christ’s blood held in glass?” Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs* 46, also mentions a crystal chalice of remarkable beauty, which a deacon allowed to slip from his hands [Col. 0790B] in the basilica of St Lawrence the Levite, so that it was broken.

Baronius, in his note on 7 August, mentions the use of glass altar chalices from apostolic times. I would have some hesitation about this, because glass at that period was not inferior in price to gold and gems. Yet what, I ask, is absurd in supposing that the Apostles saw such cups among gifts offered in churches and did not disdain to use them?

The same Council of Tribur, cited above, says that Pope Urban XVIII, who reigned from 224, made all sacred implements silver. But it does not follow that everyone was compelled to use silver, if another necessity permitted otherwise; after Urban, chalices of materials other than silver were also used. For Innocent IV even allowed the use of tin chalices in the regulations [Col. 0790C] he prescribed around 1243 for the bishop of Nicosia and the bishops of the kingdom of Cyprus during their dispute.

All sacred chalices did not serve solely for the sacred supper. Very many were dedicated also to the ornament of the church and called either standing or hanging chalices, because they either stood upon the altar and its corners, or hung from little chains. This may be seen in several passages of Anastasius the Librarian. Under Leo IV he writes:

> He also offered to the blessed apostle Peter sixteen silver chalices standing around the circuit of the altar;

and shortly afterward:

> Also a hanging chalice with little chains and dolphins.

Here “dolphins” are the chalice handles. He further records [Col. 0790D]:

> Michael, son of Theophilus, emperor of Constantinople, out of love for the Apostles, sent to the blessed apostle Peter, etc., through the hand of the monk Lazarus, etc., likewise a chalice of gold surrounded with stones, adorned with a hanging little cord of precious white gems of wondrous beauty, and with small covers for the chalice itself, as is the Greek custom.

I shall add from the Life of Leo III:

> In the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, he made twenty large chalices, fashioned from the purest silver out of the offerings made to that apostle, which hang in the arch; and forty others, hanging among the larger columns on the right and left, weighing together 267 pounds.

Likewise in the history of Paschal I:

> He made forty-two large hanging chalices of silver, all of which together weigh 281 pounds.

These chalices were not of contemptible size, since more than six pounds of silver may be reckoned for each [Col. 0791A], or nearly eighty silver thalers, in our currency. If the goldsmith’s workmanship is also valued at four Lübeck *asses* per half-ounce, the price of each chalice rises to ninety-three silver thalers.

From these things it is clear that some chalices were holy, serving only the Eucharist; others were ministerial, from which the people were served; others were principal chalices, that is, especially great and splendid; others were hanging chalices, of which I have already spoken. To these may be added “chalices founded,” which are not, as some have wished, “cast and melted,” but made from the endowment and offerings of the Church.

Likewise Anastasius calls vestments *de fundato*, woven and obtained from the Church’s property and gifts. He [Col. 0791B] explained this sufficiently in the passage cited above, where by “large chalices founded from the purest silver out of the offerings of the apostle himself” he meant from the gifts donated and offered to the apostle St Paul by faithful Christians. Thus he also intended “vestments from the endowment” to mean those provided from the Church’s own resources. This is what “to be endowed” and “to be provided from an endowment” mean in Anastasius—an expression that has troubled many until now, who have been unable to grasp Anastasius’s true meaning.

There were, besides, baptismal chalices in the ancient Church. Of Innocent I, Anastasius says that he offered three silver baptismal chalices, each weighing two pounds. In these baptismal chalices milk, honey, and wine mixed together were consecrated and offered to the newly baptized. They belonged to the ministerial chalices [Col. 0791C]; hence the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 24, says:

> The first-fruits, namely milk and honey, customarily offered on the one most solemn day for the mystery of infants, although offered upon the altar, have their own blessing, so that they may be distinguished from the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

These, therefore, were baptismal chalices. There were also chalices of penitence, concerning which Anastasius writes under Sixtus III; there he calls them a ministry for sacred baptism or penitence, because penitents reconciled to the Church were sprinkled with blessed water from these chalices.

Some have also inferred from the same Anastasius that there were reticulated chalices. Yet I hold that no such chalices ever existed and that they are not found in Anastasius. The passage they cite from Anastasius was both wrongly read by the editors [Col. 0791D], and neither understood nor explained by the editors themselves. For no one has yet explained in any word what a reticulated chalice is or ought to be; nor does Anastasius anywhere say this.

His words cited above state nothing else than that Michael, son of the emperor Theophilus, sent his gifts to blessed Peter the apostle at Rome, including “likewise a chalice of gold surrounded with stones”—that is, marked out with gems—“with a hanging net.” Thus the printed books read; but one readily sees that, with the addition of a single letter, it should be read: “adorned with a hanging little cord of precious white gems of wondrous beauty” (*resticulo pendente de gemmis albis pretiosis mirae pulchritudinis decoratum*).

For this was one of the magnificent hanging chalices mentioned above; but instead of the little chains from which other hanging chalices were suspended [Col. 0792A], it had a little cord covered with most precious pearls for the same purpose, together with small covers for the chalice itself—and also for the cord—lest, when hanging, it should be spoiled by dust and dirt. The phrase, therefore, is: “a chalice adorned with a hanging little cord of precious white gems of wondrous beauty.” Thus we reject those “reticulated chalices,” or chalices “hanging from a net,” since nothing of the kind is said or implied.

That some chalices had handles and others lacked them needs neither statement nor explanation. We all know what handles are on jugs and cups, and that many chalices are made with one handle and very many with two. Anastasius called the handles “dolphins,” as I have said, because more elaborate ones were customarily fashioned and attached in the shape of dolphins.

I wish only [Col. 0792B] to add concerning chalices furnished with two handles that they were always, in their own kind, heavier than those without handles, and pass rather into the nature of mixing-bowls than remain among the classes of cups or chalices. Such was plainly Charlemagne’s great chalice given to St Peter, with gems and two handles, weighing fifty-eight pounds.

Finally, Anastasius, under Leo III, also mentions a four-sided chalice. Rejecting the ordinary round form of chalices, he seems to have believed a quadrangular shape would appear more majestic to human eyes; hence he adds that it was exceptional:

> He made for the blessed Apostle, his patron, an exceptional four-sided golden chalice.

I say nothing of figured, gilded, golden, larger, and smaller chalices [Col. 0792C], since they explain themselves sufficiently. It may perhaps be necessary to note concerning chalices of gems (*gemmei*) and gem-encrusted chalices (*gemmati*) that writers very often confuse them.

Gem chalices, and gem vessels, are fashioned in the form of a chalice from a single gem—such as agate, emerald, or sapphire—or are constructed of several gems joined into one body; or the greater part of the chalice is a continuous gem, while a lesser addition is of gold, as when the foot of a chalice is perhaps gold but the vessel itself wholly gem, or its rim and foot are gold while the remaining body is gem.

Gem-encrusted chalices, however, are studded here and there with gems. Thus gem chalices differ from gem-encrusted chalices just as golden chalices differ from gilded ones. These are the matters concerning sacred chalices which seemed appropriate for me to discuss at this point. I do not deny that Andrew du Saussay assisted me here in his *Priestly Panoply*, book VIII.

As for the origin of the chalice and its name, whether Latin or Greek, I think it need not be greatly laboured over, since the ancients themselves disagree on the matter and hold that chalices were used for every purpose, not drinking alone. Those who derive *calix* from *caldus* and *calidus*, “warm” and “hot,” say that it was customarily placed near the fire for cooking; as Ovid too understands chalices in *Fasti* V:

> Chalices stand there: one contained beans, another vegetables.

More often, however, and more commonly, the word is used for a drinking vessel. I therefore incline to believe that the Romans made *calix* from Greek *κύλιξ*, not because of the cup’s roundness, as though from *κύκλιξ*, but because, after drinking cups, we whirl them around in a kind of dizziness before bringing ourselves back [Col. 0793A] to standing.

This *κύλισις* gave us *κύλικες* and *κυλίσκες*, that is, small cups and lesser chalices: from *κυλίνδω*, therefore, come *κύλισις*, *κυλίσει*, *κύλιξ*, and *κυλίσκη*. Such rolling *κύλικες* still survive among German drinking vessels and are called by the elegant and fitting name *Tumeler*, because, when set in motion, they turn in pleasing circles but do not fall from their position.

Why the Latins rather said *calices* is because *υ* often changes into *α*, as *κυλίνδομαι* itself is often written *καλίνδομαι*; or perhaps the Latins looked to the calyxes of flowers and to *καλυκώδεα*, which likewise resemble the form of chalices.
