But *κάλυξ* is one thing and *κύλιξ* another. Such matters need no further examination here.

(44) Crowns in the church. We heard above that there were two [Col. 0793B]. They were not excessive ornament, for a cathedral church required more. Even churches smaller than cathedrals now adorn all their arches and porticoes with such hanging crowns, so that some were and are even three hundred cubits in circumference. But this luxury did not yet suit Absalon’s age and its simplicity. It was enough that he could make them of silver-plated bronze, and here he indicates from what source the silver should be taken to complete and adorn these crowns with gold.

(45) Lord Alexander. Mentioned several times in this Testament: he is the same man noted above, Absalon’s nephew through his sister Ingefrida.

(46) Eight marks of gold. Eight and a half marks of gold, if of Hungarian fineness—as the ancients were especially concerned with the purest refined gold—amount to 1,088 silver thalers in our currency. No one should infer from this that, just as solid gold was customarily sewn or applied onto a chasuble, so the crowns too were adorned with solid gold. Silver was clothed with gold in appropriate places, which was sufficient; Germans aptly call this workmanship *zierguldt*, “ornamental gilding.”

(47) For the making of a chasuble. As it is used today, this is the vestment of priests serving at the altar. The French call it *chasuble*; the Germans retain the Latin name, *Rasel*; the Danes express it as *Meszhagel*, not inelegantly beyond the others. For they put on this garment when celebrating Mass and fasten it with clasps upon the shoulder; a clasp is *hage* in Danish, whence *Meszhagel*, named from both its shape and use [Col. 0793D].

Before it came into use among them, servants used it among the Latins, as Procopius indicates in *The Vandalic War* II:

> Wearing a garment suitable neither for generals nor for any other man engaged in military service, but entirely fitting for a slave or a private individual; the Romans call it in the Latin tongue a *casula*.

To this refer the words of Carloman and of the synod held in 742, on 21 April, as found in book V of the *Capitularies of the Emperors Charles and Louis*, title II:

> Priests and deacons shall not use cloaks in the manner of laypeople, but chasubles according to the rite of the servants of God.

Chasubles therefore belonged to servants because they could be thrown on quickly, required no effort of dressing, and did not hinder those wishing to remain active, except that they enclosed the hands. Servants’ hands were too active, and for that reason chasubles are thought to have been invented.

Therefore, that priests too might show their humility and declare themselves like servants, they introduced the chasuble into sacred rites, putting it on and professing by this garment that they were servants of God and servants of God’s servants [Col. 0794A].

Its shape was often changed when it lay in the power of ecclesiastical persons, and it was confused by many names rather than made clearer. Most identified it with the *paenula* and *planeta*; others preferred to call it the priestly garment *κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν*, “pre-eminently”; others depicted it as a sack-like garment, as Simon of Thessalonica does in *On the Temple*.

Among the Greeks the chasuble was otherwise shaped than among the Latins. Goar reproduced its image in his scholia on the Greek *Euchologion*, and Andrew du Saussay reproduced it from Goar in his *Priestly Panoply*, p. 126. It is indeed a garment not unlike a sack [Col. 0794B], closed on all sides and without sleeves, beneath which the whole body, together with the arms, is hidden except for the head. It descends to the feet and is narrower about the neck, where there is an opening through which the head is passed and the sack-like garment put on. The inscription accompanying that image reads: “Saint Sampson” (*Ὁ ἅγιος Σάμψων*).

Far different is the chasuble used among the Latins. Goar likewise published its image there, from a certain old parchment liturgical codex of the Church of Liège, which he affirms was written 650 years before his own time and attributes to Pope St. Sylvester I. I do not pledge my faith on that matter, but leave it to the author. That chasuble has much in common with our present-day chasubles: it hangs from the shoulders in front and behind [Col. 0794C], with open, gaping sides, so that the arms and hands can be used in extending them. This could by no means be done in the sack-like, hanging Greek chasuble; rather, the chasuble had to be raised in front as far as this point and held over the arms, so that the priest might have his hands free. This finally makes the Greek chasuble in some way similar to the Latin chasuble, so that we see that Latin priests learned the use of chasubles from the Greeks, but adapted them in their own fashion, to make them more convenient for priests ministering and using them. Monsieur du Saussay demonstrates this quite well in the same place, when he continues his explanation of St. Sylvester’s chasuble, p. 128.

Hence I am surprised that he wished to call the garment of Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, who was buried there in 1134, wholly wrapped in it, a chasuble, since that garment had nothing resembling a chasuble. Nor do the acts, from which he cites several words, call that distinctive garment a chasuble, but describe it as follows:

> The upper garment, which for the greater part remains, was of crimson silk, interspersed with golden threads in the likeness of flowers or roses. This garment clothed the entire body of N[orbert], together with his arms, down to the soles of his feet. Beneath it N[orbert]’s hands, crossed in the manner of a cross, were laid upon his breast. The same garment, wrapped about him, was fastened by two silver pins, ornamented at their upper end with jewelled work.

There is nothing in that garment like the Latin chasuble; rather, it may more properly be compared with the sack or the Greek chasuble.

Certainly the first writer after Procopius to mention the chasuble among garments is Isidore of Seville, *Origins*, book XIX, chapter 24 [Col. 0795A], a writer of the seventh century, who wrote from A.D. 620 to 636. “The chasuble,” he says, “is a hooded garment, called by diminution from *casa* (‘hut’), because it covers the whole person, as it were a smaller hut; whence also *cuculla* (‘hood’), as it were a smaller cell. Thus the Greeks too wish *planetae* to be so called, because they wander abroad with their faces exposed.”

By calling the chasuble a hooded garment that covers the whole body, he makes it more like the Greek chasuble and the sack of which we spoke; nor does he count the chasuble among sacred garments, but still among ordinary and pagan ones. This surprises me, since he had no lack of opportunity when he treated individually of priestly dress under the Law in chapter 21; nor in his books on ecclesiastical offices did he say anything about clerical garments.

Bede is the first to list the chasuble among priestly garments, a full century after Isidore [Col. 0795B], since he wrote from the year 725 onward. In the *Collectanea*, under the title “On the Seven Orders,” he says:

> The seventh garment is what they call the chasuble; the Greeks call it the *planeta*, because it is the outermost of all garments and covers the others with its protection.

I do not quite understand Bede’s statement, hinted at also by Isidore, that it is called *planeta* among the Greeks. For among ancient Greeks there is no word *πλανήτη* (*planētē*) meaning a garment, nor among the later Greeks. Thus both Isidore and Bede must be said to have been mistaken in this, since that name was never applied to a garment anywhere among the Greeks. *Planeta* should rather be derived from a Latin origin, from *plano* and *plane*, “plainly, completely,” because it completely covers a person. Thus it suits the chasuble, which likewise completely covered the person [Col. 0795C], as we have learned from Goar’s figure of St. Sampson and from the described garment of Archbishop Norbert.

Albert Krantz, principal canon and lecturer of Hamburg, agrees in his book *On the Institution of the Priest for the Office of Mass*, published at Rostock in 1506:

> The chasuble is the priest’s outer garment, and is so called because, in the manner of a house, it encloses all that belongs to the priest. Its shape is said to be circular, so that, when the priest’s hands are lowered, it hangs evenly on every side.

This is entirely correct according to the image which Goar caused to be drawn and attributed to the Greeks. When the hands were raised and extended outside the chasuble, this front and back fold necessarily ran down into a kind of point; the sides were left bare; and the parts of the chasuble that had been raised were carried upon the arms, twisted into folds and wrinkles. But when the hands were lowered and drawn back, these again covered the sides, resumed their circular shape, and enclosed and girded the whole person [Col. 0795D]. Nor could Krantz have been ignorant of what a chasuble was in his own day, having been nurtured in sacred things from childhood and thoroughly conversant with sacred garments.

Thus chasubles were not yet so slit at the sides as more convenient use has required them to be made today. Rather, when the priest’s hands were lowered, they fell back into their circular roundness. Amalarius Fortunatus, bishop of Trier, must therefore be explained in this sense, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 19:

> The chasuble is double: behind the back, over the shoulders, and before the breast.

For when the hands are raised [Col. 0796A] and extended outside the chasuble, the chasuble is as it were divided into two parts, namely the rear and the front. Amalarius is speaking of the appearance of a priest ministering in a chasuble. But when the hands are lowered and drawn back, those two parts are joined together and hang evenly all around, as Krantz says.

Philotheus, bishop of Constantinople, also speaks of a lowered chasuble in the rite for ordaining a deacon, found in volume VI of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*. In several places he says: “The priest also comes out backwards, wearing the chasuble lowered.” He means nothing else than that the chasuble then hangs down, containing within itself the hands and arms by which at other times he raises it, as may also be observed from Goar’s image. Further below he says: “The priest, opening the holy doors, wears the *phaelonion* lowered,” where *phaelonion* [Col. 0796B] means a *paenula* and is the same thing as a chasuble. Again he adds: “But the priest, wearing the *phaelonion* lowered and carrying the Gospel before his breast, comes out and stands in the middle of the church, with the deacon at his right holding a lighted candle.”

One might ask how he could carry the Gospel before his breast and nevertheless have the chasuble lowered. For even with his hands extended, unless the chasuble were raised, he could not show it by holding and pressing the Gospel before his breast.

Having thus explained the chasuble, it is somewhat clear from Procopius, a sixth-century writer, when that word began to be used among pagans; and we have shown from Isidore that it still remained among ordinary garments in the seventh century. By the eighth century [Col. 0796C] it had passed into sacred vestments and use, as Bede teaches. Earlier writers taught nothing about its use in sacred rites. Therefore whatever Roman Catholics insist upon concerning St. Peter’s chasuble and the Apostle Paul’s *φελόνῃ* (*phelonēi*, “cloak”) collapses at once of itself. For no one would wish to deny that Peter or Paul wore a *paenula*; but I think no Roman Catholic will prove either that the name “chasuble” was then known, or that such cloaks were assigned to sacred use. We know that the Apostles taught the nations in whatever ordinary and common clothing they had put on, and that they were sent out without bag, silver, or belt, “not having two tunics” (*μήτε ἀνὰ δύο χιτῶνας ἔχοντας*). For this is how Christ himself calls the Apostles’ garments in the Gospels.

But in what garments they celebrated sacred rites among those whom they had already taught and brought to the faith [Col. 0796D]—whether in their everyday clothing or in garments assigned solely to particular sacred uses—Scripture is silent. Nor can we rest content with the pious conjectures of certain Fathers, which we readily leave undecided whenever they bring with them nothing contrary to antiquity.

I am not speaking here of the priestly garments of the Jews and of the Old Testament, concerning which Ezekiel 44:19 expressly commands:

> And when they go out into the outer court to the people, they shall take off their garments in which they had ministered, and lay them in the treasury of the sanctuary; and they shall put on other garments, and shall not sanctify the people in their garments.

We have also shown on this occasion both that *casula* and *planeta* are of Latin origin and do not belong to the Greek language, and further, from what source the form and shape of our chasubles today [Col. 0797A] have arisen. Here we stop, lest we become too long and tedious.

(48) **“Scanian denarii.”** Scanian denarii were minted only at Lund. The traces of Lund’s coinage can be followed back to King Canute IV, who first granted the Archbishop of Lund a fourth part of that coinage around the year 1080. I judge that the first mint at Lund was established by Sweyn Estrithson, after he had founded a distinguished bishopric there in A.D. 1065. One may readily prove that the Danes had no established coinage of their own within the Danish kingdom before Canute the Great. That Canute, who died in 1036, seems first to have brought moneyers from England into Denmark and to have had the first mint and Danish denarii struck at Roskilde, in imitation of English coinage. Yet up to now no denarii have come to my notice bearing the name of Canute, king of Denmark; most instead bear “Cnut, king of England.” From those times the mints of Roskilde and Lund plainly show their origins and beginnings, and not a little is written of them. It is therefore unsurprising that Scanian denarii are mentioned here: that is, old coinage struck before Canute VI, son of Valdemar I, which was better than the newer coinage. I discussed above, note 20, the weight and fineness of Scanian denarii in that age.

(49) **“Son of Harina.”** I think it should be read *Karinae*, “of Karina.” The name *Harina* is hitherto unknown among northerners; *Carina*, however, is well known, deriving from the contracted name *Catharina*, which the Danes call *Karen*, and hence *Carina*; just as *Maren* derives from *Maria*, and hence *Marina*.

(50) **“For his soul.”** Similar formulas occur frequently: “to give for his soul”; “for the remedy of his soul”; “for eternal recompense”; “as our alms”; “for the salvation of my soul”; “for the reward of my soul”; “I have considered how I might deserve God’s favour, or divine recompense, or forgiveness of my sins”; “that in the future the reward of a good work may increase for me”; “for the remedy of my soul and that of my wife, parents, and children”; “that by earthly resources I might purchase eternal ones, and by transitory goods acquire lasting ones”; “I have considered the life to come and eternal recompense”; “among the other medicines for healing, God has also granted this remedy, that persons may redeem their souls from the hellish Tartarus by means of their own riches.”

(51) **“A fur-lined cloak.”** Having distributed gold and silver, he now proceeds to articles of clothing and other things to be given. We shall therefore first speak of the *cappa* or cloak, and then deal with linings. The cloaks, mantles, and *juppae* mentioned here differ from one another.

First, it should be observed that writers sometimes call every outer garment—whether mantle, toga, or tunic—a *cappa*. Secondly, the cloak indicated here is the archbishop’s customary and everyday cloak, not the sacred cloak, the violet one in which bishops dressed when about to preside or assist at sacred rites. Thus ordinary cloaks had sleeves [Col. 0798A], whereas sacred cloaks enclosed the body without sleeves. These ordinary cloaks resembled monks’ cloaks: divided and open in front, yet held around the body by a clasp at the neck and a belt thrown around the waist; and they were also furnished with sleeves, which made them adhere more firmly to the body. The cloaks used in sacred rites, however, being made and treated in another shape and form, were thrown round entirely open in front, fastened only by a clasp beneath the chin, and otherwise sleeveless, lavish and flowing in a long train.

There were also laymen’s cloaks, distinct from both sorts we are discussing. They are usually called *mantum*, *mantulum*, or *mantellum*; in French, *manteau*; in German, *Mantel*. They did not extend beyond the hands when hanging down, nor were they foot-length (*ποδήρης*) like the priests’ cloak. Yet Danes and northerners continue to call even this layman’s mantle *Kappe*. This word belongs to the Danes alone, and cannot be adequately understood without their language.

It is futile to derive it from *capere*, “to take,” following Isidore’s etymology, because it takes in the whole person; or from *caput*, “head,” because in mourning, rain, and other times the head is wrapped in it; and still less from *cap* and *pa*, “taking Father,” because monks and priests who use cloaks are customarily called Fathers as a title of honour. This is Andrea du Saussay’s jest in the *Panoplia sacerdotalis*, p. 144, when he could not discover the true etymology of the word. Vossius’s explanation of the word in *On Faults of Speech*, book III, is remarkable: he admits that *cappa* came from the German *Kappe*, yet adds [Col. 0798C] that *Kappe* comes from *caput*. If *Kappe* comes from *caput*, it is not a word of German origin but Latin; and if it is of German origin, it certainly does not come from *caput*.

But I see what moved them and why they wished to refer *cappa* to the head: not merely following an allusion, but chiefly because many caps, both for women and men, serve only to cover the head and extend no further. Yet it does not follow from this that there were no cloaks other than head-coverings. It is therefore evident that a word so broad in scope, whose use extends to the whole body, cannot be confined to the head alone or derive its origin from it. Here, however, ordinary sleeved clerical cloaks are meant—what we call a *Harh-Kappe*—for he includes sleeveless cloaks under mantles.

Those who said that *cappa* is a Frankish word perceived something of the truth: for *cappa* entered the Christian Church from the Franks and their language, and began to adorn the clothing of ecclesiastics. But they never noticed that the Franks and other Germans borrowed and retained much of their own language from Danish, that they flowed forth from the Danes and northerners, and that in very many respects they are distinguished only by dialects. No Frank, speaker of Frankish, or German has ever noticed this; nor do they wish to owe so much to their most richly endowed mother as even to look to her alone, from whose womb they came forth and began to speak. Rather, they prefer to appear *autochthonous* (*αὐτόχθονες*, “native-born”) and self-speaking (*αὐτόγλωττοι*, “self-language-bearing”), though they are not.

In the Danish language alone is found the true origin [Col. 0799A] of the word *cappa* and the reason for it; in no other language. For they began to call those garments *Kappe* in which one wraps oneself against rain or for other reasons; and to the Danes *Kappe* is the same as the Latin *tegere*, “to cover.” Hence it is not surprising that ancient monastic writers call the *cappa*, though ecclesiastical, a *pluviale*, “rain-cloak,” even though it is scarcely used in rain: bishops wear it in church, in dry and clear weather, while occupied with sacred rites.

Wibert, archdeacon, speaks thus in the *Life of Pope Leo IX*: “It seemed to him, while standing on high, that he received his household who fled to him from danger, and, enclosing them beneath the rain-garment called a *cappa*, saw his garments stained with their blood.” For among pagan Danes this covering began to be called *Kappe* because it defended and covered against rain, and was put on against such storms. Hence below it is expressly said: “To Jofrid the cook, two rain-cloaks.” For when they wrapped the head in a hood, or in a cloak, or without one, so that they could not be recognized, they were said to be *forkapped*; and *sig at forkappe*, “to disguise oneself”—which the Germans have retained, though the word *Kappe* has become obsolete among them—in *zu verkappen* and *verkappet*, when they go about masked and disguised [Col. 0799B].

It is therefore clear that monks and priests adopted this word, which, like many others, descended from paganism; and when wishing to speak Latin, they called it a *pluviale*, which is the Danes’ *Regenkappe*, “rain-cloak.” Yet the word *cappa* prevailed, whatever changes it underwent and whatever classes of persons adopted it.

As for the *Hartzappe* of German priests, it did not take its name from Danish, but from the Frankish *cappa*, after this little word had been granted citizenship in Latin and received among all Christians as the name of a priestly garment. This happened when ecclesiastics chose, after the manner of John the Baptist, to wear that garment and cloak woven from camel hair, produced by a new invention of weavers. Then it began to be called *Hartz-kappe* among the Germans, and it is worn to this day by many priests. From them the practice also passed to others, who afterwards put on such garments and applied them to their own use, though without the name *cappa*.

*A hairy garment, of camel hair*, whence also *Kamelot* [Col. 0799C], a merchants’ term for sellers of these cloths, arose; although it was later altered by other distinctions and restricted to watered fabrics and garments, such as *gewässerte Taft[e]*, *Tobinen*, and so forth. Properly, however, *cloths made from camel hair* were what it originally signified. Revelation 6:12 has *σάκκος τρίχινος*, “a hair-cloth sack.” Such hairy garments were made in antiquity not only from camel hair but also from goats’ hair, so that it can scarcely be said that these textiles were treated in the modern manner. For weaving cloth from such hair and making cloaks is not ancient among Germans or the European world, even though hair-shirts (*cilicia*) flourished. These too were woven from animal hair, but not camel hair, and served another use—not in cloaks or outer garments.

Nor did the Danes stop there [Col. 0800A], their language being most fertile; from *Kappe* they also produced another word, *Kaabe*, by which they especially denoted women’s mantles—something no other language has achieved, or can achieve, so easily. For it is not long since women here discarded their mantles: thirty-six years ago no married woman went out in public without her mantle and *Kaabe*. From what has now been said, I think we have sufficiently explained what sort of clothing the archbishop intended by giving cloaks: namely, ecclesiastical robes which he himself customarily wore outside sacred rites.

Now something must be said concerning linings. Here *forrata* means garments lined with shaggy, rough, and bristling skins—garments which Romans and Greeks did not know, since their temperate climates did not require such clothing [Col. 0800B]. The word *forratum* is therefore derived from the language of northerners, who called these hair-covered skins *Foder*, *Foer*, and *Foderwerck*. From that pronunciation Upper Germans learned to inflect *Futter*, *Futterwerck*, and *füttern*, whence *forrata*, *furrata*, and *foderata* occur among monastic and medieval writers. They must be carefully distinguished from *fodrum*, *Foder*, or *Futter*, which also very frequently means “fodder” in the ancient laws of Germans, Danes, and Latins. It was a tributary obligation by which subjects were bound to provide fodder for their lords’ beasts of burden. Because the Romans and Greeks knew this little or not at all, but first learned it from the Germans, we find it expressed by a Germanic name to preserve the memory of that fact.

The Latins, however, wrongly confused the Danish and northern *Forr* and *Foder*, overturning the whole matter by their euphony. *Foder* and *fodrum* mean fodder; *Forr* means shaggy skin. *Foder* derives from Danish *Fode*, “food,” that which nourishes and by which one is nourished. *Forr* is not so derived, since it is used of bristly and hairy things. Therefore *forrata* is better written here than *foderata*. The Franks and English likewise retained the proper inflection of this word, saying *fourrez* and *furring*, where the Latins say *foderare* and *foderatura*. The Latins, corrupting their word by inserting the letter *d*, misled even Germans and Danes, so that many Latinizing writers write *Foder* rather than *Forr* with the northerners, to whom the origin of the word belongs [Col. 0800C] and whose form should accordingly govern its spelling. Among Latin writers some called it not *foderatura* but *fordatura*, and used *fordare* for *forrare*; they erred less than the former.

At other times the German and Danish languages in turn were imbued with the Latin word *pellis*, “skin.” For both men and women call fur-lined tunics and garments *Petz* and *Pitz*: *einen gefütterten Peltz*, *Peltzrock*, *der Peltzer*, and similar terms.

Although *pellicea*, “fur garments,” properly means garments consisting of nothing but skins, with no cloth added above—Danish *Skindkiortel*—such garments are not *foderata* or *forrata*, but mere linings and skins. Indeed, *pellicea* is used more broadly, not only for linings and shaggy skins but also for smoothed and depilated ones, such as breeches and those called *Kollerten*. In German usage these are not *Peltzen*, but they are nevertheless included under the Latin name *pellicea*. For to the Danes *Peltzen* are only shaggy skins still bearing their hair. Nor are only those garments called *pelliceae* whose hair is turned inward and whose exterior is smooth; the term also applies to those arranged in the reverse manner, or doubled inside and out with shaggy skins, such as the mittens mentioned today in Additions I, chapter 22 of Louis the Emperor, or the tunics and boots of the Lapps. These are *pelliceae* and indeed mere skins, but they have an additional hairy, skin lining [Col. 0801A].

In the cited chapter, two *pelliceae* reaching to the ankles are ordered to be given to each monk. Emperor Charlemagne possessed a *pelliceum herbicinum*, as stated in the *Chronicle of St Gall*, book II, p. 422: that is, one made from sheepskin, not bearing hair on the outside but turned inward. Our ancestors used skins differently: for the most part the hair was on the outside and the smooth portions turned inward, thus keeping out the cold far better. In this they followed the nature of skins and their own convenience, not elegance or art. But after they became Christians, opinion did harm; people thought that, if dressed in this manner, they did not look like human beings but like brute beasts, cattle, and wild animals. Hence arose those furriers’ crafts that arranged skins in reverse order, lining garments with them inwardly so that the clothing might appear more respectable and human. Thus *Undrfoder*, *Unterfutter*, began to mean everything used to line garments, not skins alone. The Franks call it *doublure* [Col. 0801B], although they also say *fourrer* of fur-lined garments and other things; for example, they call coins and denarii *fourrés* when copper is covered beneath silver—a word that arose among them from Danish and German languages.

(52) **“Concerning marten skins.”** These are the skins of which Adam of Bremen speaks in his little book *On the Situation of Denmark*, p. 147, when he says:

> The Semigallians or Prussians hold gold and silver in little account; they abound in foreign skins, whose scent has administered to our world the deadly poison of pride. They have them, indeed, as dung, unto our condemnation, we who by right and wrong alike pant after marten fur as though after the highest blessedness.

From this one may judge that a bequest of a marten-fur cloak was not cheap at that time.

(53) **“Concerning grey skins.”** What these skins are can readily be learned from Danish, in which we call them *Graaskind*, *Graawerck*, and *Graavare*, and in German *Grauwerk*. They are pelts stripped from squirrels, which Norway and Russia send us in incredible numbers, where hunting these little animals is very actively pursued. In winter they usually become grey; mingled with reddish hairs, they grow greyish or whitish. At the far end of Jutland there are also wholly black ones, the hunting and possession of which came to adorn the armorial bearings of the noble Fris family even to this day.

In the Norwegian Chronicle, p. 94, Harald, son of Eric and king, is said to have acquired the byname *Graafell*, “Grey-cloak,” from these grey skins, because he began to wear a garment lined with grey skins and a ship loaded with such grey pelts arrived from Iceland in Norway. In the same Chronicle, p. 226 [Col. 0802A], it is related of Otto the Fool hunting squirrels in Vermaland:

> *Han fik sua mange Graaskind, at han fylte sin Sloede saa, at han kunde ikke drage meere.*

That is: “He brought down so many squirrels that he filled his sledge so completely that it could carry no more.” I have wished to note these points concerning grey pelts so that it may be understood which skins are meant. They have not disappeared today, but are esteemed among the more luxurious linings, highly prized both for their lightness and because they adequately warm the body and do not allow cold to penetrate.

(54) **“A marten-fur mantle.”** The ordinary mantle is meant, which the archbishop customarily used in winter, not the one sent from Rome and consecrated there, which archbishops could wear in church only on certain feast days. He is not speaking here of that pallium [Col. 0802B], but of the mantle which archbishops also wore outside church whenever they had to appear solemnly dressed in public. For just as clerics and bishops had certain ordinary neck-cloths and stoles for use outside church, so too they had mantles—garments entirely distinct from those worn within church while performing sacred rites, which they removed after the sacred rites and left in the church sacristy, resuming their everyday garments. Of this sort was the mantle intended for Absalon’s legatee. It is called a marten mantle because, like the cloak in the preceding clause, it was lined with marten skins, while silk or woollen cloth covered the upper and outer part of the mantle. Hence shortly afterwards follows mention of the everyday mantle that he gave and bequeathed to Peter Stamme: “a grey everyday mantle” [Col. 0802C].

(55) **“A surplice with marten fur.”** A surplice is the linen garment of clerics, descending a little below the knees and having very wide sleeves. It is distinguished in this way from the alb, which was likewise linen, but had narrower sleeves and was longer, since it extended to the ankles, *ποδήρης*, “foot-length.” The alb was not permitted except at the sacrifice of the Mass, whereas the surplice could be used in any other sacred function.

It is also called *superpliceum*, and in French *surplis*, which shows us the true origin of the word: it must be derived from folds, so that it should be written *superpliceum*, not *superpelliceum*. For it is not made of skins, since it is a linen garment; nor is it worn over fur or skin, like a shirt or under-tunic; rather, it is thrown over other garments and takes on its various folds because of the fullness it possesses. But when this passage adds that a surplice was given together with a marten-fur garment, we must observe that these linen garments were customarily adorned in various ways—on the sleeves, at the neck, and at the sides—with applied bands of velvet or gold, just as women even now continue to weave gold or other ornaments into their shifts. Thus they produced the French proverb: *Vous êtes fille de chevalier, vous avez la chemise dorée*—“You are a knight’s daughter; you have a golden shirt.”

We learn that this is ancient from Lampridius, in his account of Alexander, son of Mammaea, who judged even the putting of gold into linen to be madness, since stiffness was added to roughness and the skin would often be chafed. But this did not hinder in surplices, since other garments underneath protected the body [Col. 0803A]. Hence Anastasius, in the *Life of Benedict III*, mentions shirts ornamented with gold bands: “white shirts patterned with silk, with a gold band.” As I have spoken of albs adorned with gold bands and decorated with velvet borders, so too surplices were adorned; thus those which ought to be suitable for winter are here said to have been furnished with a marten-fur garment.

Below occurs a surplice lined with *varium* bequeathed to Nicholas, son of the archdeacon. An excellent passage illustrating this matter occurs in the General Council of Constance, session 43, canon “On the Life and Honesty of Clerics”:

> We decree that it be utterly abolished that clerics and ecclesiastical persons wear long garments with great superfluity, even slit behind and at the sides, with linings extending beyond the hem even in the slits.

We readily judge that this applies to the linen, woollen, and silk garments of clerics alike. Many can testify with me, if they care to search their memories, that these garments displaying their slits behind were not abandoned very long ago. The linings called “extending beyond the hem” remain and persist even now among men and women, clerics and nuns [Col. 0803B].

(56) **“Lined with varium.”** *Varium* and grey fur must be distinguished. What grey skins are and where they come from we have already explained in preceding note (53). I shall now say what *varium* is. The skins of panthers, lynxes, leopards, and other wild beasts, conspicuous for their spots, are called *variae*, “variegated,” by Danes and Germans, *bunt*. Not only skins naturally of varied colours, but also those sewn and joined together by furriers with a certain elegance and grace, are called *Buntfoder* and *Buntwerk*; the furriers themselves are accordingly called *Buntmacher* and *Buntwerker*.

Northerners have always loved these variegated skins so much that, whenever nature denied them, they added variegation by art. This may be learned from Tacitus, who declared of all Germans desiring such skins, chapter 17:

> They select wild beasts and adorn the stripped-off coverings with patches and with the skins of beasts which the outer ocean and the unknown sea produce.

He undoubtedly refers to seals, called *Saelhunde* by the Danes (“sea-dogs”), and the other hairy creatures of the ocean, which they sewed here and there into the skins of land animals, so that they might appear spotted and variegated [Col. 0803C].

Whether, therefore, this cloak was lined solely with lynx skins—which Norway, and Russia likewise, send marked with most elegant spots—or whether it was made of varied skins joined together, partly badger, partly cat, marten, sable, fox, wolf, and others, it could be called *vario forrata*, “lined with varium.” This lining occurs often in this testament, since most garments were sewn with varium rather than other skins. Thus it should not seem surprising that furriers acquired the name *Buntmacher* from variegated furs rather than from grey, marten, and other furs, because we read that they were chiefly occupied in sewing together variegated ones [Col. 0803D].

(57) And a Juppa. This is truly an ancient Danish word, by which they commonly signify a tunic, *een Joop*; it passed to the Germans, and the French too retained it as *la juppe*, a name mostly denoting women’s overdress, which we properly call *Skort*, and in German *Schoerten* [Col. 0804A] and *Schuertzen*, because they are girded and secured about women’s middles in various gathers and folds. They are also called *Roecke* by others, a name of rather universal application to almost all garments.

Today *Joopen* is used almost exclusively of rustic tunics. Indeed, they called beer that splendidly cheers country people *Joopen-Beer*, because it makes both persons and their tunics give themselves over to dancing; among Icelanders it would deserve to be called *Faldafeycckir*. For good drink produces such force, such a Bacchus or Ceres, that even garments feel its effects. Hence the Netherlanders say: *Hy heeft wat in syn muts: in syn timp, in syn wamhs, etc., gevattet*—“he has got something into his cap, his temple, his doublet, etc.”—when they begin to incline toward drunkenness and display excessive merriment. The Lower Saxons say of a man who has drunk deeply: *He* [Col. 0804B] *hefft syn Joop ful*—“He has filled his juppe.”

Ferrarius is therefore wrong to derive the Italians’ *giubba* and *giubbone*, and *giubbarello*, from an overdress; as those commonly do who despise our Danish and do not deem it worthy of consideration, they immediately flee to Greek, Hebrew, and Latin when deriving these names, unaware—or forgetful—how far the Danes, by both travel and arms, have introduced their language among other peoples. With the Vandals this word certainly passed into Africa to the Arabs; with the Goths, Normans, and Danes into France, Germany, Italy, and Spain. Yet these peoples seem to have learned Arabic *Aljuba* from the Arabic-speaking Moors, and the Moors from the Vandals.

Nor did Greece reject this word after Danish peoples had reached it as well. For they called a juppe ζοῦπαν (*zoupan*), deriving and pronouncing it in their accustomed fashion. They said ζοῦστρα (*zoustra*) for *justa* (“a joust”), and ζουλάπιον (*zoulapion*) for *julapium* (“julep”). This word occurs frequently in Achmet’s *Oneirocriticon*; thus in chapter 228 one may read:

> ἐὰν ἴδῃ τις ὅτι ἐνεδύσατο ζοῦπαν, εἰ μὲν ἐστὶν ἐξουσιάζων, ὄνομα καὶ φήμην καλὴν εὑρήσει, διὰ τὸ ἐπάνω φορεῖσθαι τὴν ζούπαν ἀεί.

“If anyone sees that he has put on a *zoupan*, then, if he is a person in authority, he will acquire a good name and reputation, because the *zoupan* is always worn on the outside.”

Indeed Agapius in the *Geoponica* has ζοῦπον (*zoupon*) from the *juppon* of the French and Normans, as its ending sufficiently indicates; it denotes a smaller tunic than ζοῦπαν. Hence also ζιπουνι in Crusius’s Turco-Greek, still a smaller tunic than ζουπονι, just as among Italians are *Giubbone*, *Giubeto*, and *Giubettino*.

From this garment a very great dignity among the Greeks of the later period arose: ζούπανος (*zoupanos*) came to mean the superintendent of the prince’s wardrobe. The word also passed to the Slavs—to Serbs and Hungarians—who began to call their princes and satraps ζουπάνους, Ἀρχιζουπάνους, Μεγάλους ζουπάνους—*zoupans*, *arch-zoupans*, and *great zoupans*—from this garment. Since it was an outer garment, as we heard from Achmet, this was to the glory of France and the Danish nation: men of those nations, serving and trading at Constantinople, first brought the garment and its name into these regions. There they admired the majesty and distinction associated with them so greatly that they believed it the highest and princely virtue, and a likeness to the Danes, to walk clothed like Danes, Normans, and Frenchmen.

The passage in Constantine, *On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 29, may now be understood:

> Ἄρχοντας δὲ, ὥς φασι, ταῦτα τὰ ἔθνη μὴ ἔχει, πλὴν ζουπάνους γέροντας, καθὼς καὶ αἱ λοιπαὶ Σκλαβίνιαι ἔχουσι τύπον.

“These nations, they say, have no rulers except elder *zoupans*, after the fashion also found among the other Slav lands.”

The same writer, in that chapter and often elsewhere, calls the provinces ruled by these *zoupans* ζουπανίας, *zoupanias*. Pope Innocent, in his letters [Col. 0805A] and acts, rightly calls them *jupani* and the *great jupan*, correctly following the Latin analogy of the word. Peris, ambassador of the king of Hungary to Emperor Alexius, subscribed himself in the treaty of Duke Bohemond: ζουπάνος ὁ Περὴς, “the zoupan Peris.” Ἀρχιζούπανος, “arch-zoupan,” occurs in Nicetas and John Cinnamus.

I owe these details to the most learned Monsieur du Fresne and his *Glossary*, though he neither saw nor considered the origin of these words. But let us learn what a little word for a single garment can accomplish, and how far it can extend its fringes and wings. For although clothing does not make the man, the Greek commonplace often pleases the crowd: ἱμάτιον ἄνδρα—“the garment [makes] the man.” Who would have believed that the Danish word *Joop* had travelled through so many lands and could have awakened such glory for itself?

Menage concludes well, after recounting everything in his lexicon:

> *Les Allemands disent Guipp pour dire un jupon, et je crois que c'est de ce mot allemand que l'Italien giubba a été formé.*

“The Germans say *Guipp* to mean a petticoat, and I believe that the Italian *giubba* was formed from this German word.”

Whence the Germans derived and acquired this name, along with many others, no one has hitherto carefully investigated. For no one believes that anything useful can proceed from Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, although almost everything needed to illuminate all antiquity must be sought from here, if one wishes to think correctly.

The author of the Norwegian Chronicle used the word in a manuscript concerning Magnus Barefoot, king of Norway, when describing his armour and dress, p. 399:

> *Han hafdi oc silke HIUP rauthan yfir Skyrto, oc skorit fyrer oc a back med guli silki Leo.*

“That is: he wore over his undershirt a red silk tunic, marked before and behind with a lion of yellow silk.”

This sufficiently teaches that *Joop* and *Hiup* are ancient Danish [Col. 0805C] and Icelandic words. Thus a little later the same history says:

> *Eyvindr hafdi oc silki hiup, med sama baetti sem Konungr.*

“That is: Eyvind too wore a silk tunic, in the same manner as the king.”

These juppes were larger and smaller, longer and shorter, wider and closer-fitting. Thus we also read immediately below of a smaller juppe lined with squirrel fur, which Netherlandish women commonly call *eene Jacke*, the French *jacquet*. It ends a little below the girdle, around the middle of the loins. Thus many have interpreted *jupon* as a bodice, which reaches only to the girdle; such garments are seen at Hamburg and Amsterdam among the *Karenschuyvers*, *Kruyers*, *Litzenbroeder*, and so forth.

[Col. 0805D] (58) A fox-fur covering. Unless I am mistaken, he thus calls the upper cover of a bed, lined with fox furs. Below occurs a bed-covering lined with marten fur, which he bequeathed to the archdeacon; it is the same as a covering, as likewise is the bed-covering lined with variegated fur which he leaves as a gift to Master Hugh.

(59) To the stableman. In Danish, *Stallmester*. Today the name suits servants rather than masters of the stable, so that we may observe how changed the master of the stable now goes about from what he was formerly.

(60) Esbern Mule. Enough has already been said above concerning this Esbern in note (33).

(61) To Hakon, the chamberlain. We also touched on him above in note (8), where he was present among the witnesses; here he receives a bequest.

[Col. 0806A] (62) Of brown colour. This Latin expression was then favoured because it explained and denoted the thing more precisely than if he had said “of dark” or “somewhat dark” colour. The Latins lack words by which to distinguish colours familiar and everyday to northerners. There is no small difference between *fuscus* and *bruneus*: the former denotes a saturated colour of that kind, the latter a lighter shade. Thus they introduced *blaveus* stones, distinguishing themselves by that proper colour from *caeruleus* stones, the only colour of that class known to the Romans. They called birds *blavatae* which appeared blue-footed, because they readily saw that the colour *caeruleus* did not suit them at all: *blaa* is one thing, *Himmelblaa* another. Likewise brown admits distinctions of every kind: *Hirschfarbe*, *Haarfarbe*, *Leberbraun*, [Col. 0806B] and so on; all these colours are brown.

(63) A blaccated horse. He called it so because it could not otherwise be expressed in Latin; the Danes call it *een blakket Hest*. Germans and English call black *Blak*, just as ink is *Blek* in Danish. Hence *blakked*: things which do not shine or flourish in a saturated black colour, but as it were fade toward pallor. The Germans call this colour *falb*, as *Mausz-falb*, *ein falbes Pferd*. The French call it *une couleur effacée*, properly *blafard*. They derive this from Greek βλάξ and βλακικός, words which have nothing to do with colours but mean idle, foolish, soft, and delicate. Therefore the French did not get *blafard* from that source, but rather from *blac* and *faire*: a colour, as it were, making some likeness of blackness, as are most colours with white showing through them; for such colours are truly *blakked*.

[Col. 0806C] (64) Eschil Bathsven. Thus were called the oarsmen in boats. Today we write *Baad* and *Svend*, from which this compound name is formed: servant of the pontifical boat. Particular oarsmen were assigned to him, caring for and steering it. Today we call them rather *Baadskarle* than *Svenne*, *Koerkarle*, and so forth.

(65) Nicholas Stabellarius. I found it written thus; and unless it means *stabularius*, a *Stallmeister*, as we heard earlier of Peter the stableman, I do not know what name or office they intended to indicate. For I have never noticed any name so written or formed.

(66) To his clerk Saxo. There can be no doubt that this Saxo is that most celebrated historian of Denmark, particularly because Absalon added the provision concerning books to be returned to Sorø Monastery. We conclude that Saxo was occupied in writing his history and for that purpose had books drawn, through the archbishop’s favour, from the monastery library; here he orders them restored to the monastery.

The short chronicle recently published by the Icelander Arnas Magnæus from a manuscript concerning Danish affairs expressly honoured Saxo the historian with the title of clerk, p. 10. Here Absalon calls him his clerk: that is, his scribe, secretary, amanuensis, secretary for correspondence, and attendant in other writing duties to the archbishop. For this is what it means to be someone’s clerk. Thus kings had their clerks, who especially managed writing and record-keeping. To this very day the Netherlanders, in the old manner, continue to call their scribes and secretaries *klerke*, even after rejecting the Roman religion. For formerly none but clerics were employed in this writing office, since laymen then scarcely attended to it and formed letters very badly.

It is therefore astonishing if the still pagan Danes devoted themselves to writing letters—a proposition which some wrongly claim that they can prove from Saxo, without understanding Saxo in the least. Why should kings not rather have employed skalds and men of that kind to write their letters instead of clerics? Yet nowhere is it found that kings used them, whether before Christianity or after it. Even for writing Danish at first they employed no Danish laymen, but everywhere this was the office of clerics.

But if Saxo [Col. 0807B] was such a clerk of the archbishop to the latter’s last breath, how could they have decided that he was ever provost of Roskilde? And specifically in 1161, when he was sent to Paris to bring back St William?

I marvel that this could have been Stephanius’s opinion—Stephanius, certainly a most learned man in every branch of history; I marvel. He judged, quite correctly, that our Saxo was born about the year 1150. Saxo was therefore only eleven years old when the provost of Roskilde sought St William at Paris. How, pray, do these facts cohere? How can Stephanius’s opinion be maintained or embraced?

We hear that two provosts attended as witnesses to this Testament: Tuko of Roskilde [Col. 0807C] and, unless I am mistaken, Aco of Lund. We also hear in this place that the archbishop leaves a bequest to Saxo as his clerk. When, then, was he provost of Roskilde? Is being Absalon’s clerk and holding that office more distinguished than the provostship of Roskilde? Who reasons thus? Certainly one may not reason against the truth, which we all know. For provosts, who lived established in the dignity of prelates, would not readily suffer themselves to be reduced again to the office of clerks; nor was it fitting for anyone to demand this of them.

It therefore remains more certain than certain that Saxo, historian of the Danes, was not provost of Roskilde while Absalon survived. He still called him his clerk at the end of his life. The Saxo who in the documents produced by Stephanius is called and subscribes as provost of Roskilde, and who was sent to bring St William from Paris to Denmark, was another man from Saxo Grammaticus and the historian. For Saxo the provost of Roskilde seems to have died before Absalon; at least he had Tuko as successor in the provostship, and Tuko was present as provost when Absalon dictated his Testament.

Saxo, however, was absent as the archbishop’s clerk, living, I think, in Scania and at the monastery of St Lawrence; otherwise he would have appeared among the witnesses with the others. Immediately thereafter follow Master John and Master Walter, who seem to have been priests at the monastery of St Lawrence and masters of its schools. The plenary of the monastery of Blessed Lawrence and Provost Aco [Col. 0808A] are also joined in order, so that all these bequests appear to concern the monastery of Lund.

Moreover, Saxo Grammaticus and clerk, who had already received those two and a half marks lent by the archbishop, would have received more marks bestowed and bequeathed if he had owed more to the archbishop. This is the meaning of the words: he granted his clerk Saxo two and a half marks of silver, which he remitted to him. That is, the archbishop had previously advanced Saxo this sum for his use—namely twenty ounce-thalers in our currency—and now the archbishop bestows and bequeaths it to him, so that Saxo may no longer be compelled to repay it.

(67) To Master John. The title *master* had not yet been received among the more honourable titles of learned men, as it is customary today for those admitted to advance to the master’s degree and be distinguished with such rewards, praises, and titles because of the outstanding learning they have acquired beyond others. Here, however, they are called masters from the office they exercised in the schools which they directed; for many examples show that those men were simply called masters.

Helmold, book I, chapter 14, calls Adam of Bremen a master because he presided over and governed the school of Bremen: “Master Adam is a witness, who wrote the deeds of the Church of Homburg.” Likewise Thietmar of Merseburg called Ekkehard a grammarian and master of the school, and Ansgar himself was at first a master of this kind:

> *Magistratus regimen praeceptor adeptus.*

“Having attained the administration of office as a teacher.”

So says the poet Gualdo, setting forth Ansgar’s life in verse. For among clerics in monasteries and churches no other masters occur. The Romans indeed adopted this title, recognizing many masters at home and in military service, in sacred matters, at banquets, and in guilds of craftsmen and workmen. Inscriptions testify to this; the name *master* also descended to our workmen, who are everywhere called *meister* and *mester*. Below one reads of Aco, master of bricks, *der giegelmeister*.

But after Archbishop Absalon’s time Emperor Frederick II first ordered that the title of master should be among the honours and titles of graduates, so that those who had advanced in learning might enjoy it even if appointed to no office [Col. 0808D]. Here, however, Master John had stood above among the witnesses and heard Absalon making his Testament and bequests; there he is also called a canon of the Church of Lund. Thus Master Walter, who follows immediately, was likewise a canon of the same church.

This indicates that Lund then had a distinguished and populous school, which must have had several canon-masters set over it. This is why Master John could follow Absalon and appear in his retinue; for if he alone had been in charge of governing the school, that office would not have allowed him to be absent. We should also note that at that time masters of schools, even if canons, themselves governed the schools and taught in them. But after major and minor prebends emerged and began to be distinguished, the labours of the schools began to belong to the minor canons, while the greater canon received the title of dignity and scholasticus. Such men imposed the task of teaching upon others, while themselves presiding over the schools by counsel as rectors and overseers—by philosophical judgment, not by labour. For canons commonly obtained from bishops the easy performance of these duties through vicars. Thus schoolmasters later gave way to vicars of the lord scholasticus and prelate-canon, depending upon his will. At Lund in Absalon’s age, however, this had not yet prevailed, since the canon-masters themselves were not vicars.

(68) A silver cup. Arnold also uses this word in the *Slavonic Chronicle*, book IV, chapter 14: “He performed the washing [Col. 0809B] of his fingers in a clean *biccarium*.” Here etymologists immediately, according to their usual fashion, command that *biccarium* be derived from Greek βῖκος (*bikos*), which denotes a jar, amphora, or some similar vessel—a cask, pitcher, flask, στάμνος (*stamnos*). They refer Hebrew *Backbuck* to the same source, so that from a Hebrew word the Greeks made βίκος and its diminutive βικίδιον, and thence the Latins *bicarium*, the Germans *Becher*, and then the Danes and northerners *Begere*.

No doubt they seem to themselves to reason splendidly in this way; to me, however, they appear to be dreaming. Let them tell me when *bicarium* began to be used among the Latins. Does it occur in Varro’s *On the Latin Language*, or in Gellius’s *Attic Nights*, or in similar authors? Varro often points out things that had proceeded from Celtic into Latin to adorn and enrich the language, but neither he nor anyone else has mentioned *bicarium*.

The Celtic language is nothing other than the ancient language of northern peoples, under whom Norwegians, Swedes, Danes, Germans, Gauls, and Illyrians too are included—not Hebrews, Greeks, or Latins/Romans. Let us now see whether *bicarium* is not more happily derived from those related Celtic languages, or from the more recent Danish, than from Hebrew *Backbuck* or Greek βῖκος and βικίδιον, which occurs in Suidas.

Certainly *bicarium* is not found among the Latins before the Goths had settled Italy, Gaul, and Spain; hence it may truly be called an ancient Gothic name. The most ancient histories relate—and I have proved elsewhere—that the Goths frequently came forth from the north and filled all Germany, Illyricum, and Russia with their name and language. Then, returning from Pontus and the Maeotian marsh, with the same name and language they flooded Italy, Gaul, and Spain. What wonder, then, if monks and men of that stamp and Latinity took and distorted words from that northern language, now the language of so many peoples, whenever need arose and they thought they could express things more significantly?

A *bicarium*, certainly, is among those drinking vessels which have a distinctive shape, perhaps introduced into Italy by the Goths, or by the French, Germans, and Northmen. The Romans did not know this shape of cup, nor did the Greeks; thus *Backbuck* and βῖκος do not at all fit that shape, but rather pitchers, small pitchers, or amphorae. All Hebrews indeed say that *Backbuck* took its name from the sound made by water poured through the narrow neck of a pitcher. The Greeks specifically called that sound κότταβον (*kottabos*), and called those who frequently made such sounds κοτταβίζειν (*kottabizein*), notable gluttons.

What is there like a *bicarium*? A *bicarium* is a nearly round drinking cup, narrowed below, yet so as to stand by itself, and broader above. This is the true ancient as well as modern shape of the *bicarium*, for it still survives among us. It is called *Begere* by the Danes; *Begare* by the Swedes; *Becher* by Upper Germans, *Beker* by Lower Germans; and *Bicchiero* by Italians, though they mostly use that word for a glass drinking cup—whence *Bicchierajo* is the person who either sells or makes glass cups.

But here the question is not of what material *bicaria* were customarily made, nor how narrowly and κατὰ χρηστικῶς, “according to usage,” they are employed by one people or another. It is rather from what origin the name descended and what shape the *bicarium* originally had. It is enough that I have now shown that its origin must be sought among Danes and northerners, where numerous, clear, and ancient traces of this name are found; none occur among Hebrews, Greeks, or ancient Latins. It is therefore vain to approach those sources, excessively muddy and corrupted by mere allusions, when we possess at home purer sources—the purest, indeed—as they will readily see if they wish to see.

The Danes have several words from the same origin. *Becken*, meaning a basin, is of the same root, though not of the same [Col. 0810C] shape or form as *bicarium* and *Begere*. For a basin, *Becken*, has its own shape: a vessel with broader lips and generally lower as it spreads more widely. From this the Italians made *Bacino*, according to their pronunciation; in ours it was *Bakino*, whence *bacinello* and *bacinetto*, though used for purposes other than *bacino*. This does not impede its origin, for the usage of words often becomes irregular, ἀνωμαλίζει.

The French derived their *bassin* from it; it ought to have been written *bacin*, to preserve the origin of the name, as the Italians likewise say in the proverb, *netto come un bacin da barbiere*—“clean as a barber’s basin.” Why *a* appears here rather than *e* or *i* follows from the fact that northerners change the letters *a* and *e* by a slight sound: they have, that is, a clear *a*, and *a* of a mixed sound, such as *a* and ä or ae.

For the original Danish word, from which *Begere* and *Bekken* are derived, is *Back*, which formerly also meant a vessel larger than either *Begere* or *Bekken*. It is still used among the Netherlanders, who have retained these vessels in their language: *Back*, vessels for collecting rainwater; *een Regenback*, cisterns; *een Back*, every vessel in which dry goods are put away. Sailors also call *Bak* the dishes on ships from which they take food, as in *aen den Bak gaen*, and so forth—an ancient name by which vessels were designated.

Hence already in Paulus Festus: “*Bacar*, a wine-vessel like a *bacrion*.” They called *bacrion* a kind of vessel with a longer handle; others call it a ladle. Lauremberg’s antiquary therefore correctly explained these words: “It is also called *bacar*, *bacarion*, *becario*, and *becarium*. Apuleius, Tertullian, and others mention it.” The glosses have: “*Bacarium*, εἶδος ἀγγείου”—“a kind of vessel.”

Certainly these names cannot be said to have arisen among Greeks or Latins, but passed from ancient Celtic—that is, Danish northern—speech through Germany and Gaul to the Latins. For there is the fruitful stock of such words. Thus we should more correctly be taught today to write *cen Baeck* than *Beck*, “a stream, a brook”; this word is the mother of all those mentioned, for vessels were invented to draw water. The Saxons also said *Boeck*, the Netherlanders *Beeck*, Upper Germans *Bach*. Hence the vessels and drinking cups intended for water and cleanliness which we have hitherto enumerated follow one another: *Back, Becker, Begere, Becher, baccar, bacrio, bacarium, becario, becarium, bicarium,* [Col. 0811B] *Becken*. These ought to be written *Baeer, Baegere, Baecher, Baecken*. Thus even in Iceland and its language, which still retains ancient northern speech, survive *Bekur*, “a stream,” and *Bikar* and *Boukr*, “a cup.”

Indeed *Batiola* or *baciola*, placed by Nonius Marcellus among kinds of drinking vessels, chapter 15, can now be seen to have proceeded from the same northern and Gallic Celtic language. Plautus used the word, as he says in the *Colax*:

> *Baciolam auream octo pondo habebat, accipere noluit.*

“He had a golden cup of eight pounds’ weight; he would not accept it.”

Add also the Plautine passage from the *Stichus*, act V, scene 4:

> *… Quibus divitiae domi sunt, scaphio et cantharis,*  
> *Baciolis bibunt …* [lacuna]

“Those whose wealth is at home drink from skiffs, tankards, and little cups …”

The old Latin-Greek glosses agree: *Batiola*, ποτήριον—“a drinking-cup.”

Why then do we not judge that the origin ought rather to be drawn from the one language in which so many corresponding mother-words, sister-words, and cognate words pass the torch and hand to one another, than seek etymologies for such words from the wholly foreign and far-distant sources of Greeks and Hebrews? There, once we have thoroughly strained individual words, we finally see that we have accomplished nothing: everything is forced, affected, play, and trifling.

But I may scarcely now range further into praises of the Danish language, unless I wish to invite the charge of love for my country—as though I were led more by feeling than by zeal for truth, something which I have always thought ought to be foreign to me. The most learned censors of Leipzig judged of my work devoted to the excellence of the Danish language that I had done what those usually do who are most lavish and disposed to praise their fatherland, or the place where they are well situated. This is certainly owed to one’s country, provided that we do not overstep the bounds of truth—which I hope I have also done. For I have learned not to serve my feelings but to command them somewhat. Nor would I begrudge German, Swedish, and French the same praises if I had found them anywhere praised above Danish among the ancients. But since an older praise of the Danish language may be recovered from the best and most trustworthy monuments, why should I choose to conceal the truth—especially that truth which presented itself to me as joined with the praise of my country?

Thus *bicarium* is a word belonging equally to Celtic, Danish, and [Col. 0812A] Gothic antiquity. Celtic speech had indeed already begun to expire, unless more tenacious Danish had come to its aid again and recalled what had been lost to memory, causing its own language, through the Goths in Italy and everywhere, to flourish anew or revive in the place of Celtic. For the Goths brought with them from the north the Celtic language, almost everywhere extinct, into Latin speech, Italy, France, and so forth, and preserved it, so that it can scarcely now be extinguished again.

Thietmar of Merseburg, an eleventh-century writer before Adam of Bremen, also speaks of a silver *bicarium* before Absalon, book VIII, p. 241: “With two censers and a silver *bicare*, Caesar gave generously to our church.”

(69) To Master Walter. I have spoken of him in note 67. Below follows Master Hugh, whose particular prebend is also mentioned; thus he too was a canon. Because of the office he performed in the school of Lund together with the two already mentioned, he is introduced here as a third master and likewise receives a bequest no less than Master John or Master Walter: a bed-covering lined with variegated fur, as appears here. These facts remind us that Absalon did not casually provide for and favour the school of Lund.

(70) A squirrel-fur cloak. Here he means not a cloak grey in colour, but one lined with the grey squirrel furs concerning which I spoke previously. It was suitable for wearing during the winter season of the Nativity of the Lord. For a grey cloth colour did not greatly suit either an archbishop or a priest-canon such as Master Walter; hence it must be understood of grey squirrel furs.

(71) For making a plenary. Although *plenarium* occurs often in medieval history, few have explained what it is or was. I shall first cite from Henry Wolter’s *Bremen Chronicle*, p. 43, the plenary which Emperor Henry IV gave among other gifts to the Church of Bremen, whose plate contained nine talents of Lübeck gold—that is, nine Lübeck pounds of gold by weight. Adam of Bremen likewise explained this in these words, book IV, speaking of the same gifts: “And one plenary, whose plate appeared to contain nine pounds of gold,” p. 112.

Before Adam, Thietmar of Merseburg—or whoever wrote Thietmar’s life shortly thereafter—lists the gifts bestowed by Emperor Henry II upon the church of Merseburg, p. 261:

> “This emperor gave us many things fitting for divine worship: namely, three plenaries. One, the least valuable, was of gold, adorned with an ivory plate; a second, more precious one, was varied with gold, jewels, and an ivory plate; a third, the finest, was skilfully decorated with gold, electrum, and most precious jewels.”

Conrad, the seventh abbot of Rastede, about the year 1240, is said in the *Rastede Chronicle*, p. 102, to have caused a plenary to be made for the church of Rastede from silver with gleaming gems, as may still be recognized in the monastery. Nor does the *Minden Chronicle* neglect to extol the generosity of its bishop Sigebert around 1029: “He left what pertains to the adornment of God’s house—beautiful chalices and censers, and nine very precious plenaries [Col. 0813A], painted inside with various materials and adorned outside with silver, gold, and precious stones.”

Yet from all these statements no one will readily perceive what a *plenarium* is, whether as name or thing. I shall therefore endeavour now to explain it more plainly. A *plenarium* is a missal, a book serving the sacred celebration of Mass, in which everything to be performed on feasts, Sundays, and other days was written out in full, so that nothing was lacking to the celebrating priest of what was to be said or done. This book is called a *plenarium* because it contained, fully and exactly, everything required in church: antiphons, sequences, responsories, collects, lessons, and the rest.

Because these books and plenaries were laid on the altar, they were burdened with such a display of gems, gold, ivory, electrum, and silver as we have heard in the instances already given. Concerning the plate of nine Lübeck pounds of gold which the Bremen plenary possessed, understand that this means the book’s cover. When books were bound and covered in leather, one side of a book placed upon the altar—the outward side facing the people—received a solid gold or ivory plate inserted into the leather and wooden board. This plate was encircled with various set gems, producing a great brilliance and magnificence. The other side, turned inward, displayed none of this splendour but was left in the ordinary covering of leather and board, without gems or gold. This is why only one plate, not two or more, is attributed to each plenary.

Whoever wishes to see an example may visit the library of Hamburg Cathedral Church. There one will still see, in what they call quarto format, such a plenary bound in purple leather, whose centre contains an inserted ivory plate, moderately carved and surrounded by stones once precious but now crystal and glass. One can readily perceive that the former stones were removed and others substituted. The other side of the book, however, is covered with leather alone and plainly appears entirely devoid of the adornment of the front cover.

The book comprises a collectary, homiliary, antiphonary, and many other things written on parchment. It may therefore be called a *plenarium*, just as today we are accustomed to call it *ein vollstaendig Hand- oder Kirchenbuch*, “a complete hand-book or church-book,” in which are collected all the things to be read or sung in churches.

Nor were plenaries alone adorned so sumptuously; other books were as well. Thietmar thus recalled at the end of book VI, concerning the same Emperor Henry II: “He gave a Gospel-book—that is, a book of the Gospels—adorned with gold and an ivory plate.” Similar is what Tavernier has in book VI of his *Travels*, p. 35, concerning a Gospel-book in Armenia, which the archbishop, after the Gospel is read, offers for kissing to the other patriarchs and bishops. He adds:

> *Sur un des costez de la couverture de ce livre, il y a des reliques enchâssées, et couvertes d'un crystall, et c'est le côsté du livre, qu'on donne à baiser.*

“On one side of this book’s cover there are relics set in it and covered with crystal; and it is that side of the book which is given to be kissed.”

I shall add nothing further concerning the plenary except to show that it was a book. The author of the *Minden Chronicle* demonstrates this for us, p. 105, when he says that Bishop Milo, who sat from 974 to 996, gave a beautiful plenary to the monastery on Mount Wedegon. In it are carved the verses which he offered to Saint Gorgonius:

> *Sit tibi, Gorgoni, liber hic, rogo, valde decori,*  
> *Ornari Milo quem fecit episcopus auro.*

“May this book, I pray, be greatly for your honour, Gorgonius—a book which Bishop Milo caused to be adorned with gold.”

Similarly Henry Wolter, in the *Bremen Chronicle*, when recounting Emperor Henry IV’s gifts to Bremen Church, sets them out generally: “He sent to Bremen Church many worthy and precious treasures, namely one hundred golden cloths and gilt coverings, a censer, and a book overlaid with gold and silver.” He then proceeds to raise an objection against himself: “But you will say: what are these treasures, sent by the Emperor, in their number, weight, measure, and name? I answer,” and so forth, “and one plenary, whose plate contained nine talents of Lübeck gold.” Behold: the plenary with a plate of nine pounds of gold is the same book overlaid with gold and silver.

Add Baluze on the Capitularies of the Kings of France, p. 1156, who observed that missals and books of the Mass were called *plenaria*. There is also πληνάριον (*plēnarion*) in Greek law, but not in the same sense, though it too concerns parchments and documents. In law πληνάριον means an acquittance remitting and cancelling all debts in their entirety. Hence in the sixth *Eclogue of the Basilika*, ἀμεριμνία πληναρία means “full freedom from care,” in opposition to ἀποχὴ μερική, a partial acquittance, by which only part of a debt is acknowledged as paid. In our courts today such a universal acquittance is called a receipt of all receipts. Thus the word *plenarium*, with reference to charters and books alike, began to carry this force and to enter into use among both ecclesiastics and jurists.

(72) To Provost Aco. He is the same man introduced above in note (5) among the witnesses, and I judge him to have been provost of Lund because the bequests here immediately preceding and following concern only Lund and Scania. I have already shown that Tuko of Roskilde was a provost. Saxo likewise lived at Lund when this Testament was made, and is therefore placed in that class as well.

(73) At Cluny. That monastery was founded in Burgundy in the year of Christ 895, according to the testimony of Sigebert of Gembloux [Col. 0814D] and Trithemius, by Berno, count of Burgundy and abbot of Gigny, who appointed Odo as the first abbot of Cluny.

(74) To Clairvaux. This monastery was established by St Bernard about 1117—others say 1115. Very few geographers have indicated the site of this monastery. The French themselves have neglected and omitted it, either because that celebrated place soon afterward sank into ashes and could not rise again to the fame it once possessed, or because monastic precincts generally seem unworthy of geographers. Abbot Bernard left this monastery inhabited by 700 monks, so that it was then of great and distinguished renown and was frequently visited by Danish bishops travelling to France. The monastery is situated in [Col. 0815A] Champagne, France, beside the river Aube, three leagues from the borders of Burgundy, midway between Chaumont to the east and Bar-sur-Seine to the west. It was formerly called the Valley of Wormwood, and was founded by Bernard at the request of Theobald, count of Champagne.

(75) The church of Wellinge. Its family still survives in Sweden and is not undistinguished, although at that time it was a rural parish in Scania; likewise, the following names—Stangbye, Koping, Hyphakre, Arlef, Asmundathorp, Nyehyle, and Saxelstorp—are Scanian villages, some still fairly well known, having preserved from antiquity the same names.

(76) To render one *mansus*. It is well known from many writers that a *mansus* is called a tract of land where someone can at once reside and dwell. The Germans call it *een Hove*, *een Hove Landes*: a field able to support one nearby-dwelling household. Hence *Hoba* and *Huba* in certain historians who have failed to attend to the true origin of the word. Nor do the modern Germans correctly say *eine Huffe Landes*: it ought to be *ein Hoff Landes*, since it is a *Hoflstete*, a place where those who cultivate the adjoining field live. Thus it is a *curia* when the house alone is considered, but a *mansus* when field and house are understood together. For that field is a *mansus* which has a house attached, so that lords and tenants may live there. Berghave, a place and district of Hamburg, explains the whole matter. That sloping hill on which the field was cultivated is now occupied by the church of St James, the horse-market, houses, and buildings, from the street popularly called Steenstraten to the Alster gate and [Col. 0815C] the Alster itself. Nor was this field one *mansus*, but two; therefore it is still called *kleenen Barghave* and *grooten Barghave*—namely, the places where the houses stood at the front of the field. Those who cultivated and inhabited those little hills became prosperous and, being well established through their houses and holdings, began to be called *von Bargen*; some of them later retained a celebrated name in the senate of the city. They were therefore called *Have* or *Hove*, because the field extended over a sloping hill: *Barghave*, or, in the Latin of that age, a “mountain holding” (*mansus montanus*).

(77) Master Hugh. You will find him noted above.

(78) A large cover of *Laekatte*. The *laekatt* was a spotted wild animal known by this name only to Norwegians; for so many cats inhabit the regions of Norway, and of such various kinds, that we can scarcely suffice for finding names for them. They call ermine skins *Roisekatte* and *Urkatte*, and also *Laekatte*; if these are not the same animals, they were certainly not greatly different from them. These skins are indeed the noblest of all, and are called *Hermelin* because they suit only kings, princes, and lords. They are therefore here compared with marten skins, which otherwise hold first rank in distinction: today sable skins from Russia come first; after them these cat skins, then marten and squirrel skins. Nor is it surprising that these little beasts are called *Katte*, “cats,” although they do not equal domestic cats in size but are smaller. Were they not like weasels in their length and shape, they might be classed among squirrel and dormouse [Col. 0816A] skins. They are therefore of the weasel kind—little animals which pursue mice and dormice—and are accordingly called cats or *Katte*, whose business is to hunt mice. Yet they seem to have received the name *Laefatte* from *Lae*, which among Icelanders and Norwegians means harm and damage, because these cats perhaps inflict more harm than other similar animals. Thus they call *Laeminge* the mice harmful to crops, peculiar to Norway, which they have observed in some places falling from the sky and scattered through the fields. In this respect it is distinguished from *Lä*, which means motion and rhythm, especially that of a flowing wave.

Furriers maintain that ermine skins are the same as *Laekatte*. We know that “badger skins” (*melinae pelles*) have been greatly sought both formerly and today, but they explain the term as badgers, *Dachse* in German. Indeed, skins called *melinae*, [Col. 0816B] exceedingly white, were brought from the island of Melos and served like earth-pigment and white lead. Hence Plautus, *Mostellaria*:

> At your age you ought not to touch any cosmetic,
>
> neither white lead, nor Melian white, nor any other paint.

But we know that ermines are very white and conspicuous only by the very black spot at the end of the tail; perhaps the Germans formed their name from this hybrid word. In an old London synod, about the year 1138, these skins are called *hereminae*:

> By apostolic authority we forbid nuns to use variegated, or grey, sable, marten, ermine, or beaver skins.

So it is read in Richard of Hexham [Col. 0816C], p. 328. The French still call these animals *hermines* and *ermines*, whence the English learned the name. Italians call them *ermellini*. The Latins called them “Pontic mice,” because they were first brought to them from Pontus; indeed, also “white weasels,” because they gleam with a whiteness which they acquire in winter, while in summer they display a colour like that of common weasels—brown or reddish. This commonly happens to many northern animals, hares, bears, and others, as I think is known.

But I do not wish to trim these matters belonging to the furriers’ workshop down to the very nail; for I may answer, as Xenocrates the Platonist said in Suidas to a man wishing to attend his school, whom he considered unsuitable: [Col. 0816D] “At my place wool is not carded” (*παρ᾽ ἐμοὶ πόκος οὐ κνάπτεται*). That is: “At my place skins are not dressed”; I cannot teach such things.

(79) To Nicholas, son of the archdeacon. How can this fit Absalon’s times—an archdeacon having a son? Did he live in marriage with a wife as well? Far from it! These words must not be understood in that way. Rather, this archdeacon must be regarded as one of the converted brethren, who, abandoning the world and their possessions, wife, and children, dedicated themselves wholly, in mind and body, to sacred service; afterward they were advanced to orders and dignities according to their merits. Thus this archdeacon was one of these converts and, having left his marriage, had ascended to this rank.

(80) In the castle of Haffn. This is Copenhagen, now a vast commercial city, the principal seat of the whole Danish kingdom. We see that it grew under various names: the fortress was called Axelhus because Absalon first founded it and resided there when he came thither; afterward a borough was attached to this fortification, the borough of a city—and indeed of a fortified city—which is customarily called a *castrum*, *castellum*, and *burgum*. This city was called Stegelborg [“I doubt whether it was ever called Stegelborg”], because it stood so high and steeply that it could be ascended from the sea only by steps; but from its notable harbour it was called, pre-eminently (*κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν*), Haffu.
