Thus Adam of Bremen calls the bishop’s house and the prince’s house those strongly fortified citadels of Hamburg which they built; but he calls the “castle of Hamburg” the city itself, enclosed by most powerful works and defending [Col. 0817B] the citizens’ houses and commerce from hostile incursions. This refutes those who think that in Absalon’s time Copenhagen was no city, [Col. 0818A] and that only the bishop’s fortress and house, and nothing else, existed there.

The short chronicle of Danish affairs recently published by the Icelander Árni Magnússon gives the same name, Hafn, to the commercial town in the year 1249: “The town of Hafn was devastated.” Here *villa* is used as the French use *la ville*, for a town. This, therefore, was the city’s old name; but when merchandise became abundant, it began to be called *Kisbenhaffn*, and in German *Coopmannehaven*. Thus the French and modern Germans wrongly write *Copenhagen* for *Copenhaven*; everyone willingly follows them and refuses to see the error, since the common crowd believes that the French do not err even when they are mistaken.

(81) [Acho, master of the bricks. I conjecture that he was overseer of the workmen who baked bricks, [Col. 0818B] particularly since masonry is mentioned immediately afterward.]

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1202. WILLIAM OF CHAMPAGNE, CALLED “OF THE WHITE HANDS,” ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS.

[Col. 0817]

NOTICE.

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IX, p. 95.)

[Col. 0817C] William of Champagne, called “of the White Hands,” in the vernacular *aux blanches mains* (wrongly *aux grands chemins*, “of the high roads,” in some slips), was the fourth among the sons of Theobald IV, count of Champagne, and Matilda of Carinthia. Entering the clergy while very young, he held several prebends or dignities at once in different churches. Having been elected bishop of Chartres, he moved first to the Church of Sens and then, at the beginning of 1176, to the Church of Rheims. While seated in the see of Sens he had served as apostolic legate in Gaul; as archbishop of Rheims he continued to discharge that office.

As soon as he was received at Rheims (he is said to have been received on 8 August), this most worthy prelate decreed that for an entire year he would be present in choir, so that his canons might attend the divine office more regularly, so that he might personally settle the disputes that repeatedly arose among the clergy, and so that, having himself become better informed through his presence, he might confirm the grants of his predecessors. Marlot says that he was the first among the archbishops of Rheims [Col. 0818C] to subscribe alone to his charters, without calling abbots or the dignitaries of the cathedral church of his diocese, and without even adding the year of his pontificate. He nevertheless retained the common seal, which bore the archbishop’s image on one side and that of the Virgin Mother of God on the other, with the inscription: “My secret is mine” (*Secretum meum mihi*).

At the very beginning of his pontificate at Rheims, he granted indulgences to the faithful attending the Easter fair of the leper-house of Rheims. In the same year, on 16 September, when Manasses, count of Rethélois, founded a collegiate church in the town of Mézières—which had formerly belonged to the bishopric of Rheims, according to Flodoard—William bestowed upon the newly instituted canons the altars of St Remigius of Reomont and St Marcellus. In the same [Col. 0818D] year he consecrated Nivelon bishop of Soissons; and Pope Alexander III wrote to him and to the other bishops of his province that the most dreadful schism which had flared up between himself and Emperor Frederick I had at last happily come to an end.

While visiting the province, William, as metropolitan, approved the division of prebends among the canons of Noyon, and declared in writing that the bishop of Noyon had no right to subject anyone from the choir of the greater church to excommunication. In the following year, on 24 July, he dedicated the church of Marchiennes Abbey in the presence of Frumold, bishop of Arras, and Everard, bishop of Tournai. In 1178, when he crossed into England on pilgrimage to the tomb of St Thomas of Canterbury, once closely joined to him in friendship, King Henry went to meet him and offered splendid gifts. Once his vows had been fulfilled, Baldwin, count of Guînes, received him as he returned to France at the town of Ardres with lavish and magnificent display; Lambert the priest described that banquet in his history of the counts of [Col. 0819B] Guînes.

In March 1179 he attended the Lateran council, where he was created cardinal-priest of St Sabina, and before the supreme pontiff and the other fathers of the council consecrated Roger bishop of Cambrai. At the same time, while he was still in Rome, he obtained from the supreme pontiff a special charter annulling a decree of certain citizens of Rheims which prohibited anyone from selling, bequeathing, or granting land to the church as alms:

> “Moreover, we decree null and void, as harmful, the constitution of your citizens by which they are said to have prohibited land or an estate from being sold, bequeathed, or granted to your church as alms.”

Furthermore, since a dispute still persisted between the archbishops of Sens and Rheims concerning the right to anoint the kings [Col. 0819C] of France—although Philip in the meantime, and Louis VII, had been inaugurated at Rheims without any objection whatever from Sens—he obtained for Rheims a bull of Alexander III assigning this distinguished office to Rheims alone. It was confirmed by Louis VII himself and later by other Roman pontiffs.

Upon his return to France, and having reportedly been made duke and peer of France, he anointed Philip Augustus, son of his sister Adela and King Louis VII of France, king of the French on 1 November of that same year. The archbishops of Tours, Bourges, and Sens served with him, as did almost all the bishops of Gaul. In this solemn procession the young king was preceded by Henry the Young King of England, also duke of Normandy and son of Henry II, king of England, bearing the golden crown with which Philip was to be crowned; by the count of Flanders, holding aloft the sword of the empire; and by other dukes, counts, and barons assigned to various offices. Louis VII himself could not attend, being afflicted by age and paralytic illness. From that time down to our own, the archbishops of Rheims have not only been reckoned among the dukes and peers of France, but have always held precedence among them.

Because William incurred very great expenses in crowning the king and was burdened by debt as a consequence, he requested some assistance from the common treasury of the chapter of Rheims. But, lest the canons should thereafter suffer [Col. 0820A] any loss from it, he declared in 1180 that they were exempt from such expenses.

About 1180, with assistance from both the archbishop and the canons of Rheims, the church of St Balsamia began to be rebuilt and was raised to a collegiate church. All its prebends enjoy almost the same privileges and immunities as the chapter of Rheims itself, to which they are subject. At about the same time, Pope Lucius III reproved William because he had released persons bound by the bishop of Beauvais, especially the count of Clermont, whom the bishop of Beauvais had excommunicated at the command of the archbishop of Rheims, placing the count’s land under interdict.

In 1181, the Chronicle of Nangis says that he conspired against [Col. 0820B] the king and threw all France into turmoil with the duke of Burgundy, the count of Flanders, the count of Blois, and the count of the Holy Emperor. In 1182 this prince, no less magnificent than peace-loving, restored to the city of Rheims the aldermen whom his predecessor Henry had removed. In the following year he granted the same citizens the right to cultivate land outside the city limits, so that its boundary might be extended by newly constructed buildings; he transferred there the Easter fairs which, as we have said, were held beside the chapel of the lepers. In the same year Philip Augustus appointed him chief administrator of the realm. Nangis asserts that he and Philip, count of Flanders, immediately burned many heretics in Flanders:

> “They said,” he says, “that all eternal things were created by God, but the human body [Col. 0820C] and all transitory things by Luciabel. They rejected infant baptism and the Eucharist; they said that priests celebrated Masses from avarice and greed for offerings.”

How admirably he conducted himself in affairs was attested by Philip Augustus himself. For when Pope Lucius, fervently desiring to see him, had repeatedly urged him by letters to come to Rome, but he could not satisfy the pope’s wishes because of the affairs of the kingdom, the Most Christian King wrote to the supreme pontiff in these terms [Note: [Col. 0819D] Stephen of Tournai, letter 101]:

> “The powerful attack our youth and strive to disturb the beginnings of our reign; and those who ought to have owed us loyalty for many reasons are faithless adversaries, [Col. 0820D] whose wickedness compels us both to seek new counsels and to procure assistance. Above all our friends and faithful supporters, our dearest uncle William, archbishop of Rheims, stands beside us: a watchful eye in our counsels, a right hand in our affairs. For him even temporarily to depart from us would be to yield to our enemies, who, just as they irreverently desire and expect us to be without arms, so they desire and expect us to be without friends, in accordance with their faithless wishes. We have heard, Father, that you summoned him and invited him by your sacred letters to present himself before you. He was ready to obey and to appear before you, likening disobedience to the sin of divination, and detesting a will not to comply with you as the crime of idolatry. At this moment of our utmost necessity, trusting in your exceptional affection, we have retained him, etc. … Receive, Father, our prayers—the prayers of your son, whom you have always loved from the cradle—so that you who before our birth graciously desired our rising may, by your authority, beneficially restrain those who desire our fall. Let it be pleasing to you, Father, that in so great a crisis of the kingdom we retain so great a friend, whose presence is most necessary to us and whose absence most ruinous.”

William nevertheless went to Rome in 1185 and sat in the assembly at which Pope Urban III was proclaimed. Marlot conjectures that he again attended [Col. 0821B] the election of Gregory VIII at Ferrara in 1187. On returning from Rome, he found material for litigation with his chapter, had he been inclined to lawsuits. For just as his predecessors had scarcely tolerated the power which the canons claimed of excommunicating any of their wrongdoers and likewise absolving them—a power which Pope Lucius had recently confirmed at their request by rescript—so William could not tolerate an interdict and the frequent suspension of divine office in the mother church, decreed solely by the authority of the canons. This was especially so because they maintained that, whenever the greater church ceased its services, the other churches of the city, conventual as well as parochial, ought to cease them at their command.

After more mature deliberation and examination of their privilege, the archbishop refrained from initiating litigation, and in 1187 finally granted in writing:

> “If anything is done to them, to their clerics, or to the laity belonging to them, within the province of Rheims or elsewhere wherever they possess authority by authority of the see of Rheims, which results in damage or injury to the church of Rheims, we, when requested on this matter, shall in good faith see that it is remedied. If not, the chapter may lawfully suspend the divine office and direct the other churches, conventual as well as parochial, of the city or suburb to do the same. The status of the church of St Remigius shall remain as it formerly was; parish priests shall nevertheless be permitted to administer the necessary sacraments in a low voice and with the sound of one small bell. Nor may [Col. 0821D] the interdict be lifted by the archbishop without the chapter’s consent.”

In 1188 he gave the monks of St Remigius the altar of Driencourt for celebrating his anniversary and more than twenty other anniversaries; in 1192 he added the altars of Villers-in-the-Wood and Louvois. In 1189 Philip Augustus sent him to Saumur to King Henry of England to arrange peace between the two kings. In 1190, when Philip was preparing to cross the sea to fight against the unbelievers, William gave him the pilgrim’s wallet and staff at Saint-Denis in France. Soon afterward, at the assembly of Vézelay, he was to assume the guardianship of the kingdom jointly with Queen Adela, his own sister, and the custody of the most serene prince Louis. Philip in turn granted the archbishops of Rheims a special privilege concerning the movable goods of a deceased archbishop; William granted another privilege to the abbey of Cisoing, immediately subject to his church.

In 1191, with William’s favour, Henry, count of Champagne, founded the collegiate church of St John in the town of Vitry. For it, as also for Vitry, Rethel, Châtillon, Épernay, Rocroi, Fismes, Braine, and Château-Porcien, the counts of Champagne had formerly been bound to render liege homage to the archbishops of Rheims. Meanwhile Philip, count of Flanders, died at the siege of Acre. When his dominion was divided in two, William’s efforts brought it about in 1192 that Arras and the cities of other neighbouring peoples should pass under French lordship, while the heir of the remaining territories, Baldwin, [Col. 0822B] rendered homage to the king. In the same year William consecrated St Albert bishop of Liège at Rheims and established in his metropolitan church the office of scholarch. Marlot also assigns to that year, and laments, the abolition of the common table among the canons of Rheims. The archbishop nevertheless permitted them to have free servants within his ban; he afterward extended this form of privilege to the abbeys of SS Remigius, Nicaise, and Denis. In the same year he went as a pilgrim to St James in Galicia. On returning from that journey he attended the king’s council, where the dispatch of Stephen, bishop of Noyon, to Denmark was discussed, in order to obtain Ingeborg, sister of King Canute, whom Philip Augustus had chosen as his wife.

[Col. 0822C] The marriage was celebrated in 1193; William anointed the new bride and crowned her with the diadem, while Theobald of Amiens, Peter of Arras, Stephen of Tournai, and Lambert of Thérouanne stood by and performed their episcopal ministry.

“But, astonishingly,” says Rigord, “on that same day, at the devil’s instigation, the king began to hold in hatred the wife whom he had long desired. A few days later—eighty-one days intervened in all—a synod was convened, over which William of Rheims presided. The bishops and barons calculated a degree of consanguinity through Charles, count of Flanders, and by legal judgment the marriage was dissolved.” Stephen of Tournai wrote to Archbishop William concerning this matter in the same year.

When King Canute complained to Pope Celestine III [Col. 0822D] about William and the other bishops who had approved this divorce, the cardinals Melior and Censius were sent as legates to France and convened a synod at Paris; but, “having become mute dogs,” says Marlot, “unable to bark,” they achieved nothing. There is no doubt that both King Philip and Archbishop William sinned gravely in that affair. For the following prove that the marriage of Philip and Ingeborg was lawful: first, the rescript of the supreme pontiff directing the archbishop of Sens that, if the king wished to introduce another wife, he should prevent this by apostolic authority; second, the letters by which Pope Innocent III, in 1201, honoured with legitimacy the boy and girl whom Philip had fathered by Agnes of Méran, his subsequently introduced wife; third, Ingeborg’s return to Philip and their ten-year cohabitation without objection from anyone. Hence one is surprised that most writers have narrated that divorce so evasively that they seem unwilling either to disclose the truth or to censure King Philip.

In 1196 William ratified what the canons of St Quentin of Vermandois had established concerning outsiders in their church, and he was present when Baldwin V, count of Flanders, rendered homage. At this time, down to the beginning of Innocent III’s pontificate, the number of forgers greatly increased; in the name of the apostolic see they would forge whatever letters they wished. Celestine III made a serious complaint about them to William, archbishop of Rheims. Roger of Howden relates [Col. 0823B] that a clerk of the archbishop of York, mortally ill at Rome, publicly confessed to having sent forged bulls in the name of the Roman Church to England.

Stephen of Tournai, to whom William had assigned the duty of watching in his diocese over the dealers in this filthy merchandise, wrote to him in letter 221 that he had caught certain men:

> “By your command, through caution and skill rather than force, we induced certain forgers to confess, promising immunity as far as it should be within our power to grant it, to one of whom, in the chapter, the upper and lower die of a forged bull were restored by us. Under a dreadful adjuration and solemn undertaking, he confessed that he had never used it; but he was the associate of a certain priest who sold forged letters, and he sometimes received a share of the accursed price. He also handed over to us a small notebook in which several letters are contained under the apostolic name. … We are keeping for you the forged dies, whose falsifications may be condemned by the judgment of your authority and broken with the hammer.”

In 1197 William established the rights of the chancery of Tournai. In 1198, when Innocent III succeeded Celestine III as supreme pontiff, he made William apostolic legate in both Germany and France, though in some documents of that time William does not assume the title of legate. In the same year, in October, he gave in perpetual alms to the monks of Jouy one hundred Provins sous, to be received every year at the fair of St Aigulf from the wine toll, [Col. 0823D] so that they might henceforth celebrate with wax the private Masses which they had celebrated with oil. In the same year he again confirmed for the Premonstratensians the privilege granted them—under a command sent to him in 1176—permitting them to administer parishes, especially the parish of Boconville, given in 1198 to the monks of Thenelles.

A little later, when Enguerrand III of Coucy, Roger of Rozoy, and the lord of Rethel [Manasses II, or Hugh III? See the most recent history of the lords of Coucy; Note: [Col. 0823D] *Hist. de Coucy*, note 38, p. 74] had conspired against the church of Rheims, Philip Augustus at last drove that evil away from the church; the same history, p. 55, should be consulted concerning this matter.

In 1201 William restored a hospital not far from the Basilican Gate, which the most holy apostle of the French was said to have founded. Enlarging it with new benefactions, he entrusted its administration to the religious of St Anthony. In the same year he dedicated the church of St Basolus.

Having at last returned to Italy for the third time, he was there seized by illness and planned to return to his metropolitan see. He had first confirmed at Anagni, in January 1201—that is, 1202—the immunities of his canons against the townsmen. But at Laon, before reaching Rheims, he was overtaken by a sudden illness; his speech was obstructed, [Col. 0824B] and he died intestate in the same year, in his sixty-eighth year, on 7 September. He was carried to Rheims and buried in the cathedral church beside the high altar under a stone on which the following uncouth verses are said to have been carved:

> Lofty in character, provident, gentle, prudent, and a lover of peace,
>
> For twice ten years and six, with one additional month,
>
> Archbishop William presided in the city of Rheims.
>
> The seventh Ides of September was the end of my life.

The Chronicle of Auxerre says of him:

> “When William, archbishop of Rheims, came to Laon, he was struck down by a sudden illness and, his speech being closed off, died intestate: a man noble by birth, who had long flourished, endowed with both secular [Col. 0824C] and ecclesiastical power. At the first beginnings of his pontificate he conducted himself quite modestly, shone with the ornaments of character, and would have been fortunate had the last things answered to the first and his merits remained consistent to the end. But since matters turned to the contrary and the end did not match the beginning, we have not given final praise to one rendered too notable by unjust acceptance of gifts and prodigal extravagance.”

Alberic concurs in these words:

> “William, archbishop of Rheims, died on 8 October [the month appears to be mistaken]. For twenty-six years and more he held the pontifical insignia with worldly favour and glory, though not so much with the favour of God.”

Marlot attempts to remove this blemish. William was celebrated by Stephen of Tournai, Peter of Blois, Peter of Celle, William the Breton, Rigord, John of Salisbury, Roger of Howden, Vincent of Beauvais, Bzovius, Ciaconius, the Baron of Autol, Bernerius, Donius of Attigny, Duchesne, Peter Comestor, and the poet Walter. The latter dedicated his *Alexandreis* to him, the former his *Scholastic History*. Our Martène also reports, in the *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 946, a dedicatory letter by a certain William who dedicated to him his *Microcosmography*.

[Col. 0825]

LETTERS OF WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS.

I. To Pope Alexander, written on behalf of Thomas Becket, archbishop of Canterbury, while he was still bishop of Chartres; that is, in 1166.

[Col. 0825A]

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CC, under Alexander III, among letters of various persons addressed to him.)

II. To the same.—On behalf of the same. (1168.)

(See *Patrologia*, in the same place.)

III. To the same.—Concerning the events of the conference held at Mont-Saint-Michel around the feast of Epiphany in 1169, between Louis, king of the French, and the king of England.

[Col. 0825B] (See the same place.)

IV. To the same.—In the cause of St Thomas of Canterbury. Written while he was archbishop of Sens. (1169.)

(See the same place.)

V. To the same.—In the cause of the same person.

(See the same place.)

VI. To the king of England.—Concerning those excommunicated by the archbishop of Canterbury.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXC, col. 674, among the letters of St Thomas of Canterbury. Compare King Henry’s letter to William, cols. 1049–1050.) [Col. 0825C]

VII. To Pope Alexander.—Concerning the coronation of the son of the king of the English. (1170.)

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CC, under Alexander III, among letters of various persons addressed to him.)

VIII. To the same.—Concerning the murder of St Thomas of Canterbury. (1170.)

(See the same place.)

IX. To the same.—That he had placed under interdict the king of England’s lands on this side of the sea. (1170.)

(The same place.)

X. To Abbot Ervisius and the brethren of the monastery of St Victor, Paris. (1170.)

[Col. 0826A]

[DUCHESNE, *Writers of French Affairs*, IV, 747.]

W., by the grace of God archbishop of Sens and legate of the apostolic see, to Abbot E. and the whole chapter of St Victor, beloved sons in Christ: may you abound in the spirit of love and peace through the grace of him whose dwelling-place is made in peace.

The hand of the Lord has touched me somewhat in his mercy. Therefore we have been unable to come on the day which we had appointed for you. But, God willing, we shall come to you in a spirit of gentleness and meekness as soon as an opportunity is given us, bringing [Col. 0826B] with us not a father’s blows but a mother’s words. We are prepared with the greatest zeal to labour for the peace and tranquillity of the brethren, desiring in the inward parts of Christ that religious observance may be preserved for God’s service and that external affairs may be properly arranged for the support of those serving God. Meanwhile, preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, so that the peace of God which surpasses all understanding may guard your hearts and your minds. Farewell.

XI. To Pope Alexander.—On behalf of Hugh of Campo Florido, bishop of Soissons and chancellor of the king of the French. (1170.)

[Col. 0826C] (See among the letters of various persons to Alexander III, *Patrologia*, vol. CC.)

XII. To Maurice, bishop of Paris.—Concerning the deposit of 400 marks of silver entrusted by Eskil, archbishop of Lund, to Ervisius, abbot of St Victor. (1170.)

[DUCHESNE, *Writers of French Affairs*, IV, 604.]

W., by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, to M., bishop of Paris, greetings.

Your prudent judgment knows more fully into what great and pernicious confusion Brother E., formerly abbot of St Victor, has brought the Church and all the brethren, who are recognized as pre-eminent above others both in religious observance and learning, by his disorderly conduct. Although he has attacked to the best of his ability the holy men who were with him and persecuted holiness, yet, now that the power to do them harm has by God’s grace been removed from him, he still, as we have learned, does not seek the name of the Lord; rather, his hand is still stretched out. Since he cannot overthrow their inward and eternal discipline, he strives by varied and countless forms of outward temptation to disturb their peace.

Accordingly, since he is still trying to conceal the Church’s treasure, we again command your brotherhood by the authority of this letter to go to the church without any delay and, in the presence of our beloved son G., abbot, and of the brethren of the aforesaid church, to search the chests and small repositories of the said Er.; and to deliver to the abbot and brethren the gold chalice and all other things belonging by right to the Church of Blessed Victor which you find there. But place the deposit of the archbishop of Denmark back in its place in [Col. 0827B] the greater church. If the said Er. refuses to produce these things, nevertheless break the vessel of iniquity and mammon and carry out the foregoing instructions.

XIII. To Cardinal Master Melior.—He commends to him the affair of the archbishop of Tours. (1184.)

(It appears among the letters of Stephen of Tournai, letter 110. See *Patrologia*, vol. CCXI, col. 399.)

XIV. To B., provost, and the chapter of Rheims.—Concerning the election of Peter the Cantor of Paris as dean of Rheims. (After 1196.)

[Col. 0827C]

[MARLOT, *Metropolis of Rheims*, II, 442.]

William, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved sons B., provost, S., cantor, and the whole chapter of the Church of Reims: greeting and affection.

We give thanks to God, the giver of all things, who, looking upon the desolation of the Church of Reims, deprived of the support of such a dean and teacher, has provided and restored to it such a successor, whose conduct abounds in example and whose learning in instruction. Therefore, greatly commending in the Lord the prudence [Col. 0827D] of your devotion, we approve the election of our beloved Peter—commendable before God and men and beneficial to the Church of Reims—and, receiving it favorably, willingly and generously confirm it.

XV. To Peter the Chanter.—He informs him of his election as Dean of Reims. (After 1196.)

[Col. 0828A]

[Ibid.]

William, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved son Master P., Chanter of Paris—indeed, Dean of Reims—greeting and affection.

We rise to render due thanks to God and to our Church of Reims, because, by the inspiration of the Most High, that Church has elected you as dean. We have also thought it fitting to congratulate you, because you have accepted so humbly the burden offered you by God, and neither a degenerate eye toward the Church’s more abundant revenues nor [Col. 0828B] a spirit of avarice has turned you aside. We hold this election ratified and welcome, since previously, when the whole chapter had submitted to us the matter of that same deanery, we first offered it to you, if you wished it. But then, following sounder counsel, and aiming at the end which now, thanks be to God, you have attained, you wished first, for the salvation of many, to expend among more numerous studies and schools the talent entrusted to you by God.

But now it is time that, from the seeds which you have harvested, you should gather for others sheaves of rejoicing for your own storehouse. Thus let the bread of nourishing instruction be broken for our hungry little ones, and, in a pious exchange, let the generous breasts of the mother be filled through you with the milk of doctrine which you yourselves, as little children, once drew.

[Note: [Col. 0827D] From this it is clear that Peter the Chanter sucked the milk of piety and doctrine in the Church of Reims.]

It was fitting and just [Col. 0828C] that our mother Church, the first in rank, which had for some time lent you to meet the need of others, should recall her son in her own necessities and retain him, once recalled, for her own service. Therefore, with such force of obedience as we can employ, we enjoin this upon you, advising you with a conscience secure in the Lord not to believe anyone who may suggest otherwise to you, but to persevere in this resolve, steadfast and unmoved. For we trust in the Lord that you ought to bear fruit pleasing to God both in us and, together with us, in others; for we believe that provision has been made in you not for the Church of Reims alone, but for the whole province—indeed, for the whole kingdom—and that you have been reserved even for these times. For we have decided especially to make use of the counsel of your prudence in our own and common [Col. 0828D] affairs. [lacuna] And that you may stand more firmly in this same resolve, whenever it may please you to receive, through us or through our venerable brother and kinsman, the reverend Bishop of Paris, both the title of our Church and the office of its dignity, and to be advanced to the priesthood, it will be pleasing to us, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0827D] This was Odo of Sully, Bishop of Paris, nephew of Theobald the Great, Count of Champagne, elected after [Col. 0828D] Maurice in the year 1196. He is called a kinsman of Henry II, King of the English, and of the King of the French.]

[Col. 0829]

CHARTERS OF WILLIAM.

He grants indulgences to all who attend the fair held on Easter Day near the hospital of the lepers. (1176.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolitan Church of Reims*, II, 406.]

[Col. 0829A]

William, by the grace of God Archbishop of the people of Reims, legate of the Apostolic See, to all to whom these letters shall come: greeting in the Lord.

He who has mercy on the wretched shall obtain the mercy of God, the merciful Father. Since we see persons afflicted with leprosy tortured by pitiable suffering, we ought, by the principle of humanity, to sympathize with and grieve for their pains. Moved, therefore, by this consideration, [Col. 0829B] we wish to offer relief to the affliction and misery of the lepers dwelling near the city of Reims; and we ask and earnestly exhort all the faithful in the Lord to do them good.

Trusting in the mercy of God and in the merits of the glorious Virgin Mary and of all the saints, we grant to all who come to their fair the following remission from the penances imposed upon them: namely, one year out of seven years; one forty-day penance out of three, whichever a person chooses; and a fourth part of the Friday observances. Moreover, unless they have laid violent hands upon them, we mercifully remit offenses against fathers and mothers; broken vows, if they return to those vows; and even sins forgotten by them.

Given by the hand of Alexander, our chancellor.

II. Since William had incurred greater than usual expenses at the king’s coronation and was thereby burdened with debt, he requested some assistance from the common treasury of the chapter of Reims. But, lest it should afterward suffer any loss on that account, in the following charter he declares the said chapter exempt from expenses of this kind. It begins as follows. (1180.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolitan Church of Reims*, II, 413.]

[Col. 0829C]

William, by the grace of God Archbishop of the people of Reims, Cardinal of the Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, and legate of the Apostolic See, to all, future as well as present, to whom these letters shall come: greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 0829D] Let all of you know that, since we were burdened with much debt for the anointing and coronation of the lord king Philip, our most dear nephew, [lacuna] our chapter of Reims, where we [lacuna] setting forth our [lacuna] and burden, requested assistance before all; but they, as sons sympathizing with their father’s necessity, graciously assented to our requests. And although [lacuna] they had contributed to us by obligation, they alone made this aid from their own lands—not on account of the crown, nor because of any obligation, but out of their sheer generosity. Therefore, since no one’s generosity ought to prove deceptive or harmful to him, wishing to protect them and their land in future, we grant them the safeguard of this our writing, so that a gift so freely given may not at another time be drawn by anyone into a precedent, etc.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1180.

Given by the hand of the chancellor.

III. Not willing that the people of Reims should be in a worse condition than the inhabitants of other cities, who enjoyed their own magistrates, he restored the aldermen, granting them jurisdiction to hear civil and market causes, except for three cases contained in the charter. (1182.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolitan Church of Reims*, II, 417.]

[Col. 0830B]

William, by the grace of God Archbishop of the people of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved sons and faithful subjects, all the men of Reims living under the archbishop’s ban: greeting in the Lord.

Just as rulers of lands may gain the love of God and neighbor by observing the law and liberty of their subjects, so, by violating or altering customs long maintained, they may incur the indignation of the Most High, lose the favor of the people, and impose a perpetual burden upon their own souls. [Col. 0830C] Moved by this consideration, and considering the service and devotion which you, our beloved sons and faithful burgesses, have hitherto willingly rendered us, we have deemed fit to restore to you and to your descendants, and to confirm forever, under the protection of our authority, the customs granted to you from ancient times but sometimes less faithfully observed through changes of lords.

We therefore will that aldermen be restored to the city. By the common consent of all of you, twelve shall be chosen from among those subject to our ban and presented to us; they shall be renewed every year at the beginning of Lent, and shall swear that they will judge you by just judgment and, insofar as pertains to them, faithfully preserve our rights. If anyone commonly chosen should refuse to be an alderman, we shall make him serve as alderman, provided that his bodily strength is sufficient. Yet if you are not agreed in choosing aldermen, we shall appoint aldermen according as we know to be advantageous to our city and to ourselves.

If those aldermen, or two or more of them, render any judgment which does not seem sufficiently reasonable, and acknowledge their error, they shall amend it to us without loss [Col. 0831A] of their goods. But if they persist, and anyone wishes to prosecute them for false judgment, then, if they are proved or convicted, they shall make amends to us through the judgment of our court. If the complainant cannot convict them, he shall likewise make amends for it to us and to the aldermen.

We further grant that, if a burgess living under our ban is drawn into a lawsuit for any reason, when he wishes to be proceeded against in due legal form, neither he nor his property shall be seized; nor shall his house be demolished, if he has a house or inheritance at Reims. But he shall give security that, for the execution of justice, he will provide hostages if he can; and if he cannot obtain hostages, he shall similarly pledge that he will abide by the judgment of the aldermen.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] The custom was still in force that the house of one who did not obey his lord should be destroyed as a punishment.]

If, however, he has neither house [Col. 0831B] nor inheritance at Reims, he shall give hostages; if he has no hostages, his body shall be detained until he fulfills the demands of justice. Further, if any person under our ban commits theft, murder, or treason, and the offense is manifest, he and his property shall be at our disposal. If the matter is doubtful and he is accused of it, he shall, if he belongs to our ban, give good hostages that he will abide by the judgment of the aldermen; and if he cannot give hostages, his body shall be taken and detained.

If anyone removes or withholds our *sesterlage* levy, he shall make amends to us for the offense by sixty shillings. If any money-changer, who does not pay us the *trecensum* as our money-changers do, makes an exchange, both he and the other person with whom he made the exchange shall make amends to us for the offense by [Col. 0831C] sixty shillings. The offense concerning *timonage* shall likewise be amended to us by seven and a half shillings.

We decree that whoever has possessed and held an inheritance, purchase, or any other property peacefully for seven years and one day shall thereafter possess his holding freely and quietly, so that no one may make a claim or challenge the holding, unless he can prove that during that period he was absent from the land and alleges a reasonable cause for his absence, or that during that time he was of such an age that he could not assert his right.

Therefore, lest any dispute may arise in future concerning all these matters, the foregoing provisions, as set down above, shall remain firm and ratified hereafter. We confirm them to you and your successors both by the protection of this present privilege and by the authority of our seal, ordaining and forbidding under anathema that anyone presume to oppose this document of our confirmation, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

Done in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1182.

Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] One might rightly wonder why William makes no mention of the commune of Reims in this memorable and illustrious privilege; perhaps because the aldermanship [Col. 0832D] implied the commune, and the aldermen were the protectors of the commune.]

IV. He confirms the rights and customs of the Monastery of Saint Remigius. (1182.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolitan Church of Reims*, II, 420.]

[Col. 0832A]

William, by the grace of God Archbishop of the people of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, to his beloved sons in Christ, Simon, abbot, and the whole chapter of Blessed Remigius of Reims, and their successors professing the Rule of Blessed Benedict, in perpetuity.

Pastoral care continually admonishes us to love and foster the churches and ecclesiastical persons entrusted to our care, and in every way to preserve firm and inviolate their liberties, possessions, and rights. Moved, therefore, by this consideration, graciously assenting to your just petitions, beloved sons in Christ, we receive under our custody and protection your church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and your castle and borough. We also grant to your church and to you, to possess in perpetual peace and quiet, and inviolably confirm by the authority bestowed on us by God, your liberties and customs which you possess there: ovens, mills, rents, the ban, jurisdiction, *sexterlage*, markets on Friday and Sunday, and whatsoever possessions and goods you now reasonably hold or may hereafter, with the Lord’s favor, acquire. [Col. 0832C]

We decree that your men, or other residents in the borough of Saint Remigius going to and returning from Reims, shall not be seized or detained either by our provosts or officials or by outsiders, nor shall their goods be seized, so long as they are willing to submit to the justice of your abbot, unless they are caught in a present offense.

That all these things may obtain the strength of perpetual stability, we strengthen them both by the protection of this present document and by the authority of our seal, ordaining and forbidding under anathema that anyone presume to molest your church or brethren in these matters or in any way to oppose this confirmation of ours. But upon all who preserve your rights and bestow their benefactions, may there be the peace and grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive temporal reward here and attain, on the day of the final judgment, the rewards of eternal blessedness. Amen.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182. Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] A fairly large wax seal is attached to it, bearing on its face the image of a bishop; the wax is green, as is the cord by which it is attached to the charter.]

V. Charter of Lord William, Archbishop, concerning the agreements made between the Church of Reims and Lord Rainald of Roset concerning the village of Fraislicourt. (1182.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of Reims*, vol. I, p. 387.]

[Col. 0833A]

William, by the grace of God Archbishop of the people of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, to future and present persons alike, in perpetuity.

Whereas at the village of Fraislicourt, formerly called Plumbea Fontana, a dispute had arisen between the Church of Reims and Lord Rainald of Roset concerning the ban, justice, and revenues owed by the residents; whereas ownership and lordship of the entire territory, both the land-rents and the tithes, and the church of that place, as R. himself acknowledged, belonged wholly to the Church of Reims; and whereas they nevertheless disputed concerning the aforesaid matters, the controversy was settled through our mediation in the following manner.

The Church of Reims retained as its own and to hold separately the church of the said place, all tithes of the same territory with all ecclesiastical rights, and the whole patronage of the church with all spiritual matters. It also retained the enclosed fields—that is, the meadows—in the middle of the village, formerly held as the demesne of the church but appropriated by peasants through the negligence of the canons. It also retained the land and meadows formerly held there in fief by John of Ardennes from the provost of the Church of Reims; these Arnald of Blois had bought from that same John, together with a third part of the flax tithe, and had given to the church along with the residents. It retained further the site intended for the building and dwelling [Col. 0833C] of the provost of the land, with the meadows and gardens which the aforesaid Arnald had bought from the inhabitants of that village; also the house and barn which he built there at his own expense and gave to the Church of Reims for the observance of his anniversary.

In order that the said R. and his heirs might be permitted to establish a village there, to cut down and clear the whole wood beyond the Sera, on the Roset side, which lies within the territory of the same village, and to allow the residents of the said village to work it freely and without disturbance as far as the land called Manus Firma and as far as the land of Saint Lawrence; and also, on this side of the Sera, as far as Sepau granted for fortifying the land: the Church granted the said R. the right to receive one half of the land-rent, the proceeds of the ban and justice, and the revenues [Col. 0833D] collected from holdings and residents through the village rents, saving separately to the Church such benefits as it might in any manner derive from the enclosed fields or from the fief of the aforesaid John.

This was granted under the following conditions and agreements: not only that the village should be made free and the aforesaid woodland to be cleared should be given to the said residents, but also that no one might hold any land unless he were a resident of the village and possessed of the freedom of that same village, except for lands which the residents of Rubigny and of the Valleys had already cleared. The Church granted those lands to them so long as they pay the whole tithe and the whole land-rent to the Church of Reims.

The aforesaid R., together with the Church, granted without any exception or reservation not only that the whole village with its territory should be free, but also that everyone who had, or should have, a bodily dwelling there for a year and a day should, insofar as concerned the Church and Lord R., be free and exempt from every exaction, toll, and tax, except as required by the charter establishing the village, sealed by both the Church and Lord R., while retaining the poll-taxes.

Two mayors shall be chosen, one by the canon who is provost of the village and the other by Lord R. or his heir, but only from among those possessing the freedom of the village; they shall render fealty jointly to both parties. Neither party shall have more in its own share than the other, so that if either commits an offense, he shall be judged only by the aldermen of the village, [Col. 0834B] and the amount of the amends shall belong jointly to both the provost and Lord R. During the time that they are mayors, they shall be exempt from the customary obligations of the others.

Neither the provost nor Lord R. or his heir may retain for himself anything from the entire land; it shall all be given to the residents, excepting, however, those things which, as stated, the Church shall hold separately as its own.

It was also granted on both sides that not only in the village, but throughout its whole territory, in the woodland as well as on the plain, justice in every controversy whatsoever, apart from ecclesiastical matters, shall in every respect be administered by the aldermen of the said village. If the aldermen are uncertain in giving judgment, they shall consult the Church of Reims and judge according to [Col. 0834C] it.

Apart from the constitution of the village, neither party—neither the Church nor Lord R. nor his heirs—may vex or burden the residents in any respect; nor shall either party have any greater right over them than the other. Except for those things which the Church holds separately, both their profit and authority shall be equal in all respects.

The woods on the Calvimont side of the Sera shall, as they jointly see fit, be guarded by common guards taken from the said village and from nowhere else. They shall take wood jointly for their needs, give jointly, sell jointly, and have jointly all proceeds of the woodland. If, for fortifying the land, it is expedient to construct a hedge in that wood, then, by the valuation and arbitration of lawful men, a width of hedge sufficient for fortifying the land shall be assessed in the woodland, without prejudice to either party and with the village’s use outside the hedge preserved; its length shall extend to the boundaries of the woodland. But within the bounded hedge the said R. and his heirs shall have no right without the Church; they may impose no ban contrary to the Church or to the canon who is provost of the land. Although they may prevent anyone they choose from cutting it down for the fortification of the land, both the Church and Lord R. may nevertheless take from the said hedge for the needs of their offices and use it for every domestic purpose; and in the hedge their profit and authority shall especially be equal.

The aforesaid R. also allowed all the residents [Col. 0835A] of Fraislicourt *aisances*—rights of common use—on his land, as other men had them from their free villages. He likewise granted the village, insofar as concerned himself and his heirs, perpetual peace and immunity from every *wionage* toll for all goods carried through his land for constructing buildings, for any household equipment, or for provisions, provided that security be given that they are not carrying them for trade.

Moreover, he promised protection against every robber and every evildoer, defense in good faith to the best of his ability, and aid in recovering things taken away.

Therefore Lord R. swore upon the holy hand to uphold the liberty and peace of the aforesaid village, these conditions and agreements. He promised that thenceforth he would maintain good faith toward the Church and the land, the provosts, the village, and its residents; that he would do or receive nothing to the loss or fraud of the Church, the provost, or the village; and that both he and his heirs would observe these terms. He further bound himself by oath to procure the oath and approval of his wife, of Lord G., husband of his eldest daughter, and of that daughter herself, and to make the noble, enfeoffed, and liege men of his land swear this. He also promised that he would give the Church his charter on this matter, and the Church promised him hers. And that this may not be changed forever, etc.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182. Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

VI. He grants immunities to the burgesses of the castle of Beaumont in the Argonne, built by himself. (1182.)

[D. Calmet published this charter only in French, *History of Lorraine*, II, Preface, p. DXXXVII, although in the text, II, 314, he had promised to publish it in Latin.]

[Col. 0835C]

William, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Church of Rome, of the title of Saint Sabina, to his friends and faithful men, to the mayors, aldermen, and other men of Beaumont, as well those present as those to come, in perpetuity.

Because matters which ought to retain the force of lasting stability, so that they may not be erased or altered, are committed to the record of letters, we have set down in this present document that we establish in our land a new town called Beaumont, and establish therein the franchises and customs written below.

I. We establish and grant to you permanently that every burgess who has a house in the town of Beaumont shall pay us each year twelve deniers for his garden outside the walls: six deniers at Christmas and six deniers at Saint John’s Day. If he has not paid them by the third day after the term assigned above, he shall owe two shillings as a fine.

II. Burgesses may sell and buy in the town of Beaumont without paying *vinage* or cask-duty.

[Col. 0836A]

III. For every mowing of meadow, you shall pay four deniers on the feast day of Saint Remigius.

IV. On cultivated land, you shall pay two sheaves out of twelve. On land converted from woodland to arable, you shall pay two sheaves out of fourteen.

V. We shall establish ovens in the town of Beaumont, which shall be ours, to which you shall bring your bread to bake under the ban; and out of twenty-four loaves, you shall pay one.

VI. We shall also establish mills there, at which you shall come to grind under the ban, or at the mill of L’Étang; and out of twenty *setiers* you shall pay one, without giving flour.

VII. If any man is accused of having harvested his tithes [Col. 0836B] or land-rents without paying, or of violating the ban of the mills or of the oven, he shall clear himself by his oath alone.

VIII. In addition to these things, we grant you the use of the waters and woods, as it shall be divided between you, the men of L’Étang, and the men and brethren of Belleval.

IX. In the town of Beaumont aldermen shall be established, and likewise a mayor, who shall swear fealty to us and shall answer to our officials for the rents and revenues of the town. The mayor, the *mariés* [a corrupt or uncertain office-term in the source], and the aldermen shall remain in their offices for only one year, unless all consent otherwise.

X. If anyone wishes to sell his inheritance, whether because of [Col. 0836C] necessity or otherwise, the seller shall give one denier and the buyer one denier. Of these two deniers the mayor shall have one and the aldermen the other.

XI. If anyone newly becomes a burgess, he shall at entry give one denier to the mayor and one to the aldermen, and shall receive land and a house-site from the mayor, where the mayor shall designate and assign it to him.

XII. We establish that he against whom a complaint is made, if convicted by lawful testimony, shall pay three shillings: two shillings to the archbishop, six deniers to the mayor, and six deniers to his opponent.

XIII. If anyone says an injurious thing to another, and the latter complains of it and can prove it by the testimony of two burgesses, he of whom the complaint is made shall pay five [Col. 0836D] shillings: four and a half shillings to the archbishop and six deniers to the mayor.

If the complainant has no testimony, the other shall clear himself by his oath alone.

XIV. If anyone calls another a disloyal man, or says anything as injurious as calling him disloyal, he shall pay ten shillings: six shillings to the lord, two shillings to the person to whom he said the insult, twelve deniers to the mayor, and twelve deniers to the aldermen.

XV. If he against whom the complaint is made has no witness, the other shall clear himself by his oath alone.

XVI. If anyone lays hands on another without drawn weapons, he shall pay forty-five shillings: thirty-eight shillings to the lord, twelve deniers to the mayor, twelve deniers to the aldermen, and five shillings to the person beaten. If the beaten person has no witness, the other shall clear himself by the oath of two lawful men and his own.

XVII. If anyone attacks another with drawn weapons without striking him, and this is proved by lawful testimony, he shall pay sixty shillings: fifty-eight shillings to the lord, twelve deniers to the mayor, and twelve to the aldermen. If the complainant has no witness, the other shall clear himself by the oath of two men and his own. If it happens that he draws blood and wounds him, he shall pay one hundred shillings: to the lord, four pounds less two shillings; twelve deniers to the mayor; twelve deniers to the aldermen; twenty shillings to the wounded man; and the expenses of healing the wound. If the wounded man has no witness, the other shall clear himself by the testimony of seven burgesses. If he cuts off a limb or kills him, and this is proved by lawful [Col. 0837B] testimony, his body and goods shall be at the lord’s disposal.

XVIII. If any man strikes another in defense of his own person, or draws blood from him, the other shall clear himself by the testimony of two men and his own oath; and, if the other wishes, he may challenge him by judicial combat.

XIX. He who, in defense of his own person, cuts off another’s limb or kills him—he who did so shall clear himself by judgment; and he who accuses him of such a deed shall bear the costs of the judgment and shall be at the lord’s disposal.

XX. If anyone attacks another in his house, and this is proved by lawful testimony, he shall pay one hundred [Col. 0837C] shillings: four pounds to the lord; eighteen shillings to the person whom he attacked; twelve deniers to the mayor; and twelve deniers to the aldermen.

XXI. In every offense for which the accused must clear himself, he cannot clear himself except by the testimony of burgesses.

XXII. For every false complaint, the complainant shall pay three shillings: two shillings to the lord, six deniers to the mayor, and six deniers to his opponent. If anyone falsely claims an inheritance, he shall pay twenty shillings: eighteen shillings to the lord, twelve deniers to the mayor, and twelve deniers to the aldermen.

XXIII. If anyone enters another’s inheritance without leave of the mayor and aldermen, he shall pay twenty shillings, unless he proves that it is his; and if he proves that it is his, the other shall pay twenty shillings.

XXIV. If anyone holds an inheritance safely, freely, and peacefully for a year and a day, without contradiction from men dwelling in the town, he shall hold it peacefully thereafter.

XXV. A burgess may not summon another burgess before another court as long as the burgess is willing to do right before the local court; and if he causes him loss in this matter, he shall pay ten shillings and compensate his damages: namely, eight shillings to the lord, twelve deniers to the mayor, and twelve deniers to the aldermen.

XXVI. A burgess who has served as a juror beyond his term, concerning a matter which he has heard, neither wishes nor may bear testimony or swear for more than a year and a day.

XXVII. If anyone accuses another, however the deed was done, of setting fire to another’s house, theft, homicide, or rape, and he gives pledge from his own goods, and the accused likewise gives pledge for whatever shall be adjudged, the accused shall clear himself by the water ordeal. If the accuser does not give pledge, he shall pay twenty shillings. If the accused is acquitted in the ordeal, the accuser shall pay the costs of the ordeal and nine pounds.

XXVIII. What is done before the aldermen shall be valid and binding without contradiction.

XXIX. Everyone may prove a sale up to three shillings by his own hand alone.

XXX. If anyone lends another up to ten shillings, he may prove it by two lawful witnesses of the town. Whoever claims from another a debt greater than ten shillings, and has good witnesses, may be challenged by the other through judicial combat.

XXXI. If anyone brings foreign goods to Beaumont, and the person claiming them can prove by two lawful witnesses from his own country that they are his, he shall recover them; but the other may challenge him through judicial combat. If the person against whom such goods are claimed has nothing with which to restore them, the claimant shall be given whatever may be found of his goods, and he shall not remain at Beaumont unless by the will and permission of the claimant. If the claimant does not wish him to remain there, the other shall take a safe-conduct from the town.

XXXII. If anyone challenges the judgment of the aldermen and can prove it by the testimony of the aldermen of Bruyères, the aldermen shall pay one hundred shillings. If he cannot [Col. 0838C] prove it, he shall pay one hundred shillings and the expenses of the aldermen: sixty shillings to the lord, five shillings to the mayor, and thirty-five shillings to the aldermen.

XXXIII. The judgment of the aldermen shall stand, unless someone immediately seeks counsel and speaks against it.

XXXIV. If anyone takes another’s inheritance in pledge, he shall keep it for a year and a day; and after a year and a day he shall show it to the mayor and aldermen, and the mayor and aldermen shall determine what ought to be done.

XXXV. If anyone wrongs a foreign man and it is proved, he shall make amends according to the assessment of the aldermen; and if it is not proved, he shall clear himself by his oath alone.

XXXVI. If any burgess of the place disturbs the market [Col. 0838D] of the town, he shall pay one hundred shillings: twelve deniers to the mayor, twelve deniers to the aldermen, ten shillings to the beaten person, and, if he wounds him, twenty shillings; the rest to the lord. If a foreign man disturbs the market of Beaumont, he shall pay sixty shillings: twelve deniers to the mayor, twelve deniers to the aldermen, eighteen shillings to the beaten person, and the rest to the lord.

XXXVII. If any burgess of the town beats a foreign man, he shall pay sixty shillings; and if the foreign man beats a burgess of the town, he shall pay the same amount: twelve deniers to the mayor, twelve deniers to the aldermen, ten shillings to the beaten person, and the rest to the lord.

XXXVIII. If the guard finds a man in another’s vineyard gathering grapes, or in another’s grain, he shall pay five shillings: four shillings to the lord, [Col. 0839A] six deniers to the mayor, and six deniers to the guard. If someone other than the guard finds him gathering, he shall clear himself by his oath; and if he refuses to swear, he shall pay six shillings and restore the damage according to the assessment of the aldermen.

XXXIX. If anyone is found doing damage in a garden or enclosed plot, he shall pay thirty deniers: two shillings to the lord, six deniers to the mayor, and shall restore the damage according to the assessment of the aldermen.

XL. If any man is found gathering in another’s vineyard, enclosed plot, or grain-field, and the guard makes report of it, he shall pay two deniers and swear that he did not know the custom of the town. If he refuses to swear, he shall pay five shillings: four shillings to the lord, six deniers to the mayor, and [Col. 0839B] six deniers to the guard.

XLI. Children between ten and fifteen years of age, if found there, shall pay twelve deniers according to the assessment of the aldermen.

XLII. If anyone lays hands upon the mayor or aldermen without a blow of weapons, he shall pay one hundred shillings: to the lord, four pounds less two shillings; to the assaulted person, twenty shillings; to the mayor, twelve deniers; and to the other aldermen, twelve deniers. If he wounds him, his body and goods shall be at the lord’s disposal. And if the mayor or an alderman wounds a burgess, he shall pay the same amount, and it shall be at the lord’s disposal.

XLIII. A woman who calls another woman “ugly” (Old French *lait*) shall, if this is proved by the testimony of two men or of two women, pay five sous: four sous to the lord, six deniers to the mayor, and six deniers to the person whom she called “lewd.” If she does not wish to pay the money, she shall carry the stone on Sunday during the procession, wearing only her shift.

XLIV. If a woman calls a man “ugly” (*lait*), and this is proved by lawful testimony, she shall pay five sous. And if a man calls a woman “ugly” (*lait*), he shall pay five sous, without further apportionment.

XLV. If any foreign man comes to Beaumont, or within the bounds of the town, he shall be safely received, whatever offence he may have committed, except theft and homicide; yet he may defend himself against an accusation of theft or homicide if he wishes.

XLVI. If anyone is accused of theft on suspicion, [Col. 0839D] and cannot clear himself by the testimony of two lawful men, he shall purge himself by the ordeal of water.

XLVII. If anyone cannot pay the fine for his offence, whatever of his property can be found shall be seized, and he shall be banished from the town; if he wishes to return, he shall pay the fine assessed by the jurors.

XLVIII. If cattle are found in vineyards without incursion [term uncertain], they shall pay twelve deniers; and small livestock caught in grain-fields shall pay six deniers. Of the twelve deniers, ten go to the lord and two to the keeper. Of the six deniers, five go to the lord and one to the keeper. He who owns the animal shall make good the damage, according to the assessment of the jurors. No one may distrain his own animal without justice [Col. 0840A] or without its order; if he does so, he shall incur a fine of ten sous: eight sous to the lord, twelve deniers to the mayor, and twelve deniers to the jurors.

XLIX. A tavern-keeper may take a pledge from his customer within his inn, but not outside it.

L. If anyone is found in the wood making timber, charcoal, ashes, or anything else which he carries to foreign places, except to our markets, he shall pay ten sous: eight sous to the lord, twelve deniers to the mayor, and twelve deniers to the jurors.

LI. Of all forfeitures which we and our successors, archbishops of Reims, shall have in the town of Beaumont, the burgesses shall receive one half for the government of the town, in such manner that they shall appoint two trustworthy men and we shall appoint our [Col. 0840B] serjeant as the third. These three shall faithfully expend that half upon the costs of maintaining the town.

LII. What the mayor, the jurors, and the forty prudent burgesses shall determine for the honour and profit of the town shall stand and remain fixed. Whoever opposes it shall pay twelve deniers: six deniers to the lord and six deniers for the maintenance of the town. What they have ordained and established shall stand and remain fixed.

LIII. The burgesses shall go on the lord’s mounted expedition, and shall return to Beaumont on the same day, if it pleases them.

LIV. The archbishop shall give a provision for [Col. 0840C] the general court three times a year: five sous on each occasion to the mayor and jurors. The mayor and jurors, so long as they hold office, shall each be exempt from the rent of one house-plot and one garden-plot.

We, wishing all these things to be and remain firm and stable, confirm them both by the security of this writing and by the authority of our seal; and we establish and command, under penalty of excommunication, that no one shall act against our confirmation, saving the right of Holy Church and the authority of the Roman See in all these matters. Done in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord 1182. Given by the hand of Lambellin, our chancellor.

VII. For the adornment of the city of Reims and the advantage of its citizens, he granted them a cultivated area outside the city limits, so that, by newly constructed buildings, its built-up boundary might be extended; that carpenters especially—those engaged in making casks or wagons—might live there; and that the Easter fairs, which were held beside the chapel of the lepers, might be transferred there. (Year 1183.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, II, 419.]

[Col. 0840D]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to our beloved sons, the men dwelling in the new cultivated district of Reims, both present [Col. 0841A] and future: greeting in our Lord.

We have been placed in the episcopal seat so that, with God’s aid, we may provide for the benefit and increase of the city over which the Lord has set us, advancing by making provision and making provision by advancing. Accordingly, for the increase and honour of our city, we have granted to you, our beloved and faithful burgesses, the cultivated land which we possess outside the walls, for building houses and likewise constructing there a new borough, on the condition that for each perch of land you shall pay twelve deniers annually on the feast of Blessed Remigius; and likewise, for each perch of land in our garden district, you shall pay the same number of deniers at the same term. It should nevertheless be known that, both in the cultivated district and [Col. 0841B] in the garden district, there are perches liable to pay only nine deniers.

We therefore decree that the fair formerly held at Saint Lazarus shall be celebrated in your borough, and shall last from the Saturday before Palm Sunday until the vigil of Easter Sunday. We also ordain that the carpenters who make casks and wagons shall work there and may not work in the city; for we wish all timber and building timber to be sold there and nowhere else. You may freely and peaceably make loggias, steps, and wells before your houses, without permission from the lords or their officials. Moreover, you may have your own mayor, who, according to his ability, shall redress your offences [Col. 0841C] and transgressions; matters which cannot be redressed by him shall be referred to the archbishop.

Since it is fitting that what has been justly and reasonably established by us should possess the strength of perpetual stability, we grant and confirm all these things to you and your successors, so that they may not be violated or altered by any disturbance raised by malicious persons, both by the protection of this present writing and by the authority of our seal. We decree and forbid under anathema that anyone presume with rash boldness to oppose this charter of our confirmation, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1183.

Given by the hand of Lambert, our chancellor. [Col. 0841D]

[Note: [Col. 0841D] So that the lepers, who had consented to this, should suffer no loss through the transfer of the fairs, William assigned them, as compensation, ten pounds and eight sous of Reims currency, to be received annually from the money-changers’ stalls. [Col. 0842D] He also granted that, in perpetuity, they might grind in the mills on the embankment of the Vidula the grain necessary for the use of their house without paying milling dues. Year 1182.]

VIII. Charter for the valley of Radigionis. (Year 1184.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of Reims*, vol. I, p. 407.]

WILLIAM . . . Archbishop of Reims, etc., etc. . . .

Let all know that, when our beloved brother Count H. was about to depart for Jerusalem, our beloved sons R., dean, and certain other canons of the Church of Reims [Col. 0842A] approached him at Troyes and requested that, before us, who were present there, he acknowledge what right he possessed in the valley of Radigionis and what right the canons of the Church of Blessed Mary of Reims possessed there, so that no doubt might thereafter arise concerning this matter between him or his heirs and the aforesaid canons.

The count, graciously acceding to their request, acknowledged that he and the canons held jointly and in equal shares all rights and all revenues from every advantage belonging to the jurisdiction of the valley of Radigionis, with this exception: he might take lodging there if present in person, or his men might do so once a year if he sent them through those parts on campaign; and excepting the village called Singaudicurt, which he acknowledged to belong wholly and exclusively to the canons. Furthermore, the count and the canons, as he acknowledged, have the right freely and under an equal rule to appoint officials in the same valley, who shall collect their revenues and proceeds jointly and divide them equally.

He also acknowledged and granted that neither he nor any of his heirs may give, sell, exchange, pledge, or in any way put outside his own hand what he holds in the aforesaid valley. Furthermore, he nonetheless acknowledged that at Cys-sur-Aisne the said church possesses one third of all judicial fines and forfeitures, except murder and rape, which belong to the count and his heirs. In his land of Jouy he acknowledged the whole jurisdiction to belong to the aforesaid canons, except [Col. 0842C] that they must deliver up to him and his officials a thief, stripped naked, for justice to be done. He granted all these things to the Church of Reims and its canons, as written, to possess in perpetual peace. In witness of this matter, etc.

Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1184.

IX. Privilege of Lord William, archbishop, concerning the peace made between Alan [of Rosay] and the burgesses [of Reims]. (Year 1187.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, I, 408.]

[Col. 0842D] WILLIAM . . . Archbishop of Reims, etc.

Let all know that the dispute pending between our beloved sons Alan of Rosay and the burgesses of Reims concerning the lands, meadows, and gardens situated in the territory of Saint Geneviève has been settled as follows. The possessors of the aforesaid properties shall render him all justice arising from them, at his house at Muire or at another place within the city or its banlieue, wherever he prefers. They shall be bound to satisfy and answer to him for rent, forfeitures, and breaches of the ban for as long as they possess the aforesaid properties. That this may remain ratified, etc. . . .

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187. Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

X. Charter concerning the provostship [Note: [Col. 0843C]

“The provost of the Church of Reims, although he is named after the archdeacon in Ebbo’s list—which begins with those last and lowest in dignity and ends with the archbishop—had, according to that list, very great authority over both the spiritual and temporal affairs of the chapter. He was first relieved of spiritual responsibilities by the establishment of a dean; and although the administration of the chapter’s temporal goods was left to him for several more centuries, as appears from the testament of Odalric, provost, this gave rise to several disputes. William of Champagne induced his nephew Hugh, the provost, to surrender to the chapter all his authority and also the collation of the office of bread-provider, which had formerly belonged to him, reserving only the honours of his stall in choir and the presidency in chapter.

“The chapter ceded to the same archbishop the collation of the provostship, which had previously been elective, like the deanery, and at the chapter’s disposal—as it still is today in the Church of Soissons—on condition that the provost appointed by the lord archbishop should do homage to the chapter. The authority which the provost had for administering the temporal goods having been restored to the chapter, the body has employed seneschals and receivers to carry out its orders. Thus no right or function remains to the provost other than that of presiding at [Col. 0844C] the chapter when present. The oldest statutes, reception-books, and practice attribute no other function to him. He is not an ex officio deputy for any occasion—audits of accounts, assemblies, and so forth. When he is installed in the chapter, these words are used: *Accipe locum in capitulo ad praesidendum, proponendum et concludendum super rebus in eo propositis*—‘Take your place in the chapter in order to preside, to put forward matters, and to conclude concerning matters put before it.’

[Col. 0844D] “The provost still performs to the chapter the homage specified in the charters of 1188 and 1192 and recorded in the reception-book. It states that this homage is done *ratione praesidentiae primae*, that is, the provost does homage to the chapter for the right which he has, in the first place, to perform the office of president of deliberations. At the taking of possession by the lord archbishop, he has also always observed, down to the present, in the homage he renders him, the circumstance specified in the reception-book: *Praestat hominium sinistra manu levata tantum, dextra capitulo reservata, caeteri more communi duabus manibus junctis*—‘He performs homage with the left hand raised only, the right reserved for the chapter; the others, according to common custom, with both hands joined.’ This most expressly indicates his dependence upon, and particular attachment to, the chapter.”

(Bibliothèque de Reims, portfolio YY, fol. 29, manuscripts 1, of M. de la Salle.)]

. (Year 1188.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives*, vol. I, p. 411.]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims . . . .

The concern of pastoral care admonishes us, whenever occasion allows, to provide peace and tranquillity for our subjects. Accordingly, desiring fully to settle the disputes and lawsuits which had frequently arisen between the chapter of Reims and the provost on account of the provostship, [Col. 0843B] we induced our most dear nephew Hugh to relinquish—and he did relinquish—the revenues of the provostship in all its appurtenances, likewise its jurisdictions and the grant of the office of bread-provider. He resigned all these things into our hand by means of a book, retaining for himself only the dignity of provost in choir and chapter, and his homages.

We, in turn, granted all these things to the Church of Reims for its perpetual benefit, investing it with them through the hand of the dean. The chapter, however, granted to the provost in perpetuity all that it possessed in the valley of Radigionis, except the churches and tithes which it retained for providing the meal of Blessed Nicasius; it promised thereafter to provide this meal with the same solemnity as had formerly been observed. Moreover, whenever the provost is requested and summoned [Col. 0843C] by the chapter, he shall be bound, without any demand for payment and with the utmost willingness, to assist in the needs of the church. That these provisions may be ratified, etc.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188. Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

XI. He grants the Church of Saint Remigius the personate of Driencourt [Note: [Col. 0844D] “Dricourt,” marginal note.] for celebrating the anniversary of himself and of his brother Henry; he also lists the anniversaries of others, lest they be consigned to oblivion. (Year 1188.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives*, vol. I, p. 409.]

[Col. 0844A]

WILLIAM . . . archbishop . . . considering that the venerable Church of Blessed Remigius of Reims is known always to have shown an affection of sincere devotion toward us and our predecessors; and likewise considering how devotedly the brethren of that church strive without ceasing to render service to God; wishing to become participants in their prayers, we make known to present and future alike that we have freely and peaceably granted to the beloved sons who are brethren of that church, to possess in perpetuity for their refreshment, the altar of Driencourt, for the pious annual celebration of our anniversary and for the souls of our parents, [Col. 0844B] as well as of our most dear brother, Count Henry of good memory, and of our predecessors.

Under threat of excommunication, we strictly forbid anyone to diminish or withhold the revenues of this altar, or of other benefices likewise granted—or yet to be freely granted—to the oft-mentioned church for anniversaries, or to presume to spend them on purposes other than those for which they were assigned. And so that the names of those whose anniversaries are celebrated annually in the aforesaid church may not in the future be consigned to oblivion or in any way be erased by some intervening event, we have caused them to be written below by name:

[Col. 0844C] Our anniversary; the anniversary of . . .
