Samson, Archbishop of Reims; the anniversary of Esquilius, Archbishop of Dacia; of John, Bishop of Chartres; of Peter, his successor; of Geoffrey, Bishop of Châlons; of Abbot Haideric; of Abbot Hugh and his mother; of Abbot Odo; of Abbot Azenarius; of Abbot Leo; of Saint Gisdenus; of Guy; of Saint Nicasius; of Abbot Herimar; of Count Hugh of Registens; [Col. 0845A] of Archdeacon Hildewin [Note: [Col. 0845D] If this is the archdeacon of Champagne known at Reims by that name, the charter here printed would prove that he did not die in 1196, as Marlot says, I, 465.]; of the priest Goderannus; of the priest Acarinus; of the priest Stephen; of the priest Constantius; of Garin Maloth; of Nicholas of Estampes; of Odo of Sercy; of the monk Haideric; of the monk Dragon; of the canon Gillemannus; of John the physician; of Richer Morlachar [*mordens carnem*, “flesh-biter”] and his wife Elisabeth; of Herbert Morlachar and his wife Hawidis; of Raderus and Colelina, parents of Bishop Samson; of Hawidis, mother of Archdeacon Hildewin; of Lambert the matricularius; of Theobald of Matri; of the knight Walon and his brother Elias; and of Juliana, mother of the monk Samson; of Sibilla; of Lotuiza, mother of Abbot Simon; of the knight Dragon; of Thomas the elder; of Hermann the Burgess; of Dragon Morlachar; of John Lapaut; of Hildewin and Henry; of Eustace the matricularius; of Raderus of Tarny; [Col. 0845B] of Arnulf Paisant; of Thomas the boy; of Herbert Morlachar; of Odo of Saint-Theodoric; of Wiard the mayor; of Ulderic of Mailly; of Hugh of Choilly.

Therefore, wishing this our solemn gift to remain ratified and unshaken, we confirm it by this present writing and the impression of our seal, decreeing and forbidding under threat of anathema that anyone dare violate this charter of our confirmation or oppose it in any respect, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

Done in the year 1188. Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor. [Note: [Col. 0845D] The list of obits contained in William’s charter appears to offer only the names of persons nearly contemporary with this archbishop, except for several abbots of Saint-Remi, the earliest of whom is Herimar, who died in 1071—thus a hundred years before William’s archiepiscopate. Why, then, is no mention made here of the first benefactors of the abbey, above all of the Carolingian and Capetian kings, whose diplomas would later serve the monks of Saint-Remi as a pretext for freeing themselves from the jurisdiction of the archbishops? We should have wished to clarify our [Col. 0846D] doubts by studying the sole obituary of Saint-Remi which survived the destruction of the abbey and which the enlightened care of M. Hivert, then archivist, caused to be restored to the cartulary of the city of Reims; but this obituary is one of the manuscripts withheld from us. The fragments of the Martyrology and of an obituary of Saint-Remi found in the Royal Library, supplementary French manuscripts, 1515–2, vol. II, fols. 228 and 239, could be of no help to us, since Duchesne neglected to indicate the age of the manuscripts from which he had extracted them.]

XII. Charter concerning restoration of the ban of Castellani to the monastery of Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0846D] A bull of Clement III, dated 26 January 1191—7 Kalends of February, the fourth year of his pontificate—confirms this charter. It is found in cartulary A of Saint-Remi, p. 38, and cartulary C of Saint-Remi, fol. 10, no. XXXVI.]. (Year 1189.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, p. 413.]

[Col. 0845C]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, etc.

We make known to present and future alike that Thomas Infans, of Saint-Remi, had lawfully acquired, from Theobald of Mutreio, according to the usages and customs of the land, the ban called Castellani; and for a long time he possessed the same ban freely and peaceably. But in the course of time, when he was pressed by necessity, he put the aforesaid ban up for sale to our most dear nephew Rotrold, treasurer of Tours.

Cecilia of Sillery and her sons lodged a claim and challenged the said ban; but, after a settlement had at last been made with [Col. 0846A] them, they approved in our presence the sale of the same ban and likewise declared it quit and free, as did others to whom that ban ought by hereditary right to have belonged. We also forbade, by the authority we exercise, all those who said that they had any right in that ban from making any further claim. Thereafter our most dear nephew Rotrold resigned into our hands whatever right he had in the same ban; whence, with his will and assent, we granted the said ban to the Church of Blessed Remigius to possess freely and peaceably in perpetuity.

We further granted that, should anyone presume to undertake anything contrary to the prohibition made, we would impose silence upon him, affording in every respect the aforesaid church lawful warranty. Therefore, unwilling that anyone, etc.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1189. Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

XIII. Charter of the lord archbishop for Novavilla situated near Courmisiacum. (Year 1190.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, p. 414.]

WILLIAM . . . Archbishop of Reims . . . .

Let all of you know that, when our predecessor Henry of happy memory, formerly Archbishop of Reims, had increased the candles and lights of the Church of Reims from property belonging to the treasury of Reims, that same archbishop, on an estate, as an initial recompense for the lighting endowment, granted and relinquished to the treasurers of the aforesaid Church of Reims, freely and peaceably to possess in perpetuity, the New Town near Courmisiacum and the fishpond—all of which that archbishop had acquired and built from his own resources—as well as whatever right and lordship he had in that village, with the pond and its other appurtenances.

Furthermore, wishing to provide for our peace and that of the chapter and treasurer, with the assent and will of both the chapter and the treasurer, we ordain that at the Purification of Blessed Mary the treasurer shall give the archbishop, if he is present at Reims, only ten pounds of wax for the candles of his household, [Col. 0846D] excepting the four feudal servants—[Col. 0847A] namely, the seneschal [Note: [Col. 0847C]

“The archbishops of Reims had their seneschals, to whom they granted several handsome rights. When they make their solemn entry into the city, the horse on which they are mounted belongs to the seneschal, together with the spurs; and at the feast held the same day in the great hall of the palace, he claims that the silver vessels used for the first course are due to him. When my lord resides at Reims, the seneschal must be maintained at his lodging, he being the third person, with three horses, three dogs, and three birds.

“It is to be believed that, in imitation of the other seneschals of the kings and peers of France, that of Reims had the supervision of the archbishop’s food, drink, and household; command and leadership of his vassals in war; and the exercise of his justice throughout his duchy. And, as the seneschalship of France was hereditary in the counts of Anjou, and that of Champagne in the lords of Joinville, that of the archbishops and dukes of Reims was likewise hereditary in the lords of Thuisy.

“The oldest charter I have seen in which mention is made of the seneschal of Reims dates from 1114, the seventh year of the pontificate of Raoul-le-Vert; it is subscribed by *Balduinus dapifer* [Baldwin, steward] and *Erlandus vicedominus* [Erland, vidame] . . . .

“William is named seneschal in the charter concerning the acquisition made by the abbot of Saint-Remy of the tithes of Taissy, under the Cardinal of Champagne, in 1199: ‘*Laudaverunt hoc domini a quibusdam feodum tenebant, videlicet Willelmus seneschalcus et filii sui Guido de Ceris, Simon de Bourgo, etc.*’—‘The lords from whom they held the fief approved this, namely William the seneschal and his sons, Guy of Ceris, Simon of Bourgo, etc.’ Fleuriot of Thuisy was seneschal under Pierre de Barbet in 1280; the knight Erard of Thuisy in 1310. Their descendants continued to hold the same office until the lady Jeanne of Thuisy [ [Col. 0847D]

“In the enumeration of the archbishop’s vassals doing homage in 1510, one reads: ‘Jacques de Muire, esquire, for the fief of Luches, situated at Thuizy, anciently called the fief of the seneschalship of Reims, held of the castle of Sept-Saulx, which came to him by the death of Blanchet de Muire, his father.’

“This Jacques de Muire performed the office of seneschal at the entry of R. de Lenoncourt, 1509.”]

, the last of this family, lady of Thuisy, Vraux, Lusches, and Maisnieulx, married in 1515 to Nicolas Goujon, esquire, lord of Tour-sur-Marne, Bouzy, Coigny, etc. He was seneschal in right of his wife. He was succeeded as hereditary seneschal by their son William Goujon, called Thuisi, and then by Jérôme Goujon, lords of Vraux. The latter performed the office of seneschal at the solemn entry of my lord Louis of Lorraine, Cardinal of Guise, Archbishop of Reims, in 1583. From him descended Regnault, lord of Thuisy, son of Jérôme of Thuisy, seneschal of Reims, and Claude, lord of Vraux, who are alive today.

“The fief of Thuisy, from which they took their name, is accompanied by several lands, meadows, woods, and rents, which the seneschal declares when it changes hands or when the see of Reims is provided with a new archbishop. In 1440 Lady Isabelle d’Ardenay, vidamesse of Châlons, acknowledged her fief of Thuisy as held of the lord of Reims on account of the castellany of Sept-Saulx. William Goujon did the same before the Cardinal of Lorraine in 1566, after the deaths of Nicolas Goujon and Jeanne of Thuisy, his father and mother; the appurtenances of his fief are there set out in detail, as is the fact that the horse or mount of my lord’s first entry is due to him with the spurs and the vessels of the first service.”

(Marlot, French work, book X, supplement § 5; vol. III, p. 164.)]

the vidame, the butler, and the bread-provider—who, if present on the feast-day, shall have their customary candles. If the archbishop is absent, the treasurer shall pay only two pounds of wax to the keeper of his houses. That this exchange may therefore endure perpetually, etc.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1190. Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

XIV. He accepts the satisfaction of a certain vidame of Châlons for damages inflicted by him upon the Church of Reims. He assigns to the master of the schools of Reims two measures of grain to be received from the mills of Reims. (Year 1190.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, I, 427.]

[Col. 0847B] WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to all to whom these letters shall come: greeting in the Lord.

Let it be known to future as well as present persons that, when Hugh Cachat, vidame of Châlons, had inflicted many grave damages upon the Church of Blessed Mary of Reims and had no means by which he could make full satisfaction to the church, he relinquished and resigned into our hand, with his wife’s assent, whatever he possessed in the village called Cuysiacum [perhaps Tuisiacum], which is held of our fief, for us and our successors freely and peaceably to possess in perpetuity.

Having made satisfaction to the chapter of Reims for damages inflicted by that vidame, assessed at 140 pounds, and having also received from that chapter 260 pounds for the purchase of Cuysiacum, we gave and assigned to the said chapter twenty pounds of Reims currency annually receivable from the toll of Reims, which belongs to the royal domain of the lord king. . . . . . It should also be known that neither we nor our successors may in any way, except by the will of the lord king and the assent of the chapter of Reims, transfer to another’s hand that part of Cuysiacum which belonged to the vidame Cacalis (Cazalis). Whoever shall at any time be toll-collector shall, upon assuming that office, immediately swear upon the sacred relics that, according to the tenor of this writing, he will pay the aforesaid chapter twenty pounds, setting aside every excuse and diminution. [Col. 0848B]

Furthermore, it should be known that we have given the master of the schools of Reims two muids of grain, assigning them to be received annually and in perpetuity from our mills at Reims. That all these things may remain ratified, etc. Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1190.

Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

XV. Charter by which William, Archbishop of Reims, assigns to the canons of Saint-Denis twelve pounds to be received annually, as compensation for the tithe which they possessed in the garden district and cultivated lands adjoining the city of Reims. (Year 1190.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, I, 416.]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, [Col. 0849A] Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to all, future as well as present, to whom these letters shall come: greeting in the Lord.

Since the Church of Saint Denis possessed by right a tithe in our garden district and cultivated lands adjoining the city of Reims, and since the rent of the houses might decrease or increase, wishing to provide for the peace and advantage of that church, in compensation for the same tithe and for other claims in our garden district and in the cultivated district in which the church of Saint James is built, we give and grant to that church and to the canons who devoutly and solemnly serve God therein twelve pounds to be received annually on the feast of Saint Remigius, celebrated on the Kalends of October.

[Col. 0849B] We also will that, if other cultivated districts not yet built upon should come to be built upon, the canons shall receive the tithe. We decree that the canons shall pay to us or our successors only six sous annually from their vineyards at Moiry, as they have customarily paid from ancient times.

Therefore, lest any dispute arise in future concerning these matters or injury be inflicted upon the canons, we confirm the same to the canons, to possess in perpetual peace and quiet, both by the protection of this present writing and by the authority of our seal. We decree and forbid under anathema that anyone presume in any way to oppose this charter of our confirmation, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0849C] Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1190. Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

XV *bis*. He confirms the settlement made between the bishop and chapter of Senlis. (Year 1183.)

[Gallia Christiana, new edition, X, 438.]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to all to whom these letters shall come: greeting in the Lord.

Let all of you know that, when a dispute arose between our venerable brother Henry, Bishop of Senlis, and our beloved sons, the canons of the same [Col. 0849D] church, concerning a certain custom which those canons asserted that they had possessed since ancient times, a settlement was finally made between them through our mediation as follows. If the principal church ceases services because an injury has been inflicted upon a canon or a canon’s servant, or because someone has violently entered a canon’s house or carried goods away from it, whether belonging to that canon or another, the bishop, when asked concerning this, shall immediately cause all the other churches of the city to cease services, without objection or delay.

If the bishop is absent, the archdeacon shall in this matter perform the bishop’s office; or, if the archdeacon is absent, the dean of Christendom shall do so. If the bishop, archdeacon, or dean of Christendom does not do this on the same day on which he is asked, then at the command of the dean of the principal church, or of the person acting in the dean’s place, all the other churches of the city shall cease services. Lest any dispute in future arise concerning the matters established by us, we confirm them both by the protection of this present writing and by the authority of our seal.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1183.

Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

XV *ter*. Privilege for the canons of Cison. (Year 1190.)

[*Historia ecclesiastica Cisoniensis*, in d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, folio edition, II, 883.]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, [Col. 0850B] Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved sons SIMON, abbot, and the entire chapter of Cison, in perpetuity.

Since ancient times the Church of Cisoing has been known to have belonged, and to belong, to our endowment and table; and among the other churches of our diocese it has always enjoyed this liberty: that it rendered obedience to no one except us and our predecessors. We, however, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace, security, and liberty, graciously grant you the same liberty which you have possessed from ancient times, and the same canonical order which Rainald, formerly archbishop of Reims, of blessed memory, established in your church, as Pope Alexander III, of holy memory, confirmed according to his authentic written instrument; saving the rights of ourselves and our successors. We receive you, that same order, and your possessions into our custody and protection as our own proper possessions; and, as is contained in the authentic writings of our predecessor Rainald and Pope Alexander III, we graciously assent to these things. And, by metropolitan authority, we forbid that their writings be altered. We retain, however, the right of patronage and the presentation of the person.

Moreover, concerning your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or concerning the produce from the feeding of your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. We also decree that burial in your church shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; while nevertheless preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We also forbid the bishop, archdeacon, or their officials to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you or your churches without manifest and reasonable cause, or to harass you with new and unlawful exactions. Furthermore, we strictly forbid the bishop, archdeacon, their canonical officers, or other clerics to have any power or permission, on the pretext of any custom whatever, to demand from you a palfrey, a silk cloak, [Col. 0851A] or anything else for confirmation, enthronement, or the blessing of your abbot. If indeed they demand anything from you on these grounds, since this is detestable and contrary to reason, you shall be free to refuse them what they seek from you.

Further, wishing to provide for your peace and tranquillity, by the authority which we exercise we prohibit anyone, within the enclosure of your places, from daring to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill persons. We command that the canonical order first instituted in your church by our predecessor Rainald be firmly observed there for all time, and we do not wish it to be altered by anyone except with the knowledge of ourselves [Col. 0851B] or our successors and the consent of your whole chapter. Therefore, desiring that all these things remain valid and acquire the strength of perpetual stability, we fortify them by the page of this present writing and confirm them by the authority of our seal. We ordain, and under threat of anathema firmly prohibit, anyone from daring to infringe this charter of our confirmation or rashly and presumptuously oppose it in any respect, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the Apostolic See.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1190.

Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor.

## XVI. Charter of the liberties and customs of the people and inhabitants of the village of Thuisy near Seven Willows. (1191.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, p. 417.]

[Col. 0851C]

WILLIAM . . . archbishop . . . to all . . .

A constitution which remains within the bounds of justice and serves mercy is acceptable and honourable. For in this are signs of the nature of the Lord [sic], since indulgence is granted to subjects and a limit is set for prelates, beyond which they may not stray to the injury of their subjects. Having therefore taken this into consideration, out of regard for piety, with the assent of our beloved and faithful seneschal William, whom we know to possess one half of it, we decree that the people of the village called Tusiacum [Thuisy] shall be free in perpetuity from the exaction commonly called *taillia* [tallage], [Col. 0851D] and we wish them to be restored to the lawful customs which the law imposed by us is known to have established.

> [Note: [Col. 0851D] The charter which we publish was evidently unknown to Marlot.]

> [Note: [Col. 0851D] To what law does this passage refer? Is it a charter already previously granted in favour [Col. 0852D] of Thuisy? Or does it refer to the more general provisions established by the generous William in favour of municipal administrations?]

For this purpose, each year on the feast of St Martin, every one of them who does not have a horse for the plough-cart shall pay us ten denarii, one sextary of oats, and one capon. But whoever has one horse for the plough-cart, or two, three, four, or more, shall pay for each horse two solidi, two sextaries of oats, and two capons. They shall perform four carting services each year, two of which shall be for our share; we leave the other two to William the seneschal, on the condition that they may return to their lodgings on the following night. They shall pay the other ancient customary dues [lacuna]; they shall follow our armies and expeditions.

They shall have two *scabini* [aldermen/judges], who shall swear fealty to us and to the whole village: to us concerning our rights, and to the village concerning the administration of justice in cases and judgments. One of them, however, shall be removed from the office of *scabinus* each year, unless he is of such a character as to deserve retention for the benefit of the village. They shall have two mayors, one of whom shall perform our functions and the other those of William. If anyone strikes another and does not draw blood; or if he draws blood; if he cuts off a limb; or if he commits homicide, we shall have our ban [seigneurial fine] and forfeiture according to the ancient customs. [Col. 0852B] If he wishes to deny it and the deed was not committed openly, he shall either clear himself or make amends by the judgment of the aldermen; nevertheless, the body of the murderer and all his possessions shall be in our hand. But if the injured person belongs to our household or to that of the king, amends shall be made according to our judgment and that of our court.

No one may seize a man in that village so long as he is prepared to stand judgment before our court. If anyone from outside the inhabitants of that village comes there for any reason, and has a concealed mortal hatred against one of the natives, on this first occasion he shall not touch him, but shall cause him to be prohibited, through the mayors and aldermen, from entering the village until peace or a truce exists between them. No one shall bring into the same village a man guilty of a capital offence, except ourselves and William; nor one who has plundered the village, so long as he retains the plunder. If anyone from outside the inhabitants of that village wishes to remain there, he shall remain under the aforesaid customs; and when he wishes to leave, he may leave with his goods, subject to the customs and our right.

We have wished the mayors to possess the following custom and right in that village: to each of them we remit the revenues of two *quarteria* of land; we grant them twelve loaves, twelve denarii for purchasing wine, a pig valued at three solidi and a half, and fodder-rights. If one of the mayors is absent for any reason, the other shall nonetheless perform the functions of ourselves and William. [Col. 0852D] The custom and right of the aldermen is that, from the amends for offences concerning which both complaint and answer have been made before them, they shall receive one sextary of wine, neither better nor worse, which shall be paid by the person making amends on the feasts of St Remigius, St Martin, Christmas, and Easter, when they collect our revenues in the village. The mayors shall take them with them to dinner and provide for them. If they are uncertain about any judgment and come to Reims to inquire, the person who loses the complaint shall provide for them on their journey there and back. The people of the aforesaid village shall swear this custom, and the same oath shall be renewed every fifteen years. Therefore, that all these things may remain valid, we have caused them to be confirmed by the impression of our seal.

Done in the year 1191. Given, the chancellorship being vacant.

## XVII. Privilege for the Abbey of Signy. (1191.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 879.]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to all who shall inspect these present letters, greeting.

Acts done are conveyed to posterity in writing; by its benefit ignorance is instructed and forgetfulness removed. Therefore we make known to all sons of holy mother Church that, with the will and assent of the Church of Reims, we have granted in perpetuity to our beloved in Christ, the abbot and convent of the monastery of Signy, of the Cistercian Order, immunity and liberty freely to buy and sell in our city of Reims and throughout all our land and that of the Church of Reims whatever they judge necessary for themselves; and to bring in and carry back their goods without payment of toll, *sestellage*, wine-dues, or any other exaction to be demanded from them.

We have also granted to the same abbot and convent, to possess and hold in perpetuity, their house which they acquired and [Col. 0853C] built at Reims in the place called Merochel, together with the *proprisium* [enclosed precinct/property] and appurtenances of that house; and to hold it free with this liberty: that in that house and its precinct they may sell and buy as stated above. Nor may anyone within its enclosure or precinct seize a person, shed blood, or commit any other violence without their permission. This being reserved: if the said house or its precinct should return to lay control, all our jurisdiction which we formerly had in them shall likewise revert to us.

In testimony of this matter we have caused these present letters to be authenticated by our seal and also by that of the Church of Reims.

Given in the year of grace 1191.

## XVIII. To all the faithful who come to bestow alms at the church at Virtus, founded by Count Henry of Champagne, on the feast of St John, he remits twenty days of their imposed penances. (1191.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 439.]

[Col. 0854A] WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, to all Christ’s faithful to whom these letters shall come, greeting in him who is true salvation.

No one enrolled in the Christian profession doubts that the building of a church or altar is pleasing in the eyes of the divine majesty. For there those who have wounded consciences find the physician of salvation; there the oppressed and burdened, if they cry to God amid whatever tribulations, come to be healed. Thus also in the Old Testament we read that Moses and the holy patriarchs built altars, and Solomon built a temple for the Lord, where the Lord’s name might be invoked continually and tithes and peace-offerings made for the sins of all. In view of this great benefit, which the faithful daily receive in the house of God, our most dear nephew Count Henry wished his own house near the castle of Virtus to be dedicated to the Lord, and canons appointed there to render him worthy and devout service. We also consecrated an altar there in honour of St John the Baptist; and, for the enlargement of that place, which is a new planting and cannot grow except through what the devotion of the faithful contributes, we mercifully remit to all who come to distribute their alms at the feast of St John, which falls on 24 June [VIII Kalends of July], whether they come on the vigil or on the day following the feast, twenty days from the penances imposed upon them—for sins forgotten, vows broken (provided that they return to keeping them), and offences against their parents, unless they have laid violent hands upon them—by divine dispensation.

Given by the hand of Lambin, our chancellor, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1191.

> [Note: [Col. 0853D] The same Count Henry of Troyes, munificent founder of the aforesaid church, when setting out for Jerusalem, decreed that ten pounds from his revenues should be assigned in perpetuity for the benefit of the deanery. This alms his mother Mary, countess of Troyes, not only approved, but also directed William, her brother, and her bailiffs that it should never at any future time be omitted. She also granted one hundred and twenty sextaries of oats for six pounds, and for the other four the rent, as she calls it, from Roffey. All this will be clearer from the charter of the aforesaid archbishop, which we reproduce below from the cartulary of St John under the year 1193.]

## XIX. He assigns Master Garnier, head of the schools of Reims, a dignity and the title of a personate, with an increase of endowment. (1192.)

[Note: [Col. 0854D] The chancellorship of Reims was vacant because Lambert, chancellor of Reims, had been promoted to the see of Thérouanne in 1191. MEYERUS.]

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, I, 428.]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest [Col. 0854D] of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to all sons of holy mother Church to whom these letters shall come, greeting in the Lord.

We wish it to be known that, since the beloved sons of our chapter of Reims, at our request, conferred the mastership of the schools of Reims upon our beloved clerk Master Garnier, we, with the unanimous will of all, assigned to him in perpetuity a stall in the choir belonging to a dignity, and the title of a personate, to be held by him and his successors, the chapter’s right of election being reserved as it has hitherto possessed it. Considering, however, that insufficient and very modest revenues had previously been assigned to the aforesaid personate, we have freely granted to him, and to all who shall be appointed to the aforesaid office, both for the benefit of the Church and out of regard for the honour and person of the incumbent, five *modii* of grain yearly from our mills at Reims, to be paid freely and entirely without charge at the appointed terms: namely, three on the feast of St Remigius in October and two at Easter. That this may remain valid, etc.

Done in the year 1192.

Given, the chancellorship being vacant.

> [Note: [Col. 0855D] This charter, by which the dignity of scholarch is instituted, was confirmed by Pope Celestine III on 7 June, in the sixth year of his pontificate, and by Philip Augustus in the same year, the thirteenth of his reign; present in the palace were Guy the butler, Matthew the chamberlain, and no constable or seneschal. The chancellorship being vacant.]

## XX. Charter by which William, archbishop of Reims, grants the Valley of Radigion and several other things to the chapter of Reims. (1192.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, p. 420.]

[Col. 0855B]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, of the Holy Roman Church, etc.

Let both present and future persons know that, wishing further to increase the estate of the Church of Reims, with the common will and assent of the whole chapter, the chapter having been solemnly convoked for this purpose, we have freely restored and granted to that Church of Reims the revenues of the Valley of Radigion, previously assigned for the use of the provostship. We also granted [or: “we granted also?”] [Col. 0855C] the altar of Garmereivilla, with all the rent which we had there; likewise the altar of the village of Tardenois, which Philip the vice-lord, Fulk, and Leo, canons of the Church of Reims, resigned into our hand. The chapter, however, granted the aforesaid altars to them, as they had previously held them, for their lifetimes, subject to an annual rent of two solidi, so that after their death they should freely return to the church. Moreover, we gave them the tithe of Juvigniacum, whatever the treasurer of Reims had there, and the tithe of Almericurte, which had previously belonged to the treasury of Reims. In exchange for Newville, situated near Culmisiacum, with its fishpond and mill, which we retained in our hand and which had previously belonged to the treasury, we assigned stalls in the market to the aforesaid church at an assessed annual rent of ten pounds; and also whatever the treasurer possessed at St Stephen’s on the Suippe, and one half of the altars of Bachelons and St Lupus. And we invested B. [Baldwin] as provost in the name of the Church with all these aforesaid things.

> [Note: [Col. 0855D] It seems to us that here, besides the words we have added, the name of one of the altars resigned by the three canons is missing.]

> [Note: [Col. 0856D] In cartulary G of the chapter, fols. 51 verso and 52, there is a charter of William dated 1192, like the act which we give, conferring the provostship upon Baldwin; together with a papal bull confirming this election.]

We gave all these things for distribution to the canons who are present from the beginning of the Epistle until the completion of the *Agnus Dei* of the Mass, and at the hour of sext; nor may they leave the choir unless an honourable or necessary cause calls them away, if they wish to share in the distribution to be made.

The aforesaid canons, not unmindful or ungrateful for so magnificent a benefit, granted to us and all our successors, with the approval and assent of the whole chapter, which was convoked for this purpose, the grant of the provostship and the appointment of the provost, to be held in perpetuity. In place of the revenues formerly assigned to the provostship, we assigned and granted to Provost B. and all his successors in the provostship, to hold in perpetuity, whatever the treasurer of Reims had formerly at Montigny, Betheny, and Villeir Asnorum, excepting the wine revenues of the same village, namely Villeir Asnorum, which we retained in our own hand and disposition. When the provostship is vacant, the chapter shall receive its revenues. Whoever is provost at the time, after rendering most prompt homage to the archbishop, as the other holders of personates do, shall swear fealty to the chapter; he shall swear that he will reside in the city and faithfully observe all that is contained in our aforesaid sealed charter concerning the provostship, held by the Church of Reims, except what is there contained concerning the Valley of Radigion, because henceforward no provost may lay claim to it. [Col. 0856C] These things were done while the treasury was vacant. That this arrangement and estate may obtain perpetual stability, we, together with all the priests then canons, excommunicated all who should alter this estate so solemnly established. And that all these things may remain valid and unshaken, we fortify them by the protection of this present writing and confirm them by the impression of our seal.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1192. Given, the chancellorship being vacant.

## XX bis. Privilege for the Church of St John of Virtus. (1193.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 440.]

[Col. 0856D]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to all to whom these letters shall come, greeting in the Lord.

Let all of you know that our most dear nephew Henry, count of Troyes, when setting out for Jerusalem, for the salvation of his own soul and those of his parents, entrusted to us the perpetual assignment from his revenues of ten pounds for the benefit of the deanery of the Church of St John of Virtus, [Col. 0857A] of which he himself had been founder. Upon this matter, his mother, M., countess of Troyes, our most dear sister, having been consulted by us, graciously wished that what he had ordered should be fulfilled, and charged both us and her bailiffs and servants to make the same assignment. Therefore, together with them, we assigned to the same deanery, for six pounds, 120 sextaries of oats: namely, sixty-eight in rent at Solleries, thirty-two at the Sonneys of Virtus, and twenty at the Sonneys of Bergeries; and, for four pounds, the rent of Roffey—all of which were owed in perpetuity to the same count. Those who owe these things shall be bound to render them annually to the dean of the aforesaid church, or to his official, at Virtus.

> [Note: [Col. 0857D] Here *deanery* denotes the church of St John, over which a dean presides. It is not now the office of a deacon; rather, the senior among the canons is called dean as a title of honour.]

That this may remain valid, we confirm it by the page of this present writing, ordaining and, under threat of anathema, prohibiting anyone from daring to infringe this charter of our confirmation or rashly oppose it, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the Apostolic See.

Done at Reims in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1193.

Given, the chancellorship being vacant.

> [Note: [Col. 0858D] Peter of Celle mentions the abbot of St Mary of Virtus in book II, letter 14.]

## XXI. At the request of the canons of St Quentin in Vermandois, he confirms what concerns *foraneitas*, in accordance with the decree of Alexander III. (1196.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 445.]

[Col. 0857C]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, to all to whom this present writing shall come, greeting.

We make known to present and future persons alike that we approve and hold valid the *foraneitas* [foreign/outside status] established in the Church of St Quentin by the beloved sons, the dean and chapter of that church, and confirmed by Pope Alexander, lord of blessed memory; and, in accordance with the tenor of the authentic apostolic instrument, we confirm it by the protection of this present writing and the safeguard of our seal. We have also remitted to the aforesaid church the demand for a private prebend which we made in it and from it [Col. 0857D], etc. That this may remain valid, we have caused it to be strengthened by our letters and seal.

Done in the year 1196.

## XXII. He grants the abbots of St Remigius, St Nicasius, and St Denis permission to have one servant or free burgess in their ban, with the same immunity enjoyed by the burgesses of the canons. (1196.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 437.]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0858A] to all to whom these letters shall come, greeting in the Lord.

Let all of you know that, since the Church of St Remigius of Reims has always been bound and devoted to us in every respect, considering what recompense we could render to it, we have granted and given it one of our burgesses of Reims, of middling valuation: a burgess free and emancipated from us, to be held in perpetual peace and security with the same liberty enjoyed by the servants of our common mother church, etc.

Done in the year 1196.

Given by the hand of Matthew, chancellor.

## XXIII. Charter concerning the sentence pronounced against Lord Nicholas of Rumingy. (1200.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, p. 437.]

[Col. 0858B]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims . . . . . to his beloved sons, the canons of Reims, greeting.

Since, by the office of pastoral care which we have undertaken, we are bound to provide with more diligent concern for all churches established in the province of Reims, we desire and wish to preserve whole and inviolate the goods of your church, which we embrace with special affection. But the nobleman Nicholas of Rumingy, resisting this desire of ours with a hardened heart, presumes violently to occupy and unjustly to retain certain possessions [Col. 0858C] of your church. Since we have repeatedly summoned him concerning the losses and injuries inflicted upon your church and have found him a stone—not that stone from which the Lord raises up children to Abraham, but a stone in which there is no moisture, in which the seed of God’s word has no root—when we are requested by you, we shall separate him as a rotten member from the body of holy Church with the sword of excommunication, placing his wife, children, household, and land under interdict. And lest they receive refreshment from any fragrance of priestly blessing, at your request, if it seems good to you, we shall compel all priests to leave his land, wholly forbidding the Hospitallers there any celebration of divine offices. We shall also cause what we decree to be so observed throughout the entire province of Reims that, if by chance or necessity he comes to any city, town, or place, so long as he is present there the celebration of divine offices shall be interdicted. And in order that the sentence pronounced against him may obtain twofold force, we shall have it confirmed by the authority of the lord legate, the bishop of Ostia. Lest any doubt concerning the decrees arise for anyone, we strengthen this present writing by the impression of our seal.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1200.

Given by the hand of Matthew, our chancellor.

## XXIII bis. Charter of William I, archbishop of Reims, concerning the election of the abbesses of Avenay. (1200.)

[Gallia Christiana nova, X, 51.]

[Col. 0859A]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, to his most dear nephew Th., count palatine of Troyes, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

We know and attest that, when the church of Avenay has no abbess, it ought to request from the count of Troyes permission to elect; nor ought it, nor may it, elect until it has requested permission from the count of Troyes. It is not bound to request permission to elect from the archbishop or the Church of Reims. [Col. 0859B] What we did concerning the aunt of our faithful Geoffrey of Joinville, we did because of the need of the churches of Jotro and Avenay; and we took confidence from your affection to do so. We therefore ask and affectionately request you, for the sake of our honour and out of love for the church and abbess of Avenay, to remit your offence.

## XXIV. To the lepers of Reims, because of the transfer of the fair to the village of Culture, he grants one hundred sextaries in exchange. (1201.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 452.]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims and cardinal-priest of the Roman Church of the title of St Sabina.

Let all of you know that we have transferred the fair which the lepers of Reims held during Easter week near their house to the village called Culture, for the improvement of the village; and in exchange we assigned to those lepers one hundred sextaries of grain, by the measure of Reims, to be received each year in perpetuity from the first grain coming out of our mills at Reims between the two bridges, etc.

Done in October 1201.

Given by the hand of Matthew, chancellor.

## XXV. He bestows many privileges on the hospital house of St Anthony at Reims, founded by him. (1201.)

[Note: [Col. 0859D] The hospital founded by William of Champagne was situated at the city gate called the Gate of Bacchus, where the nuns of the Congregation of Our Lady are today. It survived until the middle of the seventeenth century.]

[Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, II, 332.]

[Col. 0859D]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, to all faithful of holy mother Church to whom these letters shall come, greeting in the Lord.

Because among the other contingencies of human frailty it is not easy for the children of men to escape assaults of sin, works of piety have been set before us as a remedy for our salvation, by which we may be able to have God all the more propitious to us the more we perform them in the needs of the poor; for “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4). Since pastoral care is bound to correct, uproot, and destroy everything wicked and disordered, and to sow, build, and plant those things which pertain to love of God and neighbour, we have diligently and attentively considered that the thirteen small prebends for the poor, laudably established by St Remigius, former most holy bishop of Reims—one daily loaf and one denarius for each—were frequently, through ignorance and sometimes through the influence of friends, indiscriminately conferred on unworthy, dishonourable, and disreputable persons, contrary to the intention of the holy founder. We judged it fitting and considered it meritorious that the benefice, which was perilously distributed from the patrimony of the Crucified One, should henceforward be beneficially bestowed upon poor, infirm, and sick persons according to the rule of reason [Col. 0860B] and truth.

Therefore, desiring to satisfy the glorious confessor, striving to render to God what is God’s and to Christ’s poor what has been graciously assigned to them, for the benefit of our own soul, for the remission of all our predecessors, and for the pious instruction of our successors in doing good, we have caused a certain hospital house to be founded and built beside our barn at the Gate of Bacchus, out of regard for piety. There twenty sick poor persons shall be received and mercifully cared for in perpetuity. They shall also receive perpetually and unalterably the income of the aforesaid thirteen small prebends; and, as the means and property of the poor, God granting it, increase, so also their number and the provision of humane care shall accordingly be increased.

Recalling the fearful sentence of the Gospel and diligently bringing to mind that those who neglect to receive Christ as a guest on earth, visit him when sick, or feed him when hungry and thirsty, will on the day of the Lord’s vengeance be assigned to eternal punishments (Matthew 25), we have, with the counsel and assent of our whole chapter, added and joined for the support of the aforesaid inmates eight *modii* of grain, to be collected annually in the *sexterlagium* of Reims. The weight of the prebendal bread shall be twenty loaves to the *cartellus*. We have established that seventy *modii* [Col. 0860D] of wine from our revenue of Mont-Vols shall be paid every year; the measure of wine for each poor person shall be half a *metreta*. We have also decreed that, when he is present, the leftovers and fragments from the table of the bishop of Reims shall be distributed in perpetuity to these wretched and pitiable sick persons once a week, on Tuesday or Thursday.

Nevertheless, because the Lord has commanded us freely to give to the needy from the goods of the Church which we have freely received, for the kitchen of the aforesaid sick people, the use of clothing, their maintenance, and the necessities of the aforesaid house, we have confirmed that twenty-five Reims pounds shall be received every year from our hall which we caused to be made and acquired in our time—even if that hall is moved elsewhere, converted into any other buildings, or perhaps at some time no longer yields as much revenue. Since the need of these pitiable sick people is to be preferred to all other business, they shall receive it at the first payment of the money from the same hall. For heating the sick poor and preparing their pottages, we have permanently assigned fifty-two cartloads of wood, to be collected yearly in the archiepiscopal forest near Culmisiacum; we purchased a certain portion of that forest in our own days at great and costly price.

We have further ordained that whoever hereafter is keeper and steward of our barn situated beside the aforesaid house shall be bound to keep and feed two cows along with his other cows; the sick poor shall receive all the yield from them. Likewise, whoever hereafter lives in the episcopal residence of Jardi shall be bound to wash and clean the clothing and linens of the aforesaid sick persons.

> [Note: [Col. 0861] Even today the linens of the Hôtel-Dieu are washed in the same place.]

Whoever in future carries out the administration of the household of any lord of Reims shall be perpetual dispenser of this most meritorious benefice and commendable alms. We have granted the poor one servant, to provide for and minister to them; having assumed the religious habit, he shall enjoy complete liberty and shall answer only to the archiepiscopal [Col. 0861C] steward. If, in the course of time, anyone—a son of Belial, which may it never be!—should presumptuously attempt through negligence or avarice to diminish or wholly abolish this work, so piously instituted and solemnly confirmed by us, this work so charitable and so necessary, may he, through the intercession of the merits of the great confessor Remigius, incur the wrath and indignation of almighty God; may he be blotted out of the book of the living and not be written with the righteous. Amen.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1201. Given by the hand of Matthew, our chancellor.

## XXVI. Charter concerning the *Christianitas* granted to the canons of Reims. (1201.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, p. 445.]

[Col. 0861D]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God archbishop of Reims, cardinal-priest of the Roman Church of the title of St Sabina, to all who shall see these present letters, greeting in the Lord.

Since ancient times, the Church of Reims has always flourished in uprightness of life and ordered conduct, and rightly seems to excel among the churches of Gaul by a certain special prerogative. Considering that it especially befits a church distinguished for uprightness to be honored with distinguished and numerous liberties [Col. 0862A], for the increase of the Church’s honor and the preservation of peace we have thought fit to grant to the aforesaid Church that, in its towns and banns—both those belonging exclusively to it and those which it holds jointly with others, situated in our diocese and pertaining to the corporate body of the chapter—it shall possess the full jurisdiction of Christianity; saving to ourselves all rights over priests and clerics, likewise all cases of sacrilege and all matrimonial causes, and retaining to ourselves, as hitherto held, jurisdiction over the lands of the canons of the city of Reims; likewise reserving to ourselves appeals in every matter. But when an appeal has been made to us, the appeal shall stand, and the case shall be heard in our court in the presence of the chapter’s messenger, should he wish to attend. In the course of the proceedings, if [Col. 0862B] a monetary penalty is incurred, as commonly occurs in such cases, we may neither remit it nor apply it to our own revenues; rather, it shall belong wholly to the church.

Nevertheless, the chapter may impose a fitting penalty upon priests and their chaplains for matters within its jurisdiction if they do not obey it; and unless such a penalty has been imposed unjustly, we may not revoke it. Concerning its men or guests who reside not in its own banns but in those of others, we decree that the following shall be observed: for all matters belonging to the church, it may summon them through Christian jurisdiction; and, once summoned, may bring proceedings against them in matters, as stated, concerning its customs and rights; and, if necessary, may pronounce against them, their houses, and their households a sentence of excommunication or interdict [Col. 0862C], and may strike with a fitting sentence priests established both in its own towns and elsewhere if they refuse obedience in this respect. Sentences thus promulgated by the canons, unless imposed unjustly, may not lawfully be relaxed by us until fitting satisfaction has been made. We have judged all these concessions should be made without prejudice to the rights of the archdeacons.

Lest the course of this matter escape human memory or—God forbid!—be altered by malice, we confirm it in perpetuity under the protection of these letters and the present seal.

Given at Anagni, by the hand of Matthew our chancellor, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1201, in the month of January.

## XXVII. Agreement between the Archbishop of Reims and the Chapter of Reims concerning free servants. (Year 1201.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, p. 438.]

[Col. 0862D]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Sabina, to all who shall see these present letters, greeting in the Lord.

Since, by the favoring clemency of God, it has been granted in our time to settle the uncertainties of earlier generations and to restore irreversibly to unity and concord the old disputes which have more often [Col. 0863A] relapsed, we wish it to come to the knowledge of you all that between ourselves and our predecessors on the one hand, and the chapter of Blessed Mary of Reims on the other, discord and litigation have hitherto continued; and the more frequent they were, the more harmful were they to both parties. We asserted that in calling our citizens into their service they had exceeded proper limits; they, on the contrary, alleged [Col. 0864A] that our officers, abusing our authority, harassed both the church’s mansionarii and the common servants of the chapter and the private servants of the canons with undue exactions.

[Note: [Col. 0863A]

It is not known what disputes existed between the predecessors of William of the White Hands and the chapter concerning common and private free servants. The oath of the archbishops, in 1096, had fixed all the chapter’s rights, privileges, and exemptions in relation to the archbishop. The historians of the Church of Reims [Col. 0863B] report no dispute after 1096 other than that involving Henry of France, which they place in 1164 (MARLOT, vol. II, p. 392). He thinks that this dispute occurred only because Henry of France refused to recognize the privilege which the chapter claimed to have of excommunicating, and that it is likely that this archbishop refused to take the oath of the archbishops. Yet Cardinal Peter seems to imply the opposite in his letter to Archbishop Henry, reported at p. 394 of MARLOT, vol. II, in these words: “Your customs, which I believe you promised to observe.” One sees clearly from the letters of Alexander III to Henry, archbishop, and to his brother King Louis, that this prelate had disputes with his chapter, which complained bitterly of being harassed.

The pope himself speaks of the canons as though, at that time, they were subject to the jurisdiction of their archbishop; but he does not say wherein [Col. 0863C] these harassments, *gravamina*, consisted. It appears only from Cardinal Peter’s letter that the Church complained that the customs specified in the oath sworn by Archbishop Henry were violated, especially—*maxime*—with respect to the excommunication of the chapter’s wrongdoers. This word assumes that these customs were violated at other points, which may have concerned the chapter’s free servants. These letters are printed by Marlot (ibid., pp. 393–394). Marlot adds that it cannot be seen how the dispute between Archbishop Henry and his chapter ended. One is led to believe that it continued until William of the White Hands, Henry’s immediate successor, who, as has been seen, first settled the dispute concerning excommunication in 1197. Otherwise one could not verify these words: “Between our predecessors.”]

[Note: [Col. 0863C]

Note that the chapter complains not that the archbishop encroached upon the jurisdiction [Col. 0863D] which the chapter claimed over common and private free servants, but that he tormented them beyond reason through exactions which they were not obliged to pay—*indebitis exactionibus*. This is the subject and substance of the chapter’s complaint, and consequently the object of the agreement just made. Why, then, does the chapter maintain that William of the White Hands dealt with it concerning jurisdiction, when jurisdiction was not at issue and the matter concerned only financial dues which the chapter claimed should not be levied upon its servants as upon other burgesses? … What, then, could these undue dues and exactions of which the chapter complained have been? Undoubtedly those extraordinary levies and subsidies, those tallages or poll taxes which lords permitted themselves to raise from their vassals in extraordinary need, and of which they had the tenth or twentieth part.]

By the consenting mercy of the Holy Spirit and with the assistance of the counsel of good men, we have reached agreement in the following manner. Certainly, each canon shall be permitted to receive from our jurisdiction and bann one—and only one—servant [Note: [Col. 0864A]

The chapter claims that before this agreement each canon could have as many as three servants within the archbishopric’s bann; that the great archdeacon still has three; and that this charter of 1201 reduced the number from three servants to one only—*unum solum*. The reply is that the chapter produces no title mentioning such a right. Archbishop William of the White Hands complained that the chapter took more servants from his bann than it ought to have had, but that is no reason to say that each canon ought to have had three. It is unknown on what basis rests the great archdeacon’s possession of the right to take three servants; but even if he had that right, it would not follow that every canon had the same right. At that time the dignity of the great archdeacon was highly considerable through its revenues and through the rank of those who held it, and still more considerable through the jurisdiction attached to it.]

who shall enjoy complete liberty [Col. 0865A].

[Note: [Col. 0864B]

These words mean either that the canon may draw a servant from the archbishop’s bann to be served by him in his household, or that he may have a free servant within the bann of my lord the archbishop without that free servant residing with the canon. In the first sense, this private free servant is a true domestic servant, residing with his master and fed at his table. That appears to have been the idea held before the charter of 1201. The word *familiarium*, used by Archbishop Gervais to express private servants, means true household servants residing with their master. The oath of the archbishops does not speak of private free servants without immediately adding: “whom we have privately in our houses, and if we have any from the clergy in our houses”—a kind of servant most fitting. The ecclesiastical servant whom Pope Alexander III commended to Archbishop Henry had resided with the canon from whom he demanded repayment of money lent, “after the completion of his service.” The charter of 1201 seems favorable to the second understanding, since, after saying that each canon may have one servant from the bann of the archbishop’s jurisdiction, it adds that, if he considers it appropriate, he may have several servants from other banns or places—*plures de aliis bannis vel locis habere poterit servientes*; and lower down, that the archbishop and his officers may not trouble or harass common or private free servants residing on his bann or that of the chapter—*nec communibus, vel propriis canonicorum servientibus, in banno nostro vel suo commorantibus, injuriam aliquam irrogare*. This suggests that common or private free servants could reside on the archbishop’s bann or the chapter’s bann, unless by *commorantibus* one understands not a permanent residence but a temporary stay, such as befits servants who drive carts. In any event, *serviens* in this charter means a true domestic servant, *famulus*. That is the meaning given on the back of William of the White Hands’ charter of 1197 granting a free servant to the abbey of Saint-Denis, in handwriting apparently of the same period: “Concerning the household servant granted to us by the Archbishop of Reims”; and again on the back of Alberic’s charter of 1212: “Charter of Alberic concerning the immunity of the canons’ household servants,” in handwriting that seems contemporary with the charter.]

Subject, however, to this precaution in receiving the servant: before admitting him as servant, the canon must present him to the dean, who is our liegeman and is bound by oath most strictly both to us and to the chapter, and whoever at the time holds that office. It shall be for the dean to determine whether the person whom he receives as servant possesses the status appropriate to a servant; and neither we nor the canon may oppose his decision. The canon may, at his pleasure, replace the servant thus received and receive another in the manner stated [Col. 0866A].

If that canon should happen to resign or die, then, unless the servant has been called away from our bann by another canon who has no servant, he may, if he wishes, within forty days counted from the death or resignation of the canon, pass without impediment and without any exaction into the common custom of our city.

[Note: [Col. 0865B]

The chapter believes that in the words *omnimoda libertate*—“with complete liberty”—it finds every conceivable exemption: exemption from the archbishop’s spiritual jurisdiction, exemption from temporal jurisdiction, exemption from the right of *stellage* and from every other due levied upon other burgesses. But it is very easy to disabuse it. To establish such an exemption, especially in spiritual matters, it is not enough to allege exemption “in every manner,” *omnimoda*; the nature of the exemption must be expressed in clear and precise terms. Otherwise general words upon which one wishes to ground a particular exemption must be interpreted according to the reasons for which they were used. Now it is certain that when William of the White Hands [Col. 0865C] used the words *omnimoda libertate*, he did not mean to express a general and unlimited exemption, but only to indicate that the chapter’s free servants would be exempt from the burdens and dues to which the commune was subject in relation to him—the dues contained in the second, third, and fourth articles of the archbishops’ oath. It is sufficient to say, after Du Cange, that these dues meant the tallage and all the petty services which lords then required of their vassals, and that the servants’ franchise consisted in freedom from these dues: “and therefore they are called free servants, in French *francs-sergents*, because they were immune from tallage and every other lowly burden.”

This exemption did not extend to freeing those servants from temporal jurisdiction, still less from spiritual jurisdiction, which by divine right belongs to bishops alone. First, these words, *omnimoda libertate*, do not entail freedom from spiritual jurisdiction. The same words [Col. 0865D] occur in the charter granting a free servant, made in the same year, 1201, by William of the White Hands to the hospital of Saint Anthony at Reims; yet that free servant, like the hospital of Saint Anthony, to which he belonged as a religious, has always been subject to the archbishop’s spiritual and even temporal jurisdiction. Proofs will be found in vol. II of Marlot, p. 347 and following. Moreover, Archbishop William of the White Hands and the chapter were not in dispute about the spiritual jurisdiction over these free servants. The chapter complained that the archbishop’s officers wearied its free servants by monetary exactions and dues which ought not to have been demanded from them. It is only with reference to this subject that William of the White Hands declares the private free servants wholly exempt in relation to himself.

Second, the same reasons prevent one from inferring from *omnimoda libertate* an exemption from temporal jurisdiction. Indeed, the remainder of the charter provides grounds for destroying all the conclusions which the chapter wishes to draw from these words in order to establish such an exemption. After [Col. 0866A] William of the White Hands has said that each canon may freely appoint on the archbishopric’s bann one free servant wholly exempt in relation to the archbishop, he adds that each canon, if he thinks fit, may take from banns other than that of the archbishopric several free servants, who shall have the same exemptions in relation to the archbishop so long as they remain in the canon’s service: *plures de aliis bannis et locis habere poterit servientes, qui quandiu in ejus servitio morabuntur praetaxata libertate gaudebunt*. The Joannine [compilation] interprets *plures* so that a canon may have, in addition to the servant on the bann of my lord the archbishop, two more: one on the bann of Saint-Remi and one on the bann of the chapter. It is clear that in 1411 the canons exercised this right. They still exercise it on the chapter’s bann, especially in the case of common free servants. One sees even in the judgment of 1400 that the canons had free servants in the countryside [Col. 0866C], as at Brimont, La Vanne, and elsewhere; and these free servants had the same exemptions as those in the city. They were not subject to communal burdens.

It is believed that these free servants were the *mansionarii*, although the documents call them *francs-sergents*. This is unsurprising. Since private free servants were assigned to the canons themselves, who did not receive the greater fruits of their prebends, provided that they had estates to administer or houses to maintain—*possessiones procurandas vel domos conservandas*—servants were needed to care for these properties on site; consequently, they had to enjoy the same exemptions as those in the city. William of the White Hands grants free servants taken from banns other than his own the same freedom as those taken from his bann, *praetaxata libertate*, that is, *omnimoda*. Now it would be absurd to say that this archbishop freed such servants [Col. 0866D] from a jurisdiction which he did not possess and which belonged to other lords. In this passage, then, *omnimoda libertate* does not imply freedom from temporal jurisdiction. … If *omnimoda libertate* meant a more extensive emancipation, William of the White Hands’ charter would contradict the archbishops’ oath, which reserves to the archbishop the personal or real rent, *capitalitium*, upon common and private servants taken from his bann.]

If he wishes and considers it useful, a canon may have several servants from other banns or places, who, so long as they remain in his service, shall enjoy the liberty specified above [Col. 0867A].

[Note: [Col. 0866D]

One is led to believe that William of the White Hands understood by *serviens* a genuine domestic servant living with and in his master’s house—*famulus*—as is explained on the back of the charter concerning the free servant of Saint-Denis in 1197 and of that of Alberic in 1212. In fact, only in one place in this charter does the residence of the private servant appear distinguished from that of his master: in the words *in banno nostro*, although the servant might have belonged to a canon [Col. 0867B] residing on the archbishop’s bann. Elsewhere in this charter, nothing compels one to think that the private free servant’s residence must differ from that of his canon. One reads: “in calling our citizens into their service …”; “to receive a servant from our jurisdiction and bann …”; “he has been called away from our bann …”; “he may have several servants from other banns or places.” All these expressions can mean a servant or domestic drawn from a lord’s bann to reside with his master. Authorities cited above prove that private free servants lived with their masters. The Simonine is the first title of the chapter which, instead of saying like William of the White Hands’ charter, “to receive a servant from the archbishop’s bann,” says: “to have common and private servants in and from the archbishop’s bann.” Thus all titles which came afterward use the preposition *in* instead of *de*, making a very different sense.]

[Note: [Col. 0867D]

To set aside the foregoing conception of free servants, the chapter adduces what Archbishop Guy de Roye said in 1402 in order to destroy the alleged exemption of the chapter’s free servants. This prelate reproached the chapter for choosing as free servants the richest and most notable burgesses and thereby exempting them from the city’s burdens: “From these burdens the wealthier withdraw themselves through such exemptions, since those of the chapter more readily and willingly exempted—and exempt—the wealthier and more notable citizens of Reims than the poor, making them free.” The reply is that Guy de Roye, in recounting what took place in his own time concerning the chapter’s free servants, did not thereby intend to approve what the chapter was doing; on the contrary, he used it as a very strong means of showing the disadvantages of the alleged exemption. The practice by which the chapter then selected its free servants [Col. 0868B] from among the richest and most notable city burgesses does not prevent the free servants in origin from having been genuine domestics granted to the chapter to serve the canons and manage their temporal affairs—*famulos quoque dedit* … The same is true of the poor of Saint-Rigobert: because the chapter now grants its poor-reliefs to persons of means, does it follow that, according to their foundation, those poor-reliefs were not intended for needy poor persons? Moreover, at a time when the archbishop was elected by the chapter, it was not surprising that the most notable and wealthy should seek to be the chapter’s free servants. The chapter was then full of persons of the highest rank. Cardinals, nephews of popes, and princes of the royal blood did not consider it dishonorable to be canons, because no one could be elected archbishop unless he was a canon. For the same reason, the wealthiest burgesses did not disdain to attach themselves to canons of this rank, whose protection was powerful, just as one sees persons of very noble standing even today not despising positions as officers of cardinals and other prelates distinguished by rank and birth.]

It should nevertheless be observed that non-resident canons [Note: [Col. 0868D]

The Joannine [compilation] explains the word *foranei* as canons who do not receive their greater fruits. The prohibition, by these words, against having a free servant for those who have no houses to maintain, no possessions to administer, or who do not receive their greater fruits, completes the proof that these free servants were genuine servants, administrators of the canons’ temporal affairs.]

may not have any servant from our bann unless they have first at some time been resident canons and unless they have residences to maintain and estates to administer. Likewise, boys below the subdiaconate, and any canons who make their habitual residence with others, must obtain support from those with whom they dwell and may have no servant from our bann. By “resident” we mean those who remain continuously or intermittently for seven months, from the Nativity of Saint John until the year is completed, in our service or in that of the Church itself.

Concerning the church’s *mansionarii* residing and serving on its bann, we openly and clearly profess that, in the church’s banns wherever situated within the circuit of the city itself or [Col. 0867B] in its suburbs [Note: [Col. 0868D]

This article probably transferred to the chapter high jurisdiction over the tract of countryside called the Common Land, which later became part of the city.]

, neither we, nor our successors, nor those who administer our affairs, may upon any pretext and for absolutely no offense harass or seize anyone, bring any civil action against anyone except under the chapter’s own jurisdiction, seize property situated there, or inflict any injury upon the mansionarii themselves residing, as stated, on the church’s bann, or upon the common or private servants of the canons residing on our bann or theirs.

But because they stated that damages had been inflicted upon them by us and ours, in compensation for the damages, and no less in consideration of the regulation made concerning servants, we decree that the church’s mansionarii established on its bann, wherever they may be situated in the church’s banns and towns, whether acquired or to be acquired, shall enjoy the same liberty as the mansionarii of the city are certainly known to possess, both by ancient custom and by our grant, as set forth above [Col. 0868A]. That is: coming freely and without distinction to the city whenever they please and departing from it whenever they please, they may be sued by no person and for no matter except before the chapter’s own tribunal, nor may they in any way be harassed, unless perhaps they are caught in the act of an open and evident offense; in such a case even non-resident mansionarii situated in the city would not be spared.

Moreover, in consideration of the foregoing, we grant to the same church, in perpetual and settled right, sixty pounds of Reims currency every year, to be first received from our tolls [Col. 0868B]. Whoever shall administer our tolls shall, upon entering office, swear an oath to the chapter for payment thereof in the manner stated.

Lest the course of this matter escape human memory or—God forbid!—be altered by malice, we confirm it in perpetuity under the protection of these letters and the present seal.

Given at Anagni, by the hand of Matthew our chancellor, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1201, in the month of January.

[Note: [Col. 0868D]

The bundle in the chapter archives from which the document just published was extracted contains [Col. 0869B] in addition various confirmations made at different times.

1. April 1202. Confirmation by Philip Augustus of the acknowledgment of the annual rent of sixty pounds which the chapter has the right to take from the revenues of the archbishopric.

2. Three bulls: of Innocent III in 1201, of Gregory IX in 1229, and of Alexander IV in 1256. The following is the most important part of the first:

“Innocent III, bishop … Certainly, whereas a disagreement had arisen between you and your church on the one hand, and our venerable brother William, your archbishop, on the other, concerning certain damages and injuries which you said had been inflicted upon you and that church by him; the said archbishop alleging in reply [Col. 0869C] that you exceeded proper limits in calling his citizens into your service; appeals were made to our hearing over these complaints, and you prosecuted your appeal through our beloved sons R., precentor, Master F., Hugh, and PH., your canons. At length, induced by our admonitions, preferring to enter into a settlement among themselves rather than proceed with the case, they settled their disputes by an amicable agreement. We therefore …”

Given at Anagni, on the Ides of January, in the fourth year of our pontificate.]

## LETTER OF PHILIP, KING OF THE FRENCH, to William, Archbishop of Reims. Concerning the Saladin Tithe. (Year 1189.)

[Note: [Col. 0870B]

To meet the expenses of the holy war undertaken, it was determined, with the consent and advice of bishops and nobles, that all persons, ecclesiastical and lay alike—except those undertaking pilgrimage—should pay the king in full a tenth of their revenues and movable goods. This tenth is said to have been called the Saladin Tithe because it was imposed for the war against Saladin, king of Babylon; but because the churches were very heavily burdened by its payment, Peter of Blois, a distinguished man of piety and learning, wrote a letter to the Bishop of Orléans, urging him courageously to join the others in opposing the king who prescribed such measures. It is likely, however, that the king anticipated the bishops’ complaints, since by an authentic act he declared to William, Archbishop of Reims, and to all clerics and laymen of the province of Reims, that it was not his intention that a similar exaction should thereafter be imposed on any ground or pretext.]

(Year 1189.)

(D. MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, vol. II, p. 425.)

[Col. 0869A]

PHILIP, by the grace of God King of the French, to the venerable man and his most dear uncle WILLIAM, by the same grace Archbishop of Reims, and to all ecclesiastical and lay persons of the same province: perpetual greeting.

Since, for the restoration of the Holy Land, by the assent of the churches of the realm and of the princes, a tenth of movable goods and revenues has been levied once from ecclesiastical and lay persons alike, lest the enormity of this act be drawn into precedent, we decree [Col. 0870A] that, on the occasion of this exaction or for a similar cause, nothing whatsoever shall thereafter be exacted in any manner, etc.

Done at Paris in the year of the Incarnate Word 1189, the tenth of our reign, with those whose names are written below present in our palace:

The sign of Count Theobald, our seneschal. The sign of Guy, cupbearer. The sign of Matthew, chamberlain. The sign of Ralph, constable.

Issued while the chancellery was vacant.

## DEDICATORY LETTER OF A CERTAIN WILLIAM to William, Archbishop of Reims, prefixed to his *Microcosmography*. (About the year 1180.)

(D. MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 946, from the manuscript of Saint Matthew at Trier.)

[Col. 0869B]

To the reverend father and lord WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Reims and legate of the Apostolic See, WILLIAM [Col. 0870B], least among his own, [sends] his *Microcosmography*.

Among the other virtues of your mind, I especially cherish [Col. 0871A] and approve your love of letters and the most abundant honor which you show them. That I do so rightly is evident. For what is sweeter than learned study? I mean those letters by which we comprehend the infinity of things, contemplate the nature and power of God and our Lord, draw the mind away from bodily pleasures and compel it to remain with itself, and from which, borrowing the noblest pattern of life and conduct, we cultivate the virtues.
