Thus we not only acquire through study conduct and knowledge—which do not desert us even at the end of life—but, when we must depart from the lodging of the flesh, reviewing our actions in the occupation of a life well spent in study, we shall enjoy a delightful remembrance. In short, no life is more troublesome than an idle one, none more manageable than a studious one.

Therefore, if these are such great reasons for praise, I should strive to assign you praise equally great and to exalt the dignity of your eminence with the fullest commendations. Yet I fear lest the pleasure thereby generated should claim a share in this good, or lest flattery should gradually steal into my discourse—flattery, which ought to have no place with a wise man and has no commerce with virtue; through it I would not wish my friendship or intimacy with anyone to grow. But lest even apparent or suspected flattery produce hatred, I would avoid it all the more carefully because of the envious bites of detractors, who seek only to read what they may criticize and desire no more [Col. 0871C] good things to praise than ill-expressed things to laugh at and ambiguities to interpret maliciously. For they are excessively singular: they tolerate no equal, despise inferiors, envy superiors, and disagree altogether with their peers so as to appear clever. But it is time to cut short our delays and explain in a few words whatever it is that we have proposed.

Among the ancients I find very frequent questions concerning the constitution of human nature, its likeness to and difference from other natures, to have been discussed: some solved, others left, together with their doubts, to the inquiry of modern writers. Yet moderns have not only failed to surpass the ancients in their discoveries or judgment, or even to doubt alongside them, [Col. 0871D] but by the negligent study which they disgracefully practice have cast great darkness upon these matters—so much so that things once remembered have through their negligence come altogether into oblivion. I have judged it worthy to gather some of these questions into one work and treat them individually and plausibly, embellishing them also with a few, yet clear, solutions, while by no means omitting the opinions and solutions of the ancients. And if I can insert any conjecture based upon an opinion which is at least moderate—not erroneous, yet not arbitrary—I shall do so.

I leave the final judgment on this work to your eminence. Having assessed the smallness of my little talent, judge it more sparingly, so that at least the honor which you withhold from the style you may grant to the subject and matter. Whatever you know cannot be granted either to the style or to the matter itself, pardon to an author who confesses his ignorance.

Whether man naturally possesses intellect. That brute animals necessarily lack intellect. Why all things were made for man. On the soul. [Col. 0872B] Again, on the soul. Another opinion concerning the soul. Another opinion. Plato’s opinion. On the union of body and soul together. On the human body. On the elements. On the human body. What sight is and how it occurs. Why an image does not appear in glass as in a mirror. On the deception of sight. On touch. On hearing, and whether voice is a body. On smell. [Col. 0872C] On taste. What the discriminative faculty is. What choice and deliberation are. What deliberation is and what it concerns. On the irrational movement of the soul. On pleasure. On distress. Whether there are things within us in which free choice may rest. Which actions we control. Whether we are naturally endowed with free choice. What anger is. What fear is. On voluntary and involuntary movement. On involuntary movement. [Col. 0872D] What is involuntary through ignorance.

## CHAPTER ONE

### Whether Man Naturally Possesses Intellect

It is established that man consists of an intellectual soul, etc.

A.D. 1202. JOHN DE BELMEIS, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS.

[Col. 0873]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. II, col. 1180; vol. IV, col. 130.)

[Col. 0873A] I. John, surnamed “of the White Hands,” an Englishman by birth [Note: [Col. 0873C] The brothers de Sainte-Marthe refute the opinion of those who say that he was born of the house of Bellême, namely, the son of William, called Talvas, count of Alençon and Ponthieu, and of the Blessed Countess of Warenne. Besse produces this extract from the martyrology of the holy mother Church of Poitiers, which he believes was written before the year 1200: “The fief which Lord Bishop John of Villers-Aler gave at Samard”; from this it is understood that John was so surnamed.] and treasurer of the church of York, a cheerful, generous, and exceptionally learned man, was designated bishop in 1162, according to Robert of Mont in his Appendix to Sigebert. In 1166 he is mentioned in the records of Nouaillé Abbey, in the time of Abbot Elias. By letters issued on the Ides of April, 1167, he settled the complaint of the prior of St. Radegund against the canons of that same church and the abbess of Holy Cross concerning the assignment of a seat. He is mentioned in charters of the monastery of Étoile, whose abbot Isaac he reconciled with Hugh, lord of Calvinac. He is named as present at the dedication of the church of the monastery of St. Amantius in the territory of Angoulême in 1170, in which undertaking he assisted Bertrand, archbishop [Col. 0873B] of Bordeaux, his metropolitan.

In 1171 he acted as arbiter of peace between Agnes, abbess of Saintes, and William, abbot of Maillezais. In 1173 he settled the suit of John, abbot of Étoile, concerning the tithe of Vastines. He attended the Council of Albi in 1176 and the Lateran Council in 1179. He is also named in the instrument recording the sale of the county of La Marche, made by Count Adalbert to the king of England. In 1178 he was sent by Kings Louis VII of France and Henry II of England, together with Peter, cardinal of St. Chrysogonus, and the archbishops of Bourges and Narbonne, for the conversion of the Albigensians, as may be read in Roger of Howden’s *Annals of England*. He likewise acted as legate of the Apostolic See through Gaul, as is shown by these words of the codex of Walter:

> “In the year [Col. 0873C] of grace 1181, he was elected archbishop of Narbonne. When he was going to Rome to be confirmed by the supreme pontiff Lucius, he was made by him [Col. 0874A] archbishop and primate of Lyons; and because of his outstanding learning he was made by the same pope legate of the Apostolic See in the kingdom of France.”

Moreover, what is here said of his translation to the see of Lyons is proved by an authentic charter of St. Maxentius to have occurred not in 1181 but in the following year [Note: [Col. 0874C] Thus it is read at the end of the charter for the priory of Verrines: “This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1182, namely, the year in which John, bishop of Poitiers, was made archbishop of Lyons, and in which there occurred the disagreement between Richard, count of Poitou, and A., king of England, concerning the possession of the lordship of Poitou.” The same is confirmed by another charter, of which we speak under William, abbot of Lucion.]. Robert of Mont in his *Chronicle* calls him a man of great learning and eloquence. Before the altar of the church of this place, Hugh d’Ozai surrendered into his hand certain lordships of his fief, and bestowed them upon the monks of Absie [Note: [Col. 0874C] Cartulary of Absie.]. John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres, and Stephen of Tournai, great luminaries of the Gallican Church, wrote to him. But we shall refrain from saying more about our John, since he will be discussed again among the archbishops of Lyons.

[Col. 0874B] It should, however, be observed that in the letters addressed to him by Stephen, abbot of St. Geneviève and afterwards bishop of Tournai, John is called in the superscription legate of the Apostolic See, although he was then bishop of Poitiers. Yet the superscription may perhaps be the editor’s rather than the author’s.

II. We have already dealt with John of the White Hands among the bishops of Poitiers; here we shall report only what pertains to him as archbishop of Lyons. Designated archbishop of Narbonne in 1181, but not yet confirmed in that see by the Roman pontiff, he was soon translated to Lyons, as Robert of Mont teaches under that year:

> “John, bishop of Poitiers,” he says, “a man of great learning and eloquence, elected to the archbishopric of Narbonne, [Col. 0874C] when he had gone to Rome for the aforesaid blessing, with Pope Lucius’ consent was elected by the clergy of the primatial church of Lyons as archbishop of Lyons, [Col. 0875A] a see which holds primacy over three archbishoprics.”

Walter of Bruges says the same in his manuscript catalogue of the bishops of Poitiers, called Walter’s codex, except that he states without qualification: “He was made archbishop and primate of Lyons by Lucius”; and adds: “because of his outstanding learning he was made by the same pope legate of the Apostolic See in the kingdom of France.”

Stephen, bishop of Tournai, congratulates him on his promotion to this dignity in letter formerly numbered 92, now 75, in these words:

> “The remembrance of you presents a joyful spectacle to me . . . . . the pontifical mitres of provinces contend for one head; and while Narbonne strives to take its bishop from the chair of Poitiers . . . . . the primatial see of Gaul, Lyons, claims for itself the bishop-elect of Narbonne . . . . . [Col. 0875B] Far be it from your gentleness to decline toward the barbarism of the Goths, the fickleness of the Gascons, the cruel and savage customs of Septimania, where above faith unbelief, above reputation hunger, deceit, and grief are held in greater esteem! . . . . I confess that I trembled and was afraid when I heard that you were being invited to those places, in which, even if it should befall you to preside, it would be easy not to benefit them. Yet, when I heard that the Rhodanus of Sidonius was calling you, I rejoiced with great joy; and I desire to see our primate in glory, whom I had previously experienced as a father in affection, and as kindly disposed and generous in liberality. As you commanded, I am ready to provide your nephew, the archdeacon, a young man of good character, with both counsel and assistance.”

[Col. 0875C] The same Stephen wrote several other letters to him. He is likewise mentioned again in several letters addressed to him by John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres; and in William of Newburgh, *On English Affairs*, book V, chapter 3.

Pope Lucius ratified the exchange made by Count Guigo with the church of Lyons, by a bull issued “at Velletri through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in the year 1182, the first year of the pontificate.” Later, however, when the same count nevertheless disregarded the agreement and did not at all observe its conditions, John approached Philip Augustus, king of the Franks and lord of the count, and obtained from him confirmation of the settlement, after first rendering him an oath of fealty. Hence in the royal diploma Philip calls him [Col. 0875D] “our faithful man.”

In the year mentioned above, or about that time, the same Pope Lucius, by a decree reported by Servetus, entrusted the case of the Charterhouse of Portes against the harassment of the monks of Ivimont to the judgment and protection of “the venerable brethren John, archbishop of Lyons . . . Given at Anagni, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March.” Finally, the same pope sent a bull to him and to Oliver, the dean, in which he especially commanded the abolition of the evil custom whereby the divine office was suspended in the principal church whenever the treasurer ceased to distribute the manual portions in the refectory; “Given at Verona on the Ides of April, in the third year of [his] pontificate,” that is, A.D. 1183.

Having received [Col. 0876A] John’s homage, Emperor Frederick confirmed to him in 1184 all the rights of the county of Lyons and of the exarch and prince’s council in Burgundy, by a golden bull drawn up in the same tenor and words as that which Heraclius had received concerning the same matters. In the same year Count Guigo of Forez and his son of the same name, before Lord John, archbishop of Lyons, made several grants to the monastery of Valbenoîte. In 1186, by a charter reported by M. le Laboureur [Note: [Col. 0875D] *De Mura*, p. 313.] and M. Guichenon [Note: [Col. 0875D] *Rudiments of the Isle-Barbe*, p. 123; Library of Lyons [Col. 0876D], p. 258.], “John, by the grace of God humble priest, legate of the Apostolic See, and the chapter of the primatial church of Lyons” attest that the nobleman Stephen de Villars was received as a monk at Île-Barbe and endowed with the benefit due to a monk, in both temporal and spiritual matters, and that he had bestowed several gifts upon that [Col. 0876B] monastery.

In 1189, after the death of Stephen, bishop of Autun, King Philip Augustus of France appropriated to himself the regalian rights of that church. Upon hearing of this, John went to Paris and complained to the king of the injury done to him. After examining the matter, the king issued a diploma in these words:

> “By the testimony of lawful men, we have learned that it is the right of the church of Lyons that, as often as the see of Autun is vacant, the archbishop of Lyons shall hold in his hand both our regalian rights of Autun and the other things pertaining to the bishopric of Autun; and conversely, as often as the see of Lyons happens to be vacant, the bishop of Autun shall hold in his hand and safeguard everything pertaining to the bishopric of Lyons [Col. 0876C]. Therefore we have ordered and decreed that each church shall possess its right in full . . . so that the fact that we occupied, through ignorance, the regalian rights of the bishopric of Autun after the death of Stephen, bishop of Autun, shall not prejudice the churches. Therefore we restored the regalian rights to our faithful man John, then archbishop of Lyons, and through him granted them to his successors during the vacancy of that bishopric. Done at Paris in 1189, the tenth year of our reign.”

In the same year Kings Philip Augustus of France and Richard of England, setting out with their armies for the holy war, came to Lyons. When they and the greater part of the army had crossed the bridge over the Rhône, that bridge collapsed and drowned many people of both sexes, says Matthew Paris under Richard.

He had been present [Col. 0876D] in 1184 at Count Guigo of Forez’s foundation charter for Valbenoîte; and in 1187, as “legate of the Apostolic See,” he had, by the authority of the lord pope, confirmed the gifts made to that monastery by Girin de Bonofonte and Pons de Petraficta [Note: [Col. 0876D] *De Mura*, pp. 312 and 314.]. In 1190 he himself, together with Dean S. and the whole chapter, granted to the monastery of God’s Blessing all that a certain recluse, by gift of the church of Lyons, possessed near St. Epipodius; and he took that same abbey under his protection, according to M. de Mura (pp. 314–315). In 1192, “John, by the grace of God humble priest of the primatial church of Lyons, and Stephen, dean of the same church, with the whole chapter . . . [Col. 0877A] restored the chapel of Fourvière, begun on our land by Oliver of good memory, formerly dean, in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St. Thomas, archbishop and martyr of Canterbury . . . etc. Given at Lyons, in the pontificate of Pope Celestine III, under Emperor Henry I and King Philip. In the twentieth year since the Passion of the aforesaid martyr, and the year of salvation 1192.”

He crossed into England in 1194, according to William of Newburgh, *On English Affairs*, book V, chapter 3.

Weary of the burdens of worldly business and yearning for the contemplative life, he voluntarily resigned the episcopate and embraced the monastic life, at least by 1195, in the abbey of Clairvaux. There he persevered until death with the greatest piety and devotion, [Col. 0877B] according to Roger of Howden. He explains the reason for his withdrawal in a letter to the bishop of Glasgow, headed:

> “To the venerable lord and fellow-priest G., by the grace of God bishop of Glasgow: J., formerly archbishop of the primatial church of Lyons, but now the least of Christ’s priests.”

There he says:

> “I resolved to spend that little of life which, by God’s authorship, is granted me in repentance and tears, and to taste beforehand the sweetness of the contemplative life . . . . . For while I held the honour of the archbishopric of Lyons, I had necessarily to be entangled in the affairs of secular soldiery: to pursue robbers, sacrilegious persons, and violators of the public roads; and to demolish their strongholds. In persecuting them, deaths sometimes occurred not only among the evildoers themselves [Col. 0878A] but also among those whom we brought forth. Therefore . . . I humbly beg you to deign to intercede for pardon for my sins.”

Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, visited him while travelling through France. An ancient codex of Hugh’s life relates this in these words:

> “He also visited Clairvaux. For John, formerly archbishop of Lyons, had sent venerable men to meet him, earnestly entreating . . . that he would grant him the long-desired favour of his presence. Already weighed down by age, he had renounced the office of pastoral care, retaining only, by order of the supreme pontiff, the former insignia—or rather, as I have read elsewhere, reserving an annual pension of thirteen pounds—and in that monastery he diligently devoted himself to sacred contemplation. When the [Col. 0878B] bishop asked to what writings he had devoted the labour of his meditation, he replied: ‘Meditation on the Psalms alone has now utterly claimed me for itself, my whole being.’”

In 1201 the monks of Clairvaux petitioned Pope Innocent through him to prescribe prayers to be sung in the Mass in honour of St. Bernard. The pontiff consented and sent them in a letter “written to John, formerly archbishop of Lyons, book V, letter 160,” from which was taken the chapter *Cum Marthae*, *Extra*, “On the Celebration of Masses.” In a charter of Belle-Jeu in the diocese of Troyes, from the cartulary of Clairvaux, John is called “formerly archbishop” of Lyons and is recorded as still alive in 1197.

[Col. 0877]

## LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF JOHN DE BELMEIS, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS

I–VI. To Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 0877C]

(They are extant among the letters of Gilbert Foliot, *Patrologia*, vol. CXC, cols. 1022, 1025, 1028, 1030, 1031, 1035.)

VII. To Gilbert, bishop of London.

(See the same place, col. 1036.)

VIII. To the rectors of churches.—That they should offer prayers to God for the restoration of Angles Castle, which Richard, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitou, had usurped.

(Du Cange, *Glossary*, V, 1304.)

Since, amid every oppression and distress, recourse must be had to that unique divine remedy, Jesus Christ, who, as he wills and as it pleases him, makes calm amid disturbance and tranquillity amid storm: we, wishing in the oppression inflicted upon us and upon [Col. 0878C] our church of Poitiers by the noble count of Poitou and his men to have recourse to that same Lord Jesus Christ, whose Church’s cause we are pursuing in this matter, strictly command—firmly enjoining it under pain of excommunication and by virtue of obedience—that each rector of churches, so far as he is not subject to ecclesiastical interdict, shall make and recite every Sunday and annual feast-day an outcry and prayer for peace for us and our church, as is set out below. Let them receive this form from their deans and archpriests, or from the vicars of these.

After the *Agnus Dei* has been sung, before the peace is given, the priest shall say on bended knees:

> Before thy most sacred body and blood, Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the world, we approach; and, crying aloud, we implore thee, the living and true God, mercifully to aid us in our necessities: that thou wouldst break the hardness of the noble count of Poitou, and of his men, and of those by whose counsel he acts in this matter. [Col. 0879A] Trusting in their own strength, they have violently despoiled and still hold despoiled John our bishop and our mother church of Poitiers of Angles Castle and its castellany with their appurtenances; though duly warned, they will not make satisfaction for the matters aforesaid, or for any one of them. Therefore both our church and thine . . . which thou didst found in honour of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, sit in sadness and mourning; and there is none to console or deliver her except thou, our God. Break the hardness of that count and his companions; lead them into the way of justice and truth and of thy counsel; humble them so that they may restore the aforesaid possessions and the former rights of their church, and make due satisfaction for the aforesaid injuries. Arise, I say, to aid our bishop and the church [Col. 0879B] of Poitiers; incline the ears of thy mercy to our cry.

The response shall be: Amen.

> Strengthen them and help them.

Amen.

> Overcome those who attack them.

Amen.

> Break the hardness of those who afflict them.

Amen.

> Lord, as thou knowest, justify the aforesaid count and his men, and his counsel, in thy truth.

Amen.

> Cause them, as it pleases thee, to acknowledge their misdeeds; and by thy mercy deliver the aforesaid bishop and the church of Poitiers.

Amen.

> Do not despise us, Lord, as we cry to thee.

Amen.

> For the glory of thy name, Lord, and for the mercy whereby thou didst found the aforesaid church and exalt it in honour of thy holy apostles Peter and Paul, visit it and its bishop in peace, and rescue them from their present distress.

Amen.

Then Psalm 122 shall be said: [Col. 0879C] “Unto thee have I lifted up mine eyes.” When it has been said, the priest shall say the chapter:

> “Save thy servants; be thou unto them a tower of strength.”

Prayer:

> Crush the hardness of the enemies of the bishop and church of Poitiers, and by the power of thy right hand cast them down.

Amen.

Since we have requested and caused the noble count of Poitou to be duly admonished to restore Angles Castle and its castellany, of which Adam, his bailiff in Poitou, and his servants caused us to be unjustly disseised together with their appurtenances, etc.

IX. To G., bishop of Glasgow.—On the temporal government of the church of Lyons.—Written after his resignation of the episcopal office.

(D. Mabillon, *Analecta*, folio edition, p. 478.)

[Col. 0879D] To the venerable lord and fellow-priest G., by the grace of God bishop of Glasgow: J., formerly archbishop of the primatial church of Lyons, but now the least of Christ’s priests, greeting in him who is true salvation.

As we answered you, good brother, through your earlier letters, we know indeed that on your return—which we hope will be prosperous—you will be able to find men much wiser and more discerning than ourselves, who can reply more prudently and fully to the questions that you proposed to us, and to any others that may perhaps occur to you. This is especially so because you intend to direct your journey through the city of Paris, where there is no doubt that many persons skilled in both divine and human law may be found. [Col. 0880A] Yet, lest we leave your inquiry wholly unanswered, we shall take care to reply to you, according to our limited capacity, concerning what we have pursued by the example of our elders and by experience in our own time.

That archiepiscopal see in which you have now received the consecration of pontifical rank, and in which we ourselves, though unworthy, exercised pontifical office for some years, possesses the fullest jurisdiction—which you call a barony—both within the bounds of the Empire and within those of the kingdom of the Franks, because the parish proper to that place lies within the limits of both. Nor do we think that another church can easily be found which enjoys on either side so great a privilege of liberty.

[Col. 0880B] Accordingly, in the office of honour and burden laid upon us, we acted according to the custom of our predecessors in the following way. I had a seneschal to whom I entrusted the supervision and care of secular business. According to the nature of the cases, he handled not only monetary suits but also presided over the punishment of crimes and offences according to the custom of the region, lest, as you mentioned in your letter, immunity should increase evil men’s boldness in sinning. Yet I took care that, if the nature of an offence happened to deserve either the punishment of hanging or mutilation of limbs, no word concerning such a matter should be brought to me. He himself decided such matters with his assessors without consulting me. I knew without doubt that I was granting him authority both to investigate and to decide; but the fact that holy men who had preceded me in the same see had proceeded according to this custom without censure afforded my deliberate non-intervention [Col. 0880C] some, however slight, assurance.

For nowhere in the Latin world, apart from our greater church, are so many holy martyrs or confessors found; as you may readily discover from the martyrology of the venerable priest Bede, or that of his successor Oswald, who considerably enlarged the catalogue of saints. Further assurance came from the fact that the prefect of the city of Rome, who has special charge of punishing crimes, is said to receive the authority of his prefecture from the lord pope. Thus, on the Sunday on which “Rejoice, Jerusalem” is sung, after the solemn procession in which the same supreme pontiff carries around the golden rose has been completed, [Col. 0880D] he rewards the prefect with that same rose, as it were in payment of a debt.

Nevertheless—and this is more evident—in the city of Benevento, which properly belongs to the apostolic table, the lord pope appoints a rector who, either in person or through citizens of that city, punishes and purges the offences of that place. Such were the consolations I employed. Yet I knew that, if any revenue arose from such cases, it was applied to my expenses, after deduction of the right of my seneschal, to whom a third part of the revenues was due for his service. But this we, as well as our predecessors, carefully observed: that the person appointed to such execution was not afterwards promoted to holy orders.

[Col. 0881A] Ah, good brother! We have answered your first question, not defining what ought to be done, but stating what we did, recognizing that your conscience was in some measure troubled.

Next, we thought that your second inquiry should be answered. Clerics, and especially those advanced to holy orders, must be strictly forbidden to pursue in a secular court either robberies or thefts committed against them. Or, if they cannot altogether be restrained, they must by no means dare to proceed as far as judicial combat, an ordeal of red-hot iron or water, or any similar test. If they do not comply, and mutilation of limbs or homicide is committed through such incitement, [Col. 0881B] they deserve to be deprived both of ecclesiastical office and benefice. For the apostolic authority must be laid before them which says: “Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” We understand “defrauding” to mean loss inflicted upon [Col. 0882A] someone through another’s deceit or malice.

We have written these things out for you rather cautiously, without prejudice to better and sounder counsel. For the causes mentioned above, and several others which pressed more heavily upon me, I chose, venerable priest of Christ, to spend the little life that is granted me by God’s authorship in repentance and tears, and, if possible, to taste beforehand the sweetness of the contemplative life. For while I held the honour of the archbishopric of Lyons, I had necessarily to be entangled in the affairs of secular soldiery: to pursue robbers, sacrilegious persons, and violators of public roads with armed force; to besiege, burn, and demolish their strongholds and castles. In their pursuit, deaths sometimes occurred not only among those evildoers themselves but also among those whom [Col. 0882B] we led forth. Therefore, now casting myself as a wretched sinner at the feet of your holiness, I humbly beg you to deign to intercede for pardon for my sins. Fare well.

## STATUTES OF HUGH V, THE SEVENTEENTH ABBOT OF CLUNY, ABOUT A.D. 1203

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1457.)

[Col. 0881]

## STATUTES

### PREFACE

[Col. 0881C]

To our venerable and most dearly beloved abbots, priors, monks, and lay brothers belonging to Cluny: Brother HUGH, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting, grace, and blessing.

Since the beginnings of sacred religious life, established by the sons of the prophets and confirmed and enlarged by that great John the Baptist himself and by his illustrious successors, have descended to us, we must take pains that true sons may be born to our exalted fathers, lest—God forbid!—if we become estranged from discipline, we be reckoned degenerate and not sons; and lest we merely imitate the brilliance of gold, rather than rejoice to be truly gold. But now—to speak mournfully—not only do we cease to be gold, but moreover “[Col. 0881D] the finest colour of the gold is changed, and the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4), since the very prelates set forth as an example walk in the ways of the world, and their subjects turn to dissipation.

Therefore, since, as has been said, the splendour of virtue is obscured among religious persons, and especially in the glorious member of the Church, namely the monastery of Cluny, or in its dependent houses [Col. 0882C], we, wishing to provide for the salvation of those committed to us, for God’s honour, and to guard ourselves against danger lest, having been made watchmen, we should fail to keep our vineyard, intend, as far as possible, to reform those matters which were long ago decreed by the fathers but have in part been deformed through negligence. We do so lest, by bringing forward new or burdensome measures, we might wound weak minds.

For this undertaking we are encouraged by the example of our most holy father Innocent III, supreme pontiff, who, according to the wisdom and inspired grace given him from heaven, carefully restores with provident concern the partly decayed spiritual and temporal condition of monasteries directly subject to him without intermediary. Therefore, first honouring him whose good pleasure is “upon those who fear him, and upon those who hope in his mercy” [Col. 0882D] (Ps. 32), we decree that the matters which pertain to his name and glory are to be observed—or rather, we set forth what has already been decreed—and we prohibit more firmly and strictly those things by which he is offended, placing first what seems most in need of correction.

### CHAPTER I. An annual inquiry concerning the state of the church of Cluny

[Col. 0883A]

Since we read that the Ruler of all was subject to human beings, we, following his example and teaching—“He who is greater, let him become as the younger, and he who is leader, as one who serves” (Luke 22)—and wishing to give others a pattern for imitating us, subject even ourselves to law. We decree that four discerning and suitable persons be chosen, namely two abbots and two priors belonging to the church of Cluny. Once each year, at the appointed time—that is, in the Octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul—they shall come to Cluny and diligently inquire both into our own person, that is, whoever may be abbot of Cluny in succeeding times, and into the temporal and spiritual condition of the Church [Col. 0883B] and of its surrounding places. Matters requiring correction shall be corrected according to their counsel, and every year all these things shall be made known through them in the general chapter, so that through such visitation the church of Cluny may persevere in good condition and the rest, following the example of the head, may preserve our institutions more firmly.

### CHAPTER II. Gifts are not to be given for spiritual offices or matters

Since the holy Church claims for herself everything that is beyond reproach, and especially since nothing notable ought to be found among religious persons, while we are stained above all in this matter because many “love gifts and pursue rewards” [Col. 0883C] (Isa. 1), we decree and inviolably command that, for spiritual offices or matters, no one shall give, receive, or promise anything, or even act as an intermediary for gifts. Whoever presumes to violate this prohibition shall, without mercy, be separated from communion with all until he has made worthy satisfaction for his fault. Those consenting shall be struck with the same penalty. Persons aware of it shall suffer a like punishment unless they disclose the iniquity when they know it.

### CHAPTER III. No one is to be admitted to a monastery by contract

Since it often happens, and in many places, that admission to a monastery is granted through money or an intervening agreement, although this is forbidden by the sacred canons and endangers the souls of both those who receive and those received, we decree that henceforth no one shall be admitted to a monastery by agreement or price, nor shall anything be demanded from one entering. But if anyone freely offers something, his devotion shall not be rejected.

### CHAPTER IV. Useless persons are not to be admitted

And since this pest has chiefly crept in through the reception of weak and useless persons, we command that only such persons be received as monks as are fit for the service of God, not burdensome to the brethren, and useful to the monastery.

### CHAPTER V. Likewise on the same subject

Since by the indiscriminate reception of laymen [Col. 0884A], peasants, old men, and others weakened in any way, the service of God is performed less solemnly, houses are burdened in many ways, and little or no benefit comes from them, we decree that henceforth none such shall be admitted as monk or lay brother except for aid at the point of death. Noble and useful persons are excepted, to whom admission cannot conveniently be denied; likewise excepted are those lay brothers fit and necessary for agriculture or for the performance of useful work. Their examination shall depend on the lord abbot, if he is nearby, or on the provincial chamberlain, if he is far away.

### CHAPTER VI. Boys are not to be admitted

Since through the premature and hasty reception of children the order is for the most part corrupted and [Col. 0884B] the religious purpose of others impeded, following in the footsteps of Lord Abbot Peter of venerable memory, we decree that no future monk, even by dispensation, shall be clothed in the regular habit before the age of twenty, except only those from the school at Cluny, without whom the service of God is not customarily performed. Yet none shall succeed them before his voice has changed.

### CHAPTER VII. On the master of novices

In every conventual house where novices may lawfully be received, provision shall be made for a discerning brother of mature character, not lacking knowledge of the Order, for their instruction in religious life, the form of religious observance, moral conduct, and confessions. For through the lack of such provision, some have become more frivolous in bearing and less devout in religion.

### CHAPTER VIII. Monks are not to be received within three years

Because many of our houses are burdened by the number of monks, we decree that for the next three years no monk whatsoever shall be received in conventual houses or in places where the Order is not observed, except for aid at the point of death.

### CHAPTER IX. Women are not to be admitted

It is clear to all how much ruin of souls and destruction of houses has arisen from proximity to and association with women. We therefore decree that no woman whatsoever shall ever be received in any place as a nun, lay sister, or prebendary, except for aid at the point of death. In places where they have already been received, they shall be removed from the table and from every common dwelling or association with monks. Outlying places are excepted, where women must be kept out of necessity. Yet such women must be of such character and age that no suspicion may arise concerning them, and there shall be only one in each grange.

### CHAPTER X. No one from another religious order is to be admitted without the abbot’s permission

We decree that no person of another religious order shall be received in any of our houses without our special permission, because it is hard for such persons to leave their accustomed ways and be formed according to our institutions; and, because of their fickleness or even their grave misconduct, they are often burdensome and harmful to our communities.

### CHAPTER XI. Novices are to be blessed within three years of their reception

[Col. 0885A]

Novices received outside Cluny shall not have their blessing deferred beyond the third year. In the meantime, as the custom of Cluny requires, they shall neither be ordained priests nor, if ordained before their reception, sing Mass; nor shall they administer any spiritual or temporal obedience whatsoever. For before profession they are not fully bound to us; and often, casting off the habit and returning to the world, they minister in priestly orders and, after collecting money, make evil use of the patrimony of the Crucified One.

### CHAPTER XII. A novice is not to hold a priorship within a year

No novice, even after profession, from whatever source [Col. 0885B] he comes—whether from religious houses or from the world—shall be placed over priories or any obedience until his life has been tested for one year in the cloister of Cluny, or in some principal cloister belonging to us, or in the company of the lord abbot, and until he has been adequately instructed in the regular observances.

### CHAPTER XIII. On private property

A person received as a monk shall retain none of his worldly possessions for himself, nor shall he subsequently possess anything as his own, except what the lord abbot, or those whom he has called to share in the burden of maintaining the Order, give or permit. And in order that this vice of private ownership may be wholly uprooted from religious persons, we wish that those to whom this pertains, whether healthy or ill, be provided for according to the resources of the house, as each may need, in accordance with that saying of the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 4): “Distribution was made to each according as any had need.” If anyone dies in this vice contrary to this statute, let him be deprived of Christian burial.

### CHAPTER XIV. On silence
And because, contrary to the teaching of the prophet which says, “the fruit of justice is silence,” and contrary to the institutions of the elders, we have heard that silence has been corrupted in certain places, we command that henceforth priors and guardians of the Order employ every diligence in the observance of silence, and that all keep silence wholly in the regular places and at the appointed hours. This applies in conventual houses. In smaller houses, however, silence shall always be kept by the monks in church and after Compline. Before Prime or Terce, [Col. 0885D] they shall devote themselves to reading, meditation, or prayer.

## CHAPTER XV. On frequent confession.

Since from the cause and frequency of confession the salvation of souls chiefly proceeds, while from its omission excessive sluggishness arises, together with matter for lack of devotion and a greater boldness in sinning, we establish and most earnestly exhort that each person confess at least once a week, the Apostle exhorting and saying: “Confess your sins one to another” (James 5). Confessions shall be heard by the prior, subprior, other guardians of the Order, or certain members of the convent to whom this care has been committed—men who know how to tend their own wounds and not disclose or make public those of others.

## CHAPTER XVI. On priests who sing Mass too seldom.

[Col. 0886A]

Not without shame and sorrow do we say that certain priests among our brethren celebrate the divine mysteries less often than they ought, although they have ascended to this rank precisely in order that they themselves may minister in holy things and be holy. Therefore we admonish, urge, and counsel in the Lord that they make and prove themselves such that they may worthily frequent the sacred mysteries, and not eat and drink judgment upon themselves (1 Cor. 11).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the age of those to be ordained.

And lest, contrary to the decrees of the sacred canons, unlettered young men, who cannot yet grasp how excellent the priestly office is, approach those heavenly sacred rites as rash presumers rather than [Col. 0886B] worthy ministers, we establish that none of our brethren be advanced to the priesthood before his twenty-fifth year.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On not publicly announcing a first Mass.

When a man is about to sing his first Mass, let none cause it to be announced outside; nor shall the newly ordained retain anything from the offering. Rather, what has been offered shall be handed over at the direction of the prior sacristan. For such public announcement savours more of empty glory or ambition than of humility and devotion. For it is written: “The root of all evils is greed” (1 Tim. 6); and: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10).

## CHAPTER XIX. On observing a pause in psalmody.

[Col. 0886C] Because, in the office of the divine work, some run ahead while others delay beyond measure, and thus great confusion arises in psalmody, we establish that all verses of the canonical hours be sung with one moderate and uniform pause, so that the voices of all together end at the division of the verse and, after such a pause, together begin the next.

## CHAPTER XX. On preserving uniformity in the service of God.

And in all our places, uniformity in singing and reading shall be maintained, and there shall be no discrepancy, especially in the service of God. For, since we are of one congregation and Order, we ought to be conformed in all things.

## CHAPTER XXI. That all assemble for the canonical hours.

[Col. 0886D] For the divine work—that is, the night and day offices, the principal Mass, and especially the conference and Compline—all shall assemble. No one may be absent from Compline except for a just cause, with permission, or because he is detained by the prior. Those who remain behind after three strokes shall not drink, unless perhaps they are unable to abstain; in that case they shall drink in the infirmary and go to Prime on the following day.

## CHAPTER XXII. That those who are away do not neglect the service of God.

All, wherever they may be stationed, shall not neglect to render the appointed measure of their service, especially the canonical hours, through whose omission many are found greatly deficient. Those who do not know the Psalms shall say the Lord’s Prayer seven times for each hour: for Matins [Col. 0887A] seven times seven, and for Vespers three times seven, with bending of the knee if it is not a feast day, so that each, according to the gift he has received from the Lord, may offer Him praise and thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On maintaining order.

In choir, chapter, and refectory, let each preserve his own order, with no distinction whatsoever based on precedence or familiarity. For in church the elders withdraw to more remote places in order that they may be more freely negligent, while others climb to higher places in order to gain glory from a priorship. In the refectory, some join themselves to the more powerful in order to live more comfortably; and those more powerful themselves, because of familiarity, choose for themselves whatever companions they wish.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On not having exceptional dishes.

[Col. 0887B]

Let no costly and conspicuous individual distinction be made for anyone in the refectory, since all things ought to be common to all. If, however, anything of this kind has been given or sent to someone, it shall be offered to the person sitting at the high table, to be distributed by him to whomsoever he wishes. And, so that what remains may be preserved for distribution to the poor, no one shall presume to carry anything out of the refectory, for he commits robbery.

## CHAPTER XXV. That no one eat or drink before or after the meal without permission.

And so that frivolity in eating and drinking, which is close to vice, may be removed from those who ought to be of mature character, and the greed which is the stepmother of the moderation befitting monks may be restrained, we establish that no one eat or drink anywhere, indoors or outdoors, before or after the common meal without permission.

## CHAPTER XXVI. In what places it is permitted to eat meat.

Since we ought to provide what is good before God and men, lest anyone reproach us even concerning food, we establish that no one eat meat except in our own houses and houses of our Order, and on the appointed days.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That meat not be eaten on Wednesday and Saturday.

Wishing to restrain the insolence of certain persons living in cells, who on specified days demand meat to eat as though it were owed to them, we leave it to the discretion of the priors, according as it is fitting and they have the means, to permit them meat in charity. Otherwise, we command them to be content with their ordinary fare or with what is set before them. Nor do we wish anyone, except those utterly weak and sick, and those in the general infirmaries, to consume meat on Wednesday and Saturday, since we see that even secular persons abstain on those days.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the care to be given to the sick.

Above all, abbots and priors shall be solicitous for the sick, so that food and other necessities may be supplied to each according to the nature of his illness and the resources of the place; and they shall be served as God Himself, toward the health of body and soul. For Christ Himself will say: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the attendant of the sick.

[Col. 0888A]

In the general infirmaries, each shall receive necessities in such a way that there is enough for those of lesser standing and no excess for the more powerful. They shall not be kept without one of the guardians of the Order, so that, through reverence for him, discipline may be preserved and necessities better supplied to the brethren. A monk-attendant shall serve everyone what must be served; he shall also guard the alms and keep the number of servants in check. Each shall sit in his own place while eating, and no one shall join himself to whomever seems good to him, because this gives rise to disorder and exceptional treatment, which, as we have done in the refectory, we forbid when conspicuous. They shall assemble to eat together at the appointed hour, and after Compline has been sung in convent, no one shall presume to remain in the infirmary [Col. 0888B].

## CHAPTER XXX. On suppers for the sick.

Following also the example of Abbot Theobald of pious memory, we establish that whenever the convent has eaten once, the sick themselves likewise be refreshed only once. The dishes which were to have been served to them at supper shall instead be served at dinner for the sake of alms. For it is not fitting to say how many temporal and spiritual losses result from such suppers.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the fast of St. Benedict.

Likewise, we establish that from the Ides of September until Easter, according to the Rule of St. Benedict and the custom of the Cluniac Order, all everywhere [Col. 0888C] shall fast, since the days are short and it is shameful to depart from the institution of the fathers.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That monks not sing Mass on the day they leave the infirmary.

Since reverence must be shown to sacred things, a reverence chiefly preserved through restraint, we establish that, on the very day on which they return to the convent from eating meat, they abstain from celebrating the sacred rites. For they cannot taste the flesh of the true Lamb with the palate of faith while their stomach is still full and the flavour of flesh remains in the palate of their mouths.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On almsgiving.

It is exceedingly dangerous, and brings much reproach upon us and upon the Apostles—would that undeservedly—that we divert goods assigned for the alms of the poor to uses other than those to which we ought to apply them. Therefore we establish that no person, whether abbot or anyone else, presume with any rashness to take or alienate anything of what has been assigned for the relief of the needy. Accordingly, the alms shall be entrusted for safekeeping to a brother who fears God, who shall faithfully apply all revenues and proceeds to the uses of the poor and pilgrims. Let him be content with one mount, few attendants, and modest expenses; for whatever is done to one of the least is done to the Lord, and whatever is withheld from them is taken from God. In this matter we free our own soul, while those to whom this care has been entrusted must render, in the strict judgment, an account of their administration to God, the Judge of all.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On those who leave the gates of the monastery without permission.

[Col. 0889A]

No one who leaves the monastery gates without permission shall be received back without satisfaction. For they often wander idly about houses, villages, fields, and woods, saying and doing what is not fitting, whence reproach to us and scandal among the people arise. Therefore, even when he has received permission, a monk shall have a good reputation in going out and returning.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On wanderers.

Wishing to cut off the freedom to wander of certain men who, led not by necessity but by fickle will, return to cloisters only to roam disorderly through various monasteries, villages, and castles, producing manifold offence to those who see them, we establish [Col. 0889B] concerning them that none of this sort may travel farther than a day’s journey anywhere without our letters; or, in our absence, letters of the prior; or, if neither we nor the prior is present, letters of the subprior. These letters must contain the reason for the journey, the name of the place, and the date for return. If they are discovered otherwise, the priors who find them in this condition shall seize their horses and keep them as wanderers until we pass the sentence due upon them; or they shall send them, with their horses, to Cluny along with their messenger. We also wish these provisions to be observed in like manner concerning those who reside in our places under obedience to priors.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On those who support the disobedient.

And since such persons, as we say with sorrow, sometimes find accomplices or supporters, when these secretly or publicly encourage them in their error, thereby making them bolder, or, moved by false mercy on their behalf, strive to free them from punishments due, we wish necessarily to oppose this plague. Therefore we establish that these persons, and those who procure for their brethren obstacles to arrest or spoliation, shall undergo the punishment of like retribution.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On young men seeking obediences.

To restrain the rashness of certain young men who, wishing prematurely to cast off the yoke and not content with the fellowship of others, seek obediences or revenues assigned to themselves in order to satisfy their own desires, we establish that no assent shall be given them in such requests. Indeed, if after admonition they do not desist, they shall be subjected to graver discipline; and those who have acquired such offices shall lose them.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On those who seek offices through secular persons.

Because certain of our brethren seek to have obediences or priories entrusted to them, not on the merits of life or learning but through the intervention of secular persons, “making flesh their arm,” while their heart departs from the Lord (Jer. 17), we establish that no one who thus seeks an office shall ever obtain it, or any other within a year. For if secular persons do not obtain their request, they are stirred up against us; and the monks themselves, while they trust in man, devote less effort to good conduct and more boldly despise their prelates.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the appointment of priors.

[Col. 0890A]

Those who ought to preside over others and have care of souls shall be chosen for the merit of their lives and the teaching of wisdom, not through favouritism or nobility, so that they may form their subjects by their example and, according to the Gospel, be like the householder who knows how to bring forth from his treasure things old and new. Therefore we establish that priories, deaneries, and every other administration be conferred freely and without sale or bargain upon prudent and honourable men, who know how to preside and to benefit others, so that their service may be more reasonable and they may better provide for souls. We establish that priories, especially conventual ones, be committed only to priests. But if by necessity such priories happen to be committed to men who are not priests, [Col. 0890B] they shall be ordained priests within a year. Otherwise, from that time onward, let them know that they have been deprived of their priories.

## CHAPTER XL. On not changing priors.

Wishing to prevent the harms arising from frequent changes of priors, we establish that conventual priors appointed, as we have said above, shall not be removed—this being determined by the judgment of the definers in the general chapter—unless some manifest cause arises for which the lord abbot is compelled to remove him. We annul confirmations, except for specified causes: namely, if they are squanderers of houses, disobedient and rebellious, infamous and incontinent, or are to be promoted to greater usefulness. We wish the same to be observed concerning junior priors; hence they ought not to rely upon letters, even though they have letters of confirmation providing that they are not to be removed. On this matter we are reproached by many. For thereby lack of devotion [Note: [Col. 0889D] Perhaps, “lack of devotion.”] toward the mother church can creep in, and matter for disobedience and rebellion arise. Therefore let this appointment serve them in place of confirmation.

## CHAPTER XLI. That priors maintain fellowship with the brethren.

Since certain priors, not heeding what is written, “Not lording it over the clergy, but being made an example to the flock,” live too indulgently and, for a trivial occasion, abandon the fellowship of the brethren, eating outside the refectory and never sleeping in the dormitory, we establish that a prior shall always eat in the refectory with the brethren, unless an evident necessity or reverence for important [Col. 0890D] guests compels him to dine outside the refectory. For when priors feast in chambers, they and their servants consume more than the other brethren. During Advent and from the beginning of Septuagesima until Easter, they shall sleep in the dormitory at least, unless they freely wish to sleep there more often. From this there results for them a greater testimony of propriety and for the brethren a fuller discipline. When, however, for the aforementioned reasons they happen to eat outside the refectory, they shall take with them certain of those who are regular attendants in convent, not obedientiaries, who are rarely found in convent; and they shall be content with few servants, who do not carry off what is owed to the poor.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the same matter.

[Col. 0891A]

Let them, then, as good shepherds, make it their concern that, as they excel in dignity, so they may go before the flock in virtue. Let them frequently attend the divine office; sit with the brethren in the cloister, often giving themselves to reading; hold chapter frequently for the strictness of discipline; and not readily omit the conference. Let them always walk within the cloister wearing frocks, and not use foreign caps, so that in all things they may present themselves as an example of good works in doctrine, integrity, and gravity.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the habit and bearing of monks indoors and outdoors.

Since, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “A man’s clothing, the laughter of his teeth, and his walk declare [Col. 0891B] what he is” (Ecclus. 19), and wishing, insofar as lies within us, to bring it about that our brethren do not look to vanities and false madnesses (Ps. 39), we establish that, just as in the cloister, so when going out they shall conduct themselves honourably. No one of our priors shall presume to ride without a cowl and frock, or without a cowl and a cappa—which we command to be regular, not costly, not blue—or without a *postella* and a regular saddle not overly precious. Nor shall anyone riding use felt caps, any other little caps whatsoever, or shoes without straps. Each year at Maundy Thursday, according to custom, strapped shoes shall be given, to be used when they ride and at other appointed times. Meanwhile, until Maundy Thursday, riders shall provide themselves elsewhere with strapped footwear [Col. 0891C].

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the number of mounts.

Since superfluous mounts entail unnecessary expense, by which houses are burdened and vanity nourished, we have judged it necessary to prescribe a fixed number of riding animals for each prior and for ourselves, wishing to set an example to others. The Abbot of Cluny shall be content with sixteen mounts; the Prior of La Charité with eight or nine; the Prior of Saint-Martin with six or seven; conventual priors with three or four; and all other lesser priors with only two mounts.

## CHAPTER XLV. On servants.

Since the maturity of servants reflects the honourability of their masters, we establish that Cluniac priors and monks have servants mature in age and honourable in life: not young squires, beardless youths, overdressed persons, or others conspicuous in any way; nor shall they be clothed in parti-coloured or costly garments, so that anyone who is opposed may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about us.

## CHAPTER XLVI. That no monk have a priory before he has been at Cluny.

Since what is handled by the hands is more deeply considered, and what is seen by the eyes adheres more readily to the heart, wishing to kindle our sons’ love and devotion toward their mother, we establish that no monk at all, even if professed, obtain a Cluniac priory before he has visited the church of Cluny. If they have necessarily been appointed, they shall not fail to visit the mother church within [Col. 0892A] a year.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On not readily transferring monks from place to place.

Since, because of the importunity of priors, monks are often transferred from place to place, and thus are found conspicuous for fickleness and cruel toward their brethren when they deny them what is due to them by right, we establish that priors bear with them in charity and treat them humanely; and, if necessary, correct and chastise them. If they must be removed for a just cause, priors shall provide them with regular clothing as is fitting, and they shall be transferred only on horseback. For it is written: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4).

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On those suffering from ill repute.

If anyone suffers from ill repute, he shall be transferred to another place, and another, more honourable man, shall be substituted in his place there. In this case we wish their priors to consent to the stated exchange, and monks to be obedient to their priors, for it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6).

## CHAPTER XLIX. How fugitives are to be received and retained after reception.

Fugitive monks, whom St. Benedict commands to be received last, so that their humility may thereby be tested, when received shall not recover their former rank without our permission; nor, if they are priests, shall they celebrate the divine mysteries; nor shall they hold obediences or be advanced to orders, so that fear may be instilled in others against committing like acts. Those, moreover, who according to the statutes of our predecessors deserve expulsion for their offences, if they are near Cluny, that is, within two days’ journeys, shall be expelled with our knowledge, or, in our absence, with that of the Prior of Cluny. If farther away, this shall be done with the knowledge of the provincial chamberlain.

## CHAPTER L. That obedientiaries not be multiplied except in principal places.

Since in certain of our places the benefit of the community is lessened through the division of obediences, while the insolence of officers against priors is increased, we establish that all obediences be in the hand and at the discretion of the priors, who, with whatever assistants they wish attached to them, shall do as they see [Col. 0892D] expedient.

## CHAPTER LI. On not having suspect persons in one’s company.

Since those who bear the vessels of the Lord ought to be sanctified and to walk in wisdom toward those outside, we establish that no prior or monk have suspect persons in his household, company, or service; for, as Solomon says: “Who carries fire in his bosom and is not burned?” (Prov. 6).

## CHAPTER LII. On not loving relatives too much.

Some, abusing the testimony of Scripture which says, “No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. 5), are too tender and inclined toward fleshly affections, to such a degree that they spare neither their own reputation nor the houses entrusted to them. Therefore we admonish them, in avoiding the danger that thereby threatens their own heads, not to enrich their relatives from the sustenance of the poor [Col. 0893A].

## CHAPTER LIII. On the custody of seals.

Since we have learned that many harms have occurred in houses through negligent custody of seals, we establish that the seals of houses be secured under three keys, one of which the prior shall have and the remaining ones brethren who fear God. They shall seal nothing without the convent’s counsel, unless perhaps urgent necessity prevents waiting for chapter; then it shall be done with the counsel and knowledge of prudent brethren.

## CHAPTER LIV. That no one cross the sea or the Alps without permission.

In order that every occasion of fickleness and freedom to wander may be taken away from monks, we establish that no one presume to cross the sea or the Alps without permission. Excepted are those sent by their priors to their own places situated beyond the sea or the Alps.

## CHAPTER LV. That offices never be granted to outsiders, or to our own men for life or as an inheritance.

We establish that no men or servants belonging to clerics or laymen not connected with us shall in any way become stewards, cellarers, or provosts of Cluniac houses, because we know that many harms have been inflicted in many places by such persons or on their account. Nor shall any office be committed to our own men as an inheritance or for life, so that, when necessary, they cannot be removed at the discretion of the person appointing them; [Col. 0893C] for having sometimes obtained such offices, they become unfaithful to us, are turned into a crooked bow, and have the venom of asps under their lips. We strictly forbid prebends to be given to anyone for life under the pretext of money or any service, since this turns to the harm of the houses. But if necessity or evident advantage should require it, this shall be done with the counsel of the lord abbot or, if he is far away, of the provincial chamberlain.

## CHAPTER LVI. On provincial chamberlains and their office.

So that we may bear the burden laid upon us better and more lightly, and affairs proceed more usefully when the load is divided among several, following the example of Moses, who followed the wholesome counsel of his father-in-law Jethro lest he be consumed by foolish labour—and because the people’s business was beyond his strength, chose men fearing God, in whom was truth, who hated greed, and appointed from among them tribunes, centurions, captains of fifty, and captains of ten, so that the burden divided among others might be lighter for him—we establish that each province have one or two overseers, whom we call chamberlains: diligent men, fearing God, tested in every respect. In accordance with God and the command of the Lord Abbot of Cluny, they shall arrange what must be arranged and correct what must be corrected, for the honour of God, the benefit and honour of the church of Cluny, and the provinces entrusted to them. They shall visit every house, especially at the beginning of their office. Being informed of the condition of the houses, the amount of their debts, the conduct and number of the priors [Col. 0894A] and brethren, and also of the household, they shall report to us at the general chapter in what condition they found the houses and in what condition they left them, so that through greater diligence they may obtain greater favour. They may not permit any prior or obedientiary, without consulting us, to sell or alienate revenues or possessions of the Church; nor may they change priors, but shall reserve to our judgment what they hear, and priors shall render them account in every way and in all matters. Nor may priors, without the knowledge of the chamberlains, increase a house’s debt beyond one hundred shillings, unless they show a clear reason why they did this. Whenever it is necessary, in some grave matter concerning land, a possession, or another affair, priors shall, at their command, assist them at their own expense, meeting the poverty of the houses. And because they are human and can be tempted: when chamberlains are appointed, having looked upon the holy Gospels and touched the relics, they shall swear that in good faith, to the best of their ability, they will attend to obedience toward the lord abbot and the benefit of the church of Cluny; that neither request, price, nor favour will cause them to conceal vices, conspicuous negligence, or the ruin of houses; that they will travel with three or four mounts; and that in no house will they take anything except what is necessary for sustenance. Let the oath which we require from any brethren not appear blameworthy to anyone. For although we have from the Gospel an admonition, and from the Rule of St. Benedict, not to swear, nevertheless we do not find an oath forbidden when there is a just cause. For we read the Apostle swearing: “God knows” (2 Cor. 11), and “By your salvation, brethren”; and the canons freely permit an oath in specified cases. Besides, since the days are evil, so much so that it can now be said: “Do you think the Son of Man will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18), we judge that this reason alone suffices for lawfully taking an oath. We do not wish, however, that under cover of this office chamberlains burden the churches at other times as well.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the death-notices.

Since our life is a vapour appearing for a little while, and no one who has returned from the dead has been recognized, and since we unceasingly advance toward eternal things, we ought to think more attentively upon eternal things. First, therefore, [Col. 0894D] we must help those who have already gone before us into the world to come, so that they may have the best grace laid up for them (2 Macc. 12). Accordingly, because some have hitherto shown too little concern for the death-notices of those resting in Christ, we establish that, especially at Cluny and in all our other places wherever a brother dies, greater diligence be exercised in sending notices, and that all due obligations be rendered to the dead. Meanwhile, until the next chapter, because of the aforesaid negligence, one office with Mass shall be celebrated everywhere in every month.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the manner and time of holding the general chapter.

Since it profits little to have scattered seed unless watering follows by which it may germinate, [Col. 0895A] so that we may be like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord (Ps. 51), bring forth a shoot of honour and grace, and henceforth become praise and righteousness before all nations (Isa. 61), we have judged it necessary by the present enactment to establish that every year at Cluny a general chapter of all priors, both conventual and lesser, be held. There, without respect of persons, the offences of delinquents shall be corrected according to God, the Rule of St. Benedict, and the institutions of the Cluniac Order; and matters concerning the salvation of souls, preservation of the Order, and security of the houses shall be discussed, and whatever ought regularly to be established shall be established.

## CHAPTER LIX. On complaints.

[Col. 0895B] In these matters, let neither priors nor chamberlains spare one another; but let each, keeping the fear of the Lord before his eyes, in charity bring forward publicly or privately in chapter, as he knows best to be expedient, whatever he knows needs correction in another, remembering Scripture, which says: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. 13); “The fear of the Lord hates evil” (Prov. 8); and: “He who causes a sinner to turn from his way has saved his soul from death” (James 5). Nor shall the person corrected take this ill, but receive a brother’s correction patiently, for it is written: “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9). We have decreed that the chapter be held every year on the Sunday of the second week of Lent, on which the office “My eyes are ever” is sung (Ps. 24). We wish all abbots and priors principally subject to Cluny to attend it, even if not summoned.

## CHAPTER LX. On gifts neither given nor received in the general chapter.

We forbid this more strictly by the authority of God and our own: that at the general chapter no exactions be made on our part, or on that of any others, or even on that of the church of Cluny; and that no gifts be given, received, or promised. For “gifts blind the eyes of the wise” (Deut. 16), justice is violated by gold, and fire will consume the tents of those who willingly accept gifts.

## CHAPTER LXI. That priors provide for their servants and horses during the chapter.

[Col. 0895D]

Lest the church of Cluny be burdened by this great assembly of abbots and priors, it has been provided and established that, until provision is made by common [Col. 0896A] counsel for the source from which the necessities of so great a multitude ought to be supplied, all abbots and priors, without distinction, shall support their own servants and horses as they choose. These things, though few, we have established at present according to the will of God and the counsel of our brethren. At the next chapter we shall add other things if necessary, or remove some of these as reason may dictate. Each provincial chamberlain shall keep these statutes with him and, before the coming Easter, present them to the priors and monks under his care for observance, since in them, if they are observed, consist the form of the Order, the example of honourable conduct, and the salvation of souls.

## CHAPTER LXII. On prayers and almsgiving.

[Col. 0896B] Since among the other duties of religious profession the virtue of prayer is especially commended, Scripture teaching us to pray without ceasing (1 Thess. 5), and among works of piety almsgiving holds the first place, the Lord saying: “Give alms, and all things shall be clean to you” (Luke 11), we desire that through this chapter provision be made by these outstanding gifts of virtues both for ourselves and our own people and for all the faithful, especially those to whom we are bound by spiritual ties. Therefore we establish that in this coming year, for the lord pope and the Roman Church; the lord king of France, his son, and the kingdom; the kings of England and Spain; Catholic princes; the Cluniac, Cistercian, Carthusian, Templar, [Col. 0896C] Hospitaller, and remaining Orders; the prelates of churches; our founders and benefactors, and those of our houses; and all Christ’s faithful: one thousand poor persons be fed, and one thousand Masses, beyond those owed and customary, be celebrated. Moreover, on every day forever, everywhere in our houses, for all the persons named above, after *Levavi*, let [a text unspecified in the supplied source] be said at Sext; and at Masses for the living, after the *Agnus Dei*, let the psalm *Ad te levavi* be said until the next chapter, so that through these suffrages of prayer peace may be granted by the Lord to the living and rest to the dead. We also earnestly admonish those celebrating Mass that at the first *Memento* they devoutly remember the living, and at the second *Memento* piously keep the dead in remembrance.

[Col. 0896D] These things were enacted at Cluny in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1200, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October]. The lord Hugh, fifth abbot of that name, presided over this sacred assembly.

[Col. 0895]

# CERTAIN OTHER STATUTES OF THE CLUNIAC MONASTERY, FROM A MANUSCRIPT

## CHAPTER I. For the lord Abbot of Cluny.

[Col. 0895D]

Since the strictness of the lawful order is one thing, and a dispensatory relaxation arising from necessity within the Order another, it is right that, when necessity ceases, the integrity of the Order be preserved inviolate. For remedies which cure an illness often, once the disease has ceased, impede health if they are taken. Therefore, what we have seen hitherto relaxed in the state of our Order for specified causes, we desire to recall to its former strictness when those causes have ceased. And since the lord [Col. 0897A] abbot is the father and principle of our Order, we lay before him, as before a father, those things which we have heard were diligently instituted and firmly observed by our ancient fathers, so that in him we may recognize, as in a mirror, both the purity of teaching and the effectiveness of good work.

Namely: that he eat with the convent in the refectory and sleep in the dormitory. We desire him always to remain with the convent so that, from what he has endured together with them, he may know how to have compassion upon the infirmities of his subjects.

But if at any time fatigue or illness compels him for a little while either to take refreshment or rest apart from the convent, an honourable place shall be prepared for him, as for lord and father, in the common infirmary or in the novices’ cell, with carpets and curtains [Col. 0897B].

Never in those upper dwellings, which are more properly suited to the sacristy, shall he eat or sleep; but, as befits a good shepherd, whether healthy among the healthy or infirm among the infirm, he shall remain with them, and thus the pious shepherd shall never abandon his sheep.

Within the precincts of the monastery of Cluny, moreover, he shall admit no servant for his personal service; rather, he shall employ certain of his brothers and sons, mature in age and learning, to serve him in every respect at table, at bed, and in the care of his illness. And because “the cultivation of justice is silence,” he shall keep silence in places set apart for silence. Nor shall he make use of a cloak or mantle under any circumstances.

Horses for the lord abbot’s riding shall be assigned to the deaneries and [Col. 0897C] to other places, as he sees fit, so that they may serve the needs of the deaneries and be no burden to the house of Cluny, yet not fail to be useful. And whenever it is necessary for the lord abbot to ride—though he ought to avoid this unless grave and unavoidable business presses—then the deans and the others who maintain the horses shall send them, with their grooms, properly prepared, as befits the service of so great a Father. When they return after the business is completed, they shall again receive both grooms and horses and derive the benefit of both for the houses entrusted to them. But when those horses have been weakened, if it is the fault of their keepers, the keepers shall be compelled to make restitution; if the harm arose otherwise, it shall not be charged against the keepers. [Col. 0897D]

And because it is written, “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” (Ecclus. 32), the lord abbot shall always have in the house of Cluny twelve wise brothers, whose counsel he shall always employ in all matters to be undertaken, both internal and external.

He shall have no personal provider of food (*pastor*), but every day he shall have before him in every respect such food and drink as the community has. In addition, however, as his dignity requires by ancient custom, two *guastelli*—small loaves—from the granary, and the better wine of the common cellarer, in a suitable cup, ought to be brought before him.

He shall demand nothing from his abbots or priors; [Col. 0898A] but if any of them wishes freely to give him something for his personal use, he may accept at most one mark, from which he is to give alms to the poor. If, however, other things should happen to come into his hands, he shall hand them over to the chamberlain. For the revenues of the chamberlain are not to be diverted or diminished in any respect, whether by the lord abbot himself or by anyone else, since that chamberlain must administer all matters pertaining to the proper business of the church of Cluny. Therefore, everything brought in must flow whole to him, to be distributed at his discretion among the various needs of the church. If, however, new and great matters or unusual debts should at any time arise within the church itself, then, for the dispatch of these affairs, brothers having been called together from various places, he shall employ their assistance and higher counsel. [Col. 0898B]

He shall by no means admit new chants or new readings, either in church or in the refectory. He shall not in any way exclude the deans from the authority of the chamberlain. He shall neither dispose of nor remove the treasury and ornaments of the church without the consent of the chapter. In priories he shall not, through private favour, exempt from the authority of his prior anyone who holds an obedience or is cloistered, lest, with contention springing up between them, charity and concord grow cold.

He shall not remove from the church, by any gift, exchange, or sale, lands and revenues belonging to the church, whether possessed from ancient times or newly given. In appointing or removing priors or deans, he shall neither regard nor accept favour, influence, hatred, [Col. 0898C] prayers, promises, or money; but with equity and moderation he shall correct errors and establish what is to be established.

If the lord abbot wishes to celebrate Masses or any divine offices outside the community in the greater church, he shall take care to regulate the time and chant so that he causes no inconvenience to the brothers.

## CHAPTER II. On the election of four persons, who are to come to Cluny once yearly and carefully investigate the state of the house
