Adhering to the enactments of our venerable father, the lord Abbot Hugh, we, appointed as definers in the general chapter, decree that four discreet and suitable persons be elected—namely, [Col. 0898D] two abbots and two priors belonging to the church of Cluny. Once yearly, at a fixed time, namely in the octave of the apostles Peter and Paul, they shall come to Cluny and carefully inquire both into the person of the lord abbot of Cluny himself, whoever he may be in successive times, and into the temporal and spiritual condition of the church and of the dependent places. Whatever needs correction shall be corrected according to their counsel, and through them all matters shall be made known yearly in the general chapter, so that by such a visitation the church of Cluny may persevere in good order and the rest, following the example of the head, may observe our institutions more firmly.

Since it frequently happens in many places that spiritual benefices are conferred through an intervening bargain, [Col. 0899A] although this is forbidden by the sacred canons and contrary to divine law, we forbid and decree that, in giving or receiving priories, in return for obediences, churches and chaplains, the reception of monks, burial, or other spiritual goods or offices, anything be offered or promised by means of an agreement. The sole exception is what Blessed Benedict says concerning a monk: that his devotion, freely offered, is not to be rejected.

## CHAPTER III. That no price be received for monks and obediences. On the almoner

Since we observe that through the frequent reception of monks of every kind an unprofitable multitude is growing, we decree that no monk be received, either in the head or in the members, for five years, except for succour; otherwise never, unless evident necessity compels it—yet this must in any case be disclosed by the chamberlain of the place to the general chapter. [Col. 0899B] We decree the same concerning any women received into our cells, except that henceforth, even after the five years, the reception of such persons is to be reported to the general chapter before it takes place.

It is highly dangerous, and we are much reproached for it by many—would that undeservedly—that we turn goods assigned for alms to the poor to uses other than those proper to them. Therefore we decree that no person, whether abbot or anyone else, presume with any rashness to take away or alienate anything assigned for the support of the needy. Accordingly, the alms shall be entrusted for safekeeping to a brother who fears God, [Col. 0899C] who shall faithfully devote all revenues and proceeds to the uses of the poor and pilgrims. He shall be content with at most one riding horse, few attendants, and modest expenses; for whatever is given to one of the least is given to the Lord, and whatever is withheld from them is taken from God. In this matter we discharge our own souls; those to whom this responsibility is entrusted will answer, in the strict judgment, before God, judge of all, for their administration. When offenders are discovered, however, they shall be punished more severely than the rest.

## CHAPTER IV. On hospitality

Since we have the Lord Jesus Christ’s authority for practising hospitality, who will say in the future, “I was a stranger and you took me in” (Matt. 25), and the example of the fathers in the Old Testament, because some pleased God by receiving angels in hospitality; and since we see plainly that religious places have grown for this reason, we ought to be ashamed that we observe this less honourably, and that they now decline through the very occasion on which they grew. Therefore we decree that religious persons, secular persons, and the poor shall be kindly received, each according to their station and according to the resources of the places, and honourably provided for. In the larger places, likewise, a faithful and diligent brother shall be appointed to this office. If, when guests arrive, necessities cannot conveniently be supplied because of the poverty of the place, at least lodging and a cheerful countenance shall not be denied them, for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). [Col. 0899D] For priors and obedientiaries who do not receive Cluniac monks, we decree the following penalty for a closed gate: if the prior is present, he shall deserve deposition without mercy; if he is absent, the person acting in the prior’s place shall be deposed for failure to provide necessities, according to the judgment of the chamberlain, who knows the resources of the place and shall punish him if he considers punishment appropriate. [Col. 0900A]

## CHAPTER V. That a monk shall lodge only in a religious house

Whenever a Cluniac monk travelling outside can suitably turn aside to a religious house, he shall not go to secular households, even if those with whom he stays are unwilling or unable to provide for him from their own resources; for both expenses may be incurred more honourably and safely among religious persons, [Col. 0900B] and a stay may be made there.

## CHAPTER VI. On the forfeiture of offices

Since certain monks and priors fear the peril of disobedience that we inherited from our first parent and are everywhere transgressors of the vow of obedience which they made, and do not obey our commands or those of their superiors, we decree and strictly command that priors who have been admonished once and twice and refuse correction shall lose their offices without hope of recovery; and if they persist in contumacy, they shall even be expelled from the entire order. Monks guilty of this wicked crime shall be punished with the harshest penalties prescribed by the order; and if they refuse amendment, they shall be driven from the fellowship of the whole congregation. We say the same concerning their supporters [Col. 0900C] and those who procure for their brothers the hindrances of capture or plundering.

## CHAPTER VII. That monks shall not obtain office through lay petitions

Since some of our brothers seek obediences or priories to be entrusted to them not through merits of life or learning but through the intervention of secular persons, “making flesh their arm” and with their hearts departing from the Lord (Jer. 17), we decree that no one who seeks any office in this way shall ever obtain it, nor another office within a year. For secular persons, if they do not obtain it, are stirred up against us; and the monks themselves, while they put their confidence in a human being, take less care to cultivate good conduct and more boldly despise their superiors.

## CHAPTER VIII. To whom priories are to be entrusted

[Col. 0900D]

We decree that priories, deaneries, and every other administration shall be entrusted to discreet and honourable men, who know how both to govern and to benefit others, not because of noble birth or private familiarity, but because of merit in life and learning. Furthermore, priories—especially conventual priories—shall be entrusted only to priests, or to men who can be ordained priests within a year; otherwise, from that time they shall know themselves to be removed from their priories.

## CHAPTER IX. On those who waste the goods of houses, and on confirmation of priories

Conventual priors shall not be removed except for definite reasons: namely, if they waste the goods of houses; [Col. 0901A] if they are disobedient and rebellious; if they are notorious or incontinent; or if they are to be promoted to greater usefulness. This shall be done by judgment of the definers in the general chapter, unless some manifest cause arises that compels the lord abbot to remove them. We likewise annul confirmations of priories for life, following the example of the lord pope, and forbid their being made henceforth.

## CHAPTER X. On the election of priors

To abolish the perverse insolence of certain monks, who in many places have begun to elect priors for themselves to the prejudice of the mother church, to restrain the ambition of those who make nominations, and to curb their pride, we forbid under the strictness of anathema that such [Col. 0901B] election or nomination ever again be made. But if, God forbid, an attempt is made against this prohibition, the person who consents to the election or nomination shall know himself, by that very act, excommunicated unless he immediately comes to his senses, and shall be deprived forever of every office and administration. Those who are the authors of this accursed election or nomination shall be punished by precisely the same penalty. Those who follow them and understand less shall hold the lowest place in the congregation and shall not celebrate the divine offices until they have gone to Cluny or obtained mercy by the indulgence of the lord abbot.

## CHAPTER XI. On those who hold obediences from other monasteries

It does not seem useful or honourable that brothers subject to us, especially priors, should acquire an administrative charge in other monasteries, make profession there, or obtain obediences there, thereby evading and making a mockery of discipline and fostering greed. Therefore, by this present constitution, we decree that all our priors who have houses or obediences from other monasteries shall relinquish them, or immediately lose ours. [Col. 0901C] Our cloistered monks, if they possess foreign obediences, shall relinquish them if they wish to obtain ours. Monks who hold an administrative charge in other monasteries or have made profession there shall be content with one or the other; and if they have gone there without the will or permission of their priors, they shall be regarded as fugitives. For from this disobedience and rebellion arise, and grave losses commonly befall our houses. [Col. 0901D]

## CHAPTER XII. That priors shall act with the counsel of others

Since the benefit of houses is sometimes hindered by summoning many persons to counsel, order is thrown into confusion, and the prior’s authority is diminished, because there are certain persons puffed up in spirit and discordant, or even unskilled, who wish everything to be arranged by their own counsel, we decree that in lesser affairs the prior shall use the counsel only of the better men, and in greater affairs only of the professed. Others, since they are not fully Cluniac monks, shall not consider themselves entitled to take part in deliberations unless summoned at the prior’s will.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the seal of the prior and of the community

The prior of Cluny shall have a special seal [Col. 0902A] made in his own name, with which he may freely seal documents. The seal of the community, however, shall be kept with no small solemnity. We decree the same concerning the seals of conventual houses.

## CHAPTER XIV. On contracting loans

Furthermore, we decree that whenever a loan must be made or renewed, all priors, whether greater or lesser, shall do so with the counsel of the brothers over whom they preside, of the household, the provost, and certain good men belonging to the same place. Thus it shall be made known to all persons to whom, on what terms, and at what rate of interest the debt is owed, and for what uses the loan contracted has been applied; for in this way the houses may be better provided for.

## CHAPTER XV. On accounts

[Col. 0902B]

So that the condition of the houses may be more certainly known, each official shall render account of his office at least three times a year before the prior and elders, faithfully calculating all expenditures and receipts. Likewise, twice each year the prior shall fully make known the state of the house in chapter; and once yearly, at the general chapter, through the testimony of the provincial chamberlain, the condition of the houses shall be made more fully known to the lord abbot by the priors. Thus inconveniences may be more easily prevented and the freedom of bad administrators restrained.

## CHAPTER XVI. That a monk shall not stand surety

We decree that no prior or monk shall stand surety, or pledge his own or the common seal, for any ecclesiastical or secular person, [Col. 0902C] because, when such persons do not release them from obligation, houses are grievously burdened by these encumbrances. Nor shall monks contract secular obligations among themselves by becoming sureties, by putting up pledges, or by trading in any other way.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the alienation of houses

If anyone, for any reason, presumes, without consulting the lord abbot or the chapter of Cluny, to alienate lands, houses, possessions, or church treasures—by selling them, mortgaging them at a lower rent, granting land for a large payment, or in any other way—he shall, without remission, be deposed from office and kept for three years in the cloister of Cluny, holding no obedience whatsoever. Moreover, after the regular discipline has first been administered, both to terrify others and to inflict shame upon him, [Col. 0902D] he shall undergo, for the whole of one month, every Sunday, punishment for transgressing the command, proportioned to the gravity of the offence at the judgment of the lord abbot, by the following satisfaction: when the whole community is in procession with the people in the nave of the church, he shall come forward and prostrate himself on the ground in the midst of the brothers, to be publicly shamed; and he who sold land shall cling to the pavement, so that others may be frightened from like acts, until the lord abbot, with his counsel, takes pity and says, “It is enough.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On those who create fictitious debts

Since greater crimes must be punished with a harsher penalty, concerning certain persons who, by the basest fraud, store up mammon for themselves out of the substance of Jesus Christ and—what is worst—after wasting houses, alienating possessions, selling treasures, and filling their purses through lay intermediaries, lend money to themselves and their houses at heavy interest, and, when they have lost their priories, cause repayment to be demanded from them of what is not owed: [Col. 0903A] we decree concerning these persons, and concerning those who gamble with dice and gaming pieces, and thieves and forgers, that whoever is convicted in this matter shall be expelled without mercy from monastery and congregation, his hood cut off. We make the same decree concerning those who practise usury, accept private pledges, or disgracefully sell their goods on credit for profit, if, when warned, they do not repent and restore their peculium. We judge likewise concerning those who fabricate or conceal false debts.

## CHAPTER XIX. That a monk at the point of death shall leave his goods to no one

[Col. 0903B]

Since a monk or conversus is neither his own master nor under his own power, and ought to possess nothing as his own, much less may he give or leave to anyone, at the point of death, such goods as he possesses—lest then he incur guilt when he ought to be released from guilt by penitence. Therefore, lest this be done henceforth, we forbid it most strictly; rather, whatever goods they possess shall remain at the disposal of their superior. If anyone does this, what he has done shall be held void, and his name shall not be written in the catalogue of the dead.

## CHAPTER XX. That no one shall presume to promise benefices

We grieve more than sufficiently that our houses are excessively burdened with pensions granted to clerics, on the pretext of churches that are not vacant, which priors are not ashamed to promise them contrary to the decrees of the Lateran Council. [Col. 0903C] Therefore, wishing to counter these burdens, we forbid anyone henceforth in any way to presume either to promise benefices not vacant or to confer such pensions upon anyone. Whoever presumes this shall know that he incurs peril to his rank and will undergo the severity of regular discipline.

## CHAPTER XXI. To whom priories are to be entrusted

No priory, deanery, or other house that can be governed by a Cluniac monk shall be handed over to another person to govern, since this seems to imply either that there are no worthy men among us or that we begrudge worthy and useful men their opportunities. If necessity should at any time require it, this shall by no means be done without the counsel of the general chapter. We decree that no clerics or laymen not belonging to us, nor servants of Cluniac houses, shall ever be made procurators, cellarers, or provosts; nor shall any ministry among our own men be entrusted hereditarily or for life. [Col. 0903D]

## CHAPTER XXII. On provincial overseers and chamberlains

So that the burden laid upon the lord abbot may be borne better when the load is divided among many, we decree that each province shall have one or two overseers, whom we call chamberlains: diligent, God-fearing men, who shall arrange what needs arranging in the houses and correct what needs correction. [Col. 0904A] They shall inform the definers in the general chapter about the state of the houses and the conduct of the priors. They may not grant to any prior or obedientiaries permission to alienate revenues or possessions without consulting the lord abbot; nor may priors [lacuna] increase the debts of the houses beyond one hundred solidi without the chamberlain’s knowledge, unless they show a clear reason why they do this. Whenever it is necessary because of some grave matter, the priors shall attend upon them at their own expense. When these chamberlains are appointed, with the Gospels set before them they shall promise by oath that in good faith they will obey the lord abbot and report whatever in their provinces they see needing correction, if they cannot correct it themselves. For from what just [Col. 0904B] cause do we find an oath forbidden—

## CHAPTER XXIII. That gifts are not to be given in the general chapter

Furthermore, we forbid gifts to be given, received, or promised in the general chapter, because “gifts blind the eyes of the wise” (Deut. 17), justice is violated by gold, and fire will consume the tents of those who willingly receive gifts.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How priors are to come to chapter

Conventual priors coming to chapter shall be content with three riding horses. The prior of La Charité, however, shall bring with him two conventual priors, and the prior of Saint-Martin one. All priors and abbots shall provide for themselves at chapter until [Col. 0904C] something has been determined concerning chapter expenses. No monk or novice to be blessed shall attend the general chapter because of the large number of persons.

## CHAPTER XXV. That priories shall not be entrusted to monks from outside

Furthermore, we decree that abbots who do not hold our abbeys, even though they are our monks—much less other persons—shall immediately relinquish their priories to Cluny, and that henceforth priories shall not be entrusted to such persons unless necessity is so great that the general chapter wishes to assent to it.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On those who must come to chapter

Those in distant provinces shall arrange to come to chapter every second year. We count as distant those established in the provinces of England, Spain, and Lombardy. Others shall by no means omit to come every year. Those who disdain to come at the appointed times shall be deposed from their priories and may not be restored except through the definers of the general chapter, except only those who excuse themselves on grounds of evident necessity. [Col. 0904D]

Nevertheless, to remove the unprecedented vice of appeal from our midst, we decree that persons making appeals shall never henceforth have residence in the cloister of Cluny; rather, they shall be sent to our other conventual houses, under the discipline of the order, to remain there for their entire lives, and shall henceforth hold no administration in the Cluniac order. Those, indeed, who secretly hand letters to eminent persons passing through the church of Cluny, because by this the entire congregation is defamed, shall be punished as thieves. For this is why the general chapter is instituted: that what needs correction may be corrected and that the aforesaid persons may set forth what they see ought to be proposed. Concerning proprietors, proceedings shall be taken according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, even to the point that, should money which they have not disclosed be found with them at death, they shall lack Christian burial; but if a sentence of excommunication has been pronounced on that account, it shall be entirely relaxed. We wish common fare to be observed in the refectory; nevertheless, we approve the ancient and regular penances, rejecting the corrupt innovation [Col. 0905A] practised by obedientiaries when they purchase costly foods. Yet, with permission, the elders and the infirm may receive a dispensation. [Col. 0906A]

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the observance of these institutions

Furthermore, we decree that both priors and chamberlains shall keep these present institutions at hand, so that during the chamberlains’ visitations priors may answer concerning every matter asked of them. The definers shall do the same in the general chapter. Those who have already appealed shall be received upon making satisfaction, provided that henceforth they have no residence in the cloister of Cluny but are sent out, distributed among external obediences.

## APPENDIX TO HUGH

[Col. 0905]

### Treatise of Rostang, monk of Cluny, on the removal of the head of Saint Clement, pope and martyr, translated from Constantinople to Cluny in the time of Abbot Hugh

(Library of Cluny, 1481.)

[Col. 0905B] In order to strengthen the faith of believers and increase the devotion of hearers, I have endeavoured, according to the measure of my small ability, to make known to those present and future how, in what manner, by whom, and for what reason this translation was accomplished. The cause of this event was the capture of the holy city of Jerusalem, which has been captured many times by many people—indeed, most often it has been razed to the ground by very many. It is not contemptible to hear of the falls and disasters suffered by this city for the sins of its inhabitants, because in it our faith, salvation, and redemption received their beginning and fulfilment: “There the Lord worked our salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 23).

### Account of the translation

[Col. 0905C] We read in ancient histories and in the prophets, where the miracles of our Creator and the mighty deeds of the fathers are recounted, that the threat of destruction which the Lord had announced against Jerusalem through the prophecies of the prophets was fulfilled through Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, because the city did not correct itself. Thus Nabuzardan, a commander of his army, not only plundered the city of Jerusalem, but also destroyed its walls and carried its inhabitants captive to Babylon. Jeremiah lamented the ruins of this aforesaid city in a fourfold alphabetic acrostic; later it was honourably rebuilt under Cyrus, king of the Persians.

We also read in the Gospel that, when the Lord was passing through the midst of the city, one of his disciples said to him: “Teacher, look what stones and what structures of its wall!” The Lord said to him: “Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone shall be left upon another that shall not be destroyed” (Mark 13). This prediction, though uttered beforehand, could not pass away while heaven and earth pass away, because it came forth from the mouth of the eternal Word. Indeed, it was fulfilled through Titus and Vespasian, who not only destroyed the city to its foundations, slaughtered its Jewish inhabitants, and sold thirty of them for one silver coin—an inversion of the order, because the Lord had been bought from them for thirty silver coins—but also Aelius Hadrian, as Josephus relates, again utterly overthrew the same city. [Col. 0906B]

But how it was thereafter built or ruled, and by whom, down to the year 1099—for from the Incarnation of the Lord:

> In the eleven-hundredth year, lacking one,  
> Jerusalem is taken by the Franks with mighty strength—

seek the histories, and you will find it.

The cause of this captivity, capture, or recovery from the hands of pagans was Pope Urban II, a most religious and most venerable man, whom divine providence chose from the cloister of Cluny as priest for itself [Col. 0907A] and established at the summit of the supreme pontificate. Moved by heavenly desire, he began to deliberate how the holy city of Jerusalem might be freed from unclean and wicked people and restored to Christians and the Christian religion, so that God might be glorified and honoured by them where God had suffered much for them.

For this purpose he undertook a journey, ostensibly to visit Gaul; and, arriving in Auvergne at Clermont, he held a celebrated council. There he commanded primates, patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and priests to exhort all Christians throughout the world to undertake the journey to Jerusalem for the redemption of their souls, in order to recover the place where God wrought our salvation and our redemption. Nor were they to fear dangers by land or sea, remembering how much labour God endured there for us. [Col. 0907B]

For this reason, at that time the most devout count of Flanders, prompted by divine inspiration, the duke of Normandy, the count of Saint-Gilles, the most illustrious prince Bohemond, Adhemar bishop of Le Puy, the bishop of Albariensis, and the bishop of Janua—all these, urged by the divine Spirit, crossed the sea without king or emperor, with Christ as their leader, to free the holy city. They devastated the provinces of the Saracens, destroyed cities and castles, killed Turks, passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people, and came to Antioch, which they gained with much labour. Afterwards, with the Lord protecting them, they besieged Jerusalem and, with great effort and God’s aid, took it. They killed the faithless Saracens, cleansed the city from the filth of idols, appointed a king there, ordained a patriarch, and left people there to inhabit and guard the city. The body of the nobles, however, departed with the king of Jerusalem for other regions to be subjected to divine worship. [Col. 0907C]

Do not be displeased that I have briefly summarized all this. It is pleasant to know everything; if you desire to know it, consult the history of Jerusalem, which was written more clearly than daylight by one who took part in all these events. But now let us turn our pen to recent people and recent [Col. 0907D] times, briefly explaining the just occasion on which, and the persons by whom, the head of Saint Clement was translated from Constantinople to Cluny.

It must therefore be understood that the people left in Jerusalem, gathered from diverse places, differed in race, language, customs, and mode of life; they were joined by no affinity or blood relationship. Therefore none trusted another, but each disparaged the other. Forgetful of God’s benefits, they treated unworthily the Holy of Holies entrusted to them by God, living luxuriously and eagerly pursuing robbery and theft. They deceived pilgrims who had come there from the ends of the world to worship, at the place where the feet of him who deigned to suffer there for us had stood. Sometimes, practising the deadly trade of innkeepers and taverners, [Col. 0908A] they offered them poisoned drinks, so that, after secretly destroying them, they might freely use their possessions at will.

For this reason, because of their ingratitude, the Lord lawfully revoked the gift he had given them; and, to their dishonour, he delivered his city for a time from unworthy persons to persons still more unworthy, namely Saladin and barbarous nations. Thus in former times he took the Ark of the Covenant away from the children of Israel and delivered it into the hands of the Philistines in the time of the priest Eli, when an innumerable multitude of Jews had been struck down.

Accordingly, Baldwin, the illustrious count of Flanders, considered that the king of the Franks and the king of the English, stirred by God’s will, had intended to recover this aforesaid holy city; but the devil’s envy—he who cast humanity from Paradise—made them discordant, [Col. 0908B] while each strove in royal pride to surpass the other, and, puffed up with arrogance, each tried to prefer himself to the other. God, who “resists the proud” (1 Pet. 5), withdrew himself from their midst, because God does not dwell in division of minds. Therefore they left their enterprise unfinished; and the discord then conceived between them—alas!—still endures harshly among them as I write, as punishment for that sin.

Nevertheless, with God’s help they took the city of Achon, commonly called Acre. A little before, the Saracens had violently taken this city from us; but many bands of pilgrims, crossing the seas out of zeal for God, besieged it, and were immediately themselves besieged by Saladin. While they attacked the city in front, Saladin attacked them from behind; but they had made a rampart between themselves and him, so that he could not easily rush upon them. They lacked provisions, because no trade in foodstuffs could reach them. Therefore they wasted away under hunger with great anguish, so that they despaired not of the salvation of their souls, but of their bodies. [Col. 0908C]

But the merciful and compassionate Lord, who “gives food to those who fear him” (Ps. 145) and “fills every living creature with blessing” (Ps. 144), opened his hand to them. Looking out to sea from afar, they saw the fleet of the king of the Franks ploughing the waters. Then fear was added to fear and pain to pain; in terror they cried out, thinking that aid for the Saracens was coming to the city. Yet they sent a trireme to meet them, to discover what people it was.

When they had drawn nearer, they halted in fear until they recognized the royal sails and the crosses fixed upon the prows. Called by those aboard, they approached more confidently. When they learned how matters stood, filled with joy, they turned the reins of their wooden horses and, flying most swiftly, returned to the shore. There the people eagerly awaited news. Before they reached land, they began to cry out: “We announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people: for the king of the Franks has come to free you from the hands of your enemies.” When this was heard,
They lift their spirits and stretch their hands toward the stars (Vergil, *Aeneid*), watering their cheeks with tears which the greatness of their joy poured forth. Immediately the king put in at the harbor. Consider, if you can, with what joy—indeed, with what jubilation—they met him, coming out [Col. 0909A] with drums, choirs, and lyres. When he and his men had gained the offered shore, the king lavishly bestowed supplies upon the great men and distributed alms to the poor. Having pitched tents and spread pavilions, he besieged the city on a large scale; and at once he sent messengers to the king of England, who held Cyprus and was still staying there, asking him to come with all speed, yielding to him in this matter because, in his absence, he did not wish to attack the city. The latter came swiftly with a great army and royal equipment; with doubled joy they surrounded the city. After many hardships, with the aid of Him who alone …, they captured the city. Then the hungry were filled, the needy enriched with spoils, and the city was taken with great [Col. 0909B] triumph. If we did not now possess it, nowhere in those regions would we find a safe harbor. But the kings, made discordant by the zeal of envy, departed from one another and put aside the journey to Jerusalem.

As Count Baldwin of Flanders pondered these matters, he summoned the Count of Saint-Pol and very many other barons from France, England, Germany, and all the provinces of the world. Remembering that God is accustomed to save not by multitude but by a few, and casting his care upon the Lord, he undertook the journey to Jerusalem. The Lord gave him, as help and counsel, the count—that is, the Marquis of Montferrat—whose praise and power [Col. 0909C] are proclaimed throughout the world. He also took with him men of the highest reverence: namely, the bishop of Soissons, [f. Suession.] the bishop of Troyes, and very many other religious men. A certain knight joined this holy company, Dalmatius of Serciac, a noble and very learned man, who associated with himself a knight named Pontius of Busseria, a faithful man and good companion. Together they set out with the aforesaid army and reached Venice, where they were deceitfully received by the venomous Venetians. For a long time they refused to grant them passage, neither for freight-money nor for any price. At last, freed from their labyrinth, they fell into the Charybdis of the emperor of Constantinople. Grieved at their arrival, he concealed the sorrow of his heart beneath feigned joy; for a long time he detained them under false assurances [Col. 0909D] of assistance, and, once his own affair had been completed, lied concerning the wages he had promised them—not acting as an emperor, but as a traitor. Having provoked them, he strove by war to drive them not only from the city but even from his realm. Yet the Franks, placed between hammer and anvil, resorted to the customary mercy of God and implored divine aid. Encouraged by God, who is mighty in battle (Psalm 23), the common infantry alone attacked the Greeks before dawn. But the Greeks, by divine prompting turning their backs, fled; and one of our men pursued a hundred and ten thousand. The Franks, pursuing and slaughtering the fugitives, gained the city and compelled the emperor to flee from the palace. When he had been cast down, they established the Count of Flanders [Col. 0910A] as emperor, having captured the city.

Therefore the aforesaid Dalmatius, since he could not go to Jerusalem, devised with his companion how he might piously steal the head of blessed Clement. He had heard that a certain emperor had brought that head by sea to Constantinople and deposited it in a particularly famous place. Hear, from his own account, how Dalmatius, with God’s permission, obtained the aforesaid head of Saint Clement.

“I, Dalmatius of Serciac, and my companion Pontius of Busseria, on departing from Thessalonica, had intended to visit the land of Jerusalem; but we could not reach it because of the storm of threatening winds. Thus we labored at sea for six weeks. At last, compelled by the violence of the winds, [Col. 0910B] we again put in at Constantinople. And when I lay there as though buried in grief and sorrow because I had been unable to fulfill my vow and gain the means of going to Jerusalem, I feared that I would lose the fruit of so great a labor, for which I had undergone so many dangers by land and sea. Turning to the Lord with tears, I began to pray, saying: ‘Make thy face to shine upon thy servant, O Lord, and teach me thy statutes’ (Psalm 30); and deign to inspire in thy servant some deed equivalent to the vow that was begun but not completed; let it be equally pleasing to thee, so that I may not lose the coin of my reward. And, as I truly believe, the Lord heard the voice of my weeping and received my prayer (Psalm 6). And [Col. 0910C] there arose—that is, was divinely conceived—in my mind the thought that I should carry from there to lands beyond the sea relics of saints, of which there was such abundance there that they were handled more cheaply there; for I knew that the farther their relics were carried, the more brightly their glory and praise would shine afar.

“While I turned such matters over in my mind, I conceived the idea of consulting venerable and religious men, cardinals of the Roman Church: Lord Benedict and Lord Peter, cardinal of the Church of Capua. With one voice and unanimous agreement, they directed me that I should obtain saints’ relics, wherever I could do so without purchase; for the law forbids anyone to traffic in martyrs or buy them. They further directed me to place them honorably in a more religious place, to the praise of God and of those [Col. 0910D] saints whose relics were obtained. Having received this instruction, I began with greater insistence and zeal to carry out the work which I had conceived as a vow. Wintering in Constantinople throughout the winter until Palm Sunday, we applied ourselves to this purpose.

“It happened on that Sunday, while we were at dinner and discussing saints’ relics, that a certain priest named Marcellus, a religious man and native of the district of Chalon, said that he knew of the honorable relics of a certain saint, namely the head of blessed Clement. We asked him how he could be certain about this. He replied that he had seen a golden *barretea*—that is, a gold plate fixed into a shrine—on which was painted the image of Saint Clement [Col. 0911A] and his proper name written in Greek, namely, ὁ ἅγιος Κλεμτόπος [Greek as printed, apparently corrupt], which is rendered in Latin as ‘Saint Clement.’ The abbey in which the head of blessed Clement was kept was of great authority, in the same city; in Greek it was called Trentafolia, while in Latin it is interpreted ‘Rose.’

“We cannot explain in a few words how we obtained the head of Saint Clement; nevertheless, we shall briefly indicate certain points. We approached the monks of that place and asked them to show us saints’ relics for the sake of prayer. They assigned us a certain cleric, to guard us and show us what we asked for. But I, Dalmatius, giving the aforesaid priest and a certain Cistercian monk who was with us the opportunity to accomplish the business [Col. 0911B] for which we had come, led about with me through various parts of the church the cleric who had brought us there. Conversing with him about many other matters and turning his gaze toward images to be viewed, I caused him to wander about, lest he see what the priest was going to do. Then the priest, trembling, approached the head of blessed Clement. He did not dare take the whole thing, but cautiously tore away the chin with the jaws, leaving the head behind.

“When this had been done and we were already outside the gate of the abbey, I, Dalmatius, asked the priest what he had done. He replied that he had obtained enough of the relics. I asked him again whether he had the entire head. He answered: ‘No, but only the chin with the jaws.’ Angered, I said to him: ‘You have done nothing. Go away content with what you have; my companion Pontius [Col. 0911C] and I will see what we can do.’ Thus, after they had departed, the two of us returned to the monastery. When the monks at the gate asked why we were returning, I, Dalmatius, replied that I had left my gloves in the church. Remaining with the monks at the gate, in order to detain them, I sent my companion Lord Pontius inside to accomplish what we sought.

“He saw a certain monk, apparently the monastery’s guard, sleeping behind the gate, and hurried to accomplish the task. By God’s permission, of two saints’ heads kept in a small cupboard behind the altar, he brought out the head of blessed Clement. He recognized it as Saint Clement’s [Col. 0911D] because the priest had taken the chin from it. Thus, joyfully mounting our horses, we left the abbey in haste. When the monks learned what had been done, they ran after us with loud lamentation, tearing the hair of their beards and heads in barbarian fashion, and shouting that we had stealthily carried off holy relics. I, Dalmatius, urged my companion Pontius to ride swiftly ahead; then, to delay the monks, I held back my reins and showed them my empty lap, maintaining falsely that we had taken nothing from them. Thus, by God’s grace, we returned with the holy spoil, by the turnings of many roads, to our lodging with joy and fear. We secretly placed the holy head of blessed Clement in the chapel of our house, with not such veneration [Col. 0912A] as we ought to have shown, but such as we dared and were able to show.

“Afterward, somewhat doubtful and wishing to be assured about our deed, we dared mention nothing from Palm Sunday until Good Friday, but remained silent about these matters. On that Sunday of the Passion, changing our clothes and going on foot to visit the saints as though we were pilgrims, we came to the aforesaid abbey. We made our way toward the altar, not merely to adore, but rather to steal the other head which had been left behind. Many living monks ran after us and reached the cupboard with us. Only after much urgent entreaty did they allow us to kiss the sanctuary within, remarkably guarding it from our hands. When [Col. 0912B] we asked them why they were so afraid, they replied that they had recently lost in this manner their most precious relic, the head of blessed Clement. Having heard this, we became more certain; we left them and remained at peace until Easter Day.

“On the day of the Resurrection, I, Dalmatius, rejoicing greatly in the head we had acquired and desiring fuller certainty, sent to the aforesaid abbey an interpreter whom I kept with me, skilled in Greek and Latin. I instructed him to intimate to the abbot of that place that he should grant some relics to a certain knight in exchange for gold, silver, houses, or revenues. The interpreter came to the abbot and disclosed what I had instructed him. The abbot, as though angry, replied that he had no relics which he would be willing to part with, because they had recently lost the head of blessed Clement. [Col. 0912C] As the interpreter departed from him in this fashion, certain Venetians met him. Since the aforesaid abbey lay under their lordship and power, they asked what he was seeking. When he replied that he had come to adore the holy things, they accused him, perhaps, of being one of those who had stolen the holy head of blessed Clement. He answered that he knew nothing of these matters and withdrew from them as quickly as he could. Returning to us, he recounted everything he had heard and seen.

“Thus our joy was increased and confirmed. Yet I, Dalmatius, still did not wish to cease inquiring into the truth of our deed. I diligently asked a Syrian named Moses, who, before the capture of the city of Jerusalem, had been a canon and guardian of the tomb of our Lord Jesus Christ, and who after that capture had come to Constantinople and remained there more than fifteen years—having heard much, as a diligent investigator, concerning the condition of churches and the depositing of saints—whether [Col. 0912D] he had heard that anything from the body of blessed Clement had been brought to that city. After much reviewing among the things he had heard, he replied that the head of blessed Clement had long ago been brought to Constantinople by a certain emperor, but that he did not know where it had been deposited. With these signs and inquiries, I, Dalmatius, and my companion Pontius were greatly delighted. We vowed and promised that, should God grant us a prosperous return to our homeland, we would give the head of blessed Clement [Col. 0913A] to the holy Church of Cluny.

“As soon as we could, we embarked on a ship. Placing great confidence in God’s grace for the success of our journey and in the protection of our patron Saint Clement, we crossed many stretches of sea quite successfully as far as the vigil of Pentecost. But on that vigil, that envious enemy of the human race, the disturber of all good things insofar as God permits him, envying, as we believe, our happy undertaking, brought upon us at the twilight of that night a violent and intolerable torment of wind and sea. Disturbed by that whirlwind, ‘the dark-blue waters of the deep are troubled,’ and ‘the wondrous surges of the sea were lifted up’ (Psalm 92). [Col. 0913B] Then the breaking wave stirred the sea’s hidden depths, the tide raged over the sands, and the sea had already prepared our tomb—the bellies of fishes. Then at once the limbs of all were paralyzed with cold, since it seemed not so much that the ship was among the waves as that the waves were inside the ship. The sail, with the mast leaning over, appeared already to be lapping the sea; and the sailors, despairing of life, abandoned the ship and escaped in small boats. While all the rest of us who remained in the vessel despaired of escape and life, and, forgetful of every good and evil thing, were beside ourselves, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who ‘blows where he wills’ (John 3), deigned suddenly to inspire us to flee to Saint Clement, whose relics we were carrying, and to test his mercy. [Col. 0913C] Before the shrine, then, with bent knees, streaming tears, and palms raised to heaven, we offered the following prayer:

“‘O most merciful Clement, we implore thy mercy, in whose protection [Col. 0914A] we trust. Since thou wast overwhelmed in the sea for the name of Christ, deign to free us from being overwhelmed by the sea, so that by this we may truly prove that thou dost help us.’

“When the prayer ended, the storm immediately ended, and the sea’s calm was restored to us. We therefore confess and confidently declare that, when the north wind was at once driven away through the merits of blessed Clement, a favorable south wind promptly followed; raising the ship visibly from the opposite side, it happily enabled us to escape the aforesaid mortal danger. Joyfully we rendered joyful thanks to our deliverer, and, flying over the sea, soon reached the harbor we desired.

“Afterward, conducted prosperously by blessed Clement through various regions, on 27 July [VI Kalends of August], by the Lord’s grant and the martyr’s own permission, we offered with much devotion and [Col. 0914B] honor the often-mentioned head of the holy martyr to the holy church of Cluny and its venerable convent, to be venerated and worshipped forever. They received it honorably and with immense reverence, and joyfully deposited it with the other holy relics. A little later, however, they placed it with still greater reverence and honor in a silver reliquary. Therefore, hoping through his mercy in Him who shall judge the living and the dead, we confidently trust forever in his protection and advocacy. We pray for his mercy: that, as he once governed the universal Church, so now he may deign especially to rule and govern this Church. Amen.

“This took place by the grace of God in the year 1206, [Col. 0914C] in the presence of Pope Innocent, during the reign of Philip, king of France, through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be everlasting glory and perpetual praise, unto infinite ages of ages.”

[Col. 0913] Here ends the account of the reception at Cluny of the head of blessed Clement.

## Letters and Diplomas of Baldwin, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, Later Emperor of Constantinople

### I. Letter concerning the peace made between Count Baldwin and the people of Tournai (1197)

[Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 664. From the Hainaut cartulary of the lords of Avesnes.]

[Col. 0913D]

I, BALDWIN, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, wish to make known to all [Col. 0914D] that, having sworn an oath and pledged my faith, I have granted to every inhabitant of Tournai that I shall maintain a firm truce with them until a firm peace has been restored between the lord king and me concerning the war which has now begun between the lord king of France and me. This is on the following condition: that meanwhile they shall not further fortify their city beyond its present fortification; nor may they receive any person or persons belonging to the lord king’s party, or to any other party, from whom any harm might come to me. And they may not send to him the 300 serjeants whom they customarily sent to the lord king on his expeditions. But if the lord king wishes to have them, they shall release them to him at Tournai and nowhere else; and, if the lord king can then take them away, he shall take them away. The citizens also owe no money to the lord king for those serjeants, nor may they give him money on any other pretext or provide him with any assistance from which harm or injury might come to me while the war lasts.

My men may freely pass through the city, provided that an armed army does not pass through it; they may buy their provisions and seek their markets. Ships may travel upstream and downstream with provisions and merchandise. The citizens themselves shall meanwhile have free and secure passage throughout all my land, to seek markets and conduct their business, as they did in time of peace, before the war began between the lord king and me. Furthermore, should any dispute arise between one or more of my men, or those belonging to me, and one or more of the citizens, concord and settlement shall be made by four of my men—namely Walter of Avesnes, Th. of Diche[mue], Ren. of Trit, and my uncle William—and by four burgesses: namely [Col. 0915C] Henr. Wambe, Walt. Galet, Fob. Justitiam, and Comm. de Barra.

My brother Henry swore with me to observe this truce firmly on my behalf; and these my men confirmed it by pledging their faith: my uncle Henry; Walter of Avesnes; my uncle William; Th. of Beverna; Ren. of Trit; Roger, castellan of Kortrijk, and his son Roger; Baldwin of Commines; Baldwin of Prat; the brothers Boissard and Gill. of Borghela; the brothers Rabber. and Roger of Ruma; Gont. of Mouscin; Thom. of Lealcort; Fast. of Orcha; Osto of Arbre; the brothers Egidius and Gossuinus of Aigremont; Nich. Desplecin; Ger., provost of Saint-Amand; and the brothers Monicus and Egidius [Col. 0915D] of Guegnies.

The provosts, jurors, aldermen, electors, and all the burgesses of Tournai likewise swore and gave surety, on their own behalf, that they would firmly observe this settlement of the truce. They gave hostages: to Walter of Avesnes, 200 marks; to Roger of Kortrijk, 100 marks; to Egidius of Aigremont, 100 marks; to Bossard and Gill. of Borghella, 200 marks; to Ger., provost of Saint-Amand, 100 marks; to Gont. of Mouscin, 100 marks; to Monicus of Guegnies, 100 marks; to Frastreit of Orcha, 100 marks; to Babber. of Ruma, 100 marks; to Nich. of Flamengheria, 100 marks; and to Thomas of Lealcort, 100 marks. This was on the condition that, if the burgesses should not keep this truce as stated and ordered, these persons must pay me that money. They granted me that, wherever I could do so without violating the truce, I could take from their goods and property until full amends had been made to me for their breach of the truce, if they did not make amends within eight days. I shall acknowledge this settlement of the truce before the aldermen of Ghent, Bruges, Ypres, and Valenciennes. For these truces, as stated and ordered, they must give on my behalf to Laur. of Campagnes, John of Bavaco, and Egid. of Arras 4,000 marks, at 33 shillings and 4 Flemish pence for each mark: 1,000 at the fairs of Messines, 1,000 at the fairs of Kortrijk, 1,000 at the fairs of Ypres, and 1,000 at the fairs of Torhout. And in order that these truces may be firmly maintained as here stated and ordered, I caused them to be set down in the present writing and confirmed by the attachment of my seal.

Done before Tournai in the year of the Lord 1197, in July, on the first Sunday before the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene.

### II. Laws of Baldwin, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, concerning homicide (1200)

[D. Marten, *Anecdota*, I, 765, from a manuscript of Cambron.]

This is the form of peace throughout the whole county of Hainaut, which the lord BALDWIN, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, [Col. 0916C] the noblemen, and the other knights secured and confirmed by their oaths, and strengthened by the affixing of their seals, both those of the lord count and those of the noblemen.

I. Concerning persons who are not knights or sons of knights: a dead man for a dead man, a limb for a limb. But sons of knights who have not become knights by their twenty-fifth year shall, after their twenty-fifth year, be subject to the peace as peasants are.

II. If anyone attacks a man—what is commonly called *assalire*—and the attacked man, while defending his own person, kills the man who attacked him, he ought to have firm peace in this matter before God and before the friends of the slain man.

III. [Col. 0916D] If anyone, guarding the fruits of his own lands, woods, waters, meadows, or the like, whether in person or through his servant, wishes to take a cloth or pledge, and the cloth or pledge is refused him—that is, *sconditum* (‘refused’)—and quarrels, disputes, or conflict arise between him and the person who refused, or *scondivit* (‘refused’), the pledge, whom he finds upon his property; and if the owner of the land, wood, meadow, water, or the like kills the person whom he finds upon his property, no vengeance shall be taken against him, nor shall he make any compensation; rather, he must have firm peace.

IV. If a man kills another man and the killer flees, his friends and relatives must renounce him by oath [Col. 0917A] and declare him forsworn; thus they must have peace. Whoever refuses to forswear him shall be treated as the fleeing killer himself, until he has forsworn him.

V. If anyone flees with the killer, or absents himself on that account and leaves the country because he refuses to renounce the killer by oath, he may return within a year and make the renunciation. After a year he may no more return than may the person who committed the crime; and during that year the lord under whose jurisdiction he remains shall possess his movables wherever they are in the county of Hainaut. The friends and relatives of the slain man must assure the safety of all those who have forsworn the killer. Whoever refuses to assure their safety shall be in the same position [Col. 0917B] as the one who committed the crime. This is added: after being warned to give such assurance, he may leave the country from the following day until evening; and the lord under whose jurisdiction he remains shall possess his movables, as stated above. But if, after the warning, he does not leave the country from the following day onward, the same shall be done to him as should be done to the perpetrator of the crime. He too may return within a year to give assurance.

VI. For a limb taken away, the peace shall be maintained in the same manner, according to the value of the deed, namely in respect to the loss of the limb and the giving of assurance.

VII. The lord under whose jurisdiction the fleeing killer, or the person who took away another’s limb and fled, remains shall possess all his movables wherever they are in the county of Hainaut, and the fruits of the land for one year.

VIII. The lord may not retain for more than a year the land of a fugitive or outlaw; but once the year has passed, that person’s nearest heir shall have his inheritance and land, if he has renounced him by oath.

IX. In the case of a slain man, the lord whose serf he was, or under whose advocacy he was, shall have the “dead hand.”

X. If a fugitive who has killed a man or taken away a limb, or an outlaw, returns to the country, no free town, lord, or man may protect or guarantee him. Anyone who has sworn the peace may seize him wherever he is found. [Col. 0917D] The captor must present him to the person under whose jurisdiction he was captured, so that the latter may execute upon him the justice and vengeance aforesaid. If that person does not execute justice and vengeance, the lord Count of Hainaut must do so.

XI. If a man has been wounded or seriously injured so that there is doubt of death or the loss of a limb, the wounder or injurer must be detained and held in custody until it is seen what comes of that wound or injury.

XII. If a knight has held in custody a detained man and he escapes him, the knight must swear with two other knights that the man escaped without his fault, saving nevertheless the truth required by good peace. But if the detained man escapes from a bailiff, another official, or any person who is not a knight, that person must swear with six other men that the escape was without his fault, saving nevertheless the truth required by good peace.

XIII. Whoever carries a pointed knife, unless he is a hunter, cook, butcher, or a foreigner passing through the country, must pay sixty shillings in pence to the person under whose jurisdiction he is found. If, because of poverty, he cannot pay that compensation, his ear shall be cut off.

XIV. The compensation for wrongs in all towns in which no market is held, namely from neighbor against neighbor, whether among the count’s men or others, is as follows. For a *roisnatus* man [materially uncertain term] or a broken limb, fifty shillings in pence shall be paid: the injured man shall receive thirty shillings, and the lord under whose jurisdiction the injured man remains, twenty shillings. For shedding blood, thirty shillings shall be paid, of which the man shall receive one half and the lord under whose jurisdiction he remains the other half. For hair-pulling or a blow without bloodshed, fifteen shillings: the person whose hair was pulled or who was struck shall receive one half, and the lord under whose jurisdiction he remains the other half.

XV. All these things must be proved by good truth. But if the truth does not appear, the person who accuses another shall swear alone that the other injured him, struck him, or pulled his hair. The other shall swear with two others that he is not guilty of it, and thereby he must have peace.

XVI. [Col. 0918C] In these oaths no exceptions called *gitta* are to be introduced.

XVII. If any of the persons whose compensation is fixed at fifty, thirty, or fifteen shillings is summoned before the person to whom jurisdiction belongs on behalf of his man who has been injured, and cannot or will not pay the compensation within fifteen days, the lord shall execute justice according to the offense. If that person flees, he shall be pursued as other outlaws are pursued and shall be regarded as disgraced; his friends shall have peace.

XVIII. By these compensations firm peace must exist among lords, neighbors, and men, both concerning the count’s men and concerning others.

All these provisions the lord Baldwin, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, [Col. 0918D] and his men, noblemen and other knights whose names follow, swore upon the holy Gospels fully to observe: namely, Philip, Marquis of Namur, brother of the aforesaid count; Henry, likewise brother of that count; Walter of Avesnes; Alard of Chimay; Rasso of Gaura; Gerard of Jace; Eustace of Rues; Nicholas of Barbencione; William, uncle of the aforesaid count; Aegidius of Trasiniis; William of Kevi; Renerus of Trit; Nicholas of Ruminio; Engelbert of Aengien; Arnulf of Moreliner; Godfrey of Thuin; William of Haussi; Alulf, son of that William; Walter of Ville; Walter of Kavreng; Nicholas of Condé; Hugh of Gaia; Bernerus of Roucourt; Nicholas of Mainwaut; [Col. 0919A] Hugh of Beverna; Aegidius of Brena; his brother Henry, castellan of Binche; Osto of Wadripont; Nicholas of Flamengeria; Henry, castellan of Mons; Gillenus, castellan of Beaumont; Osto of Arbro; Baldwin of Saint-Remy; Walter of Sotenghien; Arnulf of Oudenaarde; Gerard of Saint-Aubert; Henry, uncle of the aforesaid count; Adam of Walencourt; Aegidius of Berlaimont; Hugh of Saint-Aubert; Gerard, provost of Douai; Walter, castellan of Douai; Peter of Douai; Stephen of Deneng; John of Semeriis; John of Herispont; Baldwin of Strepi; Alard, Nicholas, and Walter, sons of the same Baldwin; Aegidius; Ulbadus of Harveng; Baldwin of Valenciennes; Benardus of Strepi; Robert of [Col. 0919B] Loviniis; Nicholas of Montigny; Hugh of Harven; Franco of Felliu; Fastredus of Cambron; Renerus of Montibus; Karolus of Cruce; Drogo of Quarinum; Romundus of Quarinum; Goswinus, provost of Senogien; Walter of Blanden; his son Gerard; Obertus of Fontiniis; Aegidius of Montibus; William of Montigny; Baldwin of Curtisolva; Alard of Grandirivo; Gillebertus Cornutus; and William Flaons.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1200, at Monts Castle, on 28 July [V Kalends of August], Friday before the feast of Saint Peter in Chains.

### III. Further laws of the same Count Baldwin, concerning successions and other matters (1200)

[Marten, ibid., p. 769, from the Hainaut cartulary of the lords of Avesnes.]

[Col. 0919C]

This is a declaration of the laws in the court and county of Hainaut, more carefully set down by the common consent, counsel, deliberation, and sound recollection of the noblemen and ministeriales belonging to the county of Hainaut; and confirmed for perpetual observance by the seals and oaths of Lord Baldwin, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, and of his faithful men belonging to the county and lordship of Hainaut.

I. It has therefore been established as law that, if a man holding a fief marries a wife and has by her a daughter [Col. 0919D] but no son, that daughter shall succeed her father and mother in the fief.

II. If, after his first wife dies, a man takes another wife and has a son by her, the son shall succeed to his father’s fiefs, but not the daughter of the first wife.

III. It is likewise established as law that, if a man holding a fief has sons or daughters only, and the first son or first daughter has an heir of his or her own body and dies before the father, the heir of that first son or first daughter shall not succeed the grandfather in the fief. Rather, the nearest surviving heir—namely a son or daughter—shall succeed the deceased holder in possession of the fief.

IV. If a man holding a fief dies without an heir of his own body, [Col. 0920A] succession to the fief shall pass to his nearest heir, namely the one descended from that kinship from which the fief had previously descended.

V. The same law applies to a woman holding a fief, if she dies without an heir of her own body.

VI. If a man marrying a wife wishes to endow her with a fief, this must be done through the lord of the fief and by the testimony of that lord’s men.

VII. If a man dies without an heir of his own body, his wife shall retain nothing in his fiefs or allods which accrued by hereditary right from the husband's side, except only her dower and the movables upon the arable land of that year.

VIII. It is also established as law that, if a man and woman are joined in marriage and fiefs or allods come from the side of one or both of them, and the man or woman dies without an heir of his or her own body, the fiefs or allods which came from the side of the deceased man or woman shall immediately revert to their nearest heirs. Thus the husband shall retain nothing in his wife’s inheritance, nor the woman in her husband’s, except dower; but the movables of each upon the arable land of that year are preserved.

IX. If a man dies before his wife, his heir, if of age, shall immediately succeed his father in the fiefs; so that the wife shall retain nothing from them except the dower given to her and the movables of that year upon the arable land, which is commonly called *Wangnaule*.

X. [Col. 0920C] Likewise, if a woman dies before her husband, her heir, if of age, shall immediately succeed the mother in the fiefs; so that the husband shall retain nothing in them except the movables which are upon his arable land—that is, *Wangnale*—for that year.

XI. By law, a man’s age of majority is fifteen years, but a woman’s is twelve.

XII. It is likewise established by law that, if a man and his wife acquire a fief jointly, and the man dies without an heir of his own body, that fief must immediately devolve upon the man’s nearest heir; so that the nearest heir shall receive it from the lord of the fief, do homage to him, and possess the fortification, if there is one, and the homages pertaining to the fief. The wife, however, for as long as she lives, shall have one half [Col. 0920D] of the revenues and proceeds of that fief, without performing service or rendering justice to the lord of the fief; while the heir shall have the other half, for which he performs service and renders justice to the lord of the fief.

XIII. If a man and woman acquire an allod jointly, and the man dies without an heir of his own body, the woman shall hold the whole allod for as long as she lives; but after the woman’s death the entire allod shall pass to the husband’s nearest heirs.

XIV. If a woman dies, from whose side fiefs or allods have come, her husband shall have wardship of them, and of his children’s fiefs and goods, until his children attain their full age.

[Col. 0921A] XV. Likewise, if a man dies, from whose side fiefs or allods have come, the woman shall have the same wardship over her children and their fiefs and goods. The man, however, so long as he lives, shall hold the allods in the same manner.

XVI. If both a man and a woman die before their children have attained their age, the nearest heir of the children, who is nearest in that degree of kinship, shall have wardship over the children and their fiefs and allods until the children attain their age.

XVII. No serf may in any way alienate his allod of his own authority, or make it into a fief, without his lord’s consent.

XVIII. The bailiff of the count of Hainaut, appointed above all other bailiffs upon the testimony of the men of the lord [Col. 0921B] count, may not administer justice between one man and another, or exercise authority in all matters as though he were the lord count. Rather, the men of the lord count must fully administer justice on his behalf—namely, between one man and another, as for the lord count. That bailiff, moreover, may not plead concerning the possessions, tenures, or inheritance of the lord count in such a way that the count might lose possession through his judgment or act; nor may the bailiff summon any man of the lord count into suit or complaint concerning that man’s tenures or inheritance, except in the presence of the lord count.

XIX. In matters of movable property between the count and his men, however, the bailiff may plead at his discretion; and concerning chattels in an earlier action, judgments and complaints previously [Col. 0921C] adjudicated shall remain as they were adjudged.

XX. The lord count Baldwin of Flanders and Hainaut, and his faithful men—namely Philip, margrave of Namur, the count’s full brother; Henry, likewise the count’s full brother; Walter of Avesnes; Alard of Chimay; Rasso of Gavere; Gerard of Jacea; Nicholas of Barbençon; Eustace of Rues; William, uncle of the aforesaid lord count; William of Kevi; Rainer of Trith; Nicholas of Rumigny; Walter of Kavren; Giles of Trasegnies; Engelbert of Enghien; Henry, the count’s paternal uncle; Gerard of Saint-Aubert; William of Haussy; Adam of Vallencourt; Giles [Col. 0921D] of Blainmont; Arnulf of Oudenaarde; Walter of Sotteghem; Osto of Wadripont; Walter of Ville; Nicholas of Condé; Giles of Braine; Henry, castellan of Binche; Gerard, provost of Douai; Walter, castellan of Douai; Peter of Douai; Gerard, seneschal of Bulcheni; Stephen of Deneng; Arnulf of Kavren; Hugh of Saint-Aubert; William of Gommegnies; Gillen, castellan of Beaumont; Henry, castellan of Mons; Osto of Arbre; Hugh of Gaia; Renard of Strepy; Achard of Verli; Hugh of Crois; and many others—swore, having touched the most holy things, that they would observe all these provisions. They added to their oath that, if any of the men should presume to infringe these written laws in any respect, all the others [Col. 0922A] would stand against him for the full observance of all the foregoing.

Done at Mons in the Castle, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1200, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [28 July], Friday before the feast of Saint Peter in Chains.

## IV. Agreement between the King of England and the Count of Flanders and Hainaut. (A.D. 1200.)

*[Ibid., col. 771, from the same charter.]*

Let it be known to all who shall see this writing that this is the treaty and agreement between John, king of England, and Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, his kinsman: namely, that the said king of England shall not make, nor be able to make, peace or a truce with the king of France without the will and consent of that count; nor shall the same count make, or be able to make, peace or a truce with the king of France without the will and assent of the aforesaid king of England. And if, by the will and assent of both, peace or concord should be made between the king of France and them, and thereafter the king of France should make war upon either of them, the aforesaid king of England and count would be bound to afford one another mutual support and assistance, as best they could, and as they did when this treaty was made between them. And it is to be understood that this treaty and agreement is to endure not only in time of war, but forever between them and their heirs who shall hold their lands after them, whether there be peace or [Col. 0922C] war. Thus, if the king of England does not observe this treaty and agreement, those who have sworn, on behalf of the king of England, to maintain this treaty and agreement shall surrender themselves into the custody of the aforesaid count within a month after they have learned this in good faith, without awaiting a summons from the said count. Likewise, if the said count does not observe this treaty and agreement, those who have sworn, on behalf of that count, to maintain this treaty and agreement shall surrender themselves into the custody of the said king of England within a month after they have learned this in good faith, without awaiting a summons from the said king of England.

Robert, count of Leicester, swore that this should be observed in good faith on behalf of the king of England and upon the soul of that king; and that same count swore for himself upon his own soul. The others whose names are written below swore upon their souls that they would observe in good faith the same treaty and agreement: namely, William Marshal, earl of Pembroke; Ranulf, earl of Chester; Baldwin, count of Aumale; William of Arundel; Ralph, count of Eu; Robert, count of Meulan; Hugh of Gournay; William of Kaeu; Geoffrey of Celle; Roger, constable of Chester; Robert fitz Walter; William of Albini; Robert de Ros; Richard of Montfichet; Roger Etthoen; Saer de Quincy; William of Munchensy; Peter of Pratellis; William of Stangno; Adam of Port; Robert of Turnham; William Males; Eustace of Vescy; Peter de Brus; William of Humei, [Col. 0923A] constable of Normandy; William of Préaux; Hubert de Burgh; William of Mandeville; and Peter Savaric.

The aforesaid Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, swore with his own hand, upon his own soul, that this treaty and agreement should be observed in good faith. The others whose names are written below swore upon their souls that they would observe in good faith the same treaty and agreement on behalf of that count: namely, Henry, the count’s brother; William, the count’s uncle; Saer, castellan of Ghent; Hugh of Saint-Aubert; Rainer of Trith; Reginald of Aire; Gillen, castellan of Beaumont; Daniel of Courtrai; the provost of Bruges; Baldwin of Comines; Henry of Baillol; Thierry of Beverne; Gerard of [Col. 0923B] Rodes; Walter of Sotteghem; Bokard of Burgell; Walter, castellan of Douai; and Osto of Arbre.

These acts were performed before the king of England himself, at the castle of Roche-Andely, on the eighteenth day of August, in the first year of his reign.

## V. Charter of Baldwin, Count of Flanders, for the Monastery of Clairvaux—As he sets out for Jerusalem, moved by the holiness of the monks of Clairvaux, he makes them a donation. (A.D. 1202.)

*[MARTENE, ibid., from the cartulary of Clairvaux.]*

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I, BALDWIN, count of Flanders and Hainaut, wish it to be known to all that, as I was about to set out for Jerusalem and passed through the monastery of Clairvaux, strengthened by the sight of the holy community and, indeed, made more fervent in the love of God, I conceived, prompted by the example of so great a devotion, the intention of doing good to that place, Christian faith and religion leading the way. Since, however, after arranging my affairs and ordering my revenues, I was unable fully to provide, as I wished, for what I had conceived, I have meanwhile arranged at least a memorial beginning and earnest of the liberality I intend. I freely granted and generously assigned to them a perpetual alms for bread and wine necessary for the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood: namely, ten pounds in Valenciennes money, to be received ready money every year at my grange of Mons on the feast of [Col. 0923D] Saint Remigius, and conveyed to the aforesaid monastery by the hand of the abbot of Cambron.

For the salvation of my soul, of my dearest consort Mary, illustrious countess of Flanders and Hainaut, of my predecessors, and thereafter of my successors, I have solemnly ordained and granted this alms; and, that it may remain valid and unshaken forever, I have judged it fitting to confirm it by the protection of this present writing and the impression of my seal. By the same authority I likewise confirm all the alms and liberties which Philip, my uncle, formerly count of Flanders and Vermandois, a prince of illustrious memory and most renowned throughout the world, confirmed by his charters to that community of outstanding holiness, to be revered and observed perpetually by all posterity, as is contained in those same charters.

Done in the year of the Lord 1202, in the month of April.

## VI. Letter of M., Margrave of Montferrat, B., Count of Flanders, L., Count of Blois, and H., Count of Saint-Pol, to all Christ’s faithful—On the capture of the city of Constantinople. (A.D. 1203.)

*[MARTENE, ibid., col. 788, from an Elnone manuscript.]*

To all Christ’s faithful—to archbishops, bishops, the other prelates and clergy of churches, barons, knights, and serjeants—whom this letter may reach: M., margrave of Montferrat; B., count of Flanders and Hainaut; E., count of Blois and Clermont; [Col. 0924B] H., count of Saint-Pol; and the other barons and knights of the army of those marked with the cross in the Venetian fleet: may they so run the course that they attain the prize of the eternal calling.

With whatever brevity we can, we shall recount how great things the Lord has done for us—or rather, not for us but for his name; how great a glory he has given in our days. At the outset we observe that, from the time when we departed from the city of transgression—for so we call Zara, whose destruction we beheld, grieving indeed and driven by necessity—we remember that nothing was jointly planned among us for the army’s advantage which divine providence did not transform for the better, claim wholly for itself, and make our wisdom foolish. Therefore, rightly, we reject from ourselves all glory for the things gloriously accomplished among us, since we contributed little labor and no counsel. Hence, if any one of us wishes to glory, he must glory in the Lord, not in himself or another.

Accordingly, after an alliance had been confirmed at Zara with Alexius, son of Isaac, formerly the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, we lacked provisions and resources. We saw that we should bring burden rather than aid to the Holy Land, as did others of us who had preceded us; nor, in such want, did we believe ourselves able to reach the land of the Saracens. But, induced by entirely plausible reports and arguments that the greater and weightier part of the imperial city longed for the arrival of the said Alexius and would, by unanimous election and due solemnity, raise him to the imperial diadem, we arrived, contrary to all expectation, successfully and swiftly at the imperial city, with favorable weather and winds and sea obedient to the Lord.

Yet we did not arrive unanticipated: we found in the city up to sixty thousand horsemen besides the infantry. Passing without loss to our men over its most secure positions, bridges, towers, and rivers, we besieged by land and sea alike the city and the tyrant, who, by murdering his brother, had polluted the imperial office through long usurpation. Contrary to all expectation, therefore, we found the minds of all the citizens hardened against us; and they barred their city against their lord with walls and engines no differently than if an unbelieving people had come, intending to defile holy places and ruthlessly to uproot the Christian religion.

Indeed, the most cruel usurper of the empire—the betrayer and despoiler of his lord and brother, who had condemned him without guilt to perpetual prison, and who would have done the same to his illustrious son Alexius had happy exile not rescued him from his hands—had, after carrying on a detestable agitation among the people, infected both powerful men and commoners with speeches so venomous that he asserted that the Latins had come to overthrow their ancient liberty, restore city and nation to the Roman pontiff, and subject the empire to Latin laws. This, assuredly, so emboldened and armed all alike against us that, though we asked to be heard by the citizens concerning ourselves, our exile, and our barons, we could explain neither the reason for our arrival nor the form of our request. Whenever, standing on the wall by land or sea, we offered words, we received missiles instead of words.

[Col. 0925B] Seeing, therefore, that everything was occurring beyond our expectation, we were driven into such necessity that we had at once either to perish or to conquer. We could not prolong the siege beyond fifteen days by any means, because an incredible shortage of all provisions pressed us. Not in desperation, but with a certain divinely inspired confidence, we began eagerly to expose ourselves boldly to the dangers of war, most ready for every peril, and to prevail incredibly in all things. Often drawn up also for battle in the open field, we shut up an innumerable multitude in the city by disgraceful flight.

Meanwhile, having fitted out the instruments of war by land and sea, on the eighth day of the siege we forcibly entered the city, and fire spread through it. The emperor drew up battle-lines against us in the field; but, when we were ready to receive those advancing, he marvelled at our steadfastness despite our small numbers, turned his bridle in disgrace, and returned to the burning city. That night he undertook flight with a few men, leaving his wife and little child in the city. Once this became known, unknown to us, the Greek nobles assembled in the palace; the solemn election—or rather, the declared restoration—of our exile was celebrated, and abundant lights in the palace proclaimed their unexpected joy.

[Col. 0925D] When morning came, an unarmed multitude of Greek nobles came out to the camp and joyfully sought their chosen ruler. They declared liberty restored to the city, and showed the person of their father Isaac, the former emperor, raised from prison, with inexpressible joy at the returning son’s accession to imperial authority. Therefore, after the arrangements deemed necessary had been made, the new emperor was led in solemn procession to the church of Saint Sophia. The imperial diadem, with the fullness of power, was restored to our exile without any opposition.

Once this had been accomplished, the emperor hastened to fulfil his promises and added deeds to promises. He supplied provisions for a year, to be used in the Lord’s service.
