He proceeded to pay us and the Venetians the thousands of marks withheld; at his own expense he extended the fleet’s service for us for a year; and he bound himself by oath to raise the royal standard with us and, at the March passage, set out with us for the Lord’s service with as many thousands of armed men as he could. Under the same promise he undertook to render to the Roman pontiff the reverence which his Catholic imperial predecessors are known formerly to have rendered to their predecessor pontiffs, and to incline the Eastern Church to do the same insofar as he could.

Moved by such great advantages, lest we seem to despise the salvation which the Lord had placed in our hands and turn into everlasting reproach what appeared to have fallen to us beyond comparison with any human achievement, [Col. 0926B] we consented with ready devotion. We have bound ourselves, by a purpose as firm as it is irrevocable and by a willing oath, to winter there, God granting, and to cross toward Egypt at the next passage. And now we wish you to know that, in the bowels of Christ Jesus, we ardently desire all of you to share in this joy and glory. To this end, envoys of the said emperor and of ourselves have already been sent to the sultan of Babylon, the impious occupier of the Holy Land. On behalf of our king Jesus Christ of Nazareth and his servants—the said emperor and ourselves—they are to announce to him in a kingly manner, as is fitting, that we propose shortly, God granting, to display the devotion of the Christian people to his unbelieving nation, and that we await from heaven the power to crush unbelief.

We have done these things, trusting under the Lord rather in your strength than in our own. We desire that you be joined to us all the more devotedly and earnestly as we see better and more numerous servants of our king fighting with us, lest he who was once handed over to the Jews in Galilee to be mocked should henceforth be left to the nations. We have also taken care to communicate these same things to our brothers who await our arrival in the Holy Land, earnestly desiring by every means in the Lord that both we and they, zealous for the Christian name, should share as brothers in the consolation which the Lord has given us.

We therefore humbly beseech you, venerable fathers and prelates of churches, that the living and efficacious word of divine exhortation may be spread among the people; that you may rouse volunteers in the law to bring their purpose to completion; and that you may manfully encourage them to seize the glory of valor which the Lord deigns to offer them for very slight labor. We also seek hearers of the word who will be doers as well, with ready and manly courage. For a great door has been opened to them, so that a small measure of tribulation and labor will win for them not only a temporal name but will also produce in them an eternal weight of glory. For they do not face the hard and almost unbearable magnitude of toil that has passed over our backs, a burden which the power from heaven has mercifully made lighter for us.

## IX. Letter of Baldwin, Emperor of Constantinople, to the Bishops of Cambrai, Arras, Thérouanne, and Tournai—He announces the hope conceived for the recovery of the Holy Land and asks them to exhort the nobles to cross the sea.

*(MARTENE, ibid., col. 791, from the same manuscript.)*

[Col. 0927B]

BALDWIN, by the grace of God most faithful emperor in Christ, crowned by God, ruler of the Romans, ever august, count of Flanders and Hainaut, to his venerable and dearest friends in Christ, the bishops of Cambrai, Arras, Thérouanne, and Tournai by that same grace: his favor and every good thing.

We recall that we have fully set forth to you by our letters and envoys our position and progress, and that of the entire Christian army: by what wondrous dispensation the Lord has, through the ministry of the Christian army, procured unity for his Church. From this, as wise men infer by evident reasoning, a door and access will plainly be opened for the assistance of the Holy Land. For pilgrims will henceforth not only have a free passage through us, but, in addition to the not inconsiderable strength which we have already, by God’s grace, and which we have wholly dedicated to that land, fruitful grace will also furnish them abundance of provisions.

With all our heart we yearn for the liberation of the land in which Life, having died, triumphed over death. Since he himself became both its purpose and its price for us, we shall never desist while we live, until, besides so many favors already granted, God’s Salvation shall also reveal itself to us in this matter. Yet because we dare undertake so great and solemn a business under God not from our own sufficiency but with the assistance of all Christ’s faithful, we earnestly beseech your love to kindle, by salutary admonitions, both nobles and common people established in your bishoprics toward this same purpose. Know that we are ready and able to receive all who come to us, according to their rank and circumstances, with generous grants of possessions and honors.

Furthermore, we urgently ask you to commend in your churches, by your prayers and supplications, both our person and the coadjutors of the empire; and to urge the clergy and people entrusted to you to do the same, so that the Lord Jesus, for whose inheritance we have resolved to labor unceasingly, may not cease, as he has begun, to preserve both us and our empire.

## X. Letters of Baldwin, Emperor of Constantinople, by which he revokes his seal. (A.D. 1204.)

*[MARTENE, ibid., p. 793, from the cartulary of the lords of Avesnes at Hasnon.]*

B., by the grace of God most faithful emperor in Christ, crowned by God, ruler of the Romans, and ever [Col. 0928C] august, count of Flanders and Hainaut, to all whom this letter shall reach, greeting.

Know that, from the time of our coronation—that is, from the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June [16 May]—we have decreed that our former seal, which is appended to this letter, shall have no force. If anything has been sealed with it from the said time onward—which we do not believe—we judge it altogether false, void, and without effect.

Given in the year of the Lord 1204, in the month of June.

# APPENDIX TO BALDWIN, EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Col. 0927]

# GENEALOGIES OF THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS, EDITED BY L. C. BETHMANN

*(PERTZ, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. IX, p. 302.)*

## I. WITGER’S GENEALOGY OF COUNT ARNULF

All the genealogies of the counts of Flanders known to us originated at Saint-Bertin and in its vicinity. The most ancient among them is that composed between 951 and 959 by the priest Witger, apparently living at Compiègne.

[Note: [Col. 0927C] For in 951 Baldwin married Matilda, whom our author mentions; in 959 his mother Adela died; and the words “may his distinguished father and mother see their children’s children” appear to have been written while she was still alive.]

[Col. 0929] We have transcribed it from the autograph manuscript, formerly of Saint-Bertin and now no. 776 of the municipal library of Saint-Omer.

[Note: [Col. 0929C] Compare *Pertz, Archiv*, VIII, 419.]

There, among many leaves written at different times and bound into one volume only two centuries ago, are preserved these three folios, written in Witger’s own hand in the middle of the tenth century, in a square script, divided into lines, each marked by a single red letter. We too have retained this division. From this manuscript derives a recent copy of the twelfth century, Amiens Library no. 498, formerly no. 356. A. Hermand first published it in *Mémoires de la Société des Antiquaires de la Morinie*, vol. II; Warnkönig then published the latter part in De Smet, *Corpus Chronicorum Flandriae*, Brussels, 1837, quarto, I, 42; and again in *Flandrische Rechtsgeschichte*, III, 197.

HERE [Note: [Col. 0929] “Here” was restored by Hermand; the text had already been cut away.] BEGINS THE GENEALOGY OF THE MOST NOBLE EMPERORS AND KINGS OF THE FRANKS, COMPOSED BY KING CHARLES, RESTORER OF THE PLACE OF COMPIÈGNE, AFTER TWO FIRES.

[Col. 0929A]

The most noble Ansbert begot Arnold by Blithild, daughter of Clothar, king of the Franks; and also Feriol, Moderic, and Tarsicia.

Arnold begot Arnulf. Arnulf begot Flodulf, Walchis, and Anschis.

Walchis begot Wandregisil, confessor of the Lord.

Duke Anschis begot Pippin the Elder.

Pippin the Elder and duke begot Charles the Elder.

Charles the Elder and duke begot Pippin, [Note: [Col. 0929] Up to this point everything has been taken from the Fontenelle genealogy in Pertz, *Scriptores*, II, 308.] Carloman, Grifo, and Bernard by the queen; [Col. 0929B] Remigius and Jerome by a concubine.

King Pippin begot Charles, Carloman, and Gisela by Queen Bertrada.

Emperor Charles begot by Queen Hildegard Charles, Louis, and Pippin, Rothrude, and Bertha; and by a concubine Drogo, Hugh, and Rothaid.

Emperor Louis begot by Queen Ermengard Lothar, Pippin, and Louis, Rothrude, and Hildegard; and by Empress Judith Charles and Gisela.

Emperor Lothar begot Louis, Lothar [Note: [Col. 0929] *tharium* has been cut away in the manuscript.] and Charles by Queen Ermengard.

King Louis begot Carloman, Louis, and Charles by Queen Emma.

[Col. 0929C] King Carloman begot King Arnulf.

King Arnulf begot Louis by Queen Oda, but Zventibold by a concubine.

Emperor Charles begot by Queen Ermentrude four sons and an equal number of daughters: Louis, Charles, Carloman, and Lothar; and Judith [Note: [Col. 0929] “Concerning Judith, you will find more at length on the first page.” Witger wrote this in the margin, in ink darker than the rest, the same ink with which he wrote the cross and the entire descent of Arnulf.] as well as Hildegard, Ermentrude, and Gisela.

King Louis begot Louis, Carloman, and Hildegard by the woman called Queen Ansgard; and also the posthumous Charles and Ermentrude by Queen Adelaide.

[Col. 0930A] King Charles begot by Queen Frederuna Ermentrude, Frederuna, Adelaide, Gisela, Rothrude, and Hildegard; but by a concubine Arnulf, Drogo, Roric, and Alpaid. Finally, after Queen Frederuna died, he took another queen in marriage, named Ogiva, by whom he begot a son of handsome appearance named Louis. And afterward, by Queen Gerberga, Lothar, Charles [Note: [Col. 0929] “Karol” has been cut away. A plainly contemporary hand repeated in the lower margin the words: “And afterward, by Queen Gerberga: Lothar, Louis, and Matilda.” It thus appears that the manuscript was mutilated, as it now is, shortly after it was written. Moreover, it is certain that everything from “And afterward” through Louis Beyond-the-Seas pertains to Charles’s son Louis, husband of Gerberga, who died in 954. His father Charles the Simple died in 929.] Louis, and Matilda.

HERE BEGINS THE HOLY DESCENT OF LORD COUNT ARNULF, MOST GLORIOUS, AND OF HIS SON BALDWIN, WHOM MAY THE LORD DEIGN TO PROTECT IN THIS WORLD.

The most valiant Count Baldwin joined to himself in marriage the most prudent and beautiful Judith (863).

[Col. 0930B] By her he begot a son, giving him his own name, namely Baldwin.

This Baldwin, having taken a wife from the most noble stock of the overseas kings, begot by her two sons of good character. One he called Arnulf; the other, his brother, Adelulf.

The latter, released by God’s permission from the burden of this world, is known to have been buried in the monastery of Saint Bertin, confessor of Christ (933).

But if he had lived through a longer span of time in this world, he would have been a very great joy and strength to his own people.

But Lord Count Arnulf, most venerable and most loving toward the Lord Jesus Christ, outstanding in prudence, powerful in counsel, shining in every goodness, the most perfect restorer of God’s churches, the most pious comforter of widows, [Col. 0930C] orphans, and fatherless children, and the most merciful provider of aid to all who seek it from him in necessity—

[Note: [Col. 0929] Hermand supplied the cut-off ending *-nsator*.]

What more need be said? Even if someone had a hundred mouths and tongues, he could never recount the gifts of his benefactions.

But since we cannot adequately speak in any way of his countless good deeds, we shall mention a few out of many.

There is in the palace at Compiègne a monastery dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God, [Col. 0931A] which he has honored with many gifts, namely gold, silver, and vestments.

He also frequently distributed most generously a great abundance of money among the clerics there serving the Lord.

We know that the bier of the holy witnesses of Christ, Cornelius and Cyprian, was adorned by him with the purest silver, weighing ten pounds.

He gave to that holy place the most noble signal, which is also called a bell. This is not surprising,

because the aforesaid place had been wholly founded in marvellous fashion by his great-grandfather, Emperor Charles, who was called the Bald.

That same venerable Count Arnulf took a wife named Adela (934), [Col. 0931B] daughter of Lord Count Heribert [Note: [Col. 0931] *comitis fi-* (“daughter of the count”) has been cut away.] and niece of two kings of the Franks, namely Odo [Note: [Col. 0931] *scilic-* has been cut away.] and Robert.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] The silence of our author concerning the alleged miraculous cure of Countess Adela in the church of Saint-Bertin in 938 might be considered a kind of denial of that event, asserted by Iperius. Had this miracle occurred, Witger, who gives a panegyric of Arnulf, would probably not have failed to emphasize it brilliantly; at the very least, he would have added to Arnulf’s praises that this prince appeared especially protected by God through the healing of his wife, because of his generosity toward the ministers of religion. HERMAND. This miracle is already recorded in the Bertin manuscript, now Saint-Omer no. 746, of the end of the eleventh century; that codex is the final part of Boulogne no. 113. It is narrated under the title: “Account by the monk Eremdolf of the arrival at Sithiu in the year 938 of Athela, called in the Teutonic language, when translated, ‘Most Noble,’ countess,” written in an eleventh-century hand.]

By her, with God’s protection, he begot a son of handsome appearance, named Baldwin, beautiful in countenance, beloved by God and in every respect dear to his faithful men: a most noble count, following his father’s example a lover of God’s churches, humble, gentle, devout, modest, kind, sober, and moreover filled with every goodness.

When he reached lawful age, by God’s grant and his father’s will, he took as wife one worthy of his nobility, Matilda by name (951), daughter of the most noble prince called Herman.

May his distinguished [Col. 0931C] father and mother, through the gift of heavenly grace, see their children’s children, if [Col. 0932A] it please God, even to the third and fourth generation, with bodily health granted to them, complete safety, and absolution from all sins, now here and in the age of ages. Amen.

May this come to pass through the mercy of almighty God the Father from heaven. Amen. May this come to pass through the granting of the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son and our Lord. Amen. May this come to pass through the bestowal of the heavenly grace of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, proceeding from the Father and the Son. Amen. Amen. Amen.

The priest named Witger wishes this, [Note: [Col. 0931] I have restored the text thus; *lictus* has been cut away, leaving only the earlier part of the letter *d*.]

that salvation may be with the count so named for a long time.

Amen. Amen. Amen. Amen. Amen. Amen. Amen. Amen.

Whoever reads through this venerable genealogy [Col. 0932B] of Lord ARNULF, the most renowned prince of this age, and of his most noble son BALDWIN, let him pray for them without ceasing, and say and cry out with a pure heart:

**PRAYER FOR LORD ARNULF AND HIS SON BALDWIN.**

Almighty God, strong ruler, merciful and compassionate, King of kings and Lord of lords, save Lord Count ARNULF, most glorious, and his God-beloved son named BALDWIN. Rule, guard, protect, and defend them; keep and sustain, exalt and strengthen, fortify and make them steadfast, on every day of their lives in this present world. After a long life in this world, through the interceding merits of all the saints, may they deserve to attain the glory of paradise, by the gift of him by whom they were created. Amen. Amen. Amen. Amen. Amen. [Col. 0932C] Amen. Amen.

## II. ON COUNT ARNULF

[Col. 0931]

The most reverend Francis Vandeputte, abbot, first published the following short notice in *Annales de la Société d’Émulation de la Flandre Occidentale*, I, 3, 228 and II, 3, 69. It is written on the back of a diploma drawn up in the tenth century, in another hand, apparently of the eleventh century, as he judges; it was written by a monk of Saint Peter’s at Ghent, as appears from the conclusion. With his most gracious permission, we reproduce it here.

[Col. 0931D] Arnulf, the great margrave, who was called “the Crippled,” begot by Adela, daughter of Herbert, count of Vermandois, a son named Baldwin (962). This Baldwin begot by Matilda a son, the younger Arnulf, and, overtaken by untimely death, perished of smallpox. But Arnulf the elder entrusted Baldwin’s son, namely the younger Arnulf, to his kinsman Baldwin, surnamed Baldzo, to be reared and guarded; and he placed this same Baldzo in charge of the government of the whole dominion until the younger Arnulf should grow up. For this Baldzo was the son of Adalulf, who was the half-brother by the same mother of Arnulf the great; he begot Baldzo by a concubine, and Baldzo perished, slain by mischance by his own swineherd in a certain wood [Col. 0933A] (933). Then Arnulf adopted the son of his slain brother in the place of a son to himself, and afterwards appointed him guardian and fosterer of his grandson, the younger Arnulf [Col. 0934A]. This is that Baldwin surnamed Baldzo who granted to Saint Peter, from his own inheritance, the village of Traslingehem with its appurtenances.

## III. THE BERTINIAN GENEALOGY OF THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS

[Col. 0933]

Under Robert II, who died in 1111, there was composed at Saint-Bertin, as it seems, a genealogy [Note: [Col. 0933C] I infer this from the words “is buried at Saint-Bertin” concerning Baldwin, since the burial of no other count is indicated.] which, continued by several persons and already taken up in 1120 by Lambert, canon of Saint-Omer, became the foundation of all those that followed. This was the first to make Lidric, Ingelram, and Audacer the earliest counts of Flanders [Note: [Col. 0933C] How doubtful is the character of Lidric’s countship of Flanders is sufficiently well known; no testimonies earlier than the eleventh century survive. Yet the Annals of Blandin, before 1064, compiled from older sources, have the following in *Monumenta SS.* V, 20: “836. Count Lidric died and was buried at Harlebeke.” Moreover, in the assembly of Servais of the year 853, *Monumenta Legum* I, there occur envoys in the counties of Noyon, Vermandois, Artois, Kortrijk, and Flanders, belonging to Engilram, who can be none other than Lidric’s son. But there is no sound reason why we should believe that the Engilram cited from the assembly of Quierzy in 858 (*ibid.* I, 458) is our man, any more than Count Ingelram in 870 (*ibid.* 516) and in 864 (*SS.* I, 378). In the narrowness of these dates, the difficulties would be insoluble; they are not so in the case of our Ingelram, still living in 853 [Col. 0933D]. To resolve these chronological difficulties Vredius, Bylandt, Loys, and others maintained that Audacer never existed, but was a byname of Baldwin. But in the Annals of Blandin Baldwin is twice called son of Auaacri, in 826 and 879. Whether Audacer was count of Flanders, however, is quite doubtful, as are many matters concerning the beginnings of this county. Indeed, under the year 870—that is, while Baldwin Iron-Arm was alive—the contemporary Annals of Saint-Vaast have: “The aforesaid brothers approach Charles, king of the Franks, and Arnulf, count of Flanders, and take counsel together as to what should be done. But Charles, king of the Franks, and Arnulf, consul of the Flemings, having summoned their bishops and princes,” etc.], whereas earlier genealogies traced the line only from Baldwin onward. The principal manuscript used by Lambert has perished; the following, however, are available to us:

1. The Saint-Vaast manuscript, now lost but transcribed by Martène, who calls it eleventh-century. Lambert also used this.

2. The Bertinian manuscript, now Boulogne no. 142, a folio of the late thirteenth century.

3. The Marchiennes manuscript, now Douai no. 698, contains the same genealogy written on its final folio in a twelfth-century hand, which carried it down in a continuous hand to 1127; three further hands, succeeding one another five times, continued it.

4. The Formoselle manuscript, now Brussels no. 8673, contains the annals already published by us in the fifth volume; another twelfth-century hand added this genealogy in the margin, much altered in wording.

5. Leiden Public Library, Latin no. 20, parchment folio, twelfth century. There, on a blank page, another hand of the early thirteenth century copied the same genealogy, changing much both in wording and especially at the end, and continuing it in a continuous hand.

5*. This same Leiden exemplar, with a few additions and omissions, was copied again and carried in the same hand down to 1279 in Dijon manuscript no. 322; see Pertz, *Archiv*, VII, 353. I believe this is the same manuscript as the Cistercian one used by Brial.

It was published by Brial, XIII, 417, from 1 and 5*; and by De Smet, *Corpus chronicorum Flandriae* I, 9, from 2.

[THE GENEALOGY BEGINS.]

[Col. 0933A]

[Col. 0933B] Lidric [Note: [Col. 0933] Hildric, 1.] count of Harlebeke begot Ingelram [Note: [Col. 0933] Ingelram, 2; Lambert.]. Ingelram begot [Note: [Col. 0933] omitted in 2 and 4.] Audacer. Audacer begot [Note: [Col. 0933] omitted in 2 and 4.] Baldwin Iron-Arm, who married Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald [Note: [Col. 0933] Judith, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0934C] In 863 at Auxerre. Baldwin died in 879.]. Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0933] 1 adds “indeed”; Judith, from whom he begot, 4.] Iron-Arm begot Baldwin the Bald, who married the daughter of Edgar [Note: [Col. 0933] Etger, 3; Aedger, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0934C] False. She was Ælfthryth, daughter of Alfred the Great, who died in 929.] king of the English, named Ælfthryth [Note: [Col. 0933] Elferad, 1; Elferud, Lambert; “begetting Arnulf by her,” 4.]. Baldwin, who married Richilde, widow of Hermann, count of Mons, by whom he begot Baldwin and Arnulf. Their paternal uncle Robert married Gertrude, daughter of Bernard, count of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0936C] Rather, duke.], widow of Florent, count of the Frisians, and with her held her realm. Having received a very great sum of money from his father, he renounced Flanders under oath [Col. 0935B] [Note: [Col. 0936C] At Oudenaarde, in 1063; see Lambert’s *Annals* under 1071 on these matters.], which he granted by hereditary right to his brother Baldwin and his successors. During his brother’s life Robert kept quiet; but after his death, with the help of traitors, he killed his nephew Arnulf, count of Flanders, at Cassel, and deceitfully obtained his realm. By the aforesaid widow Gertrude he begot Philip and Count Robert. Robert married Clementia, daughter of William, duke [Note: [Col. 0936C] Count.] of Burgundy, by whom he begot [Col. 0935C] William and Count Baldwin. Baldwin, moreover, married the daughter of Alan Fergant, count of Brittany [Note: [Col. 0935] Here 1 ends.].

### CONTINUATION OF MARCHIENNES

William dies before his father. Baldwin also having died without an heir, Charles, son of Cnut, king of Denmark, by a daughter of the earlier Robert, received the county. When he had been innocently slain, William, son of Robert, count of Normandy (from here another contemporary hand), obtained the county (1127). After him came Thierry, duke of Alsace. He was succeeded by his son Philip. From here another hand of the late twelfth century.) When Philip died overseas (1191), Baldwin, count of Hainaut [Col. 0936A], received the county. His son of the same name succeeded not long afterwards to both counties. (From here, in different ink but by the same hand.) This Baldwin begot by his wife two daughters, Joan and Margaret; and afterwards he went to the land of Constantinople, where he was crowned king and emperor (1204). Afterwards he was captured in battle; by what end he died is unknown. But his daughter Joan held both counties, Hainaut and Flanders. She married the brother of the king of Portugal, named Ferdinand. (The ink changes again.) King Philip of France made war upon him, led an army into Flanders, and captured him in battle at the bridge of Bouvines. There the count himself, almost deserted by all his men, resisted for a long time by fighting manfully; [Col. 0936B] at last wounded, he was captured (1214) and taken to Paris with many of his barons, who were likewise captured, where he was held by the king himself for thirteen years. Afterwards (the hand ends at the bottom of the page; another of the late thirteenth century follows), when Joan died (1244) without heirs, her sister Margaret obtained both counties. Since Margaret had children by two husbands, it was ordained while she was alive that after her death John of Avesnes, the son she had borne to her first husband, should have the county of Hainaut, while the county of Flanders should remain to the heirs of the other husband. At her death (10 February 1280), she was succeeded by John, son of her son John, in the county of Hainaut, and by Guy, her son, in the county [Col. 0936C] of Flanders.

Bert.] Lidric [Note: [Col. 0935] Hidric, 5, through the rubricator’s error. “In the year 793 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of Charles the Great, king of the Franks, L. ruled in Flanders, who begot …,” 5*.] begot Ingelram. Baldwin Iron-Arm begot Baldwin the Bald, who married Heldrada, daughter of Otger, king of the English. Arnulf the Great begot Baldwin, who died of smallpox before his father’s death and was buried at Saint-Bertin. He married Matilda, daughter of Hermann, duke of Saxony, by whom he begot Arnulf the Bearded. Left [Col. 0937A] a widow, Matilda married Godfrey, duke of Ename. Arnulf the Bearded [Note: [Col. 0937] “this,” 5*; where “Matilda” through “the Bearded” is omitted.] married Susanna, daughter of Berengar, king of the Lombards, and [Note: [Col. 0937] “by whom,” 5*.] begot Baldwin the Bearded, who married Ogiva, daughter of Count Giselbert, and afterwards married the daughter of Richard II, duke of the Normans [Note: [Col. 0937] “and … Normans” omitted in 5*.] [Note: [Col. 0937D] Eleanor.]. Baldwin the Bearded begot Baldwin of Lille, who married Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the Franks. Baldwin of Lille begot Baldwin of Hainaut and Robert the Bearded. Baldwin of Hainaut begot Arnulf and Baldwin by Richilde. After the death of Baldwin of Hainaut, his son Arnulf was count; Robert, his paternal uncle, killed him in a battle at Cassel (22 February 1071), although King Philip of France supported Arnulf’s party [Note: [Col. 0937] “favoured,” 5*.]; and he expelled Baldwin, Arnulf’s brother, with his mother, [Col. 0937B] and married Gertrude, widow of Florent, count of Holland [Note: [Col. 0937] Hodanth, 5; Holland, 5.], by whom he begot Robert and Philip. After some years he went to Jerusalem; returning thence after two years and living quietly for a few years, he died and was buried at Cassel in the church of Saint Peter, which he himself had built (13 October 1093). His son Robert married [Note: [Col. 0937] “Robert, his son, succeeded him and married,” 5*.] Clementia, daughter of William, count of Burgundy, by whom he begot Baldwin and William. When Robert died in Francia [Note: [Col. 0937] Frisia, 5; Francia near Meaux, 5*, which is correct.] and was buried at Arras (5 October 1111), his son Baldwin received the county of Flanders, his brother William having already died. When Baldwin died childless and was buried at Saint-Bertin (1119), Charles, son of his aunt and of Canute, king of the Danes, succeeded him. When he was [Note: [Col. 0937] “by his own men at Bruges,” added in 5*.] killed [Col. 0937C] in the year 1127 of the Lord, without children, William succeeded for two years; his father was Robert, and his grandfather William, count of the Normans and king of the English [Note: [Col. 0937] “Robert, who was son of William the Bastard, duke of the Normans and king of the English,” 5*.], who married Matilda, sister of Robert the Frisian and grandmother of Baldwin. When he too had been killed without children [Note: [Col. 0937] “at the castle called Aalst,” added in 5*.], Thierry, son of the duke [Note: [Col. 0937] count, 5*.] of Alsace by Baldwin’s third aunt, received the county. He married Sibylla, daughter of Fulk, count of Anjou, by whom he begot Philip, Matthew, Peter, and [Col. 0938A] three [Note: [Col. 0937D] Four; cf. *L’Art de vérifier les dates*.] daughters (1134), of whom the eldest married Amadeus, count of Intermont [Note: [Col. 0937] Here 5* ends. “He married … Intermont” omitted in 5*, which has instead “He therefore had three daughters,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0937D] Gertrude first married Humbert III, count of Savoy.]:

**The Dijon and Cistercian manuscripts add:**

Robert, surnamed the Frisian, therefore had three daughters and one sister [Note: [Col. 0937D] Rather, a stepdaughter, Bertha, daughter of Florent by Gertrude [Col. 0938D]. Brial.]. The first [Note: [Col. 0938D] Adela.] married Canute, king of the Danes, and was afterwards married by Roger, duke of Apulia; the second [Note: [Col. 0938D] Bertha, stepdaughter of the Frisian.] married Philip, king of the Franks, by whom she bore King Louis; the third [Note: [Col. 0938D] Gertrude.] married Thierry, count of Alsace, by whom was begotten Thierry, count of Flanders. He married Sibylla, daughter of Fulk, count of Anjou, who afterwards became famous as king of Jerusalem; by her he begot four sons, Baldwin, Philip, Matthew, and Peter. Baldwin having died in childhood, Philip received the county of Flanders, Matthew the county of Boulogne [Col. 0938B], and Peter the provostships of Bruges and Saint-Omer. When Philip died childless (1191), his nephew by his sister, Baldwin, count of Hainaut, succeeded him; he afterwards became emperor of Constantinople. At his death he left two daughters, Joan and Margaret. The first, succeeding her father in the county, married Ferdinand, nephew through a daughter of the king of Portugal. Having made a conspiracy with Emperor Otto, King John of England, and Reginald, count of Boulogne, he fought against his lord Philip, king of France (1214); in this battle Ferdinand was defeated and captured with Reginald, count of Boulogne. After his death, the aforesaid Joan married again Thomas, brother of the count of Savoy. When she died childless (1244), [Col. 0938C] her sister Margaret received the county. While she was young and in the custody of Burchard of Avesnes, brother of Walter, count of Blois, Burchard begot by her two sons, John and Baldwin. She afterwards married the noble William, lord of Dampierre (1218), by whom she bore three children, William, Guy, and John. When the first of these died childless at a tournament at Trasegnies, while his mother was still alive, his brother Guy received the county in his place (1279).

## IV. GENEALOGY OF THE KINGS OF THE FRANKS AND COUNTS OF FLANDERS

[Col. 0937]

Under this title Lambert, canon of Saint-Omer, presents on folio 105 of the *Liber Floridus* a poem, here first published from the Ghent autograph of 1120. It was therefore composed in 1120; whether by Lambert himself [Col. 0939] or another is uncertain, though the former is more likely. The metre is trochaic, though not consistent: individual verses have now seven, now six theses, but everywhere eight arses.

| Princes of the Franks and Flemings, noble men, | Priam, duke of Troy, was their beginning. |
|---|---|
| After the destruction of the city, he departed from Phrygia, | he himself and Antenor came together into Pannonia. |
| Priam also having been slain, Marcomerus’ son | set out to the furthest borders of the Germans. |
| From Marcomerus came one named Pharamond, | whom the Frankish people raised as king over themselves. |
| Begotten by Pharamond, the unconquered King Clodio | reigned twenty years in the castle of Disbargium. |
| Merovech, king of the Franks, from his line | begot Childeric, given over to lust. |
| Childeric then begot the renowned Clovis; | Clovis indeed begot Lothair. |
| But King Lothair, the great Chilperic; | King Chilperic likewise begot Lothair. |
| The great King Lothair produced Dagobert; | Dagobert in turn begot Clovis. |
| Then King Theuderic, son of Clovis, | produced Childebert, who was a famous king. |
| Childebert indeed begot Dagobert, | who, reigning five years, died without offspring. |
| Afterwards Arnulf, by Blithilda, daughter of Lothair, | son of Duke Ansbert, held the sceptre of the kingdom. |
| Arnulf begot King Arnulf, then the bishop of Metz; | he begot Anchises, and Anchises Pepin. |
| Charles Martel, indeed, from noble Pepin | begot little Pepin, father of the great Charles. |
| From Charlemagne came noble Louis, | king of the Franks and renowned emperor of the Romans. |
| The emperor Louis the Pious, King Charles the Bald, | begot him who held the empire of the Romans. |
| From Charles the Bald came his daughter Judith; | she followed Baldwin Iron-Arm into Flanders. |
| Judith bore Baldwin the Bald to Baldwin; | From the Bald came great Arnulf, who begot Baldwin. |
| Baldwin then begot Arnulf by Matilda; | Arnulf begot Baldwin, builder of Blandin. |
| Baldwin begot Baldwin, buried at Lille; | Baldwin of Lille begot Robert by Adela. |
| From Robert, who was born of royal stock, | came another Robert, an unconquered knight. |
| Robert, conqueror of enemies at Jerusalem, | begot Baldwin, Clementia’s son. |
| He subdued the enemies of the realm in frequent wars; | reigning a short time, he died without offspring. |
| Then Charles, this count’s nephew, succeeded; | noble King Canute begot him by Adela. |
| And Canute having been slain, Adela with the boy | returned to Flanders, leaving the faithless Danes. |
| Thus sprung from royal stock, Charles | became heir of the realm and count of Flanders. |

## V. LAMBERT’S GENEALOGY OF THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS

[Col. 0939]

Lambert, son of Onulf, who died in 1077, canon of Saint-Omer, in 1120 wove together for God and Saint Audomar, our gracious patron, a book from the flowers of diverse authors, which, since reason so required, he entitled the *Floridus*. There, among very many disparate matters, on folio 104 is read a genealogy, arranged, as we believe, by Lambert himself: transcribing the Bertinian genealogy word for word, he expanded it from the annals of Hincmar of Reims and elsewhere, and carried it down to his own times. Shortly after 1164 this little work of Lambert served as the foundation for the genealogy which we shall give immediately after it; shortly after 1128 it was enlarged by a very brief continuation, whose author is unknown. We present it from the autograph manuscript, formerly of Saint-Omer and then Saint Bavo’s, now at Ghent University; it is discussed by Pertz, *Archiv* VII, 540; Jules de Saint-Genois, *Messager de Gand* (1845), p. 473; and by us in *Serapeum* (1845), p. 59. From it were copied Paris, *Supplément latin* 10 bis, thirteenth century; Paris, *Supplément latin* 107, of 1429; Douai 741, fifteenth century; Leiden, Vossian Latin 31, fourteenth century, formerly Alexander Petau’s, with a continuation not found in the other manuscripts mentioned; and Wolfenbüttel, among the Gudian manuscripts 1, thirteenth century, with the same continuation. The Hague no. 759, of 1460, was copied from the Wolfenbüttel manuscript in the town of Ninove; its French version survives in The Hague manuscript 759a, made in 1512 by order of Philip of Cleves. Brussels 16531, formerly of Blandin, sixteenth century, discussed by us in Pertz, *Archiv* VIII, 531, likewise derives from the Saint-Omer manuscript; a later copy of it is Paris, among the Baluze papers, arm. II, packet 1, no. 3. Labbe published the genealogy in *Concilia* X, 578, from a manuscript of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu, but only a small portion; Brial published it complete in *Recueil* XIV, 520, from a copy now preserved among the Duchesne manuscripts no. 93; Warnkönig in *Flandrische Rechtsgeschichte* I, appendix 15; De Smet in *Corpus chronicorum Flandriae* I, 1, from the autograph; and Vandeputte in *Annales de la société d’émulation de la Flandre* (1845), III, 40, who was also the first to publish the continuation. Finally, we have used all the manuscripts just mentioned; the division into chapters, absent from the manuscripts, is our own.

## GENEALOGY OF THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS

[Col. 0939A] **1.** [Gen. Bert.] In the year 792 from the Lord’s incarnation, while Charles the Great was reigning in Francia, Lidric, count of Harlebeke [Col. 0940A], seeing Flanders empty, uncultivated, and wooded, occupied it [Note: [Col. 0939] Absurd, unless you suppose that Charlemagne at that time was asleep in both ears. Paquot.]. [Col. 0941A] He begot Count Ingelram. Ingelram begot Audacer, and Audacer begot Baldwin Iron-Arm. Baldwin Iron-Arm begot Baldwin the Bald by Judith, widow of Æthelbald, king of the English, namely the daughter of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks [Hincmar]. Æthelbald had first married her, and died in the same year in which he took her [Note: [Col. 0941D] In 858. Before this, she had already had his father Æthelwulf as husband for three years.]. After his death, Judith sold the possessions which she had held in the English kingdom, returned to her father, and was kept at Senlis, *Silvanectis, Sentliz* [Note: [Col. 0941] Lambert himself wrote the words printed by us in italics above the text in the autograph manuscript.], under her father’s protection. But at the instigation of Baldwin Iron-Arm and with the consent of Louis, her brother [Note: [Col. 0941D] Judith’s.], she changed her dress and secretly followed him in the year of the Lord 860 [Note: [Col. 0941D] False: it was in 862.]. When the king learned this, he consulted the bishops and princes of the Franks and asked the bishops to pronounce, in accordance with the edict of Saint Gregory, the sentence laid down [Col. 0941B]. But they excommunicated Baldwin and Judith in accordance with the saying: “If anyone steals a widow for a wife, let him be anathema” (Exod. XXII). Hearing this, Baldwin went to Rome and sought from Pope Nicholas absolution in this matter. Moved by compassion, Nicholas sent his legates—namely Radoald, bishop of Porto, and John, bishop of Ficodense—to Charles at Soissons [Note: [Col. 0941D] 23 November 862.]. Charles kept them with him for some time; having granted Baldwin the pardon for which they had come, he dismissed them with gifts and letters to return to the apostolic see. Afterwards King Charles came as far as the city of Auxerre and there, as the lord pope had requested of him, permitted his daughter Judith to be lawfully joined in marriage, by the counsel of the Franks, to Baldwin whom she had followed [Col. 0941C], in the year of the Lord 862 [Note: [Col. 0941D] False: it was in 863.].

**2.** [Gen. Bert.] Baldwin the Bald, having married the daughter of Edgar [Note: [Col. 0941D] Rather, of Alfred the Great.] king of the English, named Ælfthryth, begot Arnulf the Great, restorer of the monastery of Blandin. Arnulf the Great begot the young Baldwin by Adela, daughter of Herbert, count of Vermandois. Young Baldwin married Matilda, daughter of Hermann, duke of Saxony, by whom he begot Arnulf; after Arnulf’s birth this Baldwin died of smallpox and was buried at Saint-Bertin. Left a widow, Matilda married Godfrey, duke of Ename, by whom she had three sons, namely Duke Gozelo, Godfrey, and [Col. 0941D] Hezelo. Arnulf, son of the young Baldwin, married Susanna, daughter of the king of the Lombards, by whom he begot Baldwin the Bearded. Baldwin the Bearded, buried at Ghent, married Otgiva, daughter [Note: [Col. 0942D] Rather, sister.] of Count Gislebert of Luxembourg, by whom he had [Col. 0942A] Baldwin of Lille. Baldwin of Lille, buried there, married Adela, buried at Messines [Note: [Col. 0942D] Present-day Messines near Ypres.], daughter of Robert, king of the Franks, by whom he begot Baldwin of Mons, Robert, and Matilda, queen of the English, wife of William the Bastard. Baldwin of Mons, buried at Hasnon, married Richilde, widow of Count Hermann [Note: [Col. 0942D] Of Mons.], by whom he begot Arnulf, buried in the church of Saint-Omer, and Baldwin, who died on the expedition to Jerusalem.

**3.** Their paternal uncle Robert married Gertrude, daughter of Bernard, duke of Saxony, namely Gertrude buried at Veurne, widow of Florent, count of the Frisians, and with her obtained her realm. Having received a very great sum from his father, he renounced Flanders under oath, [Col. 0942B] which he granted by hereditary right to his brother Baldwin of Mons and his successors. During his brother’s life Robert kept quiet; but after his death, with the help of traitors, he killed his nephew Arnulf, count of Flanders, at Cassel, expelled Arnulf’s brother Baldwin from the realm, and obtained it. Once elevated to the realm, he disinherited dying clerics, sending tax-collectors who, after their deaths, drove heirs and households from their homes. Unable any longer to bear this intolerable yoke and unheard-of form of servitude [Note: [Col. 0942D] The right of spoil, commonly exercised at that time by most princes and also claimed by Robert’s predecessors, though more rarely by them.], the clerics went to Pope Urban, threw themselves at his feet, and made a tearful complaint against the tyrant. For the liberation of the clerics [Col. 0942C] he sent him this letter in the year of the Lord 1091:

**4.** URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, valiant knight of all Flanders: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Remember, dearest son, how greatly you owe almighty God, who, against the will of your parents, made you great from small, rich from poor, and a glorious prince from humble; and, what is rarest among secular princes, endowed you with the gift of letters, knowledge, and religion [Note: [Col. 0941] “religion,” manuscript.]. Therefore be mindful of him who made you such, and labour in every way not to be found ungrateful for such great benefits. Honour him, therefore, in his churches; do not presume on any pretext to harass them, whatever their condition may be, and do not convert their estates to your own use after their death [Col. 0942D]; nor violently take money or anything whatever which they leave from their patrimony. Rather, let them be free both to serve God and to bestow the goods of their patrimony upon whomever they wish. If you allege that this has proceeded from ancient custom in your land, you should know [Col. 0943A] that your Creator said: “I am the truth” (John XIV), not “custom” or “usage.” Therefore, dearest son, we desire—and by the keys of the blessed prince of the apostles command—that you observe what we have said, and, honouring Christ in the freedom of the clerics, may you be honoured. For he himself, by the testimony of himself, will honour the one who honours him. Farewell.

**5.** Count Robert, however, persisting in his wickedness, refused to obey the apostolic letter; instead, terrifying the clerics with threats, he violently plundered their goods through impious retainers and officials. Then the Flemish clerics, sorrowful and anxious, seeking to attend the council then held at Reims by Renaud, archbishop of Reims, presented to the holy council the letter despised by the tyrant, and reported [Col. 0943B] the threats and injuries they had suffered from him for a long time [Note: [Col. 0943] The Ghent manuscript does not give here all that follows to the end, but immediately after “suffered” continues: “To the whole …” In the margin, however, the author himself wrote: “The letter of the Flemish clergy sent to Archbishop R. on behalf of Count R. is written at the end of this book, attached to the axle [?], beginning thus: ‘To their lord R., archbishop of Reims, and all bishops sitting in council, the Flemish clergy,’ and the rest.” He gives the letter itself on folio 154 and ends it thus: “not to harass.” “When the whole council had sympathized and cried out, seek this verse in the genealogy of the counts of Flanders.” Hence it appears that the author intended the letter to be inserted here. We have done so, following already the Wolfenbüttel manuscript and its Hague copy.].

6. Letter of the Flemish clergy sent to Archbishop Rainald concerning Count Robert and the rescue of clerics from his servitude (1091):

To their lord RAINALD, by God’s grace Archbishop of Reims, and to all the bishops sitting in council: the clergy of Flanders, [wishing] to do what is pleasing to the Lord.

Behold, once again, most holy father, we are compelled to flee to our mother, namely the holy Church of Reims; and we humbly beseech her that, according to the tenderness of her compassion, she may deign to look upon the tears caused by our miseries. Though now absent through fear, we nevertheless cast ourselves at your feet and, with tears of blood, appeal by this our letter both to you and to this sacred council on behalf of Count Robert, who tramples upon and devours us like a lion, and ensnares us with serpentine cunning like a dragon. But he who walks upon the asp and basilisk and tramples the lion and dragon will, through his grace cooperating with you, be able to deliver us from these evils.

For as soon as it is heard that any one of us is ill, Count Robert’s officers and executioners are immediately sent out; they seize the house and everything that seemed to belong to the sick man, so that, should he happen to wish to make any vow to God, repay his debts, or bestow some benefit upon those serving him, he is absolutely forbidden to do so. Spies are also sent everywhere to inquire whether this or that house has at any time belonged to a cleric. And if this is discovered, it is immediately assigned to the count’s claim, as though he were receiving what was his own.

What an unbearable yoke this is, what a new and unheard-of kind of servitude, sufficiently indicates [Note: “indicates” supplied by Labbe.] the ferocity of the lion, whose savagery and roar he is accustomed to conceal beneath a cloud of deceit, saying that he desires all clerics to be good, to despise transitory things, and to strive for eternal ones—adding that wicked priests do not exist; as though a sinful human being were not a human being! For if a sinful human being were not a human being, the Lord Jesus would certainly not have redeemed humankind.

Indeed, his terror has grown so great that he has stopped the mouths of our pastors. Let them themselves see what answer they will make to the supreme Shepherd, since they do not expose themselves to danger for their sheep. Nor does he act with excessive inhumanity only against us: he has also leaped up against heavenly rights into your episcopal seats, while he constrains your clergy by his own laws and, as it were, disposes of your churches. Thus it comes about that, although he has no power to loose, he nevertheless has the power to bind, seize, and despoil.

Therefore, most holy fathers, we must flee to you. Arm your hands also, and your tongues with the unconquerable sword of the Holy Spirit, if you judge it fitting; for although we are now afflicted and despised, we are nevertheless of your flock and of your body. Nor in the future should you be ashamed that such persons belong to your sees as secular power compels us to be.

He has indeed been confronted by our bishop, by our abbots, by the very presence of the metropolitan [Note: the manuscript reads “the metropolitan himself”], and most recently by the letters of Pope Urban, in which he commanded him by the keys of Saint Peter not to harass clerics further, nor to allege in his own excuse that this was the custom of his country. The same lord pope refuted him by the words of the Lord, who says: “I am the truth” (John 14), not custom or usage. Scorning all these things, he has turned to crafty arguments: although he truly harasses clerics cruelly, he nevertheless says that he does not harass clerics.

7. When the entire council had expressed its grief and approval, Rainald, the archbishop of blessed memory, commanded Arnulf, provost of Saint-Omer, John, abbot of Saint-Bertin, Gerald, abbot of Ham, and Bernard, provost of Watten, to confront Count Robert himself with the authority of the holy council—who at that time was living a private life [Note: “In retreat”], residing in the cloister of Saint-Bertin for the sake of continence and Lenten supplication—and to require him, by Palm Sunday, either to restore what he had seized or to know that, struck by the sword of anathema, his whole land would be deprived of the divine office.

Fearing this, he made satisfaction; professing that he would maintain obedience, he sought and received pardon. Thus he annulled everything he had done, so that none of his successors dared to revive this iniquity.

[Note: Oudegherst, therefore, and those who with him attribute this abolition of the right of spoliation to Robert II are mistaken.]

This occurred in the year of the Lord 1092.

[Note: False: it was the year 1093. In the same year, on the third Ides of October, Robert died, according to the contemporary Annals of Blandin.]

In that year he also died and was buried at Cassel.

8. [Genealogy of Saint-Bertin.] This Robert the Bearded begot by the aforesaid Gertrude two sons: Robert, an excellent knight, who was distinguished in the expedition to Jerusalem; and Philip, buried at Bergues. The distinguished Robert, buried at Arras, married Clementia, daughter of William, count of Burgundy; by her he begot Baldwin and William, who was buried at Saint-Bertin.

9. Count Baldwin VII, son of Clementia [Note: “Clementia” is written over an erasure], was in his day powerful above all the princes of the French. By frequent wars he exalted the realm of the Flemings so nobly that he struck terror into the neighboring tyrants on every side, and would have driven King Henry of England out of Normandy, had illness not prevented it.

For about the feast of the Nativity of Saint Mary, having assembled a multitude of troops, he planned to surround with siegeworks the town of Rouen [Note: Rouen, 1118], in which the aforesaid king was hiding, and to seize him or engage him in battle and expel him from the kingdom which he had unjustly invaded. But while he was leading his army through Arras, owing to a wound which he had shortly before received in Normandy on his forehead, he was seized in that city by a sudden illness. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October he began to be sick; struck with paralysis from thigh to feet, he remained ill for a full nine months.

When he could not be cured by physicians, he appointed Lord Charles as successor to his county. Charles had been borne by Adela, sister of his father Robert, to Cnut [Note: thus the manuscript reads], king of the Danes. Having therefore arranged the entire kingdom of Flanders, in the eighth year of his reign, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, he died in the village of Roeselare.

[Note: Roeselare. Walter says the same in his *Life of Charles the Good*; Orderic says at the castle of Aumale; Anselm of Gembloux and the contemporary Chronicle of Saint Andrew’s of the Castle of Cambrai say at Saint-Bertin.]

He was conveyed by Charles to Saint-Bertin and buried in the middle of the church, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1119, in the twelfth indiction, while Louis reigned in France.

10. When he died without an heir (1119), Charles succeeded him. This Charles and Louis, son of Philip, king of the French, were born of two sisters: Louis from Bertrada, and Charles from Adela, begotten by Cnut [Note: thus the manuscript reads]. When Cnut had been killed by the treacherous Danes [Note: A.D. 1086], the venerable queen Adela returned with her son Charles to her father Robert in Flanders. Then, after five years had passed, she married Roger, son of Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia.

The aforesaid Charles, long after the death of his father and mother, was chosen in advance by the aforementioned Baldwin; after Baldwin’s death, as I have said, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1120, he entered the church of Saint-Omer and held his first court with the princes of his realm. In the same year he utterly destroyed the castle of Saint-Pol, in which the treacherous Hugh of Campavène and many robbers were hiding (1120); he ordered the surrounding moat to be filled in, bravely demolished the other fortresses of evil-doers, and nobly subjected the kingdom to himself.

[Note: Here the autograph Ghent manuscript ends. But the Leiden and Wolfenbüttel manuscripts, and the Hague copy of the latter, append the continuation: “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1127, on the sixth Nones . . .”]

## Continuation

11. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1127, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, the sixteenth lunar day, epact 6, concurrent 5, Charles, margrave of all Flanders, ended his life—alas, by how wretched, how criminal a death!

I call it wretched and criminal because he did not die in a bed of sickness, with some native infirmity weighing down his corruptible body; nor did he fall struck down in a field appointed for battle, while the martial trumpet resounded and the hoped-for victory, promising itself to each side alike, summoned the war to swords. Rather, in the church of Saint Donatian, while he was prostrate in prayer and the priest was celebrating Mass according to custom, he was treacherously surrounded and killed in peacetime, during Lent, by his own servants and household men—namely Burchard and accomplices enticed into so great a crime—through the counsel and instigation of Bertulf, provost of that same church.

The cause was this: out of mercy he defended those whom these men wished to oppress by malice and power. Therefore the princes, disturbed; the citizens, terrified; and the peasants, grieved, assembled to avenge so great a crime and to extirpate the aforesaid murderers and their entire family. Besieging the house in which they were located, so that none might escape, they set very many guards over it, who were to harass them in attack until, compelled by the examination of public law, they surrendered themselves for condemnation. Women, children, and every class of weaker nature curse them and devote them to destruction; the clergy, doing what belonged to them, exclude them, as unworthy, from the threshold of the holy church and from participation in the sacraments by the sword of the Holy Spirit.

12. Meanwhile, as report carried the wretched event abroad, Louis, king of France, heard of it. Grieving both at the death of so great a prince and at the kingdom’s bereavement, he came to Arras (20 March) and summoned the chief men of the entire country, so that by their counsel and assent he might provide a ruler for the widowed kingdom. For this was within his right and power: to exact sufficiently worthy vengeance for the murder committed, even by their judgment.

[Note: The Wolfenbüttel, Hague, and Leiden manuscripts add “and” (Latin *et*).]

Accordingly, both those who had been summoned and those who had not flocked to the king and inquired, now publicly, now privately, who was the person to whom the inheritance of Flanders belonged. There was present William, son of Robert, count of Normandy, who by some hereditary right could succeed Charles in the kingdom. Since he was distinguished by strength of mind and body, illustrious by nobility of parents, and—more truly said—the best knight among thousands, he was indiscriminately put forward by the common people, more favorably elected by the nobles, and by the king, because he was heir and because he was elected, powerfully established as prince and ruler of the kingdom.

But lest, because he was called and was a new count, he should suffer any opposition or trouble from the citizens, he was led by the king and the chief men of the kingdom from city to city, so that, with security promised on both sides and confirmed by a pledge of faith, he might have faithful subjects and govern those he had acquired with justice and mercy.

13. While these things were being arranged, the aforesaid murderers—the provost and his nephew Burchard—were brought out of the house in which they had been besieged, after a price had been paid. Each was apprehended under sentence of condemnation [Note: the other manuscripts read “the sentence”], each subjected to disgrace, and each condemned to death [Note: the other manuscripts read “by death”].

The provost was hanged at the gallows at Ypres with Guy of Stenvoorde [Note: Wolfenbüttel and Hague read *Stevorth*; Leiden, *Stervoth*], guilty of the same crime [Note: Wolfenbüttel, Hague, and Leiden read “crimes”], as though he had been conferring with him concerning the count’s death. Burchard was punished at Lille by having his legs broken. Robert also, nephew of the same provost, underwent capital sentence for the same crime. Their accomplices were thrown headlong from the upper part of the house in which they had been besieged and put to death.

14. Before the aforesaid Count William had ruled for half a year, behold, two chief men of the kingdom—namely Iwan and his nephew Daniel—and very many citizens, namely those of Ghent, Bruges, and Lille and their dependents, rose against him in a conspiracy (August) and attempted to expel him from the kingdom. They alleged various criminal charges, I do not know whether true or false, from which they wished to infer that he deserved condemnation and could no longer lawfully rule them.

O crime! A pledged faith is disregarded; the decision of election is altered; and another count, Thierry of Alsace, son of the daughter of Count Robert the Frisian, is brought in over him (11 March 1128). The kingdom was divided, not among brothers by hereditary lot, but among enemies by a law of opposition. One advanced against the other, Thierry against William; William, stoutly defending himself and his followers, repelled those advancing against him.

At length they met at the place called Hacspola [Note: Axpoele near Tielt, in the parish of Ruiselede, as Carton demonstrates in *Annales de la Société d’émulation de la Flandre occidentale*, 1844, p. 270] (21 June), each accompanied by his own army; and there, their battle-lines drawn up in order, they fought. But William, whose cause was said to be the more just, and whose army was therefore stronger and readier for battle, prevailed. Having gained the victory there, he killed many in vengeance and as a testimony to the battle; many others he compelled, taken captive as a sign of victory, to march before him as victor.

But this did little to avert the misery prescribed by fortune. For not long afterward, drawn on by his fate to attack the city of his adversary Iwan, called Aalst, which was then besieged by Godfrey, duke of Louvain, his own ally, he arrived with a great army (12 July). There he achieved nothing and, by I know not what mischance, received from the enemy a mortal wound. That count, great in name and fame, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of August (27 July), in the second year of his reign, and was buried in the church of Saint-Bertin beside his kinsman Count Baldwin. And Thierry reigned.

## VI. *Flandria Generosa*

In the same manner in which Lambert expanded the Bertinian genealogy, so a monk of Saint-Bertin, not long after 1164, expanded the Lambertine genealogy, as is clear from the penultimate chapter. For, taking over Lambert’s work almost word for word, he inserted much material drawn from Folcuin’s cartulary of Saint-Bertin, Simon, its continuator, the Anchin manuscript of Sigebert, the now-lost poem on the battle of Cassel, and other sources now unknown; and he carried the thread down to 1164. That he himself lived at that time is sufficiently shown by the words of the final chapter, which we ourselves have seen.

[Note: Folcuin, monk of Saint-Bertin, composed the cartulary in 961. Simon, likewise a monk of Saint-Bertin and a native of Ghent, began to continue it at the command of Abbot Lambert. When Lambert was struck by paralysis in 1123, Simon managed the abbey until 1127, when the monks of Anchin made him their abbot. Elected abbot of Saint-Bertin in 1131, he laid down the staff at Pope Innocent’s command in 1136 and withdrew to Ghent, where he carried his work down to 1145. Twelve years later he returned to Saint-Bertin and died there in 1148. B. Guérard published that cartulary at Paris in 1840, quarto; the passages taken thence by our author are found there on pp. 140 and 297.]

This little work, written with a certain native vividness and not without partisanship and indignation, rests upon Lambert and in turn became the foundation of a great many Flemish chronicles. Lambert of Ardres and John of Thielrode also drew much from it; John of Ypres and Adrian of But took it over entire. Nor were continuations lacking: the Brussels continuation, written shortly after 1206, in manuscript 4, by whom is unknown; the very brief Saint-Ghislain continuation, extending to 1206, in manuscript 5, composed at Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut; and the Clairmarais continuation in manuscript 6, composed by a Cistercian monk of the Blessed Mary of Clairmarais, now Clairmarais near Saint-Omer, between 1214 and 1226.

[Note: For Louis VIII, who died in 1226, is always called “lord” here while his father was still alive.]

This contains very extensive patchworks stitched together from the Anchin continuation of Sigebert and the letter of Emperor Baldwin.

[Note: In Brial, *Recueil*, XVIII, 522.]

What the author himself contributed was written not unwillingly under Minerva’s guidance and is to be counted among the best sources, particularly for the battle of Bouvines. Bernard of Ypres, a monk of Clairmarais, continued this continuation again from 1214 to the very year in which he wrote, 1329. Finally, a third monk of the same monastery, whose name we do not know, taking up the pen from that very year at different times, carried the narrative down to 1347. Others also continued it in the Antwerp and Leuven manuscripts. Lastly, the very brief Dunes continuation, down to 1405, was written in that year itself at the monastery of the Dunes near Bruges. These manuscripts survive:

1. **Saint-Bertin manuscript**, now Saint-Omer municipal manuscript no. 746, concerning which I wrote in *Pertz Archiv*, VIII, 417. Among much else it contains a quire of eight folios; the first three have been cut out. On the recto of the fourth folio is read the end of a certain theological work; on the verso and the following four folios our genealogy is written in two columns, in a hand of the end of the twelfth century, which is that of the author himself. The lines are ruled in lead; the title and the names of the counts are written in red in the margin; the ink changes about the middle of the work; the author himself later erased the ending and wrote a longer continuation over the erasure and in the margin; twice likewise he scattered certain additions in the margin and occasionally between the lines. Thus the author took up his pen three times in composing this little work. No one before us had used this manuscript; recognizing it to be the author’s autograph, I transcribed it entire.

2. **Saint-Vaast manuscript**, now Arras municipal manuscript no. 184, parchment folio, thirteenth century. It was mutilated for bookbinders’ use by the wicked knife of Caron, formerly librarian of Arras. It contains Andrew of Marchiennes, Turpin, the *Life of Apollonius*, the Letter of Presbyter John, our Genealogy, and the History of the Counts of Boulogne. I examined it myself.

2a. **Amiens manuscript** no. 356, copied in the seventeenth century from the Saint-Vaast manuscript.

3. **Cambron manuscript**, later Lammens’s, now belonging to Leopold de Alstein of Ghent, who most graciously placed it at our disposal for inspection: parchment folio, thirteenth century; it contains Rufinus, the Genealogy, and letters of Baldwin, Henry, and Blanche.

4. **Brussels manuscript** no. 9823–9834, parchment, thirteenth century, formerly Pamel’s and then of the Jesuits of Bruges. It contains Robert’s *Passage*, Fulcher’s history, a Description of the Holy Places, a Miracle performed in the time of Heribert, catalogues of kings, *On the Lateran Sanctuary*, *On the Seven Wonders of the World*, the Genealogy of the Kings of France, a History of Muhammad, and our Genealogy, copied rather inaccurately from the Saint-Bertin manuscript. Another hand at the end of the fourteenth century added the continuation already published in De Smet, *Corpus chronicorum Flandriae*, I, 127, 130, which we have again transcribed from the manuscript itself.

5. **Saint-Ghislain manuscript**, with a short continuation; now lost, and known to us only from Galopin’s edition.

6. **Clairmarais manuscript**, now Saint-Omer manuscript no. 769, parchment quarto, thirteenth century. After the Lives of Peter of Tarentaise and Mary of Oignies, it has our Genealogy, which the same hand, continuing in the same line, carried down to “seven and more.” There this hand stopped writing at the foot of the fifth folio of a quire; the sixth and seventh folios were cut out, and the eighth is entirely blank. In place of the sixth and seventh, a quire of twelve smaller folios was inserted in the following century. One fourteenth-century hand wrote upon it the continuation published by Martène from this very manuscript, which ends at “altissimo non resurget” (“he will not rise again on high”; the precise reading is uncertain) in the middle of the final page of the quire. It left the remaining part of the page blank, and wrote in the lower margin: “Brother Bernard of Ypres, monk of Clairmarais, copied this out on the day of blessed Nicholas the bishop, in the twenty-ninth year,” etc. Finally, a third hand, also of the fourteenth century, inserted yet another continuation into the remaining space of the last page which Bernard had left blank. Beginning six years later, it carried the narrative through four added folios to the word “escaped,” where both folio and work end. But of these four folios, the first and second had already disappeared in Martène’s time.

6a. **Wolfenbüttel manuscript**, among the Weissenburg manuscripts no. 41, paper folio, fifteenth century, was copied from the Clairmarais manuscript before those two folios disappeared; Lessing therefore supplied the lacuna in the latter from it in *Beiträge zur Geschichte und Litteratur*, no. 9.

6b. The Antwerp Jesuits possessed another copy of the Clairmarais manuscript, from which was transcribed the manuscript preserved at The Hague among the G. I. Gérard manuscripts, no. 265. As we indicated in *Pertz Archiv*, IX, 511, it extends from 792 to 1329; but its final six folios do not survive in the Clairmarais manuscript.

6c. The Leuven Jesuits had a manuscript continued to Louis of Male, or to 1380, according to Henschenius in *Acta Sanctorum*, March I, 154.

6d. Brussels manuscript no. 9836, which already ends in 1305, seems to be of the same kind.

6e. Brussels manuscript no. 18417, formerly Lammens’s, parchment quarto, written in a single fourteenth-century hand, contains nothing but Bernard’s continuation, “Count Ferdinand was therefore held captive—will not rise again.” The same hand appends the unpublished Annals of Flanders: “In the year of the Lord 1334 Pope John—after they went out on the expedition,” ending in 1358.

7. **Dunes manuscript**, now Bruges municipal manuscript no. 120, paper octavo, fifteenth century. After a necrology, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and a short chronicle, it has our Genealogy, rather freely excerpted and carried down to 1405, where it ends: “may he ever deign to enlarge [it]. Amen. May this noble Flemish prince flourish and grow green without thorn, and prosper, I pray, O Christ.”

7*. **Aldenburg manuscript**, now in the Bruges seminary, fifteenth century. Among other things listed in *Pertz Archiv*, VIII, 558, it contains our genuine Genealogy with the continuation “The aforesaid Thierry—his first-born son John,” which seems to have been excerpted from the Dunes manuscript. Vandeputte published it from this manuscript in *Annales de la Société d’émulation de la Flandre occidentale*, 1845, p. 49.

8. **Paris manuscript**, among the Baluze manuscripts, armarium II, p. 1, no. 3, seventeenth century, without continuation.

9. **Tournai manuscript**, thirteenth century, concerning which I wrote in *Pertz Archiv*, VIII, 561; it extends only to 1127.

The first edition is Galopin’s *Flandria Generosa*, Mons, 1643, quarto, from the Saint-Ghislain manuscript. Paquot, *Synopsis historiae Flandriae*, Brussels, 1781, quarto, published it again with notes greatly enlarged. Martène, *Thesaurus*, III, 377, reproduced the Clairmarais manuscript. Bouquet, *Recueil*, XI, 388; XIII, 411; XVIII, 559, reprinted Martène.

**B.** The manuscripts and editions identified thus far reproduce the author’s work in its pure and genuine form. But already before 1193 an unknown interpolator copied it in such a manner that, while abstaining from altering the wording, he inserted large patches drawn from Tomellus, Lambert of Saint-Omer, Herman of Tournai, the Anchin manuscript of Sigebert, and others.

[Col. 0951]

Such a manuscript was used by Andrew of Marchiennes, Baldwin of Avesnes, and John of Ypres. We know only Brussels manuscript no. 6410–15, paper, fifteenth century, which Warnkoenig used. This interpolated work was soon afterward translated into French under the title: “The generations, the account, and the lineage of the line of the counts of Flanders.” The translation is quite accurate, omitting only very little; its translator added nothing except a single, rather extensive account of the death of Charles the Good.

[Note: Pages 55–90 of De Smet’s edition.]

He compiled this account wholly from Walter’s *Life of that Count* and Herman of Tournai. This version was excerpted by a chronicle of Flanders written in French.

[Note: It begins: “One finds by reading that in the time of Charlemagne the most mighty,” etc. It covers the years 792–1346. Its first six chapters flow almost word for word from the French version indicated above under B, with very few additions; the remainder appears to have nothing in common either with the Clairmarais continuation or with compilation C. Some have wished its author to be Jacques de Guyse. Its manuscripts are: a Lyon manuscript among the Augustinian friars, magnificently written and illuminated in 1346 at the command of Mary of Burgundy, according to Le Long, *Bibliothèque historique de France*, ed. Fevret de Fontette, III, 653; Paris, Sorbonne manuscript no. 1606, fifteenth century, entitled *Chronicles of Flanders from Charlemagne until King Edward had conquered the city of Calais*; Brussels manuscript no. 10233, continued to 1356; Brussels manuscript no. 14910, fifteenth century; the Poupet manuscript of the lords of Poupet in Burgundy, extending to 1384, published by Denys Sauvage, *Chronique de Flandre . . .*, Lyon, 1561, folio; the Paris manuscript discussed by Van Praet, *Recherches sur Louis de Bruges, seigneur de la Gruithuyse*, Paris, 1832, octavo. Perhaps Brussels manuscript no. 16789, extending to 1396, belongs here.]

The author of the Flemish rhymed chronicle made the whole translation serve his purposes.

[Note: Kaussler published it from the Comburg manuscript in *Denkmäler der altniederländischen Litteratur*, Tübingen, 1840, octavo. He investigated its sources with remarkable acuteness, but judged less correctly in thinking that its author had used only a Latin exemplar of *Flandria Generosa*. He certainly had an exemplar of type B in addition to the French version, but acquired it only after finishing the poem, as he himself says at verse 2005. From 1162 to 1278 he reproduced the Clairmarais continuators, though mixing in much else; the sources of the remainder, verses 6284–10569, are no longer known to us.]

The manuscripts are Brussels no. 9558, parchment quarto, fourteenth century, of which a later copy is preserved at The Hague among the G. Gérard manuscripts no. 264; and Saint-Germain manuscript no. 39, cited by Dom Clément in the *Art de vérifier les dates* when treating Count Arnulf III of Flanders, whose present location we do not know. De Smet published it in *Corpus chronicorum Flandriae*, II, 31, from the Brussels manuscript.

**C.** In 1423 an extensive compilation was built upon the Clairmarais manuscript under the title: *Catalogue and Chronicle of the Princes, Counts, and Foresters of Flanders, which land was once called the Land of Buc, or the Forest of the Region without Mercy.* Beginning with 621, it first recounts, not without a certain charm, popular tales about Salvard of Dijon and his wife Ermengard; about Finard the giant in Lille-les-Buc; about Lydéric le Buc, the first forester; Anthony, the second; and Lydéric of Harelbeke, the third—very pleasant tales indeed, but tales.

Then, for the years 836–1347, it took over the Clairmarais manuscript, but altered its wording extensively and interpolated it with additions so many and so great, taken from the Lives of Charles the Good by Walter and Galbert, from Vincent of Beauvais, popular tradition, and elsewhere, that under so great a mass one can scarcely recognize the principal foundation.

[Note: Both the character of the language and the form of names seem frequently to indicate French sources.]

The more delight these additions afford, the less reliability they generally possess.

[Note: Henschenius has already shown this in the material there concerning the death of Charles the Good: *Acta Sanctorum*, March I, 154.]

Finally, for the years 1348–1423, the author proceeds on his own track, and as regards those times may be counted among historical sources. For earlier periods he should only rarely be used, and never without careful caution—a rule not always observed by those who undertook to write the history of Flanders. For above all others this chronicle was read, copied, excerpted, and cited, because its agreeable prolixity and resemblance to romantic narratives made it extraordinarily attractive to an age which, in history, valued not so much what was true as what was pleasant and marvelous.

John of Diksmuide, the Chronicle of Saint Bavo, Meyer, Oudegherst, Vredius, Lambert van der Burch, Sueyro, Buzelinus, Varnewyk, and Vanloo drew very much from it.

[Note: Lambin published John of Diksmuide: *Dits de cronyke ende genealogie van den graven van den forreste van Buc, dat heet Vlaenderen, van 863 tot 1436 . . . door Ian van Dixmude*, Ypres, 1839, octavo.]

[Note: The Chronicle of Saint Bavo is in De Smet, *Corpus chronicorum Flandriae*, I, 455.]

It was continued by many, abridged,

[Note: For example, in the first four folios of the Cisoing manuscript, now Lille E. G. 34, fifteenth century, from which Warnkoenig published it in De Smet, I, 11, without observing that what he published was of absolutely no value.]

interpolated,

[Note: The following Brussels manuscripts seem to belong here: nos. 5751, 6025, 6066, 6078, 7220, 7376, 7809, 10291, 10315, 10328, 13075, 13413, 14506, 16551, 16790, 16804, 17304.]

and repeatedly translated into Flemish

[Note: The manuscripts are: Brussels no. 13163, extending to 1330; Brussels no. 6074; an Amsterdam manuscript of the Institute, written by Matthaeus, ending in 1440; Middlehill no. 4166, ending in 1466, according to *Pertz Archiv*, VIII, 764; Brussels no. 7384, formerly of the Jesuits of Bruges, extending to 1477 with a continuation to 1507, printed under the title *Dits die excellente cronyke van Vlaenderen*, Antwerp, 1531; The Hague no. 930, extending to 1497.]

and French.

[Note: In the London manuscript of the British Museum, King’s 16, F. III, *Chroniques de Flandre*, 621–1347; and Brussels manuscript no. 13068, for 621–1696.]

Nor is there any manuscript of the genuine work which has altogether refrained from adding, omitting, or altering. They are as follows: the Cisoing manuscript, now Lille E. G. 34, paper quarto, fifteenth century, used by Warnkoenig; the Bruges manuscript of the Jesuits, according to De Smet, I, preface p. 29, whose present location is unknown; Vatican manuscript of Saint Christina no. 798, formerly 1222, paper, fifteenth century, which I examined myself; the Leuven manuscript, now Brussels no. 3599–3601, paper, fifteenth century; the Bigot manuscript, now Paris no. 5237, fifteenth century; Paris manuscript no. 5994, formerly Puteanus’s; Paris manuscript no. 5041, formerly Gerard van der Strepen’s and then Puteanus’s; and the Paris manuscript among the Baluze manuscripts, armarium II, p. 1, no. 3, copied from two manuscripts belonging to Alexandre Petau and the Puteani. All these end in 1423.

Our work with a continuation is contained in the Bruges manuscript of the distinguished Mr. Vermeire, used by Warnkoenig; another hand there added a few lines in November 1424—“without his consent” in 1428. The Hamburg Public Library manuscript, *Historia Belgica* no. 14, paper folio, sixteenth century, ends in 1437. Middlehill manuscript no. 1890, formerly Meerman’s, extends to 1467; perhaps a copy of it is preserved at The Hague among the G. Gérard manuscripts no. 270; see *Pertz Archiv*, IX, 511.

Warnkoenig prepared an edition in De Smet, *Corpus chronicorum Flandriae*, I, 19, from Vermeire’s Bruges manuscript and the Cisoing manuscript; but he confused into one what he ought instead to have separated: our manuscripts 4, 5, 6, and B.

[Col. 0953]

Our edition rests entirely on autograph manuscript 1, with which we collated 2, 4, and 6. We have appended the Brussels continuation from manuscript 4, the Clairmarais continuation from 6, and the Saint-Ghislain continuation from Galopin’s edition. We shall publish Bernard of Ypres’s continuation together with the Dunes continuation from 6, 6a, 6b, 7, and 7*, among the writers of the fourteenth century. Additions from B, made still in the twelfth century, we have placed beneath the text, each in its proper location. But we have paid no attention whatever to C; for that interpolation, which did not arise before the fifteenth century, must be presented in full down to 1423 together with the later additions and continuations made to it. We have created the division into chapters ourselves; it is not found in the manuscripts. Finally, we have judged it proper, for readers’ convenience, to retain the title *Flandria Generosa*, given by Galopin and by which learned men generally cite this work.

## Here begins the Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders

1. [Lambert.] In the year 792 from the incarnation of the Lord, the first year of Emperor Constantine, son of Irene, and the twenty-fourth year of Charles the Great, king of the Franks and later emperor of the Romans, Lydéric of Harelbeke, seeing Flanders empty, uncultivated, and wooded, occupied it.
