He begot Count Ingelram. Ingelram begot Audacer. Audacer in turn begot Baldwin Iron-Arm.

2. Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 862, Baldwin Iron-Arm abducted Judith, widow of Æthelbald, king of the English, and daughter of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, son of Louis the Pious Augustus, son of Charlemagne; and by her he begot Baldwin the Bald, who was later called Charles’s nephew and an illustrious count. The aforesaid King Æthelbald died in the same year in which he had married her. After his death Judith sold the possessions which she had held in the kingdom of the English, returned to her father, and was kept at Senlis under her father’s protection. But Baldwin Iron-Arm, acting as go-between, and her brother Louis consenting [Note: [Col. 0953] “Judith, who loved the count greatly because of his worth,” is added by B.], she followed him secretly, having changed her dress [Note: [Col. 0953] “Disguised.”].

When the king learned this, he consulted the bishops and princes of the Franks and asked that the bishops pronounce a judgment according to the decree of blessed Gregory. They, following the rule, “If anyone has abducted a widow as his wife, let him be anathema,” excommunicated Baldwin and Judith. On hearing this, Baldwin went to Rome to Pope Nicholas, seeking pardon for the deed. Nicholas, however [Note: [Col. 0953] “Seeing him to be a very handsome and upright young man,” is added by B.], moved by mercy, sent his legates—namely Radoald, bishop of Porto, and John, bishop of Ficodenza—to Charles at Soissons. Charles detained them with him for some time; then, having granted the pardon for Baldwin which they had come to obtain, he dismissed them, laden with gifts and letters, to return to the Apostolic See.

Thereafter King Charles proceeded as far as the city of Auxerre [Col. 0954A], and there, at the pope’s request and with the counsel of the Franks, allowed his daughter Judith to be lawfully joined in marriage to Baldwin, whom she had followed. When Charles, king of the Franks and finally emperor of the Romans, died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 876 (877), on 5 October, and was buried in the monastery of Saint-Denis, four years after his death (879) his son-in-law Baldwin, son of Audacer, also died—a most eminent man, bold and very strong in body. He was buried in the monastery of Saint-Bertin, called Sithiu. [Note: [Col. 0953] “He is buried at Blandinium,” say the Annals of Blandinium—that is, his heart and entrails; the remainder of his body is at Saint-Bertin.]

3. [Folcuin.] Accordingly Baldwin the Bald, son of Baldwin Iron-Arm, married the daughter of Edgar [Note: [Col. 0953] “or Æthelweard,” written above by the same hand in 1 and 6.], king of the English, named Ælfthryth [Note: [Col. 0953] “or Elfelt,” written above by the same hand.]. By her he begot Arnulf the Great, restorer of Blandinium, who in the course of time and old age was called the Elder and the Old [Note: [Col. 0953] “And Adalolf. This Arnulf established twelve canons in the church of Saint Donatian at Bruges; he founded the church at Torhout and established canons there,” is added by B.]. When Baldwin died and was buried at Ghent [Note: [Col. 0953] “He died in the year of the Lord 918, 2 January,” is added by B.], his sons divided the march between themselves: Arnulf, the elder by birth, received Flanders; Adalolf received the city of Boulogne and the district of Thérouanne. When Adalolf died and was buried at Saint-Bertin (933), Arnulf received his county.

4. This Arnulf, surnamed the Old, begot Baldwin the Younger by Adela, daughter of Herbert, count of Vermandois. Baldwin the Younger married Matilda, daughter of Hermann, duke of Saxony, by whom he begot Arnulf the Younger. After Arnulf’s birth, this Baldwin died of smallpox before his father’s death, on the Kalends of January (962), and was buried in the church of Saint-Bertin [Col. 0954C]. After her husband’s death Matilda married Godfrey, duke of Ename; by him she bore three [Note: [Col. 0953] “Five; see above.”] sons: namely Duke Gozelo [Note: [Col. 0953] “or Frederick,” written above in 1 and 6.], Godfrey, and Hezelon [Note: [Col. 0953] “Arnulf the Great died in the year of the Lord 964, 27 March, and was buried at Ghent,” is added by B.].

5. Arnulf the Younger married Susanna, daughter of Berengar, king of the Lombards and of Italy [Col. 0955A]; by her he begot Baldwin, surnamed Fair-Beard [Note: [Col. 0955C] Lambert has “Baldwin the Bearded.”], who was buried at Blandinium.

6. This Baldwin was a handsome man, fine in body and tall in stature. He married Ogiva, daughter [Note: [Col. 0955C] “Sister.”] of Gislebert, count of Luxembourg. Her brothers were these: Adalbert, bishop of Metz; Frederick, duke of Lorraine; Henry, duke of Bavaria; Gislebert, count of Salins [Note: [Col. 0955C] Salm.]; and Theodoric of Luxembourg.

7. By a wife of such high birth he begot Baldwin the Pious, a prudent and valiant count, found in his time wise and most moderate in all his works. He married Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0955] “Son of Hugh Capet. This king was gentle and very learned. He was a pupil of the philosopher Gerbert; he was also a lover of religion and of churches. On the principal feasts he came to Saint-Denis, stood and chanted in the choir with the monks at Vespers, Matins, and Mass; dressed in a silk cope, he directed the choir with the cantor. He also composed certain chants: concerning the Holy Spirit, *Presentia sancti Spiritus adsit nobis gratia* (‘May the presence of the Holy Spirit’s grace be with us’); for the Nativity of the Lord, the rhythm *Judea et Iherusalem* (‘Judaea and Jerusalem’); for All Saints, the rhythm *Concede nobis, quaesumus* (‘Grant us, we beseech thee’); and he composed many others, yet in this too he greatly surpassed the rest. When Queen Constance saw him engaged in these things, she said jokingly one day that he should make some song about her. The king readily agreed and wrote the rhythm *O Constantia martirum* (‘O steadfastness of the martyrs’) in honour of Saint Denis and the other martyrs. He was most generous in giving, so much so that on feast days, when he took off or put on royal garments, if he had nothing else at hand he would distribute the very garments to the poor—unless needy persons pressing importunately were deliberately kept away by the wardrobe attendants. Queen Constance, on the other hand, was exceedingly miserly and, what least befitted a queen, excessively avaricious; for whenever she gave anything to someone, she instructed that person, saying: ‘See that Constance does not learn of this!’—and did not add the title ‘queen.’ He also adorned the kingdom with buildings and holy churches: among them he built, at Orléans, the monastery of Saint Anianus, the church of Saint Mary Mother of God and Saint Hilary the Confessor before the palace, Saint Leodegarius in the forest of Aix, Saint Medard at the castle of Vitry, the monastery of Saint Regulus in the city of Senlis, and that of Mary the Mother of God at the castle of Étampes. At Autun he built the monastery of Saint Cassian; at Paris, too, the church of Saint Nicholas in his palace, and likewise that of Saint Mary at the castle of Poissy. This illustrious king by Constance, daughter of the count of Provence, begot King Hugh, called the Flower of Youth because of the extraordinary beauty of his body and character; Robert, duke of Burgundy; Henry, later king; and Adela, most noble countess of Flanders,” is added by B.].

She bore him two sons, Baldwin [Col. 0955B] of Mons and Robert the Frisian, and a daughter named Matilda. Matilda married William, count of Normandy [Note: [Col. 0955] “who, after killing Harold … But let these things concerning Matilda, queen of England, and her sons suffice: in De Smet I, 59, from Herman of Tournai, chapters 14 and 16,” is added by B.], conqueror of England. She bore him William, king of England after his father; Robert, count of Normandy; and Henry, who, after his brother William had been killed by an arrow while hunting deer, became king of England and duke of Normandy, after his brother Robert had been captured in war and Robert’s son William—whom Elias had reared—had been removed from Normandy [Note: [Col. 0955C] “This William later succeeded Charles in Flanders.”].

8. When Henry, son of the aforesaid King Robert [Note: [Col. 0955] “Francie” (‘of France’) is written above in 1; 4 has “Francie regis” (‘of the king of France’), and 6 “regis Francie” (‘king of France’).], died (1060), the aforesaid Count Baldwin undertook to rear Henry’s son Philip until he should be of an age fit to rule the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0955] “This was done in the year of the Lord 1061,” is added by B.]. He governed the kingdom vigorously, after all the princes of the realm had sworn fidelity to him, while preserving fidelity to the boy Philip if he survived; but otherwise, without qualification, as the rightful heir of the kingdom through his wife.

9. The same Baldwin built at Lille a castle and a church of Saint Peter the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0955] “In the year of the Lord 1055, and he established forty canons in it: ten priests, of whom two were bishops, namely the bishops of Tournai and Thérouanne; ten deacons, ten subdeacons, and ten acolytes,” is added by B.] [Col. 0956B]. Buried there also, he deservedly awaits in good hope the Day of Judgment. For the dedication of the aforesaid church, he ordered all the saints from throughout his county to be brought there at his request; and he granted them in perpetual possession the places in which they had pitched their tents. [Note: [Col. 0955] “These things were done in the year of the Lord 1065, on the day after Saint Peter in Chains, in the reign of King Philip. The whole town followed the building of this church; it had previously, as if adrift, found no suitable site. For it had first been situated in the place called Salines, and later at Annappes. The aforesaid pious count, in conferring his benefactions upon the church of Saint Peter of Lille, would contribute nothing from his own table, lest perhaps the church should suffer loss or burden from his descendants wishing to reclaim his own gifts. Instead, with money contributed by the people of the district, he purchased everything which he could have spent by whatever means he wished, had he chosen; and, after the purchases had been placed in the hands of the supreme lord, namely the king, the church received them, so that it might enjoy them more safely and freely. He then obtained for it a privilege providing that whoever thereafter committed an offence should pay the church one hundred pounds of gold and incur the king’s ban.

“The count, having established his benefactions for divine service, sought suitable persons everywhere to serve God for and in those benefactions; having found them, as stated above, he established them in his church, and ordered those so established to confirm by oath that they would diligently preserve his benefactions for divine service, for himself and his successors, to the best of their ability. But this provident man, fearing the wickedness of later generations and wishing to test them, harassed them through his bailiffs over their possessions. The bailiffs invaded and forcibly seized their properties. Newly gathered together, the canons publicly pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the bailiffs. The bailiffs brought a very grave complaint to the count. The count pretended to threaten the canons severely, ordering the bailiffs to seize what was theirs but not to inflict bodily injury on them. The bailiffs returned and faithfully carried out the commands. The canons applied their sentence.

“At length the count returned to Lille. The canons assembled and approached him, unanimously resolved that, unless the count took upon himself the bailiffs’ excesses and made amends, they would pronounce that sentence against him. When the canons came and greeted him, the count answered nothing; turning away his face, he pretended that he could not endure their presence. At last he burst out in insulting speech: ‘You, whom I created from nothing, treat me so dishonourably that you dare pronounce a sentence of excommunication against my bailiffs because of my commands. But know for certain that you have not dared this with impunity. It is extraordinary that I tolerate you in my presence: not only shall I deprive you of your benefactions, but also of your genitals.’ But the canons, steadfast in their resolve, answered gently: ‘You did not establish us for this, that we should sin against God and against ourselves by allowing, in our time, to perish through negligence what you bestowed for the salvation of your soul in God’s service, and what you ordered us under oath to preserve to the best of our ability. Yet now, although you know that this was done at your command, you, warning us to desist as though we were your creation, extend coercion against our patrimony, lest the force of our oath and law compel us to pronounce the sentence which draws offenders to eternal death unless they repent.’ Then the count pretended to rage still more violently. But they, seeing that warnings and gentle words achieved nothing but rather provoked him further, excommunicated him in the sight of his own eyes and of all who were present. Seeing their constancy, the count gave thanks to God that he had chosen guardians for his church; he threw himself at their feet and humbly asked forgiveness, and thus obtained the grace of absolution. In recompense for the damage and his wrong, he enlarged the canons’ possessions by one village. In the same church the aforesaid Count Baldwin—illustrious indeed in lineage and proven virtues, surpassingly noble in greatness of spirit and strength, and in the glory of all—was buried in the year of the Lord 1067, on the Kalends of September,” is added by B.]

[Note: [Col. 0955C] The Rhymed Chronicle translates this thus:

> “With money which he received into his hand  
> From his people (which he might spend if it seemed good to him),  
> He acquired rents and land,  
> All of which he conveyed into the king’s hand,  
> So that, for greater security,  
> he had them received from the king.”]

[Col. 0957A] 10. The same Baldwin established the castle at Oudenaarde, by means of which, after destroying the castle at Ename, he appropriated for himself from the kingdom of Lotharingia the territory as far as the river Dender [Note: [Col. 0957C] The Dender, a river flowing past Ath, Grammont, Ninove, and Aalst.] in Brabant. For the river Scheldt, from its source to the sea, separates the kingdom of Lotharingia from the county of Flanders, which belongs to the kingdom of France. Therefore the king of Lotharingia, who was Caesar and Augustus, the emperor [Note: [Col. 0957C] Henry III.], came hostilely against Count Baldwin (1046). Passing before Arras, while Count Baldwin scarcely held his army within by shutting the gates, he advanced almost as far as the village of Arques [Note: [Col. 0957C] Arcques.] belonging to Saint-Bertin, falsely supposing that he could at least enter Flanders by that route. For both there and wherever a dry-land entrance into Flanders lay open, the count had fortified it against him with ditch, rampart, and palisade [Col. 0957B]. Thus the emperor, wearied by futile labour, returned as he had come.

The count pursued him as though he were fleeing, as far as the Rhine, and, after the emperor’s noble palace at Nijmegen had been burned [Note: [Col. 0957C] This was done by Godfrey the Bearded, duke of Lorraine, Baldwin’s ally, not by Baldwin himself.], returned with his army unharmed (1047). The emperor, justly ashamed and angry, came again against the count seven years later [Col. 0958A] (1054). Arriving unexpectedly at the rampart called Bulliens Rivus [Note: [Col. 0957C] Le Boulenrieu, near Évin, arrondissement of Béthune, canton of Carvin; cf. *Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium* III.68.], he invaded Tournai and quickly returned, taking Ansel [Note: [Col. 0957C] This is Ansel of Ribemont; cf. ibid. III.66, 72; Sigebert’s Aquicinctine Continuation, in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores* VI, 393.] and other nobles for battle, no one from Flanders opposing him. But when peaceful envoys intervened, he restored the prisoners to the count and granted him Brabant as a fief after receiving homage [Note: [Col. 0957C] Not Brabant in its entirety: Baldwin received in fief only the land of Aalst on the right bank of the Scheldt, together with the castle of Ghent, the Four Offices, and the land of Waas. From that time these were collectively included under the name “Imperial Flanders.” In addition he also received five islands of Zeeland. Moreover, this agreement was made not by Henry III, as our author says, but only later under Henry IV, at Cologne in December 1056. On all these matters see Kluit, *Historia critica comitatus Hollandiae* II, excursus 4, p. 56.]. [Note: [Col. 0957] “He added the castle of Valenciennes … Walcheren,” in De Smet I, 46, from Sigebert under the year 1006; added by B.]

11. The venerable countess Adela, left bereft of so great a husband but not of wealth, yet not living pleasurably amid those riches [Note: [Col. 0957] “or living,” written above in 1.], persisted in prayers night and day. Accordingly, at Messines [Note: [Col. 0958C] Messines, between Ypres and Lille. She founded it in 1065 and died there in 1071.] she built a convent for religious women. In a litter borne by two horses, suitably roofed against winds and rains lest she should thereby be hindered from holy meditation [Col. 0958B], she sought the patronage at Rome of the apostles and other saints. Having received from the lord pope the garb and blessing of widowhood, she returned to Flanders and at Messines fell asleep in Christ’s peace, to await the last trumpet.

[Col. 0959A] 12. [Lamb.] Her firstborn Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0959] “The first years of his military apprenticeship at the imperial court … solemnities,” in De Smet I, 50–52, from the *History of Hainaut* by Tomellus, chapters 8–17; added by B.], while his father was still living [Note: [Col. 0959C] In 1051.], married Richilde, countess of Hainaut, so that he might also possess that county through her. She had then become the widow of Herman, count of Mons, and had borne him a son [Note: [Col. 0959C] Roger.]. Baldwin, his stepfather, judging him through excessive simplicity insufficiently fitted for the world, contrived to elevate him to the clerical estate and to the bishopric of Châlons, thereby appropriating his inheritance for himself.

By Richilde Baldwin begot two sons, Arnulf and Baldwin; after his father’s death, he governed both counties in such peace that no one dared or cared to bear arms, close his door at night because of robbers, or carry home from the fields ploughshares and hoes removed from the ploughs. Therefore, from the whole people he jointly deserved the particular byname “the Good Count” [Col. 0959B]. Yet he and his Richilde were excommunicated by Lord Ingelbert, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, because he had married, in an incest worse than adultery, the wife of his kinsman Count Herman. But they obtained from Pope Leo IX, Richilde’s maternal uncle, this dispensation: that they should remain married, but without carnal intercourse. [Note: [Col. 0959] “The same Leo prophesied that their descendants would not possess both counties for long; later events proved the truth of this,” from Herman of Tournai, chapter 12; added by B.]

This same Pope Leo held a council at Reims in the church of Saint Remigius which he had recently built himself [Note: [Col. 0960C] “Rather, consecrated.” MARTÈNE.]. At it a certain bishop, accused of simony and having no witnesses to his innocence, was ordered to say the entire *Gloria*. He said only, “Glory to the Father and to the Son,” and was unable to add, “and to the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0959] Thus 1 and 6. In 4: “He said ‘Glory to the Father and glory to the Son’ only, but could not add ‘and to the Holy Spirit.’”]

[Col. 0959C] 13. The country was not granted the happiness of being governed long by the aforesaid Good Count. Having died (1070) and been buried at Hasnon [Note: [Col. 0959] “In the year of the Lord 1070, 17 July,” is added by B.], he sleeps and rests in peace in that very place where, after expelling robbers, he had built a monastic community from their stone tower.

14. The venerable Richilde, now for some time a widow [Col. 0960A], was at last afflicted by a remarkable penitence. Persisting in fasts and prayers, she personally served the poor and lepers daily; she even anointed herself with their pus, and after washing them in baths used those same baths after them, so that, perhaps made ill in this way, she might be inwardly restored like the king’s daughter. Thus, with the world crucified to her [Note: [Col. 0959] “At last called by the Lord, that most noble countess died in the year of the Lord 1092. Her body was carried to Hasnon, where after her husband’s death she had bestowed many benefactions, and was honourably buried in the basilica of Saint Mary Magdalene. May her soul deserve to be clothed in the garment of immortality and cherished in the delight of Paradise,” is added by B.], she committed her earthly body to Hasnon and her soul to the mercy of Jesus Christ (1086), though she had first suffered disturbances not small.

15. For when her husband died, through her womanly arrogance and the imprudence of her son Arnulf, scarcely fifteen years old, the paradise of Flanders began to be emptied of the delights of its peace, and thence to complain bitterly both within itself and before God, yearning for the renowned valour of Robert, brother of the recently deceased Good Count [Note: [Col. 0959] “It appears that [this phrase] is omitted: ‘to yearn for.’”]. When this [Col. 0960B] quarrelsome and crafty woman perceived it, she fled to the protection of Philip, king of France. Not ashamed of a third marriage, she tried still to marry a certain proud William, viscount of Normandy, thereby stirring up still more against herself certain princes and the people of Flanders.

16. For the aforesaid Robert, less dear to his father and more dear to his mother [Note: [Col. 0959] “had been; therefore his father … he withdrew to Frisia,” in De Smet I, 55, from Herman of Tournai, chapter 12; added by B.], and alienated from Flanders by his brother, [Lamb.] married Gertrude, daughter of Bernard, duke of Saxony, widow of Florent, count of Frisia, and having a daughter by her husband. She bore Robert two sons, Robert and Philip, and three daughters. One of these [Note: [Col. 0960C] Otgiva, or Mary.], having become a religious woman at Messines and a venerable abbess, fell asleep in the peace of her bridegroom. Another, married to Canute [Col. 0960C], king of Denmark, bore him a boy named Charles; but after her husband had been killed by his own men, Charles was received in Flanders by his uncle Robert [Note: [Col. 0959] “From this point the handwriting becomes slightly larger, the ink having changed. Yet it is the same hand, that of the author.”], carefully educated, and grew commendably into the strength of military discipline.

His mother afterward married the duke of Apulia [Note: [Col. 0959] Roger, by whom she bore a son named William, who succeeded his father in the duchy and greatly ennobled the dignity he had received by nobility of character and vigour of deeds. But afterward, when he heard of the death of his only brother Charles, count of Flanders, he first began to grieve inconsolably and then himself began to languish unto death. When he recognized that he was in danger, he summoned the archbishop of Salerno and the bishop of Troia; and wishing, by their testimony also, to confirm what he had done before while healthy, he assigned in perpetual right to blessed Peter the Apostle and his most holy vicar Honorius everything movable and immovable that he possessed in the land,” is added by B.]. The third [Note: [Col. 0959] “Gertrude: Henry, count of Brussels … at Auxerre,” in De Smet I, 67, from Herman of Tournai, chapter 17; added by B.] was married by Henry of Brussels; after his death, by Theodoric, duke of Alsace [Col. 0961A]. By the latter she bore Theodoric, later a most valiant count of Flanders.

17. Robert, then, living in Frisia, learned of his brother’s death and at the same time of Richilde’s tyranny. He returned to Flanders and reached Ghent. Summoning the aforesaid woman and urging her to restore to him his paternal realm, he found her, stirred by womanly fury, declaring in insulting replies:

> If he did not wish to be taken, let him swiftly be gone from there.  
> She would give him neither a part of the realm nor the whole.  
> If the matter requires it, she will hold the war by force;  
> she will not be deprived of the possessions her lord held.  
> So long as she lives, this provident woman will lose none of these things.

When the duke heard this and took the woman’s arrogance grievously, he approached the king and related everything to him in order. King Philip, deeply angered at the injury inflicted upon his nephew [Col. 0961B], ordered him to return to Flanders with all speed and gather whomsoever he could, promising most firmly to give him assistance. But Richilde, having learned the king’s plan, corrupted his mind with the promise of four thousand pounds of gold and fraudulently recalled him from the undertaking. Thus the Frisian, disappointed in his hope, returned to Frisia on the advice of his father-in-law Bernard, duke of Saxony, and wintered there for some time.

18. Meanwhile certain magnates, gravely offended by the woman’s excessive cruelty toward clergy and people, and above all distressed with great sorrow over the plundering of churches which she had committed, sent envoys to the Frisian and made known to him in letters their disposition toward her [Col. 0961C]. Greatly cheered by this message, he crossed the sea with speed and, through the prudence of Boniface the castellan, was secretly led as far as the castle called Cassel. This castle had been situated from ancient times upon the lofty summit of a mountain.

> Among the high mountains of Flanders this mountain rises above all.  
> A fortress overtops the mountain; if the sky is clear,  
> they say that one may see its summit from the hill of Laon.

[Note: [Col. 0961] “This castle … Laon” is absent from 6.]

When those who favoured his party recognized this, they hurried there in bands and strengthened the castle with arms and fortifications.

19. When the flying report reached Richilde’s ears, she and her son Arnulf, a young man of remarkable worth [Col. 0961D], gathered an army, summoned companies from diverse regions to their aid, and hastened with an immense multitude to the aforesaid castle (1072). Aid came together from every side: counts, dukes, castellans, and various troops of warriors—men of Arras, Brabant, Valenciennes, Cambrai, Tournai, Nivelles, Mons [Note: [Col. 0961D] Mons.], Saint-Omer, Boulogne, Ardennes, Saint-Pol [Note: [Col. 0961D] Saint-Pol.], Béthune, Hesdin [Note: [Col. 0961D] Hesdin.], Aubigny [Note: [Col. 0961D] Aubigny.], Guînes, Tournehem [Note: [Col. 0961] “Tornelienses” in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0961D] Tournehem, between Saint-Omer and Ardres.], Oudenaarde, Ostrevent, Choques [Note: [Col. 0961] “Locrenses” in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0961D] Choques, near Béthune?], and many others.

King Philip also came, with a strong column of armed men; Geoffrey, bishop of Paris, brother of Count Eustace of Boulogne; the bishop of Lyons [Note: [Col. 0961D] “Laudunensis” (Laon).]; the bishop of Amiens [Note: [Col. 0961D] Guy.]; Franks, Normans, men of Les Roches [Note: [Col. 0961D] Les Rochenois.], Noyon, Champagne, Senlis [Note: [Col. 0961D] Senlis.], Torote [Note: [Col. 0961D] Torote, near Compiègne.], Reims, Châlons, Chartres, Orléans, Étampes [Col. 0962B] [Note: [Col. 0962D] Étampes.], Coucy [Note: [Col. 0962D] Coucy.], Saint-Quentin, Corbie, Péronne, Nesle [Note: [Col. 0962D] Nesle in Picardy.], Montaigu [Note: [Col. 0962D] Montagu.], Ribemont [Note: [Col. 0962D] Ribemont.], Soissons, Anjou, Poitou, Barrois [Note: [Col. 0962D] Barrois in Lorraine.], Nadavernes, Burgundy, and countless others. All these encamped to defeat the Frisian in the plain below Mount Cassel.

20. Against so vast a multitude, he brought out men much fewer in number but, as the outcome proved, stronger: men of Ghent, Viven [Note: [Col. 0962D] Viven.], Coukelaer [Note: [Col. 0962D] Coukelaer.], Bergues, Veurne, Bruges, Ypres, Roeselare [Note: [Col. 0962D] Boulers or Rousselaere, between Courtrai and Dixmude.], Oudenburg, Harelbeke, Rodenburg [Note: [Col. 0961] “Erdeborgenses” in 6.], Broekburg, Courtrai, and the Cassel men themselves. At length they advanced [Col. 0962C], armed not only with steel but strengthened by faith. Casting aside linen garments, they put on woollen clothing beneath their armour; falling upon the earth, they implored with tears the help of heaven. About to fight the earthly king with so small a force, they committed their cause to the King of Heaven. [Note: [Col. 0962D] 20 February. Others: 5 February 1072.]

21. Why delay? When battle was joined with all their strength, there was a vast slaughter among the royal army. The ground was soaked with blood; the field was covered with a multitude of dead. Richilde too, responsible for so great a massacre, was captured and consigned to a dark prison. Her son, Count Arnulf, that young man greatly to be mourned even though an enemy, was also struck down and carried to the monastery of Saint-Omer for burial. Meanwhile the Frisian [Col. 0962D], while perhaps riding alone as his companions pursued the enemy farther away, was captured by Eustace and carefully taken to the castle of Saint-Omer, where he was handed over to the castellan Wulfric Rabel for custody.

When the citizens saw this [Col. 0963A], they immediately surrounded the castle with siege works and vigorously attacked it with missiles and varied engines. In short, the count was forcibly drawn out and honourably restored to his men amid universal rejoicing. Richilde too was released, and so war between them continued for a long time with varying fortune. [Sigebert.] The woman’s son Baldwin, Arnulf’s brother, rebelled as well; the count defeated and put him to flight. [Note: [Col. 0963] “Released … put him to flight” are added in the margin of 1, but in precisely the same pen and ink, not later but at the same time as the rest.] [Note: [Col. 0963] “Baldwin … set out upon the journey to Jerusalem with other princes at its beginning, and has not yet returned; to this day it could not be known whether he was killed or captured,” from Herman of Tournai, chapter 33; added by B.]

22. Therefore the king of the Franks, defeated and driven off in the battle of Cassel, proceeded to the castle called Montreuil [Note: [Col. 0963C] Montreuil.], gathered a larger army, and returned to Flanders with a strong force. When he reached the borough of Saint-Omer, he burned its suburbs and, through the treachery of the castellan Wulfric, entered the city. The enemy ran through the streets plundering; the burgesses sought hiding places in flight [Col. 0963B]; churches were despoiled, monks wronged, clerics mangled, matrons and maidens dishonoured, and the city, full of confusion, mourned.

While the king did these things, Bishop Geoffrey, residing in the town called Éperlec [Note: [Col. 0963C] Éperlec, between Saint-Omer and Ardres.] and considering in his mind how he might assist the Frisian, sent him letters promising that, if the count granted his lord the wood called Bethlo, he would restore him to his paternal realm. When the count consented to his wish, the bishop swiftly informed the king that he should look to his safety and depart with all speed, adding that the duke of Flanders and the count of Boulogne were near at hand with a great army and that, unless he hastened his flight, he would be captured. Terrified by this message, the king left the city by night, abandoning his baggage, and hurried toward France.

As the king fled, the count arrived on the following day [Col. 0963C] and recovered the city, though he grieved deeply over the injuries inflicted upon churches and people. [Note: [Col. 0963] “The king … grieved deeply,” added in the margin.] The bishop then reconciled his brother Eustace to the count and granted him the aforesaid wood, which for that reason is possessed to this day by the counts of Boulogne in hereditary right [Col. 0964A].

23. Finally Robert, surnamed the Frisian, having defeated his adversaries on every side [Note: [Col. 0963] “Envoys to the emperor … it was said,” in De Smet I, 63, from Herman of Tournai; added by B.], became monarch of all Flanders. [Note: [Col. 0963] “A few years later this same Robert went to Jerusalem, then held by the Saracens. As he wished to enter the city gate, the gate shut of its own accord. Seeing this, he was seized with great fear, understanding that the omen was not favourable to him. He therefore went to a certain hermit living near the city, whom he had heard to be a holy and religious man, in order to confess his sins. When the holy man heard his confession, he imposed upon him penance for Arnulf, his nephew, whom he had killed, and told him that, if he wished to have God propitious, he should restore to his nephew Baldwin the Flanders which he had taken from him. Greatly frightened by the omen of the gate, Robert agreed to the hermit’s counsel; he came to the gate, which opened to him of its own accord. While he was living in the city in the house of a very powerful Saracen, he heard from Saracen astrologers and others that Jerusalem would shortly be captured by Christians. It was captured not long afterward, in the thirty-ninth year of King Philip. On returning from the Jerusalem journey, Robert yielded Douai, out of great fear, to Baldwin, count of Hainaut. But while Robert was raised to the rule of Flanders, [lacuna] dying clerics … Cassel,” in De Smet I, from Lambert’s genealogy, chapters 3–8; added by B.]

After countless triumphs in war, he entrusted the reins of the realm to his son Robert, died, and was buried at Cassel (1093, 13 October).

24. [Lamb.] Robert the Younger, having become heir to his father’s principality, married Clementia, daughter of William, the most noble count of Burgundy, surnamed Testahardith [Note: [Col. 0963] and sister of Lord Pope Calixtus—[lacuna]—received burial. De Smet I, 68–74, from Heriman of Tournai, chs. 18–26, adds B.]; by her he begot Baldwin, a renowned knight, and William, who was carried off by premature death before reaching adolescence and was buried in the monastery of Saint Bertin. Count Robert accordingly distinguished himself by praiseworthy military service in the conquest of Jerusalem, and on returning from there brought with him the arm of Saint George, which he sent to the church of Aire-sur-la-Lys. [Sig. Aut. Au.] Then, because he was troubling the city of Cambrai, Emperor Henry marched against him; after capturing some of his castles, he was compelled by the severity of the approaching winter to return. [Lamb.] Having therefore designated his son for the monarchy of the realm, he died and was buried at Arras (1111, October 5). Baldwin succeeded him, illustrious in knightly prowess and not inferior in virtue [Note: [Col. 0963] Before this Robert set out for Syria, he gave the seal of his lordship and principality to the provost of Saint Donatian, whom he made chancellor of the whole dominion of Flanders. In the fifth year of Robert’s principality, Cîteaux was founded. Added by B.].

25. He took as wife the daughter of Alan, count of Brittany [Note: [Col. 0964C] Hawise, or Agnes.]; but when consanguinity between them was established, they were separated by order of Pope Paschal. This consanguinity was set out in the presence of the pope by Cono, bishop of Palestrina, as follows: Constance, queen of the Franks, and Ermengard, countess of Auvergne, were sisters. From Constance was born Countess Adela, and from Ermengard of Auvergne another Countess Ermengard [Note: [Col. 0964C] of Chartres, wife of Odo II.]; from Adela came Robert the Frisian, and from Ermengard came Countess Bertha [Note: [Col. 0965D] Wife of Alan III, duke of Brittany. Ivo of Chartres explains this kinship differently in a letter published by Dom Brial, XIII, 411, n.]; from Robert came another Robert, and from Bertha came Hawise, countess of Nantes; from Robert the Younger came this Baldwin, and from Hawise came Count Alan; from this man came this young woman.

26. [Lamb.] Thus the illustrious Baldwin, in his day powerful above all princes of the Franks, so nobly exalted the realm of the Flemings through frequent wars that he struck terror into his neighboring tyrants on every side, and would have driven King Henry of England from Normandy had illness not intervened. For, having assembled a multitude of troops and taken with him William, son of Robert, whom King Henry of England held captive, he planned to encircle with siege the town of Rouen, where the said king was hiding, and to seize him, or meet him in battle and drive him from the kingdom [Col. 0965B] which he had unjustly invaded. But while leading his army through Arras, he began to fall ill, seized by a sudden sickness arising from a wound which he had received shortly before from a certain Breton by a slight blow upon the forehead; and, stricken with paralysis from the thigh to the feet, he remained sick for a full nine months. Since he could not be cured by physicians, he put the whole realm of Flanders in order, commended himself to God and Saint Bertin, and, clothed in a monastic habit, rendered his soul to God in the eighth year of his rule, at the town of Roeselare. Carried to Saint Bertin by Charles, his successor, he was honorably buried in the middle of the church, with the whole multitude of magnates present.

[Col. 0965C] 27. When he died without an heir, Charles succeeded by right of kinship. For he was the son of Canute, king of Denmark, by the eldest daughter of Robert the Frisian and Gertrude. Having been elevated to the rule, he entered the church of Saint Omer with the princes of Flanders and held his first court; and in the same year he utterly destroyed the castle of Saint-Pol, in which the treacherous Hugh called Campdavaine and many robbers had been hiding, and ordered its surrounding moat filled in. He also manfully destroyed the strongholds of evildoers on every side and nobly subjected the realm to himself. [Simon.] In the eighth year of his rule, at Bruges, while hearing Mass during Lent, intent upon prayer within the Canon and chanting the fiftieth Psalm, he was extending his hand with alms to a poor man when he was killed before the altar by the hand of his own servants, on account of justice. Portentous signs preceded his death. For in the dungeons’ [Note: [Col. 0966D] Donjon.] ditches an abundance of blood flowed forth; when boiled by many people, it gave off an unbearable stench, foreshadowing the blood which was shed at Charles’s death or in vengeance for it, and spreading far and wide the stench of treachery.

28. When he had been killed, King Louis came into Flanders and, though with difficulty, set over the Flemings as his successor William, son of Robert, count of the Normans, whom King Henry then held captive; and he put Charles’s traitors to death, as was fitting, by various kinds of torture. Then so many massacres, so many burnings, so many wars, so many disturbances arose against William, and Flanders was afflicted by so many evils, that it is wearisome even to tell or write of them. William of Lo, son of Philip, brother of Robert the Younger, was being raised up, saying: “I shall rule.” Having won over the greater part of the people, he brought certain castles under his authority. When this became known, the king went with Count William of Ypres to meet him, captured him, and consigned him to chains and prison for some time. But afterward, falsely reconciled to him at the entreaty of his followers, this same William swore an oath of fidelity to the count [Col. 0966B] which he scarcely kept for a single day.

29. Satan also raised up against him another adversary, namely Arnold, Charles’s nephew through his eldest sister. For he claimed that by right of kinship he was heir to the realm. Received by the people of Saint Omer, he made the monastery of Saint Bertin into a fortified castle for himself, from which he rebelled. When Count William heard of this, he besieged him with his men; some attempted to set fire to it, but the count threatened anyone who presumed to do so. He compelled Arnold to come out and renounce all claim to Flanders.

30. Then certain Flemish magnates, seeing that the count relied on the counsels of the Normans, moved either by envy or enticed by the money of King Henry, summoned Thierry, son of Thierry, duke of Alsace, whom he had begotten by [Col. 0966C] a daughter of Robert the Frisian; favoring him, they caused many evils. For at that time treachery, perjury, faithlessness, and violation of agreements were considered prudence among the Flemings. What more? After innumerable exercises of evil, William and Thierry came with a strong force of armed men to battle on the field of Axpoele; Thierry and his men were routed, and victory fell to William. But he enjoyed the victory’s joy only briefly. For, while besieging Thierry in the castle called Aalst, just as the surrender of his opponents was at hand, he was wounded. Near death from this wound, he became a monk and, carried to Sithiu, was buried at the head of Count Baldwin.

31. Thierry indeed, though many resisted him, was called monarch of all [Col. 0966D] Flanders, but was very ill-suited to govern because of his uncultivated ways, being wholly unaccustomed to such matters. For, to pass over the evils that were assailing in various places, at different times, from different enemies: William of Lo, holding out from the castle called Sluys [Note: [Col. 0966D] Sluys, at the mouths of the Scheldt, between Bruges and Vlissingen.], raged against him with murders, plunder, burnings of churches, and the devastation of towns.

32. Meanwhile Clementia [Note: [Col. 0965] “sister of Pope Calixtus” was inserted into the text by hand 1; 2, 4, and 6 accepted it.] the widow of Robert the Younger, [Col. 0967A] who until then had held a third part of Flanders as her dower, died and left to the count whatever she possessed. While still alive, she built two churches of nuns, at Bourbourg and at Avesnes. Countess Suanildis also died, on account of whose consanguineous relationship many evils had occurred, having only one daughter by the count, named Lauretta. The duke of Limburg took her as wife; but because they were said to be related, they were separated. Then Iwan of Aalst married her; after his death she married Ralph, count of Péronne, and after he died, the count of Namur [Note: [Col. 0967] Reading of 5: “This: Henry, by name duke of Louvain, took this woman as wife; he died young and without an heir. Then Iwan of Aalst married her; after his death she married Henry of Limburg, but because they were related, they were separated. Moreover, she married Ralph,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0967D] Gilbert gives a different account, p. 51, ed. de Chasteler: after Iwan’s death Lauretta married Ralph, the widowed count of Vermandois; afterward Henry, duke of Limburg; then Henry, count of Namur. [Col. 0968D] Having been successively left by these husbands, she took the religious habit.]. Thierry, however, married a daughter of the king of Jerusalem named Sibylla [Simon.], by whom he had children of both sexes.

[Col. 0967B] 33. William of Lo, grievous and hateful to the count like a beam in his eye, was expelled from Flanders after the capture of the aforementioned castle. He came to England and was honorably received and retained by King Stephen, as befitted a man of such nobility. Living therefore at the royal court, he so excelled in the virtues of military discipline that he was dear and welcome to the royal majesty; and not without reason, for he most vigorously defended the king himself from every assault of his rivals. It happened that Robert, count of Gloucester, son of King Henry by a concubine, took up arms against Stephen and intended to deprive him either of life or kingdom. In short, battle was joined between them; the count captured the king and committed him to custody. When William learned this, [Col. 0967C] he took his fellow-knights with him, challenged Robert to battle, surrounded him, and, after capturing him, had him carefully guarded (1141). Then, through the intervention of the princes and magnates of the realm, each was restored in exchange for the other and returned to his own side. The king, not forgetful of these services, granted his liberator the whole province called Kent to possess and honored him among the foremost men of the realm as long as he lived. While he was thus the fear and terror of all England, by the providence of God [Col. 0968A] who scourges in order to instruct, he lost the sight of his eyes but not the strength of his spirit. Thus, as God’s grace illumined his heart, reflecting upon what was being done around him and providing for his future salvation, he set aside stores from his treasures and assigned much to Christ’s poor and to the restoration of churches.

34. At the same time, namely in the year of the incarnate Word 1152, there occurred in the town of Saint Omer a lamentable conflagration of certain churches and houses, in which the voracious flame consumed the church of Saint Bertin also, with all its workshops. Therefore Leonius [Note: [Col. 0967] Leo in 4.] of blessed memory, then abbot, deeply afflicted by so grave a disaster, went to William [Note: [Col. 0968D] of Lo.], who still held sway over all England, and set forth to him in a sorrowful [Col. 0968B] voice the circumstances of the event. Hearing this, William grieved deeply over the desolation of so venerable a place and, opening the treasures of his compassion, magnificently supplied gold, silver, and an abundance of timber for the rebuilding of the monastery, under the abbot’s direction. His memory remains forever among the inhabitants of that monastery.

35. Not long afterward King Stephen died, and Henry the Younger, son of the elder daughter of Henry, succeeded (1155). At the beginning of his reign he so hated the Flemings that he razed their castles and fortifications to the ground, deprived them of their possessions, and expelled them, together with William himself, from England. This great-hearted William, once a warlike prince, after he came to Flanders—that is, his native soil—lived quietly for about ten years. Giving much from his resources, as we ourselves saw [Note: [Col. 0967] “as we ourselves saw” is absent from 4.], to churches and the poor, he departed this life full of days at his castle called Lo, and was honorably buried there in the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February [25 January] (1164). May his soul possess the joys of paradise.

## Brussels Continuation

In manuscript 4, in a hand of the late fourteenth century.

[Col. 0967]

[Col. 0967D] After the aforesaid William died and was buried in his castle called Lo (1164), the aforementioned Count Thierry peacefully and quietly possessed the monarchy of Flanders. By his wife Sibylla he had three sons, valiant in arms, formidable to enemies, and surpassing all others in elegance of form. He inspired fear in near and distant alike, because, through fear of and awe at the courage of his sons, no one dared rebel against the said Thierry in Flanders.

When the aforesaid Thierry was removed from this world [Col. 0969A] and buried in the monastery of Watten (1168), his firstborn son Philip succeeded to the county of Flanders. Because of his illustrious deeds and martial vigor, in which he excelled above all mortals, he was deservedly compared by minstrels and by all men who knew him to Alexander the Great, king of the Greeks. He married Isabella, daughter of the count of Vermandois. After her father died (1156), he expelled Ralph, brother of this same wife, from the county of Vermandois because he had contracted elephantiasis, and obtained with his said wife the counties of Vermandois, Amiens, and Valois; throughout his wife’s life he possessed them peacefully. Philip’s next brother, Matthew, [Col. 0969B] said to be the handsomest knight of all knights, married the countess of Boulogne, by whom he had two daughters. The elder of these, against the wishes of her friends but by her own choice, married Renaud, count of Dammartin; Henry, duke of Brabant, married the younger. This same Matthew was struck by an arrow during an expedition undertaken near Rouen and died (1173). He was carried back to Boulogne and buried there [Note: [Col. 0969] Not at Boulogne, but at Saint-Josse-sur-Mer.]. The third brother, named Peter, though he was a cleric and bishop-elect of Cambrai, withdrew from the clerical state, became a knight, and married the countess of Nevers (1174); by her he had one daughter, named Sibylla.

The aforesaid Count Philip of Flanders, having governed Flanders most vigorously for forty years or thereabouts, after his wife died and deprived of the companionship of his two brothers, set out for the regions of Jerusalem (1190). There he closed his final day among his companions who had set out with him (1191, June 1); his bones, separated somehow from the flesh, were brought back to Clairvaux and buried in the church.

After him Baldwin, count of Hainaut, succeeded in the county of Flanders because he had married Philip’s sister, named Margaret. By her he had three sons: Baldwin, the firstborn, afterward emperor of Constantinople; Philip, afterward count of Namur; and Henry, afterward, like his brother Baldwin, emperor [Col. 0970B] of Constantinople (1206). When this Baldwin had governed a third part of Flanders in right of his wife for about four years, his wife was removed from this world (1194, November 15) and buried in the church of Saint Donatian at Bruges. His eldest son Baldwin obtained the county, greatly grieving and distressed because King Philip of France, who had married his sister, had appropriated for himself the better third part of Flanders. Therefore he sent envoys to his kinsman King Richard of England and made an alliance with him; the count on one side and the king on the other made war against the said king toward Poitou (1196).

## Gislebert Continuation

In manuscript 5.

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0969C] But, to pursue the sequence of the genealogy: Thierry of Alsace, count of Flanders as has been stated, after visiting the holy places of Jerusalem for the fourth time, finally ended his days at Gravelines (1168), and was buried in the monastery of regular canons at Watten, in the diocese of Saint Omer, with this epitaph inscribed above him:

> Here lies buried Lord Thierry of Alsace, count of Flanders, who visited the Holy Land four times, and, returning thence, brought the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and gave it to the town of Bruges; and after ruling Flanders vigorously for forty years, died at Gravelines in the year of the Lord 1168.

Philip of Alsace, count of Vermandois by right of his wife, after the death of his father Thierry possessed the county of Flanders [Col. 0969D]. After various conflicts with Philip, king of France, he prepared himself for a journey to the Holy Land. Returning from there, he died in Syria, leaving no offspring. His wife Matilda honorably buried his body at Clairvaux [Col. 0970C] (1191).

After Philip was taken from the living, the great-hearted Baldwin, count of Hainaut, inherited the county of Flanders also in right of his wife. For Margaret, Philip’s sister and the eldest among Thierry’s daughters, had married Baldwin, count of Hainaut.

When this Baldwin died (1194), his eldest son Baldwin became count alike of Hainaut and Flanders. In 1200, with his wife Maria, sister of Theobald, count of Champagne, he took the cross at Bruges at the beginning of Lent; in the third year after 1200, already signed with the cross, he went toward Venice in aid of the Holy Land, then proceeded to Syria and afterward to Constantinople. There, after various conflicts against the Greeks, [Col. 0970D] he was elected emperor of Constantinople in the year of the Lord 1205. But not much later he ended his life (1206), and his brother Henry, count of Flanders and Hainaut, succeeded him in the empire.

## Clairmarais Continuation

In manuscript 6.

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0969D] 1. Having inserted these matters incidentally concerning William of Lo, let us return to the genealogy of the counts of Flanders. [Col. 0970D] Thierry by his wife Sibylla had sons: Baldwin, Philip, Matthew, and [Col. 0971A] Peter; and daughters: Gertrude and Margaret. Baldwin, the eldest, who ought to have been heir to the realm, died in childhood. After him Philip, the elder in age, assumed the rights of government under his father (1155), and married Elizabeth, daughter of Ralph, count of Vermandois. A marvelous occurrence is reported concerning Philip, which seems to me an indication of his future excellence: on the third day after his birth, with all who were present hearing, he cried out terribly, “Clear the house for me!”

Matthew, praiseworthy for bodily beauty and military valor, since the principality of Flanders had passed by right, as is customary, to his elder brother, was compelled by his father to marry Mary, daughter of Stephen, king of England. Dedicated from childhood to the religious habit, she was the sole surviving heir to the county of Boulogne; she was brought out from the cloister and, with papal consent, joined in marriage to Matthew in order to provide legitimate heirs to her paternal inheritance. When Matthew had begotten two daughters by her, he restored the nun to the cloister and married again the sister of the countess of Flanders. By her he is said to have had children, but all are said to have died in childhood. Peter, the last of the sons, became a cleric and, through his brother’s provision, was promoted to be bishop-elect of Cambrai. Of the daughters, Gertrude the firstborn first married the count of Maurienne [Note: [Col. 0971D] Maurienne: Humbert III.]; after separating from him, she married Hugh of Oisy; separated from him also, she became a nun at Messines [Note: [Col. 0971D] Messines.]. Margaret married Ralph, son of the aforementioned Count Ralph; [Col. 0971C] when he became leprous and died before having known her in the manner of husbands, she married again Baldwin, count of Hainaut, by whom she produced a quite fertile offspring of both sexes. Meanwhile Count Thierry entered upon the way of all flesh at the new town [Note: [Col. 0971D] Gravelines.] situated near Bourbourg by the sea (1168), and was buried at Watten with most solemn funeral rites [Note: [Col. 0971] In the margin another hand of the fourteenth century adds: “In the year of the Lord 1167, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February [17 January]; he reigned forty years.”].

2. Philip, freely directing the administration of his county, deservedly surpassed all his predecessors in wisdom and steadfast justice. He restrained murders, thefts, and the countless other crimes with which the Flemings raged against one another; and he not only governed Flanders peacefully, but also prompted all neighboring provinces, by his example, toward the good of peace [Col. 0971D]. But because stable prosperity cannot exist in human affairs, a sad outcome troubles joyful successes, as it is written: “Sorrow occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14). For Philip, relying both on his own resourcefulness and on the assistance of his brother Matthew, would, while acting vigorously in military affairs, have subdued all Normandy, had not a certain misfortune forced him to abandon his warlike purpose.

[Col. 0972A] During the siege of a certain castle [Note: [Col. 0971D] Briencourt.], Matthew was mortally wounded and died; he was buried in the territory of his county at Saint-Josse [Note: [Col. 0972D] Saint-Josse-sur-Mer.] (1173). This untimely death was exceedingly lamentable to all the Flemings. For an heir to Flanders had been expected from Matthew, while all offspring was despaired of from Philip, whose wife was barren. Philip, therefore, already deprived of hope of succession, removed his brother, bishop-elect of Cambrai, from the clerical state, made him a knight, and joined to him in marriage the countess of Nevers (1174). Peter had one daughter by her [Note: [Col. 0972D] Sibylla.], and died, it is said, by poison.

3. Meanwhile Philip, son of Louis, king of France, was crowned king at Reims in the year of the Lord [Col. 0972B] 1179, on the Kalends of November [1 November], with all the magnates of the realm present. Count Philip attended there and appeared more glorious than the other princes, bearing the sword before the king, which ought to be carried by the noblest prince of the realm. Not many days afterward, King Philip asked the count to give him in marriage his niece, namely the daughter of his sister, that is, Margaret, countess of Hainaut. Hearing this, the count rejoiced greatly, because he felt that much honor would accrue to him if his niece became queen, queen of France. He therefore gave her to the king and granted him as dowry, to be held after his own death, whatever land and rights he possessed beyond the great ditch [Note: [Col. 0972D] The ditch of Boulogne, or New Ditch, dug in 1053 from Saint Omer to the River Lys. Compare below, ch. 9.].

4. Not long afterward discord arose between the king [Col. 0972C] of France and the count of Flanders (1182). While it continued, Countess Elizabeth died (26 March) and was honorably buried at Arras in the church of Blessed Mary, in the year of the Lord 1182. War thus existed between king and count. The king, being a young man of exceptional courage and prudence, was still uncertain in which of his barons he could fully trust; fearing almost all of them, he sought to weaken and break their power so thoroughly that he need justly fear none of them. He therefore attacked the count of Flanders, who appeared foremost among all and more powerful than all. But the latter, raging like a lion and thundering with the lightning of boldness, ranged through the royal lands, overthrowing, plundering, or burning everything in his way. [Col. 0972D] His princes, like lion cubs, ranged through the king’s territory, boldly advancing beyond Senlis and devastating as far as the village called Louvres, not far from the city of Paris; they seized Aubry, count of Dammartin, in his bed and brought him captive to the count of Flanders. Thus the count’s strength and boldness, and that of his men, were a terror to all, striking fear even into those living at Paris.

[Cont. Aquic.] The instigators of this discord on the king’s side are said to have been the count of Clermont, Ralph of Coucy, and the sons of Robert surnamed Clement, who were the king’s counsellors. In the king’s army Henry the Younger, king of England, and his brother Richard, duke of Aquitaine, acted as standard-bearers, as it were. Thus on both sides, without any remedy, there were killings, burnings, and plunderings; despoilings of churches, oppression of townspeople, and destruction of the poor. All Gaul, shaken by this wind, was bent this way and that. There was no place on this side of the Alps able to hide itself from hearing this thunder. William, archbishop of Reims, and Theobald, count of Blois, the king’s uncles, worked to restore peace. [Col. 0973B] Through the mediation of these and other religious men, truces were sometimes granted from the Nativity of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany, and from the beginning of Lent until Easter.

After Easter, when the truces had ended and there was now no hope of peace between king and count, while all were expecting war, unexpectedly Henry the elder, king of England, Philip, king of the Franks, and Philip, count of the Flemings, met between Crépy and Senlis. Through Henry, bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See and former abbot of Clairvaux, together with archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the magnates of the Franks, peace was restored among them by peace-envoys acting between them. Never in our age have we heard of such a great conflagration of war extinguished by so small a drop of peace. [Col. 0973C] Count Philip, having surrendered the county of Crépy for the benefit of the count of Beaumont, to whom it belonged through his wife [Note: [Col. 0973D] Eleanor, who was sister of Philip’s wife.], together with certain other castles [Note: [Col. 0973] The scribe first left the place of the word blank, intending to insert the number of castles as soon as he learned it. Later, in the same ink used from “But the latter” onward, he inserted *quibusdam* (“certain”). He therefore did not learn the number.] which he had held through his wife, obtained the king’s peace and favor.

5. A little later (1184), Philip, king of the Franks, at the counsel of certain of his barons who envied the count of Flanders, wished to put away the queen. But [Note: [Col. 0973] From this point the ink changes; the hand is the same.] when she learned this, she turned to God and displayed such devotion, humility, and contrition toward the Mother of God in the city of Senlis that nearly all who saw her were moved to tears. For, walking barefoot through the city streets, carrying candles in her hands, and distributing alms abundantly to every needy person, she entered the church of the blessed Mother of God, where she prayed for a long time. On that day she herself sumptuously fed all the poor of the city and herself served them. When the king and all his nobles heard this, they pitied her and, moved to repentance, abandoned their plan. Yet Count Philip now feared as enemies both the archbishop of Reims and all those who had shared in this counsel, whom he had formerly cherished as friends [Col. 0974A]. For this reason and others, peace between king and count was disturbed. After Pentecost each therefore met with his army on the borders of his lands. The king’s army was outstanding in a great multitude of knights, while the count’s was sufficiently and excellently superior in formations of armed infantry. The count had a very tall dragon displayed above his standard and carried with him upon a four-wheeled cart; the king and all France took this exceedingly ill. Nevertheless, through the mediation of King Henry of England, the truce of peace was extended from the feast of Saint John for one year. Meanwhile the count sent to Spain for Matilda, daughter of Afonso, king of Portugal. She came to him with royal display and great magnificence [Col. 0974B], and became his wife in August of the year of the Lord 1184.

6. Baldwin, count of Mons, adhered to the king; and although he had the sister of Count Philip as his wife, he nevertheless carried on hostilities against him. At his instigation the king of France again rose against the count of Flanders. But the latter, neither heedless nor unprepared, met him boldly. Having posted guards of knights in the castles which he held on the borders against the king’s attacks, he himself entered the land of the count of Mons with a military force only, from the south (1184); while from the east Philip, archbishop of Cologne, who aided the count of Flanders, entered it. The men of Douai and of Pabula devastated that land from the west with fire and plunder. [Col. 0974C] When the king learned that the count was occupied elsewhere, he entered Vermandois. Approaching the castle called Montdidier, he burned its suburbs, but was quickly driven from there by the count’s faithful men who were stationed in garrisons round about. But as winter was approaching—it was the month of November—each withdrew homeward, compelled by winter’s harshness. As the day of the Lord’s Nativity drew near, truces were granted on both sides [Note: [Col. 0973] From the twelfth day before the Nativity of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany. Gislebert, p. 142.].

When the truces were about to end and the count of Flanders was preparing his expedition (1185), Count Baldwin violently invaded the land of James of Avesnes and, mindful of an old injury, gave it over to fire. For James was said to have been the instigator of discord between the two counts. When the truces ended, king and count, all hope of peace now removed, were about to rush into mutual slaughter and encamped with their armies beneath the city of Amiens. At last, by God’s will as we believe, the count, deferring to the royal majesty, to his own honor and safety, and fearing that the slaughter of peoples would be imputed to him by both God and men, before anyone was captured, wounded, or killed, restored [Col. 0975A] to the king certain castles of the county of Vermandois. He had possessed them by right of arms from the time when his first wife—through whom he had held that county—had died; he had had no children by her. This was the entire cause of the discord between him and his lord the king [Note: [Col. 0975D] Compare Gislebert, p. 145.]. Among the castles he restored were prominent Caulaincourt, Thorote, Montdidier, Chaumont, and the lordship of Amiens. He surrendered these to the king on condition that he should refrain from arms and should grant and confirm to him, for peaceful possession as long as he lived, the remaining part of Vermandois—namely the town of Saint-Quentin, Ham, Péronne, and the surrounding region. So it was done; and thereafter the same count remained in the favor of the same king [Note: [Col. 0975D] This peace was made in 1185 according to Gislebert [Col. 0976D] and the Continuator of Anchin. Others place it in 1186.]. There also the counts of Flanders [Col. 0975B] and Hainaut were reconciled.

7. Around the same time, by the severity of divine judgment, an event occurred in the church overseas, exceedingly lamentable and grievous to all Christendom. For the king of Jerusalem, setting out to meet (1187) and engaging Saladin and an innumerable multitude of Saracens, was defeated and captured; all his princes were either killed or captured, and an innumerable common multitude was slaughtered. The bishop of Bethlehem, who bore the cross, was killed, and the cross of the Lord was taken away by pagans; and, as is written of the ark of God, “the glory of the Lord was removed from Israel.” Saladin then traversed the land, overthrowing cities and castles or retaining them for himself, strengthening and fortifying them; he destroyed monasteries, killed monks, priests, and clerics, dishonored and killed nuns [Col. 0975C]. This happened in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, in which year Louis, firstborn son of the king of France, was born on the day before the Kalends of September [31 August].

On hearing the grave news from the land of Jerusalem, the king of France and the king of England, together with many princes, bishops, counts, noble and non-noble men, took the cross in preparation to cross the sea (1186). But before they began their journey, Philip, king of France, setting out against the duke of Burgundy, took the count of Flanders with him. For that duke was exceedingly unjust and treacherous in allowing merchants of France and Flanders, whom he had received under his protection through his lands, to be despoiled by his robbers. Unable to endure [Col. 0975D] the attack of king and count, after losing certain castles he was compelled to surrender and yielded himself to the king.

Then the same king and the same count, taking with them Richard, duke of Aquitaine, led an army against Henry, king of England (1189), father of the same Richard; they plundered and burned his towns and castles. For he had always been rebellious and harmful to the kings of France. Unable to withstand their assault, he avoided their approach by fleeing from place to place. At last they pursued him as far as Le Mans. Excessively grieved by this, he fell ill and, reaching Chinon, ended his final day [Col. 0976A]. From there he was carried to Fontevraud, having scarcely the necessary expenses for burial; he who had once been rich and most powerful was buried there in the monastery of nuns. Richard, duke of Aquitaine, his son, succeeded to the kingdom in 1189. In that same year Elizabeth, queen of the Franks (15 March), niece of Philip, count of Flanders, died. She died in childbirth with twin children and, amid the excessive mourning of the Franks, was buried in the church of Blessed Mary at Paris.

8. When the aforesaid kings of France and England were making for the sea together (1190), Philip, count of Flanders, crossed over with them; and together they besieged the city called Acre, which the Saracens had very strongly fortified and were holding. During this siege, [Col. 0976B] which lasted a long time, Count Philip showed great generosity, distributing his own resources to those in need, especially to knights who had spent their pay. He died there in the third month after his crossing, in the year of the Lord 1191, on the Kalends of July [1 July], and was buried in the basilica of St Nicholas outside Acre’s walls, where more than fifty bishops, dukes, and counts were likewise interred. Later, through the care of his wife Matilda, queen of Portugal, he was transferred to Clairvaux and honorably placed in a sarcophagus within the chapel which she had prepared for him and herself. He had indeed governed the county of Flanders vigorously for twenty-four years, the noblest of all who had preceded him in Flanders, abounding in wealth [Col. 0976C] and honours, great in wisdom and power, zealous for justice, brave and worthy in arms, and not undeservedly comparable to the Maccabees alone. He honoured clerics, embraced monks, defended the poor, and upheld the causes of religious persons, even at times against his own barons and knights.

9. On hearing of his death, the whole country was thrown into confusion and turmoil; grief and fear seized everyone, especially clergy and people, and his realm was at once divided into three parts. For William, archbishop of Rheims, who guarded the rights of the king of France, occupied for the use of that queen’s son, namely Louis, the part which Count Philip had formerly granted as dowry to his niece the queen: that is, Bapaume, [Col. 0976D] Arras, Aire, St Omer, and the estate of Rihoult with its wood; the counties of Hesdin and Lens; and the homage of Boulogne, St Pol, Guînes, and Lille. For Count Philip had granted all these to be possessed by the king after his own death, when he joined his niece to him in lawful marriage. The same count had given another part to his wife Matilda on account of their marriage: namely Lille, Douai, and many fine towns lying here and there; Cassel, Watten, Bergues, Bourbourg, and the whole maritime region. Baldwin, [Col. 0977A] count of Hainaut, moreover, took possession by hereditary right of the third part, on behalf of his wife Margaret, sister of the aforesaid Count Philip.

10. [Continuation of Aquicinctum.] King Philip, returning to France, celebrated Christmas at Paris. Baldwin the count came to his court when summoned, along with others; but the king received him neither courteously nor kindly (1191). Seeing this, Baldwin secretly departed the city without saluting the king. Nevertheless, having regard for his land, he sent Simon, abbot of Anchin, and Daniel, abbot of Cambrai, to the king in order to recover the royal favour. At last, through the mediation of William, archbishop of Rheims, and Peter, bishop of Arras, peace was restored between king and count (1192), on these terms: the king received the count’s homage, and the count graciously granted him possession of [Col. 0977B] the above-mentioned western part of Flanders, retaining the eastern part for himself.

About four years later Margaret, countess of Flanders and Hainaut, died (1194). She was succeeded in the county of Flanders by her son Baldwin, although his father Baldwin was still alive for about another year. That father had taken for his firstborn son Baldwin as wife Mary, daughter of Henry, count of Champagne, whom he had begotten by a daughter of Louis, king of the Franks.

Meanwhile Richard, king of England, returned from overseas, and discord arose between him and the king of France. King Philip of France accordingly gathered an army (1197), besieged, captured, and destroyed the castle of the king of England called Aumale. The knights of the king of England captured the bishop of Beauvais, a kinsman of the king of France, [Col. 0977C] and committed him to harsh imprisonment at Rouen. At the instigation of the English king, by gifts and promises, Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, deserted the king of France and attached himself to the king of England. He therefore gathered a large army, marched through the districts of Tournai and Cambrai, and captured all the castles of that district. Thus he came to Arras and besieged it on its eastern side; but on the second day of the siege he suddenly withdrew.

When Philip, king of France, heard this and took it badly, he crossed the river Lys at Aire with a great force of cavalry and infantry and entered the count’s land to ravage it. But, struck by certain misfortunes, he held a conference with the count [Col. 0977D] outside Ypres. Thus, having accomplished nothing, he returned to his own land, while many who had feared his arrival mocked the ineffectiveness of his retreat.

Count Baldwin, however, enclosed the castle of St Omer in a siege lasting five weeks (1198), and, since Philip king of France gave it no aid—being greatly hard pressed by Richard king of England—he captured it and obtained its surrender. The people of Aire had already voluntarily surrendered themselves into Baldwin’s hands.

Meanwhile the king of England, surrounded by a multitude of knights, attacked the king of France as he was going to Gisors. The latter, hastening with his men to enter the fortress, is said to have fallen into the river when the bridge broke; but he was drawn out, although several of his more noble followers were captured. The king of France immediately gathered a large army and ravaged the part of Normandy adjoining his own land with fire and plunder. Through the mediation of Peter, cardinal of Santa Maria in Via Lata and legate of the Apostolic See, a truce was made between the kings. King Richard, while besieging a certain castle of the viscount of Limoges, who had withdrawn from him, called Châlus [Note: [Col. 0977D] Châlus-Chabrol. Brial.], was wounded there by an arrow and died (1199); his brother John succeeded him in the kingdom.

But Count Baldwin ravaged the French king’s lands with plunder and fire. Mary, countess of Flanders, went to Paris to the king in order to arrange peace between king and count. The king received her honourably and sent her home, assured of peace, with certain captives [Col. 0978B] as pledges of peace. Therefore, in the year of the Lord 1200 [1199], at Christmastide, King Philip and Count Baldwin met at Péronne to negotiate peace. There, by the exertions of Countess Mary, a firm peace was sworn by both sides—a peace that brought great joy to both France and Flanders.

11. Afterwards Count Baldwin took the cross and, setting out for Jerusalem, wintered at Venice. With Venetian help he subdued Zara, a city hostile to Venice, and handed the conquered city over to them. Then, trusting in God’s help, he approached with a small force to conquer that noble, most strongly fortified, almost impregnable city of Constantinople, formidable alike in military strength and wealth.

[Epistle of Baldwin.] Therefore, when the Flemings, [Col. 0978C] Franks, and Venetians rushed in, setting ladders against the towers, the Greeks abandoned the battlements. Our men boldly entered and opened the gates to the knights. After great slaughter of Greeks, and with evening already drawing on, our weary men laid aside their arms, intending on the following day to deliberate about assaulting the palaces. Emperor Alexius, who had withdrawn from the walls and fled into the palace, rallied his men and urged them to fight the next day, asserting that he now had our men in his power, shut within the circuit of the walls. But by night he secretly turned his back in defeat.

When this became known, the astonished populace of the Greeks discussed appointing a new emperor. As, at dawn, they proceeded to nominate a certain Constantine, our infantry, without waiting for their leaders’ deliberation, [Col. 0978D] sprang to arms. The Greeks fled; the very strong and well-defended palaces were abandoned; and in a moment the entire city was taken. So immeasurable an abundance was found of everything counted by men among riches that the whole of Latin Christendom did not seem to possess as much.

After the matters required by the event had been carefully arranged, our people unanimously and devoutly proceeded to elect an emperor. All ambition being set aside, they appointed as electors of an emperor under the Lord the venerable bishops of Soissons, Troyes, and Halberstadt; the lord of Bethlehem, who had been delegated there from overseas by apostolic authority; the bishop-elect of Acre; and the abbot of Lucedio. After prayer had duly been offered, they unanimously and solemnly elected Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, and the aforesaid bishops raised him, gloriously crowned, to the imperial dignity amid the applause and pious tears of all, in the year of the Lord 1202, on the Sunday after Easter on which *Jubilate* is sung.

12. His wife Mary, of illustrious birth, followed her husband; after wearisome journeys over land and the windings and stretches of the sea, she finally arrived at Acre. There, worn down by long and grave illnesses, she gave up her last breath.

John, king of England, after the innumerable expenses incurred over a long time in defending castles and erecting fortifications, [Col. 0979B] overcome more by cowardice than by want of money, holding the disgrace of flight cheap, abandoned Normandy, Aquitaine, and all their dependencies. As though fleeing to a refuge, he crossed the sea and quickly withdrew into England. Philip, king of France, gladly occupied and seized all these possessions.

13. Then, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1205, our emperor at Constantinople, Baldwin, count of Flanders and Hainaut, was captured in a battle fought against John surnamed Blakē, and thereafter was seen by none of our side. In the following year he was succeeded in the empire by his brother Henry, a man valiant in military affairs and distinguished by nobility of character.

In the county of Flanders and Hainaut Emperor Baldwin was succeeded by his firstborn [Col. 0979C] daughter Joan. Philip, king of France, held her in his custody and guardianship until he joined her in marriage to Ferdinand, son of the king of Portugal; this was accomplished through the efforts of Queen Matilda [Note: [Col. 0979] “his aunt,” written above in a thirteenth-century hand.], formerly countess of Flanders.

When the marriage had been celebrated in the king’s chapel at Paris (1211), and before Joan had come into Flanders with her husband Ferdinand to receive from the Flemish people the loyalty due to her, Louis, the king’s firstborn son, already made a knight, suddenly came to Aire with an army and siege engines.
