He demanded that the townsmen surrender the town to him, since, as they knew, it belonged to him by right through his mother. They replied that, if he first obtained the castle of St Omer—which was stronger and more fortified [Col. 0979D] and belonged to him by an equal right—they would surrender their town to him without delay or difficulty.

Having received this undertaking, he came to St Omer but found it closed. The townsmen did not immediately admit him, although the counts of St Pol and Ponthieu and other barons who had come with the aforesaid Louis frightened them with loud threats. A large army therefore gathered around the town and cruelly threatened to burn it and torture with most savage punishments everyone found in it. But the townsmen, seeing themselves suddenly besieged and having no knights by whose counsel and help [Col. 0980A] they could defend their town, and expecting no aid from anyone, decided to receive Lord Louis with honour on the next day, while they themselves would be received by him into favour and friendship. So it was done.

Then, on Louis’s advice, they further undertook to fortify their town more strongly with walls and larger ditches. Lord Louis himself built a high and strong tower in the middle of the wall near the Boulogne gate, through which he could enter the town whenever he wished and leave it.

14. Ferdinand, with his aunt, Queen Matilda—now old and infirm—and his wife, was proceeding slowly into Flanders and Hainaut (1211), to be received by the people of the land as their lord and to receive them as [Col. 0980B] his men. He left his wife at Douai, suffering from fever, with his aforesaid aunt Matilda; he himself hurried to Ypres, escorted by Philip, marquis of Namur and his wife’s paternal uncle; John, lord of Nesle and castellan of Bruges; and Siger, castellan of Ghent.

When the people of Ypres and Bruges had submitted their necks to his lordship, the people of Ghent refused to receive him until they saw the heiress of the land, namely the daughter of Emperor Baldwin, and were certain that he had married her. On hearing this, he returned quickly. The two most noble princes, Rasso of Gavere and Arnulf of Oudenaarde, who resented this marriage having been made without their counsel and hated the aforesaid castellans, pursued him with armed knights and many men [Col. 0980C] supplied by them, and caught up with him at Kortrijk.

He was dining with the princes who were with him. When they learned of the unexpected arrival and pursuit of the aforesaid men, they judged that nothing was more useful for them at that moment than flight. Hastening to flee, they left behind a great many of their possessions; after crossing the bridge over the river, they broke it so that their enemies could not cross after them. When the latter saw this, they returned to the town and plundered it.

15. Ferdinand then took his wife and gathered an army, and besieged Ghent. The people of Ghent gave him three thousand pounds and were received by him in peace. During the period when the land was vacant and had no count, the aforesaid castellans of Ghent and Bruges [Col. 0980D] had appropriated for themselves certain rights and customs in their castellanies, which were said to belong more properly to the count of Flanders than to themselves. Since Ferdinand would not grant and confirm these to them, they abandoned him and unanimously attached themselves to the king of France, whose men they were on account of another fief which they held from him. Rasso of Gavere and Arnulf of Oudenaarde, seeing this and hating those same castellans, returned to the count’s favour, after first making restitution for damages and satisfaction for injuries.

16. At that time (1212), Renaud of Dammartin, count of Boulogne and Mortain—whom the king [Col. 0981A] of France had exalted above all his princes because of his great worth and ability—was accused of intending to betray the king. He fled before the king, who was advancing against him with an army. In his flight he came to the count of Flanders and then to the king of England, urging them, after making an agreement with one another, to strive to recover by force of arms what their predecessors had held and what the king of France now held by violence. He promised that this could easily be done, especially since the help of Emperor Otto could not fail them. Otto was the nephew of the king of England and, hating the king of France, would willingly assist his uncle against him.

Letters were accordingly exchanged, from king to count and from count to king, concerning a league between them against the king of France, [Col. 0981B] their lord [Note: [Col. 0981D] Dom Brial prints these letters, XVII, 87.]. Meanwhile the barons of England, hating their king because of his excessive cruelty, secretly sent to the king of France, earnestly begging him to come to England. They firmly promised that they would submit themselves to his rule and, after expelling the king who was unworthy of the kingdom, would deliver the kingdom to him.

In the year of the Lord 1213, Philip, king of France, prepared at the port called Calais to cross into England with a huge multitude of ships and men. At that time a certain Pandulf, a cleric of the lord pope, was in England and, by papal authority, excommunicated all who opposed the king of England. Indeed, when John, king of England, heard that the king of France was coming against him, he was struck with great terror and resigned his kingdom to the lord pope [Col. 0981C] into the hand of the aforesaid cleric. He received it back from the same cleric to hold under an annual payment of one thousand marks to the supreme pontiff.

17. But the king of France suddenly changed his plan of going to England and turned to go into Flanders. He ordered his laden ships to meet him at the port called Damme, near Bruges. He himself went overland and came to Cassel on Ascension Sunday. Leaving knights and archers there to guard the castle, he advanced toward Ypres and Bruges, finding no one who resisted him, for he was led by the aforementioned castellans of Bruges and Ghent.

Ferdinand, count of Flanders, and Renaud, count of Boulogne, secretly emerging from [Col. 0981D] the sea, attacked the rear of the king’s army. But they were bravely and quickly driven back, and scarcely managed to escape and take refuge at sea. Nevertheless, afterwards they captured quite a few of the king’s ships. When the king heard this, he burned all the rest, guarding against their likewise being captured by the enemy. At Ypres, Bruges, and Ghent he also seized many townsmen who appeared wealthier than the rest, took them into France, and held them under very close imprisonment until he extorted a large sum of money from them.

18. Count Ferdinand then went to England and did homage [Note: [Col. 0981D] This is doubtful; cf. Dom Brial XVIII, 565.] to the king of England. The king gave him much money, as is said sharing with him his treasury and expending it to hire knights to ravage with him the land of the king of France.

This happened at Christmastide. At that time Renaud, count of Boulogne, having taken troops and certain Flemish communes, besieged Cassel. But before he could approach, the men in the fortress burned the greater part of the town, fought bravely, and defended the fortification vigorously. Although snow falling from heaven and frost gripping the earth greatly impeded the attackers (1214), they nevertheless did not cease on that account until, after thirteen days, Lord Louis, the king’s son, arrived with an armed force. Since the aforesaid count lacked the forces to resist [Col. 0982B] him, he abandoned the siege and withdrew into the interior of Flanders.

19. Returning from England, Count Ferdinand gathered a multitude of horsemen. Passing through Bourbourg and Gravelines into the land of the count of Guînes, he plundered it and destroyed its fortifications; then, passing before St Omer, he returned into Flanders. A few days later, the counts of Flanders and Boulogne came with a large body of infantry and cavalry to the town of Lens. Seeing that it was well fortified, they moved farther on to the castle called Hesdin and ravaged it and some open-country villages with fire and plunder. Coming to Aire, they encamped and made their camp there; but the knights and [Col. 0982C] archers stationed inside preserved the town unharmed.

20. At that time John, king of England, had come into Aquitaine with a great army in order to recover that land and subject it once again to his power. But Lord Louis, son of the king of France, sent there by his father with many worthy knights, bravely resisted and made the English king’s attempts futile. Philip, king of France, therefore prepared an expedition and hastened to Aire to bring aid to the besieged. When this was learned through scouts, the aforesaid counts returned to Flanders with their whole army.

Thereafter the counts of Flanders and Boulogne went to Aachen (March) to ask Emperor Otto, [Col. 0982D] who had then been excommunicated by the lord pope, to deign to come with them and give his aid to his uncle, the king of England, and to his own faithful men, who were fighting with him against the king of France. He came (July), bringing with him the duke of Lorraine [Note: [Col. 0982D] Henry II. Brial.] and certain counts and many knights, and by his arrival gladdened all Flanders. By Count Ferdinand’s proclamation, therefore, all men fit for war assembled at Valenciennes, men of Hainaut and Flanders alike.

This did not escape Philip, king of France. Taking such forces of horse and foot as he could obtain—for no small part of his army was occupied in Aquitaine with his son Louis against the king of England—he came to the bridge of Bouvines and from there to Tournai. On the next day, after hearing Mass, he returned to the bridge of Bouvines.

21. The emperor and the counts were then at Mortagne with a very large and strong army. Hearing that the king was returning to Bouvines, they thought he was fleeing. Eagerly taking up arms, they hurried in rivalry to pursue the king. They were especially urged to this by Hugh of Boves, a valiant knight whom the king of France had expelled from his land. Later, when Hugh went to England with knights and many other men, a storm arose and they were drowned and perished [Col. 0983B] in the sea.

But behold, a messenger came to the king (27 July) and told him for certain that an innumerable army was coming quickly and was now close at hand, fearing nothing except that the king’s flight might be so swift that they could not catch him. On hearing this, the king halted and made his army stand still. Calling together his princes, he said:

“What is your counsel concerning what you hear? I fight today unwillingly, since it is Sunday and we are fewer in number than they.”

Then Peter, count of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0983] “balliolensen codex”: in the Balliol manuscript, *cn* in the first hand, and *balliolens* in an erasure by a seventeenth-century hand.], replied first:

“Although it is evil to shed human blood on a feast day, yet the man sins less who does not attack the enemy or provoke him, but, when provoked by him, defends himself as he can. He [Col. 0983C] who neglects to defend himself when attacked by an enemy either proves himself defeated or admits himself foolish.”

When these words had been heard, all were inspired to fight. The king immediately drew up his battle-lines. Odo, duke of Burgundy, asked the king to withdraw himself from the battle, preserve himself for his knights and princes, and enter the nearby, well-fortified castle of Lens. But the king said:

“Far be it from me to flee while I live and am sound, and to leave my men, ready to die with me and for me. I shall remain in the battle with the last men, either dying honourably or triumphing gloriously. I trust, moreover, that it will harm our enemies that they challenge us to battle on this day, and that it will hinder them that those who lead them are either excommunicated [Col. 0983D] or traitors or deserters or perjurers. For Otto, who is called emperor, has been excommunicated by the mouth of the supreme pontiff; the count of Boulogne is a traitor and excommunicate; the count of Flanders a deserter and perjurer. These are what will today deliver them into our hands or compel them shamefully to flee before us. Therefore do not fear them.”

Having said this, he turned aside into a nearby church and prayed devoutly with tears. Rising from prayer, he first fortified his body with the sign of the cross, then with armour. Mounting his horse, he came to his men and urged them to confess their sins, so that, [Col. 0984A] if death befell them, they might die more securely, and so that, by the humility of their confession, having made God favourable to them, they might more easily overcome their enemies (1214, 27 July).

22. Meanwhile Otto had come so near that he could see the king’s army. Calling the counts of Flanders and Boulogne to him, he said:

“Was it not reported to us that the king was fleeing, afraid to await our arrival? Yet I see his camp very strongly defended, and its battle-lines most carefully drawn up and ready for battle.”

To this the count of Boulogne said:

“This, lord emperor, is what I told you already: it is the custom of the French never to flee, but to die or conquer in battle. Therefore I had advised that we should secretly fall upon them from the rear and plunder the rearmost part of their army. But Hugh [Col. 0984B] of Boves, who stands here, and certain others, ascribed this not to prudence but to fearfulness and idleness. Today their boldness and my alleged cowardice will be revealed, when they take swift flight, while I, and all who begin the fight and remain, shall be captured or perhaps killed.”

Saying this, he turned his horse and, summoning his men with the sound of a small horn, went into battle. With him went Ferdinand, count of Flanders; William, count of Salisbury, brother of the king of England; and many other Hainaut and Flemish knights, ready for battle and not sluggish in either suffering or doing whatever chance of war might bring.

The first engagement was made by these men. They were the first to begin fighting. Breaking into the first battle-line of the army with great courage, they fought fiercely, but the French received them stoutly. Then enemies were mingled everywhere, horsemen and foot soldiers alike, and they rushed against one another with all their strength. Their lances broken, they drew swords; but when the sword failed or was ineffective because an enemy pressed close at hand, they used sharpened knives against one another.

But the count of Ponthieu, who was with the king, after his lance had been broken and he had been deprived of sword and knife and made a foot soldier, repelled the blows of those striking him with his mail-clad arms and hands. For he had charged with his knights into a body of about four hundred men, said to be from Brabant. They were infantry, indeed, but not inferior to cavalry in skill and courage in fighting. They quickly made the count and his knights foot soldiers too, their horses having been killed beneath them. [Col. 0984D] The count and his men could not penetrate their dense formation, but, as stated, defended themselves with hands and arms until his communal militia arrived. They aided him in bringing down those chosen foot soldiers; otherwise he would by no means have defeated them, but he himself and his knights would, it is believed, have fallen defeated into their hands. Thus all those infantrymen were killed or captured.

Soon, however, French valour prevailed—or rather, the divine ordinance triumphed through them. The aforesaid three counts and another count [Col. 0985A] from Germany [Note: [Col. 0985C] Otto of Tecklenburg. Grotefend.] were captured, along with 127 knights and several others. When the men of Bruges, who were nearest to the battle, saw this, they were, it is said, the first to turn their backs, and by their example helped induce others to flee. Thus all the men of Hainaut and Flanders fled together; the duke of Lorraine fled with his men; the Germans fled; and Emperor Otto himself fled on his palfrey. He left on the field his destrier, a horse of remarkable quality and great price, killed by a certain knight. The king, unwilling to pursue the fugitives, returned to France. This battle took place in the year of the Lord 1214, on 27 July, the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

23. When the king returned to France [Note: [Col. 0985] After this word the ink changes, though the hand remains the same.] with a noble triumph and distinguished captives and many others, who were placed in secure custody in various places and bound with iron manacles and fetters, as though Flanders had not yet paid enough penalties, other kings were sent against it by the Lord: namely fire and water. Fire attacked its fortified towns; water invaded the open country. Thus, as fire devoured them, the houses of Ypres, Bruges, and Ghent were consumed, with very few left, which the Lord mercifully preserved lest he seem to make a complete destruction. The sea, swelling more violently than usual in the territory of Bruges, spread through fields and villages for a distance of seven leagues or more [Note: [Col. 0985] Here ends the final line of the leaf in the fifth quire; another contemporary hand adds “spread itself.” The sixth and seventh leaves have been cut out; the eighth remains, but is wholly blank. In place of the two excised leaves, after the codex had already been bound—it still has its original binding—a quire of twelve smaller-format leaves, with two attached leaves, was subsequently inserted. It contains the continuation of Bernard of Ypres, ending in 1329. Our continuation seems to have extended only a little beyond the words “or more.” For no more than those two leaves have disappeared, which Bernard appears to have cut out.] [lacuna]

## VII. SHORT GENEALOGY OF THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS

[Col. 0985]

We give this genealogy from the Bertin manuscript, now Boulogne manuscript no. 58, parchment folio, thirteenth century. There, after the works of Ambrose, it is written by another hand of the early thirteenth century. Although it is continuous, it is nevertheless apparent that everything before Baldwin, son of Robert, was copied from an older source, while the rest was later added by another hand. Before us it was already edited by Warnkoenig in De Smet, *Corpus chronicorum Flandriae*, I, 7.

## NAMES OF THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS

[Col. 0985B]

Lidric of Harlebeke was the first to occupy Flanders. After him his son Ingelram held Flanders. After him his son Audacer held the same land. After him his son Baldwin Iron-Arm was called count of Flanders [Note: [Col. 0985C] Observe that the author does not call the preceding three counts of Flanders, but says that the first Baldwin attained this dignity.]; he lies in the monastery of St Bertin. After him came his son Baldwin the Bald; he lies at Ghent. Arnulf the Elder, son of this Baldwin, nobly governed Flanders after his father. After him came his son Baldwin, who died before his father from the disease of smallpox. After the death of Arnulf the Elder, Arnulf the Younger, son of Baldwin son of Arnulf the Elder, ruled. After Arnulf the Younger ruled his son Baldwin, who lies at Blandinium. After him came his son Baldwin, who lies at Lille. [Col. 0985C] After him came his son Baldwin, who lies in Hainaut. After him came his brother Robert, called the Frisian, who lies at Cassel. After him came his son Robert, who lies at Arras. After him came his son Baldwin, who was mortally wounded in battle, became a monk of St Bertin, and was buried there.

Since he had no heir, his kinsman Charles succeeded him, the son of his aunt [Col. 0986B] and of Canute, king of Denmark. After Charles had been killed on account of justice and buried at Bruges in the church of St Donatian, a certain William from Normandy, whose great-grandfather was Baldwin of Lille, received the county. Unable to bear his tyrannical greed, the people of Bruges, Ghent, and especially Lille brought in Thierry of Alsace, son of the daughter of Robert the Elder, to resist William. When this William too had been mortally wounded and buried in the church of St Bertin, Thierry obtained the county. On his death, and burial in the church at Watten, his illustrious son Philip governed and subdued Flanders more excellently and powerfully than the rest.

When Philip was transferred from the land of Jerusalem, where he had died while abroad, to Clairvaux, Baldwin, [Col. 0986C] his sister’s husband, received Flanders to govern. After Baldwin’s death and burial in the monastery of Maubeuge, his son Baldwin received the county. When he departed abroad and was made emperor at Constantinople, having no heir except two young daughters still unmarried, his brother Philip was appointed governor of Flanders (1202).

## VIII. GENEALOGY OF THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS BY JOHN OF THIELRODE

[Col. 0987]

John of Thielrode, monk of St Bavo’s, in his compilation written in 1294, made chapter nineteen about the counts of Flanders. He excerpted it from *Flandria Generosa* down to the year 1130, adding only very little of his own and carrying the account down to his own times. We give it from the Ghent autograph manuscript, which Van Lokeren published in full at Ghent in 1835, octavo.

## ON THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS

[Col. 0987A]

[Fl. Gen.] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 792, Lidric of Harlebeke, seeing Flanders empty, uncultivated, and wooded, occupied it. He begot Ingelram. Ingelram begot Audacer. Audacer begot Baldwin Iron-Arm. Baldwin Iron-Arm carried off Judith at the city of Senlis, daughter of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, son of Louis the Pious Augustus, son of Charlemagne, and widow of the king of the English. In Baldwin’s time Flanders became a county, and Baldwin was its first count. His predecessors had been foresters of Flanders under the king of France, as we read in the chronicles of the Franks. Lidric and Audacer obtained from Abbot Einhard of the monastery of Saint Bavo permission to hunt in the wood called Heinarstryst [Col. 0987B], now called Loe, on condition that they should give one animal out of every tenth to the abbot and his successors. Baldwin Iron-Arm begot by Judith Baldwin the Bald. Baldwin the Bald married Elfrude, daughter of Edgar king of the English, and by her begot Arnulf the Great, restorer of Blandinium. Arnulf married Adela, daughter of Herbert, count of Vermandois, and by her begot Baldwin the Younger. Baldwin the Younger married Matilda, daughter of Herman, duke of the Saxons, and by her begot Arnulf the Younger. After Baldwin’s death, Matilda married Godfrey, duke of Hainaut; and she granted privileges to churches in the name of the count of Flanders. Arnulf married Susanna, daughter of Berengar [Col. 0987C], king of Lombardy and Italy, and by her begot Baldwin surnamed Fair-Beard. Baldwin married Otgiva, daughter of Giselbert, count of Luxemburg, and by her begot Baldwin of Lille. Baldwin married Adela, daughter of Robert king of France, by whom he begot Baldwin of Mons, Robert the Frisian, and a daughter named Matilda. She married William, count of Normandy, and bore him Robert, count of the Normans, who begot William, later count of Flanders. Baldwin of Mons married Richilde, countess of Hainaut, and by her begot two sons, Arnulf and Baldwin. Robert the Frisian, his paternal uncle, killed this Arnulf, the firstborn and count after his father’s death, expelled Baldwin from the realm, and thus obtained the county [Col. 0988A].

Robert the Frisian [Note: [Col. 0987C] False. His son was Robert of Jerusalem.] was a worthy and valiant knight along with Godfrey, Hugh the brother of the king of France, and Robert count of Normandy. King Godfrey died in Jerusalem in the second year of his reign, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, on 18 July. His brother Baldwin succeeded him in the kingdom. Robert married Gertrude, daughter of Bernard duke of the Frisians; she bore him two sons, Robert and Philip, and three daughters. One of these was married to Christ; another was married to Canute, king of Denmark, and bore him a son named Charles; Theoderic, duke of Alsace, married the third, and by her begot Theoderic, later count of Flanders. His firstborn Robert married Clementia, daughter of William count of Burgundy, and by her begot Baldwin, a renowned knight [Col. 0988B]. When he died without an heir, Charles, son of Canute king of Denmark, succeeded him. This Charles was killed by his own people at Bruges, in the church of Saint Donatian, in the year 1127, on 2 March; thus he reigned about eight years. William, son of Robert count of Normandy, succeeded him. Theoderic, son of Theoderic duke of Alsace, killed this William and thus obtained the county. Theoderic married Sibyl, daughter of the king of Jerusalem, and by her begot Philip and Margaret, who married Baldwin count of Hainaut. Theoderic began to reign in the year from the Nativity of the Lord 1127 and reigned about thirty-eight years. Philip, count of Flanders and Vermandois, married Matilda, daughter of the king of Portugal. [Col. 0988C] When he died without an heir, the aforesaid Baldwin, count of Hainaut, succeeded him. By Margaret he begot three sons, Baldwin, Henry, and Philip, and a daughter named Elizabeth, who married Philip king of France. Baldwin the firstborn married Mary, daughter of the count of Champagne, and by her begot two daughters, Joan and Margaret. Joan married Ferdinand, son of the king of Portugal (1211); after his death, she married Thomas of Savoy. When she died without an heir, her sister Margaret succeeded her. Margaret married William of Dampierre (1218); she bore three sons, William, Guy, and John, and two daughters, one of whom [Note: [Col. 0988C] Mary, abbess of Flines.] was married to Christ, while the other married the count of Bar [Note: [Col. 0988C] Theobald I of Bar, in 1245.]. William the firstborn married Beatrice, daughter of Henry [Col. 0989A], duke of Brabant, and widow of the count of Thuringia. When he died without an heir, his brother Guy succeeded him. By Matilda, daughter of Robert of Termonde, Guy begot five sons—Robert, William, John bishop of Liège, Baldwin, and Philip—and three daughters. One married John, duke of Brabant; another Florent, count of Holland; and the third William, count of Jülich [Note: [Col. 0989] Jülich.]; after he was killed, she married the lord of Châteauvillain [Note: [Col. 0989] Simon of Châteauvillain.]. After Matilda’s death [Note: [Col. 0990] 8 November 1264.], he married Elizabeth, daughter of Henry [Col. 0990A], count of Luxemburg, and with her obtained the county of Namur; by her he begot children of both sexes. Robert, Guy’s firstborn by Matilda, married Blanche, daughter of Charles king of Sicily. After her death (1271), he married Yolande, daughter of Odo count of Nevers and widow of John, son of Louis, king of France of pious memory; and with her obtained the county of Nevers. By her he begot—[Note: [Col. 0989] Thus the author ends; nothing is lost.]

## IX. CATALOGUES OF THE COUNTS OF FLANDERS

[Col. 0989]

At the end, Lambert appended to the genealogy given above a catalogue which Warnkoenig has already published from the same autograph manuscript used by us, *Flandrische Rechtsgeschichte*, I, appendix 19. We present a very similar one from the manuscript of Saint-Vaast, now Brussels 6439; concerning it see *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, II, 192. John of Thielrode inserted a third, worthless catalogue into his compilation about the year 1294; anyone wishing to see it should consult the edition of the Thielrode chronicle prepared by Van Lokeren, Ghent, 1835, p. 69. A fourth, covering the years 792–1506 and authored by James of Bailleul, was inserted into the Saint-Omer manuscript of Folcuin; B. Guérard published it from there in his edition of the cartulary of Sithiu, p. 11.

[Note: [Col. 0989] The following divisions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Lambert

In A.D. 791 the counts of Flanders began to reign.

1. Lidric of Harlebeke.  
2. Ingelram.  
3. Audacer.  
4. Baldwin Iron-Arm.  
5. Baldwin the Bald.  
6. Arnulf the Great.

10. Baldwin of Lille.  
11. Baldwin of Mons.  
12. Arnulf the Younger, slain.  
13. Robert the uncle, at Cassel.  
14. Robert, at Arras.  
15. Baldwin, at Saint-Bertin.  
16. Charles, Baldwin’s nephew.

Thereafter, other hands:

17. William the Norman.  
18. Theoderic of Alsace.

20. Baldwin.

### Manuscript of Saint-Vaast. COUNTS OF FLANDERS

Lidric of Harlebeke. Ingelram. Audacer. Baldwin Iron-Arm. Baldwin the Bald. Arnulf the Great. Baldwin the Younger. Arnulf the Lesser. Baldwin the Bearded. Baldwin of Lille. Baldwin of Mons. Arnulf, slain. Robert of Cassel. Robert, conqueror of Jerusalem. Baldwin, son of Clementia.

Thereafter, other hands:

Charles. William the Norman. Theoderic. Philip his son. Baldwin.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1203, ELIAS OF KOKSIJDE, SEVENTH ABBOT OF THE CISTERCIAN MONASTERY OF THE DUNES

[Col. 0991]

## NOTICE

(*Bibliotheca Cisterciensis* of C. de Wisch, second edition, published at Cologne, 1656, quarto, p. 90.)

Elias of Koksijde, deriving his surname from his native place, namely a village in the territory of Veurne in Flanders, was the seventh abbot of our monastery of the Dunes. Because of his outstanding holiness of life, he was enrolled in the Cistercian Menology on 8 October. Nearly all Europe admired and revered his sanctity and exceptional learning, as may be seen in his *Life*, which Henriquez wrote and published from the records of the monastery of the Dunes in a fascicle, and more fully in his book *On the Saints of the Hermitage of the Dunes*, published in Spanish. This is that Elias who, by his eloquence and by the influence he possessed with Leopold, duke of Austria, freed Richard, king of England, from captivity, as is described at length in the *Life*: “Formerly many sermons by him, full to overflowing with piety and learning, were read in the library of the Dunes; but they have now perished through the injury of time,” except for two, likewise delivered at the general chapter of Cîteaux. The first of these, found in an ancient manuscript of our library at the Dunes, I published in this book in 1649. The second was supplied from the library of Saint-Ghislain—where the first-mentioned sermon was also held—by the most learned George Gallopinus, a religious of that same monastery; I shall present it to readers together with the first. The venerable Elias died in the year 1203, on 16 August.

[Col. 0991]

# SERMONS OF ELIAS OF KOKSIJDE

## FIRST SERMON

[Col. 0991A] “Have they appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself; but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32).

If, according to the prophet (Isa. 51), we are commanded to look to Abraham our father and to Sarah who bore us, then in place of both, as though to the rock from which we were cut, we must together regard this Church. For she is our mother, into whose womb we have entered again, that we may be born again to life; that we may drink from milk and be satisfied from the breasts of her consolation (Isa. 66); that from her, as from the granary of the true Joseph, we may receive grain not only for ourselves to eat, but also for seed [Col. 0992A], so that we may refresh others; and, made fruitful by so great a grace of blessings, may not only ourselves bear the fruit of good works, but may also make others bear fruit by our example, so that no one may bear the mark of barrenness, accursed among the children of Israel.

For this reason we have hastened here: not to establish here the finishing-line of our running, but, refreshed at our mother’s breast, to run more strongly, eagerly, and without failing until we reach the goal set before us. Rivers do not return to the place from which they flow in order to stop there, but in order to flow forth again more freely and abundantly. A great multitude, which no one can number, from every nation, tribe, and tongue, looks to us (Rev. 5): brethren and children, our companions and fellow-citizens, awaiting and desiring our return, that with open hands they may joyfully receive us as we return laden with goods, bringing them the pastures of life and nourishment for souls. Although we may perhaps appear to preside over them by the dignity of honour—or rather by the burden of honour—we must nevertheless always consider our shared nature, our common life, and the origin of our condition, so that before God, in conscience and in merit of life, we may surpass those whom we surpass in honour. Let the dignity of honour delight and move us in such a way that the weight of its burden always frightens us more, and that we labour in every way to be useful rather than to be set over others.

For two things belong to dignity: knowledge and virtue. In the judgment of the Wise Man, dignity without knowledge is plainly quite useless, while knowledge without virtue is damnable. “For,” as someone says, “honour without humility brings itself to shame; humility without honour is sufficient unto its own honour.” Therefore the Wise Man, wisely instructing and teaching the way of wisdom, briefly sets forth and shows what prelates ought to avoid and what they ought to choose, when he says: “Have they appointed you ruler?” and so forth. In these words, as they presently occur, four things seem capable of being noted: the solicitude of care for the pastoral office; harmony of virtue for the freedom of canonical election; the safeguard of humility’s custody; and conformity of life for the observance of charity.

[Col. 0993C] Therefore, when you hear, “Ruler [have they appointed] you,” attend to the solicitude of care. When you hear, “they have appointed,” understand the harmony of unity in the freedom of canonical election. When you hear, “do not exalt yourself,” observe humility’s safeguard. And when you hear, “be among them as one of them,” mark conformity of life for the observance of charity. Certainly, he is not worthy to be reckoned by the name of ruler, nor ought he to be taken up for the work of governance, who lacks solicitous care, who possesses neither knowledge for healing the weak unto salvation nor merit of life to support the manifestation of virtue. He who has not long conducted private concerns with integrity is quite improperly and dangerously seized and drawn into public responsibilities, because “it is not fitting that he should sin who must restrain others under the rule of equity, lest he become a crooked example who is known to have been chosen for a sound institution.”

Since it befits a ruler to govern himself and others under the discipline of correction, there are certain matters by which he provides for himself, and others by which he provides for the benefit and salvation of others. He provides for himself if he is chaste in body and pure in heart; for example, if, desiring Rachel’s embraces, he serves seven years (Gen. 29), and keeps Sabbath after Sabbath, so that he not only restrains himself from evil deeds but also rests from unlawful thoughts. It also belongs to his office to be sober in food, orderly in dress, disciplined in bearing, gentle in character, grave in expression, restrained in speech, patient and strong in adversity, humble and temperate in prosperity, so that in him there may be [Col. 0994A] “evening and morning, one day.” Whether the morning of prosperity smiles upon him or the evening of adversity rises against him, the same disposition of soul should always remain in him, as one day, if he longs for the day of eternity, of which it is said: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83). When those who marvelled at the virtues of Christ the Lord wished to make him king, he fled from them; but he readily went to meet those who would crucify him. By this example, then, we are warned to avoid the blandishments of the world and to endure opposites readily.

These and similar things are those by which a ruler ought to govern himself, apart from others by which he is bound to provide for the salvation of others. Toward others he must be watchful and solicitous, prudent and circumspect, merciful [Col. 0994B] and just, so that, having care for all, he may become all things to all people in order to gain all. For governing, he must have rod and staff; for healing, wine and oil; as an example of charity and chastity, rose and lily; for offering sacrifice, fire and sword. Further, for feeding he must have bread in his bag; for restraining and urging, hay and spurs; for frightening, a dog on a leash; for striking, stones from the stream in a sling; for encouraging and destroying, a trumpet in the right hand and a pitcher in the left. Thus, for the word of salvation which he preaches, he must willingly, if necessary, even fall in death and lay down his life for his sheep (John 10).

We do not at all believe that such men, after the pitchers are broken, will lack that with which to confound their adversaries: the light of burning lamps—that is, either the brightness of good reputation because of merit, or the effect of their works in the manifestation of virtue. A multitude of such wise persons is the health of the world, because “not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these” (Matt. 6), who is adorned with such insignia. Moreover, just as the ruler is set before others in office, so he must invite them by the example of good conduct, “as an eagle provoking her young to fly and hovering over them” (Deut. 32). For how can an eagle provoke her young to fly unless she hovers above them? There is one who hovers beneath, one who hovers beside, and one who hovers above his young. The eagle hovers beneath [Col. 0994D] when the pastoral life is found inferior, humbler, and more despised than the life of those subject to it. It hovers beside them when its life is common and equal to that of the rest. But it hovers above its young when it surpasses them through a certain prerogative of holiness, so that it teaches the way by flying before the others and becomes to them a shelter from the day’s heat, protecting them by the assistance of consolation, exhortation, and prayers.

“After the death of Joshua, the children of Israel consulted the Lord, saying: ‘Who shall go up before us against the Canaanite and be leader in battle?’” (Judg. 1). They do not say, “Who shall go with us?” or “Who shall follow us?”—for that pertains to the common and undifferentiated multitude—but: “Who shall go up before us and be leader in battle?” He is deservedly called a leader in battle who is accustomed to lead others, encourage others, and in every danger go first before all others. Hence this outstanding thing is reckoned in Caesar’s praise: that in no danger did he ever say to his soldiers, “Go there,” but rather, “Come here.” Hence someone gives this very elegant admonition:

> If you command something to be observed by all,  
> Be the first to undergo what you command. Then the people  
> Become more observant of what is right, and do not refuse obedience  
> When they see the author himself obeying. The world is shaped  
> According to the ruler’s example; nor can edicts so bend  
> Human minds as does the life of the one who governs.

“Thus Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1), and he requires of us that we turn the mouth toward the armpits, that we put the sword upon our thigh (Gen. 26), and that we ourselves drink water from our own cistern (Prov. 5). And concerning the angel descending from heaven in the Apocalypse, it is read [Col. 0995B] that he had a little book in his hand (Rev. 10). The angel has the little book in his hand when the messenger of God’s word fulfils by good works the commandments of the divine law which he preaches to others. “He prepared them,” it says, “in the innocence of his heart, and guided them in understanding” (Ps. 77)—that is, in works performed intelligently; it calls practical intelligence “understanding of the hands.” Let these things be said in order that the solicitude of pastoral care may be commended to rulers, and that, when they hear “Have they appointed you ruler?” and so forth, they should remember not so much honour as a perilous burden.

For they did not rush in by rash presumption, nor presume on their own authority, nor force themselves in by violence; rather, “they have appointed”: that is, they have established by unanimous agreement, equal vote, common will, and canonical election. Since prelates are bound to complete perfection—and hence both a golden crown and a little crown are due to them—anyone who is worthily to be made pastor of God’s people must be examined with more exact diligence: to cultivate, govern, and administer the patrimony of the Crucified One. “No one takes honour to himself” (that is, no one ought to take honour to himself), “unless called by God, as Aaron was.” He is called by God if he is chosen such as he ought to be, in the manner fitting, and by those by whom he ought to be chosen—those who have both knowledge of what is true and choice of what is good. For knowledge of truth does not allow error in judgment; the choice of good makes one cleave in love to the decision of the divine will. He is likewise called by God if [Col. 0995D] he is neither thrust in by a superior’s violence nor chosen through the favour of private affection nor enters through ambition for office. These three—violence, private affection, and ambition—customarily advance the unworthy.

Therefore let those placed in a higher rank beware lest, on account of power granted to them, they dispose anything unjustly or violently thrust in an unworthy person. For, as is stated in the law: “He deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the power permitted to him.” Let those who love themselves with private affection see and reflect: with the eye of prayer darkened, they do not clearly discern what is just, while they always slip to one side or the other through favour or hatred. For favour and hatred are, as it were, a double quartan fever, to which justice alone applies a medicinal antidote. [Col. 0996A] Let those tormented by ambition for office beware, lest, while they think that they have climbed the highest rank, they slip down to the lowest; and, lifted above themselves, are cast down below, as it is written: “You cast them down, O Lord, when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72).

Let them beware of trying to enter the sheepfold by any way other than through the door, lest by the judgment of the supreme Shepherd they be reckoned not shepherds so much as thieves and robbers, and, lacking the wedding garment, be shut out from the heavenly wedding feast and “cast into the outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8). Weeping belongs to the eyes and comes from heat; gnashing of teeth occurs from cold, because those placed in torments will pass, as it is said, from snowy waters to excessive heat (Job 24).

You will be free of this blood, if you, whose concern it is to ordain a worthy minister for the house of God, do not exceed the order of law; if you do not presume to usurp anything that belongs to another’s right; if, with no respect of persons, you establish by canonical election one called by God—such a one as, according to the prophet (Jer. 1), may “pluck up and destroy, ruin and scatter, build and plant”: pluck up vice where it has already struck root; destroy what has already grown tall; ruin what has become ingrained through wicked custom; scatter what has infected others by the example of wickedness; finally build gold, silver, and precious stones where he finds a natural foundation and a mind disposed toward good; and plant in the soil of the heart—when it has been ploughed, carefully cleansed, and enriched—the shoots of faith, plants of virtue. Thus there may be in God’s house a garden of delights, in the sweet joy of those living together; a garden of nuts, in the hardness and severity of penitents; roses in bloom, in the fervent charity of those who love God; lilies of the valleys, in the shining chastity of the humble; and finally a paradise of every kind of fruit, in the sweetness of those already tasting beforehand eternal things and spreading far and wide the fragrance of good repute, an example for imitation.

But for one who is thus called by God and thus appointed by canonical election, nothing is so necessary as to preserve the virtue of humility. “For he who gathers virtues without humility,” says Saint Gregory, “is like one carrying dust into the wind.” Therefore the Wise Man, among the other matters by which he instructs the ruler, warns him not to exalt himself, saying: “Have they appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself.” Do not exalt yourself: pride is a beast with many heads, drawing its origin from diverse causes; celestial by birth, it inhabits the minds of the exalted, hides in ashes and stone, receives those first who come, and pursues those last who depart.

> When you fight well, when you think all things subdued,  
> Pride remains, assailing afterward, still to be conquered.

This is the firstborn daughter of the king of Babylon, who cast an angel from heaven and expelled humankind from paradise; for “the heart is exalted before ruin” (Prov. 16). She pours out the oil from the lamps of the foolish virgins; she empties the fasts and works of the Pharisee [Col. 0997A] and brings them to nothing; she has drawn back into the depths of vices many who appeared to have escaped the world’s flood, because they had no firm foundation of humility.

Our Lord, the humble teacher, displaying in himself the pattern of humility expressed for us, says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). When blessed Antony, in a vision, saw snares stretched as far as heaven and asked—and it was asked—who could pass through all those snares, the answer came from heaven: “Antony, humility alone.” Abraham your father calls himself ashes and dust (Gen. 18); David, chosen by God and anointed king, calls himself a dead dog and a single flea (1 Sam. 24); and before his servants and maidservants he dances and makes himself low before the Lord, who chose him rather than Saul. This was altogether prudent and just; for if the condition of things were weighed in right order and just balance, every occasion for pride would certainly be a cause and material for a person’s humility.

If you shine in knowledge, if you excel in power, if you are distinguished by the various gifts of graces, “what do you have that you have not received? Give glory to God, and the greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (1 Cor. 4). If the splendour of your household, glorious memory of your fathers, or the glory of your blood raises your spirit, remember that it is far more glorious for your nobility to begin with you than to end in you. “It is better,” says that greatest Roman master of eloquence, “better for me to flourish through my own deeds and achievements than to rely upon the reputation of my ancestors, and so to live as to become for my descendants the beginning of nobility and an example of virtue.”

> Better that Thersites be your father, provided that you are  
> Like Aeacides and desire Vulcan’s arms,  
> Than that Achilles produce you like Thersites.

So says I know not whom.

And likewise:

> What do pedigrees accomplish? What advantage, Ponticus, is there  
> In being numbered by long descent, in displaying painted faces  
> Of ancestors, or Aemilii standing in chariots?

And this too is “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclus. 1). If you rightly consider your own weakness; if you are ashamed of your past manner of life; if you remember the benefit received; if you gather to yourself and compare with yourself many who are better than you; if you set before your eyes the fear of the final [Col. 0997D] judgment, you will rightly behold your latter end and will never exalt yourself.

Of the first you have an example in the aforesaid Abraham, who, considering his own weakness, the more often he was visited by the Lord and admitted to more familiar conversation with him, thought of himself the more humbly: “I will speak to my Lord,” he says, “though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). Of the second you have an example in the Apostle Paul, who, recalling the errors of his former way of life, says: “I was formerly a blasphemer and persecutor; I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Tim. 1). Of the third you have an example in Joseph, mindful of the benefit he had received: “There is nothing,” he says, [Col. 0998A] “in my master’s house that he has not given into my hand, except you, who are his wife; and how can I commit this evil and sin against the Lord?” (Gen. 39). Of the fourth you have a notable example in Saint John the Baptist, who, though by the testimony of truth he was either greatest or at least equal to the greatest, greatly humbled himself by comparison with one better, saying: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (John 1). Of the fifth you have an example in blessed Arsenius, who, keeping the fear of God in mind, is continually said to have carried a cloth in his lap because of the abundance of his tears; and when at the point of death he was asked whether he himself was afraid, he said: “I am afraid, I am afraid; and this fear has always been in me since I became a monk. Woe to every human life, even a praiseworthy one, upon earth, if you examine it, Lord God, with mercy withdrawn. No one is clean from defilement, and all our righteousnesses are like a menstrual cloth before the Most High.”

With these authorities and examples set forth, the virtue of humility is proposed, commended, and demonstrated to rulers, so that, if they should perhaps have been called higher by God and done notable things, they may not immediately be lifted up but rather hold most firmly the Wise Man’s admonition: “Have they appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them.” “Be among them,” he says, “as one of them”: here conformity of life for the observance of charity is indicated. Nothing so promotes the observance of charity, and nothing equally gains the favour and goodwill of others, as not thinking lofty thoughts while in a high place, but agreeing with the humble; and, living in conformity with them, being among them as one of them.

[Col. 0998C] “Be among them as one of them,” so that, wholly taking on their disposition, you may rejoice with one who rejoices, suffer with one who suffers, know how to become weak with the weak, and burn with one who is scandalized. “Be among them as one of them” in friendliness of conversation, provision of assistance, enjoyment of advantages, and equity of judgment—matters which seem especially to belong to conformity of life.

In friendliness of conversation, let the salt of the spirit abound when you give counsel, and honey when you are counseled, so that your little sheep, drawn by the comforts of tender consolation, may run, be gathered, and rest in the shepherd’s bosom; so that it may receive from your mouth the sweetness of anointing and not feel the harshness of a hard prick. In provision of assistance, provide for all their necessities as you would wish provision to be made for you in similar circumstances; for this is the natural law: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7). In the enjoyment of advantages, let no more elegant clothing, more refined food, or more luxurious furnishing be sought; rather, let necessity be supplied from the common store in such a way that every excess is cut off, and thus the unity of peace and harmony of charity are preserved. “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13), says the Apostle. By saying, “Make no provision for the flesh,” he cuts off superfluities; by adding “in its desires,” he does not exclude necessities.

But in equity of judgment [Col. 0999A], “be among them as one of them,” so that you judge others in the manner in which you would wish to be judged by others, and approach the rebuking and correction of others’ offences in the spirit in which you would wish your own to be rebuked and corrected. For, as Saint Augustine says, one should never undertake the task of rebuking another’s sin unless one’s conscience clearly answers before God that one does so from love. If you rebuke, rebuke from love, and all is safe: have charity, and do what you will. Yet there are some who are less equitable in judgment in this respect: excessively lenient and indulgent toward themselves, but judging others more harshly than truthfully wherever they may have erred. They think they have done nothing unless, at each offence of their subjects, they bite, bark, and kill; and, wishing to appear to exercise justice, they do not fear to fall into tyranny. “A scale and a scale, a weight and a weight: both are abominable before God.”

Among such people the judgment of those who cried out with contempt, “Away, away, crucify, crucify him!” (John 19), receives a better hearing than that gracious judgment of the gracious judge: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8). [Col. 1000A] Not so that holy man, not so: when he heard that another had sinned grievously, he immediately burst into tears, saying: “He today; I tomorrow.” Therefore, good shepherd, imitate the example of the supreme Shepherd. Be among them as one of them: clothed in the disposition of compassion, be friendly in shared conversation; prudent and solicitous in providing aid; sparing and less indulgent toward yourself in enjoying advantages; just and guided by reason in equity of judgment—or at least let mercy triumph over judgment, that you yourself may obtain the same.

May the Father of mercies grant this mercy, which we have touched upon last because we shall need it most in our last things, to us all; and may he who called us to this work of solicitude himself advance the good in us [Col. 1000B] and for us. Since without him we can do nothing, just as neither can a branch bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, may he make us, as true branches, remain perpetually in himself, the true vine, so that at last we may come to that fountain of life, Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SECOND SERMON

[Col. 0999]

[Col. 0999C] “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

Since it is an exceedingly difficult matter to speak among a multitude in which condition of age and character is diverse, I undertake, not without embarrassment, the burden of speaking imposed upon me in so venerable an assembly, though I possess neither knowledge sufficient for instruction nor merit of life sufficient to support an example. Yet, mindful that a mute beast of burden rebuked the prophet’s madness, and that lepers announced salvation to Samaria (Num. 22; 2 Kgs. 7), I shall, more safely and freely by this example, perform the office of a whetstone, which can sharpen steel though itself incapable of cutting.

Therefore: “Remember me, O Lord, who rule over every power, [Col. 0999D] and put right and well-sounding speech into my mouth, so that my words may please you for others, and may please you both for me and for others.” They will please, moreover, if they are prudently and rightly sought out through the foresight of discernment and, with every humility, tested according to the capacity of the hearers. They will please indeed if sinners, pierced by the power of the words, turn to repentance; if the sluggish and idle are encouraged to run more vigorously; and if the strong and eager are made firmer in the love of God.

The whole sum of our intention ought surely to be occupied with three things: that the hearts of the hearers may be moved toward fuller love; and that we, gathered from different parts of the world, may by the Holy Spirit be inflamed from heaven with that fire [Col. 1000C] which our Lord Jesus Christ sent upon the earth (Luke 12) and ardently wished to be kindled.

The experience of this matter is not deceptive, but is the clearest proof of certainty, if works themselves answer to the voice of profession, and the fulfilment of the commandments confirms the worth of love. For, according to the venerable saying of Saint Gregory, “the proof of love is the showing forth of a work.” Hence it is that in today’s Gospel the Lord Jesus, the Bride’s beloved, white and ruddy, distinguishing by manifest signs and a well-trodden criterion his true and beloved lovers from those who love him falsely, says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.” In these words are shown the condition of the intention, the fulfilment of the command, [Col. 1000D] and the attainment of benefit and advantage. The condition of the intention: “If anyone loves me.” The fulfilment of the command: “he will keep my word.” The attainment of benefit and advantage is seen in the three following clauses: “My Father will love him, and we shall come to him, and we shall make our dwelling with him.”

The condition of the intention excludes compulsion and establishes freedom of choice. The fulfilment of the command produces obedience and tends toward expectation of the promise. Moreover, the attainment of benefit and advantage already, in the joy of the spirit, tastes in part the delights of the eternal reward. The Creator and Lord of the universe endowed the first man, in his creation, with free choice, by which he might be free not only from the compulsion of necessity, [Col. 1001A] but also from sin and the suffering of miseries. After the transgression of the command, that freedom was brought low and in great part lost, so that we can neither live without sin in this mortal body nor avoid daily disturbance by diverse miseries according to the varying conditions of our state; as it is written: “Man, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14).

Meanwhile, freedom from necessity remains after sin just as it did before; for as man could not then be compelled, so neither can he now. Freedom of will surely remains, as does the mind’s own capacity. For, as blessed Bernard says (*On Grace and Free Will*), “it is neither lost nor diminished by sin or misery; nor is it greater in the righteous [Col. 1001B] than in the sinner, nor fuller in an angel than in a human being. For it is as complete in the wicked as in the good, though more ordered in the good; as whole, in its own mode, in the creature as in the Creator, but in him more powerful and glorious. Therefore the will is rightly judged before God, since, free from every necessity, it can merit punishment or glory.” Therefore our Lord impels no one by force and constrains no one by necessity. He does not destroy but establishes freedom of choice, so that merit may grow from voluntary action; for he judges no one worthy of salvation whom he has not first found willing. He proposes to all under a free condition: “If anyone loves me,” etc. No one is deceived; no one is shut out or excepted; rather: “If anyone loves me, he will keep [Col. 1001C] my word.”

Among all the commandments proposed to worshippers of the Christian faith, love alone stands pre-eminent in the dignity of a certain excellence, because, by the testimony of Truth itself, “The first and greatest commandment is: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Mark 12; Luke 10). For in this command is contained the whole integrity of philosophical discipline. Here is natural philosophy, because all the causes of all natures are from God. Here is ethics, because uprightness of conduct is never formed unless the things that ought to be loved, and the manner in which they ought to be loved, are loved. Here is logic, because the light and truth of the rational soul are only in God—or are God. Here is the safety of the commonwealth, [Col. 1001D] because a city is never well preserved unless the common good is loved—and that is God.

Therefore the commandment of love is put before us and set before the other commandments, without which alone salvation cannot be obtained: “You shall love the Lord your God.” Then you love rightly if, in the present, you love nothing against God, and in the future nothing besides God. “You shall love the Lord your God.” Then you love rightly if all your movements are from God and toward God. Yet there are some movements neither from God nor toward God: when we are moved to carnal desire, theft, homicide, and the like. Some movements are from God but not toward God: when we are moved to an unlawful oath or blasphemy. There are also some movements toward God [Col. 1002A] but not from God: when we mercifully assist our neighbours in their necessities. Finally, there are movements from God and toward God; and these will be in the future, when we shall see him without difficulty, love him perfectly, and enjoy him without any interruption.

God, therefore, is to be loved both for his own worth and for our advantage: either because nothing is more just, or because nothing can be loved more profitably. If you ask the cause and the measure, as our Father says: “The cause for loving God is God; the measure is to love without measure” (St Bernard, treatise *On Loving God*). Nor is God loved without reward, though he ought to be loved without regard to reward: he gave himself as the object of merit; he keeps himself as the reward; he offers himself as the refreshment of holy souls; he gives himself up as the redemption [Col. 1002B] of captives. Love, therefore, such a Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind: that is, with understanding without error, will without opposition, and memory without labour. This is now in part upon the way; it will sometime be more perfect in the homeland. As the gracious Master invites all to this love, so he gives all a probable proof for knowing him: if they truly love God, let them demonstrate it by the truth of their works.

Hence, then, he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words.” Your word, Lord—your word is truth. God’s truth is one, by which holy souls are illumined; but among human beings there are many truths, just as from one face many images shine forth in many [Col. 1002C] mirrors. Accordingly, to keep God’s word is to walk in truth, to bring forth truth from heart and mouth, to judge according to truth, and gladly to die for truth. The first pertains to innocence of life; the second to constancy in faith; the third to the execution of justice; the fourth to most perfect charity. “For no one has greater love than this,” etc. (John 15).

Thus, in the first, a person is simple and upright; in the second, an unconquered confessor; in the third, the just judge is known; in the fourth, the victor over death is shown more gloriously. In the first, a person lives without the leaven of malice; in the second, walks without duplicity; in the third, excludes favouritism and hatred; in the fourth, offers himself to God as an acceptable [Col. 1002D] holocaust. Of the first it is said: “Lead me, Lord, in the straight way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Psalm 85). Of the second: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no” (Matthew 5). Our speech is “Yes, yes; No, no” when with the twofold truth—namely, that of heart and mouth—we affirm or deny something. And just as the elect, for this twofold confession of truth, shall be clothed doubly and possess double portions in the land, so the reprobate, who speak with heart and heart, shall for their false duplicity be clothed, as with a double garment, in their own confusion, and the Lord our God shall crush them with double destruction.

Of the third it is rightly said: “Judge your neighbour” (Leviticus 19). The Lord commends this judgment of truth in himself, saying: “As I hear, I judge, and [Col. 1003A] my judgment is just” (John 5). By this judgment of truth Daniel freed Susanna (Daniel 13); merciful Jesus freed the woman caught in adultery (John 8). Solomon restored her own son to the true mother, and by a sentence of death freed him from death by the sword, lest he perish divided by the sword (3 Kings 3). Therefore, lest he die, he is condemned to death.

Fear, hatred, and love attack this judgment of truth. Of judgment prompted by fear it is said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him” (John 11). Of judgment prompted by hatred: “Away, away, crucify him!” (John 19). To judgment prompted by love belongs what David says: “Spare my son Absalom” (2 Kings 18). Moreover, concerning the fourth member of the division, the Lord himself says: “Do not fear those who kill the body, [Col. 1003B] but can do nothing to the soul” (Matthew 10; Luke 12). Encouraged by this confidence, “the apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). Encouraged by this confidence, “the saints endured mockings and beatings, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, and died by slaughter of the sword for Christ” (Hebrews 11), who is Truth.

Therefore, in order that Christ’s word may truly be kept, let one who lives a private life strive to walk simply in truth. Let one who is called upon to bear witness to the truth strive, without fear, ambiguity, or duplicity, to bring forth truth from heart and mouth. Let one who holds the office of judge strive to judge according to truth, without respect of persons. But one to whom cause, place, and time reasonably persuade him to lay down his life for truth should not hesitate gladly to die.

According to the various qualities of persons, differences of rank, and diversities of graces, the way of God’s commandments is run in diverse ways, and God’s word is variously fulfilled by different people. Job excelled through patience; Abraham through obedience; Joseph through chastity; Moses through meekness; Joshua through constancy. Each of them pleased God in his own way and was found just. Humble David pleased God by dancing—not because of the dance, but because of devotion (1 Chronicles 5). The children of Israel sang to the Lord and, giving thanks for benefits received, were accepted by him. But you, whoever you are, who strive to please: if you have a voice, [Col. 1003D] sing; if supple arms, dance; and by whatever art you can please, please. Yet I do not mean people, but God: “For if I were still pleasing people, I should not be Christ’s servant” (Galatians 1), says that disciple of Jesus, the true servant of Christ.

Almighty God, who powerfully created all and mercifully redeemed all, does not despise the person of the poor nor honour the face of the powerful, whatever rank, order, or dignity they may possess. In every people or nation, whoever does his will is acceptable to him. He who looked upon Abel and his offerings (Genesis 4) values no more highly half the goods of Zacchaeus than the widow’s two small coins, or a cup of cold water given from the hand of a poor person—given out of good will. Good will makes the sacrifice:

> Let the poor man also come welcome to the altar,  
> And the lamb be no less pleasing to heaven than the ox.

[Col. 1004A] Since, then, our Lord presents himself as impartial and common to all, so that no one ought to despair of pardon, he invites all equally—not by coercing, but by proposing—to love him and fulfil his commandments, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word,” etc. But: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you, Lord” (Matthew 19). Behold, we love and shall love you; we keep your word and, by your gift, shall keep it for ever. But with what fruit? What reward? Good Jesus, good Jesus, what will you give us? “My Father,” he says, “will love him, and [Col. 1004B] we shall come to him, and we shall make our dwelling with him.”

This is the first attainment of benefit and advantage mentioned above. It contains a threefold good: first, in the shield of good will; second, in the frequency of visitation; third, in the permanence of blessedness. The first is in affection; the second in effect; the third without defect: that he may love, come, and remain. Happy is he whom God loves; happier he to whom the loving God comes; happiest he in whom he makes his seat and dwelling.

God’s loving is understood in three ways. “He loves,” that is, he predestines to life—and thus he loves only the predestined. “He loves,” that is, in time he bestows grace—and thus he loves those [Col. 1004C] who walk in the justice of good works. “He loves,” that is, he preserves things in their being—and thus he loves all things. Hence it is written: “You hate none of the things you have made” (Wisdom 11).

He frequently comes to those whom he loves, but the reason for his coming is diverse. He comes as an angry man, as a guest, as a merchant, as a teacher, as a physician. As a merchant, by giving an abundance of temporal things, so that through them he may draw people to faith and the keeping of the commandments; as it is said: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labours of peoples, that they might keep his justice and seek his law” (Psalm 104).

Secondly, he comes as a teacher, to instruct, inwardly instilling his will by hidden inspiration into those who fear [Col. 1004D] his name; as it is written: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Psalm 84). “I will hear what he speaks,” so that I may obey him who speaks. And in Isaiah we read: “I, the Lord, teach you things that are profitable and guide you in the way in which you shall walk” (Isaiah 48): as though [he were] God’s power—wisdom, than which learned Greece has nothing loftier; power, which is sufficient.

Thirdly, to Jews seeking signs, he comes as one angered, that he may strike with diverse temptations, injuries, losses of possessions, and bodily troubles, afflicting and tormenting in order to remove them from evil and advance them toward good. “Fill their faces with disgrace, and they shall seek your name, Lord” (Psalm 82), says the Prophet. And again: “Their infirmities were multiplied,” and afterward—what happened? “They hastened” to correction (Psalm 15). [Col. 1005A] For Balaam’s afflicted ass sometimes sees the angel whom the prophet himself does not see (Numbers 22), because flesh oppressed by troubles leads the spirit to know itself—a knowledge it could not have in prosperity.

Fourthly, he comes as a physician, to heal, pouring oil and wine into the wounds of the half-dead man (Luke 10). He not only washes away the stains of sins, but also heals bodily infirmities, as he says concerning the centurion’s servant: “I will come and heal him” (Matthew 8). Like a wise and powerful physician, he kills and makes alive, strikes and heals: “I,” he says, “will kill, and I will make alive,” etc. (Deuteronomy 32). “I will kill in them the life of sin,” because those living in fleshly pleasures and delights are dead; “and I will make alive,” changing them to a better state by bestowing on them the life [Col. 1005B] of grace, so that at last they may attain the life of glory, of which it is said: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also shall appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3).

Fifthly, he comes as a guest, passing through by the infusion of grace, granting an affection of devotion, and usefully withdrawing himself for a time to preserve humility. “For a moment,” he says, “in my indignation I hid my face from you a little while, and in everlasting mercies I remembered you” (Isaiah 54). But those through whom he often passes will easily obtain his remaining, if, when he comes, he finds the house prepared and adorned with virtues. This is figuratively suggested by that Shunammite woman, who, speaking of Elisha [Col. 1005C] to her husband, says: “I perceive that this man of God, who frequently passes by us, is holy. Let us therefore make for him a small upper room, and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that when he comes, he may remain there.” “Then one day, when he came, he turned aside into the upper room and rested there” (4 Kings 4).

The order is fitting in every respect. He comes in the day, turns aside in the day, and rests in the day—namely, that day in which there is no darkness. Therefore let the upper room be the human heart lifted toward things above; let it be small, that it may remain within humility. Let a bed be placed there, that, removed from the clamour of worldly things, he may rest. Let there be a table of refreshment, that he may feed on the diverse dishes of sacred Scripture. Let there be a chair of discernment, [Col. 1005D] that he may distinguish and judge his works and judge himself strictly. Finally, let there be a lampstand, that it may shed on every side the rays of a clear reputation.

Thus there is an upper room fit to receive the guest; small, for the foundation of humility; there is a bed, for the sweetness of contemplation; a chair, for the caution and discernment of judgment; a lampstand set on high, as an example of right living, that it may shine upon all who [Col. 1006A] are in God’s house. In this way the house of our inward person must be adorned and ordered, so that when the true Elisha comes to us and finds it thus, he may not pass by but remain there: “Remain with us, Lord, for evening is drawing on” (Luke 24), and the last day is either near us all or lies in wait for us. Remain with us, that we too may remain in you. For if we remain in you, you will remain in us; and thus we shall have full joy from that permanence of blessedness mentioned above.

For everyone’s praise is sung at the end, and among virtues perseverance alone is crowned. Judgment in any case is customarily awaited from the final sentence; for as there is a case when it is put forward, judgment when it is examined, so there is a sentence when it is concluded. Nor may one complain of the judge before the sentence has been pronounced; [Col. 1006B] then most of all it is permissible to approve or disapprove the judgment, when it has already been brought to conclusion by the sentence.

Thus a storm clouds the serene rising of the morning sun; and a gentler breeze sometimes clears the turbulence of the weather and the violence of rains, so that a fair day can always be praised in the evening. For whatever has a good end is itself wholly good. Thus Jesus, “having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end” (John 13). To this pertains the fact that Abraham died full of days (Genesis 25); that David saw the angel at the time of the evening sacrifice; that Jesus died on the cross; that among his brothers Joseph was clothed in a long robe (Genesis 37). [Col. 1006C] To this pertains the apostles’ command to shake the dust from their feet (Matthew 10), in which lies the body’s end; and that, after the resurrection, the women approached and held Jesus’ feet. “I have held him and shall not let him go,” says that loving and beloved woman.

Thus also—what I had almost passed over—Israel loved Joseph above all his sons (Genesis 37), because he had begotten him in his old age. For every righteous person, seeing God either humbly through the understanding of the Scriptures or, indeed, more sweetly through experience of conduct, especially embraces that good work which increases his reward—for Joseph is interpreted “increase”—and counts as his own salvation that which the perseverance of old age commends. By the preceding authorities and examples, the virtue of perseverance [Col. 1006D] is commended to us; we who wish to arrive at eternal rest must direct our utmost diligence toward it.

Let us therefore remain in God’s love and keep his word, so that he who first loved us (John 4) may love us more abundantly, and love us in such a way that by frequent visitation and consolation he may come to us; and come in such a way that he may not pass by, but Jesus Christ may establish in us an eternal seat and dwelling. Amen.

## A Treatise of Lord Thomas, Monk of Radolio, on the Life of the Venerable Father Lord Peter, Abbot of Clairvaux, Written at the End of the Twelfth and Beginning of the Thirteenth Century

[Note: [Col. 1007] See *Patrologia*, vol. 185, col. 1044.]

Copied from Troyes manuscript no. 1133, of the thirteenth century, and first published complete by PH. G.

[Col. 1007]

## Letter of Lord Thomas, Monk, in the Life of Lord Peter, Abbot of Clairvaux

To his lord and friend WALCHER, abbot of Longpont, brother THOMAS, monk of Radolio, greetings.

While Master Adam, your predecessor and companion and ours, was still alive, the three of us often conferred together about matters concerning the welfare of the soul. Since I frequently proposed examples of good people, you often asked me to commit them to writing. But, conscious of my inadequate eloquence, I spared the desk and pen. On the other hand, fearing the guilt of silence, I noted down in writing certain things about Lord Peter, Abbot of Clairvaux. I send you that work.

If there is any fault in its expression or beyond its expression—that is, in its writing or its meaning—I entrust it to the correction of your tongue and judgment. For certain reasons, and especially because of the dimness of my eyes, I have not been sufficiently able to attend to the labour of polishing, nor, after the manner of bears, to lick my offspring into shape and fashion its unformed, rough material as was fitting.

If the writing seems unworthy of the light, bury it. If it ought not to be consigned to the grave, make it known before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh: that is, before those who fear God, to whom the things of God taste like honey upon the palate of the heart. For the pride of those who hate God rises continually and despises and mocks things of this kind; indeed, it does not hesitate to disparage their writers. Therefore, just as pearls are not to be scattered before swine, do not give to dogs the holy thing about which I have written, but give it to those who have learned from Christ to be meek and humble. Such people may perhaps find in our writing some rest for their souls.

## Here Begins the Prologue of the Following Work

Although the Most High, who founded it, has never ceased in many ways and by many means to govern and glorify his Church, he has always provided it with men distinguished by virtues and signs. This is almost an especial effect of heavenly grace, since by it faith is strengthened and emulation of virtue is stirred up. The historical sequence, carried down and committed to letters from the bodily presence of the Saviour himself to our own time—namely, the year 1204 of his Incarnation—makes this clear.

But because at this time iniquity has abounded, the charity of many has grown cold (Matthew 24), and we therefore fear even an eclipse of faith itself; for truths have been diminished among the children of men, and the holy one has failed [Col. 1009] (Psalm 11)—that holy one, namely, who, full of grace and power, works great wonders and signs among the people (Acts 6), and confidently says: “The works which I do in the name of my Father bear witness concerning me” (John 10), or rather concerning the faith by which God decreed to save those who believe in him.

The primitive Church needed signs and revelations, and possessed them abundantly.
