But the Church, though advanced, also needs the same nourishment, so that the same medicine which bestowed health may preserve the health bestowed. For this purpose recent signs seem more effective than ancient ones, just as medicinal compounds are found through their very age to have little effect upon most people.

But since “there is none who does this good; there is not even one” (Psalm 13), I believe I am doing a useful thing in proposing, so far as can be done with my pen, to recall from the dead a man of virtue and singular in our time, whom I saw and knew: Peter, Abbot of Clairvaux. Thus, as he edified the living while alive, so may he edify them also when dead. And as he is, as we believe without doubt, in eternity, so may he be in human memory, in order to strengthen their faith and awaken divine love in them.

Yet consideration of myself strongly strives to call me back from this purpose. My bodily presence is weak and my speech contemptible (2 Corinthians 10), and I fear being accused of presumption for shamelessly taking up material that ought to be reserved for the most eloquent. I fear lest so great a man be assessed, not according to what he was, but according to the manner in which an ineffectual poet describes him. Indeed, the things I know about him are few; more have not come to our knowledge. Therefore, after many years had now passed since his death, I remained silent, listened, and waited to see whether there might be someone from his order—that is, Cîteaux, where “the multitude of the wise is the health of the world”—especially one who had been constantly and intimately near him, to compose his history. But until now I have neither found nor heard of such a person. For the philosophers of that order devote greater labour to silence than to the pen.

This necessity therefore, shattering the reasons for my silence set out above, impels me to gather, lest they perish, the few things that I learned from him himself or from good men about him, as certain fragments, and to describe them with whatever pen I possess. Perhaps from this occasion some man of noble and polished eloquence, with no rusticity mixed into his speech, will recast rhetorically what has been treated too crudely. Moreover, he will supply what is hidden from us concerning that man and missing from our little work. Indeed, with grace poured upon his lips (Psalm 44), he will turn our mud into silver, dross into gold, barley loaves into fine flour, tasteless waters into wine, or bitter waters into sweetness.

Meanwhile, let those who deign to read this not be ungrateful for my modest labour. Rather, let them repay me with favour and goodwill, if not for the usefulness of the work, at least for the intention of usefulness. Now, since, as has been said before us, it is unseemly to overflow in a preface and be scanty in the narrative, enough has been said thus far concerning the Prologue. Let us now, with Christ presiding over the narrative, put our fingers to it.

## Chapters

1. On Peter’s homeland and his holy manner of life at Igny.  
2. On his vision before he entered Igny.  
3. How, in his newness, he felt as though a certain spirit entered into him, through which he thereafter remained ever the same in every circumstance.  
4. On a certain person, probably angelic, who awakened him while he slept in choir, and whom he himself saw.  
5. On the headache that he once suffered during the vigils and from which he was miraculously delivered.  
6. On the great sweetness of God which he himself experienced, and the author’s invective against unbelievers.  
7. How he was prior at Igny, then abbot of Val-Roy, and how a certain vision preceded his election.  
8. On the hired man who wished to set fire to the grange of Val-Roy and was marvellously prevented by the man of God.  
9. On the illness which he suffered in that abbey and his deliverance.  
10. How he was transferred from Val-Roy to Igny, and on Robert the monk’s foreknowledge concerning this.  
11. A divine answer concerning the same matter to the monk Nicholas.  
12. Another answer to the same Nicholas concerning the penance to be performed.  
13. On Lord Peter’s discretion concerning himself and his subjects.  
14. On his marvellous vision concerning the knight Baldwin.  
15. The author’s testimony concerning the same vision.  
16. On Lord Peter’s vision concerning Henry, Count of Champagne.  
17. On a deceased brother whom he plainly saw after death.  
18. On a certain sick man for whom he prayed, and who in sleep saw himself being beaten by him.  
19. How it was revealed to him that he would be Abbot of Clairvaux.  
20. On the death at Igny of Gerald, Abbot of Clairvaux.  
21. On the vision of a certain brother of Clairvaux which preceded Peter’s election.  
22. On his election as Abbot of Clairvaux, and on Gilbert the Prior, whom he freed from fevers.  
23. On how the same Peter freed Gilbert’s horse from its bad habit of falling.  
24. How the Roman Pope summoned and honoured him.  
25. On the election of a certain bishop and Peter’s praiseworthy saying concerning his election.  
26. [Col. 1011] On his patience when he lost an eye.  
27. What he replied to a certain brother when choosing a prior for Igny.  
28. On his arrival at Rheims, his manner of riding, and the author’s foreknowledge of his death.  
29. On his death at Foigny.  
30. On his tooth, which one of the brothers wished to extract after his death, and on his burial at Clairvaux.  
31. On the very gracious vision of a certain monk and prior after his death.  
32. The author’s apology for the work’s imperfection and for some persons’ lesser belief.  
33. The author’s letter to the man of God while he was alive, and the epilogue of the work.  
34. Conclusion of the work.

The chapters end.

## Here Begin the Deeds of Blessed Peter, Abbot of Clairvaux

[Col. 1011A] Peter was Italian by birth, born of parents said to be eminent in the dignity of the world; yet he always concealed this, as much as he could, with the utmost dissimulation. As a young man, seeking the schools of Gaul for the sake of learning, he came to Igny. This place, not far from Rheims, was at that time a recent foundation of the Cistercian Order. There, seeing the brothers’ heavenly way of life, he was inflamed with the love of God and assumed the religious habit.

The grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow processes. For, through the working in him of the one “whose word runs swiftly” (Psalm 147), he was made perfect in a short time, as though he had completed many years. He was of middling stature, though tending toward shortness; thin in body—indeed, rather emaciated—yet in that very thinness sinewy and strong. In food and clothing [Col. 1011B] he was exceedingly frugal and sparing. In food he readily presumed upon nothing beyond the common provision, and even from the common provision he often and greatly withheld from himself.

His clothing was a tunic and cowl without distinction of seasons, except for one tunic or cowl which, beyond his usual practice, he wore in winter. He never used the footwear called *botae*, even in winter; nor did he use foot-coverings except simple ones. He attended the brothers’ vigils not merely continuously but so persistently that, when some labour gave him occasion to rest, he did not relax his unconquered spirit from psalmody. He had an almost unbelievable capacity for prayer. Although the practice of it is difficult, whenever he had leisure he easily gave himself to it, and even when business summoned him he could scarcely be drawn away from it.

Many excel in many virtues and seek after excellent charisms, but a truly and perfectly humble person is very rarely found. He is, I think, the one whom blessed Bernard thus defines: “The truly humble person wishes to seem lowly, not to be considered humble.” This holy man possessed that good singularly and wonderfully. For he neither had nor sought to possess certain graces by which temporal glory is chiefly acquired: polished eloquence, beauty of person, industry in secular affairs, the ability to manage a household and thereby rule more extensively, and liberal generosity that wins favour. Meanwhile, he did not conspicuously possess the goods by which he shone in the Lord’s eyes, and he strove as much as possible to conceal them. Thus he judged himself lowly and obscure in human estimation. Since he rejoiced in that obscurity and sought it in every way, provided only that conscience remained safe, one may conclude that he was truly humble.

Certainly, in this respect, as I think, he had in his time no equal and without doubt no superior. Yet he did not obtain the lowliness which he chiefly desired, as he supposed. For to those who knew how to judge rightly, who could discern pretence from truth, hypocrisy from gold, fruit from leaves, he appeared venerable, exceptional, and marvellous. Thus, while the excellence of his religious life made him superior even to the great, his singular humility made him equal to the weak and lowly; together these made him at once revered and admired, dear and lovable to all.

## II

Having said a few things—indeed, very few—about the character of Lord Peter, proportionate to his merit, let us recount some matters transmitted to us by suitable witnesses, in which the testimony of God, which is greater, is proved to have appeared more plainly.

When, as we have said, he came into Gaul, it happened that he drew near to Igny. One night, therefore, before he reached the house, he saw in a night vision that he was entering a hall of extraordinary beauty. A seat had been placed in it, and upon the seat sat a woman of most venerable countenance and bearing. As he entered the palace, horrible [Col. 1012C] black dogs rushed at him as if about to kill him immediately. But the venerable Lady drove away those dogs with great authority, called him to herself, caressed him with gentle hands and kindly speech, and commanded him to be wholly fearless and secure.

What this vision signified is easy to conjecture. That hall seems to signify the house of Igny; the seated woman, Blessed Mary; the black dogs, evil demons. The remaining details accord with this interpretation.

## III

Therefore, when the most devout young Peter had been received, he did not ascend to perfection gradually and by stages, but, as if in a moment and the twinkling of an eye, put on beauty. “He clothed himself with strength and girded himself with power” (Psalm 92), remaining most steadfastly the same in every place, at every time, and in every circumstance.

An abbot, intimate with him, who recounted this to me, marvelled at the constancy of his now advanced age and investigated—diligently, indeed importunately—the cause of such unchanging sameness. Peter, as he was most kindly and easily overcome by his intimates, replied: “When I was a novice, I seemed distinctly to feel a certain spirit enter into me. From then until now, that spirit, power, or influence in some manner governs, rules, and leads me as a sheep (velut ovem Joseph). It often gathers inwardly what has been scattered abroad among outward things; it compels me, when I wish to attend to other matters, to pray; and it sometimes makes me not perceive the things presented to my eyes or sounding in my ears.”

These things, which the blessed man confessed concerning himself under a certain compulsion of love, agree with what Pope Gregory says in a homily: “Whom the love of eternal life has perfectly absorbed, it renders, as though insensible, to earthly desires outside.” Thus this man too, dwelling in thought and longing in that eternal homeland and with his affection conformed to immovable things, remained unmoved within himself. With great strength of mind—not painfully, but as though it were innate and natural to him—he restrained every motion of the heart, every leap of the mind, and all storms and tempests of the soul, by which people seem to boil and toss, and which true religion commands them to lay aside.

## IV

[Col. 1013C]

While he was still a novice, or newly entered into the order, he was once present at the night vigils. As the others sang psalms, he stood in choir and, wearied, fell asleep. He felt as though someone touched him and gently roused him with a tap. He supposed it was the Prior, whose custom it was to go about the choir and awaken sleeping brethren. But when he woke and opened his eyes, he saw no one. Since this happened often, and though repeatedly awakened he did not see the one who awakened him, he understood it to be a divine power; and he was troubled that it manifested itself to him yet concealed itself from him. Therefore one night, when he felt his customary awakener, he quickly and intently opened his eyes upon waking. He saw standing beside him a radiant and handsome young man, who, to use his own words, had golden hair [Col. 1013D]. Immediately withdrawing from him, the young man went through the middle of the choir; plainly and lingeringly visible to him, after appearing for a long time he disappeared. He himself told me this; and he likewise related what I shall add.

V.

At midnight on Sunday the brethren were singing psalms in the oratory, and he was with them. A headache came upon him, so violent that he considered leaving the choir. As, unable to bear the pain, he began to move to do so, he heard a voice instructing him thus: “Praising, I shall call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my infirmities” (Psalm XVII [18]). Strengthened by this voice, he remained in choir. But after a short interval, as the pain grew stronger, he again intended to leave, and again the aforementioned voice resounded. [Col. 1014A] Why say more? Throughout that whole night and the following Sunday, until the end of the conventual Mass, that contest did not cease: the contest, that is, between the pain compelling him to leave and the voice urging him to remain. It is a solemn custom in that order that all communicate on Sunday. Therefore, when he approached in his proper order and humbly bowed at the corner of the altar, it seemed to him that a stone of great weight fell from his head. At once he straightened himself, received the holy Eucharist, and was delivered from all that pain.

VI.

How close he was to God may be judged from what I shall now relate. I was once speaking [Col. 1014B] with him concerning the rationale of our faith. When, as to a familiar friend, I confessed that I was at times assailed by some temptation against it, I also asked him whether he had ever felt any temptation of this sort. “I do not deny,” he said, “that I have often been touched by such a thought; but manifold experience of faith has strengthened all of its weakness.” Going further, I ventured to ask what it was that had produced such firmness in him. He, being gentle and humble of heart, and easy and accommodating toward friends, said: “I have experienced many things concerning God, and at one time something of such a kind that, when I ceased to experience it, I bore it more grievously than if I had been cast into a burning furnace.” I call Christ to witness, and our common hope, that he spoke these very words to me.

The unbelief of some—or, worse still, the envy of believers—compelled me to append this testimony [Col. 1014C], for through hardness of heart they cannot believe, or through malice will not allow it to be believed, that servants of God have possessed, or that those of the present day possess, so great a grace. “Human ingenuity,” as blessed Jerome says, “like those who test wines, reveres the ancients and despises the younger.” Is God only the God of the ancients? Is he not also of the younger? God shows no partiality among persons or times; but in every race and at every time, whoever fears God and does righteousness is acceptable to him (Acts X [10]). Why, then, should this man not have been acceptable to God, and so acceptable that he received from God a grace by which he experienced concerning God those things which only the most perfect deserve to experience—when he himself perhaps was most perfect [Col. 1014D]?

Indeed, in certain graces—if I may call them so—of the worldly kind, he was undoubtedly inferior to many. For, as we stated at the beginning of this work, he was not “beautiful in form above the sons of men,” nor “surrounded in garments gilded with diversity” (Psalm XLIV [45]); nor, “in chariots and horses,” was he anxious and troubled about many things (Luke X [10]) through diligent concern with outward affairs; nor was he among “the giants who groan beneath the waters” (Job XXVI [26]); nor did he “walk in great matters and in things too wonderful for” him (Psalm CXXXI [132]). Yet in all these things the Lord is not. For, as it is written, he is not in the wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but in the whisper of a gentle breeze (III Kings XIX [1 Kings 19]); and in the voice which came to Elijah and to his counterpart John, a voice which this friend [Col. 1015A] of the Bridegroom, who stood often and intimately near him, heard.

Because some did not know his inward brightness, judging according to the face, they sometimes esteemed him too little. Long ago the envious and senseless despised the great Martin, likewise saying that a man of contemptible appearance, shabby clothing, and unkempt hair was unworthy of the episcopate. Yet this man did not lack these outward graces, these worldly advantages, as we have called them: he possessed them sufficiently, but exercised temperance in them, lest, if he were continually occupied in them and by them, he should be small or nothing in those things which he loved, and ought to love, above these. This is what most prelates do; indeed, they even glory in it, rejoice in it, and boast of it: that they are efficient in outward matters and succeed in them. [Col. 1015B] Meanwhile, casting away their inner concerns, they do not feel their inward loss; and, putting after what should be put before, namely the care of souls, they entrust those souls to the care of others, though they ought themselves to care for them, relying on their own prudence and not hoping in the Lord. For this reason God sometimes abandons such men, delivers them into the hands of their enemies, and “takes the wise in their own craftiness” (Job V [5]).

But this man, trusting in God, attending to inward matters and entrusting outward matters to faithful men, because he cared for God, had God as his caretaker, as will be plainly demonstrated by convincing evidence in what follows when we come to that point.

VII.

[Col. 1015C] But now, returning to the order of the narrative, let us say that, after he had lived in a singular manner in a singular order, he was made Prior of Igny. When he had fulfilled that office also with great energy and distinction, he was elected Abbot of Val-Royal, one of Igny’s daughter-houses. Such a vision preceded his election. The abbot then presiding at Igny saw a burning and shining lampstand, set before the high altar, suddenly go out through the great window; and shortly afterwards Lord Peter was elected. Two things happened to him in that royal valley which I learned not from a common and uncertain report but from the account of a religious brother, a monk and cellarer of that same abbey, named Nicholas.

VIII.

[Col. 1015D] One of the hired labourers of that place could not obtain his wages, although he had repeatedly demanded them. The cellarer was putting him off—or rather, for certain reasons, did not wish to pay them—and asserted that by right they ought not be paid him. When the man wished therefore to bring this matter before the abbot, he could not; for the abbot was then ill, and the cellarer would not allow him to enter to see him. The servant, then, raging and inflamed by anger—which is brief madness—went to one of the abbey’s neighbouring granges, carrying burning coals in a pot, and secretly intended to set fire to the grange.

While he was planning this, the servant of God appeared and asked what he intended to do. The man was struck with violent astonishment; and since he could not conceal the matter, he confessed his intention and the reason for it. The abbot said to him: [Col. 1016A] “Do not commit this crime. But come to me tomorrow in the infirmary; I shall order your wages to be restored to you, and no one shall prevent you from coming in to me.” He did as he had been instructed; and on the next day, with no one hindering him, he came to the abbot and asked him to fulfil his promise.

Now the abbot knew nothing of all this; yet, pretending not to know, he carefully inquired into and heard the sequence of events. When the man had departed with the certain hope of receiving his wages, he said to the aforementioned Nicholas, who attended him: “Truly, brother, if we thought of the Lord, the Lord would think of us.” Nicholas, guessing that he had heard something important, wisely and skilfully followed the departing man and, promising both to conceal his plan and to expedite the business, drew from him an account of what had occurred. This was the first and great miracle. The second resembles it not in form but in grace.

IX.

The illness called a fistula had afflicted and weakened the man of God. A monk of Clairvaux, renowned in the art of medicine, passed through that place. The brethren urged him, and he himself advised and persuaded the abbot to have the illness examined. He saw it and told the brethren that it was a fistula, and that it was in a place where it could not be cut and therefore could not be healed. He added these words: “If this man sees Easter, he will never die again.” By this he meant that he could not be healed and would die before such a limit. Yet he recovered and lived many years afterwards [Col. 1016C]; but how he recovered remained unknown until now.

X.

After he had presided for some time over the brethren of Val-Royal, it happened that the Abbey of Igny had no abbot. The custom is that the subordinate abbots, or his son-abbots, assemble for the election of their chief father and abbot. Therefore the man of God, Peter, taking with him a certain Robert, a religious and learned monk of Igny whom he kept with him as a familiar companion for his consolation, was coming to Igny. He prayed to the Lord to inspire him as to whose election he himself should support. As he both thought and prayed on this matter, he heard a voice saying: “When you come [Col. 1016D] to that place”—and it indicated the place to him by some sign which I do not remember—“you shall know what you seek.”

He had almost reached the place, yet was not in possession of the thing he desired. He prayed more intently and pressed the Lord for fulfilment of the promise. Then the voice came again to him and said: “Ask the monk who accompanies you; he will tell you who is to be abbot.” At once summoning the monk, namely the aforementioned Robert, the Father addressed him in this way: “We are going to Igny, and I believe that the election of the abbot will depend greatly upon me. You, therefore, who know the brethren’s characters through much experience, tell me privately whom you judge worthiest of this office.”

But Robert, not by a prophetic spirit but from a desire for his advancement, because he loved him and knew him worthy of promotion, said: [Col. 1017A] “Without hesitation and without deliberation I shall answer: I judge no one worthier than you; and therefore I predict that you will be abbot.” The man of God kept all these words, pondering them in his heart; and although he could no longer be ignorant of what was to happen to himself, he nevertheless questioned him again, saying: “I know, brother, and am certain that you would desire my promotion; but this is not placed in your will. I therefore want you at all events to name another who is worthy to be elected.” “I shall name no one else,” he said. “You will be abbot; all desire you.”

They came to Igny, and by the unanimous consent of all, without any contradiction, he was elected abbot. Yet another such portent, as I have said, likewise preceded that election.

XI.

There was in the abbey a religious and good brother, named Nicholas, who had long exercised the office of precentor. He himself told me that, at the time when that see was vacant and the brethren were in suspense, awaiting an election, he was continually praying to the Lord in his concern over the matter, that he might provide them with a suitable abbot. Once, as he prayed to the Lord, a voice plainly said to him: “Nicholas, you shall have an abbot, and he will show you what you ought to do. Seek the blessed Peter—O admirable man! O Peter, true imitator of Peter!” Therefore the Lord rightly bore witness to him as he had formerly borne witness to Peter, the Prince of the Apostles. Indeed, he showed the truest example of Christian religion not only to the aforementioned brother but to all who were in the house, and even to outsiders who deserved to see, hear, and know him. For several years he presided over that abbey in holiness and righteousness before God, with a great name, renowned fame, and a good savour before the world. [Col. 1017C]

XII.

The aforementioned Nicholas was both kindled and admonished by Peter’s singular and arduous manner of life, to understand what was laid before him and proposed to him by Peter. Remembering the voice he had heard, and knowing that he ought to prepare similar things, he wished even to attempt something beyond the common rule. But because he was delicate and weak, he did not dare. While he was in this uncertainty, he once heard a voice saying: “Nicholas, never fear to do penance.”

I think I have fittingly included this for the confirmation of those who are “faint of spirit and troubled” (Psalm XXXIV [35]), who fear frost and are overwhelmed by snow (Job VI [6]). Yet a measure must be set to boldness, and a pious and discerning regard must be shown for bodily frailty. This too must be considered: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew XXVI [26]); and concern for the flesh, though not in desires, must be exercised in necessities. I observed that the saint of God did this.

XIII.

[Col. 1018A]

For, once when I was dining with him, I saw that he did not taste the fish set before him and was sparing likewise with other foods. Pitying him, I reproached him for excessive abstinence. “On the contrary,” he said, “I would eat more sparingly, if I did not spare my body.” Thus he spared his body even while he was, and appeared to be, extremely sparing in food and drink. From this one may rightly infer that he was temperate, discerning, and moderate in other things as well. For he desired excellence in virtue in such a way that he did not abandon temperance, which, fourth among the principal virtues, possesses such grace that without it the other three graces cannot be gracious.

I therefore heard a certain religious and wise man, namely Gilbert, Abbot of Foigny, say of him [Col. 1018B] that he had seen no one for whom singularity had turned out less badly. Certainly, he governed his singularity singularly—that is, temperately and prudently—although, to most who did not know him intimately, he seemed simple and dull. This arose from his slowness of speech and because, when he spoke, his tongue had a Latin flavour. Finally, he took particular pains to conceal all his good deeds. In truth, however, he had a penetrating intellect and very sound judgment, and was moderate and discerning in managing his affairs and governing his subjects.

Once, when I met his cellarer, a venerable man, industrious and honourable alike, I complained that, as people said, his abbot was indeed religious but harsh, excessively severe, and uncultivated. The man, who through long association and experience knew his character, life, rules, and customary practice, replied: [Col. 1018C] “Truly, he is harsh and severe—but toward himself, not toward others. Toward others he is gentle and merciful, so much so that we who have the greater care of him and are his assistants sometimes complain of what seems to us his excessive kindness and patience. We say, not in disparagement but in zeal, that the fervour of the order has grown lukewarm in his time. But when we consider his intention, hear the prior reasons he gives us for his actions, and weigh those reasons once heard, we recognize that he ought to act in this way and no other. For he pays more heed to the spirit than to the letter, and to charity—which is the law of God, the bond of perfection, and the sole source from which life proceeds—than to the rules and inventions of men. He considers the loss of certain observances easy to bear; yet he does not abandon, neglect, or despise them, but moderates them according to person, place, and time. He considers on the one hand the rigour of the order, on the other human frailty, and labours with all his strength to be a faithful steward. He believes he certainly attains this when, in exchange for certain indulgences which may seem to incur some reproach and loss, he receives the recompense of the brethren’s charity, peace, and willing service. He does not greatly care if some disparage him for this, while a pure conscience and the truth of God bear witness for him.” [Col. 1019A]

Certainly this man was not among those who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel (Matthew XXIII [23]), who tithe every herb and neglect the weightier matters of the law; who, lacking discernment between good and evil, good and better, evil and worse—and, what is worse, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Philippians II [2])—seem to keep watch over the flock but, through ignorance or malice, themselves go astray and lead others into error. They do much, make little progress, and produce many leaves but scant fruit; indeed, they often quarrel over goat’s wool and suffer nothing over the ruin of Joseph.

But Peter, taught by the revelation of the Holy Spirit that “no flesh shall be justified by works of the law” (Galatians II [2]), and that God is Spirit and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John IV [4]), was a most ardent champion of spirit and truth. He abundantly possessed a righteousness not from law and works but from the Spirit and from God. By that righteousness, being himself righteous, he justified his dispensations; and by the authority that followed holiness he obtained for them not only victory but favour. Having explained these matters, perhaps as a digression, yet still dependent upon our subject, we shall return to the subject. Meanwhile the man of God saw a vision most worthy of admiration, remembrance, and report. Since I found it written by another, I joined it to what we are writing. It is as follows.

XIV.

At a certain time Peter, Abbot of Igny [Col. 1019C], a man conspicuous for every holiness, came to Ursicamp. The whole house rejoiced, glad at his arrival, and offered him the reverence his holiness demanded. Then the Lord Abbot and the Prior, having learned that he had seen a vision which they desired to hear from the mouth of the one who had seen it, withdrew him from the company and led him aside, as though to speak of more secret matters. When they had sat down, they respectfully addressed him and began to beg that he would deign to disclose to them the course of the vision he had seen.

Trembling and afraid, and as though he did not know what they sought, he concealed as far as he could that he had seen a vision and did not at all yield to their prayers. They asked once and twice; he refused. Yet overcome by their commendable persistence [Col. 1019D]—both because the Prior showed him by the testimony of Scripture that one is guilty of sin against a brother who conceals from his brother a matter conducive to edification, and because he could refuse nothing to the Lord Abbot, whom he dearly loved and by whom he was loved no less in return—at last, with words scarcely breaking forth, he began his account thus:

“In the archbishopric of Rheims there was a knight named Baldwin, a man distinguished by birth, abounding in temporal wealth, but no less abounding in sins. For he left no evil undone except what he himself could not do. At the time when this knight was waging war against the Archbishop of Rheims, he inflicted very many evils upon the whole country and especially upon neighbouring houses. But he not only did not take the goods of our house—which he embraced with a more ample affection of love than other religious houses—but even protected them from all others, showing much reverence to our property and to us all.

“It happened, however, that he finally took to his bed, struck by bodily illness. When he knew that he was going to die, I was summoned by his messenger to visit him, and, having been summoned, I immediately came. After hearing his confession, seeing that he was moved to repentance and that henceforth he had a good will, I urged him to renounce the world and assume the religious habit. He accepted the advice and sought his wife’s permission, but could not obtain it. Therefore, seeing that he lacked permission to come, after I had anointed him with holy oil, I returned [Col. 1020B] to the monastery.

“Meanwhile, after a few days had passed, as his illness grew worse and his relatives had no hope remaining for him, he was brought by those same relatives to our monastery. We went out to meet him and received him devoutly. He was carried into a cell, clothed in the sacred habit, and guards were assigned to him. When one night they perceived that he was approaching death, they sounded the board to summon the brethren, as the custom of our order requires. The brethren were awakened and came to the sick man; I too was there among the rest. I performed the office; the convent sang the seven psalms, but the sick man had not yet departed. Seeing, therefore, that he would not die so quickly, lest the brethren who ought to attend the sacred vigils should be too much burdened, I gave them leave to return to bed.

“At that hour two of the brethren saw two visions concerning the sick man.

“The vision of one, in his bed, was this: he seemed to see the entire convent standing before the sick man and, as the sick man humbly bowed, pressing the kiss of peace upon his lips.

“The other saw, in a night vision, that the sick man lying in bed wished to rise from his bed but could not. When the brother stood near to help him, the sick man said: ‘Do not help me; I have no need of your assistance. For blessed Benedict is helping me, and he also orders the Abbot himself to make me a crown.’

“Without delay the board was sounded a second time. The brethren were again awakened and came again to the sick man. The sick man departed from the body, and his body was carried into the church. [Col. 1020D] Some brethren remained there to chant psalms around the dead man, while the convent returned to bed. That night, since I too was slightly ill, I went with the others to rest. As I lay in bed, still awake and not yet asleep, I began to reflect within myself and, as it were, to say to myself: ‘Lord my God, what will become of this man, whom the bonds of so many sins bind? What does it profit him that he confessed his evils? What that he repented at the end? What that he received the religious habit? Where is he now? Is he well or ill?’

“While I silently thought this within myself, I heard a voice saying: ‘He greatly needs help.’ Hearing, then, that he needed help, I went at once in spirit to the church and, as though bending my knees before each altar of the saints whose memorials were there, with all the devotion I could muster I invoked their patronage, that they might obtain from the Lord mercy for him who needed pardon. When this had been done, my eyes closed and suddenly toil gave way to sleep. As soon as I had begun to sleep, I felt myself weighed down as though by a great mass. I understood that it was an evil spirit oppressing me, and it said to me: ‘What is it that you intend to do?’ I replied: ‘What, I ask, do I intend to do?’ ‘Do you think,’ it said, ‘that you can take Baldwin from me for the religious habit alone which he assumed?’ ‘I do,’ I replied. ‘Should not he rightly be mine,’ it said, ‘who served me throughout the time of his life and remained in his sins until the end of his life?’ To this I replied: ‘I do not deny it. But did he not confess his sins? Did he not repent at the end and flee to God’s mercy? [Col. 1021B] And, even if I say nothing of all else, do you not know that Christ’s blood was shed for sinners for the remission of sins? By that precious blood which flowed from the side of him sleeping on the cross, I adjure you, accursed one, to depart at once from here and to have no power over him.’

“When the evil spirit heard the name of Christ’s blood, unable to bear the force of the adjuration, conquered and confounded, it departed. I, rejoicing as though in victory, burst forth from exultation of heart into a voice of jubilation and praise, and began to sing ‘We praise thee, O God’ (*Te Deum laudamus*). I sang in my sleep as far as the place where it is said, ‘Thou art the King of glory, O Christ’ (*Tu rex gloriae, Christe*). There I awoke from sleep; and, contemplating in clearer daylight the course of what had occurred, I completed the whole hymn in praise and glory of God. While I still had in my mouth that verse, ‘In thee, O Lord, have I hoped; let me never be confounded’ (*In te, Domine, speravi, non confundar in aeternum*) [Col. 1021C], the clock struck and the summons for Matins was made. I went to the vigils, not forgetting the voice which had told me that Baldwin needed help. All night I directed prayer to God for him.

“When day had come and the brethren assembled in chapter, I ordered them without interruption to offer the saving sacrifice for the deceased until the thirtieth day. I also resolved to do what I ordered others to do: that is, to offer sacrifice for him for thirty days. During those thirty days, in which we all prayed for him, Baldwin often appeared to me, coming before me and standing by me wherever I was. He appeared in the guise of a suppliant, as though to say that he needed help and to ask that prayers be made for him. He did this especially when our devotion was lukewarm and slack, or when for some reason I could not celebrate Mass. I do not say that he appeared to me every day during those thirty days, but often during those thirty days.

“It also happened that one day I set out for the granges of our house and could not sing Mass that day. As I returned to the monastery, he appeared to me on the road as a suppliant, much sadder than usual, as though he wished to say that I had been forgetful of him that day. But when the thirty-day period had elapsed, on the day when the cross is adored by all peoples, as I sat in the presbytery vested in priestly garments in order to celebrate the sacred solemnities of Mass, and the second reading was already being read in church, I looked and saw two men clothed in purple, exceedingly beautiful and desirable to behold [Col. 1022A], coming through the middle of the choir. They led between them Brother Baldwin, clothed in dark brown (*ysembrunus*). When they had brought him before me where I sat, they presented him to me and said: ‘This is Baldwin.’ And behold, while I wondered what they would do with him, they led him to the altar and offered him in this manner. When this was done, the vision disappeared. But Brother Baldwin, who had appeared to me so often, never again appeared to me from that day onward.

“Returning therefore to myself and considering what such a vision signified, I understood that, after Brother Baldwin had been offered at the altar, he had been reconciled. Yet by the black garment in which he was clothed I understood that some stain of sins still remained in him and that he was still subject to penance. Behold, you know what I saw concerning this knight.

“A little before the death of the man of whom we have spoken, a certain knight at the point of death sent for me to visit him. When I came to him and heard his confession, I could give him no better counsel than to renounce the world and flee to God’s mercy, which I believed was the only thing remaining to him. I showed him Val-Royal, a house of our order nearer his own home, and he was clothed in the religious habit; I returned to Igny. As I lay in bed that night, still awake, I began to reflect within myself and, as it were, to say to myself: ‘What good do you think the religious habit that this knight has assumed will do him? What he did he did not so much willingly as unwillingly. For if he still had had time to do evil, perhaps he would have done evil. In short, he did not so much abandon his sins as they abandoned him.’ [Col. 1022C]

“While I thought this within myself, I heard a voice saying: ‘It will greatly benefit him. And know this: in this man and in anyone who dies in the habit of the Cistercian order, the devil will have no power until judgment has been given concerning him.’ On hearing the voice, I immediately understood that what it said could be true, as the following comparison entered my mind. If a king has a servant hated by all, as long as that servant bears with him the king’s insignia and letters, and as long as it remains uncertain whether he is loved or hated by the king, he can pass safely without challenge among enemies. But if it is declared that the king hates him and has expelled him from his house, then there will be no one who does not plunder him. In the same way, one who bears with him the insignia of Christ’s knighthood, carrying his marks in his body and clothed in the religious habit, which is the Saviour’s tunic, can safely penetrate the ranks of his enemies, and the devil has no power over him, while he is still ignorant of what the Lord wills concerning him. But if the judge’s will concerning him has been made known and a sentence pronounced, proving that he does not please God, then the evil one receives authority and may exact the debt to the last farthing. [Col. 1022D]

“Strengthened by this vision, therefore, I counselled Brother Baldwin to renounce the world even though dying. For I knew that the religious habit, assumed even at the very moment of death, could benefit even the greatest sinner.”

This vision was seen by the venerable Abbot of Igny. It left us no scruple of doubt because it was not conveyed to our ears through a third person, but reported by the mouth of the very man who saw it. And although his testimony has been made most credible, nevertheless, so that fuller faith may be given to this vision, I confirm it by the following attestation: unless the vision set forth in these writings is true, may my shoulder fall from its joint and my arm be broken with its bones; may the heaven over me be bronze and the earth iron; may thorns spring up for me instead of wheat, and briars instead of barley.

XV.

[Col. 1023B] I add my testimony to the preceding attestation. Although it has no weight of authority, it certainly has the sincerity of truth. When, therefore, the foregoing account came into my hands, I was not content with the testimony of the writing, but took care also to have access to the man who saw it. Not openly or directly, but, so to speak, covertly and by certain hints—which would take too long to set down and explain here—I persuaded him to recount for my edification what he had seen concerning the knight Baldwin. Why say more? At last, overcome by my persistence and likewise by affection and arguments, he replied: “I shall say what you seek, but it will burden me to say it.” He then confessed everything to me in sequence and in agreement with the writing, and with such exact recollection that I greatly admired his memory.

XVI.

[Col. 1023C]

Henry, Count of Champagne, son of that Theobald whose memory is deservedly recorded with praise in the *Life of Saint Bernard*, once asked the servant of God to pray to the Lord for him. The latter celebrated Masses to intercede for him. When the mystery had been completed and he turned to his ministers in order to say the final collect, he saw the absent count present, bearing the sign of the cross on his garment, as those do who intend to set out for Jerusalem. Yet, as the count afterwards professed, he had not at that point affixed the cross to himself; but on that very day, after much uncertainty and long deliberation, he had firmly resolved without doubt to do so.

XVII.

[Col. 1023D]

The blessed man was once sitting in chapter. It was the anniversary of a certain brother’s death. The precentor, to whom this office belonged, reminded him to absolve the brother, as was customary. He absolved him, first saying quietly these words: “He needs absolution.” A certain elder named John, from whose report I also learned this, was sitting not far from him and heard the preceding words. At a suitable opportunity, seeking the reason for the remark, he heard from him: “Recently,” he said, “he appeared perceptibly to me while I was awake; and when I asked whether he yet saw our Lord, he replied, ‘Not yet the time,’ and with these words disappeared.”

The aforementioned John testified that the brother had lived religiously and for a long time in the Order and, during the two years preceding his death, had been much afflicted by a very troublesome illness and, as John supposed, had been tried in purgatory. But surely not only narrow but also long is the way that leads to life (Matthew VII [7]), and to the vision of the highest good and that surpassing nature, to which none but the utterly purified can attain, as Life itself testifies in saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V [5]). Who, then, shall boast that he has a clean heart? Yet let the one who boasts boast in the Lord—that is, in truth, which does not lie, not in opinion, which deceives and is deceived. For in many, iniquity lies to itself: they fashion and paint God’s mercy according to their own will, although God’s mercy does not nullify his justice and we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations—that is, purifications (Acts XVII [17]). [Col. 1024B]

Therefore, those who have put their hands to strong things (Proverbs XXXI [31]) should not despise the discipline of the Order, which in the present seems to contain something not of joy but of sorrow. Yet for those trained by it, it will yield the most peaceable fruit: in this life, of righteousness; and in the life to come, of glory. Let them not murmur at the harshness of the road, but consider the aforementioned brother: purified like gold in the furnace by prolonged and arduous observance and by two years’ bodily suffering, and tested as silver by fire, he nevertheless was not yet found perfect. Therefore even those conscious of no evil in themselves should lay the bridle of fear upon presumption, be afraid, and lower their wings.

For there is need of the long labour of a file, so that, material things and phantasms of things having been filed away from the soul, memory may retain nothing, reason see nothing, and the will love nothing except God, who is the original form of memory, the incorporeal light of reason, and the fiery impulse of the will: the highest good, the blessed good, the beatifying good of the human being. Having said these things briefly to awaken certain sleepers, let us return to our purpose.

XVIII.

In a structure, small things are sometimes proved no less necessary than great ones; therefore I shall set down here something slight, which, even if it deserves no thanks for usefulness, may nevertheless obtain pardon for its brevity. There is a brother, not unknown to you, whom the present discourse addresses. From youth to old age he has been worn down by many illnesses and has thus been proved to have endured a long martyrdom. [Col. 1024D] At times the ailments of his body increased so greatly that he was thought likely to fail altogether. I wrote to the man of God, while he was still in the flesh, asking him to extend the hand of intercession. On the night when he was praying for the sick man, it seemed to him that he stood naked before the man of God and was most severely beaten by him. He wondered at that man's unaccustomed severity toward him; but, as he wondered, his own conscience answered: “It is God who is scourging you.” He lives to this day, bearing the scourge more patiently, since he understands God to be its author. To someone this may perhaps appear an empty dream; but the concurrence of that prayer and this vision prompted me to write it. What I shall next add, the blessed man himself told me.

## XIX.

[Col. 1025A]

He was in a certain church and, in his prayer, was making confession to the Lord. The images of Saints Bernard and Malachy appeared to him as he prayed. Turning toward them, he directed his prayer and attention to them. Then one of them said to him: “You will be abbot of Clairvaux.” They vanished, and he remained terrified. Terrified, I say, because, as he later confessed to me with groaning, he would never have wished this to happen; yet he could not doubt what he had heard from God.

## XX.

After some interval of time had passed, Gerald, Abbot of Clairvaux, an honourable man adorned with many graces, came to Igny. At Igny there was then a certain [Col. 1025B] monk—indeed, a demoniac—a Judas among the apostles, a Satan among the sons of God: Hugh of Basoches. He had offended against the Order by many grave transgressions, and the aforesaid abbot had subjected him to regular discipline. Having therefore found a suitable opportunity to avenge his injury, driven by wicked furies and nursing a dreadful poison in his breast, he plotted privately for the man’s death.

One evening, then, a certain devout and humble brother, named Haymo, a native of Reims, was sitting in the entrance hall of the infirmary. As he himself confessed to me, he clearly saw two figures of horrible appearance, whom he could not doubt were demons, enter that house. At that time the said henchman of Satan, Hugh, lay there among brothers sick in body, himself [Col. 1025C] sick in mind. At midnight the abbot rose to confess to the Lord and took part in the night watches. Compelled by necessity, he went to the communal dormitory. There Hugh, lying in ambush “to kill the innocent” (Psalm 10), with a weapon ready for the deed, mortally wounded him.

He lived until the following day. Toward evening, with the brothers standing before him, he said: “Guide me, Lord, in your truth, and teach me, for you are God my Saviour, and I have waited for you all day” (Psalm 24). And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord and, as we believe, a distinguished martyr sought heaven, crowned by his blood. Abbot Peter, having prepared his body according to custom, escorted it as far as Clairvaux, greatly fearing lest what he had heard [Col. 1025D] should be fulfilled: “You will be Abbot of Clairvaux.” But a certain Henry, a man mighty in deed and word, received the lot of this ministry. When, shortly thereafter, he was elevated to become a cardinal-bishop, that see was vacant and the election of an abbot was again under discussion.

## XXI.

At Clairvaux there was Gilbert, cloistral prior and now Abbot of Foigny. Since, as the blessed man’s intimate and familiar friend, he knew his utterly sincere holiness deeply and very well, he carefully considered transferring him from Igny to Clairvaux. While he was pondering this in his mind, one of the brothers—wholly ignorant of his thought and intention—confessed to him, saying: “I bear, Father, a devout concern for our house, and I do not know whom the Lord intends [Col. 1026A] to provide for us as shepherd. Yet such a vision was shown to me: it was announced to us that the Lord Christ was coming to this house. We ran to meet him at the gates of the monastery. We saw him without beauty or comeliness, short in stature, poor in dress, contemptible in appearance; yet no one doubted that he was the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Comparing and relating this vision to his own purpose, Gilbert could interpret Christ as no other than Peter: a most true Christian, and truly Christ—that is, anointed with the heavenly chrism, namely with the Holy Spirit. In human eyes he appeared poor and insignificant, the least of men, as though struck by God; yet all his glory was within, where the precious pearl shone [Col. 1026B] in his heart, and where there was a place for the Lord, “a dwelling-place for the God of Jacob”: a dwelling-place, I say, built, adorned, spacious, beautiful, and precious through faith, charity, and the other virtues, like hangings of gold, silver, and precious stones; but externally covered with haircloth. There was a longing for the divine vision, a most sweet fragrance to the Lord; there, too, a harmony and concord of reason and affections produced a honey-sweet melody and delighted even the divine hearing.

Fittingly and deservedly, therefore, Christ appeared in the guise of poor Peter. He who “will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3) transformed the body of his glory to be conformed to the body of our weakness; and, though he was in the form of God and equal to God, he emptied himself, being made in the likeness of Peter and found in appearance as Peter himself (Philippians 2).

## XXII.

Gilbert, therefore, made more resolute by this vision, summoned the neighbouring abbots and Peter by name. Peter, indeed, fled when summoned. Nevertheless, the others came and, with the consent of the community, elected him in his absence. Nor was there anyone to oppose it, all knowing his remarkable holiness. He was therefore sought and found at a grange of that Order, living among the lay brothers. On the day he was found, he was turning hay in the meadows. Taken thence to Igny, when he could not be overcome by entreaties, he was compelled by the authority of the Order to accept the office—unwilling, reluctant, constrained. [Col. 1026D]

On the following day, when they intended to leave and make for Clairvaux, a violent fever seized the aforesaid Gilbert, who was one of those seeking him—seeking “the God of Jacob” (Psalm 23). The man of God came to him, complaining and saying that all this had been done through him and that now, contrary to the laws of friendship, he was abandoning him in his need. Gilbert’s claim of need was no falsehood. The holy abbot answered: “Rise; let us go from here. The fever will harm you no further.” He rose and went away with the servant of God, and shortly afterward the fever left him. Thus he was escorted to Clairvaux by the brothers as an angel of God, as a man sent by God, and was received with the devotion and favour of all.

He himself, however, came to them not “in loftiness of speech” nor in the persuasive [Col. 1027A] words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of spirit and power, in the truth and perfection of Christian religion, of which he showed them venerable examples.

## XXIII.

After some time, he was visiting the daughter houses of Clairvaux, and Gilbert, the new abbot of Les Boëriers, was with him. Gilbert rode a horse that was indeed comfortable but often struck its foot against stones, putting its rider in danger. Peter noticed that the horse frequently stumbled and, fearing for Gilbert’s fall, reproved him for using an animal through which he could very easily incur a fall and bodily injury.

To this Gilbert replied: “It carries me gently and well and is not treacherous, [Col. 1027B] which is why I greatly value its use. But if you fear for me and wish to help me, pray to the Lord that it may no longer suffer from this defect.” Peter said: “Are prayers, then, to be poured out rather than poured forth? For is God concerned about oxen? (1 Corinthians 9.) Nevertheless, I pray to God that it may not fall in such a way as to harm you.”

He used the horse for many years afterward and did not fall; for the animal was sure-footed. And lest this be attributed to chance rather than Peter’s merits: as soon as Gilbert had been transferred to Foigny and left both the horse and Les Boëriers, one of the brothers of that place mounted the horse, beneath which—or rather upon which—the quadruped fell so violently that the brother, his leg broken, was unhappily carried back injured to the monastery.

## XXIV.

[Col. 1027C]

Because of his outstanding holiness and manner of life, and because “no one could perform these signs unless God were with him” (John 3)—signs which also bore witness mutually to him—he gave forth fragrance like cinnamon and balsam, and, like chosen myrrh, gave sweetness of scent (Ecclesiasticus 24). This fragrance spread far and wide; throughout all the mountains not only of France but also of other regions, all these reports were published. His name was celebrated; very many regarded him as a prophet and saw him joyfully, as a friend of God and one intimate with him.

Finally, the Roman Pope, moved by such favourable renown, showed plainly how highly he valued him when, wishing to see him, he summoned him. Peter undertook that journey sadly, as they say, [Col. 1027D] but, obedient to the supreme pontiff, did not delay to go. The Pope himself was old in years, burdened with age, and afflicted by the sickness of which he later died. Yet delighted by Peter’s arrival, clothed in precious vestments, seated upon his throne, and surrounded by a circle of cardinals, he received him festively and joyfully.

Then he led him to a private place and, laying aside apostolic majesty, humbled himself before him—or rather, truly before Christ, who appeared in Peter through manifest signs. He confessed all his sins to him and received the holy Eucharist from his most sacred hand while Peter celebrated Mass before him. He also wished to assume the habit of the Cistercian Order, but the man of God, by what reason I do not know, though surely a sound one, did not allow this. The Pope also granted the necessary expenses for establishing—or rather restoring—an abbey of Peter’s Order in a place where an abbey had once existed but then lay destroyed. [Col. 1028A] After this, when the servant of God had stayed with him for some time, the Pope allowed him to return, honoured and indeed also enriched with gifts, when he did not wish to remain.

The Roman Curia is criticized for receiving the persons of great men with favour and for draining the wealth of the powerful; let it now be criticized less harshly. In poor Peter—great in this respect and not unlike Peter [the Apostle], who had neither gold nor silver—it venerated naked virtue, confessing by its actions the truth of what the moral poet says:

> Silver is less valuable than gold; gold than virtue.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.1.52

[Col. 1028B] Peter appeared before him empty-handed and found favour freely; he did not buy it. And he to whom “the kings of Tarshish and the islands offer gifts” offered gifts to poor Peter, so that Peter might build a church upon the rock of his Order.

Blessed Peter, who, although subject to every human creature for God’s sake, triumphed over golden mountains—not by his own strength, but through God. Blessed also the Roman Pope, who, though he was a golden mountain raised to the summit of the mountains, nevertheless subjected himself for God’s sake to the lowliest of all men.

## XXV.

Having set these matters down, I shall add something slight, by which nevertheless something great may be estimated. In a certain episcopal church of Gaul a dispute arose among the clergy concerning the election of a bishop. A Roman cardinal was present, to whom the clergy submitted the matter, proposing two candidates: whichever one he named, all would elect. The cardinal consulted Peter as to which of them seemed better to him. More people strongly favoured one of them because he seemed noble and generous, and they greatly desired the holy abbot to support him, as though they would advance with more plausible and sounder conscience the one whom so great a man had preferred by his testimony.

But Peter was not a reed shaken by the wind; he did not seek to please men but God. Therefore, answering according to his conscience and the truth, he said: “Between two counterfeit coins, no better one can be found.” They were confounded because Peter had rejected them. Or rather, they were not confounded and refused to blush; [Col. 1028D] for they elected that man nonetheless. He lives to this day, noble indeed by birth but not noble in virtue. It would be easy, but is unnecessary, to name the person: it is enough that the writing speak of the matter and not of the author.

In Peter’s few words one may observe the four cardinal virtues. He acted prudently, for he removed the comparison of the two as good men: since neither was good, one ought not to have been called better. He also acted justly, since he did not hide justice in his heart, but spoke truth and the salvation of God (Psalm 39). Truth breeds hatred; and because he did not shrink, in speaking the truth, from encountering some men’s hatred and offending their favour, he was courageous and, in himself,

> … wholly smooth and rounded.

[Col. 1029A] They did not believe his word, and he seemed to be defeated and to yield; yet he did not initiate litigation, put on sorrow, or disparage those who thought otherwise. By this he showed the temperance and moderation of his heart.

Perhaps it will seem unsuitable and empty to establish in so great a man such great virtues—that is, the four principal virtues—on so slight and fragile an argument, when they have been so often proved in many ways and by proofs brighter than light itself. But, as someone says, “It is the work of a skilled craftsman to enclose great things in a small one”—which, in the brief example just given, we think we have done.

## XXVI.

The virtues of this man have indeed, as we said above, been proved and shown by many and notable signs. [Col. 1029B] Moreover, patience, exercised amid hardships as humility is amid lowly things, is proved in him by a very strong argument which we have nevertheless omitted.

While he was abbot at Valroy, he was afflicted by a most severe illness. The violence of this ailment rose to the front of his head and so destroyed one of his eyes that it wholly melted away and flowed out, leaving its hollow socket empty, making the man of God—blessed in God even then—one-eyed. Let the enormity of so great a trial be considered carefully, and let the excruciating pain, the disfiguring deformity, the loss of light that made him less useful, and above all the fact that in all these things he did not sin with his lips or say anything foolish against God, be weighed with compassionate reflection in the scales of just judgment. Rather, as the holy Church sings of the martyrs:

> No murmur resounds, no complaint;  
> but, with the heart silent, the mind well aware  
> preserves patience.

[Col. 1029C] Thus this man, like the gentlest lamb before its shearer, did not open his mouth; but he was dumb, humbled, and silent from evil things (Psalm 38). Indeed, he used to say that he had escaped one of his enemies, so that he feared the remaining one more than the one already lost.

This was not because this most accomplished man felt the senses or members of his body to be adversaries to him; indeed, they were rather weapons of righteousness for God. Rather, he said this to console those who bitterly endure bodily losses, transforming himself into them through compassion and making himself like them through humility. For he had subdued his members that were upon the earth by constancy in labour, ardour of charity, and the bonds of discipline. He commanded them rather than serving them; he used them rather than enjoying them; indeed, so far as he himself was concerned, he no longer needed their use, and despised them like begged-for assistance. For, as is read of the great Martin, having surpassed human nature, with heaven as witness and God present and helping, he enjoyed God; and, carried beyond himself in mind by the Spirit of the Lord, through God to God, he reached him to whom others scarcely ascend through sensible inferences and bodily labours.

And in him was fulfilled the Scripture that says: “God’s converse is with the simple” (Proverbs 3). How familiar God was with him will appear, among other indications, from what I shall now relate.

## XXVII.

[Col. 1030A]

While he was still abbot at Igny, the brothers were at one time without a prior. Since he delayed appointing one, a certain elder asked him the reason for the delay and heard from him: “I do not cease to ask the Lord about this, and I receive no answer from him.” The elder named one man whom he considered suitable. “The Lord does not at all will this,” replied Peter.

From these things one may unquestionably affirm that, as Moses did, so this man spoke to the Lord as a man speaks to his friend (Exodus 33). For just as Moses ascended the mountain in order to speak with the Lord, so Peter stood upon a great height—not of mountain but of mind—where, like many, he consulted the Lord, but, like few, heard the Lord.

## XXVIII.

[Col. 1030B]

But, returning to Clairvaux, let us say that shortly before his death the man of God Peter came to Reims, drawn thither by domestic business. I saw him both coming and going, and I myself escorted him some distance. I looked upon him with no less reverence and affection than upon an angel. As I looked at him, the memory of the great Martin occurred to me, whom that noble orator Sulpicius Severus describes as clothed in rough dress, wrapped in a black and hanging cloak, and carried on an ass—or rather a little ass.

This man, a manifest likeness and imitator of Martin, rode a horse only a little larger than an ass. He also wore scapulars like the knapsacks of boys travelling on foot; dressed in a hanging and worn cloak, he bore more distinctly the appearance of a poor rustic [Col. 1030C] than of an abbot. Meanwhile he was short in stature, thin and worn in body, not wanton in his senses but composed; his earthly affections subdued, he was absorbed in thought and, as it were, absent from those present, so that he seemed not a man but a spirit. Such I then saw him; such I observed him; such I believed him; therefore I have spoken and described him as such.

As we went along the public embankment discussing various matters, dust stirred by the footsteps of those ahead and driven back by a wind blowing against us caused us inconvenience. I then said to him: “Let us pass those in front, so that we may escape this storm of dust.” He replied: “If we pass those walking before us, they will be in the condition in which we are, and this punishment will return upon its own head. It is no counsel of charity to inconvenience one’s neighbour for one’s own advantage.”

I confess that I blushed, observing in myself care for myself and indifference to others, but in him the more excellent way—that is, the greater charity. When would this man burden his neighbour in serious matters, who took care not to harm him in slight ones? Meanwhile we continued on, and the dust did not cease to sting us nor the wind to buffet us. Therefore, sympathizing with him and measuring his mind by my own, although he overcame the bodily suffering by a special patience of spirit, I offered a revised plan, correcting what he had reproved: “The road that leads us is broad. Let us join our companions at the side; then, while they remain unharmed, we too shall be safe from the dust, wind, and storm.” He agreed. Walking thus and discussing various matters as we had promised, we spent a great [Col. 1031A] part of the day.

When reason summoned me to return and we were just about to part, I was touched by inward sorrow of heart, and, drawing sighs from the depths, said: “Is bitter death to separate us thus?” I did not say this as one foreknowing the future, yet by it I foretold what was to come. For not long afterward he passed from this world to the Maker of the world. I shall briefly relate what those who were present attested to us concerning his passing, and so conclude this narrative.

## XXIX.

After Peter had presided over the monks of Clairvaux for several years, he left Clairvaux with certain abbots of his Order, travelling through neighbouring regions. He suddenly became seriously ill and began to lose bodily strength. Since, while he himself was silent, his illness spoke of the approaching danger, the above-mentioned Gilbert, always anxious for him and indeed loving to keep him, came to him and said: “Lord, as I judge from your condition, your departure from us is near.” Peter replied: “I think and hope so, for this year I have poured out many prayers to the Lord that he might deliver me from this body of death” (Romans 7).

Meanwhile the illness increased and the sick man was afflicted. Yet, with difficulty and exertion, they reached Foigny. There the brothers thought that he should be anointed, and wished to carry him from the upper chamber where he had lodged to a lower room, where this might be done more suitably. But he who had never been overcome by any labour or pain and would not be conquered even by death itself compelled his failing limbs to serve his spirit. [Col. 1031C] He rose, went down, was anointed, returned, and remained thus throughout the whole night until evening. When the brothers had already sung Compline, Gilbert, in the manner of a faithful friend, stood nearer to his friend, from whom he was soon to be separated and who seemed already to be in his final breath.

Believing this, the Abbot of Vaucelles, who was standing there with the others, burst out in these words: “What are we doing, brothers? This man is departing from us.” Hearing this, the man of God raised his hand to signify that he would depart not then but on the following day. The brothers therefore kept silent for the time being, while he spent the night in prayer, commending his passage [Col. 1031D] to the Lord.

When dawn broke through the darkness, the brothers gathered around him. With such effort as he could, he urged upon them the love of God; and, though he could not speak to them, he nevertheless did not cease to pray to the Lord. Thus, just as he had been gentle and quiet, so gently and quietly, in the very prayer in which he was confessing to the Lord, he gave up his spirit to the Lord who had given it. And to whom else would that spirit go but to God’s—indeed, to the Lord’s Spirit—with whom, by cleaving to him, it had been one spirit? Great and many merits raised him to that Spirit; no wickedness separated him from it; in him the Holy Spirit found his own likeness—indeed, found himself—and the deadly spirit found nothing deathly [uncertain reading: *funereum*] in him.

How far all wickedness was from him, and how great his innocence was, was attested in my hearing by Gilbert, named above several times, who heard his confession with the other fellow abbots, and who, as the Psalmist says to God, knew his sitting down and rising up without confession. [Col. 1032A] He testified, then, that for all the offences which Peter had confessed at his end and had incurred throughout his life after entering monastic life, to use Gilbert’s own words, no more than “Have mercy upon me, O God” and the “Our Father” ought to be imposed upon any penitent.

If, as the old proverb says, equals are most readily gathered to equals and like things are naturally fitted to like, one may undoubtedly conclude that this poor and lowly Peter enters heaven rich, and is joined to the saints and angels whose life and character he imitated. But now that his spirit has been worthily placed according to its merits, let us continue with the funeral rites for his body.

## XXX.

One of the brothers intended to extract one of Peter’s teeth, desiring to preserve it as a treasure and relic; he presumed he could easily do this because the dead man’s mouth was open. But when he approached to commit the pious theft, he found the mouth closed and so firmly shut that he could not accomplish his purpose. Some observed this and regarded it as a miracle; but, lest I judge presumptuously, I think that even in death he preserved the singular humility he had possessed while living.

His little body was washed. Even lifeless, it possessed not horror but grace. It was placed on a bier, and, though in his mortal humility he had wished to be buried at Igny, it was carried to Clairvaux. The brothers, as we have heard, placed Peter where Saint Bernard had first been laid, because of the grace of his merits and because it was the monument of a righteous man. In this they evidently agreed with the testimony of certain persons, to whom this man seemed of no less merit than Bernard.

For, if I may say so without offence to those who think otherwise, Bernard indeed was “exalted in words of glory” (Ecclesiasticus 47), a man of great counsel, “the chariot of Israel and its horseman” (2 Kings 13), a scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven, bringing forth from his treasure things new and old (Matthew 13). In the Cistercian Order and in [Col. 1032D] the Church of Christ he bore much fruit in his time. He, I say, was “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5), set upon a lampstand to shine for all who are in the house (Matthew 5), and like a most brilliant lamp spread the rays of his light far and wide. But this man, to speak briefly, was like a burning coal covered by the ashes of his poverty: he had less splendour, indeed, but no less heat.

## XXXI.

After the death of his outward man and the burial of his corruptible body, it was proved by the following evidence that his inward man—that is, the human soul—had indeed departed but had not died, although faith also maintains this. A monk, prior of a certain cell, used often to visit the holy man. [Col. 1033A] This monk, assailed by a severe temptation and entangled in the bonds of sin, sought Peter’s counsel and assistance. The man of God gave him a word of consolation and bade him have good hope of his deliverance.

But when news of Peter’s death came to him, as though the pledge of his redemption had been lost, he almost despaired of his own liberation. He addressed the dead man as though living, demanding fulfillment of his promise concerning release. While he thus knocked at the door of divine mercy, Saint Peter, the man of God, appeared to him in a dream and consoled him, declaring that he had been saved from all his temptation. The monk awoke and, treating what he had seen and heard as merely a dream, nevertheless awaited the outcome of the promise. And behold, within a few days, a certain person to whom he was bound by unlawful love, and while she lived he had not hoped that he could be healed, was reported dead. Thus the snare was broken, the sinner set free, and the righteous man’s word fulfilled.

## XXXII.

This discourse concerning this righteous man, maintained until now, is also complete—complete, I say, but not fully so, because it has not set forth plainly or sufficiently elegantly what might or ought to have been said about him. For, as we stated in the preface, this saint, who began as a young man and died in old age, undoubtedly performed many deeds that are unknown; and, if they are known, they are known to others, but not to me.

Indeed, to repeat what I once said when writing about Lord William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, who was one and the first of those who wrote Saint Bernard’s life: when the matters set forth above were related to me, I did not intend to write them, nor was I concerned to investigate more. But once I had resolved to put hand to pen, I had neither opportunity nor ability to seek further things. [Col. 1033C] Nevertheless, I fear that I may be judged by human judgment to have exalted this man with excessive praises, as though I had one judgment of him while he lived and another after his death; and likewise because, having undertaken to commend him, I might be permitted to say wonderful or great things rather than true ones, after the manner of certain men who rhetorically multiply lofty statements more eagerly than truthful ones, or of poets:

> Poets sing things wonderful, but not to be believed.

Yet, in order either wholly to clear away or at least somewhat to soften such objections—although no one but a very perverse person can doubt the preceding matters—and because I am debtor to the wise and the foolish alike, I shall here set down the letter which I presented to him while he still lived and was Abbot of Clairvaux. Let it serve both as an apology against unbelievers and as the epilogue of the present work; in it may be recognized the consistency of my judgment concerning him, present and past. Therefore, after the salutation, speaking and writing to him, I said as follows:

## XXXIII.

I am Thomas, brother of Philip, namely one of the two brothers of Radeul whom you used to love while Your Blessedness presided over the church of Igny and the brothers of that place rejoiced in your presence. Now they bear your absence all the more heavily because, through the experience of absence, they have learned what your presence bestowed.

But, as is read of the great Martin—whose unconquered imitator you are, to speak according to my conscience—you have been taken from us and given by God to those of Clairvaux. This is so, however, only if the men of Clairvaux recognize God’s grace in this gift of God; if they do not look to vanities and false insanities; if they know how to judge not according to appearance but with righteous judgment. What they themselves may judge about you, let them see to; I steadfastly affirm, with the testimony of all who judge rightly, that whoever does not admire and love you is certainly greatly deceived and mistaken, or else does not know either your virtue or the true nature [Col. 1034B] of virtue itself.

Let those of Clairvaux have glorious charisms in other fathers; in you, certainly—if they know how to discern them—they possess what is approved as all the more precious because it is found more rarely: an example of true and Christian virtue. Its perfect image and substantial reality do not consist in the great and wondrous things of this world, nor in things glorious by the judgment of the age, but in firm faith, burning charity, profound humility, contempt and restraint regarding visible things, and love and experience of invisible things. These are your true riches, and you possess them magnificently. Conscious of these, you despise other things in which others excel—something stronger than possessing them is to do so.

Let your brothers, therefore, see these things; and if they wish to glory in the Lord, let them glory. Above others they have this glory of distinction: in the things of God they possess an exceptional man.

But let these words suffice thus far. I do not doubt that they are few in proportion to the dignity of the subject; but I likewise do not doubt that to your most profound and singular humility they are many and greatly burdensome. Yet, as Saint Jerome writes to holy Paula, I can neither keep silent about the praises of Christ, even if I wished and were adjured, nor about yours.

Now, prostrate at the feet of Your Holiness, embracing and kissing them with pious affection and utmost devotion, I pray, my father, my father—and, if so great a sinner dared call so great a servant of God this, my friend—that you remember Thomas your son, who writes this to you, and my brother Philip; and that you render us this return for the greatest love which we bear toward you: that you sometimes pray by name for us to the common God of all, yet especially your own God.
