These things are more desirable to me than gold and much precious stone (Psalm 18).

Nor is this surprising. For just as one never prays to God without hope of his mercy, so I steadfastly believe that you never pray to him without obtaining his mercy—if not the complete fulfillment of what you ask, then at least some benefit for those for whom you pray. And it is altogether just that he should hear you above others in your prayers, since above the others of our time whom we know, you hear him in his commandments.

Let us gather into one the matters set forth above and weigh them, as it were under a single ray of the sun, with thought not only mindful but attentive. [Col. 1035A] Let us close this little work and, setting a boundary to it, conclude not merely plausibly but necessarily that Peter was a most true servant of Christ. Let us imitate him; and if we cannot follow him in the imitation of virtue, let us reach toward him in the affection of due veneration and love. Let us believe in Christ and love him in whom Peter believed and whom Peter loved; loving him, Peter was holy; and being holy, he performed the virtues described above and many others passed over.

Let us believe, I say, in Christ, but with the faith that works through love, so that, believing thus in him, after temporal life we may attain eternal life, which is in Christ—indeed, which is Christ—and to which Peter has passed.

## XXXIV.

[Col. 1035B]

To Master Henry, monk of Longpont, Brother Thomas of Radolio sends greetings. You judge that the letter placed at the end of the work which I composed concerning the life of the venerable Peter, Abbot of Clairvaux, should be removed—both because, to use your words, it does not sufficiently pertain to the subject matter, and because, addressed to one still living, it bears the mark of flattery. From this, too, the malicious and envious find an opportunity for detraction. I place great trust in the judgment of my elders, and thus in yours; but I place some trust in my own as well. Therefore, without prejudice to your judgment, I presume to say: “It does not seem so to me.”

For since I undertook to praise that man of virtue, worthy of praise, and since the letter contains an epitome of his praises [Col. 1035C], it is demonstrably and beyond doubt relevant to the subject matter. Yet, because it is offered to one living, it appears to bear the blemish of flattery. By the same reasoning, great men who wrote down the praises of great men while those men still lived will be called flatterers. To name only two and pass over the rest, Sulpicius Severus and William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, wrote histories and praises, while those praised were still alive, of the great Martin and of your Bernard. Nor did those men become futile in their thoughts because of their praises; for their glory was assuredly not human praise, even true praise, but the testimony of truth and a good conscience. Nor did these men fear the tooth of envy so as to refrain from writing what they hoped would please God and edify the humble.

With this intention, certain knowing and prudent men cast their hands into the flames [Col. 1035D] which those kindled who, spurred on by envy, despised and criticized what they themselves could not attain. Therefore I too—although I am as far inferior to them in purity as dwarfs are to giants, indeed incomparably farther—when I offered a living man his praises, was by no means serving flattery. For I knew that I was not pleasing him; rather, to confess the truth and reveal my purpose: I both spoke what was true [Col. 1036A] and wished in this way to commend him to his brethren. I feared lest, because, as Saint Bernard says, “everything humble is reckoned a reproach,” they might think little of him; seeing his outward humility—or rather, to speak more properly, humiliation—they perhaps did not know, or paid too little attention to, his inward brightness. I pressed this upon their eyes; and though I spoke directly to him, I had them more particularly in view indirectly.

Let the Letter therefore remain, if you approve, and let it contain the praises of the saint even to my own embarrassment. For in it I had in mind not my own glory but that of God and His servant. I am prepared to bear with equanimity the tongues of enemies, especially since such an occasion has sharpened them. Certainly, if I had wished to have the tongues of men pacified, [Col. 1036B] I ought altogether to have kept silent, since I do not know how to speak. And likewise, if I wished wholly to pacify them, not the letter alone but absolutely everything must be deleted: for the envious are ready to criticize everything; while to kindly learned men, sound in judgment and able to discern, everything—or most things—will deservedly be pleasing by reason of the arts. [I think the reading should be: “will not be pleasing.”]

Therefore, with the reservation stated in the preface, what I wrote, I wrote, so that readers might bear with a little of my foolishness and meanwhile, content with our ineptitudes, await those who would more fittingly rework material ineptly treated.

Consider these matters carefully, dearest brother; and so that you may either trust me or perhaps refute me more forcefully—since the rule is not only legal but also evangelical, that every word must stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses (Matthew 18)—let our little work be seen by Lord Hugh, your former abbot, who, having practice in writings of this kind, will know how to judge it. When the sons of his mother fought against him, because he did not know how to yield, he went forth after the tracks of our flocks; but now, as I hear, by a kind of return from exile, he has come back to his own country by another road. For the former he did through greatness of spirit, the latter through modesty: there strong, here modest, just in both places. But I spare him, lest I again be judged a flatterer.

But as for that passage in our little work in which the Roman Curia seemed to be criticized, because it is not safe to write against those who can proscribe, I agree that it should be deleted or, as seems good to you, altered [Col. 1036D]; and I have done this as well.

If anyone should wish to copy the little book solely out of love for the saint, may he not omit to copy this letter, so that readers may be answered by it; and let this postlogue, so to speak, sent to you, repeat what the prologue prefixed to the book does and intends.

[Col. 1035] Here ends the treatise of Lord Thomas, monk of Radolio, on the life of the venerable Father Lord Peter, Abbot of Clairvaux.

## APPENDIX TO WALTER

### BOOK ON THE TRINITY, by Walter, an early theologian

Notice. 573  

Chapter I.—God is one, incorporeal, omnipotent, eternal, Creator of all things, unchangeable; and this not by an accidental quality, but essentially. 575  

Chapter II.—In the unity of the divine substance there are three persons, or hypostases: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. 577  

Chapter III.—The Father is from no one; the Son is begotten from the Father and proceeds from Him; the Holy Spirit proceeds, is not begotten, from the Father and the Son. 578  

Chapter IV.—The Father has from no one what He has. The Son has all that is His from the Father. Whatever the Holy Spirit has, He has from the Father and the Son, not by grace but naturally; yet it does not follow from this that there is any inferiority among the divine persons. 578  

Chapter V.—The whole Trinity, and its operation outwardly, is altogether inseparable; whatever one person works, the others work also. 579  

[Col. 1038] Chapter VI.—Whatever is said of God substantially is equally affirmed of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. May one say that in the Trinity there are three individual substances of rational nature? 581  

Chapter VII.—Things which belong to God eternally in respect of nature, as also things which belong to God temporally in respect of creation, are predicated even of each individual person. The Son alone assumed flesh in time. God is affected by no accident; remaining unchangeable, He has acquired different names from the diversity of things which He made. 582  

Chapter VIII.—What should be predicated of the individual persons in the Trinity regarding relative predicates? Although all three persons are one God, and one God is the Trinity, God is not therefore to be called threefold. 583  

Chapter IX.—The mystery of the Trinity is explained by the likeness of the human soul. 584  

Chapter X.—Only the blessed in heaven will possess a perfect knowledge of the supreme Trinity. 586  

Chapter XI.—By authority and reason it is shown that in God there are no properties or relations which are not identical with God, but are things other than the substance of God. 586  

Chapter XII.—It is shown that the opinion of Saint Jerome offers no support whatsoever to the opposing view, nor do the words of the preface in the Mass of the Holy Trinity. 587  

Chapter XIII.—The error is refuted of those who absurdly maintain that omnipotence should be attributed to the Father alone, wisdom to the Son alone, and goodness to the Holy Spirit alone, and who suppose and boast that they have comprehended the mystery of the most holy Trinity. 588

XV *bis*.—He confirms the agreement made between the bishop and chapter of Senlis. 849

XVII.—Privilege for Signy Abbey. 853  

XVIII.—To all the faithful who, on the solemnity of Blessed John, come to give alms to the church founded at Virtus by Henry, Count of Champagne, he remits twenty days of the penances enjoined upon them. 853  

XIX.—He assigns to Master Garnerius, head of the schools of Reims, rank and the title of benefice-holder, together with an increase in endowment. 854  

XX.—Charter in which William, Archbishop of Reims, grants the valley of Radigion and many other things to the chapter of Reims. 855  

XX *bis*.—Privilege for the church of Blessed John of Virtus. 856  

XXI.—At the request of the canons of Saint-Quentin in Vermandois, he confirms, in accordance with the decree of Alexander III, what concerns exemption from external jurisdiction. 857  

XXII.—He grants to the abbots of Saints Remi, Nicasius, and Denis the right to have one servant or free burgess within their ban, with the same immunity enjoyed by the burgesses of the canons. 857  

XXIII.—Charter concerning the sentence pronounced against Lord Nicholas of Rumigny. 858  

XXIII *bis*.—Charter of William I, Archbishop of Reims, concerning the election of the abbesses of Avenay. 859  

XXIV.—To the lepers of Reims, in exchange for the transfer of the fair to the cultivated district, he grants one hundred sextaries. 859  

XXV.—He bestows many privileges upon the hospital house of Saint Anthony at Reims, founded by himself. 859

XXVII.—Agreement between the Archbishop of Reims and the chapter of Reims concerning free servants. 862
